en: The Padma Purāṇa: Section One, the Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa (Section on Creation).
(1) First Chapter.
Om. Salutations to Śrī Viṣṇu.
Oṃ! Pure and white as the moon, with foam produced by the agitation of elephants' trunks and sea-monsters;
frequented by the foremost of Brahmins devoted to vows and restraints who have emerged from Brahmā;
purified by the gaze of Brahmā, the teacher of the three worlds, adorned with the syllable Oṃ.
May the Puṣkara lake—delightful with its abundant enjoyments and removing all impurity—purify you! ||1||
The high-minded one named Lomaharṣaṇa, also known as Ugraśravas, spoke thus to that single Sūta, the disciple of Vyāsa, who was seated there:
"O dear one, having gone to the hermitages of the ṛṣis, [relate] the duties in brief."
Tell those who ask in detail that which you have heard from me.
O son, all the Vedas and Purāṇas have been recounted by me to you; they were obtained by me from the sages—tell them to me in detail. (4)
Just as the Lord himself was questioned at Prayāga by the best of sages, so too were those sages, seekers of dharma, instructed by him when he was thus questioned. (5)
Desiring a meritorious region, he was urged by his benevolent lord [Viṣṇu] to go to Sunābha,
which possesses divine form, is devoted to truth, and is endowed with auspicious prowess.
This incomparable wheel, as it turns, you who are unwearied shall follow behind according to the rule and attain that state which is beneficial. (7)
"Wherever the rim of the turning wheel of Dharma is shattered, that land should be considered meritorious," so said the Lord himself. (8)
Having thus spoken to all the seers, he again became invisible at the place where the rim,
which resembled a whirlpool of the Gaṅgā, shattered.
At that time, the sages were performing a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) at Naimiṣa;
go there and speak to them regarding the doubts they have concerning dharma.
Then Ugraśravas, having gone there, approached those eminent sages who were rich in wisdom;
having touched their feet and paid homage with palms joined in reverence, he stood before them. ||11||
The wise one gratified those sages with his prostrations;
and they, the performers of the sacrifice along with the members of the assembly, were pleased with that high-souled one.
Having approached him, they offered him worship according to the prescribed rites.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, from where have you come? From which country have you arrived here? (13)
"O you whose splendor is equal to the gods, tell me the reason for this in the sacred tradition.
Sūta said:
"I was indeed commanded by my father, the wise disciple of Vyāsa: (14)
Go and serve the sages; speak whatever they ask of you.
Let the venerable ones speak to me, and I shall tell them the story that I have.
The best of sages listened to those sweet words of his concerning the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and the various kinds of Dharma.
Then, having seen that learned son of Lomaharṣaṇa, who was extremely trustworthy, a desire to hear the Purāṇa arose among them.
At that sacrificial session, there was a wise patriarch named Śaunaka, an expert in all the scriptures and a teacher of the Āraṇyakas and the Upanishads. ||18||
O Sūta of great intelligence, having thus taken refuge in that state, you have properly questioned the Blessed One, the supreme knower of Brahman, regarding the dharmas he desired to hear.
Vyāsa was properly propitiated for the sake of the meaning of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. ||19||
You have milked from him that auspicious intellect which rests upon the ancient [tradition]. ||20||
O one of great intelligence, these foremost of Brahmins now desire to hear the Purāṇa; you ought to recite it for them.
All these high-souled ones, belonging to various lineages, have assembled;
let these exponents of the Veda hear their respective portions as declared in the Purāṇas. (22)
When this long sacrificial session is complete, you must indeed cause those sages to hear it;
O high-minded one, relate the Padma Purāṇa to them all.
How did the lotus arise, and how indeed did Brahmā come to be there?
How was the creation performed by him once he had emerged? Tell me that exactly as it happened.
Thus questioned, the son of Romaharṣaṇa then replied to them with auspicious words; he spoke in a subtle manner, consistent with right reasoning.
I am pleased and I am graced by your inquiry here concerning the meaning of the Purāṇas, you who are knowers of the Purāṇas and devoted to all dharma. (26)
I shall relate all that to you exactly as it was heard and well-known;
for this is the eternal duty of a Sūta, as observed by the virtuous. (27)
One must preserve the lineages of the gods, the sages, and the kings of immeasurable splendor, as well as the hymns of praise dedicated to those great-souled ones. (28)
Those who are seen as exponents of Brahman in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas have no authority whatsoever in the Vedas; such is not observed in the case of the Sūta. (29)
While the sacrifice of the high-souled Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
was being performed, both the Māgadha and the Sūta praised that lord of men.
Then, being pleased, the high-souled king granted a boon to those two:
the territory of Sūta to Sūta, and Magadha to Māgadha.
In that context, one born during the *sūtyā* sacrifice is here called a *sūta*;
this occurs when the *Bṛhaspati-sattra*, joined with the *graha* offerings, has been undertaken for Indra. (32)
That very oblation belonging to Indra, which had been mixed with and overwhelmed by the sacrificial offering of Bṛhaspati through the hand of his disciple, was born there as a Sūta. (33)
Through the inversion of the higher and lower orders, that confusion of castes was produced;
those who were born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother [were the Sūtas]. ||34||
However, those duties have been proclaimed for him by virtue of his similarity to the former [caste];
for this is the intermediate duty of the Sūta who lives by the field. (35)
My authority regarding the Purāṇas has been established here by the Brāhmaṇas;
having perceived the Dharma, I have been questioned by you, the exponents of Brahman. (36)
Therefore, I shall correctly proclaim on this earth the ancient lore honored by the seers:
the mind-born daughter of the ancestors united with Vāsava. (37)
And because she was meditated upon by her ancestors, she came to exist within the womb of a fish, like the fire-drill for the production of the sacred fire. (38)
From her was born the great seer of purified soul from Parāśara;
having paid homage to that blessed, true, and creative Lord. (39)
To the Ancient Person, who follows the words of Brahmā,
to Viṣṇu who has assumed the guise of a human, the Lord whose nature is pure white light.
As soon as he was born, the entire Veda with its compendiums approached him;
by means of that, he pierced through to the depths of the ocean of scripture.
The Great Bhārata has been brought forth as a moon that illuminates the world; for if these three—the Bhārata, the Sun, and Viṣṇu—were not to exist, [the world would remain in darkness]. 42.
From that, the state of the world consisting of the density of the darkness of ignorance arises;
know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa. 43.
Who else but the lotus-eyed one could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
Therefore, I have heard this ancient account from those who discourse on Brahman. (44)
From the Omniscient One, who is worshipped in all worlds and possesses radiant splendor, this Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the foremost of all scriptures. (45)
It is the most excellent for all the worlds, the means for attaining all knowledge, the merit that accomplishes the three goals of life, and it extends over a hundred million verses. 46.
And throughout all the worlds, Keśava, in the form of a horse, retrieved the Vedas at the command of Brahmā. (47)
The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, the Purāṇas, the extensive Nyāya, and the entirety of the Śāstras were seized by Asura and made his own. ||48||
At the beginning of the kalpa, the omnipresent Lord assumed the form of a fish and, remaining within the waters of the ocean, recounted this entire [Veda] to him. 49.
Having heard this, the Four-faced One spoke to the sages regarding the Vedas;
at that time, the origin of all the scriptures and the Purāṇa took place.
Then, seeing that the Purāṇa was not being grasped in due time,
the omnipresent Brahmā assumed the form of Vyāsa in order to collect it throughout the ages.
In each Dvāpara age, he sang it with a measure of four hundred thousand verses;
then, having divided it into eighteen parts, it was made manifest in this world of mortals.
Even now, that which extends over a hundred crores in the worlds of the gods has been set down here in brief as four hundred thousand [verses]. (53)
I shall proclaim the great merit of the Purāṇa known as the Pādma, which consists of one thousand and fifty-five [verses] and is endowed with five sections. (54)
In that regard, first there shall be the Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa, after which the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa;
thereafter the Svarga-khaṇḍa, and following that, the Pātāla-khaṇḍa. ||55||
And then, fifth, the supreme northern region is proclaimed;
this is the great lotus from which the world has arisen, of which it consists. (56)
Because it takes that account as its subject matter, it is therefore called the Pādma.
This Purāṇa is stainless, pure through its glorification of Viṣṇu’s greatness.
Whatever Hari, the God of gods, formerly proclaimed to Brahmā, and whatever was previously related by Brahmā to Marīci; ||58||
And Brahmā himself proclaimed this very thing in the world as the *Āpadya*;
for that which is the refuge of all beings is called "the lotus" (*pādma*) by the wise. (59)
That *Pādma* is recited here as consisting of fifty-five thousand [verses];
it is declared in five sections, composed in brief by Vyāsa. (60)
The first section is the Pauṣkara, where Virāṭ himself was born;
the second is the Tīrtha-parvan, which is the refuge for all the hosts of planets.
The third section concerns kings who bestowed abundant sacrificial fees;
and the lineage history is proclaimed as the fourth.
The fifth is the reality of liberation (mokṣatattva), and it is declared to be the totality of all realities.
In the Pauṣkara [Purāṇa], it is stated that the ninefold creation of all things is brought about by Brahmā.
The creation of the gods, the sages, and likewise another, the creation of the ancestors;
in the second [section], the mountains, the seven continents, and the seven oceans.
In the third [chapter], there is the creation of Rudra as well as the curse of Dakṣa;
in the fourth, the origin of kings and the recounting of all lineages.
O twice-born ones, I shall relate in this Purāṇa everything concerning the final state of liberation and the proclamation of the scriptures of emancipation. 66.
This is a purifier and a treasury of glory; this shall be exceedingly dear to the ancestors; this is always for the happiness of the gods, and it is [the destroyer] of even the great sins of men.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Purāṇa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
## Second Chapter ## Sūta said:
I bow down to the Lord of all worlds and of the entire universe.
The knower of Pradhāna brings forth that state which is the form of creation.
The creator of the world, the knower of the truth of the world, and the master of yoga, having resorted to yoga,
created all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Desiring to know the ancient narratives, I go for refuge to that unborn, all-creating Lord, the knower of the mind, the witness of the world, and the omnipresent one. (3)
Having paid homage with a concentrated mind to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and with meditative absorption to Indra, the world-protectors, and Savitṛ; 4.
And to Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent among sages and a great soul, whose ascetic heat shone from his mouth; and to Jātūkarṇya, the son of Akṣuṣa.
To that Blessed One, the arranger of the Vedas, the creator, the ancient Puruṣa, who follows the words of Bhṛgu; ||6||
Therefore, I heard this from an ancient teacher of the Veda, who was honored in all worlds and possessed radiant splendor, as he spoke of the Omniscient One. (7)
That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal and consists of both the existent and the non-existent;
it is that which brings forth the specific principles beginning with the Great One (mahat), as is well known.
In the beginning, the supreme birth of Brahmā occurred within a golden egg;
the covering of that egg was water, and the covering of the water was fire.
The wind is enveloped by space, and that [space] is enveloped by the source of the elements (bhūtādi);
the source of the elements is also enveloped by the Great One (mahat), and the Great One is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
The manifestation of the worlds is described as occurring within the cosmic egg itself;
the manifestation of the rivers and mountains is also described therein.
A concise description of the Manus and the Kalpas;
and a description of the dissolution of the Brahma-tree and the creation of the progeny of Brahmā. (12)
The wandering through the kalpas, as well as the establishing of the world, the reclining of Hari upon the waters, and again the lifting up of the earth. 13.
The tenfold cycle of births, the curse of Bhṛgu upon Keśava,
the arrangement of the ages (yugas), and the classification of all the stages of life (āśramas).
The classification of the abodes in heaven for mortals who travel to the celestial realm, as well as the origin of beasts and birds, has been fully described. ||15||
Likewise, the dissolution of all speech and the relinquishing of Vedic study; furthermore, the successive re-creations (pratisarga) of Brahmā are said to be preceded by his conscious intent.
The other three [worlds] were created by him without prior deliberation;
and from the mouths of Brahmā, Bhṛgu and the others came into being. (17)
The interval between the two Kalpas is declared to be the period of re-absorption (pratisaṃdhi) following the creation;
and there is a description of the creation of progeny by the sages, Bhṛgu and the others. 18.
The Brahmanhood of the brahmin-sage Vasiṣṭha has been fully proclaimed; thereafter follows the proclamation concerning Manu Svāyambhuva.
The emission from the navel of the Great-Souled One has been described, as well as the enumeration of the islands, oceans, and mountains. 20.
The inclusion of the various continents and oceans within the seven [great seas] is proclaimed, along with their extent in yojanas and those who dwell therein. (21)
His [the cosmic egg's] constituent parts are the five elements together with the rivers and mountains;
the islands, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are surrounded by the seven oceans. (22)
Within this egg are these worlds: the earth with its seven continents, as well as the course of the sun and moon, and likewise that of the planets and the luminaries.
The solar day is measured by Brahmā himself according to the power of the constellations and the auspicious or inauspicious nature of living beings, for the sake of the purpose of the sacrifice. 24.
The Blessed One is conceived as the sun moving through the sky;
from him comes the constant movement of the sun and other luminous bodies, as well as the fixed course of the gods. (25)
The Śiṃśumāra was fashioned such that Dhruva is situated at its tail; Sambhava is the destruction of Saṃhāra, and Saṃhāra is the destruction of Sambhava. ||26||
It is not possible to describe [this] in detail regarding the deities, the sages, Manu, and the host of ancestors; thus it has been stated in brief. ||27||
In this world, he recounted the unequal duration of the past and future Manvantaras, as well as the praises of the gods and the lords of creatures. (28)
The dissolution of all beings is recorded as being threefold: occasional, natural, and likewise absolute; this is how it is conceived. (29)
From the sun comes a terrible drought, and the fire of universal destruction;
the clouds become a single ocean, and likewise, night falls upon the Great Soul.
The characteristics of the *saṃdhyā* have thus been indicated, as well as those of the *brāhma* period in particular;
furthermore, there is a detailed description of the seven worlds of living beings.
Having proclaimed here the hells such as Raurava for all those who have committed sins, [I shall now state] the determination of the transformation of all sentient beings. (32)
The re-creation of Brahmā and the description of the universal dissolution; and the destruction even of the great ones who have perished at the end of every kalpa. ||33||
Having thoroughly reckoned and understood the impermanence of even the Brahmanas, as well as the wickedness of enjoyments and the misery of saṃsāra. (34)
Furthermore, liberation is difficult to attain; through detachment comes the perception of defects.
Having abandoned both the manifest and the unmanifest, the pure essence (sattva) is established in Brahman.
Through the vision of manifoldness, one becomes well-established; from that, he turns toward it.
Then, having transcended the threefold affliction, he is the one named Virūpa, the passionless (nirañjana).
"Having attained this bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing from anywhere.
Thus has the exposition of the purpose of the means of valid cognition been described. (37)
In which the fame of the world's transformations—its creation and dissolution, the activity of beings, as well as their cessation and the fruits [of their actions]—is proclaimed. (38)
The manifestation of Vasiṣṭha, as well as the birth of Śakti, and his restraint by Viśvāmitra on account of Saudāsa; 39.
O Lord, tell me how the birth of Parāśara occurred from Adṛśyantī, and how the sage Vyāsa was born from the daughter of the Pitṛs. (40)
Just as there was the birth of the wise Śuka as a son, so too was there the enmity directed against Parāśara by Viśvāmitra. 41.
The fire had been prepared by Vasiṣṭha with the intent to slay Viśvāmitra; it was then quenched by the powerful and wise Kaṇva for the sake of pacifying it.
O Brahmins, the Lord, desiring the welfare of the Brahmins, divided again that single Veda consisting of four quarters into four parts.
Just as the venerable Vyāsa divided [the Veda] out of favor toward all beings, so too were further divisions of the branches (śākhā) made by his disciples and grand-disciples. 44.
At Prayāga, the Lord himself was questioned by the eminent sages, and those sages, desiring righteousness, were instructed by Kṛṣṇa. 45.
All this has been explained according to its true nature, O best of the twice-born, as the unsurpassed means for the welfare of the worlds, intended for sages who are ever-devoted to dharma. (46)
This was formerly proclaimed by Brahmā to the high-souled Pulastya,
and then it was spoken by Pulastya to Bhīṣma at Gaṅgādvāra.
Its glorification, hearing, and especially its retention bring merit, fame, long life, and the destruction of all sins. (48)
This Purāṇa was revealed in due order by Sūta,
just as it had been previously taught in detail to the Brāhmaṇas by Brahmā.
He who studies it with his senses conquered and having correctly understood even a single quarter of it, by him the entire Purāṇa has been studied; of this there is no doubt. (50)
A twice-born man who knows the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs and the Upaniṣads,
and who understands the Purāṇa— he is truly wise compared to that other.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will deceive me. (52)
Having studied even a single chapter proclaimed by the Self-born One himself,
one shall be liberated upon encountering calamities and attain the desired state.
He who speaks of that which is ancient, both prior and subsequent, as the Purāṇa, by him it is remembered;
he who knows its etymology is liberated from all sins. 54.
The sages said to Sūta: "How did the venerable sage Pulastya, the mind-born son of Brahmā, come to be associated with Bhīṣma? (55)
The sight of him is difficult for men burdened by sin to obtain;
how then has this sage been brought here by the Kṣatriya Sūta? This is most extraordinary. (56)
O you of great intellect, tell us how that Bṛhadbhūta was propitiated; what kind of penance did he perform, and what other vow was undertaken by him? (57)
When the sage was not satisfied, he spoke in that manner—whether it were a full chapter, half a chapter, or the entirety [of the teaching]. (58)
O highly fortunate one, tell us that place where the venerable seer Pulastya was seen as he appeared; we are ready to hear it.
Sūta said:
There, the highly fortunate Gaṅgā, who brings benefit to the virtuous and purifies the world,
emerged with great force after splitting the mountain.
At the great sacred ford of Gaṅgādvāra, Bhīṣma, devoted to his ancestors,
remained for a very long time intent on service and established in the great observances.
For more than a full hundred years,
meditating upon the Supreme Brahman with supreme concentration, he performed his ablutions three times a day.
As that great-souled one gratified the ancestors and the gods through his Vedic study and drew his self toward [perfection], the divine Grandfather was pleased with him.
Brahmā spoke to his son Pulastya, the best of sages:
"O virtuous one, go to Bhīṣma, the heroic Devavrata born of the Kuru lineage."
"O highly fortunate one, desist from your austerity and proclaim the cause of this;
you stand firm, devotedly meditating upon your ancestors. (65)
"Whatever desire this man has in his mind, fulfill it without delay.
Having heard these words of the Grandfather, Pulastya, the best of sages, [acted accordingly].
Then, having arrived at Gaṅgādvāra, he spoke these words to Bhīṣma:
"Choose a boon—may prosperity be yours—whatever resides in your mind. (67)
O Hero, the Grandfather, the God himself, was pleased by your asceticism;
sent here by Brahmā, I shall grant you the boons you desire.
Having heard those words of Bhīṣma, which brought pleasure to his mind and ears,
he opened his eyes and saw Pulastya standing before him.
Having bowed to that best of sages with the eight-limbed prostration,
he spoke while remaining prostrate, his entire body touching the earth.
Today is the day of the fruit of your first wish, and this birth-day of yours is most auspicious; by the sight of you in battle today, may the world be filled with joy.
And the fruit of my asceticism has been attained, in that the Blessed One has been seen by me;
and having especially granted a boon, he has arrived at the riverbank. (72)
This seat, fashioned from *brasi* grass and providing comfort, is prepared; please be seated.
As for the vessel for the *arghya* offering, it should be made of *pālāśa* wood and contain *dūrvā* grass, unbroken grains, flowers, and *kuśa* grass.
With mustard seeds, curd, honey, barley, and milk—
this is indeed declared by the sages of old to be the eightfold *argha* offering.
Having heard these words of Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor,
the venerable sage Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, sat down.
Filled with joy, the Blessed One, pleased by that virtuous conduct, accepted the seat along with the water for the feet and the vessel for the respectful offering (argha).
Pulastya said: "O lord of men, you are truthful, devoted to charity, firm in truth,
modest, friendly, patient, and valiant in subduing your enemies."
You are a knower of dharma, you are one who knows what has been done, you are compassionate, and a speaker of pleasant words;
you honor those worthy of honor, you are wise, devoted to the Brahmins, and affectionate toward the virtuous.
"I am always pleased with you, who are so devoted to prostration;
speak, O highly fortunate one, and I shall grant you my discourse. (79)
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, at what time did the omnipresent Lord Brahmā abide and formerly perform the creation of the gods and others? Please tell me."
How did the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu come to abide [as the sustainer], and how was Rudra created?
Furthermore, how were the ṛṣis and the gods created by that Great-Souled One? ||81||
How is the earth, how is the sky, and how are these oceans?
How are the continents, the mountains, and the villages, forests, and cities? (82)
[He saw] the sages, the Prajāpatis, the seven eminent Ṛṣis, as well as the social classes, Vāyu, the ancient abodes, the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas.
Tell me how the Blessed One created the sacred fords, the rivers, as well as the sun and other planets and stars, just as he did so. (84)
Pulastya said:
He is the highest of the high, the supreme, the Supreme Self, and the Grandfather.
Devoid of color, form, and the like, and free from all qualifiers. ||85||
He is devoid of all qualities— decline, destruction, transformation, growth, and birth— and is accompanied solely by his own primordial nature (*svabhāva*).
He is considered equal toward all and incomparable even while dwelling [in the world];
meditating upon [the Self] as the form of Brahman, he is thus praised by the wise. (87)
That supreme secret is eternal, unborn, undecaying, and immutable;
it exists likewise in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time.
Having bowed to him, I shall proclaim how the Lord of the World formerly created the universe after rising from his lotus-bed.
O lord of men, at the time of creation, Mahat was produced from the manifestation of the qualities; it is threefold: sattvic, rājasic, and tāmasic.
Together with the primary principle (pradhāna), it is likewise enveloped by the seeds and so forth;
[these are] the vaikārika, the taijasa, and the bhūtādi, which is indeed tāmasa.
This threefold ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) was born from the principle of the Great One (mahattattva), along with the five elements, the [five] sense organs, and likewise the organs of action. 92.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—each one individually in its own form, I shall describe them in successive order. 93.
Then the Bhūtādi [tattva] enveloped the ether (kha), which consists of sound alone;
then the ether, undergoing transformation, produced touch alone.
This wind is indeed powerful, and touch is considered its quality;
space, which consists of sound alone, then enveloped the subtle element of touch.
Then Vāyu, undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of form (rūpamātra);
that [element] is light (jyotis), and it is said to have the quality of form.
Air, indeed, enveloped the subtle element of touch which is the form of sound;
and light, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste.
From that, the elements came into being; they enveloped the subtle element of form alone.
And as they were undergoing transformation, they produced the subtle element of smell alone.
From that, the aggregate is born; therefore, fragrance is considered its quality.
They say the sense organs are composed of fire, and the eleven deities are the products of the *vaikārika* [sattva]. (99)
And here, the eleven organs of perception are traditionally known as the vaikārika [devas]:
skin, eye, nose, tongue, and the ear as the fifth. (100)
Furthermore, their function is the grasping of sound and the other [objects];
then there are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals as the fifth. (101)
Emission, craftsmanship, movement, and speech are the qualities of these [elements] in reverse order:
ether, air, fire, water, and earth. 102.
By means of the qualities such as sound and so forth, they are joined with the heroic [element] through each subsequent one;
thus, they are traditionally taught to have the specific characteristics of being peaceful, terrible, and deluded respectively.
Possessing diverse powers and being separate from one another, they were unable to create living beings without striking [one another] and without coming together in their entirety. (104)
Having come together through mutual conjunction and by way of reciprocal dependence, they attain complete unity as a single aggregate numbering one hundred thousand. ||105||
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa, the Mahat and the other principles likewise produce the egg of the world through their favoring of the unmanifest. 106.
Having evolved through that sequence, he became like a water bubble;
therein, Janārdana, whose nature was previously unmanifest, assumed a manifest form.
Brahmā himself remained established in the form of both Brahman and non-Brahman;
Meru became his amnion, and the mountains became his chorion.
The waters of the womb and the oceans were the skin of that Great-Souled One;
there [within him] were the continents and the oceans, together with the entire collection of worlds including the luminaries. (109)
Within that egg were the heroes, gods, asuras, and humans;
it was surrounded on the outside by water, fire, air, and ether, which in turn were enveloped by the *bhūtādi* (the source of the elements).

The cosmic egg is enveloped by the tenfold [elements]; likewise, the source of beings (bhūtādi) is enveloped by the Great One (mahat), and the Great One, O King, together with all those, is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Endowed with all these obscurations and all the elements, it is like a coconut fruit [enclosed] by its outer husks. (112)
And Brahmā himself proceeds to the creation of the world;
he brings forth the creation age after age, until the end of the kalpa-cycle.
The Blessed One, Janārdana alone, is the knower of all;
he is the consumer of beings, the possessor of qualities, the God of immeasurable prowess. (114)
He creates a terrible form characterized by an excess of darkness and delusion;
O Indra among kings, being exceedingly fearsome, he devours all living beings.
And having devoured all beings when the world has been turned into a single ocean,
he who assumes every form lies upon his serpent-couch.
And having awakened, he who assumes various forms again effects creation;
because he performs the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, he consists of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (117)
The Creator creates himself, and Viṣṇu protects that which is to be protected; likewise, the Lord himself is withdrawn as the Destroyer. (118)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—he alone is the Lord of all beings, for he is the immutable one whose form is the universe. 119.
Therefore, the creation and so forth belong to Him alone; He is the one who abides within all beings and provides them with benefit.
He Himself is the object to be created, and He is the creator of the creation. He Himself is that which is to be protected, since He is the protector.
Having an infinite form through states such as Brahmā and others, He is Brahmā—the most excellent, the giver of boons, and the most worthy of worship. (120)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Descent of the Purāṇas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||2||
## The Third Chapter ## Bhīṣma said: Of that Great Soul who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, and pure...
How, indeed, is the status of being the creator of the initial creation possible for Brahman? (1)
Pulastya said:
The powers of all entities are inconceivable and beyond the scope of knowledge;
yet those powers of Brahmā, such as the power of creation and so forth, arise from Him.
The wise one who has arisen is called "eternal" only by way of figurative convention;
according to his own measure, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years.
That is called *tatpara*, and half of that is proclaimed as *parārdha*.
Fifteen *kāṣṭhās* are declared to be a *meṣa*, O best of kings. (4)
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* constitute the duration of one *muhūrta*.
A human day and night (*ahorātra*) is traditionally reckoned as consisting of that same number of *muhūrtas*. (5)

A month consists of as many days and nights as there are [in the aforementioned period] and is composed of two fortnights; six of those months constitute an *ayana*, and a year consists of the southern and northern *ayanas*.
The southern course is the night of the gods, and the northern course is their day;
these are known as the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages, measured by thousands of divine years.
The four yugas consist of twelve thousand [years]; learn their division from me:
four, three, two, and one [thousand] respectively for the Kṛta and the following ages.
Those who know the ancient lore say that there are thousands of divine years in the Yugas; a period of hundreds of such [years] is designated as the Sandhyā and the preceding Sandhyāṃśa.
The period equal to that [Sandhyā] is the Sandhyāṃśa, which follows immediately after the Yuga; O best of kings, the duration of both the Sandhyā and the Sandhyāṃśa is the same.
That which is known as the Yuga should be understood as comprising the Kṛta, Tretā, and the others;
the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali together constitute the Caturyuga (the four-age cycle). 11.
O King, this thousand-fold [cycle] is said to be one day of Brahmā;
O King, during one day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus.
Now hear their duration as determined by time, O King:
the seven sages, the gods, Śakra, Manu, and his sons. (13)
At one and the same time, their shame was cast off, as it had been before;
the number of the four yugas is calculated to be seventy-one and more.
O King, the duration of a Manvantara—the period of a Manu—is recorded as eight hundred thousand divine years for the gods and others. (15)
O King, thirty full crores and an additional fifty-two thousand more are reckoned by calculation. (16)
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, this duration is sixty-seven million, twenty thousand, and more. (17)
The number of years in a *manvantara* by human reckoning here is such that fourteen times this duration is known as a day of Brahmā. (18)
The Brahma dissolution is called "occasional" (naimittika); during it, you move about within that [egg].
For at that time, the entire triple world, beginning with Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ, is consumed by fire. (19)
Afflicted by heat, the inhabitants of Maharloka depart; when the three worlds have become a single ocean, Brahmā, the best among those who know Brahman, [remains]. (20)
Lying upon the serpent-bed, nourished by the swallowing of the three worlds, the Lord, the sovereign of the universe, is meditated upon by the world’s yogis. 21.
He creates again at the end of that night, which is of the same duration as the day.
In this manner is a year for Brahmā, and in this manner is his hundred-year lifespan.
The supreme lifespan of that great-souled one is a hundred years;
O sinless one, one *parārdha* of Brahmā’s life has already passed for him.
O King, at its conclusion was the great eon (kalpa) renowned as Pādma,
occurring during the second half-cycle (parārdha).
This first eon is designated as the Vārāha;
it is that eon at its beginning when the Blessed One was known as Brahmā Nārāyaṇa.
"O great sage, tell me how he created all beings.
Pulastya said:
"The Blessed One, who is without beginning and the source of all things, created progeny. (26)
At the conclusion of the past kalpa, the Lord Brahmā, having risen from his night's sleep, being overflowing with the quality of sattva, beheld the world as empty.
Perceiving the earth submerged within the waters during the deluge,
the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), having reflected upon it, desired to effect its rescue.
Then, having recognized that form as Viṣṇu’s, she entered the Vārāhī body—along with others such as the Fish and Tortoise—to bear the earth by her own splendor. (29)
Resorting to a form composed of the Vedas and sacrifices for the sake of the world’s maintenance,
the Lord of Creatures— the Supreme Self, the Self of all, whose nature is eternal— remains established.
Then the bearer of the earth, having reached the end of the waters, entered;
at that time, the Goddess beheld him who had arrived at the surface of Pātāla.
Having become prostrate and bowed low with devotion, the Earth praised him.
Pṛthivī said:
"Salutations to you, the refuge of all beings; salutations to you, the Supreme Self. (32)
Lift me up from this; I have already arisen before you.
O Supreme Self, salutations to you; O Soul of the Puruṣa, salutations to you.
Salutations to you who appear in the forms of primordial matter (pradhāna), the manifest (vyakta), time (kāla), and the elements (bhūta);
you are the creator of all beings, you are their protector, and you are their destroyer.
At the beginning of creation, he who is the Supreme Brahman, assuming the forms of Viṣṇu and Rudra, having consumed the entire world when it had been turned into a single ocean; ||35||
O Govinda, you alone remain as the one contemplated by the wise;
no one at all knows that supreme form of yours which transcends you.
The inhabitants of heaven worship that form which you assume in your incarnations; having propitiated you, the Supreme Brahman, those seeking liberation attain emancipation.
Who, without propitiating Vāsudeva, shall attain liberation? He whose form is ungraspable by the mind, yet is graspable by the eyes and other senses; ||38||
All that form of yours is entirely to be discerned by the intellect;
I am composed of you, supported by you, created by you, and have taken refuge in you. (39)
"Therefore, this world calls me 'Mādhavī'.
Thus was the Supporter of the Earth praised by the Earth. 40.

The glorious one, whose voice was the resonance of the *sāman* chants, roared with a deep, gurgling sound; then, having lifted the earth with his tusk, the Great Boar, whose eyes were like blooming lotuses and who resembled a great mountain of sapphire blue,
rose up from the subterranean realm like a vast heap of blue lotus petals.

Arise, O Father! Then let us go to those stainless sages—Sanandana and the others—who are the refuge for the world of those seeking food, who have washed away their faces, and who are the very abode of purity. (42)
The waters, accompanied by a continuous roar from the impact of the tips of his hooves, descend into the subterranean realm;
meanwhile, that multitude of clouds, driven by the wind of his breath, moves away on all sides.
As that Great Boar rises up after tearing open the earth with his belly wet from the water,
sages dwell upon the hairs of his body as they shake his Veda-made form.
Among the lords of men, you are the supreme lord, the radiant Keśava, who bears the mace, conch, lotus, sword, and discus;
you are the Lord who is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance [of the world], and there is no other supreme state than this.

O Lord, you alone are the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa): the Vedas are your feet, the sacrificial posts are your fangs, the sacrifices and the Śrutis are in your mouth, fire is your tongue, and the darbha grass is the hair on your body.
This entire world is pervaded by the very form of you, whose power is incomparable even to that of heaven and earth; O All-pervading Lord, may you exist for the welfare of the universe. (47)
O Lord of the universe, you alone are the Supreme Self; there is no other.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded by Your majesty;
yet those of unawakened intellect perceive this whole universe as being composed of the nature of [mere] knowledge. 49.
Those who perceive the nature of objects as real wander upon the raft of darkness;
but those who know reality and possess pure minds see the entire world [as it truly is]. 50.
O Supreme Lord, they behold Your form as consisting of pure consciousness;
O Soul of all beings, be gracious toward this world of Yours. 51.
O Lord of immeasurable soul, O lotus-eyed one, lift up this submerged earth!
Having come forth, O Blessed One, you have raised up this earth, O Govinda. (52)
"O Lord, uplift the world for its welfare from the ocean of existence!
While he was being praised in this way, the Supreme Self, the Supporter of the Earth, [remained there]. (53)
He quickly lifted up the earth and placed it upon the great ocean;
there she stands like a massive ship upon the mass of waters above it. (54)
Then, having leveled the earth,
the Lord, the beginningless Puruṣottama, constructed the mountains upon the earth according to their respective divisions.
Then, having divided the earth exactly as it is into seven continents,
he fashioned the four worlds beginning with Bhūr, just as before.
This very thing was previously demonstrated by Viṣṇu to Brahmā;
being pleased, the God of gods said, "O God, you are Puruṣottama."
This world must be sustained and protected with effort by you;
however, for those foremost among the asuras to whom a boon has now been granted by me, [it shall not be so]. (58)
O Lord, desiring the welfare of the gods, I have been sent by you;
I shall perform the creation, and it must be protected by you, O Lord. (59)
When he had spoken thus, the omnipresent Viṣṇu created the gods and others;
from him there appeared that which consists of darkness (tamas), arising without prior conscious intent.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and andhatāmisra—this fivefold creation exists as the meditation of the Great-Souled One. (61)
That which is external, unmanifest, with its nature concealed, consisting of the individual soul (anagātman), and not yet having reached the primary state,
is therefore called the secondary creation (mukhya-anāgāyata) by you.
Seeing that creation, the Lord considered it insufficient;
as he meditated upon another creation, the "downward-streaming" (tiryaksrotas) creation emerged.
Because its activity proceeds horizontally, it is therefore known as the downward-streaming creation.
These are known as cattle and the like; they consist mostly of darkness and are devoid of knowledge. ||64||
Those who grasp at wrong paths, possessing the conceit of knowledge regarding what is not known,
are full of egoism and pride, consisting of twenty-eight types;
they are all luminous within, yet they are mutually veiled by one another.
Considering even that to be ineffective, he meditated further; from that, another arose.
The third was the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas), which was characterized by sattva and proceeded upwards.

Abounding in happiness and joy, they are unobstructed both internally and externally; being luminous both internally and externally, they are therefore known as those whose stream flows upward (ūrdhvasrotas). ||67||
The third creation is known as the divine creation (devasarga) of the self-contented one;
when that creation was accomplished, there was then joy for Brahmā.
Then, having realized that the primary creation and its subsequent offspring were ineffective, he resolved to undertake another,
superior creation that would be effective.
As he was thus meditating, being one whose meditation was fixed on truth, there then emerged from the Unmanifest the Arvāk-srotas, the achiever.
Because they proceed from that point downward, they are called "downward-streaming" (arvāk-srotas).
They abound in light (prakāśa), yet are intensified by darkness (tamas) and dominated by passion (rajas). ||71||
Therefore, those humans who repeatedly perform many deeds that result in suffering, and who are both outwardly manifest and inwardly pure, are practitioners. //72//
The fifth section, the Anugraha-sarga, is established as fourfold:
through error (viparyaya), attainment (siddhi), power (śakti), and contentment (tuṣṭi). ||73||
Furthermore, they do not know the past or the present;
that which consists of the elements beginning with earth is called the sixth creation.

They possess no possessions and are intent on sharing with all; they are characterized by the practice of incantations and recitations, and they should be known as those who regard the elements and so forth as primary. (75)
Thus, O best of kings, these six creations have been described here:
the first is the creation of Mahat, and the second is that of Brahmā.

The second creation, consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātras), is indeed remembered as the elemental creation (bhūtasarga); the third creation, however, is known as the intellectual creation (vaikārika), which is the creation of the sense organs (indriyaka). ||77||
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen preceded by intelligence;
and the fourth is the principal creation (mukhya-sarga), wherein the immobile beings are known as the "principal" (mukhya).
That which is called the horizontal stream (tiryak-srotas) is said to be the animal womb;
therefore, the sixth [stream], that of those who flow upwards (ūrdhva-srotas), is traditionally known as the divine creation (deva-sarga). ||79||
Then follows the seventh creation, that of the downward-streaming beings, which includes both gods and humans;
the eighth is the creation of grace, which consists of the qualities of purity (sāttvika) and darkness (tāmasa).

These five are known as the modified (vaikṛta) creations, while three are remembered as the primary (prākṛta) ones; the ninth is remembered as the Kaumāra creation, which is both primary and modified.
Thus have been described the emanations of Prajāpati,
both primary and secondary, which are the fundamental causes of the world.
"What else do you wish to hear regarding the Lord who creates the universe?
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus, the creations of the gods and others, as well as those of the sprout [the lineage], have been narrated in brief. (83)
"I wish to hear this in detail from you, O best of sages.
Pulastya said:
"All of them are permeated by their own actions, both auspicious and inauspicious. (84)

Indeed, those who are not liberated from their manifest forms are withdrawn during the dissolution; the fourfold classes of beings, beginning with the gods and ending with the immobile, are thus reabsorbed, O King. (85)
As Brahmā was performing the act of creation, these [beings] born of his mind are recorded as having been produced;
thereafter, the fourfold group consisting of gods, asuras, ancestors, and humans [arose].
Desiring to create, he joined these [elements] with his own self;
from that, the evil-minded progenitors were born from the liberated soul of Prajāpati.
Then, from the thighs of the one desiring to create, the Asuras were first born;
thereafter, he cast off that body which consisted of the *mātrā* of *Tamas* and was characterized by wickedness.
O Indra among kings, as he was about to cast off that body, the night became bright;
then the gods, desiring him to assume another body, attained great joy.
O King, those beings who were predominant in *sattva* emerged from the mouth of Brahmā;
having abandoned that body, it became the day, which is primarily composed of *sattva*.
Then, indeed, the Asuras were strong at night and the gods by day; thereafter, he took on another body consisting solely of the quality of sattva.
As he regarded them as his fathers, the Pitṛs appeared before him;
then that Lord, having performed the ancestral rites, cast her away along with the Pitṛs.
Then, having cast off that state which consisted of the alternation of day and night,
she took up another body composed solely of the quality of rajas.

O best of the Kurus, from that [matter] which was produced as intensely predominant with only the quality of rajas, Prajāpati created the first human beings; he then quickly created that primordial body of the female.
That which arose from the moonlight is called Prāksaṃdhyā;
during the arrival of the moonlight, human beings as well as the ancestors become powerful. 95.
From this, O Lord of Kings, they indeed arise;
these four—moonlight, night, day, and twilight—are truly yours, O All-pervading One. (96)
The bodies of Brahmā, moreover, are supported by the three guṇas; from among these, he took up another body consisting solely of the quality of rajas. (97)
Then, hunger arose in Brahmā, and he was overcome by anger;
emaciated by hunger, the Blessed One then emitted the syllable "Dha. (98)
Desiring their own welfare, those who were deformed ran toward that powerful Lord;
because they said "rakṣa" (protect us) with longing, they consequently became Rākṣasas. 99.
Others among those yakṣas said, "Let us eat him!
Upon seeing them, the hair of the Creator, who was extremely terrified, began to fall out.

Those who were inferior repeatedly climbed onto his head; because of their crawling (*sarpaṇa*), they became serpents (*sarpa*), and because of their inferiority (*hīnatva*), they are known as snakes (*ahi*). ||101||
Then, by the enraged Vaisravana, beings were created from his own anger;
fierce and flesh-eating, they were tawny-brown in color. 102.
As he was drinking the cow that had arisen, Gandharvas were produced from him at that very moment;
because they were born from his mouth, they became known as the Gandharvas. 103.
Having created these, the Lord Brahmā, impelled by that power,
then emitted other birds of various kinds from his own pure mouth.
From his armpits and chest, Prajāpati created the *kramukha* and *toja* birds;
from his belly, he created cows and buffaloes.
And from his two feet [issued] horses, elephants, donkeys, gavayas, deer, camels, mules, nyankus, and other species of animals. (106)
O best of kings, at the beginning of the kalpa, during the dawn of the Tretā Yuga, the herbs possessing fruits and roots were produced from his body hairs by Brahmā.
Having properly created the animals and the plants, he then employed them in the sacrifice:
the cow, the goat, the buffalo, the ram, the horse, the mule, and the donkey.
These they call domestic animals; now learn from me the wild ones:
the beast of prey, the cloven-hoofed, the elephant, the monkey, and fifthly, the bird.
Cattle are the sixth, and reptiles are the seventh;
where there are cows, the *Ṛgveda*, the *Trivṛt* Soma, and the *Rathantara*. (110)
And from his first mouth, he fashioned the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices,
as well as the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh metre, and the fifteen-fold Stoma.
From his right side, he emitted the Bṛhat-sāman, the Uktha, the Dakṣiṇā,
the Sāmans, the Jagatī meter, and likewise the seventeen-fold Stoma.
From his western mouth, he created the Vairūpa-Atirātra,
as well as the Ekaviṃśa, the Atharvan, and the Aptoryāman.
From his northern mouth they produced the Ānuṣṭubh meter along with the Sāman;
from his limbs were born various beings, both high and low.
Having created the gods, the asuras, the ancestors, and human beings, the Lord of Creatures,
the Grandfather, then once again created them from his own mental resolve.
Yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, as well as hosts of apsarases; siddhas, kinnaras, rākṣasas, siṃhās, birds, beasts, and serpents—[he saw them all]. 116.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the omnipresent creator of the beginning, emitted all this— the imperishable and the perishable, both the stationary and the moving.
Whatever actions those beings performed in a previous creation, those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created once more.

Indeed, whether gentle or cruel, virtuous or non-virtuous, true or false—conditioned by those very qualities, beings enter into them; therefore, that which they have been conditioned to prefer becomes pleasing to them.
The Lord himself has personally ordained the diversity and the specific application of the sense organs, their objects, the elements, and bodies. 120.
In the beginning, he (Brahmā) brought about the manifestation of names, forms, the five elements, and activities, as well as the gods and others, solely from the words of the Veda. (121)
He established the names of the sages exactly as they were heard in the Vedas; furthermore, he assigned appropriate names to others according to their respective qualities.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons are seen to reappear in their cycle,
so too do those very same states of being appear at the beginnings of the Yugas.
Thus, at the beginning of each kalpa, he repeatedly carries out such a creation;
desiring to create, endowed with power, and impelled by the power of that which is to be created.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Brahman, you have described the human being as one whose stream of existence flows downward; tell me in detail how Brahmā created him from the darkness."
O great sage, tell us how he created the various castes and their qualities, and what the traditional duties of these classes, beginning with the Brahmins, are said to be. (126)
Pulastya said:
O best of the Kurus, when Brahmā, intent on the quality of goodness (sattva), previously desired to create offspring, there arose from his mouth creatures abounding in goodness. 127.
Likewise, others arose from the chest of Brahmā, being predominant in *rajas*; and others arose from his thighs, being predominant in both *rajas* and *tamas*. (128)
O best of the Kurus, Brahmā created other beings from his feet;
all of them were dominated by tamas, and from them arose this system of four castes (cāturvarṇya).
O best of kings, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras emerged from his feet, thighs, chest, and mouth respectively. (130)
O Great King, for the completion of the sacrifice, Brahmā created all this—the fourfold caste system, which is the supreme means for accomplishing the sacrifice. 131.
Sustained by sacrifice, the gods release rain;
thereby, human beings are nourished through the performance of dharma-sacrifices, which are the causes of all that is auspicious.
It was accomplished by those men who were always devoted to virtuous deeds, who were free from contrary conduct, who were noble, and who traveled upon the path of the righteous. ||133||
O King, from the human state men attain heaven and liberation;
O Lord, men go to whatever other place is appropriate for them. (134)
O best of kings, those subjects created by Brahmā were established in the system of the four varṇas; they were perfectly pure and devoted to the performance of proper conduct. 135.
Delighting in their own desires as they wish, free from all afflictions, with pure internal faculties, and stainless through the practice of pure dharma; ||136||
When their minds are purified and Hari is firmly established therein,
they perceive pure knowledge called Brahman, by which that supreme state is attained.
Then, that which is called the abode of Viriñca is of the nature of Time;
it is exceedingly terrible, causing one to fall into the cycle of transmigration, and possesses but a very slight essence.
It is the seed of unrighteousness, arisen from darkness and greed, and the means for the sequence of passion and so forth among subjects, sons, gods, and lords of asuras. (139)

Consequently, O King, the innate perfection (sahajasiddhi) does not arise for them to any great extent; rather, the other eight perfections, such as subjugation (vaśya) and the rest, come to pass. (140)
When those [virtues] have been entirely exhausted and sin increases, the people then become afflicted by the suffering of being oppressed by one another. (141)
Then, having constructed various fortresses—namely those on trees, on mountains, by water, in the desert, as well as cities, villages, and so forth—[he settled there]. (142)
O Great-minded One, they constructed houses in those cities and other locations according to the proper method, for the purpose of pacifying the afflictions of cold, heat, and the like. (143)
Having established this system of boundaries for those subjects beginning with the Śītas,
he then provided them with the means of livelihood consisting of the success derived from manual labor and the fruits of action.
Rice and barley, wheat and millet, sesame, priyaṅgu, kovidāra, koradūṣa, and cīnaka; ||145||
Māṣa, mudga, and masūra, niṣpāva along with kulattha, aḍhaka, caṇaka, and śaṇa—these are recorded as the seventeen [grains]. (146)
O King, these are the species of medicinal herbs belonging to the cultivated varieties; there are fourteen types of herbs, both those fit for sacrifice and those that are wild. (147)
Rice, barley, beans, wheat, millet, sesame, and seventhly, panic seeds—these are the seven; eighth are the kuluttha lentils. (148)
O King, śyāmāka, as well as nīvāra, round gavedhuka, and likewise veṇuyava and markaṭaka are said to be [suitable]. (149)
These fourteen medicinal herbs are indeed known as belonging to the village and the forest;
likewise, they are the supreme cause for the accomplishment of the sacrifice. 150.
And these [sacrifices] are the supreme cause for the creation of living beings along with the sacrifice;
therefore, the wise who know the higher and the lower perform these sacrifices. (151)
O best of kings, the daily performance of sacrifices, when carried out by men seeking their fruits, brings about great benefit. (152)
O you of great intelligence, he who created this world at the beginning of time established its boundaries in their proper places according to their respective qualities. ||153||
O best of the upholders of dharma, [you have described] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life,
as well as the worlds of all classes who correctly observe their duties.
O King, the station of Prajāpati is ordained for Brāhmaṇas;
the station of Indra is for Kṣatriyas who do not retreat in battles. (155)
The station of the Maruts belongs to the Vaiśyas who follow their own duty;
that of the Gandharvas belongs to those of the Śūdra caste who are well-disposed toward service.
The abode of those eighty-eight thousand ascetics who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) and dwell as teachers of the gods is remembered as that very place. 157.
That which is remembered as the abode of the Seven Sages is known as Vaivanauka;
that of householders is Prājāpatya, and that of renunciants is known as Brāhma. (158)
The immortal abode of the yogis is the supreme station of Brahman; for those yogis are indeed constantly engaged in meditation with one-pointed minds. 159.
That is their supreme state, which the wise behold;
it is there that the moon, the sun, and the other planets move in their courses of coming and going.
Even today they do not turn back from that [hell], being devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa:
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava. 161.
The terrible Asipatravana, Kālasūtra, and Avīci hells are for those who obstruct the Vedas and the performance of sacrifices. (162)
This place has been declared for those who abandon their own dharma;
then, as he meditated upon it, mental offspring were born from him. (163)
Together with the instruments residing in the body that had arisen from his own body,
the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) emerged from the limbs of that wise one.
All these, beginning with the gods and ending with the immobile beings, which were previously described by me as having evolved from that [Prakṛti], abide within the domain of the three guṇas. (165)
Thus were all beings created, both stationary and moving; yet when all these offspring of that wise one did not multiply, [he reflected]. (166)
Then he created other mental sons who were like himself:

Faith, fortitude, nourishment, contentment, intelligence, action, as well as discernment, modesty, form, tranquility, prosperity, and fame as the thirteenth. (183)

## Chapter Four ## Bhīṣma said:
I have indeed heard that Lakṣmī was born from the Ocean of Milk in that manner.
Born from Bhṛgu in Khyāti, he said this: "How is it, sir? (1)

For what reason did the God of gods take the daughter of Himavat as his wife?
Furthermore, may the Blessed One tell me about the conflict with Dakṣa.
Pulastya said:
O protector of the earth, hear also this which I have been asked by you here;
this account concerning Śrī was heard by me from my grandfather.
But Durvāsas, the son of Atri, while wandering over this earth,
saw a beautiful, fragrant garland in the hand of a Vidyādharī.
"I shall place it upon my mass of matted hair," thus was that Vidyādharī questioned by the sage.

Shining like a madman or a ghost, the brahmin said this:
"This is a Vidyadhara maiden with full and elevated breasts. (8)
The mind of one who has not seen [the deity] becomes agitated by the beauty, ornaments, and grace [of the visualization]; therefore, the wise person should not harbor egoism regarding this. 9.
"Go, O Amitavāda, displaying your own good fortune wherever you go.
Having spoken thus, that lord of kings wandered over the earth.
[He saw] Śakra, the lord of the inhabitants of the third heaven,
the sovereign of the three worlds, the husband of Śacī, resplendent and mounted upon Airāvata.

The elephant, its eyes rolling with intoxication upon smelling that fragrant scent,

Then the venerable Durvāsas, the best of sages, became enraged;
O king of kings, being angry, he spoke thus to the king of the gods: 15.

"Trailokyashri, deluded by passion, shall meet his destruction because he has cast aside the garland of sovereignty bestowed upon him by me upon this earth. (17)
Therefore, the three worlds will lose their prosperity,
for even the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, shall tremble with fear when he has become enraged.
Out of excessive pride, you, O King of the Gods, treat me with contempt;
therefore, Mahendra, descend from the back of your elephant with all haste. (19)
I propitiated the sinless sage Durvāsas;
being thus propitiated by me with prostrations preceded by [my submission], he was then [gracious].
"O Śatakratu, I will not endure this; what is the use of saying more?
Having said this, the brahmin departed, and the king of the gods followed him once again.
Having mounted the elephant Airāvata, he departed for Amarāvatī;
from that time forth, the three worlds, including Śakra, were bereft of splendor.
Because they did not know the right way, the ascetics practiced penance improperly;
because they did not give gifts properly, the world became as if lost.
Thus, when the three worlds were utterly devoid of glory and abandoned by sentient beings, the Daityas and Dānavas exerted their strength against the gods. (24)
Defeated by the Daityas, Indra and the other gods, led by Agni, sought refuge with the highly fortunate Grandfather (Brahmā).
After the gods had spoken as they were told, Brahmā spoke likewise to the asuras;
then, accompanied by the gods, he went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
Having gone there, the Grandfather spoke to the Blessed Vāsudeva:
"Arise quickly, O Viṣṇu; bring about the welfare of the gods."
"Without you, all the Dānavas have been conquered again and again.
Thus was the lotus-eyed Puruṣa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), addressed.
Having seen the gods with their unprecedented forms and appearances, he said to them:
"O gods, I shall provide an augmentation of your splendor."
"O gods, I declare what must be done by you:
having gathered all the medicinal herbs together with the Daityas, bring them to the Ocean of Milk."
"O gods, making me the churning-staff and making Mandara the churning-rope, and with Vāsuki as the rope, churn for the nectar while I stand as your helper. (31)
Addressing those sons of Diti with conciliatory words, he said:
"You shall be sharers in the fruits of whatever actions you perform here. (32)
Whatever nectar (amṛta) arises there from that ocean while it is being churned,
by drinking it you shall become powerful immortals.
In that very way I shall act, so that the enemies of the thirty gods shall not obtain the nectar, while the gods themselves shall be mere partakers of suffering. (34)
Having been addressed thus by the God of gods, all the deities then entered into an alliance with the asuras and strove for the sake of the nectar.
Having gathered all medicinal herbs, the gods, Daityas, and Dānavas cast them into the waters of the Ocean of Milk, which possessed the pure white luster of an autumnal cloud.
Having made me the churning-staff and Vāsuki the rope, the lords of kings then began to churn for the nectar with great speed. (37)
All the gods stood together at the tail,
while the Daityas were stationed by Viṣṇu at the front part of Vāsuki’s body.
O you of immortal splendor, by that wind and fire of his,
the luster of all those asuras was struck down, and they became devoid of brilliance.
Then, by those clouds produced from the very wind of his sighs, the gods were drenched as they rained upon the region of his tail.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, the Lord Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, and Mahādeva of great splendor, both resided upon the back of Viṣṇu. 41.
Having seized Maṇidara with his two arms like a lotus,
and having likewise fashioned a chain, he took hold of that mountain Maṇidara.
Stationed in the midst of the strength of both the gods and the demons,
the Blessed Lord Hari himself, in the form of a tortoise, dwells in the middle of the Ocean of Milk.
Hari was empowered by that very splendor while the Ocean of Milk was being churned by the gods and the Dānavas.
In the beginning, Surabhi, who is worshipped by the gods, became the vessel for the sacrificial oblation;
then, O high-minded one, both the gods and the Dānavas attained great joy.
At that time, all the Siddhas in the sky, their minds distracted as they wondered, "What is this?", became fixed-gazed.
The goddess Vāruṇī became one whose eyes were rolling from intoxication;
then, from that whirlpool, she stumbled at every step.
"Clad in a single garment, with disheveled hair, red in hue, and with eyes fixed in a stare—let the Dānavas seize this goddess, who bestows strength upon me! (48)

Then the divine Pārijāta tree, the wish-fulfilling tree of the gods, appeared;

Then Śiva became cool, bestowing joy upon the gods;
Lord Śaṅkara requested, "Let this [water] serve as an ornament for my matted locks. (52)
"Brahmā gave his consent, saying: 'This moon, which has been seized by me, shall become an ornament for Hara. (53)

Then, from the remainder of the milk of the ocean of milk that had been drunk by the Nāgas,

The hosts of immortals headed by Indra, the Vidyādharas, the great serpents, the Dānavas, the great Daityas, and the Rākṣasas along with the Guhyakas; ||64||

"Both gods and dānavas have been forbidden from entering here;

when the God, the Grandfather of all the worlds, had gone out of sight.

(5) Fifth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
How did the auspicious Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, abandon her body?

In ancient times, Dakṣa began a sacrifice at Gaṅgādvāra;

thus, as the sacrificial rites proceeded and the fires were being offered oblations, ||7||
All the Vasus have arrived, as well as the twelve Ādityas,
the Aśvins, the Maruts, and the fourteen Manus.
Thus, while the sacrifice was proceeding and the fires were being offered oblations,

Having surveyed the ground on all sides for an area of that many yojanas,

Having seen all the gods, headed by Śakra, at the sacrifice, the auspicious Satī then addressed these conciliatory words to Prajāpati: ||11||

Born in the lineage of Atri, a king among the twice-born and of great renown, he was a lord of the world upon the surface of the earth who brought joy to the eyes [of all]. (22)

The eight Vasus arrived together, and the two Aśvins also came;

Vidyādharas, hosts of bhūtas, vetālas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;

Rivers and streams, oceans and islands together with their mountains;

The Blessed Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, along with others—Pulastya, Pulaha, and the great sages beginning with Sanaka. ||27||

The meritorious royal sages and those who were kings upon the earth, as well as the various social classes and those belonging to the stages of life—all these were performers of their respective duties. ||28||

"You have surely forgotten everything; you are a destroyer of all that is auspicious.

Having heard those words spoken by her, Dakṣa Prajāpati—

Having bound a girdle of serpents around his waist, he likewise wore a bracelet of serpents on his arm, and he had Vāsuki,

"You should not harbor anger in this matter; everyone deserves their own portion, according to whatever good or evil karma was performed by them in other births. (46)
"O daughter, such is the fruit that is being experienced here in this very life;

Having seen the prosperity attained by another, which was beautiful with its form and good fortune— its exquisite beauty, supreme charm, and lovely ornaments— (he became envious).
O lady of excellent vows, birth in a great family, a most beautiful body, and wealth—these things are attainable by men through their past merits. (49)
O lady of virtuous vows, do not reproach yourself nor your own fortunes;
for who is capable of giving away that which is the fruit ordained by destiny? (50)
There is no one at all who is powerful, nor anyone who is neither deluded nor wise;
both the weak and the powerful are born as a result of their past karma. (51)
These very gods, having attained heaven, remain shining for a long time through their merit and austerity in various sacred fields.
"Whatever merit has been earned by these [monks], they shall be partakers of its fruit.

Therefore, this Lord of the worlds is the most supreme among all;

Even the tongue of Brahmā, the Creator, would not be able to describe the qualities of that God; it is incapable of proclaiming the virtues of that Supreme Lord.
Ashes, bones, and skull-basins, as well as dwelling in the cremation ground, and whatever serpents there are, such as the gonasa and others— all these have been made into ornaments.
The hosts of bhūtas and pretas, as well as piśācas and guhyakas—He is their creator and ordainer, and He is the protector of the quarters. (59)

Ten million Gaṇas, as well as Agra-hās and Vaināyakas,

Having gone there, all those gods defeated and destroyed Dakṣa’s sacrifice; once the sacrifice was slain, Dakṣa became despondent and devoid of effort.
Approaching in fear, he spoke to the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow:

With various kinds of terrible hosts, adorned with diverse ornaments, possessing various faces and tusks, and brandishing various weapons. ||71||

By those yogins who travel the path of yoga—possessing forms at will, free from desire, endowed with all objects of desire, fierce, and possessing irresistible power. ||73||
With manes like disheveled locks of hair, with faces grinning fiercely with bared fangs,
and with the skillful swelling of trunks like the flapping ears of elephants, they possessed the bodies of lions.

Some [were adorned] with garments of various wonderful patterns, possessing a luster like lamps flickering from the intense heat of a great conflagration, and [wearing] head-ornaments such as crowns that were both firm and steady.
[They were] with deer, tigers, lions,
and hyenas wearing skins, and with serpents serving as necklaces, bracelets, and sacred threads.
They held tridents, swords, and spears; they carried axes and darts in their hands;
and they bore in their palms weapons such as the thunderbolt, the saw, the bow, and the staff of Death.
Surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, who were exceedingly difficult to overcome— like the sun surrounded by the planets—
the great god of gods, Naṣṭo-yajña, ascended to heaven.

Assuming the form of a deer, Śaṅkara, terrified and seeking refuge, said: "Obeisance to the god whose luster is like a conch shell, who is accompanied by his hosts; I seek shelter at your feet today. (79)

Salutation to the one who has the bull as his seat, to the one whose essence is Soma, to the one who is the performer of sacrifice, to the one whose time is the ritual, and salutation to the one who wears the directions as his garment; salutation to you of intense splendor.

Salutations again and again to Brahmā, to the one whose body is Brahman, to the one who is devoted to Brahman, and to the immeasurable; salutations again and again to Girīśa, to the Lord of the Asuras, and to Īśāna.
Homage to Rudra, to the one with the counter-thunderbolt, to Śiva, and to Krathana; homage to the lord of gods and asuras, and to the lord of those who have gone beyond.
Salutations indeed to the smoke-colored, the fierce, the deformed, the sacrificer, the one of terrible form,
the three-eyed, the one with inauspicious eyes, and the thousand-eyed.

Salutation to the shaven-headed one, to Caṇḍamuṇḍa, to the bearer of the excellent khaṭvāṅga staff, to the one whose form is the sacrificial offering to ancestors (kavya), to the recipient of the sacrificial offering to gods (havya), and to the one who withdraws all things. ||84||
To the one who is compassionate toward his devotees, who is praised by the recitation of the Rudra-hymns, who is both deformed and beautiful, and who creates hundreds of forms; ||85||
Salutations again and again to the five-faced one, to the one with the auspicious face, and to the moon-faced one;
salutations to the bestower of boons, to the one worthy of boons, and to the Tortoise and the Deer.
Salutations again and again to the one who bears the circle of rays from his playful locks of hair, to the one whose name is Viśva, to Viśva himself, and to the Lord of the Universe. ||87||
O Maheshvara, grant us protection through Your three eyes, for we have sought refuge in You with our speech, mind, body, and inner being, O Destroyer of Tripura. (88)
Thus praised then by Dakṣa, whose body was afflicted with pain,
the God was then greatly propitiated by this divine hymn.
"O Prajāpati, I have bestowed upon you the entire fruit of the sacrifice;

Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, he prostrated before the Lord of the Gods and departed for his own abode while the hosts of gods looked on.
Due to grief for his wife, the god then remained at Gaṅgādvāra; brooding over that virtuous woman, he thought, "When will my beloved return? (92)
While he was overwhelmed by grief, Nārada spoke in his presence: "O Lord of Gods, that Satī, your wife who was as dear to you as your own life, has died. (93)
Born from the womb of Menā, the daughter of Himavat, she who knew the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāngas assumed another body. 94.
Having heard this, the god then beheld her entered into meditation;
having thus made himself one who has accomplished his purpose, the god then remained there.
The queen, having reached the prime of youth, was married once again;
thus indeed, O Bhīṣma, has been told how the sacrifice was destroyed in the past.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||5||
The Sixth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
[This concerns] the gods, the Dānavas, the Gandharvas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas.

from Dakṣa Prācetasa onwards, however, creation originated through sexual union.
Listen now, O Kaurava, to how he indeed created;
when he was creating the hosts of gods, sages, and serpents.

then Dakṣa begot thousands of sons upon his daughter Siknī.

even today they have not returned, just as the ocean does not return from the shore.
When the Haryaśvas had perished, the lord Prajāpati Dakṣa again begot a thousand sons from Vīriṇī alone. (8)
In the work of creation, the sage spoke again to those followers of Nārada who were accompanied by the Śabalāśvas, just as before.
Having measured the entire extent of the earth,

Twenty were given to Saptasoma, four to Ariṣṭanemi,
two to the son of Bhṛgu, and two to the wise Kṛśāśva.

Aruṇdhatī, Vasurjāmī, Lambābhānu, Marutvatī, Saṅkalpā, Muhūrtā, Sādhyā, and the beautiful Viśvā. (16)
These are declared to be the lawful wives; learn now of their sons:
Viśvā gave birth to the Viśvedevas, and Sādhyā gave birth to the Sādhyas. (17)
From Marutvatī were born the Maruts; from Vasu, the Vasus; likewise, from Bhānu, the Bhānus;
and from Muhūrtā, the Muhūrtajas were born.
Lambā, the daughter of Aṅgopa, was born from the lineage of the Nāgas;
she gave birth to Aruṇa, who was produced from the surface of the earth. ||19||
O Saṅkalpā, establish the creation of the Vasus within your resolve;
and may the radiant gods who pervade all directions [protect us]. 20.
The Vasus have been described to you; now hear their names:
Āpa, Dhruva, Soma, Dhara, Anila, and Anala. (21)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus;
and the four sons of Āpa were Śrānta and Vaitaṇḍa, and so forth.
The sage Vabhru was also known as Apiśānta; he was the one authorized to protect the sacrifice.
Dhruva’s son, Varcas, was born from Soma.
Draviṇa and Havyavāha—these two are remembered as the sons of Dharā;

Then Manohara, Udha, Śiva, and Hare’s sons;
Śiva [gave] his son Manojava, who bestows a course unknown [to others]. (25)
From that, the fire-god Anala begot sons whose qualities were predominantly fiery;
among them were Śākha and Viśākha, who were born of themselves from the Vedas.
Kārttikeya was then remembered as the offspring of the Kṛttikās;
Ṛbhu was the son of Pratyūṣa, and the sage named Devala was his son.
Viśvakarman, the son of Prabhāsa, was a master craftsman and a lord of creatures; he was the creator of palaces, mansions, gardens, statues, ornaments, and so forth.

O Father, these hosts of gods arise during each successive Manvantara,
and likewise they dissolve at the end of every Kalpa.

In the same way, four sons were born to Hiraṇyakaśipu:
