The sons of Prahlāda were the venerable Śibi and Vāṣkali, and Virocana was the fourth; he obtained Bali as his son.
O King, Bali had a hundred sons, of whom Bāṇa was the eldest;
they were Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Asūrya, Vivasvān, and Śrutāpana. ||43||
Nikumbha, Agurvakṣas, Kukṣi, Bhauma, and Bhīṣaṇa—thus there were many others; yet Bāṇa was the eldest and superior in qualities.
Bāṇa, however, possessed a thousand arms and was endowed with the qualities of all divine weapons;
the wielder of the trident (Śiva) dwelt in his city, being pleased by his ascetic penance.
He who was the charioteer of the wielder of the Pināka bow attained the state of Mahākāla;
Hiraṇyākṣa’s son was known by the name Andhaka.
Bhūtasaṃtāpana and likewise Mahānāga;
from these [lineages] came seventy-seven crores of sons and grandsons. ||47||
Danu obtained from Kaśyapa, who was proud of his boon, a hundred sons of great strength, massive bodies, various forms, and immense power.
Among them, the immensely powerful Vipracitti became the leader;
likewise, there were Śakuni with sixteen heads and Aśaṅkuśirodhara. ||49||
Ayomukha, Śambaras, Kapila, Vāmana, as well as Marīci, Māgadha, Hari, and Gajaśiras; ||50||
Nidrādhara, Ketu, Ketuvīrya, Śatakratu, Indramitragraha, and likewise Vajranābha. (51)
Ekavastra, Mahābāhu, Vajrākṣa, and Tāraka;
Asiloman, Puloman, and the great asura Vikurvāṇa. ||52||
Svarbhānu, Vṛṣaparvan, and others were the sons of Anu;
Svarbhānu’s daughters were Suprabhā, Śacī, and Pulomajā.
Upadānavī had two sons, Tāmraka and Dāruka;
and Śarmiṣṭhā had two sons, Āyu and Vṛṣaparvan, from Caṇḍa.
Pulomā and Kālakā, both daughters of Vaiśvānara, were the wives of Mārīca; they were of great virtue and possessed many offspring.
In former times, there were sixty thousand Dānavas belonging to those two;
and in the past, Mārīca begot the Paulomas and the Kālakhañjas.
Indeed, the inhabitants of Hiraṇyapura were not to be slain by men;
for they had obtained a boon from the Four-faced One (Brahmā), yet they were slain here by Vijaya.
Vipracitti begot nine sons upon Siṃhikā;
these thirteen were indeed the nephews of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Kaṃsa, Śaṅkha, Rājendra, Nala, Vātāpi, Ilvala, Namuci, Khasṛma, and likewise Añjana; ||59||
Naraka, Kālanābha, and likewise Paramāṇu;
and the renowned Kalpavīrya, who increased the lineage of Anu. ||60||
In the lineage of the Daitya Hlāda were the Nivātakavacas,
who were invincible to all the gods, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Relying on that power which had been taken away, Arjuna begot six daughters on the battlefield from Tāmrā through the seed of Mārīca. (62)
From Śuci, he lawfully begot Śukī, Śyenī, Bhāsī, Sugṛdhrī, Gṛdhrikā, and Ulūkā. ||63||
Śyenī gave birth to hawks and falcons, as well as vultures and crows; Gṛdhri gave birth to vultures, and Sugṛdhri to pigeons and other birds.
She gave birth to swans, cranes, ducks, and water-fowls;
these are said to be the copper-colored offspring of Vinatā—now be quiet! (65)
Garuḍa is the best of birds, and Aruṇa is the lord of winged creatures;
likewise, this daughter is renowned in the sky as Saudāminī.
Both Sampāti and Jaṭāyu were the two sons of Aruṇa;
and Vabhru, the son of Sampāti, was swift-moving and highly renowned.
Jaṭāyu, Karṇikāra, and the renowned Śatagāmī—these were among them;
the offspring of these birds, including their sons and grandsons, became innumerable.
In ancient times, a thousand serpents were born from Surasā;
Kaḍru, being of virtuous conduct, obtained a thousand [serpents] with a thousand heads.
Among them, O subduer of enemies, twenty-six are renowned as the principal ones:
Śeṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Śaṅkha, Āvataka, and Vala.
Dhanañjaya, Mahānīla, Padma, Aśvatara, Takṣaka, Elāpatra, Mahāpadma, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Balāhaka. ||71||
Śaṅkhapāla, Mahāśaṅkha, Puṣpadantṛ, Śubhānana, Śaṅkharoman, Canahuṣa, Uramaṇa, and Paṇina. ||72||
Kapila, Durmukha, Patañjali, and Mukha likewise—
of all these, their sons and grandsons became infinite in number.

likewise, the fanged beasts, jackals, crows, and others, as well as the female buffaloes and female wild boars, perished there.
In ancient times, Surabhi bore three offspring to Kaśyapa:
a sage who was the foremost among sages, and likewise a host of celestial nymphs.
Likewise, she gave birth to many Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Ariṣṭas;
and Irā produced all grasses, trees, creepers, and shrubs.
Khasātū produced yakṣas and rākṣasas by the millions;
these descendants of Kaśyapa numbered in the hundreds and thousands. (78)
In this manner, the Bhīṣma creation is recorded within the Svārociṣa Manvantara.
Then, O knower of dharma, Diti gave birth to forty-nine Maruts from Kaśyapa, all of whom were beloved by the immortals.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||6||
Chapter Seven.
Bhīṣma said:
How were the sons of Diti born as the Maruts, the beloved of the gods?
And why did they enter into unsurpassed friendship with the gods, who were their rivals? ||1||
Pulastya said: Formerly, when her sons and grandsons had been slain by the Asuras during the war between the gods and the Asuras, she, afflicted with grief, came to this excellent world of mortals.
At Puṣkara, the great sacred ford, on the auspicious bank of the Sarasvatī,
she performed severe penance, devoted to the propitiation of her husband.
Diti, the mother of the Daityas, being of virtuous vows, performed austerities for the sake of the ṛṣis' purpose,
subsisting on fruits and practicing the kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances.
For more than a hundred years she remained overwhelmed by old age and grief;
then, tormented by her own suffering, she questioned Vasiṣṭha and the other sages.
"Tell me, sirs, of a vow that destroys grief for one's son and bestows the fruit of good fortune both in this world and the next. (6)
Vasiṣṭha and the other sages said: "It is the vow of the eldest [son] on the full-moon day, by the grace of which you have become free from grief for your son. (7)
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, I wish to hear about the vow of the elder [fortnight],
by which Diti obtained forty-nine sons once again.
Pulastya said:
Listen now from me in detail to this very same vow which was previously described by Vasiṣṭha and others to Diti.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the full moon day,
one who is observant of her vows should place a flawless jar filled with white rice.
Likewise, it should be provided with various fruits and accompanied by stalks of sugarcane;
it is covered with a pair of white cloths and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Equipped with various kinds of food offerings and accompanied by gold according to one's means,
one should place a copper vessel filled with molasses upon it.
Above that, one should fashion Brahmā within the hollow of a golden lotus;

In the absence of those, how should one act? As the Grandfather (Brahmā) did for the lotus. 14.

Having worshipped the feet with "Oṃ Brāhmāya," the shanks with "Oṃ Saubhāgyadāya," the pair of thighs with "Oṃ Viriñcāya," and the waist with "Oṃ Manmathāya. (16)
To the one with a pure belly, he offered the belly; to the one who bestows [prosperity], the chest;

One should devoutly feed a Brahmin while personally abstaining from salt;

May the venerable Grandfather of all the worlds be pleased—he who is designated as the Soul within the hearts of all beings. (20)
By this method, one should perform everything month after month;
fasting on the full moon day, one should worship the imperishable Brahma.
Having consumed one fruit, he should sleep on the ground during the night;

One should give a bed along with a palanquin, fully equipped with all necessary furnishings;
having fashioned Brahmā out of gold and Sāvitrī likewise out of silver.
May he, whose nature is the lotus and who is the creator of the universe, obtain Sāvitrī;

One should give the gift of power, the gift of the self, and so forth, and utter the words, "May [the deity] be pleased.

"Desiring happiness, one should meditate upon the god Pitāmaha in the form of Kāma.

"I shall give this to you, O auspicious one; however, let this be done today, O lady of beautiful breasts: perform the Āpsava, the Bīja, and the Putrīya sacrifices."

nor should one stay, nor should one go to the roots of trees at any time. (40)
He should not settle among household utensils such as the pestle and mortar;

nor should he be without clothing, nor agitated, nor have wet feet. (45)
She should not utter inauspicious speech, nor should she indulge in excessive laughter;

I am emaciated and indeed weak; old age has come upon me. My breasts have shifted from their place, and my face is wrinkled and sagging. (49)
"You should never speak to me in this manner, saying 'I am without ego' (ahaṅkṛta).
"May it be well with you; I shall depart," he said, and she replied to him again, "So be it. (50)

With her mind filled with wonder and joy, she considered herself to have achieved her life’s purpose;

Then, having found an opportunity at that time, the husband of Śacī entered within.
The lord of the thirty gods split that embryo into seven parts with his vajra;

Then the slayer of Vṛtra, filled with anxiety, reflected thus with deliberation.

Having understood this fruit of the full-moon day through the power of merit, [he spoke]. (61)
Surely this has come to pass as a result of their worship of Brahmā;

Bhīṣma said:
O Brahman, you have described to me in detail the primary creation;
now tell me of the secondary creation and those who were the lords of each.
Pulastya said:
When Pṛthu was consecrated as the sovereign lord over the entire kingdom of the earth,
he likewise appointed Soma as the lord of medicinal herbs, of sacrificial vows, and of ascetic penances.
He saw Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who is the womb of the moon amidst the canopy of constellations, stars, birds, trees, shrubs, and creepers;
and likewise Vaiśravaṇa, the sovereign of wealth and the lord of kings. (70)
He made Viṣṇu the lord of the Ravis, Agni the lord of the Vasus, and Dakṣa the lord of the Prajāpatis;
he made Śakra the sovereign of the Maruts. (71)
Then [he saw] Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas; Yama, the lord of the Pitṛs;
and Śūlapāṇi (Śiva), the king of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Paśus, Bhūtas, Yakṣas, and Vetālas.
He made the Snowy Mountain the lord of mountains, the ocean the sovereign of rivers, and Citraratha the lord of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras. (73)
He commanded Vāsuki, the lord of nāgas of fierce prowess, and Takṣaka, the lord of serpents;
and he [commanded] Airāvaṇa by name, the king of elephants and the leader of the five elephants that guard the directions.
He made Suparṇa the lord of winged creatures, Uccaiḥśravas the king of horses, the lion the king of beasts, the bull the leader of cattle, and the fig tree the foremost of all forest trees. (75)
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā) consecrated these once more as the lords of all the directions;
he then consecrated the guardian of the eastern quarter by the name Suvarmā, who was a banner against his enemies.
Then, the Lord of the cosmic egg placed Adhipa to the south, Śaṅkhapada named Kāra-sarveśvara,
and that Lord Saketuman as the sovereign of the quarters in the west.
He made the Lord of the East, Hiraṇyaroman, the son of Megha and Prajāpati;
even today, the lords of the quarters continue to honor him, who always brings prosperity and is unwearied by the burdens of the earth.
Consecrated by these four kings named Pṛthu as the first on earth, when the Tretā age had passed, they established him on the earth under the name Vaivasvata Manu Cākṣuṣa.

When the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had passed and the Vaivasvata Manvantara had again commenced, he, born of the lineage of Sūrya and bearing its characteristic marks, became the Prajāpati of this world of moving and unmoving beings. (80)

Chapter Eight.
Bhīṣma said:
It is heard that in ancient times, the earth was enjoyed by many kings.
They are called pārthiva because of their connection with the earth (pṛthivī), due to their association with that which belongs to the earth. ||1||

Then the one of immeasurable prowess, out of anger, prepared to pierce him with an arrow;

then, standing to one side, he said, "What shall I do? (13)

"So be it," said the Earth; and that lord of men, Pṛthu, milked her, making Svāyambhuva Manu the calf with his own hands. (15)
That food became milk, by which living beings subsist;
thereafter, when it was milked by the sages, Soma became the calf.
Vācaspati became the milker, the Veda the vessel, and austerity the milk;
and the gods, with Aruṇa as the milker, then milked the earth. (17)
Indra became the calf; the milk was vigorous strength.
For the gods there was a golden vessel, and likewise for the ancestors, a silver one. (18)
Death (Antaka) became the milker, Yama was the calf, and Svadhā was the milk;

Then the milker became Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and poison was milked from her;
this [cow] was also milked by the Asuras, and iron, which causes affliction to enemies, was produced.
The calf was Māyā, Prāhlādi was the excellent milker, and Trimūrdhan was the vessel; by him (Māyā) this illusion was set in motion.
O Lord of the Earth, desiring the disappearance of the cities dug out from the earth by the Yakṣas, they made Viśvāvasu the calf and that jewel the milking vessel.
The milk was a profusion of marrow and blood, sucked out by hosts of pretas and rākṣasas;
Rūpyanābha became the milker, and Sumālī himself was the calf.
Furthermore, the Gandharvas together with hosts of Apsaras milked the earth,
making Citraratha their calf and drawing forth fragrances like those on lotus petals.
Then the milker named Vasuruci, a master of the Atharvaveda,
milked the earth through the mountains for various kinds of jewels.
The divine herbs were the milk, the mountain Meru was the milker,
Himavat became the calf there, and the vessel, moreover, was made of stone.
And from the trees, which were like cows yielding the milk of the earth, he milked the sap that causes severed branches to regrow;
Sāla trees, crowded with flowering groves, yielded their essence into vessels made of Palāśa leaves.
Then, O dear one, the Plakṣa tree became the calf, the sovereign of all trees and forests;
in this manner, the earth was likewise milked by others according to their desire.
While he rules the earth, there shall be long life, wealth, and happiness;
likewise, there shall be no poverty, nor any who are diseased, nor any who are destitute, nor any who commit evil.
While Pṛthu ruled his kingdom, there were neither calamities nor afflictions;
the people were constantly joyful and free from suffering and grief.
Pushing aside the lords of mountains with the tip of his bow, he of great power made the circle of the earth level out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. (31)

Where men do not die even when facing the difficulties of villages, forts, or those bearing weapons, and where there is no regard for the science of material prosperity (Arthaśāstra), [that is a place of happiness]. 32.
Men who are single-mindedly devoted to Dharma govern the vast kingdom;
and the vessels have been prepared, as well as the milk for you, exactly as it is. (33)
Whatever anyone has a desire for, that was given to them by me, the one who knows;
in all these glorious sacrifices, it has been offered by me to you. (34)
O Mahāmati, because she became the daughter of Pṛthu, the earth is known as "Pṛthivī" by the wise through that connection with him. (35)
Bhīṣma said: O knower of truth, you ought to recount the entire solar dynasty in its proper sequence, O Brāhmaṇa, and likewise the lunar dynasty exactly as it is.

and Prabhā bore to Tvaṣṭṛ a son named Saṃjñāta, who was likewise known as Manu.

then, the radiant form of Vivasvat became unbearable. (39)
From his own body, he produced a woman who was not subject to old age;
she was the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ in form and beauty, a beautiful lady known by the name Chāyā.
To her, who stood before him saying, "What shall I do?", he spoke:
"O fair-faced one, go and serve that husband of mine. (41)
"Protect my children with maternal affection.
Having said, "So be it," that goddess of virtuous vows departed for Kāma.
Desiring with reverence that he might be known as a god,
she gave birth to Sāvarṇi, who was Manu himself in human form.
And because of his being of the same caste as Sāvarṇi, the son of Vaivasvata Manu,
he [married] his daughter Tvaṣṭṛ’s daughter Chāyā in due order.
The Sun thought, "I shall produce a son from Chāyā," yet at that time,
he felt greater affection for his own son in Manu than for Chāyā.
Neither Manu, nor Yama, overcome with anger, could endure that;
he then threatened him, lifting up his right foot.
"May this shadow become a worm that consumes the moon;
may this one foot become a source from which pus and blood flow. (47)

"O Lord, out of childishness I once raised my hand for battle;
though restrained by Manu, I nevertheless cast a curse upon him. (49)
"O high-minded one, because we have been greatly exhausted by this lack of effort, even the god Yama spoke to us again: 'What shall I do? (50)
If even for one who possesses happiness there might be suffering, or if the continuity of karma is unavoidable even for a Buddha, what need is there to mention other living beings? (51)
The cock will devour the worm that dwells within its praise;
"khaṃ jaṃ caruciraṃ" shall indeed be this foot [of the verse]. (52)
Thus addressed, he was comforted and performed intense austerity at the holy site of Puṣkara, subsisting on fruits and foam out of a sense of detachment.
Having propitiated the Grandfather for ten thousand years,
the Lord of Gods, who is born from the lotus, was again pleased by the power of his asceticism.
He chose the status of a world-protector as well as the imperishable realm of the ancestors,
and the examination of this world consisting of both dharma and adharma.

Then Vivasvat, having learned of that deed performed out of ignorance,

Having been addressed thus, she went swiftly to the desert region, dejected;
assuming the form of a mare, she established herself upon the earth.
Therefore, if you would grant me favor so that I may share in your grace,
I shall remove this splendor of yours, making it as if the sun were in the third heaven.
"O Lord, I shall assume a form that brings benefit to the worlds.
Having been told "So be it" by the Sun, he made the sun his vehicle. (63)
He separated the splendor and fashioned the discus for Viṣṇu,
the trident for Rudra, and another, the thunderbolt, for Indra.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned a form of incomparable beauty, consisting of the thousand-rayed sun, the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, which was great beyond even that of gold.
No one was able to see that form of the Sun's foot again;
even today, no one anywhere can cause those feet to appear.
He who commits this most wicked act attains a censured state;
he suffers from leprosy in this world, which is fraught with misery.
Therefore, one who desires merit, virtue, and wealth should never have the feet of the wise God of Gods placed upon various [inauspicious] sites or anywhere else. 68.
Then the Blessed One, the Lord of the Immortals, having gone to the world of earth,
being afflicted by desire, longed for her with his face turned toward her like the sun.
Endowed with a great horse-form and possessed of immense splendor,
she recognized him in her mind and became overwhelmed with fear and agitation.
We have heard that, out of the fear that it was another man, [his semen] was discharged from both nostrils;
from that semen, the two Aśvins were born.
Because they had heard of him as the "Dasras" (the two healers), the two Nāsatyas were born from the tip of the nose;
having soon recognized that god, the virtuous ones attained supreme satisfaction. (72)
Accompanied by my wife, I joyfully ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot;
meanwhile, Sāvarṇi Manu even now performs penance on Mount Meru.
And through the power of Śani’s asceticism, as well as due to the equanimity of the planets, Yamunā and Tapatī once again became two rivers. (74)
Likewise, Viṣṭi is established as Time (Kāla) of a terrible nature;
furthermore, Vaivasvata Manu had ten sons of great strength.
Of them, the first was Ilā, who was produced through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice;
[the others were] Ikṣvāku, Kuśanābha, Ariṣṭa, and Dhṛṣṭa.
Nariṣyanta, Karūṣa, the mighty Śaryāti, Pṛṣadhra, and then Nābhāga—all these were divine-human beings. ||77||
Having first consecrated his righteous son Ila as Manu,
he went once again to Puṣkara, the forest of asceticism, for the sake of penance.
Then Brahmā, the bestower of boons, arrived for the sake of his success, saying:
"Choose a boon, O blessed one; choose whatever you desire, O son of Manu."
Then all the kings on earth, endowed with righteousness, spoke thus to the lotus-eyed, lotus-born, omnipresent Lord: "May we be blessed. (80)
"O Lord, by your grace may we become masters;
grant us this. Having said, "So be it," the Lord of Gods vanished right there.
Then, having returned to Ayodhyā, he settled there as before.
Now, on one occasion, the son of Manu, Ilavila, mounted upon his chariot—

He went forth for the sake of accomplishing his purpose across this earth, which was almost devoid of enemies, wandering through all the continents and bringing the kings into complete subjection. (83)
Then the powerful Śambhu, being drawn forth, went to the great grove named Aśaravaṇa, which was filled with wish-fulfilling trees and creepers. 84.
Where the Lord of Gods, Soma, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, delights together with Umā, there in ancient times the Śaravaṇa was created. 85.
Whatever male name is known that shall come to this forest,
all of it shall attain womanhood within a circle of ten yojanas.
King Ila, unaware of the agreement, went to Śaravaṇa;
he suddenly attained womanhood and in an instant became a mare.
Then, having forgotten her female body, she thought, "Everything was created by a man," and thus she became a woman with full, elevated, and firm breasts.
She possessed high hips and loins, eyes as long as lotus petals, a face like the full moon, a slender form, was full of grace, and had dark eyes. ||89||
Her arms were plump, elevated, and long; her hair was dark and curly;
her body hair was fine; her face was beautiful; and she spoke with a soft, faltering voice.
With a complexion of dark and golden hue, her sprout-like nails were thin and copper-colored;
she possessed eyebrows like a bow and moved with the gait of a swan. 91.
Wandering about in that place, the beautiful woman thought: "Where have my two brothers gone? Or where might my brother be here? (92)
"To whom have I been given as a husband? How many years have I spent on this earth?"—while she was thus reflecting, that woman was seen by the son of Soma (Budha). 93.
Then Budha, afflicted by desire, made an effort to obtain that woman of excellent complexion, whose mind was captivated by his form. (94)
Possessing a distinguished form, he carries a shaven-headed image, a water-pot, and a book; he is characterized by a bamboo staff, a sacred thread, and a small spade. ||95||
In the form of a twice-born, he wore a topknot and earrings,
and was accompanied by students seeking instruction who carried sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and water.
Then, having searched for her at the proper time, he called out to Satī from outside the forest,
near a bower of trees on the bank.
Suddenly, he became agitated and began to wander about; abandoning his service to the *agnihotra* fire, he cried out, "Where has she gone? Where has she gone from me? (98)
"This is the time for our pleasure; it is now passing away. Come, come, O lady of broad hips! Why are you so bewildered? (99)
This is that slender lady who dwells in the Velā-vihāra;
having smeared it with ointment, decorate my house with flowers. (100)
She said, "O ascetic, I have forgotten everything—myself, you, my husband, and my lineage; please tell me, O sinless one. (101)
Budha said to that slender woman: "O lady of excellent complexion, you are Mīlā;
I am known as Budha, the son of Candra, and am possessed of many sciences. (102)
"Born into a family of radiant ones, his father was a lord among Brahmins. Upon these words of his, she entered the wise man's palace. (103)
Seated in that palace, she considered herself to have achieved her life's purpose, for it was strewn with heaps of jewels and fashioned through divine illusion.
Oh, what a noble conduct! Oh, what a noble form! Oh, what great wealth! Oh, what a noble lineage! And oh, what supreme beauty belongs both to me and to this husband of mine! 105.
In the land of Ilāvṛta, which is equal in extent to the Cakravāḍa mountains,
there is a residence consisting of all enjoyments, just like the palace of Indra.
Then, searching for the king, his Mānava brothers,
headed by Ikṣvāku, went to the vicinity of the Aśoka grove.
Then they all saw that unsurpassed mare standing before them, shining with the radiance of a jeweled couch. (108)
Upon recognizing him, they were all struck with wonder:
"This is the son of that great-souled one named Candraprabha. (109)
For what reason did he assume the form of a mare?
Then they questioned their own priest, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
"What is this?"—this was the wonder that arose, O best among those who know yoga.
Vasiṣṭha, having seen everything with the eye of meditation, spoke it all.
In ancient times, a boon was granted by Śiva for the welfare of his beloved:
"Whatever man shall enter here shall attain womanhood. (112)
This Aśvin too attained womanhood along with the king;
just as Ila reached manhood, so did he become like Sudhanvan. (113)
In that very manner, they should exert effort even while propitiating the wielder of the Pināka bow;
thereafter, those Mānavas went to where the god Maheśvara was.
They praised Pārvatī and Parameśvara with various hymns; the two of them said, "Enough! This is the appointed time; what indeed is to be done now? (115)
Whatever fruit might result from Ikṣvāku’s horse sacrifice, that shall undoubtedly belong to us two once the heroic man has given it away. (116)
Having said, "So be it," all those sons of Vaivasvata departed;
then, having performed the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), they became men on earth. 117.
For one month the hero was a man, and for another month he became a woman; while remaining thus, he became pregnant by Budha. (118)
She gave birth to a single son endowed with manifold virtues;
having produced Budha and Pūru, she returned once more to heaven.
Then that region, named Ilāvṛta after him, came into being;
and King Ila, born of the lunar and solar lineages, became the progenitor of its dynasty.
Thus Purūravas became the progenitor of the lineage of Pūru;
likewise, the lord of men Ikṣvāku has been described as the founder of the solar dynasty. ||121||
Ila was called Sudyumna when he attained manhood; furthermore, three sons were born to Sudyumna who were unconquered.
Likewise, Utkala had a son named Āgaya, and the valiant Haritāśva was born from Āgaya;
from Utkala came the land of the Utkalas, and from Āgaya came the city of Āgayāpurī.
Having learned that the southern direction belonged to Haritāśva, he then consecrated Purūravas, the son of Iḷā, at Pratiṣṭhāna along with the Kurus.
Eating only fruits, Ikṣvāku, the eldest heir, went to enjoy the divine Ilāvṛta for a year, while [his younger brother] obtained Madhyadeśa.
Nariṣyanta’s son was Śuka, who possessed great strength; from Nābhāga came Aṃbarīṣa, and from Dhṛṣṭa came Sutaṃnaya. (126)
Then Dhṛṣṭaketu, who was bold in battle and possessed of great valor, remained true to his own duty;
and there was also the daughter Sukanyā, the daughter of Śaryāti, named Ānartā. ||127||
Ānarta had a powerful son named Roca­māna;
the country was called Ānarta, and its capital city was Kuśasthalī.
From Revā came Revat, and from Revat came Raivata;
Kakudmin was another name for him, and he was the eldest of a hundred sons. (129)
Revatī was the renowned wife of Rāma Sākanya;
from Karūṣa, moreover, the many Kārūṣas became celebrated upon the earth.
From the killing of Pṛṣadhra and from the curse of his guru, a Śūdra was born.
Among the sons of Ikṣvāku were Nātha, Vikukṣi, Nimi, and Daṇḍaka. (131)
There were fifty excellent sons of Śatajit, and their sons were likewise;
those best of kings were born to the north of Meru.
There are forty-eight others who reside within that [region];
they are proclaimed as the kings situated to the south of Meru. (133)
From Jyeṣṭha was born a son named Kakutstha; his son was Suyodhana.
His son was named Pṛthu, and Viśva was the son of that Pṛthu.
Ārdras was his son, and from him Yuvanāśva was born;
the son of Yuvanāśva was the powerful one named Śāvasta. (135)
O King, by this Nirmita, Śrāvastī was established here in the land of Aṅga; from Śrāvasta came Bṛhadaśva, and from him Kuvalāśva arose. (136)
In ancient times, having slain the asura Dhuṃdhu, [Dhundhumāra] attained the state of Dhundhumāra;
three sons were born to him: Dṛḍhāśva, Ogha, and Ghṛṇi.
The renowned Kapilāśva was the son of Dhūmrāri, who was full of majesty; Pramoda was the son of Dṛḍhāśva, and Haryaśva was his son. (138)
Haryaśva’s son was Anikuṃbha; from him Saṃhatāśva was born.
Akṛtāśva and Raṇāśva were both sons of Saṃhatāśva. (139)
From Raṇāśva was born Yuvanāśva; from him came Māndhātṛ.
From Māndhātṛ was born Purukutsa, and [from him] the king Dharmasētu.
And the renowned and powerful Mucukunda, a friend of Śakra, was born as the son of Purukutsa; he was Duḥsaha, the lord of the Narmadā. (141)
Sambhūti was his son, and from him Tridhanvan was born;
the son of Tridhanvan was born as he who is known as Trayyāruṇa. (142)
His son was named Satyavrata; from him Satyaratha is recorded [to have descended]. His son was Hariścandra, and from Hariścandra came Rohita. (143)
From Rohita was born Vṛka, and from Vṛka Bāhu was born.
His son was Sagara, a king of supreme righteousness. Sagara had two wives: Prabhā and Bhānumatī.
Formerly, the submarine fire (Aurva) was propitiated by those two out of a desire for a son.
Aurva, being pleased with them, granted each an excellent boon as they desired:
one [received] sixty-one thousand sons, and the other likewise a single son.
Prabhā took the founder of the lineage as her son, while Bhānumatī took many sons; she took one son, Asamajasa, who was peerless in valor.
Then, sixty thousand Yadavas, possessing the splendor of Indra and Agni, dug into the earth while being consumed by Viṣṇu during his search for the horse.
From Asama was born Jastutanaya, renowned by the name Śumān;
his son was Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa came Bhagīratha.
By whom the Gaṅgā, daughter of Bhagiratha, was brought down after he had performed penance;
[he] was the son of Bhagiratha, renowned as Nābhāga. (150)
From Nābhāga was born Barīṣa; from him came Saṃdhudvīpa.
His son was Ayutāyu, and from him was born Ṛtuparṇa.
His son was Kalmāṣapāda, who is remembered as having performed all sacrificial rites; his son was Anaraṇya, and Nighna became his son.
Two sons were born to Nighna, Anamitra and Raghu, the best of the Raghus;
O King, Anamitra went to the forest for the sake of destroying his enemies.
From Raghu was born Dilīpa, and from Dilīpa likewise was born Aja; Dīrghabāhu was born from Aja, and from him Prajāpāla arose. (154)
Then Daśaratha was born; he had four sons, all of whom were of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and Rāma was the eldest among them. (155)
In that same way, Rāvaṇa was the destroyer of the Raghus, while he [Rāma] was the enhancer of the Raghu lineage;
Vālmīki composed his life story, and Bhārgava (Paraśurāma) was the best among the Bhṛgus. 156.
His son was named Kuśa, who increased the Ikṣvāku lineage;
Atithi was born from Kuśa, and Niṣadha was his son.
Nala was born from Niṣadha, and from him Nabhas was born;
from Nabhas came Puṇḍarīka, and after him was Kṣemadhanvan. (158)
His son was the heroic and powerful Devānīka;
his son was Ahīnagu, and after him came Sahasrāśva.
And from him was born Nandrāvaloka, whose son was Tārāpīḍa;
his son was Candragiri, and Candrastha was his son. (160)
From him was born Śrutāyu, who was cast down to the womb of a Bhārata;
two Nalas are particularly renowned for their lineage. 161.
Likewise, Vīrasena’s son and the lord of men, Naiṣadha—
these kings of the lineage of Vivasvat were givers of abundant sacrificial fees.
Those born of the Ikṣvāku lineage have been proclaimed here primarily. ||163||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Solar Lineage," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Ninth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the supreme lineage of the Pitṛs."
And especially of Ravi, Śrāddhadeva, and Soma. ||1||
Pulastya said:
O son, I shall now describe to you the most excellent lineage of the ancestors (pitaras).
In heaven there are seven groups of ancestors; among them, some are formless (amūrta).
All four classes of ancestors possess embodied forms and immeasurable splendor;
the formless groups of ancestors belong to Vairāja Prajāpati.
Those hosts of gods renowned as the Vairājas, who sacrifice, they—having fallen from yoga—attain these eternal worlds. ||4||
Furthermore, those speakers of Brahman, having attained that state, regained their memory of the unsurpassed Yoga and Sāṅkhya. ||5||
Through yoga, they attain perfection from which return is difficult to find;
therefore, funeral offerings (śrāddhas) should be given by donors specifically to yogis.
Among these, Mānasī is considered the daughter and wife of Himavat;
Maināka was his heir, and Krauñca was his son. (7)
Krauñcadvīpa is remembered as the fourth, which is endowed with the Dhṛta ocean;
from it, Menā gave birth to three daughters who were possessed of yoga.

Some were devoted to the vow of eating from a single leaf, others to eating no leaves at all, and still others to extremely rigorous vows; some belonged to Rudra, while others belonged to Bhṛgu, Aja, and Jaigīṣavya.
The unblemished ones, who have surpassed all the world in asceticism, were bestowed by Himavat;
I shall now describe the world of the ancestors as it is celebrated—listen to this. (10)
There, the worlds of those who follow the path of Soma exist, where the Marīcis and Danas dwell;
by means of that path, the ancestors and the gods are fully nourished.
There dwell those known as the Agniṣvāttas, performers of sacrifices;
among them was a daughter of excellent complexion named Acchodā.
There, the lake Acchoda was created by the ancestors in ancient times;
there, Acchoda performed austerities for a thousand celestial years.
The ancestors, being pleased, arrived as if wishing to grant him a boon;
they all bore celestial forms and were adorned with divine garlands and unguents. ||14||
All were preeminent in strength and resembled the god of love;
seeing her father named Māvasu in their midst, that woman [was filled with joy].
Afflicted by the god of love and desiring union, that beautiful woman chose him as her husband,
for he was a steadfast man who had not fallen from yoga.
First she touched the earth and then departed to the surface of the world;
likewise, that Amāvasu formed a desire directed toward her.
By virtue of his fortitude, that day became renowned in the world as Amāvāsyā;
because it is beloved by the ancestors, it renders whatever is given there inexhaustible. (18)
Due to the exhaustion of her asceticism— rendered futile by her clear waters, downward gaze, and the shame of her wretchedness—
she too prayed to the ancestors for the sake of regaining her own prosperity.
Then, while being bashfully addressed by her fathers,
that poor girl looked toward the future and toward this task of the gods.
The highly fortunate ones spoke thus with words auspicious through their grace:
"O ascetic, by the wise, a divine body is sometimes fashioned in heaven. (21)
O lady of excellent complexion, this very fruit of that action is experienced by her;
for actions bear fruit immediately in the state of a deity, and after death in the human state.
Therefore, having performed good deeds, you shall obtain the fruit [of your actions] after death;
in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age, you will be born from the womb of a fish.
"Due to your transgression against the ancestors, you shall obtain a wretched lineage;
therefore, you will inevitably become the daughter of King Vasu."
As a maiden, you shall regain those celestial realms that are difficult to attain;
furthermore, by the power of Parāśara, you shall obtain one son.
Moreover, on the island abounding in jujube trees, your son will divide even Bādarāyaṇa— who possesses the Veda— into many parts.
Paurava had two sons, Śaṃtanu and Citrāṅgada;
the latter was the king, while Śaṃtanu was his younger brother. (27)
These two sons of that wise man— one born of his wife and one born of his field— shall become the Proṣṭhapada and Aṣṭaka, and you shall likewise exist in the world of the ancestors.
Known by the name Asatīvatī in this world, she is likewise called Aṣṭakā in the world of the ancestors;
she constantly bestows long life and health, and grants the fruit of all desires. (29)
In the next world you shall become a most excellent river of meritorious waters, known by the name Acchodā among the worlds. (30)
Having been addressed thus by those hosts of sages, she vanished right there;
she too was [the fruit of] her own misconduct, which had been ordained for me in a former life.
And on another day, they go to the world named Vibhrāja, which is full of splendor; there dwell the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, who are observers of excellent vows.
There, upon the sacrificial grass, thousands of celestial chariots are harnessed;
there, wish-fulfilling trees stand, bestowing their fruits.
Those who give with faith experience the joy of the hall of prosperity;
so too do the hosts of Dānavas, Asuras, Gandharvas, and Apsarases.
Those hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, the sons of Pulastya by the hundreds, endowed with the power of austerity and yoga, worship the gods in heaven. (35)
These high-souled ones, of great fortune, grant fearlessness to their devotees;
among them is the daughter of Pīvarī, Mānasī, renowned throughout the three worlds. (36)
She performed the yoga of the Yoginīs and a most severe austerity;
the Blessed One was pleased with her, and she then chose a boon from him. (37)
O best of speakers, since you have been pleased by embodied beings and gods, you shall possess a husband who is a master of yoga, handsome, and one who has conquered his senses. (38)
The god said: "When Vyāsa’s son becomes swift [in speech], you, O lady of excellent vows, shall become the wife of that master of yoga. (39)
Then that Yoginī, Kṛttikā, will become the daughter of the Pāñcāla king; she shall then be given in marriage to Sātvata. 40.
The mother of Brahmadatta will be remembered as Yogasiddhāntā;
and his sons will be Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, and Śambhu. (41)
Even those who are not purifiers dwell in celestial palaces where all desires are fulfilled;
how much more so those brahmins who possess faith, are generous, devoted, and endowed with ritual action? (42)
Among them, the daughter named Gau shines like the celestial cow Mānasī;
she is the beloved wife of the Sādhyas, a Sukanyā (a virtuous maiden), and the increaser of their fame. 43.
In the world-system named Marīcigarbha, within the orb of the sun,
dwell the Pitṛs, the possessors of oblations, who are the sons of Aṅgiras.
Wherever the best of Kṣatriyas perform Śrāddha at sacred fords (tīrtha), their ancestors, being pleased with them, bestow the fruit of enjoyment in heaven. 45.
Among these daughters of Mānasa, Yaśodā was the most renowned;
she was the wife of Śūrasena and the excellent daughter-in-law of Pañcajana.
Then Janaka’s mother, the great-grandmother of Bhagīratha, [spoke]:
"The worlds of those who grant all desires bestow the fruit of enjoyment even without longing. (47)
O Pitṛs, where those who possess excellent *svadhā* stand, together with their sons, in the worlds of the drinkers of clarified butter, in the realm of Kardama Prajāpati—[there may you come]. 48.
The Vaiśyas, who are the heirs of Pulaha’s elder brother, indeed cherish them;
there, all those who perform ancestral rites behold them simultaneously upon arrival.
Mothers, brothers, fathers, sisters, friends, relatives, and kinsmen—
seen and experienced thousands of times even across tens of thousands of births.
The daughter of Mānasa, Virajā, who was unknown to these [other sons],
became the co-wife of Nahuṣa and likewise the mother of Yayāti.
Afterwards, this Aṣṭakā went to the world of Brahmā;
these three groups have been described, and now I shall tell you the fourth.
The worlds of the Sumanas are situated above the world of Brahmā;
there the eternal Pitṛs known as the Somapas reside. (53)
All of them are remembered as bearers of the form of Dharma, originating from the Supreme Brahman;
having attained the state of Brahman, these yogins are subject to neither birth nor dissolution. (54)
Having performed all the work of creation and so forth, they now remain within the mind;
of them, the river named Narmadā is the daughter who carries water.
Purifying all beings as she flows toward the western ocean,
from her all human beings were fashioned during the creation of the world.
Having understood this, they always perform acts of faith with a sense of dharma;
for them, through his grace alone, there is always the attainment of yoga.
In this manner, the śrāddha was ordained for the primary creation of the ancestors;
for all of them, the vessel should be made of silver or associated with silver.
Placing the *svadhā* offering at the forefront, one always gratifies the ancestors;
however, the wise should perform the act of strengthening (*āpyāyana*) for both the Āgnīdhra and the Soma-drinkers.
Or, for one who has performed the rite an infinite number of times, it may be done in the hand of a Brahmin, or even in water,
or in the ear of a goat, or in the ear of a dog, or in a cow-pen, or near a Śiva-liṅga.
The pure abode of the ancestors is praised as being in the southern direction;
there, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), and water is offered facing north, as is the act of departure.
The meat of rhinoceroses, rice, millet, śyāmāka grain, śāli rice, barley, wild rice, mung beans, sugarcane, and white flowers and fruits [are suitable]. (62)
In this world, these are always praised as the most beloved offerings for the ancestors:
darbha grass, mung beans, ṣaṣṭika rice, cow’s milk, honey, and clarified butter.
I shall also declare those weapons and those things which are to be avoided at a śrāddha:
lentils, hemp, flat beans, cowpeas, and horse gram.
The lotus, bilva, arka, dhattūra, pāribhadra,
and aṭarūṣaka should not be offered in rites for the ancestors, nor should the milk of goats or sheep.
Kodrava, udāra, varaṭa, kapittha, madhuka, and atasī—these also should not be offered to the ancestors by one who desires prosperity. (66)
He who pleases the ancestors with devotion, they in turn please him;
the ancestors bestow upon him nourishment, physical health, and the fruit of progeny.
Furthermore, the rite for the ancestors is superior even to the rite for the gods;
it is traditionally taught that the satisfaction of the ancestors precedes that of the deities. (68)
They are quick to develop faith, free from anger, firm in their friendships, tranquil in nature,
devoted to purity, and always speak kindly.
The ancestors, who are devoted to their devotees and bestowers of happiness, are the deities of the lunar festivals;
the Sun is remembered as the presiding deity over those who offer oblations and the god of the śrāddha rites.
Thus, this entire glorification of the lineage of the ancestors has been narrated;
it is meritorious, purifying, health-bestowing, and should always be recited by men. (71)
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard all this, supreme devotion arose once again [in me] toward the time for the śrāddha,
the ritual procedure, and the śrāddha itself.
Regarding the twice-born who are to be fed at *śrāddhas* and those who are to be excluded from *śrāddhas*, at what part of the day should one commence the *śrāddha* for the ancestors? (73)
O best of those who know Brahman, how does the food given in a śrāddha go [to the ancestors]?
By what rite should it be performed, and how does it gratify those ancestors? (74)
Pulastya said:
One should perform the *śrāddha* rite day after day with food and water,
or even with milk, roots, and fruits, thereby bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.
The Śrāddha is said to be of three kinds: the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya).
Of these, I shall first describe the obligatory rite, which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana).
One should know that the Pārvaṇa rite, which is prescribed for the full-moon and new-moon festivals, is devoid of a presiding deity (adaivata).
O Lord of the Earth, listen attentively as the threefold Pārvaṇa is described.
O lord of men, hear now from me those who are to be invited at the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]:
one who maintains the five fires, a *snātaka*, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, and one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas. (78)

He was a learned Vedic scholar, the son of a learned Vedic scholar, proficient in the words of the injunctions, all-knowing, possessed of the Vedas, a minister, endowed with wisdom, and born of a noble lineage. (79)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who knows the three Madhu verses, one established in other sacred scriptures, a knower of the Purāṇas, a knower of Brahman, one devoted to private Vedic study, and one intent on silent recitation; ||80||

A Brahmin who is devoted to Brahmā, intent on his ancestors, or else a devotee of the Sun or Viṣṇu—one whose soul is established in yoga, who has conquered himself, and who is of virtuous conduct—[is worthy]. (81)
Therefore, one should strive to please these; now hear those who are to be avoided:
an outcast, his son, a eunuch, a slanderer, and one afflicted with a deformed disease. (82)
All these [unworthy persons] should be avoided by those who perceive the Dharma at the time of a Śrāddha;
one should instead invite those who are disciplined on the day before or the day after.
The ancestors approach those invited twice-born ones;
becoming like the wind, they go to them and attend upon them as they sit.
Having touched the right knee and lowered the left, he should invite [the guests], who are free from anger, devoted to purity, well-bathed, and exponents of the Veda. ||85||
"You and I must both be present for the rite of the ancestors; once the sacrifice to the fathers has been completed, the one who maintains the sacred fire should begin the libations. (86)
One should perform the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka* śrāddha;
likewise, one should smear with cow dung a place sloping toward the south.

One should begin the *śrāddha* with devotion either in a cow-pen or near water; one who possesses the sacred fire should offer the ancestral *caru* oblation, or [one without fire] with handfuls of unhusked grain.
Saying "I offer to the ancestors," he should place everything to the south;
then, having sprinkled [the offerings] with clarified butter, he should perform three offerings in front.
They should be made three spans long and four fingers wide;
one should prepare three ladles made of khadira wood and adorned with silver.
One cubit in length, perfectly smooth, with the tip shaped like a hand—this is the excellent water-pot;
as well as a strainer, a ladle, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass. (91)
One should bring the sesame vessels, fine garments, perfumes, incense, and ointments; all these, moving from right to left in a counter-clockwise direction, one should offer slowly to the south.
Having thus obtained all of that on the northern side of the house,
one should smear the mandala with cow dung and cow urine.
With water containing whole grains and flowers, he should wash the feet of the Brahmins repeatedly, moving his hands from left to right and right to left, while bowing down to them.

When the Brahmins have sat down upon seats provided with Darbha grass according to the prescribed rules, and have sipped water for purification, one should seat them and address them with the following mantra.
One should feed two Brahmins at a rite for the gods, three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each; or one may feed a single person at both.
Even a wealthy man, being wise, should not perform this with excessive elaboration.

Having first offered [the oblation] to the gods and then to the Brahmins with respectful offerings (*argha*) and so forth, the wise Brahmin, having received permission from the Brahmins, should perform the rite in the fire according to the rules. 97.

Then, having performed the ritual at the proper time according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, the wise man should perform the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the two deities Agni and Soma. 98.
O best of the twice-born, that very fire which has been brought forward to the Dakṣiṇāgni becomes [the sacrificial fire];
then, having removed the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), he should perform the sprinkling (paryukṣaṇa) and other rites.
All this should be performed by one who knows, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
Having obtained [the food], he should especially offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and water.
One should offer water from water-vessels with the left hand;
one who is free from envy and disciplined should offer everything with great effort.
Having carefully drawn the lines, he should perform the sprinkling (of water);
then, facing southward, he should indeed place the darbha grass.
Having placed each individual ball of rice upon all the darbha grass in sequence,
he should then offer them upon the darbha grass while reciting the names and lineages.

Upon those darbha grasses, he should wipe that hand for the sake of the "partakers of the smearings" (lepabhāginaḥ); in the same manner, he should perform the silent recitation (japa) and again the ritual rinsing (pratyavanejana).
Having paid homage to the one joined with water by means of perfumes, incense, worship, and so forth,
he should thus invoke all of that with the Vedic mantras as prescribed.
One who maintains only the single sacred fire (ekāgni) should likewise offer the ladle with water;
then, having performed this, the wise man should offer kuśa grass to the ancestors.
Then one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, including the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the dismissal (*visarjana*).
Thereafter, taking portions from all the rice-balls in due order, ||107||
Having first fed those very same Brahmins and caused them to sip water, the man of noble conduct should always cause them to eat desirable and pure food while describing its qualities.
Remembering Hari Nārāyaṇa, one should avoid being overcome by anger;
having ascertained that [the deities] are satisfied, one should again perform the scattering of food (vikira) for all classes.
One should place food, along with water and sesame seeds, on the ground within the *vidhṛti* lines;
then, after they have sipped water, one should again offer them water, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should perform the entire rite of pronouncing *svadhā* over the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
One should perform that [rite] beginning with the gods; otherwise, there would be the destruction of the *śrāddha*. (111)
Having dismissed the Brahmins and bowed to them, he circumambulated them;
then, with his mind fixed on his ancestors, he turned toward the southern direction.
May our donors increase, as well as our Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may there be much for us to give. (113)
May there be abundant food for us, and may we never have to beg from guests;
may those who come to us as supplicants never have to beg from us in turn.
This Anvāhārya rite for one who maintains the sacred fires has been declared;
just as it is performed at the Parvan, so too is it prescribed in other cases. 115.
One should inflict pain upon the cows, the bull, or the Brahmins, either by means of fire or water;
or one should scatter earth over them, or cause them to drink water that has been defiled.
He should cause his wife, who is endowed with humility, to eat the middle *piṇḍa*, saying:
"O ancestors, bestow upon her a fetus that will increase the lineage and the continuity of sons. (117)
One should remain until the extinguishing of the fires, or until the Brahmins have been dismissed;
then, having concluded the rites for the ancestors, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Then, being at peace, one should eat together with those who are dear, having partaken of what was offered to the ancestors;
furthermore, one should avoid a second meal, traveling, riding in vehicles, physical exertion, and sexual intercourse. (119)
One who performs a *śrāddha* or one who eats at a *śrāddha* should avoid all of this:
Vedic study, quarreling, and sleeping during the day at all times. (120)
By this method, one should always perform the śrāddha for the three classes of ancestors during the dark fortnights when the moon is situated in Virgo, Aquarius, or Taurus. 121.
Wherever the Śrāddha consisting of Sapindīkaraṇa is to be offered,
it should always be given according to this procedure by one who possesses the sacred fire.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which was uttered by Brahmā:
the Śrāddha known as Sādhāraṇa, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 123.
At the solstices and the equinoxes, on the new moon day and during the sun's transit;
on the new moon, the Aṣṭaka days, and the fifteenth days of the dark fortnight. ||124||
During the asterisms of Ārdrā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī; at the conjunction of goods and Brāhmaṇas;
during Gajacchāyā, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, Vaidhṛti, and on the day [of the week]. (125)
The third day of Vaiśākha, the ninth of Kārttika, the fifteenth of Māgha, and the thirteenth of Nabhasya. (126)

These are indeed remembered as the beginnings of the Yugas (yugādi), which are beneficial for the ancestral rites (pitṛpakṣa); likewise, a wise person should offer the Śrāddha at the beginning of the Manvantaras and other such times. 127.
Likewise, the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of Kārttika, and the third day of both the month of Caitra and Bhādrapada. (128)
The new moon day of Phālguna, as well as the eleventh day of Pauṣa, the tenth day of Āṣāḍha, and the seventh day of the month of Māgha— 129.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the full moon of Kārttika, the full moon of Phālguna, and the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha. (130)
But the Manvantaras and other such periods make what is given inexhaustible;
therefore, a self-controlled man should offer water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors. 131.

By him a funeral rite (śrāddha) has been performed for a thousand years; the ancestors declare this to be a secret, [when one observes] fasts on the full moon day of Vaiśākha and likewise at the great festival of Mahālaya. 132.
A wise person should offer the *śrāddha* at sacred fords, shrines, and cow-pens, as well as on islands, in gardens, in houses, and in secluded places that have been smeared with cow-dung. (133)

On the previous day and on the following day, he, with a disciplined mind, should consult with Brahmins who are endowed with good character, conduct, and virtues, and possessed of youth and beauty. (134)
One should feed two Brahmins at the rite for the gods and three at the rite for the ancestors, or one for each; even if very wealthy, one should not engage in excessive elaboration.
Having worshipped the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, beginning with the offering of a seat,
one should fill two vessels and place them upon *darbha* grass purifiers.
One should offer water with the mantra "śanno devī" and barley with "yavo 'si";
having worshipped them with perfumes and flowers, one should place the Viśvedevas [therein]. (137)
Having invoked [the deities] with the two verses beginning with "viśve devāsaḥ," one should scatter barley grains, [reciting]:
"O barley, you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey. (138)
The dispeller of all sins, the purifier praised by the sages—having adorned it with scents and flowers, one should offer the arghya water with the mantra beginning "yad divyam. (39)
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings and having concluded the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), one should commence the rite;
first, having prepared seats of darbha grass and so forth, one should worship three vessels.
Having first prepared the vessels with strainers, one should pour water while reciting "śanno devī";
then one should add sesame seeds while reciting "tilo 'si," and subsequently add perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
One should likewise prepare a vessel made of wood, or again one made of leaves, or one of silver, or even one originating from the ocean. (142)
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is said to be fit for the ancestors; even the mere mention, sight, or gift of silver [is meritorious]. (143)
Even water, when offered with faith by means of silver vessels adorned with silver for these ancestors, conduces to inexhaustibility.
Even today, among the vessels for the ancestors, that which is associated with silver is the most excellent and beloved by the Pitṛs, because it originated from the eye of Śiva. (145)
Having thus consecrated the vessels, free from envy, he should place darbha grasses in his hand according to what is available,
while reciting "yā divyāḥ" and pronouncing the name and lineage of the father.
"I shall invoke the ancestors," he said, and being told "So be it" by them, he should then invoke the ancestors with the two Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "uśantas tvā" and "āyantu naḥ. (147)
Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "yā divyā," one should then present the perfumes and other offerings;
having first given the garments, preceded by the *darbha* grass, one should then offer the seat at the beginning.
Having placed it in the paternal vessel, one should then set it face down to the north;
having set it with the mantra "Thou art the seat for the ancestors," one should serve the food.
Therein, one who is free from envy should first perform the fire-ritual;
having brought food with both hands, he should serve it.
Having especially placed that *darbha* grass in his hand with the mantra "uśantas tvā," he [should offer it] along with various foods and vegetables endowed with excellent qualities. (151)
The Lotus-born One has declared that food, along with curd, milk, cow-ghee, and sugar, truly gratifies all the ancestors. (152)
For two months one may subsist on fish-meat, for three months on the meat of the hariṇa deer,
for four months on the meat of sheep, and for five months on the meat of birds.
With the meat of a boar, there is excellent satisfaction for six months;
likewise, with the meat of the seven metals (or seven types of animals), and with that of a goat, [there is satisfaction] for eight [months].
The army was satiated for nine months by the flesh of spotted deer;
and for ten months they were satisfied with the meat of boars and buffaloes.
For a rabbit and a tortoise, however, one should feed them for eleven months with goat's milk or milk-rice (pāyasa). For a cow, it should be for one year. 156.
One is satisfied for fifteen months by the meat of the common pig (*saukara*);
the satisfaction from the meat of the *vārdhrīṇasa* lasts for twelve years. (157)
One should avoid boiled rice with black potherbs, or even with the meat of a rhinoceros;
likewise, anything mixed with honey, cow’s milk, curd, or milk-rice. (158)
"The ancestors, who were deities of old, have said that what is given becomes inexhaustible;
one should cause them to hear the Vedic study pertaining to the ancestors and all the Purāṇas. (159)
One should recite, according to one's ability, various hymns to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka (the Sun), and Rudra,
as well as the sūktas dedicated to Indra, Īśa, and Soma, and the Pāvamānī verses.
Therein [he recited] the Bṛhat, Rathantara, Jyeṣṭhasāman, Atharvaśiras, as well as the Śāntikādhyāya and the Madhubrāhmaṇa. ||161||
Likewise, he should recite all that which causes joy to the Brahmins and to himself, such as the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa. 162.

O King, the study of the Mahābhārata is a duty that is most dear to the ancestors; it should be performed by Brahmins after they have eaten, and offerings of food, water, and so forth should be given to them. 163.
One should bring food of all kinds, excluding meat;
one should scatter the remnants on the ground before those who have finished eating.
May those living beings of my family who have been consumed by fire, as well as those not yet consumed, find satisfaction through this gift of land; being satisfied, may they attain the supreme goal.
May this food, offered upon the earth for the satisfaction of those who have no mother, no father, no kinsmen, no friends, and likewise no food—
may it go to them from whatever direction they may be, so that they may attain union with the Divine.

On the darbha grass, there is the scattering of food (vikira) as a seat for those who have passed away into the unconditioned, those who renounced their families, and those entitled to the remnants of the meal.
Knowing them to be satiated, one should offer water and likewise perform the scattering [of food] once, upon the surface of the ground that has been smeared with cow dung, urine, and water. (168)
Having carefully placed the darbha grass according to the rules with their tips pointing southward,
he should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the regulations for all castes, as in the Pitṛyajña.

Having first performed the ritual washing (avanejana) and having uttered the name and lineage [of the ancestors], and having offered flowers and other items, one should perform the secondary washing (pratyavanejana). ||170||

Having understood this, one should perform the rite for the mother according to the rules, just as for the father, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), circling three times clockwise with the left hand while holding darbha grass.
The wise one should perform the worship with flowers like the lighting of a lamp;
likewise, having sipped water for purification (ācamana) at those points, he should offer water once each time.

Likewise, one should afterwards offer flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and water for the inexhaustible libation (akṣayyodaka) along with sesame seeds, pronouncing the name and lineage; and according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should give cows, land, gold, garments, auspicious beds, and whatever else is desired by the Brahmins, as well as for oneself and one's father. (174)
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should bring satisfaction to the ancestors;
thereafter, the *svadhā-vācana* rite is performed for the ancestors and water is offered to the Viśvedevas.

Having given his blessing, the wise man should receive [the offerings] from the twice-born with the words "May the ancestors be non-terrible; may they be well. Then he is addressed again by the twice-born with the words "So be it. (176)
Having been told by them, "May the lineage likewise flourish," he should then perform the recitation of blessings (svastivācana) with devotion, having extracted the sacred syllables (maṇḍala).
The remnants of the food should remain until the dismissal of the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should perform the domestic bali offering—thus the law is established.
The food remaining on the ground after being eaten by one who is straightforward and free from deceit is declared to be the allotted share of the group of servants.
O lord of men, this nourishment was created by the ancestors of old as a constant sustenance even for those who have not observed vows, for those without sons, and even for women.
Then, standing before the place [of the deity] and holding a small water-vessel, one should dismiss [the deity] with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting "vāje vāje. (181)
He should perform a circumambulation outside and follow for eight steps,
accompanied by his circle of kinsmen and together with his sons and wife.
Having returned and prostrated, the knower of mantras should then apply himself to the Vaiśvadeva rite and the daily bali offering for the fire.
Then, together with his servants, sons, and kinsmen, and accompanied by guests, he should eat all that is offered to the Viśvedevas and enjoyed by the ancestors.

Even one who has not been initiated should perform this common *śrāddha* on all festival days; it bestows the fruits of all desires. Even one separated from his wife or living abroad may perform it, provided he is full of devotion. (185)
O King, even a Śūdra may perform [the rite] without mantras according to this procedure;
the third, the *ābhyudayika* or *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, is thus prescribed.
During festivals, sacrifices, marriages, and other auspicious occasions, the Mothers should be worshipped first, and the Fathers immediately thereafter. (187)
Then, O King, [he should worship] the maternal grandfather and likewise the Viśvedevas with the ritual of circumambulation, using curd, unbroken rice, fruits, and water. ||188||
Facing the east, he should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to both the ancestors of the present and those of the past;
saying "It is accomplished," he should rise and offer the respectful water (arghya) to two at a time.
An even number of twice-born men should be honored with garments, ornaments, betel, and other offerings;
the application of the *tilaka* mark should be performed with barley grains, following the sequence for all of them.
And he should cause all the preeminent twice-born ones to recite auspicious hymns;
in this same manner, even a Śūdra should always perform the common *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
A wise man should perform acts of giving with the mantra *namaskāra*.
The Blessed Lord, the Master, has declared that for a Śūdra, giving is the primary duty;
for by means of giving, the attainment of all desires arises for him. (192)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of General Prosperity," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
Pulastya said:
Thereafter, I shall describe the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, as it was formerly taught by Brahmā.
If the father dies, the impurity (āśauca) lasts for ten days; if the mother dies, it lasts for one month. If the son dies, the impurity lasts as prescribed according to the specific relationship. (1)
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days for a Brāhmaṇa;
for Kṣatriyas it is twelve days, and for Vaiśyas it is indeed a fortnight.
For Śūdras, a month’s period of impurity is prescribed for those who are sapinda relations;
for those [Śūdras] prior to the tonsure ceremony, the impurity lasts one night, and beyond that, it is traditionally held to be three nights.
Even in the case of birth, it should be exactly thus for all castes at all times;
however, after the collection of the bones, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
One should perform the offering of rice-balls for the deceased for twelve days;
for that is declared to be his provision for the journey, since it brings him great satisfaction. (5)
Because the city of the hungry ghosts (preta) is reached in twelve days,
and for twelve days one beholds one's sons and wife at home.
Therefore, one should place milk in the vessel for ten nights;
it serves to pacify all burning sensations and destroys the fatigue of travel.
Then, on the eleventh day, the man should indeed feed eleven twice-born brahmins who are free from impurity regarding lineage and other such matters.
On the second day, one should again perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in the same manner;
it is performed according to the rules, devoid of the *nāndīmukha* invocation, without the offering into the fire, and without the portion for the gods.
One purifying blade of grass, one water-offering, and one rice-ball are prescribed;
one should say, "May it attend [the ancestors]," and thereafter the water with sesame seeds should be offered.
One should pronounce "svasti" during the dismissal of the Brahmins and say "abhiramyatām.
Those who know the Vedas understand that the remaining rites here also should be performed as previously described.
One should perform all this according to this rule every month;
on the second day after the period of impurity (sūtaka), one should give an extraordinary bed.
Likewise, having worshipped a golden image of a man endowed with fruit and clothing, one should give it to a Brahmin couple adorned with various ornaments.
Having seated him upon the couch, one should then offer the madhuparka, consisting of curd and milk, in a vessel of silver. (14)
Having taken a small portion from the forehead bone and having made it fine, one should mix it together;
endowed with devotion to the ancestors, one should have the wife of the twice-born man drink it. 15.
This very rule was observed by the best of the twice-born from the mountains;
therefore, that defiled bed must not be accepted by the most excellent of the twice-born. (16)
Once she has been taken, however, she requires a further consecration;
for in both the Veda and the Purāṇas, a bed [shared with such a woman] is everywhere censured.
But all those who accept [such gifts] shall go to hell;
they lie upon a bed woven with a net of wealth and served by female slaves. 18.
Those who touch [the food] without knowing [its nature] all go to hell; one should not eat at a *navasrāddha*, and having eaten, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (19)
Out of devotion to their father, sons should always perform their duty;
they should perform the rite of releasing a bull and give away an auspicious tawny cow.
O best of men, a water-pot filled with various kinds of food and fruits should be given for a year, preceded by water mixed with sesame seeds.
Then, when a full year has elapsed, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should take place;
for after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, the deceased partakes in the Pārvaṇa offerings.
Therefore, for a householder, when there are rites preceded by prosperity (vṛddhi),
he should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha preceded by the gods.
One should invoke the ancestors there, designating each deceased person individually;
one should prepare four vessels joined with water scented with perfumes and sesame seeds.
For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors;
likewise, being intent upon the ancestors, one should then resolve to offer four *piṇḍas*.
Reciting the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ," one should divide the food into three parts;
according to this procedure, one should first offer the arghya water.
Then, having attained the state of a progenitor (pitṛ) together with the fourth [deity] at that very time,
he attains supreme immortality among the Agniṣvātta and other classes of ancestors.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, no separate offering is made for him;
rather, it should be given to the ancestors themselves, among whom his status as one of the six shares is established. (28)

From that time forward, on the occasions of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), eclipses, and other such festivals, one should perform the Śrāddha rite with three pindas; and on the anniversary of the day of death, the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
He who performs the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) must abandon it;
for by doing so, he would always cause the laughter of his ancestors and bring about the destruction of his brother. (30)

One who performs the *pārvaṇa* rite on the anniversary of death falls to a lower state, even if equal to others; for when [the deceased] has attained union with heaven, the liberation of the *preta* occurs. (31)
Then the knower of the rules, the giver of the śrāddha, should perform the āma-śrāddha;
he should not perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), but should offer the rice-balls with that very [raw food]. ||32||
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed at three months, one year, or three years;
when that time arrives, he shall be released from bondage. (33)
Through the cleansing of the kuśa grass, one attains freedom from participation in the ritual smearing;
for the three beginning with the fourth [descendant] are partakers of the smearing, while [the first three] are partakers of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). ||34||
"The giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is the seventh among them; those who share the funeral cake (sapiṇḍas) are seven generations.
Bhīṣma said:
"How should offerings to the gods (havya) and offerings to the ancestors (kavya) be given by people here in this world?"
They generally receive [the offerings] in the world of the ancestors; it is said by the cranes:
"If a twice-born man eats in the mortal world, or if an oblation is offered into the fire," (36)
"How can the pretas, who consist of both auspicious and inauspicious natures, eat that food?
Pulastya said:
"The ancestors are of the nature of the Vasus, and the grandfathers are indeed the Rudras. (37)
"The Prapitāmahas as well as the Ādityas"—this is the Vedic revelation;
for it provides the names and lineages of the ancestors for the offerings of *havya* and *kavya*. (38)
Having perceived the reality of the Śrāddha through the mantras with devotion, those [ancestors] such as the Agniṣvāttas are established in their lordship over them. (39)
The names and lineages of those who have passed away, as well as those currently arising, are revealed by this;
for this worship that has been performed brings joy to all living beings. (40)
If one's father, mother, or teacher has become divine through the application of their past actions, then food offered to them becomes nectar and follows them even into their divine state. (41)

In the state of a Daitya, it appears in the form of enjoyment; in the state of a beast, it becomes the food of the ancestors; and even in the state of a Naga, the food of the Śrāddha rite presents itself in the form of wind.
In the state of a yakṣa there is drink, and likewise meat in the state of a rākṣasa; in the state of a dānava there is drink, and in the state of a preta, water consisting of blood.
For those who possess human status along with various enjoyments such as food and drink, there may be the power of pleasure toward a beloved woman, or for others, the power of eating. (44)
The power of generosity, along with wealth, beauty, and health—this is declared to be the flower of the *śrāddha*; its fruit is union with Brahman. (45)
O King, when the hosts of ancestors are pleased, they bestow long life, sons, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, happiness, and likewise sovereignty.
And it is heard that the sons of Kauśika attained liberation from the city;
through five successive births, they reached the supreme state of Brahman. 47.
Bhīṣma said:
How did the descendants of Kauśika attain that unsurpassed yoga? And through how many connections of birth does the destruction of karma occur? (48)
Pulastya said: There was a righteous great sage named Kauśika in Kurukṣetra;
learn from me now of his sons, both by name and by deed. 49.
Svasṛpa, Krodhana, Hiṃsra, Piśuna, Kavi, Vāgduṣṭa, and Pitṛvartin were then the disciples of Garga. (50)
When their father had passed away, there occurred for them a severe famine and a great drought that struck fear into all the worlds. (51)
"Though the ascetics protect this doe of the forest by the command of Garga and others, we, being severely oppressed by hunger, shall devour this Kapilā. (52)
While they were thus reflecting on the evil deed, the younger brother then spoke softly:
"If she must certainly be killed, let her be employed under the guise of a śrāddha offering. (53)
When she was being appointed to perform the *śrāddha*, her sin was certainly destroyed;
then, permitted by her younger brothers with the words "Do it thus," she became devoted to her father.
Having focused his mind on the wheel and partaken of that [food] with faith, he should again,
in due order, assign two portions for the gods and three for the ancestors.
Likewise, having made a single guest his own, the performer of the śrāddha, devoted to the ancestors, performed the śrāddha himself while reciting the mantras and remaining mindful [of them]. (56)
Then, having gone there free from suspicion, they reported it to the teacher:
"The cow has been killed by a tiger; let this calf be accepted. (57)
Thus, relying on Vedic power, those seven ascetics—fearless and performers of cruel deeds—devoured the cow. (58)
Then, in the course of time, those hunters were reborn in Daśapura;
having been purified by the sentiment of filial devotion toward their father, they attained the recollection of their former births.
There, having attained detachment through discernment, they abandoned their vital breaths according to dharma;
unseen by the world, they departed by means of that fasting at the sacred ford.
Having assumed the forms of deer on Mount Jāre for seven kalpas,
they attained the yoga of higher knowledge and abandoned those bodies of their own.
Then, having died by leaping [into the fire], their minds were filled with world-weariness;
they became seven yogins born in Lake Mānasa as cakravāka birds. ||62||
By name and by deed, they were Sarvasumanas, Kusuma, Vasu, Cittadarśin, Sudarśin, and Jñātajñānapāraga. ||63||
Devoted to their eldest brother, these seven were the most excellent and sanctifying through yoga;
yet among them, three became fallen from yoga and lost their mindfulness.
Having seen him, who was resplendent, accompanied by women, sporting with various enjoyments, and possessed of great strength and prowess; 65.
Born of the lineage of Pañcāla and possessing abundant forces and vehicles, one among those aquatic beings became desirous of sovereignty. (66)
The Brahmin Pitṛvartin, who was devoted to his ancestors and performed the Śrāddha rites,
saw two other ministers accompanied by a vast force and many mounts.
O best of the twice-born, if you both desire the office of minister in this mortal world,
there was one son of Vibhrāja known as Brahmadatta.
Likewise, Mantriputra, Puṇḍarīka, Subālaka, and Brahmadatta were consecrated in the excellent city of Kāmpilya. (69)
Then the King of Pañcāla, valiant, faithful, and devoted to his ancestors,
became a knower of yoga and a perceiver of the minds of all living beings.
That king had a wife named Sudeva; from her was born a daughter known by the name Sannati, who was formerly the daughter of Kapila. (71)
Because she was appointed to the ancestral rites, she became a speaker of the Veda;
by her, King Danu ruled his kingdom together with Cākṣuṣa. (72)
Once, while wandering through a garden with her, the king saw a pair of insects engaged in a quarrel born of passion.
Before the ant who had her face turned downward, the insect-lover, his limbs tormented by the five arrows [of love], spoke with a faltering voice: 74.
"O Nala, there exists nowhere in the world a woman equal to you—slender-waisted, possessing very broad hips, large-eyed, and of exceeding grace. (75)
With a beautiful face resembling the color of gold and a lovely smile, her countenance appears as dear as jaggery and sugar-candy. (76)
"When I eat, you eat; when I have bathed, you bathe likewise.
When I am away on a journey, you are distressed; and when I am angry, you tremble with fear. (77)
