"For what reason, O wicked woman, do you always remain with your face cast down? She replied while burning with anger: "What are you saying, you rogue? (78)
"You have consumed the powder of the sweetmeat even while leaving me out;
you have transgressed by giving it to another, O Manmatha! (79)
The ant said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, this was given by me to another out of similarity to you;
O beautiful woman, you ought to forgive me for that one offense."
"I shall never do so again," [said she] whose breasts were firm and free from agitation;
"I touch your feet with truth—be gracious to me as I bow before you. (81)
O lady of beautiful hips, if you are angry, death would come upon me from your side;
but if you are pleased, O lovely-thighed one, all my desires are fulfilled. (82)
O lady of beautiful hips, drink deeply and constantly from my mouth, which resembles the full moon and tastes like the essence of nectar, as I am attached to you.
"Having understood this, O you who are filled with compassion, one should always perform what is auspicious.
Having heard these words, she then became gracious.
Even a tiny ant, having deceived itself into thinking it was not subject to change, is deluded;
Brahmadatta, having understood all this, laughed with a smile. (85)
"Through the power of his previous karma, he became a knower of the cries of all beings.
Bhīṣma said: "How did King Brahmadatta become a knower of all cries? (86)
Moreover, there was once a group of four ruddy geese somewhere; tell me about them all, O Knower of All, and tell me the excellent vow of one among them. (87)
Pulastya said:
And furthermore, O King, those who were born in that very city were called Vākas. 88.
The heirs of the aged brahmin were wise men who remembered their former births:
Dhṛtimān, Tattvadarśin, Vidyāvarṇa, and Tapodhika. ||89||
By name and by their deeds, they were indeed very poor; thus, O twice-born one, the minds of those sons turned toward asceticism. (90)
"O best of the twice-born, we shall attain supreme perfection," they said.
Having heard those words of theirs, Sudaridra, who was performing great austerities, [spoke]. (91)
He spoke in a piteous voice, "What is this, my sons? "This is unrighteousness toward you, father," they replied. He said, "I shall kill them. (92)
Having abandoned his aged father, who was poor and living in the forest—where indeed will your dharma be now, O noble one, having forsaken both him and your own path? (93)
They said, "O King, listen to our words; we have resolved upon this course of action. This vow, O King, will bestow abundant merit upon you. (94)

O Brahmin, for you who recite this at dawn, there shall be thousands of villages filled with wealth; and those who are Brahmins in Kurukṣetra, as well as those who are hunters in Daśapura— [all shall belong to you]. (95)
"May we grow old in time as deer and cranes on Lake Mānasa.
Having spoken thus to their father, they went once more to perform endless austerities.
O King, even though he was advanced in years, that virtuous twice-born man went forth to achieve his own purpose;
he was the lord of Pañcāla in former times, named Aṇuha Vaibhrāja.
Desirous of a son, he, devoted to rigorous vows, propitiated the Lord of the gods, the lotus-born Grandfather, the omnipresent one.
Then, after a long time, his grandfather was pleased and said,
"O King, choose a boon that is auspicious for you and desired by your heart."
Aṇuha said:
"O Lord of Gods, grant me a son of great strength and prowess, one who has mastered all branches of knowledge, who is righteous, and the best among yogis. (100)
"Grant me the son born of yourself, who possesses knowledge of the cries of all sentient beings.
"So be it," said the Supreme Lord, the Soul of the Universe. 101.
While all living beings were looking on, he crossed over there as if it were water;
from him was born the powerful Brahmadatta, the son of Satasoma. 102.

Compassionate toward all sentient beings, possessing strength superior to that of all sentient beings, knowing the cries of all sentient beings, and the Lord of the lords of all sentient beings. ||103||
Then, by the power of his spiritual discipline, he arrived even as a small ant at the place where that pair of insects was staying, engaged in dalliance. (104)
Then Sāsanmati, seeing him laughing and greatly astonished,
and suspecting something, questioned that lord of men.
Sannati said:
"O King, why has this excessive laughter occurred?
I do not know the cause of your laughter; such a thing has been done by you at an improper time. (106)
The prince replied to her: "O fair-faced one, this speech of the ant has arisen from passion and is unpleasant; it is merely a joke. (107)
"O lady of pure smiles, there is no other cause whatsoever for this laughter; O Goddess, you have told me this falsehood. (108)
"I alone have laughed at this; I would not live now without you.
How could a mortal understand the conversation of ants, except for a god? (109)
"Therefore, I alone have been laughed at by you today; what more than this could there be?
Then the king, rendered speechless, desired to know the words of Hari.
Free from all taint, he remained for seven nights observing the rule of fasting.
At dawn, as Brahmā was wandering through the city, he spoke to him at the end of a dream.
"Your beloved will understand everything from the words of that most excellent of the aged brahmins.
Having said this, Brahmā vanished, and the king departed from the city in splendor.
Going out accompanied by his ministers and his wife, he saw that aged brahmin Gada at the head,
as well as that other old man.

The Brāhmaṇa said: Those foremost of Brahmins in Kurujāṅgala, as well as the fishermen in Dāśapura and the deer, along with the cakravāka birds, dwell here on Lake Mānasa as perfected beings (siddhas) who have transcended old age and time. (114)
Having heard these words of his, he fell down overcome with grief;
at that moment, the two sons of the excellent minister attained the recollection of their former births.
The author of the Kāmaśāstra was Tumburu, the son of Babhru; he was known in the worlds as Satuvālaka, a Pañcāla, and was renowned as a knower of all sciences. 116.
Puṇḍarīka, whose nature was devoted to dharma and who was a promoter of the Vedas and scriptures,
having become one who remembered his former births, fell down before him out of grief.

Having thus lamented at length, those who had fallen away from their duties through desire and were bound by the fetters of karma—those who had reached the further shore of the three yogas—[departed]. (118)
Marveling at the greatness of the śrāddha, he praised it again and again;
then, having given him wealth consisting of many villages, [he departed]. (119)
Having dismissed that aged brāhmaṇa who was accompanied by the gift of wealth,
the king [enthroned] his own son, who was endowed with the marks of royalty.
He consecrated the one named Viṣvaksena as king over the kingdoms;
all those best of yogins [remained] in the lake Mānasa.
Brahmadatta and the others were devoted to their father in that matter, free from envy;
and Sannati became joyful, as was shown by you yourself. (122)
"Whatever fruit of yoga is here perceived,
it is so," the king replied, greeting him with respect as he stood before him.
"By your grace, all this fruit is thus obtained by me. (124)
Then, all those forest-dwellers, having resorted to yoga,
attained the supreme state of Brahman through the power of their austerity.
Thus, when satisfied, the ancestors bestow upon men long life, wealth, knowledge, the happiness of heaven and liberation, as well as sons and sovereignty. (126)
O King, the wise man who causes this majesty of the ancestors belonging to Brahmadatta to be heard by the twice-born, or who listens to it or recites it himself,
is glorified in the world of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas. ||127||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Ancestors," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The eleventh chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
At what part of the day should one who performs a śrāddha ceremony perform the śrāddha?
O twice-born one, at which sacred fords (tīrthas) has a śrāddha been performed so as to yield great fruit?
Pulastya said:
There is a sacred ford named Puṣkara which is remembered as the most excellent of all;
it stands like the fulfilled desire of all the foremost of the twice-born.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or recited there becomes truly infinite;
it is eternally dear to the ancestors and is considered supreme by the sages. (3)
O King, from there is Dāthalalita, and likewise the auspicious Tīrtha of Māyāpurī; then the station of Amitra, and after that the supreme Kedāra.
They say that Gaṅgāsāgara is auspicious and consists of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
likewise, the sacred ford of Brahmasaras and the auspicious waters of the Śatadru are so.
The sacred site named Tuṇaimiṣa bestows the fruit of all holy places;
it is there that the eternal Gaṅgodbheda has arisen within the Gomatī.
Likewise, there is Yajñavarāha, the God of gods, the wielder of the trident,
where that eighteen-armed Hara stands with his golden gift.
Where in ancient times the hub of the wheel of Dharma became worn out,
that is this Naimiṣa forest, frequented by all sacred fords.
There, one shall behold the God of gods, Varāha;
he who goes there, purified in soul, shall proceed to the city of Nārāyaṇa.

Kokāmukha is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha), and it is also observed as the path of Indra; nevertheless, it is also the sacred site of the ancestors (pitṛtīrtha) belonging to Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest.
This is Puṣkarāraṇya, where the divine Grandfather resides; it is the most excellent place for beholding Viriñci, which bestows the fruit of liberation. 11.
This place, which destroys all sins, has been made a site of great merit,
where Janārdana himself manifested as the primordial Nārasiṃha.
The Tīrtha of the Ikṣumatī brings auspiciousness even to the ancestors; the ancestors are eternally satisfied at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā. 13.
Kurukṣetra is greatly meritorious, where even the path is visible;
even today, Pitṛtīrtha there bestows the fruit of all desires. (14)
O lord of men, there is the sacred ford of the ancestors known as Nīlakaṇṭha, as well as the meritorious Abhadrasaras and Lake Mānasa. (15)
Maṅgalā, Dākinī, likewise Acchodā, Vipāśā, and Sarasvatī;
similarly, Sarvamitra-pada and Vaidyanātha are of great fruit. (16)
The Kṣiprā river, the Puṇya river, the auspicious Kālasiṃjara, Tīrthodbheda, Harodbheda, Garbhabheda, and Mahālaya. ||17||
The great sages have declared that Bhadreśvara, Viṣṇupada, and Narmadādvāra are equal to Gayā by the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa). ||18||
These are the sacred sites of the ancestors (pitṛtīrthas), which remove all sins even for people through mere remembrance, let alone for those who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha). (19)
Oṃkāra, Pitṛtīrtha, the Kapilā waters of the Kāverī, the confluence with the Caṇḍavegā, and likewise Amarakaṇṭaka; ||20||
Bathing and other rites performed there yield twice the merit of Kurukṣetra.
Furthermore, Śuklatīrtha is renowned, as is the supreme Someśvara Tīrtha.

It removes all diseases, is meritorious, and its fruit is more than ten million times superior when performed in the presence [of the deity] during ancestral rites (śrāddha), giving, burnt offerings (homa), and the private recitation of sacred texts (svādhyāya). 22.
The descent of the body of the god of gods, the wielder of the trident,
known as Rocamāna, occurred in an auspicious Brahmin household.
That place became a source of great merit, as did the river Carmaṇvatī,
as well as the confluence of the Śūlatāpī, the Payoṣṇī, and the Payoṣṇī itself.
The Mahauṣadhī, the Cāraṇā, the Ānagatīrtha-pravartinī, the meritorious Mahāveṇā river, and likewise the Mahāśāla; ||25||
Likewise, there is the Gomatīvaruṇa tīrtha, the supreme Hautāśana,
Bhairava, Bhṛgutuṅga, and the unsurpassed Gaurī-tīrtha.
The sacred ford named Vaināyaka, the unsurpassed Vastraśvara, as well as the sin-removing one named Apāpahara, and the meritorious river Vetravatī. (27)
Mahārudra, Mahāliṅga, the great river Daśārṇācā, Śatarudra, Śatāhvā, as well as Pitṛpada and the city of Pura. ||28||
Likewise, there are the Aṅgāravāhikā, the Nandā, the two rivers Śoṇa and Ghargharā,
the meritorious Kālikā, the Canadī, and the auspicious Pitarācanadī.
These are the sacred fords (tīrthas) of the ancestors, commended for bathing and giving gifts;
whatever śrāddha is offered at these places is remembered as yielding infinite fruit. (30)
Śatāvaṭa, Nadinī, Jvālā, Śaradvīca, Nadī, as well as Kṛṣṇatīrtha at Dvārakā and the northern Sarasvatī. ||31||
The river Mālavatī, likewise the mountain Girikarṇikā, the holy ford Dhūtapāpa, and similarly the ocean on the south; ||32||
Gokarṇa and Gajakarṇa, as well as the auspicious Acananadī; Śrīśaila, Śākatīrtha, and thereafter Nārasiṃha. (33)
Likewise, at Mahendra and at the great river Puṇyāpuṇyā;
in these places as well, a śrāddha performed at all times is recorded as yielding infinite fruit.
Merely by seeing them, merits are indeed acquired and sins are instantly removed;
likewise, through the merit of the Tuṅgabhadrā river and the Cakrarathī.
The Bhīmeśvara, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Kāverī, the Cāñjanā river, and the holy Godāvarī river—this is the supreme Trisandhyā-pūrṇa. ||36||
There is the sacred ford named Traiyambaka, honored by all holy places,
where the Lord Bhīma himself, the three-eyed one, resides.
O King, a śrāddha offered during all of these occasions becomes ten-millionfold meritorious; even by mere remembrance, sins are shattered into a hundred pieces.
The Śrīparṇā, the meritorious Acanadī, and the unsurpassed Vyāsatīrtha;
likewise the Matsyanadī, the Kārā, and the Śivadhārā. (39)
The Bhavatīrtha is renowned as an eternal and meritorious holy site;
likewise, Rāmeśvara is meritorious, as is the excellent city of Veṇāpura.
Likewise, Aṅgāraka is renowned, as well as Ātmadarśa, Mala, Buṣa, Vatsavrāteśvara, and the supreme Gokāmukha. 41.
Govardhana, Hariścandra, Puraścandra, Pṛthūdaka, Sahasrākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, as well as the Ākāśagaṅgā river; 42.
Their names were likewise Tathātatha, Saumitrisaṅgata, Indranīla, Mahānāda, and Priyamelaka. ||43||
These also are always recommended for the śrāddha ceremony and are even more excellent,
because it is taught that the presence of all the gods resides within them.
A gift given to all of these would yield a hundred million times more merit than the merit from the Bāhudā river; likewise for the auspicious Siddhavaṭa.
The Pāśupata Tīrtha and likewise the Nadīparyaṭika;
at all these places, a Śrāddha offered yields a hundred times ten million-fold merit.
Likewise, there is Pañcatīrtha, where the river Godāvarī flows with its waters divided to the left and right, joined by a thousand liṅgas. 47.
This is that supreme sacred ford of Jamadagnya, an abode of joy, where the river Godāvarī became established out of fear of Pratīka. 48.
That is a sacred ford (tīrtha) for offerings to the gods and ancestors, frequented by hosts of Apsarases;
there, the merit of performing śrāddha, offering oblations into the fire, and other rites exceeds a hundred crores.
Likewise, there is the thousand-fold Liṅga, the supreme Carāghaveśvara;
there, in the past, Śakra went to the meritorious Indrakālā river.
Having slain the enemy Namuci, he attained heaven through his ascetic penance;
a śrāddha offered there by men shall yield infinite fruit. (51)
There is indeed the sacred ford named Puṣkara, as well as Śālagrāma;
and the famous Śoṇapāta, where Vaiśvānara has his abode.
Also the Sārasvata Tīrtha, as well as the Svāmi Tīrtha;
the holy Malada and Nandī rivers, the Kauśikī, and likewise Candrakā.
The Vidarbha, the Vegavatī, and the Payoṣṇī flow toward the east;
the Kāverī flows toward the north, as does the Jālandhara mountain.
In these shraddha-tirthas, one obtains the full merit of a shraddha ceremony;
likewise there is the Lohadanda-tirtha and Citrakuta as well. (55)
The divine bank of the all-pervading Gaṅgā, as well as the auspicious shore of that river,
the Kubjāmra tīrtha, and likewise the Ūrvaśī sandbank.
Saṃsāramocana is a sacred ford (tīrtha), and likewise is Ṛṇamocana;
at these ancestral fords (pitṛtīrthas), one enjoys the full merit of a Śrāddha offering.
Aṭṭahāsa, as well as Tīrthaṅgautameśvara,
likewise the Avasiṣṭha-tīrtha, and thereafter Bhārata.
Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, and likewise Haṃsatīrtha;
the famous Piṇḍāraka, and likewise Śaṅkhoddhāra. ||59||
Bhāṇḍeśvara, Bilvaka, and Nīlaparvata as well, and likewise Badarītīrtha, the lord of all lords of holy places (tīrthas). ||60||
The holy site named Vasudhārā, likewise Rāmatīrtha,
Jaya, Vijayā, and likewise Śuklatīrtha—
in these, those who offer the śrāddha rites proceed to the supreme state.
The sacred site named Mātṛgṛha, as well as Karavīrapura. ||62||
The place named Sapta-godāvarī is the sovereign of all lords of sacred fords;
there, a śrāddha ceremony should be offered by those desiring infinite fruit.
In the Kīkaṭa country, Gayā is meritorious; Rājagṛha is both meritorious and non-meritorious;
the hermitage of Cyavana is meritorious; and the river Punā is repeatedly purifying.
The merit gained from honoring the sense objects in this river flows on again and again, where the verses proclaimed by Brahmā circulate. (65)
One should desire many sons, so that at least one might go to Gayā,
or perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull.
This verse circulated among the sacred fords and shrines:
"O King of Men, all the praises have gathered together. (67)
"Will there be any son born in our lineage who, having gone to Gayā, will gratify those seven ancestors as well as the seven descendants? (68)
This Vedic revelation concerning the maternal grandfather is likewise brief:
"The son who goes to the Gaṅgā and casts a heap of bones [there]... (69)
He will offer a handful of water with seven or eight sesame seeds, or he will perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at the three forests.
First at Puṣkarāraṇya, and immediately after that at Naimiṣa;
having reached Dharmāraṇya once more, he will offer the śrāddha with devotion.
Likewise, that which is given at Dharmapṛṣṭha in Gayā, at the lake of Brahmā,
and at the Banyan Tree of Gayāśīrṣa, becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Even he who travels along a road after having performed a sowing of seeds quickly leads his ancestors dwelling in hell to heaven.
Who among the kings of men in the Kuleta lineage does not become a preta?
Through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one attains release from the state of a preta. ||74||
With the tip of his copper-colored hand, he alone offers water at the roots of the mango trees;
the mangoes are watered and the ancestors are satisfied—thus it is well known that a single action accomplishes two purposes. (75)
At Gayā, no other gift is superior to the offering of the piṇḍa;
by a single offering of the piṇḍa, they are satisfied and proceed toward liberation. (76)
The sages declare that the gift of grain is preeminent, and likewise the gift of wealth;
they declare that what is given by men at the sacred fords of Gayā is the most excellent cause for merit.
Those who, with total devotion and without aversion, behold that great river Mahācala after going there mentally to the south or the north; //78//
Having bowed down to the foremost of the twice-born, they have attained the fruit of their birth;
whatever an immortal desires, that he obtains without a doubt. (79)
This enumeration of the holy fords (tīrthas), along with their presiding deities, has been declared by me in brief;
even the Lord of Speech himself would not be able to describe them in detail, let alone a mortal man.
Truth is a sacred ford, compassion is a sacred ford, and the restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
even within the home of those belonging to the various castes and stages of life, tranquility is declared to be a sacred ford.
The śrāddha performed at whichever sacred sites [is prescribed] is held to yield ten millionfold merit;
however, that śrāddha which is performed at Gayā bestows final liberation.
Therefore, śrāddha at a sacred site (tīrtha) is prescribed with great effort.
The morning time consists of three muhūrtas, and saṅgava is exactly the same duration.
Midday consists of three muhūrtas;
after that comes afternoon, and evening also consists of three muhūrtas; one should not perform a śrāddha at those times.
This is the time for the Rākṣasīs, which is censured in all ritual acts;
it is explained that there are fifteen muhūrtas throughout the day at all times. (85)
Among those, the eighth muhūrta is known as the time of *kutapa*;
for from midday onwards, the sun always becomes mild. (86)
Therefore, in that regard, the effort that yields infinite fruit is distinguished;
[it consists of] the sword, the vessel, the discus, the ascetic practice, as well as the Nepalese shield and the strength. (87)
Gold, Darbha grass, sesame seeds, cows, and the daughter’s son is recorded as the eighth;
they say that "pāpa" means contemptible, and these things cause suffering for such a person.
Therefore, these eight are renowned as the *kutapas*. From the *kutapa* hour onwards, there is a period of four *muhūrtas*. (89)
The recitation of the *svadhā* formula is prescribed for exactly five *muhūrtas*.
Likewise, *kuśa* grass and black sesame seeds originate from the body of Viṣṇu. (90)
The wise declare that the definition and the time for a *śrāddha* are as follows:
an offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) should be presented by those dwelling at sacred fords (*tīrtha*). 91.
With darbha grass in hand, one shall perform the śrāddha rite within the house;
it is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, and the destroyer of all sins. (92)
And this recitation of the Tīrtha-śrāddha was indeed spoken by Brahmā;
the man who hears it or even reads it becomes endowed with prosperity. 93.
Likewise, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, this should be recited by those residing at a sacred pilgrimage site;
it is considered to be for the purpose of pacifying all sins and destroying misfortune.
This is a purifier and a treasury of glory; it is the destroyer of great sins.
Experts declare that the greatness of the śrāddha is honored by Brahmā, Arka, and Rudra. (95)

"I shall learn the mantras from Bṛhaspati for the sake of the defeat of the gods and the victory of the Asuras. (219)
Thus addressed, the god said: "O Bhārgava, perform this vow for a full thousand years, holding smoke in your mouth with your head downward."
"If it is for your welfare that you desire this, then you shall obtain the mantras. Having thus granted his permission, Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, [spoke].
Touching the feet of the god, he spoke these words: "Very well," O Lord; "O God, I shall observe the vow as commanded by you today. (222)
Commanded by the God of Gods, the sage Bhārgava performed that [task];
then, when Śukra had departed for the welfare of the Asuras, [the gods acted].
The poet Kāvya composed the meaning of the Mantras from Maheśvara by means of celibacy;
having understood that first through the science of polity (nīti), Vairāja then experienced happiness.
In this situation, out of indignation, all the gods, led by Bṛhaspati, rushed toward them with sharp weapons in hand.
Seeing the hosts of gods and deities once again with weapons raised, they all suddenly sprang up in terror and spoke these words to them: ||226||
The Daityas said: "O gods, while our preceptor has undertaken his vow and we have laid down our weapons, you have come seeking to slay us after having granted us your protection. (227)
Free from anger and resentment, we have all laid down our weapons and stand here, wearing bark garments and black antelope skins, having renounced all possessions. (228)
If we are unable to conquer even the gods in battle by any means whatsoever,
we shall seek refuge through non-violence with the mother of Kāvya.
"We shall inform [him] of this hardship until our preceptor returns; once he has returned, we, with our weapons sharpened, will quickly rise up. (230)
Having spoken thus to one another, they sought refuge with Kāvya’s mother;
then, being terrified, she granted them freedom from fear.
Do not be afraid, do not be afraid; O Dānavas, cast away your fear! As you remain in my presence, it is impossible for you to be afraid.
Seeing those [Asuras] thus overwhelmed by her and defeated, the gods then assailed the Asuras with force, without considering their relative strength or weakness. ||233||
Then, seeing those gods being bound by the deities, the Goddess, filled with wrath, said to the gods: "I shall stupefy them with sleep. (234)
Then, having gathered all the necessary provisions, that goddess, a woman rich in asceticism and disciplined in yoga, cast off her sleep.
Then, seeing Indra thus paralyzed, the gods fled in all directions like those who are bewildered,

When the hosts of gods had departed, Viṣṇu spoke to Indra.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of gods, enter into me; thus you shall protect yourself, O auspicious one."
Having been addressed thus, the destroyer of cities (Śiva) then entered Viṣṇu;
seeing him protected by Viṣṇu, the goddess became enraged and spoke these words.
"O Indra, together with Viṣṇu, burn this [demon] by force while all beings look on; let the power of my asceticism be witnessed! (239)
Overpowered by her, both those gods, Indra and Viṣṇu, became [afflicted]. Viṣṇu spoke to Indra: "How may we two be liberated together? (240)
Indra said, "Kill her, O Lord, before she consumes us both;

"Let it be so; let us go to my home, O Mattakāśinī.

Now, how is it that you have begun to undertake this very vow, which subverts the Vedas—a vow characterized by nakedness, shaven heads, and water-pots? (408)
"How is it that you carry the peacock-banner and abide in this manner?
The Dānavas replied: "We have abandoned the nature of all Asuras and are established in the dharma of the Ṛṣis. (409)
Performing deeds that cause the increase of the Dharma, may you bring joy to all beings;
enjoy the entire sovereignty of the three worlds, O Śakra, and depart!
Having said "So be it," Maghavan returned once more to Triviṣṭapa;
thus were they all deluded by the divine Bhīṣma, the priest.
Having reached the river Narmadā and stayed there, those best of Dānavas were all informed of the situation by Śukra and awakened to it.
Then they again formed a cruel intention to seize the three worlds.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Account of the Incarnations," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(14) Chapter Fourteen.
Bhīṣma said:
How was Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, born from three men? And how is Karṇa proclaimed to be a son of a charioteer, born of a maiden? (1)
"Tell me how it came to pass that one of those two was superior by nature;
I have a great curiosity, and you ought to explain it to me. (2)
Pulastya said:
In ancient times, Brahmā, overcome by great anger, cut off his own head;
sweat then appeared on his forehead, and taking it up, he struck it upon the ground.
From the sweat born of his exertion, the hero Sahasrakavacin, whose mind was fixed on the great bow of Kuṇḍalin, said, "What shall I do? ||4||
Viriñca spoke to him, pointing out Rudra with vigor:
"Let this evil-minded one be slain so that he is not born again."
Having heard the words of Brahmā, he raised his bow behind him and set forth toward Maheśa,
arrow in hand and with a most fierce gaze.
Having seen that most fierce man, the three-eyed one became afraid;
he fled from there with speed and went to the hermitage of Viṣṇu.
"Save me, save me, O Viṣṇu! Save me from this man, O slayer of enemies!
This sinful one, appearing in the form of a Mleccha, has been created by Brahmā as a source of terror. (8)
O Lord of the World, just as one might strike another when enraged,
so did Viṣṇu, having deluded that man with the sound of the syllable "Huṃ," act against him.
Invisible to all beings, the Lord whose self is yoga and who perceives everything, Keśava beheld Virūpākṣa there as he had arrived at the sacrificial ground. 10.
Then, as he prostrated himself upon the ground, he was seen by the Lord Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu said:
"You are my grandson, O Rudra; what desire of yours shall I fulfill?"
Having seen the god Nārāyaṇa, he showed his alms-bowl before him, blazing intensely with fiery energy, and said, "Give me alms."
Beholding Rudra with a skull in his hand, Viṣṇu reflected:
"Who else would be a suitable recipient for this alms-offering at this time?"
Thinking, "He is worthy," he offered his right arm;
the moon-crested Lord pierced it with an exceedingly sharp trident.
Then, from the arm of the Lord, a stream of blood began to flow, appearing like a flame of fire fashioned from the luster of gold. 15.
Having crossed that river, which was free of mud and skulls, straight-flowing, swift, and fierce, she was granted a boon by Śambhu as it reached his nose. 16.
Fifty yojanas in length and ten yojanas in width,
she flowed from the arm of Hari for a thousand divine years.
At that time, that mendicant accepted this alms from Īśa,
which had been given by Nārāyaṇa into his excellent skull-bowl.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke these most excellent words to Śambhu:
"O Supreme Lord, this vessel for the granting of boons is now completely full. (19)
Hearing these words of Hari, which resounded like thunder over the water, Hara—
whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, and who is adorned by the crescent moon upon his crest— [listened].
Fixing his gaze upon the skull with his three eyes, Janārdana struck it with his finger and said, "The skull is completely filled."
Having heard those words of Śiva, Viṣṇu restrained the stream;
then, as Hari looked on, the Lord [pierced] his own finger with blood.
For a thousand divine years, he churned [the ocean] with his glances;
as it was being churned, it gradually became turbid with blood and covered in bubbles.
Thereafter, Kirīṭin appeared with his bow,
having fastened a pair of quivers, mounted upon Vṛṣa, and equipped with finger-guards.
A person resembling fire was clearly seen within the skull;
having seen him, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu spoke these words to Rudra.
"Is this Bhava born from a skull, appearing as a human being?
Having heard these words of Hari, the Lord said to him, "O All-pervading One, listen. (26)
"This man named Nara is the best among those who know the supreme weapons; because you said 'Nara, Nara,' he shall therefore be known as Nara. (27)
Both Nara and Nārāyaṇa will become renowned in this age for their deeds in battle, for the purposes of the gods, and for the protection of the worlds. 28.
Therefore, this son of Nārāyaṇa shall come into being;
moreover, that one of great splendor will assist you in the slaying of the Asuras.
The sage shall be victorious in the world through the examination of knowledge;
this divine fifth head of Brahmā possesses superior splendor. (30)
From the splendor of the Brahman, from the blazing arm of you,
and from the falling glance of my eye— let these three splendors be united.
Born from union with that [mantra], he shall conquer his enemy in battle;
even those who are otherwise invincible and difficult to defeat shall become slayable by him.
"He shall be a source of terror even to Śakra and the immortals. Having spoken thus, Hari then stood there, filled with wonder and joy.
Remaining there within the skull-cup, that noble-minded one, placing his joined palms upon his head, then praised Hara and Keśava.
"What shall I do? he asked; having said this, he stood bowed down.
To him, the glorious Hara spoke with his own splendor through Brahmā.
"Having created him, take up the bow and arrow in your hand and pierce this man with arrows!
Having spoken thus to the cloud-bearer while praising him, Śaṅkara [addressed] that manless one.
In that very same way, having grasped the two hands joined in añjali, he lifted him up from the skull and spoke these words again: ||37||
This is that fierce Puruṣa whom I have described to you;
he has been cast into a deluding sleep produced by Viṣṇu’s *huṃkāra*.
Having said, "Awaken him quickly," Hara vanished from sight;
this was done by Nara in the very presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Struck by his left foot, that one of great strength also rose up;
then a great battle took place between Sveda and Rakta.
With his bow drawn, he made the entire earth resound with the sound [of his arrows];
he removed the armor of one born of sweat by means of one born of blood.
O King, as they fought thus in that battle for two divine years,
their sweat and blood flowed together.
Having seen the blood-born one with two arms, and the sweat-born one likewise joined together.
Having reflected thus, Vāsudeva entered the supreme abode of Brahmā.
In great agitation, Madhusūdana said this to Brahmā:
"O Brahmā, today this one born of sweat has been struck down by the one born of blood."
Having heard this, the agitated Brahmā spoke to Madhusūdana:
"O Hari, in this birth, let this man of mine live. (45)
Then Tuṣṭa spoke to him, and Viṣṇu said, "It shall be so.
Having gone to their hermitage, he restrained them both and said to them: ||46||
In another birth, during the mutual conflict between the Kali and Dvāpara ages that arose in the great battle, I shall unite them both there. 47.
Then Viṣṇu summoned the Lord of Planets and the Lord of the Gods and said to these two noble ones: "By my command, you must protect [him]. 48.
This son of Svedaja (Svayambhuva Manu) is his own [incarnation] on the surface of the earth;
he is Dvāpara, the protector of the gods, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the deities. 49.
In the lineage of the Yadus, there will be a hero of great strength named Śūra;
his daughter, named Pṛthā, is peerless on earth in her beauty. (50)
A highly fortunate one shall be born for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose; Durvāsas, moreover, will bestow upon him a boon consisting of a collection of mantras.
"By means of this mantra, he will invoke the god with devotion;
through the grace of that god, you shall have a son. (52)
Having seen you rise, she, being in her menses and filled with longing, remained overcome by anxiety, O Vibhāvasu, thinking, "I am not to be approached. (53)
He shall not enter her womb; rather, he will be born as a *kānīna* son from Kuṇḍina’s daughter, and he will become a son for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the God of gods. (54)
Having said "So be it," the Sun, a mass of splendor, spoke:
"I shall procreate a son born of Kānīna, who will be proud of his strength. (55)
By my grace, the entire world shall speak of this Viṣṇu, whose mind is purified and who is devoted to the Brahmins, as if it were in his very ear. (56)
O Keśava, there is nothing in this world that cannot be given away;
such is your power, O Lord, that you have generated even this [universe] from yourself. (57)
Having spoken thus to the thousand-eyed god, the slayer of the Dānavas,
the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, he vanished there like the sun behind a mountain.
When the sun, the stealer of waters, had gone beyond the range of sight,
he, with a joyful mind, spoke thus even to Vṛddhaśravas (Indra).
"By my grace, this man, who has arisen red-eyed with a thousand eyes,
must be addressed by you on the surface of the earth as 'Svāṃśabhūta' (the one born from a portion of yourself) during the Dvāpara age."
When the illustrious Pāṇḍu obtains Pṛthā as his wife,
and also Mādrī, O illustrious one, he will then go to the forest.
While he is dwelling in the forest, a deer will bestow a curse upon him;
through that, having developed world-weariness, he will go to Mount Śataśṛṅga.
Desiring sons born of her husband's field, she will speak thus to her wife;
and when that [wife] does not desire him, she will speak thus to her husband.
"O lord of men, I shall never, under any circumstances, deprive you of your sons through mortal enmity;
rather, by the grace of the gods, I shall provide you with sons."
Having approached you, O Śakra, he requested this;
therefore, O Lord of Śacī, by my word as well, do exactly this.
Then the Lord of Gods, being distressed, spoke these words to Viṣṇu: "In this current Manvantara, during the twenty-fourth Yuga that has passed..."
Having descended into the lineage of the Raghus and entered the household of Daśaratha,
he did so for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the peace of the dwellers of heaven.
While you were wandering in the forest in the form of Rāma for the sake of Sītā, my son was indeed killed by the god Hanumān, who acted for the benefit of the son of the Sun (Sugrīva). 68.
"O Nara, I take you as my son; for the sake of Sugrīva, Vālin, the lord of the monkeys, was long pursued by you, and I am now tormented by this very sorrow. (69)
To Indra, who was not grasping the cause and was speaking harshly,
Hari spoke regarding the removal of the earth's burden.
O Lord, I shall effect an incarnation in the world of mortals for the sake of destroying the son of the Sun and for the sake of victory for your own son. 71.
"I shall perform the duty of charioteer for the destruction of the race of Naishadha.
Then Śakra became joyful because of those words of Viṣṇu.
Having joyfully accepted the man and praised your truthful words,
the Lord Acyuta himself, having thus granted the boon, sent him away.
Having gone there, the lotus-eyed one spoke again to Brahmā:
"All this triple world, including the moving and the unmoving, was created by you."
O Lord, you do not perceive that after yourself having performed an act for which you required assistance, you have now brought about its destruction. ||75||
A loathsome deed has been committed by you, who desired to kill Śambhu;
indeed, this man was created by the God of gods out of his wrath.
For the sake of purifying this sin, perform a supreme expiation;
O Lord, accepting the three fires, maintain the Agnihotra sacrifice.
"O Grandfather, perform a sacrifice with your wife at a holy pilgrimage site, in a sacred region, or even in a forest; do so under our patronage. (78)
O Lord of the World, all the gods, as well as the Ādityas and Rudras, will carry out your command, for you are our sovereign. (79)
The Gārhapatya fire is the first, the Dakṣiṇāgni is the second, and the Āhavanīya is the third;
arrange these in the three sacrificial pits.
Then, one should worship oneself in a circular form, me in the shape of a bow,
and the god Hara in a four-cornered [square] form, using the names of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having generated fires through austerity and attained supreme prosperity,
you shall extinguish those fires after having offered oblations for a thousand divine years.
Nothing else is recited here as being more purifying than the Agnihotra;
by means of the well-performed Agnihotra, the twice-born are purified on this earth. (83)
These five fires of the world of the gods have been indicated by the Brahmins;
one fire must always be maintained by the twice-born householder.
"Without fire and without a twice-born man, this state of householdership cannot be attained here.
Bhīṣma said:
"That archer named Nara, who was born from the skull (kapāla)..."
Was he born from Ādhava, or rather from his own karma;
was he produced by Rudra, or perhaps without prior intention? ||86||
O Brahman, this Hiraṇyagarbha is born from an egg and possesses four faces;
how did his fifth face, which is so wondrous, arise?
Since sattva is not seen apart from rajas, and sattva is never found anywhere without rajas, how could the Lord Brahmā, who abides in sattva, bring about its predominance? (88)
"O Hara, I have indeed been sent here by that deluded soul, Anara.
Pulastya said:
"Both Maheśvara and Hari are established upon the path of truth. (89)
For those two great-souled ones, there was nothing unknown, whether accomplished or unaccomplished;
the fifth face of the great-souled Brahmā was directed upwards.
Then Brahmā became deluded, augmented by the quality of rajas;
thereafter, he conceived of this creation as having been fashioned by the quality of tejas.
There is no god other than Māttaṇḍa by whom this creation was set in motion, including the gods together with the gandharvas, and the multitudes of beasts, birds, and wild animals. (92)
Thus the deluded one became Viriñci again, together with Pañcāsya;
his eastern face is the originator of the Ṛgveda. (93)
The second [face] is the originator of the Yajurveda;
the third is that of the Sāmaveda; and the fourth is for the purpose of the Atharvaveda. ||94||
With his fifth face, he whose eyes gaze upward, has studied the Vedas along with their limbs, sub-limbs, histories, secret doctrines, and compendiums.
By the splendor of that mouth of wondrous radiance, all those gods and asuras were rendered without light,
like lamps at the rising of the sun.
Even in his own cities, he moved about with agitation, his mind distracted; he took no account of anyone else, and by his splendor, he eclipsed others. 97.
All the gods, being terrified, were unable to approach the great lord whose origin is the lotus, nor could they even look upon him from a distance. 98.
Considering themselves as if overcome and their splendor struck down, they all consulted together for the sake of their own welfare against the gods. 99.
"Let us go for refuge to the source of bliss, who has rendered him devoid of splendor by his own splendor.
The gods said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all beings, O Maheśvara; salutations, salutations! (100)
You are the eternal Supreme Brahman, the source of the world for those who have become liberated;
you, together with Viṣṇu, are the foundation and the cause of all the worlds.
Thus being praised by the gods, sages, ancestors, and dānavas, he vanished and spoke these words: "O gods, you have requested that which is desired."
The gods said: "O God, having granted us this direct vision, grant us whatever we desire; showing compassion toward us, let a boon also be bestowed. (103)
Whatever great vigor, splendor, vitality, and prowess we possessed—
all that has been swallowed up by Brahmā through the brilliance of his five-month-old son.
O Lord, O Maheśvara, by your grace may all beings regain their splendor; act in such a way that they may become as they were before. 105.
Then, with a serene countenance and saluted by the gods,
he went to where Brahmā was, whose intellect was deluded by passion, egoism, and ignorance.
Praising the Lord of the gods, they gathered around him;
Brahmā, shrouded in passion, did not recognize Rudra when he had arrived.

Overpowering the world with the essence of the splendor of thousands of millions of suns, that Soul of the Universe, the Creator of the Universe, and the Sustainer of the Universe, then became visible. 108.
Then Rudra, having approached Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, together with his grandfather and the entire assembly of gods who were seated there, [spoke]. (109)
"O Lord, your face shines even more with this splendor!
Having spoken thus, the moon-crested god let out a loud, boisterous laugh. 110.
With the tip of the nail of his left thumb, he severed the fifth head of Brahmā,
just as a man might cut the core of a plantain tree with his fingernails.
Then his severed head remained in Bhava’s hand, situated in the midst of the circle of planets like a second moon. (112)
With his skull-bowl tossed aloft,
Maheśvara danced like Mount Kailāsa with the sun resting upon its peak.
Upon hearing these words, the gods were delighted and praised that bull-bannered Lord,
the God of gods with matted hair, with various hymns of praise.
The gods said:
Salutations always to the skull-bearer, the destroyer of Mahākāla, who is endowed with sovereignty and knowledge, and who bestows all portions. (115)
Salutations to you who are the delight of joy, who consist of all the gods;
in the Kali age, you are remembered as Mahākāla, the bringer of dissolution.
You are the destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees; therefore, you are called Duḥkhahasta. You bring auspiciousness to your devoted followers; therefore, you are remembered as Śaṅkara.
Since you have severed the head of Brahmā and carry his skull-cup, you are therefore praised as Devakapālī; may you be gracious today.
Thus praised, the Lord Śaṅkara, his soul serene, dismissed the gods to their respective abodes; he himself remained there, filled with joy.
Then, for the sake of pacifying the anger of the worlds, he [related] the nature of the Brahman of consciousness and the birth of the Hero from the words of Śironīra.
Then, placing his joined palms upon his head and bowing down,
he praised that Prajāpati, the supreme Brahman and treasury of splendor, seeking to know him in this manner.

With the etymologies, hymns, and secret doctrines spoken in the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, Rudra said: "Obeisance to you, the immeasurable one; obeisance to the supreme Self, higher than the highest. (122)
You are the source of wonders, an inexhaustible treasury of splendors;
through victory you are the essence of the universe, the creator of all, O one of great luster! 123.
Homage to you with face turned upward; homage to you whose nature is that of sentient beings and whose nature is the earth!
Homage to you who lie upon the waters, who are born from the waters, and whose abode is the waters! 124.
O Grandfather Jayadeva, whose eyes are like the blossoming petals of a lotus, I was indeed created by you in the past for the sake of creation, O Lord. (125)
Salutations to you, the Lord of the limbs of sacrifice, whose constant food is the oblation of the sacrifice;
O Prajāpati, whose womb is gold, whose womb is the lotus, and whose womb is the gods! 126.
You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, and you are the *svadhā* offering, O Lotus-born One!
By the word of the gods, O Lord, my head has been severed by me. (127)
"I am overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin; protect me, O Lord of the World!
Having been addressed thus, Brahmā spoke these words to the God of gods.
Brahmā said:
"The Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is worthy of praise by you, shall purify you; he is the blessed one, worshipful to me, and the all-pervading Sovereign himself. (129)
Surely you have been meditated upon by that very god Viṣṇu;
for by him devotion has been produced in you, and the thought to praise me has arisen. (130)
O one of great luster, by the severing of his head you became a Kapālin, the founder of the Soma-siddhānta, and the deliverer of hundreds of millions of Brahmins.
One must perform the vow for the killing of a Brahmin; nothing else exists [as an atonement].
Sinners, the cruel, those who slay Brahmins, and evildoers are not to be spoken to. 132.

Those who have studied the Vedic sacrificial rites and the various fields of knowledge should never, under any circumstances, look at the sun while those [objects] are being seen by them; rather, they should perform the observation of the sun in that manner.
Upon touching a limb of one who has committed an offense, Rudra should enter the water with his clothes on;
in this way, he attains the purification previously observed by the wise. (134)
"O noble one, you are a slayer of a Brahmin; perform a vow for the sake of purification.
Once the vow has been completed, you shall again obtain many boons. (135)
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed; Rudra did not recognize him.
Then, by means of the path of meditation, he himself reflected upon Viṣṇu.
[He worshipped] the eternal God of gods, the bestower of boons who is accompanied by Lakṣmī;
with a prostration of eight limbs, the three-eyed God of gods [was honored]. (137)
Having become prostrate, he praised the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Rudra said:
I praise Viṣṇu, the supreme among the supreme, the immortal, the ancient, higher than the highest, and possessed of infinite valor. (138)
I constantly remember the eternal, most excellent Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, the peerless and ancient one;
higher than the highest, the first-born, of fierce speed, who goes to the fearless, the foremost among those of fearful intellect. (139)
I have taken birth as the god Hari, the sovereign ruler, the abode higher than the highest, the supreme light;
the one who is both transcendent and immanent, the ultimate light, the Lord of the transcendent and the immanent, the vast Puruṣa. (140)

I praise Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is pure, who is both transcendent and immanent, and who created this subtle world; because he eternally abides as the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), may that peaceful Pradhāna, the foremost of beings, be my refuge. 141.
Nārāyaṇa, stainless, ancient, higher than the highest, Viṣṇu, whose limit is boundless;
the primordial one, the foremost among those possessed of statesmanship, a lord of the earth devoted to fortitude, forbearance, and tranquility. (142)

I always praise that auspicious one of great majesty, who has a thousand heads and many feet, infinite arms, and eyes like the moon and sun; he is both the perishable and the imperishable, and his bed is the ocean of milk. 143.

I praise Nārāyaṇa, the supreme, the Lord of the highest, who is beyond the highest, whom even the gods cannot reach; who abides within the three creations, whose eyes are the three sacrificial fires, who is characterized by the three principles, the place of dissolution for the three, and the three-eyed one. 144.
I bow to that immeasurable Nārāyaṇa, who was white in the Kṛta age, red from the Dvāpara onwards, and black in the Kali age; I then bow to him who created the Brahmins from his very mouth.
From his arms [he created] the Kṣatriyas, from his pair of thighs the Vaiśyas, and likewise from the tips of his feet the Śūdras;
I bow to that ancient one whose body is the universe, who is higher than the highest, who has gone beyond all limits, and who is immeasurable. 146.
I bow to the armor of all the gods, which has a subtle form, a great form, the form of knowledge, and is formless, and which causes the eyes of enemies to tremble. 147.
I bow to that Supreme Lord, the Lord of Gods, who has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and mighty arms, and who stands pervading the entire universe. 148.
I bow to the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, the victorious one, the refuge and the worthy protector, who resembles a dark blue cloud and holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand. 149.
One should bow to Hari, who is pure, all-pervading, eternal, of the nature of space, ancient, and liberated from both existence and non-existence, the omnipresent one. 150.
And here, O Acyuta, I do not perceive anything distinct from you;
I see all this world of moving and non-moving beings as consisting entirely of you. 151.
When the Supreme Lord Rudra had spoken thus,
as he was being addressed in this manner by him, the Eternal One himself became visible to him, even beyond the highest.
The eternal one, whose hand holds the discus and who is seated upon Garuḍa, rose up illuminating the mountain like the sun;
he said, "Choose a boon," for I, the bestower of boons, have come to you as your boon-granter. (153)
Thus addressed repeatedly, the excellent Rudra said: "O Lord of Asuras, your purification shall be unsurpassed;
for no other supreme remover of this sin is seen except you. (154)
Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, my body has become black; the stench of a corpse clings to my limbs, and iron ornaments have appeared upon me. (155)
"How might my form become like that of Janārdana? O Great God, what shall I do, for this body of mine is from a former birth? (156)
"By your grace, may that [merit] come to pass; therefore, tell me of it, O Acyuta.
Viṣṇu said:
"The murder of a Brāhmaṇa is supreme, fierce, and the greatest of all misfortunes."
One should not even mentally entertain the thought of this sin;
by your very words, this firm resolve has been made known. (158)
Now, O mighty-armed one, act according to what was spoken by Brahmā:
rub all your limbs with ashes upon your body three times a day. (159)
"Place bones in your topknot, in your ears, and in your hand;
by doing so, no suffering shall come upon you. (160)
Having thus instructed him, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, vanished right there;
accompanied by Lakṣmī, Rudra departed, and he did not perceive him.
Wandering over this earth with a skull in his hand, the Lord of Gods reached the Himavat mountain, along with Maināka and Meru.
He meditated upon the entire Kailāsa, as well as the blue Mahāgiri, and likewise upon Kāñcī, Aṅkāśī, Tāmraliptā, Magadhā, and Āvilā. ||163||
Vatsagulma, Gokarṇa, as well as the Northern Kurus,
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and the Hairaṇyaka region— [he rained upon these].
Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, he wandered through Kāmarūpa, Prabhāsa, and the Mahendra mountain, yet found no protection. ||165||
Overcome with shame, constantly beholding the skull held in his hand, he shook his arms repeatedly and was distracted again and again. (166)
When his hands shook so that the skull-cup did not fall, the thought arose in him: "I shall observe this vow. (167)
"By this very path of mine, the twice-born shall come from all directions.
Having meditated thus for a very long time, the Lord wandered upon the earth.
Having reached Puṣkara, he entered that supreme forest, which was filled with various trees and creepers and resounded with the cries of various birds. ||169||
The ground was perfumed by a favorable breeze carrying the fragrance of the weight of tree blossoms,
and its surface was adorned with flowers that seemed as if they had been deliberately arranged.
Pervaded by the fragrance of flowers and filled with various scents from other ripe and unripe fruits, he entered the expanse of the tree.
"By worshipping here with devotion, Brahmā will grant me a boon;
through Brahmā's grace, the desired knowledge of the *Pauṣkara* has been obtained. (172)
Thus, as Rudra of immeasurable splendor was being entreated by Vaidhyāyati, [he bestowed] that which destroys sin, pacifies the wicked, and increases nourishment, fortune, and strength. (173)
Then Brahmā arrived, pleased by devotion, as did Kaṃjaja;
the Guru, having raised up the prostrate Rudra, spoke to him again. (174)
I have been propitiated by you through the performance of divine vows, and by you with extreme faith, out of a longing for a vision of me. ||175||
For gods as well as men behold those established in their vows;
therefore, by her will, I shall grant whatever boon is most excellent. 176.
Since this vow was observed for the sake of accomplishing all desires, with a satisfied inner self through the states of mind, speech, and body; (177)
"O Lord, tell me what I may give as a boon, whatever you desire.
Rudra said:
"O Blessed One, this alone is a great boon sufficient for today. (178)
O Creator of the universe, since you have been seen, salutations to you, who are accomplished through a great sacrifice performed over a long period of time. (179)
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, this skull, which causes the loss of life through asceticism, has fallen from Your hand. 180.
"O Lord, this conduct of the Ṛṣis is indeed contemptible;
yet, through your grace, this Kāpālika vow has been performed by me. (181)
This is established; let the great vow for one who has sought refuge be proclaimed here.
"In a holy place, I shall cast this [image] into the water"—say this. (182)
"By what means may I become purified among the sages of cultivated souls?
Brahmā said: "There is an ancient abode of the Blessed One called Avimukta. (183)
The sacred ford Kapālamocana shall be yours there;
I, you, and Viṣṇu as well shall be present there. (184)
Even those who are great sinners, upon seeing you there, enjoy all pleasures, having become purified within my realm. 185.
The Varaṇā and the Asī are two rivers beloved by the gods;
in the sacred field between them, one should meditate constantly in some secluded place. (186)
This is the most excellent of holy places among holy places, the most excellent of sacred fields; until the fall of their bodies, men shall serve this field of yours. (187)
Having abandoned all fear, they shall go to heaven by means of a swan-vehicle at the time of their death;
furthermore, a sacred field measuring five krośas has been granted to you by me.
When the Gaṅgā comes from the midst of the field to the lord of rivers, then this city shall become the great and meritorious Purī Rudrā. (189)
The meritorious Gaṅgā flows northward, and the Sarasvatī flows eastward;
yet the river Jāhnavī travels with such speed that she reaches the northward direction within a single yojana.
There all the gods, including Maya and Sahasrāvāsava, will come to their dwelling; release the skull there.

Having gone to those three holy fords (tīrthas), they shall indeed gratify their ancestors with the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and with śrāddha rites; for them, there shall be an imperishable world in heaven.
A man who bathes at the great sacred ford (mahātīrtha) in Vārāṇasī is liberated; by merely going there, he is released from the sins committed during seven lifetimes. (193)
That sacred ford is proclaimed as the most excellent of all sacred fords;
those living beings who, bowing down to you, cast off their lives there— [attain the highest state]. (194)
Having attained the state of Rudra, you rejoiced together with them;
even there, whatever gift was given by you with a self dedicated to Rudra [bore fruit]. (195)
There will be a great fruit for that person of cultivated mind, because people there perform the restoration of their cracked limbs. (196)
Having reached the world of the three Rudras, those embodied beings are always joyful; there, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings are performed by them. 197.
For one whose soul is endowed with devotion to Rudra, heaven yields infinite fruit;
by offering a lamp there, a man shall obtain the eye of knowledge. (198)
Having caused the son of Tugra—who was free from physical defects, youthful, gentle, and handsome—to be marked with the *oṃkāra*, he who releases him attains the supreme state. 199.
Accompanied by his ancestors, he goes to liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Now, what is the use of saying more? Whatever is performed there by men [yields that result]. (200)
When one points out the nature of karma, its fruit becomes infinite;
that is considered on earth to be a sacred ford (tīrtha), the cause of both heaven and liberation. 201.

Having gone to the sacred site of Vārāṇasī with devotion, those who are solely intent upon Rudra achieve the means for infinite fruit through bathing, recitation, and likewise through fire-offerings. (202)
Those who have attained death there are undoubtedly his ancestors;
the Vasus are to be known as the fathers, and the Rudras as the grandfathers. ||203||
"The great-grandfathers are likewise the Ādityas"—such is the Vedic revelation.
O sinless one, this threefold rule for the offering of the rice-balls has been declared by me. (204)
Human beings who have come here must always perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
and there, one's own sons should likewise perform the offering of funeral cakes with reverence. (205)
These good sons become bestowers of happiness upon their parents;
I have described to you this sacred site (tīrtha), which grants liberation even through its mere sight. (206)
Having bathed there in the water of that lake, one is released from the bondage of birth;
being liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin, one dwells there with Rudra according to one's pleasure. ||207||
"Stay here with your wife, for you have been granted by me, Avimukta.
Rudra said:
"Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth, in those I shall dwell together with Viṣṇu. (208)
"I abide by what has been spoken by you; this boon has been chosen by me: I am the God, the Great God, who must always be propitiated by you. (209)
"I shall grant you boons, for I am pleased in my innermost soul;
and I shall bestow upon Viṣṇu the boons desired by his mind. (210)
Among all the gods and among the sages of purified soul, I am the giver and I am the one to be entreated; no other should ever be conceived as such in any way.
Brahmā said:
"O Rudra, I shall do exactly as you have spoken in these auspicious words; and Nārāyaṇa will also carry out all that you have said, without a doubt. (212)
Having thus dismissed Rudra at that time, Brahmā departed;
the Great God, having gone to Vārāṇasī, established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Rudra's Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, what was done by Brahmā after sending him to the city of Vārāṇasī?
O sage, what deed was performed by Janārdana and by Śaṅkara?
Tell me how that sacrifice was performed at that sacred ford;
tell me who were the Sadasyas and all those officiating priests. ||2||
"Who were the gods gratified by him? This is a great curiosity of mine.
Pulastya said: "There is a city named Śrīnidhāna on a peak of Mount Meru, adorned with jewels. (3)
It was the abode of many deer, crowded with numerous trees, variegated by diverse minerals, and as pure as clear crystal. (4)
Richly adorned with the beauty of spreading creepers, resounded by the cries of peacocks, and crowded with herds of elephants terrified by the roars of lions. ||5||
It was cooled by the spray from waterfalls falling into the river,
and it was variegated by the clear drinking pools formed where clusters of trees were shaken by the wind.
The entire forest was perfumed with the excellent fragrance of musk,
while travelers who were Vidyādharas slept within the bower-houses, exhausted from their dalliances.
It resounded with the sweet melodies of throngs of singing kinnaras,
and its entire ground was beautified by numerous artistic arrangements.
The abode of the supreme Brahmā was named Vairāja;
there, it resounded with the sweet sounds of songs sung by celestial maidens.
She wore a garland of jasmine flowers produced from the pārijāta tree, and she was variegated with many colors arising from the mass of rays of light from her jewels. 10.
Ten million bhaktas were seated there, adorned with stainless mirrors, and made radiant by the playful splendor of the dance-performances of the apsarases. (11)
Resounding with the collective sound produced by many musical instruments, it was graced by numerous songs and instrumental performances, accompanied by rhythmic timing and tempo. ||12||
She is the bestower of refuge to the assemblies of the virtuous who are free from the gods [of the senses], joined by hosts of seers, and served by multitudes of sages. ||13||
In that [city], which resounded with the chants of the twice-born reciting the Sāman hymns,
the Lord of Gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā), was seated and absorbed in meditation.
He meditated upon the Supreme God by whom this world was created;
as he meditated, the thought arose in him: "How shall I perform a sacrifice? (15)
"In what place on the surface of the earth should I perform the sacrifice? Is it Kāśī, Prayāga, Tuṅgā, Naimiṣa, or likewise Śṛṅkhala? (16)
Kāñcī, Bhadrā, Devikā, Kurukṣetra, Sarasvatī, Prabhāsa, and other such sacred fords (tīrthas) are located here in the middle of this earth. ||17||
Whatever sacred fields and holy pilgrimage sites exist here in every respect,
as well as others on the surface of the earth created by Rudra at my command— 18.
Just as I am established as the primordial deity among all the gods,
so do I make this one supreme sacred ford the very first of its kind.
The lotus from which I was born, that very lotus born from the navel of Viṣṇu,
is declared by the seers who recite the Vedas to be the sacred ford known as Puṣkara.
As the Prajāpati Brahmā was reflecting thus, this thought arose in his mind: "I shall go now to the surface of the earth."
Having reached that most excellent place, which was filled with various trees and creepers and adorned with various flowers, he entered it just as before.
Resounding with the cries of various birds and filled with diverse throngs of sages, it perfumed the gods and asuras with the fragrances of the abundance of tree blossoms. (23)
The surface of the earth was adorned with flowers that seemed as if they had been intentionally arranged,
possessing various fragrances and flavors, both ripe and unripe, produced by all six seasons.
It was rich with fruits possessing the luster of gold, enchanting to the sense of smell and the eye;
yet there, the leaves and grass were withered, and the wood and fruits were dry.
The wind, as if by its own favor,
carried away the masses of various flowers that had fallen outside, taking up their fragrance.
He saw the earth cooled by the wind, which seemed to clothe the quarters with forests that were lush, verdant, without gaps, free of insects, and dense.
It was adorned with many kinds of trees possessing lofty peaks—some free from disease, beautiful to behold, well-rounded, and some radiant. (28)
The trees, covered with sprouts resembling minerals, shone like the households of Brahmins surrounded on all sides by officiating priests.
Men, covered by their own flawless virtues as if by noble silken garments,
touched one another closely as their peaks were tossed by the wind.
In some places, the *nāga* trees, adorned with flower-branches, were smelling one another intensely with their blossoms, while others were covered with the filaments of *druma* and *vānīra* flowers.
In some places, there were Karṇikāra trees with flower-laden tops, possessing a beauty like eyes with flickering black pupils.
In this place, the lords of the garden shone forth in pairs, like rows of excellent *vārada* trees abounding in clusters of beautiful flowers. (33)
In some places, the forest deities were worshipped in their embodied forms, shining with ornaments of flowers and appearing like blossoming jasmine buds.
In the quarters of the forest, the flowering *sarja* and *arjuna* trees shine like rising young moons, adding beauty to the directions. (35)
Just as men are covered with garments of washed silk, so too were the trees enveloped by flowering *atimuktaka* creepers. (36)
The *sāla* and *aśoka* trees, with their foliage clinging to one another, appeared like beloved women embracing their kings.
With their hands they touched one another's hands, like long-reunited close friends;
the jackfruit trees, the sarala pines, and the arjuna trees were all bent low under the weight of their fruits and flowers. (38)
The trees, with their *sāla*-tree arms embraced by the force of the wind, honored one another with flowers and fruits of intense beauty.
As the people approached nearby, they appeared as if risen up through their own splendors,
stationed there for the sake of great beauty by the very restraint of the flowers.
For, having come under its sway, men indeed vie with one another through their peaks, which are bent by the weight of floral beauty and shaken by the wind. 41.
The delighted men danced, their crests adorned with garlands;
the trees were laden with rows of flowers, shaken by the wind from the tips of the mountain peaks.
In some places, trees— covered by creepers bent down with their own flowers— dance as if they were men accompanied by their beloveds.
Like the sky in autumn variegated by clusters of shimmering stars, or like flowering mālatī creepers upon the tops of trees. (44)
Like crests, the green trees—shining with the luster of gold, laden with fruit and flowers—adorned it without being intentionally arranged. (45)
Displaying their friendship at the gathering of the virtuous, those men, as tawny as the pollen of flowers, moved through all directions. 46.
In some places, bees, intoxicated by the nectar of the flowers, fly here and there, making a loud humming sound as they conquer the silence.
In some places, they were like male cuckoos dwelling with their beloveds in thickets of trees;
in other places, resembling *śirīṣa* flowers, they appeared in pairs like parrots.
The peacocks with their variegated plumage, well-attuned to one another, utter diverse songs like honored Brahmins.
In those forests, the dancers dance beautifully,
while flocks of birds warble, uttering various cries.
They make this forest, which was exceedingly delightful—filled with various herds of deer and birds that are ever joyful—most unpleasant through their enmity. (51)
That forest was equal to Nandana, increasing the delight of the mind and the sight;
the Blessed One, the Lotus-born, [dwelt] in that most excellent forest of such a form.
With a gentle gaze that was like a mirror, he seemed as if he were purifying them;
having thus seen the Lord, the Tathāgata, all those rows of trees gazed upon him.
Having offered a wealth of flowers with devotion to the Brahmins who were seeking liberation,
the Grandfather (Brahmā), having accepted the flowers from the trees, [departed].
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you," the trees said to them.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the trees were unrestrained. (55)
Having bowed down to Viriñca, all the aquatic beings said: "O Lord, you who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge in you, if you would grant us a boon... (56)
O Blessed One, remain forever established here in this forest;
this is our supreme desire. Homage to you, O Grandfather! (57)
O Creator of the Universe, if you dwell in this forest of the Lord of Gods, then grant the supreme boon desired by us who have sought refuge with our whole being. (58)
Enough with other millions of boons being offered;
by the presence [of this] at sacred fords, this shall be the most excellent and great boon of all. (59)

Brahmā said: "This shall become the most excellent of all sacred fields (kṣetra), meritorious and eternal; its trees shall be perpetually endowed with flowers and fruits, and [its inhabitants] shall possess ever-stable youth. (60)
They move at will, assume forms at will, and bestow the fruits of their desires;
they appear according to the wishes of men whose debts have been cleared by the brilliance of their ascetic success.
"By my grace, you shall be endowed with supreme splendor.
Thus Brahmā, the giver of boons, showed favor to the trees.
Having stood there for a thousand years, he cast a lotus onto the earth;
by that act, the earth fell clearly down to the netherworld (rasātala).
Helpless, the oceans with their agitated waves abandoned their shores,
like mountains struck by Indra’s thunderbolt and overrun by tigers and serpents.
The peaks of thousands of mountains were shattered,
as were the celestial chariots of the gods and siddhas, and the cities of the gandharvas.
Pigeon-colored clouds rushed forth, wandered about, fell, and entered the surface of the earth; they descended from the sky appearing like a multitude of folded wings.
The intensely radiant suns appeared as if eclipsing the hosts of stars;
by the great sound of that [battle], the world was rendered mute and deafened.
The entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, became agitated;
so too did the bodies and minds of all the gods and asuras.
They sat down and wondered, "What is this? What is this? Unable to understand, they all then summoned their fortitude and looked toward Brahmā.
And they did not see him; where indeed had Brahmā gone?
For what reason did the earth tremble, and why was this portentous omen seen? (70)
Viṣṇu went to that place where the gods were stationed; having prostrated themselves, the inhabitants of heaven spoke these words: ||71||
O Blessed One, tell me: what is this vision of omens and portents, by which the three worlds have been seized and joined with the law of time? (72)
Did the four elephants of the quarters and the immovable mountains become for you the ocean that breaks its bounds at the end of an eon? (73)
Why is the lower region covered by the waters of the seven oceans?
O Blessed One, the arising of sound is not without purpose. (74)
Such a word as this has never been heard before, nor will it ever be;
by which a fierce wheel was raised, causing the three worlds to tremble. (75)
"O Blessed One, if you know this sound—whether auspicious or inauspicious—that has arisen for the inhabitants of the three worlds and the celestial dwellers, please tell us what it is. (76)
Thus addressed, Viṣṇu, impelled by the Supreme Being, spoke:
"Do not fear, O Maruts; hear now the reason for this."
And having ascertained by whom [this was done], I shall explain it exactly as it occurred;
for the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World, holds a lotus in his hand.
He resolved to perform a sacrifice upon a holy site on the slopes of mountains, in a forest that was exceedingly beautiful. (79)
The lotus fell from his hand onto the surface of the earth;
by its great sound, you all were made to tremble. (80)
There, the Blessed One, having been greeted by the fragrance of flowers from the trees in full bloom, then took pity upon that forest filled with deer and birds.
For the sake of favoring the world, he chose to dwell there at that sacred ford named Puṣkara, as well as at the field of Vṛṣabha.
This has been brought about by the Blessed One, who acts for the benefit of the worlds;
therefore, go there together with me and propitiate Brahmā. (83)
"The Blessed One, being propitiated, will grant excellent boons.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu [departed] together with those gods and dānavas. (84)
They went to that region of the forest where Satukañjaja dwelt;
they were joyful, their minds were contented, and they were made to speak with the warbling of cuckoos.
They entered the auspicious forest of Brahmā, radiant with heaps of flowers, which was filled with all the gods and praised by the hosts of sages. 86.
Then, having entered that forest, which was rich in lotuses, deer, and flowers, very firm, and adorned with every kind of blossom, the gods shone resplendently. 87.
"He is here!"—saying this, the gods wandered about, desiring to see him;
all those gods, together with Indra, searched for him everywhere. (88)
In that forest of wonders, the swift-moving gods did not see him;
while searching for the god, they then beheld Vāyu.
Satān said: "You shall not see Brahmā without austerity.
Then, undaunted, they searched upon that mountain slope.
Again and again, [the wind] blew between them toward the south and the north;
having placed the wind-spoken [instruction] in his heart, Vāyu spoke to them once more.
The threefold means for the vision of Viriñci is always proclaimed as faith, knowledge, austerity, and yoga. ||92||
Yogins behold the Lord as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala); ascetics behold Him as with parts, while those possessing knowledge behold the supreme, partless one.
When consciousness has arisen, one who lacks faith does not see this;
however, through supreme devotion, yogins quickly behold Brahman.
This Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa is to be beheld as changeless; those who are constantly engaged with the Grandfather through action, mind, and speech [attain him]. 95.
And for those twice-born devotees who were intent on the propitiation of Brahmā, engaged in penance and devoted to the good, he bestowed the Brāhma initiation. 96.
"Always, I recognize that I must show myself;
having heard these words of Vāyu and understanding them to be for my benefit," (97)
Then those whose minds were permeated by the desire for Brahman spoke to the Lord of Speech:
"O Knower of Wisdom, bestow upon us the initiation pertaining to Brahman."
Desiring to quickly initiate the immortals into the initiation of Brahman, the Guru initiated them according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas. (99)
With humble appearance and bowed down, they attained the state of being disciples of Aṃtevāsī;
having obtained the grace of Brahmā, they were proclaimed as possessors of the Pauṣkara knowledge. ||100||
The preceptor, the best of officiating priests, performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites;
having fashioned a lotus rich with lotus-stalks through the ritual application of the "Lotus Initiation" (Padmadīkṣā).
Impelled by the desire of the gods, the sage, who was well-versed in the application of the Vedic injunctions, favored those deities;
he bestowed [the knowledge] upon those wise ones.
Having abandoned his initiation and his astonishment, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati,
the great-souled one, prepared a single fire for the dwellers of heaven.
Being pleased, the descendant of Aṅgiras gave him that recitation prescribed in the Vedas:
the Trisuparṇa, the Trimadhu, and the purifying Pāvamānī hymns.
The noble-minded one taught him everything, beginning with the *sahijāpya*;
that which is the bath with the hymn "Āpo hi ṣṭha" is recited as the *brāhma* bath. (105)
It destroys sin, pacifies the wicked, increases nourishment, prosperity, and strength; it bestows success and fame, and utterly eradicates the impurities of the Kali age. (106)
Therefore, one should perform the Brāhma-bath with every effort;
doing so, they remain silent, self-controlled, consecrated by initiation, and have subdued their senses. (107)

All were equipped with a water-pot, wearing a sacred thread across their shoulders and holding rosaries; they carried staffs, wore garments of bark, and were exceedingly beautiful with their matted locks.
Devoted to the practice of bathing and to their seats, maintaining effort and meditation,
they should unite the mind with Brahman and desire only moderate food.
Remaining devoid of seeing, conversing, socializing, and meditating, all those observers of the vow likewise performed their ablutions at the three times of day. (110)
Endowed with supreme devotion and the highest ritual procedure,
through meditation over a long period of time, they attained divine knowledge within their minds.
When their minds were purified and singleness of mind attained through the fire of meditation on Brahman,
the Blessed One appeared within the range of vision of them all.
Sustained by his splendor, they became bewildered in mind;
then, with firm resolve, they offered their strength to the desired deity according to the prescribed rites.

With their minds delighted by the yoga of the six-limbed Veda, they were intent upon that; with their hands joined at their heads and their heads touching the ground, they prostrated themselves. (114)
They praised the Lord, the creator of the universe and the sustainer of existence.
The gods said:
"Salutations to Brahmā, whose body is Brahman, who is devoted to Brahman, and who is unconquered. (115)
With self-restraint, we pay homage to the one who bestows sacrifices and the Vedas; salutations indeed to the compassionate one toward the worlds, whose form is the creation of the gods. 116.
To the one who is compassionate toward his devotees, who is praised by the chanting of the Vedas, whose own form consists of many forms, and who assumes hundreds of forms. ||117||
Salutation to the Lord of Sāvitrī, to the Lord of Gāyatrī;
salutation to the one seated upon a lotus, to the Lotus One, to the one with a lotus-like face. ||118||
Salutations to the bestower of boons, who is worthy of the highest boons; to the one who is both tortoise and deer;
to the one endowed with a crown of matted hair, and who holds the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles.
Homage to the one whose eye is the law of the deer-marked moon;
homage and homage again to the one named Viśva, who is the universe and the Lord of the universe.
O Grandfather, you ought to provide protection for the eye of the Dharma even beyond this; we have taken refuge in you with our speech, mind, body, and being. (121)
Thus praised by the gods at that time, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, said:
