"I shall grant it; very well. For the sight of you is never in vain."
"But tell me, O sons, what excellent boons shall I grant you?
Having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, the gods spoke these words. (123)
O Blessed One, this very auspicious sound produced by you as you approach has today become for us a great and sufficient remedy. (124)
"For what purpose has my father been slain and the worlds thrown into turmoil? O Lord, this cannot be without cause; please tell me the reason for it. (125)
Brahmā said:
"This lotus was indeed deposited by me for your benefit;
it is for the protection of the gods—listen now to the reason for this. (126)
This Asura Vajranābha, the snatcher of the lives of the foolish,
remains stationed there, having seized and taken refuge in the depths of the netherworld (rasātala).
Knowing that you had arrived, that man of evil conduct, desiring to slay even the gods including Indra, laid aside his weapons while engaged in ascetic penance. (128)
The destruction of him who had fallen from his lotus-seat was brought about by me;
he, arrogant with royal sovereignty and power, was slain by me for that reason. 129.
In this world, those Brahmins who are devoted to their vows and have mastered the Vedas do not fall into a miserable state; rather, they attain a happy rebirth once again. (130)
O dwellers of heaven, I am equal toward all— the gods, the dānavas, humans, serpents, rākṣasas, and the entire multitude of living beings.
For the sake of your welfare, he was slain by me with the *pāpasaumya* mantra;
by the sight of his lotus-like face, he has attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds.
"Because of the lotus that was released by me, this place on earth shall become known as Puṣkara;
it will be a great, purifying, and merit-bestowing holy site. (133)
On this earth, it is proclaimed that [this work] bestows merit upon all living beings;
for, O God, you have indeed shown favor to your devotees who desire devotion. 134.
O sinless one, Mahākāla has come to this forest, which has been requested by the trees for his eternal residence, now that I have arrived.
O gods, as you perform ascetic penance, great wisdom has been revealed to you; therefore, keep in your hearts both your own welfare and the welfare of others. 136.
"You must show yourselves on earth assuming various forms;
for that man who hates a learned brahmin is indeed afflicted by his own sin. (137)
One shall not be liberated from sin even in hundreds of millions of births;
one must neither kill nor defile a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedāṅgas.
Since by the killing of one [such person], ten million are considered slain, one should, endowed with faith, feed a single learned Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas. (139)
He who bestows alms sufficient to fill the bowl of ascetics shall undoubtedly have fed ten million Brahmins; of this there is no doubt. (140)
Liberated from all evils, he shall not fall into an evil rebirth;
just as I am the eldest, the most excellent, and the grandfather among all the gods. 141.
Likewise, the man of knowledge who is free from the sense of "mine" and without possessions is always worthy of worship;
for the sake of liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra, this is the vow protected by Brahman. (142)
Having undertaken the Agnihotra sacrifice prescribed by me as the cause for the Brahmins' liberation from rebirth, one who has not conquered his senses might abandon it. (143)
He who is frivolous in worldly affairs and performs base actions is quickly led away by the servants of Yama and goes to the Raurava hell. (144)

Possessing a mind full of passion, he is amorous and fond of women, wealth, and fine clothes; eating alone, he partakes of delicious food and devotes himself to agriculture, trade, and service. ||145||
One who is ignorant, a reviler of the Vedas, and one who consorts with another's wife—by merely conversing with such a person who is defiled by faults such as these, [one is tainted]. (146)
A man who violates his virtuous vows shall go to hell—he who is discontented, divided in mind, evil-minded, and a doer of evil. (147)
"One should not touch [another] by contact of limbs; having touched [one], one becomes pure through bathing.
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One, Brahmā, together with those immortals—
I shall describe to you exactly how he established the field:
from the north of the Candra river as far as the eastern Sarasvatī. (149)
Formerly, however, from Nandana onwards, extending as far as Kalpa together with Puṣkara, this altar was fashioned for the sacrifice by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds. (150)
The eldest should be known as the first sacred ford (tīrtha), which purifies the three worlds;
it is renowned as having Brahmā as its presiding deity, while the middle one likewise belongs to Viṣṇu. (151)
He caused the youngest [temple] to be built first, dedicated to Rudra;
this is proclaimed in the Vedas as the primordial, supreme, and secret field (kṣetra). ||152||
In the forest named Puṣkara, the Lord Brahmā himself is ever-present; indeed, he has personally bestowed his grace upon this region of the earth. 153.
For the sake of favoring all the brahmins who roam the earth, the ground was made marked with altars featuring golden vajras. (154)
Adorned with various jewels and a wonderful mosaic floor, it is made entirely beautiful;
there the Blessed One Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, takes his delight. (155)
Viṣṇu and Rudra, as well as the gods Vasus and the Aśvins,
and the Maruts along with Mahendra— those dwellers of heaven took their delight there.
This has been truly declared for the sake of favoring the world, following the sequence of the *Saṃhitā* and with mantras according to the prescribed rules. 157
Those Brahmins who study the Vedas and are devoted to the service of their gurus,
all of them, empowered by that [merit], dwell in the vicinity of Brahmā.
Bhīṣma said: "O Blessed One, by what rule should men dwelling in the sacred field of Puṣkara in the forest reside, desiring to attain the world of Brahmā?"
Of what use are men, or women, or those belonging to the various castes and stages of life? What should be practiced by those who dwell [in this world]? Tell me all of this. (160)
Pulastya said:
Men and women residing according to their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) must dwell [there], devoted to the practice of their own duties and free from the delusion of pride. 161.

By those devoted to Brahman, who have conquered their senses, who are free from malice, who are not mean-spirited, and who are intent on the welfare of all beings—through action, mind, and speech—[they should practice]. ||162||
Bhīṣma said: "What must a man do to be called a devotee of Brahman in this world through his actions? And what kind of people are remembered as devotees of Brahman among men? Tell me."
Pulastya said:
Devotion is declared to be threefold, arising from mind, speech, and body;
it may also be worldly, Vedic, and likewise spiritual. (164)

That which consists of the recollection of the meaning of the Vedas through the intellect aided by meditation and concentration, and which brings pleasure to Brahman—this is called mental devotion (mānasī bhakti). 165.
Vocal devotion is held to consist of salutations with mantras and the Vedas, reflections on the fire-sacrifice (agniśrāddha) and other rites, as well as essential recitations (jāpya). //166//
By those restrained by vows and fasts who have controlled their minds and senses, and likewise by ornaments rich with gold and jewels, as well as by the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances. ||167||
Through the Brahma-kṛcchra fasts and likewise through other auspicious vows,
the bodily devotion of the twice-born is said to be threefold.
With cow’s ghee, milk, and curd; with jewel-lamps and water from *kuśa* grass;
with various perfumes, garlands, and prepared mineral pigments. ||169||
With incense of ghee and guggulu fragrant with black aloe-wood, with ornaments rich in gold and jewels, and with variegated garlands as well. (170)

And with dance, instrumental music, and song, with offerings of all kinds of jewels, and with various foods, edibles, meals, and drinks—whatever worship is performed by men, [it is not equal to the merit of this]. (171)
Devotion directed toward the Grandfather (Brahmā) is considered worldly;
devotion performed through the application of Vedic mantras and oblations is considered Vedic.

The Agnihotra sacrifice should be performed either on the new moon day or the full moon day; the giving of sacrificial fees is highly recommended, as are the offering of the *puroḍāśa* cake and the preparation of the *caru* oblation. (173)
The sacrifice, fortitude, the drinking of Soma, all sacrificial rites in every respect, the recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the study of the Saṃhitās; ||174||
Devotion directed toward the ritual procedure is considered Vedic;
[it concerns] fire, earth, wind, ether, water, the moon, and the sun. (175)
O King, every action performed with that [Brahman] as its intended object has Brahman as its deity;
furthermore, spiritual devotion to Brahman is established as being of two kinds. (176)
Now hear from me concerning another [type of] division arising from the application of number:
the twenty-four principles beginning with Pradhāna are designated by that number. (177)
The objects of enjoyment are insentient, while the twenty-fifth principle is the Person (puruṣa). The Person is conscious, the enjoyer, and not the agent of that action. (178)
The Self is indeed eternal and the presiding controller;
the Unmanifest, the Puruṣa, and the eternal Grandfather (Brahmā) are the cause. ||179||
In reality, there is the creation of the principles (tattva-sarga), the creation of the non-existent (abhāva-sarga), and the creation of the elements (bhūta-sarga);
by enumeration, it is reckoned as having the Pradhāna as its primary constituent, which consists of the Guṇas.
Similarity, measurement, sovereignty, primacy, and difference;
causality, brahminhood, and desirability—this is what is being described. (181)

This is stated as the dissimilarity of the Pradhāna [to Brahman]: that while the Pradhāna is subject to being employed [by another], Brahman—the Puruṣa—is everywhere the agent, whereas the Puruṣa itself is non-agency. (182)
This quality of consciousness is said to be the point of similarity with the Pradhāna; it is a distinct principle among the principles and is indeed the cause of action. (183)
The purpose [of this work] is not to be applied to the enumeration of the categories of Īśvara;
rather, it is said by the wise who deliberate upon the meaning that "the number exists" after having reached a definitive conclusion. (184)
Having heard the equipment for reality according to the enumeration and nature of reality, as well as that which exceeds the principle of Brahman, the wise have understood it. (185)

This devotion, which was established by the followers of Sāṅkhya and adopted by the virtuous as spiritual, has been described; now hear of the devotion born of yoga that belongs to the devotees of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Constantly devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), possessed of meditation, with senses restrained, subsisting on alms, or even observing vows, he has withdrawn all his senses. ||187||

Meditating upon the Lord of Creatures, one should perform the mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) in the heart, [visualizing Him] seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, red-hued and with beautiful eyes. (188)
His face is brilliantly illuminated, with the sacred thread reaching down to his waist;
he has four faces and four arms, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. ||189||
The perfection of the mental faculty born of yoga is remembered as the supreme devotion to Brahman;
he who possesses such devotion toward the Divine is called a devotee of Brahman. (190)

And, O Indra among kings, hear the livelihood ordained for those who dwell in the sacred field (kṣetra), as it was personally declared by the Lord in the assembly of Viṣṇu and the other brahmins. ||191||
All of this was previously explained in detail in the presence of everyone;
they were free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, unattached, and without possessions.
They were devoid of affection for their circle of kinsmen, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
they granted fearlessness to all beings through various constant virtuous deeds. (193)
Constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and intent upon supreme meditation, they are perpetual performers of sacrifice, pure, and dedicated to the dharma of ascetics. ||194||
And those Brahmins dwelling in the sacred field who know the methods of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, who are experts in Dharma, and whose doubts have been dispelled, worship according to this rite. (195)
Listen to the fruit of their merit when they die in the Pauṣkara forest:
they attain the imperishable union with Brahman, which is so difficult to reach. (196)
Having attained which they do not undergo birth again, which brings death, but having abandoned returning to this world, they remain established in the knowledge of Brahman. ||197||
For others who dwell in the stages of worldly expansion (*prapañca-āśrama*), there is a return [to rebirth];
they always remain devoted to the six duties by relying upon the rules of the householder stage (*gārhasthya-vidhi*). (198)
One who is properly consecrated by the sacrificial rite through mantras obtains superior fruit, being freed from all suffering. (199)
And his movement throughout all worlds is not obstructed;
mounted upon his own [vehicle] together with his retinue, he possesses divine power and sovereignty. (200)
Surrounded by thousands of women, he went to his own abode in a radiant celestial chariot that shone like the rising sun.
He wanders through all the worlds at will, unimpeded;
he is most desirable to men, possessing the wealth of the supreme of all dharmas. (202)
Falling from heaven, he shall be born into a great family, endowed with beauty, a knower of dharma, devoted to dharma, and one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge. ||203||
In the same way, engaged in celibacy and service to the guru, devoted to the study of the Vedas, subsisting on alms, and having his senses subdued; 204.
Constantly engaged in the vow of truth, he is vigilant in his own duties;
he is fulfilled by the attainment of all desires, yet remains independent of all desires. (205)
Like the sun with its second [disc], he was unobstructed by his celestial chariot;
among the Guhyakas, the group known as the Abrahmas is considered the most excellent.
Worshipped by gods and dānavas, they possess immeasurable power and sovereignty;
he is endowed with a sovereignty equal to theirs, being identical to them in sameness. (207)
Among gods, dānavas, and mortals, he possesses weapons that appear unpredictably for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of years.
Thus endowed with sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
having dwelt there in such splendor, when he eventually falls from that state again— ||209||
From the world of Viṣṇu, by virtue of his own deeds, he is born in the abodes of heaven. ||210||
Having reached the Puṣkara forest and established himself in the stage of celibacy (brahmacarya),
he dwells there through the study of the Vedas, or even dies there.
He has died and departed by means of a most divine celestial chariot through his own splendor, as pleasing to behold as the moon, with the radiance of the full moon. ||212||
Having reached the world of Rudra, he rejoices together with the Guhyakas;
he attains great sovereignty and becomes the lord of the entire universe. ||213||
Having enjoyed [the fruits of his merit] for thousands of yugas, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
then, having descended from that world of Rudra, he proceeds by gradual stages.
Having always rejoiced there and enjoyed happiness free from affliction, he is born into a great and divine family among the twice-born. ||215||
Among humans, he will be a virtuous soul, a lord of speech with a beautiful form;
possessing a body desired by women, he will be powerful and a master of great enjoyments.
One who follows the conduct of a forest-dweller and avoids cultivated herbs finds that his movement is unimpeded throughout all worlds.
Subsisting on withered leaves and fruits, eating flowers and roots, he lived as a pigeon-ascetic, a stone-grinder, and one who uses a wooden mortar for his food.
He should live by the means of subsistence appropriate for his stage, clothed in garments of bark and rags;
wearing matted hair, bathing three times a day, having abandoned all faults, and carrying a staff.

Whether he be one devoted to the *kṛcchra* vow, or even another such as a *śvapaca*, or one who sleeps in water, performs the five fires penance, or plunges into the clouds during the rainy season; ||220||
He sleeps on the ground covered with insects, thorns, and stones; he delights in the postures of standing and the heroic pose (vīrāsana); he is equanimous and firm in his vows.
He is a consumer of forest herbs, a bestower of fearlessness upon all beings, constantly devoted to the acquisition of dharma, with anger conquered and the senses subdued. ||222||
A devotee of Brahmā, a resident of the sacred field, that sage dwells at Puṣkara;
having renounced all attachments, he is self-restrained and free from desire.
O Bhīṣma, hear also the destiny of him who dwells here,
[illuminated] by a sacrificial altar shining with the brilliance of the rising sun.
A devotee of Brahmā, traveling in a celestial chariot that moves at will,
shone in the sky like a second moon.
Accompanied by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases skilled in song, instrumental music, and dance,
he remained joined with those celestial nymphs for hundreds of millions of years.
By the very grace of Brahmā, he goes unimpeded to the world of whichever deity it may be, and shines resplendent in each of those places.
Having descended from the world of Brahmā, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
having fallen from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Therefore, even after passing away from that state, he is born among the continents, as well as in the heavens and other realms, having enjoyed desired pleasures. (229)
Having enjoyed sovereignty among them, he is then born again among mortals;
he is born as a king, or a prince, or one who is wealthy and happy. (230)
Handsome, fortunate, desirable, and possessed of fame, he is permeated by devotion—whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even a forest-dweller. (231)

O King, those who delight in their own duty, who are well-conducted and long-lived, who are devoted to Brahman with their whole being, and who act for the benefit of all living beings—[they shall dwell there]. (232)
Those seekers of liberation who dwell in the great field of Puṣkaretu go, upon death, to the abode of Brahmā by means of splendid celestial chariots. ||233||

Or else, he who offers his own body as an oblation into a fire that is blazing on all sides, [travels] by means of vehicles that move at will, assume any form at will, and resound with the songs of hosts of Apsarases. ||234||
The great being who meditates on Brahmā shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
his world of Brahmā is inexhaustible and eternal, along with its splendors. (235)
It becomes most delightful to all the world and an achiever of desired goals for those who give up their lives in the waters at the highly meritorious Puṣkara. 236.
For those high-souled ones as well, the world of Brahmā is imperishable;
they behold the God himself, the destroyer of all suffering.
The gods, accompanied by all the immortals and joined by the hosts of Rudra and Viṣṇu,
[honored] the Śūdras who had died through fasting at Puṣkara and Tuvana.
Then they depart in celestial chariots yoked with swans, possessing the brilliance of the sun,
enriched with various jewels and gold, sturdy, and perfumed with fragrances.
With other incomparable qualities, resounding with the songs of celestial nymphs, and made to ring with various bells fixed upon banners and flags; ||240||
And there were many [elephants] endowed with great speed, skilled in the arts of play, radiant, possessed of excellent qualities, and carrying the finest peacocks. ||241||
O undaunted ones, we delighted in the world of Brahmā; having died there, we dwelt for a long time and enjoyed pleasures according to our desires. (242)
A man who, having come to the state of a mortal, performs the *puṣkara* rite with a forest of *kārīṣī* grass, is born as one who enjoys wealth and is free from obstacles. (243)
Having abandoned all worlds, he goes to the world of Brahmā;
he shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for as long as the dissolution of the kalpa occurs. ||244||
Indeed, one does not see a mortal being tormented by his own karmas;
for his movement is unimpeded—sideways, upwards, and likewise downwards. (245)
Worthy of worship in all worlds, spreading his fame, self-controlled, skilled in the rules of right conduct, and captivating to all the senses; ||246||
Skilled in dance, instrumental music, and song, he was fortunate and pleasing to behold; his flowers were never withered, and he was adorned with divine ornaments. ||247||
Dark as the petals of a blue lotus, with hair gathered in a dark topknot;
they were not of low birth, possessed slender waists, and were filled with every form of beauty.
Endowed with all sovereign qualities and exceedingly proud of their youth,
the women dwelling there serve [the men] and delight them upon couches.
Awakened by the sounds of lutes and flutes, he enjoys the bliss of a great festival, which is difficult for those of undisciplined mind to attain. (250)
"By the grace of Brahmā, the God of gods, the performer of auspicious deeds.
Bhīṣma said:
"Conduct is the supreme dharma, devoted to the duties pertaining to the sacred field (kṣetra). (251)
For those who are devoted to the practice of their own dharma, who have conquered anger and subdued their senses, it is not surprising in my view that they go to the world of Brahmā. (252)
Without doubt, O twice-born ones, people go to other worlds even without the fast of Padma and likewise without [other] religious observances.
Women, barbarians, Śūdras, birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, the mute, the dull-witted, the blind, and the deaf—those who are devoid of austerity and self-restraint [are all equal]. (254)
Remaining at the edge of the Brahman-lotus, they spoke their discourse.
Pulastya said: "Women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, beasts, birds, and wild animals [were there]. (255)
They go to the world of Brahmā, having passed beyond Puṣkara, Ārta, Amṛta, and Abhīṣma, with bodies of divine form and in celestial chariots of radiant splendor. (256)
[He ascended] by means of excellent golden banners endowed with divine arrays, which were adorned with stairs of gold and vajra-jewels. ||257||
Abounding in the enjoyment of all desires, traveling at will and assuming forms at will, they go forth accompanied by thousands of women and endowed with limbs rich in various flavors. (258)
Those great-souled ones go to the world of Brahmā and to other worlds as they desire;
even when they fall from the world of Brahmā, they proceed in due order to the various continents.
A virtuous twice-born man becomes wealthy in a great and extensive family;
whereas those who have entered the wombs of animals—snakes, insects, and ants—[do not]. ||260||

Those born from land and from water, those born from sweat, from eggs, from sprouts, and from the womb—whether with desire or without desire—they all reach death in the waters, in the lotuses, in the forests, and in the groves. (261)
Residing in celestial chariots of solar radiance, they proceed to the world of Brahmā;
yet in the most terrible Kali age, living beings are impelled by their sins.
By no other means than this method are dharma and heaven attained;
those men who dwell at Puṣkara are devoted to the worship of Brahmā. (263)
In the Kali age, those who have achieved their purpose suffer, while others are rendered useless;
whatever sin a man commits at night with his five senses, [it is all in vain].
Driven by their actions of mind, speech, and body, and subject to the power of desire and anger,
they approached Pitāmaha at Puṣkara in the morning when it was covered with water.
Having approached [the deity] and become pure, one is liberated from that sin;
starting from sunrise until the upward-moving vision [of the deity]. (266)
By meditating upon the Brahma-yoga known as Mānasa-prasa, one removes sin;
by beholding Viriñci at midday, a person is liberated from evil. (267)
Whatever sin one may commit with the senses from midday until sunset, one is liberated from that merely by beholding the meditation upon the Grandfather (Brahmā). ||268||
Even while enjoying all objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, according to his desire,
he who dwells at Puṣkara devoted to Brahman remains established in austerity.
One who dwells in the midst of the Puṣkara forest, eating food that tastes like sweet delicacies, yet consumes it only three times a day, is considered equal to one who subsists on air alone. ||270||
Those men who have performed meritorious deeds dwell here in Puṣkara; by the power of this sacred field, they enjoy great pleasures for as long as the world lasts. ||271||
Just as there is no other body of water equal to the great ocean, so too there exists no sacred ford equal to Puṣkara. 272.
There is no sacred ford superior in virtues to the Puṣkara forest;
now I shall describe others that are situated within this field.
All the celestial dwellers, headed by Indra, together with Viṣṇu;
Gajavaktra, Kumāra, Revanta, and the Sun-god. ||274||
Likewise, the goddess Śivadūtī is always a bringer of well-being to those who perform worship through penance, observances, and virtuous deeds. (275)
Having performed even great acts of vows and fasting, he remains without effort in the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara forest. (276)
The twice-born who always remains right here attains the fulfillment of all desires;
he goes to that supreme, imperishable station which is equal to that of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
O Bhīṣma, that which is accomplished in twelve years during the Kṛta age is achieved in one year during the Tretā, in one month during the Dvāpara, and in a single day and night during the Kali age.
"The fruit is obtained in this world by those who dwell at the holy ford (tīrtha) of Kṣetrasimha," thus was it previously declared by the God of gods to me, O Brahmā. (279)
There is no sacred field on this earth superior to this;
therefore, one should take refuge in this forest with every effort. (280)
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
all who act according to their prescribed rules attain the supreme goal.
He who, free from desire and aversion, duly observes the dharma of any one of the stages of life (āśrama), is exalted in the next world. (282)
This ladder, established by Brahmā at the crossroads, leads upward;
by relying upon this ladder, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||283||

One who is free from malice and skilled in the knowledge of dharma and artha should live as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) for at least one-fourth of his life with a teacher or the teacher’s son.
One who desires prosperity should study under a teacher beyond [the requirements of] ritual duties;
having been invited, he should provide the sacrificial fees and take refuge with the teacher. (285)
In the teacher’s residence, he should be the first to go to bed and the last to rise;
furthermore, he must perform whatever duties are to be carried out by a disciple, such as personal service and so forth. (286)
Having performed all this, he should stand at the side, saying "It is done," acting as a servant, performing all tasks, and being skilled in every kind of work. ||287||
Pure, skillful, endowed with virtues, and having conquered his senses, he should speak the desired answer; then, with an undistracted mind, he should look upon the teacher with his eyes.
One should not eat when one has not yet eaten, nor drink when one has not yet drunk; likewise, one should not sit while standing, nor enter [a place] while sleeping.
With both hands turned upward, one should touch the feet very gently;
one should press the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand.
Having paid homage to the guru, one should speak while stating one's own name, saying: "O Blessed One, I shall do this, and this too has been done by me. (291)
One should not perform any act without first informing and reporting it to the guru;
furthermore, whatever has been performed must be reported to the guru again.

Whatever fragrant substances or flavors a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) does not consume, he may consume them after completing his studies; such is the certainty regarding these rules of conduct.
Whatever rules have been stated in detail for the celibate student (brahmacārin), the devotee and disciple of the guru should observe them all. 294.
Having thus brought satisfaction to the teacher according to his ability,
the disciple should conduct himself through his actions within the non-vulgar stages of life (āśramas).

Likewise, O twice-born one, having studied the Vedas, the Vedānta, the various branches of the Vedas, and the meaning of the Vedas from the mouth of his guru—even while subsisting on alms and sleeping on the ground—he [attained perfection]. (296)
Having applied himself to the Vedic vows for a fourth part [of the time] through yoga,
and having given the sacrificial fee to the guru, he should perform the return ceremony (samāvartana) according to the prescribed rule.
Having invoked and worshipped the sacred fires with noble men endowed with righteousness, the householder should perform his duties during the second portion of his life. (298)
Formerly, four modes of livelihood for householders were established by the sages:
the first is that of one who possesses a granary of grain, and the second is that of one who possesses a jar of grain. (299)
The third is said to be "not for tomorrow" (aśvastanī), the fourth is the "pigeon-like" (kāpotī), and the fifth is the "gleaning" (uñchavṛtti).
Among these, each subsequent one is superior to the preceding in terms of dharma and is the most excellent for conquering the world.
One [brahmin] performs the six duties; another proceeds with three;
the fourth indeed proceeds with two; such is the twice-born one established in the state of Brahma.
They declare that there is no greater sacred ford than the vow of a householder:
one should not cook food for oneself alone, nor should one slaughter an animal in vain.
One should perform sacrifice with conditioned phenomena that are either animate or inanimate;
one should never sleep during the first or the last watch of the night. (303)
One should not speak a falsehood here even at the cost of one's life;
nor should any Brahmin dwell in a house without being honored, even if he does not eat. (304)
Likewise, those who carry out the offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) are remembered as his guests;
they are those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas, and who have mastered the Vedas. (305)
Those ascetics who live by their own prescribed duties and possess ritual action—
for them, the *havya* (offering to the gods) and *kavya* (offering to the ancestors) are ordained for the purpose of honoring them.

For one who has associated with those destined for destruction, who has fallen away from his own duty, who has abandoned the sacred fire-offering, who is a teacher acting falsely, or [for such a person], [there is no merit]. ||307||
For one who lacks adherence to the unreal, there is no qualification for the two types of action;
rather, it remains that all beings are distinguished according to their respective lineages. (308)
In the same way, the householder should give to those who cook for themselves;
thus he shall always be one who eats the remnants (vighasa) and always one who eats the nectar (amṛta). ||309||

The remnant of the sacrifice is nectar; its consumption is equal to the eating of sacrificial oblation (havis). One who eats what remains after others have eaten is called a "consumer of vighasa. (310)

Devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, highly skillful, and having thoroughly conquered his senses, he [should associate] with the officiating priests, the family priest, the teacher, maternal uncles, and guests. (311)
By the elderly, children, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and friends;
by mother, father, son-in-law, brother, son, and wife. (312)
One should not engage in disputes with one's daughters or the group of slaves;
by avoiding these disputes, one is liberated from all sins. ||313||
When these are conquered, one conquers all the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā, and the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati.
The guest is the lord of all the worlds, the officiating priest, and the refuge of the Vedas; he is the master.
The son-in-law is the lord of the world of the Apsarases, and the paternal kinsmen are the lords of the Vaiśvadeva deities. (315)
Relatives, kinsmen, and others are on the earth; the mother and maternal uncle are in the atmosphere; and the elderly, children, and the sick are the powerful ones in the sky. (316)
The priest was the lord of the world of Ṛṣis; the Sādhyas and the world-protectors were his dependents.
The physician was the lord of the world of the Aśvins, and his brother was the lord of the world of the Vasus. ||317||
He was the son of the wife of Candralokeśvara, born in the home of an apsaras;
his eldest brother was equal to his father, and his wife, son, and his own body were all one with him. (318)
Scribes, servants, and daughters are the ultimate objects of pity;
therefore, one should always endure being insulted by these without feverish agitation.

A wise man who delights in the duties of a householder, who is steadfast in dharma and has overcome fatigue, should not undertake many tasks; rather, he should undertake some task that is consistent with dharma.
There are three modes of life for householders; among them, the highest leads to ultimate liberation. Likewise, they speak of the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) as being mutually [complementary].

All those restraints (yamas) which have been mentioned must be practiced by one who desires to prosper, whether they live with stored grain sufficient for a year, or follow the unchha, śila, or kāpotī modes of livelihood.
In that kingdom where the king acts thus, the realm prospers;
he purifies ten generations of ancestors before him and ten generations after him.
One who practices this very way of life of a householder, free from the pain of worldly attachment,
shall attain a destination equal to that of the worlds of the Cakradharas.
Or rather, this is ordained as the destiny for those who have conquered their senses: the heavenly world for householders and stability for those of self-restraint. (225)
This is indeed the ladder struck down by Brahmā;
he from whom it is released, having gradually reached the second [step], is glorified in the heavenly world.
I shall also speak of the third; listen to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, [he should enter this stage]. (227)
One should take refuge in that very forest which is the offspring of one's offspring;
it is for those who dwell in the stage of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha), exhausted by the vows of household life. 228.
Listen, Bhīṣma—may it be well with you—to those who have taken up the vow of renunciation, who dwell in holy places, and whose souls are the refuge of all the worlds. (229)
For men endowed with the power of wisdom, possessed of truthfulness, purity,
and forbearance, the third part of their life is spent in the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
The sacrificer, self-restrained, restricted in diet, and devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, should attend upon those very fires which are the dwellers of heaven.
Then, the Agnihotra oblations and all the constituent parts of the sacrifice, as well as uncultivated rice and barley, wild grain, and the remnants of offerings— 332.
In the summer he should offer food fit for sacrifice, and likewise during the five months of the rainy season;
these three modes of subsistence are prescribed for the stage of life of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
Some are eaters of what is fresh; some store up [food] for a month;
some store up for a year; and some store up for twelve years.
For the sake of honoring guests and for the purpose of performing sacrificial rites, they take refuge in the heat during the summer months,
remaining under the open sky when there are clouds and rain during the monsoon.
In summer, scorched by the fires of the sun, they subsist on nectar in autumn; they roll about upon the ground and stand even on their tiptoes.
Some remain standing or sitting even while staying in their dwellings; some are "mortar-eaters," while others are likewise "stone-grinders. (337)
Some drank boiled barley-gruel during the bright fortnight, while others drank it during the dark fortnight; some ate according to the traditional rules. (338)
Some, firm in their vows, subsist according to the rule on roots, some on fruits, and some on water, observing the ascetic discipline of the Vaikhānasas.
These and various other initiations belong to those wise ones;
and the fourth, the dharma of the Upaniṣads, is considered common to all.
In that very age, the forest-dweller and the householder constantly engage in other [duties] as well,
according to the Brahmins who perceive all matters.
Agastya, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), Madhucchandas, Gaveṣaṇa, Sāṅkṛti, Sadivobhāṇḍi, and Yavaprotha of the Atharvan lineage. ||342||
Ahovīrya, Tathākāmya, Sthāṇu, Medhātithi, Budha, Manovāka, Śinīvāka, Śūnyapāla, and Kṛtavraṇa. ||343||
Being wise in their actions, they attained heaven;
these were the Āyāvara clans, who perceived dharma directly before their eyes.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Gods, those sages of fierce austerity, who perceive the subtleties of Dharma, took refuge in the protection of the Brahmins.
Having cast aside their deceptive practices and taken refuge in the protection of the Brahmins,
those hosts of exiles appeared invincible, like those who have left behind the stars.
Wasted by old age and afflicted by disease,
they departed from the third stage of life and proceeded to the remaining fourth stage, that of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).

One who performs the *sadyaskāra* sacrifice, one who has offered all his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇā*), one who sacrifices for the self, one whose mind is gentle, one who sports in the Self, and one who takes refuge in the Self. (348)
Having established the fire within himself and renounced all possessions,
he should always perform sacrifices here, including the Sadyaska and the Iṣṭi.
For those who sacrifice constantly, the sacrifice proceeds within the self through the act of worship;
one should properly abandon the three fires within the self itself by means of the self in an instant. (350)
Whatever he may obtain, he should eat it without disparaging it; or, devoted to the hermitage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he should cast away his hair, body hair, and nails.

Having given a promise of fearlessness to all beings, the twice-born who goes forth into the wandering life immediately becomes purified of his karmas as he passes from one stage of life to the next. (352)
His worlds shall consist of light, and after departing this life, he enjoys immortality;
being of virtuous conduct and cleansed of all taint, he does not strive for rebirth either here or in the hereafter.

If one who has abandoned the mental conflict arising from anger and delusion remains like a neutral observer through self-reflection, and does not suffer when others act toward him, then his mental confusion is empty of its own treatises.

For one who is devoted to dharma, has conquered the senses, and performs the sacrifice of the self, there will be movement at will; of this there is no doubt. Beyond this, there is that which is presided over by supreme and most excellent virtues, transcending the three stages of life.
Listen now to the description of the fourth and final stage of life, the supreme refuge;
having received the purificatory rites from these two preceding stages, one proceeds beyond them.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to that task for the sake of the Supreme Self:
having donned the saffron robe, [one should act] within the three stages of the spiritual hierarchy. (357)

Now listen likewise to how one who would go to that supreme state, the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant, should conduct himself after having performed the renunciation through that contemplation.
One should practice the Dharma alone, without companions, for the sake of accomplishment; and one who finds delight in solitude, seeing thus, neither abandons nor is abandoned. (359)
Without fire and without a dwelling, he should enter a village for the sake of alms;
the sage, endowed with pure being, should not provide for the morrow.

Having seen the Puṣkara holy site shining equally on all sides,

The high-souled Vālakhilyas, others who grind with stones, some who use their teeth as mortars, and others who wash [their food]—[all these were there]. 102.

Having seen her beautiful face reflected in this lake, they were momentarily struck with wonder; then, wondering "What is this?", they looked at one another.
By the sight of his face at the holy ford, the sword attained a beautiful form;
thus the ascetics gave it the name "Mukhadarśana" (Face-Bearer).
Having bathed, they then became endowed with beautiful forms and joined by the Yama [twins];
they were born resembling sons of gods, possessed of incomparable qualities.
All those forest-dwellers stood there, shining, O best of men;

They performed the agnihotra sacrifices and engaged in various religious rites,
contemplating [the goal], O Indra among kings, their sins having been burnt away by asceticism.
"There is no other sacred ford superior to this; because of its status as the eldest, the twice-born gave this lake the name Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara. (109)
There, seeing many hunchbacks standing near the holy ford,
the people who had gathered there were filled with wonder.
Having given various vessels to the twice-born, and having heard that the Sarasvatī flows eastward, the twice-born arrived, desiring to bathe. 111.
It was joined by hosts of twice-born men from various excellent tirthas on the Sarasvati,
and was filled with jujube, inguda, kāśmarya, plakṣa, aśvattha, and vibhītaka trees.
With *pauloma* trees, *palāśa*, *karīra*, and *pīlu*, as well as with *dhanvana* and *syaṃdana* trees growing at the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) along the Sarasvatī; 113.
It was adorned with *kapittha*, *karavīra*, *bilva*, and *amlātaka* trees,
as well as groves of *atimuktaka* and *pārijāta* trees.
Then, in a place abounding in groves, delightful to all living beings,
he lived with those who subsisted on wind, water, fruits, and leaves, and even those who used their teeth as mortars.
Likewise, it was surrounded by the most eminent sages, headed by Aśmakuṭṭa;
it resounded with the chanting of Vedic study and was filled with hundreds of herds of deer.
It was exceedingly beautified by those devoted to dharma who lived there;
it was known as Suprabhā and Kāñcanā, and it was the ancient, vast city of Dvārakā.
There, upon the surface of the earth while the assembly of the Grandfather was taking place, the river Puṣkara flowed through five channels.
In the spacious sacrificial enclosure, when the twice-born and others had arrived,
there were widespread proclamations of "Auspicious Day" as well as the observances of the gods.
While the gods were thus preoccupied with that performance of the sacrifice, and while the Grandfather, O great king, was initiated therein; 120.
While he was performing that sacrificial session (sattra) which fulfills all desires,
those skilled in dharma and worldly affairs likewise attained whatever objects they had conceived in their minds.
There, in various places, they waited upon the king of kings and the twice-born;
the divine gandharvas sang and the throngs of apsarases danced.
They played divine musical instruments with vigor; even the gods were satisfied by the perfection of that sacrifice.
They were struck with supreme wonder; how much more so those of non-human origin, while the Grandfather was thus engaged in the sacrifice at Puṣkara?
O King of kings, the Ṛṣis, being highly pleased, spoke to Sarasvatī, who was named Suprabhā and also known by the name Sarasvatī. (125)
Seeing Sarasvatī flowing with great force and illuminating the Grandfather (Brahmā), all those sages held that sacrifice in high esteem.
Thus this Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, appeared among the Puṣkaras for the sake of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and for the satisfaction of the wise. 127.
The Sarasvatī with five streams makes merit meritorious;
she is named Suprabhā, O King of Kings, and also by the name Sarasvatī. (128)
Where those peaceful sages were engaged in various recitations of their sacred texts, the seers, having arrived there, remembered Sarasvatī.
That great river, beloved by her devotees, was established in the eastern direction by the highly fortunate ṛṣis who were performers of sacrificial sessions (sattra). 130.
O Great King, listen to this other most excellent account on earth concerning Prācī, Pūrvā, Avahā, Amunī, Vaṃdyā, and Sarasvatī. (131)
O King, we have heard that when the Brahmin Maṅkaṇaka was wounded by the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, vegetable juice flowed from his wound instead of blood. (132)
Seeing the entire universe filled with the essence of Śākara, he was overcome with joy and began to dance;
then, as he danced, everything that is stationary and everything that moves also danced.
The entire world, deluded by his splendor, began to dance, along with Śakra and the other gods, and the sages whose wealth is their asceticism. (134)
O King, having been thus informed there, Vaibhrāja said, "Let him dance; do so. He was commanded by Brahmā for the sake of the sage Rudra.
"You should tell him the truth as it is desired so that he will not dance;
go and see the sage Rudra, who is utterly overcome with joy. (136)
"O bull among Brahmins! For what reason do you dance?
Because of your dancing, the entire world is dancing as well. (137)
Restrained by him, that best of sages, while dancing, spoke:
The sage said:
"O King, do you not see that vegetable juice is flowing from my hand? (138)
Seeing him, I began to dance, overwhelmed by great joy;
the Lord, smiling, spoke to that sage who was deluded by passion. (139)
"I do not feel any astonishment while beholding this here.
Thus was the best of sages addressed by Mahādeva, O Kaurava.
While he was thus meditating, O Indra among kings, he was forbidden by that very person who had likewise struck his own thumb with the tip of his finger. 141.
Then, O King, something white as snow emerged from the wound in the ashes;
seeing that, he was filled with shame and fell at his feet, saying: (142)
I consider no other being greater or more supreme than the god Rudra;
O wielder of the trident, you are the refuge of the entire world, both moving and unmoving. 143.
The wise declare that all this was created by you;
at the end of the eon, everything enters back into you alone.
Even by the gods you cannot be fully known; how then could it be by me?
For within you are seen all the deities, even Brahmā and the others.
O Lord, you alone are the creator and the cause of all the gods;
by your grace, all the deities have become free from fear here in this world.
Having thus praised the Great God, the Ṛṣi bowed down and said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, my ascetic merit shall not diminish here. (147)
Then the God, with a pleased mind, spoke again to that sage: "O Brahmin, may your ascetic power increase a thousandfold through my grace."
"I shall indeed always dwell here with you, O Prācī, especially in this most meritorious field of Sarasvatī. (149)
O Natasya, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain for one who casts off their own body here on this bank of the Sarasvatī, north of the river, both in this world and in the next. 150.
One who bathes here at Prācī-taṭeja shall not die again, and having immersed oneself, one will obtain the abundant fruit of a horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). ||151||
By means of observances and fasts, the ascetic emaciated his own body, subsisting on water, feeding on air, and eating leaves. 152.
Likewise, that best of the twice-born who observes separate rules such as sleeping on the bare ground and other various restraints, as well as those vows—[he attains the fruit]. (153)
And one whose body has become exceedingly pure attains the supreme station of Brahman;
for those who give even a mere atom of gold at that sacred ford (tīrtha), [they shall attain that same state]. ||154||
Prajāpati declared of old that this shall be equal to the gift of Mount Meru;
those men who shall perform a śrāddha at that holy ford (tīrtha). (155)

Endowed with twenty-one generations of their lineage, those men shall go to heaven; and by being gratified with a single funeral cake (piṇḍa) at this auspicious tīrtha of the ancestors, they shall attain that goal. 156.
Having been brought here by their own son, they will go to the world of Brahmā;
moreover, they no longer desire food and proceed upon the path to liberation.
Listen now to the true nature of Sarasvatī’s antiquity:
in ancient times, Sarasvatī was proclaimed by all the gods, including Indra. (158)
"You must proceed to the shore of the salt ocean in the western direction;
having led this submarine fire there, cast it into the sea. (159)
When this is done, all the gods will become free from fear;
otherwise, the submarine fire will consume them with its own brilliance.
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, protect these gods from this imminent danger;
be like a mother, granting fearlessness to the deities. 161.
When she had been addressed thus by the all-powerful Viṣṇu, the goddess Aditi said: "I am not my own mistress; let my father alone be chosen as the sovereign."
"Ever obedient to his commands, I, Kumārī, have maintained my vow;
without my father's instruction, I do not speak even a single word anywhere. (163)
"I shall go; therefore, oh, let some other means be devised.
Having understood his intention, they then gathered together and spoke to the Grandfather (Brahmā). 164.
O Grandfather, it is impossible for anyone else to lead away the submarine fire (Vaḍavāgni), except for your daughter Kumārī, who has never seen the face of a man. 165.
Having brought Sarasvatī near and placed that woman of excellent complexion upon his lap, he smelled her head with affection and then spoke to Sarasvatī.
And the gods said to me, "O Goddess, speak to that illustrious being:
'Having taken him, cast him into the salt ocean. (167)
Having heard her father’s words, which were for her welfare, the maiden wept with a distressed mind, like a female osprey separated from her mate. 168.
Her face, with eyes clouded by tears of grief,
shone like a white, blossoming lotus sprinkled with water-drops.
Beholding him in such a state, all the gods, led by Brahmā, fell completely under the sway of grief. ||170||
Then, steadying her heart which was tormented by grief, the Grandfather said to her: "Do not weep; there is no fear for you."
And through your power alone, there shall be honor and gain;
O son, take this fire and cast it into the midst of the salt-water ocean.
Having been addressed thus, that young girl, her eyes clouded with tears, bowed to the Lotus-born One and said, "I am going. 173.
"Do not fear," they said to her, and she likewise replied to her father; casting aside her fear, with a joyful heart, she stood ready to depart. (174)
At the time of her departure, the world was filled with auspicious sounds—the blare of conchs and kettledrums, and the resonant cries of other auspicious instruments. (175)
She was white, wearing a garment of fine cloth, adorned with white sandalwood paste, possessing the luster of an autumn lotus, and decorated with a necklace of pearls. 176.
With a face like the full moon and eyes as long as lotus petals, she filled the ten directions with the auspicious fame of the Lord of the Gods. 177.
By her own splendor, she caused the world to appear as it issued forth from his heart;
following him as he passed away, O dear one, that woman of excellent complexion was called the Gaṅgā.
"O friend, I shall see you again; where shall I go?
When she had spoken thus, Gaṅgā replied with sweet words.
O auspicious one, as soon as you come to the eastern direction and behold me, surrounded by the gods, I shall resort to invisibility. 180.
Then, facing north, O lady of pure smiles, abandon your grief;
for I am facing north due to my merit, while you, O Sarasvatī, are facing east. (181)
There, O observer of noble vows, the merit of a hundred sacrifices is gained through bathing and giving;
likewise, whatever is given to the ancestors through the performance of *śrāddha* becomes eternally inexhaustible.
Those humans who will act for the sake of liberated beings, having freed themselves from the three debts, shall proceed upon the path to liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (183)
Then Gaṅgā said to her: "May there be a future meeting with you; go now to your own abode, O blessed one, and I, O sinless one, am to be remembered by you. (184)
Yamunā likewise, as did the beautiful Gāyatrī;
all of them, together with Sāvitrī, sent their friend forth in that manner.
Then, having released those gods, Sarasvatī became a river;
that spirited lady manifested herself at the hermitage of Uttaṅka.
Then, while the gods were looking on, those two highly fortunate ones descended from the Plakṣa tree, casting down their bodies. (187)
That tree, which is the very form of Viṣṇu, is praised by all the gods;
it should be constantly served by the twice-born for the sake of fruit, as it brings about great prosperity. (188)
And it was spread with many branches like another four-faced Brahmā; for the twice-born who had entered the crevices of its hollows as their dwellings— (189)
Various words were heard from the gods whose hearts were filled with passion; even the lord of the forest, though not yet in bloom, appeared as if it were flowering.
That best of rivers was adorned with *jāti* flowers as ripe as fruit, with auspicious parrots perched upon the branches, and with fragrant *ketakī* blossoms. (191)
She appeared as if in bloom with the foam of her ornaments and the sounds of cuckoos,
just as the Gaṅgā is graced by Śiva and the earth by the Plakṣa tree.
Then, standing there upon the goat-skin, he spoke thus to Janārdana:
"Hand over that fire; I shall carry out the command of the gods."
When this was said, Viṣṇu then replied to Sāta:
"Do not fear the burning; you must not abandon this king of fire yourself."
O auspicious one, to lead the submarine fire to the western ocean, you must proceed in this manner;
then, O auspicious one, you will attain that goal.
Then Govinda, having placed that submarine fire within a vessel of gold,
deposited it into the vast belly of the Sarasvatī.
Taking Sātaṅga with her, that lady of beautiful hips went facing westward;
that great river reached Puṣkara by means of disappearance.
On that boundary mountain, the stainless river was born; there is also the vast Puṣkara forest, frequented by gods and siddhas. 198.
This great river has come here for the sake of the success of the foremost sages, at the place where the Grandsire performed a sacrificial session.
All those sacrificial pits in which oblations had been offered by Viriñci were flooded with water that rose up along with the serpents.
In that field, the great merit arose from Puṣkara;
therefore, its filling by Vāyu, who possesses the life-force of the world, has been proclaimed. (201)
Having reached that meritorious field, the auspicious great river Sarasvatī, the goddess who destroys the sins of mortals, remained there. (202)
In that regard, those who have performed virtuous deeds behold the Sarasvatī situated on Puṣkara; by that, they do not see that most terrible state of downfall.
Furthermore, that man who performs his bath there with devotion reaches the world of Brahmā and rejoices together with Brahmā. (204)
But he who gives delightful curd to a Brāhmaṇa there, having reached the world of Agni, enjoys most splendid pleasures. ||205||
If a woman should devoutly give an excellent upper garment to a twice-born man,
she too shall obtain ten times the fruit of the gift of fine cloth.
The man of pure intellect who, having bathed in the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa, offers libations to his ancestors,
delivers them all from even hell.
"Having reached the holy Sarasvatī in the pure ancestral field, what else would a man pray for? Thus spoke the son of Brahmā. (208)
Therefore, whatever fruit a person obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords (tīrthas), a mortal may obtain all of that by bathing even once in the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa. ||209||
What is the use of saying more here? This field, this sacred ford, and the auspicious state—by whomsoever these three are attained, by him the supreme goal is reached. (210)
He who, having bathed at the proper time, in the proper place, and at a sacred ford, and having offered oblations there, bestows wealth upon a brahmin, enjoys infinite happiness. (211)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, and in Vaiśākha, O Moon-adorned One,
as well as during an eclipse of the moon or sun at Kurujāṅgala.
Among all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in these fields that have been described by the lords of sages,
the Grandfather (Brahmā) has declared this one to be the most meritorious.
O twice-born one, that man who bathes in the middle of the Kuṇḍeta on the full moon day of Kārttika and bestows wealth there shall obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Likewise, having bathed with meditative concentration in a sacrificial pit of this smallest size, whoever offers even a well-formed Śālikā bird to a Brahmin, [attains the same merit]. (215)
A person who performs this journey quickly reaches the delightful world of Agni;
accompanied by twenty-one generations of their lineage, they enjoy great fruit there. (216)
Therefore, with every effort, a person must cultivate a firm and auspicious resolve not to go [to lower realms], in order to attain the state of Puṣkara. (217)
Having reached the Puṣkara forest where the Sarasvatī flows toward the east, there dwell Mati, Smṛti, Śubhā, Prajñā, Medhā, Buddhi, and Dayāparā. (218)
These six synonyms of Sarasvatī have been proclaimed;
from that time onwards, she became the Prācī (Eastern) Sarasvatī wherever she was.
Those who, standing on the bank, behold that water situated there, they too obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. (220)
Furthermore, whatever man should perform a bath there, endowed with meditative concentration, he shall indeed become a follower of Brahmā. ||221||
For even if a person worships the ancestors there with vegetables and the like, he too attains vast enjoyments through the very power of those [ancestors]. (222)
Furthermore, those men who perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) there according to the prescribed rule cause their ancestors to go to heaven, even from a hell that bestows suffering. (223)
The ancestors are satisfied by him who, having bathed there, offers them pure water mixed with kuśa grass and sesame seeds. (224)
Of all sacred fords (tīrthas), this alone is remembered as the most preeminent; therefore, it is renowned throughout the world as the primordial sacred ford among all sacred fords. ||225||
The playfulness of the intellect regarding both phenomena and liberation remains established;
moreover, when united with Sarasvatī, it becomes even more endowed with excellence. 226.
That man, who bestows all four—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—entered the water for the sake of destroying the impurities of those [who sought them]. 227.
The fruit of these [acts] shall be equal to the gift of a cow, attained through happiness alone;
likewise, the wise have said it is equal to the gift of gold.
Through the offering of libations and the giving of funeral cakes, even those ancestors residing in the hells go to heaven, having been delivered there by their son.
Those people who drink the water at Puṣkara and at the Sarasvatī obtain imperishable worlds, praised by Brahmā and Viśveśa.
The Sarasvatī at Puṣkara has become a ladder to heaven;
that great river can be reached by men who possess merit. 231.
She is practiced here and there by the sages who know the true nature of reality;
therefore, this Goddess is pure everywhere and is present in all places. 232.
This river Sarasvatī is more purified than even the Puṣkara tīrtha; she is meritorious, easily accessible, and established for the stability of the world.
It is difficult to find at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, or Puṣkara;
that sacred site is ordained as the most excellent among all sacred sites on earth. (234)
Having reached the Eastern Sarasvatī, which accomplishes all four goals—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—who would seek any other sacred ford? (235)
Having utterly abandoned the nectar situated in the mouth, one desires poison;
the *jyeṣṭhā* [vowels] are known to reside in the *jyeṣṭha* [mouth], and the *madhyamā* [consonants] are remembered as being in the middle. (236)
Then, the wise and younger [disciple] should proceed in circumambulation;
he should bathe at all three of these and also perform circumambulation.
He who offers water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors, they, being satisfied, in turn bestow upon him immeasurable fruit. (238)
He who, having bathed and being constantly pure, should then behold the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) through both direct and reverse orders, as well as in their separate and combined forms.
One who desires the world of Brahmā should bathe daily at Puṣkara;
it has three white peaks and three springs.
The Puṣkara lakes are well known, yet we do not know the reason for that;
[namely,] the smallest, the middle, and the third, the greatest Puṣkara. (241)
A man who possesses auspicious springs known as Śṛṅgaśadba, yet remains fruitless regarding his intentions for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; ||242||
Whoever there renounces the body attains liberation without a doubt;
being self-restrained and disciplined, having bathed in that [river], one should give auspicious food to the twice-born.
By giving even a single cow purified by mantras, one attains the worlds that grant liberation;
what need is there for much speaking here, for one should give even at night to a seeker?
Having bathed there, one who bestows wealth enjoys infinite happiness;
the best of sages praise the gift of sesame seeds at that place. (245)
A bath is always prescribed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
whoever offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) here with oil-cake or even with molasses [attains merit].
Having become purified, he goes to the world of the ancestors;
then, having reached the Puṣkara forest, from there the Sarasvatī flows again.
Then, facing westward, she began to disappear;
not far from that beautiful lotus pond, she vanished.
Having reached a date-palm grove adorned with fruits and flowers,
and having stayed there, the goddess then went to the forest of the sages, which was delightful to the mind.
Strewed with flowers of every season and frequented by siddhas and cāraṇas, there is the Nandā, the best of rivers, renowned throughout the three worlds. (250)
"Filled with pure water and abounding with fish, crocodiles, and large fish," Sūta said: "Then Devavrata asked: 'What other river is superior to this? (251)
O Brahman, this is my sole curiosity: why and by what cause was Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, transformed into a female fish? 252.
When this had been said, Pulastya began to relate this ancient account to Bhīṣma, as it was traditionally remembered from the beginning of time.
The king, who was always a bearer of the kṣatriya vow, became lusterless before the people;
that one of great strength then set out in this forest to hunt deer.
Then he saw a doe standing at the edge of a thicket;
with an exceedingly sharp arrow, he pierced her as she stood before him.
Having surveyed all directions and seen him with arrow in hand, she said:
"O fool, what is this difficult deed that has been done by you? (256)
"First, let me give my breast to my son while standing with my face turned downward;
for I, though fearless toward all, have been pierced by him with speed through his greed. (257)
"O King, I have previously heard that one should not kill such a deer as this—one that drinks while protecting its young and engages in mating in secret. (258)
While I was offering my breast to this infant, I was struck by you with an arrow like a thunderbolt, though I had come to the forest innocent of any fault. (259)
Therefore, O evil-minded one, you too shall attain the state of a flesh-eater;
in this forest strewn with thorns, you shall assume the form of a tiger. (260)
Having heard this pronouncement of the curse, the king stood before her with his hands joined in salutation and,
his senses distressed, spoke to that doe.
"O auspicious one, while I was here giving my breast to my son, I was struck down by ignorance;
be gracious through your excellent meditative concentration. (262)
"O deer, when shall I cast off this tiger-form and regain my human state?
O deer, tell me of the auspicious means for liberation from such a curse."
When this had been said, the cow addressed these auspicious words to him:
"O King, a hundred years have passed since I arrived here under the influence of that curse. (264)
Having encountered that conversation which was both compassionate and forceful, the king reached his end; for when the doe had spoken thus, he then became like a tiger.
Equipped with claws and fangs as weapons, he was a tiger-form, exceedingly terrifying;
there he remained devouring four-footed beasts after having slain them.
Even the bipeds situated there were struck down by him in due course;
in this manner, a hundred years passed for him in that forest.
When shall I again attain such a human state as this, while I am censuring myself and eating the flesh of deer? (268)
I shall not perform that great act which causes one to fall from one's caste—a despicable deed committed by those who, driven by greed, run about on the hunt. (269)
The sight of deer together with humans is fraught with calamity, brings fear to men, and causes me great distress. (270)
Though born into a virtuous family that was itself sinless, he has been led to sinfulness by his own evil;
he has been brought to a state of corruption—behold the reversal of time! 271.
Therefore, there is no merit for me; indeed, she alone is to be censured. By her, suffering will be obtained, and liberation will not come to pass. ||272||
"How shall my liberation come to be? How shall the deer-maiden become real?"—thus he thought while dwelling in that forest for a hundred years at that time.
For the sake of fodder, water, and shelter for the herds of cattle afflicted by disease, that cow-pen enclosure was established there. (274)
This forest, filled with the sound of this place near the edge of the woods, is crowded with intoxicated cowherds; even its trees seem drunk.
Accompanied by the sound of flutes and auspicious for the cowherd women,
he thus dwelt in that place filled with date-palm groves.
Delighted, satisfied, and nourished, she was known by this name;
she was the foremost of the herd of cows, white in color, with a flowing udder. (277)
She has a long nose, well-proportioned limbs, graceful body parts, and thin skin; she possesses a beautiful neck like that of a blue jay and a voice as sweet as a *ghaṃṭālī* bird. 278.
Standing at the front of the entire herd, fearless and full of joy, she should graze in a hidden place alone, as she pleases. (279)
There, on the bank of a river, is another mountain named Rohita, which moves about like a grass-eater, covered by the fear of the Asuras who desire it as they wish. ||280||
It was frequented by various creatures dwelling in caves and deep fissures;
in its north-eastern quarter, it was formidable and thick with grass.

In narrow passes, treacherous places, and difficult terrains, amidst terrifying situations that cause the hair to stand on end, and in regions infested with deer, lions, and birds, frequented by many beasts of prey. (282)
In this fortress, dense with thickets of creepers and trees and resounding with the howls of hundreds of jackals,
dwells a fierce, terrifying being capable of assuming any form at will.
He, whose weapons were his terrible tusks and claws, smeared with the blood of a leopard,
was not one whose nature conformed to the truth, yet he was devoted to the welfare of the cowherd women.
With long grasses whose tips were uncut, he protected his wealth of cattle;
yet one of them, strayed from the herd, desired to eat the grass of that giver. (285)
As he was walking ahead of Tīvra, a cow with its calf appeared before him;
a leopard rushed toward it and cried out, "Stay! Stay! (tiṣṭha tiṣṭha). ||286||
"O wish-fulfilling cow, you have yourself arrived today as my ordained food," [said he],
having heard the harsh and hair-raising words of the leopard.
The cow, longing for her calf, remembers the young one who is endowed with a white form, auspicious, and possessing a luster like that of the moon, uttering words faltering with affection.
Burning with grief for her son,
she who was so affectionate toward her children wept piteously, having lost all hope of seeing her son again.
Seeing that cow crying out piteously, the leopard spoke these terrible words: "O little cow, why are you weeping? (290)
By fate you have obtained happiness, and by chance you have become my food;
yet if you were to weep and cry out to me, that life of yours might be preserved.

That which was ordained is being experienced by you in this world; the wish-fulfilling cow has come to you of its own accord, and death is ordained for you this very day—why do you grieve in vain? (292)
The leopard asked them again: "For what reason were you weeping?
Great curiosity has arisen in me; tell it to me indeed. (293)
Having heard the tiger's words, he then spoke these words to him: "O Lord who can assume any form at will, you ought to forgive me; salutations be unto you! (294)
Having approached you, there is no protector for the world;
I do not grieve for the sake of life, for death must be encountered by me. (295)
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Therefore, O Lord of Beasts, I do not grieve over that which is inevitable. (296)
"Since even by all the gods death must certainly be faced helplessly, therefore, O tiger, I alone grieve for my life. (297)
But why have I wept out of affection and sorrow? There is a burning anguish in my heart, and you ought to hear it. (298)
"O Lord of Beasts, having reached my first period of life, I have given birth;
this young boy is my beloved first-born son. (299)
My calf, who drinks milk, does not yet even smell the grass;
bound in the cowherd's fold and afflicted by hunger, he gazes at me. (300)
I grieve for him and wonder how his son will live;
overcome by maternal affection, I longed to give him my breast to suckle. (301)
Having allowed the calf to drink from her udder and having licked its head,
she entrusted it to her companions and instructed them on what was beneficial and what was harmful.
"I shall return again; you may eat as much as you desire.
Having heard these words of the lion, the lord of beasts spoke once more: (303)
What is to be done by you with a son? Do you not perceive that death exists?
All beings tremble at it, and they die upon seeing it. (304)
But you, overcome by compassion, cry out "Son!
Son!"—yet neither sons, nor asceticism, nor charity, nor mother, nor father, nor teacher [can save one]. (305)
They are unable to protect a man oppressed by Time;
how then could you go to Aṅgokula, which is crowded with the community of cowherd women? (306)
Resounding with the cries of bulls, adorned with young calves, it is the ornament of the world of the gods; there is no doubt that it is equal to heaven. (307)
It is eternally joyful, divine, and worshipped by all the gods; it is the most sacred of sacred things and the most auspicious of auspicious things. (308)
That sacred ford which is the most auspicious among all auspicious tirthas,
endowed with every excellence, is a great abode of the Lord.
That which is renowned as the unsurpassed heaven upon earth for all holy places [is attained] by the sound of the cowherd girls' singing and the lowing of the young calves. (310)
By the sound of the cows' *huṃ* cries, misfortune (*alakṣmī*) is repelled—where the calves also utter the *huṃ* cry piteously out of longing for their mothers. (311)
It was guarded by heroic cowherds who had exerted themselves in wrestling;
it resounded with singing, dancing, and conversation, and echoed with the sounds of clapping and slapping.
With calves standing here and there,
the royal cow-pen was being stirred up on all sides, like a lake with its lotuses moving about.
Having seen that pleasant abode of Śrī, crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, resembling Goloka itself—how will you return? (314)
The five elements drank your blood, O Maibhadra; the elements were not satiated. I shall satisfy them with mere words. (315)
She said to him:
"O King of Beasts, listen to me regarding this first-born calf;
having seen my friends, the young son, the cowherds, and the protectors. (316)
Having taken leave of the cowherd women and especially my mother, I shall return by means of oaths; do you believe this of me? (317)
Whatever sin there is in the killing of a Brahmin, and in the killing of one's mother or father—may I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again. (318)
Whatever sin belongs to hunters and to those barbarians who cause pain to living beings, may I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again. (319)
If those who create obstacles for the cows and strike them while they are sleeping should be tainted by that sin, may I too be so tainted if I do not return again. (320)
If I do not return again, may I be stained by the sin of him who, having once given his daughter in marriage, desires to give her to a second [man]. (321)
That man who would yoke oxen unfit for the task to a rugged path,
or who creates an obstacle while a story is being told— (322)
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again—
[the sin] of him whose friend, having arrived at his house, departs disappointed.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again.
Through these terrible transgressions, I shall return once again.
Having gained confidence, the leopard spoke these words again.
The tiger said:
"O Dhenuka, our trust has been established through these oaths. (325)
Sometimes you may think, "I have deceived this fool," yet even in this case, some will say that there is sin incurred by means of an oath. (326)
In matters concerning women, arrows, and marriages, as well as in the release of cows, and when the loss of life has occurred, you must not place your trust [in me]. (327)
In this world, there are certain nihilists, fools who consider themselves scholars;
they will cause your mind to whirl in an instant, like a wheel upon which it has mounted. (328)
Those base men, whose minds are shrouded by ignorance and who are unskilled in the scriptures, delude others with the practice of fallacious reasoning and sophistry. (329)
Displaying things that are untrue as if they were true,
these exceedingly skillful men are like those who know the art of painting, who depict depressions and elevations on a level surface.
Generally, this world considers one who has achieved their own purpose to be a benefactor; like a calf that sees the exhaustion of milk, it abandons its mother. 331.
I see one in this world who returns a favor for what has been done; for once a person has achieved their purpose, their mind turns toward something else. (332)
In the past, oaths were made by sages, gods, asuras, and humans to one another for the sake of accomplishing their goals; we pay homage to them. (333)
But he who utters a curse even with truth in the presence of the gods, the fire, or his guru—
for him King Vaivasvata cuts away half of his dharma.
"O Mother, let your mind not be thus; this is bound by oaths.
You yourself have revealed everything; now do as you wish. (335)
He said to him:
"In this very way, O great virtuous one, you are capable of deceiving yourself; for he who deceives another will surely deceive himself. (336)
The female leopard said:
"O cow, you who are so fond of your calf, go see your son;
let him drink from your udder and lick his head."
Having seen your mother, brother, friends, kinsmen, and relatives, place truth alone before you and return quickly. (338)
Having thus made this oath,
the cow, speaking the truth and affectionate toward her calf, was permitted by the king of beasts and departed.
With her face filled with tears, miserable, trembling, and deeply distressed, she let out a great cry and fell into an ocean of sorrow. (340)
Seized by the trunk of an elephant in a body of water,
she was crying out again and again, for the female elephants were unable to rescue her.
Having reached Gokula there, situated on the bank of the Harinī river,
and hearing the lowing of her calf, she ran toward it with her face turned back.
Approaching his mother, whose eyes were clouded with tears, the calf, full of apprehension, questioned her. (343)
I do not perceive any composure in you, nor do I observe any fortitude today;
your gaze appears agitated, and you seem utterly terrified. (344)
Nanda said:
"O son, drink my breast-milk if you ask for the cause of its sweetness; I am unable to explain it to you, so satisfy yourself as much as you desire. (345)
"O son, this is the final time you will behold your mother, for she is difficult to see again.
Having drunk [only] once today, what will you drink at dawn? (346)
"Having abandoned you, my son, I must go; indeed, I have come here bound by oaths. My own life must be given to this tiger who is emaciated with hunger. (347)
Having heard his words and the speech of Dāya, Vatsa spoke these words:
Vatsa said—"I shall go there, wherever you desire to go. (348)
Even for me, death along with you is praiseworthy, without a doubt;
for I must die alone, afflicted as I am without you.
O mother, if a tiger kills me in the forest while I am reciting this sacred collection, that destination which belongs to those devoted to their mothers will surely be mine. (350)
Therefore, I shall certainly go with you; of this there is no doubt.
Or rather, O father, stay here and let me swear oaths to you.
What is the purpose of life for one separated from his mother?
For me, who am constantly without a protector in the forest, who will become my protector? (352)
For children who live on milk, there is no kinsman equal to a mother;
there is no protector equal to a mother, and no refuge equal to a mother. (353)
There is no affection equal to that of a mother; there is no face equal to a mother's;
