there is nothing equal to a mother, whether in this world or in the next. (354)
Thus is the supreme dharma ordained by Prajāpati;
those sons who always abide by it attain the highest goal. (355)
He said to him:
"O son, death has been ordained for me alone; you shall not come [to this end].
Nor can this death of mine be brought about by the death of another living being. (356)
"This is my final son; this is the supreme instruction from your mother. Stay here at my word, and thereafter perform service [to him]. (357)
O father, do not be negligent while moving about on land or in water;
through negligence all beings perish, of this there is no doubt. (358)
One should never act out of greed, even for a blade of grass situated in difficult terrain;
through greed comes the destruction of all, both in this world and in the next. (359)
Deluded by greed, sons enter the ocean and the forest;
out of greed, even a learned man may commit an extremely terrible misdeed. (360)
Through greed, negligence, and betrayal—by these three, the ruin of men occurs.
Therefore, one should not be greedy, nor should one trust in negligence. (361)
One must always exert effort to protect oneself from all predatory beasts, as well as from the perils posed by barbarians, thieves, and the like. (362)
O son, having understood that the minds of those in animal births and those of evil origins are contrary [to the Dharma], even though they dwell together in one place. (363)
You should never place your trust in those with claws, in rivers, in horned creatures, in those who bear weapons, in women, or in servants. (364)
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place excessive trust even in the trustworthy;
for danger arising from misplaced trust cuts down even the very roots. (365)
One should not trust even one's own body when it is powerful yet the mind is fearful;
for they will speak excessively in secret when one is asleep, intoxicated, or through negligence.
One should constantly and diligently smell the scent everywhere; for cows see by means of scent, and kings see by means of the eye of spies. (367)
One should not remain alone in a fearsome forest; one should contemplate the Dharma alone.
You should not feel agitation, for death is certain for everyone.
Just as a certain traveler rests by taking refuge in the shade, and having rested, departs once more—such is the meeting of living beings. (369)
The entire world is eternally possessed of sons; why then do you alone grieve for it?
Therefore, cast off your grief and follow my words.
Smelling her son on the head and licking his crown,
she was overcome with great grief, her eyes clouded with tears.
Sighing repeatedly— long and hot like a female serpent—
he became filled with intense anguish as he perceived the world to be empty, being bereft of his son.

Standing as if submerged in a great mire and sinking down, she lamented and spoke these words again to the son of the Sun: 373. "I am sinking, as if immersed in a vast quagmire; I am perishing. Lamenting, I address this further speech to the Son of the Day."
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no happiness equal to that for a son;
there is no joy equal to that for a son; there is no attainment equal to that for a son. ||374||
For one without a son, the world is empty; for one without a son, there is no happiness in the home. Through a son, one attains the world [of the ancestors]; without a son, one goes to hell. (375)
The words of worldly advice are cool like sandalwood and camphor;
yet the embrace of a son's body is cooler than sandalwood. (376)
Having thus described the virtues of her son and gazing at him again and again,
she hurriedly asked her mother, her friends, and the cowherd women.
The lord of beasts has assailed me as I was leading the way at the head of the herd;
having been released by him through oaths, I shall indeed go back there once more.
"I have come to see my son, my mother, my friends, and Gokula;
by means of this truthful word, I shall indeed go back there. (379)
O Mother, forgive all this that I have done through my misconduct and other faults;
he is but a child, your own grandson—what else can I say in this matter? (380)
O vast one, O mother, O auspicious one, O you who possess a fragrant mind;
O bestower of wealth, O giver of beloved things, O great one, O you whose streams flow like jars! 381.
O highly fortunate ones, whatever unpleasant thing has been said by me, whether through ignorance or even knowingly, and whatever else has been done, please forgive that. (382)
All of you, endowed with every virtue, mothers of all the world, who eternally bestow everything—protect my child! ||383||
"Protect my son, who is helpless, impaired, and miserable;
O sisters, you shall protect him who is tormented by grief for his mother. (384)
Since you will protect the helpless and the weak like your own sons, O highly fortunate ones, forgive me by virtue of my reliance on truth. (385)
Neither by great efforts nor by any means whatsoever can one's friends prevent death from standing before this first-born being. (386)
Having heard those words of his, his mother and her friends were grieved; they fell into a state of extreme despondency and, filled with wonder, spoke as follows: ||387||
O you who speak the truth, do not give up that great vow which you have undertaken to carry out—that terrible speech like a tiger’s. (388)
Having appeased this great danger with oaths and truthful words, one should strive to destroy it; by no means should one proceed [to the mountain].
Therefore, you must not commit unrighteousness by abandoning your own young son out of greed for truth. (390)
In this regard, a verse was formerly proclaimed by the seers who discourse on Brahman: "When the loss of life has occurred, there is no sin in [taking] oaths. (391)
Whereby the lives of living beings would be saved by speaking a falsehood, there falsehood becomes truth, and even truth becomes falsehood. (392)
In the case of the marriage of a woman, the slaughter of cows, and likewise upon the death of Brahmins, there is no sin incurred through oaths. (393)
He said to him:
"For the sake of protecting the lives of others, I would indeed speak a false word; but for my own sake, or even for the sake of my life, I would never venture to speak it. (394)
Alone one is joined with the womb, and likewise with death and sustenance;
alone one experiences pleasure and pain. Therefore, I speak the truth: [395]
The world is established upon truth; dharma is established upon truth.
By his word of truth, the ocean does not overstep its boundaries. (396)
Having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali took refuge in the netherworld (Pātāla);
though Bali was bound by a stratagem, he did not abandon his word of truth.
The lord of mountains, Śataśṛṅga, having arisen and grown great, remains established in truth; he does not overstep his commitment.
Heaven, liberation, and hell are established upon truthful speech; he who violates his word has violated everything without exception. (399)
If one perceives the self as something other than what it truly is, what sin has not been committed by that thief who robs himself? (400)
I shall go to a terrible hell, having destroyed myself by my own self;
King Vaivasvata will cut away half of that person's merit.
Having bathed in the lake of forbearance—a pure sacred ford with unfathomable waters and truth as its banks—one is liberated from sin and attains the supreme goal. (402)
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Truth bears the fruit of goodness; it is the supreme learning, free from afflictions and the like;
it is the proximity of the virtuous, the family wealth of the noble, and the fruit of all stages of life.
Since one attains heaven by acquiring it, how can it be abandoned?
In this assembly of the world, you must always speak the truth daily and with certainty. ||404||

The friends said: "O you who are worthy of salutation by all, even by the gods and the asuras, since you are casting off your life-breaths—which are so difficult to abandon—with such supreme goodness. (405)
What more can we say? O auspicious lady, you who bear the yoke of Dharma—by this renunciation, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that remains unattainable for you. (406)
Indeed, I see no separation from this son resulting from my abandonment;
for there are no calamities anywhere for a woman of virtuous mind. (407)
Having seen all the cowherd women and having circumambulated Gokula, she then set out,
taking leave once more of the trees and the gods.
The earth, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and also the moon;
the deities of the ten directions, the trees, and the constellations together with the planets. ||409||
Having prostrated again and again,
he made his request to all those perfected beings (siddhas) who had taken refuge in the forest, as well as to all the deities of the woods.
That forest-dweller, my son, who is like a protector of the three [worlds], is surrounded by *caṃpakas*, *aśokas*, *puṃnāgas*, *saralas*, *arjunas*, and *kiṃśukas*. (411)
Hearing that my son was wandering alone and distressed in the rugged forest, all of you, with feet weary from travel, came to my region. (412)
Protect this young calf out of affection, as if it were your own biological son;
for he is bereft of mother and father, helpless, and dejected in mind. (413)
As he wandered through this region, taming himself and deeply afflicted by suffering—
taming himself here in the great forest, my son— 414.
For one overcome by great sorrow, afflicted by hunger and thirst,
solitary and alone, perceiving the entire world as empty— ||415||
"Protection must be provided with compassion for one who is traveling; having thus instructed him out of affection, she was overcome by maternal love. (416)
Blazing with the fire of grief and deprived of the sight of her son,
she wandered about like a female cakravāka bird separated from its mate after it has fallen from a tree.
Free from the view of a self and unswerving at every step,
she proceeded once more to that place where the flesh-eater was.
He sat there with his mouth agape and sharp fangs baring a terrifying threat;
meanwhile, her son, O dear one, was a calf with an upturned tail and great speed. (419)
Having arrived, he stood before the lion, the foremost of beasts;
and seeing his son returned, he saw Death standing right in front of him.
Seeing the tiger, the cow Sudhenu spoke these words: "O King of Beasts, I have come; I am established in the vows of truth and righteousness. (421)
Now, satisfy yourself with my flesh as much as you desire;
gratify the elements, and drink my blood.
"Since she has died, let us eat this calf.
The tiger said:
"Welcome to you, O auspicious one; O cow, you are a speaker of truth. (423)
For nothing inauspicious ever befalls those who possess truth;
O Dhenuka, what was previously spoken by you shall likewise come true upon your return.
"Having reached that single festival, how could she return?
Furthermore, I have sent her again for the purpose of testing your truthfulness. (425)
Otherwise, having encountered me, how will you escape with your life? And that curiosity which has arisen in us is my search for the truth. (426)
Therefore, by this truth, may you now be freed from fear;
you are my sister, and your son is my nephew.
For me, who have received this instruction and whose actions are most virtuous, the world is established in truth;
dharma is established in truth.
By truth, the cow pours forth a stream of milk as her beloved oblation; she is the most blessed cow who lives upon your milk. 429.
Those regions of the earth, along with their grasses and creepers, are blessed; they are fortunate and have fulfilled their purpose, for by them alone has a virtuous deed been performed.
Those who drink your milk have obtained the very essence of birth;
having gained conviction, the king of beasts was filled with supreme wonder. (431)
This is our rejection, truly shown by the gods:
having seen the desired cow, it truly desires nothing other than my life. (432)
I shall perform that action by which I might be liberated from this sin;
by me, thousands and hundreds of living beings have been devoured. (433)
"Having seen such a truth regarding the cow, I am going to that destination;
for I am a sinner, of wicked conduct, cruel, and a slayer of living beings. (434)
"To what worlds shall I go after having committed such a terrible deed? I shall go to holy pilgrimage sites and perform the purification of my sins. (435)
I shall either fall after climbing a mountain, or enter the fire;
for I must perform penance by giving away cows in order to purify myself from sin.
"Therefore, instruct me in brief, for this is no time for prolixity.
The Cow replied:
"In the Kṛta age, austerity is praised; and in the Tretā age, knowledge alone. (437)
They say that sacrifice is the duty in the Dvāpara age, while giving alone is the duty in the Kali age;
among all forms of giving, this one alone is supreme.
There is no gift superior to the granting of fearlessness to all beings;
he who bestows fearlessness upon all creatures, both moving and stationary, [attains the highest merit]. (439)
Freed from all fears, one attains the Supreme Brahman;
there is no gift equal to non-violence, and there is no austerity equal to non-violence. (440)
Just as all other footprints are subsumed within the footprint of an elephant, so too, O Vyāghra, are all phenomena subsumed within non-violence. 441.
The shade of the tree of yoga destroys the threefold affliction;
its flowers are dharma and knowledge, and its fruits are heaven and liberation.
For one scorched by the threefold suffering, the tree of union with the Shade (Chāyā) is remembered;
having attained supreme Nirvāṇa, one is no longer afflicted by sufferings. ||443||
Thus, this supreme good has been proclaimed to you in brief; and since you have already known all of it in its entirety, you ask me about it [only] for the sake of my satisfaction. 444.
The leopard said:
"In former times, I was cursed by a doe and have remained in the form of a tiger;
consequently, from the killing of living beings, everything has been entirely forgotten by me."
Through association with you and through my instruction, memory has arisen once more;
and by this truth, you too shall go to the supreme goal.
Therefore, O auspicious lady, I ask you again this one question that dwells in my heart; for a full hundred years and more have passed while I have been lost in thought.
O beautiful lady of heaven, by the power of my misfortune, I have at some point established a firm foundation for dharma, firmly rooted in the path of the virtuous. ||448||
"What is that auspicious name? Tell me, O lady of good vows, for I am ignorant. She replied: "Know me as the wife of the Lord of the Gods, who has committed no sin. (449)
"Why do you stand here now saying, 'I shall eat'?
Having heard that, the person whose curse had been released spoke to the radiant one.
Having once again attained the status of a king, endowed with strength and beauty,
in the meantime, Dharma, having learned that she was a speaker of truth, [acted].
Having arrived there to see her, he spoke to the cow:
"O you who are true to your vow, I am Dharma, come here out of joy. (452)
"Choose [a boon], may it be well with you; choose indeed the most excellent of boons.
Having been addressed thus, that goddess requested this boon from him: [453]
"By your power, I have come with my sons to this supreme abode;
may this auspicious holy site become a bestower of dharma for sages. (454)
And this river shall be named after me; it shall not be called Sarasvatī.
O Lord of Gods, this was requested by me through the granting of a boon. (455)
Pulastya said: At that very moment, the goddess departed for the auspicious abode of the truthful;
the king attained his previously acquired kingdom, which was filled with splendor.
Because he went to heaven by means of that gift, and because he obtained the Sarasvatī through that gift, she was called by the wise "Naṃdāsarasvatī" after his name. 457.
Then Sarasvatī again flowed from that forest known as Kharjūra,
moving toward the south and flooding the surface of the earth.
Even while approaching, that man does not grasp her name;
he attains happiness while living and, upon death, becomes a wanderer in the sky.
In that regard, those men who perform virtuous deeds and abandon their own bodies become happy people, kings of the Vidyādharas. (460)
For men, the Sarasvatī is a ladder to heaven; by bathing in it and drinking from it, they attain liberation.
Those who, being well-composed, perform their ablutions there on the eighth lunar day [attain this]. (461)
Having reached heaven, those delightful women rejoiced;
there, the Sarasvatī always bestows good fortune upon women. (462)
Even by fasting on the third lunar day, one becomes a vessel of good fortune;
by merely beholding him there, one is liberated from the accumulation of sins.
Those men who touch it should also be known as lords among sages;
by the gift of silver, a man becomes handsome.
This daughter of Brahmā, endowed with the waters of merit and demerit,
flows toward the south in a vast current that never ceases.
Having gone not very far from there, she turned back once more;
from that time forth, the goddess remained manifest by force.
On its holy banks, sacred fords and shrines were frequented by sages and perfected beings alike.
Among all of them, Sarasvatī, the great river, is the cause of dharma through bathing, drinking, or the giving of gold. 468.
For those who have bathed here, a gift bestowed upon the donors of gold, land, and maidens at this great festival of pilgrimage produces inexhaustible fruit. (469)
The sages declare that the gift of grain is praised, as is the gift of wealth;
whatever is bestowed by men at those sacred fords is proclaimed to be the most excellent cause for merit.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever, being self-restrained, should diligently perform the rite of fasting unto death there at the sacred fords,
he shall attain union with the Divine.
He enjoys the fruit at will in the house of Brahmā. ||471||
Even if all beings, both stationary and moving, were to die together at his side through the exhaustion of their karma,
it would still be impossible for them all to forcibly obtain the fruit of the sacrifice, which is so difficult to attain.

Therefore, for those men whose minds are afflicted by the sufferings of birth and so forth, and for whom there is an absence of the fruits of merit, the great river Sarasvatī—who bestows the fruit of dharma—should be served with all one's soul and with diligent effort by persons seeking the fruits of virtue. 473.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Nandāprācī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The nineteenth chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
"I have heard the excellent majesty of the gift of Puṣkara."
When ten million sages arrived at Puṣkara to behold his face. ||1||
"By all [these means] beauty has been obtained; all this I have heard from you.
Now tell me those things which are to be offered with sacred threads. (2)

How was the classification of sacred fords (tīrtha) established by those great-souled ones? Furthermore, how were these sacred fords within the hermitages (āśrama) created by the great seers (maharṣi)? ||3||
Formerly, Viṣṇu set foot upon Yajñaparvata;
there, those highly venomous serpents established five sacred bathing places (tīrthas). ||4||
How is it that the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, which were previously created by Piṇḍapradāna-vāpīcaka, have now gone underground and flow facing north? (5)
"O Brahmins learned in the Vedas, how should one conduct a journey when the three worlds are parched? Tell me that by which its fruit may be produced."
Pulastya said:
A great burden of questions has been set forth by you;
therefore, becoming one-pointed in mind, listen to the great fruit of the sacred fords (tīrtha).
He whose hands, feet, and speech are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame, enjoys the fruit of the true sacred ford.
One who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is content with whatever comes his way,
and who has turned away from egoism, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.
O king of kings, one who is free from anger, truthful, firm in his vows,
and who treats all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.
O best of the Bharatas, this is the supreme secret of the sages,
concerning that which occurred formerly at the great ancestral sacrifice of the Great King.
Those ascetics of fierce penance, whose crores have assembled and remain stationed at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara, having sought the sight of his face.
Having attained supreme beauty, those best of sages were filled with joy;
possessed by great delight, they longed for a vision of Brahmā.

Having reached the earth with their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) spread out in all four directions, they established a division for the holy bathing place (*tīrtha*) and remained there, devoted to worship.
Then, seeing the devotion of those wise ones, the Grandfather (Brahmā) became pleased with them and approached them ten million times over.
From this day forward, there shall be an increase in your merit.
Whoever, having come here, first places a limb of their body into the water—whether man or woman—[shall attain success]. (16)
Having performed the function of a ford (tīrtha) for the sake of flooding [the world] with his form,
his body will no longer exist within a circle extending for one yojana.
This sacred ford, frequented by ten million sages, measures half a yojana in width and one and a half yojanas in length.
O enemy-subduer, by merely going to Puṣkara, the king of gods, a person obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. ||19||
Having entered the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara, which is exceedingly meritorious due to the presence of Sarasvatī, the gods headed by Brahmā, as well as the ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, [reside there]. (20)
They approach on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra;
there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform the consecration.
One obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice (Gomedha) and uplifts one's entire lineage;
thus was the classification of the sacred fords (tīrtha) established by those great seers.
Having gratified the ancestors and the gods, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
having bathed there, a mortal becomes as stainless as the moon.
One attains the world of Brahmā and shall go to the supreme goal;
this is the holy ford (tīrtha) of the God of gods, renowned throughout the three worlds in the realm of men. ||24||
O Lord of the Earth, there is a place renowned by the name Puṣkara, which destroys great sins; it is equal to ten thousand times ten million holy fords (tīrthas). 25.
O delighter of your lineage, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts maintain their presence at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day.
O Lord, Gandharvas and Apsarases are always present there,
where the gods, Daityas, and Brahman-sages likewise performed austerities.
Endowed with great merit through divine yoga,
those high-minded ones attained the Puṣkara lakes even by the mere desire of their minds.
All his sins are purified, O great king, and he rejoices in the vault of heaven; for at that holy site (tīrtha), the Grandfather (Brahmā) dwells eternally. ||29||
Residing at Puṣkara, O great king, he dwelt there with supreme joy, honored by gods and dānavas; so too did the gods, preceded by the sages. 30.
Having attained perfection and being endowed with great merit, whoever performs an ablution there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, [attains success]. (31)
The wise declare that feeding even a single Brahmin while residing in the Puṣkara forest is ten times more meritorious than the Aśvamedha sacrifice. (32)
When a koṭi [of beings] is satisfied and honored with food and drink, by that deed one rejoices both here and after passing away, O Bhīṣma. (33)
One should personally cultivate it with vegetables, roots, fruits, or even barley;
then, being faithful and free from malice, one should give that to a Brāhmaṇa.
By that alone, O best of kings, a wise man— whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra— shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
The meritorious lake of the Grandfather, known by the name Puṣkara,
is indeed the bestower of merit upon the Vaikhānasas, the Siddhas, and the sages.
Today we have reached the most meritorious Sarasvatī, which flows toward the great ocean, where the primordial god, the great yogi Madhusūdana, resides. ||37||
He is renowned by the name Ādivarāha and is worshipped by the thirty gods;
and those of low caste who have gone to the tīrtha of Pitāmaha [attain high status]. (38)
Having bathed at the tīrtha of the Great-Souled One, they go to a new womb;
and he who especially visits Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārtika [attains the same].
We have heard that for him, the fruit thereof becomes inexhaustible—he who, with palms joined in reverence, should remember the Puṣkara lakes both morning and evening. (40)
O descendant of Kuru, by touching [the water] here, one obtains the merit of all sacred fords; whatever sin has been committed since birth, whether by a woman or a man, [is destroyed].
By merely bathing at Puṣkara, all this perishes;
just as among the gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) is the foremost of them all. 42.
In the same way, the sacred site of Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of all tīrthas;
having seen it, one who is self-controlled and pure for ten years at Puṣkara [attains the highest goal].
He obtains all sacrificial rites and goes to the world of Brahmā;
this is true for one who performs the Agnihotra for a full hundred years. ||44||
Or one may dwell for a single Kārttikī [lunar month] at Puṣkara; that is indeed equal [to the merit of a lifetime].
At Puṣkara, the fire-sacrifice is difficult to perform; at Puṣkara, austerity is difficult to practice. (45)
Giving a gift at Puṣkara is difficult, and residing there is indeed very difficult;
yet a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, having gone to Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara, [achieves this]. (46)
By bathing, one becomes a partaker of liberation; by performing a śrāddha, one becomes a savior of the ancestors.
Even a brahmin who merely bears the name [of this place], having gone there, performs the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
"By this, meditation has been practiced here for twelve years; let there be no doubt in this matter, for it was previously declared by Svayambhū himself. (48)
The fault described by Sāvitrī does not arise in that family where a wife gives her husband the materials for his twilight worship as he is about to perform it. (49)
By offering water with a copper vessel, one may go to heaven as if released from a pearl;
having reached the world of Brahmā, he remains there for the duration of a day of Brahmā.
Even when you have come alone,
meditate upon it in due order with the water from the lotus and that which has been placed in the pitcher.
By him, moreover, the twilight worship has undoubtedly been performed for twelve years, even while he was performing the libations to the ancestors with his wife standing nearby. (51)
O best of kings, by facing the southern direction while reciting the Gāyatrī,
the supreme satisfaction of the ancestors is accomplished for twelve years.
By means of a collective śrāddha performed for a thousand yugas, one attains infinity;
it is for this purpose that a wise man takes a wife.
Having gone to the sacred ford (tīrtha), we shall indeed offer the funeral cakes preceded by the śrāddha;
for them there shall be sons, wealth, grain, and an uninterrupted lineage. (55)
The Grandfather (Brahmā) has declared that this body would indeed be free from disease;
having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O King, listen with a focused mind as I describe the hermitages to you;
here, a hermitage equal to that of the gods was established by Agastya. (57)
In ancient times, there was here the hermitage of the Seven Sages, esteemed by the gods; likewise, it was the supreme abode of the Brahman-sages and the Manus.
And on the slopes of Mount Yajñaparvata, there is the delightful city of the Nāgas, which displays the power of the great king Agastya, whose soul is immeasurable. (59)
I shall tell it to you in brief; listen with a well-composed mind.
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, there were Dānavas as fierce as Bhīṣma, intoxicated by the pride of battle.
The hosts known as the Kāleyas, who were exceedingly fierce, having taken refuge with Vṛtra, prepared to slay the gods. (61)
Then the gods, greatly agitated, approached Brahmā; and as they all stood there with palms joined in reverence, the Supreme Lord spoke to them.
"O gods, everything that you desire to accomplish is known to me;
I shall declare the means by which you will slay Vṛtra."
There was a great ṛṣi of noble intellect, renowned as Dadhīci;
having gone to him together, they all requested a boon from him. (64)
That righteous-souled one, being well-pleased in his inner self, will offer himself as a slave;
he must be addressed by all of you together, who are desirous of victory.
"Give your own bones, desiring the welfare of the three worlds;
having cast off your body, you shall give your own bones. (66)
"Let a firm and most terrible vajra be fashioned from her bones;
that divine weapon, known as the thunderbolt (aśani), shall slay the great enemy. ||67||
With that very thunderbolt, Śatakratu shall slay Vṛtra.
All this has been told to you; therefore, let everything be carried out accordingly.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then took leave of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and,
placing Śatakratu (Indra) at their head, went to the hermitage of Dadhīci.
On the far bank of the Sarasvatī, it was covered with various trees and creepers and resounded with the humming songs of bees, as if proclaimed by Sāman-chanting priests.
It was filled with the cries of male cuckoos and the calls of jīvañjīvaka birds,
as well as with buffaloes, boars, sṛmara deer, and even mṛga deer.
There, they were accompanied by female elephants and male elephants with temples and mouths flowing with rut, who moved about free from the fear of tigers.
It resounded with the playful outbursts of their own voices,
and it was echoed by lions and tigers roaring with great cries.
And with peacocks dwelling in mountain caves nestled within those various groves, it was made to resound with most delightful cries.
They arrived at Dadhīci’s hermitage, which was as magnificent as heaven itself;
there they beheld Dadhīci, whose splendor was equal to that of the sun.
O King of the Asuras, seeing him blazing with his body and possessing four arms due to his splendor,
I bowed down and prostrated at his feet; then I requested of him all the boons exactly as they had been described by Parameṣṭhin.
Then Adhīci, supremely pleased, said to those best of gods, "O gods, I shall do whatever you desire today; I will even cast off my own body. (77)
Having spoken thus to them, that best of bipeds then suddenly cast off his life-breaths;
and the gods, including Indra, took those bones of his for their respective uses.
And the gods, appearing joyful for the sake of victory, approached Tvaṣṭṛ and spoke of that matter;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, having heard their words, being joyful in appearance, with self-restraint and great effort, [acted].
Having fashioned a vajra of exceedingly fierce power and made it his weapon, he spoke joyfully to him:
"With this most excellent of weapons, reduce the fierce enemy of the gods, the Asura, to ashes this very day! (80)
Then, having slain his enemies, you, remaining in heaven with your hosts, may happily rule over the entire celestial realm;
thus addressed by Tvaṣṭṛ, Purandara, being delighted and composed, took up the thunderbolt.
Then, accompanied by his thunderbolt and honored by the deities,
he approached Vṛtra, who stood encompassing both heaven and earth.
It was filled with the Kālakeyas of massive bodies,
who stood together like mountains with peaks, their weapons raised high.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, a great battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas for a moment, causing terror to the worlds.
From the heroic arms raised and brandishing swords, and from the bodies being torn asunder, there arose a tumultuous sound. (85)
As their heads fell from the sky to the surface of the earth,
the ground appeared as if covered by palm fruits— those very heads of the kings.
Having donned golden armor and wielding iron clubs as weapons,
the Kāleyas then rushed against the gods like trees consumed by fire.
They were unable to withstand the force of those rushing together with great speed;
broken, they fled in fear.
Seeing them fleeing in fear and beholding Vṛtra growing in power, the thousand-eyed Purandara was overcome by a great dejection. ||89||
Seeing Śakra possessed by that dejection, the eternal Viṣṇu infused his own splendor into Śakra, increasing his strength.
Then, seeing Śakra nourished by Viṣṇu,
all the hosts of gods as well as the stainless brahmin-sages bestowed their respective splendors upon him.
Having been fully nourished by Viṣṇu along with the deities and the highly blessed ṛṣis, Śakra became powerful once again. 92.
Perceiving that lord of the thirty gods to be established in his power, Vṛtra let out a most tremendous roar;
by that thundering sound, the earth, the quarters, the sky, the heavens, and the mountains—all trembled.
Then Mahendra, greatly distressed upon hearing that most terrible roar, was submerged in fear;
he quickly released his great thunderbolt upon the head of the elephant. (94)
Struck by Śakra’s thunderbolt, he fell with a great roar, wearing a golden garland, like a massive, preeminent mountain released from the hand of Viṣṇu and crashing down into a chasm before him. (95)
When that foremost of Daityas had been slain, Śakra, afflicted by fear, fled toward the cave;
and out of terror, he did not even perceive that the thunderbolt had slipped from his hand or that Vṛtra was already dead.
All the gods, together with the ṛṣis, were delighted and overjoyed, and they praised him;
meanwhile, the remaining Daityas, having gathered quickly, struck the gods who were distressed by the slaughter of Vṛtra.
Then, being pursued by the gods, those great asuras, possessing a speed equal to the wind, entered the ocean alone, afflicted by fear; and having entered the immeasurable sea, they remained there.
Then, together, they performed that mantra which was crowded with crocodiles and filled with jewels;
there, some among them, being of firm resolve, reflected upon various means for the sacrifice. (99)
Afflicted by fear and tormented by the divine hosts, they set their minds upon the destruction of the three worlds;
as they brooded there, a terrible thought arose within them due to the onset of the time of dissolution.
Those who possess knowledge and asceticism must first be destroyed;
for all the worlds are sustained by asceticism. Therefore, hasten to bring about the destruction of asceticism! 101.
There are some on this earth who dwell in asceticism, who know the Dharma, and who understand it;
let their slaughter be carried out quickly, for when they are destroyed, the world is ruined. (102)
Thus, with their minds fixed on the destruction of the world, they were supremely delighted;
taking refuge in that formidable ocean, the abode of Varuṇa and mine of jewels, which was surging with great waves. (103)
Having reached the ocean, that abode of Varuṇa and reservoir of waters,
the Kāleyas gathered there for the destruction of the three worlds.
Then, enraged for three nights, they devoured those sages in their hermitages and in sacred sanctuaries.
In the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, one hundred and eighty-eight brahmins and other ascetics were devoured by those evil-minded ones in the forest. (106)
Having gone to the holy hermitage of Cyavana, which was frequented by the twice-born, he ate the food of a hundred sages who subsisted on fruits and roots. (107)
Thus, avoiding the heat of the night, they entered the ocean by day;
having reached the hermitage of Bharadvāja, they remained disciplined as celibate students.
At that time, twenty Dānavas were slaughtered by the sages for the purpose of food, including those who subsisted on air and those who subsisted on foam. 109.
At night, relying on the strength of their arms and their weapons, they roamed about;
over a long period of time, they indeed slew many groups of sages.

O lord of men, do not fail to recognize these younger brothers of yours, who are devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, and for whom the performance of sacrifices and festivals has perished. (111)
The world was devoid of energy, oppressed by the fear of Kāleya;
thus, O lord of men, those humans were being utterly destroyed. (112)
Terrified by the fear for their own lives, they fled in the ten directions;
some entered caves, while other brahmins were scattered about.
Others, agitated by fear, abandoned their lives out of terror;
yet there were some great archers there, heroes exceedingly proud of their prowess. (114)
Seeking them with the utmost effort, the [gods] exerted themselves against the Dānavas;
yet they could not pursue them, for the Dānavas had taken refuge in the ocean.
They did not attain supreme peace, but rather reached utter destruction;
for the world was born into a state of lack of tranquility, where the performance of sacrifices and festivals had perished.
O lord of men, the gods, being exceedingly agitated, arrived; having assembled with Indra at their head, they held a consultation out of fear. (117)
Placing the invincible Vaikuṇṭha Nārāyaṇa at their head,
those assembled gods then spoke to Madhusūdana.
O Lord, you are our creator, our protector, and the sustainer of the universe;
by you has the entire world been created—whatever moves and whatever is immobile.
O Lotus-eyed One, in former times the earth was lost in the ocean;
assuming the form of a boar, you raised it up for the sake of the world. (120)
In ancient times, O Puruṣottama, the first Daitya, Hiraṇyakaśipu of great prowess, was slain by you after you had assumed the body of a man-lion. 121.
Even Bali, the great asura who was invulnerable to all beings,
was cast down from the three worlds by you after you assumed the form of a dwarf.
The Asura Jambha, renowned for his great skill with the bow, a cruel disturber of sacrifices, has been struck down by you with your arrows. 123.
O Madhusūdana, for us who are terrified by such deeds as these, of which there is no end, you alone are our refuge. 124.
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, we inform you for the sake of the world:
protect the worlds, the gods, and Śakra from this great fear.
By your grace, all four classes of beings flourish;
humans become healthy, and the denizens of heaven are sustained by offerings to the gods and ancestors.
For the worlds proceed in this manner, mutually dependent upon one another;
through your power they are free from anxiety, and by you alone are they protected.
And this supreme terror has come upon the worlds; know that these Brāhmaṇas are not to be slain by you, O Nacaka! Śi. 128.
When the Brahmins have perished, the destruction of the earth will follow;
through your grace, O mighty-armed Lord of the World, all the worlds [will be saved]. (129)
"Protected by you, they shall not meet with destruction.
Viṣṇu said:
"O gods, the entire cause for the destruction of my subjects is known to me. (130)
And I shall also speak to you; listen, free from all anxiety.
There are hosts known as the Kālakeyas, who are exceedingly fierce.
Seeing Vṛtra slain by the wise thousand-eyed Indra,
they entered the abode of Varuṇa, seeking to preserve their lives.
Having entered the terrible ocean, which is infested with various kinds of crocodiles,
those sages here slay the night-demons for the sake of destroying the world.
"However, it is not possible to bring about the destruction of the oceans, O you who act for the benefit and harm of others;
therefore, let your minds consider a means for the depletion of the ocean. (134)
Having heard these words uttered by Viṣṇu,
the gods approached Parameṣṭhin and went to the hermitage of Agastya.
There he beheld the high-souled son of Varuṇa, blazing with splendor, being worshipped by sages like the Grandfather [Brahmā] by the gods. (136)
They approached that great-souled one, the supreme son of Mitrāvaruṇa,
who was vigilant and a mass of asceticism through the performance of his own prescribed duties.
The gods said:
"In former times, you were the refuge of the worlds oppressed by Nahuṣa;
for the sake of the worlds, that crusher of worlds was cast down from the sovereignty of the gods. (138)
Out of anger, the great mountain Vindhya, the best of peaks, having grown excessively, no longer increases, not transgressing your word, O Sun. (139)
When the world was shrouded in darkness and all beings were oppressed by death,
they came to you alone as their protector and attained supreme peace.
For us who are terrified by fear, you alone are our constant refuge;
therefore, we now entreat you for a boon, for you are indeed the granter of boons. (141)
Bhīṣma said:
"O great sage, I wish to hear in detail for what reason Vidura suddenly became so agitated, overwhelmed by anger."
Pulastya said: The sun performs a circumambulation of Meru, the king of mountains, the great peak, the golden mountain, from its rising until its setting.
Seeing him then, the mountain Āviṃdhya spoke to Sūrya: "Just as Himavat and Meru are circumambulated by you, so too should I. (144)
"Perform a circumambulation of me; do so, O Bhāskara.
Being addressed thus, Sūrya then replied to the lord of mountains: 145.
I do not perform this circumambulation of the mountain by my own will;
rather, this is the path ordained for me by Him who created this world. (146)
Thus addressed, O ascetic of supreme penance, that mountain suddenly grew out of anger,
desiring to block the path of the sun and the moon.
Then all the gods together with Indra assembled and restrained that great king of mountains as it was about to leap up; however, he did not heed their words.

Then those gods went together to the sage Agastya, who was staying in his hermitage, the most eminent among ascetics and practitioners of dharma, and possessed of most wonderful and radiant power; and they spoke to that noble one. (149)
The gods said: "This king of mountains, Vindhya, following the impulse of anger, obstructs the path of the sun and the moon, as well as the course of the stars. (150)
"O Lord of Sages, no one else is capable of restraining him.
Having heard those words of the gods, the brahmin went to the mountain.
Approaching with reverence, he spoke to the wise one who was standing nearby:
"O best of mountains, I desire that a path be granted by you. (152)
"Go toward the southern direction for some business;
wait there until my return. (153)
"Therefore, O Vṛddha, you may now turn back from me, the king of mountains, according to your desire.
Pulastya said:
"Even today, the son of Varuṇa does not turn back from the southern region."
All this has been told to you, just as the Vindhya mountain does not grow,
by the power of Agastya— concerning that which you asked me.
O King, listen as I relate how all the Kāleyas were destroyed by the gods after they had reached the gateway of Agastya. (156)
Having heard the words of the thirty gods, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa said:
"For what purpose have you come together? What do you desire from me? (157)
Thus addressed by him, the gods then spoke to that sage:
"O divine sage of great soul, we desire one wonderful boon: drink up the ocean. (158)
O great seer, if you should thus desire the entire great ocean to be drunk up by me,
then we shall destroy the continuous lineage of Kāleya, that force of the enemies of the gods.
Having heard the words of the thirty gods, the sage said, "So be it;
I shall fulfill your desire, which brings happiness to the worlds. (160)
Having spoken thus, O observer of noble vows, he then went to the ocean, that treasure-house of waters, together with the gods and the sages who had perfected their asceticism.
Humans, nāgas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and likewise kiṃpuruṣas followed that great-souled one, desiring to behold that wonder. (162)
Then he beheld together with his companions the ocean, making a terrifying sound; it seemed as if it were dancing with its waves and leaping about with the wind.
It was laughing, as it were, with its masses of foam, stumbling in its depths,
filled with various crocodiles, and frequented by various flocks of birds.
Accompanied by Agastya, the gods, along with the Gandharvas and great serpents,
as well as the highly fortunate sages, approached the great ocean.
Having reached the ocean, the venerable sage Vāruṇi spoke to the assembled gods and the ṛṣis who had gathered there.
Desiring to cross the ocean, Agastya, the best of sages, said: "For the sake of the welfare of the world, I shall drink up the abode of Varuṇa. (167)
"Whatever is to be performed by you, let that be carried out quickly.
Having spoken these words, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa stood at the front.
Enraged, he drank the ocean while all the world looked on;
and seeing the ocean being thus drunk, the gods, together with Indra, [were struck with wonder]. (169)
They were filled with supreme wonder and honored him with hymns of praise:
"You are our protector and creator, the sustainer of the worlds;
through your grace, may the universe attain its full expansion. (170)
While being honored by the gods, amidst the chanting of the chief Gandharvas,
and being strewn with celestial flowers, that Great-Souled One rendered the great ocean waterless.
Seeing the great ocean rendered waterless, all the gods were exceedingly delighted;
grasping their divine and excellent weapons, those of undaunted spirit struck down the Dānavas. (172)
Being thus assailed by the high-souled, mighty, and roaring thirty gods,
who were endowed with great speed, they were unable to withstand the force of those powerful, high-souled inhabitants of heaven.
Being thus assailed by the gods, O Bhārata, the Dānavas, whose roars were terrifying, waged a most tumultuous battle for a mere moment.
Previously burnt by the ascetic power of sages of purified souls, they were destroyed by the gods despite their striving with all their might. (175)
Adorned with golden neck-ornaments and wearing earrings and armlets, they lay slain, no longer radiant, like flowering *kiṃśuka* trees.
Then some of the remaining foremost Kāleya demons, having split open the goddess Earth, took refuge in the depths of Pātāla. ||177||
Seeing the Dānavas slain, the gods praised that bull among sages with various words and spoke these words: ||178||
O highly fortunate one, through your grace, the worlds have attained great happiness;
and by your splendor, the Kaleyas of terrible prowess have been struck down. (179)
Fill this great ocean of Brahmins, the sustainer of the world;
release back into it that water which was drunk by you. (180)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the bull among sages, replied: "That water has turned to ice; let another means be devised. (181)
"Exert yourselves for the purpose of filling the ocean.
Having thus heard the words of the great seer of purified soul, [the gods spoke].
The gods, both amazed and despondent,
took leave of one another and bowed down to that bull among sages.
All the subjects departed for their respective homes as they had come;
the thirty gods, together with Viṣṇu, followed after the Grandfather (Brahmā).184
For the purpose of filling the ocean, all those aquatic creatures consulted one another and spoke of the filling of the sea. (185)
To them, gathered together, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, said:
"Go, all you gods, according to your desire and as you wish. (186)
Through the great yoga of timely action, the ocean shall return to its natural state; having made his kinsmen the cause, the great king Bhagīratha [will achieve this]. (187)
And he shall again fill the ocean with the flood of the Gaṅgā.
Thus were those best of sages dispatched by Brahmā to the gods.
The Blessed One, being pleased, spoke to Agastya, the best of sages: "May the work of the gods—the destruction of the Dānavas—be accomplished by you. (189)
"O Sage, I am indeed pleased that those gods have been delivered by you; therefore, ask for whatever boon you desire, and I shall grant it to you. (190)
Thus addressed, Agastya then, preceded by a prostration, said:
"While remaining here, O God of gods, this task has been accomplished by me."
"O Blessed One, this hermitage of mine shall become the most excellent among all hermitages;
as it has been spoken by you, so shall it be—of this there is no doubt. (192)
Brahmā said:
Those men who, having performed a pilgrimage to Puṣkara, come here and bathe in these pools, and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods; ||193||
And worship among the gods indeed makes everything inexhaustible;
then, taking various kinds of water-offerings (arghya), as well as fried cakes and sweetmeats, [one should proceed].
Those who give [these gifts] to the foremost of the twice-born shall have their residence in Triviṣṭapa;
through the Śrāddha, the ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
Whoever shall satisfy this sage with roots and fruits will rejoice for eternal years after reaching the abode of the Seven Sages. (196)
Having ascended the mountain of sacrifice and beheld the outflow of the Gaṅgā,
the divine river emerged facing north toward Puṣkara.
Whoever performs an ablution here, being devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice; of this there is no doubt. ||198||
But he who feeds even a single Brahmin, O Lord of Sages, it is as if ten million have been fed; moreover, the food and drink given here becomes inexhaustible. (199)
Whatever desire he may wish for shall be his; there is no womb into which a man who has merely bathed here on earth shall enter. 200.
O best of sages, the supreme among all places and the most excellent of all holy sites has been granted by me; of this there is no doubt. 201.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth—all of this perishes for one who has merely bathed here. (202)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
took his leave of the sage Agastya, the best of sages, and departed.
Agastya performed supreme austerity there in his own hermitage;
thus has this origin of Agastya’s hermitage been recounted to you. 204.
And I shall describe the hermitages of the seven seers, O best of the Kurus:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (205)
Aṅgiras, Gautama, Sumati, and likewise Sumukha;
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, and Pratardana. ||206||
Raibhya, Bṛhaspati, Cyavana, Kaśyapa, Bhṛgu, Durvāsas, Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Gālava. ||207||
Uśanas, Bharadvāja, the sage Yavakrīta, Sthūlākṣa, Sakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, and Kṛta. ||208||
Nārada, Parvata, Svagandhin, Cyavana, O twice-born one, Tṛṇāmbu, Śabala, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, and Kṛtavraṇa. ||209||
Jamadagni, as well as Ārāma, Aṣṭaka, Māḍhaya, and others, and Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana himself, accompanied by his sons and disciples. ||210||
Then, having reached Puṣkara at the hermitage of the Seven Sages,
those ascetics, endowed with compassion, were restrained by Yama.
Kindness, victory, fortitude, austerity, truth, patience, straightforwardness, compassion, generosity, and recitation—these are all established upon that [dharma]. ||212||
Whatever action is performed here is experienced there;
having understood this to be so, the sages are devoted to the supreme goal. (213)
Neither atheists, nor those who have perished, nor those who have not conquered their senses enter there;
nor do the cruel, the malicious, the ungrateful, or the arrogant. (214)

They were true to their word, radiant with splendor, heroic, compassionate, and devoted to forbearance; they were performers of sacrifices, habitually engaged in ritual, free from worldly desire, and devoid of affliction.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, they go there to Puṣkara;
for those great-souled ones, there shall be neither disease, nor old age, nor death.
In that state, deluded persons— who are devoid of the true nature of the self and are afflicted by desire, greed, pride, malice, anger, and delusion— do not enter.
Those who are equal toward honor and dishonor, free from the pairs of opposites, with senses restrained, and devoted to the yoga of meditation—they indeed go to Puṣkara. ||218||
Those twice-born ones who conduct themselves as prescribed in the aforementioned stages of life (āśramas) according to the sacred injunctions—
by them these worlds of great exaltation are attained.
For those who, toward all beings, act with deeds, mind, and speech that are most free from cruelty, they shall always speak what is not unpleasant. (220)
They were constantly devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, always honoring guests, ever intent on the study of the Vedas, and perpetually dedicated to ritual bathing. ||221||
They constantly look upon the wives of others as their own mothers, sisters, and daughters, being forever free from desire.
Those who are reviled do not become angry, for they are indeed not harmed;
being equal in suffering and happiness, these noble beings have their senses conquered. (223)
All of them beheld that [state] because they had previously wandered this earth,
contemplating the eternal world of Brahmā through meditative absorption.
Then, at one time, there occurred a great drought;
indeed, the entire world there became afflicted by hunger and was reduced to a state of extreme hardship. (225)
Then, desiring to save their own lives, they looked about in that smokeless world;
taking up the dead boy, they then fell into a state of great distress.
Then, seeing the sages there who were suffering and distressed, the king, afflicted by despair, spoke these words at that time: ||227||
The king said:
"Acceptance of gifts is seen as an unobjectionable means of livelihood for Brahmins;
therefore, O best of sages, accept gifts from me. (228)
O twice-born ones, do not cook for me all those excellent villages, rice, barley, juices, jewels, gold, cows, and milch-cows. ||229||
The sages said:
"O King, accepting gifts is terrible; it has the taste of honey but is like poison.
Knowing this, why do you attempt to entice us? (230)
One who possesses a gambling wheel is equal to ten slaughterhouses; one who possesses a banner is equal to ten who possess a gambling wheel;
a courtesan is equal to ten who possess a banner; and a king is equal to ten courtesans. ||231||
A king is equal to a vintner who operates ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible.
The Brāhmaṇa who, deluded by greed, accepts gifts from a wicked king, is cooked in the most terrible hells, such as Tāmisra and others. (233)
"Therefore, go; may it be well with you, O King.
Let this be given to others by means of a gift. Having said this, they departed for the forest. (234)
Then, at the king’s command, the ministers went there and scattered udumbara fruits containing gold within the ground.
Then, while searching for food, they even began to take up heavy stones;
however, having recognized that these were too heavy, Atri declared that they should not be taken.
Atri said: "We are not of deluded understanding; we are not of dull intellect.
We know these things to be made of gold; we are awakened, for they are our riches. (237)
This very thing leads to the gratification of wealth in this world, while after death it results in the dawning of Vaikuṇṭha;
therefore, one who desires the bliss of liberation must certainly not accept this [pleasure]. (238)
He who receives from another a *niṣka* multiplied by a hundred and accompanied by a thousand [other coins] attains the most sinful state of existence. (239)
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women exist upon the earth—surely all this is not enough for even one person; realizing this, one should attain tranquility.

Vasiṣṭha said: He who possesses an accumulation of austerities and he who possesses an accumulation of material goods—the accumulation of austerity alone is superior to the accumulation of wealth. (241)
For one who abandons all accumulations, calamities come to an end;
indeed, no one possessing accumulations is ever seen to be free from calamity.
To the extent that a Brahmin does not accept improper gifts,
to that same extent his spiritual power increases through the satisfaction of the virtuous.
He weighed poverty and sovereignty on a scale and found them unequal;
for one who has realized the Self, poverty is superior even to sovereignty.
Kaśyapa said:
This great accumulation of wealth is a misfortune for a brāhmaṇa.
For a twice-born man who is utterly deluded by wealth and power falls away from the highest good; the acquisition of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell. (246)

Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should avoid from afar that which is called "wealth" when it is actually harmful; for him whose pursuit of wealth is for the sake of dharma, non-pursuit is superior.
Indeed, it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off;
that dharma which is accomplished through wealth is proclaimed to be perishable. (248)
That renunciation for the sake of others is imperishable and characterized by liberation.
Bharadvāja said: "The hair of a decaying man decays; the teeth of a decaying man decay. (249)
The hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay even as one decays;
the eyes and ears decay, but craving alone remains a source of affliction.
Just as a needle-bringer brings the thread to the cloth through the eye of the needle,
so too is the thread of saṃsāra brought [to its end] by the needle of craving for existence.
Just as the horn of a ruru deer grows as its body grows, so too does craving—which is shoreless, insatiable, and brings forth hundreds of sufferings—increase. (252)
"And because it is full of unrighteousness, one should therefore avoid it.
Gautama said:
"Who, being satisfied, is able to transcend even by means of fruits? (253)
One who is greedy plunges into perils through the fickleness of the senses;
for him whose mind is contented, there is prosperity everywhere. (254)
For one whose feet are hidden by sandals, the earth is as if covered with leather;
such is the happiness of those whose minds are peaceful and who are satiated by the nectar of contentment.
For those greedy for wealth who run hither and thither, discontent is the supreme suffering; contentment is the supreme happiness. (256)
Therefore, a person seeking happiness should remain contented and ever-satisfied.
Viśvāmitra said: "If the desire of one who longs for a wish is fulfilled... (257)
Then another desire pierces him even more deeply, like an arrow;
desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desires. (258)
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more;
a man who, out of delusion, longs for desires does not prosper in happiness. (259)
Like a monkey entering the shade of a tree that is the dwelling of a hawk, he who enjoys this earth bounded by the four oceans [is like one entering a place of danger]. (260)
He who regards stone and gold as equal is a king whose purpose is already accomplished.
Jamadagni said: Even though he is capable of accepting gifts, he does not take what is offered.
A Brahmin who seizes from a king the wealth of those virtuous people whose nature is to bestow the worlds shall incur eternal suffering; he is to be mourned by the great seers.
The fool does not perceive the fear of torments in hell;
even though he is capable of receiving gifts, he should not become addicted to accepting them.
Through the acceptance of gifts, the Vedic luster of Brahmins is extinguished;
yet for those who are capable of receiving gifts but refrain from doing so, that luster remains intact.
"Those very worlds that belong to those who give are the same as those for those who do not accept.
Arundhatī said:
"Just as one who has entered a lotus stalk might constantly enter into its fibers, so it is with this. (265)
Craving, which resides always within the body from the very beginning, is difficult for the foolish to abandon; it does not decay even as one decays with age. (266)
For one who abandons that thirst which is the foremost disease of the vital breaths, there is happiness.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"O Great Lords, because we are terrified by the fear arising from such fierce [conditions]," ||267||
"And because of that very fact, I am afraid of the strong acting like the weak.
Paśusakha said:
"Whatever learned men who are ever devoted to dharma practice," [268]
"Therefore, that very thing should be done by a wise person desiring his own welfare.
Having said this, he indeed cast away those fruits which were filled with gold.
The sages, all of whom were firm in their vows, went to where [the others] were;
then, wandering about, they arrived at Madhyama Puṣkara.
They suddenly beheld a wandering mendicant, a friend of Śunaḥ, who had arrived there;
accompanied by him, they went a short distance further into the forest.
I saw a supreme lake, a reservoir filled with lotuses;
we sat upon the shore of the lake, contemplating the auspicious goal.
Then Śunaḥsakha said to all the sages who were hungry:
"Let everyone speak together; what is the nature of the sensation of hunger? (273)
They spoke together to that wandering mendicant, the friend of Śunaḥ.
The sages said:
"With spears, swords, clubs, discuses, tomara-lances, and arrows... [274]
Even when afflicted by hunger, she was overcome by pain;
likewise by asthma, leprosy, consumption, tumors, fever, epilepsy, and colic. (275)
Even the hunger produced by diseases would not be more than this [ordinary] hunger;
[they were] adorned with bright armlets, bracelets, crowns, and earrings made of gold. (276)
The sun does not shine for those men who remain there in hunger;
just as on the earth, wherever one goes, the rays of the sun draw [heat] upon them. ||277||
In the same way, the channels born of the body are dried up by the digestive fire;
he does not hear, nor does he smell, nor indeed does he see with his eyes.
The fool is consumed, wasted away, and parched, afflicted by hunger;
he does not go to the east, nor to the south, nor to the west, nor even to the north. (279)
One who is possessed by the eye-demon does not see what is below or above;
moreover, there is muteness, deafness, dullness, and lameness. (280)
In the state of Bhairava, when hunger increases beyond all bounds, one [seeks to devour] even one's father, mother, sons, wife, and likewise one's daughter. (281)
Afflicted by hunger, he would abandon his brother or even his own kinsmen;
he would not properly honor his ancestors, nor the gods, nor likewise his guru. (282)
And even when sages have approached him, one overcome by hunger does not perceive them;
thus do these [afflictions] arise for embodied beings who are deprived of food. (283)
Thus, endowed with faith, one should bestow food;
having become Brahman, he then rejoices together with Brahman.
One should give well-prepared food to a twice-born man day after day; moreover, one should recite this "Gift of Food" (Annadāna), especially during a śrāddha ceremony. ||285||
Having become single-minded, on the new moon day at the waning of the moon,
one should always cause [the teaching] to be heard during a śrāddha rite that is complete and free from injury to living beings.
His ancestors remain satisfied for as long as he lives, there is no doubt;
one who gives food while standing near a deity or a twice-born man is liberated. (287)
Whether one is awakened or vigilant, whether one has come there by chance or even if devoid of devotion, one who listens is liberated from sin. (288)
Brahmins endowed with generosity are happy and partakers of the Dharma;
self-restraint, tranquility, and discipline have been proclaimed by those who perceive the true meaning of reality. (289)
This self-restraint is especially the eternal dharma of the Brahmins; self-restraint increases one's splendor, it is purifying, and self-restraint is supreme. (290)
Free from evil and full of splendor, a man shall become self-controlled;
whatever observances exist in this world and whatever dharmas are associated with auspiciousness—[he should practice them]. (291)
And even the fruit of all sacrifices is surpassed by these;
likewise, austerity, sacrifice, and giving proceed from self-restraint alone. (292)
What is a forest to him who gives, and what is a hermitage to him who gives?
Wherever one dwells while giving, that is the forest and that is the great hermitage.
For one who is endowed with moral conduct and proper behavior, whose senses are restrained, and who abides in uprightness—what need has such a person for the stages of life (āśramas)? ||294||
Even in the forest, faults arise for those possessed by passion; even in the home, the restraint of the five senses is asceticism.
For one who engages in blameless actions and is free from desire, his very home is a grove of asceticism.

For those whose lives are earned through virtuous deeds and righteousness, who are always content and delight in their own homes, who have conquered their senses, who are fond of guests, and who remain established in dharma and discipline even within the household— (296)
Liberation is not for one intent on the science of grammar, nor for one intent on attachment to the [four] castes;
it is not for one devoted solely to food and clothing, nor for one intent on adopting the ways of the world.

For one who is singular in virtue, firm in his vows, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses, whose mind is absorbed in internal yoga, and who is eternally non-violent, liberation is certain. (298)
He sleeps in happiness and awakens in happiness—he whose mind is awakened and remains equanimous toward all beings. (299)
One does not travel happily by means of a bad horse, nor does one travel happily by means of a braying camel;
just as one travels happily on the great road when one has disciplined oneself. (300)
Hari does not act when touched, nor does a serpent even when greatly provoked, nor an enemy when not enraged, just as the Self does not act when devoid of the ego (ahaṃkāra). ||301||
They say that this "Yama" is indeed the Self; it is called the Self because by means of it one restrains (yamyate), and thus it is distinguished as Yama. ||302||
It is said that "this one is Yama," yet people tremble before him in vain;
for what can Yama do to one who has realized that the Self is indeed Yama? 303.
There is constant fear from flesh-eating beings and from those who are unrestrained; for the purpose of restraining them, the rod of punishment was created by the Self-existent One. (304)
The rod protects all beings; the rod guards the subjects;
the rod restrains the most wicked; indeed, the rod is invincible. (305)
Dark-complexioned, youthful, and red-eyed, he brings fear to all beings;
Punishment is the ruler of men, upon whom Dharma is established. (306)
Now, among all the stages of life (āśramas), self-restraint (dama) alone is the supreme vow.
I shall describe those characteristics by which self-restraint is proclaimed.
Freedom from meanness, absence of harshness, contentment, proper conduct, lack of envy, honoring the guru, compassion for all beings, and freedom from backbiting. (308)
O King, it has been declared by the six sages of tranquil intellect that dharma and liberation, as well as heaven, depend upon compassion and self-restraint. (309)
One who is not provoked by insult and does not rejoice in honor, remaining steadfast in both suffering and happiness—that wise one is called "enduring" (titikṣu). //310//
For one who sleeps in peace wakes up in peace;
therefore, it is better to remain [in patience], for the scorner perishes. (311)
One should never contemplate the sin of one who has shown disrespect;
moreover, having regard for one's own duty, one should not find fault with the duty of another. (312)
One should know oneself and not reproach others for their faults,
whether they be deficient in mantras, in ritual actions, or even by birth.
Self-control covers everything, just as a cloth covers a defective limb;
those who do not understand self-control study it in vain.
This is indeed the root of sacred learning: self-restraint is the eternal dharma.
For he who weighs his own self-restraint against gold on a scale [is truly wise]. (315)
One who possesses steadfastness is renowned, but not one who is deluded by material wealth;
indeed, among all vows, self-restraint alone is the supreme goal. (316)
Even if a twice-born man has studied the six Vedāṅgas and knows the true meaning of the Vedas, if he is devoid of self-restraint, he does not attain honor in this world. (317)
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of self-restraint, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences;
likewise, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, noble lineage, birth, and ritual bathing at sacred fords are all useless [for such a person]. (318)
The knower of yoga should find satisfaction in insult as if it were nectar;
the twice-born man should always loathe honor as if it were poison. (19)
Through disrespect, ascetic merit increases; through honor, ascetic merit perishes.
A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped departs like a cow that has been milked dry.
Just as a cow is restored by water and grass,
so too is a twice-born man restored by means of recitations and burnt offerings.
In this world, there exists no friend equal to one who takes upon himself another's misdeeds and gives his own merit to that person. (322)
One should not revile those who revile; one should turn back one's own anger.
By thus restraining oneself, one sprinkles oneself with immortality.
An alms bowl, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude, indifference, and the practice of celibacy lead one to the supreme goal. (324)
Having utterly conquered desire and anger, what need will there be for the forest?
Indeed, the Veda is maintained by practice, and the family by character. (325)
Mantras are sustained by virtues; anger is sustained by courage. He who restrains the anger that has arisen within himself— //326//
The hero should conquer with non-anger; who on earth is equal to him?
He who, when anger has arisen, restrains it and remains steadfast. (327)
The man who sits upon this, considering it to be the most excellent essence—
that is the secret of the Grandfather (Brahmā), the eternal Lord of Brahmā.
Indeed, that lack of fixed rule regarding dharma which has been extensively declared by me—there are worlds for those who perform sacrifices that are distinct from those for the ascetics. ||329||
O people, these alone are most highly honored among those who have descended to this world:
for those who possess forgiveness, there is one fault, and a second does not exist. (330)
When people consider one who is endowed with patience to be powerless, this should not be regarded as a fault; for patience is the strength of those possessed of wisdom. (331)
He who understands tranquility is honored for his sacrifices and charitable works;
whereas that which one who is possessed by anger mutters, offers as oblation, or worships [is of no avail]. (332)
Just as water in a broken jar becomes entirely tainted, so too does one who rises in the morning and recites this meritorious chapter [become purified]. 333.
Having boarded the ship of the True Dharma, he shall cross over all difficulties;
a twice-born man should constantly cause this meritorious chapter on self-restraint to be heard.
One attains the world of Brahmā and does not fall from there again. Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be held fast. (335)
One should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself;
one should regard the wives of others as one's own mother and the property of others as a clod of earth. (336)
He who sees all beings as himself truly sees;
for his cooking is for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva offering, and his very life is for the sake of others. (337)
O King, having studied this—which is the welfare of all beings—one partakes of the nectar of immortality; it becomes one's entire possession, just as gold is the essence of all minerals. (338)
Having thus explained the entirety of the heterodox doctrines to Śunahsakha,
they all, together with him, settled down on the bank of the lake.
Seeing a very extensive lake covered with lotuses and water-lilies,
they descended into it and gathered the lotus stalks in bundles.
Having cast their water-pot on the bank, they performed the meritorious water-libation rites;
then, having emerged from that water, they gathered together with one another.
I saw these lotus stalks and spoke these words.
The sages said:
"By whom [were they taken] from us, who are tormented by hunger and of sinful deeds? (342)
Fearing that the lotus stalks had been carried away by a cruel army seeking food,
those best of the twice-born questioned one another.
O King, they all made it their path toward the Lord;
Kaśyapa said:
"May he take everything everywhere, and may he effect the omission of the ritual deposit. (344)
He who gives false testimony, he who steals lotus stalks, he who practices unrighteousness, and he who serves a king—[these all go to the same state]. (345)
He who eats honey and meat, commits theft of lotus stalks, always speaks falsehood, and indulges in sensual pleasures; ||346||
"Let him who steals lotus stalks give his daughter for a bride-price.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Let him engage in sexual intercourse with a woman during her courses, and let him indulge in sleeping during the day. (347)
He who commits the theft of lotus stalks incurs the state of being mutual guests;
such a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman shall dwell in a village that has but a single well. 348.
"May he who steals lotus stalks attain the same world as that [deity].
Bharadvāja said:
May he be cruel toward all beings, and may he be possessed of great prosperity and ego. (349)
May he who steals the lotus stalks be both envious and slanderous;
may he who reviles me be reviled in return, and he who strikes me strike another. (350)
He who sells poison and he who commits theft of lotus stalks;
Gautama said:
and he who, upon the arrival of a guest, practices partiality in cooking. (351)
He who constantly eats the food of a Śūdra, commits theft of lotus stalks, boasts of gifts received, and takes pleasure in the wife or son of another; 352.
"He who eats his favorite food all alone commits the theft of the lotus stalks.
Viśvāmitra said:
"May he be eternally devoted to desire and engage in sexual intercourse even during the daytime! (353)
He who constantly commits sins, steals lotus stalks, utters slander against others, and consorts with the wives of others; ||354||
He who steals the lotus stalks from another's pond treats his mother and father with contempt; he is a man of evil mind. (355)

He who steals lotus stalks while harboring the notion that they belong to someone else, he who always eats the food of another, and he who serves the wife of another—[these three] would be equal [in sin]. (356)
He who sells the Vedas and he who commits the theft of lotus stalks—Jamadagni said:
"In birth after birth, may he become a servant to others. (357)
"He who steals even a blade of grass is devoid of all righteous action.
Śunasakha said: "A householder should study the Vedas according to the rules and be fond of guests. (358)
Let him speak the truth constantly; let him commit the theft of lotus stalks;
let him offer oblations into the fire according to the rules, and let him perform sacrifices perpetually. (359)
"He who goes to the abode of Brahmā commits the theft of the lotus-stalks.
The sages said:
"This which has been made a solemn oath is indeed desired by the twice-born."
"O friend of Śunaḥ, you have committed the theft of the lotus stalks for all of us.
Śunaḥsakha said:
"O birds, these lotus stalks were indeed destroyed by me. (361)
O best of sages, you who desire to hear the Dharma, know me to be Vāsava; through non-attachment, we have conquered the imperishable worlds. (362)
"Take possession of the celestial chariot; let us go to the abode of the thirty gods.
Then those great seers, having understood [his intent], departed for Amarāvatī.
Those experts in speech spoke these words to Purandara:
"A man who, having come here, enters the middle Puṣkara, [attains the highest state]. (364)
Having fasted for three nights, one should obtain the necessary fruit;
this is remembered as being equivalent to a twelve-year initiation for those dwelling in the forest.
O destroyer of Māra, there is no doubt that one obtains the complete fruit of that [merit];
such a person does not fall into an evil rebirth, but rejoices together with their own retinue in heaven. (366)
Having reached the abode of Viriñci, they remained there for a day of Brahmā.
Pulastya said:
Then, filled with joy, they went together with Indra to Triviṣṭapa. 367.
Thus being enticed here by various kinds of temptations, they did not yield to greed at all; therefore, they went to the third heaven.
Whoever should constantly hear this auspicious life-story of the sages, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world. ||369||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue with the Seven Sages," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(20) The twentieth chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
This story is exceedingly wonderful, beautiful, and destructive of evil;
tell it to me in detail and according to the truth, as I am asking you.
The greatness of the middle [caste] has been proclaimed by the sages;
the fruit of food has been told, as well as the greatness of *dama* (self-restraint).
O great sage, tell me how Viṣṇu set foot there,
and likewise describe exactly how the birth of the youngest [brother] occurred.
Pulastya said: In a former age, O Ratha, there was a king named Puṣpavāhana,
renowned throughout the worlds and equal to the sun in splendor.
O descendant of Bharata, O King, being pleased by his ascetic penance, the four-faced Brahmā gave him a golden lotus that could travel wherever he desired.
He constantly wandered at will through the world of seven islands;
however, at the beginning of the kalpa, his island was equal to that of the dweller of Puṣkara.
Therefore, Puṣkaradvīpa is called "honored by the world";
that very lotus-vehicle was given to him by Brahmā.
Therefore, the gods and the dānavas call him Puṣpavāhana;
indeed, there is no comparison for that king even here in the three worlds, nor for him who dwells within the lotus of Brahmā.
Then, by the power of his asceticism, the queen— whom thousands of women were praising—
became known as Acalāvaṇyavatī, who was as beloved by Bhava as Pārvatī herself.
He had ten thousand sons who were righteous-souled and skilled archers;
beholding those sons of his, the king was filled with wonder again and again.

To the preeminent sage Pracetas, who had arrived and was worthy of worship, he spoke these words: "From what cause has this prosperity arisen, which is honored by immortals and mortals alike and is like that of the lotus-born Brahmā? And how is it that you are a king of such noble character? (11)
