The sage Dadhīci granted me a palace of emeralds, which was bestowed by the Creator who was not fully satisfied with my wife’s meager asceticism;
for even when a hundred million kings, accompanied by their ministers, elephants, chariot-arrays, and retinues, have entered it, [it remains spacious].
It is not perceived where it has gone even by the hosts of stars moving through the sky, for it is inaccessible even to those with rays of difficult-to-withstand light.
Therefore, what else could have been performed by one born from the womb of a mother that transcends all people—namely, Dharma and so forth? (13)
"O Pracetas, tell all of that—whether by me, or by my sons, or even by this virtuous wife.
Then he replied: "O Lord of the Earth, behold the son of Bhava; hear the account of the cause of that wonder. (14)
Your birth occurred even in the family of a hunter, which is terrible; you yourself have become a daily perpetrator of foul sins.
Furthermore, O father, your body has become like that of a common being—possessing ill-smelling limbs and adorned with deformed nails. (15)
Neither your friend, nor your sons, nor your kinsmen, nor such a sister, nor even your mother was ever so accused; yet she,
who was highly esteemed and most beloved, now stands before you.
O Lord of the Earth, this beautiful woman has been born for you. ||16||
Once, there occurred an exceedingly terrible drought;
when you were afflicted by hunger on account of food in that [time], you gave.
Some forest fruits and other such food that has been obtained. ||17||
Then he beheld a great, excellent lake, rich in lotuses and its banks surrounded by mud;
thereupon, he took many lotuses from it.
He indeed went to the city named Diśā. ||18||
Then, in order to obtain its price, you wandered through the entire city for the whole day;
yet no buyer at all arose among those born of the lotus.
Exhausted and extremely tormented by hunger. ||19||
Seated alone with your wife in the courtyard of your residence,
you then heard the sound of auspicious music there during the night.
Accompanied by his wife, he went to that place where the sound of auspicious chanting was heard;
there, he beheld the image of Viṣṇu situated in the center of the mandala.
Veśyānaṅgavatī, having observed the vow of the twelfth day,
completed it on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha by offering a mountain of salt.
Having adorned Hṛṣīkeśa with a golden image equal [in size] to himself, he respectfully presented it, along with a bed provided with all its furnishings, to his guru.
Then, having seen this, those two reflected:
"What is the use of these lotuses? It would be better for Viṣṇu to be adorned [with them]. (24)
O Lord of Men, at that time such devotion arose toward the couple;
through that association, they worshipped Keśava as the Salt Mountain (Lavaṇācala).
The bed was worshipped on all sides with scattered heaps of flowers;
then Anaṅgavatī, being pleased, gave them a hundred measures of grain there.
Then he commanded, "Let three palas of gold be given";
however, because of his great courage and strength, it was not accepted by the two of them. (27)
Then Anaṅgavatī brought four kinds of food for the two of them and said, "O King, let this consecrated food be eaten. (28)
They both said this as well: "O fair-faced one, we shall eat tomorrow;
moreover, fasting today on this occasion will bring auspiciousness. (29)
O Goddess of firm vows, we two have been most sinful since birth;
yet, through association with you, may there be at least a trace of dharma here in your abode.
Thus, the vigil was performed by the two of them in connection with that [rite].
And at dawn, a salt-mountain bed was offered by her.
And out of devotion to the Guru, he should give a village to the Brahmins; likewise, twelve cows adorned with garments, ornaments, and gold.
And he provided food for his friends, well-wishers, the poor, and the wretched;
having honored that couple, who were free from greed, he dismissed them. (33)
By virtue of that multitude of lotuses and the worship of Keśava, the lord of men was born as the king Sabhāvat along with his wife. ||34||
O King, because of the greatness of that truth and through his austerity free from greed, all your sins have been destroyed and your body has become most auspicious. (35)
The Lord of the World, the Four-faced One, being well-pleased, bestowed upon you a vehicle that travels at will; therefore, take refuge in this Puṣkara, the sovereign king of hymns. (36)
O King of Kings, having encountered this twelfth-day vow of Vibhūti which brings about the welfare of sentient beings, you will certainly attain nirvāṇa within a single kalpa.
Having spoken thus, the sage vanished right there;
and King Puṣpavāhana performed everything exactly as he had been told.
O King, for one who performs this in whatever manner possible throughout time, there shall be the state of unbroken observance of the twelve Dvādaśīs, O Ruler. (39)
O King, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the gods and Brahmins according to one's capacity;
cows should be given in the case of the eldest [rite], and excellent land in the case of the middle one. 40.
A small amount of gold should be given; this is remembered as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The first [oblation] has Brahmā as its deity, and the second likewise belongs to Viṣṇu.

The third [chapter] has Rudra as its presiding deity; the three gods are established in the three [worlds]. Whoever recites this, which tears away the impurities of people, or listens to it with devotion, [attains the highest state]. ||42||
Furthermore, O Atideva, he dwells in the world of the gods for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme vow among all vows. (43)
That Rudra has declared this destroyer of great sins:
by practicing [this vow] at night for one year, even a wife who wears the hem of her husband's garment [attains the goal]. 44.
One should give a golden discus and trident, as well as two garments, to a Brahmin;
he who performs such meritorious deeds rejoices in the world of Śiva. ||45||
This very vow is called the destroyer of great sins;
he who, by means of a single meal, should offer a cow together with a bull [performs it]. (46)
One should give a cow made of sesame seeds; one attains the state of Śaṅkara along with his attendants.
This is known as the Rudra-vrata, which destroys fear and sorrow. 47.
And whoever offers a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar, it is equal to fasting for one night and day while observing the vow of truth. ||48||
This is known as the Nīlavrata, which leads one to the abode of Viṣṇu;
during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a man should avoid oil massage.
One should provide food and utensils for the abode of Hari;
this, which brings joy to people, is called the Prīti-vrata here.
Having avoided liquor, one should offer curd, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice;
one should also give fine garments together with a vessel for juices.
Having worshipped a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Gaurī be pleased," this is known as the Gaurī-vrata, which bestows the world of Bhavānī. (52)
On the thirteenth day of the month of Puṣya and others, having observed the practice of eating only at night (naktavrata),
one should then give a golden Aśoka flower, ten finger-breadths in length, accompanied by sugarcane.
Having given [this] along with a garment to a Brahmin, saying "May Pradyumna be pleased," one shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu for a kalpa and then become free from sorrow once again, O King. (54)
This is known as the Kāmavrata, which eternally destroys sorrow;
he who, during the vow beginning in Āṣāḍha, should avoid eating fruit.

When the Cāturmāsya vow has concluded, one should present a jar filled with ghee and jaggery on the full moon day of Kārttika; furthermore, that [jar] should be made of gold and offered to a Brāhmaṇa.
He attains the world of Rudra; this is remembered as the Śiva-vrata.
He who avoids flowers during the spring, summer, and winter seasons [attains this]. (57)
Having fashioned three flowers from gold according to one's means on the full moon day of Phālguna, one should offer them at the two junctions of the day; may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
Having given [this gift], one goes to the supreme state; this is known as the Saumya-vrata.
He who avoids salt on the third lunar day beginning with Phālguna [attains the same]. (59)
One should provide a level bed and a house furnished with household utensils, having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Bhavānī be pleased."

Having observed silence during the three junctions [of the day] and having offered a pot of ghee on the full moon day, that man shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa; this is called the Saubhāgya-vrata.
Having crossed the Laṅghaṭā, one should present a pair of garments to a Brāhmaṇa;
such a person goes to the world of Sarasvatī, from which return is difficult to attain.
This is known as the Sārasvata [rite], which bestows knowledge of names and forms;
having worshipped Lakṣmī, a man should observe a fast on the fifth lunar day.
One should give a golden lotus together with a cow on that same day;
he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu and shall possess prosperity in birth after birth.
This vow named Lakṣmīvrata is the destroyer of suffering and grief;
having performed the anointing of the ground before Śambhu and Keśava, [one should observe it].
Furthermore, for as many years as one gives a cow and likewise a water-pot,
that person shall be a king for ten thousand births, and thereafter shall go to the city of Śiva.
This is the vow known as Āyurvrata, which bestows all desires;
having prostrated before the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā with a one-pointed mind, [one should perform it]. (67)
A man free from envy should observe the vow of eating only one meal a day for one year;
he should worship a Brahmin couple along with three cows as part of this vow.
Whoever should eat a golden tree would obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
this is the vow named Kīrtivratam, which bestows the fruit of prosperity and fame. (69)
Having performed the ceremonial bath with ghee while reciting the *Śambhoḥ* or *Keśavasya* [mantras], and having prepared a circle of cow-dung together with unbroken rice grains and flowers; 70.
One should give a level golden lotus together with a cow, along with a trident eight finger-breadths in length; such a person is glorified in the world of Śiva.
The chanting of the Sāman hymns is here called the Sāma-vrata;
having taken a single meal on the ninth lunar day, one should also honor virgins according to one's ability.
Having fed [the Brahmins], one should give a golden vessel along with seven horses;
and by giving a golden lion to a Brahmin, one shall go to the abode of Śiva.
One will be free from birth-defects, handsome, and unconquered by enemies;
this is known as the Vīra-vrata, which bestows happiness upon men. (74)
Filled with compassion, one should offer water for the four months beginning with Caitra;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a maṇika-pitcher of water, along with food and clothing. (75)
One who offers a vessel of sesame seeds and gold is honored in the world of Brahmā; for as many eons as there are grains, one attains prosperity and birth—this is called the *mānada* vow. (76)
O Lord, having performed the ritual bathing with the five nectars for one year,
one should then give a cow accompanied by the five nectars at the end of that year.
One should give a conch shell to a Brahmin; he attains the state of Śaṅkara.
He becomes a king for a kalpa; this is remembered as the dhṛti-vrata.
Having avoided me, a man should become a giver of cows while observing those vows;
likewise, he who gives a golden deer shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
It is said that one who observes this vow shall become a lord of the earth for a kalpa;
having risen at dawn and performed his bath, he should worship the Lord of the Discus (Viṣṇu).
Having fed [the deity] according to one's ability and honored them with garlands, garments, and ornaments, one shall dwell in the world of the Sun for a kalpa; this is known as the Sūryavrata. ||81||
A man who bathes at dawn during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha,
and gives a meal to a Brahmin on the full moon day of Kārtika, becomes a giver of cows.
This is known as the Viṣṇu-vrata; by it one attains the station of Viṣṇu.
From one solstice until the next, one should avoid flowers and clarified butter.
Having given at its conclusion flowers, food, and a cow made of ghee, along with ghee and milk-rice to a Brahmin, one goes to the abode of Śiva. (84)
This is known as the vow of conduct (*śīlavrata*), which bestows the fruits of virtue and health;
it belongs to one who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*) on the fifteenth day for as long as it may last. (85)
The performer of the śrāddha should give five milch cows of equal age, along with saffron-colored garments and water-pots. (86)
He shall eternally go to the world of Viṣṇu and deliver a hundred of his ancestors. ||87||
This is remembered as the vow for the ancestors of the king of kings, performed for ten kalpas;
he who offers a lamp at twilight should use ghee and avoid oil.
One should offer a lamp on the full moon day, along with a golden wheel and trident, and a pair of garments to a Brahmin; such a man shall become radiant.
One attains the world of Rudra; this is known as the Dīpti-vrata.
On the third lunar day of the month beginning with Kārttika, one should consume cow’s urine and barley-gruel (yāvaka).
One should observe this vow at night for one year; at the end of the year, one becomes a giver of a cow.
One shall dwell in the world of Gaurī for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
This observance known as the Rudra-vrata always brings about auspiciousness;
he who avoids perfumes and ointments for four months [attains its fruit]. (92)
One should give oyster-shell, perfume, and unbroken rice, along with two white garments, to a Brahmin;
one who maintains this firm vow attains the station of Varuṇa—this is what is remembered.
Furthermore, one who gives a cow should avoid flowers and salt during the month of Vaiśākha;
having resided for a kalpa at the foot of Viṣṇu, he shall become a king in this world.
This vow named Śānti bestows the fruit of fame and desired objects;
having fashioned a golden Brahmāṇḍa accompanied by a heap of sesame seeds, [one should give it]. 95.
Having become a giver of other [gifts] with clarified butter, he should satisfy the fire and the virtuous twice-born;
and having honored the wife of the brahmin with garlands, garments, and ornaments. (96)

According to one's capacity, on an auspicious day, one should give [the gift] weighing more than three palas, saying, "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased. On another [occasion], by means of the Brahma [gift], one goes to the state beyond rebirth.
This is called the Brahma-vow, which bestows the fruit of Nirvana upon men;
and he who gives a cow with two faces, endowed with all abundant qualities, [attains that same fruit]. (98)
One should observe the milk-vow for a day; by doing so, one goes to the supreme state.
This is indeed called the *suvrata* (the excellent vow), from which return is difficult to attain. 99.
Having observed the vow of subsisting on milk for three days, one should offer a golden wish-fulfilling tree weighing more than a *pala*,
accompanied by a *prastha* of rice according to one's capacity.
Having given this, one goes to the state of Brahmā; this is remembered as the Bhīmavrata.
He who, having fasted for a month, gives a beautiful cow to a Brahmin, [attains the same]. (101)
This is remembered as the Bhīmavrata, which leads one to the station of Viṣṇu;
having fashioned a golden image of the Earth, one should give it weighing more than twenty palas.
One who remains for a day observing the vow of milk is glorified in the world of Rudra;
this is declared to be the bestower of wealth, following one for seven hundred kalpas.
In the month of Māgha or Caitra, one should become a giver of a cow made of jaggery;
by this "jaggery-vow" on the third lunar day, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī. (104)
This is indeed the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), which produces supreme bliss;
he who observes the fast for a fortnight and gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin [attains this]. (105)
Worshipped by gods and asuras, he attains the world of Brahmā;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall be a universal monarch—this is remembered as the Prabhāvrata.
One who eats only one meal a day for a year and gives food and a water-pot shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is known as the Prāpti-vrata.
One who gives a milch cow on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina for a full year attains Paurandara;
this is called the Sugati-vrata.
He who bestows wealth upon the foremost of Brahmins during the four seasons beginning with spring,
and he who gives a cow of ghee, goes to the Supreme Brahman.
The vow known as Vaiśvānara destroys all sins;
he who, eating only at night on the eleventh day, should offer a discus [to the deity]. (110)
Having performed this for me, he shall attain the golden abode of Viṣṇu;
this is known as the Kṛṣṇa-vrata, which grants the attainment of a kingdom at the end of the kalpa.
He who eats milk-rice and gives a pair of cows to a Brahmin shall dwell in the world of Lakṣmī for a kalpa; this is remembered as the Devī-vrata. ||112||
On the seventh lunar day, one should eat only at night and, upon completion, give a milch cow;
one thus attains the world of the Sun—this is remembered as the Bhānu-vrata.
On the fourth day, one who eats only at night should likewise give gold and a pair of bulls;
this is known as the Vaināyaka vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Śiva. (114)

He who, having renounced great rewards during the four-month period, gives golden [gifts] to a twice-born man in the month of Kārttika, as well as a pair of cows at the conclusion of the fire-oblation; ||115||
O King, this is known as the Saura-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the solar world;
he who completes twelve Dvādaśīs by fasting [on each] attains it.
A man should worship the Brahmins with cows, garments, and gold according to his capacity;
he attains the supreme state—this is remembered as the Viṣṇu-vrata.
One who eats only at night on the fourteenth day and gives a pair of cattle at the end of the month attains the state of Śiva; this is remembered as the Trayodaśī-vratakam. ||118||
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man;
they call this the "Excellent Vow," which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā. (119)
Having reached Āśī, he who gives a milch cow shall dwell in the world of Śakra for a kalpa; this is remembered as the mantra-vow.
Having completely abandoned even the face, one becomes a bestower of light.
One attains the world of Varuṇa; this is called the Vāruṇa vow.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa fast and offer a golden moon;
this is declared to be the Candra-vrata, which bestows the fruit of the lunar world. ||122||
He who practices the five-fold austerity in the month of Jyeṣṭha and gives away a golden cow goes to heaven;
this is remembered as the Rudra-vrata on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days.
One should perform the single rite on the third lunar day in a temple of Śiva; upon its completion, a cow should be given as a gift—this is called the Bhavānī-vrata. 124.
On the night of Māgha, one should wear wet clothes; on the seventh day, one should become a giver of limbs. Having worn [wet clothes] for two days, one becomes a king; this is the Pavana-vrata.
Having fasted for three nights, one should give a beautiful mansion on the full moon day of Phālguna;
one attains the world of the Sun—this is remembered as the Dhāma-vrata.
By worshipping the divine couple at the three junctions of the day while observing a fast and adorning them with ornaments, one attains liberation;
this is known as the vow of liberation (mokṣavrata). ||127||
Having given a vessel of salt on the second day of the dark fortnight,
one who gives a cow at its conclusion goes to the auspicious abode of Śiva for a kalpa.
Likewise, at the conclusion, one who gives a golden vessel with cloth and accompanied by a royal gift, as well as a cow,
goes to the eternal abode of Śiva.
By this, one becomes a king of kings for a thousand kalpas; this is known as the Somavrata.
Eating only one meal on the first lunar day (pratipad), it bestows its fruit upon completion. 130.
This is known as the Śikhivrata, which leads one to the state of Vaiśvānara;
it consists of a golden chariot weighing more than two palas and yoked with a pair of horses.
Having observed the fast, one should give [the gift]; he shall dwell for a hundred divine kalpas, and at the end of that, he shall become a king of kings—this is remembered as the Aśva-vrata.
Likewise, a king who gives a golden chariot joined with two elephants shall dwell in Satyaloka for a thousand kalpas.
Having come here to this earth, one should observe this vow known as the "Sprout" (Aṅkura-vrata).
Eating only a single meal on the tenth day, at its conclusion, one should give ten cows. 134.
One who gives a lamp made of gold shall become the sovereign of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa);
this is known as the Viśvavrata, which destroys even the greatest sins. 135.
He who shall perform the gift of a daughter in marriage at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika will go to the world of Brahmā, endowed with twenty-one virtues. ||136||
There is no gift anywhere superior to the gift of a daughter in marriage;
this is especially so at Puṣkara, and particularly on the full moon day of Kārttika.
It should be given to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite; for them, there shall be no end to their worlds.
Having fashioned an elephant out of sesame flour, endowed with jewels— ||138||
Those men who, standing in the midst of water, offer [libations] to a Brahmin, for them there shall be an imperishable world until the dissolution of all beings. 139.
Whoever should read or even hear this unsurpassed Vrataṣaṣṭhī shall become the lord of the Gandharvas for a hundred Manvantaras.

O best of kings, this meritorious Ṣaṣṭhī-vrata, beneficial to all people, has been declared to you today; if you wish to hear it, O noble one, listen to what must be performed by the twice-born. (141)
Purity and the purification of the inner being do not exist without bathing;
therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, bathing is prescribed at the outset. (142)
One should perform the ritual bath with water that has either been drawn out or not drawn out;
the wise knower of mantras should designate the sacred site (tīrtha) by means of the root mantra. 143.
"Salutation to Nārāyaṇa"—thus the root mantra is proclaimed.
With darbha grass in hand, having sipped water according to the rule, he should be self-controlled and pure. (144)
Then, having fashioned a level square measuring four cubits,
the wise practitioner should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras.
Born from the foot of Viṣṇu, auspicious, belonging to Viṣṇu, and having Viṣṇu as her deity—save us from that sin which extends from birth until death! 146.
Vāyu declared that there are three and a half crores of sacred fords;
O Jāhnavī, these exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
She is named Naṃdinī among the gods, and Nalinī as well; she is Dakṣā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, and Asitā. (148)
Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, as well as Lokaprasādinī, Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī. ||149||
One should recite these names of merit at the time of bathing;
there, the Ganges that flows through the three paths becomes present. 150.
Having joined the palms together, one should sprinkle water upon the head three, four, five, or seven times, after it has been consecrated with the mantra recited seven times.
Likewise, one should perform the bath with earth after addressing it according to the ritual injunction:
"O Earth, you who are stepped upon by horses, stepped upon by chariots, and stepped upon by Viṣṇu! (152)
O Earth, take away this sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me;
you were raised up by the boar Varāha, by Kṛṣṇa of a hundred arms.
"Salutations to you, O source of all worlds, O goddess of excellent vows!
Having bathed in this manner, one should thereafter perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules. (154)
Having risen and put on two pure, bright garments,
he should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the nourishment of the three worlds.
First, one should satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Prajāpatis;
as well as the gods, yakṣas, nāgas, and the hosts of gandharvas and apsarases. (156)
Cruel serpents, birds of prey, trees, jambhakas and the like, vidyādharas, clouds, and likewise those who travel through the sky; ||157||
And for those living beings who have no support, and those who are devoted to sinful ways—for their nourishment, this water is offered by me. (158)
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, one should then wear it around the neck (nivītī);
then, with devotion, one should satisfy the humans, as well as the sons of the sages and the sages themselves.
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha. ||160||
May they all always attain satisfaction through the water offered by me:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
One should satisfy Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada, as well as all the divine and brahminical ṛṣis, with water mixed with unbroken grains. (162)
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and the left knee upon the ground,
[he should offer to] the Agniṣvātta, the Saumya, the Barhiṣmat, and the Uṣmapā [ancestors].
Furthermore, one should devoutly satisfy the Sukālins, the Barhiṣads, and the Ājyapas—
these ancestors— with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste.
Then, with darbha grass in his hand, he should satisfy his own ancestors according to the rule,
[addressing] the father and others by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfather and others.
Having gratified them according to the prescribed rite with devotion, one should utter this mantra:
"Those who were my kinsmen or non-kinsmen, and those who were my kinsmen in other births... (166)
Those who desire our water, even if they have not yet attained full satisfaction,
should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) properly according to the rules and draw a lotus in front of them.
One should diligently offer the *arghya* with water containing raw rice grains, flowers, sesame seeds, and red sandalwood, while reciting the names of the Sun. (168)
Salutations to you of universal form; salutations to you who take the form of Viṣṇu. Salutations to you, O God of all; be gracious to me, O Bhāskara.
"Salutations to you, O Maker of Day; salutations to you, O Maker of Light.
Having thus paid homage to the Sun and having circumambulated him three times, [he should proceed]. (170)
Having seen and touched the golden image marked with two birds, one should go home;
then, one should worship the meritorious image situated in one's own house. 171.
After that, one should cause the meal to be served, beginning with the twice-born.
By this procedure, all the ṛṣis attained perfection. 172.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bathing," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(21) The Twenty-First Chapter.
Pulastya said:
In former times, during the Bṛhatkalpa, there was a lord of men named Dharmamūrti,
who was a friend of Śakra and by whom thousands of Daityas were slain.
By whose splendor the moon, the sun, and others have their radiance eclipsed by the hundreds, and by whom the Dānavas have been utterly defeated; ||2||
He was unconquered, capable of assuming any form at will, and though human, possessed extraordinary power;
his wife was Bhānumatī, a virtuous woman who was the most beautiful in the three worlds.
With a form like that of Lakṣmī, she surpassed even the celestial nymphs;
she was dearer than life itself to that king, his chief queen. (4)
In the midst of ten thousand women, Śrī shines like a king;
she is never surpassed by even ten million kings. (5)
Once, while seated in his assembly hall,
he, overcome with wonder, bowed down to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, and questioned his own domestic priest.
"O Blessed One, by what dharma is my fortune unsurpassed?
And why is there always such vast and supreme splendor in my body? (7)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Formerly, there was a woman named Līlāvatī who was devoted to Śiva, though not a courtesan;
on the fourteenth lunar day, she offered a mountain of salt to him at Puṣkara.
Then the Śūdra and the goldsmith became performers of the ritual together with the Hemavṛkṣa deities, according to the rules and in the prescribed manner. 9.
O King, by this servant in the house of Līlāvatī, trees made of gold and bearing golden flowers were fashioned with great devotion.
Endowed with exceeding beauty, well-fashioned, and most splendid,
they were not taken as wages, for it was known that they were for the sake of religious duty.
O King, golden trees were set ablaze and placed within the apartments of Līlāvatī for her service.
O sinless one, through those two [sons] and by serving the twice-born without guile, that prostitute Līlāvatī, in the course of time, [attained her goal]. (13)
Freed from all evil, he went to the auspicious abode;
he who was that goldsmith, though poor, possessed of exceeding virtue. (14)
Having now taken an immeasurable price from a courtesan, I have become the lord of the seven continents, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. (15)
This Bhānumatī here is the wife of the goldsmith Yayāsu, by whom these [ornaments] fashioned from gold were perfectly polished. 16.
Therefore, you shall be unconquered in the worlds of men, endowed with health, good fortune, and immovable prosperity;
therefore, O King, you should perform the rites concerning the mountain of grain and other such offerings according to the prescribed injunctions. (17)
Pulastya said:

"So be it," replied he whose form is the embodiment of dharma; having honored Vasiṣṭha's words, he bestowed all the mountains of grain and other gifts according to the prescribed rite for the Enemy of Smara (Śiva). Honored by the gods, he departed for that world.

If one should see these [images] being brought forward, touch them when they are being offered by men here, or hear of them with devotion and fix one's mind upon them, even such a person, freed from sin, goes to heaven. (19)
A person attains the pacification of bad dreams by reciting these Kings of Mountains, which shatter the fear of existence;
what then need be said of one who would properly perform this, O bull among kings?
The tranquil-souled one [performed] the gift of all the lords of mountains. ||20||
Bhīṣma said:

Is it fasting or a vow that can uproot the fire of grief born from separation from what is desired? And for a man on this earth, what is there that brings about stable prosperity and even destroys the fear of worldly existence? 21.
Pulastya said:
"This which you have asked is dear to the world, yet difficult even for the gods to obtain because of its greatness;
nevertheless, because of your devotion, I shall describe this secret vow among Indra, the asuras, and human beings."
In the month of Āśvayuja, there is the meritorious Viśoka-dvādaśī vow; on the tenth day, the wise man, eating light food, should begin it with self-restraint. (23)
Facing either north or east, having first cleansed his teeth,
he should remain without food on the eleventh day, having properly worshipped Keśava.
Having worshipped Śrī according to the prescribed rites, I shall eat on the following day;
thus, having made this vow and slept, the man rises in the morning.
One should perform a bath with all medicinal herbs and with the water of the five products of the cow;
wearing white garlands and fine garments, one should worship the Lord of Śrī with blue lotuses.
Salutations to Viśoka at the feet; salutations to the Bestower of Boons at the shanks; likewise, salutations to Śrīśāya at the knees and to Jalaśāyin at the thighs.
"Salutation to Kandarpa for the secret parts; salutation to Mādhava for the hips;
[salutation] to Dāmodara for the belly, and to Vipula for the sides. (28)

Salutations to the one with a lotus-navel for the navel; salutations to the one who possesses the god of love for the heart; salutations to the bearer of Śrī for the chest of the Lord; salutations to the slayer of Madhu for the hands. 29.
Salutation to Vaikuṇṭha for the Ka and Ṭha [phonemes], and to the lotus-faced one for the mouth; salutation to Aśokanidhi for the nose, and to Vāsudeva for the two eyes.
One should offer the forehead to Vāmana, the two eyebrows again to Hari,
the curls to Mādhava, and the crown to Viśvarūpin.
"Salutation to the Soul of All; O Lord, this is Your head"—with these words one should worship.
Having thus worshipped Govinda with incense, garlands, and ointments, [one should proceed]. (32)
Then, having prepared the site, one should fashion a leveled altar out of clay;
it should be square, even, a cubit in measure, and sloping toward the north.
The parapet should be smooth, pleasing to the heart, and completely surrounded by a railing;
the height of the parapet is three finger-breadths, and its width is two finger-breadths.
Above the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), there should be a wall eight finger-breadths high;
upon it, one should place an image of Lakṣmī made from river sand.
On the sacrificial ground, the wise man should worship Lakṣmī, who resides in the center of the sun:
"Salutation to the Goddess, salutation to Peace, salutation to Lakṣmī, salutation to Śrī. (36)
Salutations to Tuṣṭi, salutations to Puṣṭi; salutations again and again to Sṛṣṭi and Dṛṣṭi. O Viśokā, you who destroy suffering, salutations to you, the bestower of boons.
"May there be freedom from sorrow through prosperity; may there be freedom from sorrow for the sake of all accomplishments.
Then, having surrounded the bright sun with excellent fruits, one should worship it. (38)
The wise man should place various kinds of foods along with a golden lotus into silver vessels, as well as water with *darbha* grass. (39)
Then, one should have dances and songs performed throughout the entire night; but when three watches have passed, the person should rise.
Having approached, he should honor the couples of the Brahmins—three or one—according to his ability, with garments, garlands, and ointments. (41)
The places where He lies down should be worshipped; "Obeisance to You who recline upon the waters!
Then, singing and playing musical instruments, a vigil should be kept during the night.
Then, having performed his bath at dawn, he should worship his wife and feed her according to his ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
Having heard the Purāṇas with devotion, one should pass that day;
by this procedure, one should perform everything month after month.
One should give a bed for the observance of the vow, accompanied by a cow made of jaggery, provided with pillows, a place for reclining, and an auspicious, well-spread coverlet.
Just as misfortune does not depart from you without abandoning your lordship over men, so may there always be for me beauty, health, and freedom from sorrow. 46.
Just as misfortune sometimes arises when one is deprived of a king, so may there be unwavering devotion to Keśava for me, who am free from sorrow. 47.
With this mantra, one who desires prosperity should offer a bed accompanied by a cow made of molasses, along with the Sun-god together with Lakṣmī.
The blue lotus, the karavīra, the amānaka, saffron, the ketakī, the sindhuvāra, the mallikā, and the fragrant pāṭalā. ||49||
"Kadaṃba, vaṅkubjaka, and the lordly Jātī—these are always [to be offered].
Bhīṣma said:
"O Lord of Sages, please explain the ritual procedure for the cow made of jaggery (guḍadhenu)."
"What is the form of that mantra by which it should be given? Let that be told here.
Pulastya said:
"The form and the fruit of the ritual procedure for the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu) shall be described here."
I shall now proclaim that which destroys all sins:
one should place upon the ground a black antelope skin, four cubits in size, with its neck pointing toward the east. (52)
On ground smeared with cow-dung and strewn everywhere with darbha grass,
one should likewise prepare a small deer-skin and a calf.
One should fashion the cow facing east out of soft earth, together with its calf;
the best sugar-cow (guḍadhenu) should always consist of four bhāras.
One should prepare [the offering] with a full measure; it is known as the middling [type] when made with half a measure, and the inferior [type] with one measure for the calf. ||55||
The calf should be one-fourth [the size] of the cow, according to the extent of one's household wealth;
both the cow and the calf should be made well-formed, white, and covered in fine cloth.
Śukti has ears like oyster shells and feet like sugarcane; Muktāphala has eyes like pearls; Sitasūtra has a network of veins like white threads; and Baluka has hair like white gravel.
These two have backs like copper-colored cheek-plates with white chowrie-wool;
they possess a pair of eyebrows like coral and are endowed with breasts of fresh butter.
Equipped with a pair of golden eyes and pupils of sapphire, they had tails of fine linen;
they were swift runners, white, and exceedingly beautiful. (59)
Their horns were adorned with golden ornaments, their hooves were richly decorated with silver,
they were laden with various fruits, and their nostrils were like caskets of fragrance.
Having thus prepared [the offerings], one should likewise worship with incense and lamps:
"That Lakṣmī who belongs to all beings, and she who resides among the gods... (61)
May that goddess, in the form of a cow, remove this sin;
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu and Svāhā in the fire. (62)
May she who is the power of the moon, the sun, and Indra, the wish-fulfilling cow who grants boons, be mine;
for she is the *svadhā* of the foremost ancestors and the *svāhā* of those who consume the sacrifice.
"The cow is the remover of all sins; therefore, grant me prosperity.
Having thus addressed the cow, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
This procedure is prescribed for all cows whatsoever;
however, those ten cows which destroy evil are specifically recited here.
O lord of men, I shall describe their essential nature and names:
the first is the molasses-cow (guḍadhenu), and the next is the ghee-cow (ghṛtadhenu).
The third is the sesame-cow, and the fourth is named the water-cow;
the fifth is the milk-cow, and another is likewise the honey-cow.
The seventh [cow] is made of sugar, the eighth is fashioned from curd,
the ninth is the cow of essence (rasadhenu), and the tenth is according to its actual form.
Some men desire a golden cow for those cows that have the breast-ornament (urasat) as their mark, while others prefer one whose nature is that of the celestial spheres. ||69||
With fresh butter and oils, other great seers likewise performed this very same rite; it is recorded that the ritual procedures and the necessary implements were identical.
Combined with the invocation of mantras, they should always be offered on every festival day according to the śrāddha rite; they bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In connection with the cow made of jaggery, all these hymns have been proclaimed;
they bestow the fruit of all sacrifices, remove all sins, and are auspicious. (72)
Since the Viśoka-dvādaśī vow is the most excellent of all vows,
the offering of a cow made of molasses (guḍadhenu) is highly praised here as an ancillary part of it.

On the auspicious occasions of the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise on the Vyatīpāta yoga, as well as during eclipses and other such festival days, gifts such as the "jaggery-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others should be bestowed.
This auspicious Viśokadvādaśī removes all sins;
by fasting upon it, a man goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (75)
In this world, one attains sovereignty, good fortune, long life, and health;
and at the time of death, through the remembrance of Hari, one reaches the city of Viṣṇu.
O King, for one who knows the Dharma, ten thousand nine hundred and eight *arbudas* of [aeons] pass by; for him, sorrow, suffering, and misfortune never arise. (77)
If a woman observes this Viśoka-dvādaśī, remaining constantly devoted to dance and song, she too shall obtain that same fruit. 78.
Because the dance of Hari, accompanied by infinite singing and instrumental music, is performed at the beginning of the day—
he who recites this here, or hears it correctly,
or beholds the worship of the enemy of Madhu, Muru, and Naraka; ||79||
He who bestows even a single measure of land upon those who have lost their minds dwells in the world of Indra for one kalpa, honored by the hosts of gods.
Bhīṣma said:
O Blessed One, I now desire to hear about the supreme majesty of this [practice]. ||80||
"That which is inexhaustible in the other world and honored by the hosts of gods and sages.
Pulastya said:
"O best of kings, I shall describe the gift of Meru in its tenfold form. (81)
The giver of which attains infinite worlds honored by the gods—[as described] in the Purāṇas, the Vedas, the sacrifices, and the sacred shrines. (82)
One does not enjoy the fruit of those [meritorious deeds] performed here that have not been dedicated;
therefore, I shall describe the gift of mountains in their proper order. (83)

The first is the mountain of grain (dhānya-śaila), the second is the mountain of salt (lavaṇa-acala), the third is the mountain of molasses (guḍa-acala), and the fourth is the mountain of gold (hema-parvata). ||84||
The fifth shall be a mountain of sesame seeds, the sixth a mountain of cotton;
the seventh shall be a mountain of ghee, and likewise the eighth a mountain of jewels.
Likewise, the ninth is made of silver, and the tenth is a mountain of sugar;
I shall describe the ritual procedure for these in due order and according to the rules.
On the solstices, on the full moon days, during Vyatīpāta, at the end of the day, on the third day of the bright fortnight, during an eclipse, and at the waning of the moon; ||87||
During marriage festivals or sacrifices, or again on the twelfth day, or on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under auspicious constellations, according to the prescribed rule. ||88||
Mountains of grain and other such gifts should be offered on the full moon of Kārttika at Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara, or at sacred fords (tīrthas), temples, cow-pens, or courtyards of dwellings. 89.
One should devoutly cause a pavilion to be constructed, square and facing north,
auspiciously sloping toward the east or north, or facing east, according to the prescribed rules.
Having spread kuśa grass upon ground smeared with cow dung,
one should fashion a mountain in its center, complete with subsidiary peaks and surrounding mountains.
With a thousand *droṇas* of grain, an excellent mountain [of merit] is formed here;
a middling one with five hundred, and the smallest with three hundred. (92)
Mount Meru, consisting of great rice, should be provided with three golden trees at its center;
furthermore, the foremost of the twice-born should perform many other rites upon its summit.
Its four peaks are made of silver, and its slopes are also of silver;
it is joined with pearls and diamonds on the east, and with gomedaka and ruby on the south.

Furthermore, it was adorned with emeralds and sapphires, gentle lapis lazuli and topazes; it was surrounded on all sides by pieces of sandalwood and coral, possessed of climbing vines, and enriched with pavements of pearls. (95)
Where Brahmā, Viṣṇu the Blessed One, Purāri (Śiva), and the Sun-god are golden,
there likewise are groves surrounded by sugarcane plantations, and in all directions flow streams of ghee-water.
The row of wise men should wear white garments in the east, yellow in the south,
variegated in the west, and thick red ones in the north.
Then, having installed the eight world-protectors, headed by Mahendra, in order upon silver [pedestals],
there should be a delightful arrangement of various rows of forests, along with garlands and ointments.
And having arranged a white canopy above, adorned with unfading flowers of five colors, he thus established the foremost mountain of the immortals, Meru, with its vast foothills, in due order. (99)
One should establish it with its fourth part facing the four directions, enriched with flowers and ointments; to the east, a mandara tree endowed with many fruits, shining with a golden trunk.
To the south, Gandhamādana should be situated, consisting of heaps of wheat and possessing golden peaks;
it should be joined with the golden Mānasa lake, the silver Vastrāpada mountain, and silver forests. ||101||

Thereafter, one should fashion a mountain of sesame seeds adorned with many fragrant flowers, golden *pippala* trees, and golden swans; likewise, it should be provided with a forest of silver flowers and, in front of it, lakes of curd and white water.
One should establish the Vipaśaila mountain to the north, as well as the Supārśva mountain made of mung beans and covered with cloth;
one should fashion it so that it is crowned by golden banyan trees and resplendent with the Golden Banner.

Having likewise fashioned a radiant canopy made of silver, treated with a mixture of honey and *bhadrasara* resin, a fire-sacrifice (*homa*) was then performed by four eminent brahmins who were knowers of the Vedas and Purāṇas, self-controlled, and whose conduct and appearance were celestial. ||104||
To the east, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) one cubit in measure should be prepared; it should be offered oblations with sesame seeds, barley, ghee, fuel-sticks, and kuśa grass.
At night, a vigil should be kept with songs that are not overly boisterous. Now I shall describe the invocation of the mountain deities.
O you who are the treasury of the splendor of all the hosts of gods, quickly destroy the enemy in our homes as you did the mountain of the immortals (Kailāsa).
Bestow security and grant us unsurpassed peace; being fully honored by me with supreme devotion, depart! 106.
You alone are the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
you are the seed consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest. Therefore, protect me, O Eternal One! (107)
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors and of Viśvamūrti, as well as of the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, therefore grant me this request. (108)
Since your head is not empty of immortals and women, therefore deliver me from this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra. (109)
Having thus worshipped that Mount Meru, one should also honor Mandara,
O Mountain, because you are [adorned] by the Caitraratha and Bhadrāśva groves.
Shine brightly here; quickly become a source of joy, for you, O Gandhamādana, are the crest-jewel of Jambudvīpa. (111)
May my fame thereafter be as firm as that of the Gandharva hosts, since you [have been honored] by Ketumāla, Vaibhrāja, and Vana. (112)
Since it is adorned with golden stones, may there be firm prosperity for you from that;
and because of the Northern Kurus and the forest of Sāvitra. (113)
"May the King Supārśva always protect my fortune from harm.
Having thus addressed them all, [he did so] again at the clear dawn. (114)
Having bathed, O King, one should give the middle of the best of mountains to the preceptor,
and one should give the subsidiary mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) to the officiating priests in due order.
O King, twenty-four cows should be given, or twelve;
according to one's capacity, seven, eight, or five should be given by one who is unable [to give more]. 116.
Even a single Kapila cow that yields milk is to be given to the Guru;
this same rule is prescribed for all mountains without exception. ||117||
These very same mantras are prescribed for the worship of the planets, the world-protectors, and all others beginning with Brahmā; these very same items are recorded as the ritual implements.
In all cases regarding the mountains, it is taught that the fire-oblation (homa) is to be performed with one's own mantra;
one should always observe a fast, though if unable, eating only at night (nakta) is prescribed.
O King, listen now to the procedure for all the mountains in due order, as well as the mantras to be used in their gift-giving and the fruits obtained from each mountain. 120.
Food is declared to be Brahman; food is proclaimed to be the vital breaths. From food all beings arise; by food the world grows. (121)
Food alone is Lakṣmī; food alone is Janārdana.
Therefore, O best of mountains, protect us in the form of this mountain of grain. 122.
Whoever should give a mountain made of grain according to this rite is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred Manvantaras. (123)
O best of kings, he comes to the heights of heaven in a celestial chariot, resplendent and crowded with hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, one attains the sovereignty of kings in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of salt. 125.
By the gift of which a man attains the world endowed with auspiciousness, a salt-mountain (lavaṇācala) of the highest grade should be made with sixteen droṇas. 126.
The medium [size] is half of that, and the inferior is recorded as being four [dronas];
one who lacks wealth should have it made according to his ability, exceeding one drona.
One should cause the mountain-enclosures for the constellations to be made separately with a fourth part [of the area];
one should always perform the ritual procedure for Brahmā and the others as previously described.
In the same way, one should construct the entire abode of the world-protectors out of gold;
likewise, one should install lakes, groves, trees, and other such features.
One should keep a vigil here as well; learn now the mantras for the gift:
"This water is endowed with the essence of auspiciousness and the essence of salt. (130)
Therefore, O best of mountains, protect me who have fallen into distress, for you consist of that very essence;
since all other tastes are intense only when devoid of salt. (131)
Since you are eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, therefore grant peace;
for since you have arisen from the body of Viṣṇu, you are the increaser of health.
Therefore, by this procedure, whoever should offer a mountain of salt in the form of a mountain shall be protected from the ocean of saṃsāra. (133)
One may dwell in the world of Umā for a kalpa, and thereafter attain the supreme goal. Hereafter, I shall describe the excellent mountain of jaggery (guḍaparvata).
By the gift of which a man, honored by the gods, attains heaven;
the best [gift] is considered to consist of ten bhāras, while the middling is held to be five.
With three loads one would be of the lowest [class], and with half of that one possesses little wealth.
Likewise, one should perform invitations, worship, [plant] golden trees, and the veneration of the gods.

Likewise, one should perform the offerings to the boundary-mountains, the years, and the forest deities; similarly, there should be the fire-oblation (homa), the ritual vigil (jāgaraṇa), and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the world-protectors (lokapāla).
One should fashion [the mountain] like a mountain of grain and recite this mantra:
"Just as among the gods Janārdana is the foremost, the Soul of All; (138)
Just as the Sāmaveda is among the Vedas, Mahādeva is among yogis, the Praṇava is among all mantras, so too is Pārvatī among women. (139)
Just as sugarcane juice is always the most excellent among all juices, may this mountain of jaggery grant me supreme prosperity from that very source. (140)
Since this Guḍaparvata was created by Śiva together with Pārvatī as the abode of Saubhāgyadāyinī, therefore protect me always. 141.
Whoever should give a mountain made of jaggery according to this rite, being honored by Gandharvas, is glorified in the world of Gaurī. (142)
Furthermore, for a hundred kalpas he shall be the sovereign of the seven continents, endowed with long life and health, and unconquered by enemies. (143)
Now I shall describe the supreme Suvarṇācala, which removes all sins, by the gift of which men go to the abode of Viṣṇu. (144)
The best [image] consists of a thousand palas, the middling of five hundred;
the lowest is half of that, and likewise for a man of small means. (145)
One should give more than one *pala*, according to one's capacity and free from envy;
O best of kings, one should perform everything else just as in the case of the mountain of grain (*dhānyaparvata*).
Likewise, one should present the Mount Viṣkambha to the officiating priests, saying:
"Salutations to you, the seed of all things; salutations indeed to you, whose womb is Brahman. (147)
Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect me, O mountain;
since you are the offspring of Agni, and since you are the son of the Lord of the World. (148)
Therefore, O best of mountains, protect [us] in the form of the Golden Mountain;
whoever should give a mountain of gold according to this rite, [attains the supreme goal]. (149)
One who always performs the supreme *brahmalokāmana* with the syllable *da* shall remain there for a hundred kalpas; thereafter, he goes to the highest goal. 150.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the ritual for the mountain of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rules; by the gift of which a man goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu. (151)
The best [tila-śaila] is known to consist of ten droṇas; the middling, of five;
and the lowest, O king of kings, is proclaimed to be three droṇas. 152.
And as before, all else—the boundary mountains and so forth—is likewise;
O best of kings, I shall now proclaim the mantra for the gift. (153)
Since sesame seeds, kuśa grass, and black grams were produced from the sweat of Viṣṇu’s body at the slaying of Madhu, therefore, be the bestower of peace. (154)
Since sesame seeds alone provide protection against obstacles in offerings to gods and ancestors, O Lord of Mountains, you who possess the splendor of sesame—salutations to you! (155)
Having thus addressed [the preceptor], he who should offer this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds attains the station of Viṣṇu, from which a return to worldly existence is difficult to find. (156)
Furthermore, the "cotton mountain" (kārpāsaparvata) here is considered excellent when it consists of twenty bhāras;
the middling is said to be ten, and the inferior is regarded as five. ||157||
One of modest means should give according to his capacity, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
O best of kings, everything should be prepared in the same manner as for the mountain of grain. 158.
And when the night has turned to dawn, one should give [the offering] and recite this:
"Since you alone are always the protection for the worlds here. (159)
"O you who destroy the flood of sins, arise from this mountain of cotton!"—he who should thus offer the lordly mountain of cotton in the presence of Śarva [Śiva], [attains the highest state]. (160)
One shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter become a king here on earth.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Ghṛtācala (Mountain of Ghee). 161.
Ghee is full of splendor, meritorious, and the destroyer of great sins;
a mountain of ghee made from twenty jars of ghee would be considered the best. (162)
With ten [materials] it is declared to be middling, while with five it is remembered as the lowest;
even one with little wealth may perform it here according to the rule with two.
In the same manner, one should fashion the supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) as a fourth part [of the main mountain];
one should place vessels of śāli rice upon the kumbhas.
One should have them constructed high and well-proportioned according to the rules so as to be beautiful;
one should encircle them with white cloths, sugarcane stalks, fruits, and the like.

The entire ritual procedure is recited here as it is for the Mountain of Grain (dhānyaparvata), preceded by the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) and including the performance of oblations and worship of the deities. 166.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should announce it to the preceptor;
likewise, with a tranquil mind, one should present the model mountains to the officiating priests.
Since ghee has arisen from the union of [the elements] within the splendor of the nectar of immortality (amṛta), may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be pleased here by this flame of ghee. 168.
Since you consist of light and are established as the very essence of clarified butter,
O upholder of the earth, protect us in the form of a mountain of ghee.
By this rite, one should offer the unsurpassed mountain of ghee;
even one joined with great sins attains the world of Śambhu. (170)
He was surrounded by Apsarases, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas, traveling in a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells.
One shall dwell together with the ancestors until the dissolution of all beings;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of jewels. 172.
A mountain made of a thousand pearls is considered unsurpassed;
one of five hundred is middling, and one of three hundred is recorded as the lowest.
On the fourth part, the mountain-ranges of the constellations (bha-parvatas) should be situated all around;
to the east, they consist of vajra-gomedaka stones, and to the south, of indranīla stones.
The Gandhamādana mountain should be fashioned by the wise joined with topazes;
thereafter, the Vipula mountain should be mixed with lapis lazuli and corals.
One should also place [the offerings] to the north with rubies set in gold;
everything else here should be prepared just as in the case of the mountain of grain. 176.
In that same way, having performed the invocation, one should worship the trees and the golden deities with flowers, perfumes, and so forth; the dismissal should take place at the end of the light.
As before, one should recite this mantra to the preceptor and the officiating priests:
"Just as all the hosts of gods abide within all precious gems... (178)
Therefore, O Great Mountain, protect us constantly with your jewels, for by the gift of jewels, Janārdana attains satisfaction. (179)
Therefore, O Mountain, protect us through the grace of this worship-mantra;
whoever should give a mountain made of jewels according to this rite—180.
Worshipped by the lords of the immortals, he goes forever to the world of Viṣṇu;
O lord of men, he shall dwell there for more than a hundred kalpas.
Endowed with beauty, health, and virtues, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents;
whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed by him here or in another world— [it shall be destroyed]. (182)
All that goes to destruction like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of silver. 183.
O best of men, by the gift of which a person goes to the world of Soma, the supreme silver mountain consists of ten thousand palas. (184)
The middling [rite] is said to be with five [verses], and the inferior is recorded as half of that.
One who is unable [to perform more] should always cause it to be done with twenty or more, according to one's capacity.
In the same manner, one should fashion the boundary-mountains (viṣkaṃbha-parvatas) as a fourth part;
and as before, one should prepare the silver [mandala] and the other elements according to the prescribed rule.
In that same manner, the wise man should have the world-protectors fashioned from gold;
he should also have Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun made of refined gold.
For the others, those mountains should be made of silver, not of gold;
one should perform the remaining rites, such as the fire-oblation and the night vigil, as previously described.

In the same manner, at dawn, one should give a mountain of silver to the preceptor, and after honoring the assistant priests with garments and ornaments, [one should give] mountains of the supporting peaks to them. (189)
Reciting this mantra, one who is free from envy and holds *darbha* grass in his hand should offer it;
for it is beloved by the ancestors, as well as by the Moon and by Śaṅkara. (190)
"O Silver One, protect us from that ocean of sorrowful saṃsāra.
Having thus addressed [the deity], one should offer an excellent mountain of silver. (191)
That person attains the fruit of ten thousand times ten thousand cows; he dwells in the world of Soma with Gandharvas and throngs of Kinnaras and Apsarases. (192)
Being thus honored, the wise man may dwell there until the dissolution of all beings.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the most excellent mountain of sugar. (193)
By the gift of which Viṣṇu, the Sun, and Rudra are always pleased;
with eight loads of sugar, it shall be an excellent great mountain. (194)
The middling [type] is said to consist of four [loads], while the inferior is recorded as consisting of two loads.
One who possesses little wealth may construct it with one load or even half a load. (195)
A person should fashion the intermediate mountains from the fourth part [of the gold];
everything else, including the golden peak, should be like that of the mountain of grain.
Above Mount Meru, three golden trees are to be placed there:
the Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpapādapa.
One should place these three trees upon the heads of all [the deities]: Haricandana on the eastern side and Sāta on the western side. (198)
Having established [the deity] on all mountains, especially on the Śarkarācala mountain, Kāmadeva should always remain facing westward within the Maṇḍala. 199.
On the peak of Gandhamādana, Dhanada would be facing north;
on the Vipula mountain, Haṃsa, the embodiment of the Vedas, would be facing east. (200)
On the Supārśva mountain, however, the [image] should be made of gold and face the south;
everything else, such as the invocation, the sacrifice, and so forth, is to be performed just as on the mountain of grain (Dhānyaparvata). (201)

Then, having prepared [the materials], he should give the middle of the best mountains to the preceptor, and four mountains to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), while reciting the mantras taught by me. ||202||
This supreme mountain of sugar is the essence of the nectar of good fortune;
therefore, O Lord of Mountains, may you always be the source of bliss. (203)
O Śarkarācala, protect us— you who arose from those drops of nectar that fell upon the earth as the gods were drinking it.
Furthermore, having emerged from the center of the bow of the Mind-born [Kāmadeva],
you protect us from the great mountain of saṃsāra, which is like a sea of gravel.
The man who gives a mountain of sugar according to this rite, being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Brahmā. (206)
Then, having ascended a vehicle resembling the sun and moon, he should rise into the sky with his attendants and the Lord Viṣṇu.
Then, for a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with long life and health for as long as his lifespan lasts there.
One should provide food according to one's ability at all these mountains without any stinginess;
and with their permission, one should oneself eat food that is free from pungent salt.
One should cause all the mountain-appurtenances to reach the abode of a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus has been fully described to you this unsurpassed gift of a mountain. 210.
"O King, ask me whatever else pleases you.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Blessed One, [tell me that which] effects the crossing over the ocean of worldly existence (bhava-saṃsāra)."
"Tell me of some vow that bestows the fruits of heaven and health.
Pulastya said:
"I shall proclaim the solar dharma known by the name Kalyāṇasaptamī."
In the same manner, one should observe the Viśoka-saptamī, the third, the Phala-saptamī,
the Śarkarā-saptamī, and likewise the Kamala-saptamī.
The Dārasaptamī, the Ṣaṣṭhī, the Saptamī, and the Śubhasaptamī—all these are declared to yield meritorious fruits and are honored by all the gods and sages. ||214||
I shall describe their ritual procedure correctly and in due order:
when the seventh day of the bright fortnight happens to be a Sunday. (215)
For those women who desire auspiciousness, this is declared as the "Avijayā" vow:
one should perform a bath in a river with cow's milk in the morning. (216)
Wearing white garments, one should fashion a lotus with unbroken grains;
facing east, it should have eight petals, and in the center, a circular pericarp likewise.
One should place flowers, unbroken rice grains, and water around the Lord of Gods in due order:
first with "Obeisance to Tapan" (tapanāya) and then with "Obeisance to Mārtaṇḍa" (mārtaṇḍāya). ||218||
"To Yāmya" for the southern direction, "to Vidhātṛ" for the southwestern (nairṛta), "to Varuṇa" for the western, and "to Bhāskara" for the northwestern (ānīla). (219)
"O gentle one, O Vikartana, O God"—thus [is the mantra] on the eighth petal;
"Salutation to the Supreme Self" should be recited at the beginning, the end, and the middle. (220)
One should worship with these mantras accompanied by salutations,
using white garments, fruits, edible offerings, incense, garlands, and ointments.
One should worship with devotion on the sacrificial ground using jaggery and indeed salt;
then, having dismissed the eminent brahmins with the vyāhṛti mantra.
One should satisfy [the Brahmins] according to one's ability with devotion by means of molasses, milk, ghee, and so forth;
and one should present a vessel of sesame seeds and gold to the Brahmin.
Having thus observed the vow and slept, the man who rises at dawn,
having performed his ablutions and recitations together with the Brahmins, [should offer] ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having eaten at the house of one who knows the Vedas and is free from the "cat-vow" (hypocrisy),
one should present a vessel of ghee along with gold and a water-pot.
"May the venerable Supreme Self, the Sun, be pleased.
By this rite, one should perform everything month after month. (226)
Then, in the thirteenth month, he should give thirteen milch-cows, provided with garments and ornaments, having horns tipped with gold. (227)
Even one who is destitute of wealth, being free from envy, should give even a single [gift];
he should not practice deceit regarding his wealth, for through such delusion he falls downward.
Whoever performs the Kalyāṇasaptamī according to this rite, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of the Sun. ||229||
In this world, infinite longevity, health, and sovereignty arise;
she is the remover of all sins and is worshipped by all the deities. 230.
This auspicious seventh day (Kalyāṇasaptamī), which pacifies all evils and always bestows well-being—whosoever [observes] this Kalyāṇasaptamī, which yields infinite fruit; ||231||
Whoever hears or even recites this is liberated from sins;
likewise, O best of kings, I shall now describe the Viśoka-saptamī.
Having fasted on this [day] and bathed with black sesame seeds on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, a man never experiences grief here in this world. (233)
Having eaten *kṛsarā* and performed ablutions, he should observe a fast and, remaining celibate, sleep at night. (234)
Then, having risen at dawn, performed his ablutions and recitations, and become pure,
he should fashion a golden lotus and worship it with the mantra "Arka-aye" (Obeisance to the Sun).
O Āditya, just as the world is always rendered free from sorrow by you alone, through the red karavīra flower and the pair of red garments; 236.
In this way, devotion to you shall bring freedom from sorrow in every birth;
thus, having worshipped on the sixth lunar day, one should devoutly honor the twice-born.
Having himself consumed cow's urine and risen,
having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should diligently honor the Brahmins with vessels containing molasses.
One should present a pair of fine garments and a lotus to a Brāhmaṇa;
having eaten food without oil or salt on the seventh lunar day, one should remain observant of silence.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should listen to the Purāṇas according to this procedure during both fortnights. (240)
One should perform this until the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-pot accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should give a bed with its furnishings and a tawny cow that yields milk; he who does so according to this rite, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, [attains the fruit].
One who performs the Viśoka-saptamī shall attain the supreme goal;
this remains so for as long as a full hundred crores of thousands of births.
Until then, he attains freedom from sorrow, being devoid of disease and misfortune;
whatever desire he may long for, that very thing he obtains in its full measure.
He who performs [this rite] without desire attains the Supreme Brahman;
and whoever reads or even hears this account of the seventh day known as Viśoka, [attains the same]. (245)
Having reached the world of the gods, he too shall never experience suffering anywhere.
Furthermore, I shall describe another [observance] called the Phala-saptamī.
By fasting on this day in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a man, firm in his vow, shall be liberated from sins and become a partaker of heaven. (247)
Having fasted on the sixth lunar day and having adorned a golden lotus,
one should give it, together with sugar, to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a family.
Having made an offering of gold with his own hand, the knower of Dharma should give it at the time of two watches for the sake of a single fruit, saying: "May the Sun be pleased with me. (249)
Having honored the Brahmins according to one's capacity on the seventh lunar day and partaken of a meal of milk,
one should observe the renunciation of fruits until the Kṛṣṇa-saptamī arrives.
Having fasted according to the prescribed rule and in this very sequence,
one should likewise give a gift of gold consisting of a golden lotus.
Provided with a vessel of sugar and accompanied by a cloth and a garland,
one should perform this very rite on both the seventh lunar days throughout the year.
Having observed the fast, one should offer [the oblation] in due order and recite the mantra of Sūrya:
"Bhānu, Arka, Ravi, Brahmā, Sūrya, Śukra, Hari, Śiva. (253)
"May the glorious Vibhāvasu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Varuṇa be pleased"—thus one should recite each name individually on the seventh lunar day of every month. ||254||
O Brahmin, performing this renunciation of the fruit as an antidote, you should practice it; you should honor a married couple with garments and ornaments. (255)
One should offer a jar of sugar accompanied by a golden lotus and fruit, so that the desire of your devotees may always be unfailing. (256)
Likewise, may there be the attainment of infinite fruit for me in birth after birth, for whoever performs this Phala-saptamī, which bestows infinite fruit. (257)
He who hears or even recites this shall deliver twenty-one generations of men—both past and future—and he too shall become a partaker of auspicious fortune. (258)
With his soul purified of all evil, he is glorified in the world of the Sun; whatever [sin] such as drinking liquor was committed by him here or in the hereafter, [it is all cleansed]. (259)
All that perishes for one who performs the Phala-saptamī;
I shall now describe the Śarkarā-saptamī, which likewise destroys all impurities.
By means of which infinite longevity, health, and sovereignty are produced—
one who is firm in his vow on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mādhava.
Having bathed in the morning with white sesame seeds, and being adorned with pure garlands and unguents,
one should draw a lotus with a pericarp upon the sacrificial ground using saffron.
In that [place], one should offer incense and flowers with the mantra "Obeisance to Savitṛ," and one should place a water-pot together with a vessel of sugar.
Having adorned it with white garments, white garlands, and unguents, one should worship it, together with golden flowers, with this mantra: ||264||
Since you are proclaimed in the Vedas as the omniscient one, and since you alone are the essence of all immortality, therefore grant me peace. (265)
Then, having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should sleep on the ground at its side;
he should remain there reciting the Saura-sūkta and listening to the Purāṇas.
After the passing of a day and night, having performed his daily obligatory rites on the eighth day,
he should offer all of that to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability with sugar, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa);
or else, remaining restrained in speech, one should eat oneself without oil or salt.
By this procedure, one should perform everything month by month;
for a full year, [one should maintain] the couch accompanied by a jar of sugar.
One who is capable should give a milch cow with one of her horns intact, provided with all necessary utensils, as well as a house equipped with all its furnishings. (270)
Then, having prepared it with a thousand niṣkas, or with a hundred, or with ten, or with three, or again with a single niṣka, he should give it. ||271||
One should offer a lotus according to one's own capacity, reciting the mantra as before; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, for by doing so, one incurs faults.
From the mouth of the Sun as he was drinking nectar, drops of nectar fell upon the earth; those became rice, mung beans, and sugarcane.
From that [milk] came the juice of sugar-candy; from that, the essence of sugarcane, which possesses the nature of nectar.
Therefore, sugar is dear to the Sun and is meritorious for both the offerings to gods (havya) and the offerings to ancestors (kavya). //274//
This Śarkarāsaptamī bestows the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
it pacifies all evils and increases one's sons and grandsons. (275)
Whoever performs this with supreme devotion goes to the Supreme Brahman;
he shall dwell in heaven for one kalpa and thereafter attain the highest state.

Whoever hears this, remembers it, or recites it here in the world of the Lord of the Gods, he too—possessing even but a glimmer of understanding—is honored by the gods and the lords of sages in the city of the immortals. (277)
Henceforth, I shall likewise proclaim the Kamala-saptamī, by the mere recitation of which the Sun-god becomes pleased in this world. (278)
On the seventh day of the month of Tāmasa, having bathed well with white mustard seeds,
one should place a beautiful golden lotus within a vessel of sesame seeds.
Having clothed [the image] in a pair of garments, one should then worship it with perfumes and flowers:
"Homage to you who hold a lotus in your hand; homage to you, the bearer of the universe. (280)
"Salutations to you, O Maker of Day; salutations to you, O Maker of Light.
Then, at the time of the two watches [of the night], accompanied by a water-pot— 281.
One should give [the gift] to a Brahmin after honoring him with garments, garlands, and ornaments;
according to one's capacity, one should give a tawny cow (kapilā) after adorning it according to the prescribed rite.
After the passing of a day and night, on the eighth day, one should feed the twice-born;
and according to one's capacity, one should eat meatless food, avoiding oil.
By this method, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight month after month,
one should perform everything with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth.
One should give a bed for the vows, accompanied by a golden lotus. ||285||
One should also give cows that yield milk, along with gold according to one's ability;
and one should give desired household utensils such as vessels, seats, and lamps.
Whoever performs the Kamala-saptamī according to this rite attains the eternal Lakṣmī and rejoices in the world of the Sun.
Having gone separately through each of the seven worlds during every eon,
surrounded by celestial nymphs (apsaras), he then attains the supreme goal.

Whoever should behold this, hear it for even a moment, recite it with devotion, or bestow their intellect [upon it], shall attain stainless prosperity and go to the world of the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas. (289)
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the meritorious Dārasaptamī, which destroys all sins, grants all desires, and is [known] by name. (290)
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
a wise man who eats light food should then prepare a tooth-stick and fast on the sixth day.
Having fully honored the Brahmins, he should request his wife at night;
then, having risen at dawn and performed his ablutions, he should again [honour] the twice-born.
One should feed [the guests] according to one's ability and should fashion eight images made of clay and flowers;
likewise, there should be a very beautiful golden figure holding a lotus in its hand.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in a copper vessel with black sesame seeds, one should worship the Sun in the east with golden and mango flowers, saying "To Bhāskara. (294)
Likewise, with the salutation "To Sūrya," [he should worship] on the spotless petal;
similarly, with "To Arka" and "To Aryaman," on the south and the southwest respectively.
In the western quarter of the temple, in the northwestern quarter, and in the north, one should worship Caṇḍabhānu, Pūṣan, and Ānanda, respectively; this is the supreme injunction.
A person should be placed upon the pericarp and also within the entire [mandala], having been wrapped in white garments and provided with food, garlands, fruits, and so forth. (297)
Having thus worshipped, he should again give all of that to one who knows the Vedas;
then, remaining silent and facing the east, the householder should eat his meal without oil or salt.
By this procedure, one should perform everything every seventh day of each month for as long as a year, free from any stinginess regarding wealth.
Having placed this very [image] upon a water-pot, it should be given away along with cows according to one's means by one who desires prosperity. (300)
Homage to you, the protector of wives, and to you, the abode of wives;
as the sun, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra. (301)
Any mortal who performs the Māndāra-saptamī according to this rite becomes free from sin,
attains happiness, and rejoices in heaven for an eon.
A man walking through the night of saṃsāra will not stumble if he takes hold of this lamp that dispels the terrifying darkness of the mass of the flood of sins. (303)
Whoever reads or even hears this Dārasaptamī, which bestows the fruits of desired objects, shall also be liberated from sins. (304)
Now I shall also describe another auspicious Śubhasaptamī, by fasting on which a person is liberated from the flood of disease and grief. (305)
Having performed his bath and recitation in the month of Āśvayuja, being pure and meritorious,
he should then cause the Brahmins to recite [the prayers] and commence the auspicious Saptamī vow.
One should worship Kapilā with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
I bow to her who is born from the Sun and is the abode of the entire world. (307)
