O auspicious and virtuous lady, for the purification of my own body, I have prepared a prastha of sesame seeds together with a copper vessel. (308)
Likewise, [one should offer] a golden bull, provided with cloth, garlands, and molasses, together with a pillow and accompanied by a resting place, vessels, and a seat. (309)
At both times of day, one should offer various kinds of fruits and foods prepared with ghee and milk-rice, saying: "May Aryaman be pleased."
Having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should sleep on the bare ground without a bed;
then, when morning has dawned, he should devoutly gratify the twice-born with offerings.
By this rite, a man should always, month after month,
give a golden bull along with two garments, as well as [an image] produced from Ganges gold.
One should provide a bed for a full year, accompanied by sugarcane stalks and molasses,
along with a prastha measure of sesame seeds in a copper vessel, and likewise a golden bull.
One should give everything to a knower of the Vedas, saying, "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased. By this rite, the wise man who performs the Śubhasaptamī [attains the fruit]. (314)
In birth after birth, he shall possess the fortune of stainless fame;
being honored by hosts of apsarases and gandharvas in the abode of the gods. (315)
Having become the Lord of the Gaṇas, he shall reside until the dissolution of all beings;
and having descended at the beginning of the kalpa, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
This meritorious and auspicious Saptamī, when recited, is sufficient for the destruction of a thousand killings of embryos and a hundred killings of Brahmins. ||317||

Whoever should recite this, listen to it for even a moment, or even see it being given away incidentally—that person, with a body liberated from all sins, attains the leadership of the Vidyādharas. (318)
He who performs the seventh [offering] for seven years, employing the sevenfold method, becomes successively the sovereign of the seven worlds and attains the supreme state of Murāri. (319)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, concerning the majesty of Puṣkara. ||21||
The Twenty-Second Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
The world of Bhūḥ, the world of Bhuvaḥ, the world of Svaḥ, as well as Mahas, Jana, Tapaḥ, and Satyam—these seven are proclaimed as the worlds of the gods. ||1||
But how can all these—auspicious form, longevity, and health in this world—come to be under their sovereign influence in turn? (2)
"O Brahmin, honored by the gods, how may vast prosperity be attained?
Pulastya said: "In ancient times, on the surface of the earth, the Fire-god was together with the Wind-god. (3)
Commanded by Indra for the destruction of the enemies of the gods,
he then consumed the Dānavas by the thousands.
Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, Parāvasu,
Virocana, and Saṃhrāda— these went and dwelt there at that time.
Having entered the ocean, they established their dwellings;
though they were powerless, they were nevertheless overlooked by Agni and Māruta.
From that time forward, having oppressed the gods, humans, and serpents, as well as all the sages, they would enter the water once again.
Thus, O King, for fifteen thousand ages, those heroes,
by the strength of their fortress in the waters, have oppressed the three worlds.
Then, moreover, the Lord of the Immortals commanded Fire and Wind:
"Let this ocean be dried up without delay. (9)
Since this ocean is the refuge of our enemies,
let it be brought to exhaustion by you two this very day.
Then those two said to Śakra, the slayer of Maya and Śambara:
"O Lord of the Gods, this destruction of Sāgara is unrighteous. (11)
Since there would be the destruction of a great multitude of living beings, therefore, O Purandara, resort to another means. (12)
O most excellent one, how can he deserve destruction, when even within a single yojana there dwell hundreds of millions of living beings? (13)
Thus addressed, the lord of the gods, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke these words out of anger to the immortals Agni and Māruta: ||14||
The immortals never encounter the conjunction of merit and demerit; those two high-souled ones remain superior even amidst the various states of existence. 15.
Therefore, because of my ignorance, you have become like the wind;
having taken up this body, remain devoted to the vows of a sage.
Therefore, O Vibhāvasu, [I shall enter] a womb devoid of the knowledge of Dharma and Arthaśāstra;
thus, with a single body in human form, I shall appear in the guise of a sage.
There shall be no one equal to you in this world,
even when you are born as a human being, for even in that state, you dried up the ocean with a mere mouthful.
"O Fire, you shall become the ocean; then you will attain divinity.
Thus, by the power of that curse, he fell at that very moment to the surface of the earth.
Then, having obtained the vessel of birth from Taudehaka,
Vasiṣṭha was born as the son of Mitrāvaruṇa through their power.
Then Agastya became a sage of fierce asceticism, the best of munis;
he was the younger brother of this [Rāma's] brother, the muni Vasiṣṭha. ||21||
Bhīṣma said:
How were his parents, Mitra and Varuṇa, reduced to such a state?
Tell me now how the birth of Agastya came about.
Pulastya said: In ancient times, on Mount Gandhamādana,
the primordial Puruṣa Viṣṇu, having become the son of Dharma, performed extensive and profound penance.
Fearing his ascetic power, Śakra dispatched both Mādhava and Anaṅga, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, for the purpose of creating obstacles.
When Hari could not be led into passion or delusion by Kāma and Mādhava through song, instrumental music, and amorous gestures such as *bhāva* and *hāva*, [he remained steadfast].
Then the host of women, longing for him as their honey, fell into despondency;
and from the region of their thighs, which were extended in agitation, the best of men departed. (26)
He brought forth a woman who could enchant even the three worlds;
deluded by her, both the gods and the asuras offered praise.
In the presence of the Apsarases, Hari said to the gods:
"She shall go forth to fame in the world by the name of Urvaśī. (28)
Then Urvaśī was summoned by her lover, who desired her;
he said, "Delight me," and she replied, "So be it."
Then, as she was going toward the world of the Sun, she was seen by the daughter of the ocean;
subsequently, having been chosen by Varuṇa, she spoke these words to him. (30)
"O Lord, I was previously chosen by Mitra; my husband is Sūrya," she said.
Varuṇa, having set his heart upon me, replied, "You may go. (31)
When she had departed, saying "So be it," Mitra then uttered a curse:
"Go this very day to the world of mortals, to the son of the Moon's daughter."
"O Bhajamāna, this false dharma has been committed by you;
therefore, let this water-jar be filled with vigor by your friend Varuṇa. (33)
Then, when those two best of sages had thus been cast out and were no longer present,
there was once a king named Nimi who played at dice with women.
Then Vasiṣṭha, born of Brahmā, arrived from another region;
the sage cursed the king who failed to offer him worship. (35)
"May you become bodiless," he was thus cursed by him;
and due to their mutual curses, the splendors of both became disembodied.
They went to Brahmā, the lord of the world, for the sake of destroying the curse;
then, by the command of Brahmā, Nimi closed his eyes.
O King, the twinklings of the eyes of all beings occurred for the sake of his rest;
and Vasiṣṭha also remained within that water-jar as before.
And from him was born Turvāhu, who, bearing a rosary, a water-pot, and the sacred thread,
became the son of Agastya and an excellent sage.
In a certain region of Malaya, accompanied by his wife and surrounded by brahmins, he performed most difficult austerities according to the rules of the Vaikhānasas.
Then, after a long time, beholding the world oppressed by Tāraka and others, he drank up the ocean with great wrath.
Then all [the gods], beginning with Śaṅkara, became granters of boons to him;
both Brahmā and the Lord Viṣṇu also came to bestow boons. ||42||
"Choose a boon, O Muni; may it be well with you, and whatever is desired by you, I shall grant.
Agastya said: "For as long as twenty-five crores of thousands of Brahmās [endure]... (43)
"I shall become the presiding deity of the celestial chariot on the southern path;
whoever performs my worship upon the emergence of my chariot [shall receive the fruit]. (44)
He who shall proclaim your hermitage by the name "Puṣkaravat" will, in due course, become the sovereign of the seven worlds. (45)
And he alone shall attain the highest merit, for he has been chosen by me;
those who shall perform the Śrāddha rite here with devotion, preceded by the offering of the Piṇḍas. (46)
All their groups of ancestors, residing together with Maya in heaven, shall dwell there for this duration of time; this indeed is my boon.
Having said, "So be it," those gods departed as they had come;
therefore, the wise should always offer the *arghya* to Agastya. 48.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Muni, how should the offering of arghya be performed for him?
Tell me that procedure for the worship of Agastya. (49)
Pulastya said: At the time of dawn, during its rising at night, the wise man should perform a bath with white sesame seeds, likewise wearing white garlands and garments.
One should place a flawless jar, adorned with garlands and cloth,
joined with the five jewels, and accompanied by a vessel of ghee.
Likewise, one should place a person the size of a thumb, golden, with long staff-like arms,
four-armed, holding a vessel with the mouth of a jar, and accompanied by the seven mountains filled with grains.

Having lifted the water-pot with his long arms, he, with one-pointed mind and facing the north, should offer it along with unhusked rice and white flowers to an eminent twice-born, using the mantra. (53)

If one has the means, a man should bow down before a brahmin and give him a white cow with silver hooves, a golden face, accompanied by her calf, yielding milk, and adorned with garlands, garments, and ornaments. (54)

This entire [offering] must be given by a man with the rising [of the planet], for up to seven nights, or until seventeen years have passed; beyond that, some authorities say it may even be done later.
O you who resemble the kāśa flower, born from fire and wind, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from the womb of the pitcher—salutations to you! (56)
By performing the renunciation of fruit in this manner every year, a person does not falter;
thereafter, having performed the fire-oblation, he may consume the fruit.
Whatever man should offer the arghya according to this rite attains this world, which bestows the fruits of beauty and health. (58)
By the second [offering], one attains the Bhuvarloka; thereafter, he who bestows seven arghyas attains all seven worlds. (59)

Whoever thus recites or hears this correctly, or beholds the ritual for the worship of Agastya, or even bestows their attention upon it—that person, having entered the abode of Viṣṇu, is honored by the hosts of gods. (60)
Bhīṣma said: O one of great intelligence, tell me that which bestows the fruits of good fortune and health, causes the destruction of enemies, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Pulastya said: Formerly, when auspicious and charming stories were being narrated, the God who is the slayer of Andhaka spoke thus to Umā.
I shall now proclaim that which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Gaurī said:
"O Lord of the Asuras, a curse has been pronounced upon me and Lakṣmī by Sāvitrī. (63)
"Tell me how I may go so as to have misfortune as my primary characteristic.
Śaṅkara said:
"Listen attentively, O Goddess, for I shall tell you exactly what was done by yourself."
For both men and women, the means of attaining the unsurpassed [state] is [worship] in the month of Nabhasya,
or Vaiśākha, or likewise in the meritorious month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, having bathed with white mustard seeds,
one should likewise take yellow pigment (gorocanā), cow’s urine, cow’s milk, and ghee.
One should apply a tilaka on the forehead mixed with curd and honey,
for it bestows good fortune and health, and is always dear to the graceful Lalitā.
On the third [lunar day], as an antidote, a man or even a married woman should wear red garments and white flowers.
A widow should wear only a single white garment;
a maiden, however, should put on two fine white garments.
Then one should bathe the Goddess with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), then with milk alone,
likewise with honey, and with water scented with flowers.
One should worship with white flowers and various kinds of fruits,
as well as with grains, parched grain, salt, molasses, milk, and ghee.
O Goddess, you should always perform worship with white unbroken sesame seeds;
O fair-faced one, you should perform the worship of the feet every fortnight.
Salutations to Varadā for the two feet; likewise, salutations to Śrī for the two ankles;
salutations to Aśokā for the two shanks; and likewise, salutations to Pārvatī for the two knees. (73)
Salutations to the thighs for Māṅgalyakāriṇī, and likewise to the waist for Vāmadevī;
salutations to the belly for Padmodarā, and salutations to Śrī on the throat. (74)
I bow to the one who bestows fortune upon the hands, to the one whose beauty is a gracious countenance,
to the one who destroys pride in the face, and again to the one who grants the god of love through her smile.
Salutation to Gaurī for the forehead, and likewise to Utpalā for the nose;
salutation to Tuṣṭi for the hair on the forehead, and to Kātyāyanī for the head. (76)
Homage to Gaurī, homage to Puṣṭi, homage to Kānti, homage to Śrī; homage again and again to Raṃbhā, to Lalitā, and to Vāmadevī. ||77||
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should draw a lotus in front [of the deity],
provided with sixteen petals and a pericarp in due order.
One should place Gaurī to the east, and after that Aparṇā;
likewise Bhavānī to the south, and after that Rudrāṇī.
One should place Madanavāsinī in the western part,
the fierce Pāṭalā in the north-west, and likewise Umā in the north.
Having established Sādhyā, Pathyā, likewise Saumyā, the virtuous Maṅgalāṅkuśadā,
and Bhadrā in the middle, one should place Lalitā upon the pericarp.
One should place [the offerings] with flowers or with unbroken grains (akṣata) and water, even without a formal salutation;
and having caused a woman in her confinement (suvāsinī) to make the sound of auspicious songs.
One should worship them with red garments, red garlands, and red unguents;
and one should scatter *sindūra* powder for their bath upon their heads. (83)
Since saffron from afar and bathing are exceedingly desired,
one should likewise diligently honor the preceptor who provides instruction.
Where the Guru is not honored, all ritual actions there are fruitless;
one should always worship Gaurī with prayers and blue lotuses. 85.
In the month of Kārttika, one should diligently worship the beloved [deity] with Bandhujīva flowers;
in Mārgaśīrṣa with Jātī flowers, and in Pauṣa with yellow Kuraṇṭaka flowers.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship the Goddess with *kuṃda* and *kumuda* flowers;
in Phālguna as well, a person should worship her with *sinduvāra* and *jāti*.

One should worship with *caitrea*, *mallikā*, and *aśoka* flowers in Caitra; with *gandhapāṭala* in Vaiśākha; with lotuses (*kamala*) and jasmine (*māndāra*) in Jyeṣṭha; and with water-born flowers (*jalāmbuja*) in Āṣāḍha.
One should always worship me with my consorts, along with *athama-latā*, during the months of Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa;
[offering] cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass. (89)
One should always consume, in successive order, bilva leaves, arka flowers, lotuses, water from a cow's horn, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and bilva fruit.
This consumption [of the substances] is declared to take place at the beginning of the month of Bhādrapada;
and every fortnight, O fair-faced one, there is a pair on the third lunar day.
Having fed them, one should honor them with devotion by means of garments, garlands, and ointments;
one should give yellow cloth to the men and silken garments to the women.
One should give to a woman a fruit accompanied by sinewless ginger, salt, sugarcane stalks, and jaggery; to a man, one joined with a golden lotus.
Just as Lord Anādideva departs, having completely abandoned you, so may he deliver me from the entire ocean of saṃsāra with its manifold sufferings. 94.
Kumudā, Vimalā, Dā, Bhavānī, Vasudhā, Śivā, Lalitā, Kamalā, Gaurī, Satī, Rambhā, Ambā, and Pārvatī. (95)
During the months beginning with Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa) and lasting for five months, one should utter the words, "May [the deity] be pleased.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a bed accompanied by a golden lotus.
One should worship twenty-four pairs, or twelve,
or eight, or eight again, or alternatively, one should worship them during four months.
Having first given to the Guru, one should thereafter worship others;
this is called the "Third Ananta," which always bestows infinite fruit. (98)
The Goddess who removes all sins increases good fortune and health; one should never, even for a moment, transgress this [instruction] through stinginess regarding wealth. 99.
A man or a woman, or even a pregnant woman, one who has recently given birth, a young girl, or a sick person, may observe the vow of fasting. (100)
When one is impure, one should have it performed by another while remaining self-restrained; he who observes this third [day], which yields infinite fruit, [attains that result]. (101)
One is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of kalpas;
even one devoid of wealth should perform this fasting for at least one year.
Even by following this procedure for the mantra of flowers, one shall obtain that same fruit;
or a woman who desires her own welfare may perform it as well. 103.
"One attains the fruit of human birth through the grace of Gaurī.
Thus, he who reads or hears of this vow of the Daughter of the Mountain shall dwell in the realm of Indra. (104)
Even he who bestows but a single thought [upon this vow] is worthy of worship by the gods, the celestial women, and the kinnaras;
I shall now describe another third [vow], which destroys all sins. (105)
The wise know this Rasakalyāṇinī to have originated in a former kalpa;
it is to be undertaken upon reaching the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha. (106)
In the morning, one should perform a bath with fragrant substances, milk, and sesame seeds;
likewise, one should bathe the Goddess with honey and sugarcane juice.
Furthermore, one should perform worship with scented water and saffron;
having worshipped the right limbs, one should then worship the left limbs. (108)

One should worship the feet of the Goddess with "Salutation to Lalitā," and then the two ankles with "To Her. Likewise, one should worship the shanks with "To Śānti," and the thighs with "Salutation to Śrī. (109)

I bow to Madālasā, whose waist is stainless; likewise, I bow to her belly; I bow to the breasts of the dweller of passion; and I bow to her face, which is like a white lotus, and to her earth-like hips.
I bow to the eyebrows and the forehead of Mādhavī, who possesses a smile of singular purity;
likewise, I bow to the locks of hair of Carudrāṇī, the consort of Śaṅkara.
To Madanāya, [he offered] the forehead; to Tumohanāya, the two eyebrows;
to Candrārdhadhāriṇī, the eyes; and again to Tuṣṭyai, the face. (112)
Salutation to Utkaṇṭhinī at the neck; salutation to Amṛtā at the throat; salutation to Tanu at the chest; salutation to Bhā at the great arms; salutation to Viśokā at the hands. (113)
[He worships] the heart with "Obeisance to Manmathāhvayā," the belly with "Obeisance to Pāṭalā," the hips with "Obeisance to Suratavāsinī," and the thighs with "Obeisance to Paṅkajaśrī. ||114||
One should worship the knees and shanks with "Oṃ Gaurīya," and likewise the ankles with "Śāntyai";
the feet with "Dharādharāya" and the head with "Viśvakāya Namaḥ. (115)
Salutations to Bhavānī, who desires only one [Lord], to Vāsudevī, the Fortune of the Universe;
salutations again and again to Subhadrā, who bestows this inheritance of bliss.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should honor the husband of the twice-born woman;
likewise, being free from envy, one should feed him with sweet food.
Having given a water-pot filled with water, two pairs of white garments,
and a golden lotus, one should then worship [it] with perfumes and garlands.
May she be pleased; one should undertake the salt-vow (lavaṇavrata).
According to this procedure, one should always worship the Goddess month after month. 119.
One should avoid salt in the month of Māgha, molasses in Phālguna, fresh butter in Caitra, and honey in Vaiśākha. (120)
One should avoid drinking water in the month of Jyeṣṭha, as well as cumin in Āṣāḍha;
one should avoid milk in Śrāvaṇa, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada.
Likewise, ghee should be avoided in Āśvayuja; honey should be avoided in Ūrja;
coriander in Mārgaśīrṣa; and sugar should be avoided in Pauṣa. 122.
Every month,
at the hour of twilight, one should give them a full water-pot as a fulfillment of their vow, accompanied by a vessel of food.
Sweetmeat balls, servants, and likewise saṃyāva, apūpa, and pūrikā;
cakes filled with coconut and ghee, and cakes filled with flour—this is the offering for Dikī. 124.
One should offer milk-vegetables, curd-rice, and likewise vegetable-balls,
placing these in turn upon the water-jar starting from the month of Māgha.
Kumudā, Mādhavīrā, Bhāsubhadrā, Caśivā, Jayā, Lalitā, Kamalā, Anaṅgā, Maṅgalā, and Ratilālasā. (126)
One should recite "May [the deity] be pleased" during the months beginning with Māgha in due order;
in all cases, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is prescribed.
She should always observe the fast; if she is unable, a meal at night (nakta) is prescribed.
In this manner, a woman who desires well-being should perform this vow. 128.
Furthermore, when the month of Māgha has arrived, having fashioned an image of Gaurī out of gold and endowed it with five jewels, [one should place it] upon a jar of sugar.
And [one should visualize] oneself as four-armed and radiant, with a rosary, a water-pot, and a thumb-sized [image], covered by a white eye-cloth. (130)
In the same manner, one should give a pair of cows, gold, a white garment, and a vessel with cloth, saying, "May Bhavānī be pleased. (131)
Whoever performs this *Turasakalyāṇinī* vow according to this procedure is liberated from all sins at that very moment. (132)
One never becomes a sufferer of misery even for a thousand existences;
one shall obtain that fruit which is gained by a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices. ||133||
Whether she be a woman, a maiden, or a wretched widow, O fair-faced one, she shall partake of that fruit. (134)
Endowed with good fortune and health, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Whoever thus recites this or hears it even incidentally, being liberated from all impurities, goes to the world of Pārvatī. 135.
That which bestows even a mere thought upon men for the sake of their welfare shall be unfailing when it reaches the people who are lords of the wise;
likewise, I shall proclaim another third [vow], which destroys all sins. (136)
This foremost *anaṅgakarī*, renowned throughout the world by name, should be performed whenever the asterism Aṣāḍhā occurs on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha. (137)
Or else, under the Rohiṇī asterism, or Maghā, Hastā, or Mūla,
one should then properly perform the bath with darbha grass and scented water.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes and unguents, one should worship Bhavānī with devotion using fragrant white flowers. 139.
And to the Great God seated upon the great throne, [he offered] "Salutation to Vāsudeva" for the feet, and "Salutation to Śaṅkara" for the thighs of Hara. (140)

O Lord, one should worship the shanks with "Salutation to the Destroyer of Sorrow" and "Salutation to the Bestower of Honor"; and the thighs with "Raṃ" for Śiva and "Bhāyai" for the Wielder of the Pināka bow. ||141||
[He offered] the ānaṃdinya-fruit to the Goddess, the trident-bearing Śūlapāṇi;
likewise the mādhavī-fruit to Nābhi, and the śambhu-fruit to Bhava. 142.
Salutations to the one who holds the breasts of Umā, to the one who bears the crescent moon of Śaṅkara; salutations to the one who is longed for by Umā, and to the blue-throated one of Hari. (143)
O Lord of the world, may Hara—who delights in the dance of Hari—be pleased by those who hold blue lotuses in their hands and embrace his arms. 144.
O Lord, the face of the Goddess was for the sake of the playful one, and again for the sake of the Bull;
O Lord, the smile was for the sake of the one worthy of remembrance, and indeed for the sake of the one whose face is the universe. 145.
Salutations to the one whose eyes are fixed on the dwellers of the forest, the abode of all, the wielder of the trident;
salutations to the lover of dance, to Śambhu, who holds the noose and the trident. 146.

O All-pervading Lord, [I bow] to the forehead of the Goddess with the mantra *indrāṇyai*, to her crown with *svāhāyai*, and to the goddess who wears an elephant's tusk as an earring with *ibhagaṅgādharāyai*. (147)

The auspicious Śiva and Pārvatī, the Supreme Lord and his consort, possess universal bodies, universal arms, and universal feet and faces; they are gracious, bestowing boons, and radiant with splendor. 148.
Having thus worshipped according to the rule before the two Śivas,
one should again have lotuses and water-lilies made from powder of various colors.
The conch, the discus, the earring, and the svastika are auspicious signs;
as many grains of dust as fall there upon the ground [indicate the years]. 150.
For that many thousands of years he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
[he who offers] four vessels of ghee along with gold according to his ability. (151)
Having given [the offering] along with water into the hand of the twice-born,
one should present these every fortnight until the end of the four months.
Then, for four months, as before, he should place four vessels of ghee and immediately thereafter four vessels of sesame seeds upon his hand. (153)
Scented water, flower-water, water with curd and saffron, uncooked curd and milk, and likewise water from a cow's horn. ||154||
Likewise, water with cow dung, again water mixed with powdered kuṣṭha, water with uśīra, and again water with barley powder. ||155||
Having consumed sesame-water, one should sleep during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa; it is taught that this consumption should take place twice a fortnight throughout the months.
White flowers are always recommended for worship everywhere;
and at the time of making offerings, one should everywhere recite this mantra. (157)
May Gaurī be eternally pleased with me; may Maṅgalā destroy my sins; may Lalitā grant good fortune; and may Bhavānī bestow all spiritual perfections. 158.
For one year, he should offer a water-pot filled with oil, salt, jaggery, saffron, sandalwood, gold, and lotuses. (159)
For the pleasure of Umā, one should offer a golden bed provided with pillows and coverlets, along with a place for rest, and accompanied by the fruits of the Vidikṣu tree. (160)
By saying, "May Gaurī be pleased with this Brahmin together with his wife," a man shall obtain prosperity known as the *dakari*. 161.
One who possesses this longevity-elixir shall never encounter sorrow;
nor does a woman suffer as a widow, a young maiden, or an elderly woman. 162.

there, the second altar of the God is a lotus with its pericarp.

The Twenty-fourth Chapter.
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, tell me that which bestows boons upon both man and woman here,
by means of which grief, disease, fear, and suffering shall not exist.
