which follow one through seven hundred kalpas as a result of gifts such as cows, land, and gold.
One should perform the worship, beginning with the invocation, as previously described;
this is proclaimed as the "Non-Empty Bed" rite, which is without a second.
Upon that [image], one should worship Viṣṇu according to the prescribed rule with these mantras:
"O Bearer of the Śrīvatsa, O Desired by Śrī, O Lord of Śrī, O Supporter of Śrī, O Imperishable One! (5)
O Puruṣottama, let my householder life not perish—may it grant dharma, artha, and kāma—and let the sacred fires not be extinguished for me, O God. (6)
O Father, may I never be separated from my husband, just as the Lord Hari is never separated from Lakṣmī. May I not perish through any breach of that union.
Likewise, O Bestower of Boons, let my connection with my wife be severed from me, so that your bed may never be empty of Lakṣmī. (8)
O Madhusūdana, having prepared the bed, one should likewise cause the sounds of singing and musical instruments to be made for the God of gods. 9.
Since the *ghaṇṭā* (bell) consists of all musical instruments for one who is incapable [of playing them all], having thus worshipped Govinda, one should eat food devoid of oil. 10.
At night, one should consume [food] that is free from pungent spices and salt until the fourfold [period] is completed;
then, when morning has dawned, [one should worship the goddess] together with the Lord of Lakṣmī.
One should give an extraordinary bed provided with lamps, food, and vessels, along with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, and a seat. (12)
Equipped with desired furnishings, adorned with white flowers and fine cloths, [it should be given] to a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin who is free from physical defects and has a family. ||13||
It should never be given to one who is not a knower of the Vedas, nor to one who is not a husband.
Having seated the husband there and having adorned him according to the prescribed rule, [the gift should be made]. ||14||
One should give a vessel for the wife, provided with various kinds of food and edibles; and for the Brāhmaṇa, one should also give a golden vessel provided with all necessary utensils.
One should offer a water-pot to the image of the God of gods;
thus, that man who performs this rite of Aśūnyaśayana for Hari [attains the fruit]. (16)
Free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, he never at any time experiences separation from his wife. (17)
O Brahmin, as long as the moon, sun, and stars exist, may you never become like a widow, nor ever be deformed or afflicted by grief, for you two shall remain husbands. (18)
O Grandfather, sons, cattle, and jewels do not go to ruin for seven thousand and seven hundred kalpas. (19)
By performing the Aśūnyaśayana rite, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said: How can there always be health, sovereignty, intelligence, and steadfastness in dharma? (20)
"How can one who is devoted to others who are not free from defects also have devotion toward Viṣṇu?
The Lord said: "O Brahmin, you have asked well; I shall now tell it to you."
[He recounted] the dialogue between Virocana and the wise Bhārgava,
after seeing the son of Prahlāda at the age of sixteen years.
O Brahmin, this was his appearance as he sat there, the descendant of Bhrigu:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! May it be well with you, O Virocana. (23)
The destroyer of the Asuras asked him about that laughter:
"O Brahmin, for what reason was this laugh of yours directed toward me? (24)
"You have spoken thus to me, saying 'Excellent, excellent!'; speak now.
To him who spoke thus appropriately, the best among speakers replied: (25)
Out of wonder at the greatness of the vow, this laughter was made by me formerly when the wielder of the trident was enraged for the sake of destroying Dakṣa. (26)
The drops of sweat born from the forehead of that one with a terrifying face fell and,
having pierced the seven netherworlds (pātālas), burned the seven oceans.
With many mouths and eyes, terrifying with blazing fire, he was known as Vīrabhadra, endowed with ten thousand hands and feet. 28.
Having performed the destruction of the sacrifice, the subsequent dissolution of all beings was again averted by Śiva through the burning of the three worlds. 29.
You have accomplished the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice through Āvīrabhadra;
now, enough with this deed that burns the world. (30)
"By bestowing peace upon all the planets, become their foremost;
those of noble birth who have perfected themselves will perform worship with great joy. (31)
O son of the sword, you shall attain the renown of Aṅgāraka;
in the world of the gods, you will possess a second form.
Those people who shall worship you on the fourth lunar day, under the asterism of Puṣya,
will possess infinite beauty, health, and sovereignty.
Thus addressed, O King, he who could assume any form at will attained peace; born at that very moment, he then returned once more to his state as a child.
Once, you observed that excellent offerings, such as water for honor and worship, were being performed by a Śūdra while you remained standing there. (35)

Therefore, you have been born as a handsome Asura, a thunderbolt to the race of your enemies; and since she who is so dear to you has been born not far from you, she too has become one of diverse and beautiful forms.
Therefore, both gods and demons call you Virocana, because of the sight of this vow being performed by a Śūdra. (37)
"I was struck with wonder at such perfection of form; 'Excellent! Excellent! he said, 'Ah! What supreme majesty! (38)
Even for one who merely beholds it, such sovereignty arises; what need is there to mention one who performs [meritorious acts]?
For this reason, out of devotion to the Son of the Earth (Yudhiṣṭhira), he bestowed gifts of cattle and other things while being censured. (39)
"Beheld by him within the womb of the enemy of the Asuras, this birth of yours has arisen from the race of Daityas.
Then, having heard those words of the high-souled Bhārgava, [she spoke].
The heroic Virocana, the son of Danu, again questioned Bhārgava, who brings delight to Prahlāda.
Virocana said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear that vow correctly and in accordance with its true essence."
Furthermore, you ought to explain correctly the greatness and the procedure of that gift which was seen by me being given in a previous existence. (42)
Having heard those words, the Brahmin spoke respectfully:
"O Dānava, when the fourth lunar day falls on a Tuesday," (43)
Then, adorned with rubies, he should perform a bath with clay;
having bathed and facing north, he should mutter the mantra beginning with "agnirmūrdhā divaḥ. (44)
But a Śūdra, remaining silent and remembering the Earth, should remain free from sensual enjoyments;
then, when the sun has set, he should smear [the ground] with cow-dung.
Then, having honored the courtyard with flower garlands, unbroken rice,
and water, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with saffron.
In the absence of saffron as well, red sandalwood is desired. Four water-pots (karaka) should be prepared, provided with various kinds of food and edibles. ||47||
Having placed them in the four corners along with rice grains soaked in water, red lotuses, and various kinds of fruits; ||48||
One should likewise arrange all the perfumes, garlands, and so forth;
then, having worshipped a tawny cow with golden horns and silver hooves, yielding milk in a bronze vessel and accompanied by a cloth.
One should likewise fashion a gentle bull bearing the yoke, with red hooves, joined with the seven kinds of grain,
and a golden human figure the size of a thumb, with long, staff-like arms.
To one who has four arms, is made of gold, and possesses four copper vessels filled with jaggery and ghee on top;
who knows the melodies of the Sāma Veda, has conquered his senses, and is endowed with excellent form, character, and lineage. (51)

O highly fortunate son of the Earth, all of this must be given by a householder to a brahmin who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities; for it originated from the sweat of the wielder of the Pināka bow. 52.
"O you who desire form, I have approached you; accept this water-offering (arghya); homage be to you!
Having offered the arghya with this mantra and with water mixed with red sandalwood, [he should proceed]. (53)
Then one should worship the best of Brahmins with red garlands and other offerings;
with that same mantra, one should give land together with a pair of cattle.
One who is capable should give a bed equipped with all necessary furnishings,
as well as whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is most cherished in one's own home.
One who desires that what has been given become inexhaustible should bestow it upon those possessing such-and-such virtues;
thereafter, having performed a circumambulation, one should dismiss the most excellent of the twice-born.
One should consume milk at night; likewise for the eight Aṅgāraka days, or for four of them—whatever merit there is in that, I shall describe it to you. (57)
In birth after birth, that man shall be endowed with beauty and good fortune;
devoted to Viṣṇu or Śiva, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
For seven thousand kalpas he is honored in the world of Rudra;
therefore, O Lord of Daityas, you too should observe this vow.
Having been addressed thus by Bhṛgu, the Daitya Danu performed that entire vow;
and you too, O King, perform all this, for those who know the Vedas declare that from this [vow] comes imperishability.
And whoever hears this with undistracted mind, for him too the Blessed One ordains everything.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of Aṅgāraka-Caturthī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Five.
Bhīṣma said:
For one who is unable to fast, yet desires the same fruit [as fasting], or for one who is unable due to lack of practice or illness—tell me, what is the desired vow? (1)
Pulastya said:
For those who are unable to observe fasts, eating at night is prescribed. Listen now to that great vow which is associated with this practice.

Those conjunctions of constellations in which the experts in the Purāṇas declare the ritual of lying down for the sun (ādityaśayana) and the worship of Śaṅkara should be performed according to the rules. ||3||
When the seventh lunar day falls on a Sunday,
and that lunar day coincides with the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), it fulfills all desires.
One should worship the image of Umāmaheśvara using the names of the Sun;
for one should worship both the image of the Sun and the Śiva-liṅga with equal devotion. ||5||
No distinction whatsoever is maintained between Umāpati and Āditya;
therefore, O best of kings, one should worship the Sun in the temple.
Salutations to Sūryāya for the hands; to Arkāya for the feet during the Citrā constellation;
to Puruṣottama for the region of the ankles during Svātī; and to Dhātṛ for the region of the shanks and knees during Viśākhā. ||7||
Likewise, in Anurādhā, one should worship the two thighs of the thousand-rayed Sun;
in Jyeṣṭhā, "Salutation to Anaṅga" for the private parts; and in Mūla, "Salutation to Indra Bhīma" for the waist.
To Tvaṣṭṛ, the seven-horsed one, salutation in the pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā at the navel;
to Śava, the sharp one, in Śravaṇa at the belly; and to Vikartana in Dhaniṣṭhā at the back. (9)
The chest is to be worshipped in the asterism of the Lord of Waters (Śatabhiṣaj) for the destruction of darkness;
and the two supreme arms are to be worshipped in the two *uttarā-bhādrapadā*s for the sake of [attaining] the fierce rays of the sun.
The two hands of the Lord of the Three Worlds, bearing His armor, should be worshipped during the Revatī asterisms;
likewise, the fingernails are to be worshipped during the Aśvinī asterisms with the mantra: "Obeisance to the one who bears the yoke of the seven-horsed chariot. (11)
One should worship the syllable *ṭhaṃ* as "to Divākara, the bearer of fierce radiance" in the *Bharaṇī* nakṣatra;
one should worship it in the *Rohiṇī* nakṣatra within the *sampuṭa* (enclosure) of the *grīvāgni* (neck-fire) constellation.

"Obeisance to you who are fierce, piercing with that [trident] which is the enemy of the city of Rasanā; obeisance to Savitṛ"—with these words, having worshipped the nose of Śaṅkara under the asterism Punarvasu. (13)
The forehead is for the beloved of the lotus (the Moon); the hair-tufts are for the one who bears the body of the Vedas;
the serpent-adorned crown is for the beloved of the gods (Śiva); and the two ears are for those who bring auspiciousness on the Maghā constellation—thus they are to be worshipped. 14.
May the eastern quarter, the cow, the Brāhmaṇa, the moon, and the leader of men—these most worthy of worship—grant you well-being!
Now, in the asterism of Uttarā-phālgunī, the two eyebrows, and the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) are to be worshipped. (15)

Salutation to Śiva, who holds a noose, a goad, a lotus, a trident, a skull-bowl, a serpent, the moon, and a bow; salutation to the root cause of the destruction of Gayāsura, Anaṅga, Purandhaka, and the others. 16.
Having worshipped these and other limbs, one should worship the head with the mantra "To Viśveśvara.
Here too, one should eat food that is free from oil, meat, salt, and pungent seasonings, and which is not the remains of what has already been eaten.
Having thus performed these nocturnal rites on the Punarvasu [nakṣatra],
one should then offer a prastha of śāli rice grains and ghee from an udumbara vessel.
Having placed it in a vessel, he should present it to a Brahmin along with gold;
furthermore, there should be seven pairs of garments for the breaking of the fast. ||19||
On the fourteenth day, when the breaking of the fast has arrived at the beginning of the Bhārata and other [festivals],
one should devoutly feed a Brāhmaṇa with molasses, milk, ghee, and other such foods.
Having fashioned a pure eight-fingered lotus with eight petals and a pericarp out of gold, it should be provided with petals made of rubies.
Having prepared a bed marked with auspicious signs, free from discordant knots, provided with a pillow and a canopy, and furnished with a mattress, a coverlet, and a support; ||22||
She was also provided with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, a mirror, ornaments, fruits, garments, and ointments. (23)

Having fashioned a lotus upon that [altar] and adorned it with excellent qualities, one should provide a tawny cow, endowed with fine qualities, covered in cloth, possessing excellent character, and yielding milk. (24)
One should give away that cow—having silver hooves, golden horns, accompanied by her calf, and yielding milk—with the sacred mantra; one should not let the forenoon pass by.
Just as the bed of the Sun is never empty [of you], so may these increases—through grace, fortitude, splendor, and nourishment—be mine. 26.
Just as the gods know no one other than you who is more excellent and sinless, so likewise deliver me from the ocean of saṃsāra with its endless sufferings. 27.
Then, having circumambulated and prostrated, one should bid him farewell;
all that pertains to the bed and its components should be taken to the house of a twice-born man.

This vow of the Lord whose crest is a tree is not to be revealed to those of immoral conduct, nor to those who do not give alms, nor to those who proclaim their own faults; it is likewise forbidden for those who engage in improper acts toward cows, Brahmins, gods, or sages, and for those who harbor excessive malice. (29)
This secret, which is easy to perform and auspicious, should be told to that devotee who offers devotion;
those who know the Vedas declare that this brings about the destruction of the sins of men who have committed great crimes. (30)

O women, by practicing devotion here, you shall not be separated from kinsmen, sons, or wealth; you shall not be deprived of your husbands, and you shall offer delight to the gods. You shall encounter neither disease, nor suffering, nor delusion. (31)
This city was formerly built by Vasiṣṭha, Arjuna, and the fearless Kubera;
by the mere recitation of its name, all sins go to destruction—of this there is no doubt. (32)

Thus, he who recites or hears this account of Ravi’s reclining shall become beloved by Indra; moreover, he who performs this rite here brings even all his ancestors who have gone to hell back to heaven. (33)
The great seers have declared that the aśvattha, the vaṭa, the udumbara tree, the nyagrodha, the jambu tree, and the bilva [are suitable]. (34)
One should perform the worship of each of these trees, one by one, in sequence during two months starting from Mārgaśīrṣa.
Upon completion, one should give curd-rice, a canopy, a banner, and chowries;
and to the twice-born, water-pots accompanied by the five jewels.
One who practices deceit toward the Teacher incurs faults by doing so. ||37||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Sun’s Reclining," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Six.
Bhīṣma said:
A man shall be endowed with long life, health, and the great prosperity of his lineage, as well as beauty and noble birth.
O Moon, please explain correctly the vow of him who has taken birth again and again.
Pulastya said:
"What you have asked is perfect; it brings about an imperishable heaven."
I shall now proclaim the secret which those who know the Purāṇas understand.
The vow known as Rohiṇīcandraśayana is described here; on that occasion, one should worship the image of Nārāyaṇa with the names of the [twelve] months.
Whenever the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight occurs on a Monday, or when the constellation Rohiṇī (Brahma-nakṣatra) arises on the full moon day; ||4||
Then a man should perform his bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and white mustard seeds;
furthermore, the wise man should recite the mantra "āpyāyasva" one hundred and eight times.

Even a Śūdra, through supreme devotion and avoiding conversation with heretics, should worship: "Obeisance to Soma" for the feet; "Obeisance to Yaśastāyana" for the two shanks; "Obeisance to Anantadhāman" for the two thighs;
and "Obeisance to Jalodara" for the belly, and "Obeisance to Anaṅgadhāman" for the penis.
Salutations again and again to the hips that bestow the pleasure of desire; the moon is always to be worshipped there.
Likewise, the belly is for Amṛtodarā, and the navel is to be honored as the abode of the moon. 9.

Homage to the moon-faced one, who is eternally honored as the lord of the twice-born; homage to the one worthy of worship like the moon, whose lips are beloved by the forest of the *kaumoda* [teeth]. 10.
The nose of Śauri, the protector of the world and the best among medicinal herbs; the two eyebrows, which are the seeds of joy;
and likewise the two eyes, resembling lotuses, belong to him whose hands are as broad as blue lotuses. 11.
Salutations to the one worshipped at all sacrifices; the two ears are for the slayer of the Daityas;
the forehead, the arms, and the neck are to be worshipped as the beloved of the ocean; and the hair is to be worshipped as belonging to the Lord of Suṣumṇā. (12)
Salutations to the head of Murāri, which is the vehicle of the moon;
salutations to the crown of the Lord of the Universe, an ocean of nectar consisting of the fortune and happiness of the lotus-loving Rohiṇī. ||13||

Having worshipped the divine consort of Indra with fragrant flowers, offerings, incense, and other such items, he who sleeps on the ground and rises again, bathes, and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) for the sake of the Brahmins; ||14||
At dawn, he should give a water-pot containing gold as a gift, saying: "Obeisance to the Destroyer of Sin.
Then, having consumed cow's urine that is not salty and free from meat, he should eat twenty-eight mouthfuls of food. (15)

Having fasted and then eaten three morsels mixed with ghee, one should listen for a moment to an ancient history (itihāsa) concerning the kadamba, blue lotus, ketakī, jasmine, lotus, and śatapatrikā flowers. ||16||
Then, flowers that do not fade, the *siṃduvāra* flower, the *mallikā* flower of Bhārata, the white flower, the *karavīra* flower, and the *śrīcaṃpaka* should be offered to the Moon. (17)
In the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one should always worship Hari with these [flowers] respectively;
in whichever month a vow or other observance occurs, one should worship Hari with the flowers appropriate to that month.
Having thus fasted according to the rules for as long as a year,
a man should give a bed as a religious gift, provided with all its necessary furnishings.
Having caused a golden image of the pair Rohiṇī and the Moon to be made,
the Moon should be six finger-breadths in size and Rohiṇī four finger-breadths.
It should be provided with eight pearls, accompanied by a white eye,
and further endowed with a vessel of milk, a golden bowl, and unbroken grains of rice.
In the forenoon, one should give [the cow] together with rice, sugarcane, and fruit, accompanied by the mantra—a white cow with a golden face and provided with silver hooves. (22)
Having adorned a cow with a cloth and a vessel, as well as a conch and a bowl, and having decorated a virtuous Brahmin couple with ornaments, [he should give them]. (23)
One should imagine that this Moon, in the form of a brahmin, has arrived with his wife,
just as Kṛṣṇa never abandoned his bed even when Rōhiṇī was present.
This forest is indeed a manifestation of the form of Soma through its various powers;
just as you alone are the supreme bliss for all and the bestower of liberation. (25)
"May enjoyment, liberation, and likewise devotion toward you be firm in me, O Moon—thus [I pray], O sinless one, for one who is terrified by saṃsāra and desires liberation. (26)
O King, this alone is the unsurpassed provider of beauty, health, and long life,
and it is always beloved by the ancestors.
Having become the sovereign of the three worlds for seven hundred kalpas there,
he attains the realm of the Moon, from which a return [to this world] is difficult to find.
Any woman who performs this worship of the moon-bedded [Viṣṇu] shall also obtain that fruit, from which rebirth is difficult to attain. (29)
Thus, whoever recites or hears this hymn of praise to the Slayer of Madhu, he too—by the mere mention of the name of Śauri—attains wisdom;
and having entered the celestial abode, he is honored by the hosts of gods. (30)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Vow of Rohiṇī and the Moon’s Reclining," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-Seven
Bhīṣma said: O Brāhmaṇa, tell me the procedure regarding tanks, groves, wells, ponds, lotus-pools,
and temples.
Who are the brahmin officiating priests there, what should the Vedivāk be like, what are the sacrificial fees and offerings, and what are the time, the location, and the preceptor? (2)
"O you of excellent vows, tell me everything regarding the materials that are prescribed for all [these rites].
Pulastya said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed King, to the procedure that applies to tanks and other such works."
O best of kings, this history is recited in the Purāṇas when the auspicious bright fortnight has arrived and the sun has entered its northern course.
On an auspicious day, having had the Brahmins recite the benedictions (vācana), one should perform [the rite] near a lake in a place free from inauspicious things. ||5||
The altar should be four cubits in length, level, square, and four-faced;
likewise, the pavilion should be sixteen cubits [in length] and four-faced.
O Prince, the altars (vedī) should be surrounded by trenches (garta) one cubit (aratni) deep, having three,
seven, or five tiers (mekhalā), and their faces should be straight.
The yoni should be one *vitasti* in measure and six or seven *aṅgulas* in width;
the pits should be one *hasta* in measure, with a girdle (*mekhalā*) three finger-joints (*triparva*) high.
On all sides, they should be of uniform color and provided with banners and flags;
moreover, they should be fashioned from the branches of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
One should cause these doors to be made for each direction of the pavilion;
there, eight auspicious hotṛ-priests and likewise eight gatekeepers [should be appointed].
Eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
who are endowed with all auspicious marks, who know the mantras, and who have conquered their senses, should be appointed as reciters.
One should station the best of the twice-born, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, at each pit; and one should place jars and sacrificial implements in each of them.
A white fan, a seat, and a very large copper vessel;
then there should be offerings (bali) of many colors for each deity. 13.
The wise preceptor, having consecrated it with mantras, should cast [the post] into the ground;
the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be one cubit (aratni) in length and fashioned from a tree that yields milky sap.
One desiring prosperity should establish the sacrificial hall at the height of the sacrificer; twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) adorned with golden ornaments should be appointed. ||15||
And these earrings, as well as armlets and bracelets, finger-rings, and various kinds of garments. (16)

One should give equal shares to all, but it is traditionally taught that the preceptor should receive double; one should also give what is appropriate for the occasion and whatever is personally dear to oneself.
The tortoise and the crocodile are made of gold; the fish and the dolphin are made of silver; the tortoise and the frog are made of copper; and the crow and the mongoose are made of iron. (18)
Having thus obtained all of that, O lord of the people, at the very outset,
one should wear white garlands and garments, and be anointed with white perfumes and unguents.
The patron, together with his wife, sons, and grandsons, was bathed with all the waters containing every medicinal herb by those who had mastered the Vedas.
Having reached the western gate, he should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
then, with auspicious sounds and the resonance of kettledrums.
The knower of reality should adorn the mandala with five colors;
it should have sixteen spokes, a wheel, a lotus center, and four faces. (22)
Having made it square on top and circular at the base, and beautifully adorned in the middle,
one should then place the planets and the lords of the worlds upon the altar.
The wise one should place all [the deities] according to the mantra in every direction;
he should install a water-pot (kalaśa) in the center, relying upon the Vāruṇa mantra.
The wise man should install Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu there, as well as Vināyaka, Kamalā, and Ambikā. (25)

Then, for the sake of the peace of all worlds, one should install the assembly of beings; having thus performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) provided with flowers, edible offerings, and fruits. (26)
One should wrap the pitcher, the syllable *Bhāṃ*, and the Ratnagarbhā [image] with cloths;
then, having adorned them with flowers and perfumes, one should likewise [adorn] the door-keepers.
He should say to them, "Sacrifice! and honor the teacher.
Two Rigvedins should be stationed in the east, and two knowers of the Yajurveda in the south. (28)
The two Sāmavedins should be stationed in the west, and the two Atharvavedins in the north;
the sacrificer should sit down in the south, facing north.
He should say "Sacrifice! to those priests, and likewise to those chanters, "Remain steadfast through the recitation of the most excellent mantras. (30)
Having thus instructed them all, he who knows the mantras should milk the fire and offer oblations with mantras,
as well as clarified butter and sacrificial fuel.
The officiating priests must likewise offer oblations with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa on all sides;
having offered according to the rules to the planets, as well as to Indra and Īśvara.
He offered oblations according to the prescribed rite to the Maruts, the world-protectors, and Viśvakarman;
[reciting] the Śāntisūkta, the Caraudra, the Pāvamāna, and the Maṅgala hymns.
To the east, the Bahvṛca priest shall separately recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta,
as well as the Śākvara, Raudra, Saumya, Kauśmāṇḍa, and Jātavedasa hymns.
Those who know the Yajurveda should recite the Saura hymn on the south side;
[they should also recite] the Vairāja, the Pauruṣa hymn, the Sauparṇa, and that which is beneficial to Rudra.
The Śaiśava with its five-fold finale, the Gāyatra, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, the Vāmadevya, the Bṛhatsāman, the Raurava, and the Caratha-tara. (36)
O King, the chanters of the Sāmaveda, stationed at the western gate, should sing the *Gavāṃvratam*, the *Vikīrṇam*, the *Carkṣoghnam*, and likewise the *Cayam*.
And to the north, the followers of the Atharvaveda should likewise recite the Śāntika and Pauṣṭika mantras mentally, taking refuge in the Lord Varuṇa.

Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in this manner on both nights preceding [the main ceremony], [one should collect earth] from an elephant, a horse, a chariot, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, a cow-pen, and a herd of cattle. (39)
Having taken clay, one should likewise place medicinal herbs into the jars,
as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), white mustard seeds, fragrant substances, and guggulu resin.

The bathing of that [image] should be performed using the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), preceded by the great mantras of the performer, having thus carried it out according to the ritual injunctions. (41)
Having thus passed the night with rites performed according to the injunctions,
then, when the clear dawn had arisen, [he should proceed] with a hundred bulls.
It should be given to the Brahmins—either sixty-eight, or again fifty, or thirty-six, or twenty-five. ||43||
Then, when the auspicious and pure lagna had arrived at its proper time, [the ceremony was performed] with Vedic chants, accompanied by Gandharvas and various musical instruments. ||44||
Having adorned her body with gold ornaments, O lord of the people, one should cause her to descend into the water and give her to a Brāhmaṇa who chants the Sāman hymns.
Then, taking a golden vessel endowed with all kinds of gems,
he placed within it crocodiles, fish, and all other such creatures.
It was supported by four Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and it was provided with the water of great rivers and adorned with curds and unbroken grains of rice.
One should have her placed face down in the middle of the water facing north,
having been well-bathed with the Ātharvaṇa mantras, as well as with the *punarmā* hymn.
Having cast [the materials] with the mantra beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having returned to the pavilion and honored the members of the assembly,
he should then offer the bali-oblation equally.
O best of kings, one should offer oblations for four more days;
on the fourth day, the ritual (caturthī-karma) must be performed, and there too, gifts should be given according to one's capacity.
Having prepared the vessels for the sacrifice and the sacrificial implements,
he should distribute them equally among the officiating priests and then divide the pavilion as well.
One should present a golden vessel and a bed to a Brahmin;
thereafter, one should feed either a thousand Brahmins or likewise eight hundred.
Fifty or twenty-five portions of food should be given according to one's capacity;
thus is the rite for a tank described in the Purāṇas. (53)
This same procedure is prescribed for all wells and tanks, as well as for lotus-pools, and likewise for their consecration ceremonies.
There may be a distinction based on the mantra in the case of palaces, gardens, and grounds;
however, this procedure for those who are incapable was seen by Svayambhū as being performed with half [the usual dimensions].
Even when one's resources are very meager, those free from stinginess regarding wealth should perform [the rite] as if with a single fire;
staying [in this manner] during the rainy season is remembered as being equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
That which occurs during the autumn season yields the aforementioned results;
gold [given] during the winter and the cool season yields the fruits of the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices respectively.
They say that residing during the rainy season is equal to the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha);
likewise, residing during the summer excels even the royal consecration (rājasūya). (58)
O Great King, he whose intellect is exceedingly pure performs these distinguished dharmas on this earth;
being purified, he goes indeed to the abode of Brahmā and rejoices in heaven for many eons. (59)
Having wandered through many worlds and enjoyed the pleasures of sound and other objects with celestial women for two *aparārddhas*,
he eventually attains again that supreme station of Viṣṇu by the power of yoga.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of a Tank," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Twenty-eighth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, describe in detail and according to the rules the ritual for trees;
explain the procedure by which the planting of trees should be performed by the wise.
"Tell me now those worlds which are said to belong to them.
Pulastya said:
"I shall describe the ritual for trees as well as for garden grounds. (2)

O Lord of the World, having completed everything according to the procedure for constructing a tank—including the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, and a preceptor of the prescribed qualifications—[he should proceed]. (3)
Likewise, one should honor the Brahmins with gold, garments, and ointments,
having sprinkled them with water containing all medicinal herbs and adorned them with curd and unbroken grains.
Having adorned the trees with garlands, one should envelop them with cloths;
and for all of them, the piercing of the ears should be performed using a golden needle.
One should also give that same [mixture] to another person with a golden probe;
one should cause seven or eight fruits to be prepared from *kāladhauta* gold.
One should consecrate each of all those trees upon the altar;
guggulu incense is the best, and they should be placed within copper vessels.
O Lord of the Earth, having filled jars with the seven types of grain and adorned them with cloths, perfumes, and unguents,
one should place them at all the trees.

Having performed worship and offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the world, beginning with Indra and the others, according to the prescribed rule and according to their respective powers. ||9||
The consecration of the tree must be performed by the twice-born in this manner.
Then [they should bring] those wearing white garments and golden girdles.
One should release from the midst of the trees a milch cow, facing northward, possessing a beautiful gait, adorned with golden horns, and yielding abundant milk. 11.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments and auspicious songs,
and with the Vāruṇa mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, [the rite was performed] on all sides at that time.
The eminent brahmins should perform the ceremonial bath with those very jars;
having bathed and wearing white garments, the patron should pay worship.
He gratified all the attentive officiating priests with cows,
golden threads, bracelets, rings, and sacred grass rings.
One should perform the milk-consecration with garments, beds, as well as household utensils and sandals for four days.
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with clarified butter, barley, and black sesame seeds;
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of the Palāśa tree are recommended, and on the fourth day, a festival should likewise be held. 16.
Likewise, one should again give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) there according to one's ability;
whatever is most dear to oneself, that one should give without envy.
Having given double [the fee] to the preceptor and prostrating, one should ask for his forgiveness.
The wise person who performs the tree festival according to this rite— ||18||
The wise man who installs this tree, O king of kings, attains all desires and enjoys the infinite state. (19)
That king shall also dwell in heaven for as long as Indra lives there,
rescuing as many men of the past and the future as are equal in number to the hairs on his body.
That person who would constantly hear this or cause it to be heard attains the supreme perfection from which return is difficult to find. (21)
He too is worshipped by the gods and is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
even trees provide the status of a son to one who is childless.

O King of kings, they bestow the fruits of their efforts upon those who give offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and so forth at sacred fords (*tīrtha*); therefore, with great care, plant the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*).
One shall perform the task that would otherwise require a thousand sons;
the wealthy man [is served] by the Aśvattha tree, and the Aśoka tree is the destroyer of grief. (24)
The Plakṣa tree is said to bestow sacrifice, and the Kṣīrī is remembered as the giver of longevity; likewise, the Jaṃbukī, Kanyakā, Dātrī, Bhāryā, and Āḍimī grant wives. (25)
The Aśvattha tree destroys diseases, while the Palāśa likewise bestows Brahman-knowledge;
however, he who consumes the Vibhītaka will be born as a ghost.
Through the growth of *aṅkola* trees, the prosperity of the family; through *khadira*, freedom from disease;
and through the sprouting of *nimba* trees—the Sun shall always be pleased with those who plant them. (27)
Lord Śiva resides in the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, while Pārvatī is in the Pāṭalā;
the Apsarases are in the Śiṃśapā, and the best of Gandharvas are in the Kuṃda. (28)
The *tiṃtiḍīka*, the group of trees beginning with *kedāra*, and likewise the *jula* and *dasyu*;
the *caṃdana* tree, which bestows merit and prosperity, as well as the *panasa* tree. (29)
The *saubhāgyada* is a mango tree; the *karīra* is an adulterer;
the *tālova* causes the destruction of offspring; and the *kula* is a *kulavardhana*. ||30||

Bahubhāryā cures scabies; nārikela (coconut) is for all body ailments; drākṣā (grape) bestows pleasure; sarvāṅgasundarī is likewise; kolī is a giver of sexual delight; and ketakī destroys enemies. ||31||
Other mountains such as these have also been mentioned by the Sage;
they too shall attain stability for those who have planted trees. (32)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Planting Trees," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||28||
The Twenty-Ninth Chapter.
Pulastya said:
Likewise, I shall describe another [rite] that bestows the fruit of all desires, which those learned in the Purāṇas know by the name Saubhāgyaśayana. 1.
Formerly, when these worlds— Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahas, and the rest— had been consumed by fire,
the collective good fortune of all living beings then became concentrated in one place.
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha, he remained upon the chest of Viṣṇu;
then, after some time, O King, during the process of creation once again—

In this world enveloped by egoism, which is possessed of both primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa), and while the rivalry between the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) and Kṛṣṇa had intensified; ||4||
A terrifying flame of fire, appearing tawny in form, arose;
from the chest of Hari, heated by that [flame], it issued forth.
That which, having resorted to the chest of Viṣṇu, attained the state of supreme beauty in the form of nectar—so long as it does not reach the surface of the earth, [it remains as such]. (6)
It was cast up from the sky by the wise son of Brahmā;
as soon as it was drunk by Dakṣa, it produced beauty and loveliness.
Great power and splendor were born from Dakṣa Parameṣṭhin;
that which remained and fell upon the earth was divided into eight parts and thus came into being.
Then the medicinal herbs were born, which bestow the sevenfold prosperity:
sugarcanes, the king of trees (the coconut), beans, and śāli rice.
Like curdled milk, cow’s milk, the *kuṣumbha* flower, and likewise the *kuśuma* flower, with salt as the eighth— this is called the "Eightfold Saubhāgya" (the eight auspicious substances).
She was formerly drunk by the son of Brahmā, who was a knower of yoga and knowledge; from him she became his daughter, she who is called Satī.
Because she transcends the worlds through her grace, she is called Lalitā;
the wielder of the Pināka bow married that goddess, who is the cave of the three worlds.

By worshipping her with devotion—the one who consists of the triple-world’s good fortune and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—what indeed does a man not obtain? Nor even a woman. 13.
Bhīṣma said:
O Muni, tell me how she is to be propitiated;
and tell me what her ritual procedure is for the peace of the world. (14)
Pulastya said: Having reached the month of Vaiśākha, on the third day of the bright fortnight during the forenoon, one who is dear to the people should perform a bath with sesame seeds.
On that day, the goddess Sāvitrī, being the soul of the universe,
married that woman of excellent complexion with the mantras used for taking the hand in marriage.
Then, on the third lunar day, one should worship Viśveśa together with her,
using various kinds of fruits, lamps, incense, and accompanied by food offerings (naivedya).
Having bathed the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise with fragrant water, one should worship Gaurī together with the Lord whose crest is the moon.
"Salutation to Pāṭalā"—thus [one should say] at the two feet of the Goddess and of Śiva;
and having proclaimed "to Śivā," [one should say] "to Jayā" at the two ankles. (19)
With the mantra "Tryambakāya," he worships the pair of shanks of Rudra with Bhavānī;
with "Śiraḥ rudreśvarāya," he worships the two knees with Vijayā. (20)
Salutation to Harikeśāya for the thighs; salutation to Varada for the shanks; salutation to Īśāya for the waist; salutation to Śaṅkarāya for Śaṅkara (the phallus) for the sake of bliss.
One should worship the two sides of the belly with "Obeisance to the one who possesses a trident in the forest," and the belly with "Obeisance to you, Maṅgala, the conqueror. (22)
One should worship the pair of breasts with the mantra "sarvātmane namo rudram īśānyai," and likewise worship the single letter *ṭha* as Śiva and Rudrāṇī with the mantra "vedātmane. (23)

"Salutation to the destroyer of Tripura," "O Lord of the Universe," "Salutation to the one who has two arms," "To the three-eyed one," "The remover [of sins]," "O beloved of the fire of time at the end of the age. (24)
One should always worship the ornaments with the mantra "To Saubhāgyabhavana," the face with "Svāhā Svadhāyai," and the wielder of the trident (Śūlin) with "Īśvarāya. (25)
To her who dwells in the Aśoka grove, the two lips are to be worshipped as the givers of prosperity;
likewise, the face is for Sthāṇu, O beloved of the moon-faced one. (26)

"Obeisance to Ardhanārīśa," [he said] to the nose; "Obeisance to Hara," to the tip of the nose; "Obeisance to Asitāṅgī," to the eyebrows; "Obeisance to Ugrā," to the lord of the world (the forehead); and "Obeisance to Lalitā," again to the two eyebrows.
One should worship Śarva as the leader of the hosts, Vāsudeva as the one with matted hair (Laka), and likewise worship the Lord of the Śrī-kaṇṭha [lineage] and Śiva-keśa. 28.
Salutation to the head of her who possesses a terrifying, fierce, and formidable form, and to the Self of All;
having worshipped Hara according to the prescribed rites, one should place the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) before him.
One should place smooth *niṣpāva* beans, *kusumbha*, sesame, *jīraka*,
the king of trees (*tarurāja*), sugarcane, salt, and *kustumburu* as the eighth.
Since it bestows good fortune, one should offer the "Eightfold Good Fortune" (saubhāgyāṣṭaka);
having thus presented all of this before the two Śivas once more, [one should proceed]. (31)
Having consumed the *śṛṅgāṭaka* fruits of the month of Caitra, one should sleep on the ground to subdue the enemy;
then, at dawn, having likewise performed ritual bathing and recitation, one becomes pure. (32)
Having honored a brahmin couple with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
one should present two golden images accompanied by the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka).
"May Maitralalitā-Brāhmaṇāyani be pleased with me"—
thus, O King, one should always [recite this] on the third lunar day for the duration of a year.
Listen now to this specific instruction regarding the mantra for the offering of the Prāśana:
it is said that in the month of Vaiśākha, one should offer cow-dung upon the tip of a cow's horn. (35)
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, this flower of the dāru tree is prescribed; in Śuci, the bilva leaf is remembered [as the offering].
In Śrāvaṇa, one should consume curd, and in Nabhas, water infused with kuśa grass.
In the month of Āśvayuja one should consume milk; in Kārttika, speckled butter (pṛṣadājya);
in Mārgaśīrṣa, cow’s urine; and in Pauṣa, one should consume clarified butter.
Likewise, one should offer black sesame seeds in the dark fortnight of Māgha and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in Phālguna;
[the goddesses are] Lalitā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Kumudā, and Śivā. (38)
Likewise, at the time of giving, one should proclaim: "May Vāsudevī, Gaurī, Maṅgalā, Kamalā, Satī, and Umā be pleased. (39)
On the twelfth day of that month, on the twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, one should worship Lakṣmī there together with her husband.
Therefore, on the full moon day, the grandfather (Brahmā) together with his consort should likewise be worshipped by the learned man who desires freedom from fear in the hereafter. 41.
Likewise, one desiring prosperity should offer the eightfold auspiciousness (saubhāgyāṣṭaka), consisting of jasmine, aśoka, lotus, kadamba, blue lotus, and campaka. 42.
Kubjaka, karavīra, bāṇa, amlāna, paṅkaja, and sinduvāra are known as flowers [to be offered] in all months. (43)
Japākusuma, bhakusuma, mālatī, śatapatrikā, and karavīra—these are all recommended whenever they are available, and karavīra is especially so at all times. 44.
Having thus observed the fast according to the prescribed rules for a full year, a man— or a woman, or a maiden— should worship Śiva with devotion day and night.
One should give a bed for the observance, complete with all necessary furnishings,
along with golden images of Umā and Maheśvara, and a bull together with a cow.
Having set up the bed, he should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa;
for one year, on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), he should worship Keśava as Mahālakṣmī.
Having worshipped Brahmā with the Sahasrāvitri here on earth, a man attains all the desires he has mentally sought after. 48.
Furthermore, according to one's ability, other couples [should be honored] with garments and the like, with gifts of grain, ornaments, and cattle, and with other accumulations of wealth. ||49||
Free from stinginess regarding wealth and devoid of pride, one should perform worship;
he who thus correctly observes the Saubhāgya-śayana-vrata [attains success]. (50)
One who performs this practice while renouncing even a single fruit attains all desires or reaches the eternal state. 51.
O lord of men, every month he attains fame and renown, as well as good fortune, health, and beauty, along with garments, ornaments, and decorations. (52)
O King, he who performs the Saubhāgya-śayana vow for twelve years shall never be separated from his wife and shall bestow good fortune upon his bed.
Having performed seven, eight, or nine [such acts], a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā; being duly honored, he shall dwell there for ten thousand kalpas.
Having reached the world of Viṣṇu and likewise attained the world of Śiva,
O Lord of Monkeys, she acts like a woman or like a young maiden.
She too, cherished by the grace of the Goddess, attains that fruit;
and whoever should even hear it, or indeed bestow their mind upon it, [attains the same]. (56)
Having become a Vidyādhara, he shall dwell for a long time in the heavenly world.
This was created here in ancient times by Madana; it was likewise performed by Śatadhanu and by Nara.
Then, having been honored by the Wind-god, the Lord of Men performed a great marvel; would it not be new? ||58||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Vows," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||29||
Bhīṣma said:
"Having reached the Yajñaparvata mountain, the almighty Viṣṇu placed his footsteps here;
for what purpose was this trail of footprints made?"
O you of great intellect, tell me that which was done by the God of gods; which gift was indeed given to him by Viṣṇu? ||2||
O great sage, having made that supreme abode for me,
O Lord, the high-souled Viṣṇu shall have his residence in Vaikuṇṭha in the heavenly world.
How did he set foot in the world of men?
And among the worlds of the gods, who were the god of gods, led by Indra? ||4||
O Brahmin, it is proclaimed that the residence of those who are constantly devoted to the Lord through great austerity is in the Maharloka of Śrī-Varāha. ||5||
Likewise, the residence of the high-souled Nṛsiṃha in Janaloka was thus declared;
the dwelling of Trivikrama in Tapoloka is celebrated.
Having abandoned these worlds, how [could you remain] with both feet on the ground here at Puṣkara, on this ancestral field, the mountain of sacrifice?
O Brahmin, recount in detail the verses;
by hearing them, the destruction of all sins will certainly come to pass.
Pulastya said:
You have asked well, O sir; listen with a concentrated mind to how the placement of his steps was formerly performed by Lord Viṣṇu.
Having reached Yajñaparvata on the slope of the Śilā mountain,
in the former Kṛta age, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the divine task of Bhīṣma.
Formerly, Viṣṇu performed supreme austerities for the sake of the earth;
[thereby] the entire celestial realm was recovered from the exceedingly powerful Dānavas. (11)
Having brought the three worlds under his control and conquered the gods along with Indra, the Dānavas—
who were the enjoyers of the sacrifice— became exceedingly powerful there.
When the world of the three realms, including all things mobile and immobile, had thus come to pass, it was [ruled] by the exceedingly powerful Dānava Ābāskali. (13)
Śakra fell into extreme distress, rendered hopeless regarding his life;
together with Bāṣkali, the lord of the Dānavas said, "He is invincible to me in this age. (14)
By virtue of Brahmā’s granting of a boon to all the inhabitants of heaven,
I was chosen for that position in the world of Brahmā by all the gods.
"I go for refuge to the God; no other resort exists.
Having reflected thus, Indra was surrounded by all the inhabitants of heaven. (16)
He went quickly, O Bhīṣma, to where the divine Grandfather was; having reached the abode of Brahmā, he was surrounded by those dwellers of heaven.
He spoke regarding the world's duty and the supreme calamity that had arrived:
"O Vaidehī, do you not know that both [sides] have come upon us? (18)
"O Lord, since everything was taken away by the Daityas through the granting of that boon, I have related to you all that was said by the evil-minded Bāṣkali. (19)
O Grandfather, let us not be disregarded; act without delay.
O Lord of Gods, you must consider this matter here for the sake of the peace of the world.
And as they did not perceive anything at all, the ritual acts prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis did not proceed; thus, day after day, there was a loss for us. (21)
Just as an ordinary person speaks with a view toward his own self-interest, so too have we always spoken, having set aside all personal benefit. (22)
If one who has been benefited by another does not, in turn, perform a thousandfold benefit for that person,
he is of vain intellect.
Furthermore, for that wicked person who performs evil deeds— shameless and consumed by his own ingratitude— there shall be a dwelling even in the hells.
A remedy for this is not accomplished by this much alone;
nor does it even occur to those whose intellects are fixed solely on their own self-interest. (25)
If that place which was not his own abode, where the world finds suffering,
had split his heart into a hundred pieces, it would still not have reached satiety.
Or rather, wherever they may be submerged, you must lift them out by speaking of skillful means; by this, his splendor will be set in motion. (27)
Behold this world as it was described and seen by me, existing in such a state:
devoid of Vedic recitation and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, with its festivals and auspicious rites ceased. (28)
Having abandoned the practice of Vedic study, having relinquished all conversation and possessions, and having cast aside the science of statecraft,
he was left with nothing remaining but his breath.
The world has fallen into affliction and reached an even more miserable state;
yet, in all this time, we have not succumbed to exhaustion.
Brahmā said:
"I know that Bāṣkali is indeed arrogant because of the granting of the boon;
I consider him invincible to you all, but he shall be subdued by Viṣṇu. (31)
Then, as he remained established in cessation, this reality of non-existence arose;
for him who was situated in samādhi, by mere meditation, the four-armed [Lord] appeared.
Being meditated upon by Svayambhū for only a very short time,
he arrived in a mere moment while everyone was looking on.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Brahman, desist from this meditation; you have been restrained. I am he for whose sake you desired to meditate, and I have come before you. (34)
Brahmā said: This is indeed a great favor here—the very sight of our Lord. For whom else in this world, O Master, could such a thought even arise? (35)
My very own birth was fashioned for the sake of the world;
yet this world exists for your sake—this is a wonder, for it does not exist in reality. (36)
The protection of the world must be performed by you; indeed, Rudra alone shall take it away.
Thus, while this world exists, [this shall apply] to this high-souled Śakra. (37)
"The kingdom of the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, has been seized by Bāṣkali;
O Keśava, let assistance be rendered to your servant by granting him counsel. (38)
Vāsudeva said: "By virtue of your boon, this Dānava is currently incapable of being slain;
he can only be overcome by means of intelligence, for his purpose here is solely to be bound. (39)
"I shall become a dwarf, the destroyer of the Dānavas; come with me to the dwelling of Bāṣkali. (40)
Having gone there, O King, you should request this boon from him: three paces of land for this dwarf Brahmin. (41)
"O illustrious one, grant this which has been requested by me.
Thus addressed by Śakra, the lord of the Dānavas replied, "I would give even my own life. (42)
O Grandfather, having bound that Dānava— who had seized his household— and having diligently cast him down into the netherworld (Pātāla), [he departed].
"O Śakra, assuming the form of a boar for the sake of slaying that evil-minded one, go quickly with haste, for my body will not remain. (44)
Having spoken thus, he ceased and indeed vanished;
then, after some time, Viṣṇu entered the womb of Aditi.
Extremely terrible omens appeared in great numbers when Viṣṇu, the support of the entire world, had entered the state of being an embryo. (46)
For then an auspicious and powerful omen indeed occurred:
a fragrant and sweet scent of *mālatī* flowers wafted forth. (47)
Then, having reached the appointed time for the ordained rite, the God,
compassionate toward all beings, for the sake of the welfare of the host of the thirty [gods],
possessed of pure and sparse hair, and possessing the splendor of the rising moon or a conch shell—
The God of gods assumed the state of being the son of Aditi. ||48||
When Viṣṇu was about to descend, the faces of the Siddhas, gods, and Asuras—whose eyes were unblinking—beamed with joy;
and as winds carrying away the excessive dust blew, that day during Viṣṇu’s birth became truly auspicious.

A man who constantly performs worship of the deities, guests, and the great guru, and who is truly devoted to the worship of the ancestors, is born as a noble preta. 42.
When the fourth lunar day (Caturthī) occurs conjoined with a white Mars (Śuklāṅgāraka),
a man who performs a Śrāddha ceremony on that day with faith does not become a preta.

The pretas said: "O Sage, we have heard of various unrighteous acts; O Great-minded One, please tell us that by which one truly becomes a preta, for we are afflicted with suffering. (46)
The Brāhmaṇa said:

From officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, from abandoning those worthy to sacrifice, and from serving a Śūdra while engaged in sexual pleasure, a man is born as a preta after death. 49.
A man who steals deposits, betrays friends, is constantly devoted to cooking for Śūdras, is treacherous, a killer of Brahmins, and is deceitful, is born as a preta.

Having received a common sacrificial fee, he who hides it all to himself alone,
being devoted to the disposition of an atheist, is reborn as a hungry ghost.
O best of Brahmins, even as he was speaking thus, a shower of flowers released by the gods in their thousands fell upon the earth from the sky with a sweet sound.
But the celestial chariots of the pretas arrived from all directions because of their conversation with this brahmin and the proclamation of his merit. (54)
Therefore, O son of Gaṅgā, if you desire to perform what is beneficial for yourself, converse with the virtuous with every effort and without weariness. 55.
One who recites this story of the five pretas as a tilaka of all dharmas a hundred thousand times—no man born in his family shall be reborn as a preta. (56)
Whether he hears it repeatedly or even with a lack of supreme faith, or even if he is not endowed with devotion, that man is not reborn as a preta.
Bhīṣma said:
"Why is Puṣkara celebrated in the intermediate space?
And how is it attained here by sages who are devoted to righteousness? (58)
Tell me all of that by which it is obtained, how what has been obtained is secured, and how that which is secured yields its fruit; for I ask you out of curiosity, O Lord. (59)
Pulastya said: O King, ten million sages dwelling in the southern region arrived at Puṣkara, which has ascended to the sky, for the purpose of bathing.
Realizing this, all those sages became devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and,
meditating upon the Supreme Brahman, remained thus for twelve years.
There, Brahmā, the great seers, and the gods led by Indra assembled;
the seers, remaining invisible, spoke to them of these extremely difficult observances.
O twice-born ones, let the ritual bathing of Puṣkara be performed with the mantra;
by means of the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he will attain proximity to it.
By the recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, it indeed becomes a bestower of fruit;
thus, at the conclusion of the speech by all those brahmins, they acted accordingly.
O twice-born ones, because they have attained a state of meritlessness through their actions,
those brahmins— whether facing south or north— are censured in the treatises on dharma.
And those others who are mountaineers and are worthy of invitation at a *śrāddha*—for this reason, O King, it is established thus in the sky. (66)
O King, by bathing at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika, one attains purity;
together with Brahmā, it bestows merit upon all.

Listen, O Lord, to what has been seen here by me, and how it was seen:
O Rāma, King Indradyumna, whose mind is inconceivable, has arrived here. (97)
O descendant of Raghu, there were three such beings endowed with bodies like those of brahmins, each adorned with all kinds of ornaments. 98.
"O Raghava, my ancestors were seen by me within the limbs of the Brahmana;
seeing them, I was overcome with shame and departed from your presence. (99)
"The Brahmins have not been fed by you, nor has the Śrāddha been performed according to the rules;
how then can these women, clad in bark garments and deerskins, be the leaders of the king's procession? (100)
"O slayer of the enemy heroes of worldly existence, this truth has been proclaimed:
the silken garments of Kaikeyī have indeed been taken away. (101)
From that time forth, having learned that my refuge was the Cīriṇī forest, I thought, "O Mother, let not even the slightest suffering befall you. (102)
O scorcher of enemies, O Raghava, I do not recall ever having asked my mother or my father when the end of this forest exile would come.
I swear by my own feet that these very days pass again and again, longing for the sight of Rāma’s face. 104.
How could this food be given by the king with his own hand? For even among servants, one never eats while remaining indifferent toward those who serve him. (105)
How indeed can I venture to bestow such a person upon him, when I was seen by the king in the city adorned with all my ornaments? (106)
Fanning the lord of men with a fly-whisk in her hand, how can I look upon the king, whose limbs are covered with sweat and dirt? 107.
Clearly you have reached the third heaven, having been delivered by me, your son, after seeing me—a young girl, suffering, distressed in the forest, and innocent. (108)
"O Raghava, this king will surely grieve, thinking, 'She is lost.
You are like his very life-breath, O Rama; therefore, there is nothing here that should be hidden from me."
"By this very truth, I now touch your two feet.
Hearing that, Rāghava was pleased with his beloved wife who spoke so sweetly.
Having brought him close and embraced him very firmly with great respect, O hero,
he then ate his food, and after that, Jānakī ate.
Having remained there for that night, the two descendants of Raghu,
when the thousand-rayed sun had risen, set their minds on departing.
Facing westward, he traveled for one krośa as far as the Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara;
meanwhile, Rāghava remained on the eastern side of the Puṣkara.
Then he heard the words spoken by the divine messenger:
"O Raghava, may it be well with you; this sacred ford is very difficult to attain. (114)
O hero, staying in this place, perform meritorious deeds for yourself;
you must accomplish the work of the gods, and the enemies of the gods must be slain by you. 115.
Then the heroic one, his mind filled with joy, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O son of Sumitrā, I have been graced by Brahmā, the god of gods. (116)
O Lakṣmaṇa, having established a hermitage here for one month, I wish to perform an excellent vow for the purification of the body. (117)
When Lakṣmaṇa had said, "So be it," he completed the vow by performing the offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and other gifts, as well as the ancestral rites (śrāddhas), for his grandfathers.
Then Puṣkara, in that grove, duly offered libations;
and Kanakā, Suprabhā, Nandā, Prācī, and Sarasvatī likewise did so. ||119||
The Pañcasrotas [river] among the Puṣkaras bestows satisfaction upon the ancestors;
that daily worship of the ancestors, preceded by the ancestors themselves, [is performed there]. 120.
Having thus addressed Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke these words:
"Come quickly, Lakṣmaṇa, and bring water from the Puṣkara lake. (121)
Having washed my feet and prepared a bed of kuruṣa grass,
when the night has passed, I shall depart toward the southern direction.
Lakṣmaṇa, however, spoke these words: "O Rāma, let Sītā be made to carry the water;
I will not act as your slave at all times. (123)
"She is well-nourished and exceedingly corpulent;
what will you do with her as a wife? Tell me now. (124)
"Will this beloved wife of yours go to the heights of immortality?
Or will you always keep her well-nourished for the Rākṣasa at all times? (125)
"O best of the Raghus, she, being delighted, constantly torments me; and you, O Rāma, have caused her torment, for harm arises from another. (126)
And for your sake, I always endure thirst along with hunger; behold, my body [endures this] even for the sake of the hereafter. (127)
"No one is seen following behind those who have died;
even so, the wife, sons, and wealth [do not follow]," thus say the wise. (128)
And when you died, having abandoned the kingdom of the triple world and the single *kaṇṭaka* thorn, you were cast into the forest by me out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Kaikeyī. (129)
Remaining here are Kaikeyī, all the wealth, and all the kinsmen;
the great king Daśaratha alone has gone to his final destination. 130.
I think it is certain that Sītā will not go with you;
what indeed will you do with her now, O Raghava? (131)
Having heard those words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, which he had never heard before,
Rāghava stood despondent, as did the lovely-faced Sītā.
Then Sītā did everything that Lakṣmaṇa had said;
having bathed and eaten, O hero, those two lotus-eyed ones [proceeded] to Puṣkara.
Having spent the night there, they set their minds on departing;
"Come, arise, O son of Sumitrā, let us go toward the southern direction. (134)
The son of Sumitrā said to Rāma: "I will not go by any means;
you, O lotus-eyed one, go together with this unchaste wife. (135)
"O Raghava, I shall not go to any other forest, nor indeed to Ayodhya;
I will dwell here in this very forest for fourteen years. (136)
"O Lord, O King, if you do not go to Ayodhyā without me, you must return by this very path."
"If I live for this long, I shall go again to my father's city; there I will honor [him] with asceticism. What will you do here? (138)
"O gentle one, may you have an auspicious journey; I bid farewell to those who stand in my path.
O lotus-eyed one, I see that you have returned again with your wife. (139)
O lord of men, Śatrughna and Bharata both remain in Ayodhyā, intent on carrying out your command regarding the ancestral kingdom of their father and grandfather. (140)
"O supreme ascetic, I am constantly adverse to you, especially during your dwelling in the forest, both by day and by night. (141)
"I am unable to perform my duties; go, gentle one, as you please.
To the son of Sumitrā who was speaking thus, the descendant of Raghu replied:
"How is it that you previously departed from Ayodhyā with me? O Rāma, I shall dwell in the forest for nine and five years. (143)
I shall never dwell anywhere, even in heaven, if separated from you; therefore, by that sacrifice, there will be a curse for me as well as for him. (144)
"O Rāghava, show me favor; lead me as well.
O slayer of enemies, how will you remain on this path now, half-way through?"
But Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma, "I shall not go back.
Knowing that Lakṣmaṇa remained steadfast, Rāma spoke these words. ||146||
"Follow me, O son of Sumitrā; I shall go to the forest alone.
Let this Sītā go as my second," was Lakṣmaṇa addressed by Rāma. (147)
Then, having accepted Rāma’s words, they both rose up along with Lakṣmaṇa;
reaching the boundary mountain that marks the limit of the sacred field, those two supreme ascetics arrived.
And having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation before Ajagandha, the Lord of Gods, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the three-eyed Rāma; 149.
Standing with a composed mind and having joined his palms in reverence, he, his body covered in horripilation, offered praise to Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī. (150)
Having attained a state of sattva and shaken off rajas and tamas,
he understood the Lord, the cause of the worlds, the sovereign of the gods.
Rāma said:

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, who is the creator of this entire world with its moving and non-moving beings, as well as the author of what has been created; he who bestows both happiness and suffering, and who is the cause of dissolution once again at the end of time. 152.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who bore upon his head the Gaṅgā— whose body consists of waters once pure, lovely, and surging— as she fell from the sky with her great waves tossing like a garland of flowers shaken by the wind. I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, by whose lotus feet the peak of Mount Kailāsa was held firm even as it was being shaken by the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who resembled the very summit of Kailāsa itself.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, by whom the sons of Danu were repeatedly cast down in battle, as well as the hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas who were deprived of all their boons, and by whom the best of sages were united with the fruits of subsisting on roots and fruits. (155)

He who deprived Dakṣa of his eyes at the sacrifice, and likewise knocked out the row of teeth from Bhaga and Pūṣan—I, terrified, go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge, whose hand held the thunderbolt against Indra. (156)

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, by taking refuge in whom men become enjoyers of happiness—even those who have committed sins, whose minds are attached to sense objects, and who are not endowed with knowledge, lineage, learning, or virtues. (157)

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, whose splendor is equal to ten million suns born of Atri, who struck terror into the foremost of gods and dānavas, and who forcibly drank the fiercely blazing Kālakūṭa poison. ||158||

The illustrious Maheśa could grant boons to Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Maruts, and even to Kārttikeya; yet he did not rescue this [child] from the jaws of Death. Therefore, I seek refuge in that Śaṅkara, the giver of refuge. ||159||

I take refuge in that high-souled Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, whom the great sage Bhṛgu propitiated through severe penance in the caves of the Himalayas by means of the smoke-vow—a practice inaccessible even to others—and who then bestowed upon him the Jīvanī mantra. 160.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who is worshipped by various hosts of powerful Gaṇas with faces resembling those of elephants and cats— those who crushed Dakṣa’s sacrifice— and by the multitudes of gods bearing maces, together with the world-protectors.

I go for refuge to Śaṅkara, the bestower of protection, who, followed by the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, mounts his preeminent bull—white as a conch shell or a jasmine flower—and proceeds toward that supreme state adorned with the clouds of cosmic dissolution. 162.

I seek refuge in Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who forcibly protected the peaceful sage as he was being led away by those terrifying and most fierce men intent on the execution of his punishment—the sage who remained bowed with devotion and intent upon praise. 163.

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of protection, who, before the very eyes of the gods, forcibly severed with the tip of the nail of his lotus-like left hand the fifth head of Brahmā, which resembled a young lotus. (164)

I go for refuge to that Śaṅkara, the giver of shelter, whose feet one who is unwearied in soul bows to with devotion and praises with pure words, just as the radiant sun, dispelling the darkness with its own rays, shines forth after bowing to the feet of the Giver of Boons and praising him with stainless hymns. 165.
Yet, O Supreme Guru of the gods, deluded men do not recognize you as the Lord of this world with its moving and unmoving beings;
later, their minds being impure, they experience torment through the lingering influence of their attachment to worldly power and honor.
As he was thus offering praise, the trident-wielder whose banner is the bull,
being delighted and with a satisfied mind, spoke these words to Rāghava.
Rudra said:
"O Rāma, I am delighted; may it be well with you, for you are born of a stainless lineage.
You are indeed the god of the worlds, the deity who has assumed a human form. (168)
"O Lord, with you as our protector, the gods shall remain happy for eternal years;
we shall serve you for a long time once the fourteen years have passed. (169)
When you have arrived in Ayodhyā, the celestial beings dwelling on the earth shall behold you;
they will enjoy happiness here, and likewise, their residence in heaven shall be imperishable.
"Having performed this great task for the sake of the gods, you should return again to the city. Having thus bowed to the god, Rāghava quickly departed.
Having reached the river Indramārgā and bound his matted locks, Rāma said this to Lakṣmaṇa: "Hand over this bow to me."
Having heard those words of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Sītā: "For what reason, O Queen, has Rāma abandoned you without any cause? (173)
"I do not know the offense for which that mighty-armed one has become angry;
I have been abandoned by Rāma, and I shall undoubtedly give up my life. (174)
"No purpose is served by this life;
fie, fie upon me, a disgrace to my lineage, by whom the noble one has been provoked to anger, a sinner that I am! (175)
"Which worlds shall I go to, having been ill-treated by that great-souled one?
Placing both hands over his mouth, he spoke these words with tears in his throat. (176)
I have not offended Rāma in deed, thought, or word; O Goddess, my feet have been touched by him, and there can be no other refuge for me. (177)
Then Sītā said to Rāma: "Why has your younger brother been abandoned? O Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of the Ikṣvāku lineage, let this partiality toward the child be relinquished. (178)
Rāghava, however, said to Sītā: "I shall never abandon Lakṣmaṇa;
not even for a moment, O beloved, would I do so even in a dream, against Lakṣmaṇa’s will. (179)
And I have heard before of the peculiar conduct of this land of Suśroṇi:
in this land, all people are indeed truly intent only upon their own self-interest. (180)
Sons do not look upon one another, nor do they listen to the beneficial words of their own selves; likewise, fathers do not listen to the words of their sons. 181.
The disciple does not heed the word of the teacher, nor likewise does the teacher heed that of the disciple;
affection is merely bound to one's own interests, for no one is truly dear to another. (182)
Speaking thus, Kakutstha reached the great river Revā; together with his younger brother and Sītā, he performed his ablutions there.
Having gratified his own ancestors and the deities with water offerings,
he gazed repeatedly at the sun and the gods with a concentrated mind.
Having performed his ablutions, the King of Horses, Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
resembles the Blessed Lord Śiva, who has performed his ablutions together with the Daughter of the Mountain and Guha.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Vision of Mārkaṇḍeya’s Hermitage," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||33||
The Thirty-Fourth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
At what time did the Blessed Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, begin to perform sacrifices with those fit for sacrifice? You ought to tell me that.
What were the names of those priests appointed by Brahmā, and what sacrificial fee was given to them by that high-souled one?
Proclaim to me, exactly as it occurred and according to reality, that true nature [of the sacrifice];
for a very great curiosity has arisen regarding the sacrifice of the Grandfather.
Pulastya said:
Previously, when this Manu Svāyambhuva was told by me,
"Having created all the Prajāpatis, you must indeed perform the act of creation," [he replied as follows].
Having gone to Puṣkara himself and brought back the full details of the sacrifice,
he gathered all the necessary materials and took his place at the center of the sacrificial fire-altar.
The Gandharvas sing eternally and the hosts of Apsarases dance;
the Brahman, Udgātṛ, Hotṛ, and Adhvaryu are the four who carry out the sacrifice.
In that [rite], each one has his own distinct retinue prepared by himself:
the Brahman, the Brahmanācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, and the Āgnīdhra. (7)
This fourfold [Vedic] knowledge of Brahman indeed comprises all branches of learning, including Ānvīkṣikī;
it consists of the Udgātṛ, the Pratyudgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya.
This second [set] of four is proclaimed as belonging to the Udgātṛ;
likewise, the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, and the Acchāvāka. (9)
The Grāvastut is the fourth; then there is a group of four beginning with the Hotṛ; and likewise the Adhvaryu, the Pratiṣṭhātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and the Unnetṛ. ||10||
This fourth [chapter] concerning the fourfold [sacrificial fees] has been proclaimed by Śantanu;
these sixteen priests have indeed been declared by those who contemplate the Vedas. (11)
Three hundred and sixty-three sacrifices were created by the Self-Existent One;
and among all these, the twice-born always proclaim this [sacrifice] alone.
Some desire him as the Sadasya, and likewise the Adhvaryu of the three Sāmans;
he made Nārada the Brahmā and Gautama the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
Devagarbha, Capotarama, Agnīdhra, and Devala; Udgātā was the son of Aṅgiras, and Pratyudgātā was Pulaha.
Nārāyaṇa is said to be the Pratihartṛ, and Atri the Subrahmaṇya;
in that sacrifice, Bhṛgu is the Hotṛ, and Vasiṣṭha is the Maitra.
Kratu was proclaimed as the Acchāvāka priest, and Cyavana likewise as the Grāvastut;
Pulastya was the Adhvaryu, and Vaiśaṃbhi was the Pratiṣṭhātṛ. ||16||
Bṛhaspati was the Neṣṭṛ there, and Aśvaśapāyana was the Unnetṛ;
Dharma was the Sadasya there, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and kinsmen. ||17||
Bharadvāja, Śamīka, Purukutsa, Yugandhara, Enaka, Tīrṇaka, Keśa, and Kutapa. ||18||
Gargavedaśiras and Trisāman were made Adhvaryu priests;
likewise Kaṇva and others, as well as Mārkaṇḍa and Gaṇḍi. ||19||
Accompanied by their sons and grandsons, along with their disciples and kinsmen,
they performed their duties there day after day, free from weariness.
When the Manvantara had passed away, the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice took place;
the sacrificial fee was given to the Brahman priest, and the eastern direction was the fee for the Hotṛ priest.
Brahmā gave the western direction to the Adhvaryu priest and likewise the northern direction to the Udgātṛ; he then bestowed the entire three worlds as their sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
A hundred cows should be given by the wise for the successful completion of the sacrifice, as well as forty-eight carriers of the sacrifice. (23)
Twenty-four are proclaimed for those standing in the second position;
sixteen auspicious cows should be given for those in the third.
Likewise, one should cause twelve others to be given to the Āgnīdhra and other priests;
and by this same number, villages, female slaves, goats, and sheep. (25)
Having bathed at the concluding ritual (avabhṛtha) of the sacrifice, a feast for a thousand [brahmins] should be provided;
the sacrificer should give away his entire possessions—thus Svāyambhuva declared.
The voluntary acceptance of gifts from the Adhvaryus and the members of the assembly is prescribed;
then, having summoned Viṣṇu, the Brahman spoke these words with joy. (27)
"O you of excellent vows, having propitiated Sāvitrī, bring her here;
once she has seen you, that lady of beautiful countenance will no longer harbor anger."
With words that are affectionate, conciliatory, and especially endowed with sound reasoning, you always speak with sweetness; from your tongue, nectar flows forth. (29)
"Whoever can carry out this command, which is unparalleled in the three worlds—go, accompanied by the Gandharvas, and bring back my beloved. (30)
Propitiated by you, she will certainly come here satisfied;
