do not delay, but go quickly to Vraja to see Mādhava.
"Let Lakṣmī go before you; let the auspicious Sāvitrī go to her abode;
and you, follow her path, for she is dearer to me than my own life. (32)
O Queen, he never does anything displeasing to you;
desiring to serve you in solitude, he always remains by your side, watching your face with humble devotion.
In this manner, many such sweet words should be made to hear by the queen, so that she may soon become satisfied. (34)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, Viṣṇu then departed in haste to where Sāvitrī was staying.
Seeing Keśava approaching from afar with his wife, she rose up in haste and was greeted by Viṣṇu.
Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, O Consort of Brahmā; salutations be to you!
Indeed, by bowing down to you, every person is liberated from sin. (37)
O highly fortunate one, devoted to your husband, you reside within the heart of Brahmā;
contemplating you day and night, he yearns for your grace. (38)
And ask this dear friend of yours, the virtuous Lakṣmī, daughter of Bhṛgu;
for if you, O fair-eyed one, have no faith in these words of mine.
Having spoken thus, Śauri then touched both of Sāvitrī’s feet with both his hands, saying, "Salutations to you."
Having touched her and saluted her with the words, "O Mother of the World, I bow to you," that goddess drew back her feet and, with her own hands, covered the hands of Hari.
Having taken him, he said to Viṣṇu: "O Acyuta, everything has been forgiven by me;
this Lakṣmī shall always dwell here within your heart. (42)
Without you, she will never find delight anywhere else;
born from the wife of Bhṛgu, she is your devoted wife, O you of excellent vows. (43)
Furthermore, produced through the efforts of the gods and dānavas within the ocean, she,
the Blessed One, made her descent wherever she desired.
In her state as a goddess, she was a goddess in body; in her state as a human, she was a human.
With you as her companion, this body of hers, devoted to her husband’s vows, has not been abandoned for a long time. (45)
"O Lord, tell me truly what must be done by me here.
Viṣṇu said: "The conclusion of the sacrifice has arrived; I have been sent to your presence."
"Bring Sāvitrī quickly so that she may perform her bath with me;
O Goddess, come swiftly and go there filled with joy. (47)
"Go and see your own husband accompanied by all the gods.
Lakṣmī said:
"O Noble One, arise quickly; go where the Grandfather (Brahmā) is. 48.
"Without you, my feet have been touched by this woman.
Having said this, he raised her up and took her right hand in his own right hand. (49)
Knowing that Sāvitrī was delaying, the divine Grandfather (Brahmā) then spoke these words to Mahādeva, who was standing nearby: ||50||
"Go with this Pārvatī, O destroyer of asuras;
let Gaurī go before you, and you follow behind, O Śaṅkara. (51)
"Awaken him and bring him here quickly; do that!
When they were addressed thus, Parvati and the Supreme Lord then [acted].
Having gone there, they spoke thus to the beloved wife of Brahmā, who was weeping:
"O devoted wife, you must perform a great task there. (53)
O lady of beautiful hips, ask this Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain;
and ask this large-eyed Lakṣmī, or Indrāṇī, O lady of auspicious countenance. (54)
Or those who, out of lack of faith, ask, "Obeisance to you, O God," yet receive a blessing from the trident-bearing God of gods; [55]
"O Śaṅkara, Gaurī shall always remain as half of your body;
O God, O beautiful one of the three worlds, you shall shine with her. (56)
"O slayer of enemies, by you, our protector, may the entire world be made partakers of happiness.
While she was speaking thus, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was seized.
While Gaurī saluted the goddess with her left hand and Lakṣmī with her right hand, Śaṅkara spoke these words.
"Come, O lady of great fortune; go to where your husband stays, for he is the supreme refuge for women, O beautiful one. (59)
O Goddess, you ought to go out of affection even if there is no formal invitation;
for Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Pārvatī are all present before you, O Goddess.
O Goddess of auspicious countenance, beloved of Brahmā, it is not fitting for us two to cause the breaking of their pride by means of these words.
"O Goddess, go there filled with joy at our request.
Gaurī said:
"And I am always your beloved, O Goddess; I myself shall go."
And Lakṣmī was held by me from the right side of your waist;
come, O illustrious one, come to where your husband stands! 63.
By means of the two [mantras] *nīta* and *asātuta*, the Goddess was brought under control;
Viṣṇu and Rudra were made her precursors, as were Indra and the other gods, as well as the asuras.
The Gandharvas and Apsaras, as well as the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, arrived there; and the goddess Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was also present.
Having beheld Sāvitrī with her beautiful countenance, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, together with Gāyatrī, spoke these words: ||66||
"O Goddess, I am your servant; I stand under your command. O lady of beautiful hips, please instruct me as to what task must be performed by me here."
Thus addressed by the god Brahmā himself,
the goddess, her face cast down in shame, said nothing at all.

Having fallen at his feet, the goddess Gāyatrī, urged by Brahmā, committed an offense against you; forgive her, O God, salutations to you! Having affectionately embraced her and pressed her to his chest, he held her in a close embrace.
I have composed this Gāyatrī for you; may it be my lord of nourishment. ||70||
"The word of her husband must be carried out by women, for the husband is the lord of their life;
this was stated previously by the Blessed One, Viriñci, at the time of creation. (71)
Women have no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even fasting;
whatever word her husband speaks, she should do that without reproach.
She who utters insults against her husband, and likewise insults against her sister, or engages in slander or idle chatter, goes quickly to hell. (73)
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living,
she takes away his longevity and, upon death, desires hell.
Knowing this, you must not do anything displeasing to your husband;
nor, my dear, should you ever, under any circumstances, attend to his right limb.
"In all matters, I shall take his right side;
you, O noble lady, shall take the left, while Ārya, Nārada, and Puṣkara shall remain by his side."
And other abodes of Brahmā and established dwellings shall be obtained by me, shining brilliantly, as long as creation continues to arise. (77)
"You must remain here with me, there is no doubt; take refuge on my left side by the side of Brahmā at Puṣkara. (78)
By this instruction, she became endowed with happiness and stability.
Gāyatrī said: "I shall do exactly as you have directed."
"By your very command, you have become my friend, dear as my own life;
O Goddess, I am your younger sister, and you ought to protect me always. (80)
Then Brahmā, the god of gods, together with Viṣṇu at Puṣkara,
granted boons to all the deities at the conclusion of their ablutions.
Śakra, the lord of the gods; the maker of day among the luminaries;
likewise Soma among the constellations; and Varuṇa among the flavors. ||82||
He made Dakṣa the lord of the Prajāpatis, the ocean the lord of the rivers,
Kubera the superintendent of wealth, and likewise [Rāvaṇa] the lord of the Rākṣasas.
He is the Pinākin among all beings, Manu among the Gaṇas, Manu among human beings, and likewise Garuḍa among birds. ||84||
Having thus declared Vasiṣṭha among the sages, Prabhākara among the planets,
and other such [leaders], the Grandfather, the God of gods, [spoke].
Brahmā spoke respectfully to both Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara:
"Among all the sacred fords on earth, you two are the most excellent ones to be worshipped. (86)
"By you two, has a new holy site ever been made sacred, or is a linga or even an image seen anywhere? (87)
That sacred ford shall attain holiness and bestow all fruits upon those men who perform worship with offerings. (88)
With me placed at your head, how could there be any fear of disease for them?
In whatever kingdoms you hold festivals, worship, and other such ceremonies, [how could there be fear? (89)
All activities will proceed; hear now what their fruit shall be:
there will be neither mental anxieties nor physical diseases, nor calamities, nor fear of hunger. (90)
There shall be no separation from loved ones, nor union with those who are disliked;
no eye disease, no headache, no bilious colic, and no genital ailments. (91)
Therein, there is no malevolent magic, no fear, no epilepsy, nor cholera;
there is increase according to one's desire, and unsurpassed, perfect wisdom. 92.
There shall be health in every respect, long life, progeny, and wealth;
there shall be no untimely death, nor shall cows yield little milk. (93)
The trees did not bear fruit out of season, nor was there even the slightest fear of portents.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu then prepared to praise Brahmā.
Viṣṇu said:
Salutations to the one who is infinite, whose mind is pure, whose form is the very essence of all forms, and who possesses a thousand arms;
to the Creator who is the source of a thousand rays, whose body is vast, and whose actions are stainless. (95)
Salutations to the one who brings peace, the remover of all the world's afflictions; salutations to the one whose brilliance is as intense as the sun and fire combined.
Homage to the wielder of the discus, whose knowledge is vast; always homage to the one who establishes the seat of all intelligence. 96.
O Lord whose crest-jewel is the infallible primordial God, O Great Īśvara, Lord of all that is yet to be, now arising, and already come into being;
O Lord of the Great Principle (Mahat), Lord of All, Lord of the World, Lord of the Earth, Lord of the Universe—salutations to You forever! 97.
O Lord of Sacrifice, Nārāyaṇa, Jiṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Sovereign of the Earth, Viśveśvara, Viśvalocana;
O Moon, Sun, Acyuta, Vīra, You whose forms are the source of the universe, whose form is nectar, the Imperishable! 98.
O Nārāyaṇa, whose face is turned everywhere and who fills the entire region with the circle of blazing flames of fire;
O Lord, who removes the suffering of all gods and is the imperishable nectar—protect me, who have thus come to you for refuge! 99.
O All-pervading Lord, I behold Your many mouths, You who are the ancient goal of sacrifice;
O Lord, source of the worlds, salutations to You, the Great-Grandfather! 100.

Through the many revolutions of the wheel of saṃsāra, you have at times been the supreme deity among the best of gods; since you are worshipped by beings whose minds are purified by the knowledge of all things, why do I not bow down to you? (101)

Thus, he who knows that Being prior to primordial nature is the most excellent among all knowers; though possessing a vast form, he is here known as one whose nature is subtle, even among those endowed with qualities. (102)
How is it that you, though devoid of speech, hands, and feet, possess such excellent conduct and perform good deeds?
Furthermore, O best of gods, how is it that you are to be known as one whose senses are withdrawn from the bonds of saṃsāra? ||103||

From the embodied, the unembodied is not attained; but by those of pure disposition who worship with the highest intent that supreme form which severs the cycle of worldly existence, the state of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) may be reached.
Yet they do not know that from which this body arises, O Lord who assumes such wondrous forms—even the gods and others!
Alas, O All-pervading One, one should worship that most ancient primordial source seated upon the lotus-throne. 105.
One of purified being understands that single source of even the Creator of the universe;
but how shall I know that ancient, primordial Bhava, who is purified by austerity? 106.
The son of Vañjana, Padmāsana, is indeed well-known; for such is his renown repeatedly from the Purāṇas.
Even if one contemplates that all-pervading Lord Bhava, one who is devoid of austerity does not know Him in this way.

O you of noble fame, even the most eminent ones like us must awaken you; yet those god-like fools, having divided their own wits, desire to awaken you while remaining devoid of intelligence themselves. 108.
Whether through many births or through the discerning intellect of the Vedas, there may arise a light that is as if unmanifest;
for one greedy for its attainment, even the status of a human being is not enough, nor would even Śiva, the lord of gods and gandharvas, suffice.
O Lord, You who are not merely of the form of Viṣṇu, who are exceedingly subtle, yet You are the manifest God for the fulfillment of all purposes;
though gross, You are subtle and easily attained. O God, those who act otherwise than this fall into hell.

Or rather, while remaining in this [state], one is liberated; for within the nature of the Self, the essence of the moon, fire, sun, wind, and earth—bearing identical forms as their own essential natures—is pervaded by that very nature. (111)

Therefore, O Blessed One, please accept this hymn of praise from me, your devotee who possesses infinite qualities—especially from one whose mind is joined in meditative concentration, whose heart is purified, and whose thoughts follow solely the realization of your true nature. (112)

"O Blessed One, you who always abide in my heart—salutations to you! O Blessed One, O Ancient One, salutations to you eternally! Thus, O All-pervading One, this praise of You has been proclaimed by me, O Awakened Lord. (113)
Furthermore, protect us from the fear associated with wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra and other such [sufferings]. ||114||
Brahmā said:
O Keśava, you are omniscient and a mass of wisdom regarding the body;
you shall forever be the foremost and most worshipful among the gods. 115.
Immediately after Nārāyaṇa, Rudra,
having bowed down with devotion, praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus and known as Viriñca.
Salutations to the lotus-eyed one; salutations to the one born from the lotus;
salutations to the supreme self, the teacher of gods and asuras, the creator. 117.
Salutations to you, Lord of all gods; salutations indeed to the destroyer of delusion, who was born from the lotus-seated Brahmā situated at the navel of Viṣṇu. 118.
Salutations to you, who are adorned with sprout-like hands whose limbs are as red as coral;
I have come to you for refuge—protect me from the cycle of worldly existence. 119
O Grandfather, having first seen the blue bud of the *budā* flower, he then beheld it again with its red face, complete with petals and filaments. (120)
And there is a lotus with many petals, immeasurable and without end;
by you, stationed therein, this very creation was set in motion.
"Except for you, there is no other protection for the world; salutations to you!
I have been consumed by the curse of Sāvitrī, and my linga has fallen to the earth. (122)
"Now, O Lord of Kuruma, protect me along with my wife;
O Brahmā, protect my feet, for you are like the lotus-seated one protecting his own shanks. (123)
May Viriñca protect my left thigh, and may the Creator protect my secret organ;
may the Lotus-seated One protect my navel, and the Four-faced One protect my belly. 124.
May the protector of the universe protect my chest; may the lotus-born one protect my heart;
may the Lord of Sāvitrī protect my throat; and may Hṛṣīkeśa protect my mouth. 125.
The lotus-colored one is the supreme self in the eyes;
thus, having performed the placement (nyāsa), the name of the Guru is Śaṅkara, the benefactor. 126.
Having said, "Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O Brahmā," he ceased speaking.
Then Brahmā, being pleased, spoke these words to Hara: 127.
"What desire shall I fulfill for you today? Ask whatever you wish.
Rudra said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Giver of Boons, or if you are my benefactor..."
O All-pervading Lord, tell me that one place alone where you reside;
and in which various places do the twice-born always behold you? (129)
O Lord of All, tell me that place which shines upon the surface of the earth by the mere mention of its name, for I am devoted to you. (130)
Brahmā said:
At Puṣkara I am the best of gods; at Gayā, the four-faced one;
at Kānyakubja, Devagarbha; and at Bhṛgukakṣa, Pitāmaha. (131)
The Creator (Brahmā) is at Kāverī, Bṛhaspati is at Dvipurī, the Lotus-born (Brahmā) is at Prabhāsa, and the Beloved of the Gods (Viṣṇu) is at Vānaryā. ||132||
In Dvāravatī was the lord of the world Pauṇḍraka, a follower of the Ṛgveda; in Vaidiśa was Puṇḍarīkākṣa; and in Hastināpura was Piṅgākṣa. (133)
I am Jaya in Tyā and Vijaya in Asmijaya; I am Puṣkarāvarta in Taḥ; I am Padmahasta among the Ugras and Tamonuda in the Tamonadī. ||134||
I was Dīpa at Ahicchattra, Janapriya in Cīpurī, Brahmā in Pāṭaliputra, and likewise a sage in Ṛṣikuṇḍa. (135)
Mahitāre is Mukunda; Śrīkaṇṭha resides in Śrīnivāsa;
in Kāmarūpa he is Śubhākāra; and in Vārāṇasī he is Śivapriya. ||136||
Viṣṇu is at Mallikākṣa, as is Mahendra and Bhārgava;
Pitāmaha is at Gonarda, while the Elder (Vasiṣṭha) is in the form of a pillar in Ujjayinī. ||137||
The Great Awakening is at Kauśāmbī; Rāghava is at Ayodhyā;
the Lord of Sages is at Citrakūṭa; and Vārāha is on the Vindhya mountain. (138)
At Gaṅgādvāra he was Parameṣṭhin, and on the Himavat he was Śaṅkara;
at Devikā he had a sacrificial ladle in his hand, and at Turvaṭa he held a sruva-ladle in his hand.
In Vṛndāvana he is Padmapāṇi, and in Naimiṣa he is Kuśahasta;
in Goplakṣa he is Gopīndra, and on the bank of the Yamunā he is Sa-candra.
In Bhāgīrathī, he is Padmatanu; in Jalāna, he is Dojala;
in Kauṅkaṇa, he is Madrākṣa; and in Kāmpilya, he is Kanakapriya. ||141||
Veṅkaṭeśa is the giver of food, and Śambhu is indeed at Kratusthala;
Pulastya is in Laṅkā, and I, the swan-vehicled one, am in Kaśmīra. ||142||
Vasiṣṭha shall be at Arbuda, Nārada at Utpalāvata; I am Melaka, the giver of the Vedas, and the Lord of Waters [Varuṇa] shall be at Prapāta. ||143||
In the Sāmaveda he is Yajña; in Madhura he is Madhurapriya;
in Aṅkoṭa he is Yajñabhoktā; and in Brahmavāda he is Surapriya. ||144||
And Nārāyaṇa is Goman in Māyāpurī, beloved of the twice-born;
he is Ṛṣivedu in Durādharṣā and Suramardana in Devā. (145)
In Vijayā he is Mahārūpa; in Rāṣṭravardhana he is Svarūpa;
in Tumālavyā he is Pṛthūdara; and in Śākambharī he is Rasapriya.
Piṇḍāraketugopāla at Śaṅkhoddhāra, Aṅgavardhana at Kādaṃbaka, Prajādhyakṣa at Devādhyakṣa, and Samasthala. (147)
I am Gaṅgādhara on Bhadrapīṭha, Jalaśāyin on Arbuda, Tripurādhīśa at Tryambaka, and Trilocana on Śrīparvata. ||148||
Mahādeva is in Padmapura, Vaidhasa likewise in Ekāpāla;
Śauri is the lord of Śṛṅgiberapura, and Cakrapāṇika is in Naumiṣa. ||149||
In Daṇḍapurī there was Virūpākṣa, in Dhūtapāpaka Gautama,
in Mālyavat Haṃsanātha, and likewise in Valika the lord of the twice-born.
In Indrapurī, Devanātha resides; in Udyūtapā, Purandara;
in Haṃsavāhastulā, Caṇḍa; and in Aṅga, the one dear to Garuḍa. ||151||
In Mahodaya, he is the Great Sacrifice; in Suyajña, the Banner of Sacrifice; in Siddhisvara, the Lotus-colored One; and in Vibhā, the Awakener of the Lotus. ||152||
In the Devadāru forest is the Liṅga; at Mahāpatta is Vināyaka; Tryambaka is in the abode of the Mothers; and in Alakā is Kulādhipa. ||153||
And on Trikūṭa is Gonarda; likewise Vāsuki resides in Pātāla;
Padmādhyakṣa is in Kedāra, and Suratapriya is in Kūṣmāṇḍa. ||154||
Śubhāṅga is at Kuṇḍavāpī, Takṣaka likewise at Sāraṇī, Pāpahā at Akṣoṭa, and Sudarśana at Ambikā. (155)
In Varadā, the Great Hero is the destroyer of difficult passages;
in Parṇāṭa, he is Ananta; and in Prakāśā, he is Divākara. ||156||
Padmanābha is in Virājā, Svarudra in Vṛkasthala, Mārkaṇḍa in Vaṭaka, and Mṛgaketana in Vāhinī. ||157||
Padmagṛha is in Padmāvatī, and Padmaketana is in the sky;
thus, one hundred and eight places have been proclaimed by me to you. (158)
O Destroyer of Tripura, wherever my presence resides at the three junctions of the day, a devoted man who beholds even one of these [shrines] there— ||159||
Having attained that most stainless state, he rejoices for eternal years;
whatever evil he has committed through mind, speech, or body [is thereby purified]. (160)
All that goes to destruction; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
But that man who, having gone to all these places, beholds me—161.
"Wherever you, who possess the factors conducive to liberation, may be stationed, there I shall remain, with offerings of flowers, incense, and by satisfying the brahmins. (162)
Through unwavering meditation, the Supreme Lord is swiftly attained;
its foremost fruit is merit, and likewise, its fruit is liberation. (163)
Having reached the world of Brahmā, he remains there for that duration;
then, at the time of renewed creation, he becomes a god among the Vairājas, possessed of great ascetic power.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, even those committed in this world,
whether unintentionally or intentionally, perish at that very moment.
Whether one is impoverished in this world or has fallen from his kingdom,
by going to these places, he indeed beholds me through meditative absorption (samādhi).
Having performed worship and offerings, as well as bathing and the libations for the ancestors,
and having also offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), he will soon be freed from suffering.
He shall become a king under a single umbrella; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
In this world, he will possess kingdoms, good fortune, wealth, grain, and excellent women. (168)
Various [merits] accrue to him by whom the pilgrimage to Puṣkara has been performed;
whoever performs or causes this procedure for the pilgrimage to be done [attains these fruits]. ||169||
By merely hearing [this], one is liberated from all sins; even that man who has committed the act of approaching those who should not be approached is known [to be purified]. (170)
By not neglecting the performance of sacred rites and by practicing them for many years, one attains the Vedic consecration after performing this pilgrimage even once. (171)
O Śaṅkara, what is the use of saying much more in this regard?
By attaining this, even that which was unattainable is attained, and even one's sins are destroyed.
It is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices, bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas), and through it alone, the completion of all the Vedas is accomplished. (173)
By those who, having performed the Puṣkara meditation, have worshipped Sāvitrī with the water from a lotus offered by the hand of their own wife. (174)
O Śaṅkara, at the close of day, that meritorious water was brought by means of an excellent water-pot, even though it was made of clay, for the purpose of the evening worship.
She is to be composed through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Listen now, O foremost of the days, to the merit that arises when she has been so constituted as her limb. (176)
By that, it becomes as if twelve years have been spent in meditative absorption;
likewise, the fruit of a horse-sacrifice is obtained by bathing, and the merit of giving is tenfold.
O sinless one, I have myself declared that even by fasting, the merit is infinite for him who, in the presence of Sāvitrī, offers food to his husband. (178)
"Therefore, O Lord, I have been fed there; of this there is no doubt. Whoever feeds a second person has, by that act, fed Keśava. (179)
The Lord who has Lakṣmī as his companion bestows boons upon him;
the Lord who has Umā as his companion, having been fed on the third day, grants them—of this there is no doubt. (180)
Alternatively, if one should give food out of devotion to young maidens, there shall never be a widow or an unfortunate woman in her family. (181)
She who is neither the mother of a daughter nor the beloved wife of her husband—therefore, with every effort, one should first offer food to a Sāvitrī. 182.
Those men who desire benefits either in the next world or in this one should always give [gifts] at all times, excluding pungent oil and mustard oil. 183.
Women should never eat anything sour or alkaline; rather, their food should consist of the five kinds of edible grains, well-prepared with all the various seasonings. 184.
She should eat well-cooked cakes filled with ghee and accompanied by plenty of milk,
as well as śikhariṇī prepared with curd and milk.
It brings delight to men and is exceedingly dear to women;
it is filled with wealth, grain, and people, and abounds with hundreds of women. (186)
In that [state], cakes and fried pastries are produced; of this there is no doubt.
There is neither fever nor distress, neither suffering nor separation from loved ones. (187)
He causes his own kinsmen, numbering twenty-one generations, as well as his relatives, sons, and endless male and female servants, to cross over.
He who gives a *pūrikā* to her, whose lineage is thus filled, shall prosper for a long time, endowed with sons and grandsons. (189)
The entire lineage of one who offers even a single *śaṣkula* cake becomes possessed of sons; his daughters become mothers of sons, and his family is united with its kinsmen. (190)
For those young women who bestow the *śikhariṇī*, there is no doubt that their entire family rejoices, filled with all perfections. (191)
O Hara, it is by the offering of modakas alone that the Lord of Creatures, Brahmā, attained his status;
indeed, this very food is praised for the Gaurīs. 192.
Fortunate, possessed of sons, virtuous, and endowed with wealth and prosperity, she shall happily enjoy a thousand meals in birth after birth. (193)
And there were auspicious cakes, sweetly prepared, primarily consisting of grape juice and combined with pieces of jaggery. (194)
Having prepared an unbroken mixture of autumnal grains along with husks, these shall serve as the drinks and foods for women and for the twice-born. (195)
And here, one should cause to be given all those various garments that are suitable for the rainy season, provided they are not made of sheep's wool in every respect. ||196||
Having honored them according to the prescribed rite with gifts of wealth and saffron,
their limbs were smeared with saffron and they were adorned with garlands of flowers.
Having given sandals for the feet, one should likewise offer a coconut; having given collyrium for the eyes, one should place a sword and a bell upon the head. (198)
Having placed molasses, pleasant fruits, and soft, cut pieces of food into their hands along with vessels, he should bid them farewell after prostrating himself.
One should eat oneself only after one's kinsmen have eaten along with their children;
or else, there is no prosperity, nor is there a worthy recipient for giving at a sacred ford.
"Having gone home, I shall offer [this] with joy; O God, be gracious to me.
In this very manner, having returned to his own abode, he likewise offered it to the ancestors.
One should perform the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules, preceded by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
thus his ancestors remain satisfied for a day of Brahmā.
O Śiva, the merit for those giving at their own home is eightfold that of a sacred ford;
however, base people do not witness the Śrāddha performed by the twice-born.
The Śrāddha for the ancestors is desired to be performed in a secluded place within the house;
that which is struck by a low-caste person's gaze does not reach the ancestors at all. (204)
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the Śrāddha to be performed in secret;
this is declared by Svayambhū himself to be that which grants satisfaction to the ancestors. 205.

Through her devotion to Gaurī, she attained superior excellence; having mastered the ritual acts prescribed by the scriptures, she was known in the minds of people as one who bestows fame, being of a passionate (rājasī) nature. 206.
One who desires their own welfare should always give gifts in secret;
for cooked food, when being given by people on this earth, becomes visible. (207)
That which is being seen here is never seen for the sake of satisfaction;
when one Brahmin is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed. (208)
In this world, the body is indeed real; such is the word of the Purāṇas.
At a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should never examine a Brāhmaṇa in any way whatsoever.
Regarding this, Manu said that one should provide food to the seeker who has arrived,
offering him a ball of rice mixed with either groats, barley-meal, or milk-rice.
This is what has been prescribed by the sages: it should always be offered with oil-cake or inguda-nut cake, using sesame oil-cake, by men who are full of devotion. (211)
A *śrāddha* ceremony should be performed there, however, excluding the offering of water (*arghya*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*).
For vultures or crows will carry away the *svadhā* offering with their very sight. (212)
That śrāddha is declared to be pertaining to the Tīrthikas; it is supremely satisfying to the ancestors and should be performed with great effort, for devotion alone is the cause here. (213)
The ancestors are satisfied by devotion; being pleased, they grant all desires: sons, grandsons, wealth, grain, and whatever other desires one wishes for in the mind. (214)
Pleased by devotion and right conduct, the Grandfather (Brahmā) bestows his favor upon men;
therefore, a Śrāddha should always be offered by men at a sacred site, whether it be at an improper time or the proper time. (215)
Having reached [the water], one should always perform the ritual bathing and offer libations to the ancestors;
furthermore, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), which is exceedingly dear to the ancestors, should be performed. ||216||
The ancestors, filled with supreme hope and longing for water, gaze expectantly at their kinsman who has arrived. (217)
One must not cause delay, nor should one create any obstacle;
for them, there shall always be an uninterrupted continuity at all times.
The ancestors, desiring the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* performed by one who grants them a son, never bring about the severance of their lineage through him. (219)
Therefore, the Śrāddha was previously proclaimed by Svayambhū himself as that which must be performed with superior qualities by the twice-born who are devoted to their ancestors. (220)
Whether at a sacred ford, a holy field, or even in one's own home; during a solar transit, or during an eclipse; at the equinoxes, at the solstices, or when one's birth star is afflicted. ||221||
In ancient times, Svāyaṃbhuva spoke of these as the times for the śrāddha;
when the śrāddha has been performed, no bodily affliction occurs for men. 222.
Then one abandons all evil deeds committed even by one's son, so that there will be no suffering from planets, thieves, kings, or others. (223)
All misdeeds are destroyed, and one attains an auspicious rebirth in the next world;
of this there is no doubt, according to the word of Prajāpati. (224)
In the Kṛta Yuga, Puṣkara is the sacred site; in the Tretā, Naimiṣa is remembered; in the Dvāpara, Kurukṣetra; and in the Kali Yuga, one should take refuge in the Gaṅgā. 225.
Dwelling at Puṣkara is difficult; performing penance at Puṣkara is difficult.
For whatever sin has been committed elsewhere attains lightness there at the sacred ford.
Wherever one may be, one removes all sin by bowing to the Tīrthaṅkara;
he who, with palms joined in reverence, remembers the Puṣkaras in the evening and in the morning [attains the same]. (227)
O Bhārata, by bathing there, one has effectively bathed in all sacred fords;
having bathed at Puṣkara morning and evening with restrained senses, [one attains the fruit]. (228)
He attains all sacrificial rites and goes to the world of Brahmā;
[this applies for] twelve years, twelve days, a month, or even half a month. ||229||
He who dwells eternally at Puṣkara shall go to the supreme goal;
it stands above all worlds, situated even beyond the world of Brahmā.
He who desires to go to Puṣkara should attend upon Puṣkara;
as it is with the direct and reverse orders, so it is with the individual and collective [arrangements]. (231)
But one who has bathed properly at Puṣkara obtains the fruit of ten million [baths],
which is the fruit obtained at all sacred fords when they are visited according to the prescribed rules.
By merely looking at Puṣkara, a human being obtains that same fruit which is gained from ten thousand times ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) upon the surface of the earth. 233.
O descendant of Kuru, the presence of these three at Puṣkara shall endure as long as the mountains stand and as long as the oceans remain. ||234||
For as long as one is free from death by drowning in water, there is no doubt that the world of Brahmā belongs to them;
this remains so through thousands of future births, until the very end of birth and death.
By bathing but once at Puṣkara, one would burn away all evil deeds;
Puṣkara is a field difficult to reach, which destroys all sins.
Now listen, O King, to the account of the sacrifice to the God of gods, which destroys the five great sins and bestows wealth upon the sons of Brahmā. 237.
Whatever man on this earth may be afflicted in this life by poverty, disease, leprosy, and the like, or who is unfortunate and childless; ||238||
For him, prosperity shall arise immediately, along with full longevity, sons, and happiness, having performed the rite within a maṇḍala accompanied by the world-protectors. (239)
He who beholds Brahmā, the supreme deity, according to the prescribed rite,
sees his own self in the form of the mantra, worshipped by the Lord of the Forest (Rāma).
Especially on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, or indeed on all full moon days, one should sacrifice to the deity according to the prescribed ritual. (241)
O King, at the time of a solar transit, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, whoever beholds the all-pervading Lord worshipped by his preceptor— ||242||
For him, there shall be immediate satisfaction and the destruction of evil arises;
and he becomes equal to the gods here on earth, O lord of men. (243)
The preceptor shall examine the devotion of his disciples from the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes for one year, by means of their birth, purity, ritual actions, and so forth. (244)
Having recognized that [the disciple] is fit, he should fix it in his heart; and they too, endowed with devotion, should meditate upon the Teacher as the Supreme Lord. (245)
They should perform devotion toward Viṣṇu throughout the year in whatever manner is appropriate,
and then, when the year is complete, they should propitiate the Guru.
O Blessed One, by your grace, [may there be] the crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra through the worship of the Supreme Brahman and the propitiation of Viriñci. ||247||
"By the recitation of the *Sahasraśīrṣa* and the *Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa*, and likewise through meditation—may such instruction be granted to us. (248)
"We desire Vedic prosperity; may you be pleased with us.
Thus was the preceptor Medhāvī then entreated by them.
One should worship Brahmā according to the prescribed rites, preceded by Viṣṇu;
with their eyes bound, they should be made to sleep on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, they sit in the bound lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and meditate upon their guru in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*), wearing white garments and a sacred thread.
Wearing white garlands and garments, and anointed with white perfumes, they should go outside to the river and perform their daily rites without weariness. (252)
The preceptor should cause [the disciples] to take a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree;
they should eat it after going to a river that flows into the ocean. (253)
Alternatively, one may consume another pond or even water from a house, consecrated by the mantra of Parameṣṭhin, according to the prescribed rite. (254)
Having consecrated [the water] seven times with the mantra beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having recited the mantra "devasya tvā," one should place it on the hand with the mantra "yuje tvā. (255)
Having rinsed [the mouth] with the mantra "irāvatyā," and having eaten the *brahmaudana* while facing away,
one should throw it far away and look at where it has fallen.

Whether facing [the deity] directly, or facing east, or even having come from an intermediate direction, the attainment of the deity in one's presence and the accomplishment of the mantra arise. (257)
If he turns his back on this [target], all the gods turn their backs;
if he has gone past it to the north, success may or may not occur. (258)
If death should occur on the right side of the Guru, there is no doubt that it will happen for him;
therefore, one should sleep on the ground, looking toward the inauspicious [side], in the presence of the God of gods.
Having seen dreams, the wise ones should report them before their guru;
then the supreme guru should discern therein what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. (260)
Having bathed on the full moon day, one should then proceed to the temple;
and the preceptor shall draw the mandala upon the prepared ground.
Having marked out the ground according to the rules by means of various characteristics,
one should draw a lotus with sixteen spokes or even nine spokes.
Then, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, the wise one should show it;
he should carefully perform the binding of the eyes with a white cloth.
The wise one should cause the disciples to enter with flowers in their hands according to their respective castes;
when he, being learned, constructs the nine-naveled maṇḍala with colored powders.
O King, one should worship the god Indra preceded by Indrāṇī in the eastern direction;
likewise, one should worship Agni together with the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One should place Vahni in the eastern direction, Yama in the southern, Nirṛti in the south-western,
Varuṇa in the western quarter, and Vāyu in the north-western region.
One should place Dhanada in the north and Rudra in the region of Īśāna;
likewise, one should place the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in the east and the sacrificial ladle (sruk) in the south.
One should place the *haṃsa* in the west, the *sruva* in the north, the *brasi* in the southeast,
and the *pādukā* in the southwest.
In the northwest, one should worship the yogapaṭṭa, and in the northeast, the *cagalantī* plant;
Viṣṇu is to be worshipped in the east, and Śaṅkara also in the south. (269)
In the west is the god Tura, and likewise the ṛṣis in the north;
in the center is the Self-born Padmajanman himself, and likewise Sāvitrī in the south.
And in the north is the goddess Gāyatrī, whose eyes are like lotus petals;
having placed the Ṛgveda in the east and the Yajurveda in the south. (271)
In the west, the Sāmaveda; likewise, the Atharvaveda in the north;
as well as the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, the Chandas, and Jyotiṣa. ||272||
One should place other Dharmaśāstras in the directions beginning with Indra (the east); having worshipped Bala on the eastern petal, one should worship Pradyumna on the southern petal.
In the west, one should place Rudra, and Vāsudeva in the north;
Vāmadeva in the east, and Sadyojāta in the south.
One should place Īśāna in the western position and Tatpuruṣa in the north;
Aghora is to be worshipped everywhere—this is the worship in the maṇḍala.
One should worship Bhāskara in the east, Divākara in the south,
Prabhākara in the west, and Grahārāja in the north.
Having thus worshipped Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, according to the prescribed rite,
one should duly place eight water-pots (kumbhas) within the circle of the directions.
One should arrange the Brahma-pitcher as the ninth in the center;
one who desires liberation should bathe [the deity] with that pitcher of Brahmā. (278)
O King, one who desires prosperity should be bathed here with a Vaiṣṇava jar, while one who seeks a kingdom should be bathed with a Kaubera jar. ||279||
However, for one who desires the power of wealth, one should bathe that person with the water from an Āgneya jar according to the ritual for conquering death, so as to purify them from sin. (280)
The rite for the destruction of evil is prescribed by means of the Nairṛta [mantra];
one should quickly bathe the person with the Vāruṇa [mantra] for the sake of destroying sin.
One who desires health of the body should be consecrated with the Vāyavya [mantra];
for one who desires the acquisition of wealth, the Kaubera [consecration] is prescribed.
For one desiring knowledge through the Raudra [rite], these are the jars of the World-Protectors;
by bathing in each one individually, a person becomes free from all defects. (283)
A king is born who is equal to Brahmā, or else he becomes a monkey immediately;
or else,
having worshipped all the guardians of the quarters (lokapālas) with jars according to their respective order and by their own names, in this manner, [he attains his goal].
Having thus worshipped the gods and the world-protectors with a serene mind, [he should proceed].
Afterwards, one should cause the examined disciples to enter with their eyes blindfolded;
having burned them with the fire-element concentration (dhāraṇā), one should then shake them off with the wind-element.
Having caused them to be nourished with *soma*, he should then cause them to hear the pledges:
"One must not revile the Brāhmaṇas, the gods, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā. (287)
One should worship Indra, Āditya, Agni, and likewise the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the planets;
as well as one's preceptor, a Brāhmaṇa, or a sage who has previously been initiated. ||288||
Having thus caused the *samaya* to be heard, one should afterwards perform the fire-oblation (*homa*):
*Oṃ namaḥ bhagavate brahmaṇe sarvarūpiṇe huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (289)
One should perform the fire offering (homa) in the blazing fire with the sixteen-syllable mantra;
one should cause all the oblations, beginning with those for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), to be offered.

Having performed the oblations with the three vyāhṛtis in the presence of the God of gods, the initiated disciple should thereafter cause the teacher to receive the preceptor’s fee (guru-dakṣiṇā). ||291||
O King, a wise man should cause the preceptor to receive elephants, horses, vehicles, carts, gold, grain, and so forth; likewise, in a middling [rite], he should give a middling amount.
One should cause another pair, along with gold, to be given to the preceptor;
when this is done, great merit is likewise produced. (293)
That cannot be described even in hundreds of years, were one to first undergo initiation and then hear the *Pādma*. 294.
The ten Vedas, the Purāṇas, and all the mantras along with their compendiums, become as if recited at the holy sites of Puṣkara, Prayāga, Sindhu, and the ocean. (295)
Whatever fruit may accrue to those who recite [this] at Devahrada, Kurukṣetra, and especially at Vārāṇasī, as well as during an eclipse or at the equinoxes; ||296||
Having seen the Grandfather (Brahmā) seated upon that lotus, one obtains a hundredfold fruit and attains various desires, if one so desires. 297.
Having performed the worship according to the rules, whoever listens to it—even the gods, having performed austerities, meditate upon it and speak of it. (298)
O King, when will our birth take place in this land of Jambūdvīpa? And when shall we be initiated and hear the *Padma-purāṇa*? (299)
Having once projected the sixteen-fold lotus-self within the body, we shall go to that supreme station, having reached which there is no further rebirth. (300)
Thus the wise spoke and reflected in their minds:
"O King, when shall we behold the Brahma-sacrifice performed on the full moon day of Kārttika? (301)
Thus has this rite been taught by me to you, O best of beings;
for it is indeed always difficult to obtain even for gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas.
Thus, whoever knows it as it truly is, whoever beholds the maṇḍala, and whoever hears this—all these are liberated; such is the sacred tradition.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim this supreme secret, by which men may attain fortune, fortitude, contentment, and nourishment. (304)
O King, by him all the planets always become auspicious,
provided he first performs this with devotion on a Sunday coinciding with the Hasta nakṣatra.
One should offer a portion of food seven times;
then, when the seventh [offering] is complete, one should provide a meal for a Brāhmaṇa.
A person should diligently fashion a golden image of the Sun, covered with a pair of red garments, along with a small umbrella and sandals. (307)
One should give a pair of sandals and place them in a copper vessel;
having performed a ceremonial bath with ghee, they should be presented to a twice-born man whose limbs are complete.
One should cause it to be given specifically to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the ritual procedures;
when this is done, his reward shall be supreme health. (309)
This ritual prescribed by the Purāṇas for the attainment of all material wealth is non-contradictory; it bestows peace and prosperity upon men. (310)
In the same way, the wise one, having carefully observed a Monday,
should diligently consume [only] at night for eight consecutive Mondays.
The wise should feed Brahmins individually according to their capacity;
then, when the ninth [vessel] is full, one should perform the feeding of Brahmins.
A pair of garments should then be given, and thereafter one should cause Soma to be offered,
placed within a golden vessel and filled with milk.
Likewise, an umbrella along with sandals and shoes should be given, especially to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses all his limbs intact. ||314||
On the day of Svāti, one should worship Mars and subsist on a single meal at night;
in this manner, one should continue for eight days, providing meals for Brahmins.
And having placed a golden Aṅgāraka in a copper vessel,
he should then cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa who indeed possesses all his limbs complete.
One should cast seven small images according to the sequence of the lunar mansions;
then, on the eighth day, the wise man should cause golden planetary figures to be given in due order.
One should perform the fire-ritual according to the prescribed injunctions as they have been observed.
O lord of men, listen to what will come to pass when this has been done. 318.
All malevolent planets become entirely auspicious in form;
all diseases perish, and the deities attain satisfaction. ||319||
The Nāgas do not obstruct him, nor do the ancestors fail to be gratified; likewise, for those who hear or recite this, there is the destruction of bad dreams.
If Mars, Saturn, and the Sun, along with Rāhu and Ketu at the head, stand there—these fierce planets that cause affliction. (321)
Indeed, by merely performing this, they become possessed of good fortune;
for he who always performs it thus, O King, endowed with devotion, [attains these results]. (322)
When they are accompanied by their respective attendants, they bestow [the desired results] upon all; it is not otherwise.
One should place Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu in vessels made of iron. (323)
One should have these fashioned out of iron and cause them to be given to Brāhmaṇas;
a pair of black garments should indeed be given for their gratification.
Those who desire peace, prosperity, and victory should offer golden-bodied [images];
O King, all these planets must be made of gold for those observing the vow. (325)
Those who desire peace should provide a meal for the twice-born as part of their vow;
likewise, they should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to their ability for the pleasure of the planets.
O lord of kings, one may attain all desires with little effort;
one should seek knowledge from Śaṅkara and likewise health from Bhāskara.
One should seek wealth from the Consumer of Oblations (Agni), and one should seek the supreme goal from Janārdana;
and from Pitāmaha (Brahmā), one should seek that which pertains to Brahmā, which brings peace to all living beings.
Bhīṣma said:
"The sacrifice which you have described yields great fruit for those who perform it;
however, because of the brevity of life, it cannot be accomplished by others. (329)
O best of sages, tell me of that great fruit which would result from the merit born of fasting for an entire year with very little effort. (330)
Pulastya said:
O great king, for this very purpose, the highly illustrious King Śveta,
being severely afflicted by hunger, questioned Vasiṣṭha regarding this inquiry.
In the region of Ilāvṛta, there was a king named Śveta of great strength;
he conquered the entire earth with its seven continents and its cities. ||332||
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, was his domestic priest.
Once, that best of kings, being exceedingly righteous, having conquered [his enemies]... [333]
He spoke these words to his family priest Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who recite prayers:
Śveta said— "O Blessed One, I desire to perform a thousand horse-sacrifices."
O Guru, I desire to give gifts of gold, silver, and jewels to the twice-born, and to bestow upon the earth the gift of food, as if it were my very own wish. (335)
O Lord, when a gift of food is given to a twice-born, one should realize that nothing at all has been given;
knowing this, one should never give such a thing as that.
That King Śveta of great renown gave red garments, ornaments, villages, and cities to the brāhmaṇas. (337)
Never did that king provide food or water [to others];
thereafter, O best of men, he became a performer of many horse-sacrifices.
Having gone to heaven after performing penance for three arbudas won through merit,
he attained residence in the same world as Brahmā, adorned with every ornament.
There the celestial nymphs danced and the wives of the Siddhas sang;
both Tumburu and Nārada were always present there as well.
The two highly wise ones sang, and the sages endowed with austerity praised the performer of many sacrifices with mantras declared in the Vedas. (341)
Thus, although that high-souled king was possessed of great wealth,
his body was tormented by hunger and especially by thirst.
Though oppressed by hunger, that best of kings abandoned even heaven and its celestial chariot and went to Mount Ṛkṣa.
Where his own body had gone to the great forest long ago to be consumed by fire,
there that king remained, personally gathering and licking his own bones.
Then,
after a long time, that king of firm vows, the lord of men, ascended his celestial chariot and departed for heaven.
Having seen him licking his own bones, the family priest Vasiṣṭha said: "O lord of kings, O ruler of men, why indeed do you eat your own bones? (346)
Having been addressed thus by the great seer Vasiṣṭha,
King Śveta then spoke these words to that sage.
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, formerly, afflicted by hunger and thirst, I did not give food; therefore, this hunger now oppresses me. (348)
Thus addressed, the great sage Vasiṣṭha,
the bull among munis, then spoke these words again to that king.
"O Lord of Kings, what can I do for you, especially since you are hungry?
For even a mere trifle, nothing remains unoffered that stands before you. (350)
By the gift of jewels and gold, a man becomes possessed of enjoyments;
by the gift of food, he is illuminated with all his desires fulfilled. (351)
"O King, you have not given that [gift], thinking it to be a trifle, O lord of men.
Śveta said:
"O my teacher, how did the acquisition of what was not given come about for me? (352)
"O Vasiṣṭha, by your grace, tell this to me who asks.
Vasiṣṭha said:
There is one cause by which this occurs; of this there is no doubt."
Listen to that, O tiger among men, as it is being told by me to you:
in a former age, there was a king renowned as Vinītāśva. (354)
If the king had indeed begun to perform the horse sacrifice, he would have given those cows, horses, and other things requested by the best of the twice-born as sacrificial fees. (355)
Because he did not give even a little food, considering it too small as you did,
he died after a long time on the bank of the Ganges.
In Māyāpurī, Vinītāśva became a sovereign king;
he too went to heaven, O Lord, just as you have become a king. (357)
He too, overcome by hunger, arrived in this very same way at the bank of the river Gaṅgā on Mount Nīla in the world of mortals. (358)
O King, like a god, he beheld his own body in a radiant celestial chariot with the luster of the sun, as well as his own domestic priest.
Seeing that Brahmin Hotṛ, the priest who performs sacrifices, on the bank of the Jāhnavī,
she questioned that best of the twice-born once again.
O King, he spoke to Sahotā regarding the cause of his hunger; O best of beings, he [described] the sesame-cow and the ghee-cow.
O King, quickly give me a water-cow, a milk-cow, and a grass-cow, so that you may be freed from thirst and hunger in heaven. (362)
"Enjoy yourself as long as the sun and the moon shine in the sky.
Having been addressed thus, the king then questioned him again.
"Tell me the procedure for the sesame-cow gift; having performed it accordingly, I shall give it.
The priest said:
"O lord of men, listen to the ritual for the sesame-cow as it has been declared."
The cow should consist of sixteen *āḍhakas* of grain, and the calf should consist of four;
the feet and teeth should be made of sugarcane stalks, and the auspicious [limbs] of flowers. (365)
Her nose should be made of incense, her tongue of molasses, and her tail fashioned from a red cloth; she should be adorned with ornaments of bells.
Having fashioned such a cow, one should then fashion a golden-horned cow with silver hooves, yielding milk, according to the previously prescribed ritual for a cow.
O King, having prepared that [cow], one should cause it to be given to a Brahmin with the appropriate mantra;
the auspicious cow should stand upon a black antelope skin and be covered with cloths. (368)
Having marked it with a thread and endowed it with the five jewels, one should cause it to be sprinkled with all medicinal herbs and purified by mantras. ||369||
"May food be produced for us instantly, as well as drinks and all flavors;
fulfill our desires, for we are distressed by hunger. (370)
O Goddess, I accept you with devotion, especially for the sake of my family;
O Tiladhenu, salutations to you who bestow all the desires of this body. (371)
O best of kings, an *atiladhenu* given according to this procedure brings about the attainment of all desires; of this there is no doubt. (372)
In this world, a water-cow fashioned in this manner from jars, when given according to the prescribed rite, immediately bestows all desired objects. (373)
Likewise, a hundred cows were given by Yama on the full-moon day;
indeed, she became like Sāvitrī in heaven, granting all desires.
Likewise, when a cow of ghee is given according to the prescribed rite by the wise, it brings about the fulfillment of all desires; indeed, it becomes a source of great joy.
Likewise, O King, if a cow of nectar is given in the month of Kārttika, she shall grant all desires and eternally bestow a favorable state of rebirth. (376)
All this has been explained to you in brief, though it is very extensive;
its boundless fruit has been indicated by Brahmā through every rite.
O best of kings, O lord of men, whatever gift is given out of thirst or hunger—whether one is afflicted by these or not—that gift should first be given to the body. (378)
O All-pervading Lord, this entire universe is fully endowed with living beings, jewels, and medicinal herbs,
and it is always inhabited by gods, dānavas, and yakṣas.
Having fashioned this entire [image], adorned on all sides with silver and enriched with excellent jewels, suns, and moons, one should worship it on the twelfth day of the month of Kārtika.
Alternatively, on the fifteenth day of the month of Kārttika,
a devoted man should cause it to be given to his domestic priest or to his preceptor.
O King, whatever beings exist within the interior of the cosmic egg, they have all been given away by you; thus has the rite of the Vaitana sacrifice been briefly described to you. (382)
O King, whatever fruit is obtained by one who performs sacrifices with complete and excellent sacrificial fees—that entire fruit belongs specifically to that region of the universe. (383)
Furthermore, whatever man might bestow this entire Brahmāṇḍa, by him it would be as if recited, offered in oblation, studied, and proclaimed. (384)
The King said:

"O sinless one, having performed the ritual for the gift of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍadāna), one becomes a partaker of liberation; tell me everything regarding the time, the place, and the Brahmin worthy of the gift. (385)
By whatever action I have performed, I shall become a partaker of its fruit;
may there be for me soon liberation from this contemptible state of being. (386)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, O King, the priest of that [king], a virtuous twice-born man,
then caused a golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) to be fashioned from all kinds of metals.
There he fashioned a lotus adorned with a thousand gold coins;
in its center was Brahmā, embellished with rubies.
Together with Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, along with the Ṛṣis and Munis, all the sons beginning with Nārada, and all the celestial dwellers beginning with Indra [were present]. (389)
All those golden-bodied attendants of Brahmā stood before him;
and the eternal Lord, in the form of a boar, was laughing with Lakṣmī.
One should have blue gems and emeralds fashioned as ornaments for him; the wise man should also cause his splendor to be enhanced by *gomeda* stones.
One should cause pearls to be offered for Soma, diamonds for the Sun, and gold for all the other planets. (392)
Silver is seven times [the value] of gold; copper is likewise [seven times the value] of silver;
from that, bronze should be made seven times [the value], and tin likewise seven times [the value].
O lord of men, one should cause tin to be made seven times the weight of lead;
and one should cause iron to be made seven times the weight of tin, and [seven times] the weight of iron to be lead. (394)
The seven continents, the oceans, and the seven golden mountain ranges were then fashioned by artisans through merits of incalculable number. (395)
One should have trees and other such beings fashioned out of silver, and one should have wild animals fashioned out of gold. (396)
Having prepared trees, forest lords, shrubs, grasses, leaves, and creepers according to the prescribed rule, everything should be offered at the sacred site by the wise.
At Kurukṣetra, at Gayā, at Prayāga, at Amarakaṇṭaka, at Dvāravatī, at Prabhāsa, at Gaṅgādvāra, and at Puṣkara; ||398||
O Vaidehī, at these sacred fords (tīrthas), during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on all the intercalary days (dinacchidras), and during the southern and northern solstices (ayanas); 399.
O King of kings, this should be given during the Vyatīpāta yoga with great merit, and especially during the Viṣuva; one should not entertain any doubt regarding this. 400.
Having established a householder who maintains the sacred fires, endowed with handsome form and the five qualities,
and having honored him along with his wife and adorned them with ornaments.
Having appointed the chief priest as the foremost, and likewise other twice-born men endowed with the twenty-four qualities, they were consulted along with their wives.
Likewise, one should cause rings and earrings to be given;
having been thus praised and honored, he stands well-composed before them. (403)
Having prostrated again and again with the eight-limbed salutation, and having placed his joined palms before the domestic priest, he stood in front of him.
O Brāhmaṇas, favor me with affection and friendliness; O best of the twice-born, through your graciousness, may this day become even more purified for me.
Through the bond of your affection, the Grandfather himself was pleased;
and because the Cosmic Egg was offered by you, Janārdana attained satisfaction.
O best of the twice-born, through their meditative concentration, the Lord who holds the Pināka bow in his hand and Śakra, the lord of the thirty gods, both attained satisfaction.
Having praised him in this way, the king then immediately presented the Brahmāṇḍa vessel to his preceptor, who was a master of the Vedas, according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, satisfied with all his desires, the lord of men went to heaven;
and that [wealth] was distributed by that very preceptor together with the brahmins.
O lord of men, he has also given the entire universe to others;
and among those who receive gifts of land within universes, he alone shall indeed be the recipient of sovereign power.
One who takes it incurs the fault of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
It should indeed be given after being proclaimed in the presence of everyone. 411.
Even those who merely behold it being given become purified;
by the mere sight of it, they certainly attain liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Those who have observed these aforementioned Dvādaśīs ending with Svarṇa, as well as the Mṛgājina—
having performed these, they shall behold the fruit of their actions through these very visions.
O King, by means of this mantra, one shall effortlessly attain the very same world as the Creator, and cows should always be bowed to. 414.
Homage to the cows, to the illustrious ones, and indeed to the daughters of Surabhi;
homage to the daughters of Brahmā, and repeated homage to those who are pure. 415.
By remembering this mantra, one obtains the fruit of giving a cow;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too [should do so] at the most excellent holy site of Puṣkara.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, you shall especially obtain the fruit of giving a cow;
whatever sin exists, whether of a woman or of a man, [it shall be destroyed].
By merely bathing at Puṣkara, all that perishes entirely.
O Bhārata, whatever sacred fords exist on earth as far as the ocean— [418]
These lotuses arrive, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika. ||419||
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Gift of the Cosmic Egg," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Thirty-Five
Bhīṣma said:
Everything concerning the Purāṇas has been stated by the Blessed One;
likewise, the entire Brahmāṇḍa was imparted to Guru by Aśveta.
O twice-born one, having heard this, curiosity arose as to how he performed the licking of bones for the sake of dispelling hunger without the giving of food.
Therefore, I wish to hear about those kings on earth who have attained heaven through the gift of food, and how sacrifices are rooted in food. (3)
How was the mind of that high-souled one destroyed, and why was no gift of food given by him, nor was it shown by the sages? (4)
Whatever fruit results from the greatness of *ahoma* and from food given here [in this world] is enjoyed by men in the next world; moreover, heaven shall attain imperishability.
O Brahmins, those who are ever-vigilant proclaim that the gift of food is supreme;
by the gift of food, the Lord of the Gods enjoys the three worlds here.
"He is called Śatakratu by all the best of the twice-born;
therefore, the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods attained a state corresponding to that. (7)
I have heard from you everything concerning the attainment of heaven through giving; furthermore, I have heard of other past events, whether they occurred or have ceased.
"O high-minded one, I wish to hear more; please tell me that.
Pulastya said:
"This narrative was formerly [related] by the great-souled Agastya."
"O King, I shall now relate to you that which was told by Rāma.
Bhīṣma said:
'In whom was that Rāma, the best of kings, born?'"
To whomsoever this ancient history was told by Agastya, Pulastya said:
"In the lineage of Raghu was born the one named Rāma, possessed of great strength. (11)
The work of the gods has been accomplished by him; Rāvaṇa has been slain in Laṅkā. As he is established in the sovereignty of the earth, the Ṛṣis have come to his house.
Those great-souled ones arrived at the residence of Rāghava;
then, by the word of Agastya, the doorkeeper quickly [informed] Rāma.
Having seen Rāma, who was like the risen full moon, the gatekeeper hurriedly announced that the sages had arrived.
"O son of Kausalyā, may it be well with you; the night has turned to dawn today.
Having arrived here, I have come now to behold the prosperity of the descendant of Raghu."
O King, Agastya stood at the gate together with the sages;
having heard that the sages had arrived, Rāma [went out] to meet those who were as radiant as the sun.
Then, filled with haste, he spoke these words standing at the gate:
"For what reason have you blocked the entrance to these most excellent sages? (17)
At Rāma’s word, he ushered those two sages in with comfort;

Rāma, having saluted them with a prostration, seated them upon comfortable seats that were beautifully spread and variegated with gold. ||19||
Seated together upon excellent kusha grass, the family priest offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering to those preeminent sages.
When all those great seers, who were knowers of the Vedas, were asked about their welfare by Rāma, they spoke these words. (21)
All is well with you everywhere, O mighty-armed descendant of Raghu;
and by good fortune, we behold you safe and sound, having slain that enemy.
O tiger among the Raghus, your wife Sītā was abducted by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa through his extreme wickedness; yet he has been slain by her very power.
By you alone and without assistance, Rāma was slain;
there exists no other doer of such a deed as that which you have committed. (24)
O King of Kings, having seen you who have arrived here to converse with us, we ascetics have now all become purified by the mere sight of you. (25)
By slaying Rāvaṇa today, you have wiped away my tears;
having bestowed this meritorious gift of safety upon the world, O Hero. (26)
"By good fortune you have prospered through the victory of Aṅkūṭastha, O you of immeasurable prowess!

O ascetic of supreme penance, when you had entered the forest, I presented to you Indra’s bow,
as well as two inexhaustible quivers and armor.
"O descendant of Raghu, you must come again to this hermitage on Mount Meru.
Having spoken thus to him, all those sages vanished. (29)
When the foremost of sages had departed, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, reflected upon that matter: "What could have been intended by the sage? (30)
"O descendant of Raghu, you must come again to this hermitage;

"The secret of the gods must be heard, and whatever else he may say must be carried out"—
as Rāma of immeasurable splendor was thinking thus, ||32||
He will certainly practice the Dharma, for the Dharma is the supreme goal;

As that high-souled Raghava gave gifts, offered oblations, and protected his subjects, those years passed for him as if they were but a single year.
On that very day, an aged twice-born man from the countryside arrived at the gate of Rāma, bringing his deceased son with him.
She spoke various words filled with affectionate syllables:
"O son, what evil deed was committed by me in a previous life? (36)
That I behold you, my only son, who have met your end—still a child who has not yet reached youth, with a lifespan of only five years. (37)

It is evident that Rāma has committed some evil deed, for by it death has come upon you;

"He will enter [the fire] without doubt, along with his wife, after I have died"—
Rāghava heard all this, filled with pain and grief.
Rāma spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha, who was being restrained:
