Listen, O Rāma, to how at the proper time the destruction of the Bāla clan occurred;
formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, O Rāma, the Brāhmaṇas were supreme everywhere.
O Raghava, at that time there was no one at all who was not a brahmin; they all performed austerities, were free from death, and lived for a long time. (45)

When the Tretā Yuga arrived once more, the unsurpassed Brahmanical and Kṣatriya orders [flourished]; however, in the Dvāpara, unrighteousness entered among them, as well as among the Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Thus, when untruth had arisen and prevailed continuously,
one quarter of Adharma arrived there, and a single quarter of Dharma followed.
Then, because the easterners were greatly terrified and the Brahmins and others [were oppressed], the second foot of Dharma was once again established. (48)
In that Dvāpara age, the asceticism of the Vaiśyas entered; thus the unrighteousness of the three ages established itself within Dharma.
O bull among men, since the Kali age has arrived and this current yuga is prevailing, unrighteousness and falsehood have indeed increased.
O King, in the Kali age, he will be born from a Śūdra womb; having performed intense austerity at the edge of the region, he will dwell there. (51)
A Śūdra of wicked intellect and evil intent committed the murder of a child; indeed, he performed an unrighteous act that was forbidden for him and outside the king's jurisdiction.
A man of evil mind who acts like a tiger toward a pure brāhmaṇa goes quickly to hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts. 53.
O tiger among men, the king partakes of a fourth portion of that sin; therefore, go to your own kingdom.
Wherever you perceive wrongdoing, there apply effort;
in this way, there will be an increase in your righteousness as well as an increase in your strength. (55)
"O best of men, this child shall live.
When Nārada had spoken thus, Raghunandana was filled with wonder.
He experienced incomparable joy and said this to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Go, gentle Lakṣmaṇa, and console that best of brahmins."
And you must place the body of the child in a vat of oil, with most excellent perfumes and fragrant oils. (58)
O gentle one, act in such a way that the child does not perish, and that the body of this boy of unblemished deeds remains protected. (59)
"Act in such a way that there may be neither misfortune nor division;
having thus instructed Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who is endowed with auspicious marks," [he spoke].
The highly illustrious one meditated with his mind upon the Puṣpaka chariot, thinking, "May it come here";
and perceiving that intention, the golden-adorned vehicle arrived, moving at will.
In a moment, he indeed came into the presence of Rāghava;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words: "O lord of men, here I am. (62)
O King, having heard what was spoken for a long time by the Puṣpaka, the servant of the great-armed Agretava presented himself.
Having paid homage to those great sages, he ascended his celestial chariot,
taking with him his bow, two quivers, and a sword of great luster.
Having left both the heroic son of Sumitrā and Bharata in the city, the valiant one,
well-composed and searching diligently, departed swiftly toward the west.
Afterwards, he went to the northern direction situated at the Himavat;
having also gone to the eastern direction, the lord of men likewise beheld it.
Then, [the army] of the joy of the Raghus marched toward the southern region, which was entirely pure in conduct and as stainless as a mirror.
On the northern side of the mountain, he saw a great lake;
in that lake, he beheld that ascetic performing very great penance.
Rāghava saw the formidable Lampaṇa hanging with his face turned downwards;
approaching him, the descendant of Kakutstha spoke to that ascetic who was performing penance.
Rāghava spoke these words: "Blessed are you, O one with the splendor of an immortal!
In what womb was your birth, that you possess such growth in asceticism and such firm resolve?"
"I am Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; out of curiosity, I ask you: what is it that you have resolved upon—is it the heavenly world or something else? (71)
"For what reason do you suffer, O ascetic? I wish to hear this. Are you a Brāhmaṇa—may prosperity be yours—or are you an invincible Kṣatriya? (72)
Whether he be a Vaiśya of the third caste or a Śūdra, let it be told truly:
asceticism, whose essence is truth, is eternally required for the attainment of the heavenly world. (73)
That austerity, consisting of the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and that which is essentially truth,
was created by Viriñca himself as a cause for the benefit of the world.
That which arises from the fierce energy of a kṣatriya is called tāmasa;
and that which is intended for the destruction of others is declared to be āsura.
Or, one who conceals his limbs when they have been partially burnt by the fire may either accomplish the five fires or attain success, or even death itself. (76)
For this disposition of yours is indeed demonic; you are not considered a twice-born man. Truth brings success for one who speaks it, but there is no life for one who speaks falsehood. (77)
Having heard these words spoken by Rāma of unwearied deeds,
he remained with his head bowed down and spoke this speech.
Welcome to you, O best of kings; it has been a long time since you were last seen, O Rāghava.
I am like a son to you, and you are like a father to me, O sinless one.
Or rather, it is not so; for the king is the father of all.
You are indeed worthy of honor, O King, and we are performing penance within your domain.
We wander there; a portion [of us] was created of old by Svayambhū.
We are not fortunate, O King; you alone are fortunate, O Rāma. (81)
O Rāghava, since ascetics desire success even in such worldly objects through austerity,
may you attain success through my austerity.
"As for what was said by you, that 'this penance of yours is in a single womb'—I have been born from a Śūdra womb, yet I have undertaken this fierce penance. (83)
O observer of excellent vows, do not pray for divinity with this very body;
O King, I shall not speak falsely out of a desire to conquer the world of the gods. (84)
"O descendant of Kakutstha, know me to be a Śūdra named Śambūka.
As he was speaking thus, the descendant of Kakutstha [drew] his sword of radiant luster.
Rāghava drew it from its scabbard and severed the stainless head;
when that Śūdra was slain, the gods, led by Agni and including Indra, rejoiced.
"Excellent, excellent! they praised the descendant of Kakutstha again and again;
and a great, fragrant rain of flowers from the gods fell. (87)
Having released the arrow from the sky, they scattered it everywhere;
and being well-pleased, the gods spoke these words to Rāma, the best among those skilled in speech: ||88||
O gentle one, this task has been accomplished by you;
O Rāma of great vows, accept a boon, for we desire it from you.
"Indeed, because of your deed, this Śūdra has gone to heaven in his very body.
Having heard the speech of the gods, Rāghava became deeply composed. (90)
With palms joined in reverence, he addressed these words to the thousand-eyed Purandara:
"If the gods are indeed pleased with me, or if I am worthy of a boon... (91)
"O son of a twice-born, let these who are pleased by my deed live!
For this is the supreme boon desired by me from you. (92)
"Due to my transgression, this young son of a Brahmin, his time not yet come, has been led by Time to the abode of Vaivasvata. (93)
"Bring him back to life; may it be well with you. I shall not be a liar toward my preceptor.
For I have heard the word of the twice-born, and I shall restore your son to life. (94)
"O Asuras, let this boy live for the duration of my own life, or for half of it; this boon, which I have chosen, is superior to ten million other boons. (95)
Having heard those words of Rāghava, the best of the gods,
delighted and filled with affection, replied to that high-souled one.
O descendant of Kakutstha, the only son of that brahmin, who had been extinguished, has regained his life and has once again been reunited with his kinsmen. (97)
In the very moment that this Śūdra, the descendant of Kakutstha, was struck down, he was suddenly reunited with life. 98.
"May you attain well-being; may it be auspicious for you. We shall accomplish the supreme austerity, so that we may behold the great sage in the hermitage of Agastya. (99)
Having thus made his vow before the gods, the joy of the Raghus ascended that Puṣpaka aerial chariot, adorned with gold.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaughter of the Śūdra Ascetic," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||35||
Chapter Thirty-Six.
Pulastya said:
Then the gods departed at that time in their great celestial chariots.
Rāma also quickly followed the pitcher-born Agastya to the penance grove. ||1||
The Blessed One said: "He who has previously come before me in the assembly shall not have to come again. (2)
Therefore, by the command of the deity and for the sake of that task, I shall go and see that great sage, who is worshipped by gods and demons. (3)
And that most excellent being, being pleased, will himself grant instruction;
by which mortal I shall never again become a sufferer. 4.
My father is Daśaratha and my mother is Kausalyā;
though I am born into the solar dynasty, I am nonetheless so deeply distressed. (5)
During my time as king, I lived in the forest with my wife and younger brother;
furthermore, my wife was abducted by Rāvaṇa.
Having crossed the supreme ocean without assistance from me,
and having besieged that entire city, he brought about the destruction of his own lineage.
Then, in the presence of the gods, I was seen abandoned by Rāvaṇa;
they declared me to be pure, and thus I was taken home by Rāma as Sītā.
Having been brought here by one who was displeased and dismissed from the words of the people,
that queen dwells in the forest, while I indeed dwell in the city.
"I am born as the foremost, and thus I am the best among archers;
yet having fallen into supreme misery, my heart does not break. (10)
"I have certainly been created by the Creator, who possesses the essence of the essence of the Vajra;
now, at the command of the Brahmin, I wander upon the surface of the earth. (11)
While I was established in austerity, that sinful Śūdra was struck down by me;
however, at the word of the gods, my life-breath has once again been established within my heart. (12)
Behold this Sage, who is devoted to the welfare of this world;
by seeing him, suffering will likewise swiftly go to its destruction. (13)
Just as the snow melts at the rising of the thousand-rayed sun,
even so the onset of suffering will come to an end in every way.
And seeing that the gods had arrived, the venerable sage Agastya, taking up the guest-offering (arghya), was well-pleased and honored them all. ||15||
Then, having received worship and conversed with the great sage,
they departed for the heights of heaven, delighted along with their followers.
When they had departed, that descendant of Kakutstha descended from the Puṣpaka chariot and approached the supreme sage Agastya to pay his respects.
The king said:
"O best of sages, I am the son of Daśaratha; I have come to pay my respects to you. Behold me with a gracious eye. (18)
"Having seen you, I shall undoubtedly become one whose sins have been shaken off;
having said this much, he saluted the sage again and again. (19)
All is well with my circle of servants, the deer, and my son;
however, desiring a vision of the Blessed One, I killed a Śūdra and have come here. (20)
Agastya said:
Welcome to you, O best of the Raghus, eternal refuge of the world! By the sight of you, O descendant of Kakutstha, I, along with the sages, am purified.
O tiger among the Raghus, accept this guest-offering prepared by me, O one of great splendor!
Welcome, O tiger among men; by good fortune you have arrived, O slayer of enemies! (22)
Since you are always highly esteemed for your many supreme qualities, you are indeed worthy of worship, residing eternally within my heart. (23)
The spies report to you that a slayer of a Śūdra has arrived;
yet by means of dharma, you have restored the life of a Brāhmaṇa’s son. (24)
"O Blessed One, O Raghava, please stay here for a while in my presence;
O high-minded one, tomorrow morning you shall go from here to Ayodhya by means of the Puṣpaka."
And this ornament, fashioned with skill by Viśvakarman, is gentle and beautiful;
it is divine, shining with its own splendor upon his divine body.
O Raghava, accept this King of Kings, who is dear to me;
it is said that there is a very great fruit in giving back what has been received. (27)
For you are indeed capable of protecting even the supreme gods, including Indra;
therefore, O bull among men, I shall bestow [this] upon you according to the rite—please accept it.
Then the mighty-armed great chariot-warrior of the Ikṣvākus, having performed his salutation, spoke to the best of sages while recollecting his own dharma. (29)
O Blessed One, the acceptance of gifts is indeed censured by the wise; how then can a Kṣatriya who understands this accept gifts from a Brahmin? (30)
O great sage, you ought to tell me what was given by that brahmin; for I am now possessed of sons and a home, and I am capable, O great ascetic. (31)
How can one accept a gift when overwhelmed by calamity?
My wife has been lost for a very long time, and no other woman exists for me. (32)
I alone shall be the partaker of the fault here; of this there is no doubt.
Even a Kṣatriya who accepts gifts falls into a miserable state.
One who acts [in this way] incurs no fault; Manu himself is the authority on this point:
"An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son. (34)
Even after committing a hundred improper acts, he spoke kindly to her who was to be supported:
"O brahmin-sage, I do not accept the gift bestowed by you. (35)
O you who are worshipped by the gods, you must certainly not harbor anger toward me. 36.
Agastya said: "O King, there is no fault in accepting gifts when they are offered by rulers of the earth;
for you, O Rāghava, are capable of rescuing even the three worlds from the Vaitaraṇī river."
"O Rāma, deliver this Brāhmaṇa, especially this ascetic;
therefore, O Lord of Men, I shall bestow [this] upon you according to the prescribed rites—accept it. (38)
Rāma said:
"How should a Kṣatriya who understands his duty accept what is given by a Brāhmaṇa? You ought to tell me that. (39)
Agastya said:
In the ancient Kṛta age, which was purified by Rāma and Brahmā, all subjects were without a king, and Śatakratu was the lord of the gods. ||40||
Those subjects approached the Lord of the gods for the sake of a king;
for among the gods, Śatakratu, the god of gods, exists as their king. (41)
O Lord of the World, O King, act now for our welfare in this world, so that men, by offering worship unto you, may enjoy the earth. (42)
Then Brahmā, the best of the gods, having summoned all the world-protectors along with Indra, said: "Let a portion of your splendor be bestowed upon him."
Then the world-protectors each contributed a fourth part of their own splendor;
from that, O King, Brahmā was born as the eternal and imperishable Yatojāta.
Brahmā assigned that portion of the guardians of the world to Puṃsā;
thereafter, the king became an expert in ensuring the welfare of those subjects.
In that regard, with the portion belonging to Indra, the king should issue commands to all;
and with the portion belonging to Varuṇa, he nourishes all embodied beings. 46.
Likewise, the king assigns wealth through the quarter of Kubera;
and he governs the subjects with that portion of Yama which belongs to the king. (47)
And there, O best of kings, O Lord, accept this ornament from me with the portion belonging to Indra, for the sake of my deliverance. 48.
Then Rāma took from the hand of that high-souled sage a divine and variegated ornament, which was as radiant as the sun.
Then Rāghava, the slayer of enemy heroes, having accepted it from Agastya,
gazed upon it for a very long time and reflected upon it again and again.
There were various pearls, equal in size to *dhātrī* fruits,
set in gold and joined with diamonds, coral, and sapphires.
It was well-fastened and beautifully proportioned with rubies, gomedas, lapis lazuli, and topazes, and was excellently crafted by Viśvakarman.
Having seen them, he was filled with joy and further reflected thus:
"Never before have I seen such jewels as these. (53)
These exquisite ornaments, bound together and equal in value to the entire earth,
were never seen by me before in Vibhīṣaṇa’s Laṅkā.
Having thus reflected with a composed mind, Rāghava once again began to inquire about that divine arrival from the sage.
O Brahmin, this is most wonderful and unattainable even for kings;
how was it obtained by your holiness, and by whom was it created? (56)
And out of curiosity, O Great-minded One, I ask you this: how is it that many hands, though resting upon the palm [of one hand], are clearly visible? (57)
One should know that to be the lowest, condemned in all the scriptures;
O best of sages, that which illuminates the directions is the middling. 58.
That which is upward-pointing and three-pronged is declared to be the most excellent;
these, indeed, have been proclaimed by the sages as being of the highest class.
"For the Blessed One is indeed a treasury of many divine wonders. Having spoken thus, O descendant of Kakutstha, the sage then addressed these words.
Agastya said: Listen, O Rāma, to this great ancient account of what occurred formerly in the Tretā Yuga,
which I witnessed when the Dvāpara Yuga had arrived.
O noble one of mighty arms, listen to this, O descendant of Raghu:
in ancient times, during the Tretā Yuga, there was a vast forest here.
In that uninhabited forest, extending for an equal hundred yojanas and devoid of deer and tigers,
he desired to perform supreme austerity.
O gentle one, I have come to enter this forest;
indeed, the center of that forest is always well-supplied with roots and fruits. (64)
In the midst of that forest, extending for five yojanas, there were various kinds of vegetables and groves of diverse forms and beautiful appearance.
There I beheld a most beautiful lake, crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and adorned with *cakravāka* birds. (66)
In ancient times, he went to the vicinity of that lake to perform austerities— a place strewn with scattered tortoises and filled with flocks of rows of cranes.
Having thus reached a holy region entirely free from all harm,
O bull among men, I dwelt there for one night during the summer season.
Having risen early at dawn, I approached that lake;
then I beheld a corpse there, untouched by old age.
O Raghava, standing not far from that place, which was filled with supreme splendor,
I remained there for a moment, reflecting upon his sake.
Is this a living being on the shore, or perhaps a bull among the gods; is it a sage, or a king, or is it a sage who has become a king? (71)
Alternatively, if the son of a king has been conceived in this manner, yet dies on the same day, or at night, or even in the morning; ||72||
"O best of the Raghus, you must certainly know that I am unable to depart from this lake;
therefore, while I remain thus, reflect upon it. (73)
Then, after a moment, I beheld a divine and wonderful-looking celestial chariot,
most magnificent, yoked with swans, and swift as thought.
O King, there before him were a thousand celestial nymphs of great splendor,
and an equal number of Gandharvas, who delighted that excellent man.
Some sang divine songs while others played musical instruments;
then I saw a man descending from that celestial chariot.
O descendant of Raghu's lineage, having bathed,
you shall then eat as much as you desire of this very fat female corpse.
Having descended into the lake, he quickly ascended to heaven once more;
I beheld him, who resembled a god and was endowed with supreme splendor.
"Oho! O fortunate one who dwells in heaven, I ask you this:
how is it that your food is loathsome, yet your destiny is so excellent? (79)
If this is not a secret that you may speak of today, O Blessed One, I desire to hear it at will; what is this supreme word? (80)
"O gentle one, you say that the body and food are contemptible; yet this is being consumed by you. For what purpose do you exist anywhere? (81)
Whose sovereign power is this that has been fashioned into the state of a corpse?
And how is food to be consumed? I wish to hear the truth of these matters. (82)
Having heard those words spoken there, O best among the virtuous, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, joined his palms in reverence and replied thus to the gods: 83.
Listen now to this account of mine, arising from both happiness and sorrow, exactly as it occurred;
for desire is difficult to overcome, O twice-born one, which you have asked about. (84)
In former times, there was a king of Vidarbha named Pitāmaha, of great fame;
he was known throughout the three worlds as Vāsudeva, a man of righteous conduct. ||85||
O Brahmin, he had two sons born of two wives; I was known as Śveta, and the younger was Suratha. (86)
When that father had passed away, the citizens consecrated him;
there he ruled the kingdom with self-consciousness, being fully composed in righteousness.
Thus, while I was exercising my sovereignty and protecting the subjects, many thousands of years passed by.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, having resolved upon death in my heart due to detachment from some particular circumstance, I went to the forest of asceticism. (89)
Thus, I have entered this delightful forest, which is utterly devoid of birds, in order to practice asceticism in the vicinity of this very lake. (90)
Having consecrated his brother Suratha as king over those realms,
that lord of men reached this lake and performed most rigorous austerities.
Having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest, he attained the auspicious and healthy realm of Brahmā, his own divine abode. 92.
"O Brahmin, O best of the twice-born, even while I was staying in heaven, hunger and thirst tormented me intensely, and my senses became deeply distressed. (93)
Then I spoke to the Grandfather, the most excellent in the three worlds:
"O Blessed One, this heavenly world is devoid of hunger and thirst. (94)
"O Lord, O illustrious Grandfather, tell me: what is the ripening of which karma that there is this hunger and thirst for me? And what shall be my food? (95)
Then, O great sage, the Grandfather, having meditated properly for a long time, spoke these words to me: "O sir, there is no food produced from one's own body. (96)
O Tuhini, you have been eating these my own flesh-essences constantly;
by nourishing your own body, you have performed a most excellent penance.
O father, I have never seen anything on the surface of the earth that was not given;
even in the past, when a living being begged out of persistence, I would give him alms. (98)

"Indeed, because you did not give this to a guest at that time out of delusion and confusion regarding the householder's state, you now suffer from hunger and thirst even though you have gone to heaven. (99)
O King of Cāraṇas, eat your own unsurpassed body, which has been well-nourished by foods; thus you will attain satisfaction and bliss. 100.
Having been addressed thus, I then spoke to the god Brahmā:
"O All-pervading Lord, once my own body has been consumed, what other food shall there be? (101)
The mere warding off of hunger does not constitute the nourishment of this body;

Then Brahmā spoke again: "Your body has been made indestructible;
day by day, this corpse shall become nourished and turn white. (103)
O King, for a full hundred years you ate your own flesh;
then Agastya, the great ascetic, arrived at Śvetāraṇya.

The Blessed One is exceedingly difficult to overcome; you shall be liberated from him only with great difficulty, for he is capable of contending even against the gods and asuras, including Indra himself.
This food is contemptible; how much more so for you, O royal sage?
A great task for the gods has been accomplished by you, a high-souled one, through no small merit. (106)
The ocean was rendered waterless and the Dānavas were struck down;
furthermore, the Vindhya mountain, which had grown out of hatred for the Sun, was restrained.
This earth, having been consecrated by the weight of the syllables Laṃ and Baṃ, moved toward the southern direction and so forth, leaving the three worlds in a state of instability. (108)
Having gone to the southern direction together with the gods, O highly fortunate one, I was sent forth as the teacher equal to the world, along with its sprouts.
Thus, having remained there, that sage made the entire earth level;
by that king of sages, it remains visible even today in this manner. (110)
Having heard these words spoken by the Blessed One, the God of Gods, I shall consume even contemptible food, while my own body remains unsurpassed. (111)
For a full hundred years, even this loathsome food has been my sustenance;
yet it has not diminished, and my supreme satisfaction remains. (112)
Tormented by hardship, he thought day and night: "When will that sage grant me a vision in the forest? (113)
Thus I thought, O Brahmin: "Though I have remained here for a hundred years, the sage Agastya will certainly be my refuge. (114)
"O twice-born one, my state will be like that of an elephant after the death of its trainer";
having heard these words spoken by Rāma and seeing his loathsome necklace, [Agastya said: 115.
Filled with supreme compassion, I shall make that king, who is departing for heaven,
a consumer of ambrosial food, and I shall destroy his loathsome [karmic] state.
Reflecting thus, I said to him: "What will Agastya do?
O high-minded one, we have eaten this contemptible thing because of him. (117)
"Ask of us whatever you desire that shall bring supreme delight to your heart.
Then she said to him: "How can the word of Brahmā be otherwise? (118)
"It is impossible for me to do this for the sage, nor will anyone else save him, except for that one born from the womb of Kaśyapa and the union of Mitra and Varuṇa. (119)
O Brahmin, even though I had not asked him, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) spoke thus;
to Śveta, who was speaking in this manner, I said, "I am he."
"You have come here by your own good fortune; I have been seen by you, of this there is no doubt.
Then, recognizing me as a celestial being, he fell upon the ground like a staff."
Having raised him up, Rāma then said, "What shall I do for you?
The king replied:
"O Brahmin, deliver me today from this evil deed arising from contemptible food."
"By this act performed by you, the world shall become an inexhaustible heaven for you; therefore, O King, I have indeed bestowed this gift upon you. (123)
May you show me favor; please accept this gift.
At that time, having accepted the ornaments placed in his hand by Rāma, the son of Raghu, he set his mind on crossing over out of greed for them. ||128||
O King, his former human body was then lost;
and when that body had perished, the royal sage was filled with supreme joy.
Having been thus addressed by me, he departed once again for the third heaven in his celestial chariot;
and by him, who was equal to Indra, that auspicious ornament was given to me.
On that occasion, O descendant of Kakutstha, a gift was given by the one of wondrous deeds;
at that time, King Darbhaka became white and was freed from all taint.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Rāma and Agastya," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(37) Chapter Thirty-Seven.
Pulastya said:
Having heard those most wonderful words of Raghunandana,
he proceeded once more to inquire out of both reverence and amazement.
Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, that forest where he performed his austerities was terrible;
how did it become so wonderful that Śveta, the king of Vidarbha, became [a great ascetic] there?"
O great sage, tell me how the king entered that rugged forest—desolate and devoid of wild animals—to practice asceticism. (3)
"How did that entire hundred-yojana region become devoid of human beings?
How did you enter it? Tell me the purpose for which you went there."
Agastya said:
In former times, in the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Manu, the lord who wields the rod of justice.
His son was Ikṣvāku, of immeasurable splendor, whose name was Thā.
Having installed that eldest son on the earth as king, in accordance with his own will,
he declared him to be the "King of Kings" among all royal lineages on earth.
"O Raghava, the son has thus promised his father's request;
thereupon, being exceedingly delighted, he spoke to him again. (7)
I am pleased by that most noble deed; there is no doubt about it. You have protected your subjects with the rod of punishment, yet you have not applied punishment without cause. (8)
When punishment is meted out here by men against offenders, that punishment, when duly released according to the law, leads the king to heaven. (9)
Therefore, O mighty-armed son, be diligent with the rod;
for you, dharma will be established as supreme in this world. (10)
Having thus instructed his son Manu with deep concentration,
he, being joyful, departed for the third heaven, the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
"How shall I produce sons?"—thus he became consumed by anxiety;
through various manifold ritual acts, he became endowed with sons.
He gratified the ancestors with his sons, who were like the offspring of gods; among them all, O descendant of Raghu, the youngest was the most excellent. (13)
Then his wise father, considering that he was brave, learned, and a teacher honored by the people, gave him the name Daṇḍin.
And seeing that the fall of punishment would come upon his own body,
Rāghava beheld that terrible fault of his son.
The Lord bestowed upon him the sovereignty over the region between the Savi and Dhyanī rivers;
there, on the summit of a beautiful mountain, he became king with full authority.
And he himself made that incomparable city his residence,
and gave that city the name Madhumattama.
Endowed with such instruction, the hero took up his residence;
thus the king, together with his domestic priest, governed that kingdom.
It was filled with joyful and virtuous subjects, like the king of the gods in heaven;
then the descendant of Kakutstha ruled for many tens of thousands of years with justice.
The righteous-souled king ruled his kingdom, having struck down all enemies;
then, in due time, King Kuśa went to the hermitage of Bhārgava.
In the delightful month of Caitra, he went to that charming place,
where he [beheld] the daughter of Bhārgava, whose beauty was peerless on earth.
While wandering in that forest region, he beheld an unsurpassed woman—
tall and full-figured, youthful, with a face like the moon, and auspicious.
Seeing her with a beautiful nose, lovely in all her limbs, with full and elevated breasts, slender-waisted and broad-hipped, let him feel joy. (23)
Seeing her alone in the forest, clad in a single garment and standing in the prime of her youth, he was afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god (Kāma) through unrighteousness.
Having approached her as she was well-rested, he spoke these words to the maiden: "From where have you come, O lady of beautiful hips? And whose daughter are you, O most radiant one? (25)
"O beautiful one, being tormented by the god of love, I ask you:
O lovely lady, my heart has been stolen by you from the very moment I saw you. (26)
This food of yours is delightful and captivating to the hearts of sages;
if I do not obtain it to eat, consider me as dead. (27)
O fair-eyed one, restore to life my life-breaths which have been taken away by you!
O beautiful woman of excellent limbs, I am your slave; favor me, your devotee, O auspicious lady! 28.
As he was speaking thus, intoxicated by passion and lust, the daughter of Bhṛgu addressed these words with humility to the king. (29)
Know her, O lord of kings, to be the daughter of Śukra Bhārgava, whose deeds were difficult to accomplish; she was named Arajā, the eldest of those dwelling in the hermitage.
Śukra is the father of the great-souled one, and you, O Indra among kings, are his disciple;
and according to dharma, O crusher of enemies, I am his sister. (31)
O King, you ought not to speak such words;
for I must always be protected by you even from others who are very wicked. (32)
"An angry and fierce father might reduce you to ashes;
or else, by the law of kings, he will forcibly establish a connection with me. (33)
"O best of kings, you should entreat my father with an act consistent with righteousness;
choose my father, who is possessed of great luster."
Otherwise, vast and terrible suffering would certainly befall you;
for if my father were enraged, he could utterly consume the three worlds. (35)
Then, having heard that most terrible and exceedingly dreadful evil, Daṇḍa, intoxicated with pride, bowed his head once more and replied: (36)
"O fair-hipped one, show favor to me, who am maddened by desire for you, O lovely woman!
My life-breaths are perishing, obstructed by you, O lady of beautiful countenance. (37)
Having encountered you, my enmity here has either vanished or become even greater;
O timid one, favor me, your devotee, for my devotion toward you is supreme. (38)
Having spoken thus, he seized that maiden by force with his arm; meanwhile, she was stripped of her clothes by another king’s hand. (39)
Embracing limb with limb and kissing mouth with mouth, he began the act of sexual union, quivering according to his desire.
Having inflicted that most terrible and extremely cruel calamity,
Daṇḍa quickly returned to his own city like an elephant intoxicated with rut.
Distressed and dejected, the daughter of Bhṛgu waited nearby the hermitage for her father, who was equal to a god, with an anxious heart. 42.
After a short while, having performed his ablutions, the celestial sage of immeasurable luster,
afflicted by hunger, returned to his own hermitage surrounded by his disciples.
He beheld Arajā, dejected and overwhelmed by dust, like the moonlight eclipsed when joined with thick clouds. ||44||
Anger arose in that great-souled one who was afflicted by hunger;
as if burning the three worlds with his gaze, he spoke to those disciples.
Behold the terrible-looking calamity of one who is perverse and lacks foresight, appearing like a blazing crest of fire. (46)
He who has touched the flame of a blazing fire will undoubtedly meet his destruction and fall into an evil state, along with his followers. (47)
Since he has committed such a terrible and grave sin, that one of wicked intellect shall therefore receive an unsurpassed rain of dust for five years. 48.
Accompanied by the commands of an evil king, along with his servants, army, and vehicles, that wicked-minded man, whose conduct consists of sinful deeds, shall meet his death. 49.
May Indra, the subduer of Pāka, shake off the sins of this evil-minded one with a great shower of rain over his entire realm of a hundred yojanas.
Whatever beings there are here, whether moving or stationary—for all of them, destruction will quickly come through a heavy rain of dust. ||51||

For as long as [the king] remains outside the scope of the rod of punishment, so long will there be a shower of jewels from the sky for seven nights, like a rain of gold, throughout the sacrificial ground and the hermitage.
Having spoken thus, burning with anger, he said to the people dwelling in that hermitage and to those from the countryside, "Stay here! (53)
As soon as Uśanas had spoken, the people dwelling in the hermitage quickly vacated that region and established their residence outside.
Having spoken thus to that forest-dweller, she said this to Arajas:
"O you of very dull wit, remain here in the hermitage, devoted to your duties."
Remain for a hundred kalpas in this hermitage, which extends for a yojana and possesses a radiant luster, free from dust and devoid of passion, as if it were not dusty at all.
Having heard the instruction of the brahmin-sage,
the daughter of Bhṛgu, being deeply distressed, then said "So be it" to her father.
Having spoken thus, the descendant of Bhṛgu departed from that dwelling and proceeded to another, as had been described by the knower of Brahman; within seven days, [the city] was reduced to ashes.
Therefore, Daṇḍa was the object of the curse of Vindhyaśaila;
for he had been cursed by Uśanas at that time because of his act of violating Rāmā.
From that time forward, O descendant of Kakutstha, it is called the Daṇḍaka forest.
All this that you asked me, O Rāghava, has been related to you.
For the hero’s vow indeed transcends the practice of meditation;
therefore, these great sages, like jars filled with nectar, have all departed together from there.
Having performed the water-libations and worship for the tiger among men, they proceed toward the Sun with hymns composed by Brahmā and others, which have been practiced by all the ṛṣis.
"The sun has set; go and perform your ablutions with water.
Accepting the sage's words, Rāma went to perform the twilight devotions.
He approached that meritorious lake of Raghunandana;
then, in that delightful forest region adorned with trees, [he arrived]. (64)
On that supreme mountain, Nadapunya, adorned with hundreds of cuckoos, filled with the cries of various birds, and crowded with diverse groves and rivers. (65)
It was infested with lions and tigers, crowded with various birds,
and for many series of years, it had been abandoned by vultures and owls.
Then the vulture, who was wicked and deceitful,
having made this plan, provoked a quarrel with that owl.
"Rāma, the lotus-eyed one, is the king of the entire world;
let us seek refuge with him quickly, for to whom else could this palace belong? (68)
Provoked to anger and filled with resentment, the vulture and the owl approached Rāma, their minds agitated by grief, seeking refuge with him at once.
Then, as they were engaged in battle, touching one another with mutual hatred, the vulture, seeing the lord of the Raghavas, spoke these words: ||70||
Among the gods and the asuras, you are considered by me to be the foremost;
O one of great intelligence, you are superior even to Bṛhaspati and Śukra.
Among all beings, high and low, he was like another Śakra among mortals;
he was difficult to look upon, like the sun, and like the Himavat in his majesty.
You are the ocean and you are the earth; you are the fear of the world and you are the guardian of the world. You are equal to the earth in forbearance, and you are like the wind in swiftness.
O Rāghava, you are the Guru, endowed with all perfections, the very form of Viṣṇu;
you are indignant, invincible, a conqueror, and one who has reached the further shore of the ritual application of all divine weapons.
Listen, O Lord of Gods, O bull among men, to what I have to inform you:
O Lord, my abode was indeed established by me through the power of my own arms in former times.
O King, this owl has especially come into your presence;
such is this man of evil conduct, O monarch, who transgresses your command. (76)
"You ought to punish Rāma with the rod of death.
When the vulture had spoken thus, the owl addressed these words.
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind to this instruction from me, which has been received from Soma, Śakra, Sūrya, Dhanada, and likewise from Yama. (78)
A king is born as some mere human being,
but you are the God who consists of all things, whose ultimate refuge is Nārāyaṇa.
O King, it is said that when a matter is properly deliberated, one should protect it thoroughly from those who cause distress, for you are indeed a destroyer of obstacles. (80)
Since you remove the fear of sin from your subjects through the punishment of their faults, you are therefore Indra to us—bestower, punisher, and protector. (81)
Invincible among all beings due to his fiery splendor like that of fire,
Rāma, the sun, constantly burns away the sins of those who steal through his ascetic heat.
O best of kings, you are directly equal to the Lord of Wealth, or even superior to him; for your fortune and your wife are eternally under your own control.
In his treasury he was like Kubera, and in his majesty he was like Kubera;
he was equal toward all beings, both the stationary and the moving. (84)
O Raghava, you should look upon enemy and friend with equal vision and always govern according to righteousness through the established procedures of legal conduct.
He against whom you feel anger is said to be one whose death is imminent;
because he is sung [of] by that [anger], he is widely known as *vairāja* (the enemy-born). 86.
And that superhuman nature which both of you possess, O best of kings,
is due to the king’s supreme compassion and his being endowed with mercy toward all.
For the weak and the protectorless, the king becomes their strength; for the sightless, he becomes the eye, and for those lacking understanding, he becomes the intellect. (88)
"You are our lord as well; listen to me, O righteous one! You must consider it thus: that these birds are indeed [your own]. (89)
The Lord of Yogins, having appointed Droṇabhava as his partisan, said:
"O Lord, let there be no ownership for us in the presence of Devanā. (90)
"O King, it was previously by you alone that the fourfold collection of living beings was created; yet now, a vulture has entered my abode and is tormenting me. (91)
"O Teacher among gods and men, O bull among men, you are indeed such a one.
Having heard this, the King of Vārāṇasī himself summoned his ministers. 92.
Viṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Rāṣṭravardhana, Aśoka, Dharmapāla, Sumantra, and Mahābala. ||93||
These high-souled ministers of King Daśaratha were endowed with statesmanship and were experts in all the śāstras. ||94||
Having descended from the Puṣpaka chariot, that righteous-souled one summoned those who were well-disciplined, of noble birth, and skilled in policy and counsel. 95.
The best of sages asked the vulture and the owl as they were disputing:
"How many years have you made this dwelling place for yourself, O vulture? (96)
"Tell me this, which is my sole curiosity, if you know it according to reality.
Having heard these words, the vulture spoke to Rāghava as he stood there.
Since that time, this earth has been filled with all its quarters by the many raised arms of Rāma, who is possessed of superhuman strength; it has become my home. (98)
The owl, however, said to Rāma: "From the very moment this earth was adorned with trees, O King, that has been my home. (99)

Having heard this, Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, spoke to the members of the assembly: "That is no assembly where the elders do not sit, nor where those who know the law do not speak of dharma with humility. (100)
That is not dharma where there is no truth, and that is not truth which resorts to deceit; but those who, having entered the assembly, remain silent and meditative, are truly honorable. (101)
All those who do not speak exactly as they have perceived are speakers of untruth; likewise, he who does not speak what he has heard out of desire, anger, or fear is also a speaker of untruth.
A thousand nooses of Varuṇa bind that man;
when a full year has passed, only one of those nooses is released.
"Therefore, one who knows must speak the truth, even if it is unpleasant.
Having heard this, I then spoke to my ministers alone: 104.
"O King, it is the owl, not the vulture, O high-minded one! You are the authority, O great king; you are the supreme refuge for kings and serpents. (105)
All subjects have the king as their root; the king is the eternal source of Dharma.
The king is the ruler of those who owe him no debt, and they do not go to an evil rebirth. (106)
And those who have been released by Vaivasvata become the best of men.
Having heard the words of his ministers, he spoke these words to Rāma: 107.
Listen, for I shall relate that ancient account which has been proclaimed:
[the world] consisting of heaven with its moon, sun, and stars, along with the oceans, mountains, earth, and trees. (108)
The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, were submerged in the ocean of water;
at that time, everything existed as one, like a single vast expanse of water.
Punarbhu, together with Lakṣmī, entered the belly of Viṣṇu;
having restrained her, the one of great splendor entered the ocean of waters.
Having been cast out by him who was well-slept, Brahmā entered Viṣṇu’s belly after he had slept for many hundreds of years; then, from that [state], he emerged.
Having known that [lotus] to have many streams, the Great Yogin entered it—the lotus born from the navel of Viṣṇu, adorned with gold. ||112||
Having emerged from Satī and become a yogi of great power,
the Lord desired to create the earth, the wind, the mountains, and the trees.
Then, that one of great ascetic power created all creatures—both human and non-human, including those born from wombs and those born from eggs. (114)
Then, from his body, there arose the two Dānavas Kaiṭabha and Madhu,
who were of great heroism, terrible, and had obtained boons.
O King, seeing Prajāpati there, both of them, overcome with anger,
rushed with great speed toward Svayambhū to devour him.
Having seen all beings emerging one by one,
Viṣṇu, having slain those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, was praised by Brahmā.
For the sake of their stability, you two caused the earth to increase with fat; because it bears the scent of fat (medas) and supports all things, it acquired the name Medinī.
Therefore, that vulture, being truly a man of evil deeds and a wicked soul, makes another's property his own; he must undoubtedly be punished. ||119||
Then an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"Do not kill the vulture Āma; he was previously consumed by the power of his asceticism."
This lord of subjects, the ruler of men, was formerly consumed by the fire of Gautama;
his name is Brahmadatta, a hero, pure and devoted to truth. ||121||
Having returned home, he requested food from the brahmin-sage;
and for a full hundred years, O best of kings, he ate there.
Then, O one of great luster, he himself properly prepared the water for the feet and the guest-offering for this very Brahmadatta, for the purpose of his meal.
Having entered the house of that great-souled one to take food,
he saw a woman with full breasts and then touched her with his hand.
Then, by the enraged sage, a most terrible curse was pronounced: "Go, you deluded king, and become a vulture! Thereupon, the king spoke to the sage.
"The extraction of the curse will be accomplished by one of great fortune who possesses the sprout of compassion.
Having heard those words, the compassionate king spoke again, O lord of men. (126)
In the lineage of the Raghus, there will arise a highly illustrious one named Rāma, a lotus-eyed king of great fortune among the Ikṣvākus. (127)
"Therefore, O bull among men, you shall not see the ripening of that [karma];
it has been seen by Rāma. Having heard this, the lord of the earth became [tranquil].
Quickly abandoning the state of a vulture and anointed with divine perfumes, he,
a man of divine form, addressed that lord of men.
O Lord, through your grace, I, though a sinner, have been made virtuous by you; because of your kindness, I have been liberated from a terrible hell, for you are a knower of dharma. (130)
Having dismissed the royal attendant, the lord of the earth in human form, who was knowledgeable in dharma, said to Ulūka: "O Kauśika, enter your own home. (131)
"Having performed my meditation on non-violence (ahiṃsā), I shall go where the Sage is.
Then, having sipped water and sat down facing the west, he meditated upon non-violence.
Rāma entered the hermitage of the high-souled Kumbhayoni;
there Agastya respectfully [offered] him fruit and roots of many virtues.
He brought flavorful vegetables for the meal;
that tiger among men partook of that food, which was like nectar. 134.
Pleased and thoroughly satisfied, he spent that night there;
then, having risen at the break of dawn and performed his daily rites, O subduer of enemies, [he set out].
The best of the Raghus approached the seer to pay his respects;
having offered salutations, Rāma spoke to the great seer born from a water-pot.
"I take my leave, O Brahmin; may you grant me permission to depart.
I am blessed and favored by the sight of you, O great sage. (137)
"By good fortune, I shall become the purifier of that great-souled one," said the descendant of Kakutstha, as he spoke these words of wondrous appearance. (138)
Filled with supreme joy and with eyes brimming with tears, the ascetic spoke these most wonderful words, O Rāma, consisting of auspicious syllables:
139. "This speech of yours, O Rāma, is composed of auspicious syllables and is truly marvelous."
O descendant of Raghu, you have spoken that which purifies all beings—that by which men behold you, O Rāma, with a friendly eye for even a single moment. (140)
O inhabitants of heaven, you who have been purified by all the hymns must now be told:
those living beings on earth whom you gaze upon with your terrible eyes [shall suffer].
By that very rod of Brahma, they would have immediately gone to hell;
yet you, O best of the Raghus, are such a purifier of all embodied beings. (142)
And as people speak of you thus, O Raghava, they shall attain perfection;
go then, free from anxiety and fear from any quarter, upon your path without obstacle.
"Rule the kingdom with righteousness; you are the refuge of all beings.
Thus addressed by the sage, the king joined his palms in reverence. (144)
He made obeisance to Agastya, the best of sages,
and having saluted that most excellent of munis, he also paid homage to all those ascetics distinguished by their penance.
Then, undistracted, he ascended the gold-adorned Puṣpaka chariot;
as it departed, the hosts of sages then followed with blessings.
The people honored that lord of men as the immortals honor the thousand-eyed Indra;
then, when half the day had passed, Rāma, who was skilled in all matters, [proceeded].
Having reached Ayodhyā, the descendant of Kakutstha descended from the sky to the earth on foot,
after leaving behind the beautiful Puṣpaka chariot that travels at will.
Emerging from the inner apartment, the king spoke these words to the gatekeepers:
"Go with quick steps to Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata. (149)
"Having announced my arrival, bring him here without delay," said the gatekeepers upon hearing the speech of Rāma, whose deeds are difficult to perform. (150)
Having gone and summoned the two princes, they reported [the matter] to Rāghava; by Rāghava’s command, the two princes were brought in by the doorkeepers. ||151||
Seeing that his dear Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa had arrived, Rāghava embraced them both and spoke these words: ||152||
I have performed this unsurpassed service for the twice-born exactly as it should be; therefore, O Raghavas, I desire to perform further deeds for the sake of dharma.
Together with you two, who are as my very self, I desire to perform the Rājasūya, the supreme of sacrifices, wherein eternal Dharma resides. (154)
Formerly, while staying at Puṣkara, Brahmā, the creator of the world,
performed sixty-one sacrifices there.
Having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice according to dharma, Soma, the knower of dharma, attained the unsurpassed station of fame in all the worlds. (156)
Having performed the Ahi-rājasūya sacrifice, Amitra, the destroyer of enemies,
attained the status of Varuṇa within a single auspicious moment.
"Therefore, O venerable one, speak what is beneficial regarding this matter that must be considered.
Bharata said:
"O virtuous one, you are the supreme Dharma; in you, the entire earth is sustained. (158)
O mighty-armed one of immeasurable prowess, all the protectors of the earth are established in you, just as the immortals are established in Prajāpati. 159.
O Great-minded King, those high-souled lords of the world look upon you in this way, and the subjects likewise behold you as a father. 160.
O Raghava, you have become the refuge of living beings here on earth;
therefore, O supreme ascetic, you shall not perform such a sacrifice.
O tiger among kings, O lord of men, it is heard that the destruction of all beings on earth is seen to occur during the period of Soma. 162.
In the war of the stars, during the conflict known as Tārakāmaya,
Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, was carried off by Soma out of lust.
There, a great battle took place, destroying both gods and dānavas;
in that terrible sacrifice of Varuṇa, there were fish and tortoises in the conflict.
O tiger among kings, O Raghava, because of Hariścandra’s performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice, all the aquatic creatures perished. 165.
The great battle of Āḍībaka, which brought destruction to all the worlds,
[swept away] whatever beings there were on earth, even those belonging to the animal realm.

O tiger among men, O king, it has been heard that the exhaustion of both celestial and earthly kings occurs at the conclusion of the Rājasūya sacrifice; therefore, O ruler of the earth, reflect upon this with your intellect.
"Practice the complete dharma, which is beneficial and gentle toward all living beings.
Hearing Bharata's words, Rāghava replied respectfully. 168.
"I am pleased, O slayer of enemies, by these words of yours which are consistent with dharma; O lover of righteousness, your mind has been turned away from the Rājasūya sacrifice. (169)
"I shall fulfill the Dharma and establish the Vāmana [avatāra] in Kānyakubja; O Hero, my fame shall reach the heavens. (170)
The body shall not exist, just as the Gaṅgā did not for Bhagīratha.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Prevention of the Sacrifice," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||37||
The Thirty-Eighth Chapter.

Then, having prostrated with his head and having touched the earth with his five limbs,

The various castes, consisting mostly of non-Brahmins, have assembled to see him;

"O son, I have bestowed the kingship upon these two; O Māthura, you must consecrate them.
Having spoken thus, Rāma then reached the midday sun.

This bridge of Dharma, which increases prosperity, has been constructed by me;

"You must not go further; stay where the Lord of Wealth resides.

The entire earth is seen within his belly, and then, at some point, he emerges from that belly once again. (102)

Then, with a heart full of joy and eyes wide with wonder,

Mārkaṇḍeya said:

The Blessed Lord said: O Brāhmaṇa, I am Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all beings;

When the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya had entered the mouth of the Blessed One,

Then the high-souled and exceedingly powerful one, born from the lotus, covered his own body with water in order to depart from the world of mortals.
And of the great beings, Viśva contemplated the universe;

When the world had been destroyed, becoming subtle, consisting of water, and devoid of space,

from that aperture, the wind was produced, which takes sound as its object.
Having obtained that agitation, the wind increased;
the ocean was violently stirred by the forceful wind with great speed.
From that ocean, as it was agitated and its waters churned within that vessel,
the great lord Vaiśvānara, whose path is black, came into being.
Then the Fire-god dried up much water;
the entire ocean became a void, and the sky spread out [unobstructed]. (145)
The pure waters, which arise from the splendor of the Self, are like the essence of nectar;

Then, seeing that fire produced from friction and its origin, the divine Grandfather, the creator of the great elements, [appeared].
Having seen the beings, the Blessed One, possessing many forms, meditated upon the supreme [means] for the purpose of creating the world, together with the birth of Brahmā.
At the end of a cycle of thousands of four-yuga ages, that which belongs to the lords of the twice-born on earth whose souls have been purified by austerity [is attained]. 149.
Hari, whose self is purified through many births, is called Brahman;
having perceived knowledge, the Self of the Universe attains the state of fitness for yogis. (150)
Having recognized him as a master of yoga and possessed of supreme, perfect sovereignty,
the knower of yoga established him in the station of Brahman over the entire universe.
Then, in that great body of water, Maheśa Hari,
the infallible creator of all worlds, duly engaged in aquatic sports.
Then he produced a single lotus arising from his navel,
which was thousand-colored, stainless, radiant as the sun, and golden.
Rising up with a brilliance blazing like the cresting flames of a sacrificial fire, possessing the splendor of the stainless autumn sun,
the lotus of the Great-Souled One shines with noble luster, its beautiful hair serving as lovely moss.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Lotus," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||39||
Chapter Forty.
Pulastya said: Then he created Brahmā, the creator of all the worlds, who possesses great splendor, faces in every direction, and is the foremost among those endowed with yoga.
Upon that golden lotus, extending for many yojanas,
consisting of all qualities of splendor and endowed with the characteristics of the earthly realm.
The great seers declare that this lotus, which existed in the beginning as the supreme form of the earth, was produced from Nārāyaṇa. (3)

Himavat, Nīla, Meru, and Niṣadha; Kailāsa, Śṛṅgavat, and likewise Mount Gandhamādana. ||5||
Puṇya, Triśikhara, Kānta, Mandara, Udāra, Piñjara, Vidhyamasta, and the mountain [named] Caparvata. ||6||
These alone are the abodes of the Gaṇas, the Siddhas, and the great-souled ones of virtuous conduct; they bestow the fruits of all desires.
Among these, this island is known as Jambūdvīpa; such is the configuration of Jambūdvīpa, where the sacrificial rites of the wheel-turning monarchs are performed.
The water that flows from them is like the taste of divine nectar;

Those which are here the filaments of this lotus, spread out equally, are the innumerable and various mountains upon the earth. (10)
O King, those many ancient petals of the lotus are proclaimed to be the impassable mountain ranges, the mounds of earth, and the lands of the Mlecchas. (11)

Therefore, this manifestation is known by the name Puṣkarasaṃjñita;
for this reason, it has been [described] in sacrifice by the ancient supreme sages.
Just as the construction of the sacrificial posts was performed through sacrifices seen in the Vedas by those entitled to sacrifice,
so too was the earth constructed by that Blessed One who pervades the universe.
The arrangement of mountains and rivers was fashioned by him who possesses incomparable power over the universe, who is like the sun in splendor, and whose radiance is like that of Varuṇa. (17)
Slowly, the Self-Existent One, who consists of the universe, emitted from the great ocean the lotus-treasure while it was in a state of deep sleep;
meanwhile, a great demon named Madhu arose as an obstacle to his ascetic penance.
Simultaneously with that [creation], the demon named Kaiṭabha arose;
born from those qualities of rajas and tamas, they were both followers of tamas.
Those two of great strength agitated the entire world, which had become a single ocean;
they wore divine red garments and possessed white, blazing, and fierce tusks.
Exalted by their crowns and diadems, radiant with armlets and bracelets,
with large, wide-open coppery eyes, broad chests, and mighty arms.
Like two moving mountains striking against a great mountain,
resembling fresh clouds and possessing faces like the sun.
With their arms adorned with massive coils and armlets, they were exceedingly terrifying;
with the placement of their footsteps, they seemed to churn the ocean.
They beheld Madhusūdana lying there like a swan upon the water,
while those two, Viśvatomukha, were moving about in the lotus-pool.
Then they both beheld that most excellent of yogis, radiant and blazing, who, commanded by Nārāyaṇa, was creating all living beings. (25)
Then those two best of asuras spoke there to Brahmā regarding all the deities and the mental sons who were sages.
The two wicked ones, eager for combat and enraged, their eyes agitated by fury, asked:
"Who are you, standing in the midst of the lotus, wearing a white turban and possessing four arms? (27)
"O Lotus-born One, disregarding us both out of delusion, you have crossed the bridge free from desire; come, come, grant us battle! (28)
"Even we two, the supreme lords, would be unable to remain in that ocean;
who else could there be for you who has been appointed to this task? (29)
"Who is the creator and who is the protector? By what name is he designated?
Brahmā said:
"In the world, he is called Īśvara, as well as Viṣṇu, the bearer of infinite power. (30)
"Know me, born from his presence, to be the Creator.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O great sage, there is nothing superior to us in this world."
By us both, the entire universe is indeed covered with darkness and passion;
we two, consisting of passion and darkness, have transgressed beyond the sages. (32)
Concealing the virtuous conduct of all embodied beings, we two, who are difficult for the world to overcome, shall remain joined together in age after age. (33)

We two, as well as wealth, desire, sacrifice, and the possession of all things—wherever there is happiness, wherever there is intoxication, and wherever there is prosperity and fame [shall remain]. (34)
"Whatever anyone desires, we two shall consider that for them.
Brahmā said:
"Having seen you two previously defeated, we were struck with fear. (35)
Having concentrated upon that virtuous Being, I have taken refuge in Him who is the Supreme,
whose self is united in yoga, who is the Imperishable, and who is indeed the very essence of *sattva*;
He who is the creator of both *rajas* and *tamas*, and the source of the universe.
From that, the elements were born, both those characterized by sattva and the others.
That very Vāsudeva will bring about your destruction;
even while sleeping, that god [will do so] within a space extending many yojanas.
Nārāyaṇa created two arms for him through his own creative power (māyā);
being drawn along by those two arms, he appeared possessed of great strength.
Those two, fat as birds and dripping with ichor,
then went and spoke to the eternal Vāsudeva.
Having prostrated themselves before Padmanābha Hṛṣīkeśa, both of them bowed low and said:
"We know you to be the source of the universe, you alone, the Supreme Person. (41)
Knowing you to be the cause of both of us and the source of intelligence,
we recognize you as the eternal one, whose vision is unfailing and who is the truth.
Therefore, we desire to behold you closely, O God;
your vision is never in vain. Homage to you! Be victorious in battle! 43.
The Blessed Lord said:
For what purpose do you two, the best of asuras, address me? Your lives have departed; how is it that you both desire to live again?
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"O Lord, we desire our death at the hands of one in whom no one has ever died before;
and we also desire to become your sons, O you of great asceticism. (45)
The Blessed Lord said:
"This shall indeed come to pass for both of you when the Kali age arises;
you two shall possess bodies that are not mortal. I speak this truth to you."

Then, having granted a boon to the two great Asuras, the eternal Viśvadhara, the supreme among gods and lord of the immortals, crushed those two who were like the people of the world—being free from passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas)—beneath his thighs. 47.
Standing upon the lotus of Ātasi, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, raised his arms and, possessing great splendor, undertook a formidable penance. 48.
Blazing as if with splendors, dispelling darkness with his own radiance,
that righteous-souled one spoke like the thousand-rayed sun with its beams.
Then the Lord Narayana, the imperishable one of great splendor and great fame, having assumed another form, arrived as the teacher of yoga. (50)
And the wise teacher of Sāṅkhya, Kapila, the best of Brahmins—both of those great souls were honored there, being devoted to that [task]. (51)
Having arrived there, those two, who were experts in the distinctions between the higher and the lower and were honored by the great seers, spoke to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
O Viśālākṣa, you two are established in that Brahman which is to be fully realized;
you are the leaders of all beings, Brahmā, who is worshipped throughout the three worlds. (53)
Having heard those words of theirs, who had reached the state of supreme awakening,
he created these three worlds, just as this Vedic revelation of Brahmā declares.
He produced from himself a single son upon the earth;
then, at the very beginning, the one born of Brahmā’s mind arrived there.
As soon as he was born, the mind-born son spoke to Brahmā:
"What assistance may we provide for you? Let the Blessed One speak."
Brahmā said:
"O you of great intellect, since this one named Kapila is indeed Brahmā and likewise Nārāyaṇa, do as you both say. (57)
Thus addressed by Brahmā, they arose and spoke to the king:
"With palms joined in reverence, we are eager to serve you; what shall we do? (58)
The Blessed Lord said: That which is the truth, the imperishable Brahman, is eighteenfold;
remember that truth, the immortal, which is the supreme state. (59)
Having heard these words, he went toward the northern direction;
having gone there, he beheld Brahmā with the eye of knowledge.
Then the Lord Brahmā, the great-minded one, having formed it with his mind, created that which is called Bhuvar, the second [world]. ||61||
Then he also spoke these words: "O Grandfather, what shall I do? Having been commanded by the Grandfather, he approached Brahmā.
The Brahmin experienced the taste of the nectar; by that very act, he attained the supreme state and came into the presence of those two.
When he too had departed, the Lord created a third [son], skilled in the practice of liberation; the Lord was endowed with excellent splendor.
Relying upon the Dharma that had been taught, they attained the very state of those two;
thus all three sons of the high-souled Śambhu have gone to bliss.
Taking those sons of his, who possessed powerful movements,
the Lord Nārāyaṇa and Kapila, the lord of ascetics, went there.
Furthermore, at that time, he attained the state of Brahmā; and indeed, at that very time, he again resorted to most terrible asceticism for the sake of the supreme goal.
Then Brahmā, being alone and lacking power, performed austerities;
thereafter, he produced from half of his own body that auspicious wife.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) created sons equal to himself;
from them the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) emerged, from whom the worlds issued forth.
First, the Great-Souled One created Viśveśa, his son born of austerity;
he then created Dharma by name, who is everywhere auspicious and all-pervading.
Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhṛgu, and the sage Aṅgiras. ||71||
Those great sages are to be known as most wonderful by virtue of their own deeds;
thus, the lineages of the great sages consist of thirteen qualities.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyuḥ, Siṃhikā, Khasā, Prācī, Krodhā, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū. (73)
This is the offspring of Dakṣa; from Kanyā alone were born twelve kings, and twenty-seven powerful constellations for the Moon. (74)
Kaśyapa was indeed the son of Marīci, born through his ascetic penance;
and Dakṣa gave him twelve daughters, whom he bestowed upon him.
And likewise, O descendant of Kuru, the Ṛṣi gave all the auspicious lunar mansions, beginning with Rohiṇī, to Soma.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Saṃdhyā, Viśveśā, and Mahāyaśā—the goddess Sarasvatī and these others were created by Brahmā in ancient times. 77.
O King, these five most excellent and best of goddesses have been given to you, the righteous one and foremost of the gods;
may prosperity be yours, for they were bestowed by Brahmā, whose actions are beyond perception.
Surabhi, the wife of Brahmā who possessed a beautiful form and could assume any shape at will,
suddenly appeared before Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, who is honored by the worlds and who knows the cause for the creation of the world, approached her for sexual union for the sake of cattle, O best of beings.
And he begot eleven sons who were vast, well-versed in dharma,
resembling clouds of blood-red hue, great, and of fierce splendor.
Because they wept (rudana) and because they fled (dravana), and because they went to their grandfather (tat-pitāmaha), they are remembered as the Rudras. ||82||
Nirhṛti, Saṃdhya, and the third who is not born from a womb (ayonija), as well as Mṛgavyādha, Kapardin, and he who is Mahāviśveśvara. ||83||
The venerable Ahirbudhnya, Kapālī, Piṅgala, and Senānī of great splendor—these are remembered as the eleven Rudras. ||84||
From that very Surabhi were born the cows and the Suras;
likewise, O best of kings, were born Aja and Haṃsa. (85)
From Dharma were born the most excellent and fragrant medicinal herbs; likewise, Lakṣmī, Kāma, and the Sādhyas were born from Sādhyā.
Bhava, Prabhava, Kṛśāśva, Suvaha, Aruṇa, Varuṇa, Viśvāmitra, Caladhruva, and [Dhruva]. (87)
He [gave] Haviṣmān, Tanūja, and Vidhāna, as well as Abhimata, Vatsara, Bhūti, and Sarvāsuraniṣūdana. ||88||
The goddess, followed by Vāsava, gave birth to the great-bodied Suparvan, who was honored by the world of the Sādhyas and the gods. 89.
The first god is Dhara, the second is Dhruva the imperishable, the third is Viśvāvasu, and the fourth is Soma the Lord. ||90||
Then immediately after that, the seventh is the "Just as it is" (tathatā), and likewise the eighth is the "Extraction" (nirhṛti). ||91||
This offspring of Dharma was indeed born from Surabhi;
and the Viśvedevas are recorded in tradition as having been born from Dharma through Viśvā.
And Dakṣa, the mighty-armed, Puṣkara, Tamas, Cākṣuṣa, Atri, as well as Bhadra and Mahoraga. (93)
Viśvāntaka, Vasubāli, and the highly illustrious Nikumbha; Ruru, who possesses the power of great siddhis, and Bhāskara, whose splendor is like that of the sun. ||94||
Devamātā gave birth to all the Viśvedevas as her sons;
Marutvatī gave birth to the Maruts, the gods, as her sons.
And Agni, Kṣuravin, Jyotis, Sāvitrī, Mitra, Amara, Śaravṛṣṭi, Sukarṣa, and Mahattara. (96)
Virāja and Rāja, Viśvāyu and Sumati, as well as Aśvaga, Citraratha, and King Macatathācaniṣadha. ||97||
Furthermore, he likewise [taught] the rule for the self, conduct, that which consists of a quarter, the extensive, the form of the Vṛhat, and similarly that which resides in the navel. 98.
Aditi gave birth to Marutvatī, who bore Jyeṣṭha, the leader of the Maruts; Aditi also gave birth to Kaśyapa, from whom she indeed bore the twelve Ādityas.
Indra, Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Aryaman, Ravi, Pūṣan, Mitra, Dhātṛ, and Parjanya are indeed the givers of boons. ||100||
Thus these twelve Ādityas are the most excellent among the inhabitants of the third heaven;
and two noble sons were born to Āditya by Sarasvatī.
Danu gave birth to the Dānavas, and Diti gave birth to the Daityas— both of whom were preeminent in asceticism, preeminent in virtue, and highly esteemed in the third heaven.
The Kālās, Atukās, Kālakeyas, as well as the Asuras and Rākṣasas, and the sons of Anāyuṣā, who were diseases of great strength. ||103||
The sage [Vasiṣṭha] was the mother of Siṃhikā and the mother of the Gandharvas;
Prācī was the mother of the Apsarases, while Bhāratī was the mother of the Puṇyas. 104.
O King, lord of the people, all beings became filled with wrath, as did the Piśācas, the hosts of Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas. 105.
Four-footed creatures, these very cows of the herd, the Ancient Puruṣa, and Māyā—[all these are] Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari. (106)
He was spoken of by him in due order and praised by the great seers;
and whatever man should always hear this foremost Purāṇa, or should recite it on the festival days.
For having attained this world, he is indeed free from passion, and in the next world he enjoys the fruits of heaven;
[he does so] in four ways: through sight, mind, speech, and action. (108)
He who pleases Kṛṣṇa is pleased by Kṛṣṇa;
the king obtains his kingdom, and the poor man obtains the highest wealth. 109.
One whose lifespan is exhausted obtains longevity; one desiring a son obtains progeny;
likewise, those seeking the fruits of sacrifice obtain their desires, as do those performing various austerities.
Whatever desire one may long for, that very thing one shall obtain from the Lord of the World;
having abandoned everything else, one should recite this *Pauṣkara* hymn of Hari. (111)
O best of men, for one who bows before this manifestation, no inauspiciousness shall occur;
this is the manifestation of the Great Soul known as Pauṣkaraka.
The great king has been celebrated through the illustration of the Vedas by Vyāsa; hear from me that Viṣṇu possesses the nature of Viṣṇu and the nature of Hari in the Kṛta Yuga.
The state of being Vaikuṇṭha among the gods and the state of being Kṛṣṇa among humans—
this is the difficult-to-comprehend course of the deeds of the benevolent Lord.
Now, O King, hear truly concerning the past and the future:
this Lord, the Sovereign, who is unmanifest yet abides within manifest signs. (115)
For Nārāyaṇa is the self of all beings, the source of their origin and dissolution;
having become this Nārāyaṇa, he was the eternal Hari.
O descendant of Kuru, Brahmā, Vāyu, Soma, Dharma, Śakra, and Bṛhaspati—though unborn, they too attained the state of being sons of Aditi. ||117||
This powerful one, known as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra,
was born for the sake of a son for Aditi through the grace of that all-pervading Lord.
Then, for the purpose of slaying the enemies of the gods— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—
he created the deities, Brahmā, and the Prajāpatis in that Kalpa.
There he mentally created unsurpassed lineages of Brahmās;
from those great-souled ones emerged the supreme, eternal Brahman.
Thus has been recounted the deed of Viṣṇu, who is the source of all activity;
listen now as I proclaim that which is worthy of praise among the worlds. 121.
When the Vṛtra-slaying had occurred and Bhīṣma was present during the Kṛta Yuga,
there arose a battle renowned throughout the three worlds known as Tārakāmaya.
There, all those terrible Dānavas, invincible in battle,
were slaying all the gods and Asuras, along with the Yakṣas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
Being thus tormented and turned away from their purpose in battle with their weapons covered,
they mentally sought refuge in the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa, as their protector.
In the meantime, clouds with the luster of glowing embers covered the expanse of the sky, along with the sun, moon, and the host of planets.
Accompanied by masses of fierce lightning and producing terrible roars,
the seven winds blew, striking one another with great force.
The sky was as if being consumed by portents of fire and thunderbolts, accompanied by the crashing of blazing waters and most terrible sounds.
Thousands of meteors fell, and even celestial beings descended;
divine chariots were falling down and flying upward.
Whatever fear may arise for the worlds at the time of the end of the four ages, or whatever formless and formed portents appear during that period of calamity— [all these are overcome by this].
Therefore, everything was poorly illuminated and nothing at all could be discerned; and the ten directions shone forth as if enveloped by a mass of darkness. (130)
Kālī, in her embodied form, entered, enveloped by dark clouds;
the sky did not shine, overwhelmed and shrouded in terrible darkness. 131.
Having severed that mass of waves along with the crocodiles by means of his two arms,
the Lord Hari revealed his own divine body, the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Resembling a rain-cloud, with hair like a cloud,
he was dark in both splendor and form, like a black mountain.
Wearing radiant yellow garments and adorned with ornaments of molten gold, his body was like smoke-filled darkness, rising up like the fire at the end of an eon. ||134||
With thighs that were round, twice as thick [as the calves], and with hair covered by a diadem,
he shone, adorned with weapons resembling refined gold.
It was as lofty as a mountain peak illuminated by the rays of the sun and moon,
its chest radiant with the Kaustubha gem that dispels darkness.

Exalted by the variegated fruits of his power, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, he is the mountain of Viṣṇu, whose nature is forbearance, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, and holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand. ||137||
Bestowing noble fruits upon the thirty gods, it is the beloved of the beautiful celestial women;
it is the delight of the minds of all the worlds and the captivator of the hearts of all living beings. 138.

When it has branches vast with illusion, a radiance equal to a flood, and is rich with the growth of the great elements—consisting of knowledge, ego, and pride—[it is the tree of worldly existence]. (139)
It was strewn with special leaves, blossomed with the planets and constellations, a great mountain for the world of the Daityas, yet visible to the world of mortals. 140.
It had a resonance like the ocean, its foundation reached down to the subterranean realm (rasātala),
it was spread out with the nooses of the lords of serpents, and it was provided with the feathers of birds.
Rich with the inexhaustible fragrance of moral virtues, it is a great tree for all the world;
it has the unmanifest as its root-water and the manifest ego as its froth. (142)
It was filled with the surging flood of the great elements, with planets, constellations,
and bubbles, and it was crowded with the pomp of celestial chariots and mounts.
That which is teeming with shoals of fish, joined by families of rocks and shells, whirled within the domain of the three qualities (guṇas), and having all the worlds as its timingila fish; ||144||
It has heroes as its trees, creepers, and shrubs; moss released by serpents;
twelve suns as its great islands; and eleven Rudras as its cities. 145.
I meditated upon the great ocean of the three worlds, filled with the waters of the waves of the mind, adorned with the mountains of the eight treasures.
It was a multitude of Daityas and Yakṣas, teeming with crocodiles that were hosts of Rākṣasas;
it possessed the great prowess of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and was crowded with the jewels among celestial women. ||147||
It was filled with the rivers of the splendors of glorious fame and fortune,
and possessed the force of the arising of the great dissolution through the heavy rains of the conjunction of time.
The great shore of the ocean of association with the virtuous, the great ocean that is Nārāyaṇa, the god beyond gods, the bestower of boons, who is affectionate toward his devotees. 149.
To the god who bestows grace, who brings about tranquility, and who is auspicious;
he who is mounted upon a chariot drawn by bay horses and adorned with the banner of Suparṇa. 150.
On the vast axle-wood of Mount Meru, which is difficult to behold because it is joined with countless rays and surrounded by the noble eyes formed by the wheels of the moon and sun; (151)
[Salutation] to the Goddess who is beautiful with the stars as her variegated flowers and the planets and constellations as her ornaments;
who grants fearlessness in times of danger; and who is unconquered by gods and demons in the sky.
They beheld the God seated upon a divine, celestial chariot, yoked with horses as swift as tigers and adorned with the splendor of pearls. 153.
