All the gods, led by Indra, having performed their rites, approached that protector for refuge, placing cries of victory at their head. (154)
And having heard these words of theirs, Viṣṇu, the deity of the gods, set his mind upon the destruction of the Dānavas in the great battle. (155)
Standing in the sky, Viṣṇu, assuming his supreme form,
spoke these words with a solemn promise to all the deities.
Go in peace; may it be well with you; do not fear, O dwellers of the celestial courtyard! All the demons have been conquered; let the three worlds be taken possession of.
Then, gratified by the words of Viṣṇu, who is devoid of falsehood and delusion,
the gods attained supreme joy, as if having tasted the most excellent nectar.
Then, having withdrawn the darkness, the clouds vanished;
auspicious winds blew, and the ten directions became clear. (159)
The planets moved clockwise around the moon, which was as pure as a merchant's commodity;
the planets did not seize it, and even the lions became placid. (160)
The three realms, beginning with heaven, became free from passion and illuminated by the path;
the rivers flowed according to their true nature, and the ocean was not agitated. (161)
The senses of men were pure within their inner selves;
the great seers, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud. (162)

And at the sacrifices, the purifier (Agni) rendered the cooking of the oblations auspicious; the people were delighted in their minds by the light of the world, which was characterized by the practice of active righteousness.
Then, having heard from the mouth of Viṣṇu— who is true to his promise— the words concerning the destruction of their enemies,
the Daityas and Dānavas were struck with fear.
They made great efforts for the sake of battle and for victory;
meanwhile, Maya constructed a golden bridge, three *nalvas* wide and imperishable.
And he [mounted] a four-legged steed, vast and well-equipped with great weapons, resounding with the tinkling of a network of small bells, and adorned with leopard skins. (166)
It was beautiful, adorned with networks of rays and lattices of gold,
filled with herds of artificial deer, and resplendent with flocks of birds.
Resplendent with divine missiles and weapons, resounding with the thundering of clouds,
it was a noble and excellent chariot with beautiful wheels, well-constructed, and resembling the sky.
It was filled with maces and iron clubs like a personified ocean,
adorned with golden armlets and bracelets, and possessed a pole as large as the orb of the moon.
Adorned with banners and flags, it was like the sun rising from Mount Mandara;
its body possessed the majestic bulk of a lordly elephant, and in some places it shone with the brilliance of a lion's mane.
He [ascended] a divine chariot that moved through the sky, blazing and destroying the chariots of enemies, which was yoked to a thousand stars and resounded with the roar of clouds. 171.
Desirous of battle, Tāra occupied Meru, which was like the blazing sun;
it was one krośa in width and likewise in length.
Resembling a mountain in its pole-axle, dark as a mass of people,
with its pole-axle bound together by a collection of black iron and jewels.
Like a thundering cloud emitting rays of darkness,
he was obscured by a great iron net through a window.
It was filled with iron bars, projectiles, and mallets;
with spears, snares spread wide, and unyielding thorns.
Adorned with terrifying javelins and battle-axes,
it was raised for the sake of his enemies like a second Mount Mandara.
Yoked with a thousand horses, he ascended that excellent chariot;
meanwhile, Virocana, enraged, stood ready with a mace in his hand.
At the head of that army was the Dānava Hayagrīva, who, with his flaming crest, resembled a mountain, and was yoked to a thousand horses.
The valiant Śveta, son of Vipracitti, adorned with white earrings, strode about the arrayed host of the Dānavas. (179)
The crusher of enemy forces drove his chariot forward,
stretching his great bow which possessed a thousand extended yokes.
At the front of the battle, Khara stood like a mountain with sprouting growth,
scattering [missiles] from his anger and shedding tears born of rage from his eyes.
With his teeth, lips, and eyes quivering, that Dānava, having mounted a chariot drawn by eighteen horses, eagerly desired battle. 182.
Facing the battle, which resembled a divine array,
stood Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, most excellent and wielding irresistible weapons.
Facing the battle, he stood firm like a mountain peak, while the young colt, impelled by his own young companions, was filled with great joy.
Lamba, who resembled a fresh cloud and was adorned with flowing garments, stood in the midst of the Daityas like the sun in the midst of the planets. ||185||
Having entered the array of the Daityas, he shone like the moon amidst a thick mist;
thereafter, he whose teeth, lips, eyes, and weapons were like the earth and its treasures [appeared]. (186)
The great and cruel planet stood laughing in the midst of the Daityas;
some there were mounted on horses, while others were mounted on lordly elephants in rut.
Some were mounted on lions and tigers, others on boars and bears;
some rode upon donkeys and camels, while others had clouds as their vehicles.
And other Daityas, terrifying with their deformed faces—
some with one foot and some footless— danced, longing for battle.
Many slapped their arms, while others likewise roared;
those preeminent among the Dānavas bellowed with the sound of proud tigers.
With their arms like iron bars, the deities, holding stones and mallets in their hands, threatened him with terrible iron enclosures. (191)
They sported with spears, swords, nooses, javelins, hooks, and sharp-edged spears; with *śataghnīs* and mallets possessing a hundred edges.
With rhinoceros-hide shields, rocks, and iron clubs raised as weapons,
the sky was filled and surrounded on all sides by hosts of clouds.
Thus that army of Dānavas, all of them fierce with pride,
stood facing the gods like a mass of clouds arisen.

He repelled that dense army of a thousand Daityas—which was like wind, fire, mountains, clouds, and water—an army agitated by a flood of strength and risen up, appearing as if intoxicated with the desire for battle. ||195||
O joy of the Kurus, you have heard the extent of the Daitya army;
now hear the extent of the divine army belonging to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Daitya Army," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||40||
Chapter Forty-One.
Pulastya said: The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins of great strength, together with their forces and followers, bound on their armor in due order.
And Puruhūta, the thousand-eyed guardian of the eastern quarter,
the leader of all the gods, mounted his excellent elephant.
To his left side was his chariot, with its excellent banner resembling a bird's wing,
its wheels adorned with the brilliance of the sun, and decorated with a golden parasol.
He was followed by thousands of hosts of gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas,
and was praised by radiant brahman-sages dwelling in heaven.
He was accompanied by hosts of clouds that moved at will like mountains, which had arisen from the expansion of vajras and possessed the radiance of lightning and Indra’s bow.
Mounted upon whom the Blessed One traverses the entire world—the Brahmins stationed at the mouth of the sacrifice sing [his praises] during the offerings of oblations. (6)
When the sounds of divine trumpets resound as he has gone to the battle for heaven,
hosts of Apsarases by the hundreds dance before him along with Indra.
Shining like the sun by means of the elephant-king Ketu,
he was yoked to a thousand horses that were swifter than thought or the wind.
Then that excellent chariot, yoked by Mātali,
shone brilliantly, like Mount Meru entirely surrounded by the splendor of the sun.
Raising his staff and his mallet, which was appropriate for the occasion, Yama stood there,
displaying himself before the hosts of gods and the daityas.
Endowed with the four oceans and with licking serpents, wearing armlets of conch and pearls, he bears a body composed of water.
Brandishing the nooses of Time with horses resembling moonbeams,
he performed thousands of playful maneuvers that took on the appearance of water stirred by the wind.
Clad in pale white garments, with beautiful coral armlets,
his excellent body dark as a sapphire, his chest adorned with a pearl necklace.
Varuṇa, the wielder of the noose, stood in the midst of the host of gods,
longing for the time of battle like the ocean that has overstepped its shore.
He is joined by an army of yakṣas and rākṣasas, as well as by the hosts of guhyakas;
he is the lord and master of the treasures, accompanied by the two treasures Śaṅkha and Padma.
The glorious Lord of the Kings of Kings was seen with a mace in his hand, a warrior in a celestial chariot, seated upon the Puṣpaka like Kubera. ||16||
Accompanied by the king of kings, the lord of yakṣas who has a man as his vehicle shone forth;
the thousand-eyed Indra was in the east, and the king of the ancestors was in the south.
Varuṇa is on the western wing, and the one whose vehicle is man (Indra) is on the northern;
these four world-protectors of great strength each have four wings. ||18||
Then,
as that divine host was moving toward the eastern quarter, the Sun arrived on a chariot yoked with seven horses that travels swiftly through the sky.
Blazing with splendor and shining with rays that reached as far as the boundaries of Mount Meru, he brought about both sunrise and sunset.
Through austerity, he [attained] the imperishable world by means of the wheel that is the gate to the third heaven,
shining with the brilliance endowed with a thousand rays.
In the midst of the gods, the twelve-fold Sun moves; Soma, with his white horses, shines like the moon with its cool rays in the sky.
Gladdening the world with rays filled with cool water, he was like the lord of the twice-born (the moon), accompanied by a conjunction of stars, during the winter season.
His body was marked by the shadow of the hare; he was the destroyer of the darkness of night, the lord of the luminaries, the imperishable master who has no abode in the sky.
The repository of purifying herbs and of nectar,
the supreme portion of the world, gentle and consisting of all essence.
The Dānavas beheld Soma standing there with snow as his weapon—he who is the vital breath of all beings, which is divided fivefold among men. (26)
He supported and created the seven worlds;
him they call the creator of fire, the Lord who is the source of all.
He whose source is proclaimed by hymns consisting of the seven notes;
whom they call the moving being, and whom they call the bodiless. (28)
That which they call moving through space, swift-moving, and born from sound, together with the wind, is the life-force of all beings, exalted by its own brilliance. (29)
Accompanied by the gods, Gandharvas, and hosts of Vidyādharas, the wind-god Māruta, bearing water, agitated the Daityas in a contrary direction.
They sported with their bright rays, which were like snakes that had cast off their skins;
meanwhile, the lords of serpents emitted a fierce poison consisting of intense wrath.
And with their mouths wide open, they moved about like Śarabhas, clinging to one another;
and the mountains [fell] with their rocky peaks and trees with a hundred branches. 32.
The hosts of gods approached to strike the Dānava Bala—
that Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, Trivikrama, who is with the gods.
He is the yoke, the one whose path is black, the lord of the entire world,
the source of all, the destroyer of the demon Madhu, the consumer of the oblation, and he who is established in sacrifice.
The dark-complexioned Lord, whose self consists of earth, water, space,
and the elements, who bestows peace here, and who bears the discus and mace, has ensured that there is no obstacle for the immortals and others.
With her left hand she held aloft the great mace that destroys all weapons;
by her form she was like Kālī, and with her armlets she brought death to her enemies.

With his remaining arms, which were blazing with light, the Lord whose banner bears the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa) and who possesses great strength held a multitude of weapons, such as the Śārṅga bow and others.
He was a twice-born son of Kaśyapa, a devourer of serpents,
resplendent with his mouth set wide open like that of the lord of snakes.
He was joined with the ashes of Amṛtāra, rising high like Mount Mandara;
his prowess had been witnessed many times during the conflicts between the gods and the asuras.
It was marked with the sign of the thunderbolt by Mahendra for the sake of the nectar;
it was clothed in variegated leaves and resembled a mountain rich in minerals.
By means of his arm, which was swollen with intense anger, possessed of a cool brilliance,
and radiant with a jewel that clung to the coils of a serpent.
He was covered by two beautiful-winged sides as if by divine play,
appearing like the two ends of the world-age poles adorned with Indra’s rainbows.
Adorned with blue, red, and yellow banners,
the illustrious Lord mounted the younger brother of Aruṇa for the battle.
The hosts of gods and the composed sages followed him, whose body was golden-hued and who was the best of sky-travelers with beautiful wings.
And with supreme mantras and hymns, they praised Gadādhara,
who was joined by Vaiśravaṇa and preceded by Vaivasvata.
It was surrounded by the king of waters, adorned by the king of gods, its roar bound by the wind, and its sacrificial fires blazing brightly. ||46||
The powerful army of Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, and Sahiṣṇu, enveloped by the brilliance of Bhrājiṣṇu,
advanced for battle with great intensity.
"Blessings be unto the gods," thus spoke Bṛhaspati; "Blessings be unto the Daityas," thus Uśanas uttered his reply. (48)
Then, from those two hosts, a tumultuous battle broke out between the gods and the asuras, both sides desiring victory over one another.
Raising various weapons, the Dānavas and the gods met together in combat, like mountains clashing against mountains.
That battle, joined by gods and asuras, appeared most wonderful;
it was characterized by both righteousness and unrighteousness, as well as by pride and humility.
Then, with swift horses and urged elephants,
and with those leaping into the sky with swords in hand, they advanced together from all sides.
With maces being hurled, with arrows falling,
with bows being drawn, and with most terrible [missiles] being cast down.
That battle became terrible, crowded with gods and dānavas,
generating terror for the world, and resembling the onset of the end of an eon.
In the battle, the Dānavas struck the gods, led by Indra, with iron clubs, mallets, and even mountains hurled from their own hands.
Being tormented by the powerful Dānavas who appeared victorious, they,
with dejected faces, suffered extreme distress before the Lord in battle.
Pierced by their spears and missiles, with heads shattered by iron clubs and chests split open by the sons of Aditi, they bled profusely in the forest.
Slain by nets of arrows and rendered motionless by shafts,
they entered into a demonic illusion (dānavī māyā) and were unable to counteract his maneuvers.
The army of the gods, rendered like something shattered, breathless, and devoid of life by the Asuras, was left with its weapons rendered useless.
Having seen those terrible arrows discharged from the bow of the Daitya,
the thousand-eyed Śakra entered the formidable army of the Daityas with his thunderbolt.
Having slain all the great hosts of Daityas along with their leaders,
he then rendered that vast Daitya army into darkness by means of a net of Tāmasa weapons.
Then, enveloped by a terrible darkness through the splendor of Puruhūta, neither the Daityas nor their mounts could perceive one another.
Then those best of gods, having been liberated from the snares of Māyā with great effort,
struck down the heads of the hosts of Daityas, which had become like darkness.
And the Dānavas, their vision obscured by a darkness of bluish luster,
immediately fell down like mountains whose wings had been clipped.
There, with the lords of the Daityas overcome, the abode of the Dānavas became like the darkness of the end of time,
as if it had become a mass of blinding gloom.
In that manner, Maya, burning away that darkness-born great illusion,
created it as the producer of light, like the world at the end of an eon when it is consumed by the submarine fire.
Afflicted by constant burning, the Daityas, who were products of Indra’s illusory power (māyā), suddenly rose up in battle with bodies possessing the form of the sun.
Encountering the illusory bowstring, the inhabitants of heaven, as if being scorched,
fled toward the region of the moon, to the cool and pleasant waters of a lake.
Being scorched by the Aurva fire and deprived of their senses,
the gods, tormented and seeking refuge, praised the wielder of the thunderbolt.
While the army was being scorched by illusion and struck down by the dānavas, Varuṇa, urged by the king of the gods, spoke these words: ||70||
In former times, the radiant Urvashi, who was equal to Brahmā in his qualities, performed most severe austerities for Śakra, born as she was from a Brahmarṣi.
The hosts of sages, together with the gods and celestial rishis, approached that imperishable world-sustainer who was blazing like the sun with his ascetic power.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Dānava and lord of the Dānavas,
once informed the sage of supreme splendor.
Those brahmin-sages spoke these words, beneficial for dharma:
"O venerable one, among the descendants of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, this family line has been severed at its root. (74)
"You are alone and childless, and no other lineage exists for you; having undertaken a vow of lifelong celibacy, you pursue nothing but hardship. (75)
Many lineages of Brahmins, sages of purified souls, remain as single bodies, solitary and without offspring. (76)
Thus, among all beings, you are the cause of the sons' faith in Me,
O best of ascetics, possessing a splendor equal to Prajāpati.
Therefore, proceed; increase your lineage and augment yourself by means of yourself.
Concentrate your exalted splendor and produce a second body. (78)
Thus addressed by the sages, the sage, struck in his mind, censured that assembly of ṛṣis and spoke these words: (79)
Just as the eternal dharma ordained for sages in ancient times was purely that of the seers—consisting of ritual acts and subsisting on wild roots and fruits. (80)
For a Brāhmaṇa born from the womb of Brahman who abides in the Self,
well-practiced celibacy may even cause Brahmā to tremble.
There are three modes of livelihood for people living in the householder stage of life,
while our mode of livelihood is that of forest-dwellers residing in the forest hermitage.
There were those who subsisted on water, those who subsisted on air, those who used their teeth as a mortar,
those who used a wooden pestle, those who ground with stones, and others who practiced the austerity of the five fires.
Standing firm in this austerity, and with vows that are exceedingly difficult to perform,
they place celibacy (brahmacarya) at the forefront and seek the supreme goal.
The status of a Brahmin for a Brahmin is ordained through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya);
thus say those who know brahmacarya regarding the world beyond.
Dharma is established in celibacy; austerity is established in celibacy.
Those who are established in celibacy are established in the state of Brahman and the like. ||86||
Without yoga there is no accomplishment; without yoga there is no fame. In this world, fame has its root in [yoga]; there is no austerity higher than celibacy (brahmacarya). ||87||
Restraining the group of senses within the womb and the group of five elements, he practices celibacy; what austerity could be greater than this? (88)
Wearing matted hair without yoga, performing vows without intention, and practicing non-celibacy—these three are known as the "ash-eater's" [vices]. (89)
In one place there are wives, in another union, and in another the reversal of states;
indeed, this offspring was created by Brahmā from his own mind.
If you possess the ascetic power of those who have conquered their selves,
then create mental sons through the rite of Prajāpati.
The mental [meditations] have been established as the source to be cultivated by those practicing austerities;
for ascetics, neither the seed of noble yoga nor the vow has been prescribed. (92)
This which you, who are fearless here, have uttered—though it is called the "extinct Dharma"—is considered by the wise to be exceedingly like that which is non-existent. ||93||
Having made my own self into a body of light consisting of mind, I shall,
without the aid of a woman, emit a son born from my own body.
In this way, the Self will produce a second self by means of the rite pertaining to Prajāpati, as if desiring to consume all creatures with that very fire.
Varuṇa said:
"Urvaśī, being impelled by her ascetic penance, entered her own wide vulva into the fire;
then, with a single blade of darbha grass, she produced the means for the birth of my son."
Suddenly piercing his thigh, that fire rose up;
desiring to consume the world, it became his son Agni.
Having pierced through the thighs of Urvaśī, the fire named Aurva,
as if desiring to incinerate the three worlds, became exceedingly wrathful.
As he was being born, he spoke to his father with a piteous voice: "O Father, hunger oppresses me; eat me immediately so that I may devour the world. (99)
With flames ascending to the third heaven and expanding through the ten directions, he grew like the fire at the end of an aeon, consuming all living beings. 100.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived before the sage Mura and said:
"Restrain your son; show compassion for the world."
"O best among speakers, my son, listen to these truthful words: 'I shall provide you with supreme assistance; you will see the fruit of this. (102)
Aurva said: "O Blessed One, O Supreme Soul, I am blessed and I am graced, since you grant this wisdom to me, a mere child, for my very welfare."
When the time of dawn has arrived and the desired meeting is at hand, O Blessed One, by what sacrificial offerings will your son be satisfied so that he may attain happiness? (104)
Where will his dwelling be, and what will be the nature of his food? What will the Blessed One provide here that is equal to the prowess of one of such great majesty?
Brahmā said: "O Brahmin, his residence shall indeed be in the ocean within the Mare’s Mouth;
water is my source, and let this [fire] go to that which is immeasurable."
There, this Āstīka, drinking the water which is indeed an oblation,
shall release that expanse of water and its abode for the sake of the Brahmins.
Therefore, O son, you and I shall wander together here through the ages of these beings, acting as the authors of the Purāṇas.
This fire, created by me at that time as one subsisting on water, was the burner of all beings, including gods, asuras, and rakshasas. 109.
Saying "So be it," that Agni, his circle of flames withdrawn,
bowed to his lordly father Urva and entered the mouth of the ocean.
Then Brahmā and all those great sages,
having understood the power of Aurva’s fire, returned to their respective abodes.
Then, having witnessed that great marvel, Hiraṇyakaśipu,
with all his limbs bowed low, spoke these words.
O Blessed One, this wonderful event has occurred before the eyes of the world:
the Grandfather (Brahmā) has been thoroughly pleased by the asceticism of that best of sages.
But I, O observer of the great vow, must be understood as the servant of both you and your son; you are praiseworthy here for your deed. (114)
Therefore, look upon me as one who has attained meditative absorption and is solely intent on your propitiation;
O best of sages, if I should fail, that defeat would be yours alone. (115)
Urva said:
"I am blessed and I am graced, since you consider me your guru here;
by this austerity of yours, O observer of excellent vows, there shall be no fear for you in this world."
"Accept this illusory form created by my son, named Nirindhri, which is composed of fire and is difficult to touch even for flames. (117)
She will bring her own lineage under her control by subduing those who act against them; she will protect her own side and utterly consume the enemy faction. 118.
Varuṇa said:
This is an unbearable illusion, difficult even for the gods to overcome,
which was created in the past by Aurva, the son of Urva, the fire-god.
"O Daityas, because they were distressed by him, she is undoubtedly devoid of power;
for a curse was previously given to her by him with his own splendor when she was created."
"If this is not to be obstructed, let the Blessed One be made happy;
let the moon, the source of the waters, be given to me as a friend. (121)
Therefore, having come together with him and surrounded by aquatic creatures, I shall destroy this illusion through your grace; of this there is no doubt.
Saying "So be it," Śakra, the enhancer of the thirty gods, was filled with joy and commanded Soma, whose weapons are cool, to go before him for battle.
"Go, O Moon-companion, to the one who bears the noose, for the destruction of the asuras and for the victory of the inhabitants of heaven. (124)
You are considered the counter-force and the sovereign even of the luminaries;
those who know the Vedas recognize that in all worlds, the essences consist of you.
In this world, there exists no one equal to you, O wielder of the cool weapon (Śiva);
for even in the ocean and in the supreme ether, increase and decay are unmanifest.
You cause time to revolve day and night, deluding the world;
your mark, consisting of the shadow of the world, is the form of the moon. 127.
Those whose origin is in the stars do not know this illusion of yours;
you are situated above the path of the sun and above all luminous bodies.
Having suddenly dispelled the darkness, you illuminate the entire world;
you are the cool-rayed moon, the one with a body of frost, the lord of luminaries. 129.

Furthermore, he is the soul of the conjunction of time, the one to be worshipped, the imperishable chariot of sacrifice, the lord of herbs, the source of ritual action, the source of the waters, and the cool-rayed moon. (130)
You are the cool one, the source of the nectar of heroes, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the one with white steeds;
you are the protector of the body, the protector of the world, and for those who drink the Soma juice, you are Soma himself. 131.
You are gentle toward all beings; you are the destroyer of darkness, O King of the Bears.
Therefore, go forth with the great army and Varuṇa as your protector.
"Subdue the illusory power of the Asuras by which we were scorched in battle.
Soma said: "O bestower of boons, King of the Gods, as for what you say to me regarding war—"
This is the rain, this is the cold, and this is the removal of the Daitya's illusion;
behold these [Daityas] consumed by my frost and enveloped in ice. (134)
Likewise, showers of snakes accompanied by nooses, released by the sea-monsters,
enveloped those Daityas just as the wind surrounds masses of clouds.
The two immensely powerful ones, Śuci and Varuṇa, struck the Dānavas with falls of snow and throws of nooses, making them cold as if bound by a snare of frost. ||136||
The two lords of the Aṅgas, both warriors armed with nooses,
clashed in battle like two great oceans agitated by the winds of destruction.
That great army of Dānavas was completely filled by those two,
just as the world is enveloped by the downpours of clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
Then both the lords of the waters, Śaśāṅka and Varuṇa, having raised their water-jars, quelled that tumultuous illusion created by the lord of the Daityas. ||139||
Scorched by the network of Śītā’s rays and ensnared by her nooses in the forest,
the Daityas were unable to move, like mountains deprived of their peaks.
All those Daityas were struck down by Śītā;
their entire bodies were drenched in frost, like fires extinguished by heat. 141.
Indeed, auspicious and variegated celestial chariots belonging to those gods and Daityas were falling down, and they were also falling and rising up.
I, the illusory Dānava Mayā, saw those Dānavas bound by nooses held in hands and covered by cool rays, as they were falling from heaven.
It was filled with networks of mountains, laughing with the broad blades of swords spread out,
marked by the peaks of heaps of fallen trees, and its forests were slightly scattered about.
It was crowded with herds of lions and tigers, with the leaders of the gods' hosts roaring,
filled with throngs of wild beasts, and its trees shaken by the wind.
Then, he created a mountain-like illusion, fashioned by his own son Kūja, which moved at will through the sky and was renowned as Pārvatī. ||146||
With the sounds of swords, showers of falling rocks, and descending trees,
he struck down the hosts of gods while simultaneously reviving those Dānavas.
Then that illusion, like the moonlight or the wine of Varuṇa, vanished;
the earth became terrible to behold, as if filled with mountains. ||148||
Neither was the god seen by the multitudes of trees obstructing the view, nor was he visible;
for his bow had been shattered and he was distressed by his broken weapons.
The host of gods is rendered effortless, having abandoned the wielder of the mace; for that glorious Lord, when engaged in battle, does not fall [unawares] before us. 150.
Out of forbearance, the Lord of the World, the wielder of the mace, did not become angry;
knowing the proper time and resembling a dark rain-cloud, he observed the moment for battle.
Then Hari, desiring to witness the conflict between the gods and the asuras,
commanded Agni and Māruta to go to the battle by the Blessed One.
Then, urged by the words of Viṣṇu, they drew forth their māyā;
those two, awakened in the great battle, possessed a bewildering speed.
The illusion of Parvati was burnt; her face was reduced to ashes and she perished. That wind, joined with fire, became fire itself, yet it was not composed of fire. ||154||
Having fainted from the heat of those [flames] like the fires at the end of an eon, they both consumed the army of the Daityas;
there, the wind blew with great speed, and subsequently, the fire followed from that wind.
While the armies of the Cērus and Dānavas were playing with fires, the elements were reduced to ashes as they fell and leaped about. (156)
Then, as the celestial chariots of the Dānavas fell simultaneously,
they were scattered by the force of the wind once the fire had performed its task.
While the Wielder of the Mace was being praised as he set out for the slaying of Māyā,
the Daityas became effortless and the three worlds were released from their bonds.
While the gods were exultant, crying out "Excellent!
Excellent!", there was victory for the thousand-eyed Indra and the defeat of the Daityas.
When all directions were pure, when the expansion of the Dharma had proceeded, when the path of the moon was opened, and while the sun remained in its proper station; (160)
While living beings remain engaged in worldly activity, even among men of virtuous conduct,
death— whose fetters are unbreakable— is being offered as an oblation into the sacrificial fire.
While the gods, who adorn the sacrifice, were pointing out the path to heaven, and while all the world-protectors were stationed in their respective directions; ||162||
When those who have perfected their ascetic practices are flourishing and those of evil deeds are absent,
the faction of the gods rejoices while the faction of the Daityas desponds.
While Dharma, consisting of three parts, stands with its single part—unrighteousness—fully grasped; while the great door is thrown open, and the path of the virtuous remains untraversed. (164)
While the worlds were established in the practice of Dharma, while the stages of life (āśramas) were being followed, and while kings reigned devoted to the protection of their subjects; ||165||
While those three worlds were being pacified and the darkness was stilled by the Dānava,
Agni and Māruta engaged in that act of battle.
Pervaded by that [splendor] and possessing stainless light, they performed acts of victory;
having heard of the intense and great fear of the Daityas caused by Māruta and Agni. (167)
The Dānava known as Kālanemi appeared,
wearing a crown with the form of the sun and adorned with armlets and ornaments of refined gold.
Resembling Mount Mandara, he was surrounded by great silver;
fierce with a hundred weapons, he possessed a hundred arms and a hundred faces. ||169||
The glorious one stood with a hundred heads, like a mountain with a hundred peaks;
he grew exceedingly great in his power, like a fire in the heat of summer.
With smoky hair and a tawny beard, possessing fangs and a formidable face,
he bore a massive body that spanned the breadth of the three worlds.
Weighing the sky with his arms, tossing mountains with his feet, and driving away rain-bearing clouds with the breaths from his mouth. 172.
With wide, elongated, red eyes and a dull yet formidable luster,
he seemed as if he wished to consume all the hosts of gods in battle.
Threatening the hosts of gods and shrouding the ten directions,
he was seen like the risen god of death, bristling with fury at the time of universal dissolution.
With a palm that was elevated, with broad finger-joints, adorned with various ornaments, and performing some slight movement; ||175||
With his right hand raised and beautiful in form, he spoke to the Dānavas who had been slain by the gods, saying, "Arise! and "Stay! (or "Be firm!").
Beholding Taṅkaḷanemi, who brought terror to his enemies in battle, all the asuras stood with eyes overwhelmed by fear. (177)
Beholding him—who was swallowing all beings, who possessed a wheel with a razor-sharp rim, and who displayed the three strides like another Nārāyaṇa—they were struck with fear. (178)
Having regained his great height once more, that excellent asura, shaken by the wind,
advanced to fight, terrifying all the gods.
Having encountered the lord of the gods and being embraced by him while wandering in battle,
the Daitya Kālanemi shone like Mount Mandara with Viṣṇu.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra,
were indeed distressed upon seeing that Kālanemi approaching like another Death.
Desiring to gratify the Dānavas, the great Asura Kālanemi,
possessed of immense splendor, grew like a rain-cloud at the end of the hot season.
Seeing him traversing the three worlds, those lords of the Dānavas rose up,
unwearied, as if they had drunk the most excellent nectar.
Having transcended fear and terror, they were led by Amitābha;
in the battle against the host of Māra, they constantly displayed the splendor of victory. (184)
The Dānavas, stationed on the battlefield and longing for combat,
shone as they practiced their mantras and moved about the battle formation.
And as they gazed upon Dānava Kālanemi, joy arose;
for those who were the chief followers of Maya there had been the vanguard of battle.
Having abandoned all fear, they all stood ready to fight with joy:
Maya, Tāra, Varāha, and the Dānava Hayagrīva.
Śveta, the son of Vipracitti, and Kharala—both of these as well as Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, and likewise the one named Kiśora; 188.
Surabhānu, Cāmaraprakhyas, and the great asura Krayodhin—all of these were knowers of the Vedas and all were firmly established in austerity. ||189||
The skillful Dānavas went toward the arrogant Kālanemi;
they [assailed him] with very heavy maces, clubs, and battle-axes.
With clubs resembling mallets, with slings and hammers,
with stones like missiles, and likewise with dreadful mountain peaks.
With spears, slings, and iron clubs of the finest steel,
as well as with heavy, lethal *śataghnī* weapons.
With yokes, with three-pronged goads, with plows struck fiercely, with outstretched arms, and with nooses, iron clubs, and other weapons; ||193||
With serpent-faced [weapons] licking [the air], with gliding arrows, with thunderbolt-like missiles, and with blazing javelins; ||194||
With sharp swords drawn from their scabbards, with bright and stainless spears, and with blazing bows grasped by the Daityas, [the battlefield shone]. ||195||
Then, placing Kālanemi at its head in battle,
the army of the Daityas shone forth, with its excellent weapons set ablaze.
With all her limbs closed like a lotus at the arrival of winter, yet she rejoiced even as a host of deities protected her. 197.
It was endowed with the splendors of the moon and sun, which were free from cold and heat;
it possessed the force of the wind, and its banners were the gentle hosts of stars.
Clad in garments of water, she smiles with the constellations as her ornaments;
she is guarded by Yama, Indra, Kubera, and the wise Varuṇa.
That army, with its blazing fires and winds, was devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
resembling the surging tide of the ocean, it shone brilliantly day and night.
Resplendent with weapons and graced by yakṣas and gandharvas, there then occurred a meeting between those two mothers. (201)
As at the end of a yuga, when the union of heaven and earth occurs,
so did that terrible battle take place, crowded with gods and dānavas.
The gods and asuras fled from these two, who were supreme in both forbearance and prowess, and who possessed both pride and humility through their respective powers.
Seized by those two forces from the front and the rear like clouds by the two oceans,
those gods and dānavas moved about, utterly frantic with joy.
Just as mountains are struck by two flowering forest trees from the mountains,
so too did they beat kettledrums and blow conch shells many times over.
The sound of the bowstring striking his palm, the twang of the bow, and the roar of the arrows completely filled the cosmic egg, the earth, and all the directions. (206)
The roar of the *duṃdubhī* drums drowned out the sound of the Daityas' mantras;
driven by that, they rushed at one another, tormenting each other.
Desiring to fight with one another, they engaged in hand-to-hand combat with their arms;
[the gods hurled] the terrible thunderbolts of the gods, iron clubs, and other supreme weapons.
In the battle, the Dānavas hurled swords and heavy maces;
their limbs shattered by the falling maces and torn to pieces by arrows, [they fell]. (209)
Some fled in great haste, while others struck back;
then they advanced with chariots, horses, celestial palaces, and infantry.
Seizing one another in the battle out of rage, they encountered each other,
closing in for combat with their lips and faces bitten in fury.
Chariots fought with chariots, and foot-soldiers with foot-soldiers;
the tumultuous roar of those chariots, carrying their sounds, resounded.
Like clouds in the sky with their thundering,
some shattered the chariots by means of [other] chariots, while others crushed them with chariots.
Other chariots, having reached a congested space, were unable to move;
they struck one another in the midst of the fray, lifting each other up with their arms.
Roaring together with their forces, those sword-and-shield bearers struck there; pierced by other weapons, they vomited blood, slain in battle.
Having come together like clouds pouring down rain,
they appeared to create a day of battle-storms through their mutual showering of arrows.
In the meantime, the enraged Kālanemi, the son of Danu,
grew like a cloud being filled by the surging waters of the ocean.
Clouds resembling mountains and peaks, wreathed in lightning-streaks and raining down blazing thunderbolts, fell upon him with their massive bodies. (218)
As he hissed in anger, with his eyebrows knitted and sweat pouring down,
rays of light accompanied by sparks of fire issued forth continuously from his mouth.
His arms extended across, upwards, and into the sky,
like five-headed serpents emerging from a mountain.
With various nets of arrows, bows, and even iron clubs,
he covered the divine sky as if with towering mountains.
Clad in garments produced from his own body, he stood longing for battle,
like the immovable Mount Meru itself with its peaks consumed by the fire of his meditation.
With the peaks, crags, and trees shaken by the force of his thighs,
he struck down the hosts of gods as if with a thunderbolt, like great mountains.
With their hair matted and torn by arms still clutching swords,
the gods, struck down in battle by Kālanemi, were unable to move.
Some were struck down by his fists, and some were torn asunder—
yakṣas, gandharvas, birds, along with great serpents and kinnaras.
Terrified by Kālanemi in that battle, they fled;
though they exerted themselves, they were distraught and unable to perform any effort.
By him, the thousand-eyed Śakra was bound with a multitude of arrows; rendered powerless in battle, he was unable even to move.
Resembling the waterless sky and possessing the splendor of a waterless ocean,
Varuṇa was rendered inactive and stripped of his noose by him in battle.
Surrounded in battle by Vaiśravaṇa, who had assumed the form of Death,
the Lord of the World-Protectors lamented and was forced by him to relinquish his office as the Giver of Wealth.
Yama, the destroyer of all, who wields the weapon of death in battle,
abandoned his southern state and, filled with fear, retreated to his own quarter.
Having driven away the world-protectors (lokapālas) and taken their respective functions, he then divided his own body into four parts and placed them in all directions.
Having reached the divine path of the constellations shown by Svarbhānu,
he seized the splendor of the Moon and that which was his great domain.
He caused the blazing sun of the Dharma to move through the gates of the assembly hall, and he withdrew his teaching from the realm of the Day-maker (the Sun). ||233||
Having conquered the god of sleep, he made his own face the refuge;
and having conquered the wind with his own strength, he brought it under his own control.
Having forcibly brought together all the rivers from as far as the ocean, he made them flow toward him through his heroic power, so that even the seas became like his own body.
Having brought both the celestial and terrestrial women under their power,
they covered the earth, which was well-guarded by mountain ranges.
He shone like the self-existent Brahmā, a great lord of the great elements;
he was a Daitya composed of all the worlds, bringing fear to all the worlds. ||237||
Possessing a single body with the world-protectors as its eyes, having the nature of the moon, sun, and planets,
he was born from the fire, a king among Danavas who gave joy to his enemies.
Established in the supreme station, which is like the source of all worlds,
the hosts of Daityas praised him just as the gods praise the Grandfather Brahmā.
I did not turn back from that path due to contrary action;
for dharma is the Veda, and patience and truthfulness, as well as prosperity, have their refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
Because they did not attend upon him, the lord of the Dānavas became enraged;
seeking the station of Viṣṇu, he departed from that place of the gods.
He beheld [Viṣṇu] seated upon Garuḍa, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace; for the destruction of the Dānavas, he brandished that auspicious mace.
He was mounted upon a sky-faring bird belonging to Kaśyapa, which resembled a water-bearing cloud, possessed garments like lightning, and was adorned with golden feathers.
Seeing Viṣṇu standing as if stationed in the sky for the sake of destroying the wicked Daityas, the Dānava, his mind agitated, spoke to the unshakeable one.
This Śarīru was the destroyer of our ancestors, as well as of Madhu and Kaiṭabha who dwelt in the ocean. 245.
"This Śariputra is indeed said to be our peerless one;
by him, through many hundreds of thousands of ages, many Dānavas have been slain. (246)
This man is utterly merciless in this world, devoid of shame before women and children,
by whom the parting of the hair was made upon the wives of the Dānavas.
He is Viṣṇu among the gods, Vaikuṇṭha among the celestial dwellers, Ananta among the serpents, and Svayambhū among the self-existent ones. (248)
This protector of the gods is being drawn away by us;
having encountered his wrath, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain.
Resorting to its shade, the gods stationed at the front of the sacrifice partake of the clarified butter offered in three ways by the great seers.
This is the cause of the destruction of all the enemies of the gods;
for our lineages have entered his discus in battle. (251)
In battles involving enemies, this one, having renounced his life for the sake of the gods, hurls the discus—endowed with radiant splendor—at his foes. (252)
While Kālabhūti remains here as the master of the Daityas known as Sakāloda,
Keśava shall reap the fruit of that transgressed time.
By good fortune, Viṣṇu has now come before my very eyes;
crushed by me in countless ways, he shall perish right here.
"By good fortune, I shall today in this age pay my debt of honor to my ancestors by slaying this Nārāyaṇa, who brings fear to the Dānavas. (255)
"I shall swiftly slay the hosts of enemies in battle;
for even from afar, this one born of noble lineage afflicts the Dānavas in combat. (256)
Having previously been Ananta, he became known as Padmanābha;
in the terrible single ocean, he slew both those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
In former times, having divided his body into two parts— one half a horse and the other half a man— one [of them] slew his father, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Aditi, the source of the gods, bore him who is the essence of auspiciousness;
he, taking three strides, seized the three worlds with his three steps.
Furthermore, now that this battle for Tāraka has arrived,
having encountered me, he shall perish along with all the gods.
Having spoken thus in many ways with harsh words, he quickly urged Nārāyaṇa toward battle in the fray.
Though being hurled by the lord of the asuras, the wielder of the mace did not become angry;
instead, through the power of his great forbearance, he spoke these words with a smile: (262)

The power of pride is slight, O Daitya, while the strength born of freedom from anger is firm; you have been slain by the faults born of pride, yet having abandoned them, you speak with such harshness.
"You are base in my eyes; fie upon this strength of your words! What men are there where women roar? (264)
I see you, O Daitya, following the path of your ancestors;
who could remain secure after abandoning the bridge established by Prajāpati? (265)
Today I shall destroy you, the destroyer of the gods' activities;
and I shall re-establish the deities each in their own respective places.
While she, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, was speaking these words in the midst of battle,
the Dānava laughed out of rage and struck her with his hand and his weapons.
Raising all his hundreds of arms and a multitude of weapons in battle,
his eyes doubly red with rage, he struck them against the chest of Viṣṇu.
And the Dānavas also, led by Maya and Tāra,
with raised weapons and missiles, rushed toward Viṣṇu in the battle.
Though being struck by the exceedingly powerful Daityas with all their weapons raised,
he did not waver in that battle, remaining like a mountain being drenched by rain.
And the great asura Kālanemi, joined with Suparṇa,
raised up a massive iron chain with all his strength and arms.
Seizing Garuḍa, he released a terrible, blazing, and fierce [missile] upon him;
by that deed of the Daitya, Viṣṇu was filled with wonder.
Then that mace was hurled by him at the head of Suparṇa;
seeing Suparṇa pained and his own body wounded, [he withdrew it]. (273)
Then the omnipresent Lord, with eyes red with wrath like those of Viṣṇu, gradually increased his speed and grew equal to Suparṇa.
And his arms grew so as to pervade the ten directions,
filling the intermediate quarters, the sky, and the earth as well.
He grew by his own power, as if desiring to stride across the worlds once more;
he increased in the sky for the sake of conquering the lords of the asuras.
The ṛṣis, together with the gandharvas, praised Madhusūdana,
while he was immediately scratching his head with his radiant crown.
Trampling the earth with his feet and covering the quarters with his arms,
he [wielded] that thousand-spoked wheel, which resembled a thousand rays and brought destruction to his enemies.
Terror-inspiring like a blazing fire, yet beautiful to behold;
its rim encircled with golden dust, it was formidable with a hub of diamond.
Sprinkled with the fat, marrow, and blood produced by the Dānavas,
that unique weapon was a circle of razor-edged blades.
Adorned with garlands and wreaths, he is the fulfiller of desires, assuming forms at will;
created by Svayambhū himself, he strikes fear into all enemies. (281)
He was constantly possessed by wrath and arrogant in battle;
at his mere hurling, all the worlds, including both the stationary and the moving, would fall into confusion. (282)
And the flesh-eating beings attained satisfaction in that great battle;
he, whose deeds were incomparable, was equal to the sun in splendor.
Raising his discus in battle and wielding his mace which blazed with fury,
he caused the splendor of the Dānava to perish by means of his own splendor.
In that battle, he severed the arms of Kālanemi as if with a thief;
and that terrible hundredfold face, along with its fire-like, ash-colored, loud laughter, [he likewise destroyed].
With his discus, Hari forcibly struck down that Daitya;
with his arms severed and his headless, the Dānava fell to the earth.
Stationed in battle like a trunkless tree,
he spread his great wings and attained a speed equal to that of the wind.
Garuda struck Kālanemi with his chest;
his body, facing him, was deprived of arms as he whirled about in agony.
Leaving heaven, he fell down as if shaking the surface of the earth;
when that Daitya had fallen, the gods along with the hosts of sages likewise [rejoiced].
"Excellent! Excellent! they cried, and having assembled, they honored Vaikuṇṭha;
while other Daityas, who had witnessed his prowess in battle, [did likewise]. (290)
Covered by all those arms, they were unable to move in the battle;
some he seized by the hair, and others he squeezed by the neck.
He severed the mouth of one and likewise seized another by the middle;
those [demons], scorched by his mace and discus, were deprived of their strength and their life-breaths.
With all their limbs shattered, they fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth;
when all those Daityas had been slain, Puruṣottama [remained].
Then, having performed what was pleasing to Śakra, the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu), whose deeds are uncreated,
entered into that conflict during the Tārakāmaya war.
Then Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, went to that place together with all the Brahman-sages and hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Worshiping Hari, the God of gods, the Lord spoke these words:
"A great deed has been accomplished by you, O God; the thorn of the asuras has been extracted. (296)
And by the destruction of the Daityas, we too have been thoroughly gratified;
for this great Asura Kālanemi, who was slain by you, O Viṣṇu. (297)
Indeed, without you, there is no one at all who can be his instructor in this world; he treats with contempt the gods, the worlds, and all things mobile and immobile. (298)
Having caused distress even to the sages, he roars back at me;
therefore, I am well-pleased with this deed of yours.
Since this Kālanemi, who was like the eon itself, has been struck down, come now;
may it be well with you, let us go to the supreme heaven.
The Brahman-sages, remaining there and having gathered in that assembly, await you;
and what boon shall I grant you, O best among the bestowers of boons? (301)
While the gods remained in their own abodes, you became their protector;
this triple world has now emerged prosperous, with its thorns destroyed.
In this very battle, for the sake of Viṣṇu and the high-souled Śakra;
having been addressed thus by the Blessed Brahmā, the imperishable Hari [acted].
Viṣṇu spoke with auspicious words to all the gods, headed by Śakra:
"Listen, O all you thirty deities, as many as have assembled here. (304)
There, accompanied by the Suparṇas and placing Purandara at their head,
we all together struck Kālanemi and his followers.
Endowed with the prowess of Danavas and even greater than Śakra himself,
they emerged from the two gates in this great battle.
Virocana the son of Diti and the mighty Svarbhānu occupied their own quarters,
as did Śakra and Varuṇa their respective quarters.
May Yama protect the southern quarter, and the Lord of Wealth the northern;
likewise, may the Moon always go his course together with the constellations. (308)
This sun, the mouth of the seasons, joined with the solstices;
the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgas), honored by the members of the assembly, proceeded.
The fires were gratified by the learned priests through rites prescribed in the Vedas;
the gods were gratified by offerings and oblations, and the great sages by the private recitation of the scriptures.
Through the śrāddha, the ancestors attained satisfaction according to their pleasure; and Vāyu, established on the path of passion, blazed forth in three ways like fire.
And you, satisfying the three castes and the worlds with your own virtues,
set the sacrifices in motion through the twice-born who perform the initiatory rites.
The sacrificial fees were distributed separately by the officiating priests:
Sūrya [received] the cows, Rasa [received] the sunbeams, Soma [received] the waters, and Vāyu [received] the vital breaths within living beings.
These rivers, originating from the Mahendra and Malaya mountains, flow forth in due order according to their own functions, nourishing that Pravarta with their watery essences.
"O mothers of the three worlds, all of you have gone to the ocean as your husband;
let your fear of the Daityas be abandoned, and may you, O goddesses, attain peace. (315)
May there be well-being for you; I shall go to the eternal world of Brahmā, whether in my own home, in the heavenly realm, or in battle—without distinction.
One must always remain vigilant against base serpents and Dānavas, for they strike at vulnerabilities;
thus, their persistence remains constant.
"O gentle ones, may your minds be straightforward toward your own true natures.
Having spoken thus to the hosts of asuras, Viṣṇu, whose prowess is truth, [departed]. (318)
The illustrious and powerful Lord, having generated great joy among the gods, went together with Brahmā to the world of Brahmā. ||319||
This was the course of events in the Tārakāmaya war between the Dānavas and Viṣṇu, about which you have questioned me.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Battle Between the Gods and Asuras Arising from the Lotus," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Forty-second Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
O Brahmin, you have related in detail the account of the lotus-born Brahmā,
as well as the majesty of Bhava and the birth of Guha in brief.
O Brahman, I wish to hear how he was born and what he did;
and how the Dānava Tāraka became so exceedingly powerful.
O Brahman, how was the great Asura destroyed by Kārttikeya? And how, O sages, were you sent by Rudra to Mount Mandara?
How was Umā obtained there by Rudra, the supreme lord?
O great sage, tell me all of this exactly as it happened.
Pulastya said: In former times, Kaśyapa spoke to Aditi, the auspicious firewood for the Daityas:
"O Goddess, a son shall be born to you with limbs as hard as adamant."
A son named Vajrāṅga, who is devoted to the Dharma, shall come to be;
and the goddess Sācalā, having obtained a boon, gave birth to Vajraduśchida.
As soon as he was born, he became one who had reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures;
with devotion, he said to his mother: "Mother, what shall I do for you? (7)
Then Aditi, being delighted, said to that lord of the Daityas:
"O dear son, many of my sons have been slain by the thousand-eyed Indra."
"Go and perform service for them so that they may slay Śakra.
Having said "So be it" to them, he went by force to the celestial realm.
Having bound the thousand-eyed one with a noose of unfailing splendor,
he approached his mother like a hunter approaching a small deer.
In the meantime, Brahmā and Kaśyapa of great asceticism arrived at that place where the fearless mother and son were staying.
Having seen them, Brahmā and Kaśyapa spoke this: "Release him, O Devendra; what need have you for him?"
O son, for one who is held in high esteem, being insulted is said to be equivalent to death;
he who has been released by my word from your hand is as good as dead. (13)
One who is released from the enemy's power due to the latter's respect is, in battle, the enemy of enemies;
for he is as good as dead day after day, even while still alive. 14.
Having heard this, Ativajrāṅga bowed and spoke these words: "I have no business with this; my mother's command has been carried out by me. (15)
"You are indeed the lord of the gods and asuras, and the grandfather who is beyond reproach;
O God, you shall carry out these words," thus was Śatakratu addressed.
"O God, may my delight be in austerity, and may that remain free from obstacles through your grace, O Blessed One. Having spoken thus, he ceased.
While those Daityas remained silent, the Grandfather spoke this:
Brahmā said: "Undergo penance; having fallen into distress, he remains steadfast in our command."
"By this purity of mind, the fruit of birth has been fully attained," having said this, the Lotus-born One created a large-eyed maiden. (19)
The lotus-born god Brahmā gave her to him as a wife;
having bestowed upon her the name Varāṅgī, the destroyer of sins departed.
Together with Vajrāṅgī, he went to a place for ascetic practice;
with his arms raised, the lord of the Daityas remained there for a thousand years.
With eyes like the petals of a black lotus, pure in intellect, and performing great austerities,
he remained with his face turned downwards for that duration of time, standing amidst five fires.
Free from food, performing terrible austerities, he became a mass of ascetic merit;
thereafter, he made his dwelling within the waters for a thousand years.

When he had entered the water, his wife, who was devoted to great vows, remained at the edge of that very lake, having taken up a vow of silence. Possessed of great luster, she undertook a terrible penance, abstaining from all food.
While you were engaged in penance there, Indra and Kṛvi both terrified you.
Having gone to that great hermitage, the powerful one, who had the form of a monkey, dragged away the seat and the basket containing perfumes and other articles for worship.
Then, in the form of a boar, he terrified the passionate woman;
thereafter, in the form of a serpent, he bit her two feet.
By the power of his asceticism, he attained invincibility against all weapons;
meanwhile, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, tormented him with many terrifying threats.
Then Vajrāṅga’s queen,
having become enraged, perceived the wickedness of the mountain and prepared to utter a curse.
Seeing her intent on pronouncing a curse, the mountain, who had assumed a human form,
spoke with eyes full of fear to that woman of beautiful hips and lovely limbs.
Śaila said:
"O you of great vows, I am not wicked; I am to be served by all embodied beings.
It is this enraged Indra who is doing what is displeasing to you. (31)
In the meantime, a period of a thousand years had elapsed;
at that time, the Blessed One, born from the lotus, became aware of it.
Having arrived at that body of water, he was pleased and spoke to Vajrāṅga.
Brahmā said:
"I grant you every desire; arise, O son of Aditi!"
Thus addressed, that lord of the Daityas, a treasure-house of asceticism, then rose and,
with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the Grandfather of all the worlds.
Vajrāṅga said:
"May I have no fear of demons, may my worlds be free from decay, and may I have devotion to asceticism as well as the maintenance of this body. (35)
Saying "So be it," the Lord departed for his own abode;
Vajrāṅga, too, having completed his penance, remained firm in his self-restraint.
Desiring to see his own wife, he did not see her in his own hermitage;
overcome by hunger, he entered the thicket of the mountain.
As he was looking about to gather fruits and roots,
he beheld his beloved wife, miserable and weeping, her face concealed by the foliage of a tree.
Having beheld her, the Daitya then spoke to his assembly.
Vajrāṅga said:
"O blessed lady, by whom was this penance performed while desiring to go to the world of Yama? (39)
"What desire shall I grant you? Speak quickly, O proud one!
Varāṅgī said:
"I have been terrified, cast aside, struck, and tormented. (40)
With the king of the gods having become fierce, I was like one whose protector had perished; I saw the darkness of suffering and stood resolved to give up my life. (41)
"Give me back my son Metāraka from this great ocean of suffering!
When he had spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas, his eyes agitated with anger, [replied]. (42)
Although that great Asura was capable of retaliating against the king of the gods, he,
possessed of great strength, resolved instead to perform ascetic penance once again.
Having understood his extremely cruel resolve, Brahmā again returned with great haste to where the son of Diti was.
Brahmā said:
"For what purpose have you undertaken this vow to increase the number of your sons? Therefore, I shall grant you again the son you desire by my power. (45)
Vajrāṅga said:
"Having risen from my meditative absorption at your command, I was seen by Indra, who had been terrified; that beautiful-limbed woman spoke to me, seeking her son. (46)
"O Grandfather, grant me a son who will satisfy my desires; O Hero, enough of this penance; enter into this difficult-to-cross hardship.
Brahmā said:
"Enough of your penance, O Hero; enter into this difficult-to-cross hardship. (47)
There will be a son named Tāraka, possessed of great strength, who shall loosen the braided hair-knots of the wives of the gods. (48)
Having been addressed thus, the lord of the Daityas bowed to the Great-Grandfather and went to his beloved queen, who was exceedingly emaciated by grief. 49.
Then, having accomplished their purpose, the two went to their own hermitage;
meanwhile, that woman of excellent limbs and beautiful complexion conceived a fetus.
For a full thousand years she indeed remained within her womb;
then, after those thousand years, that beautiful-limbed woman gave birth.
As that Daitya, who brought terror to the world, was being born,
the entire earth trembled and the great oceans were violently agitated.
The mountains trembled, terrifying winds blew,
the best of sages muttered their prayers, and even the beasts of prey and wild animals roared.
When that great Asura was born, the earth, the moon, and the sun vanished, the quarters were shrouded in mist, and all the great Asuras [perished]. ||54||
The wives of the asuras likewise arrived there filled with joy;
overcome with delight, they sang, and the throngs of apsaras danced.
Then, O one of great luster, when that great festival of the Dānavas had occurred,
the gods, including Indra, became despondent in mind.
Seeing the son of Varāṅgī, who was born from her, the lord of the Daityas was then filled with joy; at that time, he considered him to be well-born because of her.
As soon as he was born, Tāraka, the lord of the Daityas and one of fierce prowess,
was consecrated by the chief Asuras, such as Kujambha, Mahiṣa, and others.
O best of kings, Tāraka has attained the great sovereignty over all the Asuras, a realm capable of rivaling the very earth.
The best of the Dānavas spoke these reasoned words.
Tāraka said:
"Listen, all you Asuras of great strength, to my speech."
O gods, for all of us Dānavas, an inexhaustible enmity has taken root through our very nature of birth, which brings about the destruction of our lineage. (61)
"Let us all, relying on the strength of our own arms, undergo penance for the sake of subduing the gods; of this there is no doubt. (62)
Having heard that, he made up his mind and went to the Pāriyātra mountain;
there, fasting, practicing the five-fold heat, eating leaves, and subsisting on water, [he remained].
For a hundred times a hundred years, he performed these same austerities;
thus, his body being emaciated, he attained the state of a mass of asceticism.
Brahmā, having arrived, said to the lord of the Daityas: "O you of noble vows, choose a boon!
Let there be no death for you from any being whatsoever. (65)
Then Brahmā said to him: "Death is certain for embodied beings;
therefore, choose even that death from which you do not fear."
Then, having reflected, the lord of the Daityas, deluded by arrogance, chose the death of the infant within seven days. (67)
Having uttered the words "I shall go," Brahmā went to his own home;
then I quickly commanded my ministers, "Let my army be mobilized. (68)
If you wish to do what is pleasing to me, O best of gods, then these foremost of asuras must be subdued; for when they are restrained, incomparable joy arises within me.
Having heard the words of Tāraka, the Dānava named Grasana,
the commander-in-chief of the Daitya king, made his army ready.
Having struck the terrifying drum, he quickly summoned the Daityas;
ten koṭis of Daitya lords of fierce prowess arrived.
Their leaders were Aja, Bha, Kuja, Bho, Antara, Asura, Mahiṣa, Kuṃjara, Megha, Kālanemi, and Nimi. (72)
Maṃthana, Oja, Bhaka, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas, Daśanāyaka, and hundreds of others capable of supporting the earth were there. (73)
Adorned with eight wheels and a thousand garuḍas,
it was equipped with a railing and its retinue, and measured four yojanas in width.
Dana’s son, Tāraka, possessed chariots yoked with tigers, lions, donkeys, and horses; he crushed the sons of Bhaga and the Bhagus.
Meghasya was joined by dvīpis, Kālanemina with kūṣmāṇḍas,
Parvatābha with four tigers, and Nime’s [son] had a great elephant.
The king of the Daityas, Maṇthana, mounted upon a hundred-hoofed horse,

Pulastya said:
A doorkeeper appeared, wearing excellent white silken garments;

Salutations to You, the source of the sprouting of the syllable *Oṃ* and all else; salutations to the one who first existed as the infinite variety of the world’s abodes, and who subsequently arose from the root of *Satva* through the will of *Saṃhāra*; salutations to You whose form is *Satva*. (8)

Heaven is your head; the moon and sun are your eyes; the serpents are your hair; the quarters of space are your ears and heart;

You are the renowned creator of illusion; you are the peaceful light, declared to be the sun;

The gross [universe] is entirely composed of misfortune; other than that, the subtle is the true object which is praised even by those who seek welfare.

You join together that which is real, the reality, the possessor of prosperity, and the state of being, cultivated through every state of existence;
and having joined them, you cast them out from their manifest nature, establishing their functional activity in each respective place.

Thus the Lord, the refuge, protector, and guardian of those who possess individual forms, whose infinite manifestations have been meditated upon, was praised; and having thus extolled Brahmā as the cause, the immortals ceased.

Even a maiden equal to ten sons may be devoid of virtue;
this speech is fruitless, whereas for men, it yields the fruit of glory. (154)
A daughter is miserable, pitiable, and a source of grief that increases her father's sorrow, even if she should possess all desired objects and be endowed with a husband and sons. (155)
How much more so for those unfortunate ones who lack a husband, sons, wealth, and the like?
And you yourself have described this collection of defects regarding the body of a daughter. (156)
Alas, O Nārada, I am bewildered, I am parched, I am weary, and I am sinking;
though it be improper, and even unattainable at this moment, it must be spoken. 157.
O Sage, for the sake of favoring us, please cut away this suffering rooted in the maiden;
even though it is limited, it is indeterminate because it is rooted in the humiliation of the mind. (158)
For women, who possess both natures, their birth and lineage are most excellent when they are thoroughly immersed in the heat of passion and again take refuge in the desire for its fruit. (159)
It is said that for the sake of happiness in this world and the next, one should seek the attainment of a virtuous husband;
yet, because such a man is difficult to find, it is said that even a husband devoid of good qualities is better than none at all for women.
A husband is never obtained by a woman without merits;
for dharma is without means, and the resulting pleasure arises from its transformation.
Wealth lasts until the end of life; it is established by noble wives for their husbands.
A man who is destitute, foul-mouthed, foolish, and devoid of all auspicious marks [is not favored]. 162.
"The husband is always declared to be the supreme deity for a woman;
this was indeed stated by you, O divine sage, even though her husband had not yet been born. (163)
O Sage, this incomparable and countless misfortune, difficult to bear, pervades the entire creation of moving and non-moving beings. 164.
Having heard that he is "born of the ancient ones," my mind has become agitated;
for this [omen] indicates the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of both human and divine races. (165)
"O bull among sages, it is said that one's destiny is determined by the marks on the hands and feet; this woman, whom you have called 'the one with upturned hands,' [possesses such marks]. (166)
The state of having hands held outstretched is said to be the perpetual begging of those fortunate ones for whom auspicious results arise, who never give [anything away]. (167)
Moreover, the two signs you have mentioned regarding her beautiful complexion and her voice are not infallible;
even in that regard, it seems to me that hope is better placed elsewhere.
"And there are others characterized by bodily marks that indicate various distinct fruits.
Having spoken thus, while the Mountain, who contemplates great suffering, remained silent, [the Lord continued]. (169)
Preceded by a smile, Nārada, who is honored by the gods, spoke this.
Nārada said:
"A cause for great joy has occurred, yet you describe it as sorrow. (170)
O Great Mountain, I have fallen into delusion regarding the meaning of this undifferentiated sentence; listen to these words from me, which are established in the secret doctrine. (171)
"O Himācala, I have said that there is no husband for this goddess who has been described as being composed of great mountains; such a person has not yet come into existence. (172)
The Great God born of truth, the source of the past, the future, and the present;
the refuge, the eternal, the Teacher, the benefactor, the Supreme Lord. (173)
Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the sages—all of whom are afflicted by conception, birth, and old age—are but playthings for that Supreme Lord, O Mountain. (174)
From the cosmic egg and by his will, the Lord of the World was born;
O Mountain, even you, who are stationary, exist because there is no destruction of the Self.
For the embodied being who is born and dies within saṃsāra, it is only the body that perishes here; the destruction of the self is not spoken of.
This world-process, which is proclaimed to extend from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings, revolves incessantly, afflicted by the sufferings of birth and death. (177)
The great god Śiva, the immovable Sthāṇu, the unborn, the progenitor, the ancient one, that Lord of the World who is free from all affliction, shall become his husband. (178)
And as for what was said: "Listen now to a thorough investigation of those words spoken by you, who are devoid of the characteristics of a goddess. (179)
A divine mark is indeed a sign residing in the limbs of the body; it reveals the ultimate outcome of one's lifespan, wealth, and fortune. (180)
O Upholder of the Earth, for one who possesses infinite and immeasurable good fortune, the form of the aṅkola mark is not at all produced upon the body. (181)
Therefore, O Mahāmati, there is no mark on her body such as a mountain-tuft; and as for what I have said regarding her hands always being turned upward—
This hand of the Goddess, ever palm-upturned and granting boons, shall become the bestower of boons upon the hosts of gods, asuras, and sages. (183)
O best of mountains, listen from me to the explanation of what I have said regarding my two feet, which possess beautiful shadows and are never-failing. (184)
Her two feet resemble lotuses, clear and radiant with bright nails, [being illuminated] by the rays from the jewels in the crowns of the gods and asuras bowing down before her. 185.
O Mountain, this is the wife of the Lord of the World, whose husband bears the bull as his emblem; she is reflected here with beautiful clarity by those of various complexions who gaze upon her. 186.

The mother of all the world, the source of what has been, what is becoming, and what is yet to be—this auspicious one, possessing purifying luster, has appeared in your field solely for the sake of purification. (187)
O best of mountain lords, you must act according to the prescribed rites in such a way that she may swiftly enter into union with the wielder of the Pināka bow.
"O Himavat, there is a great task for the gods that must be performed.
Having heard this from Nārada, the Lord of Mountains indeed understood everything.
Then Menā’s husband, Himācala, considering himself born again, spoke joyfully to Nārada.
O Lord, I have been rescued by you from the terrible, impassable hell;
having been lifted up from Pātāla, I have been made the sovereign of the seven worlds. (191)
"O best of sages, I am now renowned by you as Himācala;
I have attained a loftiness a hundred times greater than that of the mountain Himācala. (192)
O Great Sage, my heart, which has long been carried away by the pursuit of pleasure, does not resolve upon the discernment of the distinctions between duties. (193)
O Sage, the sight of those such as you is certainly never in vain;

I am myself the performer of the purification for both sages and deities;

"This very same purpose is even more significant for you as well in the work of protection.

Nārada said:

The Lord Indra, the subduer of Pāka, called to mind the mango-sprout weapon;

The fish-bannered god of love, filled with passion and displaying his charms, approached her;

The fish-bannered god of love, accompanied by Rati and full of amorous grace, drew near; and seeing him thus appeared, Śakra addressed Manmatha.
Śakra said:
What is the use of much instruction to you, who are so very dear? By means of that [instruction], you already know what has arisen in the minds of living beings.
