"Joined with this honey, go accompanied by Rati"—
thus was Madana addressed by Śakra for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose.
Then the five-arrowed one, being afraid, spoke these words to Śatakratu.
Kāma said:
"O God, by means of this collection [of weapons], which strikes fear into sages and dānavas—" (206)
O Lord of the world, if even the god Śaṅkara is difficult to propitiate, what would he not know?
You alone know the cause of that god and his imperishable abode.
Generally, even when provoked by anger, the greatness of those struck by snow remains;
for such nobility, born of heaven, is the very essence of all enjoyments. (208)

Hearing these words of those who, fearing a distinction [from him], were anxious about a fall from their status as equals to Śakra regarding the fruit [of their merit], Śakra, accompanied by the immortals, spoke to them:
Śakra said:
"We are your authority in this matter; there is no doubt regarding the desire for pleasure.
The power to destroy with a mere glance is not desired by a blacksmith. (210)
"The capacity of any being is seen only in some places, not everywhere.
Having said this, Kāma departed, taking refuge with his friend Madhu. (211)
Filled with delight, he quickly went to the plateau of the snowy mountain;
having arrived there, he reflected upon the means for accomplishing his task.
For great-souled beings, the "scab" of pride is extremely difficult to conquer;
therefore, by first agitating it in this manner, victory over it will be achieved.
Success is generally achieved only when one has first purified oneself;
how else could this be accomplished through such states of being without following after aversion? (214)
Anger is her most cruel companion; terrible envy is her great friend;
and from fickleness she gains great strength that destroys the very foundation of steadfastness. (215)
Having first closed the doors of fortitude and withdrawn my satisfaction, I shall not employ that tamasic modification of the mind before me.
No wise person here can truly understand that snow mountain;
it is merely a conceptual construction arising from the mind of Virūpākṣa. 217.

"Having entered this terrible ocean of worldly activity, which is difficult to cross due to its whirlpools, I shall become the refuge for one who is steadfast in soul and established in austerity. (218)
Having reflected thus upon his hermitage, where the collection of sense-faculties is restrained and the means of accomplishment are not delightful, Madana then went to the abode of his master.
He went to the mountain, the essence of the world, which had platforms of straight trees,
was filled with peaceful beings, and was teeming with living creatures.
The lord of the mountain hosts, whose ridges were covered with a network of various flowering creepers,
resounded with the cries of calm bulls, and possessed slopes of dark green grass.
There he saw the beautiful Vīraka, the companion of the Three-eyed Lord, the sovereign of the world of heroes, whose splendor was like that of Īśāna.
His matted locks were tawny like a mass of saffron and liquid gold;
he held a cane in his hand, was unperturbed, formidable, and adorned with inauspicious ornaments. ||223||
Then, with eyes like the petals of a lotus, half-closed and half-open, he gazes straight ahead,
keeping his sight fixed on the tip of the bridge of his nose.
He wore an exceedingly beautiful upper garment made of Indra’s skin, tawny from the fire of the breath exhaled by the hoods of the serpents upon his ears. ||225||
With his matted locks resting upon his chin as it swayed against his cheeks,
he had made Vāsuki his sacred thread, which was fastened at the base of his navel.

Kāma, gradually approaching his presence, beheld Śaṅkara, who stood with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali* gesture, his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose, and adorned with ornaments of serpents. ||227||
Then, following the humming of bees that accompanied the trees,
Madana entered the ear-cavity of Bhava, captivating his mind.
Then Śaṅkara, hearing that sweet speech centered on Madana,
remembered his beloved daughter of Dakṣa with a mind full of longing.
Then, from the cultivation of samādhi, there arose for Śiva a most pure vision of the subtle, which was perceptible to the senses and yet gradually became hidden. (230)
Then, having become absorbed in that state, his mind obscured by obstacles,
the Lord of the Gods entered into a transformation consisting of passion.
Slightly overcome with anger, Dhūrjaṭi,
maintaining his composure, remained enveloped by his yogic power (yogamāyā) after casting out Madana.
Then Madana, possessed by that true illusion, blazed forth;
he was one whose body was composed of will, difficult to comprehend, an abode of defects, and vast in scope.
Then, having emerged from his heart, that [being] consisting of the addiction to latent impressions (vāsanā) reached the external space, and the one whose banner is a fish (Kāma) appeared.
For he has now been followed by his friend, the spring, who, seeing the mango tree shaken by the gentle breeze, [has come to its aid]. (235)
The one whose banner is the sea-monster quickly released upon Hara’s chest a cluster of arrows, delightful with passion, called "the Enchanter."
From the pure heart of Satya, there fell the great arrow of the one renowned as Aśoka—a harsh, lofty, and bewildering flower-arrow. 237.
Then, when his senses were pierced by the flow of passion, the Lord of Beings became agitated in his heart; even though he was steadfast, he turned toward love. (238)
Then, due to his mastery over all things, he perceived his own possession [of power] and spoke many words consisting of the production of obstacles.
Then, from the fierce *huṃ* sound produced by the fire of his wrath, a third eye, filled with flames, appeared upon his face. (240)
Then Dhūrjaṭi drew his bow, which was terrifying due to its power to destroy the world, as he stood near Rudra, whose form was fierce with passion.
By a spark from his eye, as the inhabitants of heaven cried out,
Kandarpa— the one who inflames the pride of desire— was swiftly reduced to ashes.
Having reduced Satī to ashes, the fire born from the eye of Hara expanded,
knowing him to be a devourer by his *huṃ* sound, in order to burn the world.
Then Bhava, for the sake of the world, divided the fire (Jātavedas) among the mango tree,
the *madhu* flower, the moon, and the *sumanā* jasmine— both in himself and in others.
Through the distinction between the bees and the mouths of the cuckoos, Hara was pierced by the arrows of Smara both externally and internally, as if by the fire of love itself.
Pervading these portions, he appeared as the destroyer of many, divided into parts that cause agitation to the world, difficult to restrain, and formidable. 246.
With his heart filled with the longing for its attainment, Bhīma, burning day and night, indeed fell under the sway of suffering. (247)
Beholding Smara reduced to ashes by the flame of Hara’s “huṃ”-utterance,
Rati lamented piteously along with her kinsman Madhu.
Then, having lamented extensively before the assembly, he now went for refuge to the three-eyed God whose crown is the moon.
Having gathered a flowering mango creeper followed by bees, which was covered with leafy trees and had become a friend to the cuckoos; 250.
Let him bind his mass of matted hair with locks that are exceedingly curved,
and let him smear his body with the beautiful, white ashes of Smara.
Falling to her knees upon the ground, Rati spoke to the one adorned by the moon.
Rati said: "Salutations to Śiva, who consists of the mind, who pervades the universe, and whose path is wondrous; salutations to him! (252)
Salutations to Śiva, who is worshipped by the gods, who is ever intent on showing compassion to his devotees;
salutations to Bhava, the source of worldly existence; salutations to you, the destroyer of the god of love (Manobhava). ||253||
Homage to you who are the refuge for those intoxicated by illusion; homage to you who are adorned with innate purity.
Homage to you, the immeasurable one, the source of all virtues; homage to you, the perfected one, the ancient one. 254.
Homage to the one worthy of refuge; homage to you who possess infinite qualities; homage to the one followed by the formidable hosts.
Homage to the creator of prosperity for the various worlds; homage to the bestower of the desired objects of your devotees. 255.
Homage to you, whose activity is born of action; homage always to you of infinite forms!
Homage always to you of irresistible wrath; homage to you who bear the mark of the moon! 256.
Salutations to the one whose playful sword is praised as supreme, who rides upon the king of bulls, and who is the destroyer of the cities;
salutations to the renowned great medicine, and salutations to the one who possesses manifold forms. 257.
Homage to Kāla, homage to Kalā; homage to you who transcend both time and its parts.
You are the preeminent teacher of the moving and the unmoving, the teacher to be contemplated, who has envisioned the creation of all beings. 258.
O Maheśa, I have suddenly sought refuge in you, the moon-crested one, for the sake of obtaining my beloved;
grant me the fulfillment of my desire for a husband, for without him, O Blessed One, I cannot live. (259)

O Lord of Men, who else in these worlds is as dear to his beloved as you are—eternal, the sovereign lord, the powerful master, the source of all that is pleasing, and the penance that is the ultimate synonym for mastery? (260)
"You alone are the protector and guardian of the world, compassionate and having uprooted the fear of your devotees.
Thus praised by Śaṅkara, the bull-bannered Vṛṣākapi, whose body was as lovely as the god of love, [departed].
The wearer of the crescent moon, the source of night, was pleased; looking at her, he spoke sweetly.
Śaṅkara said:
"O beautiful one, this desire of yours shall indeed be fulfilled by you after a long time."
"Thus he shall attain renown throughout the worlds as Anaṅga (the Bodiless One).
Having been addressed thus, the beloved of the Lord of Mountains bowed her head. 263.
And Rati went to another grove on the Snowy Mountain; distressed, she wept many times at various beautiful spots. (264)
Having desisted from the resolve to die at the command of Śiva, the Mountain King was then urged by the words of Nārada. 265.
She had completed her adornment with ornaments and performed the auspicious marriage rites; she wore a crest-jewel fashioned from celestial flowers and was clad in excellent, pure white Chinese silk.
Then, having taken his daughter who was accompanied by her two friends, the mountain went away; O fortunate one, at that time his heart’s desire was completely fulfilled.
Approaching the forests, groves, and woodlands along with their thickets, he beheld a woman of inconceivable and great splendor who was weeping. ||268||
In human form, on such delightful mountain slopes in this world, the Mountain, touched by curiosity upon seeing her weeping, [approached]. (269)
Then, having approached her, he also asked about the mat:
Himavat said—"Who are you, O auspicious one? And for what reason do you weep? (270)
"O beauty of the world, I do not consider this cause to be insignificant.
Having heard these words of Sātaka, he then spoke with Madhu: [271]
Weeping with words of grief and sighing in a manner that increased her wretchedness,
Rati said:
"O you of noble vows, know me to be Rati, the beloved wife of Kāma."
The Lord Giriśa, established in austerity on Mount Girīva, was enraged;
with his eyes wide open in anger, he created an obstacle for him.
Having escaped from the blazing flames of the fire's crest, I was reduced to nothing but ashes;
yet, overwhelmed by fear, I sought refuge in that god. (274)
Then, being pleased by her praise, Aṅgiras said to Mā: "I am pleased; O beloved of Kāma, the birth of Kāma shall come to pass. (275)
And a man who, taking refuge in me with devotion, studies this hymn of praise to you, shall obtain his desired wish, even to the point of averting death itself. (276)
O one of great splendor, awaiting his words, I shall preserve my body for some time through the power of intense longing.
Thus addressed by Rati, Śaila, terrifying with agitation,
took his daughter by the hand and desired to go to his own city.
Because that which is destined to happen must inevitably occur, the future Bhavitrī, having become the past Bhāvinī,
spoke bashfully through the faces of her friends to her father, the Mountain.
The daughter of the mountain said:
"What use have I for this unfortunate body? And how may my husband Śaṅkara be restored to that former state? (280)
Through austerities, one's desired goal is attained; indeed, nothing is unattainable for one who practices austerity.
Misfortune in this world is in vain when the prescribed means have been employed.
To his daughter, who had fallen away from asceticism and said, "Therefore, out of a desire to achieve my own purpose, I shall perform penance here; I am going," [the father spoke]. (282)
Himavat spoke with words whose sounds and syllables were faltering, like the lord of mountains:
"O daughter, Umā, such fickleness is not befitting your form. (283)
O gentle-looking one, for you who are capable of enduring asceticism in accordance with your afflictions,
all future tasks and worldly affairs shall indeed always be accomplished.
Indeed, many things that are destined to happen occur even against the will of those who desire otherwise;
therefore, there is not the slightest purpose for you, O fool, in performing ascetic penance.
"I shall go to Bhavana and indeed take care of you there. When she had spoken thus, the daughter of the mountain did not follow him to his home. (286)
Then, overcome by that anxiety, he praised his own daughter;
thereupon, a divine voice arose in the sky, heard throughout the three worlds.
"Because you have spoken of this daughter as 'Umā' from the word *tanayā*, she shall be known by the name Umā throughout the worlds. (288)
"Success, personified as she is, will accomplish whatever you desire.
Having heard these words, he then [looked] toward the expanse of the sky.
Having taken leave of his daughter, Śaila quickly went to his own abode.
Pulastya said: Śailajā also departed for the mountain, though it was inaccessible even to the gods. (290)
Followed by her two friends,
the daughter of the Lord of Mountains ascended the sacred peak of the Himalayas, which was adorned with various minerals.
It was strewn with divine flowering creepers, its trees resounded with the humming of bees,
endowed with celestial springs, and radiant with hundreds of fulfilled desires.
It was filled with various birds and graced by ruddy geese,
and it was adorned with the holy blossoms of both aquatic and terrestrial plants.
It was variegated, with hidden recesses, endowed with celestial dwellings,
resounded by flocks of birds, and densely crowded with wish-fulfilling trees.
There he saw a great-branched tree with green foliage,
endowed with every kind of flower and graced by ruddy geese.
Strewn with hundreds of various flowers and endowed with many kinds of fruits,
its clusters of sprouts were broken and scattered by the rays of the sun.
There, having cast off her bracelets and ornaments, Śailajā donned divine bark garments and a girdle fashioned from *darbha* grass. (297)
For a hundred autumns, she remained bathing three times a day and subsisting on *pāṭala* flowers;
she then sustained herself for another hundred years by consuming a single withered leaf.
That treasure-house of austerity remained without food for a hundred years;
consequently, all living beings were distressed by the fire of his penance. (299)
Then the Blessed One, who has performed seven hundred sacrifices, remembered the sages;
they all arrived, joyful and well-disposed.
Honored by Mahendra, they asked him about the purpose [of their visit]: "O best of gods, for what reason have we been summoned by you? (301)
Śakra said: "O Blessed One, listen to the purpose: the daughter of the Mountain King is performing severe penance on the Himālaya. (302)
Therefore, you ought to bring about his birth through the desired union; hasten to complete the penance for the sake of the Goddess and the world. (303)
Having said "So be it," the sages then approached that mountain, which was frequented by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas),
and spoke to her with words that were sweet and gentle.
O lotus-eyed one, Kāma, having resolved to become their adopted daughter,
then spoke with respect and reverence to those sages, O Goddess.
The Goddess said:
O highly fortunate ones, you who are performing penance, cast off your silence; for those like you, when appointed by the Lord, must perform their duty without hesitation. (306)
Having first accepted seats from us with very serene faces,
and having sat down and dispelled their fatigue, you shall then question me as you wish.
Having been addressed thus, they then cried out and took their seats; she, meanwhile, first honored them according to the prescribed rules and ritual injunctions.
Having broken his vow of silence and having bowed according to the prescribed rites to the sages, he spoke softly to the seven ṛṣis who were as radiant as the sun.
Then the Blessed Ones, as well as those seven sages,
questioned her once again in that manner, for she had become a vessel of great respect.
She too, with a mind full of reverence and a beautiful smile, looked at all the sages and spoke while restraining her speech. (311)
O Blessed Ones, you should know the mental desires of living beings;
those embodied ones have been excessively tormented by their bodies and other such things. (312)
But some who are skillful, through various efforts and means, being untiring, obtain there even things that are difficult to attain. ||313||
Others, however, having discerned various forms and approaches,
resort to the essential core for the sake of another body, adhering to their beneficial vow.
With his hand repeatedly reaching out as if wishing to touch the peak of Mount Vindhya, which is adorned with flower garlands born from the sky of possessiveness (mamatva). 315.
"I am indeed prepared to obtain your majesty, the god, as my husband;
yet he is now engaged in asceticism, which by its very nature is difficult to propitiate. (316)
That which was not determined by the gods and asuras, yet is the basis for the activity of ultimate reality, has now been utterly consumed by the one free from passion— Madana himself.
"How may one such as I propitiate the Lord Śiva, who is so unlike her? Having been thus addressed, those women then attained steadiness of mind.
To learn his intention, they spoke words consistent with the subject at hand.
The sages said: "O son, two kinds of happiness are perceived in this world. (319)
There is no contact with this body, nor is there any peace for the mind;
by nature he is clothed in the quarters of space, terrifying, and adorned with ashes and bones. (320)
He was a skull-bearing mendicant, naked, with distorted eyes and unstable conduct;
he had the appearance of one intoxicated or insane, loathsome, and a collector of [impure] things. ||321||
There is no purpose served by bowing down to embodied beings who are driven by harmful intent, if you desire eternal happiness for your own body. (322)
So how [could one desire] that great god, who partakes of living beings, who is loathsome, and whose ornaments are made from skulls, bones, and flowing human fat and flesh? (323)
[He is] adorned with ornaments made of the lordly serpents hissing fiercely,
and he dwells in the cremation ground followed by fierce Pramathas.
The slayer of enemies, whose feet are rubbed by the multitude of crowns of the lords of gods, Hari exists as the sustainer of the world, the beloved of Śrī, possessing infinite forms. (325)
Likewise, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, exists as the enjoyer of sacrifices for those who recite prayers;
and Agni, the fulfiller of all desires, exists as the treasure-store of the gods.
There exists Vāyu, the sustainer of the world, who is the vital breath (prāṇa) of all embodied beings;
likewise, there is King Vaiśravaṇa, the lord whose majesty consists of all objects of desire. ||327||
Do you wish to attain happiness from one of these, or from something else here that is not desired by the mind? (328)
Thus it is, O daughter; by this power, may there be the attainment of worldly prosperity for you in this body, and the attainment of supreme auspiciousness in the next world.
Everything that was reported to the gods by the father himself has now come to pass;
even the hardship endured for the sake of obtaining the bridegroom has become a fruitless tree here.
Generally, an object that is not sought after is indeed very difficult to obtain, even if one is capable.
Because it is assigned to its own place, it is also obtained there as a son. ||331||
When the excellent sages had spoken thus, Śailajā,
her eyes red with anger and her lips quivering, spoke.
The Goddess said:
What is the policy for one with a false grasp? Where is the remedy for calamity? By what means are those who perceive things perversely led onto the path of the virtuous? (333)

Thus, do not direct your analytical investigation toward me, who am fond of false attachments to improper objects and possessed of a corrupted intellect, for I am one whose pride and conceit have been destroyed.
All of you are equal to Prajāpati, omniscient;
surely you know that eternal God, the Lord of the world. (335)
Let that Unborn Lord remain unmanifest, whose emergence is of immeasurable majesty;
for the true nature of his activity remains obscured until awakening occurs. (336)
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the Asuras do not know that [Lord],
whose self-arisen power expands throughout the worlds.
Even though it is manifest to all beings, who does not know this?
To whom does this sky belong? To whom is form? To whom is fire? To whom is the wind? (338)
Whose son is Bhūti? Whose is Varuṇa? And whose are the sun and moon as his eyes?
Whose linga do the gods and asuras worship with devotion in the worlds? (339)
And as for Brahmā, Īśvara, Deva, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other great sages—even their power or their origin, do you not know? (340)
From Kaśyapa and Aditi were born the gods, beginning with Nārāyaṇa;
for Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and Aditi was the daughter of Dakṣa.
Marīci and Dakṣa were indeed the two sons of Brahmā;
Brahmā, possessing the power of a perfected deity, arose from the golden egg.
From whom did the ordinary Śakra appear through ordinary meditation? Then,
by the very will of Nārāyaṇa himself,
impelled by Him, he proceeded toward that birth which is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
That [cognition] also is said to arise from karma alone for those whose minds are rendered helpless by the impulse [of past actions]. (344)
Just as the mind of one afflicted by insanity and other such disorders becomes violent, he indeed perceives even desired objects as being contrary to their true nature. (345)
One always laughs at the worldly transactions that are observed;
know that Viṣṇu alone is the cause for the attainment of the fruits of dharma and adharma. (346)
O sages, repeatedly offer such words to me in the presence of the Lord of Mountains, who is the soil of the Vedas;
just as farmers on the surface of the earth scatter handfuls of good seed into excellent fields for the sake of a bountiful harvest.
Having heard those beneficial and delightful words concerning the successive stages of practice, those who resembled the Lord of Speech spoke with gentle smiles. (348)
The sages said:
"Once the creation of the world has been accomplished, that [destruction] is indeed the supreme task;
for it is generally the work of the Snowy Mountain appearing in the form of Time. (349)
It is true that all those who are striving for the sake of this task stand with longing; yet, what need is there for haste on the part of those great-souled ones? 350.
Since that [scripture] is intended to follow worldly practice without distinction, those who uphold its authority maintain that its validity consists in its excellence of dharma. (351)
Having spoken thus, those sages departed quickly for the Snowy Mountain;
there they were honored with great respect by that lord of mountains.
The excellent sages, being pleased yet filled with haste, spoke briefly.
The sages said:
"O Goddess, the wielder of the Pināka bow himself seeks you as his daughter."
Therefore, quickly purify yourself as an oblation cast into the fire;
for that which is beneficial to the gods endures for a very long time.
"Such an effort must be undertaken for the sake of uplifting the world"—
having been addressed thus, the mountain, under the influence of an onset of joy, [spoke] to the sages.
Unable to speak further, as if seeking an answer, she then addressed those sages, overwhelmed with affection: (356)
And Menā herself spoke these meaningful words to those sages regarding her daughter:
"The purpose for which you desire the birth of my daughter is indeed one of great fruit. (357)
All that has now arrived before us in due order;
for even one who is endowed with noble birth, youth, beauty, and power— (358)
Even to him, though he was naked, matted-haired, trident-bearing, and one who had burnt away desire, she gave her daughter when he asked for her; for he was the giver of desire. (359)
"How indeed can Aghora be worshipped by one who possesses a son?
The sages said: "O Lord, understand the sovereignty of Śaṅkara; [even] the gods and demons [revere him]. (360)
And those whose pair of lotus-feet are being propitiated are perfectly at ease;
whatever form is required for a particular purpose, that very form is long sought after by him. (361)
The young woman performs terrible austerities, finding contentment in that very form, since she will bring her divine vows to completion. (362)
"Therefore, let us remain here for a while with focused attention.
Having said this, they went together with the mountain to where the daughter of the mountain resided.
Indeed, Umā consists of the splendor of light, her heat being like the blazing fire of the sun;
she has been described by the sages as "the affectionate one" (snigdhā), for her name signifies both honor and meaningful speech.
Indeed, I do not desire [anything] from anyone base other than Śarva, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
for he stands as the bestower of supreme prosperity upon all living beings according to their respective degrees of merit.
Steadfastness, sovereignty, and activities constitute the incomparable and great authority;
for there is nothing else superior to it, and from it everything proceeds. (366)
I have gone for refuge to him whose sovereignty is beginningless, who is impartial, resolute, and free from long-standing error. (367)
Having thus heard these words from the goddess, the best of sages,
their eyes overflowing with tears of joy, then embraced that ascetic woman.
And being exceedingly delighted, they spoke these sweet words to the daughter of the mountain.
The sages said:
"O great daughter, you are truly wonderful; you are like the stainless embodiment of knowledge. (369)
"Because he has abandoned the state of being a wielder of the sword due to his reliance on the nature of existence, we indeed know the wonderful sovereignty of that deity. (370)
O slender-limbed one, we have come here to ascertain the firmness of your resolve; before long, your desire shall indeed be fulfilled. (371)
O Lord, what light could there be separate from the jewels of the sun?
And who, having abandoned his own colors, could exist as such apart from Giriśa? (372)
We have sought to entreat him through many means;
indeed, this very purpose dwells even more deeply within our hearts. (373)
Therefore, you alone are that intellect, for you alone are indeed policy;
thus, Śaṅkara will undoubtedly carry out what must be done.
Having spoken thus and being honored by the daughter of the mountain, all the sages departed for the great plateau of Himavat to behold Giriśa.
Their bodies were submerged in the Ganges, their matted locks and manes were tied with yellow bands,
and they wore garlands of *māndāra* flowers held in their hands, which were followed by bees.
Having reached the mountain plateau, they beheld the hermitage of Śaṅkara,
where the entire multitude of living beings was tranquil and the forest was completely still.
There they saw Vīraka at the gate, holding a cane in his hand, as the water flowed silently and undisturbed in every direction.
Then those sages, worthy of honor and disciplined, being the best among eloquent speakers, spoke these words with sweet voices out of respect for the gravity of the matter. (379)
We have come here to behold Śaṅkara, the leader of the Guṇas;
know us to be the three-eyed one, impelled by the task of the gods. 380.
"You alone are the one to go there, so that there may be no transgression of the proper time;
O Lord, this request is generally made through the medium of a doorkeeper. (381)
Having been addressed thus by the sages, he spoke to them out of respect: "I have gone to the Dakini to perform the evening twilight devotion of the sacrifice. (382)
"O Brahmins, once you have meditated for a moment, you shall then behold the wielder of the trident.
Having been addressed thus, those sages, experts in their duties, remained there with great effort.

Just as thirsty cātaka birds [rush] toward a deep, wise lake during the rainy season, so too did they [approach] him who had, in a single moment, perfected the ritual procedures of proper conduct. (384)
Having designated the *vīrāsana* posture and secured himself with a deer-skin, he then joyfully lowered his knees, supporting himself upon the earth. (385)
Vīraka said to the god, whose sole refuge is affection:
"The sages have arrived to behold you, who possess blazing splendor. (386)
"O Lord, you ought to instruct me so that I may behold that meditation.
Thus was Dhūrjaṭi addressed by that high-souled Vīraka.
Then, perceiving their knitting of the eyebrows, the great sage Vīraka gave them permission to enter by nodding his head. 388.
Standing nearby, they called out to the wielder of the Pināka bow to appear;
with their matted locks bound in haste, those excellent sages moved about, their dark garments fluttering.
Then they entered the divine pavilion of the all-pervading Lord of the Mountains,
casting heaps of celestial flowers with their joined palms.
The inhabitants of heaven worshipped the pair of feet of the wielder of the Pināka bow;
thereafter, the sages were gazed upon with affection by the trident-bearer.
Then, having beheld Girīśa, they all praised him with joy. ||392||
The sages said:
"Oh, we have now truly attained our purpose, seeing the sprout of your feet worshipped by the lords of the gods!
O you whose excellence is increased by your virtues, command us as to how we may accomplish the protection of all. (393)
Then, laughing, the Omniscient One said to the best of sages:
"Now perform that task which is in your hearts. (394)
Having been addressed thus, the sages quickly went to where the daughter of the mountain was;
those who knew the divisions of time spoke to Girijā in a mountain cave, [describing] her beautiful, beloved, and captivating form, which had been produced by her ascetic penance. (395)
"Śaṅkara, being pleased with you, will accept your hand;
we have come here first because we had previously requested your father. (396)
"Let us go to our own home with our father.
Having been told this, she reflected, "There is indeed fruit to asceticism. (397)
Hurrying, she went to her father’s divine and beautifully adorned home;
there, that virtuous woman perceived the night as equal to ten thousand years.
Then, at that very moment, the daughter of the mountain, her longing aroused by the sight of Hara, performed the rites for her friend as prescribed by Brahmā.
Having performed various auspicious rites according to the proper sequence, he recited many auspicious mantras due to his union with divine auspiciousness. (400)
The personified seasons, granting all desires, waited upon the mountain;
and the winds were pleasant during the process of cleansing the mountain. 401.
In the palaces, the goddess Śrī herself performed various adornments; beauty pervaded all things, and prosperity was intent upon providing for all. 402.
Then the Cintāmaṇi jewel and other gems, as well as the mountains, creepers, and great trees such as the Kalpaka, approached him from all sides. (403)
The medicinal herbs in embodied form, endowed with divine powers,
as well as the juices and the minerals— all these are the servants of the mountain.
The attendants of that mountain remained undistracted, dwelling within the hermitage;
as did all the rivers, oceans, and everything else, both stationary and moving.
All of them—sages, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras—increased the greatness of Himavat. 406.
On Mount Gandhamādana, even for Śaṅkara, the gods stood with their pure forms, having prepared the materials for their adornment. 407.
Then the Grandfather (Brahmā), his eyes wide with noble affection, bound a crescent moon upon the matted locks of Śarva.
Binding a vast garland of skulls upon the head of Cāmuṇḍā, she said to Giriśa: "O Śaṅkara, beget a son! (409)
Having slain the race of the lord of the Daityas, Śauri will satiate me with their blood;
he shall wear a radiant crest-jewel as his ornament. (410)
O Śambhu, standing before you with serpent-ornaments ready to be grasped, Śakra [offers] the tips of his sprout-like hands smeared with the fat of elephant-skins. 411.
He rushed forward impetuously, his broad lotus-face perspiring;
and sharp winds blew fiercely, as did the sharp [rays] of the Himavat mountain. 412.
They adorned the bull, the vehicle of Hara, which was as swift as thought;
the rays of the sun and fire shone brilliantly, residing within his eyes. 413.
He placed his own splendor—the silver-like radiance of the Lord of the World, the witness of the deeds of the universe—into the skull-bowl filled with the ashes of the funeral pyre. (414)
The Lord of the Pretas stood nearby, free from fear, wearing a necklace made of human bones fastened upon his arm.
Having cast aside with his own hand the great jewel-ornament of various forms brought by the Giver of Wealth—which was like a crest of a blazing lord of serpents—[he departed]. 416.
The Lord himself made the stainless Takṣaka his ear-ornament;
and once the ornament was completed, he adorned the Lord with various decorations.
There too, indeed, these [trees], with their forms intent upon self-restraint,
released all kinds of new, delightful, fragrant, and medicinal herbs.
Then Queen Pṛthivī, who was charming in every aspect, took up various ornaments rich with jewels, while Varuṇa himself [took them as well]. (419)
And there were various flowers made of many kinds of jewels; the God, the knower of all embodied beings, stood there adorned with ornaments. 420.
And Jvalana, being self-restrained, presented divine golden ornaments and purifying vessels made of gold.
The all-pervading wind was fragrant and pleasant to the touch;
and Indra held aloft a parasol as brilliant as the rays of the moon, which seemed to laugh with its radiance.
The illustrious one, adorned with vajra ornaments, joyfully grasped [him] with his arms;
the chief gandharvas sang and the hosts of apsaras danced. ||423||
The gandharvas and kinnaras sang most sweetly while playing their instruments;
for a moment, the seasons there indeed sang and danced.
And the fickle hosts stood there, agitating the Himālaya mountain;
then, in due course, the Creator, the maker of the universe and the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, sat down.
Having performed the marriage rites with his wife as prescribed,
he was honored by the king of mountains with the offering of arghya and entertained by the hosts of gods.
There, Taka dwelt together with his wife and his city;
then [he was overcome] by the singing of the Gandharvas and the dancing of the Apsarases.
Awakened by the hymns of praise from the gods and the Daityas, the Lord of the Gods took leave of the King of Mountains, the Himālaya, at dawn, together with his wife.
He went to Mount Mandara with his horn-bow at the speed of the wind;
then, when the Lord Nīlalohita had departed with Umā, the mountain experienced relief.
For whose mind in this world is not bound by kin? Indeed, for a father, his daughter is [his kin] even in delightful city gardens and in secluded forests. (430)
The Goddess, whose heart was deeply attached [to him], abandoned her eyes upon his private parts;
then, after a long period of time had passed, the Daughter of the Mountain [Pārvatī] [was born] under the name of a son.
Accompanied by her friends, she played with artificial dolls;
at another time, the daughter of the mountain anointed her body with fragrant oil.
He massaged his body, which was filled with impurities, with medicinal powders;
by means of that powder, he transformed the man into an elephant-faced being.
The Goddess played with the man and cast him into the ashes;
then, by the power of his friendship with Śiva and Jāhnavī, he became possessed of a massive body.
Then, filling the world with his exceedingly vast body, he said to her, "O Mother! and Jāhnavī replied to him, "O Son! (435)
Gajānana was worshipped by the gods, beginning with Gāṅgeya;
and his grandfather, Pitāmaha, granted him the lordship over the Vināyakas. 436.
Furthermore, that woman of excellent complexion and auspicious countenance fashioned a tree for her play,
producing a lovely, well-rooted sprout of the aśoka tree.
And they caused him, for whom the auspicious rites had been performed,
to grow up under the care of Brahmins headed by Bṛhaspati, the domestic priest of the Lord of Heaven.
Then the gods and sages spoke these words to the Goddess:
"Now that the path has been shown, you ought to establish the boundaries of conduct. (439)
"What will become of me with these imagined tree-children?"—
having been addressed thus, she, her limbs filled with joy, spoke to the one of exceedingly auspicious luster.
A wise man who causes a well to be dug in a waterless village dwells for a year in heaven, drinking water from two vessels at a time. (441)
A pond is equal to ten wells; a lake is equal to ten ponds;
a maiden is equal to ten lakes; and a tree is equal to ten maidens. ||442||
"This indeed is the auspicious boundary that brings light to the world";
thus were the brahmins addressed, with Bṛhaspati at their head. (443)
They went to their own abodes, having saluted Bhavānī, whose mother is the Earth.
When they had departed, Lord Śaṅkara [addressed] the daughter of the Mountain.
Being supported by his hand, he went to his own residence, a palace with towers and gateways that produced clarity of mind. (445)
With long strings of pearls, its balconies crowded with garlands,
and its golden surfaces well-fastened, he envisioned a pleasure-pavilion within his mind.
Resounding with the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of scattered flowers,
it was a concert hall where Kinnaras sang aloud, its walls echoing with their melodies.
A mass of fragrant incense, imperceptible to the mind,
was offered with impetuosity from all sides by women sporting with peacocks.
Resounding with the cries of flocks of swans, its crystal pillars shimmering,
it was unstained by dust, free from agitation, and crowded in many places by kinnaras.
Where, because of the parrots perched upon them, the walls made of rubies appear as if they were mirrors reflecting pearls through a confusion of species.
There, on a ground of pure sapphire, the god began to sport with his beloved using dice; the two remained there engaged in play. (451)
While the Goddess and Śaṅkara were thus sporting there, finding delight in the aesthetic flavor of their diversion, they were accompanied by their own physical forms. 452.
A great sound arose, falling within the range of their hearing;
hearing that, the Goddess asked Śaṅkara out of curiosity, "What is this? (453)
He questioned Hara, the best of gods, with wonder preceding him;
the god said, "O lady of pure smiles, this has never been seen by me before. (454)
These leaders of the Gaṇas, who are always dear to me, sport upon this mountain through austerity, celibacy, [recitation of] names, and service to the sacred field. 455.
O lady of auspicious countenance, those who were previously struck by me—these very same best of men have now arrived in my presence, appearing unpleasant to me. (456)
Possessing great energy and endowed with the qualities of a magnificent form,
I shall experience wonder at the deeds of those who are powerful.

They are capable of the creation and destruction of this world through their state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya), [accompanied] by Brahmā, Candra, Indra, Gandharvas, along with Kinnaras and great serpents (mahoragas). 458.
O delightful one, though I am eternally free from these [defilements], I am never separated from them;
they sport upon the mountain of my heart, adorning all my limbs with their beauty. (459)
Having been addressed thus, the goddess then abandoned him, overwhelmed with wonder;
reaching the window, she gazed out with a startled countenance.
Some were emaciated, some tall, some short, and some stout; some had large bellies, some had the faces of tigers or elephants, and some had the forms of rams or goats.
They have the forms of various living beings, with flames for mouths, and are dark-brown in color;
they are both gentle and terrifying, with smiling faces and perpetually dark-brown matted locks. 462.
Some have faces like various birds, others have faces like various gods;
some wear silk or skins, others are naked, and still others are deformed.
Some had ears like those of cows or elephants, while others possessed many mouths, eyes, and bellies; they had many feet and many arms, with various divine weapons in their hands.
They were adorned with many flower-garlands, agitated and terrifying in their various ways; they bore diverse weapons and were decorated with various types of armor.
Mounted upon various vehicles, possessing divine forms, they move through the sky;
they are resounded by the sound of lute music and consist of dancers performing in various postures.
Having seen those Gaṇeśas in that manner, the Goddess spoke to Śaṅkara.
The Goddess said:
"How many Gaṇeśas are there in number? What are their names? And what is their nature? (467)
"Tell me of each one individually, separately, once they have reached their conclusion.
Śaṅkara said:
"They are numbered in the tens of millions upon millions, possessing various and renowned heroic powers."
The entire world was filled with these terrifying beings of great strength, in the seats of the perfected ones, on the streets, in ancient gardens, and in houses. 469.
These enter joyfully into the bodies of Dānavas, as well as into those of children and the insane, partaking of various kinds of food and conduct.
Those who drink vapors, those who drink froth, those who smoke, and those who drink honey;
those who feed on fat, those who drink blood, those who eat everything, and those who do not eat at all.

The hosts of gods, who subsist on the food of ascetics and delight in various musical instruments and pleasures—indeed, these multitudes cannot be described individually here because of their infinity. (472)
The Goddess said:
"With a garment of elephant-skin as his upper robe, his limbs pure, wearing a girdle of *mūñja* grass, and with his face made radiant by a paste of red arsenic, he is impetuous. (473)
He has the sweet appearance of garlands of blue lotuses bitten by bees;
he causes the sounding of cymbals upon fragments of stone turned face upward.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, who is this follower of the Kinnaras named what, who repeatedly lends his ear to the songs of the Gaṇas? (475)
Śarva said:
O Goddess, this is that very Vīraka, who is always dear to my heart;
he is the repository of various wonderful qualities and is worshipped by the hosts of the lords of the Gaṇas. 476.
The Goddess said:
"I have such a longing for a son like this;
when shall I see such a son who bestows joy? (477)
Śarva said:
"O slender-waisted one, this very son of yours is the cause of the destruction of the eyes of the gods;
for even Vīraka has been rendered purposeless by you."
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the king, eager for joy, dispatched her friend Vijayā, who was anxious with excitement, to quickly bring Vīraka.
Hurrying with urgency, she descended from the palace that touched the clouds,
[to see him] standing in the midst of the assembly of Gaṇas, who radiate like ten million suns.
Vijayā said: "Come! By your heroic impetuosity, the Goddess has been propitiated;
she calls for you. Thus addressed, [the boy] cast aside the fragment of stone.
Accompanied by Vijayā, he slowly approached the presence of the Goddess,
his splendor resembling a full-blown red lotus atop the pinnacle of the palace.
Seeing him, Girijā, whose breasts were filled with abundant and sweet milk, said:
"Drink this milk, my child; it flows from me, so drink as much as you desire. (483)
The Goddess spoke with words of affection and sweet syllables:
"Come, my son; you have now been born, bestowed upon me this very day by the God of gods, Vīraka."
Having spoken thus, she placed him on her lap and embraced him;
kissing his cheeks again and again, she smelled his head, massaged his limbs, and adorned him with divine ornaments herself.

Adorned with small bells, waist-bands, and anklets; with excellent armlets and necklaces set with jewels; with priceless virtues; with tender sprouts; and with beautiful, auspicious bracelets produced by divine mantras.
Then, with many pure white mustard seeds mixed together, he performed the rite of personal protection for him;
and having thus prepared a garland, he spoke, having placed upon his head a decoration of gorocana in the form of leaf-patterns.
O child, play now with the calves in the courtyards, remaining vigilant and avoiding the pits of Vraja;
for the mountain ridges and trees, crowded with swarms of predatory beasts, have their branches broken by elephants and are exceedingly treacherous.
Do not enter the waters agitated by the whirlpools of the Gaṅgā, like a forest infested with many tigers;
for a person of pure mind, even when dwelling among the hardships of childhood, attains the state of being a son of Vīraka.
"What was desired by the fortunate one will come to pass; even he shall be deprived of all his virtues.
Thus addressed, Naya-vīraka, his mind possessed by the power of Līlā, spoke to his mother with a smile.
By these very [flowers], a bracelet has been fashioned for my arm, and a leaf-pattern has been drawn with pale-red spots;
this delicate garland has been placed upon my head, made of lovely *mālatī* blossoms.

Thinking quickly, "I shall please the Goddess," Vīraka, filled with joy, went out to the playground accompanied by his own attendants; from the south he went to the west, and from the west to the north.
Coming from the north to the east, she beheld Vīraka at the window, who was playing outside with the daughter of the Mountain;
he, out of affection for the world and longing for a son, was like a father to her.
I am a fool, ignorant of even a little of delusion and illusion, bearing this body which is a mere aggregate of feces and urine;
yet I desire to see the Moon-crested Lord, who is superior even to the lords dwelling in heaven, once he has entered the inner court.

As the world-protectors were thus mounting their vehicles, [the sage] said: "In this very moment, this sword—once stainless and now rendered swordless by its own cutting—has been taken away; tell us, by whom and for what purpose was it stolen? (495)
"Of what use is a staff for one whose hand is [already] the weapon? What can we say of this courtyard with its terrifying forms?
This is merely a noose; who here is to be bound by it? Cease your efforts, O World-Guardians, and stay back! (496)

Saying "It is even so," those lords of beings (the gods) spoke thus upon the ground at the entrance of Agni’s hall on the mountain in the forest of the goddess, having observed Vīraka, the protector who follows the gods.
Do not plunge into the waterfalls amidst the falling streams, nor even into the abodes covered with clusters of flowers;
likewise, do not intentionally enter the deep hollows of the high-peaked mountains, for fear of being struck by the force of the wind. (498)

With a golden hue turned tawny by contact with the masses of golden dust rising from the earth at the foot of its lofty golden peaks, this mountain—a source of beautiful forms for both forest-dwellers and sky-goers—is fit to be inhabited by a multitude. (499)
I saw a certain man on the bank of the lovely Kunda lake,
drinking the nectar of her form with his wide, unblinking eyes alone, while she was being drunk in by perfected women with their own wide, unblinking eyes.
Desirous of a son and seeking diversion, she remembered Vīraka, the son of Śilāda, who was capable of crossing over the waves;
he too, having attained such a rise of merit at that very moment, was born as her son in a subsequent life.

How can there be satiety for him as he sports—even with the Goddess who possesses the splendor of the Creator—amidst moments of divine song, moments of gazing upon her, and moments of activity with the hosts of Gaṇas eager for dance? (502)
On Mount Gaṇḍaśaila, which was filled with the lion-roars [of the gods] and possessed nets of blazing jewels, he beheld the great *sāla* and *tāla* trees;
he beheld the blossoming various *tamāla* trees frequented by swarms of bees, and at the foot of the trees, he beheld the swaying ruddy geese.
In a small lotus pond, his eyes fixed upon the lotuses; on his mother’s lap, his pure and stainless gaze;
playing amidst a multitude spreading out in childish frolics—the Lord Gaṇeśa, the bestower of joy to the gods, sports there.

In the mountain caves where the conduct of the Vidyādharas is sung, the wielder of the Pināka bow, full of playful grace through his amorous sports, sported about; at that time, when the sun had departed, he illuminated the world with his rays.
Then, that mountain situated far away reached another region,
as if manifesting within its heart a very firm friendship for him.
The glorious Meru, the son of the cloudless sky, though constantly propitiated by the Brahmins,
did not offer assistance to the sun as it was about to fall.
It is heard that among people there is this lack of stability; for the sun, following the day and filling its own kin, descends downward. 508.
Before those two sages, with their hands joined in prayer and their faces turned toward the sun,
sit down quickly to dispel the heat that afflicts them.
Then, in this world, the darkness of night gradually expanded,
corrupting the minds of men just as turbidity corrupts the heart of a crooked person.
On a couch whose walls were illuminated by the jewel-lamps of the hoods of hissing serpents, and which was covered with a canopy of precious cloths and heaps of moon-like gems; 511.
It was adorned with the shimmering splendor of various jewels that mocked the rainbow,
and it was graced by networks of tinkling bells and clusters of glistening pearls.
I bow to Him who, accompanied by the Daughter of the Mountain, moves with a graceful gait upon a noble chariot covered by a canopy of lovely, swaying creepers. 513.
There the Lord, whose arm was entwined with the vine-like arm of the Daughter of the Mountain, stood,
his field of vision filled by the expansive, white moonlight of the moon-faced goddess.
Girijā too, with her dark-cornered eyes and the luster of a blue lotus petal,
appeared exceedingly beautiful when joined with the night.
Then the God spoke to her, who was engaged in the arts of playful sport.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Gaurī’s Marriage," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
And the forty-fourth chapter—
Śarva said:
O slender-limbed one, you who possess a white radiance have a white luster upon my body.
Like a female serpent, she clung closely to the two breasts, which were adorned with beautiful, fragrant sandalwood paste.
Clad in a garment of blood mingled with moonlight, like the night during the dark fortnight,
you bring harm to my eyes.
Having been addressed thus by him as he stood with his hands raised, the daughter of the mountain,
her eyes reddened with anger and her face distorted by a frown, spoke to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
The Goddess said:
"O Moon-adorned One, every person is overcome by the dullness resulting from their own actions; inevitably, the seeker meets with frustration. (4)
Since I have sought you through long-practiced austerities,
this [union] is indeed a constant humiliation for me at every step.

"I shall go to the mountain to abandon my life through asceticism, having been rendered lifeless by this wicked deed and humiliated by that rogue. (9)

If conceptual thought arises in one whose mind is composed, O Daughter of the Mountain, it is not mine by way of my sequence;
if it should thus become agitated, O Fearless One, then I am not yours again.
"I shall speak jestingly; abandon your anger, O lady of pure smiles! With my head bowed low, I offer this salutation with joined palms to you. (14)

Though the goddess was entreated by the king with many flatteries,

Then, her garment having been seized and torn by the hand of Śaṅkara,

"All this has indeed been transferred from the Himavat mountain to you, O slender-limbed one.

The turbidity of the heart arising from the moon is more difficult to overcome than even poison;

You have no fear because you dwell in cremation grounds; you have no shame because of your nakedness; you have no compassion because you carry a skull-bowl; and long ago, you abandoned all mercy.
Having spoken thus, the daughter of the Himalaya departed from that place;
as the Goddess of the Gods was going away, the courtesans raised a tumultuous cry of "kila-kila."

I said, "O Mother, what is this? Where are you going, so angry and distressed?

"If not, I shall fall from the peak of this mountain, abandoned by you.
Raising her face, the Goddess [spoke] with her right hand. (29)

"It is fitting for you, my son; listen to the business for which I am going.

The Forty-Fifth Chapter.
Bhīṣma said:
Now I wish to hear about the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
as well as the majesty of Narasiṃha, which destroys all sins.
Pulastya said: O King, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, the lord Hiraṇyakaśipu,
the primordial ancestor of the Daityas, performed a very great penance.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
he dwelt in the water, observing the vow of ritual bathing and maintaining silence.
Indeed, being endowed with tranquility and self-control, as well as with celibacy,
Brahmā became pleased with him because of his austerity and his disciplined restraint.
Then the Blessed One himself, having arrived there in person by means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans, [spoke].
Together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, Maruts, and deities,

And by the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, by the rivers as well as the oceans, by the lunar mansions, the auspicious moments, and the great planets that move through the sky; ||7||

"I am pleased with this austerity of yours, O observer of noble vows who are devoted to me.

Hiraṇyakaśipu said: "O best of gods, neither the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, nor rākṣasas, nor humans, nor piśācas shall be able to kill me. (11)
O Grandfather, let the sages and the sons of Manu not be able to curse me with their curses;

Neither with a weapon nor with a missile, neither with a mountain nor with a tree, neither with something dry nor with something wet—nor by any other means whatsoever—should he be slain. (13)
May I alone become the sun, the moon, the wind, and the fire; may I become the water, the atmosphere, the stars, and the ten directions. (14)
Ego, anger, and desire; Varuṇa, Vāsava, and Yama;

Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas and the Cāraṇas,

The fruit of this asceticism must necessarily be obtained by him;
at the conclusion of his penance, the Lord Viṣṇu will effect his destruction.
Having heard those words from the lotus-born one, all the gods,

As soon as he had obtained the boon,
the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu, arrogant because of that gift of a boon, oppressed all his subjects.
In the hermitages, the Dānava constantly harassed the highly fortunate sages, who were firm in their vows, devoted to truth and righteousness, and self-controlled.
Having defeated the gods dwelling in the three worlds, that great asura, the dānava,

When, intoxicated by his own inferiority complex and impelled by the law of time, he made the Daityas worthy of sacrifice and the deities unworthy of sacrifice. (27)

It was a delightful place provided with dwellings and seats, blazing as if with fire by its splendor,

They do not suffer from hunger, thirst, or exhaustion;

Possessing a self-radiance more beautiful than the moon, the sun, and fire,

when that illusion was thus thwarted in battle, the Dānava—

She who resides on the forehead, who dwells upon the three peaks, and who is like the Gaṅgā flowing through the triple path.

Parāvaha, Saṃvaha, and the mighty Udvaha, as well as the illustrious Aparivaha, who foretells the fear of portents. ||123||

Then a great black trunk was seen in the sky;

They open their eyes and close them; they laugh and weep;

The Carmaṇvatī, the Asi, the Dhu, as well as the lord of rivers, the Anada;
and the Śoṇa, originating from Melaka, whose waters are like jewels. ||153||
The Narmadā with its auspicious currents, the river Vetravatī, the Gomatī abounding in herds of cows, and likewise the eastern Sarasvatī. (154)
The Mahākāla mountain and the Tamasā river flow with flowers;
Jambūdvīpa is like a jewel, adorned with every kind of gem. (155)
There is Suvarṇapuṭaka, adorned with gold mines, and the great river Lauhitya, along with the mountain resplendent with gold. ||156||
Pattana, Kośakāra, Aṅkaśa, Caru, and Rajatākara;
as well as the great villages of Magadha, Puṇḍra, and Ugra. (157)
Srughna, Malla, Videha, Mālava, Kāśī, and Kosala—this was the abode of Vainateya, which was coveted by the lord of the Daityas. (158)
The ocean named Lauhitya, which was fashioned by Viśvakarman and resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa, is exceedingly terrifying with its jewels and waters. (159)
And Mount Udaya rises a hundred yojanas high like a great mountain; it possesses a golden altar-platform, is glorious, and is frequented by rows of clouds. ||160||
With trees made of gold that shone like the blazing sun, and with flowering *sāla*, *tāla*, *tamāla*, and *karṇikāra* trees; ||161||
And there is the famous Ayomukha, adorned on all sides with minerals;
and the auspicious Malaya mountain, which possesses the fragrance of tamāla forests. ||162||
The Surāṣṭras along with the Bāhlīkas, as well as the Śūdras and the Ābhīras;
the Bhojas, the Pāṇḍyas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Tāmraliptakas. ||163||
In the same way, the Pauṇḍras, the Śubhras, the Vāmacūḍas, and the Keralas were agitated by that Daitya, as were the gods and the hosts of Apsarases. (164)
And there was the abode of Agastya, which had been established by Agastya in ancient times;
it was enchanting and crowded with throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas. 165.
It was filled with various kinds of colorful birds and great trees in full bloom,
possessing peaks made of gold and frequented by hosts of celestial nymphs.
And the mountain Giri-puṣpitaka, endowed with beauty and pleasing to behold, rose up having pierced the ocean, serving as a resting place for the moon and the sun. 167.
It shone with its great peaks as if scraping the sky,
appearing like the rays of the moon and sun, and was surrounded by the waters of the ocean.
The glorious mountain Vidyuttvān extends for a hundred yojanas;
it is there, on that best of mountains, that the flashes of lightning are cast down.
There is Mount Ṛṣabha, and the glorious Mount Ṛṣabhasaṃsthita;
there is the glorious Mount Kuñjara, and the auspicious home of Agastya. 170.
The city of Mālatī belonged to the serpents known as Vimala and Adurddharṣa;
likewise, Bhogavatī was cherished by the lord of the Daityas.
And Mahāsenagiri, as well as the Pāriyātra mountain;
Cakravān, the best of mountains, and the Vārāha mountain. ||172||
And even before the city of Jyotiṣapura was the auspicious city made of gold,
in which the evil-minded Dānava named Naraka dwelt.
And there, O lord of the people, on that best of mountains called Megha-ga, which resounds with a terrifying roar like a cloud, there are sixty thousand other mountains. 174.
And Mount Meru, the great mountain, resembling the rising sun, is a cave that is constantly frequented by yakṣas, rākṣasas, and gandharvas. 175.
Hemagarbha, Mahāsena, Meghasakha, Giri, and Kailāsa, the lord of mountains, were all seized by the lord of the Dānavas. ||176||
By him, the Vaikhānasa lake was covered with golden lotuses,
as were Lake Kaṃpita and Lake Mānasa, which were crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks.
Triśṛṅga, the best of mountains; Kumārī, the foremost of rivers; and Mount Mandara, covered with masses of snow. (178)
And the mountain Uśīrabīja, as well as the king of mountains Bhadraprastha;
likewise Prajāpatigiri and the Puṣkara mountain. ||179||
Devābha and Parvata, as well as the Vaivālukā mountain, Krauñca, the Saptarṣi mountain, and the Dhūmravarṇa mountain. ||180||
These and other mountains, regions, and provinces,
as well as all the rivers together with the oceans, were all assailed by the Dānava.
And Kapila, the son of Mahī, Vyāghravān, Prakaṃpita, the sky-dwellers, the sons of Niśā, and those who dwell in the depths of Pātāla. 182.
Likewise, there was another host called Raudra, whose leader was named Megha and who was armed with a goad;
he possessed a terrifying upward-moving speed, and all these were the fathers of elephants.
Gadīśūlīkarāla and Hiraṇyakaśipu likewise;
Jīmūtaghananirghoṣa and Jīmūta, who was possessed of great speed. 184.
The enraged enemy of the gods, the son of Diti, rushed toward the lion-like man;
then he was struck by that king of beasts with his sharp, great claws.

Then, having been torn apart and slain in battle by the one with the aid of the syllable Oṃ, the earth, time, the moon, the sky, the planets along with the sun, and all the directions [were likewise destroyed]. (186)
The rivers, the mountains, and the great oceans attained clarity through the destruction of the sons of Diti;
thereafter, the gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism were filled with joy.
They praised the eternal primordial deity with divine names, saying: "O Lord, this body of yours as the Man-Lion has been assumed. (188)
Those people who know the higher and the lower shall worship this very one.
Brahmā said:
You are Brahmā, you are Rudra, and you are Mahendra, the best of gods. (189)
You are the creator and the destroyer, the origin and the dissolution of the worlds;
you are supreme accomplishment, supreme being, the supreme secret, and the supreme oblation. (190)
They call you the supreme Dharma and supreme glory, the foremost, the highest, and the ancient;
the supreme truth and supreme austerity, the supreme purity and the supreme path. (191)
They call you the supreme sacrifice and the supreme fire-oblation, the supreme Agni, the ancient one;
the supreme body and the supreme Brahman, the supreme yoga and the supreme speech. (192)
They call you the supreme secret, the supreme goal, the ancient one, the highest and undecaying;
having spoken thus, the Blessed One, the grandfather of all the worlds, [remained silent]. (193)
Having praised the god Nārāyaṇa, the Lord went to the world of Brahmā;
then, while the musical instruments resounded and the Apsarases were dancing, [he departed].
The Lord Hari, the radiant deity, having assumed the form of Narasiṃha, went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk. 195.
Assuming his ancient form, he whose banner is Garuḍa set forth in a radiant,
majestic vehicle equipped with eight wheels.
The Lord, whose nature is unmanifest, returned to his own abode.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Narasiṃha," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Forty-sixth Chapter.
Śrī Bhīṣma said:
You have described in detail the majesty of Narasiṃha; likewise, let the majesty of Bhava as Bhairava be recounted.
Pulastya said:
Listen also to the supreme deed of that God of gods.
There was a Daitya named Andhaka, who was like a mass of shattered mountains.
Endowed with great ascetic power, he was indeed incapable of being slain by the inhabitants of heaven;
once, [he beheld] the omnipresent Great God together with Pārvatī.
Seeing him playing there, he set out to seize the goddess, thinking:
"If I take this goddess today, she will meet her death through separation from me. (4)
Then this wife of mine, who brings beauty to the world, shall become steadfast;
her face has lovely lips, a beautiful countenance, and a most radiant complexion.
"If she were not my wife, what purpose would life have?
Having formed this resolve, he then consulted with his ministers."
Having formed his military array, he spoke to his general who was with the army:
"Bring me my victorious chariot, which strikes down the gods."
I shall conquer all the gods, led by Viṣṇu and Rudra;
I shall seize the daughter of the mountain, for my mind has been stolen away by her.
The minister related to him the killing of Kanaka by the gods;
he had been slain by the gods, including Indra, because he was infatuated with another's wife.
Then, his soul overcome with anger, he would slay the gods along with Śaṅkara; having slain that Dānava, he took the bow of the Asura out of fear.
Seeking refuge, he went to Kailāsa, the abode of Śaṅkara;
having seen the Lord of Gods, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, he bowed down before him.
Terrified, he who holds the thousand eyes (Indra) made his plea:
"O God, grant me freedom from fear; I shall consume the Dānavas."
We are terrified that his son has been struck down in battle by Yama;
therefore, as long as that great Asura does not realize his son has been slain— (13)
Therefore, while you are still right there, let that cruel Dānava— who brings me fear, who is lustful for women, and who abducts the wives of others— be swiftly slain.
"O best of asuras, you must be slain by him in every way.
Having heard these words of Śakra, Śaṅkara, the protector, then [spoke].
He granted immunity from fear to Śatakratu, saying, "Do not fear";
and having been granted this assurance of safety, he returned from Kailāsa to Kuśasthalī.
Surrounded by hosts of spirits, Īśa, for the purpose of slaying Andhaka, assumed a massive body, a universal form that was most terrifying. ||17||
It was terrifying with blazing, darting serpents like a fearsome great serpent,
and the sky was filled with the mass of his matted locks by the radiance of the crest-jewels of the hooded snakes.
Scorching with intense splendors like the fire of time at the end of an aeon,
he possessed faces marked by sprout-like fangs and radiant as the crescent of the second day of the moon.
With thousands of arms that resembled the interior of the netherworld (pātāla) and which uttered terrifying roars, he grasped many weapons.
Adorned with many ornaments and rich in various terrible sounds,
he was clothed in a lion’s skin and wore a tiger’s hide as an upper garment.
Having assumed such a form—displaying the majesty of an elephant hide, filled with the humming of falling bees, and bringing fear to the demons who oppose the Lord—[he appeared]. (22)
Bhīma,
the destroyer of his enemies, descended to the earth upon hearing that the son of the Asura Aṃdhaka had been slain in battle.
Overcome by anger and darkness, he urged on his battle-instruments; having arrived with focused intent, he reached the place where those gods stood.
Together with a vast army equipped with chariots and elephants,
those gods beheld the Dānavas who were intent on waging a great battle.
With their armor fallen away, they sought refuge for their well-being;
having said "Do not fear" to those gods, the three-eyed god spoke to them. (26)
Seizing his trident, he stood there with great fury, his fangs bared;
then, by the enraged Andhaka, the Gaṇas were struck with hundreds of millions of arrows.
And even as he was discharging arrows emitting sparks and flames from his fire-like bow, the wielder of the Pināka struck down many gods who had been joined together as one.
Then the sky was covered with arrows by that chariot-borne [enemy];
meanwhile, the lord of the Danus, standing upon his chariot, became weak and his weapons grew slack.
Having invited all the demons, he proceeded to fight;
that army was shattered in many ways by those who fought with various weapons.
Seeing his army shattered by the gods—heroes in battle led by Yudhi—and having formed an alliance with Sthāṇu, the Dānava Andhaka watched as it was destroyed by the deities. ||31||
And I, my body overwhelmed by tens of millions of arrows discharged by the Great Lord, relied solely upon him. (32)
Seizing the Pināka bow of Rudra, he struck Rudra;
by the blow of the Pināka, Rudra then fell to the ground.
When the god was cast down to the ground, the three worlds trembled;
the oceans overstepped their shores, and the mountains shed their peaks.
When the Lord of Gods had fallen to the earth, Aṃdhaka again struck him repeatedly with his mace, so that the stars fell away from him in great numbers like pearls.
Enraged, he struck the elephant; having killed it, he caused it to fall to the ground.
Abandoning Śiva, the king of elephants fled and went elsewhere.
After a moment, having regained consciousness, the Supreme Lord arose;
taking up his divine axe, he did not see the Dānava at all.
Having employed a tamasic illusion, he who was skilled in a hundred illusions caused the gods to be utterly deluded by it; then the Dānava advanced.
"O Śambhu, once fear has been reached, what can a sinner do?
As long as the gods remain shrouded in darkness, they will fall into a state of agitation. (39)
Then, their minds agitated by the gravity of the task, they spoke;
in that interval, the Sun stood there in the form of radiant splendor.
He rose up in the form of a man, making the quarters of the sky free from darkness; while the glow-worm stood revealed with its body thrilled because the darkness had vanished.
The gods, their faces and eyes clearly visible, attained great joy;
all the deities and the hosts led by Skanda were indeed radiant with splendor. 42.
They praise with various hymns the Sun in human form—
the incomparable, all-pervading Brahman, who is beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Having then beheld that Prabhāsa, which possessed the luster of smooth coral and a radiant glow like the rising sun, he touched the earth with his five limbs in prostration.
Then the three-eyed god, with a gaze tender with affection, looked upon the God of gods as he was inclined toward prostration and preceded by his solemn vow.
The Lord Hara, filling the three worlds with his splendors, spoke thus slowly in a voice that was affectionate yet terrifying. (46)
For living beings who have been overcome by the illusions of the Daityas and whose minds are agitated by what they see, this alone is the one unfailing deity. 47.
And this very Lord, the Sovereign, acts as the helmsman for all sentient beings, delivering them from the entire ocean of saṃsāra. (48)
Worshipping this god with various forms of austerity and devotion, they always bow down to that omnipresent Lord Bhāskara, who is capable of bestowing the highest bliss. 49.

But he who, with the playful rays of his light resembling the brilliance of blossoming flowers, acts as a crown upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise, and having pervaded the intermediate and cardinal directions with his multitude of beams, shines intensely—he is the Sun, for the sake of manifestation in the world. (50)

[He was worshipped] daily by hosts of sages seeking the highest good—experts in the rituals of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, the Maruts, Viṣṇu, Agni, and Varuṇa—who, like the unguents of the day, had their entire bodies anointed with divine ointments. (51)
Those who, devoid of their own homes, praise your worshipful form— which is eternally present even at the time of universal dissolution— with hymns adorned by a manifold array of words,
always become recipients of your outstretched hand in this world.

O Lord of Gods, those men whose limbs are afflicted by diseases such as leprosy and eruptions, whose skin is withered, who have deformed nails, and whose hair has fallen out, become instantly endowed with the appearance of sixteen-year-olds upon bowing at Your feet. (53)

The Sāmavedic assemblies approached you for the sake of the *makhā* sacrifice; the groups of chief Ṛgvedins sought you with the word "Ṛk"; those who know what must be done recognized you as the noble one (*ārya*); the Nāgas and even the ancestors came to perceive you as the essence of all fragrances.
O Lord, the Māyāvī Upāsanakas, the Ṛṣis, the six classes of gods, and the immortals worship you here just as we do;
likewise, the hosts of Gandharvas and Kinnaras along with the Cāraṇas worship you, and you, O Blessed One, assume such forms accordingly.

Deprived of wealth, they constantly worship you, who are worthy of worship and whose radiance scorches the quarters; yet, lacking means, they wander for alms at the houses of others with bellies emaciated by hunger and carrying broken shards of pottery. (56)
Her wide eyes were like the calyxes of full-blown red lotuses, with brown pupils slightly tremulous and curved with a touch of coquetry;
her form was exceedingly beautiful, charming with a fine necklace, yet weary from the weight of her high, swelling breasts. (57)
"Raṃ" [is the sound] of the broad, full buttocks of the women of noble families; "biṃ" [is the sound] of their girdles with rows of tinkling jewels bound upon them;
"bṛṃ daṃ" [is the sound] of the flapping of the hems of their garments against the surface of their foreheads; and "bi" [is the sound] of the golden anklets on their moving feet. (58)

O Blessed One, who among those women in their homes—whose speech was sweet and faltering, whose voices resounded with the tinkling of anklets—did you honor with a glance like a spark from fire, O You who liberate one from worldly existence? (59)
You alone are Brahmā; you are Hari, Anila, Agni, Rudra, Oṃkāra, Varuṇa, and the Lord of the Immortals.
You are Soma, Vāyu, Bhū, Īśvara, the Sacrifice, the Lord of Wealth, and the Unconquered. 60.

Then, having crossed with great speed over the earth released by the seizing of the seven-horsed Sun-god, they traverse this sky which is devoid of resistance; even for these [beings], it causes no fatigue, even though they travel through it constantly.

O You of infinite form, those embodied beings who are devoted to the singular yoga of meditation and who, through the cultivation of samādhi, have meditated upon Your fourth state, become free from the cycle of rebirth;
thus, they are liberated and unafraid, having attained that eternal, inconceivable, beginningless, and endless Brahman.

Free from birth and other ailments, supreme, ancient, the Lord beyond old age, death, grief, and fear; uncounted by the multitude of gross perceptions, pure, and that which is fully realized through the Upanishads and other scriptures. (63)

O Lord of pure and beautiful form, whose pair of lotus feet are rubbed by the crowns of the hosts of gods and demons, your devotees have gone to heaven after worshipping you for a very long time—you who possess the speed of fire and are the abode of austerities. (64)

O Lord of beings, bestower of boons upon beings, the unchanging Self who acts as the creator, O You whose loud laughter resounds through the sky, the progenitor, the sole lamp of the world, the supreme substratum of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus mantras, the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, and the protector of the worlds! 65.
O Lord of Ascetics, may I cross over the ocean of existence— into which I, wretched and miserable, am submerged— wherein beautiful desires are devoid of reflection,
and which is perpetually a site of terrible calamities like the rays of the moon and the fear of old age, death, grief, and disease.
Whoever recites this at dawn, at evening, or at midday, attains the same world as the radiant Sun and obtains virtue, wealth, and desire.
Therefore, that which is eternally declared as arising from the Sun and from the Mind—to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who grants fearlessness to your devotees, I bow. 68.
O Subrahmaṇya, salutations to you, who are honored by all the gods;
salutations to you of fierce radiance, and salutations to the hunger of the world.
"Obeisance to you, O Prabhākara, O Bhānu, O Conqueror, O Lord of the World!
O Lord of the World, I am tormented by this chief of the Danus. (70)
"What shall I do, and how shall I slay him, O Divākara?
Sūrya said:
"O most sinful one, [slay] him who is skilled in a hundred illusions with the victory-trident."
O Lord of Gods, having slain Andhaka with his trident, he attained victory;
then, seizing that trident and casting it far away, he withdrew its splendor by means of his own power.
Then Andhaka, the doer of evil deeds, struck him with a trident;
in that battle, Rudra was thus afflicted by Andhaka.
Bending his bow Pināka with both arms,
Śaṅkara himself, the wielder of the Pināka, released the exceedingly fierce arrow known as the Pāśupata.
From the blood of Andhaka, which issued from his being pierced by Rudra’s arrow,
hundreds and thousands of other Andhakas were born.
As they were being torn apart, from their blood there arose other terrible *andhakas*, by whom the entire world was pervaded.
Seeing that deceptive being, the God of Gods then created the weapon Aṃdhaka for the purpose of drinking that Aṃdhaka, and at that time the Mātṛkās [also appeared].
Likewise, [one may employ] the Māheśvarī, the Brāhmī, the Śaurī, or the Ābāḍavī;
or the Sauparṇī, the Āyavyā, the Śaṅkhinī, and the Taittirī. ||78||
Saurī, Saumyā, Śivadūtī, Cāmuṇḍā, or Āruṇī;
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Vibhāvarī. ||79||
Śatānandā, Bhagāndā, Picchilā, Bhagamālinī, Bālā, Atibalā, Raktā, Surabhī, and Mukhamaṇḍitā. ||80||
Mātṛṇāṃ, Dāṃsunāṃ, Cabidānī, Śakunī, as well as the highly meritorious Revatī, and likewise Śikhipaṭṭikā. ||81||
Then Tripurāntaka pierced that Daitya with his trident;
the Mothers then drank the blood that flowed from him. 82.
O King, the Daitya Nīrarakta became withered;
impaled upon the trident, that Daitya remained there for a thousand divine years.
O observer of excellent vows, although he was held fast by Rudra of great strength, the Daitya did not die; rather, O virtuous one, he then praised him with devotion.
Homage be to you, O Śambhu, the cause of the destruction of worldly existence! Homage to you, O best of gods; be gracious.
You are the eightfold form consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, sun, moon, and the sacrificer—the source of the manifestation of the world. 85.
Having pleased you with many musical instruments, the Lord of the Rākṣasas obtained this bow, which is to be guarded within his own city;
for he brought it here after lifting Mount Kailāsa with his arms, his form distressed by your leap.
