Having attained sovereignty over all the hosts of *rakṣasas*, and having obtained a son of great prowess who bound even Śakra himself—O Hara, supreme and most noble dispeller of the fear of worldly existence, you who bring about my happiness and are the essence of all the gods! 87.

O Lord, whose lotus feet are the essence for wandering in this world—the feet that have conquered the winds and reached the further shore by bestowing desired boons—when Your lotus feet take up residence in the heart of one who is purified by devotion, You grant whatever he desires. (88)
The lords of sages, having thus reverently worshipped Hara—who exists in the form of the *liṅga*—fulfilled their desires;

then, meditating upon him who is the sole source of existence and whose form is the fivefold manifestation of the universe, they remained within the hollow of a tree, contemplating that life-giver of all living beings.
O Lord, who fulfills all desires through the mere thought of Your feet, I have come step by step to Your state which is accompanied by Your servants;
yet I am a fool and do not know how to praise You, O Compassionate One toward devotees. (90)
Thus was Maheśa praised with devotion and respect by the Daitya, who had become a vessel for compassion even through a mind directed toward the Lord.
He granted him the status of Gaṇeśa and the names Bhṛṅgin and Ṛṭin;
such is the greatness of this Hara, the remover of worldly existence.
Thus it was told that he who is called the Obstacle (Vighna) brings happiness to those devoted to him.
Bhīṣma said:
"Even for a human being, divinity, happiness, sovereignty, wealth, and fame [are attained]. (93)
O best of Brahmins, tell me of victory, enjoyments, health, long life, knowledge, prosperity, sons, kinsmen, and all that is auspicious. (94)
Pulastya said:
Endowed with these qualities, the illustrious Brāhmaṇa is ever pure on earth; indeed, the divine Brāhmaṇa is always pure throughout the three worlds in age after age. 95.
Having honored the twice-born, the gods enjoy imperishable heaven;
kings protect the earth, as well as both worlds, wealth, happiness, and auspiciousness. 96.
There is no one equal to him in the world; he is the deity even of the gods.
He is truly composed of the Dharma and is the manifest bestower of liberation upon the earth. 97.

The teacher of the worlds, worthy of worship, a holy place of pilgrimage, and a sinless person; a dwelling for all the gods, he was created by Brahmā in ancient times through his essence of goodness (sattva). 98.
Regarding this matter, the Grandfather was previously questioned by Nārada:
"O Brahmin, when which [deity] is worshipped does Mādhava become gracious? (99)
Brahmā said: "Viṣṇu is pleased with him with whom the Brahmins are pleased;
therefore, one who serves the Brahmins attains the Supreme Brahman. (100)
Viṣṇu always dwells within the bodies of Brāhmaṇas, and not otherwise;
therefore, Viṣṇu is pleased at that very moment by the worship of a Brāhmaṇa.
He who constantly honors Brahmins with gifts, respect, worship, and the like,
has performed a hundred sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas that are accompanied by beloved sacrificial fees.
The mouth of a Brahmin is a field that is neither saline nor thorny;
one may sow all seeds therein, for such agriculture yields fruit in all seasons.
Whatever is given upon approaching [a worthy recipient] and whatever gift is pleasing to the mind—for such giving, there is an end to the ocean, but no end is found for it. 104.
Indeed, even in their minds they do not exist for one who seeks to harm a Brahmin;
they attain a state of favorability toward him that is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (105)
The wise man who comes to one's house and does not depart with disappointment—his every sin is destroyed, and he enjoys eternal heaven. ||106||
Whatever wealth one offers to a Brahmin at the proper time, in the proper place, and to a worthy recipient—that wealth becomes inexhaustible and remains so birth after birth. (107)
He shall not fall into poverty, nor shall he be afflicted by illness or cowardice;
having worshipped a woman who is pleasing to his mind, he shall obtain twice-born men [as attendants]. 108.
If one performs acts of daring and gives them to a Brahmin on sacred festival days (parvan), that gift is declared to be highly meritorious; it is indeed both fearlessness and gain.
That hand which becomes wounded by being rubbed against the soles of the feet of Brahmins is called the "Hand of Fortune" (Śrī-kara); any other hand is merely a "hand for labor" (Karma-kara). 110.
Purified by the dust of the brahmins' feet and purified by drops of that water, they are forever freed from calamities and sins and go to heaven. 111.
The courtyards of houses, purified by the dust from the feet of Brahmins and rendered pure, become equal to sacred fields; they are highly praised for sacrificial rites.
O sinless one, in ancient times, the Brahmin was born from the mouth of Brahmā;
from him the Vedas, which are the causes of creation and preservation, were likewise produced.
Therefore, the Vedas were indeed deposited by the Supreme Person into the mouths of the Brahmins for the sake of the worship of all the worlds and certainly for the purpose of all sacrifices. 114.
In ancestral sacrifices, marriages, fire-rituals, and propitiatory rites,
as well as in all ceremonies for auspiciousness, Brāhmaṇas are always highly commended.

The gods consume the sacrificial offerings (havya), the spirits such as the pretas and asuras consume the tribute (bali), and the ancestors consume the ancestral offerings (kavya); all this certainly proceeds from the mouth of the brahmin alone. 116.
Whatever gift, oblation, or offering one may give to the gods and the ancestors during sacrificial rites, it is fruitless without a Brahmin. 117.
There, the Asuras, Pretas, Daityas, and Rākṣasas feast;
therefore, having summoned a Brāhmaṇa, one should have him perform these rites. (118)
At the proper time, in the proper place, and to a worthy recipient, [the merit] becomes a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold;
moreover, upon seeing a twice-born man, one should perform a salutation with faith.
By the word of such a long-lived person, a man shall live for a long time;
yet [he may lose this] through failing to offer salutation, through hatred toward Brahmins, and also through lack of faith. (120)
For men, there would be the exhaustion of life-span, the destruction of prosperity, and an evil rebirth;
[but through this,] there is the increase of longevity, the increase of fame, and the increase of knowledge and wealth. (121)
By honoring the twice-born, one shall become excellent; of this there is no doubt. There are no mud-pits of the water from the feet of Brahmins, nor are there any echoes of the Vedic scriptures. 122.
Those houses which are devoid of the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *svasti* are equal to cremation grounds.
Nārada said: "And who is the most worthy of worship among brahmins, or who indeed should not be worshipped? (123)
"Tell me also the true characteristics of a Brahmin and of a Guru.
Brahmā said:
"One who is well-versed in the Vedas (śrotriya) and always endowed with virtuous conduct is eternally worthy of worship. (124)
One of virtuous conduct, free from impurities, a living sanctuary, and sinless—such a person is truly holy.
Nārada said:
"O Father, who is born as a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya)—in a noble family or even in an ignoble one? (125)
A Brahmin on earth who is the performer of both good and evil deeds is worthy of worship.
Brahmā said:
"One born into a family of learned Vedic scholars (śrotriya) who is devoid of ritual action is certainly not honored. (126)
Just as Vyāsa and Vaibhāṇḍaka were honored despite being born in lowly fields and families,
so too was Viśvāmitra, though born in a family of Kṣatriyas, equal to me.
Vasiṣṭha was the son of a prostitute, as were other perfected ones, twice-born men, and so forth.
Therefore, listen to the characteristics of the sons of true Śrotriyas and others, O dear child. (128)

On this earth, among those who have become sacred fords (tīrthas), he who removes all sins is to be known as a Brāhmaṇa by birth; yet it is said that one becomes a twice-born (dvija) through sacramental rites (saṃskāras). 129.
Through knowledge one attains the state of a great scholar (*vipra*); by three [qualities], one possesses the characteristics of a *śrotriya*:
being purified by knowledge, purified by mantras, and likewise purified by the Vedas. (130)
A Brahmin who is purified by bathing at sacred fords and other rites is considered most worthy of worship;
likewise, one who is constantly devoted to Nārāyaṇa is pure in heart.
He had conquered his senses and subdued his anger; he was impartial toward all people, devoted to his guru, the gods, and guests, and dedicated to the service of his parents. (132)
He whose mind never delights in another's wife, who is constantly a narrator of the Purāṇas, and for whom there is a continuous succession of dharma-expositions; ||133||
By the mere sight of this very [place], one constantly attains the fruit born of the horse-sacrifice and other rites;
he attains the same state as one who has bathed in the Bhāgīrathī.
Purified by various vows, by daily bathing, and by the worship of the twice-born,
he should be compassionate toward both friend and foe, and impartial toward all people.

That man who does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another found in the forest, being one whose senses are unsubdued yet liberated from desire, anger, and the like—[he is a true sage]. (136)
He does not even mentally covet the wives of others, even when they have come to his house.
Nārada said: What is the characteristic of the Gāyatrī, or what is the merit arising from each of its syllables?
"Tell me truly about her womb, her feet, and her lineage.
Brahmā said: "The *chaṃ* syllable is the *dogāyatrī*; the deity of the *gāyatrī* is certainly Savitṛ. (138)
She is white in color, with Agni as her face; Viśvāmitra is her seer (ṛṣi).
She is mounted upon the head of Brahmā, and her crest-lock (śikhā) resides in the heart of Viṣṇu.
The marriage alliance should be with one born of the Sāṅkhyāyana gotra; she is to be known as Trailokyacaraṇā, residing within the womb of Pṛthivī. (140)
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the twenty-four syllables upon the twenty-four locations, beginning from the feet and ending at the crown of the head, one bestows the world of Brahmā.
Having known the deity of every syllable, one attains union with Viṣṇu;
furthermore, I shall declare the fixed characteristics of the Gāyatrī.

Standing in water, one should recite one hundred times that [mantra] which consists of fifty-seven syllables, beginning with the word *tathā* and ending with the syllable *ha*, and containing the *brahmayajus* as its eighteenth syllable. 143.
Even those who have committed millions of minor offenses (upapātaka),
as well as major sins (atipātaka) such as the killing of a Brahmin and other such evils, are liberated and go to my abode.
Oṃ, from the speech of Agni, which is favored by the Puṃsīya-Yajurveda, drink the Soma, svāhā!
[Recite] the mantra of Viṣṇu, the great mantra, and likewise that of Maheśvara. (145)
O son, in whichever family one is born— whether that of the Goddesses, the Sun, Gaṇeśa, or the enjoyers of sacrifices— one becomes endowed with those very virtues.
A Brahmin who is directly composed of Brahman should be worshipped with great effort;
one should always give gifts according to the prescribed rules on every festival day.
The donor obtains inexhaustible merit for hundreds of millions of births;
likewise, the Brahmin devoted to sacred study who recites this or causes others to recite it [obtains the same]. (148)

And he should always cause the Dharma to be heard in the world— the conduct of the virtuous, the Śruti, the Smṛti, the Purāṇas and Saṃhitās, and likewise that which is truly consistent with the Dharma.

Having caused [this] to be heard throughout the incomparable worlds and having caused it to be heard among the twice-born, he, who is equal to Viṣṇu upon the earth, is to be worshipped by men and gods alike. (150)
Having performed equal worship to that one who possesses inexhaustible power and who is a holy ford (tīrtha) free from all evil, a person goes to the abode of Acyuta.
Sometimes a sin may be committed, yet the Brahmin is not defiled by those sins, just as the sun and fire remain unsullied even when situated within the house of a Cāṇḍāla. 152.

O twice-born ones, for Brahmins who are like blazing fires or the sun, there is no fault incurred from officiating at sacrifices, teaching, marriage alliances, or likewise from accepting improper gifts. (153)
Established in breath control (prāṇāyāma), they destroy here those evils born of receiving gifts, just as the wind destroys clouds in the sky. 154.
Whoever constantly recites the Gāyatrī accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma), joined with the deities residing in each syllable, and even performs its placement upon one's own limbs; ||155||
Completely liberated from all evil, even that committed over ten million lifetimes, and having attained the state of Brahman, he shall go beyond primordial nature (prakṛti). ||156||
"Therefore, O Nārada, recite the Gāyatrī joined with breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Nārada said:
"O Brahmin, how are the breath-controls [performed], and what are the deities for each syllable? (157)
"O Father, tell me how their placement upon the limbs is performed according to the proper sequence.
Brahmā said:
"The apāna wind of the embodied being resides in the region of the anus, and the prāṇa resides in the heart. (158)
Therefore, one should contract the anus and join it with the breath; then, having performed inhalation (*pūraka*), one should perform the supreme retention (*kumbhaka*). (159)
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), the twice-born should recite the Gāyatrī;
by this very [recitation], whatever accumulation of great sins exists is purified. (160)
By merely uttering it once, a minor offense (upapātaka) goes to destruction; he who, having known each letter and vowel, performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body. 161.
We are unable to describe the fruit that a virtuous person attains as Brahmanhood;
however, O son, listen as I tell you what the divine nature of each syllable is. 162.
Having recited which, the twice-born no longer drinks from his mother’s breast;
that first [mantra] is to be known as Āgneya, while the second is Vāyavya. (163)
The third has the Sun as its deity, the fourth likewise belongs to the Wind;
the fifth has Yama as its deity, and the sixth is said to belong to Varuṇa.
They know the seventh to be that of Bṛhaspati, and the eighth as that of Tvaṣṭṛ and Parjanya; the ninth should be known as that of Indra, and likewise the tenth as that of Gāndharva. (165)
Know the eleventh to be Pauṣṇa; the twelfth is recorded as Maitra;
the thirteenth should be known as Tvāṣṭra; and the fourteenth is Vāsava. (166)
The fifteenth is known as Māruta, the sixteenth as Saumya,
the seventeenth as Āṅgirasa, and after that, Vaiśvadeva.
The nineteenth is that of the Aśvins, while the twentieth belongs to Prajāpati;
the twenty-first, which consists of all the gods, should be known as the imperishable syllable (akṣara).
The twenty-second is to be known as Raudra, and beyond that, Brāhma;
the twenty-fourth is Vaiṣṇava—these are the deities of the syllables. (169)
If one meditates [on the deity] at the time of recitation, one shall attain union with it;
having known that deity, the entire Veda shall become known to him. (170)
Freed from all sins, he shall go to the state of Brahman;
first, the wise man should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Gāyatrī upon his own body. (171)
The wise yogi should place that *kāra* upon the twenty-four locations from the feet to the head, specifically on the big toes of the feet. 172.

One should place the syllable *sa* at the region of the ankles, the syllable *vi* on the two shanks, the syllable *tu* in the middle of the knees, and the syllable *va* at the region of the thighs. (173)
One should place the syllable *re* in the secret region, the syllable *ṇi* on the testicles,
the syllable *ya* at the hip region, and the syllable *bha* in the circle of the navel.
One should place the syllable *go* in the belly, the syllable *de* on the breasts, the syllable *va* in the heart, and the syllable *sya* in the region of the hands. (175)
Uttering the syllable *dhī*, one should place the syllable *a* on the palate;
the syllable *hi* at the tip of the nose, and the syllable *dhi* on the two eyes.
The syllable *yo* is in the middle of the two eyebrows, the syllable *ya* is on the forehead;
the syllable *naḥ* is on the eastern face, and the syllable *pra* is on the southern face. (177)
One should place the syllable *ca* in the west and the syllable *da* in the north;
having placed the syllable *ya* upon the head, one remains pervading all.

Having thus deposited these, the righteous-souled one, whose nature is that of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, being a great yogi and a possessor of supreme knowledge, shall attain the highest liberation. ||179||
Now listen to the re-assignment during twilight, according to its true meaning:
one should assign "Oṃ Bhūḥ" to the heart and "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ" to the head. (180)
Oṃ Svaḥ, for the crest-lock; "This most excellent splendor of Savitṛ" upon the body;
Oṃ Bhargo devasya dhīmahi, for the two eyes. (181)
One should place [the mantra] "Oṃ dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt" upon the two hands.
By merely touching water with the mantra "Oṃ āpo jyotī raso 'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ," one becomes purified from sin and shall go to Hari. 182.
Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ svaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyam.
Oṃ, we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he inspire our intellects.
Oṃ, water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Oṃ.
Having recited this [Gāyatrī] together with the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava, consisting of twelve Oṃkāras, three times during the period of meditation while performing the Kumbhaka breath-retention;
and having recited the twenty-four-syllabled Sāvitrī during the worship of the Sun, one becomes superior even to the Mahāvidyās and attains the state of Brahman. ||183||
Listen with diligence to the *putragāyatrī* characterized by six bellies, knowing which a twice-born man goes to the supreme abode of Brahman. 184.
Oṃ tat! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. 185.
Now, the definition of the five-headed Gāyatrī:
Oṃ bhūḥ | Oṃ bhuvaḥ | Oṃ svaḥ | Oṃ mahaḥ | Oṃ janaḥ | Oṃ tapaḥ | Oṃ satyam | Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt ||186||
One should perform the re-installation (nyāsa) again with the Gāyatrī mantra accompanied by the Vyahṛtis;
thus liberated from all sins, one shall attain union with Viṣṇu. ||187||
Oṃ bhūḥ to the two feet; Oṃ bhuvaḥ to the two knees; Oṃ svaḥ to the waist; Oṃ mahaḥ to the navel; Oṃ janaḥ one should assign to the heart; Oṃ tapaḥ to the two hands; Oṃ satyaṃ to the forehead;
and with "Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt," [one should assign] to the crest-lock (śikhā). ||188||
Thus, the Brahmin who does not know this is the lowest of Brāhmaṇas;
his sin is not destroyed, and he becomes one who accepts excessive gifts. ||189||
Whoever knows this Gāyatrī, which is endowed with all seeds, knows the four Vedas, the knowledge of Yoga, and the threefold recitation. 190.
He who does not know this is considered lower than a Śūdra; the ancestral *pārvaṇa* rite should not be offered to that impure Brahmin. 191.
No one would obtain the fruit of bathing, and everything would become fruitless;
for learning, wealth, birth, and the status of a twice-born are the causes [of merit]. (192)
All of that is fruitless for him, like an impure flower cast upon filth;
even the four Vedas and the Gāyatrī are outweighed by the Tulasī. 193.

The Gāyatrī, superior to the four Vedas, is remembered as the bestower of liberation; she removes [the sins] produced in ten lifetimes with ten recitations, and those committed in a previous life with a hundred. (194)
The Gāyatrī destroys sin three thousand times over a period of three ages;
one should recite the Gāyatrī on a rosary both in the evening and in the morning. (195)
A twice-born man who daily recites the Gāyatrī for one year during the three periods of the day undoubtedly attains the fruit of all four Vedas. (196)
By the mere utterance of the Gāyatrī, his evil arising from ten million births goes to destruction, and he is purified from a mass of sins.
The best of the twice-born attains heaven and liberation by reciting daily;
he who recites the mantras of Vāsudeva day after day [attains these]. (198)
One who bows at the feet of Hari shall attain liberation;
moreover, the hymns of Vāsudeva and the most excellent narratives should be kept in one's mouth.
Yet, by merely touching the mud with his body, he obtained the fruit of bathing in the triple-streamed Ganges through plunging into the Vedas and Shastras. (200)
One obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices in this world by honoring those who recite the Dharma.
O best of the twice-born, I am unable to describe all the virtues of such Brahmins in their entirety. (201)
Viśvarūpa, Kodehī, Samūrta, and Harireva—by whose curse there shall be the destruction of one's lifespan, knowledge, fame, and purity. 202.
Likewise, all prosperities come through the granting of boons;
and Viṣṇu always attains devotion to Brahmanas by the grace of the Brahmins. (203)
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, the protector of cows, who is devoted to Brahman, who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins, and who works for the benefit of the world. 204.
The man who constantly worships Hari with this very mantra—Hari, being pleased with him, shall lead him to union with Viṣṇu. (205)
Whoever shall hear this meritorious narrative, which is the very embodiment of Dharma, for them the sins committed throughout many births shall go to destruction. (206)
Whoever recites this, or causes it to be recited, or acts as a teacher to others, shall have no return to this world; he enjoys imperishable heaven. (207)
There, one obtains wealth, grain, royal enjoyments, freedom from disease, virtuous sons, auspicious fame, and rejoices in heaven like a god. (208)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Consecration of Brāhmaṇas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||46||
The forty-seventh chapter.
Nārada said:
By your grace, I have come to know that brahmin who is most meritorious.
As I understand it, by the act of the Lord of Gods, he became the lowest of Brahmins. ||1||
"Speak quickly, O best of gods, if you desire my affection.
Brahmā said:
"One who is liberated by the ten kinds of ablutions as well as by libations and other rites..."
He who lacks meditation and self-restraint is indeed the lowest of Brahmins, even if he is devoid of worship of the gods, vows, and the knowledge of the Vedas. (3)
The great seers have proclaimed five types of baths for Brahmins: those consisting of truth, purity, and so forth, as well as the satisfaction of the fire of yogic knowledge. ||4||
The Agneya, Varuna, Brahma, Vayavya, and Divya [baths]—the Agneya bath is said to be with ashes, and the Varuna bath is with water. (5)
The *āpohiṣṭhā* hymn is indeed the Brāhma bath; the dust of a cow is known as the Vāyavya bath;
and bathing with water from rain or sunlight is declared to be the Divya bath.
By bathing with these mantras, one obtains the fruit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas). One should also take water that has come into contact with a *tulasī* leaf or a *sālagrāma* stone.
The water from the horns of cows and the water from the feet of Brahmins—
such is the Smṛti tradition that it is purer than the pure, even for those who are preeminent among gurus.
Whatever fruit a wise man obtains through sacrifices such as those at the tirthas of renunciation, as well as through vows and fire-offerings— that same fruit he obtains through these baths.
One who is constantly deprived of the libations for the ancestors is a killer of ancestors and goes to hell; likewise, one who lacks meditative concentration is a killer of Brahmins.
Even if he is liberated through the qualities of Vedic knowledge, sacrifices, gifts, and so forth, a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of mantra and vows is the lowest of the low. 11.

Those who perform sacrifices for hire, those who act as temple priests, those who serve as village priests for Kṣatriyas, and those who are constantly devoted to the wives of others—these five are the lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (12)
Those Brahmins who are devoid of mantra-consecration, who lack purity and self-restraint, who eat in vain, and who are evil-minded, are the lowest of the low. ||13||
Deluded by the desire for wealth, devoid of all dharma, and constantly treading the wrong path, these Brāhmaṇas are the lowest of the low. (14)

Those who are devoid of rites such as the *śrāddha*, who have abandoned service to their guru, who are without mantras, and who do not observe the boundaries of conduct—these are the lowest of the low among all. (15)
These wicked ones are not to be conversed with; they all go to hell.
They are impure, of evil conduct, and likewise unworthy of honor. 16.
Those who subsist by the sword, those who serve as messengers, those twice-born who delight in driving cattle, those who live by the craft of artisans, and those who are usurers for guilds; ||17||
Those who deal in children, those who practice sorcery, those who have taken refuge in the letter "aṃ," the ungrateful, and those who kill their gurus— these are all considered the lowest of men.
And those others who are of evil conduct, who revile the dharma of the heretics, who are detractors of the various gods—these twice-born ones are haters of Brahman. (19)
Nevertheless, O Brahmin, I must never be slain;
by killing this best of the twice-born, a man would become a slayer of a Brahmin. (20)
Whether among the Ābhīra, Mleccha, or Caṇḍāla castes, or even among those fallen from their caste or birth, I am not to be treated with contempt in any way whatsoever. (21)
Even by approaching women of every caste and by eating all that is forbidden to eat, the status of a twice-born man is not destroyed; through merit, he becomes a Brahmin once again.
Nārada said: "O Grandfather of all the worlds, having committed such an evil deed, if a brahmin subsequently performs meritorious acts, what destination does he attain? (23)
Brahmā said:
"He who, having committed all manner of sins, subsequently conquers his senses, is liberated from all those sins and is worthy of attaining the state of Brahmā once again. (24)
Listen to this delightful, wonderful, and ancient tale concerning a certain brahmin who had a son endowed with great youthfulness. (25)
Then, due to the attainment of youth, delusion, and his past karma,
he immediately approached a Caṇḍālī woman and became more devoted to her than to anyone else.
Having begotten sons and daughters upon her,
he abandoned his own family and remained in her house for a long time.
He did not eat any other forbidden food, and out of disgust he abandoned liquor;
the king said to him, "Always eat one or the other kind of liquor."
He said to her: "O beloved, you ought not to mourn this impurity;
for from hearing of it, a thrill of joy constantly arises within me. (29)
Once, exhausted from searching for deer, he slept during the day in his house;
having seized a demoness, she laughed and placed her in his mouth.
Then, from the mouth of that brahmin, fire blazed forth all at once;
that flame then consumed her along with her family, the house, and her wealth.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", the brahmin rose up and then lamented;
indeed, he then began his lamentations out of a desire to understand [the situation].
"From where has this fire arisen, and how does it burn my house?
Then Kheṭa said this to him: 'This is the splendor of that Brāhmaṇa. (33)
When this account of events had been told, the brāhmaṇa was filled with wonder;
having reflected upon its meaning, he spoke these words again for his own benefit in the sky. (34)
"Your great splendor has been lost; therefore, practice the Dharma.
Then that twice-born man went to the best of sages and asked about his own welfare.
All the sages said to him, "Practice the dharma of giving.
The seers said:
"O Brāhmaṇas, you shall be purified from all sins by means of restraints and vows. (36)
For the sake of purification, practice the observances seen in the scriptures, as well as the Cāndrāyaṇa, Kṛcchra, and Taptakṛcchra penances again and again. (37)
Quickly go to the purifying holy sites—both those belonging to Prajāpati and those celestial—which dry up all defects; there, perform the worship of Govinda. 38.
Then, by the power of the holy pilgrimage site and the power of Govinda, their sins will perish entirely and without delay. (39)
Your sins shall perish and you will attain the state of Brahmā;
listen, for we shall relate to you an ancient account exactly as it occurred.
Like a calf seeking milk, like Garuḍa seeking his mother, like Vinatā’s son, like a moth, and like a young chick emerging from its shell, he likewise emerged directly from the egg. (41)
Seeking food, he said to his mother, "Give me something to eat.
Then [he saw] Garuḍa, who was like a mountain and possessed great strength.
Seeing her son, the illustrious daughter of her maternal grandfather, with a joyful heart, she said:
"O son, I am unable to satisfy your hunger at this time. (43)
On the northern bank of the Lauhitya, your grandfather, the righteous-souled Kaśyapa, who is the Grandfather of the worlds in person, performed austerities. (44)
Go there and ask your father as you wish;
by his instruction, O dear one, the hunger and thirst of this [being] will be pacified.
Then, having heard his mother’s words, the mighty Vainateya,
swift as thought, went to his father's presence within a mere moment.
Having seen his father, the best of sages, blazing like a fire,
the bird bowed his head to his father and spoke these words.
"O Lord, I have come here seeking food from that Great-Souled One;
afflicted by hunger, O Master, let food be given to me. (48)
Then, having entered into meditation and recognized him as the son of Vinatā,
that best of sages spoke these words out of affection for his son.
Hundreds of thousands of most wicked beings stand upon the banks of the lord of rivers; devour them and become happy. (50)
Those difficult-to-overcome crows of heretics were destroying the sacred fords;
O Niṣāda, eat them unobserved, except for the Brahmin.
Thus addressed, the bird immediately began to devour them;
then, his form becoming invisible, the Brahmin was swallowed by that bird.
Then the brahmin firmly grasped Satasṛṅga by the throat; yet that best of brahmins was unable either to swallow him or to vomit him up. 53.
Having gone, he said to his father who was standing there, "Father, why is this?
I would not be able to counteract my impending misfortune. (54)
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa said to him:
"O child, you do not understand that this is a Brāhmaṇa whom I have declared to be your city. (55)
Having spoken thus, the wise and righteous sage laughed and said to the twice-born:
"Come near me; I shall grant you what is for your benefit. (56)
Then that Brahmin said to Kaśyapa, the bull among sages:
"All these sons of mine are my constant kinsmen and are dear to me. (57)
My fathers-in-law, my brothers-in-law, my kinsmen, and others along with their children—all these shall go with me, whether to hell or to an auspicious state. (58)
Having heard those words of his, Kaśyapa was astonished and said:
"Though born in a family of twice-born brahmins, you have become an outcaste among the Cāṇḍālas. (59)
Those men will certainly fall into a terrible hell; for them, there is no way whatsoever here for their purification to occur even after a long time.
Having abandoned all those of evil conduct, as well as Cāṇḍālas and evildoers, and having cast off faults, a man subsequently becomes happy; it cannot be otherwise.
If one has committed a most terrible sin through ignorance or delusion,
he who thereafter practices righteousness shall go to the supreme goal.
One who commits evil should not practice dharma, nor should one again set one's mind upon evil;
like one who has boarded a boat made of stone, he sinks away in the ocean.
Having committed all manner of evils and likewise accumulated rebirths in miserable states,
one will later become pacified and will bring that fault to rest.
He spoke to that highly wise brahmin, the best among the foremost of sages: "If this bird does not abandon me here, along with all my kinsmen... (65)
Therefore, I shall give up my life-breath by striking a vital organ,
for if I do not, I must abandon these kinsmen and remain firm to my vow.
Then, out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the sage said this to Tārkṣya:
"Vomit forth these Mlecchas along with the Brahmins all at once."
O Lord of Birds, knowing the faults [of the situation], you then quickly flew up from there into the forests, on the mountain peaks, and in all directions, at your father’s command.
Then all those who were somewhat bearded became manifest, devoid of hair and shorn of beards, yet remained fond of Yavana food. (69)

Those who maintain no sacred fires yet perform sacrifices, those who speak ill on the right side, the terrible ones who delight in the slaughter of living beings, and the evil-minded ones who subsist on cattle; (these dwell in the southern direction).
In the southwest dwell those who speak like Rākṣasas, who are wicked and intent on killing cows and Brāhmaṇas;
in the west and the east dwell the terrible Kharparas.
In the northwest are those with four testicles, their faces covered in beards, who subsist on cow-dung;
they are mounted upon the backs of horses and never retreat in battle.
In the northern mountains dwell the Mlecchas, who live among the hills;
they are said to be eaters of all things, of evil conduct, and devoted to killing and binding [others]. (73)
In the north there are hells belonging to the doers, where tree-dwellers reside;
these are the Mlecchas situated there, fierce with hunger and holding weapons in their hands.
And those by whose mere touch one should enter the water even while clothed—even in these places, throughout the entire region, at an improper time when dharma is absent. (75)
Then, out of greed for wealth, they all together entered into contact with those barbarians;
having released them, he was tormented by hunger.
The twice-born Tāta spoke again, saying, "Hunger afflicts me exceedingly.
Thereupon, Kaśyapa quickly addressed Garuḍa out of compassion. (77)
Standing there, those two immeasurable beings of great essence, an elephant and a tortoise, remained intent on devouring the vast regions of the ocean's edge. (78)
They will quickly go into the water and ward off the calf's hunger;
having heard their father's words, they both went there and entered [the water]. (79)
Having torn apart the great beings, the tortoise and the elephant, with his claws,
that one of great speed and immense strength leapt into the sky, seizing them like a flash of lightning in its velocity.
And the mountains, Maṇḍara and the others, could not serve as a support;
therefore, having gone two hundred thousand yojanas, [he reached] Mārutaraṃhasa.
The mighty lord of birds suddenly alighted upon a great branch of a jambu tree; as he was flying away, that branch broke. ||82||
Fearing the slaughter of cows and Brahmins, the powerful one seized him with great speed; having captured that beautiful and exceedingly mighty one, he ran away with haste. 83.
Having gone there, Hari Viṣṇu, assuming a human form, said this:
"Who are you that wander in the sky, and for what purpose, O Lord of Birds? (84)
Holding up a massive branch, the great elephant and tortoise spoke to that Hari, who was present there in human form, as he addressed the twice-born one.
"O mighty-armed one, by my own karma I am Garuḍa, in the form of a bird;
I am the son of the sage Kaśyapa, born from the womb of Vinatā. (86)
"Behold these two great beings whom I have seized for the purpose of devouring them;
neither the earth, nor the oceans, nor the trees, nor the mountains can serve as my support. (87)
Having seen the Jambu tree many yojanas high, I leapt onto its branch to eat from it along with my gold. (88)
Having seized the branch of the Sahasrākṣa tree that had been broken, I wandered about due to the slaughter of thousands upon millions of Brahmins and cows. (89)
O wise one, fear and despondency suddenly entered me there; "What shall I do? How will my watchman endure this surge? (90)
When this was said, Hari then spoke thus to the best of birds:
"Mounting upon my arm, let us eat the elephant and the tortoise."
Garuḍa said:
"The oceans and the best of mountains do not even reach my support;
how then will you sustain such a great being? (92)
"Except for Nārāyaṇa, who else by truth is capable of supporting me?
What man alone in the three worlds could withstand my force? (93)
Hari said:
"A wise man should accomplish his own task; perform your own task now.
O best of birds, having done what ought not to be done, you will surely recognize me."
Seeing that great being and reflecting with his mind, the bird said, "So be it," and alighted upon the great arm. (95)
The arm of that lord of birds did not falter even upon the collision;
remaining there, he released the branch onto the mountain abode. (96)
By the mere falling of the branch, the earth with its forests of moving and non-moving beings trembled,
and the oceans surged violently.
Then, having suddenly devoured the two beings—the elephant and the tortoise—he did not attain satisfaction; his hunger was not appeased by that. (98)
Having understood this, Govinda spoke to that lord of birds:
"Eat my arm's flesh and be at ease. 99.
When this was said, [he replied: "O son, because I ate that meat in great abundance, there is indeed no wound from hunger upon him. (100)
The immensely wise one spoke to Hari, the preceptor of gods and men:
"Who are you? Or what unpleasant thing might you do now at this moment? (101)
Nārāyaṇa said: "O Vidhi, knowing that I, Nārāyaṇa, had come for the sake of your welfare,
I revealed my own true form to him indeed as a sign of proof."
Clad in yellow garments, dark as a rain cloud, four-armed and enchanting, he holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and is the sovereign of all the gods. 103.
And having seen him, Garuḍa bowed his head to Hari and said:
"O Supreme Person, what dear service shall I perform for you? (104)
To him spoke Hari, the Lord of the God of Gods and of great splendor: "O friend of the brave, I have indeed created you as one who exists for all time. (105)
The best of birds said to him: "O Lord of the gods, I am blessed;
O Master, having seen you today, my birth has become fruitful. (106)
Having requested his parents, "I shall return to your presence," Viṣṇu, being pleased, said this: "Become free from old age and death. (107)
May you be invulnerable to all beings, may your power of action be equal to mine, may you possess movement everywhere, and may there be for you constant and total happiness. 108.
Let everything that is pleasing to your mind come together quickly; you shall obtain food according to your desire and to your heart's content, without any hardship. (109)
"Otherwise, you shall not immediately liberate your mother from this calamity.
Having spoken thus, Hari instantly vanished on the spot.
Having gone to Tārkṣya who was distressed, he then related everything;
having heard that, his heart filled with joy, he spoke again to his son.
"I am blessed, O best of birds, and blessed is your auspicious mother;
blessed indeed is this field and family, which has such a son as you. (112)
He in whose family is born a son who is a Vaiṣṇava and the best of men shall uplift ten million ancestors of his lineage and attain union with Viṣṇu. ||113||
He who constantly worships Viṣṇu, meditates upon Viṣṇu, sings [of] Viṣṇu, always mutters the mantra of Viṣṇu, and shall recite His hymn of praise—[for him... 114.
One should always maintain serenity and observe a fast on the day of Hari;
by the destruction of all sins, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (115)
He in whose mind Govinda always dwells—he alone, by virtue of his merits, attains the servitude of that Supreme Person. 116.
Having accumulated a store of virtuous deeds over thousands of millions of births,
and through the exhaustion of all sins, one shall attain the status of a servant of Viṣṇu.
O fortunate one, in the world of Viṣṇu, one attains similarity with Him;
he is eternal, worshiped by the best of gods, the Lord of the World, the infallible, and the imperishable. 118.
He with whom [the Lord] is well-pleased is indeed the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), even more so than by means of many austerities, religious duties, or various kinds of sacrifices. ||119||
"He cannot be obtained by the gods, yet he is being deceived by you;
release your mother from this terrible calamity caused by her rival wife."
Then, having performed the requital for your mother,
having received the command of Janaka, and having obtained the great boon from Viṣṇu, you shall go to the Lord of Gods.
Having gone to his father’s side, he was delighted; bowing down, he stood before him.
Vinatā said:
"O Lord, today there has been a feast, for both my son and my father have been seen. (122)
"O Kīrti, Vavila, and Basteci, I have indeed been distressed by you.
Having heard these words of the afflicted woman, Garuḍa, as if laughing, [spoke]. 123.
Having heard that account as it was being told, she was struck with wonder and asked:
"How indeed was this difficult deed performed by you while still in the state of childhood? (124)
Blessed am I and blessed is Mekula, since you have become a friend of Viṣṇu;
having obtained such a high-souled one as a boon, my mind rejoices upon seeing him. 125.
"By your manly prowess, you have extracted both my lineages.
Suparṇa said:
"O Mother, what shall I do for you? Let that which is pleasing to you be told. (126)
"Having accomplished my task, I shall then go to the side of Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard this, the virtuous Vinatā spoke to Garuḍa.
"O father, great suffering has come upon me; perform a remedy! Previously, my sister, who was my co-wife, cast a curse upon me. (128)
"I shall go there to become her servant; who can deliver me from this?
Having made Kṛṣṇa the horse for her, along with her sons, the great serpents. (129)
At the time of dawn, she said, "This horse shall turn black"; then I spoke there, "I am always dark by nature. (130)
Then, O Mother, that false nature fulfilled her vow;
thereupon I spoke an oath to Kadrū, the mother of the serpents.
"If this horse of Hari becomes black, then I shall become your slave"—this is what I said at that time. (132)
Then, when Kṛṣṇa had been made a horse by Hari,
I entered into servitude at that time through her deceitful sons and rogues.
"At whatever time I give her the desired object, at that very time you shall become a slave; thus I shall bring about the destruction of your lineage. (134)
Garuḍa said:
"O mother, ask quickly; I shall provide the remedy.
I will devour those nāgas; my vow shall be made true."
Then Vinatā, being distressed, said this to Kadrū: "O auspicious lady, tell me what you desire, so that I may be released from this hardship. (136)
That woman of wicked conduct said, "Let nectar be given.
Upon hearing these words, she became devoid of luster.
Then, approaching her son slowly, she spoke in distress:
"O sinner, what will you do by seeking immortality? (138)
Having heard these words, Garuḍa, filled with great wrath, said:
"I shall bring the nectar; O Mother, do not turn away from me. (139)
Having spoken thus, he went with even greater speed to the presence of his father, thinking:
"O sinless one, I shall now bring the nectar for the sake of my mother."
The sage spoke these words to you, the Lord of Birds:
"Above Satyaloka, there is a city constructed by Viśvakarman. (141)
There is a city, beautiful with its assembly halls, for the benefit of the gods;
it is difficult to reach due to its wall of fire and is unassailable even by the asuras and the gods.
For the sake of protection, a god of great strength was created there by the deities;
whatever hero he beholds, that very person shall be reduced to ashes. (143)
Suparṇa said:
"O best of sages, a boon was obtained by me from Nārāyaṇa;
therefore, I have no fear here even from the hosts of gods and asuras."
Having spoken thus, that Garuḍa, the bird, having drawn up water from the ocean,
entered the sky and went upward with the speed of thought.
By the wind from his wings, much dust was raised up;
yet it did not fall near him, nor did it reach him—that accumulation [of dust] remained away from him.
Having gone there, the powerful one extinguished the fire with the water from his crest;
however, with his eyes filled with dust, the Asura did not see him.
The powerful one struck down those groups of guardians and carried off the nectar;
having gone to the celestial river, Śatakratu brought that vessel of ambrosia back.
Having mounted Airāvata, he spoke these words:
"Who are you, assuming the form of a bird, who carries off the nectar by force? (149)
Having acted in a way displeasing to all the gods, how can one live with ease?
With arrows resembling fire, I shall lead this man to the abode of Yama.
Having heard the words of Hari, that one of great strength spoke out of anger:
"Bring the nectar; show me your prowess! (151)
Having heard this, the mighty-armed one struck him with sharp arrows,
just as a rain-cloud strikes the peak of Mount Meru with a downpour of water.
With claws resembling thunderbolts, Garuḍa tore apart the elephant,
as well as Mātali, the chariot, the discus, and the gods who were leading the way.
The mighty-armed Aśva was distressed, as was Mātali and the preeminent elephant;
then all the hosts of gods were turned back by the wind from his wings.
Then Jishnu, provoked to anger, struck him with his thunderbolt;
yet by the falling of that thunderbolt, the great bird was not shaken.
Seeing his own [body] futile and shattered, Hari then became afraid;
withdrawing from that battle, he disappeared right there as if into the water.
Having gone even further with great speed, he arrived upon the surface of the earth;
then that best of gods spoke in the presence of all the hosts of deities.
Śakra said: "O mother of the Nāgas, if you were to give this nectar now,
all the serpents would certainly become immortals by means of it."
If this were not promised, the fruit of your life would have been lost;
therefore, O sinless one, I shall take this with your consent. 159.
Garuda said: "O Hari, at what time will your mother Aditi, being sorrowful, become known throughout all the worlds as 'she who shall take away the nectar'?"
Having spoken thus, the one of great heroism went and then said to his mother:
"O Mother, the nectar has been brought; let it be given to her alone. (161)
Having seen her son together with the nectar, her heart blossomed with joy;
she called out to that Amṛtā, gave her the nectar, and then she herself became one who had arrived there.
Then all the gods and great sages, seeing the grass, wood, beings, cattle, and reptiles, were filled with wonder. ||163||
Having released her, the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) departed well-composed;
in the meantime, Śakra suddenly carried off the nectar.
Having placed the poison there, he remained unobserved by her;
then, with a joyful heart, Kadrū hurriedly summoned her sons.
In their mouths was the sound of a roar that, though fierce, bore the characteristics of nectar;
their mother said to those sons, "May you always reside in the family. (166)
Then the great sages, the gods, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and humans, having beheld him with their own eyes, were filled with joy and stood there, their desires fulfilled. ||167||
They said: "O Mother, by our grace, let there be peace for our lineage;
the gods, along with the Siddhas and the sages, have been dismissed by the Nāgas. (168)
The delighted and joyful nāgas went to their own abodes and remained there; meanwhile, during this interval, Garuḍa forcibly seized the nāgas from the sky.
The remaining ones have fled in all directions—to the mountains and forests, to the oceans, to the netherworlds and caves, and into the hollows of trees. (170)
The serpents dwelling in secluded hollows are at ease;
they have always been ordained by fate as his food. ||171||
Having greeted his friends and conversed with his parents,
and having honored the gods, he then went to the imperishable Hari.
Whoever should read or even hear this auspicious account of Suparṇa’s deeds shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of the gods. (173)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Origin of Garuḍa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Forty-Eighth Chapter.
Brahmā said:
Thereafter, O brahmin-sage, that twice-born man who had become a Cāṇḍāla and fallen from his status, lamenting many sorrows, went to the sage Kaśyapa. (1)
Having gone there, O best of sages, speak words that are beneficial to us;
O best of sages, act in such a way that I may be liberated from this sin. (2)
Then, with a slight smile, the one of great splendor spoke to him with equanimity.
Kaśyapa said:
"By the mere sight of the Mlecchas, you yourself have become pacified."
By means of recitations of the Gāyatrī, burnt offerings (homa), and vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, and by constantly remembering the feet of Hari while fasting on the day of Hari. ||4||
Meditate on Hari day and night, and offer salutations to the Lord;
by bathing in the sacred ford with the mantra, you shall go to His abode.
Then, through the very destruction of your sins, you shall indeed attain the status of a Brahmin;
O twice-born one, by means of vows superior to those of a bull, you shall destroy your impurity and attain liberation.
Having heard the words of that sage, he then became one who had accomplished his purpose;
having performed various meritorious deeds, he attained the state of Brahmā once again. ||7||
Then, having performed intense austerity, he went to the heavenly world after a long time;
for one of virtuous conduct, all sin perishes day by day.
Indeed, the merit of one who follows an evil path perishes like the life of a common person;
a Brahmin slain by improper conduct may attain the state of a god through right conduct.
Therefore, O twice-born one, perform right conduct even with life-breaths that have departed;
always practice good conduct through action, mind, and body.
Through the instruction of Kaśyapa, the twice-born became disciplined; having then established himself in right conduct and performed austerities, he departed for heaven.
A Brahmin who has abandoned right conduct is censured in the heavenly worlds;
however, by practicing right conduct once again, he is honored in the world of the Asuras.
Nārada said:
"O Lord, by honoring the best of the twice-born, people attain their destination;
but by causing pain to the twice-born, what destination does one go? (13)
Brahmā said:
A man who does not worship with devotion according to his capacity those high-souled brāhmaṇas whose bodies are tormented by hunger shall go to hell. 14.
But he who, having reviled with harsh words, releases [the offender] without anger, shall go to the terrible hell Mahāraurava, which is full of great suffering. ||15||
Having returned from there, he is born among the lowest classes of beings, such as insects;
thereafter, he becomes diseased, impoverished, and tormented by hunger.
Therefore, one should not despise a Brahmin who has come to one's house out of hunger;
he who says "I will not give" regarding the gods, the sacred fire, or a Brahmin [is a sinner]. 17.
Having passed through hundreds of animal births, he enters the womb of a Cāṇḍāla woman;
he who, raising his foot, strikes a Brahmin, a cow, his parents, or his teacher. (18)
There is no atonement for one whose dwelling is fixed in the Raurava hell;
even if, by some merit, he should obtain birth [as a human], he would become a cripple. (19)
Extremely wretched, despondent, and oppressed by pain and grief—having thus experienced three births, there shall be his atonement. (20)
That man who strikes a Brahmin with his fists, slaps, or blows him with his head,
shall dwell for an entire kalpa in the terrible Tāpana and Raurava hells.
Then, having reached the birth-state of a dog, cruel and fierce, though born among the [human] species, he is poor and suffers from colic in his belly. (22)

If one exerts oneself as if lifting a foot, a *śilīpada* (elephantiasis) occurs in that foot; or a man may become *khañja* (lame), *jovāman* (dwarfed), *da-jaṅgha* (having a deformed shank), or *khaṇḍapāda* (having a maimed foot). ||23||
His limbs were constantly trembling from the wind of his wings;
he [avoided] his mother, his father, a brahmin, a bath-graduate (snātaka), and an ascetic.
Having killed a multitude of elders out of anger, one will dwell for a long time in the Kumbhīpāka hell;
and having dwelt there, one shall thereafter be born among the species of insects.
O son, if one should speak contradictory and harsh words to the twice-born,
eight types of leprosy will firmly arise upon his body.
Vicarcikā, atha-dadrū, maṇḍala, śukti, sidhmaka, kālakuṣṭha, as well as the very dreadful śukla and taruṇa [types of leprosy]. ||27||
Then, through the physician’s application [of treatment], merit flees from sin;
by that very act, one meets death as if from demerit, like a line drawn upon water. (28)
Among these, three are proclaimed as the great leprosies (mahā-kuṣṭha):
Kālakuṣṭha, Śukla, and the extremely dreadful Taruṇa. ||29||

Indeed, for those who have committed heinous crimes (atipātakin), three [defects] arise within the body, whether through the commission of great sins (mahāpātaka) or even through association with them. (30)
From association and contact, disease spreads among men;
therefore, a wise man should avoid it from afar, and having touched it, he should perform a ritual bath.
Having touched one afflicted with leprosy, a fallen person, a Cāṇḍāla, a cow-eater,
a dog, a woman in her menses, or a Bhilla, one should perform a bath.
In accordance with their misdeeds, they remain afflicted by leprosy in their bodies both in this world and the next; there is no doubt that it exists [as a consequence] even there. ||33||
He who seizes the property of a Brahmin, even if it be a livelihood acquired through righteous means, shall fall into an inexhaustible hell from which there is no rebirth. (34)
One who is a slanderer of Brahmins and intent on seeking out their faults—
upon seeing or even touching such a person, one should enter the water without one's clothes.
A Brahmin’s property, when consumed out of friendship, burns the family up to the seventh generation; however, one who enjoys it by force destroys ten ancestors and ten descendants. (36)
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
Having out of delusion approached his mother, a Brahmin woman, or the wife of his teacher,
he falls into the terrible Raurava hell, from which rebirth is difficult to obtain again.
The ancestors of that person fall into Kumbhīpāka and Tāpana, as well as into Avīci, Kālasūtra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava. (39)
They never at any time permitted an expiation for these [crimes];
by killing the life of a twice-born, one goes oneself to a state from which there is no return. (40)
Thousands of men fall into the Raurava hell for that [offense].
Nārada said:
"The sin is equal even in the killing of all Brahmins. (41)
"From where would such an inequality arise? You ought to tell me the truth.
Brahmā said: "By killing a Brahmin, one certainly incurs the sin that is proclaimed as the 'son-slaughter' (putrapātaka)."
The slayer of a Brahmin incurs a terrible [sin]; hear now another thing that must be said:
he partakes in the slaughter of thousands of lakhs of crores of Brahmins. ||43||

Having killed a learned Brahmin who is endowed with the knowledge of the Vedas and the Shastras, has conquered his senses, and is a Vaishnava, the sin is ten times greater than that [of killing an ordinary Brahmin]. ||44||
Having caused his own lineage to fall, he does not find rebirth;
having killed a *snātaka* learned in the three Vedas, he does not find that end even in hell. (45)
For one who kills such a Brāhmaṇa— one learned in the Vedas, of virtuous conduct, and purified by sacred fords and mantras— there is no end to the sin.
If a twice-born man should give up his life on account of an injury inflicted by another, that other person shall be considered a slayer of a Brahmin. (47)
If a twice-born man, tormented by harsh words or struck by blows,
gives up his life on account of someone, they call that person a slayer of a Brahmin.
The sages, the ascetics, the gods, and all those who know Brahman likewise declare that he shall be slain here in this world by the rulers of various lands. 49.
Even though he has incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin, he is cooked together with his ancestors;
therefore, a wise man should certainly honor a Brahmin who has undertaken a fast unto death.
One should even give up one's life for the sake of that which is free from faults;
one who is smeared with terrible sins should not proclaim it.
He who would commit suicide by climbing a tree, living in hollows, or otherwise taking his own life, becomes a slayer of his own self and a killer of a Brahmin. (52)
He who kills an embryo, or an infant, or a sick person, or an elder, shall himself be a slayer of a Brahmin; he is not merely described as such by others.
If a base Brāhmaṇa should kill a member of his own lineage or a non-Brāhmaṇa, that sin belongs to him alone; it does not accrue to the one who merely proclaims [the act]. ||54||
If a Śūdra, having oppressed a twice-born man, should accomplish his own purpose, then the sin of that transgression belongs to the Śūdra; it cannot be otherwise.
O best of the twice-born, having killed Tāra, an assassin, at that very moment, I am not tainted by those sins.
Even if one kills in battle an approaching assassin who intends to kill him, he does not become a slayer of a Brahmin by that act. //57//
The arsonist, the poisoner, the thief of wealth, the murderer while one sleeps, and the stealer of land or wife—these six are indeed *ātatāyin* (assassins). 58.

One who strives to kill a chaff-eater (khalu-rāja), one intent on killing his own ancestors, a king who follows [an enemy], and a king's [treacherous] follower—these four are assassins (ātatāyin). 59.
It is not fitting to kill again a Brahmin who has already died at that very moment;
for by killing him again, one certainly incurs a terrible sin through such intentional knowledge.
In this world, there is no one equal to the Teacher, the Guru of the universe, who is worthy of worship;
the sin that would result from killing him is unsurpassed. (61)
He is to be worshipped like a god by the hosts of gods and asuras, as well as by men;
it is certain that there is no one equal to a brahmin in the three worlds. 62.
Nārada said:
O best of gods, you ought to tell me truly what mode of livelihood a twice-born man should adopt in order to live his life. (63)
Brahmā said: Begging for alms without asking is proclaimed as excellent;
therefore, the gleaning of grains (uñcha-vṛtti) is more auspicious than that, being the most blessed among all modes of livelihood.
Relying upon which, the best of sages attain the state of Brahman;
indeed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) from the remnants of the sacrifice must be accepted by one engaged in the sacrifice. 65.
Having performed teaching and officiating at sacrifices, wealth should be accepted by the twice-born;
yet, having taught and studied, they must not accept it without performing auspicious rites for well-being.
This is the livelihood for Brāhmaṇas: the conduct of the learned and the acceptance of gifts. Those who subsist on the sacred scriptures are blessed; those who subsist on trees are not blessed.
For those who subsist on grain, trees, creepers, or live in groves and depend on cultivated crops, the sin born of killing arises; for the pacification of that fault: [68]
One should cause the nine kinds of grains to be bestowed upon Brahmins;
for if they are not given, there is certainly a loss of life wherever there is the taking of living beings.
Therefore, one should give very abundantly to the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born;
for in the absence [of other means], the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is subsisted upon by Brāhmaṇas. (70)
In righteous battles, one should fight and observe the auspicious vow of a hero; whatever wealth a twice-born man obtains from a king through his honest livelihood, [that he may keep]. (71)
That wealth which is given in sacrifices to the ancestors and other rites is called pure;
the sinless one should always practice the science of archery in conjunction with the Vedas.
Then, there were javelins, spears, maces, and clubs on all sides, as well as horsemen, elephant-riders, and illusions equal to those of Indra.
One should cause all types of combat appropriate for chariots and the ground to be carried out;
likewise, one should observe the conduct of the twice-born, the gods, the fixed stars, women, and ascetics.
How can that merit which is surely obtained by heroes through the protection of virtuous men and women, gurus, and kings, be attained by those who discourse upon Brahman? (75)
Having brought about the destruction of all evil, he enjoys imperishable heaven;
and in a fair fight face-to-face, the Brahmins fall upon the enemy in battle.
They go to the supreme state, unattainable even by those who discourse on Brahman.
Listen now to the meritorious account of what occurred during that righteous battle, exactly as it happened.
They do not strike one who is fighting face-to-face with them, nor those who are fleeing in cowardice;
they do not strike from behind, nor those who are unarmed or in flight. (78)

One who does not fight, a coward, one who has fallen, one whose sins have been removed, an unworthy Śūdra, one who is pleased by praise, and one who has come for refuge in battle—[these should not be slain]. ||79||
Having killed [the enemy], those of evil conduct who desire victory go to hell;
this is the duty of a Kṣatriya as proclaimed by those of virtuous conduct. (80)
Relying upon which, all kṣatriya heroes go to heaven;
for a kṣatriya, death in a righteous battle is auspicious and faces him directly.
He shall become purified and liberated from all sins;
he shall dwell in the heavenly world, adorned with palaces and jewels. 82.
[He saw] a golden throne set upon a ground adorned with jewels,
completely filled with desired objects and graced with divine articles.
And before him stand wish-fulfilling trees that grant all desires, in a place adorned with ponds, wells, lakes, and gardens. (84)
And the throngs of Apsarases, rich in youth, constantly danced with joy before him like daughters of the gods. (85)
The Gandharvas sing songs and the gods act as reciters of praises;
by proceeding in this manner for a kalpa, that king shall become a sovereign ruler of the entire earth.
He was the sole creator of all enjoyments, free from disease, and possessed a body like that of the god of love;
his wives were richly endowed with beauty and always possessed of youth. (87)
Virtuous, radiant, prosperous, and esteemed by their fathers—such Kṣatriyas enjoy [the fruits of their merit] for seven births in this sequence. (88)
But those warriors who stand by unrighteousness dwell for a long time in hell;
thus is the livelihood of the Kṣatriyas subsisted upon by the Brāhmaṇas. (89)
By Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise by others who are outcastes or of Mleccha origin—
whosoever they may be— whoever fights as warriors, they always fight according to righteous conduct.
All twice-born men of every caste go to the highest state;
yet there is no twice-born man who is a coward, being timid and devoid of missiles and weapons. (91)
In times of adversity, the best of the twice-born may adopt the livelihood of a Vaiśya;
that is, the occupation of a merchant, as well as agriculture and other such pursuits.

A twice-born man should engage in agriculture and trade, yet he must never abandon the duties of a Brāhmaṇa. If, due to his status as a merchant, he speaks falsely, that twice-born man shall fall into a miserable state of existence.
By renouncing moist goods (or raw commodities), a Brāhmaṇa attains auspiciousness.
Then, having generated the ritual procedure, he should give everything to the Brahmin.
Likewise, at the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), the twice-born should offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rules.
One should not practice falsehood in the balance, for the law of the balance is firmly established.
Having weighed a deceitful disposition against it on a scale, one falls into hell;
for even if a substance is beyond measure, one should not abandon it through falsehood.
Thus, falsehood should never be committed, for it gives birth to sin; there is no dharma higher than truth, and no evil greater than untruth. (97)
Therefore, in all undertakings, truth alone is preeminent;
for a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held together on a scale. (98)
Truth indeed excels a thousand horse-sacrifices;
one should speak the truth in all undertakings and abandon falsehood. 99.
He easily overcomes all difficulties and attains imperishable heaven;
a Brahmin should engage in trade, but must certainly abandon it if it becomes fraudulent. 100.
One should cast the interest into sacred fords and personally feed the remainder;
due to the physical hardship involved, that merit always becomes a thousandfold. (101)
For the sake of acquiring wealth, mortals enter treacherous waters, as well as which forest infested with beasts of prey? (102)
Out of greed for wealth, he went from there to a mountain, to a difficult mountain cave, and to the terrifying home of weapon-wielding Mlecchas; all these places were alike to him.
Greedy people abandon their wives and children and travel far away;
they carry the burden on their shoulders while causing others to fall by means of treacherous paths.
O son, the accumulation of wealth through hardships such as casting [goods] into the sea, great sufferings, and the constant loss of life is dearer to me than my own life. 105.
Wealth acquired by these means through the occupation of a merchant, when bestowed without effort upon ancestors, gods, and the twice-born, yields inexhaustible merit. (106)
These two great faults exist in the business of trade and the pursuit of profit:
the failure to renounce greed and the acceptance of false weights for sale. (107)
Having abandoned these faults, a wise man should engage in the acquisition of wealth;
through giving, he attains inexhaustible merit and is not defiled by the faults of trade.
A Brahmin devoted to meritorious deeds should indeed undertake agriculture;
he should cause four oxen to pull [the plow] for half the day. (109)
One should not allow the three [fires] to remain without rest due to their absence;
rather, one should maintain them with uncut grass in a place free from thieves and tigers.
One should give grass as desired and personally satisfy them constantly;
one should also construct for them a cow-pen that is free from any obstacles.
One should always cast pure cow dung and urine,
free from food remnants, into the cow-pen, which is the abode of all the gods.
A wise person should have a bed made suitable for himself;
he should carefully ensure that it is even and free from cold, wind, and dust. (113)

One should perceive the vital breath (prāṇa) as being similar [to oneself], and the cow as having a common form; thus, whatever pleasure or pain exists in its body is likewise imagined to belong to that very [self]. 114.
Whoever should cause agricultural work to be performed according to this method shall not be tainted by the defects of oxen or vehicles, and he shall become wealthy. 115.
He who oppresses one who is weak, as well as one afflicted by disease,
or one who is too young or too old, incurs the same guilt as the killing of a cow.
He who yokes an ox to uneven ground, whether it be weak or strong, incurs a sin equal to that of cow-slaughter; of this there is no doubt in this world. ||117||
Whoever should drive away a cow from a field of grain or restrain it from eating grass or water out of delusion, he incurs a sin equal to that of killing a cow. 118.
On the day of the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), on the full moon day, and likewise on the new moon day,
the sin arising from driving a plough is equal to the slaughter of a thousand cows.
The man who worships these with white substances, paintings and the like, with collyriums, flowers, and oils, enjoys an imperishable heaven. (120)
He who daily gives a handful of grass to another's cow effects the destruction of all his sins and enjoys eternal heaven. ||121||
As is a learned man, so is a cow; the fruit of worship for both is equal.
Yet, upon examination, the Brāhmaṇa is preeminent among men, while the cow is likewise [preeminent] among animals. 122.
Nārada said: O sinless Lord, you have told me that the Brahmin was born from the mouth of Brahmā; how then, O Master, did he become equal to cows? My wonder at this is indeed great. (123)
Brahmā said: Listen here to the truth regarding how the unity of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) among Brāhmaṇas was established by men in ancient times. 124.
In ancient times, a great mass of radiant energy emerged from the mouth of Brahmā;
that which was produced as four parts became the Veda, fire, the cow, and likewise the twice-born.
Prior to the origin of light, the Veda and fire existed;
likewise, the cow and the brahmin were born separately from that which is beyond. 126.
There, at the beginning of creation, the four Vedas were produced by me individually for the sake of the stability of all worlds and universes, extending everywhere. (127)
Just as Agni consumes the oblations for the sake of the gods, so too does the twice-born;
know that clarified butter originates from the cow, and therefore these two are of common origin.
If these four great ones do not exist in the worlds, then the entire universe, both stationary and moving, would perish. (129)
Supported by these, the worlds always abide by their very nature;
that nature is the form of Brahman, and thus they are remembered as being composed of Brahman.
Therefore, this cow is worthy of worship even by Brahmins, gods, and asuras;
noble in all undertakings, she has truly arisen as a mine of virtues. (131)
He is visibly composed of all the gods and is compassionate toward all sentient beings;
his task was created by me long ago for the sake of nourishing him.
Therefore, I have granted this most excellent boon;
it is firmly resolved that liberation shall be yours within a single lifetime. (133)
Right here, these cows that have died come to my abode;
not even a single atom of sin remains within their bodies. (134)
The goddess Gaurdhenukā, the gods, and the primordial goddess Triśaktikā—by whose grace the origin of sacrifices is indeed certain. (135)
The urine, dung, milk, curd, and likewise the clarified butter of cows—these, the most purifying of all things, sanctify the entire world. (136)
No sin remains in the body from eating these;
therefore, the righteous always consume clarified butter, curd, and milk. (137)

Among all substances, that which comes from the cow is desired as the most distinguished and supremely auspicious; for one who has no food [offered] from her mouth, his very form is indeed foul-smelling.
Food is obtained after five nights, milk after seven nights, curd after twenty nights, and ghee after one month. (139)
If a person eats food that is not fit for cows continuously for one month,
the hungry ghosts (pretas) indeed devour the food of that mortal.
Having eaten supreme food that is exceedingly pure and cooked with rice grains not exposed to the sun, whatever merit is performed shall become multiplied by ten million times ten million.

Furthermore, whatever substance fit for oblation is prepared according to the scriptures, if one performs any rite after consuming that, all such action becomes a hundred-thousandfold more meritorious. 142.
Whatever fruit one may obtain from any purely disinterested mental state, a single cow is praised for all purposes throughout every age. 143.
He is the bestower of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa at all times and for all desires.
Nārada said: "In which [practices] and by what application is the supreme merit proclaimed? (144)
"Speak all this according to your knowledge as it truly is.
Brahmā said:
"Having performed a single circumambulation, one should salute the wealth of cattle. (145)
Completely liberated from all sins, he enjoys the imperishable heaven; he is as worthy of worship as the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati) and as the Lord Mādhava himself. 146.
Having performed seven circumambulations, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) rose at dawn from his seat of sovereignty, took the vessel along with water amidst the cows, and departed.
If a practitioner of yoga, abstaining from food, should receive that water upon his head with his very crest, learn now the merit thereof. (148)
O Nārada, those sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist throughout the three worlds, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas and served by great ṛṣis, have been heard by you.
The consecration of all those limbs and of the water from the horns [is complete];
that mortal who, having risen in the morning, touches a cow, ghee, and honey [attains purity]. (150)
By giving mustard seeds and *priyaṅgu* grains, one is liberated from sin;
likewise, cows that yield ghee and milk, those whose source is ghee, and those produced from ghee. (151)
Rivers of ghee with whirlpools of ghee flow constantly in my house;
ghee is in all my limbs, and ghee resides in my mind. (152)
May cows always be before me, and cows likewise behind me;
may cows be in all my limbs, and may I dwell in the midst of cows. 153.
Having thus sipped water and being pure, one should mutter this mantra morning and evening;
for him, there is the destruction of all sins, and he shall be honored in the heavenly world. ||154||
As is the cow, so is the Brahmin; as is the Brahmin, so is Hari;
as is Hari, so is the Gaṅgā. By this, indeed, they are remembered as non-different.
Cows are the kinsmen of humans, and humans are the kinsmen of cows;
that house in which there is no cow is a house devoid of prosperity.
The Vedas, together with their six limbs and the Pada and Krama recensions, are supported by the mouth;
and Hari and Keśava are eternally situated upon the two horns. 157.
Skanda is always situated in the belly, Brahmā resides in the head,
the bull-bannered Śiva is on the forehead, and Indra is at the tip of the horns.
In his two ears are the twin gods, the Aśvins; in his two eyes are the Moon and the Sun;
in his teeth is the divine Garuḍa; and on his tongue is Sarasvatī. (159)
All sacred fords reside in the anus, and the Ganges is in the urine;
the sages dwell in the pores of the skin, while Yama is in the mouth and behind.
Dhanada and Varuṇa themselves took their positions on the right side, while on the left side stood the Yakṣas, radiant and possessed of great strength. (161)
The Gandharvas reside within the mouth, the Pannagas likewise at the tip of the nose, and the Apsarases are situated on the rear side of the hooves. 162.
In cow dung resides Lakṣmī; in cow urine dwells Sarvamaṅgalā.
On the tip of the foot I am known as Kha-carā (the Sky-walker), and in the sound "bhā" I am Prajāpati.
The four oceans are filled with cows for those who stand upon them;
and he who constantly touches the earth becomes as one who has bathed perpetually. (164)
One who is not subject to death is liberated from all sins by those [acts] that are well-nourished;
he who bears upon his head the dust raised by the hooves of cows [is likewise purified]. (165)
"Having bathed in the waters of Sacatīrtha, one is liberated from all sins.
Nārada said:
"What is the fruit of giving cows of the ten colors?"
"O best of gurus, O Parameṣṭhin, tell me the truth if it is pleasing to you.
Brahmā said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, by giving a white-bodied [image], a human becomes a lord. (167)
One who constantly worships Prāsāda-vāsā becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and prospers in happiness;
Dhūmrā, however, leads those desiring heaven across the ocean of saṃsāra and grants liberation from sin. (168)
By giving a brown cow that yields inexhaustible milk, one does not perish; by giving a white cow, which is rare in this world, one attains a golden complexion and a noble lineage. (169)
For one desiring the form of Raktākṣī, Nīlikā is prescribed;
by giving a single tawny cow, one is liberated from all sins. (170)
Whatever sin was committed in childhood, or in youth, or in old age; whatever was done by speech, or done by action, or conceived by the mind—(171)

Sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, treachery toward friends, which are indeed heinous sins; cheating with weights and measures, falsehood regarding a maiden, and falsehood regarding cattle. (172)
He who bestows a Kapilā cow swiftly destroys everything,
even a great river ten yojanas wide with vast banks.
While the iron shaft was still far away in the vast ocean of water, as long as the two feet and the face of the calf had not yet emerged. (174)
The cow should be known as the Earth as long as she does not release her calf;
she should have golden horns, be richly clothed, and adorned with all ornaments. (175)
With a copper-colored back and silver hooves, with a bronze milking vessel, its body adorned with fragrant flowers and decorated with all ornaments. (176)
One should give such a tawny cow to a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedas;
for him, there is the destruction of all sins, and he shall become imperishable in the world of Viṣṇu. ||177||
As that earth was being milked, birds fell from the sky;
they were born from groves and the like, possessing many excellent flowers and fruits. (178)
Where there are trees that yield fruits according to one's desires, rivers with mud of milk-rice, and even palaces made of gold— there go those who have given gifts of cows.
If one should give ten cows and even a single ox capable of bearing a yoke,
it is declared by Brahmā that the fruit of both is equal.
One should give one [gift] for every ten thousand; its fruit is a hundred thousandfold.
According to that principle, O Nārada, the fruit should be understood with effort.
The son who, on this earth, releases a bull dedicated to the ancestors, his ancestors are honored according to their desires in the worlds of Viṣṇu. 182.
And four heifers for one bull alone;
they shall be released from all bonds—this is the eternal rule regarding sons. 183.
For as many hairs as there are on their bodies in every respect,
for that many thousands of years do those humans enjoy heaven.
Whatever water a bull surely tosses up with his tail,
that water shall become nectar for the ancestors for a thousand years.
