If one scrapes the earth with a hoof, or if there is a clod of earth or mud there,
the offering of *svadhā* to the ancestors becomes a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold more meritorious.
If the mother perishes while the father is still living, a cow marked with sandalwood paste should be given for her sake to secure her residence in heaven. ||187||
The giver indeed discharges his debt to the ancestors and, being honored like Indra himself, attains imperishable heaven. (188)
A cow endowed with all auspicious marks, young, and yielding milk, which has recently calved and is of noble breed—that cow is considered equal to the earth. 189.
By the gift of this mantra, one obtains a fruit equal to the gift of the earth;
such a mortal becomes equal to Indra (Śatakratu) and uplifts a hundred generations of his lineage. ||190||
Having stolen cows, except for a cow, a chariot, or a calf,
one must remain in a well filled with worms until the dissolution of all beings.
Having committed the slaughter of cows, one is cooked together with one's ancestors in the terrible Raurava hell for that same duration; such is the retribution. (192)
And because he had broken the cow-pasture and bound the stallions and their mounts, he went to an inexhaustible hell in birth after birth. (193)
Whoever causes this most meritorious narrative to be heard even once, all their sins are destroyed, and they rejoice together with the gods. 194.
Whoever should hear this supreme, most meritorious, and great [teaching] shall indeed be liberated at that very moment from the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes. (195)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Cow," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The forty-ninth chapter.
Nārada said:
By what conduct does the Brahmanic luster of a brāhmaṇa increase?
By what conduct is his very Brahmanic splendor destroyed? ||1||
Brahmā said: Having risen from his bed at night, that best of the twice-born should constantly remember the gods and likewise the meritorious ones with certainty. (2)
Govinda, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Dāmodara,
as well as Nārāyaṇa, Jagannātha, Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading Lord.
Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Sāvitrī—the mother of the Vedas—Brahmā, Bhāskara (the Sun), Candra (the Moon), the guardians of the quarters, and likewise the planets. ||4||
And Śaṅkara, Śiva, Śambhu, Īśvara, and Maheśvara;
Gaṇeśa and likewise Skanda, Gaurī, Bhāgīrathī, and Śivā. ||5||
King Nala is of virtuous fame; Janārdana is of virtuous fame;
indeed, the Veda is of virtuous fame; and Yudhiṣṭhira is of virtuous fame. (6)
Aśvatthāman, Bali, Vyāsa, Hanumān, Vibhīṣaṇa,
Kṛpa, and Paraśurāma— these seven are long-lived.
A person who, having risen in the morning, constantly remembers these [names], is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (8)
By reciting this even once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
one enjoys the merit of giving away hundreds of thousands of cows.
Then, one should discard feces and urine in a secluded place;
facing south at night, and facing north during the day. (10)
One should meditate upon the goad as firewood, and upon the whip as grass such as udumbara; beyond this, one should meditate upon the chariot, and by doing so, the twice-born becomes self-restrained.
In the forenoon, the twice-born should meditate upon Sarasvatī as red in color; at midday, as white in color; and in the evening, as black in color, according to the prescribed rule.
Then, one should diligently perform the bath according to one's knowledge;
having washed the limbs, one should subsequently smear them with clay.
In the region of the head, on the forehead, in the nose, in the heart, between the eyebrows, in the two arms, on the sides, as well as in the navel, the two knees, and the two feet; 14.
One application of clay should be given to the penis, three to the anus, ten to the left hand, and seven to both hands by one who desires purification. (15)
O Earth, who art trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu, bearer of wealth;
O Clay, take away this sin which has been accumulated by me in the past. (16)
Whoever should apply clay to his body with this very mantra, for him all sins are destroyed and that person becomes pure. ||17||
Then, however, the wise man should perform his bath preceded by the *Tuvet* [mantra] in a river, a stream, a well, a lotus pond, or a tank. (18)

Furthermore, for the destruction of all sins, a mortal should cause the ritual bath in a jar [filled with] the water-accumulation [of the Ganges] to be performed according to the prescribed rules. 19.
The morning bath is of great merit and destroys all sins;
the Brahmin who performs it constantly is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (20)
As long as the morning twilight remains within a distance of four *daṇḍas*,
the water offered stands as nectar for the ancestors.
From the time the pair of water-clocks (ghaṭikās) has passed until one watch (yāma) of the day,
water that is like honey increases the satisfaction of the ancestors in that period.
Then, for one and a half watches (six hours), it is traditionally held that the water consists of milk;
the water mixed with milk remains so for as long as four daṇḍas (three hours).
After this, until three watches have passed, it is called *capānīya*;
beyond that, until the sun has set, it is declared to be *lohita*.
In the fourth watch of the night, one should satisfy the ancestors with water;
that water is remembered as belonging only to the Rākṣasas, except when it is taken [for other purposes]. ||25||
This water was created by me long ago for the sake of all accomplishments;
and the yakṣas, who bear the burden, were likewise created for the protection of that water. (26)
The ancestors who have passed away to other worlds do not obtain [offerings];
for them, water is difficult to reach except through you, O dweller among mortals. (27)
Therefore, it should be offered as libations by disciples, sons, grandsons, daughters' sons, and so forth, as well as by circles of kinsmen and others who are devoted to their ancestors.
Nārada said:
"O Lord of Gods, tell me the deity of the water and the ritual for the libation (tarpaṇa); as I understand it, you ought to explain this to me according to its true essence. (29)
Brahmā said:
Viṣṇu is celebrated in all the worlds as the deity of water;
he who is purified by water becomes Viṣṇu, and he becomes Śaṅkara. (30)
By drinking even a single mouthful of water from the courtyard, a man becomes purified;
especially when mixed with *kuśa* grass, that water is superior even to nectar.
This abode of all the gods was fashioned from darbha grass in ancient times;
Brahmā resides at the root of the kuśa, while Keśava resides in its middle. (32)
One should pierce the tip of a *kuśa* blade with a needle; these [blades] are thus consecrated.
One who always holds *kuśa* grass in hand remains pure; if he recites a hymn or a mantra, [it becomes effective]. (33)
It is declared that all [these] possess a hundredfold merit, while a thousandfold is said to be found at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Likewise, there are kuśa grasses, kāśa grasses, dūrvā grasses, barley leaves, and rice grains.
Balvajas, puṇḍarikas, and kuśas are proclaimed as the seven [types of grass];
they are pure in succession and are established in the world as kuśa.
Any bath performed without mantras shall be entirely fruitless;
[only that bath] becomes as sweet as nectar through contact with sesame seeds. (36)
Therefore, a wise person should always satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds and water;
for with as many as ten sesame seeds, the satisfaction of the ancestors is supreme.
Out of fear of him, the gods do not desire excessive expansion;
he who, having bathed, daily gratifies the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds. (38)
By dwelling in the Nīlaparṇa forest with water mixed with rice, and by the gift of lamps during the rainy season, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors. (39)
He who gratifies the ancestors with sesame seeds on the new moon day for one year attains the status of Vināyaka and is worshipped by all the gods.
Whoever offers libations to the ancestors with sesame seeds on all the Yugādi days obtains a hundred times more merit than what has been declared for the new moon day (Amāvāsyā). 41.
By likewise satiating the assembly of ancestors on the solstices, the equinoxes, and on the Rākā and Māyā days, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Likewise, during the Manvantara known as Tāraka, or during any other auspicious occasion, at the time of an eclipse of the moon or sun, or at holy pilgrimage sites such as Gayā and others; ||43||
Having gratified the ancestors, one should go to the abode of Mādhava;
having obtained from there a day of merit (*puṇyāha*), one should satisfy the multitude of ancestors.
Having first performed the libation for the deities with a concentrated mind, the wise man subsequently becomes qualified for the libation for the ancestors. 45.
At the time of eating during a śrāddha, one should cause [the food] to be given with one hand;
during the libation (tarpaṇa), one should give with both hands—this is the eternal rule.
Facing the south and being pure, one should satisfy the ancestors with the words "May they be satisfied," while again [pronouncing] their names and lineages.
If, out of delusion, one should satisfy the assembly of ancestors with non-black sesame seeds, or if a donor gives water while standing on the ground instead of remaining in the water; (48)
That gift is given in vain; it does not reach anyone.
For that man who, standing on dry land, offers water into the water [is acting fruitlessly]. (49)
If one performs the water-libation for the ancestors while wearing wet clothes, that water does not reach them; it is useless. (50)
O sinless one, his ancestors are always gratified along with the gods;
yet they consider a garment washed by dyers to be impure.
After washing one's hands, the cloth becomes pure once again;
wearing dry clothes in a clean place, one should offer libations to the ancestors.
Then the ancestors certainly become satisfied tenfold more by bathing and performing *saṃdhyā* with water from a stone, a sword, or a copper vessel.
He who performs the libation for each [ancestor] more than a hundred times,
holding a silver ring on his forefinger, shall satisfy the ancestors.
And all this becomes increased a hundred-thousandfold, and not otherwise;
likewise, O wise one, having placed a gold ring upon the ring-finger (anāmikā). (55)
One should satisfy the assembly of ancestors; the merit shall be a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold.
Between the thumb and the forefinger of the right hand is the sword (khaḍgaka).
Having held that jewel which yields inexhaustible fruit,
the gods, together with the hosts of ancestors, approached it for the purpose of bathing.
Afflicted by thirst and seeking water, they follow after those who have become like the wind; yet, having lost all hope, they turn back just as one does upon wringing out a garment.
Therefore, one should not wring out one's garment without having performed the libation to the ancestors (pitr-tarpana).
There are thirty-five million body hairs on a human being. (59)
All sacred fords flow from that [head]; therefore, one should not cause it pain.
The gods drink from the head, and likewise the ancestors from the beard.
From the eyes, moreover, the Gandharvas were born; from below [the eyes], all the gods and the hosts of Pitṛs, as well as the Gandharvas, were born from the skin. (61)
They are satisfied by mere bathing; through bathing, no sin remains.
That man who performs the daily bath is the most excellent of persons. (62)
Completely liberated from all sins, he is honored in various celestial worlds;
the gods and great sages know this to be the culmination of bathing and libations.
Beyond this, the wise man should cause the worship of the gods to be performed;
he who worships Gaṇeśa encounters no obstacle.
One should worship Sūrya for the sake of health, Mādhava for the sake of dharma and liberation,
Śiva for the sake of rites and desired objects, and Caṇḍikā for the sake of all desires.
Having worshipped the deities, one should indeed perform the Vaiśvadeva offering;
then, having performed the fire-rite, one should conduct the sacrifice and the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having made his coming and going firm, he shall go again to the third heaven of the gods and all sentient beings; having attained liberation and the bliss of heaven according to his desires.
Therefore, with every effort, one should constantly perform ritual acts.
Nārada said:
"And for what purpose, O Father, do the gods together with the hosts of ancestors offer water?"
"Those men do not attain the acquisition of omniscience.
Brahmā said:
"In the past, this water, consisting of the nectar of all the gods, was created by me. (69)
For the sake of guarding him alone, the yakṣas who carry bows as protectors slay even his father, the god, at our command, for he is not a human being.
Animals, birds, and insects established in the world of the immortals, as well as those born as mortals—gods and likewise humans—are indeed constant [in their nature]. (71)
Having constantly gratified their guru, they are established in the world of the gods;
whereas one who does not bathe eats filth, and one who does not recite prayers consumes pus and blood.

That righteous-souled one, his intellect undeluded, spoke to the prince:
"This difficult deed which has been performed by me was for the sake of your welfare. (125)
I consider everything to be in vain according to the common talk of people;
today I shall go into the fire, O men and gods, while you look on! (126)
Having spoken thus, that illustrious one entered the fire;
as he was entering the flames, a flower remained in his mass of hair.
Neither fire consumed her limbs, nor her garments, nor her body;
the gods in the sky were filled with joy and cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (128).
Then, showers of flowers fell simultaneously upon his head by those who had spoken harsh words directed at both of them.
Various kinds of leprosy were produced in their mouths;
then the gods, having arrived there, joyfully drew it away from Agni.
The sages, filled with wonder, worshipped him with beautiful flowers;
likewise, all the best of sages and various kinds of men did so at that time.
That one of great splendor was honored, and he in turn honored all;
he was named Sajjanādrohaka by the gods, asuras, and humans.
Purified by the dust of his feet, she became filled with grain; and the gods there said to him, "Accept this woman as your wife."
There has never been his equal in the world, nor will there ever be;
at present, there is no man on earth who has conquered the stain of greed. (134)
For gods, asuras, humans, rākṣasas, beasts, birds, and all others beginning with insects, this desire is exceedingly difficult to conquer. (135)
From desire, greed, and likewise from anger, [attachment] constantly arises toward sentient beings; this desire is the binder in saṃsāra, for there is no such thing as desirelessness anywhere. (136)
By him alone all fourteen worlds have been conquered; Vāsudeva dwells eternally within his heart with joy. (137)
Having thus touched or seen him, men are freed from all impurity; they become sinless and indeed attain the imperishable heaven.
Having spoken thus, the gods departed joyfully for heaven in their celestial chariots;
the humans likewise, being satisfied, went to their own homes with their husbands.
Then he possessed divine vision and beheld the gods; moreover, he came to know the news of the three worlds with great ease.
Then, having seen him on that very street, he approached him together with him and asked:
"O noble one, speak of the teaching of Dharma that is beneficial."
Sajjanādroha said:
"Go to Puruṣottama, the Vaiṣṇava who knows the dharma of Bāḍaba;
upon seeing him, your desire will now bear fruit. (142)
"Know that the drying up of the ocean and likewise the non-drying of this cloth—whatever other desire resides in your heart, you shall know it. (143)
Having heard these words, he went toward the Vaiṣṇava and departed joyfully along with that brahmin who possessed the form of Viṣṇu.
He saw a pure person standing before him, blazing,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and shining with his own splendor.
That righteous-souled one spoke to the beloved of Hari, who was absorbed in meditation, saying:
"I have come from afar, reporting everything that has occurred and how I have arrived before you. (146)
The Vaiṣṇava said:
"O twice-born one, the Lord of the gods, the foremost of the Asuras and the enemy of the Dānavas, is always pleased with you;
and now, upon seeing you, our mind rejoices as it were. (147)
If today’s auspicious and incomparable [deed] had borne fruit, my desire would have been fulfilled;
otherwise, my garment would not dry so quickly in the path of the gods. (148)
Having seen Lord Hari, the best of gods, stationed in my house, the Vaiṣṇava spoke thus; then, having been praised, he spoke again. (149)
"Where does that Viṣṇu eternally reside? Show him to me today through your grace.
The Vaiṣṇava said:
"Having entered this beautiful temple of the gods, [behold] the Supreme Lord. (150)
"Upon seeing him, you shall be liberated from terrible sin and from the bondage of birth.
Having heard those words of his, he entered the house.
He saw that twice-born Viṣṇu standing upon a lotus-bed;
bowing his head, he then joyfully grasped his feet.
O Lord of Gods, you were previously recognized by me as one who has become gracious; O Lord of Gods, O Master, I am your servant both here and in the hereafter. (153)
And this favor has been shown to me by you, O Madhusūdana;
if you have compassion for me, I wish to see your form. (154)
Viṣṇu said:
"O god among men, you are indeed always dear to me;
out of affection for those who possess merit, I have caused you to be seen by me. (155)
Through seeing, touching, meditating upon, praising, or conversing with them—even once—the meritorious alone enjoy eternal heaven. (156)
By this constant creation, there shall be the destruction of all sins;
having experienced infinite happiness, one dissolves into my own body. ||157||
Having bathed in sacred fords and having beheld me everywhere, and having seen the lands of the meritorious, one dissolves into my body. (158)
Having always spoken virtuous discourse in the presence of the world, he indeed dissolves into the body of that tiger among men. (159)
Having fasted on our day and having certainly heard my life-story, one who performs a vigil at night is absorbed into my body. 160.
Constantly reciting the name of the best of the twice-born amidst the sounds of horses, dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the like, he dissolves into my body. 161.
"You alone have become a sacred pilgrimage site because of the slaying of Baka;
for the sake of his liberation from whatever sin he committed, he spoke while remaining in the sky. (162)
"Go to the high-souled Gacchamūka, the best of holy places for the meritorious;
O father, by the sight of Mūka, all great people have been seen. (163)
"Simply by seeing them, by conversing with them, and through the state of my association with them, you have come to my house. (164)
For one whose sins have been exhausted over thousands of millions of births, the Knower of Dharma regards him with equanimity; such is the clarity of his vision. 165.
"O sinless child, it is solely by my grace that I have been seen by you;
therefore, choose a boon, whatever dwells in your mind. (166)
The brahmin said:
"Let our mind, which is entirely without a protector, rest in you;
for apart from you, it has never found delight in anyone else in all the worlds. (167)
Mādhava said:
"O sinless one, because such an understanding always flashes within you,
therefore you shall obtain enjoyments equal to mine in my own abode."
"But will your parents receive worship from you, O sinless one? Only after you have worshipped your parents shall you enter my body. (169)
By the wind of their breath and by their intense anger, their ascetic merit constantly leaks away; therefore, O twice-born one, worship them. 170.
In that son upon whom the anger of his parents constantly falls, neither the Creator nor Śaṅkara can provide protection here from hell. 171.
Therefore, go to your parents and perform worship for them with diligence;
then, by their very grace, which is beneficial to both, proceed to my state.
When this had been said, the best of the twice-born spoke again to the Teacher of the World:
"If you are pleased with me, O Lord, then show me your own form, O Acyuta. (173)
Then, his heart gladdened by the affection of the twice-born, that self-controlled one,
devoted to the Brahmanas, revealed his true form for the sake of the Brahmin's ritual.
The Supreme Person, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, is the cause of all worlds; he fills the universe with his splendor. 175.
Having prostrated like a staff, the brahmin spoke again to Acyuta: "Today my birth has become fruitful; today my two eyes have become auspicious. (176)
"O Lord of the World, today my two hands have become praiseworthy and dark;
today these men go to the eternal world of Brahmā. (177)
"O Janārdana, by your grace today my kinsmen have been restored;
and now all my heart's desires have indeed been fulfilled. (178)
O Lord, why is it that you do not feel great astonishment at the knowledge of the Mūka and others?
How do they know my history, even though I have arrived from another land? (179)
A most excellent Brahmin resided within the space inside his house,
and likewise, [the same was true] in the house of the devoted wife upon the head of Tulādhāra.
Likewise, O foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, you are one who does not harm even his enemies;
therefore, O Brahmin, by my grace, you ought to speak the truth as it is.
The Blessed Lord said:
"He was always devoted to his parents and remained silent; she was a chaste and auspicious wife;
Tulādhāra was a speaker of truth and equal toward all people. (182)
One who has conquered greed and lust, who is free from malice, and who is devoted to me is known as a Vaiṣṇava.
Delighted by these qualities of theirs, I dwell joyfully in their homes. (183)
O best of the twice-born, together with Bhāratī and Kamalā, the Brahmin said: "Due to the association with great sinners, men become as if they were even greater sinners. (184)
"Thus do those who know the Dharma always declare in the Smṛti scriptures, the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Vedas; why then do you remain at home? (185)
The Blessed Lord said:

Even a person who is mute and born of a Cāṇḍāla womb, if he is established in virtuous conduct and is the performer of all auspicious deeds in the three worlds, the gods know him to be a Brāhmaṇa. (186)
In this world, there is no one equal to a mute person in terms of meritorious deeds;
by one who is constantly devoted to his parents, the three worlds are conquered. (187)
Pleased by their devotion, I, together with all the hosts of gods,
remained in the interior of his house in the form of a twice-born brahmin.
Likewise, [one should go] to the house of a devoted wife, to the palace of Tulādhāra, to the home of Adroha, and to the residence of a Vaiṣṇava.
I always abide in the Knower of Dharma; I do not abandon him even for a moment. Therefore, those others who are doers of evil do not see me constantly. 190.
Because of your merit, you have been seen by me for the sake of showing favor;
devoted to your parents, pure, though a Cāṇḍāla, you have attained the state of a deity. (191)
Therefore, out of affection for him, I remained with him in that palace;
again and again, I engaged in conversation with that twice-born man.
I always abide in his celestial chariot, contemplating him;
he knows your conduct, as do those devoted wives and others.
I shall tell you their history; listen to it in due order, for by hearing it, an immortal is in every way liberated from the bondage of birth. (194)
There is no sacred place higher than one's father and mother among all the gods of gods;
he by whom the worship of his parents is performed is indeed the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). 195.
The fruit of honoring one's parents and the command of a deity or a guru is equal.
Through the worship of heaven, one attains sovereignty; through its violation, one goes to the Raurava hell. (196)
Even though he dwells within my heart, I dwell within his heart;
there is no interval between us, and in this world and the next, there is none equal to me.
Together with all his kinsmen, he shall enjoy inexhaustible pleasures in the most beautiful city of Madagrēma. ||198||
For this very reason, O tiger among men, that mute man knows the news arising from the three worlds; whence comes this wonder of yours? (199)
The twice-born said:

"O Lord of the world, whether out of delusion or ignorance I have failed to perform the worship of my father, what should be done now that I am aware of it? Tell me, O Lord of the good and the evil. (200)
The Blessed Lord said:
He by whom devotion to his parents has been practiced for even a single day, a month, a fortnight, half a fortnight, or a year, shall go to my abode.
Having caused mental anguish, one will inevitably go to hell;
for before this [act], there was no other worship of the parents, whether performed or not performed. 202.
By performing the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), a man obtains the fruit of devotion to his ancestors;
he should likewise offer food, clothing, and products of the cow, whether with meat or without meat.
Whatever is given by a wise son to his kinsmen is said to possess a hundred thousandfold merit; indeed, he has performed the Śrāddha rite with his entire being.
One attains the memory of past births and receives the fruit of devotion to one's ancestors;
there is no great sacrifice superior to the Śrāddha in the three worlds. (205)
Whatever is given here, all of it enjoys imperishability;
know that ten thousandfold is for others, while a hundred thousand is said to be for kinsmen.
It is said that [the merit] at Piṇḍatīrtha is ten millionfold, while for a twice-born man it is declared to be infinite;
likewise at the waters of the Gaṅgā, at Gayā, at Prayāga, and at Puṣkara. (207)
Whoever offers a ball of rice at Siddhakuṇḍa in Vārāṇasī, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, will certainly attain liberation. (208)
The ancestors obtain imperishable heaven as the fruit of their birth for him who especially offers water with sesame seeds in the Bhāgīrathī. (209)
If one attains the path to liberation even by the offering of a single morsel of food, how much more so when it is offered by the thousands on riverbanks?
It is held that [the merit] at rivers is ten thousandfold.
Through the association with common auspicious fruits, the śrāddha becomes a hundredfold meritorious on the new moon day,
on the anniversaries of the Yugas, and during solar and lunar eclipses.
He who performs the Pārvaṇa rite attains an imperishable world;
all his ancestors remain satisfied for ten thousand years.
Having bestowed upon his son beloved blessings and infinite enjoyments,
he then joyfully performed the Pārvaṇa rite with his sons on the auspicious lunar day.
By performing this sacrifice for one's parents, one is liberated from the bondage of birth; that śrāddha which is performed day after day is known as the *nitya-śrāddha*. (214)
He who performs [the rite] with faith attains an imperishable world;
likewise, one should perform the optional *śrāddha* during the dark fortnight according to the prescribed rules.
Having performed this without desire, one attains whatever dwells in the mind;
taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, that which follows is the fifth fortnight.
In that regard, one should perform the *śrāddha* during the period when the sun enters Virgo;
for there are sixteen days while the sun remains in Virgo. (217)
These are equal to sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial fees;
this highly meritorious optional *śrāddha* has arrived as auspicious for him. (218)
Due to the absence [of offerings] during the dark fortnight, starting from the month of Tulā, the ancestors fall into despair as the new moon arrives in Vṛścika. (219)
Having uttered a most terrible curse, they returned again to their own abode;
it is recorded that by the father’s curse, everything belonging to the son was destroyed. ||220||
Wealth, sons, fame, desired objects, and even long life—all these are to be obtained by human beings birth after birth. (221)
Because it is the most excellent [offering] for the ancestors, one should not exclude it;
having performed the *nāndīmukha* rite, a twice-born man [should perform it] at marriages, vows, sacrifices, and other such occasions. (222)
One obtains inexhaustible merit, and one's spiritual lineage increases;
the person who acts in the opposite of this way goes to hell.
The destruction of his family would occur, and he would remain miserable even while alive;
therefore, one should first worship Gaṇeśa, Śambhu, and Damanaka.
Furthermore, one should [offer] the sixteen Mothers and, after them, the assembly of ancestors, beginning with the great-grandfather, into all the mouths of the flames. (225)
The wise man should have all the twice-born seated facing east at the mouth of the *nāṃdī*; he should cause them to utter the word "namaḥ" and employ the word "svadhā" where appropriate.
Even if a man has not offered the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and water during an eclipse of the moon or sun, he obtains an imperishable heaven that increases the nourishment of his ancestors. ||227||
If a man does not perform a ritual bath there, nor offers rice-balls and water according to his ability,
he goes to the state of a caṇḍāla for his ancestors.
Every gift is equal to the earth, all Brahmins are equal to Vyāsa, and everything is equal to the Gaṅgā when the moon is seized by Rāhu. (229)
A single arm-slap is said to have a merit of one hundred thousand; ten lakhs [of such merits] are attained when the sun is in Tula (Libra).
However, when the sun is in Gaṅgā (Aquarius), ten crores of such arm-slaps are attained.
The fruit that is said to come from the correct gift of a hundred thousand cows, that same fruit they say comes from bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is eclipsed. (231)
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one who plunges into the Ganges has bathed in all sacred fords; what need is there to wander the earth?
A solar eclipse on a Sunday and likewise a lunar eclipse on a Monday is known as the "Cūḍāmaṇi" (the crest-jewel); in that case, the fruit is remembered as infinite.
That man who, having fasted at the former Puṇyatīrtha, offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa), water, and gifts, is established in Satyaloka. ||234||
The twice-born said:
"Thus has the great sacrifice and the śrāddha for your father been described. O dear one, what indeed should be performed by a son at the time of his final departure? (235)
"O God, having performed what supreme good is obtained in birth after birth?
You ought to explain this with effort to me through your son, who is possessed of wisdom. (236)
The Blessed Lord said:
"When one has reached an advanced age, the relationship is remembered as 'father and son';
furthermore, in later life, the son becomes the father because of his role in protection, and not because of worship. (237)
One should worship one's father like a god and show him affection like a son;
one should never transgress his word, even in thought.
The son who provides medical treatment for his sick father attains imperishable heaven and is forever honored by the gods. (239)
Even for a dying father who beholds the signs of death,
a son who performs the funeral sacrifice attains equality with the gods.
Listen, I shall describe the merit of that wise son who, by means of fasting according to the prescribed rite, bestows heaven upon his father. (241)
The merit of those two who fast would equal that of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecrations, and it would be ten million times the merit of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
O Puruṣottama, that man who dies in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī shall not drink the milk from his mother’s breast again; he shall attain liberation.
He who, however, should give up his life spontaneously at Vārāṇasī, having enjoyed his desired fruit, dissolves into my own body. (244)
That goal which belongs to the sages who are disciplined in yoga and whose vital energy is drawn upward,
that same goal belongs to one who gives up his life-breaths among the seven sons of Brahmā.
Whoever, relying on the banks of the Lohita river without distinction, should abandon their life according to the prescribed rite, shall attain equality with me. 246.
O best of the twice-born, one who dies and is reborn at that very sacred ford called Urvaśīkeśa does not become defiled by any faults; he attains everything.
If one's life were certainly to be lost within the interior of a house, as long as that book remained in the house, bondage would remain upon the body. (248)
Year after year, even a single portion continues to diminish;
for those watching their sons and kinsmen, there is no compensation for this loss of wealth.
One who dies on a mountain, in a forest, in a difficult pass, or in a place devoid of water, attains a miserable rebirth; he is born again as a worm or similar creature. (250)
And for whomsoever the funeral rites are performed on the day after death,
he remains in the Kumbhīpāka hell for sixty thousand years.
Merely by touching one who is untouchable, he becomes impure, fallen, and dead;
having remained in hell for a very long time, he is born among the mleccha tribes.
In the same way, one is born among species of beings with many insects;
therefore, one should understand that merit and demerit bear fruit before long. (253)
Through merit and the application of meritorious deeds, for all inhabitants of the mortal world, such is the destination reached by men at the time of death. (254)
One who dies at a holy pilgrimage site while meditating upon the names of Viṣṇu shall go to heaven purified of sin;
he is not tainted by any faults.
Whatever strong son carries the body of his deceased father, he undoubtedly obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step. ||256||
Before the piling of the funeral fire, the son should cause the father’s body to enter the mouth-fire;
afterwards, he should burn the body again according to the rite purified by mantras.
May I burn away all the limbs [of this body] joined with greed and delusion and enveloped by both sin and merit; may he go to the divine worlds.
Having cremated [the body], even a son should cross over [the river] before the collection of the bones;
when the tenth day has arrived, he should discard his wet garment.
Having cut off the blood-stained garment, he should then cast it into fire or water;
thereafter, on the eleventh day, the wise man should perform the śrāddha rite.
For the sake of nourishing the body of the deceased, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa;
and according to the prescribed rite, one should give gifts such as clothing, a seat, and sandals.
One should give land, elephants, horses, and the like, along with all necessary implements, together with a black-bodied cow, for the sake of liberation from all sins.
The fourth, the ninth, the third fortnight, the sixth month, and likewise the annual [śrāddha],
as well as the twelve monthly ones— these are the sixteen śrāddhas.
For one who does not desire these [offerings] with faith according to their capacity,
their state as a piśāca remains firm even by means of hundreds of śrāddhas performed for them.
One should offer a water-pot every month and food accompanied by meat;
if the daily offerings are absent, one should pass the month by making these monthly offerings.
When one year has passed, the wise and best of the twice-born should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha according to the rules of the Pārvaṇa rite.
Impurity for a father lasts one year, and for a mother it is six months;
for a wife it is three months, and half of that for both a brother and a son. (267)
Impurity for sapindas shall last as long as [the corpse] remains in the house;
now listen, for I shall tell you that which is prohibited for a son. ||268||
A celibate student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) who observes proper conduct should never approach a woman, either after seven ghaṭīs or before nine ghaṭīs [of the night]. (269)
The Kutapa period should be known as the proper time for the ancestors; what is given then becomes inexhaustible.
In a Śrāddha ceremony, three things are purifying: a daughter's son, the Kutapa period, and sesame seeds.

And here, three things are praised: truthfulness, freedom from anger, and lack of haste; as well as evening twilight devotion, avoiding food given by others, and abstaining from eating a second time and from sexual intercourse. (271)
Having performed a *śrāddha*, one should avoid both giving and receiving gifts;
a wise person should perform a *śrāddha* even after having committed a hundred deeds that ought not to be done.
"That it must be performed was spoken by Viriñci himself;
listen, my son, to this ancient account, which I shall relate to you concerning many [beings]. (273)
Having performed the cow-sacrifice for their guru, they gave the śrāddha offering and went to heaven;
by the mere recitation of their names, the śrāddha becomes inexhaustible.
The seven disciples of the sage Vasiṣṭha were Brahmins of excellent vows; when the ancestral Śrāddha ceremony arrived, they [approached] the sacrificial cow, the preceptor’s beloved.
Having entreated him and led him home with joy, the seven brothers,
without reflection, killed that cow for the sake of its products during a sacrifice to the ancestors.
They gave me to the Brahmin, and the Brahmins fed me the remainder; having completed the rites for the ancestors, O child, those twice-born ones took hold of me. (277)
They offered the cow to their preceptor, saying, "It has been devoured by a tiger.
Then, through the power of his asceticism, he understood the truth and performed a rite for them.
"Along with the sages, you shall become outcasts (caṇḍālas) as you fall from your discipleship. Then the Brahmins stood trembling, their palms joined in reverence.
O sinless one, those who always bestow a cow upon me for the sake of ancestral rites [overcome] thousands of forbidden acts and even great sins. (280)
"By performing the ancestral rites (pitr-karya), they have gone to heaven purified of sin;
I have heard this various ancient account from the mouth of my Lord. (281)
"O knower of dharma, you ought to forgive me; let an end be ordained for this curse.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"A curse, like sin, is exhausted through the discernment of dharma. (282)
Even those born from outcasts and the like will remember past events; there shall be no loss of knowledge for you, and the scripture of memory (Smṛti) shall not perish. 283.
"O twice-born ones, having crossed over that evil birth, you shall afterwards attain liberation;
then, O brahmins, you shall give up your lives due to the curse of your preceptor. (284)
Though born into the Cāṇḍāla caste, they were all endowed with knowledge;
they did not drink breast milk, as they remembered their previous births.
All the cakravāka birds that had died and not yet been reborn were born again as deer in the forest;
however, the white haṃsa birds, having been twice-born brahmins, were reborn at the Mānasa-tīrtha.
Desirous of death, O highly fortunate one, they died because of that cause of distress.
At that time, O great king, there was one known as Dharmaketu. ||287||
Then, accompanied by his wife and his retinue, he went to that sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to bathe;
meanwhile, out of delusion, three swans [seized] the kingdom, the enjoyments, and his wife.
Having reflected upon the objects of enjoyment and having known the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, they then departed for the other world, thinking, "We shall attain liberation. (189)
Thinking thus, they departed from here toward another world.
Then three kings were born, and four most excellent brahmins. (290)
In Kurukṣetra, they knew the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas equally through the power of their austerity, as well as the news of both this world and the next.
Three kings born in royal families were deluded by pride; due to the loss of their wisdom, they did not know the higher world or what was beneficial. 292.
Then those Brahmins, having summoned their own servant from the house, said with agitation:
"Go to the king and, out of your own wretchedness, give him the document. (293)
The seven hunters were born as deer in the Daśārṇa region; they became Kinnaras on Mount Jārudhi;
they were Cakravāka birds on Śaradvīpa; and they were swans in Lake Mānasa. (294)
"O Brahmins born of the three [classes], who have mastered the Vedas in Kurukṣetra!
You have set out upon the road as messengers; why do you falter? (295)
Having taken the letter from the servant, he showed it to the king;
and having seen the letter, the king immediately abandoned his kingdom and went to the twice-born brahmins.
Having heard their words, those whose wealth was asceticism then departed;
and in a very short time, they attained liberation along with them.
O twice-born one, whoever hears this account of the seven hunters and the rest during a śrāddha ceremony,
inexhaustible food and drink reaches his ancestors.
The twice-born said: O Keśava, how can the ancestral rites (pitr-kārya) be performed by a brahmin who is destitute of wealth, whether he be an ascetic, a forest-dweller, or a householder?
The Blessed One said:
"Having gathered grass and wood without requesting even a single cowrie shell, one performs the ancestral rites; that [merit] shall become a hundred thousandfold. (300)
Even if one has committed a hundred forbidden acts, the man who performs the ancestral *śrāddha* rite sees all his sins destroyed and goes to heaven. ||301||

Even when no other [guests] are present, the man who gives fodder to cows on the anniversary of his father's death obtains a fruit even greater than that of offering the funeral cakes (piṇḍa). ||302||
Formerly, in the forest regions, he was extremely wretched and wept;
now that his father has arrived as a guest, he weeps because of his total lack of possessions. (303)
Having wept for a very long time, he too questioned the learned brahmin: "O Brahmin, what indeed might be done today on this day of the ancestors and guests that would be beneficial? (304)
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, I have a cowrie shell and some wealth;
please grant me instruction by which I may remain established in dharma. (305)
The twice-born said:
"Go quickly now to the forest during this Kutapa muhūrta;
having taken water, offer it swiftly for the sake of your father, saying, 'May you attain heaven.'"
Then, having taken a bundle of fodder according to his instruction and having given it to the cow for the sake of her nourishment, he was as delighted as if he had received it himself. ||307||
By the grace of this merit, he went to the celestial realm;
having enjoyed heaven for a very long time, he was reborn into a family of wealthy men.
Due to his former merit and for the sake of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña),
the wealthy man offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father with all his possessions and wealth.
There, having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu through practice in a single birth,

so too must a gift of dowry (yautaka) be given by one who is truly virtuous.
Having failed to give, one falls into hell and enters into servitude;
this applies to those who are too near, those who are too far, those who are excessively wealthy, and those who are extremely destitute. (94)

A daughter should not be given to one who is of low birth, nor to a fool; nor to one who is excessively old, nor to one who is extremely destitute, nor to one who is most diseased, nor to a resident of a foreign land. (95)
Even if he is extremely angry or dissatisfied, a daughter must not be given to these six types of men;
by giving a daughter to such as these, one goes to hell. (96)
Out of greed for honor and gain, and by means of exchanging a young girl, he [seized] a woman who was a beloved of the sages, youthful, and endowed with beauty. ||97||

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Women," within the *Pañcākhyāna* section of the first book, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.

There is no one equal to Tulādhāra established in the world of the gods;

By merely reciting it once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
in the presence of the worlds, brahmins, and gods, one shall attain the state of being worthy of worship.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śūdra Named Alobha," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||53||

He was renowned as Śaṃtunaḥ, and his wife was a devoted pativrata;

And while Brahmā had gone to her house to search for her husband, at that time the best of sages had gone to the forest for the sake of flowers and other offerings. ||21||
Seeing Sāta, the best of gods, she offered him water for his hands and feet and other honors;

"In the eastern direction, within the interior of a cave, there is the Devaśa-tīrtha.
Having heard that, the tiger among men went and beheld the pool.
The clockwise-turning whirlpool of water was bright, auspicious, and a destroyer of sins;
by the mere touch of that water, Kuṭhāra attained purity. (49)
Then Rāma, filled with great joy, performed the consecration;
and in that pure-souled and sinless one, a purified intellect was born.
Having stayed for a very long time at that king of holy places (Prayāga) and having propitiated it thoroughly,
he then departed from that mountain and reached the city with great speed.
Having made it famous, he then went from the earth to the salt ocean;
this excellent sacred site was manifested on earth by the Grandfather himself.
It is indeed the bestower of happiness in every respect, pure, and the provider of the path to liberation;
know that such is the power of desire, which is both irresistible and unbearable.

The son born of lust is wicked; the son born of merit is virtuous through the application of merit; likewise, the son born together [with the mother], the son of a *lohita* woman, and the legitimate (*aurasa*) son. (54)
May there be peace for Śantanu, who was born from the field [of Ganga] and originated from the womb of Amoghā;
he who is the unconquered Kāma by Viriñci, yet free from envy even toward Śantanu.
Because of her devotion to her husband, she is indeed the most excellent of all holy places;
thus, whoever constantly recites this auspicious and meritorious narrative, [attains the same]. //56//
Or whoever hears it on this earth shall go upon the path of liberation. ||57||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of the Lauhitya," in the *Pañcākhyāna* section of the first book, the *Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The Fifty-sixth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: In ancient times, Śarva saw women endowed with youthful beauty belonging to Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and humans everywhere. (1)
Having drawn them toward him by means of a mantra from the far reaches of the sky,
the Lord, under the pretext of practicing asceticism, fixed his mind upon them.
Having fashioned exceedingly beautiful bower-huts, Maheśvara, who had previously conquered the god of love, suddenly engaged in play together with them.
In the meantime, Gaurī’s mind became bewildered;
through the power of meditation, she beheld that Lord of the Universe sporting there.
Perceiving that he was surrounded by women, she fell under the sway of anger;
then, assuming the form of Kṣemaṅkarī, she entered [the city].
In the midst of the vast expanse of space, far away, he beheld the Supreme Person, white and radiant like the god of love, situated between the Vāmā and Atimadhyā [channels].
Embracing him repeatedly with the women, they sported with him again and again;
they kissed that god Hara intensely, as he was overcome by passion.
Seeing Vṛttaṅkṣemaṅkarī, he then fell before her;
pulling her by the hair, he struck her with his feet.
Afflicted by shame, Śarva stood with his face turned away;
then, pulling them by the hair out of anger, he cast them down upon the ground.
Having suddenly reached the lowest state, their faces transformed, their limbs scorched by Umā’s curse, all the women fell under the power of the Mlecchas. ||10||
And those women known as Cāṇḍālas, whether widowed or accompanied by their husbands, all of them continue even today to suffer the curse uttered by Umā. (11)
Then Umā, having assumed a form with a hundred streams, united with the Lord;
O twice-born one, know that such is the constant power of Kāma.
Then, after a long time, he went with her to Mount Kailāsa;
therefore, those men who behold Kṣemaṅkarī [attain] bliss. (13)
O you whose entire body is reddened with saffron and whose face is as white as the moon, [you who grant] the presence or absence of wealth, prosperity, and power for them in this world and the next.
O Goddess who bestows all auspiciousness, salutations to you, the bringer of security!
Through that very [power], there is equality with the Yoginīs, whether one faces toward them or away from them. 15.
Having seen her, one who does not bow down suffers defeat in battle; by bowing down to her in royal palaces and in the pursuit of knowledge, victory shall be attained. (16)
Thus, O Bhava, you have fallen under the sway of delusion regarding the greatness of Kāma;
this [Kāma] has attained power over the gods and asuras through his forbearance.
There has never been his equal in this world, nor will there ever be;
he who held Rāma on his lap while reclining upon a beautiful couch upon the surface of the earth.
Having thus renounced [the world], they have attained worlds that are very difficult even for gods and demons to reach;
such indeed is the foremost of the Vaiṣṇavas, worshipped by the hosts of gods and demons. (19)
He gives the food to the digestive fire and enjoys the remainder himself;
thus, through the steadiness of practice over a long period, happiness is attained. (20)
Having seen his own wife before their union, he joyfully gave her to me; having resolved upon a twelve-year period of celibacy, he was previously established by me in the enjoyment of my own power.
Therefore, I always remain in his house for the sake of protecting it; likewise, I always desire the fresh juice of the *dhātrī* fruit.
Therefore, O Brahmin, I have previously stated that other Vaiṣṇavas and even those who are not Vaiṣṇavas, as well as devotees of the gods, are followers of the wrong path. ||23||
Whatever has been done by them has been done by this supreme one;
therefore, I have composed this delightful "Essence of Vaiṣṇavism" (Vaiṣṇavasarvasva). ||24||
"I shall remain in this house for a moment; I do not move from here.
O twice-born one, I am easily accessible to those who are devoted to me. (25)
Today I have indeed bestowed our own status upon them for my own sake;
the Brahmin’s benevolence toward us both, as well as the food enjoyed in dreams and so forth, is equal. (26)
Beholding the supreme state of union and friendship with the gods,
Mūka and all the others then welcomed Hari, the Lord.
Even those meritorious beings who, together with their wives and retinues, desire to go to heaven—even the house-lizards in their own homes that dwell near them—[attain that state]. (28)
The gods followed those various insects and other creatures.
Vyāsa said:
In the meantime, the gods, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis [arrived]. (29)
They rained down showers of flowers and cried out "Excellent! Excellent!", while divine drums resounded both in the celestial chariots and in the groves.
Having each mounted his own chariot, they went to the city of Harivīthī.
Beholding that miracle, the Brahmin spoke to Janārdana: ||31||
"O Lord of gods, O Madhusūdana, tell me your instruction.
The Blessed One said:
"Go, my son, to your parents whose minds are overwhelmed with grief."
Having propitiated them with diligent effort, you will reach my abode before long;
for the gods who dwell in the celestial realm stand equal to one's father and mother.
By whom this body, though always most contemptible, was protected in childhood, nourished, and even made to grow, accompanied as it was by the faults of ignorance. (34)
There were none equal to those two in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile; therefore, all the hosts of gods were filled with joy by those five [deeds]. (35)
Praising Mādhava, they went to the delightful city of Hari,
which was inlaid with jewels and constructed by Viśvakarman.
Abounding in jewels, filled with desired things, endowed with wish-fulfilling trees and the like,
variegated with houses made of gold and all kinds of gems.

It possessed stairs made of diamond and lapis lazuli, was joined by the waters of golden rivers, was filled with songs, instrumental music, and the like, and was crowded with all kinds of difficult terrains. ||38||
Abounding in the warbling of cuckoos, frequented by *siddhas* and *gandharvas*, and filled with virtuous people rich in beauty, it was like the city of the gods, Prayāga, in the sky. (39)
Then, having remained there, all those who had fallen from their positions were firmly established above all the worlds;
and the twice-born one, having gone to his parents, propitiated them with great effort. (40)
In no long time at all, he went to Haridvāra with his family.
This meritorious Pañcākhyāna has been fully recounted by me to you. 41.
Whoever reads or even hears this shall have no miserable rebirth here;
he shall never be tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Whatever fruit a person obtains by the gift of ten million cows, that same fruit one attains from immersing oneself in the *Pañcākhyāna*. 43.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing daily and at all times in the Puṣkara and Bhāgīrathī, that one attains simply from hearing [this] once.
It swiftly destroys bad dreams and likewise bestows health; since it brings about both prosperity and well-being, it must certainly be heard. 45.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Five Narratives," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||56||
The Fifty-Seventh Chapter.
The twice-born said:
"O tiger among sages, if you have favor toward us, then fame, dharma, and all the most excellent things in the worlds shall be ours. (1)
Vyāsa said: He in whose dug-out forest-pit the cows remain satisfied for even a month,
or for as little as seven days, becomes purified and honored by all the gods.
Listen now to all that fruit which is obtained here by the gift of water at this Puṣkariṇī, which is uniquely purified by sacrificial rites. (3)
Year after year and indeed kalpa after kalpa, this is ordained:
by giving water at all times on earth, one attains heaven.
As many thousands of years as there are drops of spray produced when a cloud rains upon the earth,
for that long does that man enjoy heaven.
Through water and the cooking of food and other such things, Umānava becomes gracious;
for the maintenance of the vital breaths does not occur without food.
The libation for the ancestors, purification, beauty, the removal of foul odors, and all the seeds accumulated here—everything is established within them. (7)
Washing clothes and likewise washing vessels is pleasing;
by that alone all tasks are accomplished, and even drinking water becomes pure.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have ponds, wells,
and tanks constructed by means of all available labor as well as all available wealth.
Furthermore, for one who provides a reservoir of water in a region devoid of water, one should designate a kalpa in heaven for every single day [of that merit]. (10)
A brahmin who has fallen from heaven, having mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras,
who is a friend to the world and whose soul is devoted to righteousness, shall go to heaven after performing austerities.
Thus, by obtaining eight births, one is said to attain imperishability;
born into a lineage of Kṣatriyas, he shall become a sovereign king.
The common people should know that wealth is imperishable, and whatever is dear to them from birth to birth;
even Śūdras, Antyajas, and others repeatedly attain the path to heaven.
That man who digs a well measuring four cubits in depth, which constantly benefits others, dwells in heaven for a kalpa. (14)
One should know that the merit is doubled for a well twice the size, and fourfold for one a hundred cubits;
he who gives a lotus-pond measuring twenty cubits [attains great merit].
He too shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu as well as divine enjoyments;
thereafter, he shall become a king, wealthy, and a master of speech.
In this way, it is held that the enjoyment [of the fruits] increases twofold, threefold, fourfold, or even fivefold;
know, O Acyuta, that in its vast extent, it is more abundant than heaven by a thousandfold.
By twice a thousand [repetitions], a man becomes worthy of worship by the gods;
as many as have gone there and have attained life through that recitation, [so shall he be]. 18.
A number of people equal to that [number] become his servants, constantly following him in his home, city, and throughout the countryside. (19)
Just as birds leave their father when his wealth of food is exhausted and go to the forest,
so too do the sow, the buffalo, and the female elephant.
The instructor, the performer, and these six go to heaven;
one should designate a hundred divine days for the birds as well.
For a thousand years he remains as a boar, for ten thousand years as a great buffalo; having assumed a divine form, he is said to dwell with female elephants for a hundred thousand years.
This reservoir, which yields ten million [units] for the instructor and is inexhaustible for the maker, was constructed by the son of Purādhanī and is well known. (23)
With an expenditure of ten thousand coins, with his very life and strength, and endowed with faith in Śiva for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings. (24)
After some time, it is said that his wealth was exhausted;
then a certain creditor, desiring his money, urged him to pay the price.
Having reflected, the wealthy man said: "Listen now to my declaration:
for her sake, I shall give ten thousand dīnāras. (26)
You have obtained the merit of that lotus pond, yet you disregard it because of your gain; having paid its price according to your ability, you have resolved to make it your own. (27)
When this was said, he spoke again: "Even by reciting it ten thousand times during the day, the fruit is indeed eternal; those who know merit recognize it as such. (28)
In this waterless place, Śiva caused a well to be dug for me;
there, everyone performs their desired activities such as bathing and drinking. (29)
Therefore, I too desire a constant fruit for that which has ten thousand meanings;
consequently, there arose laughter from him as well as from those present in the assembly. (30)
Though oppressed by shame, he spoke these words:
"This speech of ours is true; perform the examination according to dharma."
Out of envy, my father said to Satuta, "I have not even heard such a thing. Give me ten thousand dinars, and having given them, bring back a stone slab. (32)
I shall cause you to fall into this pit so that you may wallow as is fitting;
yet at such a time as you emerge, even a stone would float.
"Otherwise, my wealth will go to ruin; for this is indeed my duty.
Having said "So be it," he took ten thousand [coins] from him and went to his own home. (34)
In the presence of the witnesses, the thief likewise cast down his bundle of grass;
it was seen by men, gods, and asuras in a great lotus pond.
Then, it was weighed upon the scale of Dharma by the witness of Dharma:
the gift of ten thousand dīnāras compared to the water of the Puṣkariṇī pond. (36)
But for the wealthy, even a single day is extremely difficult to endure according to the nature of things; their minds suffer, and on the following day, their wealth becomes useless. (37)
A mountain of rock emerged like an island upon the water;
then a tumultuous roar arose from the people. (38)
Having heard those wonderful words, they both departed from there with joy; and seeing the mountain thus transformed and likewise multiplied ten thousandfold by him, they were amazed.
Then, by the very lord of the moat, the mountain was cast far away;
for when the merit of the moat had been uprooted, it was indeed destroyed by his son.
Having ascended the chariot drawn by pigeons, he was completely at peace throughout birth after birth;
[he likewise brought peace] to the lineages, the groups of mothers, the kings, and his friends.
Having heard of the inexhaustible fruit for those who assist friends and benefactors, and especially for ascetics, the helpless, and Brahmins; ||42||
Having caused a pit to be dug, one enjoys heaven that is imperishable;
therefore, O Brahmins, whoever shall perform the digging of pits and other such works according to their capacity [attains this]. (43)
Through the destruction of all evil, he shall attain merit and liberation; of this there is no doubt—[this applies to] whoever causes this most exalted narrative of Dharma to be heard in the world.
The righteous person enjoys the fruit of giving away all his possessions on the excellent bank of the Bhāgīrathī during an eclipse of the sun. ||45||
Having heard the fruit of the gift of ten million cows, a man shall obtain it;
he shall not encounter poverty, nor sorrow, nor an accumulation of diseases. (46)
One who does not attain both [truth and] honor experiences great suffering.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Glorification of the Khāta and Other [Rites]," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Fifty-Eighth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O highly fortunate ones, I shall describe the specific fruit of each and every tree; listen to that, categorized individually according to their planting. (1)
The fruit of merit for one who plants virtuous trees evenly along both banks of a river is such that it cannot possibly be described or even fully known. (2)
Whatever fruit one might obtain by planting trees elsewhere, that same fruit, multiplied ten million times over, shall be obtained near water. ||3||
One enjoys infinite fruit by doing so personally on the bank of a lotus pond;
we say that for those who perform meritorious deeds by planting trees, the reward is a hundred times greater than that.
The fruit that a mortal obtains by planting an *aśvattha* tree near a body of water cannot be attained even by a hundred sacrifices. (5)
Those leaves which fall into the water at every change of the moon (parvan),
these become like funeral cakes (piṇḍa) here and become inexhaustible for the ancestors.
There, birds certainly eat fruits at their will;
for him, that merit becomes equal to the food of Brahmā and is imperishable. ||7||
Whatever fruit is obtained through the eating and planting of the *aśvattha* tree itself, that is not attained even by hundreds of sacrifices nor even by hundreds of sons. (8)
When it is hot, cows, gods, and the twice-born take shelter in the shade;
for the performer [of this act] and the hosts of his ancestors, heaven becomes imperishable. ||9||
Because it is imperishable, it is impossible for one who is healthy to cause any obstacle to its planting;
therefore, with every effort, one should plant the Ādhava tree.
By planting a single tree, a man does not fall from heaven;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, plant such a great tree. (11)
That noble-minded person who plants trees along roads, near bodies of water, on delightful mountain slopes, and at places for buying and selling, [attains great merit]. 12.
Having planted the Aśvattha and other such trees, one goes to the delightful heaven;
O twice-born ones, I shall now declare the merit that accrues from honoring them. 13.
He who, having bathed, touches the Aśvattha tree is liberated from all sins;
even a mortal who touches it without having bathed obtains the fruit born of bathing.
By seeing you, one destroys sin; by touching you, one attains prosperity;
by circumambulating you, one gains long life. O Ashvattha tree, salutations to you forever! (15)
Salutations always to you, the Ashvattha tree—the Bodhisattva worthy of worship, in whom Viṣṇu eternally resides, and whose leaves and branches are ever-moving. (16)
Having offered oblations of horse-gram (aśvattha), parched grain, milk, and food offerings (naivedya), as well as flowers, incense, and lamps, one does not fall from heaven. ||17||
Know that the worship of the Aśvattha tree brings inexhaustible wealth, increase of prosperity, and fame; it bestows victory, honor, and auspiciousness, along with one's sons. (18)
Whatever has been recited, offered in sacrifice, praised, or performed through yantras, mantras, and the like—
all that is said to be multiplied ten millionfold by one who stands upon the root of the moving leaf.
Who in this world would not worship that [tree] at whose root Viṣṇu resides, at whose middle Śaṅkara stands, and at whose top portion Brahmā is situated? 20.
The merit that is obtained by one who observes silence while bathing on a Monday,
as well as the fruit of giving a thousand cows, is attained by the worship of the Aśvattha tree.
By performing seven circumambulations alone, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand cows;
by many millions and tens of millions more, therefore, non-violence should always be practiced.
Whatever is given there— be it fruits, roots, water, or the like—
all that yields inexhaustible fruit, arising as goodness birth after birth.
Aha! There is no tree-form Hari on earth equal to the Aśvattha;
he is as worthy of worship in the world as the twice-born, as cows, and as the immortals. 24.
Likewise, the deity in the form of the Aśvattha tree is remembered as most worthy of worship, always during its planting, its protection, its touching, and in the act of its worship. (25)
A man who performs even a small act of cutting upon the body of the Aśvattha tree bestows wealth, sons, heaven, and liberation in succession. (26)
Having suffered in hell for one kalpa, he is born as a cāṇḍāla;
by the cutting off of his very root, he attains non-rebirth.
Men stand in the Raurava hell, which is terrible to behold;
such is the fruit that results from planting even a single pipal tree. 28.
Likewise, in the planting of three *pākarka* trees, there are eight *bilva* trees and seven *nyagrodha* trees. (29)
O twice-born ones, there are ten types of trees, and their fruit is equal;
the fruit of each individual tree has been declared in relation to the planting of trees. (30)
Having understood this, a righteous soul should create an artificial forest;
[the merit thereof lasts] for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Having ascended a thousand [circumambulations] of the mango tree that has reached the sky,
one should then perform two or three times that number, even if it is slightly less or not very abundant.
Having enjoyed [the fruit], a king or a lord may enjoy it again;
thereafter, there is heaven to be experienced, as well as sovereignty, auspiciousness, prosperity, and welfare. (33)
Health and perfected valor arise from the very garden of this [tree], whose fruits thousands of living beings consume. (34)
The birds that dwell upon it, the insects, the winged creatures, the locusts, and so forth—those beings who take refuge in its shade are counted as ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana). ||35||
Hundreds of deities worshipped by the gods become his attendants;
and those trees which are great beings, all of them take on divine forms. ||36||
Therefore, his worship should be performed like that of one's father, as well as service and the offering of water and rice-balls;
such sons are found in the world of mortals in birth after birth. (37)
Handsome, well-disciplined, and always pure through meritorious deeds—those who cling to the mango tree of your vow attain such lordship over these qualities. (38)
Dhātrī, harītakī, and others produced from pungent, bitter, and sour [flavors]—all these, when purified by fire, always grant fruits and bestow auspiciousness. (39)
There, the palaces are made of gold and adorned with every kind of jewel;
they are equipped with all ornaments and are like celestial chariots beyond compare.
The trees there are made of gold and grant everything at all times;
they provide the pleasure of every season, and the gentle maidens are like celestial nymphs. (41)
Devoted to song and dance, the tree-deities dwell there,
especially in the lotus ponds and whatever other excavated pools exist.

The rivers were strewn with pure stones, their mud was made of milk-rice (pāyasa), and they possessed foam consisting of milk once again; they were endowed with the six flavors beginning with food. ||43||
Just as there is enjoyment in the world of mortals, so again in heaven and again on earth;
and through that very practice, there is once more the digging of pits and the planting of gardens.

Just as a man who performs meritorious deeds and the like becomes a lord of heaven or mortals, so too one who is unable [to perform great works] shall obtain the fruit of a lotus pond by constructing a small water-trough (prapā). ||45||

And here is the characteristic of the water-distribution stand (prapā): it is supreme, the remover of all sins, the bestower of all enjoyments, pure, the giver of heaven and liberation, and stable. ||46||
I shall now describe the characteristics of a water-stall that increases one’s fame: having constructed a pavilion at a place on a waterless road frequented by travelers. (47)
Even during the summer, the rainy season, and autumn, when many travelers have arrived,
[he provides] water fragrant with agallochum and other scents, as well as betel nut with camphor.
By giving her a seat and betel-leaf, one is not deprived of heaven;
thus, in just three years, one obtains the fruit of [constructing] a lotus pond.
A mortal who does not fall even from heaven is honored by the gods as well;
he who provides a water-station for one month during the waterless heat of summer [attains this]. (50)
One shall dwell in heaven for a single kalpa, and having fallen from heaven, one is honored on earth; those who give water-pots reside there where those who give lotus ponds reside.
Otherwise, a meritorious water-pot of dharma (dharma-ghaṭa) should be given for the destruction of sin;
this dharma-ghaṭa is to be known as being composed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"By your grace, my desires have become fruitful;
[I offer] a fourth part of a gold māṣa as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the jar. (53)

Thus, by merely reading or causing others to hear this, one shall obtain in just three years the fruit of providing water for drinking, as well as the merit arising from the construction of lotus ponds and other such works. (54)
One shall be directly liberated from sin and attain a good rebirth through his grace;
so too for whoever causes this auspicious, meritorious narrative to be heard among people. (55)
He dwells in the world of the gods for thousands of millions of eons. ||56||
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Duties Concerning Puṣkariṇī and Others," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Fifty-Ninth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme and auspicious dharma of fame, the meritorious fruit of building a bridge, exactly as it was spoken by Brahmā. (1)
Whom would she not ferry across the impassable mire crowded with the stakes of men?
By embracing her, a mortal becomes purified and attains divinity. ||2||
He would dwell in the divine heaven for a full hundred years;
by following this method of calculation, a man does not fall from heaven.
Sometimes, due to contact with impurity, one is born on earth from heaven;
then the illustrious Bhaṭṭāraka is freed from disease and sorrow. ||4||
By constructing steps for crossing the mud and other obstacles, one does not fall from heaven;
all his sins are destroyed day by day. ||5||
Likewise, the fruit of the thirteen transits is proclaimed to be equal;
it is always performed by the wise even at the cost of wealth and life. (6)
Listen to this ancient narrative, esteemed by the elders, which occurred in the past:
there was a certain thief who, being greatly terrified, was intent upon the act of stealing.
Having placed his foot upon the head of Kāntārī, he indeed proceeded to commit theft;
for by him, the wealth of a householder was plundered.
Having gone there for a long time, people come upon the path;
it is certain that for all of them, there is happiness on that single footpath. 9.
The head is the supreme boat for crossing the difficult passage of the body with its single foot;
that head is situated in the *kāntāra* (the wilderness) of *cāndrāyaṇa*. ||10||
Then, when the thief’s death was brought about by Citragupta,
there was not even a mere trace of dharma to be found in him.
The ancestral rites, bathing at sacred fords, worship of the twice-born, giving gifts, honoring elders, and auspicious knowledge beneficial to others—none of these are so [efficacious] as this. (12)
How could that which was not committed by mind, nor by action, become a rash act of theft or the violation of another's wife? (13)
False accusations against the virtuous and likewise the Dvāpara age—thus a hundred thousand such acts were committed by that Tathāgata. (14)
Thereupon, Dharmarāja, whose radiance is like the fire of universal destruction, said: "Lead this hero to the fruit [of his actions]—to the miserable rebirth from which there is no returning. (15)
In the meantime, the compassionate Citragupta said:
"O Lord, there is some merit from the Gośīrṣa [mountain] belonging to this man; please forgive him now. (16)
O wicked-minded mortal, go there; for the King of Dharma has declared that such a person shall obtain on earth the merit arising from twelve years of royal offerings.
"Enjoy the kingdom of Akaṇṭaka for twelve years, because you were released by him alone through the path of the *gośiras* mantra. (18)
Then, having come together there and formed an alliance for the sake of non-rebirth, he, oppressed by sorrow, spoke with joined palms to the God: (19)
"O sinful woman, having thus deceived the feet of Dharmarāja, you have acted as the mistress of the Lord of the Kurus; I know this with great joy. (20)
And the King of Dharma said to him, "Very well, go from here;
by my grace, you shall remember your own history even while being deeply distressed. (21)
In that very interval, he was indeed released by a servant;
his birth then took place with two certain merchants who were destitute and in great distress. (22)
From birth, various kinds of suffering were experienced due to past misdeeds; having endured that great affliction for twenty-one years. (23)
In that kingdom, the king died, oppressed by his own karma;
meanwhile, he was observed by the ministers and the wise counselors.
Having wandered upon the earth with many investigations,
he now firmly enveloped him [the opponent] before the eyes of everyone.
Then the royal consecration was performed by those free from envy,
and the excellent Dharmarāja took possession of the kingdom along with its sovereignty.
He constructed a bridge of stone and earth bound together with iron chains, and likewise others built a causeway across the water-fortress.
He constructed ponds, wells, tanks, water-stations, groves, and trees;
thereafter, he performed various sacrifices and meritorious acts of charity.
And Smara remembered his various past deeds, the manifold dharmas performed for the sake of destroying all evil, and his diverse vows. ||29||
By satisfying the gods, the brahmins, and my elders,
I have been purified from sin and have come here to the abode of the wise Dharmarāja.
Then, seeing him standing over his prostrate body, he became red-eyed with rage;
with palms joined in reverence, he said to him: "O Dharma, grant me protection! (31)
Citragupta spoke these words in the presence of Dharmarāja:
"Let him, purified in deed and in mind, go to the world of Viṣṇu. (32)
Having heard this a hundred times and having understood the reason for it, he smiled with affection, his soul serene, and said: "Go, go to the abode of Acyuta! (33)
Having ascended a celestial chariot, variegated in color, which had come from the world of the gods,
he went to heaven, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, he by whom a staff of the measure of a *kiṣku* was given in former times follows after that great king in heaven, along with his royal lineage. (35)
Likewise, by providing even a cow-pasture for grazing, one does not fall from heaven;
whatever destination belongs to the giver of a cow, that shall certainly be his.
For that wise person by whom [the mind] is released so as to move within the span of a single fathom, heaven becomes his desired goal; what is the use of other many words? (37)
If one gives even as much land as can be grazed by a cow for the purpose of abandoning [sin],
his merit from feeding Brahmins day after day is increased a hundredfold.
Therefore, one does not fall from heaven after having declared the pasture for cattle; however, he who cuts down a sacred tree cuts off the very pasture for the cattle. (39)
Twenty-one generations of his family shall be cooked in the Raurava hells;
however, the village guardian who destroys the pasture-land, having recognized the offender, should punish him.
One who cuts down the trees of Dharma, especially one guilty of the offense regarding the cow-pasture—there is no happiness for him; therefore, the king should punish him.
That man who constructs a temple for the Viṣṇu-liṅga—whether it has three sections or five sections, beautifully adorned and provided with well-fashioned pitchers—[attains the highest state]. (42)
But if one should give more than this— whether made of clay or of stone—
it should be filled with wealth and provisions, delightful to the gods, and like a divine terrestrial realm.
The consecration rite (pratiṣṭhākarma) is completed, surrounded by servants and attendants;
it is a fine image of one's chosen deity, especially that of Viṣṇu.
Having done so, that best of men attains union with Viṣṇu;
likewise, by having fashioned an image of Hari or of one of the other [deities]. (45)
The fruit that a person obtains by constructing a beautiful temple cannot be attained through thousands of sacrifices, nor through gifts, nor through vows and other such acts performed on earth. (46)
For thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons, [they dwell] in palaces endowed with jewels and filled with an abundance of all necessary articles. (47)
He shall dwell in celestial vehicles that move at will and enchant the entire world;
having descended from heaven, he becomes a sovereign monarch, masterful through his virtues. 48.
Having caused a temple for the Śiva-liṅga to be built according to one's own capacity, whatever has been prescribed for the Viṣṇu-liṅga should be understood to apply to the abode of Śiva as well. 49.
The highly fortunate one enjoys in heaven a supreme pleasure that brings mental bliss, filled with the delights of beautiful women and granting happiness in every respect. (50)
