A king or a man of great wealth who, having fashioned an image of Hara, installs it in a temple, enjoys inexhaustible pleasures upon the earth. (51)
Whether possessing auspicious marks or deformed features, he shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas;
when fallen from heaven, he shall become a king, a wealthy man, or one most worthy of honor.
Having constructed a temple for the Goddess at all the Liṅgas of the Goddess, a man shall attain the state of a god in the world that originates from all the bliss of the Goddess. (53)
He attains a state of extreme non-falling, reaches supreme bliss, and becomes free from all affliction,
within a palace fashioned from jewels upon a ground variegated with gems.
In that place, which was created by the Goddess for the enjoyment of ten thousand Rāmas, free from fear,
delightful with dance and song, and pleasing to all the senses and the mind.
In a house made of jewels, rich with gem-studded mṛdaṅga drums and cymbals, always sounded by women, stainless, delightful, pleasant, and beautifully adorned with precious gems. (56)
Likewise, by [visiting] the supreme temple of the Goddess who has no equal image,
a human being goes to the heavenly world for ten million billion kalpas.
Having fallen from heaven, the king, who was solely devoted to the Goddess,
would be born thus on earth for a thousand births as Śiva himself.
A man who, full of devotion, performs the *Āṅgāṇapatya* and the propitiation of the goddesses within the temple, becomes honored by the hosts of gods and is born as a celestial being.
In that very way, one attains sovereignty and likewise enjoys pleasures in the city of the Goddess,
remaining forever free from obstacles in all undertakings, just like Gaṇapa himself.
O best of men, for one who has not stumbled from his command among gods, asuras, and humans, the fruit is likewise obtained in the temple of Saura. 61.
Free from disease, with a perfectly serene soul, and possessing a splendor equal to that of Kāmadeva,
he was a bestower of boons in all the worlds, just like the sun.
Having constructed a stone temple for the peerless image of Śūra,
one shall enjoy heaven for a hundred crores of kalpas and then become a lord of the earth.
I shall now describe, for the benefit of men, the individual worship of all the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, each one separately. (64)
He who offers a lamp of ghee for one day and night throughout his life shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand divine years,
honored by the best of gods.
That man on earth who performs a bath with ghee for the Liṅga shall dwell in heaven for thousands of crores of kalpas.
The fruit of another [lamp] is half that of a lamp made of sesame oil;
by the fruit of giving water for one month, one shall attain lordship.
Through the gift of incense one becomes a Gandharva; through sandalwood, the merit is doubled.
By the gift of musk and agallochum, there shall be great fruit. (68)
By the offering of a garland of flowers, a man shall become a lord of the three worlds;
by giving a cotton garment in the cold season, one is liberated from all suffering.
He who gives a garment according to his ability shall never suffer, even after giving a cool cloth during the heat that is difficult to endure life after life. (70)
A beautiful covering for the feet, measuring four cubits in height and girth, does not cause one to fall from heaven. (71)
By the gift of gold according to one's capacity, a man shall become honored in heaven;
he shall possess a celestial pavilion extending ten yojanas in width.
By giving gold endowed with jewels, one obtains a tenfold reward;
likewise for diamonds, lapis lazuli, emeralds, rubies, and other priceless gems.
By giving [this] according to the prescribed rite to a Brāhmaṇa who possesses fame,
one shall become the sovereign over a circle extending for a hundred yojanas.
Likewise, although born on this earth as a person belonging to all the worlds, he was eloquent and handsome due to his gift of fragrant substances. (75)
By giving red nectar and a *kaṃṭha* fruit, as well as betel nuts, a man shall become a god;
by the gift of a boon-granting slave girl, a man shall dwell in heaven for a kalpa.
By the gift of a female servant who grants boons, one becomes a lord of wealth on earth;
likewise, by the gift of a male servant, one shall possess many servants in heaven.
Through the gift of all kinds of musical instruments, one is born with inexhaustible supernatural power (ṛddhi) in birth after birth; being virtuous, one is honored by the world. (78)
Through mastery of the sciences of dance, song, and so forth, one becomes a lord of the Gandharvas in heaven, endowed with male and female servants, wealth, women, and excellent things. (79)
In the same way, by the gift of a cow, one shall dwell in heaven for that same length of time;
and by offering milk at a linga, a man shall dwell in heaven for a kalpa.
By bathing with curd, one gains double [the merit], but by bathing with ghee, one gains a hundred times more;
by giving food endowed with the six flavors, one becomes a lord of the earth.
In that very manner, the most excellent sage on earth, who had mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, joyfully gave milk-rice (pāyasa) and sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) to the sages. ||82||
Through the gift of that which is free from worldly desire, one becomes a celibate observer of vows;
through the gift of honey, molasses, and salt, one attains good fortune.

The sweetness [of the Lord] is celebrated throughout all the worlds by means of sugar and other substances, after having performed the worship of the Śambhu-liṅgas according to the prescribed rite for the gods. (84)
In due course, he shall become the lord of the worlds, beginning with heaven;
and for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, the gods remain standing before his face.
Having performed a single circumambulation at Aśvabhūliṅga, the wise and best of men goes to heaven for a full hundred divine years. (86)
In this very manner, by means of these prostrations performed in sequence, one goes from the earthly realm to the celestial world and then to heaven; therefore, one should practice this constantly.
The man who steals the wealth of the God in the form of the Liṅga shall reach the Raurava hell,
and due to that act of theft, he shall become a worm.
He who takes away the worship offered by a donor for the sake of a *liṅga* or of Hari shall not return from hell for ten million generations of his lineage. (89)
If one has taken water, flowers, lamps, or other offerings for the sake of the ritual, but later fails to give them out of greed, he shall go to an inexhaustible hell. (90)
Having abducted the female servant of an Atuliliṅga, one does not return from hell;
one who is afflicted by lust might go to his mother, but he would never go to the female servant of Śiva.
Then, having gone to the wife of Śiva, as well as by stealing the property of Śiva,
and by consuming his food and drink, a man shall attain a miserable state.
Therefore, a Brahmin who [frequents] the company of gods does not return from hell;
for that reason, indeed, the wickedness of courtesans would be beneficial. 93.
Therefore, having touched a courtesan, a man becomes pure through bathing;
yet, by resorting to many men, she goes to a defiled and miserable state.
A courtesan who is an ascetic woman, always devoted to the worship of the gods, dedicated to her husband, and pure, attains imperishable heaven. 95.
But he who always regards the courtesan as his mother, enjoys every kind of pleasure in the celestial worlds like a god. (96)
Just as Hari is worthy of worship by gods, demons, and humans, so too is this Arhat worthy of honor in all the worlds, the sole purifier of all beings. 97.
He who is always devoted to the service of the gods and is ever eager for divine rites, that lord of the world goes to the world of the gods and is glorified there. (98)

Having caused these very images to be made and having constructed a pavilion for the ablution, one obtains heaven according to one's capacity; now hear from me what is attained at the end of the eon. 99.
By means of grass alone, one hundred years [are attained];
by a reed-stalk, ten thousand; by other wood, ten thousand; and by khadira wood, a hundred thousand.
With extremely firm stones numbering in the millions of millions, and joined with great effort,
the wise man should therefore cause the pavilion to be constructed with every possible exertion.
For as long as a person who has constructed a pavilion for humans dwells in heaven,
for that same length of time a person who steals one shall fall into an evil rebirth.
It was delightful with the multitudes of people buying and selling goods, and it served as a refuge for travelers at the confluence of rivers and streams. (103)
Whatever fruit a person obtains by constructing a pavilion for the gods, O eminent Brāhmaṇa, he attains that same fruit doubled by constructing one for the Brāhmaṇas. (104)
By having a beautiful house built for one who is helpless, miserable, and especially for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), a man does not fall from heaven.
Whoever should constantly hear this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative shall attain imperishable heaven and obtain the fruit of constructing temples and other such works. (106)
Furthermore, by teaching or by studying [this] for the wealthy, the powerful, and likewise for those who possess merit, a man does not fall from heaven. (107)
That Brahmin who always recites [this] in the temples of the gods, and among the male and female servants, constantly proceeds upon the path to liberation. ||108||
Having recited this in the presence of kings, lords, the wealthy, and the virtuous, one attains liberation; by merely hearing it, one obtains that same fruit.
The twice-born said: O best of the twice-born, there is one supreme and holy being in the world of mortals who is easily accessible and worthy of worship by mortals as well as by ascetic sages. (110)
Of the four castes and the stages of life, of men possessing both sin and merit, as well as those possessing virtues and vices, and likewise those with caste and those without caste; ||111||
Vyāsa said: Among all beings indeed, one who is endowed with a rudrākṣa is most excellent;
by the mere sight of him, the mass of sins of people is dissolved. (112)
By touching it, one enjoys heaven; by wearing it, one attains the state of Rudra. Whoever wears Rudrākṣa on the head, the chest, or the arms [attains this]. (113)
If one who is equal to Īśāna, whose range of activity is everywhere in the world, should reside there, that place where this brahmin stays would become meritorious. (114)
Having seen or even having touched it, a person is purified from sin; whatever chanting, libation, giving, bathing, worship, or circumambulation one performs [therein], [it becomes infinite]. 115.
O twice-born ones, whatever merit one performs becomes entirely infinite; such is the fruit of the Rudrākṣa, the greatest of all sacred fords (tīrthas). 116.
By the mere retention of this, the embodied soul becomes purified of sin and partakes of great merit;
and having taken up the auspicious rosary of beads joined at the Brahma-thread, [he attains the goal]. (117)
Whatever has been recited, whatever gift has been given, whatever hymn of praise, mantra, or worship of the gods has been performed—
all this becomes inexhaustible, and one shall attain the destruction of all sins.
O best of the twice-born, listen as we describe the characteristics of the rosary; by knowing its characteristics, you shall attain the path of Śiva. 119.
One should avoid, in due order, a [liṅga] that has no source, one pierced by insects, one with a broken emblem, and one whose seed-syllable is stuck to another within the rosary. 120.
One should avoid from afar that [garland] which is woven by oneself, or one that is loosely strung with strands intermingled, or one woven by Śūdras and others who are impure. 121.
The seed-syllable fixed at the center should be recited in due order;
likewise, by the rapid movement of the hands, one should repeatedly perform the touching of Mount Meru. 122.
A mantra that has been counted is effective, whereas one that is uncounted is fruitless;
for all deities, one should recite the mantra using one's own rosary. (123)
For one who is self-restrained, [this] shall be ten million times ten million times superior to all holy fords (tīrtha),
provided it is on pure ground, or even in a place of impurity at the root of a tree.
In a cow-pen, at a crossroads, or at a temple site, one shall obtain infinite fruit by reciting the mantra of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, or Sūrya before their respective liṅgas.
Whoever recites the mantra of the Goddess in an empty house, before a lord, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads, becomes an accomplished practitioner instantly. (126)
Furthermore, every mantra— whether non-Vedic, from the Purāṇas, or arising from the Āgamas—
that is recited upon a rosary of Rudrākṣa beads bestows all desired and cherished objects.
One should carry on one's head the pure water flowing from rudrākṣa beads;
purified from all sin, one’s merit becomes inexhaustible. 128.
That mortal who wears even a single seed of a rudrākṣa, which is individually immortal, shall become the most excellent among the gods. (129)
The twice-born said:
From where was the rudrākṣa born, or why did it attain a state of impurity? For what purpose did it become an immobile being on earth, and by whom was it propagated? (130)
Vyāsa said: O Brahmins, in former times, during the Kṛta-yuga, there was a Dānava named Tripura who, having brought about the destruction of the gods, resided in a city in the intermediate space.
While all the worlds were perishing, yet remaining firm by virtue of his boon of Brahmanhood,
Śaṅkara, the Lord, heard the terrifying report presented by the gods.
Then, having fixed an arrow resembling a meteor to the Ajagava bow and holding it,
he struck him while observing him with divine vision.
Like great meteors fallen from heaven onto the surface of the earth with a crash, the drops of sweat fell from Rudra, who was agitated by the act of creation. (134)
There, from a drop of his tear, a great rudrākṣa was born upon the earth;
living beings do not know its fruit because it is exceedingly secret. (135)
Then, having prostrated with his head upon the ground before Maheśvara, the God of gods, on the peak of Kailāsa, Kaṇḍu spoke these words.
O Lord, I desire to know the fruit of the rudrākṣa in its true essence—whether through recitation, wearing it, seeing it, or even touching it. (137)
The Lord said:
"From the sight of it, one gains a hundred thousand merits; from touching it, ten million;
and by wearing it, a man obtains the merit of a billion. (138)
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, ten million times, a billion times, or even ten billion times, one obtains merit; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Whether one is impure from food remnants, engaged in improper actions, or burdened by all manner of sins, one is indeed liberated from all evils by wearing Rudrākṣa beads. 140.
If even a beast of prey dies while holding a single old rudrākṣa, it too attains the state of Rudra;
how much more so then humans and others? (141)
Even one who is devoid of meditation and mental retention, if he should wear rudrākṣa, being liberated from all sins, attains the supreme goal. ||142||
Kārttikeya said:
[I shall describe those with] one face, and likewise two, three, four, five, or six faces;
as well as seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven faces.
The Rudrākṣa with twelve faces, as well as that with thirteen faces, and that endowed with fourteen faces, was spoken of by Śaṅkara himself. 144.
O Lord of the World, tell me also who are the deities of those four faces,
what their qualities are, or what their defects may be.
"If there is favor toward me, speak according to the truth.
Īśvara said:
"Śiva, when manifest with even a single face, removes the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Therefore, one should wear it on the body for the destruction of all sins;
one shall go to the world of Śiva and rejoice together with Śiva. ||147||
O Six-faced One, by means of a great accumulation of merit and through the grace of Hara, a mortal may obtain Kailāsa with a single face.
The man who bears upon his head this two-faced image of the God of gods attains the destruction of all sins, including even the secret sin of cow-slaughter. (149)
Furthermore, by wearing two faces [of the deity], one attains imperishable heaven;
for fire itself, manifest as three faces, is established within his body. (150)
It burns away the sins accumulated in that person's life, just as fire consumes fuel—even the sins of killing a woman, killing a Brahmin, or the slaughter of many others. (151)
Whatever sin a mortal incurs, all of it perishes at that very moment;
[it is as if one has obtained] the fruit of worshipping the fire, performing the fire-ritual, and offering oblations of clarified butter. 152.
The wise man who wears that [mark] obtains its fruit and enjoys infinite heaven;
he who wears the three-faced [mark] is equal to Brahmā on earth. 153.
All accumulated misdeeds from birth after birth shall be consumed by it;
neither will disease arise in the belly, nor will one fall into a state of physical incapacity. (154)
One does not suffer defeat, nor is one's house consumed by fire; all these and other such things, as well as [protection] from thunderbolts and the like, are warded off. 155.
By the wearing of the three-faced [liṅga], no inauspiciousness whatsoever exists;
for Brahmā himself becomes four-faced in whose body it is established. (156)
He may be a knower of all scriptures, a twice-born one who is the best among those who know the Vedas;
he may be a knower of the true essence of all dharmas and arthas, a follower of the Smṛtis, or a knower of the Purāṇas. (157)
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a human being, or among many beings in their dwellings—all that is quickly consumed by the fire of the dhāraṇī of the Four-Faced One. 158.
Maheśa is eternally pleased; he becomes the lord of all beings. Likewise, Sadyojāta, Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Aghora [are likewise pleased]. (159)
The Vāmadeva [mantra] is resorted to by the five faces of the gods;
therefore, it is most abundant everywhere on the surface of the earth as the five-faced one. 160.
Since this is the very form of Rudra’s own son, the wise man should wear it for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas.
For that duration, he shall be worshipped by gods and asuras in the presence of Śiva;
possessing the splendor of Śarva, he shall become a sovereign ruler on earth within the abode of Śiva.
Therefore, with every effort, one should wear the five-faced [Śiva];
and wearing the six-faced Kārttikeya on the right arm, ||163||
He is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
When the end of the kalpa has arrived, he shall be a hero equal to Skanda.
There is no defeat here; he becomes a mine of virtues upon the earth, attaining the state of a prince just as the son of Gaurī attained it from Nandana. 165.
The Brāhmaṇa becomes honored by kings, and the Kṣatriya attains victory;
the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other castes are always filled with sovereignty.
To him, Gaurī, the giver of boons, becomes as easily accessible as a mother. (166)
Then, by the power of his arms alone, that man shall become possessed of universal splendor;
he shall be eloquent and steadfast in the assembly, in the royal palace, and in the council.
He shall not fall into cowardice, and certainly no defeat shall occur. ||168||
All these and others are obtained solely through the wearing of the six-faced one;
Mahāsena is seven-faced, while Ananta is the king of the nāgas. (169)
On each of its individual mouths reside the following nāgas:
Ananta, Karkaṭa, Puṇḍarīka, and Takṣaka. ||170||
Viṣolbaṇa, Kārīṣa, and Śaṅkhacūḍa as the seventh—by these seven of great prowess, [the fire] is established within its seven mouths. 171.
Merely by holding this [mantra], poison does not spread through one's body;
and Hara becomes supremely pleased, just as he is with Nāgeśvara. 172.
Through love for her, all sins go to destruction day by day, including the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and that which arises from violating the Guru’s bed. (173)
Whatever sin a mortal incurs, all of it perishes at that very moment;
he shall certainly obtain food equal to that of the gods throughout the three worlds. 174.
The eight-faced Mahāsena is the god Vināyaka himself; hear from me the merit that arises simply from the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) upon him. 175.
Birth after birth he shall not be a fool, nor diseased, nor of impaired intellect;
for him, there shall always be freedom from obstacles in all undertakings. (176)
Skill in the work of writing, proficiency in great undertakings, and capability in all tasks beginning with agriculture increase for him day by day. (177)
One who uses a half-scale, a false balance, or likewise any kind of deception,
and one who touches a woman with his penis, belly, or hand, is a teacher of falsehood.
All such [practices] as these destroy all evils in every way;
having enjoyed the imperishable celestial realm, one is liberated and goes to the supreme state. (179)
All these qualities are obtained through the wearing of these [ornaments] of the Eight-Faced One; indeed, he who wears the nine-faced Bhairava upon his arm is so described. (180)
By wearing the Kapila [ash] which bestows liberation, one becomes equal in strength to me;
even he who has committed thousands of millions of Brahman-murders [is purified]. ||181||
By holding this nine-faced [mantra], one quickly destroys all those [obstacles]; he is always honored by the gods in the world of the immortals, just like Maghavan. 182.
Gaṇeśa resides here in the excellent abode of Hara; of this there is no doubt.
And the serpents perish through the meditation upon the ten-faced one. 183.
Eleven Rudras are traditionally said to reside in the mouth;
one should always wear them on the crest-lock. Hear now the fruit of that merit. ||184||
The fruit that results from a thousand horse-sacrifices and hundreds of millions of other sacrifices is equal to the fruit of a hundred thousand cows properly given as a gift.
One attains that fruit swiftly by reciting it eleven times;
such a person becomes like Hara in this world, and for them, rebirth no longer exists.
Whoever wears a twelve-faced rudrākṣa on the region of the throat, the Sun-god is eternally pleased, for he resides within that twelve-faced bead. ||187||

Whatever fruit one obtains by performing a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), a cow sacrifice (gomedha), or a human sacrifice (naramedha), one quickly attains that same fruit through the warding off of thunderbolts and other such calamities. 188.
There shall be no fear of fire, nor shall disease arise;
he enjoys the acquisition of wealth and happiness like a lord, and not poverty. (189)
Having killed or even caused the slaughter of elephants, horses, men, cats, mice, rabbits, as well as tigers, venomous snakes, jackals, and so forth; ||190||
One is liberated from this body by wearing twelve beads on the face; if thirteen beads are obtained, one attains the state of Rudra, the Great Rudra. (191)
He is the most auspicious one, easily known, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
he is indeed the elixir of nectar, the alchemy of base metals, and the magical sandals. (192)
O Six-faced One, all these succeed for that fortunate person even after he has slain his mother, father, sister, brother, or teacher.
By holding this in one's mouth for thirteen days, one is liberated from all sins and attains imperishable heaven, just like the god Maheśvara. 194.
If one should constantly wear upon the head or the arm fourteen Rudrākṣas of the Vatsa variety, it is equal to the power of Śiva himself, even for one who is impotent.
What need is there for further words or repeated description?
It is constantly worshipped by the gods and attained through the weight of one's merit. (196)
Kārttikeya said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear from you as you speak, according to the prescribed rule:
by which mantra is the ritual placement (nyāsa) performed, or how is the wearing [of the ashes] to be done? Please tell me."
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Six-faced One, according to the truth, as it pertains to each and every organ of speech in due order;
these qualities are proclaimed to arise simply from the non-utterance of mantras. 198.
Furthermore, as for that person on earth who would maintain [this] endowed with mantras, it is simply impossible to describe the greatness of his qualities. (199)
Now, the mantras for these are taught to you: Oṃ rudra for the one-faced; Oṃ khaṃ for the two-faced; Oṃ vuṃ for the three-faced;
Oṃ hrīṃ for the four-faced; Oṃ hrāṃ for the five-faced.
Oṃ hrūṃ ṃ, for the six-faced one; oṃ hraḥ, for the seven-faced one; oṃ kaṃ, for the eight-faced one; oṃ jūṃ, for the nine-faced one;
oṃ kṣaṃ, for the ten-faced one; oṃ śrī-ṃ, for the eleven-faced one.
Oṃ hrīṃ for the twelve-faced one; oṃ kṣauṃ for the thirteen-faced one;
oṃ nrāṃ for the fourteen-faced one.
In this manner, the mantras should be deposited in their proper sequence.
If a man, taking a garland upon his head and chest, should go forth, he obtains at every step the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; it is not otherwise.
By wearing [the beads] from all the faces, one becomes equal to me;
therefore, my son, wear the Rudrākṣa with every effort. (201)
The man who dies on this earth while wearing fourteen rudrākṣas goes to my beautiful city,
honored by all the gods.
Formerly, in the land of Maru, at a place known as Vatsavaṇijyāya,
a merchant’s son traveling there was tormented by a hungry ghost (preta).
From that dancing preta, the brahmin saw another and asked:
"Who are you, O wretched one, who dance while clothed in tattered rags? (204)
Then she said to that twice-born man: "I have heard from the messenger of the gods that, by the fall of the thunderbolt, this very handsome man has now [perished]. (205)
"Death will certainly come to this brahmin from his master.
In that very interval, a thunderbolt fell from the sky upon his head.
It fell with a great crash upon the earth, upon a half-fragment of a rudrākṣa;
then, O son, my celestial chariot quickly descended from my city.
Having ascended it, the glorious one remains there for a long time.
Having reached me, Śakra, what lord could ever become impoverished? 208.
O son, in this way, even for one who has died with a fragment of a rudrākṣa, a good rebirth is attained;
however, we are unable to describe the fruit for that man who wears it with true knowledge.
Whether one belongs to the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Saura tradition, if they wear even a single Rudrākṣa bead as a garland after death, [they attain liberation]. ||210||
Whoever recites it, causes it to be recited, hears it, or even listens to it—
having their soul liberated from all sins— shall gradually attain the blissful heaven.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Rudrākṣa," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||59||
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Skanda said:
O Lord of the Universe, for the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, please speak regarding the purity of even another tree that bears fruit. 1.
Īśvara said:
The dhātrī fruit is supremely pure and renowned throughout all the worlds; by planting it, a man or woman is liberated from the bondage of birth. (2)
This is the purifying fruit of Vāsudeva, delightful and auspicious;
by the mere eating of it, one is liberated from all impurity.
By eating [it], one gains longevity; by drinking [it], there is an accumulation of merit;
by bathing [with it], misfortune is destroyed, and one shall attain all sovereignty. ||4||
In whatever house the nurse Mahāsenā always resides, there the pretas, daityas, and rākṣasas do not go. ||5||
Neither the Ganges, nor the Naga, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Prayāga, nor Puṣkara—on the day of Hari, the Earth alone is attained by men as their sole refuge. (6)
Whoever performs the bath with *dhātrī* fruit on the eleventh day of both fortnights attains the destruction of all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||7||
The fruit of the *dhātrī* tree should always be used, both for eating and for bathing;
it is especially prescribed for the breaking of the fast on the day of Viṣṇu, and even for a mere bath on the day of Hari. (8)

A man who, having eaten on the day of breaking the fast or while still under restraint, or while being touched by his nurse alone, should then skip the Ekādaśī of both the bright and dark fortnights; (9)
O Six-faced One, by performing even a single fast, one is liberated from the sins committed during seven lifetimes; there is no doubt about this. (10)
One obtains inexhaustible heaven and attains union with Viṣṇu;
therefore, perform the Dhātrī vow with every effort. 11.
O Six-faced One, no one whose hair has been constantly moistened by the juice of the *dhātrī* fruit would ever again drink from his mother’s breast, having conquered the gods.
Whether by seeing the nurse, by touching her, or even by uttering her name,
Viṣṇu— the bestower of boons— becomes well-disposed and is pleased with that beloved one.
Wherever the fruit of the Dhātrī tree is found, there Keśava resides; there Brahmā dwells within the firm lotus; therefore, one should place that [fruit] in the house. 14.
Misfortune perishes wherever the Dhātrī plant is established;
all the gods, being well-pleased, joyfully do not leave that place for even a moment. (15)
Viṣṇu becomes pleased with one who offers an oblation of *dhātrī* fruit even if it possesses great wealth; he is not so pleased by hundreds of other sacrifices. (16)
He who, having bathed, worships Mādhava with the juice of the *adhātrī* fruit, obtains his desired fruit—whatever resides in his mind. (17)
Likewise, having remembered and worshipped it with its characteristic marks, the fruit for that best of men is indeed the merit of a hundred thousand pieces of gold. ||18||
A man who delights in the service of the Dhātrī attains that same goal which is reached by those of great wisdom, by the Skanda-sages, and by those devoted to yoga. (19)
That same goal is attained by men through various vows such as visiting sacred fords and pilgrimage sites, as well as by the diligent consumption of the dhātrī fruit. (20)
And there was joy for all the gods, goddesses, and the host of celestial musicians upon seeing his face, as he bathed and partook of the dhātrī fruit. ||21||
Whosoever are corrupted by planetary influences, and whatever fierce Daityas and Rākṣasas there may be,
they all attain a state of non-malice through the excellent consumption of Dhātrī fruits.
The amalaka fruit is recommended for all sacrificial rites and for the worship of every deity, with the exception of the Sun, O son.
Therefore, especially on the seventh lunar day falling on a Sunday, one should always avoid *dhātrī* fruits from afar.
But he who bathes or eats on the day of Dhātrī-vrata, his lifespan, wealth, wife, and everything else shall perish. (25)
During a solar transit, on a Saturday, on the sixth, the first,
the ninth, and also on the new moon day, one should avoid the dhātrī tree from afar.
He upon whose nose, ears, snout, or even in the hair of one who has died, the dhātrī fruit remains, goes directly to the realm of Viṣṇu. (27)
Merely by contact with a *dhātrī* fruit, one who is dead goes to the abode of Acyuta;
all his sins are destroyed, and he goes to heaven by means of a chariot. (28)
A righteous man who, having smeared himself with the juice of the *dhātrī* fruit, performs a bath at the Yaśas river, obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step. ||29||
Merely by the sight of him, all these most wicked, evil, and terrible planets flee from his presence. (30)
Formerly, a certain Pulkasa went to the forest for the sake of hunting;
having killed multitudes of deer and birds, he was overcome by thirst. (31)
Seeing before him an amalaki tree laden with plump fruits, he climbed it out of hunger and immediately ate the excellent fruit.
Then, by fate, he fell from the top of that tree onto the surface of the earth;
deeply pierced by intense agony, he then met his death.
Then all the hosts of pretas, as well as the hosts of rakshasas and bhutas— all of them,
the very servants of Yama— joyfully [prepared] to carry his body.
Even those of great strength were unable to look upon the dead Cāṇḍāla; they fell into mutual conflict, each saying, "This is mine! (35)
They were unable to seize or lead one another away;
then, looking about, they went toward the hosts of sages.
The pretas said:
"O sages, for what reason are you so steadfast? We are not able even to look upon this outcaste who commits evil deeds, nor is he our servant. (37)
They die, cast down by those who are firm yet turned away from battle; struck down by acts of violence, they are terrified and crushed like wood by the fire of a thunderbolt.
Whether by lions, tigers, or predatory beasts, or by water-born creatures, the spirits dwelling in water or on land are struck down by trees and mountains. (39)
Those killed by beasts or birds, those who died in prison, those who died by suicide, and those for whom rites such as the śrāddha were not performed; ||40||
Those who perform secret deeds, those who die [unnaturally], rogues, those who hate their guru, brahmins, or kings;
heretics, Kaulikas, the cruel, poisoners, and perjured witnesses—[these are the ones to avoid]. ||41||
Those who eat food during a period of ritual impurity undoubtedly become the objects of enjoyment for the deceased;
yet, even while crying out, "This is mine!", we were unable to take him away. (42)
"He is as difficult to gaze upon as the sun; what then could be due to his own power?
The sages said: "O ghosts, he has eaten a ripe *āmalaka* fruit. (43)
They go to his company and receive his abundant fruits;
for that very reason, he is certainly difficult for you to behold.
Then, out of affection, he did not abandon the life of the one who had fallen from the treetop;
for this [sun] does not [abandon] the messenger of the sun, nor others who are evildoers. 45.
"Merely by eating the *dhātrī* fruit, one is purified from sin and shall go to heaven.
The ghosts said: "We ask you out of ignorance; we are not revilers at any time. (46)
"O tigers among sages, before the celestial chariot has even arrived from the world of Viṣṇu, let that which is held in your minds be spoken immediately. (47)
As long as they proclaim the sounds of discernment fashioned from Vedic mantras and the like—wherein the Vedas and various mantras are to be proclaimed—[so long shall this continue]. (48)
Wherein we are unable to remain for even a moment amidst the Purāṇas and Smṛtis,
and amidst the rites of sacrifice, oblation, recitation, the stationing of deities, and worship.
We stand right here before you; therefore, let the matter be explained.
O twice-born ones, what did those men do to obtain birth in the womb of a preta? (50)
"We wish to hear correctly how his body became deformed.
The twice-born said:
"By the afflictions of cold, wind, and heat, and by the particular torments of hunger and thirst," (51)
Furthermore, those false witnesses who were tormented by other miseries, and who died through execution or imprisonment, have gone as pretas to hell. (52)

Those who are intent on seeking out the faults of the twice-born and who destroy their merit, as well as those who act similarly toward their gurus, become pretas who do not attain rebirth [in higher realms]. (53)
O best of the twice-born, when [the food] is being given, it pierces the donor;
having entered a state of long-term ghosthood, he does not return from hell. (54)
Those fools who, having made another or themselves a beast of burden, do not protect them from being oppressed or driven, become preta-beings born of their karma on this earth. (55)
Those men who have made low vows, who are untruthful, and likewise those whose observances are broken,
as well as those who eat from lotus leaves— they become pretas on earth, born of their own karma.
Those who sell a pure daughter, a virtuous wife, or an honest woman, as well as paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others—they become pretas on earth due to their karma. (57)
"These and many other ghosts have been born through their own past actions.
The ghosts said:
"O twice-born ones, how is it that we do not become ghosts? By what action [do we attain this state]? (58)
He spoke quickly for the welfare of all, that supreme benefit for the entire world.
The twice-born said:
"By which wise man has the bath been performed in the water of the sacred ford? (59)
Having paid homage to the supreme Liṅga,
and having fasted specifically on the eleventh day and the twelfth day, a man does not go to the state of a ghost.
Having worshipped Hari with hymns, mantras, and the like produced from the syllables of the Vedas, mortals indeed do not fall into the state of a ghost.
Those who are devoted to the worship of the gods do not become pretas;
having heard these divine words from the Purāṇa, which are beneficial for dharma. (62)
Even by teaching or by reciting [this], one does not go to the state of a piśāca;
likewise, those purified by various vows and by the wearing of lotus seeds (rudrākṣas) [attain the same].
Having recited [the mantra] with a rosary of lotus seeds, one never goes to the state of a preta;
those who bathe daily with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits and are devoted to eating them [attain the same].
Therefore, by thoroughly worshipping Viṣṇu, they do not fall into the state of being Piśācas.
The Pretas said:
"The seers of the Purāṇas know that merit arises from the sight of the virtuous. (65)
Therefore, you ought to perform that which will bring about our welfare; act so that the liberation of us all from this state of being hungry ghosts may occur. (66)
"O wise ones, we have come to you for refuge as our instructors in the vows.
Thereupon, all those most excellent of the twice-born, being full of compassion, spoke to them. (67)
"O Brahmins, for the sake of our liberation, we shall quickly consume the *dhātrī* fruits.
The *pretas* said:
"O Brahmin, upon seeing the *dhātrīs*, we are unable to remain [in this state]. (68)
"How can you eat these fruits now, since their power cannot be shared?
The twice-born said:
"By our word, the eating of these dhātrī fruits here shall be auspicious. (69)
"It will bear fruit in the next world; therefore, you ought to go there.
Then, having obtained a boon from them, the Piśācas [went] to the Dhātrī tree.
Having ascended [the tree] and reached its fruit, he then ate it with ease;
thereafter, from that temple, he quickly mounted a very beautiful, stout chariot.
Having mounted that [vehicle] which had arrived, even those accompanied by Cāṇḍālas and Piśācas went to heaven—
that which is very difficult to attain— by means of the vows for sons and sacrifices.
Skanda said: "By merely eating the *dhātrī* fruit, they attained merit and went to heaven; why then do men and others who eat it not go to heaven? (73)
Īśvara said:
Formerly, due to the loss of their knowledge, they did not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful;
[they ate] leavings, food touched by dogs, or even phlegm, urine, and excrement. (74)
Thinking him to be the best, they are indeed always deluded; the ghosts eat his excrement, urine, and water, as well as his offerings made with pigs and cocks. (75)
If one does not abandon the recitation of mantras during periods of impurity caused by death or birth, the hungry ghosts (pretas) shall always consume his food and water. (76)
He whose wife is difficult to control, impure, devoid of self-restraint, expelled by her elders, and wicked—there, indeed, hungry ghosts dwell. (77)
Lacking preeminence in lineage and birth, and devoid of strength and vigor,
they are deaf, emaciated, and wretched— these Piśācas born of their own karma.

For them, there is not even a moment of auspiciousness, as they are intensely possessed by physical bodies and suffering; for that very reason, they possess deformed appearances and are utterly deprived of all enjoyments.
Naked, afflicted by disease, scorched, parched, and soiled—these and other such beings of the preta class are perpetually tormented by suffering. (80)
By the ripening of that karma, you are born with such desires as these: those who revile their fathers, mothers, and teachers, and those who are intent on insulting the gods. (81)
Those heretics, Kaulikas, and evildoers become pretas born of their karma on this earth;
likewise, those who commit suicide by means of nooses around the neck, water, weapons, or poison [become such]. ||82||

In this world, there are those born as hungry ghosts (preta), as outcastes (caṇḍāla) and the like, as outcasts from the Aṅga region, as those who have fallen from their status, and those who die of sinful diseases. (83)

Those killed by being abandoned, those slain in battle, those who have died on a funeral pyre, those joined with great sins, and those excluded from marriage—[these are the ones for whom this applies]. (84)

Those who are reckless due to their valor, those who are born as pretas on earth as a result of their karma, those who commit treason against the king, and those who harbor malice toward their ancestors; ||85||

Those devoid of meditation and study, those lacking in vows such as the worship of deities and so forth, those without mantras and devoid of ritual bathing, and those devoted to sexual intercourse with the wife of their guru; ||86||

Likewise, those who associate with wicked women and those who have died through cruel fasting, as well as those who have died while residing in the lands of barbarians (mleccha), [go to the same state]. //87//
Those who speak impure Mleccha languages, those who subsist on the livelihood of Mlecchas, and those who live off women and wealth—such people follow the ways of the Mlecchas. (88)

Those by whom women are not protected are undoubtedly among the hungry ghosts (preta) here; likewise, one who, with a body tormented by hunger, comes to a house exhausted and is a Brahmin—[he too is such]. (89)
Having abandoned a guest who is a vessel of virtue and merit, they go to the state of piśācas;
they sell cows to barbarians and to those who eat cow-flesh.
Having remained in the world of the hungry ghosts and attained non-rebirth,
those born as animals and those who have died shall cross over the impurity.
For a long time they have been hungry ghosts and piśācas, dying and being born again and again,
entirely devoid of the purificatory rites beginning with the birth ceremony.
And in each individual conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskāra*), the state of being a preta is abandoned through bathing, meditation, worship of the gods, the Vedas, sacrifices, vows, and syllables. (93)
Those who have been excluded from birth since conception are those sinful pretas who are not subject to rebirth;
they [subsist on] the remnants of food in vessels and the impurities of the body. (94)
Those who cast [others] down at a sacred ford (tīrtha) undoubtedly become pretas here;
they are not satisfied by gifts, honors, worship, or even by the satisfaction of Brahmins on this earth. (95)
The ancestors and the gurus are indeed hungry ghosts (preta) born intensely from their own karma;
likewise, those ignoble women who, having abandoned their husbands, live with other men [are reborn as such]. (96)
Having remained for a long time in the world of hungry ghosts, they were born among those [other] wombs;
and having fallen from that state as well, they became deluded by the objects of the senses.
Those wicked ones who eat sweet foods [without offering] shall remain as pretas on earth for a long time;
they are consumers of feces and urine, being devoted to devouring the property of Brahmins.
Others, who eat what is unfit to be eaten, become these pretas who do not return to rebirth; they forcibly seize the property of others and do not give anything away. (99)
Those who, relying on their wealth, treat guests with contempt become ghosts;
therefore, having eaten an *āmalaka* fruit and bathed in its juice, [one should proceed]. 100.
Being completely liberated from all evil, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
therefore, with every effort, one should serve the auspicious Āmalakī tree. 101.
Whoever should constantly hear this auspicious and meritorious narrative, with their soul purified of all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. 102.
One should constantly cause this to be heard in the world, especially among the devotees of Viṣṇu;
the knowers of the Purāṇas declare that such a person attains union with Viṣṇu (sāyujya). 103.
Skanda said:
O Lord, it is known that the fruit of trees is purified in two ways;
now I wish to hear about the leaves and flowers that grant excellent liberation. 104.
The Lord said:
Among all leaves and flowers, the most excellent is the auspicious Tulasī;
she is pure, the bestower of all desires, belonging to Viṣṇu, and very dear to Viṣṇu. 105.
She is the foremost bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the supreme auspiciousness for all the worlds;
relying upon her, the best of sages have gone to the imperishable heaven. (106)
In ancient times, Tulasī was established by Viṣṇu for the welfare of all the worlds; indeed, all dharma is established within its leaves and flowers. (107)
Just as Lakṣmī is dear to Viṣṇu and just as I am dear to him, so too is this Goddess Tulasī; a fourth [such beloved] is not possible. (108)
A single Tulasī leaf indeed yields the fruit of a hundred pieces of gold; it cannot be equaled by other flowers, nor by other leaves, nor by other perfumes and ointments. (109)
Viṣṇu, the slayer of the Daityas, is not pleased without the leaves of Tulasī;
by whomsoever Hari is worshipped daily with this [leaf] and with supreme devotion. (110)
Whatever he has given, offered in sacrifice, known, or performed—such as vows and rituals—[brings] the state of being radiant birth after birth, happiness, fortune, fame, and prosperity. (111)
Family, virtue, wife, as well as son and daughter;
wealth, sovereignty, health, and both knowledge and discernment. ||112||
One should consider the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the Āgamas, and the Saṃhitās as being contained within every limb during the worship of Hari with Tulasī. 113.
Just as the Gaṅgā, with her purifying limbs, bestows liberation in the world of the gods,
and just as the Bhāgīrathī is meritorious, so too is the auspicious Tulasī.
Moreover, what is the use of the water of the Gaṅgā, or what is the use of serving the Puṣkara?
One is truly delighted by water alone that is mixed with a Tulasī leaf. (115)
Mādhava said: "In every birth of that wise man whose mouth is ever directed toward Me, faith arises upon hearing about the worship of Hari with Tulasī. (116)
O Skanda, it is impossible to describe the fruit of the merit of one who worships Viṣṇu with these very leaves of Tulasī. 117.
There, wherever there is a grove of *tulasī*, Keśava is present; there also is Brahmā, together with Lakṣmī and all the hosts of gods. (118)
Therefore, one should always worship that Goddess who is near at hand;
for by means of hymns, mantras, and so forth, she bestows all honor and prosperity. (119)
Furthermore, the pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, bhūtas, daityas, and so forth, always fled from that place. (120)
Alakṣmī, Nāśinī, Ghūrṇā, the Ḍākinīs, and the other Mothers—all of them shrink away upon seeing a leaf of tulasī. (121)
The diseases of sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, which arise from evil deeds and are brought about by wicked counsel— all these indeed perish there.
He who has planted a grove of *tulasī* on the earth for the sake of Hari has,
in effect, performed a hundred sacrifices according to the rules, accompanied by generous sacrificial fees.
By taking hold of a tulasī leaf at other lingas as well as on śālagrāma stones, one shall attain sāyujya with Viṣṇu.
That wise man who plants a *tulasī* tree for the sake of Lord Mādhava during the month of Vaiśākha goes to the abode of Mādhava. 125.
Having worshipped the Lord Hari, whoever wears the remains of the offering (nirmālya) or a leaf of Tulasī upon his own head shall be purified from sin and go to heaven.
In the Kali age, Tulasī destroys sin through worship, chanting, meditation, planting, and wearing; she bestows both heaven and liberation.
He should give instruction to her and, furthermore, practice it himself.
The supreme state that is the abode of Mādhava, which brings pleasure to Hari—that indeed shall be most dear to me. (129)
Therefore, among all the gods and goddesses,
O Six-faced One, my leaf alone is equal [to others] in śrāddha rites and sacrificial ceremonies.
Therefore, serve Tulasī with every effort;
by him who has served Tulasī, everything has been served.
Therefore, O Six-faced One, serve the guru, the brahmin, and the deity as sacred sites;
for he who casts off his life-breaths while wearing *tulasī* upon his crest [attains the highest goal].
Freed from the flood of evil deeds, he goes to the healthy realm of heaven by means of sacrifices such as the Rājasūya, various vows, and restraints. ||133||
The destination that is attained by the wise shall belong to those who serve the tulasī; for by worshipping Hari with even a single tulasī leaf, a man [attains it]. (134)

One attains the state of being a Vaiṣṇava; what is the use of other extensive scriptures? One would not obtain the merit of drinking ten million draughts of a mother’s milk by drinking the water from ten million Tulasī plants. 135.
The mortal by whom Keśava has been honored with the tender sprouts of branches shall bring men to mind by the hundreds and thousands. (136)
Having worshipped Hari daily with tender tulasī leaves, O dear one,
I have described to you the preeminent qualities of tulasī.
We are unable to describe his entire multitude of qualities, even over a vast period of time;
yet whoever should constantly hear this narrative, which is an accumulation of merit, [shall attain great reward]. (138)
One is liberated from the bondage of birth resulting from sins committed in previous lives;
by merely reciting it once, one obtains the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice. 139.
For one who has performed this dance, there shall never be diseases or the foolishness of a son;
he always attains victory and shall never suffer defeat. 140.
In whosever house this letter remains, prosperity shall prevail for him;
there shall be neither mental anguish nor ghosts, nor grief, nor humiliation. (141)
They do not remain for even a moment where this script prevails. ||142||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(61) The sixty-first chapter.
The twice-born said:
O Hari, we have heard from you the auspicious greatness of the Tulasī flower;
now we desire to hear the meritorious hymn composed for her. (1)
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, that Purāṇa which was previously proclaimed by me in the Skanda Purāṇa, they shall now relate in its entirety for the sake of liberation. 2.
All those disciples of Śatānanda, who were firm in their vows, bowed down to their preceptor and asked the Brahmin about that which is meritorious and beneficial.
O best among the knowers of Brahman, we wish to hear from you that hymn of praise to Tulasī which was previously heard by us from the mouth of Brahmā.
Śatānīka said: By the utterance of her name, the destroyer of the pride of the asuras is pleased;
sins go to dissolution, and merit becomes inexhaustible. (5)
How indeed can that Tulasī be worshipped by people through gambling, when merely seeing her yields the merit of giving ten million cows? (6)
Blessed are those men in this world who, in the Kali age, possess in their homes a śālagrāma stone and tulasī for daily use upon the ground. (7)
Blessed are those whose sprout-like hands gather Tulasī,
and who, in this age of Kali, plant it upon this earth for the sake of Keśava.
What will he do when enraged, even with his own attendants?
For by him who has worshipped the Lord of Gods with a single leaf of *tulasī*, all suffering is destroyed. (9)

A kinnara is perfected through the fruits of traveling on pilgrimages and the like, as well as through bathing, giving gifts, meditation, consuming [sacred substances], and the worship of Keśava. (10)
O Tulasī, in this Kali age, you destroy sin through being carried, through praise, and through being planted.
O beloved of Keśava, you are born from nectar; may you always remain upon my breast.
"O beautiful one, grant me a boon; I gather you for the sake of Keśava, so that I may constantly worship Hari with the products arising from your body. (12)
Likewise, O destroyer of all impurities and sins,
whoever shall pluck a Tulasī leaf with this mantra— ||13||
The worship of Vāsudeva shall be multiplied a hundred thousand crore times;
O Goddess of gods, the best of the deities sing of your power. (14)
The sages, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, and even the King of the Nagas himself in Patala—
none of these deities know his power, except for Kesava.
Even in hundreds of millions of kalpas, the measure of her virtues cannot be reached;
she emerged from Kṛṣṇānanda during the effort of churning the Ocean of Milk. (16)
O Goddess, since Viṣṇu formerly bore the tulasī upon his head,
you have now obtained all these limbs of Viṣṇu in their entirety.
Purity has been attained by you; I bow to you, O Tulasī, so that with leaves produced from your body, I may worship Hari. (18)
Act in such a way for me that there may be no obstacle, so that I may attain the supreme goal—[this tree] which was planted on the bank of the Gomatī by Kṛṣṇa himself and nurtured by him. (19)
For the welfare of the world and for the benefit of the gopīs, Viṣṇu himself, while wandering in Vṛndāvana, personally served the tulasī plant. 20.
For the sake of the prosperity of Gokula and for the destruction of Kaṃsa,
[this was done] previously by Rāma on the bank of the Sarayū at the word of Vasiṣṭha.
O beloved of the world, you were planted for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas;
I bow down to you, Tulasī, who were planted for the increase of ascetic merit. 22.
While separated from Vāsudeva, the daughter of Janaka meditated upon you,
and in the midst of the Aśoka grove, she was reunited with her beloved.
O Goddess, in ancient times you were planted by Pārvatī on the Himālayas for the sake of Śaṅkara and for the increase of her ascetic merit; I bow down to you, O Tulasī. 24.
In the Nandana grove, you are served by all the wives of the gods and by the kinnaras for the purpose of destroying bad dreams; homage be to you! 25.
In the Forest of Dharma and at Gayā, the meritorious Tulasī was personally worshipped by the ancestors; it should likewise be worshipped by one who desires their own welfare. (26)
Tulasī was planted by Rāmacandra, tended by Lakṣmaṇa,
and protected with devotion by Sītā in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Just as the Gaṅgā is sung of in the scriptures as pervading the three worlds, even so is the goddess Tulasī seen throughout the realm of the moving and the unmoving. 28.
And while dwelling on Ṛśyamūka, the king of monkeys cultivated the Tulasī plant for the sake of destroying Vālin and for the purpose of union with Tārā. (29)
Having bowed down to the goddess Tulasī, Hanumān crossed the ocean; having accomplished his task and being greatly delighted, he returned once more. (30)
Having taken up the *tulasī*, one is liberated from sins;
or else, O tiger among sages, it removes even the slaughter of a Brahmin. (31)
Whoever carries on his head the water dripping from a tulasī leaf obtains the merit of bathing in the Ganges, which bestows the fruit of donating ten cows.
Be gracious, O Goddess, Queen of the Gods; be gracious, O Beloved of Hari!
O Tulasī, born from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, I bow down to you. (33)
Keśava forgives even the thirty-two offenses of that person who recites the Tulasī-stava during the night vigil on the twelfth lunar day.
Whatever sin has been committed in youth, childhood, adolescence, or old age—all that goes to dissolution through the recitation of the praise of Tulasī. ||35||
When the Lord of Devas is pleased, he bestows joy; when satisfied, he grants prosperity.
He effects the destruction of enemies and bestows happiness and knowledge. (36)
By the mere name of Tulasī, the gods grant the desires of their devotees;
even for those who are censurable, O Lord of Gods, [Tulasī] grants liberation to embodied beings.
Satisfied by the hymn of praise to Tulasī, she bestows happiness and prosperity;
know that even the sin that has arisen and stands upon the path of Yama is cast away with ease. 38.
In whichever house a hymn of praise to Tulasī is found inscribed, no inauspiciousness shall exist there; he certainly attains auspiciousness. (39)
For him, everything is auspicious; there is nothing whatsoever inauspicious.
He always enjoys abundance of food, as well as wealth and grain in great plenty. (40)
There is devotion to Nīlakaṇṭha and the Lord of the World (Śiva), as well as never being separated from Vaiṣṇavas;
he lives free from disease, and his mind is not born to unrighteousness. 41.
Whoever recites the Tulasī hymn while keeping a vigil on the twelfth lunar day attains that fruit which is obtained by ten million times a hundred thousand crores of holy pilgrimage sites.
One obtains that very fruit by reciting the hymn of praise to Tulasī. ||43||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Hymn to Tulasī," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-second chapter.
The twice-born said:
"By bathing, all sin certainly goes to destruction;
tell us your command regarding other great sins as well. (1)
Purified from sin, he enjoys the imperishable heaven in the celestial realm like Śakra; there shall be no loss of his divine birth—O Sage, speak such instruction for me.
In this regard, after death, everything is to be enjoyed as the supreme heaven for the best of gods;
and it is said to be the staircase to heaven for those struck down by the sins of the Kali age.
Vyāsa said:
O brahmins, for those of ordinary birth who contemplate their destiny, the sin of women and men is quickly dispelled by the mere sight of the Gaṅgā. 4.
By the mere remembrance of Gaṅgā, sin goes to its destruction;
by her glorification, great sins [are destroyed]; and by the sight of her, heavy impurity [is removed]. (5)
Through bathing and drinking from the Gaṅgā, as well as by offering libations to the ancestors,
multitudes of great sins perish day by day.
Just as cotton or dry grass is consumed by fire in an instant,
so too is the sin of men burnt away in a moment by contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
By bathing in the Gaṅgā at Keśava, one attains imperishable heaven;
through merit, one obtains fame, sovereignty, heaven, and the supreme goal.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who offers a funeral cake (piṇḍa) in the Gaṅgā, intended for his ancestors, according to the prescribed rite preceded by the recitation of mantras. ||9||
By offering a single grain of rice, one is honored in the abode of the gods for ten thousand years;
know that by offering sesame seeds the merit is doubled, and likewise by offering pure fruit.
O Brahmins, by the rite of the cow-offering, there is no end to heaven;
likewise, by the constant offering of funeral cakes, it becomes as if one has performed a hundred sacrifices.
O fathers dwelling in hell, blessed are those who live as mortals, endowed with wealth and sons, possessing health, happiness, and honored with respect. (12)

Those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), those insects upon the surface of the earth, those in the stationary world, the flocks of birds, and likewise mortals—whether wealthy or kings—[all enter this state]. (13)
And by various sons and grandsons, kinsmen and daughters' sons, as well as by sons-in-law, nephews, friends, and associates—both dear and unpleasant. (14)
If water and funeral cakes, along with the necessary ritual implements, are offered by them on the banks of the Ganges or in its waters, their residence in heaven shall be imperishable. (15)
And those ancestors born of the mother's lineage who remain above the funeral rice-ball—all mortals by the hundreds of thousands become happy. (16)
The beings dwelling in heaven, those situated below, and those living in the middle—all constantly desire you both, who possess the limbs of the true Gaṅgā, that celestial river. (17)
Those men who go alone to the Gaṅgā to perform worship—this [act] is thus of great merit; it enables one to cross over [saṃsāra] and causes others to cross as well. 18.
Even the four-faced Brahmā is unable to describe all the qualities of the Gaṅgā;
therefore, I shall speak of a small portion of the virtues of Bhāgīrathī.
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and other excellent gods,
having performed austerities on the banks of the Gaṅgā, became imperishable in the heavenly world.
Even today, they have not returned with their divine bodies and their chariots that travel at will, despite the exhaustion of the treasures filled with jewels.
There, the palaces are made of gold, auspicious, and reaching above all worlds;
they are perfectly filled with desired objects, and there the women are enchanting.
The *pārijāta* trees, flowering trees equal to the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*), indeed bestow sovereignty upon those who perform penance there on the banks of the Gaṅgā. 23.
That goal which is attained through many austerities, sacrifices, various kinds of vows, and manifold gifts, is attained by those who serve the Gaṅgā.
Abandon him who is born of an adulterer, fallen, wicked,
a slayer of his elders, possessed of malice toward all, and endowed with every sin.
Sons abandon their father, wives their beloved husbands, and all other kinsmen and friends; yet one should never abandon the Gaṅgā. 26.
Just as a mother herself performs the cleansing of the impurities of birth,
so too does the Gaṅgā, having embraced them, wash away their impurities.
Among them, they become renowned, honored with enjoyments, ornaments, and worship;
for those men who repeatedly behold the Gaṅgā with devotion, [they attain this]. (28)

The auspicious one, who removes the suffering of those who remember her, delivers a hundred thousand generations of their families when she is meditated upon, praised, and rejoiced in by the virtuous. (29)

On the days of the sun’s passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), during the vyatīpāta yoga, and at the eclipses of the moon and the sun, he causes both lineages of men to cross over the ocean of existence by means of the Gaṅgā.

Having bathed in the Gaṅgā on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, by day, at the time of the gods, or during the northern course of the sun, one may uplift ten million members of one's lineage.
Blessed are those people who cast off their bodies while Janārdana dwells within their hearts;
he who, by this very method, [perishes] in the auspicious waters of the Bhāgīrathī, [attains liberation].
Having abandoned his life-breaths, he shall go to heaven from which there is no return;
for he who constantly follows the limbs of yoga is indeed a follower of all the gods. ||33||
Since Viṣṇu consists of all the gods and Gaṅgā consists of Viṣṇu, by offering rice-balls (piṇḍas) and water with sesame seeds to the ancestors in the Gaṅgā, [one attains the highest goal]. 34.
Those who are intent on harming others' wives, seizing the property of others, and practicing malice go from hell to heaven, and from heaven they may attain liberation. (35)
For one who is merely a human being, for one devoid of the Vedas and scriptures, and for one intent on censuring their guru, the Gaṅgā alone is the supreme refuge.
For one who has fallen away from the conduct of the observance (samayācāra), there is no destination equal to that of the Gaṅgā;
what is the use of sacrifices rich in great wealth, or of austerities most difficult to perform? (37)
The Gaṅgā, who bestows heaven and liberation and is worshipped for her bliss and auspiciousness—what need is there for constant supreme restraints or for yogas that restrain the mind? (38)
Gaṅgā, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, stands before one for the sake of easy deliverance;
the sins accumulated over many series of births perish for men. (39)
By merely bathing in the Gaṅgā, a man immediately becomes a partaker of merit, as does one at Prabhāsa when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, [or] when a thousand cows [are gifted]. (40)
Whatever fruit one obtains from giving gifts day after day by bathing in the Gaṅgā, that very sin is destroyed upon seeing [the deity]; and by touching [it], one attains the incomparable heaven. 41.
Even by way of incidental discussion, this immersion in the Gaṅgā bestows liberation;
it also [removes] the fickleness of all the senses, which arises from the power of latent impressions (vāsanā). 42.
Consequently, cruelty perishes upon seeing the Gaṅgā, as do the longing for another's wealth and the desire for another's wife. (43)
Delight in the dharma of others perishes at the mere sight [of the truth];
one who is content with what comes by chance engages in his own duties. (44)
And equanimity toward all beings arises from bathing in the Gaṅgā;
for that man who, having taken refuge in the Gaṅgā, dwells in happiness. ||45||
He alone is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) here, the most excellent among all;
for him who remains having resorted to the Gaṅgā, there is no further duty to be performed. 46.
That man has accomplished all that was to be done, is liberated from everything, and is liberated while living;
for him, sacrifice, charity, austerity, recitation, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods [are no longer required]. 47.
Whatever is performed daily at the Gaṅgā becomes multiplied by millions upon millions;
even the sin committed in other places perishes upon the banks of the Gaṅgā. (48)
Sin committed on the banks of the Gaṅgā is destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā;
[this occurs] on the day of one's own birth-star when it coincides with the day of the Jahnavī’s confluence. (49)
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā, a man shall uplift his own lineage; a man who praises that Lord of Wealth with devotion shall always [attain prosperity]. (50)
By praising the Gaṅgā even once in such a manner, one becomes a recipient of heaven;
so too for him who, even without faith, utters the name of the Gaṅgā.
He who causes the river of merit to flow indeed becomes a vessel for heaven;
while nourishing mortals on earth, he also delivers the nāgas from below. (52)
The river Gaṅgā, which traverses the three paths, is remembered as the one who leads the gods to heaven;
whether through knowledge or ignorance, and whether intentionally or unintentionally. (53)
A mortal who dies in the Gaṅgā attains heaven and liberation; such is the destination of the wise man who is established in purity and disciplined in yoga.
For an embodied being who gives up his life in the Gaṅgā,
it is as if he has performed thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa penances for the purification of his body.
One may drink as much as one desires; yet the Gaṅgā is distinguished from the earth. Such is the power of sacred fords (tīrthas), and that of the gods is especially so. 56.
Such is the power of the Vedas that it does not reach the Jahnavi;
Vayu declared that there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas).
O Jāhnavī, those [worlds] exist in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space;
O Gaṅgā, born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, you travel along the three paths.
O Ganges, you are renowned as the liquid of Dharma; you wash away my sin.
You were born from the foot of Viṣṇu; you belong to Viṣṇu and are worshipped by Viṣṇu. (59)
Protect me from that sin which extends from birth until death;
O Śrīmatārajasā, you who are filled with the splendor of the Dharma through faith. (60)
O Great Goddess Bhāgīrathī, purify me with your nectar!
Whoever bathes in the waters of the Jāhnavī while reciting these three excellent verses [shall attain the highest state]. 61.
One is liberated from the sins committed over ten million lifetimes; there is no doubt about this.
I shall now proclaim the root mantra spoken by Jāhnavī.
By reciting this once, a person becomes purified and established within the body of Viṣṇu.
And this mantra is:
*Oṃ namo gaṅgāyai viśvarūpiṇyai nārāyaṇyai namo namaḥ* ||63||
That man who carries on his head the clay produced on the banks of the Jāhnavī is liberated from all sins, even without bathing in the Gaṅgā. (64)
If one touches the wind shaken by the waves of the Ganges water,
he is purified from terrible sin and attains imperishable heaven.
As long as the bones of a human remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
By casting the bones of one's parents, kinsmen, orphans, or even one's teacher into the Gaṅgā, a person does not fall from heaven.
That man who carries a fragment of bone of his ancestors toward the Gaṅgā obtains, at every step, the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. ||68||
Blessed are the inhabitants of the countryside, as well as the beasts, birds, and insects, and all other beings, both stationary and moving, who have taken refuge on the banks of the Gaṅgā. (69)
O best of the twice-born, there are gods who have become mortals within a distance of one krośa along the Gaṅgā; all others on earth are merely human beings. (70)
If one dies on the path while traveling to bathe in the Gaṅgā, he attains heaven and obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (71)
Those living beings who die on the path shall go to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
even insects, birds, and locusts [shall go] by the mere touch of the feet of those traveling there. (72)
O twice-born ones, even those who merely mention the name of the Gaṅgā to every person attain supreme merit; such men obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (73)
Those whose minds are destroyed by heretics who revile the Gaṅgā go to a terrible hell from which rebirth is difficult to obtain. (74)
Even one who is like dust, if he constantly remembers and proclaims "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā," and recites [her name], attains heaven; what is the use of other extensive discourses? (75)
Even if one should say "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" from a distance of hundreds of yojanas,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Those men who have gone to the Ganges after dying from a miscarriage are born in vain as those who are blind and lame. (77)
Those lowest of men who do not praise the Gaṅgā are like the dull-witted;
those who do not instruct others regarding her are like the insane, their minds deranged.

O Brahmins, those of evil intellect, fallen and base, who do not recite this scripture for the sake of people, find its fruit to be entirely in vain; [yet] the fruit of the merit of the Gaṅgā belongs to them. 79.
Those wise ones who teach people with faith and themselves study with faith go to heaven; they deliver their ancestors and their teachers.
He who provides provisions for those traveling according to his wealth and power,
and he who travels without consuming the food of others, obtains the merit of bathing in the Bhāgīrathī.
One should know that the fruit of the bath belongs to the performer, but it is twofold for the instigator—whether by his own desire, unintentionally, through instigation, or by serving another. (82)
One who goes to the holy Jāhnavī through yoga shall go to the abode of the gods.
The twice-born said:
"O Vyāsa, we have heard from you this stainless glorification of Gaṅgā. (83)
"From where does the Gaṅgā come, what is her form, and from whence is she so exceedingly purifying?
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, I shall now tell you this ancient and meritorious story."
Having heard which, the best of men attains the path to liberation;
formerly, having gone to the world of Brahmā, Nārada, the bull among sages, [heard it]. (85)
Having bowed down, he asked the pure one, the purifier of the three worlds:
"O Father, what was created by you? What is the doctrine (mata) that brings welfare to both Śiva and Kṛṣṇa? (86)
For the sake of the welfare of the entire world, she was desired for a place upon the earth;
she is the most excellent among all goddesses or non-goddesses. (87)

Having resorted to her, the gods, Daityas, humans, and serpents, as well as those born from eggs, those born from sweat, trees, and others such as those born from sprouts, [attain their respective states]. (88)
"O Brahman, they all go to Śiva, who is the complete, eternal, and sovereign power.
Brahmā said: "In the past, while creating, he spoke of her whose form is Māyā and Prakṛti. (89)
"From you, I shall create the worlds and the beings of the first existence.
Having heard this, she then became sevenfold.
She is the Gāyatrī, the Speech, the Melody, and the Fortune who bestows all crops and wealth;
she is Knowledge, Wisdom, the Goddess Umā, the Seed of Power, and the Ascetic Woman. 91.
These seven are proclaimed as the fluids of the dharma of the castes;
the Vedas originate from the Gāyatrī, and from the Vedas the entire world exists.
*Svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *dīkṣā*—these are remembered as born from the Gāyatrī.
One should always recite the Gāyatrī in the sacrifice along with the Mātṛkās and other [mantras]. (93)
O gods, having obtained the *svadhā* offering at the sacrifice, you shall become free from old age and death;
thereafter, O gods, release the essence of nectar (*sudhārasa*) upon the surface of the earth. 94.
Then the earth became rich in crops, and the herbs were exceedingly auspicious; by means of fruits, roots, grains, and edible foods, the people became much more comfortable. 95.
The Goddess of Speech resides within the mouths and minds of all people;
likewise, she brings about the proclamation of Dharma in all the scriptures. (96)
Without her, the entire world—consisting of consciousness, conflict, sorrow, delusion, non-delusion, auspiciousness, and inauspiciousness—is said to proceed as something unreal. (97)
The birth of Kamalā, as well as the abundance of garments and ornaments, happiness, and sovereignty over the three worlds—therefore she is the beloved of Hari. 98.
O Bhairava, that knowledge which is pervasive throughout the worlds has Umā as its cause and destruction;
O Bhairava, she who dwells in half his body is both the mother of knowledge and the object of knowledge. 99.
The power of Varṇikā is exceedingly fierce, deluding all the worlds;
she brings about the maintenance and destruction of the worlds among all the worlds. ||100||
Previously, the two asuras Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain by the Goddess;
and Ruru, who was terrible and renowned throughout all the worlds, was also slain. (101)
She slew Mahiṣāsura, the sole conqueror of all the gods;
those foremost of asuras and daityas who were slain by the Goddess were killed with effortless ease.
Thus, having forever destroyed the forces of the Daityas, she protected and gladdened this entire triple world. (103)
Having beheld that great one, whose essential nature is the fluid of Dharma and who is established in all dharmas, I have held her within my water-pot. (104)
Born from the lotus-foot of Viṣṇu, she is borne upon the head of Śiva;
and she is joined by us three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (105)
In the water-pot whose form was like water renowned as the essence of Dharma,
there arose [the goddess] through the powerful Viṣṇu during the Bali sacrifices.
Previously, Bali, the best among the powerful, was deceived by a ruse;
thereafter, he stepped across the entire surface of the earth with only two steps. (107)
And the Sky-footed one (Nabhaḥpāda), having pierced the cosmic egg, stood before me;
his feet were indeed worshipped by me with the water from my water-pot. 108.
Having washed her feet, she offered them worship; the water fell upon Hemakūṭa, and reaching Śaṅkara from that peak, it remained within his matted locks as it circled about.
Then, having propitiated Śiva on earth, Bhagīratha brought [the Gaṅgā] down;
and the preeminent elephant was constantly worshipped by him with austerity.
Therefore, having pierced through the mountain with vigor by means of those three teeth, she made a hole;
because she went through that triple-chambered opening, she became world-renowned as Trisrotā.
Purified by union with Hari, Brahmā, and Hara, she is the sanctifier of the world; having approached that goddess, one obtains the fruit of all dharma. 112.

That goal which is attained by all beings through Vedic study, sacrifices, mantras, fire-oblations, and the worship of the gods, cannot be achieved even by those devoted to such acts without service to the Gaṅgā. 113.
For there exists no other means for accomplishing Dharma than this;
therefore, O Nārada, go to her, through the conjunction of merit from the three worlds. (114)
Through contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā and their bones, those sons of Sagara attained heaven, together with their ancestors and their descendants born before and after them. 115.
Then, having heard this from the mouth of Brahmā, Nārada, the bull among sages,
performed penance at Gaṅgādvāra and became equal to Brahmā.
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere; she is difficult to find only in three places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
By means of a three-night fast or a one-night fast, a man attains the supreme goal;
therefore, with every effort, he should contemplate immediate liberation.
Therefore, O knowers of dharma, go here to the auspicious Bhāgīrathī;
in a very short time, you shall attain heaven and liberation.
Especially in the Kali age, for those people who grant liberation through the Gaṅgā, there arises infinite merit for those whose strength has been exhausted by hardship. (120)
Then those brahmins, delighted upon hearing that auspicious speech from Vyāsa,
performed austerities at the Gaṅgā and subsequently proceeded upon the path to liberation.
Whatever mortal should hear this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative, he shall cross over the entire flood of suffering and obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. 122.
By reciting it even once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices:
[the merit of] giving, chanting, meditation, hymns, mantras, and the worship of the gods. (123)
Whoever should perform [the rite] there indeed obtains infinite fruit;
therefore, men should perform recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth in that place. 124.
And its fruit is said to be infinite; it is easily obtained birth after birth. ||125||
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṅgā," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-third chapter.
The sixty-third chapter.
Pulastya said:
In the meantime, the great sage Saṃjaya, a disciple of Vyāsa, having first paid homage to his teacher, questioned Bhīṣma. (1)
Tell me with certainty the method and sequence for the worship of the gods;
who is the most worthy of worship at the beginning, and who is the one to be worshipped constantly in the middle?
O Brahmin, who is the object of this worship, and who is its performer? What fruit does a person obtain after having performed this worship? (3)
Vyāsa said:
One should worship Gaṇeśa here at the outset for the sake of removing obstacles;
thus one attains the state of Vināyaka, just as he did when he was the son of Gaurī. 4.
