Formerly, Pārvatī gave birth to these two sons of Maheśvara, the heroic gods who support all the worlds and are the lords of the hosts of Skanda. (5)
Having seen that, the daughter of the mountain spoke for the sake of her success:
"O son, this water has been given by the gods, who are filled with joy. (6)
It is renowned as Mahābuddhi, fashioned from nectar;
I shall proclaim its virtues, so listen with concentrated minds. (7)
By merely smelling this, one will certainly attain immortality;
one becomes a knower of the true essence of the meaning of all scriptures and an expert in all weapons and missiles. ||8||

A scribe who is skillful in all branches of learning, wise, and a creator of beautiful compositions, who knows the principles of theoretical and practical knowledge—he is undoubtedly omniscient in this world. ||9||
"Having attained a status superior to that of a son through dharma, he shall attain a hundred perfections;
I shall grant this very boon to him, your father—this is my resolve. (10)
Having heard these words from the very mouth of his mother, Skanda, who was supremely wise,
immediately went to every sacred ford (tīrtha) situated throughout the three worlds.
Having mounted his own peacock, the wise Lumbodharadhara performed his consecration in an instant; then, having circumambulated his parents, he departed.
Then, thus prepared, he stood before his parents;
and likewise Skanda stood before them, saying, "Give me [a portion]. ||13||
Then, having observed that, Pārvatī was amazed and said:
"By the ablutions performed at all sacred fords and by all the gods who have likewise bowed down," [14]
All sacrifices, vows, mantras, yogas, and likewise other restraints, do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit gained by one who performs the worship of the parents. 15.
Therefore, he is superior even to a hundred sons by a hundredfold measure;
for this reason, O Heramba, I give you this modaka fashioned by the gods.
For this very reason, his worship is performed first in sacrifices and in the recitation of Vedic scriptures and hymns,
as well as constantly during the various rites of worship.
The Lord, together with Pārvatī, granted him a great boon:
"By worshipping him alone first, may the gods indeed become pleased. (18)
Then, all the goddesses and the ancestors likewise performed penance constantly, once the Lord of the Gaṇas had been worshipped.
Therefore, in all sacrifices, a twice-born man should worship Gaṇapa;
the merit of those [sacrifices] is multiplied by millions upon millions, according to the words of the God of gods and the Goddess.
Having joyfully bestowed all virtuous merit upon the God and Goddess,
he was then appointed as the lord of the Gaṇas in the presence of all the gods.
Therefore, in extensive sacrifices, in hymns of praise, and in daily worship, a person who worships Gaṇeśa shall obtain all accomplishments. ||22||
Knowing this, the gods, desiring to attain their beloved, then worshipped him with all their hearts for the certain sake of heaven and liberation. (23)
And on the fourth [lunar day], having observed a fast at night and having worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, the God should be worshipped either in a linga, or in an image, or in a painting. 24.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, who pacifies all obstacles;
O wise one, grant me protection from the ocean of existence and bestow the pride of Umā. 25.
O Lord who bestows the knowledge and realization of the water-born meditation, O King of Obstacles, homage to you; be gracious at all times. (26)
Whoever, having observed a fast, joyfully worships Gaṇeśa, being liberated from all sins, is honored in the world of the gods. ||27||
I shall proclaim his auspicious hymn of praise consisting of twelve names; "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati"—this is the mantra declared. (28)
Gaṇapati, Vighnarāja, Lambatuṇḍa, Gajānana, Dvaimātura, Heramba, Ekadanta, and Gaṇādhipa. ||29||
Vināyaka, Cārukarṇa, Paśupāla, and Bhavātmaja—one who recites these twelve names upon rising in the morning, [attains success]. (30)
The entire universe shall be under his control, and no obstacle shall arise anywhere.
Great spirits (mahā-preta) shall be pacified, and he shall not be afflicted by diseases.
Liberated from all sins, he indeed enjoys imperishable heaven. ||31||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Sixty-Fourth Chapter
Vyāsa said:
Once more I shall proclaim another hymn to the Lord of the Gaṇas,
which bestows all perfections, is purifying, and grants the fruit of all desires.
Once, that one of great body, resembling molten gold, with a protruding belly and wide eyes—him, the leader of the hosts of deities—I salute. (2)
I bow to that child who wears a black antelope skin, who has a serpent as his sacred thread, whose crown is a cluster of *dūrvā* grass, and who is the leader of the courtyard of the body. (3)
The god who removes all obstacles and is himself free from all obstacles,
having mounted his supreme mouse in the great battle between the gods and the asuras.
The great-armed one who desires to fight, the leader of the field of battle—[the letter] Yaṃ, which is the heart of the syllable Viṃ, surrounded by the Mātṛkās. ||5||
He who is fond of devotion, intoxicated with joy, the lord of the courtyard of the body,
whose limbs are variegated with diverse jewels, and adorned with wonderful garlands.
I bow to the god who assumes any form at will, the leader of the celestial hosts,
the elephant-faced one, the best among the gods, adorned with beautiful ears.
One should [meditate upon] the Lord Gaṇanāyaka, who holds a noose and a goad, and who is always attended by Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas. (8)
A person who recites with the water of devotion this meritorious hymn to the eight Gaṇas—the great-bodied one being praised and the leader of the Gaṇa-hosts—[attains the highest state]. 9.
He attains all perfections and is glorified in the world of Rudra;
furthermore, such a person does not fall into poverty for seven births.
The man who recites this constantly shall become a great king;
by reciting or even hearing it, he brings the three worlds under his control.
This supreme hymn of the high-souled Gaṇeśa is of great merit. (11)
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gaṇapati," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Sixty-Fifth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
One should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas at all the openings of the Naṃdī;
everything shall come under his control, and his merit shall become inexhaustible. (1)
By means of the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," a person attains all perfections in all sacrificial jars, and shall obtain heaven and liberation. ||2||
A wise person should cause the image of Hari to be drawn upon a clay model, a painting, a stone, a wooden door, or a vessel.
Even in another place that is constantly within the range of one's vision, a wise person should establish the image of Hara and worship it according to their ability. ||4||
Consequently, his beloved undertakings will all be accomplished;
nothing whatsoever shall arise as an obstacle, and he may bring even the three worlds under his control.
The seeker of knowledge obtains knowledge arising from the Vedas and the Shastras, as well as other arts and crafts, victory, and that which bestows heaven. (6)
One seeking wealth shall obtain vast riches; a virtuous and charming daughter; sovereignty achieved through righteousness; and a son who grants liberation to the lineage. (7)
No one is afflicted by diseases, nor by planetary spirits or those born as ghosts;
neither by horned beasts, nor by Rākṣasas, lightning, or forest-thieves.
When Vināyaka has been worshipped, the king does not become angry, pestilence does not prevail in the home, there is no famine, and there is no weakness.
Salutation to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired aims, and who cuts through all obstacles. (10)
And this is the mantra: *Oṃ namaḥ gaṇapataye*.
With flowers dear to Nārāyaṇa, as well as other fragrant ones, with sweetmeats, fruits, roots, and likewise with substances produced in their season. (11)
He who worships Gaṇeśa with curds and milk, with beloved musical instruments, and with fragrant incense, shall attain all perfections. 12.
Especially for his linga, whoever gives what is dear to Vasu—articles of worship, clothing, or anything else—all shall become a hundred thousand times more effective. (13)
In the land of Bhāratavarṣa, in the presence of a woman, on the southern bank of the Lauhitya river, there is Vināyaka in the form of a Liṅga. 14.
By the command of Hara and Gaurī, and with the consent of the gods, he remained for the sake of the peace of the world and for the destruction of all obstacles. (15)
Having worshipped that deity with offerings according to one's capacity, one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras attains the status of Vinayaka. (16)
Having performed a single circumambulation, and having seen and touched it, a human being attains imperishable heaven and is always honored by the gods. ||17||

There, for the sake of the welfare of those who associate with Mlecchas, for those of great asceticism who are on the path to liberation, and for the sake of sons for all people, Vināyaka is Śambhu. 18.
Having performed an ablution in the Lauhitya, whoever touches the Lord of the Gaṇas is liberated from the sins committed in seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. ||19||
Having approached Vināyaka, one shall obtain in every birth a mind free from widowhood, poverty, sorrow, and envy. 20.
Furthermore, for a person who worships Gaṇeśa, there is success again, enjoyment again, fame again, and strength again; of this there is no doubt.
Without performing worship of this [liṅga], all one's desired objects perish;
therein reside the gods, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and others, who are well-pleased. (22)
Then, while the Lord of the Gaṇas was devoid of worship by the Maghons,
he was assailed in battle by the highly powerful Asuras, headed by Hiraṇyākṣa.
This was taken by Hiraṇyākṣa from Maghavat through his own conquered valor;
thereafter, for a hundred years in the past, the gods were rendered powerless.
In the great war between the gods and the asuras, the gods were defeated; thereupon, Śiva, the God of gods, was informed by the deities. (25)
"O Blessed One, our kingdom has not been seized by the asuras, nor have the sacrifices been destroyed. In the meantime, the Lord spoke these words to the gods: [26]
"O Heraṃbā, by me who am pleased with both of you, may supreme perfection for the gods and others be attained through this worship. (27)
That man who, out of delusion, disregards this great festival shall find no success, and even in battle he shall suffer defeat. (28)
A great sacrifice was performed by you for the worship of Gaṇapati;
because it was done with negligence and delusion, defeat was consequently obtained. ||29||
"Go quickly, O you who possess vast merit; perform worship for that great-souled lord of the courtyard. O knowers of dharma, victory will swiftly be yours. (30)
Then, having heard from the mouth of Hara words that were auspicious and beneficial,
all the gods, standing before the Lord of the Gaṇas, were filled with joy.
The gods said:
"Obeisance to you, O Lord of the Gaṇas, the sole protector of all the gods!
We bow down to you, who out of affection bestow the enjoyments of heaven; indeed, we have come to you for refuge. (32)
We bow down to you, Heraṃba, the bestower of victory in all battles, the granter of success in all undertakings, who possesses great illusion and a massive body. 33.
Once, we bowed down before that wise Vināyaka Laṃbatuṇḍa, the god who is honored by great seers and gods, and even by Indra himself. (34)
"Forgive us for that worship which was previously performed by you through sacrifice. Having heard the words of the gods, Gaṇapa spoke these words: ||35||
"O gods, let a boon be chosen by you from me, for it is desired by both of us.
Thereupon, Śakra and all the others, led by Bṛhaspati, [spoke].
The gods said to Gaṇapati, "May victory be ours.
Having heard the words of the gods, Gaṇeśa spoke these words: ||37||
"Very well, O best of asuras; may victory be yours quickly!
Then all the hosts of gods, their minds overflowing with joy, [spoke thus]. (38)
They worshipped Gaṇeśa with the finest fragrant substances and ornaments,
with divine incenses, excellent garments, and flowers born in the Nandana grove.
Worshipped by the gods with *pārijāta* flowers and other blossoms that enchant the deities, Gaṇapa spoke to the best of the asuras.
"Go, O gods, to Viṣṇu, the lord of the wise, whose daring is marvelous;
he will fulfill your desire and whatever you wish for, O deities. (41)
Having mounted their respective chariots, they went to the immutable Hari;
and having offered salutations to him who is clad in yellow garments, the hosts of gods spoke with joy.
O Great-souled Keśava, having approached and worshipped the son of Hara, the Lord of Gaṇas, we have now come into your presence. 43.
Having heard these words of the gods, the imperishable Hari spoke this according to the truth: "I shall slay the foremost of the Daityas."
Having heard the nectar of speech fallen from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, the gods were thrilled and filled with great joy; they worshipped him with their desired offerings.
Viṣṇu spoke again to the gods, headed by Indra:
"Gathering your respective forces, prepare yourselves, free from anxiety. (46)
"You shall seize these men of wicked conduct and their equal force;
having gathered the multitude of weapons, you shall stand there free from fear. (47)
Having heard the words of Mādhava, the preeminent gods departed;
all of them, bearing divine weapons, ascended their celestial chariots.
The spies of the Daityas indeed heard the words of joy uttered by the gods, and they reported them to the immensely powerful King Hiraṇyākṣa. 49.
Having heard this, the lord of the Daityas, possessed of immense strength, became enraged;
summoning his ministers, he spoke these words in his anger. (50)
Now all the gods, beginning with Indra, though possessed of cruel intentions, desiring to seize Mādhava, reported everything to Śambhu. (51)
"How shall we obtain victory over this most terrible host of Daityas?
Thus [asked], Tripurāri said, "O gods, worship Gaṇeśa! (52)
"Having worshipped that god, you shall conquer the asuras and dānavas.
Then the leader of the gaṇas was honored by the joyful hosts of gods.
The Great One, being pleased, granted this boon to Krūra:
"Today you shall conquer all the Asuras. Then the gods were filled with joy.
Desiring our destruction, they reported this to Hari;
and having heard Hari’s "So be it," the chariot-warriors took up their weapons in hand.
O fearless and healthy lady, the gods stand ready for battle;
let each god here say clearly what power he possesses to conquer him.
Then, having heard the king's words, Madhu spoke these sweet words:
"O King, I shall conquer Hari; appoint me as your ally. (57)
"Since the gods, even the thirty [Tridaśas], are certainly filled with fear when Nārāyaṇa conquers, therefore Nārāyaṇa is our share; he is the victory over all cities. (58)
Then Dhundhu, Dhu, Suṃda, and the mighty Kālakeya, along with Madhu as their ally, said, "O King, we shall conquer Mādhava. (59)
And all the leaders of the Daitya forces,
heroes of firm prowess equal to Time and Death, were masters who had reached the further shore of the knowledge of all weapons.
Thereupon Bala spoke these words:
"O King, I shall surely conquer that Jishnu against whom victory is at hand; this is my firm vow."
Namuci and Muci, the two brothers, arrogant in their strength, said to the king: "We two, being powerful, shall surely conquer you by our might. (62)
And Jambha spoke these words to Indra and those led by Indra: "I shall conquer; do not fear, O Daityas, be free from anxiety."
Tripura spoke these words: "I shall conquer Vināyaka.
Then the commander-in-chief said: "By me, the gods have been rendered powerless. (64)
[He saw] Kubera with the Rākṣasas and all the Hiraṇyakas;
in the meantime, Nārada, the best of sages, arrived there.
Having gone there, he said to Hiraṇyākṣa: "I have come as the messenger of Jiṣṇu;
renounce the kingdom, for your life-breaths are at our disposal if you so desire. (66)
"If you do not fight me, you shall go to the subterranean realm (rasātala) intoxicated with pride.
Then, out of anger, he spoke these words to Nārada, the best of sages.
"O serpent, go quickly from here before me, O Brāhmaṇa;
[report] the calamity, the slaughter, and the destruction of the gods before [the Lord]. (68)
"Behold! By a mere glance, he has reached Hari, Hara, and the others.
Having spoken thus, the lord of the Daityas addressed the commander of his forces.
Having heard the words of the king of the Daityas, the commander of the forces immediately prepared the entire army and quickly brought forth all the chariots.
Summoning their forces, they arrived swiftly and in great alarm;
there were thousands of crores of crores of akṣauhiṇīs and various armies.
And for each hero there were great and magnificent vehicles—various chariots, as well as elephants, camels, horses, and donkeys. (72)
Then, mounting lions, tigers,
and leopards, they set forth with a great multitude of all kinds of musical instruments and terrifying lion-roars.
The quarters of the sky, along with the oceans, the shore-mountains, and the earth, were filled with his roars;
all the worlds were terrified, and the oceans trembled.
The gods sounded their celestial drums, which were struck by all the deities,
along with various other musical instruments filled with air and producing deep, resonant sounds.
Wherein all the worlds abide, and where the inhabitants of the three realms dwell;
having lost their desires, they have come to the sky toward that terrible, intense, and great conflict.
In the battle, they struck one another with iron clubs, nooses, spears, swords, staffs, axes, and sharp, terrible arrows.
With many weapons and missiles discharged in every direction—into the quarters, the intermediate points, on the earth, upon the mountains, and in the waters—[the battle raged]. (78)
The battle between those two took place in temples, as well as in the sky, on mountain peaks and ridges, in caves, and in great forests.
Just as torrents of water fall from thick clouds such as Puṣkala,
so too did weapons fall upon the armies by the hundreds and thousands.
Some fell upon the earth with their bodies pierced by arrows;
others [fell] by means of spears, clubs, umbrellas, tridents, and battle-axes.
Those heroes who have fallen in battle while acting with justice,
being fearless for the sake of their master, go to the abodes of the gods.
And those others who are cowardly, sinful, or turn their backs on the battle, and those warriors who fight with unjust means—they go to the abode of Yama. (83)
Those stationed on elephants attacked those stationed on horses; likewise, chariot-riders attacked others stationed in chariots, and foot-soldiers attacked those who were on foot.
Desiring battle, those heroes strike one another down;
they are joyful, endowed with courage, most righteous, and possessed of strength. (85)
Some, their heads shattered by maces concealed within the arms [of their attackers], fell to the surface of the earth with hair, skulls, and garments [scattered]. (86)
Thus, those of great strength fell upon the earth— some cut through the middle, others split asunder—
pierced and mangled by the falls of swords and fierce battle-axes.
The ground of the region became ablaze with brave men, elephants, serpents, horses, and foot-soldiers, who were as unsteady as women fallen into a village yet adorned with divine ornaments. (88)
Then, with its various ornaments, banners, and standards lost, the entire earth, including its mountains, forests, and groves, [appeared desolate]. 89.
There, in the battle between the gods and the asuras, the heaps of provisions were devoured by many carnivorous beasts while drenched in floods of blood.
Abundant blood was drunk by the Rākṣasas, wolves, and other great hosts, along with the wind-blown gore. (91)
And it was joyfully devoured by throngs of jackals and vultures;
meanwhile, the wise Bṛhaspati, honored by the gods, [arrived]. (92)
He thoroughly mastered the science of reviving the dead among the gods—the divine *viśalyakaraṇī*, the great and powerful knowledge of Brahman. ||93||
Then the wise Dhanvantari, the divine physician who is as swift as thought,
roamed joyfully throughout the battlefield with medicines and their various applications.
There, the gods live and those who were dead in the great battle; free from wounds and endowed with strength, they fight again most fiercely. 95.
Thus, by the power of merit, that arrogant host of a hundred thousand Daityas fell, their bodies pierced through by arrows.
Then, with cries of "Victory!", the Siddhas, Cāraṇas,
Ṛṣis, other sky-dwellers, and hosts of Apsarases honored him.
The Gandharvas sang songs and the supreme sages offered praises;
then the chief of the Daityas, possessed of great splendor and great strength, became enraged. 98.
The commander-in-chief of the Daitya king, renowned as Kālakeya, stood upon his chariot there, wielding a bow and possessing great heroism. (99)
He struck those hosts of asuras and made them dance upon the earth;
at that time, the sky was completely covered by an incessant shower of arrows.
Arrows fall by the thousands upon tens of millions of troops;
then the gods fall, never retreating in the battles.
Vomiting blood, all the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras, as well as the gods, being tormented by his arrows, fell upon the surface of the earth. 102.
Some, pierced by hundreds, thousands, and even tens of thousands of arrows, those heroes of great prowess—foremost among the gods—fell upon the earth in that battle. (103)
And all those dwellers of heaven, beginning with Śyandana, became distressed;
tormented by his arrows, they were unable to stand before him.
Thereupon, his army plunged in like an elephant into a lake or a forest;
the gods were afflicted by his arrows, which possessed a brilliance equal to the thunderbolt and fire.
They were unable to stand in battle against Maghavan; they then fled from him.
There was a god renowned as Citraratha, the best among the wielders of weapons. (106)
Mounting his excellent chariot, that wielder of the bow went forth toward the battle; he then spoke these words to the commander of the army, the great Asura.
Just as a great hero joyfully slays the army of the gods, so you, being full of courage and worthy of praise, are considered a Śūra (hero) among the Asuras. 108.
The deed that was dear to Hiraṇyākṣa has now been performed by you in battle;
now, by my arrows, go yourself to the abode of Yama.
Then Kālakeya spoke these words with a smile:
"The entire host of gods has already been conquered by me with effortless play."
Now all this army stands at ease in the battle through your grace;
O bull among the gods, you have joy in their destruction here. (111)
"By these sharpened arrows, I shall lead you to the abode of Yama," he said,
and being exceedingly enraged, [he drew] an arrow resembling a venomous serpent.
In that battle, the hero struck him with three arrows and cut off his bow;
then, in a fury, he quickly fixed more arrows to his bow in the encounter.
With great agility, he struck down many Daityas;
thereafter, they [the two] struck one another with sharp arrows possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
The best of archers, with great force, cut it down upon the ground;
that battle between the god and the demon became exceedingly righteous.
Sages, gods, celestial musicians, and serpents have come to his side desiring to see him;
likewise, hundreds of thousands of arrows have been drawn [by him].
The two heroes shone forth against one another in battle for the sake of victory;
then, the lord of the Gandharvas, possessed of great splendor, became enraged.
He pierced him with three arrows in the forehead, five in the heart,
seven in the belly, and five in the private parts.
Struck by arrows, the Daitya became bewildered and fell into a state of dejection;
with his bow slackened, the powerful one regained consciousness only after a long time.
With three arrows, he pierced Madhusaṃjña, the best of the asuras; and while the king of the Daityas looked on, he shattered his bow with celestial weapons.
Then, with thousands of arrows possessing a luster like that of the sun at the end of time,
that most excellent and powerful of gods pierced the lion-like Daitya.
With his consciousness impaired, the lord of the Daityas, streaming with much blood,
agitated and afflicted by many arrows, the Dānava seized a trident.
Having struck the horse of that very one who held a spear in his hand with four arrows, he caused it to fall;
and with three [more], he struck Tāraka himself.
Then, standing upon the earth, the powerful Citraratha struck that best of Gandharvas with a trident; however, the latter cut that trident apart with three arrows.
Seeing the trident shattered like a serpent deprived of its fangs,
the powerful one seized a formidable mallet and rushed toward the asura.
Then, as Samudgara arrived at the head of the Daitya army,
he swiftly severed his head from his body with a crescent-headed arrow.
The earth, along with its mountains and surface, trembled violently;
then all the hosts of Daityas turned their backs and fled in every direction.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Kālakeyas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Sixty-sixth Chapter.
Vyāsa said: Seeing his brother slain, the Dānava named Kāleya rushed toward Citraratha, seizing his bow and an arrow.
Seeing that demon rushing forward with a splendor like the God of Death at the time of destruction,
the highly heroic Jaya, son of Pākaśāsana, obstructed him.
The one of great splendor, the best of the gods, spoke these words to the son of Diti—
words that were true, endowed with righteousness, and certainly beneficial for both worlds.
He who strikes down one afflicted by the pain of a weapon-wound, or one covered in filth, or one joined with another,
or one who is broken, or one who has fled, is indeed a fool.
Having suffered in Raurava for a very long time, one shall thereafter become its slave for a long duration;
therefore, do not fight with me, but remain established in the dharma of battle.
Overwhelmed with rage, Kāleya spoke these words to Jaya:
"Having slain Tāraka, the slayer of my brother, I shall now kill you."
Then Jayanta, the best of the gods, struck that foremost of asuras, who possessed a radiance like the fire of time, with sharpened arrows.
That Asura also pierced Nicakartta with three arrows,
just as a mountain stream carries away a multitude of trees when it encounters them during the rains.
Thus, those two of great heroism, neither exhausted nor cowardly, and each desiring victory over the other, found no rest. ||9||
Then, with an arrow, he severed the bow of that Daitya;
with five arrows, he struck Tāra and caused him to fall to the ground.
With eight sharp arrows, he struck down the four horses;
then, standing on the ground and seizing a spear, he struck Kumāra.
Having struck down Siṃha along with his horses, his chariot-fender, and his pole by means of his mace, he let out a roar upon the earth. ||12||
Moving with agility to the earth's surface, he stood there mace in hand;
his roar became as unbearable for the worlds as the crash of a thunderbolt.
Thus, from the impact of their maces, there arose a sound again and again;
in this manner, the mace-duel between them continued for four years.
Then, both of them, standing on broken pieces of their chariots and wielding swords and shields,
engaged in a wonderful battle between the infantrymen that caused the hair to stand on end.
Upon seeing this, the gods, asuras, and great serpents were filled with wonder;
for in a mere moment, the armor of those two was completely shattered by the falling strokes of the sword.
A sword-fight ensued between those two who were exceedingly skilled in combat;
Jayanta, possessed of terrible prowess, struck off his [the opponent's] head.
With his sword, he struck off his head and cast it to the ground;
then all the gods rejoiced with shouts of victory.
And the hosts of Daityas, utterly shattered, fled in all directions.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Kāleyas," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||66||
The sixty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the exceedingly powerful Daitya lord Hiraṇyākṣa, filled with rage and his eyes extremely copper-red, commanded the asuras. (1)
"I myself shall go to battle with the desire to destroy the gods;
since they do not come to fight, let them enter here by this path."
Having heard these words, all the remaining lords of the Daitya hosts, highly skilled in wielding spears and nooses, set out for battle.
And even more than that, by hundreds of times the former army,
they proceeded without interval through the sky, desiring battle.
Then the Rudras, along with the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the Vasus;
and Skanda and Gaṇeśa, preceded by Viṣṇu and Jiṣṇu. ||5||
All those warriors set out, joyful and eager for battle;
in the meantime, a conflict also broke out between the gods and the dānavas.
Never before had anything been seen or heard so terrifying to all the world,
equipped with many kinds of weapons and missiles, like a forest in the winter season.
The battle raged as they hemmed in the earth, heaven, and the sky;
they struck one another in the air and likewise upon the surface of the earth.
With spears, maces, and bhallas; with many showers of arrows;
with terrible blows from swords, as well as with discuses and battle-axes; ||9||
They struck one another with various other weapons;
they became of terrible form and appeared as if indestructible in the sky. 10.
With weapons, arrows, and the falling of blood, accompanied by herons, crows, and jackdaws,
the clouds rain down redness like streams of molten metal.
Likewise, with blood dripping from their own limbs, some gods and dānavas fell down,
fainted, stumbled, and laughed.
Some uttered cries of distress, while others repeatedly let out lion-like roars; some had their arms severed, and others likewise had their feet cut off.
With their flanks and bellies mangled, some fell upon the earth by the hundreds;
likewise, thousands of crores of elephants, horses, and asuras [perished]. (14)
Falling upon the surface of the earth in many streams of blood,
thereupon the surface of the earth became an ocean of blood.
Then, contrary to their nature, the rivers there suddenly overflowed;
there, piles of wood consisting of grass and timber were carried away by the currents.
Mudgaras, maces, tridents, makaras, and so forth appear; and there are those with the forms of jackals, fish, tortoises, and crocodiles. (17)
Obstructed here and there by arrows and the like, as well as by numerous great camels,
those [rivers] were then filled with hair, yak-tail whisks, and moss.
And by those falling [arrows] and various others, an ocean of blood was then formed,
covering the entire earth along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
A most terrible river of blood, causing fear to all the worlds, reached the abode of Yama for the Daityas by the falling of Skanda’s spear. ||20||
Bound with the supreme axe, with fire, with arrows having crests of flame, and with the noose of Varuṇa, he was cast into the inexhaustible fire of Yama.
By whose sons, grandsons, and likewise by their leaders and ministers,
the Daityas were struck down with showers of arrows, spears, and double-edged swords.
And by the planets, the winds, the yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras, as well as by Mahādeva and the wise Kubera. ||23||
Driven by the masses of thick thunderbolts, by frost impelled by the moon,
and by the terrible poisons of serpents, the Daityas fell to the surface of the earth.
And by other various gods, numbering in the thousands of millions upon millions,
they were all struck down and fell to the earth, their lives departed.
Having abandoned their bodies, some go to heaven, others to this world, and some go to the netherworld (pātāla) according to the application of their merit and demerit. ||26||
In the meantime, the supreme sages spoke among themselves:
"May there be well-being for the Brahmins, for the cows, for women, and for those practicing austerities. (27)
While all other beings are currently engaged in combat,
the remaining Daityas, afflicted by the gods, have taken refuge in the mountains.
And they fled in all directions, cowardly and terrified of the forest;
for when the Daitya array had been broken, the one named Bala possessed great strength.
He afflicted the gods, restraining them with arrows equal to fire;
many of those gods, though proud of their strength, were tormented by his shafts.
Some fell upon the surface of the earth and others were broken on the field of battle, having witnessed his great deed, which was terrible and terrifying to the world. ||31||
The gods and the excellent sages praised him, while the disciplined ones there cried out in joy.
Then the immensely powerful Śatakratu, the subduer of enemies, became enraged.
With his arrows and staffs, he struck Bala, the foremost of the powerful;
and Bala, too, being enraged, fought with such agitation against Śakra in that battle.
With their limbs drenched by flowing blood, those two of great strength appeared like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom during the month of Mādhava.
And that best of asuras, impetuous in battle, buried thousands of discuses, spears, and maces into the earth.
The powerful king of the gods, having suddenly become bewildered in battle, effortlessly cut down those discs and spears with his excellent arrows. (36)
Then the great-splendored Daitya Sacat,
with a spear, swiftly struck Puraṃdara as he stood upon his elephant between its two frontal lobes.
Struck by her, Śakra trembled upon his elephant;
Jiṣṇu, having regained his composure and strength, pierced the Danuja in an instant.
Standing upon his chariot, [the other] cut off his hands and bow with an arrow;
then the slayer of heroes severed his shield and sharp standard with a single shaft.
With four sharp arrows he pierced the four horses,
and with a single shaft he instantly severed the head of the charioteer.
With his bow severed, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he fell to the earth unconscious and met his death after a short while.
Then the great Daitya Namuci, the destroyer of the pride of the gods, being enraged,
suddenly took up a mace and struck the great elephant.
Just as the fall of a thunderbolt upon the peak of Mount Meru would certainly occur,
even so did that great sound arise, causing the hair to stand on end.
Afflicted by the blow, Padmin trembled, utterly overwhelmed;
his limbs drenched in blood, he turned away, tormented by pain. ||44||
They rushed toward Śatakratu by the hundreds and thousands;
the Subduer of Pāka cut them down with crescent-headed arrows and razor-sharp shafts.
O foremost of gods, since you have been afflicted by his illusions,
some have fallen to the ground while others lie asleep upon their chariots.
Seeing his great feat as well as those arrows, Mādhava cut them down with his discus as they remained fixed in his body.
Then Jiṣṇu struck him down to the ground with three arrows;
fallen upon the earth, the Daitya fainted and staggered again.
Brandishing his terrible mallet, he rose up intent on slaying Śakra;
then Maghavat struck the great Asura with his thunderbolt.
His great strength was displayed as his chest was pierced upon the surface of the earth with a thunderbolt;
and the gods, the Siddhas, and the great seers cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (50).
Then they honored Śakra with many showers of flowers;
thereafter, all the hosts of Daityas fled from that place in fear.
The Gandharvas sang songs and the throngs of Apsaras danced.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Bala and Namuci," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||67||
The Sixty-Eighth Chapter
Vyāsa said:
Having seen Bala slain as well as his own elder brother Namuci, Mucis spoke these words there: "My eldest brother has been destroyed by you. (1)
"Now, out of your sight, I shall send you to the son of the Sun with my arrows.
To him, Śakra, of great splendor and worshipped by all the gods, replied:
"O brother, you will certainly now obtain the state of Dharma,
just as a moth, through delusion and without knowing the heat of fire, [seeks it]."
"You wish to enter the fire and likewise to fight me so suddenly!"—
to Indra, who was speaking thus, he struck with three arrows.
Śakra, the conqueror of enemy cities, cut his [the demon’s] heart with three arrows;
then he struck Indrajit with ten and Airāvaṇa with three.
Having severed Mātali with seven arrows, he roared loudly with a terrible sound;
then the Daitya, in great agitation, whirled Śakra around once more.
Then Śakra, possessing great strength and prowess,
struck that iron club from the armpit with his thunderbolt, as it was light as a balance-scale.
With the falling of the fragile [weapon], the demon fell down lifeless;
by that fall of the Danuja, the earth trembled.
The gods performed dances, and the Dānavas fled in all directions.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Muci," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||68||
The Sixty-Ninth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Tāraka, endowed with great strength and possessing valor equal to Śakra, struck Skanda,
the slayer of his father, with arrows in battle.
Then the mighty-armed Skanda, whose prowess was equal to that of Indra,
cut down those various arrows and pierced them with his own excellent shafts.
Then Viśākha, remaining unperturbed, suddenly covered Skanda along with the Daityas with his arrows and cut them down with his shafts.
Tāreya struck Skanda with fire-arrows at the head of the battle;
he then plunged a spear, resembling a thunderbolt, into the mouth of the demon.
There, the commander-in-chief Vaiśvānara surrounded him;
then the Daitya again hurled the Raudra weapon at him.
That [weapon] was repelled by him with that struck arrow;
then the Daitya hurled the Aghora weapon, which was terrible in form and extremely fierce.
Mountains, trees, mountainsides, as well as serpents and other creatures, fled by the thousands of millions upon millions toward the son of Pārvatī, using them as arrows.
Having severed those arrows, he pierced that bull among the Daityas with arrows resembling fire and the sun, from his feet up to the top of his head.
The gold-feathered arrows lodged deeply in the body of the lord of the Daityas shone like fragments of gold upon a mountain of black stone.
Then, from his body, blood flowed profusely,
just as the śamī tree blossoms abundantly in the month of Caitra.
They, along with Danda and Ashva, lay prostrate upon the ground.
Then the great Daitya, filled with rage, [seized] a terrible and dreadful trident.
Having seized it, he hurled back that trident— which shone like Time and Death— toward Pāśupati with a roar, even as Pārvatī looked on.
Thrown by him, it was destroyed and burnt in an instant on the field of battle;
then the Dānava hurled another spear given by Brahmā.
Then he struck back with a trident possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred peaks;
thereafter, two weapons resembling thunderbolts clashed even in the sky.
As those two, exerting their full prowess, fell upon the ground,
the lord of the Daityas then struck Skanda with arrows resembling flames of fire.
He suddenly struck him like a mountain with a torrent of rain;
having repelled that [attack], the mighty-armed commander drew his bow.
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he likewise severed his great head;
furthermore, with many arrows, he struck down the horses to the ground.
Seizing a mace, that lord of the Daityas rushed with speed toward Guha on the ground and struck Śikhin, whose vehicle is the peacock.
Then the peacock, having fallen into delusion, cried out repeatedly;
thereafter, Skanda struck that foremost of asuras once more.
With the force of his sword, he cut down the most terrible mace;
then Tāreya, seizing a spear, struck the destroyer of Krauñca.
Then he too released an unerring spear, the slayer of the wicked;
thereupon that spear, which brings about the dissolution of the universe, began to burn him.
Having shattered the staff of Yama as it were, he entered the cave again; his life departed, he fell upon the earth, shaking the mountains and the bearer of wealth.
Skanda was worshipped by all the gods with flowers, incense, and other offerings. ||23||
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Tāraka," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventieth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then the powerful Daitya Tāraka, his lips bitten in rage, roared toward the battle and engaged in combat according to the rules of dharma.
Having gone there, he spoke words censured by all the world:
"Out of wicked delusion, you do not recognize the great Dharma in its proper sequence. (2)
Capable of restraining and favoring through the application of sin and merit,
I have been created by the Creator and carry out your command.
You do not know that this Dharma has death as its precursor at any time;
for death knows neither disease, nor old age, nor time, nor does it act as a servant.
One who deviates from the Dharma undergoes suffering day and night;
thus it was said to Vasu of great heroism, that Yama has the Dharma as his sole witness. (5)
The virtuous-souled one struck him with three arrows, radiant as Time and Death,
and cut them down with another three shafts.
Then, with abundant high-flying arrows possessing the luster of glowing embers,
he struck Yama in battle and cut down his arrows with his own shafts.
In the meantime, enraged and desiring victory over one another, those two of great strength and prowess struck each other in battle. (8)
A most terrible battle between the two continued for a day and night;
in the midst of this, the enraged [Śiva], with fury, [struck] Praśamana with a spear.
Then that powerful tiger among the Daityas, filled with ego,
quickly seized that very spear in his wrath.
He struck him violently between the breasts with his very fist;
with all his limbs trembling and blood gushing from his mouth, [the opponent fell]. (11)
Then, filled with rage, the one of great splendor took up a most terrible and infallible staff and hurled it at the body of that Daitya.
Intoxicated by his wrath, Śamana reduced to ashes that chariot with its horses, the charioteer, the warrior, and the collection of weapons.
When that Daitya had thus fallen, a Dānava named Durdharṣa,
bearing a trident in his hand, rushed forward with the intent to kill Śamana.
Then Death, fearless and holding a spear in his hand, approached him who stood with a trident in his hand, resembling the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala). ||15||
Having seen him, Asuro instantly struck him with a spear; then Mṛtyu hurled a javelin at him on the field of battle.
Suddenly burning with a sharp pain, possessing a radiance equal to a mass of fire,
it pierced the heart of the Daitya and entered the surface of the earth.
With his chariot and horses fallen upon the earth, his body shattered by the spear, another mighty warrior, Durmukha, then drew his bow with death in view. (18)
Kāla, bearing a sword and shield, arrived on his chariot;
seeing him, he struck Yama with an abundance of arrows in the battle.
Then the god, having struck Sacāplavya from his chariot with a sword, suddenly severed his head— complete with its earrings— and cast it to the ground.
The entire remaining force fled in the ten directions.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Antaka, Durdharṣa, and Durmukha," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||70||
The Seventy-First Chapter.
Vyāsa said: Then Namuci, enraged,
standing upon his chariot, afflicted the denizens of heaven with terrible arrows resembling venomous serpents.
Then, at that time, the gods, siddhas, kinnaras,
and pannagas were unable to endure the force of the arrows as they fell simultaneously.
Having mounted a chariot yoked with the horse Uccaiḥśravas and driven by Mātali,
Puruhūta (Indra) approached that great army.
Having seen Śakra of great heroism, Namuci, the foremost of the Daityas, then spoke to Vāsava and his followers in the midst of battle: ||4||
Having destroyed what is natural, devoid of decay, and neither dishonorable nor dear, there is neither the attainment of Nala nor victory, O you who are praised by the people. (5)
Therefore, everything here shall become eternal;
I shall obtain the sovereignty of the gods and enjoy happiness in the abode of the deities.
To him spoke Śakra, of great splendor and conqueror of enemy cities:
"Bravery is easily attained everywhere by mere words alone. (7)
"Or rather, O lowest of Dānavas, display your great prowess and valor in battle; I shall lead you to the city of the Sun. (8)
Having heard this, the highly effulgent bull among the Daityas became enraged and struck the best of the gods with five sharpened arrows.
Desiring the objects of the senses, those two of great heroism swiftly proceeded in battle toward her with five sharp, iron-tipped arrows that cut through her breast.
With sudden impetuosity, they both cut each other's arrows with shafts;
then, with arrows resembling thunderbolts, they pierced one another's limbs.
By those very two, through their most unprecedentedly performed deeds, the obstruction was thoroughly removed;
[he attained] lightness, the essence of arrows, and the extremely rare mastery over the drawing and releasing [of them]. (12)
Upon seeing this, the hosts of gods and asuras were then filled with wonder;
in that very interval, the Daitya unleashed his illusory powers.
Hundreds of arrows issued forth from there simultaneously;
then the powerful Śakra, out of anger, quickly raised his bow once more.
Blazing with fury, he struck him in all his limbs with fierce arrows,
and then likewise with eight thousand more shafts.
They pierced one another from there and cut each other down;
in that battle, they saw the sky completely covered by arrows.
They fell upon the surface of the earth by the thousands from the strokes of swords;
thus, after that great battle had lasted for a very long time.
Then Namuci, the doer of cruel deeds, displayed the illusion-weapon (māyāstra),
which rendered the three worlds entirely and continuously shrouded in darkness.
The hosts of gods and asuras could not see one another at all, nor could they see the sun, the moon, the planets, the fires, or the other celestial dwellers.
In that darkness, the sun’s rays were not seen at all;
and then, by means of arrows resembling flames of fire, the Daitya quickly [pierced] them.
All the gods and Śakra were shattered at the front of the battle;
their bodies pierced by arrows, they fell upon the surface of the earth.
And other heroes, being utterly broken, fled in the ten directions;
having recognized his deceptive form, Hari, who is worshipped by all the gods, [intervened].
Then, seeing that [the enemy] had been delayed, he released a gentle weapon, possessing the brilliance of a hundred suns in the sky, with a multitude of spears.
He struck the chest of the Daitya, who fell down overcome with pain;
after a long time, regaining consciousness, that son of Diti became senseless with rage.
Having gone with speed, he seized Airāvata, the preeminent elephant of the gods;
in his rage, he terrified Indra’s mount exceedingly.
Having seized the elephant with Indra, he cast them down upon the surface of the earth;
then Śakra, having fallen to the ground, was overcome by dejection for a moment.
Leaping down from the elephant's trunk and standing upon its back,
he [the Daitya] remained there for the sake of slaying the leader of the herd, Śakra, who was desirous of seizing him.
Having severed the head of the chief of the Asuras with his sword, he cast it down;
all the gods rejoiced, the Gandharvas sang charmingly,
and the delighted sages praised the best of the deities.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Slaying of Namuci," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||71||
The Seventy-second Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having mounted his divine chariot, bow in hand and endowed with great strength,
he went before the hosts of gods and asuras to the battle against Mādhava.
Overcome by great anger, Madhu, the crusher of the ageless ones,
spoke these harsh words to the imperishable Lord Hari.
O Nārāyaṇa, how is it that you do not know the code of combat? Having employed an unjust and wicked means of slaying, why do you grieve when you have perished? (3)
By this method of non-clinging, both conventional activity and the state of being a god would be destroyed; therefore, I shall create another creation. (4)
"I shall slay you alone here, along with the hosts of gods," he said,
and taking up his bow, he struck the Lord with arrows.
Then Mādhava pierced them with arrows possessing the brilliance of thunderbolts;
he struck Madhu with many shafts in all his limbs.
O best of gods, that Daitya was concealed by illusion;
so too were those who are truly heroic—the Rudras and other deities who uphold the quality of goodness (sattva). ||7||
There were also various goddesses, equipped with weapons and vehicles,
as well as the commanders of the armies, the lords of the hosts, and the gods Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
All the other gods, such as the Grahas and others, fought together;
yet at that time, those gods were surely destroyed by the illusory power of Madhu.
In front and from behind alike, showers of arrows, spears, and double-edged swords fell suddenly upon the earth, and those afflicted by the weapons collapsed instantly.
In the meantime, Viṣṇu, taking up the Sudarśana discus,
struck the gods— who had become asuras— by means of his illusory power at the forefront of the battle.
Then the Lord of the Gods, having severed their heads by the thousands, caused them to fall— the Daityas who were of demonic nature.
In this manner, the Lord put the other Daityas to flight from the battle;
seeing him, all the sages and gods were filled with wonder. ||13||
The gods and hosts of sages whisper into one another's ears:
"Hari, the imperishable Lord, is always the sole protector of the gods. (14)
But this god, the conqueror of the Daityas, is the witness of all in age after age;
how is it that he slays all the gods here at the end of the kalpa? (15)
In the meantime, Madhu, having employed his illusory power from afar and assumed the form of Hara, spoke to the imperishable Hari.
Having slain the gods on all sides in the sinful battle before the Daityas, today your virtue, fame, glory, and qualities have become a source of ill omen for Śiva. (17)
Due to your state of extreme madness, you do not distinguish between others and your own;
therefore, with these sharpened arrows, I shall send you to the abode of Yama. ||18||
Having spoken thus, he struck Keśava in battle with fierce arrows;
but Mādhava cut down those arrows and spoke these words: ||19||
I know you, O Daitya, as a beloved one who assumes the form of Hara in battle—
a hero of heroic deeds, Madhu, who is employed with illusory powers.
"I shall strike down the world of falsehood and deliver it onto the field of battle";
in that interval, he pierced [his opponent] with sharp arrows in the encounter.
Jaṭila and Vṛṣaketu, and Maheśvara seated upon his bull—then there occurred a truly great battle between those two, like that between a god and a dānava. ||22||
As they were piercing one another with arrows as soon as they were discharged,
the imperishable Hari cut off his bow with a razor-headed shaft (kṣurapra).
Then the Daitya,
with trident in hand, struck down the horse in the form of a bull and rushed toward the Lord of the World.
Then, having whirled his trident, he struck the Supreme Lord;
[the latter] cut that trident, which blazed like the fire of time, with three arrows.
Then the cruel, mighty-armed Hari, who is exceedingly illusory through his power of māyā,
assumed the form of the goddess and, standing upon his chariot, set forth.
He struck Viṣṇu with various kinds of arrows and spoke these words:
"O Lord, O best of Asuras, you alone have been felled in battle!"
"I shall slay you and your two sons, Dvivida and Nalakuvara.
Having said this, he struck that son of Diti with many arrows.
Seeing his two fathers slain by Māyāvaṭṭha and lying on the surface of the earth with their lives departed, vomiting blood, he of great strength [fell] with a loud cry. (29)
Taking up his spear, Skanda set out to fight Hari;
then Dhātṛ spoke these words to Skanda, who was afflicted by delusion.
The two Pitṛs saw from afar such a battle;
they remained stationed in the intermediate space as witnesses to the world.
Having heard this and seen it, he then vanished right there;
then Dhundhu and Sunda, two brothers exceedingly arrogant, [arose].
In the battle, Vadhū and Pratiharī both flew above Garuḍa;
one held a sword in hand, while the other held a mace, shouting "ca-dhuṃ dhuṃ ca-sa-gadaṃ suṃ dhumeva."
With a single blow of his mace, he brought about the severing of [the other's] arm;
both great heroes, wounded and mangled, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Then Madhu, suddenly appearing and shrouded in infinite darkness,
caused hundreds of mountains to fall upon Viṣṇu through his illusory power (māyā).
Then, having seen those mountains within the darkness in battle,
he cut off their heads with the Sudarśana [discus] out of anger and struck them down.
Then, by the gods beginning with Brahmā and by the thirty deities as well,
Viṣṇu’s renown as "Madhusūdana" was established throughout the worlds.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Slaying of Madhu," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventy-third Chapter.
Vyāsa said: Then Vṛtra, of great splendor and the foremost of the Daityas in battle,
mounted upon an elephant as large as a world-elephant, rushed toward the slayer of Bala.
Then, in that great battle, he approached Vṛtra and pierced him in all his limbs with arrows possessing the brilliance of the fire of cosmic destruction, as if he were an elephant.
Then Vṛtra, possessed of great strength, suddenly pierced the head of the victorious [Indra] with that winged [thunderbolt], and he [Indra] wavered.
Having comforted himself and raised his bow,
the valiant one rained down a shower of arrows upon the body of that Daitya.
Having cut his arrows, the one of great heroism quickly pierced Śatakratu, the lord of all the gods, in battle with arrows resembling venomous serpents. ||5||
Then the king of the gods pierced the Daitya with thousands of arrows,
so that their shafts flew at one another like the rays of the seven-horsed sun.
Thus, with thousands of arrows, they pierced one another;
swift as the speed of thought, those firm shafts were like mountain peaks.
The arrows of those two archers were like the submarine fire to the touch and capable of piercing even the thunderbolt; in their battle, the arrows were endowed with equal qualities.
In this manner, the battle continued for a day and a night;
then Mahendra struck his elephant with a trident.
Having come together upon the surface of the earth, he quickly mounted his own chariot;
standing in that chariot, he struck the chest of that god firmly with a spear.
With the swiftness of his piercing [the elephant], he quickly shattered it like a great mountain with a thunderbolt;
thus both the elephant and that great Indra shone resplendently. 11.
Then, taking up his spear and hurling it at the Asura, Indra pierced the Daitya in the chest; he fell upon his chariot.
In an instant, regaining his consciousness and crying out,
he pierced Śakra in battle with a featherless arrow and immediately fell into a swoon.
Having regained his consciousness, Indra struck him with sharp arrows;
afflicted by those shafts equal to hundreds of millions, he was overcome with pain.
Then Vṛtra hurled a great trident at the Lord of the Gods;
the Lord of the Gods neutralized it with the Śiva-weapon and discharged the Vaiṣṇava weapon. ||15||
In that encounter, both [warriors], whose weapons possessed a luster like the peak of a blazing fire, struck one another while emitting sparks.
The soldiers of both armies were unable to stand before the sparks of the arrows, just as moths cannot remain before a blazing fire.
Burnt, they fell upon the earth, and all the directions fled;
the heroes of both gods and dānavas perished, and the battlefield there became empty. ||18||
Seeing his missile repelled, the Daitya, overwhelmed with rage, discharged at Śakra the illusory mountain-showering weapon (śailasaṃdoḥ). ||19||
In the battle, Hari cut down the mass of mountains with floods of arrows;
then the Daitya unleashed the Aghora weapon against the mighty Puruhūta.
There were thousands of millions of excellent bows, as well as lions, tigers, bears, wolves, leopards, great elephants, and so forth. (21)
Then scorpions and other creatures rushed toward the Lord of the Gods with razor-edged arrows,
crescent-shaped shafts, broad-headed arrows, and likewise with locust-tailed arrows.
The lord of the gods, the slayer of enemy heroes, cut down those who had approached him;
then the mighty-armed and valiant Vṛtra, raising his bow, [attacked].
With thousands of arrows resembling thunderbolts, he pierced Śatakratu; and Śakra, having cut [the demon's] bow with razor-sharp shafts, severed it.
At that very moment, the best of the asuras, having worshipped Kaṇṭakāṅgadā, caused the charioteer and the horses to fall upon the earth. ||25||
In his delusion, he struck the head of Padmina with his mace and fell to the earth;
then the Lord of all gods, holding his mace, arrived upon the ground.
Then a mace-duel between the two of them proceeded again and again;
as they struck one another, the sound produced by the impact of the maces was indeed constant.
They repeatedly performed whirls and circumambulations, striking downward and upward, and delivering most terrifying blows to each other's sides. (28)
This battle between the two, which caused terror to the worlds and the intermediate spaces, took place;
seeing it, the hosts of gods, siddhas, and dānavas were struck with amazement. ||29||
Those two heroes, fighting and having entered into a state of mortal danger,
could not even be looked upon by the heroic warriors of the gods and the dānavas.
Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods, stationed in the sky, sought to behold that wonder;
yet they were [obstructed] by the sound of their *huṃ* and by the roar of the falling mace.
A sound ascends higher and higher as the eating proceeds;
when the two sticks are broken, the hands of those two are joined together in a hollowed gesture.
And thus, at the very half-watch of the night, those two weapons fell upon them; in that interval, O hero, they both then took up sword and shield.
To fight back in that most terrible battle, they both advanced; their swords were like lightning and meteors, and their bodies were shielded by armor.
They were seen by all the people, who were filled with wonder at their agility,
as they cut through each other's many-colored shields.
Thus, between those two, a hand-to-hand combat ensued,
characterized by circular movements, the use of discus and bow, agility, and leaping maneuvers.
The battle between Vṛtra and Vāsava was like that between Vṛtra and Vāsava;
[Vāsava], having leaped up and seized Vṛtra’s hair, swiftly struck with his sword.
Indra suddenly severed the head upon the head of the elephant;
then, simultaneously, there arose the cry of "Victory! from the gods.
With their hearts blossoming with joy, the gods worshipped Indra;
divine drums resounded and throngs of apsarases danced. (39)
The Gandharvas sang songs, and the sages who recited hymns of praise [did likewise];
all the Daityas, terrified, fled in every direction, casting away their weapons and other gear.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Vṛtra," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||73||
The seventy-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Then the son of Tripura ascended a chariot yoked with four horses, radiant as the sun, and spoke these words to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
"O Lord of the Gaṇas, because my father was slain by your father,
I shall today send you to the abode of Yama with my arrows."
Then the god Gaṇeśa spoke to that son of Tripura: "In former times, your wicked father committed what was harmful to the gods."
Indeed, Janaka heard that a great sin had been committed;
having realized through the power of his knowledge that [the perpetrator] was wicked and devoted to sinful deeds.
He killed his father with a single arrow by means of that very strength;
deceived by delusion from the mud, he was sent far away to the other world.
And I, having been repeatedly sent here by the Daityas,
spoke to you— that highly wise leader of the hosts of gods— concerning that path.
He pierced him with ten sharp arrows, radiant like the fire of cosmic destruction;
then, with a thousand arrows, he struck the Daitya with great force.

With arrows resembling the staff of Yama, with razor-sharp *kṣurapras*, with *śilīmukhas*, with *kaṅkapatras* that were exceedingly keen, and possessing a radiance like the fire of a thunderbolt; ||8||
Lambodara, who is worshipped by the gods, cut his arrows to pieces;
then he suddenly pierced him again with arrows resembling thunderbolts.
With all his limbs tormented by arrows, he fell to the ground in a swoon;
then Bhadra, Saubhadra, Bhīṣaṇa, and Nirjarāntaka [attacked].
Each taking up his own club, they rushed toward that Vināyaka and simultaneously struck the leader of the Gaṇas with blows from their maces.
But the one of great strength, having rendered their maces useless through his agility,
then struck Bhadraka on the head with an axe.
The head of Saubhadra was struck down by the edge of a sword; Bhīṣaṇa by a battle-axe, and Nirjarāntaka by a scimitar. 13.
Then, having felled Airāvata, who was like a great mountain,
Gaṇeśa struck down the four leaders of the Gaṇas and other enemies as well.
Then, having regained his consciousness at that place where the supreme asura Ipurī was,
he mounted his own chariot and struck down that best of the asuras.
With straight shafts, crescent-headed arrows, razor-edged arrows, and bhalla-javelins,
the righteous-souled one cut those [weapons] to pieces and pierced him again with arrows.
With four arrows he struck down Saṃdhava, with one arrow the charioteer, and with many arrows he felled the leaders of the hosts to the surface of the earth. 17.
Moving swiftly from one chariot to another, he pierced the Lord of the Gaṇas with arrows resembling thunderbolts as he approached the city of Tripura.
With his limbs drenched in blood, he possessed a fierce and terrible radiance like that of Yama;
he was struck with three arrows in the forehead and seven between the breasts.
With four [blows] at the region of the navel and five on the head,
the one of great wrath pierced the powerful Śambhunandana.
With all his limbs tormented by arrows at the forefront of the battle against the Daityas,
he fell into a state of extreme exhaustion and collapsed upon his chariot.
Then, having been led away from the arena by the steady charioteer,
the heroic Vināyaka, who is worshipped by the gods, did not strike him as he turned his face away.
After a long time, having regained consciousness, he spoke these words to Tāra:
"Go to the fearless Vināyaka, the son of Hara."
Then he spoke these words to him—truthful, beneficial, and gentle:
"Who is capable on the field of battle of enduring the arrows of Hara’s son? (24)
Therefore, O son of Prabhā, you have fallen into delusion and been led astray by me;
having understood this, O sir, do now whatever is appropriate. (25)
In the meantime, the best of poets, urged by the king, restored consciousness to the elephant by means of the application of medicinal herbs and other remedies. ||26||
He caused [the wound] to be treated with a hundredfold healing power and commanded a victory;
then, having first applied consecrated water, he healed the wounds on her limbs.
With the very tusks of his elephant, he shattered the mountain;
likewise, he destroyed hundreds of thousands of armies and army commanders.
The elephant, exceedingly difficult to conquer, brought them down in the battle;
meanwhile, the Daitya, stationed upon its back, [struck] with arrows possessing the splendor of the fire of cosmic destruction.
Then, with arrows possessing a luster equal to the rod of Yama, he struck down the foremost of the lords of the gods upon the earth.
Those of great prowess fell, drenched in floods of blood;
wherever that sword went, there the Daityas along with their elephants perished.
In various places, he created a terrifying mass of arrows;
some were struck down by elephants, and others by elephant-riders.
Some gods were scorched by the mere force of his whirling;
thus the leaders of the hosts of gods [assailed] him with various weapons and missiles.
Fearless in battle, they struck him with many arrows;
nevertheless, those of great strength were unable to fight that elephant.
With his arrows, Tripura swiftly struck down that mountain peak along with its elephants;
and the gods, their bodies shattered, fell to the earth.
Terrified and afflicted by that pain, they went to the courtyard of Śarabha;
seeing the slaughter of the gods, the powerful lord of the Gaṇas [intervened].
He struck [the opponent] along with his elephant with arrows equal to the fire of a thunderbolt;
obstructed by the force of the elephant, he was raised up again by an arrow.
Then those two pierced each other with arrows;
both of them, roaring, desired victory over one another.
With all their limbs smeared with blood, those two foremost heroes among the Suras and Asuras then struck the intoxicated elephant with their own tusks.
The serpent, pursued by the mouse, engaged in a most terrible battle with him;
their extraordinary combat took place both below and above, divided into four parts. 40.
A tumultuous battle, terrifying to all the worlds, raged with a great clamor, fought tooth against tooth and arrow against the finest of arrows. (41)
That terrible battle took place in the conflict between the gods and the dānavas;
Mahānāga, possessing great strength, caused a split between the mouse and the owl.
Standing upon the tip of the Daitya’s backbone with his axe, he struck him again; by means of his agility, he struck him at the opening of the teeth and in the heart.
Along with his mount and his arrows, vomiting blood upon the earth, he lost his life;
the gods and the celestial sages cried out, "Excellent! Excellent! (44).
There, with other unerring weapons, they struck down the Daityas in battle,
until the conflict between the two armies could not be brought to a conclusion through victory alone.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Destruction of Tripura," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-fifth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words from Maheśvara, the gods, led by Śakra,
all rushed together at once toward those hosts of Daityas.
The mighty-armed great asura named Kuṃbha arrived;
he, the lord of the Nairṛtas and king of the yakṣas, struck Aṅgada violently with his mace.
The Lord of the Guhyakas struck that supreme being violently with blows from his mace;
thereafter, a terrifying club-duel ensued between the two of them.
The wheel-binding, the great binding, the binding of those to be executed before one; the abundant, terrifying vehicle, and the application of bursting oil.
Having waged a great battle, at its conclusion, the Lord of Wealth struck that *sphoṭa* upon the chest of Kumbha.
Then, with his fangs shattered, Kuṃbha fell to the surface of the earth;
meanwhile, the immensely powerful Syandana seized Hariya’s horse at that time.
And likewise, he struck Airāvaṇa violently with multitudes of arrows;
with the thunderbolt of Indra, he pierced that foremost of asuras.
He fell upon the surface of the earth, his life departed and drenched in blood;
likewise, he entered the most terrible forest, which was both non-terrible and indeed terrible. ||8||
And in that age, he pierced the leaders of the four divisions with his power;
moreover, with agility, he struck down each of the generals individually.
With multitudes of arrows, Jayanta brought Saurabha under his control;
he also subdued Śakrahasta, Saṃhrāda, Yamadaṇḍa, and Narāntaka.
Having struck him, he caused him to fall, his body reduced to ashes;
and Kāla, with a blow of his sword, brought Bābhrava down.
Śakti brought death to Amṛtyu and likewise to Anirghṛṇaka in battle;
and these seven of great strength were consumed by Agni.
Bhadrabāhu, Mahābāhu, Sugandha, Gandha, Bhaurika, Vallika, and Bhīma—these were the leaders at the head of the army. ||13||
And in the battle, those of great prowess, their bodies burnt and bound by the nooses of the high-souled Varuṇa, fell upon the earth, deprived of life. 14.
The great beings, heroes who were terrifying even to other heroes, fell upon the earth;
the five Dānavas were struck down by the net of Śūra’s rays. ||15||
Turutuṃ, Burudurmedha, Sādhaka, Asādhaka, Abhidhā, Krūra, Caraṇeśāna, Moda, Saṃmoda, and Ṣaṇmukha. ||16||
The Daityas were struck down by arrows like trees felled by the wind at the end of an eon;
Nairṛta, with his mace, brought Bhīma to the surface of the earth.
And by the hundreds of spears hurled by the Rudras, the Daityas and Dānavas, skilled in the art of battle, fell down terrified in that conflict. ||18||
By the falling arrows of the Vasus and the heroes garlanded with rays, and by the very terrible thunderbolts and hailstones of the clouds. (19)
Hundreds of powerful Daityas, having been struck down in battle,
fall by the thousands from the blows of Kubera’s mace.
The foremost of the Daityas were split asunder by Śakra’s thunderbolt alone;
likewise, countless others fell to the earth, struck down by Skanda’s spear.
By the falling of Gaṇeśa’s axe, the foremost of the foremost fell,
as did those struck by the fiercely acting discus released from the hand of Viṣṇu.
The heads of the foremost Daityas fell by the thousands upon thousands of crores at Kaurava, struck by the staff of Yama, the God of Death.
Then Kāla struck down the Dānavas upon the earth with his sword;
likewise, Mṛtyu struck the Daityas with his spear, and Pāśin with his noose.

With the Sudhā weapon he struck Takṣaka and the others; with the Śoṣa weapon, he [dried up] the cold season; with the Aśvārohin weapon, he [overcame] Khara; with the Manyuhan weapon, he [subdued] the nooses; and likewise with the Gaja weapon, [he subdued the elephants].
Then, with his iron club, he shattered the temples of the elephants of the Daityas and destroyed them;
likewise, with great agility, he struck down their horses and elephants.
Thus [he was honored] by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases of great power, as well as by other deities together with the leaders of the hosts of Mothers. ||27||
These most terrible great demons of the dissolution have been struck down by arrows,
by the falling of swords, and by spears, javelins, and battle-axes.
The gods struck down the asuras with staffs, iron clubs, and spears;
thus, as they were being utterly destroyed, the king of the Daityas arrived.
Resembling the chariot of the sun, adorned with the finest jewels, made of gold, divine, and decorated with whisks and bells. ||30||
Having mounted that beautiful chariot, which was filled with banners and flags and resembled the chariot of Śakra, the great hero Hiraṇyākṣa, the lord of the asuras, [set forth]. 31.
Invincible by gods and asuras alike, the hero struck down with nets of arrows the elephants,
chariots, and thousands of swift-footed soldiers along with their armies.
He caused them to fall upon the earth by the hundreds and thousands;
thus he moved through all the hosts of the gods.
Then the lord of the Daityas rained down floods of arrows resembling death itself,
and in due course, he overwhelmed the divine armies in battle.
Just as an elephant in a cluster of lotus ponds agitates them with swift,
sharp-falling arrows, so too did he [the enemy] repeatedly roar like a lion with great speed.
Then, due to the force of falling upon the earth, he struck that lord of the Daityas,
Jaya, with ten extremely sharp-pointed arrows.
He struck Rema with five arrows, Śakra with fifteen,
Citraratha with twenty, and Guha with twenty-five.
With three arrows he struck Hara, with forty arrows Yama,
and likewise Kāla and Mṛtyu with twice that number of arrows from his hand.
He pierced Guhyakeśa, the life-breath of the world, with ten arrows each; and he struck all the Rudras individually with six and seven arrows respectively.
In battle, he pierces all the Vasus with arrows, as well as the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas— ten, eighteen, and six gods respectively.
Because of the flood of vital energy (*ojas*), their extreme heroism, and their swift display of agility, the gods, having fallen into calamity, were unable to counteract them out of fear. (41)
Struck in that battle by arrows resembling the trident of Maheśa,
which pierced their vital organs, they fell to the earth in a swoon.
The foremost gods were unable even to stand before his face;
then the gods, together with the Lord of the Three Heavens, were utterly routed.
Being struck, they went there for refuge to Hari, who is the protector;
in the meantime, Viṣṇu spoke to Jiṣṇu, the lord of birds.
Now, in order to destroy the face of that Daitya at the front of the battle,
he went quickly and with speed into his presence.
Having pierced Viṣṇu along with his chariot with arrows, the Daitya checked his speed;
then, from the front of the chariot, he spoke to the imperishable Viṣṇu.
"Today I shall create another creation after killing you, even though you are ageless.
Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to that roaring bull among the Daityas.
"If you are capable of competing with me in battle, O sinful one, then stand firm!
Then he struck the imperishable Viṣṇu with hundreds of arrows.
Unperturbed, he cut down those arrows resembling staffs of Yama;
then, in that battle, he discharged thousands of arrows once again.
Having severed those [weapons] with his arrows,
Śauri pierced him with shafts that were indestructible due to their great weight and resembled the submarine fire upon contact.
And with sharp, piercing arrows that travel through the air with the speed of thought, he rendered Keśava’s weapons, through his own agility, like cotton or dry grass.
Struck by thousands of golden arrows and tormented by that affliction,
the preeminent Daitya became enraged and seized a mountain peak in the battle.
The immensely powerful Hiraṇyākṣa violently struck Mādhava;
however, Hari effortlessly pulverized him with his mace.
In this manner, a thousand mountains were indeed struck down one after another;
likewise, by the dānava Hariṇa, they were reduced to powder with such ease.
Furthermore, that best of the Dānavas, having assumed thousands of arms, [assailed him] with arrows, extremely fierce spears, tridents, axes, and other weapons. ||55||
With his mind possessed by anger, Viṣṇu showered [him] with many [missiles]; however, that best of asuras cut down those very weapons discharged by him while he was being praised.
With blazing, most terrible arrows that struck fear into the asuras—arrows resembling spears—he pierced them in all their limbs. (57)
The Lord Hari, the master of the Dānavas, who is beyond number and imperishable,
having attained a state of dejection along with Cakra, [realized] his unsurpassed and all-pervading power.
Terrifying like the tongue of Time (Kālajihvā), she was endowed with eight *ghaṇṭā* sounds; fleeing from the chest of Hari, she quickly fell down. 59.
That best of asuras shone like a dense cloud accompanied by lightning;
then the Daityas cried out, "Victory!", uttering words of praise.
Then Kṛtānta, the enemy of the Dānavas, discharged his army of Daityas;
as their heads were being severed, they returned again toward Mādhava.
After a long time, having regained consciousness, he struck Keśava with a fire-arrow in the battle, bringing down the Daitya along with his weapons by the discharge of that shaft.
Enraged in battle, Hari struck down the son of Kubera and repelled him;
then he discharged the exceedingly terrible *māyā-astra* of the Asuras.
In that battle, the powerful Hiraṇyākṣa likewise slew lions, tigers, and leopards, as well as elephants and serpents, against Viṣṇu.
Then, in that battle, Hari cut down the floods of weapons and missiles produced by Māyā with his own arrows alone,
and likewise struck them with his spear.
At that moment, with all his limbs trembling and drenched in blood,
Viṣṇu, his body overflowing with gore, dragged Hara away.
The lord of the gods pierced that spear with three arrows,
as well as his chariot-guard, his banner, his standard, his chariot, and his parasol.
When Tāraka had been cut down by Hari with ten arrows,
the Daitya, his chariot having been struck down, then leaped up toward another chariot.
The powerful lord of the Daityas climbed up and opened his mouth;
then a most terrible battle occurred, causing the hair to stand on end.
And there was the great battle with missiles between Hiraṇyākṣa and Hari, which caused wonder to the world, as they performed counter-attacks against one another. (70)
Then, as they fought continuously, a hundred divine years passed;
thereafter, the Daitya of great prowess grew like Vāmana.
In his rage, he seized the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, with his mouth; having uprooted the circle of the earth, he entered the subterranean realm (rasātala).
And the remaining Daityas entered after him, filled with joy;
then Viṣṇu, of great splendor, perceiving the vast army of the Daityas, [acted].
Assuming the form of a boar with the intent to slay the king of the Daityas,
Viṣṇu took on the body of a wild boar and swiftly entered after him.
Having gone there, he saw the earth situated in the netherworld (rasātala) at the base of the Rasā river;
he then took up the Vasundharā, the supporter of the worlds, upon his two tusks.
As Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor was proceeding while holding her,
the lord of the Daityas arrived, taunting him with harsh words.
Viṣṇu, whose body was that of a boar created by Māyā, desiring to devour Durvaca in his wrath,
supported this earth upon the water like a true upholder of the world.
Having placed his own being within her, he then made her immovable with the syllable *ca*.
Thereafter, the king of the Daityas arrived, having fixed his gaze upon her.
Possessed by great anger, he struck Hari with his mace;
Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar through his illusory power, shattered that very mace.
Just as one engaged in yoga slays Death, he slew him with the Kaumodakī;
thereafter, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa was again possessed by rage.
O Lord, he struck the god with his fist on the right arm;
