thus the battle proceeded, most terrible, with movements to the left and right.
Likewise, they imitated the movements and distractions of their wandering;
then Brahmā and the other gods, stationed in the sky, watched the battle.
"May there be well-being for the subjects, the gods, and the sages," they said;
and they spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods of gods, who was in the form of a boar.
"Do not play like a child; abandon this demon Ṭaka.
Then Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, assumed the form of a magical boar.
Having obtained the consent of Brahmā and the other gods, he hurled the formidable discus, which resembled a thousand suns, possessed a thousand spokes, and was of great radiance. ||85||
That fierce discus, which causes the destruction of the Daityas and possesses a radiance like the fire of universal dissolution,
was released by Viṣṇu against the exceedingly powerful Hiraṇyākṣa.
While Brahmā and the others looked on, he instantly reduced the Daityas to ashes; and that fierce, infallible discus returned to Acyuta.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, headed by Śakra and the world-protectors, having witnessed the victory of Viṣṇu, assembled and offered him praise. (88)
The gods said:
"We bow to Viṣṇu, who is the primordial source of the universe, the lord of gods and asuras, and the protector of the worlds;
we have indeed gone for refuge to him from whose navel-lotus, it is said, the lotus-born Brahmā arose. (89)

Salutations again and again to You who assumed the form of a fish; salutations to You who bore the form of a tortoise. We offer our salutations to You in the form of Nṛsiṃha, and likewise, salutations to You in the form of Vāmana. (90)
Homage to you, the destroyer of the kṣatriyas, Rāma; homage to Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-faced one; homage to the slayer of Pralamba and Bali; homage to the Buddha, who deludes the daityas. 91.
Salutations again to the one named Kalki, who assumes the form of a boar;
for the welfare of the world, you manifest these forms in age after age to destroy the asuras.
Indeed, this arrogant Daitya named Hiraṇyākṣa has now been utterly destroyed by you—he who, with mere sport, held even the world-protectors headed by Indra in utter contempt. (93)
O God, know that he was struck down by you solely for the sake of the world's welfare; O God of gods, be gracious!
You are the creator of the emission of this universe through your form as Brahmā. (94)
You alone protect this world, assuming beautiful forms age after age;
and you alone, becoming the fire of time and Hara, shall lead the universe to its destruction at the appointed time.
Therefore, O Lord, you alone are the cause of the universe; there is no other, whether living or non-living.
Whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever is currently existing—all such forms [originate from you]. (96)
Everything known as the moving and the unmoving is you alone; apart from you, nothing at all exists in this universe.
Whether it be "it is" or "it is not," that which rests upon the duality of existence and non-existence appears within you alone, being the very nature of both the real and the unreal. (97)

Therefore, even one whose intellect is unripened ought to know that state which is difficult for even the gods to understand; except for a person who has taken refuge at your feet, there is no other way—thus we have come to you, the worthy refuge, for protection. 98.
Vyāsa said:
Thereupon Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, spoke to the inhabitants of heaven: "O gods, I am pleased; may it be well with you now through this hymn of praise to you."
O gods, for one who recites this Vijaya-stotra with devotion and respect, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds shall be difficult to attain. 100.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows, a person attains that same fruit by reciting or hearing [this]. 101.
The constant glorification of the God of gods bestows all desires;
beyond this, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a greater supreme knowledge.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Hymn of Victory," at the conclusion of the battle between the gods and the asuras, in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventy-sixth Chapter.
Saṃjaya said:
O Brahmin, I wish to hear in truth the destination of those Asuras who died in battle, whether facing the enemy or with their backs turned. (1)
"O Lord, O Teacher of the World, where are these innumerable Daityas of the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, who even now remain attached [to worldly things]?"
Vyāsa said:
Those foremost among the Daityas who died as heroes at the front in battle, having themselves attained divinity, enjoy eternal pleasures. (3)
There are palaces made of gold, adorned with various jewels;
there are trees that grant all desires, and [rivers] joined by the waters of the celestial Ganges.
The auspicious lotus pond was filled with lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies, as well as other flowers rich in fragrance, along with curd, milk, ghee, and sugar-candy.
Endowed with exceedingly beautiful forms and always possessing the freshness of youth,
they exercise sovereignty there as well as upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, having attained this Janmāṣṭaka, wealthy men, high officials,
and ministers enjoy the eternal heaven with half their faces and bodies [still remaining].
Those who turn their backs in battle, those who are cowardly and afraid, those who are deceitful in combat,
and those who hate the gods and the twice-born— they go to a terrible hell.
Those who cause another warrior to fall, faint, or break in battle—
those Mlecchas and Kuvācakas go to the Haṃtāra hell.
In reality, those who steal what has been deposited are turned away from the truth; they are like thieves and reckless doers lost in a forest at night. 10.
Those who eat everything, those who are addicted to intoxicants, the deluded barbarians, cow-killers, slayers of Brahmins,
and those who speak ill of others— these other barbarians are of deceitful origin.
Among them, there exists neither the Paiśācika language nor worldly conduct;
there is no purity, no austerity, no knowledge, and no libations to the gods or ancestors.

Giving gifts, performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and so forth; the sacrifice (*yajña*) and the thorough worship of the gods; and service toward the ancestors, the twice-born, the deities, and ascetics. (13)
Due to the loss of their knowledge, they possess no purity from impurity;
they lust after their mother, their sister, and other women as well.
Every form of perversion from the world is stained by improper conduct, as is the case with the descendants of Tārkṣya, those born of Udvavana, and others dwelling in the mountains. 15.
Those born of noble lineage who are always Daityas, whose merit is groundless,
and who kill the wives and children of the twice-born, go to a miserable state after death.
Those evil-minded ones who eat cows and are devoted to consuming what is unfit for food go to the womb of insects, or become other creatures such as ants. (17)
Among those enemies of the gods, there was no one who bowed to the mantras or the gods;
their elder brother, Sahaja, was like them, and they all possessed fierce and vulgar conduct.

Those who cause the growth of body hair and head hair, who delight in eating raw flesh on earth, and whose vows, gifts, ablutions, sacrifices, and so forth are merely acts of violence—[they are not true ascetics]. (19)
They take pleasure in fish, meat, and other such things; they speak false words; they are always full of lust, always full of greed, and always possessed by anger and intoxication.
Men who delight in killing, binding, and sexual passion; who are fond of gambling and music;
who possess wicked servants; who take pleasure in base people; and who are devoted to foul odors. (21)
And those nights which were spent not among gods nor among wise men, nor in hearing the Dharma, nor in meritorious acts such as hymns and mantras, but according to their worldly duties. (22)
Afflicted by many diseases and full of great wrath, and possessing various forms and accoutrements—these are the signs of the Daityas among the human race on this earth. (23)
They do not know the next world, nor their own teacher, nor anyone else;
they desire only the filling of their own wombs, and not guests, teachers, or brahmins. 24.
In that dream, they do not recognize their own son, nor their lineage, nor their friend, nor their kinsman; they do not recognize the gift, nor the food they have eaten, nor their belongings. (25)
Because those yakṣas in human form guard their wealth, they do not grant even a little of that wealth as long as the king lives. (26)
They are yakṣas dwelling in miserable states, carrying the burdens of others for their sake; such is the characteristic of pretas, or rather, that which is despised by all the world. ||27||
Listen with a one-pointed mind to [the description] of both women and men:
they are constantly covered in the mire of impurity and are utterly devoid of truth and purity. (28)
For cotton garments, woolen clothes, the body, and accumulations of dirt, as well as for household items, seats, and vessels, a single cleansing is not considered sufficient. (29)
Seeing no happiness in women, they quickly enter the forest; for on this earth, there is nothing but the eating of leftovers, remnants, and putrid things.
Food, drink, and a bed are pleasing in the darkness;
sometimes there is health, and sometimes there is impurity in the body. (31)
Such indeed is the characteristic of pretas in the worlds of men:
they do not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful, nor between friend and enemy, nor between virtue and vice. (32)
By their very nature, they do not perceive such states as sin and merit, nor bathing, nor the worship of gods and brahmins, nor enemy, friend, or neutral party. (33)
Those animals dwelling among mortals are to be known through their mental conceptions;
and because of the diversity of states of the intellect, they wander falsely upon this earth.
Those men who have the form of yakṣas are excluded from all ritual acts;
I shall now declare their distinctions and characteristics upon the surface of the earth. (35)
Born among the immortal worlds, yet corresponding exactly to his own sin, he was a Nāgara of impure birth who lived as a Brahmin in disguise. ||36||
O Lord, the wise say that one who eats the remnants of food (vighasa) becomes a crow; the sinner who is devoted to forbidden food becomes a dog, fond of putrid things.
Engaged in all domestic rites, subsisting on both what is fit and unfit to be eaten, they undergo rebirth upon the earth in various lineages among the wombs of animals and other beings. (38)
They seize dogs with their hands; they are fond of eating the flesh of mlecchas, especially that of pigs and those who fight on foot. (39)
They were delighted by nourishment and eating, and by foul odors, censurable things, and wicked people;
they took pleasure in mountains, in making fires, and in the gathering and piling up of wood.
These mlecchas, overwhelmed by fear of the kṣatriyas, should always be known as such in an age when dharma has perished among the people and they are forever devoid of purity. ||41||
At that time, even those of noble birth will become Mlecchas and thieves;
others likewise [will become so] through association with them, through marriage alliances, and from eating their food. (42)
Through sexual intercourse with his wife, they indeed attain that very state;
at that time, all people will be tormented by suffering and disease. (43)
Bewildered by famine and lacking food, oppressed by wicked kings, the mortals there will delight in falsehood and be devoid of all purity. (44)
They were not heard to have been established by the ancient scriptures; those wicked and most cruel men were fond of wine and meat, eating all kinds of food. (45)
Devoted to cruel conduct and constantly intent on deception, sons do not support their father, nor even their mother or other elders. (46)
Servants do not wish to serve their master who is endowed with virtues;
nor do some women [wish to serve] their husbands, nor their fathers-in-law, nor their mothers. 47.
There, people will be constantly afflicted by hardships, and there will be quarrels in every house;
likewise, the kings, the Mlecchas, and those who drink liquor, as well as the ministers and domestic priests [will be so]. (48)
And by humans, [he is worshipped] with offerings of fish and meat; he is free from worldly desires.
He is superior to the heretics and those engaged in ascetic toil, as well as to the proponents of primordial matter (pradhāna) and the qualities (guṇas). ||49||
The surface of the earth was pervaded by those cuckoos, who were like wealthy lords;
consequently, they carried off their beloveds one after another in both forests and cities. (50)
Men eat food resembling excrement, such as fish, meat, and the like; and other twice-born ones eat what is impure in the forest. (51)
All those sinful ones, who were formerly gods, cause that devoted animal and all others to fall into the state of no-return for their ancestors. 52.
Piśācas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, guhyakas, and dhruvas—these beings, who delight in misconduct, are neither gods nor humans. (53)
Saṃjaya said:
"O Lord, how do those who know the truth recognize the *lakṣya* amidst the conditions of mortality?
Therefore, please dispel this doubt of mine. (54)
Vyāsa said:
Whether among the twice-born or other castes, Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Pretas take on forms corresponding to the sins they have committed; they do not abandon their own nature.
Those who are born among asuras and mortals, always eager for strife, deceitful, treacherous, and cruel—these should be known as rākṣasas on earth. (56)
Through giving that causes distress to people and the like, as well as through the worship of deities on earth out of a fierce disposition,
they obtain wealth and enjoy eternal sovereignty.
Victory, valor, and other such merits, as well as the destruction of sins, shall come again;
thus it is on earth, as well as in the celestial realm and in the abode of the world of the Nagas. (58)
By means of fierce austerity, someone may attain the state of a god in heaven;
Prahāda, honored by the gods, attained it by propitiating Vāsudeva.
Having thus praised Hara, the Daitya Andhaka became his courtier;
the mighty Bhṛṅgin obtained the position of being one of his principal attendants.
These and many others, such as Bali and Indra,
always attain the supreme state both here and hereafter, O dear one.
Certain excellent gods, born on earth in the lineage of Daityas,
honor all their ancestors by the hundreds and thousands.
Even by a single wise son who has mastered even one *sūtra*, the family is protected;
indeed, even a single Vaiṣṇava son may uplift ten million members of his lineage.
Though he was self-controlled, righteous in soul, and devoted to the worship of Brahmins and gods,
righteousness decayed in cities and throughout the countryside until only a single portion remained.
The righteous-souled Ekoraka protected the city, the village, and the multitude of people;
and there was a great city of Brāhmaṇas that was rich in learned men.
There, all the twice-born were constantly devoted to meditation and worship; they were wise, intent on the recitation of the Vedas, and honored their gods, guests, and fellow brahmins.

For those who perform sacrifices, observe vows, and maintain sacred fires, and who are devoted to the six duties—should their minds ever turn toward even the slightest sin, they undergo the *atikṛcchra* penance. (67)
The heroes constantly perform the eternal sacrifice of the vow;
yet, by the turn of fate, at some point a wise householder [is encountered].
The brahmin seer, knowing the mantras, offered clarified butter into the fire with the mantra;
at that very moment, he suffered a most terrible affliction from urinary obstruction.
Leaving that [oil] aside, she stationed a maidservant there for the sake of protection;
however, due to her negligence, the dog ate the clarified butter. (70)
Then, with haste, that brahmin took his own vessel, which was filled with his own urine, and offered it into the fire while remaining unobserved.
And at that very moment, by means of that fire characterized by smoke,
a peak consisting of gold— actual gold with the luster of refined gold (jāmbūnada)— was produced.
Having taken it with joy, the brahmin committed a sinful act;
out of astonishment, he asked the maidservant, "O dear one, tell me, how did this happen? (73)
O twice-born one, she joyfully related there everything exactly as it had happened;
thereafter, that [practice] was performed by him constantly and at the proper times. (74)
The prosperity was wonderful and caused amazement among the people;
then, having heard of it from one another, everyone in that city [was moved]. (75)
Having heard that one who has committed evil deeds through greed has been cast into a great mire by the wicked, and out of excessive greed, he himself too enters that very mire. (76)
Then, due to delusion and the resulting confusion of intellect, that city was utterly consumed by a mass of sins, as if out of fear of the mire of rebirth.
At that time, women were corrupted and all people were corrupted by the power of sin;
there, the elder Brahmin Jñātā set his mind upon that task.
Then his virtuous wife, overwhelmed by great sorrow and tormented by the hardship, spoke an improper word to her husband. (79)
The Brāhmaṇī said:
Alas, O Lord, it pains me to see you joined with such sorrow;
you ought to perform this village custom, or perhaps another. (80)
Then, the knower of faults, having smiled there, spoke these words:
"But he who lives by means of sin, having abandoned dharma, which is the supreme benefit... (81)

O highly fortunate one, accompanied by all those worthy of instruction, he proceeds to the city of Apūrvabhavana; these brahmins are of excellent conduct, together with their wives and their retinues.
Due to their association with extreme transgressions, they are considered great sinners;
together with their immense evil, they shall go to the netherworld (rasātala).
Oṃ! Having attained non-rebirth, no further transgression exists;
I alone shall remain here for the sake of preserving my own merit. (84)
Then she said this to Sāta: "You ought not to speak these words, which will be laughed at by the world, in our presence, rather than before anyone else. (85)
The twice-born said:
"O beloved, if I were to go from here to that place at this very moment, then this city, along with its wealth and kinsmen, would immediately fall into ruin."
Having spoken thus, exceedingly delighted and taking his own wealth,
that twice-born man quickly went with her to the shore of the ocean.
Having stayed there, she saw that the city remained as firm as before; that virtuous woman said, "My husband has not been killed, yet this city is perishing. (88)
Reflecting on this, the best of brahmins, greatly amazed, said:
"What kind of substance is this that stands there outside our house? (89)
Having reflected that the sandals were not brought by me through delusion, he said, "While you two remain there, shall I indeed wear them? (90)
Having spoken thus to her husband, the virtuous woman took him and approached;
from near her husband, she saw the city devoid of suffering and free from distress.
Then the castes beginning with the Brahmins, the Kaccaras, and the inhabitants of the city remained in a terrible hell, suffering and without hope of rebirth.
They go to the city of Yamapura through great hardship, and for them there is no atonement;
therefore, that which is foul-smelling and impure is declared to be avoided. 93.
Delighting in eating as before, yet committing sin today, having the habit of theft and wandering at night—he is to be known by the wise as a *vañcaka* (deceiver). 94.
One who is ignorant in all undertakings, unlearned in all rituals, and devoid of the conduct of the observance is indeed a beast, that fool. (95)

In this way, there exist [beings] such as camels and others that are prey for predators like mongooses; and those who are timid regarding violence, the distress of people, and the fear of battle. (96)
A man who is constantly fond of the remains of offerings and the like is called a "dog" by the wise;
he who is always devoted to the act of theft and is a deceiver of many friends [is likewise so called]. (97)
A mortal is described as one who is constantly quarrelsome with his wife, by nature always fickle, and ever restless for food. (98)
A monkey delights in the forest; on earth, he is a man and a tree-dweller. He is a betrayer through his speech and his intellect, both toward his own kin and toward strangers. 99.
Because he causes agitation, that man is known as *anuraga*;
he is powerful, of a wandering disposition, and always devoid of shame. (100)
Nṛsiṃha is proclaimed as one who delights in the enjoyment of putrid flesh;
at his very roar, other beings such as wolves perish in fear. (101)
Those of far-reaching vision know this regarding elephants and other beings;
one should understand it among men in this very same sequence. (102)
We shall describe the characteristics of the gods, who abide in human form:
[toward] the twice-born, the deities, guests, teachers, the virtuous, and ascetics. (103)
Constantly devoted to worship and austerity, versed in the treatises on Dharma and in ethics, characterized by forgiveness, having conquered anger, truthful in speech, and with senses subdued; (104)
He is compassionate, beloved by the people, handsome, and sweet-voiced;
he is the lord of speech, skilled in all undertakings, virtuous, dexterous, and possessed of great strength. (105)

He was both learned in the sacred syllables and a scholar, possessing knowledge of the true principles of song and dance, as well as of the practices of self-knowledge and all the three-syllabled mantras of the various tantras. (106)
Among all sacrificial offerings, among products of the cow, and among those free from meat;
among substances that are fresh, flavorful, and newly acquired, and which are exceedingly beautiful.
He was delighted with perfumes, garlands, garments, scriptures, and ornaments,
as well as with guests, almsgiving, and rites such as the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha.
Time should pass through baths, gifts, and other such duties, through vows, sacrifices, worship of the gods, and recitations; not a single day should be spent in effeminacy.
This very conduct of humans is constant; it is praised by the best of sages as the divine conduct of men. 110.
However, a god who is superior in strength and a human who is terrified are always fearful; a god is always firm, while a human is always mild. (111)
Indeed, through the praise of these two, great joy arises even among the Daityas and others;
it brings about a state of supreme affection, happiness, friendship, merit, and auspiciousness. (112)
Likewise, there is affection between gods and humans, as well as between Daityas and Rākṣasas;
among ghosts and the like, there is affection for their own kind, and even between animals and animals. (113)
Crows and others are pleased with their own kind, as are others with their own species; they are displeased with those who are different—this is known as their characteristic. (114)

Thus, through the distinction of merit, one should discern the pleasant and unpleasant within various types of births, as well as the meritorious and non-meritorious, and the virtuous and non-virtuous. (115)

On this earth, there is no happiness whatsoever for husbands due to the differences in the castes of men; rather, affection arises toward those of one's own caste, whether one is liberated or even if one is not. (116)
Those who perform meritorious deeds obtain a beautiful lifespan through great merit;
however, those of sinful nature, such as the Daityas and other men, meet their end.
In the Kṛta age, the gods, Daityas, and other species were born on the earth;
in the Tretā age, they had one foot [remaining], and in the Dvāpara age, two feet.
He meditated upon the entire Bhārata, which had been composed and set in motion, consisting of all its feet and sections, as it was born from the gods and others. 119.
The warriors of Duryodhana himself, as well as his soldiers and so forth, all those Daityas and others, and whoever on earth were led by Karṇa—[all these were slain]. (120)
Bhīṣma, the foremost of the Vasus; Droṇa, the lordly sage Devamuni;
Aśvatthāman, who is directly Hari himself; and Nakula’s son Saha-deva. ||121||
The five Indras were born as the Pāṇḍavas, Vidura was Dharma himself, and Gāndhārī and Draupadī were born from the surface of the earth. 122.
During the middle of the Kali age, gods and Daityas, as well as Daityas, humans, Śeṣa,
spirits, carnivorous beasts, and birds will constantly come into being.
Among them, there was a maidservant of loose character who was exceedingly wretched;
she constantly spoke of their conduct with affection amidst the various pairs [of lovers]. (124)
Those Daityas and others who delight in all kinds of sins, in quarreling, and in unjust actions— all of them go to hell.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Since the Daityas and others were of a false nature, they did not possess the status of gods nor their celestial abode.
How then could there be enjoyment for them, or happiness, health, and the accumulation of strength? (126)

Sovereignty, longevity, fame, desired objects, beloved strength, the knowledge of ethics and so forth, as well as one's future existence, birth, growth, and the eternal [self]—[all these depend on it]. 127.
O Lord, how are the acts of giving, study, and sacrifices such as the *yajña* performed?
O Master, you ought to explain this to me, your worthy disciple. (128)
Vyāsa said:
For the Daityas, it is certain that their asceticism arises solely from audacity;
likewise, their vows, sacrifices, and so forth, as well as their affection for their own kin, are rooted in the same. 129.
When one is self-controlled, free from vices, has grasped the true meaning of the treatises on ethics, and is purified by these various qualities, he shall possess the characteristics of a god. (130)
O twice-born one, he who is capable of uplifting the world himself performs meritorious deeds according to the ancient scriptures and rituals, both in the heavens and here on earth. (131)
He who, seeing a Vaiṣṇava especially, rejoices and worships him, is liberated from all sins and is capable of uplifting the virtuous. 132.
The brahmin is devoted to the six duties and always intent upon all sacrifices;
he is eternally fond of narrations on dharma and capable of upholding the righteous path. ||133||
Those men who betray trust, who are ungrateful, who violate their vows, and who harbor hatred toward the twice-born and the gods, cause the earth to perish. (134)
Those men who are addicted to wine and passion, as well as those who delight in sinful gambling, and who engage in conversation with heretics and the fallen, cause the earth to decay. (135)
Those men who are devoid of good deeds, who are constantly agitated yet outwardly fearless, and who are distressed by the meaning of the Smṛtis and Śāstras, cause the earth to suffer. (136)
Those base men who, abandoning their own proper conduct, perform vile deeds, and out of hatred for their guru and wife, cause the earth to tremble. (137)
Those men who obstruct the giver and impel him toward sin, who oppress the poor and the helpless, and who cause the earth to tremble; 138.
These and many other men who have committed evil deeds cause other men to fall and cast them down to the earth.
Whoever should hear this delightful teaching, the supreme benefit more secret than the secret, for them there shall be no miserable rebirth, suffering, misfortune, or wretchedness on earth. (140)
In the state beginning with "Na da," there shall be birth in the heavenly world and eternal happiness;
for him there is no untimely death, nor is he defiled by sins. (141)
The lord of the three heavens, who is the witness of all people here,
having enjoyed heaven kalpa after kalpa, proceeds toward the path of liberation.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Merit," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventy-Seventh Chapter.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O best of the twice-born, O Lord, this sky is eternal and all-pervading; who is its creator, what is its power, from where was it born, and who is its compassionate Lord? (1)
What indeed is the task to be performed by the gods, the best of sages, the *sādhus*, the *cāraṇas*, the *daityas*, and the *rākṣasas* who are intensely filled with rays of light? (2)
He is always to be worshipped by all human beings, including the Brāhmaṇas and others.
Vyāsa said:
"The supreme splendor of Brahman has issued forth from the body of Brahmā. (3)
Know this [disc] to be directly composed of Brahman, bestowing dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation;
its peak is exceedingly fierce and very difficult to endure due to its stainless rays.
Seeing him, the worlds fled, tormented by his fierce rays;
thereafter, all the oceans, excellent rivers, streams, and so forth [were likewise affected].
The people of Jambudvīpa withered away there and the sickly folk died;
then Śakra and the other gods approached Brahmā.
Then the gods spoke on this matter, and Brahmā said:
"O gods, the Lord Janaka is the progenitor who abides in the quality of goodness (sattva), the primordial source of the body of Brahmā."
This one is truly composed of passion (rajas), while the other possesses a body as white as nectar;
by these two, the worlds of the three realms, including all things moving and unmoving, are protected.
Just as there are gods born by divine apparition, so too here are those born from a womb;
likewise, there are those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts and the like. ||9||
We are truly unable to describe the power of this Sun;
by him the worlds were created, protected, and certainly sustained. (10)
There is none equal to him because he protects all;
and upon seeing whom at dawn, even a heap of sins is dissolved. (11)
Having propitiated Him, the twice-born attain liberation;
indeed, at the time of meditation and worship, the Brahmins who know Brahman [meditate upon] Him.
With uplifted arms, they indeed became worshipped by the gods;
and one should meditate upon the Goddess, whose form is that of meditation, situated within this very mandala.
All the twice-born who have worshipped him together shall obtain both heaven and liberation;
even those who have fallen on the earth with his remnants become purified by his rays.
Merely by performing the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), one attains purification from sin, even after seeing a Cāṇḍāla, a killer of a cow, an outcaste, or one afflicted with leprosy. ||15||
By beholding the Sun, men who are defiled by great sins (mahāpātaka) and enveloped by minor sins (upapātaka) become purified from their heavy transgressions. ||16||
By the mere worship of this, one is liberated from all diseases;
there is neither loss of caste, nor poverty, nor suffering, nor any cause for grief. (17)
And by worshipping Virocana, one obtains [the fruits] both here and in the hereafter;
moreover, even the gods such as Hari, Hara, and others cannot be seen by those worlds.
"Accessible through the form of meditative absorption (dhyāna), this one who has been seen is indeed remembered as a god.
The gods said: "Let him be propitiated for the sake of grace; let there be service and worship. (19)
O Brahman, the vision of this very [reality] is like the fire of universal dissolution;
all beings, including humans, have reached the state of immortality on earth.
By the power of his splendor, the oceans and other [elements] have been destroyed;
we ourselves are not capable of enduring it—how much less others who are mere ordinary beings? (21)
Therefore, by your grace, we worship him as we do the Sun;
let that means be ordained by which men may sacrifice to him with devotion.
Having heard the words of the gods, he went to Brahmā, the lord of birds;
having arrived, he began to offer praise for the welfare of all the worlds.
He is the divinity who has become the eye of the entire world, free from all affliction;
he directly assumes the form of Brahman, yet is as difficult to behold as the fire of universal dissolution.
For you indeed abide within all gods, and you are ever the friend of Vāyu in their bodies;
from you alone comes the digestion of food and the like, and life itself becomes certain.
The Lord of the World is the sole deity over creation and dissolution;
without you, there is not even a single day of life for all the worlds. 26.
You are the Lord of all worlds, the savior, the protector, the mother, and the progenitor;
by your grace, the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings is sustained.
O Blessed One, there is no one equal to you among all the gods;
the existence of all vows resides in you alone, for by you the entire world is sustained.

Just as you [perceive] the capacity of tastes to produce forms, smells, and so forth, as well as their sweetness, so too is the Sun, the Lord of the Universe, the cause of the maintenance of all things. (29)
O Lord of the world, you alone are the cause of purification for sacred fords, holy fields, and sacrifices; you are the witness of all and the mine of all virtues.

The omniscient one, the creator of all, the destroyer, the protector, ever-eager [for the welfare of beings], the dispeller of darkness, sin, and disease, and the annihilator of poverty and suffering. ||31||
In this world and the next, there is no other kinsman; you are the all-knowing, the all-seeing one. Apart from you, there exists no benefactor for all the worlds. (32)
Āditya said:
O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O Creator of the universe, Indra, and of all beings! Speak quickly, O Vidhi, of that supreme purpose which you have; I shall perform it as you desire.
Brahmā said: "O Lord of the Gods,
act in such a way that these rays, which are exceedingly fierce and utterly unbearable for the worlds,
may become mild."
The Sun said:
"O Lord, my rays, numbering millions upon millions, are supreme destroyers of the worlds; they do not bring about what is desired in the world through their application, so please cut them down."
Then, by the power of Ravi’s words, Viriñci quickly summoned Viśvakarman and had him fashion a whetstone made of adamant.
He cut off the suns of Cicarava, which resembled the fire of universal dissolution;
with those very [discs], he fashioned there for Viṣṇu the Sudarśana discus.
The Amogha, the Yamadaṇḍa, and likewise the Śūla of Paśupati;
the supreme Khaḍga of Kāla, and the Śakti that delights the Guru. (38)
At the command of Brahmā, Viśvakarman quickly fashioned for Caṇḍikā a supreme weapon, a variegated trident (śūlaka).
The thousand-rayed [sun] remained, while the other was utterly destroyed;
and again, O Sage Kaśyapa, it was restored through the agency of Aja.
Born from the womb of Aditi, he is indeed remembered as Āditya;
he moves through all these worlds and even revolves around the peak of Mount Meru. ||41||
Six hundred thousand yojanas above the earth, day and night are equal;
there the planets, beginning with the Moon, move according to the divine law.
The Sun moves through the twelve months, consisting of twelve parts each;
from his transition [from one sign] to another, his transit (saṅkrānti) is recognized by everyone.
Or rather, O Sage, we shall describe the entire fruit for all people during those [periods]:
the six-aśīti periods occur in the signs of Sagittarius, Gemini, Pisces, and Virgo. (44)
In the signs of Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo, Viṣṇupadī is remembered;
know that there, libations, gifts, and the worship of the gods yield inexhaustible merit. (45)
The fruit of [reciting] eighty-six thousand times is eighty-six-fold;
at Viṣṇupadī it is one hundred thousand-fold, and at Ayana it is ten million times ten million-fold.
I shall describe the presence [of Viṣṇu] for the donor, which is proclaimed to be inexhaustible when a gift is given at the Viṣṇupadī; it remains constant in birth after birth. 47.
By the gift of cool cotton cloth, no suffering arises for the body;
through the gift of a balance scale and the gift of a seat, the fruit of both is indeed inexhaustible. (48)
He who, free from envy, gives a bed equipped with all necessary furnishings to a Brahmin of noble appearance, shall attain the rank of a king.
Likewise, having offered fire and water on the bank of a river at dawn while on a journey, and having offered betel-leaf with oil upon the ground, one shall become a sovereign lord. (50)
By bowing to a twice-born man with a sincere heart, one who is poor shall attain inexhaustible wealth;
this occurs on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha at the break of dawn. (51)
Having gratified the ancestors with sesame seeds and water, which yields inexhaustible merit in heaven, and having given a cow of auspicious marks with golden horns and the luster of jewels; 52.
Having given this [cow] with silver-plated hooves and a beautiful bronze milking vessel to an eminent brahmin, a king shall become a sovereign ruler of the entire earth. (53)
Having given food and ornaments, the king, the lord who purifies the circle of his realm,
should then give a sesame-cow (tiladhenu) together with all its necessary appurtenances.
One who is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven births shall become imperishable in heaven;
by giving food to a Brāhmaṇa, one enjoys an inexhaustible heaven.
Grain, clothing, servants, a house, a seat, and so forth—whatever one gives to the foremost of the twice-born, prosperity does not forsake him. (56)
Whatever gift is given, whether it be small or great,
becomes inexhaustible in the worlds beyond, as does that which is given on the anniversaries of the Yugas.
Furthermore, the worship of the gods, hymns of praise, and listening to the exposition of the Dharma purify one from all sins; such a person becomes worthy of honor in heaven. (58)
The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is known as Anvantarā;
whatever gift is given on that day is said to be entirely inexhaustible.
Wealth, enjoyments, and likewise sovereignty do not endure for even a kalpa;
therefore, giving and honoring the virtuous bestow infinite fruit in the life hereafter. (60)
The seventh lunar day of the month of Māgha, which follows the Manvantara, is declared by the Purāṇas to be the most meritorious of all dates. 61.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, there is the Koṭibhāskarā [tithi];
by fasting on that meritorious day, a person is liberated—of this there is no doubt.
The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing on that day at the time of dawn yields great fruit.
And whatever sin has been committed by me there during seven previous births,
may that be destroyed by this Saptamī dedicated to the Sun, which removes both Meru and Śoka.
O Mother of all beings, on the seventh day of the seven-times-seven [forty-nine days], when the orb of the sun has risen on the seventh lunar day, O Goddess! ||65||
Arka leaves, barley, fragrant flowers, jujube fruit, and rice grains—
these should be brought together in either a leaf-cup or a copper vessel.
Having offered a very beautiful arghya with a sacrificial thread and a lion [image] at a distance, whatever sins have been committed throughout seven lifetimes go to destruction. 67.
One is thus tormented by hells, by diseases, and by sins that bring suffering;
therefore, one should offer pure food consisting of sacrificial oblations made from sun-dried rice.
One should avoid ginger that has been ground on a stone, as well as leafy vegetables, the leaves of the *koradūṣaka* plant, and the milk of a goat. Likewise, [one should avoid] clarified butter. (69)
One should avoid hair, insects, and the like, as well as bathing with hot water;
during the vow of celibacy, one should avoid all small seeds and similar things.
Furthermore, one who observes the vow should not perform any other action there without reflecting upon dharma;
for the Saura-vrata is of great merit, as praised by the Purāṇas. (71)
For thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of years,
he shall obtain eternal enjoyment in heaven equal to that of the Sun.
Thus, immediately upon the exhaustion of his merit in heaven, that king became a very wealthy man on earth;
due to his former practice, he performed the Bhāskara-vrata in the world of mortals. (73)
Likewise, by the grace of Bhāskara, the one who is born shall obtain eternal happiness to be enjoyed in heaven, as well as health and prosperity. (74)
If it falls on a Sunday during the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, it is renowned as Mahājaya; otherwise, it is remembered as Vijayā.
A crore of *vijayā* would be [the result], while *mahājaya* would be infinite;
by such a single vow in that regard, one is said to be liberated from the bondage of birth. (76)
The lord of heaven and mortals gives, in succession, a horse-gem, gold, red cloth, and grain, out of affection for the Sun. (77)
I shall explain their distinctions; listen, O Brahmin, according to the facts.
He who gives here a horse endowed with excellent ornaments and a noble mount [is described as follows]. (78)
One shall obtain land frequented by the seven oceans and free from enemies;
one shall cross over existence and become a sole sovereign over mortals.
One who lacks a horse, or whose vehicle is without wings, or even one adorned with bulls,
has prescribed as his sacrificial fee either one gold māṣa or two māṣas by the ignorant.
Having given a vessel of jewels of great value, or one made entirely of gold,
or even pure gold alone, he becomes a lord of wealth in the third heaven.
He who, according to his ability, offers red cloth and grain along with water, attains lordship over heaven and earth; Fortune never abandons him.
Free from disease, with a very serene soul, a conqueror, and possessed of majesty—he is most worthy of worship for as long as the sun shines. 83.
One should observe the twelfth lunar day in the month of Māgha, as well as the seventh;
having enjoyed the desired fruits in this world, he is honored even by the gods.
Having performed the Arkāṅgasaptamī vow according to the prescribed rules, the wise man,
purified from sin, shall obtain his desired objects here and attain liberation.
I shall also declare the characteristics and the procedure for each month;
by the grace of this vow, one is honored among the gods in heaven. (86)
When the bright fortnight has begun and the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa),
one should undertake the Saptamī vow under a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) bearing a masculine name.
The wise declare that Hasta, Maitra (Anurādhā), Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśiras, and Punarvasu are the asterisms with masculine names.
On the fifth day, a single meal is prescribed; on the sixth, a night-meal (nakta) is proclaimed;

One should consume the tip of an *arka* plant, pure cow dung, excellent pepper, and its fruit; likewise, having performed fasting at night and the single-meal rite according to the rules,
one may also consume milk or food smeared with ghee— these are declared [as the regimen] in this sequence.
Having performed the seventh-day rite dedicated to the Sun, one obtains the desired fruit. ||90||
One should drink two special, fine leaves from the tip of a branch of an *arka* tree located to the northeast of the village, still containing their sap, without touching them with the teeth.
One should drink one *pala* of pure cow dung that has not fallen on the ground, still containing its moisture, without touching it with the teeth, using the thumb and ring finger.
One should drink a single drop of fresh, unboiled water that has not been touched by teeth;

this water should be drunk as it flows from the base of the fingers during the *brahma* and *pitṛ* offerings. One should drink any one of the fruits—date, coconut, or others—as long as it is untouched by teeth. As for food, it should be anointed with ghee and measured by the size of a peacock's crest;
the ghee itself should also be of that same measure. (91)
When the sun casts a shadow twice the length of one's own body, then one should know that it is *nakta*; *nakta* is not merely eating at night.
First, one should worship the deity with fruits, flowers, and other offerings accompanied by mantras;

Then the meditation:
[He is] complete with all the marks, adorned with all ornaments, two-armed, red in color, and holding a red lotus in his hand. (94)
The seed-syllable *baṃ* is the orb of fire, situated in the midst of abundant water, together with its retinue;
it is the deity seated upon a lotus throne, anointed with red perfumes and unguents. ||95||
One should meditate upon the Sun-god, especially at the time of worship.
Now, this is the mantra: "We know Bhāskara; we meditate upon the thousand-rayed one; may Sūrya impel us. (96)
This supreme recitation (japya) is proclaimed as bringing victory on the seventh lunar day,

Afterwards, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā) should be performed on the eighth day, especially;
indeed, the breaking of the fast must be done on the eighth day, and never on the ninth.
If the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is performed on the ninth day, one does not obtain the fruit of the vow;

One should carefully cleanse the rice, discarding grass, seeds, and the like;
one should also avoid mung beans, black gram, sesame, and ghee.

One who is capable should feed the brahmins with devotion using offerings such as milk and the like; according to one's means, they should also be provided with food, drink, and non-meat side dishes. 101.
That man who performs this Saptamī, which yields infinite fruit, should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin after distributing them according to his means. 102.
O best of the twice-born, by performing this vow month after month for the satisfaction of the Sun, one pacifies all sins and increases wealth and progeny. (103)
Whoever performs the breaking of the fast with devotion goes to the world of the Sun;
he shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas and thereafter attain the supreme goal.
This very other secret was spoken by Śambhu in the past:
"The fruit is proclaimed to be equal for one who constantly hears it, for one who observes that vow, or even for one who causes others to hear it. (105)
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Arkāṅga-saptamī Vow," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventy-Eighth Chapter.
Vaiśampāyana said: "O Blessed One, by your grace I have heard the purifying vow;
now I desire to hear another, as well as that which is dear to Bradhna."
Vyāsa said:
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground before Maheśvara, who was seated comfortably on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, Kaṇva spoke these words.
O Lord, this ritual known as Arkāṅga has been heard by me from you in detail;
now I wish to hear in truth the fruit that results from the [astrological] day and other factors.
Īśvara said:
A man observing the vow should offer arghya with red flowers on every Sunday;
by taking his meal at night and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), he does not fall from heaven.
And for one who always performs every virtuous practice on Sunday, the Supreme Lord, together with his retinue, attains great pleasure. (5)
By observing the fast on the day of the week [dedicated] to Śūra, one attains a state equal to his;
by [observing it] alone, one attains the status of a Gaṇapati as long as the sun remains in the sky.
The meritorious and beneficial vow of the Sun on Sundays bestows all desires, confers sovereignty, destroys disease, grants heaven, and bestows liberation. (7)
On a Sunday coinciding with a solar transit (saṅkrānti) or the seventh lunar day (saptamī),
O Śivā, all such acts as vows and worship performed on that day shall attain imperishability.
On a bright Sunday, one should perform the worship of the Lord of Planets;
having expelled [the deity] through the mouth of the vital breath, one should place him within the mandala.
Having meditated upon [the deity] with two arms, seated on a red lotus, with a beautiful neck, clad in red garments,
and adorned with all-red ornaments, one should hold a flower with both hands and cast it toward the northeast for the sake of gathering [the essence].
We know the Āditya; we meditate upon Bhāskara. May that Bhānu inspire us. 11.
Then, according to the ritual prescribed by the guru, there is the anointing;
for that anointing there is true incense, and for that incense there is the lamp.
Then one should offer a lamp, incense, and food offerings, and thereafter present water. Then one should perform the recitation, praise, ritual gestures (mudrās), and prostrations. ||13||
"Aṃ" is the first mudrā, and the second is known as the dhenukā;
he who worships the Sun in this manner shall attain union with the Sun.
By the grace of that Sun, this terrible skull of mine, which had been stuck to my hand due to the slaughter of a Brahmin,
was released on the bank of Vārāṇasī.
There is no deity higher than Ravi (the Sun) to be found in the three worlds;
by his grace, I have been liberated from terrible and heavy sin. (16)
Skanda said:
O Lord, having heard these words from you, O Master, wonder has arisen within me.
O God, there is no one other than you; how then could the murder of a Brahmin be committed against you?
And you are the omniscient Lord, the yogi, the enjoyer in the world, the imperishable and undecaying;
you are the sole preceptor of the gods, the pervasive-formed Maheśvara. ||18||
O Lord, you are eternally omniscient and the master of all living beings;
how then could there be any evil deed in you, much less anger? (19)
Śiva said:
"O son, for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, we—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—manifest separately in age after age and perform all [our respective duties]. (20)

For us there is neither bondage nor liberation, neither that which is to be done nor that which is not to be done; nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world, we act according to the prescribed rules.
It is supreme in every respect, the destroyer of all obstacles, the pacifier of all diseases, and the accomplisher of all goals. ||22||
Having become manifold from a single source, undivided yet distinguished by temporal divisions,
he, being one, undergoes twelvefold forms month after month as he performs penance.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the eternal Viṣṇu is Mitra; in the month of Pauṣa, he is Varuṇa; and in the month of Māgha, he is likewise Sūrya. In the month of Phālguna, he is indeed the Sun. (24)
In the month of Caitra, the Sun shines; in Vaiśākha, he is known as Tāpana;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, Indra shines; and in Āṣāḍha, the Sun becomes Tapana.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa he is Gabhasti; likewise in Bhādrapada he is Yama;
in Āśvayuja he is Hiraṇyaretas; and in Kārttika he is Divākara.
Thus, these twelve Ādityas are proclaimed month by month;
they possess vast forms and great splendor, and are endowed with the brilliance of fire.
For one who recites this constantly, no sin exists;
there shall be neither disease nor poverty, nor shall there be any contempt anywhere. (28)
One obtains inexhaustible heaven, happiness, sovereignty, and fame in succession;
I shall now proclaim the supreme Great Mantra, which brings delight to all. (29)
Ūṃ, salutations to the thousand-armed one; salutations again and again to Āditya. Salutations to you who hold a lotus in your hand; salutations again and again to Varuṇa. ||30||
Salutations to the illustrious Sun, the destroyer of darkness; salutations again and again. Salutations to the thousand-tongued Bhanu; salutations again and again. (31)
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Rudra; salutations, salutations to you!
You are Agni within all beings, and you are Vāyu; salutations, salutations to you! ||32||
Pervading all beings, for there is nothing whatsoever that exists without you;
you are established within every body in this world of the moving and the unmoving. (33)
Having thus recited [the mantra], one may obtain one's desire, such as the enjoyments of heaven, in due order:
Āditya, Bhāskara, Sūrya, Arka, Bhānu, Divākara. (34)
Suvarṇaretas, Amitra, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, Aja, Eka, Daśa, Svayambhū, and Timirāśa are proclaimed as the twelve. ||35||
The man who recites these names of the Sun—Śuci and the rest—is liberated from all sins and diseases and attains the supreme goal. (36)
Furthermore, I shall speak of another [aspect] of the Great-Souled Bhāskara:
those known as Raktas, who resemble blood and possess bodies that are intensely crimson. (37)
O Six-faced One, hear those names which are primary:
Tapanas, Tāpanas, Kartṛ, Hartṛ, and Agraheśvara. ||38||
The witness of the world in the three realms, the lord of the sky, the maker of day;
the great Brahmin whose womb is fire, heaven itself, he whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses. (39)
The Lotus-handed One, the Dispeller of Darkness, who is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the singer of the Sāmaveda;
he has meditated upon Kālapriya Puṇḍarīka as the primary abode.
For one who always remembers [this] with devotion, whence can there be fear of disease?
O Kārtika, listen with diligence to this auspicious [account], which removes all sins. 41.
O high-minded one, there is no body, mind, or action belonging to the Sun;
*oṃ* *oṃ* salutations to Indra; *oṃ* *oṃ* salutations to Viṣṇu. ||42||
This recitation, this fire-oblation, and likewise this twilight worship, brings about all auspiciousness and destroys all obstacles. ||43||
It shall destroy all diseases, such as spider-bites and eruptions,
as well as diseases like jaundice and whatever other ailments are severe.
Daily fever, three-day fever, and likewise quartan fever;
leprosy, consumption, abdominal disease, and likewise fever. (45)
[It cures] urinary stones, dysuria, and various other diseases; likewise, those diseases arising from wind (vāta) and those diseases arising from the womb (garbha). 46.
Crushing great diseases and consisting of the pain of those afflicted,
all of them go to dissolution through the utterance of Āditya.
O Lord of the gods of gods, when this is recited at the time of the sun, all fears of Rakṣasas, grahas, and diseases shall be pacified. (48)
I shall proclaim the root mantra of the great-souled Bhāskara, which eternally bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and accomplishes all desires and aims. (49)
And this is the mantra: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Sūrya.
By means of this mantra, all accomplishments will certainly be attained at all times. (50)
Indeed, diseases will afflict him, and through that, undesirable fear shall arise;
for he who takes up the water of the *sūryāvarta* [plant] and proceeds in the wrong order.
By merely consuming it, a person is liberated from disease;
it should not be given away, nor should it be disclosed, but rather recited with diligent effort. ||52||
To those who are non-devotees, childless, heretics, or worldly-minded, one should administer [the medicine] mixed with pungent oil as a nasal drop or for drinking. 53.
By drinking water from a *sūryāvarta* plant, one’s son is liberated from all diseases;
furthermore, the root mantra should be recited while meditating upon him during fire-offering rituals.
When this is recited, diseases as well as malevolent planets are destroyed;
what need is there for other numerous scriptures or for mantras of great extent? (55)
It is beneficial for all, even for animals, and accomplishes every purpose;
it must not be given to atheists, nor to those who revile the gods and brahmins. (56)
It should be given only to one who is devoted to the guru, and never to others;
it should be recited daily by a person who has risen in the morning.
Even a killer of a cow and a person ungrateful for favors is liberated from all sins;
it bestows physical health, increases wealth, and brings about fame. (58)
For him whose body satisfies the Sun-god, no fear arises here;
[this applies] whether he worships once, twice, thrice, or indeed daily. (59)
Whoever recites this in the presence of the Sun shall obtain their desired fruit;
one seeking a son obtains a son, and one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter.
One who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge, and one who seeks wealth obtains wealth;
provided that he listens with devotion, being endowed with pure conduct. (61)
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes even to the world of the Sun;
this is the result of the vow of Bhāskara, as well as its ritual observances and sacrifices.
If one recites this in sacred places and at holy fords (tīrthas), it shall yield ten millionfold merit;
likewise when feeding those afflicted by planets, during worship, or when feeding Brahmins before the foremost of the twice-born.
The wise man who recites this in the presence of ascetics, Brahmins, and gods, shall obtain infinite fruit. (64)
Whoever recites this, or causes it to be recited, is glorified in the world of the gods.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Peace of the Sun," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: In the Middle Country, there was a sovereign emperor known as Bhadreśvara,
who had been purified by many austerities and various kinds of vows.
He indeed always worshipped the gods with a pure heart;
yet on his left side there appeared leprosy, and white spots arose upon his hand.
Then, after the physician had applied his treatment and the symptoms were seen to have vanished as before,
he summoned the foremost of the twice-born and his ministers and spoke these words.
The king said:
"O brāhmaṇas, my sin is unbearable and condemned by the world;
therefore, [show me] a sacred great field where I may cast off this body. ||4||
"O heroes who know the Dharma, command me for the sake of my welfare in the next world—that which will be beneficial to me after death—since I am now without a lineage. (5)
"Therefore, speak with great favor regarding that which I have declared and which I shall perform.
The twice-born said:
"The kingdom has been abandoned by you, who are wise and of virtuous character."
"O King, this world is ruined; therefore, you ought not to speak thus. Indeed, we perceive that there is a remedy for this. (7)
"O Lord, diligently propitiate the great god Sūrya with mantras.
The king said:
"O best of brahmins, by what means shall I satisfy Bhāskara?"
O twice-born ones, I have become invisible to all beings and despised by them because of my foul leprosy, which is loathed by the world. (9)
"What shall I do with the kingdom, and what would be gained by its propitiation?
The twice-born said:
"Staying here in your own kingdom, you should worship Virocana. (10)
"Having been liberated from terrible sin, you shall obtain heaven and liberation.
Having heard this, O Indra among kings, that best of monarchs prostrated before the most excellent of the twice-born.
And he performed the supreme propitiation of that Sun-god, offering daily worship with mantras, oblations, and ointments. (12)
With various kinds of fruits and offerings, with unbroken rice grains scorched by the sun, and with hibiscus flowers, arka leaves, oleanders, and *karañja* flowers. ||13||
With red saffron, vermilion, and likewise with āvāsantika flowers and others, with fragrant plantain leaves and their most beautiful fruits; ||14||
Having prepared the *arghya* offering in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood,
the king always presented it to the Sun with his face turned toward the sun, accompanied by his ministers and domestic priest.
Then, together with the chief queens who were likewise enjoying the arghya offering, and with all those residing in the inner apartments along with their wives and the guards, [he proceeded]. ||16||
Thus, the offering of honor (argha) is presented day after day by groups of servants and others, accompanied by extremely fierce hymns of praise, mantras, and other rites dedicated to the Sun. (17)
With both root mantras and other mantras, they worshipped the Sun;
likewise, they, being well-composed, performed another vow known as Arkāṅga.
Gradually attaining a state of health, the king recovered; once that terrible disease was overcome, the entire world was freed from its affliction.
He caused the vow of sacrificing on auspicious days to be observed;
likewise, he offered *japā* flowers and fragrant *kadalī* fruits.
Having performed such great merit, which is dear to all people, by offering arka leaves and flowers without stalks along with his wives and arrows; ||21||
A person who worships the Sun while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) or fasting,
and likewise honors him with these three groups [of offerings], is thus worshipped by Vibhākara.
Approaching the king, he was filled with joy and spoke these words out of compassion:
"Choose a boon that is desired, whatever dwells within your mind."
For the sake of the welfare of all the city-dwellers,
the king, followed by his ministers, said: "If you wish to grant a boon that is pleasing to the eyes of all," [24]
"May the supreme heaven be ours all together in your presence.
Sūrya said:
"Those ministers, the twice-born brahmins, along with their wives and their retinues," (25)
Possessing fresh youthfulness, pure, and free from disease, may you dwell in my beautiful city until the dissolution of all beings, endowed with every enjoyment. (26)
O highly fortunate one, [he was surrounded] by celestial trees, by palaces as perfect as wish-fulfilling trees,
and by women with excellent dancing, singing, and other arts.
"O King, you shall become the first of five future kings; and these men standing before you, the lords of the earth, shall be your priests. (28)
Likewise, you learned and wealthy men who dwell in the countryside—having obtained the supreme intoxication therein, you shall attain the happiness of heaven. (29)
Having spoken thus, the Eye of the World vanished right there; thereafter, King Bhadreśvara rejoiced in heaven together with his retinue.
There, even those such as insects who were yellow-colored, along with their sons and others, enjoy the celestial trees in heaven; it is a great marvel.
In this very manner, O King, the Brahmins, the sages of pure vows,
and those of the Kṣatriya and other castes who followed him, quickly went to the sun and heaven.
Some requested wealth, others sons and wives, while others sought happiness, heaven, and health through the grace of the Sun-god. (33)
The pure person who recites this auspicious *puṇyakūṭa* will have all their sins destroyed; they shall be honored on earth like Rudra himself. (34)
He shall become a witness to all things in heaven, a granter of boons, and dear to the Sun;
that mortal who listens with self-restraint shall obtain his desired fruit. (35)
One who has reached the further shore beyond all evils shall be like the sun in an assembly;
by hearing this, one will always become eloquent, meritorious, and wealthy. (36)
This most secret of secrets was promulgated by Bhāskara;
this was told to Yama and proclaimed on earth by Vyāsa. (37)
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Bhadreśvara," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(80) The Eightieth Chapter. Vaiśampāyana said:
O twice-born one, by your grace, this power of Śrutagraheśvara has been attained; now tell us the ritual procedure for the planets, beginning with the Sun.
How is it that their [the senses'] objects—such as sound and the rest—are sixfold? How is the beloved?
And when time and place have arrived, how is that vision of the auspicious and the inauspicious? (2)
Vyāsa said:
In this world, the planets and other celestial bodies experience both merit and demerit;
they bring about both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness for the destruction of all worldly actions.
The Sun is the master of time, of the planets, and of the *yojanas*;
through his fierce and gentle conjunctions, he is the lord over both restraint and favor.
I shall now declare the true nature of the planetary states for that very person who offers oblations with the sprouts of the Udumbara and Palāśa trees. (5)
Then, for the sake of peace and to obtain one's desired fruit, one should offer oblations of radish combined with clarified butter while reciting the mantra beginning with "ākṛṣṇena."
For the pacification of all diseases and for liberation from slaughter and bondage,
one hundred oblations should be offered with each individual mantra.
On Sunday, one should offer cool goat’s milk to the Sun and feed Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability with delightful offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya). ||8||
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight, and likewise on the fifteenth,
the sick person is freed from disease and shall no longer encounter hardship due to illness.
The heroic one will manifest as the supreme, stainless being within the mere span of a *bāla* from Brahmā down to the earth, and even within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) as small as an atom.
He is the withdrawal [of all things] through the sequence of stages, the cause of the origin and maintenance of everything;
he moves throughout the universe within the bodies of people at the emission of breath.
At the time of death, it departs from the midst of the body along with the vital breath (prāṇa).
The moon, always situated within the head, is endowed with sixteen digits (kalās).
Day and night, facing downwards, he pours down a rain of nectar upon the body;
by that, all beings, from the great to the minute, are sustained in life. (13)
Just as the earth nourishes crops, so does it sustain all things stationary and moving;
by these two, which are like flowers, the entire world is supported and brought forth. (14)
Through the propitiation of those two, there is constant nourishment and the attainment of supreme merit; the practitioner, remaining ever pure, shall accomplish all his objectives at all times. (15)
That lowest of men who, out of delusion, does not worship the Sudhāśuṃ [the Moon] finds his lifespan diminished and goes to hell. ||16||
O Lord of the World, you who are the crest-jewel of Gaṅgādhara and the bearer of the stainless digits [of the moon], salutations to you, O Moon, on the second lunar day. 17.
That man who, having reached another lunar day (tithi), performs even a single prostration to the Moon, shall obtain his desired fruit. (18)
Obeisance to you, O Moon, born from the eye of Atri, produced from the churning of the ocean of milk, and residing upon the crown of Maheśa. 19.
Obeisance to you of divine form, O Lord of the World who is like the moon;
the wise know [this] during the bright fortnight as well as the dark fortnight, at the third watch of the night.
"Ūṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ somāya namaḥ"—this is the mantra to be recited. It should be recited at dawn. Thus, whoever worships Soma, or causes others to hear [this], or listens [to it] themselves—
In every birth, throughout the worlds, may he be equal to nectar. ||21||
Thus, he who on earth praises and worships with the Thousand Names attains imperishable heaven, from which a return to this world is difficult to achieve. (22)
This is the Soma-pūjā:
there should be a vessel made of bell-metal filled with ghee for Śiva;
whether it be small or large according to one's means, one should perform the rite without envy upon hearing [the instructions]. 23.
O Hero, O Auspicious One, having established Mercury in the house of Saturn, one should bestow [the merit] upon a man with many sons in every situation, as if he were shining like gold.
Supreme good fortune arises, far exceeding even nectar; for both women and men, misfortune shall never occur. 25.
Desiring beauty and good fortune, I give this vessel filled with curd;
grant me beauty and good fortune contained within the bowl of my own body. (26)
A man, free from envy, should give [the gift] preceded by the words of the twice-born;
according to his ability, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, as well as new garments and other such items.
One should offer food that is complete in every respect, a most enchanting betel-roll, and flower garlands and the like, for the sake of attaining beauty and good fortune. (28)
Thus, whoever makes such a gift dedicated to Soma for a twice-born man shall enjoy beauty and good fortune in the heavenly world or in the world of men. (29)
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Worship of Soma," in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||80||
The Eighty-First Chapter.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O virtuous ones, I desire to hear in truth about the origin of the Red-limbed One (Mars), his delight among people, as well as his power, majesty, and splendor.

"Then that host shall abandon its asura nature.

O beautiful lady, others are bewildered by your splendor and beauty;
O Goddess, I am the son of Viśvāmitra and Śivaśarman. (14)
O feeble one, even for one who has attained perfection in yoga or achieved success through austerity,
great defects such as desire and the like have been conquered right from the very beginning.
"O large-eyed lady, resort to another; I am going to the world of Indra.
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born then departed in haste. (16)
Born of Menakā, she was fruitless; questioned by the wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, she repeatedly displayed various forms of intimidation.
O twice-born ones, just as heaps of grass, once consumed by fire, become mere ashes,
so too have those terrors been reduced to nothingness.
O best of men, by the spiritual power of that brahmin who was devoted to his father, those terrible and fierce demons were brought to their destruction. (19)
The thousand-eyed Indra repeatedly manifested obstacles, but the highly illustrious Brahmin, by means of his own splendor, destroyed them again and again.
In this way, the wise one destroyed even the many obstacles of that high-souled Indra by means of the power of his asceticism.
When the arrows were destroyed and the obstacles were both terrible and great,
he recognized those dreadful obstacles created by him, which possessed fearsome forms.
Then the highly effulgent Viṣṇuśarman, the best of the twice-born and a man of great fortune, became enraged; with his eyes bloodshot from passion, he glared toward Indra.
"I shall cause Indra to fall from the world of Indra; otherwise, one who is devoted to his own duties today would be committing an obstacle against me. (24)
"I shall inflict punishment upon him who strikes one who is being struck;
likewise, I shall act so as to be the protector of the gods once again. (25)
While that best of beings was thus exerting himself for the destruction of the lord of the Brahmins,
Indra, the subduer of Pāka, arrived at that very moment.
O Brahmin! By virtue of your great wisdom, austerity, and self-restraint, as well as by your self-control, truthfulness, and purity, there is no other person equal to you. (27)
I have been incited by this devotion of yours toward your father, along with the gods;
O most excellent one, you ought to forgive all my transgression. 28.
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one; even that which is difficult to obtain, I shall grant you.
Then Viṣṇuśarman spoke thus to the king of the gods who had appeared before him: [29]
O Lord of gods, O All-pervading One, the great splendor of one devoted to the ancestors is unbearable for the gods and deities, and is impossible to withstand in any way. (30)
The majesty of these high-souled Brāhmaṇas must not be diminished by you, along with all your sons and grandsons; for they are, in turn, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
O best of the twice-born, if you had not returned today because your body was destroyed by his wrath, then this unsurpassed kingdom would not have come to me. (32)
"By the power of your own asceticism, you have become desirous of giving [this] to another great-souled one, with eyes filled with rage. (33)
"Your Honor, having arrived today, you wish to grant a boon here:
grant me the nectar of immortality, O Lord of Gods, as well as unwavering devotion to the ancestors. (34)
"O Destroyer of Enemies, if you are pleased, grant me such a boon as this. [The Lord replied:
"I grant you this merit-bestowing boon, which is joined with nectar. (35)
Having spoken thus to that brahmin, he himself gave him the nectar;
with a joyful heart, he gave it to him along with the vessel.
"O Brahmin, may your devotion to the ancestors always remain unshakable.
Having thus addressed that Brahmin and dismissed him, the thousand-eyed one [Indra] departed.
Seeing that unbearable splendor of the Brahmin, Viṣṇuśarman became filled with faith; he then approached his father and spoke these words.
"O father, this nectar, which destroys disease, has been brought from Indra by me. By this, O highly fortunate one, may you always remain free from illness. (39)
"Attain supreme satisfaction this very day with the nectar!
Having heard these great words of his son, Śivaśarman,
with a joyful heart, summoned all his sons.
"O sons, you are devoted to your father and obedient to my words."
"Choose a boon, my sons, for you are well-pleased; choose that which is difficult to obtain on earth.
Thus addressed by him, they all listened with focused minds.
Having deliberated upon all this, they spoke thus to their father:
"While we are alive, our mother has gone to that other world. (43)
O you of excellent vows, by the grace of the Goddess, you have become free from disease;
may you be my father and she my mother, birth after birth, O beloved. (44)
"We all wish to become sons and likewise performers of meritorious deeds.
Śivaśarman said: "Even this very day, your mother, who was so affectionate toward her sons, has died. (45)
"Living and joyful, she will surely return; there is no doubt about this.
When these auspicious words were thus spoken by the sage Śivaśarman, [the king] was filled with joy. 46.
Their mother, having arrived, spoke these words with great joy:
"For this very purpose was this son of great heroism born.
Men desire a virtuous son who brings glory and power to the lineage. (47)
In this world, women are highly fortunate, very meritorious, and devoted to virtue. ||48||
Everywhere they desire that which is heard [the sacred word], for it is a limb of merit and an achiever of merit;
for into whose womb the most meritorious embryo has entered, there it develops. (49)
That meritorious woman shall give birth to virtuous sons who uphold family traditions, support the lineage, and deliver their fathers and mothers [from saṃsāra]. (50)
Without merit, how could a woman obtain an excellent son?
By what such merits as these has this husband become a possessor of great fortune?
Born with the vigor for the Dharma, his very self being the Dharma and affectionate toward the Dharma, it was through his vigor that I attained you, my sons, who are even greater than he. (52)
Such is the power of merit; O you who are devoted to merit, my sons have been born thus, entirely dedicated to filial devotion toward their father. ||53||
In this world, through merits, a virtuous son is obtained—one who is superior to each [of his predecessors], who has attained the fifth stage, and who possesses a great resolve. (54)
Performers of sacrifice, virtuous in character, and possessing the power of austerity and prowess—
thus were they repeatedly nourished by her alone.
Overcome with great joy, the sons bowed down to their mother.
The sons said: "By great merits is a mother obtained; indeed, a good mother is like a good father. (56)
By our merits, you have become our mother, brought forth by our good fortune;
having entered her womb, we were nurtured by her great virtues. (57)
"In birth after birth, you two shall indeed become my mother and father.
The father said:
"Listen, my sons, to this excellent boon that bestows merit. (58)
"May you, being pleased, enjoy inexhaustible pleasures with your sons.
The sons said:
"O father, if you are pleased and desire to grant a boon here," (59)
"Send us to Goloka, the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning.
The father said:
"Go to the realm of Viṣṇu, you who are now cleansed of all sin. (60)
"By my grace, by your ascetic penances, and by this devotion of yours toward your father"—
when these words had been spoken by that seer, he was then liberated.

Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace, and mounted upon Garuḍa, he arrived and spoke thus again and again to Śivaśarman and his son: śaṅkhacakragadāpāṇirgaruḍārūḍhaāgataḥ | saputraṃ śivaśarmāṇamity uvācapunaḥ punaḥ ||62||
"O twice-born one, I have been conquered by you today through your devotion;
come now together with your four sons who perform meritorious deeds. (63)
Śivaśarman said: "Together with this meritorious wife who desires her husband's welfare, let us go to those very sons and to the highest world. (64)
For some time I shall dwell upon this earth with my wife and with this excellent son, Somaśarman.
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the truthful sage,
the Lord of Gods then spoke to those excellent sons of Śivaśarman.
"Go to that world which bestows liberation and is free from burning and dissolution.
Having been addressed thus, O Brahmins, the four of them, whose minds were fixed on truth, [departed].
At that very moment, they all assumed the form of Viṣṇu,
possessing a complexion like sapphire and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Possessing the beauty of all ornaments and the form of Viṣṇu, they were of great majesty,
enriched by the splendor of necklaces and bracelets, and adorned with garlands of jewels.
Resembling the splendor of the sun and enveloped in flames of light,
they entered the body of Viṣṇu as Śivaśarman looked on.
Just as lamps pass on their light to other lamps, O Great-minded One,
even so those best of the twice-born, having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu through devotion to their ancestors, [continue their lineage].71.
But I shall proclaim the true power of Somaśarman. ||72||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śivaśarman," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Sūta said:
When they had departed for Goloka, that realm of Viṣṇu beyond darkness...
The highly wise Śivaśarman spoke these words to his younger brother: ||1||
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Somaśarman, you are highly wise and devoted to your father;
now, protect this great jar of nectar given by me. (2)
"I shall set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords together with this wife of mine. "So be it, O illustrious one; I shall provide auspicious protection. (3)
Having given a water-pot into the hand of that high-souled one who was endowed with wisdom,
he performed intense penance for a period of ten years.
The righteous-souled one protected the water-pot with diligence throughout the day and night;
then the highly illustrious Śivaśarman returned once again. ||5||
Having practiced a deception together with his wife, that highly wise man caused his son to become afflicted with the disease of leprosy; and his wife likewise became such [as he].
These two, who possess strength like that of a sapinda, were created by illusion;
they have come into the presence of that terrible brahmin Somaśarman.
Seeing his two sons together and extremely distressed on all sides, the highly illustrious Somaśarman was overcome with supreme compassion. ||8||
