Having bowed with devotion to the feet of those two whose heads were bent low, Dhara said: "I do not see anyone like you, endowed as you are with such ascetic power."
What is this that has occurred in you, endowed as you are with such masses of excellent merit? All the deities have come to you and are always offering you service like slaves.
O best of Brahmins, having received your command, they have been drawn by your splendor;
by what sin in your body has this disease, accompanied by agony, arisen? (11)
O best of Brahmins, having been born, tell me the reason for that:
this mother Puṇyavatī is highly meritorious, a great devotee, and faithful to her husband. (12)
She who desires to create the three worlds by the grace of her husband—how could she experience suffering? Is there no fruit of asceticism? (13)
Having completely abandoned passion and hatred through various actions, she who serves him like a god, being full of affection for her guru—[to her he speaks]. (14)
He experienced the suffering of leprosy, which brings great misery.
Śivaśarman said:
"Do not grieve, O highly fortunate one; the fruit born of one's own karma must be experienced. (15)
Indeed, by means of the human being joined with karma consisting of both sin and merit, you have performed the purification of these two who were afflicted by disease. (16)
"O highly fortunate one, you desire here that merit which consists of service.
When these auspicious words had been spoken, the highly illustrious Somaśarman [replied]. (17)
"O best of the twice-born, I, a sinful, wicked, and wretched man, shall perform service for you two who are endowed with merit. (18)
"What should be done here this very day? We must indeed worship our guru.
Having spoken thus, they were afflicted by sorrow, pained by grief upon grief.
He cleaned away both the phlegm, urine, and excrement;
likewise, he performed the washing of their feet and the massaging of their limbs. (20)
Filled with devotion, he himself attended to their bathing place and other needs;
these two were his gurus—the Brahmin and the highly illustrious Somaśarman. (21)
The righteous and most excellent one, having placed the two of them upon his shoulders, leads them to the sacred ford; he himself bathes them with auspicious rites using his own hands.
One who is well-versed in the three Vedas should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules, as well as the libation for the ancestors and the worship of the deities. (23)
That virtuous soul constantly caused both of them to perform their duties;
he himself offered oblations into the fire and cooked excellent food.
Being well-pleased, he instructs them: "These two are my great gurus;
O Brahmin, you must always cause them both to rest upon their bed and seat. (25)
He should constantly offer them all things such as clothing and flowers;
he should present both of them with abundant and excellent betel-leaf.
The highly fortunate Somaśarman would also satisfy them both;
he constantly gave them roots, milk, excellent food, and other such things. (27)
But Somaśarman, of great renown, constantly offered them their desired portion; by this method of practice, he propitiated them perpetually. (28)
The virtuous Somaśarman would worship his parents;
however, his father, being cruel, would call Somaśarman and revile him.
One should strike him with reproachful and harsh words in the presence of sages;
yet, when his purpose is accomplished, he should always treat his son as one who has performed meritorious deeds.
"O defiler of your lineage, you have done me no good at all!"—with such various words, harsh and painful, [he spoke]. (31)
Śivaśarman, being constantly distressed, struck him with blows of his staff; yet even when this was done, the righteous-souled one did not become angry at all.
Being always satisfied through the threefold means of mind, speech, and action, he should likewise worship his father. 33.
In that same way, day after day, Śivaśarman observed the conduct of his half-brother Somaśarman and perceived his own behavior as well.
"Even for my sake, Viṣṇuśarman has brought the nectar;
he is endowed with merit, a righteous soul, and always devoted to his father. (35)
Thus, when a great many hundreds of eons had passed, Śivaśarman too, seeing his devotion, reflected as follows: (36)
"I have indeed said this before: O good son, you who are skilled in sacrifice, cast these fragments of the Mother wherever you please, my son. (37)
My word was honored by him, and he showed compassion toward his mother;
this is a very slight suffering for one who desires the destruction of the lifeless. (38)
"That son Vedaśarman has indeed committed a rash act;
I consider this even more serious than that, because he is wavering. (39)
In even a mere moment, he may again bring about a reversal;
furthermore, there is another power of asceticism that is truly effective.
Even though he was constantly engaged in propitiation, something even greater was observed in him;
therefore, an examination of this ascetic was conducted at that time. (41)
Because of his state of devotion, even though that was so, his son did not perish;
yet, by means of Māyā, leprosy was manifested even upon his own body. (42)
The highly illustrious one felt no disgust toward phlegm, urine, or excrement;
he constantly cleansed his own wounds with his own hand. (43)
The high-minded one should provide foot-washing and likewise attend to his purification;
he always endures my harsh and unbearable speech. (44)
Though he was always speaking of what was desired [by others], my son of great intelligence was thus constantly engaged in the practice of suffering through reviling and beating. (45)
I consider this ocean of sufferings to be afflicted by many defilements;
yet, through the grace of Viṣṇu, I shall remove this suffering. (46)
Then, while reflecting with his mind, the highly intelligent Brahmin Śivaśarman again employed his illusory power (*māyā*) so that the water was drawn back out from the jar. (47)
Afterwards, having summoned him, he said to Somaśarman:
"I have given you in my hand the nectar that destroys disease. (48)
Therefore, grant it to me quickly so that I may perform my ablutions,
by which I shall become free from disease today through the grace of Viṣṇuśarman.
When these words had been spoken by the sage Śivaśarman,
Somaśarman rose up in haste and took his water-pot.
Seeing him thus deprived of his chariot and separated from the nectar, [they wondered]:
"By whose sin, or by what deed, has this unpleasantness been brought about? (51)
Having become overcome by such thoughts, Somaśarman was deeply distressed;
he thought, "I shall relate this account before my father when the time comes. (52)
Then, having reflected for a long time, the highly intelligent Somaśarman thought: "My preceptor, afflicted by disease, will become angry with me. (53)
If truth exists in me, and if there has been service to my guru, and if austerity was previously practiced by me with a heart free from deceit; 54.
When truth and dharma itself have been protected through self-restraint, purity, and other virtues, then this water-jar shall undoubtedly become filled with nectar. ||55||
As soon as that highly fortunate one had thought thus and looked, the jar once again became filled with nectar. ||56||
Seeing that, the highly illustrious Somaśarman was filled with joy;
he went, paid homage to his preceptor, and quickly took up the water-pot. (57)
"O father, please accept this jar of water that has been brought;
O highly fortunate one, drink it and be freed from disease without delay. (58)
Having heard these words—highly meritorious, consistent with truth, dharma, and purpose, and uttered in sweet syllables—from the son of Śivaśarman, [he was moved]. (59)
Overcome with great joy, he spoke these words: ||60||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Śivaśarman," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||4||
The fifth chapter. Śivaśarman said:
Through austerity, self-restraint, purity, and likewise through service to the guru...
But I am pleased by the absence of devotion; therefore, O good son, speak the truth. (1)
"Abandon this deformed appearance and obtain happiness from me.
Having spoken thus to his son, the Brahmin revealed his true form to him.
He saw his two teachers standing exactly as they had been before;
both great-souled ones were radiant, resembling the orb of the sun.
With great devotion, he bowed at the feet of both those high-souled ones;
then, filled with great joy, he addressed his son.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, through his own merits, and by the practice of yoga, that best of men, whose soul was devoted to dharma, went to Keśava together with his wife. ||5||
The sage has indeed entered the abode of Viṣṇu, that station which is difficult to attain;
that state which grants liberation cannot be reached by others through other merits or austerities.
Through meditations on Viṣṇu, as well as through ritual consignments, contemplation, knowledge, hymns of praise,
gifts, and pilgrimages to sacred fords, Madhusūdana is perceived.
Through the yoga of meditative concentration and knowledge, the supreme state is perceived,
just as the great yogi, the Brahmin, has entered the body of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
Thereupon, the highly resplendent Somaśarman performed penance there;
he regarded neither clothing nor ornament as anything other than a stone or a clod of earth.
Having conquered his appetite, possessing a virtuous nature, and being entirely free from sleep, he abandons all sense-objects and resorts even to solitude. ||10||
Seated in yogic postures, free from desire and without possessions—
this [state] belongs to him when the time of death has arrived at its appointed hour.
When the time of death had arrived for Somaśarman, who was subsisting on his life-breath, the Brahmin Āgatādāna came into his presence.
In the great sacred field of Śāligrāma, which increases the honor of the sages, some say they are Daityas, while others say they are Dānavas. (13)
At that time, such a great sound reached the range of the ears of that very best of brahmins,
Somaśarman, after a long interval.

Fear born of the Daityas entered him who was absorbed in knowledge and meditation; yet, by means of that very meditation, even for him, this [fear] vanished through the power of that meditation itself.
And very quickly those vital breaths departed from that great-souled one;
overcome by fear of the Daityas, he fell under the power of death. ||16||
Therefore, though born in the house of a Daitya as the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
he was slain by the wielder of the discus in the great war between the gods and the Asuras.
Even by that high-souled Prahlāda while he was fighting,
the nature of Vāsudeva, endowed with the universal form (viśvarūpa), was clearly perceived.
Through the practice of yoga, the great-souled one attained knowledge as before;
he remembered his entire former life as Śivaśarman. (19)
Formerly, I was known by the name Somaśarman; having entered this body of an asura, when shall I [attain] from this physical frame that pure, supreme abode? (20)
We shall go, by means of our great merits known as wisdom, to that which bestows liberation,
together with the high-souled Prahlāda who is dying in battle.
O best of the twice-born, listen now to this unprecedented account of what was thought;
thus has it been told, destroying all doubts. (22)
Sūta said:
When Prahlāda had been slain in battle by the god of gods,
the wielder of the discus, that passionate woman, her son having been killed, wept piteously.
Prahlāda’s mother, the beloved wife of Hiraṇyakaśipu, grieved day and night with great sorrow for Prahlāda. ||24||
To that highly fortunate Kamalā, the devoted wife who was weeping day and night, Nārada spoke as follows: 25.
"Do not grieve, O illustrious lady, you who share in merit, for the sake of your son;
though your son has been slain by Vāsudeva, he shall be reunited with you. (26)
Furthermore, your son shall be endowed with his own specific characteristics and possess great intelligence; moreover, his name shall be Prahlāda. (27)
Deprived of asuric dispositions and endowed with divinity,
O auspicious one, he rejoices in the state of Indra, saluted by all the gods.
O highly fortunate lady, you shall always be happy because of this son; O Goddess, you must not disclose this excellent news to anyone.
"O you whose nature is ignorance, always keep this well-concealed;
having spoken thus, the brahmin Nārada, the best of sages, departed. (30)
Furthermore, from the womb of Kamalā, there was born his unsurpassed son;
his name was Prahlāda, and this is the narrative of that great-souled one.
O brahmins, from his very childhood he thought only of Kṛṣṇa;
by the grace of Narasiṃha, he became the king of the gods in heaven.
Having attained divinity and the unsurpassed station of Indra, he,
whose self is knowledge, shall go to liberation— the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The manifestations of creation are indeed innumerable and of great magnitude;
thus, delusion should not be entertained by high-souled ones who possess knowledge. (34)
All this has been narrated to you as it was asked, O best of the twice-born. Ask another question, O highly fortunate ones; I shall dispel your doubt.
The victory of the gods and the great destruction of the Dānavas were achieved by the God of gods; indeed, the three worlds were established by him. (36)
The sages said:
Whose Indrahood has arisen, which sustains the sound of the gods?
O best of the twice-born, tell us in detail by whom it was bestowed. (37)
Sūta said:
O best of beings, I shall relate in detail how this highly fortunate one attained the status of Indra through his most meritorious deeds.
When all those Daityas had been slain in that great battle and the wicked ones utterly destroyed by the high-souled Govinda;
Then all the gods, along with the gandharvas, nāgas, and vidyādharas, having joined their palms in reverence, spoke thus to Mādhava: ||40||
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, salutations be unto you!
We inform you of this; let all of it be taken into account. 41.
O Kurukeśava, you are our teacher, protector, and meritorious soul;
you are the king of meritorious dharma, Indra, and the ruler of the world. 42.
By taking refuge in this, one shall obtain happiness as a subject of the gods in the three worlds.
Vāsudeva said: "O highly fortunate one, in my world, you shall be endowed with the Vaiṣṇava [nature]. (43)
O best of Brahmins, that great-souled one, having dwelt for a long time by means of his splendor, has now completed his time in the world of the immortals. 44.
O best of gods, as that brahmin devoted to me dwelt there, he became his protector through the very splendor of Viṣṇu. 45.
He will be one whose soul is devoted to the True Dharma and who takes delight in that Dharma; he will be a protector and a preserver, and he shall be the most excellent of Brahmins. 46.
There will be a virtuous soul named Suvrata, the son of Aditi and a great-minded one, for the sake of being a protector for you all. (47)
"He shall be possessed of great strength and great heroism, and he shall become the Indra of all.
Sūta said:
"Thus, O Lord of the Gods, having granted these supreme boons to the gods," (48)
All those victorious gods, together with Viṣṇu, the most excellent of beings,
went there to see their father Kaśyapa and their mother.
They bowed down to those two high-souled ones as they sat comfortably;
filled with great joy, they all spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"Indeed, it is by your grace that we have attained divinity.
Overcome with great joy, he spoke these words to the gods. (51)
Kaśyapa said: "Indeed, you have always been conducting yourselves according to the dharma of falsehood; yet, by the grace of us both and through the power of our asceticism," (52)
They have attained lordship, divinity, and the imperishable state;
filled with great joy, I grant them this very boon.
"You shall indeed become immortal, ageless, and imperishable;
your every desire fulfilled and endowed with all perfections. (54)
"By my grace, O great Asuras, you shall become gods, nāgas, and gandharvas.
Viṣṇu said:
"Choose a boon; may it be well with you, O illustrious daughter of a god."
"Whatever is desired by the mind, all that is well-determined for me.
Aditi said:
"O Mādhava, by your grace, I have previously become a mother of sons. (56)
"O Madhusūdana, listen: all these sons of mine are immortal, ageless, imperishable, devoted to merit, and free from disease. (57)
Furthermore, O Govinda, you are the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires;
please dwell within my womb and grant me the cessation of suffering.
O Keśava, just as you always fulfill the desire for food for your own son Dāman, so too, O Lord, fulfill this most exalted wish of mine. (59)
Vāsudeva said:
"O Goddess, for the sake of the work of the gods, you must assume a human body;
then I shall certainly enter your womb."
When the twelfth Yuga had arrived, O Goddess, for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth,
there appeared the son of Jamadagni, the best of the twice-born named Rāma.
"Endowed with the splendor of majesty and for the sake of slaying all the kṣatriyas, I shall become your son, the best among all wielders of weapons. (62)
O devoted wife, when the age known as Tretā arrives, consisting of twenty-seven thousand years,
I shall become a son named Rāma to you.
"Furthermore, you shall become my son once more; listen, O storehouse of merit!
This will happen when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara Yuga has arrived."
For the sake of destroying all the Daityas and for the removal of the earth's burden, I shall become your son known as Vāsudeva; of this there is no doubt.
Now, O virtuous one, listen to my words which are endowed with righteousness,
possessed of all auspicious characteristics, and consistent with truth and dharma.
Having produced a beautiful son who is omniscient and a lord of all gods, I shall grant him the status of Indra; he too shall become Indra.
Having heard these words spoken, she was filled with great joy, thinking:
"By the grace of the God of gods, a son equal to Indra shall be born. (68)
"So be it, O Great Being; I shall do as you have commanded. Then all those deities indeed returned to their own abodes.
Accompanied by the deer, all were free from fear and filled with joy.
Sūta said:
Having reached her season, the high-minded Aditi spoke to Kaśyapa.
"O Blessed One, let your son be given, he who enjoys the station of the Lord of the Gods.
Having reflected for a moment, the Brahmin spoke to that high-minded woman.
"Let it be so, O highly fortunate one! He shall become your son;
he alone shall be the creator of the three worlds and the enjoyer of the sacrifice. (72)
Having placed his own hand upon her head, that best of the twice-born,
radiant and endowed with truth and righteousness, performed austerities.
The radiant one named Suvrata shall dwell eternally in the world of Viṣṇu;
O best of the twice-born, when his merit is exhausted, he shall depart from the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of the twice-born, due to the power of his karma, he then fell from there and entered a meritorious womb with Aditi, O Brahmin, as one of great asceticism.
Desiring to enjoy the state of Indra through her true merit and virtuous deeds,
that goddess indeed conceived a fetus by means of her merit and ascetic power.
Free from indolence and devoted to dwelling in the forest,
she performed austerities for a hundred divine years while you were performing penance, O Mother of the Gods.
Then she performed intense and severe penance, difficult even for gods and asuras;
thereupon, she became endowed with splendor through that asceticism and that luster.
Resembling the splendor of the sun, she shone like a second sun,
established in supreme meditation as if ablaze.
Then, by the power of her asceticism, she surpassed all in beauty;
devoted to penance and meditation, that female ascetic subsisted on air alone.
Then the goddess shone even more brilliantly than the daughter of Dakṣa;
so too did all the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, and the gods of great majesty.
They praised that highly fortunate woman and protected her with great diligence;
when a full hundred years had passed for her, Viṣṇu arrived there.
He spoke to that highly fortunate Aditi, who was endowed with ascetic power:
"The divine embryo is fully developed; the time for birth is approaching. (83)
"Nourished by your very asceticism and increased by your splendor, release this embryo this very day, O illustrious lady! (84)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods went to his own abode;
and when the time of great auspiciousness had arrived, that goddess gave birth to a son.
Accompanied by his son, he was endowed with brilliance like a second sun;
he was fortunate, with beautiful limbs on every side, and possessed of all auspicious marks.
Four-armed and of massive body, he is the world-protector and lord of the gods;
he is enveloped in a blaze of splendor, with a discus and a lotus in his beautiful hands. ||87||
The one of great intelligence, with a face resembling molten gold, shone forth, O wise one, endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu. (88)
Adorned with other divine marks and divine qualities, he was complete with all the characteristics, his eyes like the petals of a lotus. ||89||
Then the three gods arrived, along with the ṛṣis who have mastered the Vedas, as well as the gandharvas, nāgas, siddhas, and vidyādharas. (90)
The seven divine sages of ancient times, possessed of great majesty, as well as other holy ascetics who bestow merit and auspiciousness; ||91||
When that illustrious and highly energetic Blessed One was born, those great-souled ones arrived with their minds overflowing with joy. 92.
All the deities arrived, as did the ascetics dwelling on the mountains, all the oceans beginning with the Ocean of Milk, and likewise the pure rivers. 93.
Then all those others, both mobile and immobile, were filled with joy;
and all the lords of the gods celebrated with auspicious rites and great enthusiasm.
Multitudes of Apsarases danced and Gandharvas sang charmingly; the gods and the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas praised him with Vedic mantras.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Vedas themselves, having assembled together, praised that great-souled son of Kaśyapa. ||96||
O best of beings, when that one of great majesty was born, all those beings in the three worlds who were endowed with merit became likewise possessed of the primary and secondary limbs.
When that one of great majesty was born, all who had gathered there performed auspicious rites with meritorious songs and great festivals.
Filled with intense joy, all the three gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as Kaśyapa and Bṛhaspati, honored those of great luster.
The karmic actions of that very same Great-Souled One were named Cakrin;
he was renowned as Vasudatta, and furthermore, O son, as Vasudeva. (100)
He is named Ākhaṇḍala, and he is also called Marutvān;
you are Maghavān, Viḍaujas, and Pākaśāsana as well. (101)
Śakra, Vikhyāta, and Indra—these were the sons born to him; these indeed are the names of that very same great-souled one. 102.
All the deities, satisfied and joyful in mind, performed the bathing ceremony and the purificatory rites for the great asura. ||103||
Having summoned Viśvakarman, they gave him those auspicious and divine ornaments; they bestowed them upon that high-souled one. (104)
When that illustrious and high-souled king of the gods was thus born, all the gods of great majesty attained supreme joy. 105.
On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation and at a propitious moment, he was installed as Indra by the high-souled gods and consecrated with highly auspicious rites.
Having attained the station of Indra through the grace of that wielder of the discus, the radiant Vasudatta, lord of the gods, performed austerities. (107)
Endowed with fierce splendor, he holds the vajra, the noose, and the goad as his weapons. ||108||
Sūta said:
Having observed the entire formidable power of his asceticism, Śukra uttered this verse: "In the worlds, there shall be no other such as he; for indeed, he is so exceedingly beautiful. (109)
By the grace of Viṣṇu, that great-souled one attained supreme and divine sovereignty right here in this world.
"By this [merit], there shall be no one else in the worlds equal to him in the gravity of his ascetic power. ||111||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Coronation of the Lord of the Asuras," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||5||
The sixth chapter.
Sūta said:
And Kaśyapa had another wife, a female ascetic named Danu.
Tormented by grief for her son, she reached this most terrible state. ||1||
Then, weeping and bowing down to her pair of lotus feet, Aditi,
overcome by great sorrow, was consoled by her [the Goddess].
Diti said:
"O highly fortunate one, why is this cause of weeping yours alone?
Indeed, O noble lady, women who possess sons are honored by the world even with a single son. (3)
O beautiful lady, you are the mother of the hundred sons who possess virtuous qualities;
O auspicious one, you are the mother of the high-souled Śumbha and the others.
"Tell me this reason why you have not met with such suffering:
King Hiraṇyakaśipu and the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa. (5)
"Tell us why such great sorrow has arisen for her, whose two sons are high-souled and possessed of great strength and prowess."
"Tell me the entire reason why you weep so bitterly.
Having addressed the goddess in this way, the high-minded lady fell silent.
Danu said:
"Behold, O highly fortunate one, behold the desire of my co-wife;
it has been completely fulfilled by that God of gods, the wielder of the discus."
Just as a boon was previously granted to Aditi by Lord Viṣṇu,
O Goddess, so now a great boon has been granted to her son.
A son renowned from Kaśyapa was born as the protector of the three worlds;
Indrahood was granted to him by you, having been taken away from your own son.
Aditi, who increases happiness, was completely fulfilled by her desires;
and her youngest son was Vasudatta, who was devoted to him.
"He enjoys that station, so difficult even for the gods to attain.
Diti said: "From what position has my son, who is of great intelligence, fallen? (12)
"O friend, O illustrious one, why have those other Dānavas and Daityas been deprived of their splendor?
Tell me the cause of that in detail."
Having addressed her with these words, Diti, deeply distressed, fell silent.
Danu said:
"All the gods and the dānavas have gone to the battlefield, filled with wrath. (14)
There, a great battle took place, causing the destruction of the Daityas;
and in the conflict with the gods and Viṣṇu, the sons of Mamatā were struck down.
In the very same way, those sons of yours were driven from the forest by the God of gods, the wielder of the discus, as a lion would with its own splendor.
In that same way, these sons of mine were slain by the one who holds a conch in his hand;
as was the army led by Kālanemi, which was invincible even to the gods and asuras. ||17||
Everything was destroyed, crushed, melted away, and rendered powerless, just as fire with its own flames would consume the grasses in a forest. ||18||
In that same way, Keśava utterly consumes all the hosts of Daityas;
O Goddess, because my son has died, the Danus have offered many hymns of praise.
Just as all moths meet their destruction upon reaching a fire,
so too did all those Dānavas go to their ruin upon reaching Hari.
Thus did Diti hear this dreadful account of what had transpired.
Diti said:
"O blessed one, how can such a thing happen to me, which is like the falling of a thunderbolt?"
When addressed in this way, the queen fell down unconscious;
"Alas! Alas! This misery has arisen—this great suffering that brings such torment! (22)
Deeply afflicted by grief for her son, she wept piteously;
seeing her, that best of sages spoke these auspicious words.
Do not weep, O blessed one; for this very reason those like you grieve.
You are a being of great fortune, free from greed and delusion. (24)
Whose sons indeed are they? Whose queen is Subāndhavā?
They belong to an atheist; O beloved, let all of this be heard from me.
"You are the daughters of Dakṣa and likewise my own beautiful daughters; O auspicious ones, I am your husband, the fulfiller of your desires. (26)
O lady of beautiful countenance, he is the uniter, the protector, and the guardian of this world;
why then has enmity been created toward him by these cruel asuras who have not conquered their own selves? (27)
O highly fortunate one, your sons are devoid of truth and righteousness;
therefore, O auspicious lady, they have all fallen into this misfortune solely through your own fault. (28)
They have been slain by Vāsudeva and struck down by the gods;
therefore, you should not give way to grief, for it destroys truth and liberation.
Sorrow destroys merit, and through the exhaustion of merit, one perishes;
therefore, O fair-faced one, abandon sorrow, which is the very form of an obstacle. (30)
By the power of their own faults, the Dānavas met their death;
and the gods, having become mere instruments, were destroyed by their own karma. (31)
"Knowing this, O illustrious one, come toward happiness.
Having spoken thus to his beloved, who was a partaker of sorrow, the great yogi— [32]
And having turned away from despondency, that one of great intelligence ceased [his lamentation]. ||33||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Lamentation of Diti," in the Devāsura section of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(7) The Seventh Chapter. Diti said:
"O Anātha, everything you have said is true; there is no doubt about it.
O twice-born one, she has departed, having abandoned her affection for her husband out of a desire to avoid co-wifery. (1)
O best of beings, tormented by the suffering of pride, by the loss of honor,
and by great anguish, I shall release my life.
Kaśyapa said:
Listen, I shall declare how peace will come about; for no one can be anyone's son, nor mother, nor father, O auspicious lady. (3)
Whose husband is he who has no brother? And whose husbands are those who have no kinsmen?
Thus, bound by the delusion of Māyā, one is attached to this cycle of saṃsāra. (4)
One is oneself indeed the father and the mother, oneself the husband, oneself the circle of kinsmen, and oneself the eternal Dharma. ||5||
O Goddess, through right conduct, human happiness arises;
likewise, through misconduct and sin, one certainly meets with destruction.
Thus, O Goddess, a man goes to a cruel womb through his delusion, by means of actions devoid of truth and characterized by great sin; of this there is no doubt.
A mortal who dwells constantly among living beings exists in a state of enmity; wherever he may be, his enemies are likewise present there—of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful woman, when a mortal conducts himself with loving-kindness toward what is dear and auspicious in this world, then his very existence becomes friends everywhere.
O Goddess, when a farmer has sown well-placed and well-covered seed, he reaps a fruit that is exactly of such a nature as that seed. ||10||
You vied with virtuous sons of the Tathāgatas;
now, O steadfast one, enjoy the well-established fruit of that action which has come upon you. (11)
O highly fortunate lady, because your sons were devoid of austerity and tranquility, they have all fallen from that great state due to that sin. (12)
Knowing this, attain peace regarding both this suffering and happiness; for whom are there sons, and for whom are there friends, kinsmen, and relatives? (13)
O Goddess, those who are wise through the knowledge of reality live happily according to their own past actions, contemplating the welfare of others. 14.
Great-souled beings do not act in vain; of this there is no doubt.
[They know that] the body, composed of the five elements, is merely a collection of decaying bones. (15)
O Goddess, he has made himself his own friend out of a desire for happiness;
he is the great merit of the self, all-pervading, and the seer of all. ||16||
The embodiment of all perfections, the soul of all, the sattvic one who bestows all success—thus, O Goddess, the One, free from all taint, wanders as the essence of everything. 17.
O best of the twice-born, as he was wandering through that uninhabited place, he beheld four meritorious and embodied beings of great majesty. (18)
The fifth was Śvasana, who was indeed the friend of the former ones;
then the Self arrived, bringing with him the very assistance of knowledge.
Seeing the virtuous ones, the Great-Souled One spoke to Jñāna and Ātman:
"O Jñāna, behold these five; they are three, yet they are mutually distinct. (20)
Having gone to them, he said, "Ask them, 'Who are you?
and having heard that supreme speech and its meaning from that great-souled one, [he understood]. (21)
Then he said: "O God, you have been propitiated by these; what is your purpose? Tell me truly, for you are eternally pure at all times. (22)
The Self said:
"These five highly fortunate ones are handsome and wise;
having gone there, I shall show them to you. Listen, O Jñāna, as I speak. (23)
I shall describe these fortunate ones who have attained the fifth destiny: "O wise one, skilled in the duties of a messenger, go forth as a messenger! (24)
Jñāna said:
"O son, listen to my words; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
You must never, under any circumstances, associate with these people. (25)
O pure-souled one, for one who desires auspiciousness, there is no improper act;
O high-minded one, this person desires association with you out of delusion. (26)
The Self said:
"O wise one, tell me truly the reason why you prevent these from associating with knowledge. (27)
Jñāna said:
"From mere association with these, great suffering will arise;
they are indeed like serpents rooted in misery, causing grief and torment. (28)
"So be it, O one of great wisdom; I shall indeed do this for you.
Having spoken thus, he united himself with his own self through meditation, accompanied by the light of knowledge. (29)
Kaśyapa said:
Then, after five days, they saw that very self there;
they summoned the intellect and said to it, "Come, unite with the self indeed. (30)
O auspicious one, perform the duty of a messenger for us along with yourself;
the five great-souled principles are the sustainers of the universe and are auspicious. (31)
"Go and speak these words to the high-minded one: 'They desire your friendship.
Having gone and understood his intent, you must do what needs to be done; do not depart from here. (32)
"So be it, O highly fortunate one; I shall perform this supreme task.
Having spoken thus to them, he went and addressed himself [to that very task]. (33)
O illustrious one, I am Buddhi; I have come here as an envoy from those great beings. Listen now to their words. (34)
The five classes of beings desire your inexhaustible loving-kindness;
O highly wise one, abandon the Kurus' love and meditation from afar. (35)
Dhyāna said: "O Ātman, you must not bring these together;
by their mere association, great suffering will arise. (36)
Devoid of the knowledge of sacrifice, how will you perform the ritual?
In this very way, you must not have any association with them.
O Lord, they will lead you to dwelling in a womb; that shall not be otherwise.
Deprived of knowledge by me in this way, you will certainly go to ignorance.
Having spoken thus to that high-minded one, he ceased;
then the Self, being resolute, spoke to that Intellect which had approached him. (39)
The two great-souled ones, Jñāna and Dhyāna, are my auspicious protectors;
it is fitting that I bow there. Therefore, O Buddhi, what shall I do? 40.
Having heard this, their illustrious intellect then related that entire discourse on knowledge and meditation in its full detail.
Then all those sages returned to themselves, saying:
"We indeed always desire only friendship with you. (42)
Since you are pure like Lokeśvara, we have approached you;
having reflected upon this yourself, please grant us an answer. (43)
The Self said:
"You five desire to obtain my friendship;
therefore, describe your own qualities and power before me. (44)
The Earth said:
"I am the foundation of all things, composed of skin and flesh, with firmness rooted in bone, and provided with nails and hair. (45)
O one of great wisdom, within my very body is indeed his power;
the fragrance that reaches my nose is from my high-minded servant. 46.
Ākāśa said:
"I have become Ākāśaka, possessing power within my own body;
listen, for I shall describe that which has the nature of the Supreme Brahman. (47)
I resided in an empty place outside the city, in an open space;
there, my two ministers, Utanka and Karṇa, were stationed for the purpose of hearing [news]. 48.
Vāyu said:
"I abide in five forms and thus bring about both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Residing within the body of skin, the minister [of touch] experiences the quality of touch."
Tejas said:
"O Kāyasa, you who are eternally impermanent, I perform the process of digestion;
I manifest everything, both internal and external, as well as all that is substantial and insubstantial."
Semen, marrow, saliva, and likewise skin, blood, and fat are situated [within me];
I indeed send forth the blood, for I abide within the midst of the body. 51.
In this regard, Netra and Amātya are the two who accomplish the attainment of the medicinal substances;
thus has my supreme personal activity been described before you. (52)
Jala said:
"O beloved of Kāyapattana, I constantly satisfy my body with nectar; such is my activity here. (53)
The Nose spoke to the Minister, the supreme tongue that experiences the taste of flavors:
"I too shall provide nourishment for the body, which is intent upon fragrances. (54)
Having completely abandoned the foul odor of the body, one should manifest the fragrance of the body; O noble one endowed with wisdom, [this] is cultivated through the absence of that [odor]. (55)
In this body which is for the sake of the Master’s work, I abide immovably;
know that my quality, fragrance, is of two kinds as it is manifested. (56)
The two ears said:

"We shall hear the sounds spoken by people regarding what ought and ought not to be done, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as well as the true and false, and the pleasant and unpleasant, residing within our own bodies. (57)
Sound is declared to be my quality; indeed, it is my very activity. When the intellect becomes full, I join [the soul] with that which is without body. 58
The skin said: "The wind, consisting of five forms, is established within this body. (59)
I know in truth their every movement, both external and internal,
as well as cold, heat, sunshine, rain, and even the throbbing of the wind.
I know all the touch of men, such as clinging, embracing, and so forth;
touch alone is my quality—this I tell you truly. (61)
"Thus has the non-activity (avyāpāra) been declared by me for the sake of benefit.
The two eyes said:
O most excellent one, describe the forms of those who are fit for liberation (bhavya) and those who are unfit (abhavya) within saṃsāra. (62)
When the intellect is impelled, then [the self] perceives through it and not otherwise;
we two dwell within the body, and this is our form and quality here.
"In this way, O Mahāmati, there is a connection of activity within the body.
The tongue said:
"O father, endowed with intelligence, I shall discern the various distinctions of tastes. (64)
I shall contemplate all alkaline, sour, and other substances as being sapless yet sweet; even through this activity, I remain eternally absorbed in equanimity.
For of all the senses, this intellect is the leader.
Thus, O beloved, hear concerning the five senses as they come together.
They spoke again and again of their own improper deeds;
then, having regained her composure, Buddhi addressed the high-minded Tama.
When the body is bereft of me, it perishes and not otherwise;
therefore, O high-minded one, abide in me and conduct yourself accordingly.
Then, having arrived, Karmā spoke thus to himself:
"O highly wise one, I, Karma, have come into your presence. (69)
"I send you by that very path through which you have come here.
Having heard all this, the Self spoke to them in reply. (70)
Since you yourselves are composed of the five [aggregates] and are indeed common to all, why do you desire friendliness toward those who likewise consist of the five? (71)
But [the Lord] spoke the reason for all this before them: "All that is indeed composed of the five elements.
Then the five elements said:
"Even through association with our union, the physical body (piṇḍa) alone is produced. (72)
In that place, O you of great wisdom, you who are firm in your vows dwell;
indeed, by your grace, we all remain there. (73)
"For this reason, we desire your constant friendship.
The Self replied: "So be it, O noble ones; let there be exactly what is pleasing to you. (74)

"O noble one, though being restrained even by that great-souled one through his wisdom, you shall nevertheless perform here this act of self-immolation out of a desire for friendship and affection. (75)
And through his meditation, O Sūta, that Great-Souled One entered into association with them;
there he was then deluded by them through passion, hatred, and other such emotions.
Endowed with the five elements, the Lord entered the state of a body;
when he entered the womb, which was filled with feces and urine.
Having fallen into a difficult, slippery whirlpool along with them, he became distressed in body and spoke to his five sons:
"O you five elements, all of you, listen to my words!
I have been deluded by the great suffering resulting from your association. (79)
Having fallen there into that slippery, terrible, and most fearsome place, the five elements said:
"O King, remain here until the fetus has reached full development. (80)
Thereafter, your departure will indeed take place, of this there is no doubt;
for you, our lord, are established in the land of Kāya. (81)
"The kingdom itself must be established; he will become an enjoyer of happiness.
Having heard those words of theirs, his own self was tormented by grief. (82)
Desiring to go, he became intent on fleeing from that place. ||83||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Bodies of the Lord of Gods and Asuras," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||7||
The Eighth Chapter. Kaśyapa said: He became distressed while in the womb, suffering day after day.
Overcome by suffering, his nature being such, he was tormented by every kind of affliction. ||1||
With his face turned downward, held fast within the womb by a web of delusion, he was overcome by mental and physical afflictions; crying out "Alas! Alas!", he became unconscious.
Overwhelmed by great suffering and tormented by ignorance, he spoke;
the Self said:
"O highly wise one, those words were then uttered by me. (3)
Even while being restrained by meditation, he has fallen into the perilous strait of delusion;
therefore, O one of great wisdom, protect him from this most dreadful dwelling in the womb.
Jñāna said: "O Self, you were indeed forbidden by me, yet you did not follow my word;
thus, you have been cast into the peril of the womb by these five extremely cruel beings. (5)
Go now to meditative absorption; from that you shall obtain happiness.
There will be liberation for you from dwelling in a womb; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard those words of his and having understood the true nature of ignorance, he summoned Meditation and said: "Listen to my words. (7)
"I have come to you for refuge; protect me constantly in meditation.
"So be it," said the one of great wisdom, the highly intelligent Adhyānamāha. (8)
Having heard these words, he then attained self-meditation;
for through meditation, he remained within the womb, free from delusion.
For when, through the limbs of meditative absorption, the self is no longer forgotten, the fear born of the womb ceases;
there, accompanied by both [faith and knowledge], one is freed from self-delusion.
Thinking thus constantly of my own happiness alone, I shall cast off this body of mine as soon as I have emerged from here, for it is truly not worth preserving.
Thinking thus constantly, O fair-faced one, the Lord remained within the womb; then, when the time for birth had arrived, he was born under the constellation Prajāpati.
When the embryo is moved by the wind and further impelled by the powerful vital breath (prāṇa),
the birth canal then undergoes an expansion of twenty-four finger-breadths.
When the fetus is twenty-five finger-breadths long, it experiences oppression by the thief [of vitality].
Thus oppressed, O beloved, it faints in a swoon.
Having fallen upon the ground, yet endowed with knowledge and meditation,
he was not separated from the divine wind belonging to Prajāpati.
Merely by touching the ground, his knowledge and meditation were forgotten; smeared by the bonds of worldly existence, he remained there out of attachment to his own self. (16)
Overcome by both virtues and faults and possessed of great delusion, he desires all things such as food and drink day after day. (17)
Thus, while being nourished by the five [senses] along with their respective objects, the self is pervaded by all the senses and by the objects that produce evil. (18)
O Goddess, likewise, husbands together with their wives and others become increasingly agitated and distressed day after day due to delusion. (19)
Smeared by great delusion and caught in the snare of delusion, the Lord is bound like a fish caught in the nets of a fisherman. (20)
He was unable to move at all; likewise, the self remained firmly bound by all those nets of delusion, held fast by strong bonds.
Thus, by this and other such elaborations, he is not pervaded by the Pervader;
for he has fallen away from knowledge and discernment, and is destroyed by passion, hatred, and the like. ||22||
Whether oppressed by desire or likewise by anger, bound by his very nature and by his actions, he became a great fool. (23)
Sūta said:
Thus, when this self is deluded and has fallen under the sway of desire and anger, it is occupied by all those evil-natured things such as greed, passion, and the rest.
"This is my wife, this is my son, this is my friend, and this is my home"—thus is he bound by the great delusion of the web of worldly attachments. (25)
At that time, he was agitated by various sufferings such as grief for his son,
and likewise seized by old age, diseases, and mental afflictions.
Thus the self is scorched by most terrible suffering and delusion, and is shattered by conceits, humiliations of pride, and manifold miseries. (27)
Afflicted by old age and likewise by infirmity, O Goddess, he constantly broods on suffering, crying out "Alas! Alas! and losing his senses.
O Goddess, day after day, one sees dreams at night and is devoid of consciousness during the day, being thus pervaded by the impairment of the limbs. 29.
While wandering through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), he demonstrated detachment therein—free from doubt, devoid of attachment, tranquil, and indeed contented. (30)
He then spoke to him, who was free from desire and anger: "Who are you, appearing in the form of a naked ascetic? Why do you not feel shame before your friends? (31)
Where there are women—old and young—as well as mothers, you, being unencumbered, have no fear of entering into their midst. (32)
Vītarāga said:
"Who indeed here could be seen naked, saying 'I am naked,' at any time?
For even you are well-restrained and fully clothed. (33)
Because he has no shame regarding nakedness and other such things, he appears naked;
he is subject to the power of the senses and their objects, and is utterly devoid of moral restraint. (34)
The Self said:
O observer of excellent vows, tell me in detail, O highly wise one, if you know it for certain, what the limits of a person's lifespan are. (35)
The great sage, free from passion and possessed of vast wisdom, said to him:
"The mind maintains perfect stability at all times, amidst both pleasure and pain. (36)
One should abandon all those things that cause affliction; now I shall explain shame, by which the mind enters fully into its proper course. (37)
"I should not have done this today—standing naked and deprived of my place.
Thus, deeply immersed in remorse, he speaks with great shame. (38)
Whom should one feel shame before? There is never a second [person]. And who is this divine person that could destroy whatever one has thought? (39)
Now I shall describe the worlds which have been mentioned by you;
just as a potter places clay upon his wheel.
Having rotated it with the thread, one should reveal various different forms;
established in his own will, he may manifest thousands of vessels.
In this way, the Creator fashions various forms that are not otherwise;
subsequently, they come to destruction by some cause or another. ||42||
One must feel shame before those who are eternally established and the worlds that are eternal; they do not return to this earth again.
Space, wind, fire, earth, and water as the fifth—these worlds shine forth; they are established everywhere. (44)
These five are well-established in the various limbs and parts of sentient beings;
they circulate everywhere—of whom is shame felt? (45)
I shall describe the form of women; listen, O dear one, with focused attention, how it shines forth as if in thousands of jars filled with water. 46.
And one [hero], the illustrious Droṇa, shone everywhere in that same manner;
the high-souled one, having entered the wheel of delusion, was like a thousand suns. 47.
And among all stationary beings as well as moving ones, you indeed [enter] through the door of birth by means of sin consisting of the delusion of Māyā. 48.
She shines with her two breasts, her two arms, and her youth;
there is no doubt that an increase in the flesh of her heart has been observed here. 49.
The form of delusion that causes the worlds to fall has been revealed;
that woman who was described by you does not exist at all. (50)
The Creator performs these acts as a sport for His own diversion;
just as there are women, so too are there men—the individual soul (jīva) is present everywhere. 51.
Those who are forever devoid of the womb of the body are indeed liberated while living;
a man is called *puruṣa*, while a woman is said to be *prakṛti*. (52)
He never sports with women;
you, however, are seen among men as one endowed with *prakṛti*. (53)
Who feels shame before whom? Knowing this, proceed happily.
O fair-faced one, I shall describe an old woman who is eternally old. (54)
O lady of beautiful countenance, even on his body the skin has reached a state of decay,
and he is covered with white hair and graying locks.
Even if she is weak, lordless, and miserable, because she possesses pervasive power, this woman does not become old; rather, she is called "the Aged" (Vṛddhā). ||56||
The characteristics of this [Prakṛti] have been declared; now I shall speak of the young woman (the individual soul).
She constantly increases through knowledge and remains closely dependent upon the side of the Jīva.
She is called by the name Sumati; she exists as both old women and young maidens, and is forever established among all women and men in the world. (58)
Out of shame for her, this must be done; furthermore, I shall tell you another thing:
I will speak of that mother who was mentioned by you. (59)
That consciousness which always resides within the limbs and regions of living beings and bestows supreme knowledge is called Prajñā.
She is declared to be the mother of wisdom, for the protection of living beings;
she is established in all worlds for their nourishment or for their welfare.
She who is named Sumati is declared to be their mother;
she is she who constantly describes the forms of the paths that lead to the gateway of saṃsāra. (62)
These mothers indeed manifest many forms of suffering; their nature as mothers has been fully described. Now I shall speak of another [form]. (63)
The Self said:
"Who are you that have come here, the destroyer of my torment?
Tell me in detail your own true nature."
Vītarāga said:
"Because they are free from desire, all these people turn away from their cravings;
it is because of their wickedness that they do not perceive these actions, and not otherwise. (65)
Hope never approaches his presence,
nor do anger, greed, and delusion, for they have met their destruction out of fear of him.
"I am free from passion; may it be well with you. Discrimination is my elder brother. The Self said: "What is this brother of yours named Discrimination like by name? (67)
"Tell me the characteristics of him, your brother, and of yourself. Vītarāga said:
"I shall not describe his characteristics or form before you."
O illustrious one, I am calling out to that brother of mine:
"Ho there, O Brother Viveka! Listen to these words of us two. (69)
"Come, come, O highly fortunate one, out of affection for me, O great-minded one!
Kaśyapa said:
"I have arrived together with my two wives, Śānti and Kṣamā. (70)
He is the all-seeing, the pervader of all speech, and devoted to all principles;
he is the enemy of all bodies and is fond of knowledge.
The two daughters of that very high-souled one were Dhāraṇā and Adhīcchad;
his eldest son was Yoga, whose great preceptor was Mokṣa.
Stainless, free from ego, without expectations, and without possessions;
with a mind serene at all times, he has transcended duality—he is the one of great intelligence. (73)
He has arrived endowed with discernment and adorned with the jewels of virtue;
his two high-minded ministers are Dharmasatya and Mahāmati. (74)
Endowed with patience and tranquility, possessed of discernment, and having arrived, he said this to Vītarāga: "I have come as I was summoned. (75)
Therefore, brother, tell me the entire reason for this before me—relying upon which you have today issued this very challenge to me. (76)
Vītarāga said:
"A man who stands before me is constantly bound by great fetters, bewildered by the arrows of delusion and by the bonds of saṃsāra. (77)
This Self alone is the pervasive lord of all, and it belongs to me;
it is permeated by the five elements and is devoid of knowledge and meditation. (78)
"Please ask him about the self; you are an expert in the true nature of things.
Having heard the words of the one free from passion, Viveka spoke these words: (79)
Viveka said:
"O Lord, Leader of the Universe, you remain in a state of ease;
now that you have arrived at the essence of all things, what happiness have you yourself enjoyed?"
The Self said:
"O wise one, dwelling in the womb is a great suffering—unbearable and terrible—which has been experienced by me, who am always devoid of knowledge. (81)
Even within this body, having fallen away from knowledge, I have been born in many ways;
O Lord, while in the state of childhood, I committed both what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Having failed to enjoy pleasures in youth and having taken many wives,
he was tormented upon reaching old age by the grief for his sons and other such sorrows.
I am tormented day and night by the separations from my wife and others;
I am scorched every single day by manifold and diverse sufferings. (84)
O one of great wisdom, day and night I find no happiness anywhere;
thus, O high-minded one, being thoroughly tormented by sufferings, I move about like a fish [on hot ground]. (85)
Tell me that means by which I may indeed find happiness;
release me today from this flood of the net of worldly existence and from the bondage of life.
Viveka said:
"O Lord of the World, you are pure, free from dualities, and sinless. Go now to that Great-Souled One, who is free from passion and the bestower of happiness. (87)
Without a doubt, you have seen one who is naked and devoid of proper conduct;
yet he is indeed a bestower of happiness and a destroyer of all suffering. (88)
Having heard this, the pure-souled one, though free from passion, spoke again to him while sighing dejectedly: "Listen to my words. (89)
"I shall show you that path by which I have found happiness; let it be so, O one of great wisdom, and I shall surely do as you have requested. (90)
Go back once more to solitude, for you have brought news of happiness; by your departure from the path of pleasure, this [happiness] shall be yours.
Sent by the merit of one free from passion, the Lord went to that high-souled Viveka, who was of pure essence; he spoke to him.
"O Bhava, show me happiness, for I have been sent by one who is free from passion;
having come to you for refuge, protect me from this terrible ocean of existence. (93)
Viveka said:
O highly wise one, go to Jñāna; he will tell you everything.
He is called the Self (Ātman), and he has arrived where knowledge is firmly established. 94.
O Knowledge of great splendor, who reveals all states of being!
I have come to you for refuge; show me the path to happiness. (95)
Jñāna said:
"O you of noble vows, you do not know that I am your servant;
previously, I indeed restrained you again and again through meditation."
O highly wise one, you have encountered this calamity through attachment to the five [senses] which consist of the self; therefore, go to meditation, for that is the giver of happiness. 97.
"The self, indeed, dispatched by knowledge, remains established by resorting to meditation; show me that meditation which bestows supreme, perfected happiness. (98)
"Protect me alone, who have come to you for refuge from worldly existence.
Hearing these words spoken by him, he [the sage] focused his meditation upon that speech. (99)
Having regained his composure, he spoke again with great joy:
"O Father, I am by no means to be abandoned; I am firmly resolved upon all my duties. (100)
Indeed, you yourself, being free from passion and possessed of discernment, should always remain engaged in meditation; behold your own self! 101.
Becoming self-possessed, firm, free from fear, and undisturbed by conceptual constructions, you shall remain steady, just as a lamp placed in a windless spot steadily emits soot.
Having thus burned away all defects, he will indeed attain nirvāṇa;
remaining alone, he shall abstain from food and always eat only a limited amount.
Free from the pairs of opposites, devoid of sound, and remaining motionless while seated, he meditated upon the Self by means of the self with a mind fixed on me alone. 104.
You shall attain the supreme station, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Inner Self," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||8||
The Ninth Chapter.
Kaśyapa said:
Thus enlightened there by means of self-meditation and other practices, [he remained].
Desiring to abandon that which consists of the five elements along with their functions, the wise one [proceeds]. ||1||
Seeing only signs, he proceeds toward that which is to be attained; yet, having abandoned the body, he does not see it fallen, for it is without defining characteristics. ||2||
There is no connection between the vital breath and the body that have grown together;
for what reason, then, should there be a connection with wealth, sons, and wife? (3)
Knowing this, attain peace; do not yield to weakness, O beloved.
This alone is the Supreme Brahman; this alone is the Eternal.
This one abides among the Daityas and gods in his own essential nature;
he is Brahmā, he is Rudra, and he is indeed the eternal Viṣṇu. (5)
This Janārdana, whose nature is dharma yet who assumes the form of adharma, creates all things, protects all creatures, and withdraws them all.
By this [act], O beloved, both gods and dānavas have been produced;
the gods are free from unrighteousness, while your sons are devoid of righteousness. (7)
This is the duty of Mādhava, O dear one, which has been protected by all the gods at all times;
one should reflect upon dharma, O Goddess, and one should indeed protect dharma.
Viṣṇu, whose nature is identical with that [of the Lord], was always favored by all the gods;
indeed, the gods were maintained through righteousness, truth, and austerity. 9.
Those by whom Viṣṇu is pleased have protected Dharma here in this world;
for this Dharma is the very body of Viṣṇu, and Truth is his heart.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly protects truth and righteousness, but he who defiles them would surely foster only sin.
Viṣṇu, being exceedingly powerful, would become enraged at him and destroy that dharma protected by the Vaiṣṇavas who are firmly established in austerity and truth.
Their virtuous souls, being thus purified, performed protection alone;
likewise, the sons of Anu, your son, and the Saindhavas did the same. (13)
Those of sinful mind, who lived by unrighteous and wicked ways,
were slaughtered in battle by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus.
That very Self which was previously described by me before you is this Viṣṇu; he is not the body, but is the righteous soul, the protector of all. (15)
O Goddess, he who was established in his own nature yet remained fixed in evil, that highly intelligent one, being enraged, struck down the Dānavas. ||16||
Having become both external and internal, your sons have been struck down;
O Goddess, by whom they were produced, by that very same one they have been brought to ruin.
You should not feel any delusion regarding them; listen to my words:
he who conducts himself with wickedness shall surely meet his destruction. (18)
"Therefore, abandoning delusion, always take refuge in the Dharma.
Diti said: "So be it, O illustrious one; I shall indeed do as you say. (19)
Addressing Kaśyapa, the best of sages, she spoke thus in her distress;
awakened by the sage, she abandoned her suffering and remained composed. (20)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Address to Aditi by the Gods and Asuras," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
The Sages said:
Then all those Dānavas, headed by Hiraṇyakaśipu, [spoke].
But what could those broken by battle possibly achieve through resolve, O high-minded one? (1)
O twice-born one, tell us in detail their unsurpassed conduct; we all desire to hear from you their history. (2)
Sūta said: Then all those Daityas, their pride gone and afflicted by great sorrow, being devoid of strength, went to their father from that shattered battlefield. ||3||
Having bowed down with devotion, all of them then spoke to Kaśyapa. The Dānavas said:
"O best of the twice-born, our origin is from your own prowess."
We are all Dānavas, possessing strength, heroism, and prowess, just like the gods who receive great shares of sacrificial offerings. ||5||
We are many, skilled in means, wise, and endowed with diligence; whereas those gods are likewise few in number.
"How is it that they all have triumphed while we have been shattered in this great battle? What is the cause of this, O father, for we were endowed with strength and splendor? (7)
O Mahāmati, the strength possessed by each single Daitya is equal to that of a thousand intoxicated elephants;
such strength does not exist among the gods.
O Father, since victory is seen thus even among the gods in this great battle, you ought to explain all of that in order to dispel my doubt. (9)
Kaśyapa said: "Listen, all you sons, to the cause of Jayanta as well,
by which indeed all the deities became victorious in battle."
This is always the field for the mother who extinguishes one's vigor;
it is indeed [the field] for upholding, protecting, and nourishing.
What indeed could a father do for his son in a matter of such adversity?
In this case, it is karma alone that is primary; thus has my mind resolved.
The twofold connection with action arises from both sin and merit;
it is by relying solely upon truth that the highest dharma is performed. (13)
O sons, that which is joined with austerity and meditation is for the sake of crossing over and is beneficial;
however, that which leads to a downfall is declared to be a sin at all times—of this there is no doubt. (14)
O sons, for a man devoid of merit, this strength—consisting of his retinue, his noble birth, and his own power—is rendered ineffective. (15)
In the lofty mountain fastnesses there are trees that bear excellent fruit;
yet they fall, along with their very roots, by the force of the wind, just like thick clouds.
Deprived of truth and righteousness, they likewise go to the abode of Yama;
for this, O good sons, is the common lot of all living beings.
That by which one crosses over fear both in this world and in the next—truth endowed with righteousness—has been abandoned by you. (18)
"O sons, you have resorted to unrighteousness, being devoid of truth;
fallen away from truth, dharma, and austerity, you have plunged into an ocean of suffering. (19)
And the gods are endowed with truth, possessed of excellence, equipped with austerity, tranquility, and self-restraint; they are highly meritorious and free from evil. ||20||
Where truth, righteousness, austerity, and merit likewise reside,
and where Viṣṇu Hṛṣīkeśa is present— there victory is seen.
The eternal Vāsudeva was born as their ally;
therefore, those gods, endowed with truth and righteousness, are victorious. ||22||
Indeed, by means of allies, strength, and likewise by manly prowess, you sons are said to be devoid of austerity and truth. (23)
Those who know the Dharma understand that victory belongs only to him whose ally is Viṣṇu, and whose asceticism as well as his strength are likewise [his allies]. 24.
But you, being devoid of Dharma and bereft of austerity and truth, previously attained the station of Indra solely through force. ||25||
O highly wise one, without austerity, without righteousness, and without glory, sons cannot attain the station of Indra, which is unattainable even through strength, pride, or virtues. (26)
"O sons, even after attaining the station of Indra, one indeed falls from it;
therefore, O sons, you should all together perform penance."
Those who are disciplined through non-opposition and endowed with knowledge and meditation should never harbor enmity toward Keśava. 28.
When you have acted in this manner for our son, you will become blessed;
then, all of you shall attain supreme perfection, of this there is no doubt. ||29||
Having thus been addressed by the high-souled Tṛṇakaśyapa,
those Dānavas of great prowess listened to the words of their father.
Having bowed with devotion to Kaśyapa and risen up with haste,
the Daityas, concentrated upon one another, performed an excellent mantra.
Then Hiraṇyakaśipu spoke to the Dānavas who had been born:
"I shall perform austerities that are difficult to practice and which grant all things."
Then Hiraṇyākṣa said: "I shall perform severe penance;
then, by that power, I will seize the three worlds—of this there is no doubt. (33)
Having conquered Govinda in battle, I shall slay this evil-minded one and,
having [pleased] all the deities, proceed to the station of Indra.
Bali said:
"O lords of the sons of Diti, it is not fitting for you to act in this way;
that enmity with Viṣṇu is not the cause for the destruction of our enmity. (35)
By means of the duty of giving, as well as through meritorious deeds, austerities, and the performance of sacrifices, men attain happiness by propitiating that Hṛṣīkeśa. (36)
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"I myself shall never perform the propitiation of Hari;
rather, having abandoned my own nature, I shall practice service toward the enemy. (37)
The wise indeed consider that [devotion] to be superior even to death;
it is not subject to change through the service of Viṣṇu, nor can it be attained by others, such as the Dānavas. 38.
Bali spoke again to that high-souled Grandfather regarding what has been seen in the treatises on dharma by the sages who know the truth.
One should employ counsel endowed with political wisdom, primarily directed against the enemy,
while recognizing oneself as inferior and the adversary as powerful.
Having gone to his side, one should wait for the time of victory;
always remaining in the darkness, one should take refuge in the shadow of the lamp. 41.
Even when observing that the oil of a lamp has reached its final stage, though it possesses great power, its light quickly fades away while the darkness increases once more. ||42||
Thus, remaining concealed, he should inspire confidence by pointing out their affection according to the truth;
having established affection with the Asuras, he should win over the enemies of the gods through righteous dispositions.
O king of kings, this excellent mantra was previously spoken by the sage Kaśyapa; therefore, being self-possessed, perform your duty with that mantra. 44.
Having heard those words of his, the powerful Daitya said:
"O grandson, I shall not act in such a way as to bring about my own humiliation."
Then all the other husbands spoke to that wise counselor:
"Whatever merit was spoken of by Bali brings delight to the gods. (46)
"It has been declared that it causes pride even to Śakra and strikes terror into the Dānavas;
we shall all perform such unsurpassed austerity. (47)
"Having conquered the gods through asceticism, we shall seize our own place.
Thus they all deliberated, having then cast aside Bali.
Having established a great enmity toward Viṣṇu in their hearts, all those great asuras then performed austerities in mountain fastnesses and on mountain peaks.
Thus all those Dānavas were completely free from passion, firmly resolved,
devoid of desire and anger, abstaining from food, and having conquered fatigue.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Daityas' Ascetic Penance," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Eleventh Chapter.
The Sages said:
"O Omniscient One, you have narrated the conflict between the Daityas and the Dānavas."
Now we wish to hear about the great-souled Suvrata. ||1||
Whose son was this man of great wisdom, and from what lineage did he arise? What was the austerity of that brahmin, and how was Hari propitiated by him? (2)
Sūta said:
O brahmins, by the power of the wisdom arising from this narrative, I shall relate exactly as it was heard before the account of the high-souled Suvrata.
By the grace of Viṣṇu, I shall relate before you the entire divine and purifying life-story of Viṣṇu, which brings about the highest good. 4.
In a previous kalpa, those highly fortunate ones [dwelt] at the excellent field that destroys sin,
on the very meritorious bank of the Revā, at the sacred ford known as Vāmana.
Born in the family of Kauśika, Somaśarman was the best among the twice-born;
yet, being destitute of sons, he was overwhelmed by great sorrow. ||6||
Constantly tormented by the suffering of poverty, he would contemplate day and night the means of obtaining wealth and a son. (7)
Once, however, his beloved wife, named Sumanā, who was firm in her vows, observed her husband overcome with anxiety and with his face cast downwards. (8)
Beholding him thus desirous, the ascetic woman said to him:
"Your mind has been overwhelmed by countless nets of suffering. (9)
O high-minded one, abandon this thought born of delusion;
tell me your sorrow, become composed, and attain happiness. (10)
There is no suffering equal to the anxiety of "it does not exist," for it truly withers the body;
he who lives having abandoned such anxiety rejoices in unhindered happiness. (11)
"O Brahmin, tell me the cause of your anxiety in my presence.

Having heard his beloved's words, Somaśarman spoke to his beloved: [Note: The provided source text contains only the first line of verse 12. The following is the translation of that partial line. "O Brahmin, tell me the cause of your anxiety in my presence."
Somaśarman said:
"O blessed lady, that which was thought of by desire is the cause of this anxiety and suffering.
I shall tell you all of it; having heard it, let it be well considered. (13)
O lady of excellent vows, I do not know by what sin I have become destitute of wealth and likewise bereft of sons; this is the cause of my suffering. (14)
Sumanā said:
Listen, for I shall declare that which destroys all doubt—the true nature of instruction, which reveals all knowledge. (15)

Greed is the seed of evil, and delusion is indeed its root; falsehood is its trunk, and deceit spreads its branches far and wide. Crookedness is its leaves, and it is always in bloom with wicked intellect;
untruth is its fragrance, and ignorance is its fruit.
Deceit, heresy, valor, and envy—these cruel, fraudulent, and sinful birds have taken refuge upon the branches of illusion on the tree of delusion. (18)
Ignorance is its excellent fruit, for unrighteousness is the juice of that fruit;
it increases with the water of craving, and lack of faith is its beloved liquid. (19)
Unrighteousness is its nectar; though pungent, it tastes sweet, just as the tree of greed bears fruits that appear to be excellent.
Whatever man takes refuge in its shade is completely satisfied;
day after day, he eats its well-ripened fruits. (21)
Even if a mortal is protected by unrighteousness through the mere taste of fruits,
he may indeed be satisfied, yet he goes toward his downfall.
Therefore, having abandoned anxiety, a man should not harbor greed; he should not entertain even a single thought concerning wealth, sons, or wife. ||23||
For what wise man would ever follow the path of fools? A fool constantly thinks only of how wealth might belong to him alone. (24)
"May I obtain a good wife here, wealth, servants, and sons"—thus he constantly thinks, deluded day and night. (25)
For a single moment, one may behold that great bliss within the midst of thought;
yet again, consciousness returns and is tormented by great suffering. ||26||
O twice-born one, having completely abandoned the delusion of thought, follow [this path];
O high-minded one, there is no connection with anything whatsoever in this cycle of existence. 17.
Friends, kinsmen, sons, fathers, mothers, servants, as well as all relatives and likewise wives—these alone have become our bonds. (28)
Somaśarman said: "O auspicious one, tell me in detail what kind of relationship it is, by which all our relatives—possessing wealth, sons, and other blessings—have become so. (29)
Sumanā said:
"Some of us are debtors, some are embezzlers of deposits;
some are providers of profit, and others are indifferent. (30)
Through four types of divisions, sons, friends, and women arise;
likewise wives, fathers, mothers, servants, kinsmen, and relatives. (31)

O twice-born ones, whatever property has been deposited on this earth by anyone, if it is taken away through the act of misappropriating a deposit, that entire debt shall belong to you individually on the surface of the earth.
The owner of the deposit shall become a virtuous and handsome son on this earth;
there is no doubt that he will find the deposit that was stolen right in the house of the one who took it.
Due to the misappropriation of a deposit, he experienced suffering that was constant and terrible; moreover, the owner of the deposit became like a good son to the one who had embezzled it. (34)
Possessed of virtues and beauty, and endowed with all auspicious marks, he shall manifest devotion toward him by becoming his son day after day. (35)
Speaking with pleasant and sweet words, displaying great affection and free from illness,
he took up his own wealth and generated the highest degree of joy.
Just as in the past, due to the misappropriation of a deposit, he experienced great and terrible suffering that was indeed life-destroying, so too did it happen for him by whom it was given. (37)
Having become his son through such friendship and by means of great virtues,
he likewise becomes short-lived and approaches death.
Having thus repeatedly caused suffering again and again, he departs;
at which time he utters the lamentation, "O son! O my son! while gasping for breath. (39)
Then he said: "Indeed, whose son is this? He is a father to Hika.
By him has my deposit, the means of my livelihood, been stolen. (40)
"Indeed, even by the theft of our wealth, O King, our lives were nearly lost in the past through great and unbearable suffering. (41)
Having thus caused such suffering and having seized excellent wealth, I have now become the son of one who is exceedingly wretched; how can I be such as this? (42)
Nor was this son of his ever previously turned into a *piśāca* by me for anyone else; rather, it was to this very evil-minded one that I granted the state of a *piśāca*. (43)
Having spoken thus, he departs, laughing at him again and again;
he goes along this path, inflicting most terrible suffering.
Thus, for one who performs this ritual placement (nyāsa), what indeed become his sons?
They are invisible in this world and everywhere else, amidst the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) which abounds in suffering. ||45||
I shall declare before you that all sons are the creditors of their father. ||46||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Suvrata," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||11||
The twelfth chapter.
Sumanā said:
I shall describe before you a son who is bound by debt.
Indeed, he who goes to his death having incurred a debt [is lost]. ||1||
Having become a giver of wealth, a son, a brother, a father, and a beloved, he,
being exceedingly wicked, always behaves in the guise of a friend.
That cruel man of harsh appearance would not perceive any virtue at all;
he always spoke harsh words even toward his own kinsmen. (3)
He constantly eats sweet after sweet and enjoys pleasures perpetually;
he is ever devoted to the practice of gambling and has a longing for the act of theft.
When one forcibly consumes household property while being restrained, he becomes angry;
day by day, he even reviles his father and mother. (5)
He is a seducer and a terrorizer, speaking many harsh words;
yet, having consumed such wealth, he remains at ease.
In childhood, through the birth-rites and other ceremonies, this cruel one seizes his substance;
again, through marriage and various manifold distinctions of wealth. (7)
Thus he thinks: "This very substance gives even to me;
indeed, my house, fields, and all else are mine alone—of this there is no doubt. (8)
Day after day, he indeed strikes his father and mother with cruel blows from all sides, as if with pieces of sugarcane or pestles.
But when that father or mother has died, he becomes exceedingly cruel, devoid of affection, and indeed harsh; of this there is no doubt. (10)
A person who performs ancestral rites and acts of charity for the sake of the gods—
such sons as these indeed arise upon the surface of the earth.
O best of the twice-born, I shall declare to you that one who is an enemy even while still a son;
from the very moment he attains childhood, he always exists in the state of an enemy. (12)
While playing, he would strike his father and mother;
having struck them, he would depart, laughing again and again. (13)
Terrified, he returned again toward his father and mother; he behaved with constant anger and reviled them again and again. (14)
Thus he was constantly and always engaged in acts of enmity;
having killed his father and then his mother as well. (15)
Thus the one of wicked soul departs due to the influence of former enmity;
now, therefore, I shall explain that by which what is dear may be obtained. (16)
As soon as he is born, he brings joy; in childhood, he delights his parents with fondling and play; and upon reaching maturity, he thereafter continues to bring them happiness.
One should constantly satisfy them both with devotion; one should please them both with affection, with kind words, and with pleasant conversation. (18)
