Upon the death of the guru, he wept again out of affection;
he performed all the funeral rites, including the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and other ceremonies. (19)
Afflicted by great suffering, he indeed provides them with their livelihood;
burdened by the three debts, he constantly causes them to eat out of affection.
Because whatever may be obtainable, he bestows it without doubt; indeed, having become a son through this rite, O one of great wisdom. (21)
I shall declare the indifferent one before you, O beloved;
it always revolves with an indifferent disposition. (22)
O best of the twice-born, he neither gives nor receives, he neither becomes angry nor is he pleased; having abandoned both giving and receiving, he remains indifferent.
Everything has been told before you: such is the destiny of sons;
as is the son, so are the wife, the father, the mother, and likewise the husbands. (24)
Other servants are likewise declared to be cattle, as are horses, elephants, buffaloes, slaves, and all those who are bound by debt. (25)
No debt was incurred by him toward either of us; nor was anything deposited as a pledge by anyone in our previous birth. (26)
Listen indeed to the debt of Unaka that he owes you; it was incurred by him in a previous birth through the offering of a new *āmramastika* fruit. (27)
O Lord of the World, we two have not abandoned what is beneficial;
knowing this, abandon this useless anxiety and attain peace. (28)
Whose sons are they? Whose beloved wife is she? Whose kinsmen and friends are they?
Nothing has been taken away by anyone, nor has anything been given back by you. (29)
O Madhava, how indeed did wealth come to you with such great wonder?
O best of the twice-born, wherever a substance is destined to be obtained, it surely comes to pass. (30)
That which is already present arises effortlessly in the hands of some, while a person must protect their wealth with great effort. (31)
While walking, one indeed continues to walk, yet the wealth remains right there.
Knowing this, attain tranquility and abandon useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a beloved wife? Whose are kinsmen and friends?
Who belongs to whom? There is no such thing as "mine" in this world; tell me all this, O best of the twice-born. (33)
Deluded by great delusion, men of sinful mind think: "This house, these sons, and these noble women belong to me alone. (34)
"Untruth is seen as something beautiful, though it is a bond that destroys one's essence.
Thus was he then enlightened by his beloved wife, the goddess.
Then Somaśarman spoke again to his beloved wife Sumanā, who was eloquent in wisdom:
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth, which destroys all doubt. (36)
Nevertheless, virtuous people who are wise in truth desire this:
that my son may have such wealth as he desires, and likewise, O beloved, that I may have such wealth as I desire. (37)
"By whatever means possible, I shall produce a son.
Sumanā said:
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; a son delivers the family. (38)
O highly fortunate one, by means of a virtuous son, both father and mother are liberated from rebirth;
what is the use of many sons who are devoid of merit, even if they are excellent and learned? (39)
One person alone can deliver those who cause suffering;
this has already been declared by me previously, while others merely follow after their kin. (40)
A son is obtained through merit; a noble family is obtained through merit; a virtuous conception is obtained through merits; therefore, practice merit. (41)
For one who is born, death is certain; likewise, for one who has died, birth occurs again. Birth is attained through merits, and death is attained in the very same way. (42)
"A collection of wealth is enjoyed with ease through meritorious deeds.
Somaśarman said:
"O beloved, tell me how to practice merit, as well as about other births. (43)
"O Bhadrā, what is the nature of great merit? What are the characteristics of merit?
Sumanā said:
"First, I shall describe merit as I have heard it. (44)
Whether it be a man or a woman, just as one constantly conducts oneself, so too does one obtain fame, beloved sons, and wealth through meritorious deeds. (45)
I shall now describe all the characteristics of merit:
through celibacy, truthfulness, and the performance of the five great sacrifices.
O beloved, [one attains this] through charity, religious observances, forbearance, purity, non-violence, according to one's capacity, and by conduct such as non-stealing. ||47||
One should fulfill the Dharma itself by means of these ten factors;
when fulfilled, the Dharma arises just as food is digested by the digestive juices within the stomach.
The righteous-souled one creates Dharma through threefold action; his Dharma, being serene in nature, shall surely lead him to merit alone. (49)
"Whatever the wise man thinks of, he attains even that which is difficult to obtain.
Somaśarman said: "O beautiful lady, what is the form of Dharma, and what are its limbs?"
Out of affection, I spoke this to you, for a desire to hear it has arisen within you.
Sumanā said:
"O best of the twice-born, by whom has the formless nature of Dharma been seen in this world?"
His path was invisible, his nature was untruthful, and he was unseen by gods or dānavas;
he was born in the lineage of Atri as the twice-born son of Anasūyā.
Therefore, those two great-souled ones, Dṛḍha and Dharmadatta Ātreya, were always performing the highest forms of austerity; they were never seen [by others]. 53.
Abiding by righteousness, through austerity and power, they two shall exist with a form more praiseworthy than that of Indra. (54)
For ten thousand years those two remained in the forest;
subsisting on air and taking no food, they became auspicious to behold.
For ten thousand years, for that duration, they performed intense asceticism;
and while they were thus successfully practicing, Dharma was clearly perceived there.
O best of the twice-born, for that long he practiced fire-worship twice a day,
and likewise, he remained without food while practicing it three times a day.
Meanwhile, the ascetic Dattātreya was staying in the midst of the water,
as was Durvāsas, the best of sages, who was emaciated by his austerities.
The bull among sages, whose very self was the Dharma, became enraged at the one who opposed the Dharma;
when that most fortunate and excellent sage was thus provoked to anger, [the earth shook]. (59)
Then Dharma arrived there in his own form;
that wise one was endowed with celibacy and other such ascetic practices.
Truth is in the form of a Brāhmaṇa, and likewise celibacy;
austerity belongs to the best of the twice-born, while self-restraint is the wise one, O foremost of the twice-born. (61)
But Niyama, Mahāprājña, Dāna, and likewise Tathaiva, together with Agnihotri, approached Ātreya in his own form. (62)
Forgiveness, tranquility, as well as shamelessness, non-violence, and lack of discernment—all these arrived there in female forms, O best of the twice-born. (63)
At that time, intellect, wisdom, compassion, faith, intelligence, honor, and tranquility, as well as the five sacrifices and the meritorious Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, were praised. 64.
All these, maintaining their own true nature, have attained perfection;
likewise, the meritorious rites such as the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) and others like the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). ||65||
Endowed with beauty and charm, adorned with all kinds of ornaments,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Adorned with crowns and earrings, and decorated with divine ornaments,
they were radiant, beautiful in form, and enveloped by flames of splendor.
Thus Dharma arrived accompanied by his retinue,
whereupon the irascible Durvāsas remained there like Time itself.
Dharma said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, why have you become angry, you who are endowed with asceticism?
For anger destroys the merit of asceticism; of this there is no doubt. (69)
Therefore, one should avoid anger in that situation, for it causes total ruin.
Be at ease, O best of the twice-born; the fruit of austerity is supreme. (70)
Durvāsas said:
Who are you that have arrived here together with these excellent brahmins?
Seven women, beautiful and well-adorned, are standing there as well. (71)
"O Great-minded one, tell me this in detail.
Dharma said: "He, endowed with all splendor, appeared here in the form of a Brāhmaṇa. (72)
With staff in hand, serene, and likewise bearing a water-pot, here before you stands this very Brahmacharya; behold him as he has arrived.
"O best of the twice-born, look at another who is radiant—this Kapila with tawny eyes, who is truly the supreme among the twice-born. (74)
O virtuous one, behold such a thing, possessing a splendor equal to that of Vaiśvadeva, which you have produced through penance and which is the refuge of all the gods. (75)
Behold this one of great fortune, who has come to your side;
he is endowed with gracious speech and radiance, and is devoted to compassion for all living beings. (76)
Likewise, this Dama himself always nourishes your splendor;
he is matted-haired, harsh, tawny, exceedingly fierce, and a great lord.
O best of the twice-born, he who holds a sword in hand is incapable of destroying sins;
however, one who is endowed with great merit and constant ritual practice is capable of such destruction. ||78||
O best of the twice-born, Niyama arrived at your side, unbound, greatly radiant, and resembling pure crystal. (79)
"O twice-born one, carrying a water-pot in hand and holding a wooden staff, you have arrived here in my presence for the sake of purification. (80)
"O most virtuous and illustrious one, adorned with truth as her ornament, you whose limbs possess the splendor of all ornaments—this servant has arrived to attend upon you. (81)
Extremely steadfast, with serene limbs, fair-complexioned, and with a smiling face;
holding a lotus in her hand, she is this Dhātrī, lotus-eyed and like a beautiful lotus-pond. 82.
O best of the twice-born, she was adorned with divine ornaments, had attained self-control,
was exceedingly peaceful, well-established, and endowed with many auspicious signs.
O Great Sage, your Peace, whose form is primordial wisdom, has arrived—adorned with divine ornaments and possessing the splendor created by celestial jewels. (84)
Constantly intent on performing favors for others, filled with many truths, and always moderate in speech, she has arrived as if she were not even imagined. 85.
She is gracious, endowed with eyes like lotus seeds, adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus, beautiful in form, dark-complexioned, and renowned for her glory. ||86||
It is well that you, O highly fortunate one, have come here;
you are like molten gold in the color of your limbs, red and a most beautiful woman. (87)
The ascetic woman, her hand [raised] through merit and overcome by the state of knowledge, beheld here and there the nectar of supreme tranquility. 88.
Abounding in the splendor of pearl ornaments, pure and possessing a beautiful smile—O illustrious one, behold, behold! Here has arrived Śraddhā. 89.
She is pervaded by great intelligence, filled with vast knowledge, possessed of a form attached to excellent enjoyments, well-established, and beautiful with auspiciousness. ||90||
Endowed with all desired meditative concentrations, she is the mother of the world and renowned;
she is richly adorned with all ornaments, possessing full hips and breasts.
Fair-complexioned, adorned with garlands and garments, this Medhā stands here by your side, O one of great wisdom. (92)
I am truthful, resembling a mirror, adorned with a long pearl necklace,
decorated with all ornaments, very serene, and high-minded.
Enveloped in white cloth, she rests upon a hundred-petaled lotus; with a book held in her lotus-like hand, she shines eternally.
This highly fortunate Prajñā has arrived, possessing great merit;
her complexion is like the juice of lac, and she is ever truly serene. 95.
Adorned with garlands, necklaces, and armlets made of yellow flowers, she is endowed with finger-rings and bracelets, and graced by earrings. ||96||
The Goddess always shines brilliantly in her yellow garment;
she is the peerless one for the sake of benefiting and nourishing the three worlds. 97.

O best of the twice-born, she whose virtuous conduct has always been celebrated by the most excellent brahmins—she, full of compassion, has now arrived at your side, O foremost of the twice-born. (98)
"O best of the twice-born, this aged ascetic woman, whose nature is that of a great sage, is my mother; O you of virtuous vows, I am your dharma. (99)
"Knowing this, come to me and protect me.
Durvāsas said:
"Since Dharma has arrived here in my presence, let that be so. (100)
"Tell me this one cause: what dharma shall I perform for you? Dharma said:
"O best of Brahmins, why are you angry? What unpleasant thing have they done? (101)
"Therefore, tell me the reason for this, O Durvāsas, if you so intend.
Durvāsas said:
"O Goddess, listen to the reason why I became angry. (102)

Having purified his own body through self-restraint, purity, and severe hardships for a duration of one hundred thousand years, he performed ascetic practices consisting of various forms of austerity. (103)
"Since you view it thus, this very compassion proceeds [from me].
Therefore, being angry with you, I shall grant you this very curse this very day. (104)
Having heard this from him, the high-minded Dharma spoke to him. Dharma said: "O wise one, if I am destroyed, the world will meet its destruction. (105)
"O father, O twice-born one, I shall utterly uproot the root of suffering;
afterwards, I shall grant you happiness—if this is true, then let my head split asunder. (106)
This evil has its root in happiness, whereas merit is obtained through suffering; a living being who performs only meritorious deeds may even lose his life. (107)
"I grant great happiness in this way, and there is no doubt regarding the next world.
Durvāsas said:
"By that very means through which one attains happiness, one encounters supreme suffering. (108)
Having abandoned that which is mortal, it is enjoyed by another as well; who indeed understands that happiness? One perceives no certainty at all.
We see nothing better than this: for what you have done is unjust;
by the very body with which an action is performed, its pleasure cannot be enjoyed.
Affliction is produced by one [person], yet it is experienced by another;
who then understands that happiness, or likewise injustice or even the Dharma? (111)
Affliction is produced by one [agent], yet a person experiences happiness through another;
such is the nature of dharma, and all that is joined with the highest good.
By this [person], merit is indeed acquired, yet by this [other person] one enjoys the fruit;
furthermore, merit being performed by one is enjoyed by another. (113)
All that which has been declared as happiness, whatever its characteristics may be,
and whatever is ordained in the treatises on Dharma, is performed everywhere exactly as it is taught and not otherwise.
With whatever body they perform [actions], with that very same body they endure suffering; in the next world they experience it by means of that, and likewise even in this one. (115)
Having understood this, you, whose nature is devoted to the Dharma, should reflect:
"Just as those great evildoers, the thieves, endure terrible and intense suffering with their own bodies, how could it be otherwise for happiness? (116)
Dharma said: "By whichever body sinful people indeed commit a transgression... (117)
Therefore, even while enduring suffering, one should indeed endure the fruit that results from a sin;
for the learned have seen in the treatises on Dharma that punishment alone is the supreme [remedy]. (118)
"You yourself must indeed recognize that [act] as being preceded by righteousness according to these principles.
Durvāsas said: "O King of Dharma, I do not consider this to be right; listen to my words accordingly. (119)
"Enraged, I shall bestow three curses upon you; it cannot be otherwise.
Dharma said: "Since I am angry, O highly wise one, please forgive me. (120)
O best of Brahmins, you certainly cannot endure that the son of a slave-girl be made the moon;
O great sage, he must instead be made a king or even a Cāṇḍāla.
For Durvāsas was always favorably disposed toward the Brahmin who bowed before him; however, having become enraged, he then cursed Dharma. 122.
Durvāsas said: "O son of a slave-woman, you were not otherwise; you were a king because of your righteousness. Go now to the womb of a Caṇḍāla, and practice dharma according to your own will."
Having thus pronounced these three curses, that best of the twice-born departed;
it is said that even through this incidental occurrence, Dharma was beheld in the past.
Somaśarman said:
"O beautiful lady, tell me what kind of dharma arose from that high-souled one by which he was cursed; if you know it, speak of its nature to me. (125)
Sumanā said:
Yudhiṣṭhira, though born in the lineage of the Bharatas, became [the embodiment of] Dharma; Vidura was the son of a maidservant; and I shall tell you yet another thing as well. (126)
When King Hariścandra was tormented by Viśvāmitra,
he, that highly intelligent Dharma, attained the state of a Caṇḍāla.
Thus was the fruit of karma experienced even by that great-souled one through his own dharma;
indeed, the truth has been spoken before you regarding the curse of Durvāsas.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Somaśarman and Sumanas," within the Narrative of Somaśarman in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||12||
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"Tell me in detail the characteristics of celibacy (brahmacarya)."
And what kind of celibacy is it, O beautiful lady, if you know? (1)
He whose delight is always in truth, that virtuous soul attains contentment;
free from fault, he may approach his own wife when her season has arrived. (2)
One never abandons the virtuous conduct and the giving of gifts of one's own family;
this alone, O best of the twice-born, is declared to be the duty of a householder. (3)
I have already declared what is indeed the supreme celibacy for householders; now I shall proclaim that which pertains to ascetics—listen to me as I speak. ||4||
Endowed with self-restraint and truth, always fearing evil, and having abandoned attachment to his wife, he is firmly established in meditation and knowledge. ||5||
The practice of celibacy for ascetics has been declared before you;
now I shall speak of austerity itself—listen to me as I describe it.
Free from desire and anger, he should proceed according to right conduct; established for the benefit of living beings, he remains devoted to diligent effort.
Thus has austerity been fully described; I speak the truth indeed:
it consists in non-covetousness toward the property of others, and likewise toward the wives of others. (8)
Having seen this, the intellect of a statesman becomes true, as it is proclaimed;
now I shall speak only of giving, by which human beings live. (9)
He who would accept his own happiness, whether in this world or the next, should indeed give even a great gift of food; for it is the certain cause of happiness.
Likewise, one should undoubtedly give even a mere morsel to one afflicted by hunger;
when given, there is great merit, and he always partakes of nectar.
Every day, one should offer according to the extent of one's means:
grass for a bed, water for a drink, a place of speech, and the cool shade of one's house. (12)
Ground, water, as well as food, most excellent and pleasant speech, a seat, and conversation free from deceit; ||13||
He who performs [this] solely for the sake of his own livelihood, or he who gives such a gift after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors—[these are not true givers]. (14)
He who spends this day in acts of giving, study, and ritual performance rejoices right here in this way, and likewise in the next world. (15)
Having become human, one shall become a god; there is no doubt in this matter.
And I shall declare the rule, the supreme means for accomplishing dharma. (16)
He who delighted in the worship of the gods and brahmins, who was constantly disciplined by his observances, and who was firm in his vows regarding acts of charity and religious observances; (17)
This rule regarding beneficial and meritorious acts has been proclaimed;
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall now describe the nature of forbearance. (18)
Upon hearing the harsh abuse of another, one should not become angry;
even when struck, one should not strike back. (19)
One who is patient and whose soul is established in righteousness attains freedom from passion;
he enjoys supreme happiness both in this world and in the hereafter. (20)
Thus has impurity been described; now I shall speak of that very purity which is both internal and external, consisting of complete purification and freedom from passion. 21.
One conducts oneself through the very practices of bathing and sipping water; this is declared to be purity (śauca). Now, I shall speak of non-violence (ahiṃsā). ||22||
Even a blade of grass should not be cut by one who understands it without a purpose;
one should be intent on non-violence toward others just as one is toward oneself. (23)
I shall inquire only after peace, for through peace one attains happiness;
peace alone must be cultivated, and one must never abandon the afflictions.
Having thus abandoned enmity toward living beings, one should act in this manner;
in this way, peace has been fully described. Now, I shall speak of non-stealing.
One must never take the property of others, nor likewise the wives of others;
one should cultivate this very mindset through thoughts, words, and physical actions. (26)
O best of the twice-born, I shall first explain self-restraint (dama) to you; for by the restraint of the senses, even the transformations of a troubled mind are overcome. (27)
Then, like a conscious person, he should destroy their restlessness;
furthermore, I shall explain the kind of service that is prescribed in the treatises on Dharma. (28)
I shall proclaim that very [path] as it was taught by the former teachers:
one should accomplish the service of the guru through speech, body, and mind. (29)
Where grace arises, that is declared to be service;
O best of the twice-born, that which has been fully described before you is Dharma with its constituent parts.
O Lord, I shall speak of something else that you wish to hear:
how a man always conducts himself even under such circumstances as these. (31)
The manifestation of that which has been accumulated arises once again;
through dharma one goes to heaven—this I tell you as the truth, the absolute truth. (32)
Knowing this, O one of great wisdom, proceed toward the Dharma alone;
for everything that is unattainable on the surface of the earth shall indeed be obtained through it. (33)
"Therefore, out of faith in the Dharma, you must indeed follow my word.
Having heard these words of his wife, the highly intelligent Somaśarman—
Again he spoke to his wife Sumanā, who spoke in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dṛḍhasumana," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||13||
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"Such is this most excellent exposition of dharma, which is of great merit."
How do you know this, Bhadra? And from whom was it heard by you? ||1||
Sumanā said:
O high-minded grandfather, born in the lineage of the Bhṛgus, there was one renowned by the name Cyavana, who was an expert in all branches of knowledge. (2)
O you of excellent vows, she is my beloved daughter, dearer to me than even my own life; wherever she goes—to sacred fords or groves—[I follow].
I always go alone with him to the assemblies of pure sages, as well as to the temples of the gods, where we constantly sport together.
Vedaśarman, of great intelligence and born of the Kauśika lineage, a friend of my father, arrived here while wandering about by chance. (5)
Overwhelmed by great suffering and reflecting again and again, he said to that high-souled one who had arrived: "O my grandfather! (6)
"O observer of excellent vows, I know that you are tormented by suffering;
tell me the reason why you have become so miserable. (7)
Having then heard these words of the high-souled Acyavana, my son of excellent vows spoke to that great-souled father: 8.
The highly wise Vedaśarman said: "The cause of all my suffering is my wife, who is most virtuous and devoted to her husband. (9)
"O son, this unbearable sorrow has arisen for me; no other cause exists. This reason has been declared to you because you asked me."
In the meantime, a certain Siddha arrived;
likewise, my father Vedaśarman rose up and came to meet him. ||11||
Furthermore, he was propitiated by those two with offerings accompanied by devotion, including food to be eaten and words of sweet syllables. (12)
When both of them had asked about what was within [his mind] and what he had previously mentioned,
that righteous-souled one told everything to my father along with his companion.
I have indeed told you all the causes of dharma;
through dharma one obtains a son, wealth, grain, and likewise women. (14)
Then, by that Vedaśarman, dharma was fully accomplished;
from that dharma, great happiness was well-born for him along with his son.
Through this unattached discourse, my conviction has become exceedingly firm;
thus, whatever was spoken by me according to your desire is indeed supremely auspicious.
Therefore, having heard from the great Siddha that which destroys all doubt, take refuge in the dharma of the Brahmins and follow it at all times. (17)
Somaśarman said: "O Dharma, tell me what kind of death and birth there are; tell me all that, for I desire to know the characteristics of both. (18)
Sumanā said:
"I shall describe the death of him by whom truth, purity, forgiveness, tranquility, pilgrimage to sacred sites, merit, and so forth, as well as dharma itself, have been protected. (19)
For him, no disease shall arise, nor shall there be any affliction in the body;
indeed, there shall be neither fatigue, nor exhaustion, nor perspiration, nor dizziness.
Having assumed divine forms, the Gandharvas and likewise the Brahmins were engaged in the recitation of the Vedas and were experts in the knowledge of song. ||21||
They approach his side and offer incomparable praise;
he is indeed established in his seat, composed, and devoted to the worship of the deity. 22.
The wise man, devoted to dharma, obtains a sacred bathing place for the purpose of ritual ablution at the fire-sanctuary, the cow-pen, and the temples of the deities. (23)
In a grove, by a pond, or where there is an Aśvattha or a Vaṭa tree, as well as having resorted to a Brahma-tree (Ficus religiosa) or likewise a Śrī-tree (Ficus glomerata). ||24||
When a man, having taken refuge at a stable for horses, stands situated at a place where elephants are kept, or when he stands taking refuge under an Aśoka tree or a mango tree; ||25||

Whether he has gone to the house of a Brāhmaṇa for a funeral feast, or has entered the royal palace, or has taken refuge on the battlefield—he should first perform that rite by which he may become immortal. ||26||
The sacred sites of death are meritorious and solely for the sake of Dharma;
likewise, having reached Gograha, Susaṃprāpta, Āmarakaṇṭaka, and Ṭaka. ||27||
Constantly performing pure deeds and being affectionately devoted to the Dharma according to its true nature, he attains such a state when he encounters death. (28)
That best of men beholds his mother with merit, as well as his father, his brother endowed with excellence, and other kinsmen and friends. (29)
While being praised again and again by the twice-born and those of merit with the syllable "Baṃ," he would no longer see his mother, father, or other such sinful relatives. (30)
The Gandharvas sing songs, and the panegyrists praise him with hymns;
likewise, the Brahmins honor him with the recitation of mantras out of affection for their mother.
The father and the circle of kinsmen likewise [protect] the righteous and high-minded one;
thus have the messengers been described, O Lord, as those who abide in merit.
He sees the messengers visibly before him, clouded by laughter and affection; yet he is neither deluded by a dream nor affected by the moisture of infatuation. (33)
The King of Dharma, possessed of great wisdom, summoned him, saying:
"Come, come, O highly fortunate one, to where Dharma abides! (34)
For him, there arises no delusion, no confusion, no exhaustion, and no loss of mindfulness;
of this there is no doubt. With a serene self, he abides. (35)
Endowed with both spiritual knowledge (jñāna) and worldly discernment (vijñāna), remembering the god Janārdana, he goes along with them, satisfied and joyful in mind. ||36||
There, the oneness arises for him who abandons his own physical body;
resorting to the tenth door, his self departs. (37)
A charming palanquin comes for him as his vehicle;
likewise, a celestial chariot or an excellent horse, bull, or elephant arrives. (38)
With a parasol being held over him and being fanned with chowries and fans,
that meritorious soul was thus attended by merits themselves from all sides.
The righteous-souled one was being sung of and praised by the learned,
by divine bards and celestial beings, and by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Being praised by the virtuous and endowed with all happiness, he there obtains the fruit according to the power of his gift. ||41||
He proceeds with ease into the midst of the garden groves, surrounded by celestial nymphs and endowed with divine auspiciousness. (42)
Being praised by the gods, he beheld Dharmarāja;
and the gods, endowed with righteousness, went directly toward his face.
"Come, come, O highly fortunate one! Enjoy pleasures that are agreeable to the mind.
Thus he perceives dharma as having a gentle form, O great-minded one. 44.
By the power of his own merit, he enjoys heaven itself;
when his enjoyment is exhausted, that righteous-souled one indeed undergoes rebirth.
Through faith in their own respective duties, the merit of a highly virtuous Brāhmaṇa and likewise that of a Kṣatriya truly extends to their entire family. (46)
O high-minded one, in that very place, a wealthy and highly meritorious Vaiśya rejoices according to his merit and performs further meritorious deeds. (47)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dṛṣṭasumana," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||14||
Fifteenth Chapter.
Somaśarman said: "O blessed one, what kind of characteristics are possessed by the death of sinners?"
Therefore, O beautiful woman, tell me that in detail, if you know it.
Sumanā said:
"Listen, for I shall relate what I have heard from that perfected being regarding the manner of death and the specific signs of sinners."
I shall now describe the abode and the activities of those who have committed great sins: a ground filled with excrement, urine, and impurities, and pervaded by evil.
Having encountered the virtuous, that evil-souled one gives up his life with great suffering;
having reached the land of the Cāṇḍālas, he meets his death in a state of extreme misery. ||4||
Having resorted to ground frequented by donkeys, having taken refuge in a courtesan’s house,
and having gone to the home of a keeper of the world-destroying fire, he approaches his own death.
Filled with bones, skin, and nails, and inhabited by sinful defilements—
having reached that [body], the wicked-minded one certainly goes to death.
Having encountered another woman of sinful conduct, he goes to his death.
Now, I shall describe the behavior of messengers who desire his welfare. (7)
Terrible, fierce, and horrific Bhairavas with extremely black complexions and large bellies; those with tawny eyes, yellow-blue complexions, and those who are exceedingly white with large bellies.
[He saw] those who were exceedingly tall and terrifying, resembling skeletons with dried-up flesh;
those with fierce fangs and gaping mouths, laughing, and having serpents for hands.
O high-minded one, seeing the virtuous, he trembles and is repeatedly distressed by terrible, loud cries like the howling of jackals. (10)
Then all the messengers indeed whispered into his ear,
having bound him by the neck with nooses, and likewise bound him around the waist and the belly.
That which is unassailable and cannot be cast down, which speaks repeatedly without cause—that very movement of one who is dying, I declare to be such. (12)
The seizing of another's property, the violation of another's wife, and all the wealth of another that has been taken by sinners; (13)
Furthermore, one should never accept what has not been given due to greed, attachment to taste, or delusion; likewise, the acceptance of gifts from others is a great sin.
What can all those [relatives] do for him as he dies, and for whatever evils were previously committed by him? (15)
They come to the root of that great evil; it is not otherwise.
Producing suffering, they bring about this terrible fruit of the tree of karma. 16.
Afflicted by agonizing pains, one groans with a harsh and rattling sound;
one weeps excessively, crying out for one's mother and father again and again. (17)
There he remembers his brother, his wife, and his sons again and again;
yet, deluded by great sin, he falls into forgetfulness once more. (18)
His vital breaths depart, overwhelmed by great agony;
he falls down, and thus he falls again and again, fainting repeatedly. ||19||
Thus, joined with such torment, the deluded one experiences suffering;
his vital breaths are shaken by great agony and extreme distress. (20)
Resorting to the path of exhalation (apāna), hear how they proceed;
thus does the living being, greatly deluded and possessed by greed and infatuation. ||21||
But when he is led away by the messengers of Yama, I shall describe his suffering.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Intention to Die a Sinful Death," within the Legend of Indrasumanas, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||15||
The sixteenth chapter.
Sumanā said:
"On a path strewn with heaps of embers, one who is being dragged is led away."
Being burned, that evil-souled one struggles again and again. ||1||
There, scorched by the twelve suns and heated by the rays of the sun, he is led along that path by means of an intensely fierce heat.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, that fool is led along that path through mountains and difficult terrains devoid of shade. ||3||
Being struck by the messengers with maces, swords, and axes, and being beaten with whips while being tormented by those messengers. (4)
Then, on the path of cold, he is again assailed by the wind;
becoming miserable because of that cold, he proceeds—of this there is no doubt. (5)
Dragged by messengers, he is led through various difficult terrains;
thus is the evil-souled sinner who reviles gods and Brahmins. (6)
One who practices every kind of evil deed is led away by the servants of Yama;
that wicked-souled one beholds Yama, who resembles a mass of black clouds.
It was fierce, cruel, and terrifying, surrounded by fearsome messengers,
filled with all manner of diseases, and attended by Citragupta.
O best of the twice-born, the god Dharmarāja was mounted upon a buffalo;
his mouth was exceedingly fierce with terrifying fangs, resembling the very face of Time (Kāla).
Wearing yellow garments, with a mace in hand, smeared with red unguents,
adorned with red garlands, holding a mace in his hand, he was terrifying.
The evil-minded one sees Yama in such a form, with a massive body;
having seen him arrived, he is excluded from all righteous laws. (11)
Yama beholds that wicked, most sinful, and cruel person and shall punish him with great sufferings, torments, and wooden mallets.
For as many thousands of yugas as that [number], he is cooked for that length of time;
furthermore, he is cooked again and again in various kinds of hells. ||13||
The evildoer goes to the hellish womb among millions of worms;
he is cooked eternally in filth, crying out "Alas! Alas!", deprived of his senses.
Thus that evil-souled one certainly goes to his death; in this way, the wicked-minded person experiences the consequence of his association with sin. 15.
I shall further describe the rebirths and the wombs into which one goes; having entered a hundred births as a dog, he indeed continues to experience the consequences of his sin.
The evil-minded one becomes a tiger, and then again enters the womb of a female donkey;
likewise, he enters the womb of a cat, a pig, and even a serpent. (17)
Furthermore, they go again and again into all the various kinds of animal births, among sinful birds, and into other great [animal] existences. (18)
The evildoer goes to the womb of a Cāṇḍāla, a Bhilla, or a Caṇḍāla;
thus has all this regarding the birth of sinners been told to you. 19.
Listen now to the truth regarding death and their most dreadful behavior;
the conduct of both the sinful and the meritorious has been described by me before you. (20)
O giver of honor, if you ask, I shall speak of something else entirely.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Desire for Sin and Merit," in the *Aindra-sumanopākhyāna* of the *Śrī-Padmapurāṇa*, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. ||16||
The seventh chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"O Goddess, you have fully explained the supreme foundation of dharma."
How may I obtain a son who is endowed with all-knowing wisdom and every virtue? (1)
"Speak to me, O highly fortunate one, if you know, O lady of excellent vows;
[tell me of] the duty of giving and so forth, O auspicious one, for the sake of the next world and this one—of this there is no doubt. (2)
Sumanā said:
"Go to Vasiṣṭha, the knower of dharma; entreat that great sage.
From him you shall surely obtain a son who knows dharma and is devoted to dharma. (3)
Sūta said:
When these words had been spoken by her, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, replied:
"O auspicious lady, I shall do exactly as you have said; of this there is no doubt."
Having spoken thus, Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, quickly approached Vasiṣṭha— the all-knowing, divine one, the foremost among those who practice austerity.
He saw that best of the twice-born, situated in a holy hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
enveloped in a blaze of splendor like a second sun.
Having bowed with devotion again and again like a staff to that great-souled lord of Brahmins, the best of the twice-born, who was shining with majesty and devoted to the Vedas.
To him spoke the son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor and free from all taint: "Sit down upon this auspicious seat with ease, O you of great intelligence. (8)
Having spoken thus, the king again addressed the ascetic, the possessor of penance:
"O dear one, [be present] always in my house, among my sons, and likewise among my wives and servants."
O highly fortunate one, may there be well-being for you amidst these fires of virtuous deeds;
may you be free from ailment in your limbs, and may you always protect the Dharma. (10)
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom laughed again at Suśarman and said:
"O best of the twice-born, what dear service may I perform for you that is most pleasing? (11)
When that illustrious Vasiṣṭha, the bull among sages, had thus spoken, Agastya, the son of Kumbha, ceased speaking. (12)
He spoke thus to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity:
"O Blessed One, please listen to my words with a well-pleased mind. (13)
If this is a very pleasing task for you, O bull among sages, then dispel the doubt regarding the meaning of my question, O best of the twice-born. (14)
"By what sin does poverty arise, and why is there no happiness from a son? O father, tell me this doubt of mine: from what specific sin does it come? (15)
O twice-born one, deluded by great ignorance and awakened by my beloved, I have been sent by her to your side, O father, being deeply distressed. (16)
Tell me all of that, which destroys every doubt;
may you become the giver of liberation for me from this bond of worldly existence. (17)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Sons, enemies, friends, brothers, and others such as kinsmen and wives—these five divisions arise from the differentiation of a person. (18)
O best of the twice-born, all those who are bound by debt have already been described by Taittisevana before you; they are all like bad sons.
I shall now proclaim before you the meritorious characteristics of a son:
he whose soul is devoted to merit and who is always delighted in truth and righteousness. (20)
Endowed with purity and discernment, he was an ascetic and the best among those skilled in speech;
steadfast, he was well-composed in all his actions and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
He was a knower of all the scriptures, a worshiper of gods and brahmins, a performer of all sacrifices, a donor, one who practiced great renunciation, and a speaker of pleasant words. ||22||

He was constantly devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, ever peaceful, self-controlled, and always a friend to all; he was eternally dedicated to his father and mother, and affectionate toward all his kinsmen.
An expert in delivering [the fetus] from the womb, a nourisher of the family, and endowed with such qualities as these, he brings happiness to his sons along with his own offspring. (24)
Others are joined with relationships that bring about grief and torment;
what is to be done with such a thing, which is devoid of fruit? (25)
They all come and go after inflicting most terrible suffering;
O best of the twice-born, they all move about in the form of sons. 26.
Whatever merit was performed by you in a previous birth and preserved, all of that I shall indeed declare; listen once more to this wonder. (27)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O highly wise one, you were a Śūdra in your previous birth; otherwise, it would not be so.
You were a farmer, devoid of knowledge, and possessed by great greed. (28)
You always harbor hatred toward your single wife, yet you have many sons;
indeed, you do not understand dharma, nor have you ever heard the truth. (29)
O high-minded one, you have not given any gift, nor have you ever promised to study the scriptures, nor have you even undertaken a pilgrimage to sacred fords. (30)
O best of the twice-born, you have thus repeatedly performed the tending of livestock and the care of all the cattle over a long period of time.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the repeated tending of buffaloes and horses was likewise a deed previously performed by you alone. (32)
And when was that vast wealth, accumulated through greed, ever spent by you for the sake of great merit? (33)
Seeing that the recipient is indeed weak, one does not give a gift;
yet, out of compassion, even if one gives nothing, it shall become wealth for oneself. (34)
All the cattle, such as cows and buffaloes, have been gathered by you;
and having sold them, a vast amount of wealth has been accumulated by you from the Brahmins. (35)
Having sold buttermilk, ghee, milk, and then curd, he,
deluded by the illusory power of Viṣṇu, brooded over the famine.
O best of Brahmins, you have indeed prepared very costly food here;
yet, being merciless, you have never given any gift at all. (37)
Never was the worship of the gods performed by you through the agency of Brahmins; nor was any wealth offered to the Brahmins upon the arrival of auspicious festival days. (38)
"Having reached this time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha), you have not performed them with faith; today, that virtuous wife of yours has passed away, and this very day has arrived. (39)
O high-minded one, this is the time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) of your father-in-law and likewise of your mother-in-law;
having heard those words of hers, you have abandoned your home and fled.
The path of Dharma has never been seen by you, nor has it ever been heard by you;
greed is your mother, father, and brother; greed is your kinsmen and your wife. (41)
Having always abandoned unrighteousness, he protected greed alone;
therefore, having become miserable, he was born afflicted by extreme poverty. ||42||
Day by day, great thirst increases within his heart;
whenever he acquires wealth in the house, it only grows further. (43)
Burning with that very thirst which takes the form of fire,
you were indeed sleeping soundly at night, yet you remained certain in your contemplation.
Having reached this day, you have indeed always been pervaded by great delusions;
when will it be a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, or even a hundred million? 45.
When will there be a kharva and a nikharva in my house?
Likewise, a thousand, a hundred thousand, ten million, and even an arbuda? (46)
From a *kharva* it becomes a *nikharva*, yet craving does not depart;
having abandoned your body, it always continues to increase.
Neither was anything given as a gift, nor offered in sacrifice, nor eaten by Brahmins by you at any time;
nor was anything dug out from within the earth and buried—your sons do not know [of such deeds]. 48.
O wise one, you always seek out other means for the acquisition of wealth; indeed, you consult all the people of the world. 49.
Deluded by craving, he wanders all alone, questioning people about digging for treasure and, beyond that, the doctrine of alchemy.
Constantly contemplate touch, which bestows the accomplishments (siddhis) of the kalpas;
you inquire well about the entry into the subterranean openings and the destruction of darkness. 51.
Burning with the fire of craving, you find no happiness at all;
inflamed by the fire of craving, you cry out "Alas! and lose your senses.
Thus, O best of Brahmins, you have become deluded and fallen under the power of the dark dust;
for when your wife, sons, and that wealth were being questioned by them, you remained silent.
Having abandoned his life-breaths, he has gone to Yama;
thus have I related to you his entire previous history.
By this karma, you have become a Brahmin who is destitute and poor;
yet he whose virtuous son is always indeed devoted to him [shall attain liberation].
Those endowed with good character and knowledge, who are always devoted to truth and righteousness, are born in the home of him with whom Viṣṇu is pleased. (56)
He whose Viṣṇu is pleased enjoys wealth, grain, a wife, sons, grandsons, food, and water in this world of mortals. (57)
Without the grace of Viṣṇu, one shall not obtain a wife, sons, a good birth, or a noble lineage, O Brāhmaṇa;
that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. (58)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Indrasumanas," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The eighteenth chapter.
Somaśarman said:
"O sage, you have related the sin committed by me in a previous birth."
But by my very self, O best of Brahmins, it has been completely excluded from the status of a Śūdra.
O best of the twice-born, how was the state of being a brahmin attained by Himaya?
O scholar of wisdom and realized knowledge, tell me the cause of all that.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O twice-born one, I shall fully relate that action based on dharma which was performed by you in the past; listen, if you so desire. (3)
There was a certain Brahmin, sinless, of virtuous conduct, and highly learned;
he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous in soul, and eternally devoted to Viṣṇu. ||4||
Under the pretext of visiting sacred fords, that one of great intelligence wanders alone over the earth; while traveling, he has arrived at your house. (5)
O best of the twice-born, a single dwelling place was requested for the sake of our livelihood;
it was granted by your wife alone, along with you and your sons. (6)
"O Brahmin, stay here for as long as you wish; may you dwell happily in my home.
Thus he spoke again and again to that meritorious Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa.
"O observer of noble vows, please remain here at ease; this house is yours. Today I am blessed, and today I have reached a sacred place of pilgrimage. (8)
Today, by the sight of your two feet, the fruit of visiting all sacred fords has been attained;
[I have reached] the most excellent and meritorious abode of cows, offered as a place of residence. (9)
Having massaged his limbs and rubbed his feet,
he washed them again with water and bathed with the water used for washing the feet.
You likewise gave fresh ghee, curd, milk, food, and buttermilk to that very same high-souled brāhmaṇa. (11)
Thus was that illustrious brāhmaṇa, a devotee of Viṣṇu and an expert in knowledge, fully gratified by you together with your wife and sons. (12)
Then, when the morning had arrived on that auspicious and fortune-bestowing day,
it was the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, which destroys all sins.
On that day, the destroyer of all sins arrives,
on which the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa enters into yogic sleep.
Having attained that [state], O twice-born one, those wise in intellect abandoned all worldly activities and became devoted to the meditation upon Viṣṇu. (15)
They celebrated a supreme festival with songs and auspicious musical instruments;
all the Brahmins praised him with Vedic hymns and most auspicious eulogies.
Having thus experienced such a great festival, that best of virtuous brāhmaṇas remained there on that day, having undertaken a fast.
The greatness of Ekādaśī was indeed recited by the Brāhmaṇa;
it was heard along with his wife, daughters, and sons as the unsurpassed dharma. ||18||
Having heard this highly meritorious [account], urged by his wife and son, he performed this vow through the association with that brahmin. 19.
Having heard those great words which bestow all merit, his mind became firmly resolved: "I shall perform this vow. (20)
Having come together with your wife and sons, you performed your bath in the river;
with a joyful mind, O Brahmin, you worshipped Madhusūdana.
Having performed a night vigil with all kinds of offerings, meritorious acts, such as perfumes and incense, as well as with dance, song, and the like. ||22||
In connection with the brahmin, he bathed again in the river;
the Lord of the Gods was worshipped with auspicious offerings such as flowers and incense. (23)
Having prostrated with devotion before Govinda and bathed him again and again,
such an offering was given to that high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
Having bowed with devotion to that brahmin, he gave him a generous sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and performed the breaking of his fast together with the sons of the brahmins, his wife, and the others.
"He was sent by you yourself with sincere devotion;
thus has this vow been performed by you, O best of the twice-born. (26)
"Through association with a brāhmaṇa and by the grace of Viṣṇu himself, you have attained the status of a brāhmaṇa, endowed as you are with truth and righteousness. (27)
By virtue of that vow, you have attained a great lineage of Brahmins, O highly wise one, which is filled with truth and righteousness. (28)
Therefore, food that has been well-prepared and given with faith and a spirit of truth to such a great-souled Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa [yields great fruit].
Through the power of that gift, desirable food presents itself;
yet his mind is utterly deluded by great ignorance and pervaded by craving. (30)
O Brahmin, in your previous birth, wealth was indeed accumulated for your own sake;
it was not given by you to the brahmins, nor to others who were in need. (31)
Because you died out of a longing for a son and a wife,
poverty has taken hold of you through the power of that very sin.
Having abandoned the longing for a son and cast off affection nearby, you have become sonless;
this is the fruit of that sin.
A virtuous son, a noble family, Brahmins, wealth, grain, excellent women, a good birth and death, as well as excellent enjoyments and happiness itself—[all these arise from that]. (34)
Sovereignty, heaven, liberation, and whatever else is difficult to attain—all these come through the grace of that god, the high-souled Viṣṇu. (35)
Therefore, by propitiating Govinda, the stainless Nārāyaṇa,
you shall attain the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu.
Excellent sons, wealth, grain, fine enjoyments, and even happiness—all that was performed by you in previous lives and has now been fully experienced. (37)
Therefore, O Brahmin, I have related this which is firmly established before you;
having understood this, O noble one, become devoted to Nārāyaṇa as your supreme goal. 38.

Indeed, that noble-souled one, the best of brahmins, having been enlightened by the son of Brahmā, was filled with joy; and that great-souled man, bowing there with devotion to Vasiṣṭha, [remained]. (39)

Having reached his own home with his wife Sumanā, he was filled with great joy; and having approached that brahmin, he related everything—the entire account of my former conduct—saying, "It was all by the grace of that very brahmin."
O noble lady, my delusion has been utterly destroyed this very day by Vasiṣṭha’s instruction;
for I shall now worship Madhusūdana, so that I may attain liberation, that supreme state. (41)

Having heard those most excellent, great, and highly auspicious words which indeed bestow blessings, she was filled with joy and said to him: "You are meritorious; you have been awakened by a brahmin. (42)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Episode of Dṛḍhasumana," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The nineteenth chapter.
Sūta said:
O best of beings, the highly wise Somaśarman was together with Sumanā.
At the confluence of the Kapilā, on the very meritorious banks of the Revā, which bestows great merit.
Having bathed there and offered libations to the gods and ancestors, the wise one,
with a tranquil soul, performed austerities while chanting the auspicious name of Nārāyaṇa.
Possessing great resolve and observing excellent vows, he was absorbed in meditation upon that very God of gods, Vāsudeva, by means of the twelve-syllable mantra. (3)
Whether on a seat, in a bed, in a vehicle, or in a dream, one should always behold Keśava, remaining perfectly steady and free from desire and anger. ||4||
And that virtuous, highly fortunate woman, devoted to her husband,
served him alone— who was endowed with ascetic power— with a cheerful mind.
Even as that high-souled one was meditating, fear was manifested by obstacles;
there, black snakes with virulent poison approached him.
As Somaśarman was thus being tormented on his side,
lions, tigers, elephants, and other beasts granted him freedom from fear.
Vetālas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, and bhairavas display these terrifying and dreadful forms that destroy life. ||8||
Various kinds of great and terrifying lions, having gathered there, with mouths formidable with fangs, roared most dreadfully. 9.
Through meditation on Viṣṇu, the great-minded one, whose soul was possessed of righteousness, remained unmoved;
yet that bull among sages was shaken by well-established, great obstacles.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, Somaśarman did not waver from his meditation,
though he was greatly afflicted by cold winds and heavy rain.
Terrified by the terrifying roar of a great lion that had approached his hand,
the twice-born man, trembling with fear upon seeing it, remembered Nṛhari.
Resembling a sapphire, clad in yellow garments, and possessed of great majesty;
the god bearing the conch and the discus, and holding a mace and a lotus.
Janārdana was shining with a great pearl necklace that imitated the color of the moon,
and also with the Kaustubha gem.
His chest shines with the divine Śrīvatsa mark;
his limbs are adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, and his eyes resemble a hundred-petaled lotus. (15)
With a face of gentle smiles, serene, and adorned with jeweled garlands, Hṛṣīkeśa was resplendent; he certainly performed meditation upon Him. (16)
You alone are the refuge, O Kṛṣṇa, you who are affectionate toward those who have come for shelter;
salutations be to the God of gods—what fear will it cause me? (17)
In the belly of that Great Soul reside the three worlds and the seven others;
I have entered his refuge—where, indeed, could fear come to me? 18.
I have gone for refuge to him who destroys all fears, from which such powerful [forces] as Kṛtyā and the like arise. (19)
I have gone for refuge to Him who is the protector of the devotees of Viṣṇu and who causes great fear to all sinners and demons. (20)
I have gone for refuge to that Yoga-path of all the great-souled Dānava children who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa. ||21||
Fearing for my safety and desiring the destruction of fear and the destruction of sin, I, possessing knowledge, have gone alone for refuge to him in the form of Indra. (22)
I have gone for refuge to Him who possesses the nature of medicine solely for the destruction of diseases, who is free from ailment and free from sorrow. (23)
The sinless one, being immovable, can shake the worlds and even knowledge itself; having come to him for refuge, what fear will he do to me? (24)
I have gone for refuge to Him who is the protector of all virtuous ones, who is indeed free from ailment, who protects the universe, and who is the soul of the universe. (25)
I have come for refuge to Him who displays fear before me in the form of a lion-king; I bow down to that Narasiṃha. 26.
Intoxicated with rut, a massive-bodied forest elephant approached the Lord, who moves with the grace of an elephant and is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge. 27.
I have come for refuge to the elephant-faced one, endowed with wisdom, holding a noose and a goad, whose face is dark and whose trunk is like that of an elephant. ||28||
I have gone for refuge to the Boar, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa;
I have sought shelter in that Vāmana, who is compassionate toward those who come to him for protection. 29.
Dwarfs, hunchbacks, ghosts, kūṣmāṇḍas, and others—all assuming the forms of Death—show me their terrifying faces. (30)
I have drunk that nectar; what fear will it cause me?
Hari is devoted to Brahman, the giver of Brahman, Brahman itself, and consists of the knowledge of Brahman.
I have taken refuge in him; what fear will he cause me?
For he who is fearless toward the world is the destroyer of fear and the giver of fearlessness. (32)
"I have fallen into a state of fear; what will this fear do to me?
He is the savior of all worlds and the destroyer of all sinners. (33)
I have sought refuge in that Janārdana, who is the embodiment of Dharma, the enemy of the gods, who bears a wondrous golden body. (34)
He is my refuge; this Sadāgati is my constant resort.
Jhaṃ! Jhāvāta, the great and fierce one, consumes my body intensely. 35.
I have taken refuge in you; this Sugata is my constant resort, for the extreme cold, the excessive rain, and the heat are all tormenting me. (36)
I have gone for refuge to that god who possesses their form; these protectors of mine, who grant fearlessness, have arrived in the form of Time.
I have taken refuge in these, who are eternally of the nature of Hari. 38.

I take refuge in Him whom they call Nārāyaṇa, the primordial perfected one, the Lord of the perfected, the supreme God of all gods, who is exclusively composed of pure knowledge and is like a lamp. ||39||
Thus meditating and constantly praising Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, Hari was brought by him through devotion into his own heart. (40)
Having witnessed the exertion and prowess of that Somaśarman,
Hṛṣīkeśa appeared and spoke to him with great joy.
O Somaśarman, O highly wise one, listen along with your wife:
"I am Vāsudeva; O best of Brahmins, O observer of excellent vows, ask for a boon. (42)
Having been addressed thus by him, O best of Brahmins, he opened both his eyes and beheld the Lord Viṣṇu, dark as a rain cloud and of great splendor.
His limbs were adorned with the beauty of all ornaments, he was equipped with all weapons,
endowed with divine marks, and possessed eyes like lotuses.
Clad in yellow garments, the resplendent Lord of the Gods was mounted upon Vainateya,
bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
The one of great renown [worships] the creator of nectar for Brahmā and the others, the eternal transcendent of this world, the teacher of the universe who is beyond form. (46)
Overcome with great joy, he prostrated himself like a staff before Him who was endowed with splendor, shining with a radiance equal to ten million suns. 47.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he addressed Jayamādhava, the bestower of honor, along with that Sumana, saying, "Victory! Victory! (48)
Victory to You, O Lord of Yogins, Sovereign of Yogins, who recline upon the body of the serpent Śeṣa;
victory to You, whose limbs are the sacrifice, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Eternal, and the All-pervading! 49.
Victory to you, O Lord of All, whose nature is sacrifice; salutations to you!
Victory to you, the best among the possessors of knowledge; victory to you, the leader of knowledge! 50.

Victory to you, O Giver of All, O Omniscient One! Victory to you, the Creator of all beings! Victory to you, the Lord of the nature of the individual soul; O Great Life, let there be salutation unto you! 51.
Victory to You, O Hari, who bestows victory, wisdom, and the limbs of wisdom;
who grants victory and the vital breath; who destroys sin; the Lord of merit; and the Master of virtue! 52.
Victory to the Lord whose nature is knowledge, who is accessible through wisdom; obeisance to Him!
Victory to the one with eyes like lotus petals, who has a lotus in His navel; obeisance to Him! (53)
Victory to Govinda, the cowherd; victory to the stainless bearer of the conch!
Victory to the bearer of the discus, whose form is both unmanifest and manifest; salutations to You. (54)

Victory to you, whose limbs possess the splendor of victorious prowess, O Leader of Victorious Valor! Victory to you, who are filled with love for the lady Jayalakṣmī, the embodiment of playful grace! 55.
Victory to you, whose limbs possess the splendor of victorious valor! Victory to you, who bestows the pride of heroic exertion!
Victory to you, the time of exertion; salutations again and again to exertion itself! ||56||
Victory to You, the one endowed with the power of exertion, the upholder of the threefold exertion;
salutations to that Dharma who is engaged in the exertion of battle. ||57||
Homage to that Hiraṇyaretas; homage to you, O Splendor! Homage to the one whose very nature is supreme brilliance and who consists of all splendor. ||58||
Salutations be to the Supreme Self, who destroys the splendor of the Daityas, who removes the radiance of the wicked, and who acts for the welfare of cows and Brahmins. (59)
Salutations to you, the consumer of oblations; salutations to you, the bearer of the sacrificial offerings.
Salutations indeed to you, the bearer of the ancestral offerings; salutations to you, whose very form is the *svadhā* invocation.
Salutations again and again to the sacrifice whose form is *svāhā*, the purifier;
salutations to you, Hari, who holds the *śārṅga* bow in his hand and removes all evil.
Salutations indeed to the one who impels both the existent and the non-existent; salutations to the one endowed with supreme consciousness;
salutations to the one whose very nature is the Veda; salutations again and again to the purifier. 62.
Homage be to you, Hari-keśa, the remover of all afflictions;
homage to you, Keśava, the supreme sustainer of the universe. (63)
Homage to you who are the very source of compassion; homage to you who consist of joy!
Homage forever to the infinite, the pure, and the destroyer of afflictions. (64)
Salutations eternally to you, Ānanda, who are pure and absolute;
salutations to you whose feet are worshipped by the Rudras and by Viriñci. ||65||
Homage to you, whose lotus feet are bowed to by the lords of gods and asuras;
repeated homage to the Supreme Lord, the unconquered one, whose nature is immortality.
Salutations to You who dwell in the Ocean of Milk, salutations to You who are beloved of Padmā;
salutations again and again to the pure syllable Oṃ, to the stainless, and to the immovable one.
Salutations, salutations to the all-pervading one, to the very pervader who removes all calamities; salutations to you, the Boar, and salutations to you, the Great Tortoise. ||68||
Homage to the Great Soul in the form of Vāmana, to Nṛsiṃha;
homage to the divine Rāma and to him who brought about the slaughter of all the kṣatriyas.
Homage to you, the omniscient Fish; homage to you, Rāma;
homage to Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha; homage to the destroyer of the Mlecchas. ||70||
Salutations to you, the brahmin Kapila; salutations to you, Hayagrīva.
Salutations to you in the form of Vyāsa; salutations to you who consist of all things. ||71||
Having thus praised Hṛṣīkeśa, he spoke to that Janārdana:
"Even Brahmā does not know the further shore of your qualities, O Purifier. (72)
Even the omniscient Rudra, the thousand-eyed one, is not able to praise you; for who indeed is capable of describing you? O All-pervading Lord, what kind of intellect do I possess? 73.
O Keśava, this hymn of yours, both devoid of attributes and endowed with attributes, was composed by me alone;
forgive my use of correct and incorrect words, for I am your servant, O you of noble vows. (74)
O Lord of the World, O Purifier, show me compassion in birth after birth. (75)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Dṛḍhasumana," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. 19.
(20) The Twentieth Chapter. Hari said:
O twice-born one, I am pleased by this austerity, by this merit, by this truth, and also by this purifying hymn; let a boon be chosen.
"O highly fortunate one, we shall grant you a boon that accords with your heart's desire; whatever wish you may desire, I shall fulfill each and every one for you. (2)
Somaśarman said:
"First, grant me one single boon, O Kṛṣṇa, which is my heart's desire;
if you are well-pleased in mind, grant it to me today with great compassion. (3)
Having reached birth after birth, may I practice devotion unto you;
show me your supreme abode, which is immovable and bestows liberation. ||4||
[He gave birth to] his own son, Śatāraka, who was endowed with divine marks, eternally devoted to Viṣṇu, and a bearer of my lineage. ||5||
He is omniscient, the giver of all, self-controlled, and endowed with the splendor of asceticism;
he is the eternal protector and worshiper of the gods, the Brahmins, and the worlds.
O Hara and Keśava, grant me such a son— one who is a friend to the gods, a vessel of merit, a donor, and a scholar of wisdom— thereby removing my poverty.
"Let it be so; let there be no body for me; rather, I choose this [other boon]. Hari said:
"So be it, O best of the twice-born; it shall come to pass, of this there is no doubt. (8)
By my grace, you shall have a virtuous son who will deliver you from the cycle of existence;
and you shall enjoy excellent pleasures, both divine and human, in this world.
O son, having beheld the supreme auspicious happiness born of your offspring, you shall not behold suffering for as long as you live, remaining in the state of a Brahmin. (10)
You will become a giver, an enjoyer, and a grasper of virtues; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, you shall meet death at a sacred ford and attain the supreme goal.
Having thus granted the boon to his beloved brahmin, the Lord Hari vanished;
the deity appeared like a vision in a dream.
Then that best of the twice-born, Somaśarman, being joined with this devotion,
[resided] at this most holy and purifying site on the bank of the Revā, which bestows great merit.
That Brahmin Amaraka performed meritorious acts of charity;
after a very long time had passed for that Somaśarman, [the following occurred]. (14)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Kapilā and Revā,
the brahmin emerged and saw before him a single white elephant.
It was brilliantly radiant, beautiful, divine, and intoxicatingly delightful, endowed with charming marks; its limbs were adorned with various ornaments, and it was possessed of abundant splendor.
Its two frontal globes shone with saffron applied at a distance,
and it was adorned with blue lotuses on its ears and equipped with flagstaffs.
A divine person, standing atop a serpent, possessed of firm and excellent radiance, endowed with divine marks, and adorned with all ornaments. ||18||
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, he was exceedingly gentle, like the full moon, and accompanied by an umbrella and chowries.
Then that best of beings saw him again, mounted upon a serpent,
proceeding most auspiciously while being praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas.
Seeing that beautiful man with his bull, who possessed divine marks, Somaśarman, his mind overcome with wonder, reflected: ||21||
"Who is this one with divine limbs who, having reached the path, proceeds as one of excellent vows?
While he was reflecting thus, he arrived at his home.
Entering that house door, which was divine in form and captivating to the mind,
Somaśarman, the best of the twice-born, was filled with great joy.
The righteous-souled one proceeded in haste toward his own home;
yet, as soon as he reached the door of the house, he did not see him. ||24||
The high-minded and best of the twice-born saw that the flowers which had fallen in the courtyard were indeed friendly and appeared as if they were divine garments. (25)
Having seen her own courtyard smeared with meritorious, fragrant sandalwood and saffron, and strewn with dūrvā grass and unbroken grains of rice; ||26||
Thus filled with wonder and reflecting again and again,
that wise one beheld Sumanā, who was a collection of divine and auspicious qualities.
Somaśarman said: "By whom were these divine ornaments given? [By whom was given] this grace, beauty, and charm, along with the clothing, jewelry, and decorations? (28)
"Therefore, O blessed lady, tell me the reason for this without hesitation.
Having thus addressed his wife, the best of the twice-born ceased speaking. (29)
Sumanā said:
Listen; some most excellent of gods has arrived here, mounted upon a white elephant and adorned with divine ornaments. (30)
With his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and endowed with divine wonders, he is indeed that one God who is served by Brahmins and Gandharvas. 31.
Being praised by gods, gandharvas, and celestial singers, he arrived,
accompanied by women rich in virtuous beauty and endowed with the grace of physical form.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and having all their desires fulfilled, they were together with me and that high-souled person, in the presence of Akṣa.
The fourfold area was filled with jewels and endowed with every splendor;
there, it is said, I was placed upon a meritorious throne by the brahmins. (34)
Indeed, all those who are burdened by fatness [and pride] through garments, ornaments, and finery [are purified] by Vedic auspicious songs and by meritorious songs from the Śāstras. ||35||
O best of the twice-born, having been consecrated by all these smiles, they vanished;
yet they all spoke to me once more from every side.
"We shall all indeed always remain in your house;
O auspicious one, be pure at all times together with your husband. (37)
Having spoken thus, they all departed; indeed, I myself witnessed this.
Having heard the account related by her, the one of great intelligence [reflected]. (38)
Then, having fallen into deep reflection, that highly intelligent Somaśarman pondered: "What is this? Has it been created by a god? (39)

Being fully engaged in the work of Brahmā, she bore a child from that illustrious one, who was endowed with the supreme dharma of similarity to his nature, for she herself was distinguished by her observance of vows. (40)
Then that queen shone even more brilliantly with the embryo within her,
endowed as she was with the splendor and flames of the radiant son.
By means of his ascetic penance, Sāhi begot a son who resembled a god;
then, from the firmament, the celestial drums resounded.
The great gods blew their conchs, the gandharvas sang charmingly, and all those who were fond of water danced at that time.
Then, together with the Brahmās and the Asuras, that best of the twice-born arrived;
being composed, he gave him the name Suvrata.
Then all those gods of great majesty departed after having performed the naming ceremony.
When those gods had gone, Somaśarman [performed the rites] for his son.
O best of the twice-born, when a son was born to you—O highly fortunate one, O observer of excellent vows, created by the gods—he performed the birth-rite and other ceremonies. 46.
In his house was great prosperity, abounding in wealth and grain;
there were elephants, horses, buffaloes, cows, gold, and jewels as well. (47)
Just as the abode of Kubera shines with heaps of wealth,
so too does the house of Somaśarman resplendently gleam.
The best of the twice-born performed meritorious deeds such as meditation; the Brahmin was filled with various merits arising from his pilgrimage. 49.
There, O best of the twice-born, that wise man, endowed with knowledge and merit, performed various other meritorious acts of charity. (50)
Thus he should accomplish his duty and protect it again and again;
the best of the twice-born should perform for his son the birth-rites and other ceremonies. (51)
He indeed caused the wedding to be performed with great joy;
sons endowed with virtues and auspicious marks were born to his son.
Somaśarman performed meritorious deeds for those who were always devoted to the dharma of giving and endowed with truth, righteousness, and austerity.
O highly fortunate one, he rejoices in the happiness of his grandsons;
and being free from old age and disease, he enjoys every kind of bliss. (54)
Just as one who has mastered the twenty-five sciences, so indeed was his body;
the highly intelligent Somaśarman resembled the splendor of the sun. (55)
And that goddess Sumanā shone with meritorious auspicious signs,
along with her highly fortunate sons and grandsons, who were devoted to great vows and self-restraint.
Possessing exceedingly large eyes and the merits of devotion to her husband and other virtues,
she was endowed with youth as if she were sixteen years of age.
Those two great-souled lords were rejoicing, beautiful and auspicious;
endowed with joy, they were meritorious souls of great fortune.
O best of the twice-born, I shall thus describe to you the practice of the vow of Suvrata, which is endowed with meritorious conduct and characterized by excellent behavior.
Just as he propitiated the flawless Nārāyaṇa. ||60||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Origin of Suvrata," in the Legend of Indrasumanas, within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||20||
The twenty-first chapter.
Sūta said:
Once, that divine Vyāsa [approached] Brahmā, the lord of the world.
Greatly amazed, he asked for the entire narrative concerning Suvrata. ||1||
Vyāsa said:
O Soul of the World, O Great Lord of the gods, who ordains the arrangement of the worlds!
I now desire to hear the life-story of Suvrata in its entirety.
Brahmā said:
O highly fortunate son of Parāśara, listen to this most excellent and meritorious account concerning the practice of penance by the virtuous and noble brāhmaṇa Suvrata.
The wise Suvrata, even while still in his childhood,
reflected deeply and beheld within the womb the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person.
Then, through the practice of his previous karma, he became absorbed in meditation upon Hari—
the god who bears the conch and discus, whose navel is a lotus, and who bestows great merit.
He indeed meditates and contemplates upon that Gīta during its recitation and study;
thus, O best of the twice-born, that excellent brahmin always meditates upon the Lord Hari.
Thus the supreme child always played together with the sons of Āḍimbi;
and the great-souled one likewise took his own name from the children.
The wise Cakāsa, a meritorious soul who is devoted to virtue,
being of great intelligence, challenged his adversary with the name of Hari.
"O Keshava, come, come! O Madhava, wielder of the discus!
You alone, O Supreme Person, sport with me. (9)
"O Madhusūdana, we two must rise at the very same time;
likewise, the twice-born [Nārada] invoked Hari by his names in that very same manner. (10)
In playing, reciting, laughing, reclining, singing, and watching; in traveling, riding, sitting, meditating, incantation, study, and in virtuous deeds—(in all these, he remains absorbed). ||11||
Thus he beholds and thus he speaks of Janārdana, the Lord of the World;
he meditates upon Him alone, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the Sovereign of the Universe. 12.
Whether in grass, wood, stone, dry or moist, he who is of virtuous soul beholds Keśava, the lotus-eyed Govinda, in this very way. (13)
The one of great intelligence [perceives] thus: in the sky, on the earth, in the midst of mountains and forests, in water, on land, in stone, and likewise among living beings. (14)
The wise brahmin Sumanasuta, firm in his vows, beheld Nṛsiṃha;
thus, day after day, he took delight in the child’s play. (15)
And they sang of Kṛṣṇa with songs possessing beautiful melodies and sweet syllables, accompanied by rhythmic beats and tempo, with excellent tones and melodic modulations. ||16||
Suvrata said:
"I go for refuge to Madhusūdana, the Lord of Yoga, the destroyer of all sins, whom the knowers of the Vedas constantly meditate upon as the one in whose body the entire universe resides. (17)
I perpetually bow at the pair of feet of that Supreme Lord alone, who conforms to all the worlds and in whom all worlds dwell, and who is free from every single defect. 18.
Those of pure intellect constantly recite the Vedas, which are the treasury of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities and His immeasurable power;
for the sake of crossing over that entire ocean of worldly existence—which is shoreless, difficult to traverse, and bottomless—I take refuge in Him. 19.
O King of swans upon the lake of the minds of yogis, whose entire power is ever pure—O enemy of the asuras, grant protection to my pair of stainless and expansive feet, for I am wretched. (20)
I meditate upon the Lord of all worlds, the Divine Master, who is the destroyer of the darkness of suffering even here on earth;
the Lord of gods, the teacher of all the world, who is endowed with truth and has taken up the duty of protecting the world. (21)

I sing incessantly of Śrīraṅga, the sole God of the universe, who destroys ignorance, who is like the sun in his splendor, who bestows all that is desired, and who is endowed with greatness—using the rhythms and measures of divine songs. (22)
I shall sing with melodies of no other flavor that song of skillful artistry concerning that very full treasury of nectar;
it is joined with the instruments of one's own yoga and eternally perceives the entire universe, both moving and unmoving, as the vision of ultimate reality.
Those people of this world who are deeply wicked do not see this at all; they constantly seek refuge in that very Keśava. ||24||
Beating the rhythmic clapping with his two hands in perfect time, he sings praises of Kṛṣṇa with song and rejoices together with the boys.
Thus, while constantly engaged in play during his childhood, Sumanā’s son Suvrata remained devoted to meditation upon Viṣṇu. ||26||
As he was playing, his mother said to him, who was firm in his vows and possessed of beautiful marks:
