"Eat now; hunger will surely afflict you. (27)
The wise one spoke again to Sumanā’s mother:
"I am indeed satisfied by the great nectar, the essence of meditation upon Hari. (28)
Having ascended to the seat of food, he beholds the desired meal;
this food is Viṣṇu himself, for the Self has taken refuge in the food. (29)
May Viṣṇu, who dwells within the ocean of milk, be satisfied by this food in his own essential form.
By this meritorious water, may Keśava attain satisfaction;
likewise by these betel leaves, sandalwood, fragrances, and charming flowers.
When Keśava, whose nature is dharma, attains satisfaction while lying down, being himself satisfied by his own essential nature, then one should meditate upon that Kṛṣṇa.
I have gone for refuge to that Kṛṣṇa who is endowed with yogic sleep;
likewise, O twice-born one, [I seek refuge] in his eating, clothing, sitting, and reclining.
One should meditate upon that Vāsudeva and offer everything to him;
having attained youth, the righteous-souled one indeed renounces the enjoyments of desire.
Keśava was joined [in meditation] on the excellent Vaidūrya mountain,
where there is the Vaiṣṇava Liṅga Siddheśvara, which destroys all sins.
Having meditated upon Rudra, who is identical with the syllable Om, the Great Lord, the God who was magnified by Brahmā on the southern bank of the Narmadā; ||36||
Having taken refuge at Siddheśvara, he contemplated the state of asceticism. ||37||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Aindrasumanas," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||21||
(22) The Twenty-second Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O highly fortunate one, I shall ask you a single question; please answer it.
For you yourself have previously spoken of the excellent vow dedicated to the Lord. (1)
Meditating upon the flawless Nārāyaṇa through his previous practice, in what birth was he born as one of noble vows in his former life? (2)
Therefore, tell me this now: how was Hari propitiated by him? And who is this lord of gods, so filled with the abundance of merit? (3)
Brahmā said:
In the meritorious city of Vaidiśa, which was filled with all kinds of prosperity,
there lived a king of great splendor and power, the son of Ṛtadhvaja.
The son of that highly wise king was renowned as Urucakrabhūṣaṇa;
his wife was the illustrious Dharmapatnī, who was devoted to him.
Having then procreated a son resembling himself upon her,
the king named that prince Dharmāṅgada.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and devoted to his father, this son of Rukmāṅgada is the best among the blessed. (7)
For the sake of his father's happiness, he offered his own head to Mohinī;
indeed, he was satisfied through devotion to his father and by means of Vaiṣṇava dharma.
With his senses perfectly tranquil,
that knower of all dharmas, a Vaiṣṇava and the best of the Sātvatas, was led with his very body to the station of Viṣṇu.
The highly wise Dharmāṅgada, who was proficient in wisdom and knowledge, remained there; he was truly great in wisdom, a Dharma, and an ornament of Dharma. ||10||
Rejoicing in divine enjoyments that follow his mind, he serves the Lord for a full thousand yugas; such is Dharma, whose ornament is righteousness. (11)
Falling from that state, yet by the grace of Viṣṇu himself, he was born as the wise and cheerful Suvrata, who increased the joy of the gods. (12)
The son of Somaśarman, the most excellent among the best of the blessed, being wise, performed penance and became intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu. (13)
Having abandoned defects such as lust and anger, that best of the twice-born restrained the group of his senses and performed penance incessantly.
On the excellent Vaidūrya mountain, in the presence of Siddheśvara, having unified his mind, he united himself with Viṣṇu. (15)
Thus, after this great-souled one had remained in meditation for a hundred years,
the Lord of the World, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, became perfectly pleased.
To him, Keśava, together with Lakṣmī, granted another boon:
"O you of good vows, O righteous-souled one, O best among the wise, wake up! (17)
"Choose a boon, O auspicious one; I am Kṛṣṇa, who has come to you.
Having thus heard these unsurpassed words of Viṣṇu, Medhāvī—
Overcome with great joy upon seeing Lord Janārdana,
he then joined his palms in reverence and offered his salutation.
Suvrata said:

This ocean of worldly existence is filled with waves of various nets of great misery, with billows of manifold delusions, and with the foam of one's own faults and virtues; therefore, O Janārdana, quickly rescue the wretched person who has reached it.

My karma thunders loudly, rains down as it were, and flashes with streaks of lightning through the masses of my sins; my vision is obscured by the thick veils of the darkness of delusion. O Madhusūdana, grant the hand of Your grace to me, who am thus wretched. (21)

O Kṛṣṇa, protect the dense forest of saṃsāra, which is crowded with trees of manifold suffering and haunted by lions of delusion; it is ablaze with the intense heat of the many fires of egoism and is being scorched incessantly. 22.

O Enemy of Mura, O Blessed One, protect me here who have climbed this exceedingly ancient tree of saṃsāra—tall with the trunk of illusion, possessing many branches of suffering and a lack of compassion, with the foliage of attachment to wife and kin, and now bearing fruit; I have fallen from it. (23)

I am constantly being burned by the fires of suffering consisting of various delusions, by thick smoke-like sorrows resembling separation and death at its end; O Kṛṣṇa, grant me liberation from my body, and you, always sprinkle me with the nectar of knowledge from the wise. 24.
O Kṛṣṇa, I have fallen perpetually into the great and terrible abyss named Saṃsāra, which is a dense thicket of the letter *dhakāra*.
You are truly compassionate; therefore, having become weary of that world which afflicts me with fear, I have come to you for refuge. (25)
Those whose mental disposition is restrained and focused meditate upon you alone with a mind of wisdom, and thereby they attain the state of knowledge;
they bow before your pair of feet, which possess great merit and which the hosts of gods and kinnaras constantly contemplate. (26)
I speak of no other, I worship no other, nor do I think of any other; I bow constantly at the pair of your lotus feet.
O Kṛṣṇa, may you yourself fulfill my desire today; let the accumulation of my sins depart far away.
"I am your slave, O God; I am your servant, birth after birth. I constantly remember the pair of your lotus feet. (28)
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa, if you are pleased with me, grant me this boon:
let my mother and father come here into the presence of Kṛṣṇa. (29)
"And there is no doubt that you shall attain Me, O Great God.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "In this way, your supreme purpose will be accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (30)
Hṛṣīkeśa was pleased with him, being fully gratified by his devotion;
he indeed departed for the world of Viṣṇu, which is free from burning and dissolution.
Together with Suvrata, those two, Sumanas and Somaśarman, remained for as long as two kalpas had passed; meanwhile, that brahmin Suvrata—
O high-minded one, he enjoyed divine worlds as a ruler of the earth;
and for the sake of the gods' mission, he returned once more to the house of Kaśyapa right here.
Having descended at the command of that wielder of the discus, the one of great wisdom enjoys the station of Indra and indeed that of Viṣṇu through his grace. (34)
Renowned as Vasudatta and saluted by all the gods, he indeed enjoys the station of Indra, equal to that of Vāsava in heaven, for an entire kalpa.
All this has been told to you regarding the cause of the connection between creation;
I shall now explain another matter concerning which you have inquired.
Vyāsa said:
The highly wise and powerful Dharmāṅgada, the son of Rukmāṅgada, was born in the first Kṛta age; at the time of creation, he was Vāsava.
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, how is it that Dharmāṅgada on earth is one person, while King Rukmāṅgada is another, and this [being] is the lord of the thirty gods? (38)
"This doubt has arisen in me; you ought to explain it.
Brahmā said:
"Indeed, I shall tell you that which destroys all doubts. (39)
O best of the twice-born, it exists for the purpose of the Lord’s playful creation, just as there are days, fortnights, months, and seasons. (40)
The years, the Manus, and likewise the Yugas pass away again;
afterwards the Kalpa arrives, and thus I shall go to Janārdana.
I alone am the great embodiment of wisdom within which all things, moving and unmoving, reside; then, as the soul of yoga, I indeed create the entire universe anew, just as before. 42.
Again I was born, again the Vedas, again those deities and the twice-born;
likewise all these kings, whose splendor was equal to their own conduct. 43.
O highly fortunate one, the wise prevail therein and are not deluded,
just as in a former kalpa, O highly fortunate one, [there was] King Rukmāṅgada.
Likewise, this illustrious twice-born Dharmāṅgada was born;
as were the highly wise Rāma and others, as well as Yayāti and Nahuṣa. (45)
Great-souled beings such as Manu and others come into existence and dissolve;
kings devoted to dharma attain that supreme state, the Lord. 46.
Just as the heroic Dharmāṅgada [sought] his lord, the great station of the Jatis, so too do the Vedas, the gods, and the Purāṇas, preceded by the Smṛtis [seek him]. 47.
O best of the twice-born, this entire meritorious life-story of Suvrata, which bestows a happy rebirth, has now been narrated before you. (48)
O highly fortunate one, I shall now declare the Unmanifest before you. ||49||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narrative of Indrasuvrata," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. || 22 ||
The twenty-third chapter.
The sages said:
"This story is wonderful, meritorious, auspicious, and bestows fame."
"O best among speakers, it has been declared by you that [this] removes all sins. ||1||
O Sūtanandana, you ought to explain to us this connection regarding creation,
just as you previously described the process of creation in detail.
Sūta said:
I shall explain in detail the cause of creation and dissolution,
by the mere hearing of which a person may attain omniscience.
Even by Hiraṇyakaśyapa, the three worlds were pervaded;
having propitiated Brahmā through austerity, he obtained a boon that is very difficult to attain.
From that highly fortunate god, he likewise obtained immortality;
having pervaded the worlds of the gods, he acquired sovereignty for himself. (5)
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, the sages who have mastered the Vedas,
the nāgas, the kinnaras, the siddhas, the yakṣas, and others as well, [approached].
Placing Brahmā at their head, they went to the Lord Nārāyaṇa,
the Master who was sleeping upon the Ocean of Milk, absorbed in yogic sleep.

Then the gods and the inhabitants of the celestial realms, having awakened him with great hymns of praise, related the conduct of that evil-minded one to the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of Gods. (8)
Having heard this, the Lord of the World, the one of great wisdom, assumed the form of Narasiṃha and slew Hiraṇyakaśipu. ||9||
Furthermore, in the form of a boar, the immensely powerful Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by Him,
and at that time the holy earth was lifted up from the depths of the asuras.
He caused other Dānavas of terrible appearance to be slain;
and thus, when these great Dānavas had been destroyed, [the world was freed].
When those other sons of Aditi had perished,
and these great gods had again attained their positions, ||12||
While all sacrifices were being performed and all religious rites were proceeding,
and while all the worlds were in a state of well-being, Aditi was tormented by suffering.
Tormented by grief for her son, she became distraught and unconscious;
she [beheld] her husband, who resembled the sun and was endowed with the splendor of ascetic power.
Then, having bowed with devotion to that high-souled donor and husband, Kaśyapa, the best of Brahmins, she spoke to that great-minded one.

O Blessed One, by that very Lord who wields the discus and is free from the egoism of being the "father of eight," all the Daityas and Dānavas were struck down, just as [the enemies] are by the gods. ||16||
O best of sages, O Lord, I am scorched by the fire of grief for my son—my son who was so dear to me and who has taken away all my splendor. (17)
Subala, whose every limb was beautiful, possessed a splendor equal to that of the king of the gods; he was intelligent, all-knowing, a knower of all things, and the most learned of scholars. ||18||
Endowed with the splendor of austerity, possessed of strength and auspicious marks, devoted to Brahman, a knower of wisdom, and a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins. ||19||
O twice-born one, O Lord, grant me a son who shall be a conqueror of all worlds, who will perform my commands, and who is endowed with all auspicious marks. (20)
Having thus heard these excellent words of hers, O best of the twice-born, Kaśyapa’s mind was filled with compassion; he was both pleased and pained by her distress.
Placing his own hand upon her head, he who was intent on her welfare spoke to that illustrious woman, who was miserable and dejected in mind. (22)
"O highly fortunate lady, you shall have a son exactly as you desire.
Having spoken thus, he departed for Meru, the best of excellent mountains.
Performing supreme vows, he practiced penance without support;
during this very interval, he conceived an excellent embryo.
Sāditi, who was wise, possessed of beautiful deeds, and a knower of all dharmas,
remained impure for herself for the duration of one hundred years.
By her was born a son endowed with Brahmanic luster;
then Kaśyapa arrived, filled with great joy. (26)
The most excellent sage, the wise Cakrānāman, spoke to his son who was equal to himself in greatness, saying, "O son, you shall be known by the name Bala. (27)
Thus he performed the naming ceremony and the binding of the vows;
he said to his son, "O highly fortunate one, accomplish the life of celibacy."
"O best of the twice-born, O most excellent one, I shall indeed act according to your word;
I shall perform the study of the Veda through the practice of celibacy. (29)
Thus, after a full hundred years had passed while he was performing his austerities,
he returned into the presence of his mother, endowed with the splendor of his ascetic power.
Diti, filled with great joy, beheld the divine celibacy of her high-souled son, which consisted of the power of austerity.
He spoke to that high-souled Bala, his ascetic son,
who was wise, magnanimous, and proficient in wisdom and knowledge.
While you, O wise one, live, my sons continue to live;
for it was by you, the wielder of the discus, that Hiraṇyakaśipu and the others were slain.
While he was indeed accomplishing his enmity against the gods in battle, Sādana spoke these words to his son, the exceedingly powerful Bala: sādanus tam uvācedaṃ balaṃ putraṃ mahā-balam ||34||
"O son, first quickly slay Indra, the lord of gods;
afterwards, having struck down those other gods, he whose vehicle is Garuḍa [shall do so]. (35)
Having heard those two, Queen Aditi, who was devoted to her husband,
overcome with great sorrow, spoke to her son Indra.
The son of Diti, possessing a massive body, grew by means of his Brahmanic luster;
for the sake of slaying the gods, he performed penance in Nirañjana.
"O Lord of the Gods, know this: if you desire welfare here [in this world],"—having heard these words of his mother, Pākaśāsana [Indra]... [38]
Then the king of the gods fell into great distress of mind;
terrified by a great fear, he reflected upon this matter.
"How shall I slay this reviler of the divine dharma?"—
having thus resolved regarding the destruction of Bala, the Lord of the Gods [proceeded].
Once, that Ahibala also resorted to the forest of Siṃdhu for the sake of meditation,
adorned with a divine black antelope skin and a staff of *daṇḍaka* wood.
By virtue of that stainless merit and his practice of celibacy,
he arrived at this seat of meditation on the shore of the ocean.
The subduer of Pāka (Indra) beheld him, peaceful and engaged in silent recitation;
he was struck by that divine thunderbolt of Indra.
Seeing the army fallen, its living beings departed and gone to the earth, the king of the gods was then filled with great joy and rejoiced. 44.
Having thus struck down the Daityas Diti and Danu,
the righteous Pākaśāsana ruled the kingdom in happiness.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Daitya Bala," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||23||
The twenty-fourth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard that her sons Subala and Bala had been slain, Aditi...
Having uttered piteous cries of weeping, she cried out, "Alas! Alas! What misery for me! (1)
Having thus practiced great compassion for a long time, that illustrious ascetic woman went to Kaśyapa and spoke to him.
Your son, the lord of the hosts of gods and a great sinner,
having seen my weak body endowed with the marks of Brahmā upon the shore of the ocean, [acted].
He struck him with a thunderbolt and indeed made his face dark;
having heard this, the son of Marīci then became enraged.
Overcome by great anger, that best of the twice-born blazed as if with fire; he loosened a single matted lock and cast it into the pure flame.
"I shall produce a son for the very purpose of slaying Indra;
he shall be born from that vessel and also from the mouth of the sacrificial fire."
Accompanied by a multitude of people, he was dark-complexioned, with tawny eyes and a terrifying form;
with a mouth formidable with fangs, he was the bringer of fear to the three worlds.
Terrible with his great club, likewise bearing a sword and shield,
blazing with the splendor of his entire body, he is powerful like a great cloud.
He said to the Brahmin Kaśyapa, "Let my command be given; tell me, O Brahmin, for what reason have you brought him forth? (9)
“I shall accomplish that through your grace, O you of excellent vows.
Kaśyapa said: “O my son, fulfill this very desire of mine.”
O Aditi, you of great wisdom, slay the evil-minded Indra; once the king of the gods has been slain, enjoy the position of Indra yourself.
Thus instructed by the high-souled Kaśyapa,
Vṛtra made an effort for the sake of slaying that Indra.
Endowed with manliness, he practiced the science of archery (dhanurveda),
as well as strength, heroism, the prowess of a kshatriya, and energy combined with fortitude.
Having seen that Daitya Ahi, the thousand-eyed one became distressed with fear and devised a stratagem against that evil-minded Vṛtra.
For the purpose of slaying him, the God of gods summoned the great sages and dispatched the seven Ṛṣis toward Vṛtra, the lord of the Daityas.
"O lords of sages, go there where Vṛtra stays, and together with him, establish a bond of friendship for my sake. (16)
Thus instructed by him, those seventy sages,
having been dispatched by the thousand-eyed Indra, then spoke to Vṛtrāsura.
"O best of Daityas, let friendship be established; let it be done.
Thus spoke the seven seers, knowers of reality, to the mighty Vṛtra. (18)
O thousand-eyed one, O most excellent of beings, you who possess great wisdom, you desire to act with friendliness; why then do you not perform it? 19.
"Enjoy the eastern half of Indra's domain as a heroic being with true happiness;
let Indra rule the other half, as do the Asuras and the gods."
"May you all live in happiness, having truly cast aside enmity.
Vṛtra said:
"If it is true, O best of beings, that this lord desires friendship with me..."
"Relying on truth, I shall indeed act with self-assertion; there is no doubt in this.
But Indra, placing deceit before him, would commit treachery. (22)
O Brahmins, what proof can be given for the meaning "what is done then"?
State the proof for the meaning "the sages spoke to you thus. (23)
"Therefore, tell us the truth if you desire friendship here.
Indra said:
"If I were to act with falsehood toward you through a disguise... (24)
"I shall be tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
Having employed such a deception, Indra will commit an act of treachery. (25)
"I shall be tainted by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; there is no doubt in this matter," said the Great Wise One, Śiva, to you alone along with the city [of the gods]. (26)
"By this very reason, O great-minded friend, [I have come] to you.
Vṛtra said:
"By this truth of yours, which follows the path of the disciplined, and by that [truth] of his... (27)
"O best of the twice-born, I shall indeed act with friendliness toward him;
Vṛtra has been brought to the abode of Indra by the preeminent Brāhmaṇas. (28)
Seeing that Vṛtra had arrived for the sake of his friend, Indra rose quickly from his lion-throne and, taking the water of honor (argha), prepared himself. ||29||
O best of the twice-born, that unrighteous one gave half [of his merit] to Vṛtra;
O highly wise one, enjoy this great station. (30)
"O best of Daityas, we two must also conduct ourselves with ease.
Thus did he speak to the Daitya Vṛtra with friendly words to inspire confidence in him.
O best of the twice-born, once those brahmins had departed for their own abodes,
that evil-minded one was constantly watching for a vulnerability even in Vṛtra.
Even Indra should contemplate vigilance day and night;
he would not find a single flaw even in the great-souled Vṛtra.
He devised a stratagem for the very purpose of killing him;
he dispatched Rambhā to delude that great asura.
"O auspicious lady, by whatever means possible, act in such a way that you may obtain happiness after slaying the enemy of the Asuras through delusion.
[Go to] the sacred, great, divine forest, frequented by holy trees."
It was endowed with many trees and fruits, and teeming with wild animals and birds. ||36||
The celestial palace was adorned on all sides with divine jewels;
it was filled with the songs of divine gandharvas and was always swarming with bees. (37)
It was everywhere filled with the meritorious cries of cuckoos, sweet and drawn-out,
and with the sounds of peacocks and antelopes, making it tumultuous in every direction.
It was adorned everywhere with divine sandalwood trees and with charming ponds, pools, and lakes filled with water. ||39||
It was adorned with blooming lotuses and hundred-petaled flowers, and frequented by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, cāraṇas, and kinnaras. ||40||
It shone with divine sages and a most excellent celestial garden,
crowded with throngs of apsaras and various auspicious wonders.
It was crowded with golden palaces,
and everywhere adorned with staffs, umbrellas, chowries, jars, and banners.
Reaching that sacrificial ground, which was filled with the sound of the Vedas and crowded with the sound of singing, she of the lovely smile approached Sāraṅga. 43.
There, that playful woman sported in this manner together with the Apsarases.
Sūta said:
Once, however, Vṛtra, drawn away by Kāla, went to the forest.
Accompanied by several dānavas and filled with supreme joy,
he wandered about the side of that very same high-souled one, remaining unobserved.
Even the king of the gods, though seeking the faults of his enemies along with the foremost of the brahmins, was nevertheless highly wise and trusted Vṛtra in all undertakings. (46)
Knowing Indra and Mitra to be supreme, he felt no fear;
wandering about, he saw the forest to be entirely and supremely auspicious.
The most delightful Kautuka forest, crowded with throngs of women, possessed the cool and highly meritorious shade of even the sandalwood tree. 48.
Reclining upon a broad couch, the illustrious and highly fortunate lady of large eyes shines resplendently, having ascended a swing together with her friends. 49.
A song was being sung in a beautiful melody, enchanting the entire universe;
Vṛtra arrived there, his mind agitated by desire.
Having beheld me, the beautiful-eyed one, mounted upon the swing, he quickly [approached]. ||51||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Deception of Vṛtra," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||24||
The twenty-fifth chapter.
Sūta said:
This Hikkā, with her beautiful eyes, pervades the entire universe with her playful gestures and emotional expressions.
With her exceedingly youthful, radiant, and charming full forms, she utterly deludes people. ||1||

Having seen this woman with long, lotus-like eyes, full breasts, and limbs smeared with saffron—she whose face is like a lotus and who is the very abode of desire—is she not my delight, so beautiful and captivating? (2)
"She possesses a full form, her limbs are perfectly proportioned, and her character is exceedingly virtuous;
sent here today by the god of love, I shall come under her power right now."
Thus the Daitya, possessed by deep reflection, deluded by passion, and urged for a long time, went there in haste, agitated; with a distressed mind, he spoke to that beautiful-eyed woman. (4)
"By whom were you sent, O beautiful one? What is your name? Tell me, what is most meritorious?
By your very form, which possesses great splendor, I am infatuated; O young girl, come under my power! (5)
When she had spoken thus to Vṛtra, who was agitated by desire, the large-eyed lady said,
"I am going to the excellent forest for the sake of playing with my dear friend."
While [the others] have come together with their friends to this excellent forest of Dandaka, why have you come to the side of the Himavat? (7)
Vṛtra said:
"Listen, O auspicious one; I shall tell you who I am that have come here as a child—I am born from the Fire-god, the son of Kaśyapa."
"O fair-faced one, I am the friend of Indra, the god of gods; O lady of excellent limbs, half of my state has come to you for enjoyment. (9)
"O lady of excellent complexion, how can I, who am Vṛtra, not bow down even to this goddess, by whose mere will the three worlds have been brought under control? (10)
"I have come for refuge; protect me from desire, O fair-faced one!
O beloved with large eyes, accept me who am agitated by passion. (11)
Raṃbhā said:
"O hero, from this day forth I shall undoubtedly remain under your command;
whatever I say, that must indeed be done by you. (12)
"So be it, O noble one! I shall do all that.
Having thus established this bond with her, the one of great power [proceeded]. (13)
In that forest of great merit, the best of the Dānavas took delight in his singing, dancing, charming laughter, and graceful movements.
The great Daitya, being exceedingly infatuated with her through sexual union,
spoke to that illustrious Vṛtra, the best of the Dānavas.
"Drink this liquor; drink the sweet *mādhavī* wine!
He spoke thus to that large-eyed woman whose face resembled the moon. 16.
"I am the son of a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas; O auspicious lady, how could I ever commit the censured act of drinking liquor? (17)
Out of fear of that goddess, he took the liquor from her by force;
then, due to his lack of courtesy, he drank the liquor.
When he had become utterly deluded and fallen from the knowledge of the gods,
he was then struck down by the lord of the gods with his thunderbolt.
Then, being smeared with the sins of killing a Brahmin and other such crimes, the slayer of Vṛtra was addressed by the Brahmins: "O Indra, a sin has been committed by you."
"From this very statement, the immensely powerful Vṛtra, being utterly trusting, was slain by you through that very act of instilling confidence; thus has this sin been committed by you. (21)
Indra said:
"By whatever means possible, I must always be an enemy to that [demon], who is a slayer of gods and brahmins, a thief of sacrifices, and a destroyer of dharma. (22)
The wicked Dānava, the leader even of the three worlds, has been slain;
that you are angry for his sake is the very definition of justice.
"O best of the twice-born, you must first deliberate;
afterwards, you may express your anger, provided you consider it unjust toward me. (24)
Thus were those most excellent ones enlightened by the high-souled Indra,
and they were likewise enlightened by all the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
They went indeed to their own place, having struck down the pillar of Dharma.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Vṛtra," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The twenty-sixth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard that her son had been slain, Aditi was overwhelmed with grief.
O best of the twice-born, she was utterly consumed by that very grief for her son.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, they spoke again to the high-souled Kaśyapa, the bull among sages, for the sake of slaying even the most wicked Indra. (2)
"O Lord, grant me this one son, who is composed of Brahmanic splendor, intense, and unbearable for all the gods—since I am so very dear to you. (3)
Kaśyapa said: "The two very powerful sons of mine, Bala and Vṛtra, have been slain by that wicked-souled Indra, the god, who has resorted to unrighteousness."
And for the sake of his very destruction, I shall give you one son;
O illustrious lady, remain pure for a hundred years. (5)
Having spoken thus to the yogin Droha, he placed him upon his head and,
together with Aditi, went to Mount Meru, the forest of asceticism.
O best of the twice-born, the goddess, who dwells in the penance grove, performed austerities and remained ever pure for the sake of obtaining a son.
Then, O highly fortunate one, the thousand-eyed god, having perceived that very exertion and having observed Diti, became a witness to her inner state. ||8||
Having become a master of the twenty-five sciences, the king of gods, who was like a deity,
approached her presence in the form of a Brahmin.
Having bowed to his virtuous mother, who was endowed with ascetic power, the thousand-eyed one was addressed by her: "O best of the twice-born, why have you become angry? (10)
The thousand-eyed one said to her: "O beautiful lady, I am your son; O passionate woman, I am a Brahmin learned in the Vedas and I know the Dharma. (11)
"I shall assist you in your asceticism; of this there is no doubt.
The goddess is serving her mother, who is endowed with ascetic power, as is the way of the virtuous. (12)
She recognized that Indra had arrived as one who had committed a wicked deed;
she knew him to be the son of Dharma, serving her day after day. (13)
One should massage the limbs of the Goddess and then wash her feet;
likewise, one should offer leaves, roots, fruits, bark, and even a deerskin. (14)
Thus, the Self whose nature is Truth always grants this very thing to him who has pleased Him with devotion; being satisfied, He spoke to him. (15)
O highly fortunate one, when my son has been born with great merit and Indra has been slain,
let the kingdom of the Kurus be yours through my son’s divine power.
"So be it, O illustrious one; through your grace, this shall come to pass.
But Indra, the subduer of Pāka, became intent on finding a vulnerability in her. (17)
When less than a hundred years had passed, Acyuta appeared before him;
Diti, without having performed the purification of her feet, entered her bed. (18)
Making her bed with his head at her feet, her hair disheveled and extremely distraught, she fell asleep; and he entered her womb.
Then Vajrapāṇi split that embryo into seven parts with his sharp-edged vajra; staying within the womb, he wept.
O eminent brāhmaṇas, while the great embryo was still within Indra’s hand, he spoke again and again to that weeping child.
Śatakratu, of great splendor, spoke thus: "Āro!
And Śakra again divided that embryo of the son of Diti into seven parts.
Having cut each one into seven pieces while he was weeping, O King of the Gods, the Maruts were thus born; they are gods of great majesty.
Just as they were addressed by Indra, they thereafter became known by those names;
they possessed extreme vigor, massive bodies, and intense brilliance and prowess. ||24||
Then those fifty-nine Maruts became known by the name Marutas; they remained dependent upon Indra alone.
For the sake of all beings, Prajāpati Hari assigned a great multitude within each and every class.
In due course, those kingdoms were indeed ruled by the descendants of Pṛthu;
[but] Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, the all-pervading teacher of the universe, is with the gods.
He is the conqueror through austerity, possessed of great splendor, the one Prajāpati of all;
he is indeed Parjanya, Pāvaka, the meritorious, the Self of all, and everything itself. 28.
O best of the twice-born, for one who correctly understands this entire world of merit, consisting of the moving and the stationary, and this creation of beings, all this belongs to him. 29.
There is no fear of returning here; whence could there be fear of the next world? This creation is of great merit, auspicious, and the remover of all sins. (30)
The man who hears this with devotion is liberated from all sins; he is fortunate, meritorious, and endowed with truth. (31)
He who hears this creation attains the supreme goal;
with his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||32||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Origin of Maruts," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||26||
The twenty-seventh chapter.
Sūta said:
Then the Lord, the sovereign of all the worlds, consecrated the king.
Pṛthu, the son of Vena, the great lord over the entire kingdom. ||1||
Having bestowed the Brahma-kingships one after another, he indeed reflected upon him who possessed great arms and a great body, like Indra, the lord of the gods.
Whatever was suitable for her to drink, he began to offer—of trees, of Brahmins, and likewise of planets and constellations. (3)
The one of great intelligence consecrated Soma as king over austerities, over duties, over dharma-sacrifices, and over meritorious splendors. ||4||
O best of the twice-born, having likewise consecrated Varuṇa as the lord of the waters, of the deities, of holy fords, of welfare, and of jewels.
Furthermore, the Grandfather [Brahmā] appointed Vaiśravaṇa as the king of all other yakṣas,
and the highly wise Viṣṇu as the king of the Ādityas.
For the sake of the welfare of the people,
he established Dakṣa alone as the lord of subjects (prajāpati) over all meritorious realms.
He installed Prahrāda, who was capable, a knower of all dharmas, and the lord of the hosts of Prajāpatis,
as the king over the entire kingdom.
He consecrated Yama, the son of Vivasvat, endowed with the splendor of Viṣṇu, as the Dharma over the ancestral kingdom of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas; of piśācas, uragas, and sarpiṇīs; of all the yoginīs, and of the great-souled vetālas. ||10||
He likewise [worships] all the Kaṅkālas, all the Kūṣmāṇḍas,
and all the Pārthivas, as well as Giriśa, the wielder of the trident.
Of all mountains, he saw the great mountain Himavat;
likewise, of rivers, lakes, and ponds. (12)
In the divine regions of Kuṇḍa, Aṅkuśa, Rājya, and Iha, the Lord of the Gods established the meritorious ocean, the unsurpassed source of all sacred fords (tīrthas). ||13||
Then Brahmā, the lord of the gods, consecrated Citraratha as the king over the entire kingdom of all the Gandharvas and likewise over their merits.
The Four-faced One consecrated Vāsuki as the king of the Nāgas of meritorious power,
and likewise consecrated Takṣaka as the king of the serpents.
Then, among the elephants in the kingdom, he [beheld] Airāvata; and among all the horses, he likewise beheld Uccaiḥśravas.
Furthermore, he appointed Vainateya as the king of all birds, and likewise,
he assigned Brahmāsiṃha as the king over the beasts.
Having consecrated the bull among cows in the midst of the cattle, the Grandfather Prajāpati likewise consecrated the Plakṣa tree among all the lords of the forest.
Having thus established all the kingdoms,
the Grandfather Brahmā, the most excellent one, then installed the guardians of the directions.
Likewise, he consecrated Sudhanvan, the son of Vairāja and the best of beings, as the king and guardian of the eastern quarter. (20)
In the south, he consecrated as king the high-souled Śaṅkhapada, the son of the patriarch Kardama.
Likewise, in the west, that Prajāpati consecrated the son of Brahmā and Varuṇa, named Puṣkara, as the Prajāpati.
In the northern direction, O Brahman, he likewise consecrated Nalakūbara;
in this manner, he consecrated the guardians of the quarters, all of whom possessed great majesty.
By whom this entire earth, with its seven continents and its cities, is even today protected according to region through righteousness. ||24||
And thus the highly fortunate Pṛthu was consecrated as lord of men;
he was consecrated by means of all the great sacrifices, such as the Rājasūya and others. ||25||
The lord of the earth ruled the kingdom of men according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
and when the meritorious and highly powerful Cākṣuṣa Manvantara had passed away, [the next followed].

then those great-souled ones milked from her pure song as their excellent milk.
By this [milk], the Gandharvas, other Apsarases, and even the highly meritorious mountains subsist; thus has this Earth been milked for wealth.
Various kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs like nectar were provided, and the highly fortunate Himalaya was appointed as the calf. 68.
Meru became the milker and a mountain-born vessel was made;
by that milk, all the mountains of great power were nourished and grew.
Furthermore, great and meritorious trees, such as the wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees,
milked forth a palāśa leaf-bowl that sprouts again even when cut or burnt.
At that time, the Śāla tree became the milch-cow, and the Plakṣa tree became the calf;
[this was witnessed] by the Guhyakas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and hosts of Vidyādharas.
This is the milch-cow of all-sustenance, the bestower of all desires;
whatever people wish for, they obtain through the specific qualities of the recipient and the calf. (72)
By those very means, she indeed gives them milk of such a true nature;
this is the nurse, but this earth is the creator and the best sustainer of wealth.
This cow, who milks all desires, is adorned by merits;
she is the supreme foundation, she is creation, and she is progeny. (74)
She is the purifier, the bestower of merit, the meritorious one, the cause of the growth of all crops, and indeed the foundation and source of all that is moving and unmoving. ||75||
This Mahālakṣmī is the Vidyā who is eternally composed of the entire universe;
she is the cow of plenty who grants all desires, the remover of all diseases, and the one from whom all seeds sprout.
She is the mother of all blessings and the sustainer of all the worlds;
she is the light and the very form of even the five elements.
This earth, renowned as Tāmedinī,
was submerged in the ocean and entirely drenched with the fat of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Therefore, this earth is called "Medinī" by those who discourse on Brahman;
and because of his acceptance [of it], O best of men, she is also known as "Pṛthivī" after Pṛthu, the son of Vena.
Having attained the status of a daughter, she is called Queen Pṛthvī;
by that king, O best of the twice-born, this earth was protected. (80)
O twice-born ones, it is the support of villages and houses, garlanded with cities and towns, abundant with crops and mines, prosperous, and consisting of all sacred fords.
Thus Queen Vasumatī was always composed of all the worlds;
such is the majesty of the King of Kings as it is recited in the Purāṇas. ||82||
The highly fortunate Pṛthu, son of Vena, was the illuminator of all actions;
he was like Viṣṇu, like Brahmā, and like the eternal Rudra. ||83||
The three gods are to be saluted by the foremost of the gods and by those who discourse on Brahman;
likewise, the best of kings is to be saluted by all brahmins and sages. (84)
He who is the establisher of the castes and the stages of life, the sustainer of all the worlds, [is worshipped] by highly fortunate kings desiring sovereignty here on earth. ||85||
The first king, the majestic Pṛthu, son of Vena, was worthy of homage by warriors seeking mastery in the science of archery and always desiring victory. (86)
The great king, who bestows sustenance upon those who support the earth, is worthy of salutation.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, have the specific types of recipients been described by me. (87)
The calves were indeed most excellent, as were the milkers standing before you; and even the milk possessed a special quality, just as had been described by the king. ||88||
Thus has it been fully explained by you for those who have come before;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame, health, merit, and the destruction of sin. (89)
O best of the twice-born, for him who hears the life-story of Pṛthu, the son of Vena,
a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||91||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Pṛthu," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
The Thirty-First Chapter.
The Sages said: "That Vena, whom you have described as having lived according to sinful conduct—"
O twice-born one, what was the nature of that sin, and what fruit did he obtain?
O best among the wise, O one of great intellect, recount in detail that former conduct of Vena, for this matter is not small.
Sūta said:
I shall duly recount the most meritorious life-story of that great-souled Vena, the son of Vena, as it was heard in ancient times.
When that high-souled Pṛthu was born as his son, O highly fortunate one,
the king attained purity once again, having returned to righteousness.
All the great sins accumulated by the lowest of men go away through the occasion of contact with a holy place. ||5||
From association with the virtuous, merit alone is produced; of this there is no doubt.
But from attachment to the wicked, only evil is produced.
Indeed, from conversation, sight, touch, sharing a seat, sharing food, and even from association with sinners, one incurs their guilt. (7)
Likewise, merit alone shall accrue even to those whose nature is demerit;
through association with great sacred sites, the sinful are purified, and not otherwise.
"By this [means], they go to a meritorious state, having shaken off all impurities.
The sages said:
"O best of the twice-born, how do those sinners attain supreme perfection?"
Tell that to us in detail; our faith proceeds to hear it.
Sūta said:
And those hunters, great sinners, were born as slaves and fishermen;
they remained within the waters of the Revā, Yamunā, and Gaṅgā. 11.
Having bathed again and again with knowledge, they indeed sport in the water;
through association with the great river, they attain the supreme goal.
Having abandoned their state of servitude and the accumulation of sins, they all depart,
for they have all been bathed through contact with the holy waters.
O best of beings, by the flow of the Mahānadī, the sins of even great sinners are destroyed, as well as the [sins] of others who possess great merit. 14.
From seeing or touching [this] incidentally, no deliberation is required here;
regarding this matter, O Brahmins, an ancient legend that destroys sin is heard.
I shall now proclaim that which bestows great merit:
there was once a hunter named Sulobha in the great forest. (16)
With dogs, snares, nets, and likewise with bows and arrows, he constantly slaughters deer, being thoroughly intent on the taste of flesh. (17)
Once, that extremely wicked-souled archer, bow in hand and arrows in his grasp,
entered the impenetrable forest of the Vindhya mountains surrounded by dogs.
Having reached the banks of the Revā, a certain fisherman killed many deer, antelopes, and wild boars, as well as numerous fish, without fear. (19)
Having killed the fish, he went out from the water;
meanwhile, the doe, terrified by the fear of the hunter-greedy man, departed.
Devoted to saving her life, distressed, terrified, and with a trembling mind, she fled in haste, seeking refuge from one shore to another. ||21||
Agitated by dogs and distressed by wounds from the strikes of arrows, he was easily slain by the hunter, even with the force of his own breathing. ||22||
The female deer was coming from behind and moving ahead;
seeing her, Śapharaghna stood ready with an arrow in his hand.
While he was bending his bow with speed and pursuing that female deer,
a hunter named Lobha arrived together with his dogs.
"I am not to be given away; I have come for the hunt.
Having heard those words, the fisherman took up his net. ||25||
The evil-minded one of great strength discharged an arrow aimed at her;
she was struck by that sharp shaft from the hunter.
When those two evil-minded ones were slain by the arrow of Amṛgīta, she,
being pursued by snarling dogs, fled away in great haste.
From the peak, at the meritorious confluence of the Revā that destroys sins, dogs, while running about, fell into the pure lake. (28)
Overwhelmed with rage, the hunter spoke thus to the fisherman:
"This doe is mine; why have you, wicked man, killed her with your arrows? (29)
He spoke again to that fisherman, the slayer of deer: "This body is mine; you speak with arrogance. (30)
Then, O highly fortunate one, those two, fighting each other out of anger and greed, fell into the pure water. 31.
At that time, the great festival occurs which bestows a favorable rebirth;
it is joined with the new moon (Amāvāsyā) and grants the fruit of great merit. ||32||
O best of beings, at that time all of them fell [from their state],
being devoid of recitation and meditation, and abandoned by sincerity and truth.
In connection with bathing at the sacred ford, the doe, the dog,
and the hunter were all liberated from every sin and attained the supreme goal.
O best of the twice-born, by the power of sacred fords and through association with the virtuous, one may destroy the sins of sinners, just as fire consumes dry wood. (35)
Sūta said:
By the mere conversation, the sight, and even the touch of those high-souled ṛṣis, the sin of that king was destroyed. (36)
In ancient times, the stain of Vena was indeed destroyed through association with the virtuous;
for the sin of evildoers perishes through the accumulation of exceedingly intense merit.
Through association with those who commit extremely heinous sins, one will surely practice sin as well;
by the fault of his maternal grandfather, that very man becomes defiled. (38)
The sages said: "What was the fault of the maternal grandfather? Tell us that in detail—how Death, Time, Yama, and Dharma himself [were involved]. (39)
No one at all is established upon this [world];
the worlds, both moving and unmoving, are subject to the power of their own karma. (40)
They live and they die; thus, by their own actions, those wicked ones behold that terrible state as the ripening of their karma. (41)
In all the hells as well, this Sūta Yama, being thus highly meritorious through his own karma,
day after day appoints and strikes them.
In all highly meritorious deeds, such a virtuous person, being righteous in soul, engages himself; no fault is seen in him. (43)
"By what fault did this sinful Samṛtyu come to be born?
Sūta said:
Samṛtyu was always the punisher of the wicked-minded who were guilty of sins. (44)
It proceeds in the form of Time and examines their karma;
it causes even that person of evil deeds to be slain by means of that very karma.
Having recognized his evil, Yama leads him away; likewise, one whose soul is virtuous shall surely attain heaven by means of his well-performed deeds.
Death itself unites them all with its own messengers, accompanied by a great sense of well-being and the singing of auspicious hymns. 47.
And he should employ those of disciplined mind in acts such as giving and enjoyment, as well as in various forms of affliction, hardships, and terrible torments. (48)
If one were to frighten or strike Brahmins out of anger, they would indeed become Death itself;
thus, even for one intent on what is beneficial, their activity turns into its opposite.
O highly fortunate one, even from death, [a being] is born through greed or merit;
this [woman] was born from the non-deficiency of the noble-minded Sunītha. (50)
Having reflected upon the deeds of their father, they played for a time until fate brought forth one who would be the punisher of living beings and the observer of merit and sin.
That highly fortunate daughter of Sātuka, Sunīthā, having reached the forest while sporting, was surrounded by her companions. ||52||
There he saw the illustrious and excellent son of a Gandharva, Suśaṅkha by name, even amidst the clamor of singing. 53.
He saw him, whose every limb was beautiful, performing that great austerity,
meditating upon Sarasvatī for the sake of perfect mastery in the science of song.
Day after day, Suśaṅkha subjected him to such harassment; yet he always forgave him and said, "Go, go. (55)
She should not go to those who have been sent away, but should perform her duties without obstacle. Even when addressed by him with anger, she struck the one established in asceticism.
Then Suśaṅkha, enraged and overwhelmed with anger, said to her:
"O wicked woman of sinful conduct, why have you suddenly created this obstacle? (57)
When struck by the wicked, great men do not strike back;
even when reviled, they do not become angry—such is the established order of dharma. (58)
"By you, O sinful one, I—who am innocent and endowed with ascetic merit—have been struck down.
Having spoken thus to the unrighteous Sunīthā, who was a doer of evil, that virtuous-souled one [departed].
Having realized she was not a woman, he desisted from his great rage and turned back;
then, whether out of the delusion of sin, or out of childishness, he remained right here.
He spoke to the high-souled Suśaṅkha, who was established in asceticism:
"The father of the inhabitants of the three worlds is indeed my own slayer. (61)
One should always slay the wicked and protect the virtuous;
no fault shall accrue to him, for he shall abide in great merit.
Having spoken thus, he went to his father and addressed him with these words:
"O Father, the son of a Gandharva was struck by me in the forest. (63)
Constantly performing austerities, always alone, and free from desire and anger,
that righteous-souled one spoke to Samā, who was possessed of both passion and anger.
"One should not strike back at one who strikes, nor should one shout back at one who shouts," my father said to me; tell me the reason for that. (65)
O best of the twice-born, having been addressed thus, the virtuous Saumṛtyu did not say anything by way of answer to Sunīthā’s question. (66)
Having reached the forest where Śaṅkha was stationed,
he struck that best of ascetics with blows from his hands out of malice.
O Brahmin, when Suśaṅkha was struck by Mṛtyu with a conch shell, he became enraged;
then, that one of great splendor cursed the slender-waisted girl.
Since you have struck one who is faultless while he was already afflicted by the wicked,
and since I am dwelling here in this forest, I therefore pronounce a curse upon you.
And listen, when you had entered the householder's life with your husband, you gave birth to a son who was full of sinful conduct and a reviler of gods and Brahmins. (70)
"O you who delight in all evil, a wicked one shall be born from your womb.
Having thus cursed him, he departed; and he too remained there, taking refuge in that very place.
When that illustrious one had departed, Sūnīthā went home;
with a distressed mind, she informed her high-souled father.
All that which had been spoken by Death was heard by that son of the Gandharvas, who had been cursed as previously described. (73)
"Why have you inflicted this injury upon one who is free from the fault of heat? O daughter, it was not at all right for you to strike one who is devoted to truth."
Having addressed the righteous-souled one in this manner, Mṛtyu became deeply afflicted by grief, reflecting upon that very command which had been given to him.
Sūta said:
O brahmins, once the son of Atri, a twice-born man of great splendor and prowess named Aṅga, went toward the land of Nanda.
There he beheld that king of the gods, Indra, the subduer of Pāka,
accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, as well as Gandharvas and Kinnaras.
He was being sung to by singers with melodious voices in the seven musical scales,
and he was being fanned on all sides with fragrant fans.
I was fanned with yak-tail whisks by women endowed with beauty,
and I was shaded by a golden parasol that resembled the orb of the moon.
I beheld the god of immeasurable splendor, shining, thousand-eyed, adorned with all ornaments, and engaged in amorous play.
Beside him was the highly fortunate Paulomī, beautiful and auspicious,
illustrious for her beauty, her splendor, her asceticism, and her fame.
He saw that virtuous woman, Satī, shining with her auspicious fortune and devotion to her husband;
together with her, the thousand-eyed Indra entered the forest of Danu.
Beholding his divine play, the excellent brahmin Aṅga exclaimed, "Blessed indeed is this king of the gods, surrounded by such [attendants]! (83)
Oh, how great is the power of this ascetic’s penance, by which such a high station has been attained, since I have such a son as this, the sustainer of all the worlds! (84)
"Then there will be great happiness for me; I shall obtain it here, of this there is no doubt. Thinking thus, he became intent on reflection and returned home in haste. (85)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within this very narrative. || 30 ||
Chapter Thirty-One.
Sūta said:
Then Tvaṅgu, possessing great splendor, having beheld the prosperity of Indra, [proceeded].
And indeed, the enjoyment, the splendor, and the playful grace of that Great-Souled One. ||1||
"How might I have a son like Indra, endowed with righteousness?
Having reflected thus for a moment, Aṅga, the best among the upholders of dharma, [proceeded].
Having returned to his own home, Satyaṅga, who was devoted to truth,
bowed with humility and, supporting himself on his staff, questioned his father Atri.
Who is this person who, through meritorious conducts, enjoys such great sovereignty as Indra?
From what abundance of merit does this arise, what was performed, and of what nature was that deed? (4)
What kind of austerity did he perform, and whom did he propitiate in the past?
O best among the truthful, tell me this in detail. (5)
Atri said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, since you ask me thus!
O child, listen as I narrate the life-story of Indra."
In former times, there was an excellent brāhmaṇa named Suvrata who was highly intelligent;
by means of his austerity, he satisfied Kṛṣṇa Hṛṣīkeśa.
Furthermore, having obtained a womb of merit from Kaśyapa through Aditi,
he indeed became the king of the gods by the grace of Viṣṇu alone.
Aṅga said:
"O you who are fond of your son, how might my son become equal to Indra?
O best among the wise, please explain the means for that. (9)
Atri said:
O high-minded one, listen briefly to the entire meritorious life-story of this very same great-souled one of excellent vows. 10.
Just as that wise one of excellent vows propitiated Hari, so too [the sage described] the disposition, devotion,
and meditation of that high-souled being.
Having beheld the Lord of the World, he indeed attained the great state—the entire three worlds, including all moving and non-moving beings, along with Śakra and all riches of enjoyment. 12.
And by the grace of Viṣṇu alone, the upholder of the three worlds enjoys his station;
thus has all the conduct of Indra been related to them.
O best of beings, Govinda is pleased by devotion and meditation upon His true nature;
when Hari is satisfied by devotion, He grants everything with a contented soul. 14.
Therefore, one should propitiate Govinda, the giver of all, the source of all, the omniscient, the knower of all, the supreme Person among all. ||15||
Therefore, you shall obtain everything, whatever you desire, O Nanda.
He is the giver of happiness, the giver of the ultimate truth, the giver of liberation, and the protector of the worlds.
Therefore, go and propitiate him, my son; you shall indeed obtain a son equal to Indra.
Having heard these words, which were endowed with the ultimate truth and spoken by the high-souled, well-wishing seer,
he grasped the essence of that speech and, having prostrated himself, departed for that eternal state.
The high-souled Āma, equal to Brahmā himself, reached the peak of Mount Meru, which was adorned with various jewels, after having approached his father, who was likewise born of Brahmā. ||19||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses.
Chapter Thirty-two.
Sūta said:
His limbs were brilliantly illuminated by various jewels and also entirely by gold.
Shining like the sun with its own rays upon the best of mountains. ||1||
Having reached the cool and bliss-bestowing shade of the Aśoka tree,
all the yogins sat upon firm seats and engaged in meditation.
In some places sages practice austerities; in other places kinnaras sing;
and the ṛṣis and gandharvas, well-pleased, hold lutes and cymbals in their hands.

Absorbed in rhythm, tempo, and measure, accompanied by the seven musical notes joined with melodic modulations (*mūrchanās*) and ornaments (*ratnas*), the song was clearly articulated and captivating to the mind. (4)
On that best of mountains, resorting to the shade of sandalwood trees,
the Gandharvas— who are experts in the principles of song— sing songs with total devotion.
There, upon that supreme mountain, women dance for the gods;
it is divine, the destroyer of sins, the bestower of merit, and the granter of the highest welfare. (6)
On that most excellent mountain, the sweet resonance of the Vedas is heard,
[amidst] sandalwood, aśoka, punnāga, śāla, tāla, and tamālaka trees.
That best of mountains shines with banyan trees resembling clouds,
and with *santānaka* and *kalpa* trees crowded with celestial *aṃbhāpādapa* plants.
The mountain was filled with various minerals and heaps of diverse jewels, and it was covered everywhere with celestial trees in full bloom.
It was endowed with various wonders and accompanied by various auspicious rites; it was well-honored by hosts of Vedic scholars and crowded with throngs of apsarases.
It shines with ṛṣis, munis, siddhas, and gandharvas;
it is resplendent with elephants resembling mountains and with the roars of lions. 11.
It was adorned with śarabhas, intoxicated tigers, and rogue deer,
and possessed ponds, wells, and lakes filled with pure water.
It shines everywhere, crowded with *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* birds;
it is resplendent with golden lotuses, white lotuses, and red lotuses. (13)
Likewise, with the confluences of river currents and pure waters,
and with forms of *śāla* and *tāla* trees, as well as crystal elephants.
The king of mountains shines forth, filled with vast, divine golden plateaus that possess a radiance equal to the sun and fire. 15.
Adorned with the celestial chariots of the gods, with palaces, and with the finest of mountains,
it resembled a flight of swans and was embellished with golden staffs.
It was adorned with palaces equipped with water-jars and chowries, and graced by hosts of gods delighted by its various virtues. ||17||
Adorned everywhere by many hosts of gods, as well as by gandharvas and cāraṇas, Meru, the most excellent of great mountains, shines forth with merit. (18)
Therefore, I am the great river Gaṅgā, possessing highly meritorious waters; I have issued forth from a most sacred bathing place and am filled with lotuses. (19)
This great river is frequented by hosts of sages and seers;
such is this best of mountains, possessing these qualities and characterized by merit, auspiciousness, and blessings. (20)
The meritorious great sage Aṅga, the son of Atri,
entered a solitary and beautiful cave on the most sacred bank of the Gaṅgā.
Sitting there, the wise one, free from desire and anger,
having restrained all the senses, [should meditate on] Hṛṣīkeśa who has entered the mind.
Meditating upon the Lord Madhusūdana, whose nature is the True Dharma, who removes all afflictions,
and who is the master of the seat, the bed, the vehicle, and meditation.
One whose self is disciplined, who is engaged in yoga, and whose senses are conquered,
constantly beholds Keśava within all those living beings, both moving and unmoving.
Whether they were wet or dry, or all others as well, O twice-born one,
a hundred years passed while he remained thus engaged in ascetic penance.
Beholding the best of the twice-born, the Lord of the World, the wielder of the discus,
constantly manifests many most terrible obstacles.
By the splendor of that high-souled deity Nṛsiṃha,
the righteous-souled one, free from all affliction, burns away [evil] like fire consumes dry wood.
Through various observances, restraints, and fasts, O best of the twice-born,
he became emaciated and blazed with his own splendor.
O dear one, he was seen thus, resembling the sun and fire, being perfectly devoted to austerity and meditating upon Janārdana. (29)
The Lord appeared and said, "Choose a boon, O Mānada.
Seeing Hṛṣīkeśa, Aṅga was supremely delighted.
With a serene mind, he remained standing without bowing and praised Vāsudeva.
Aṅga said:
O you who are the refuge of all beings, O purifier of the creator of beings, O soul of all beings, O Lord of all beings, salutations to you, the essence of the qualities! 32.
Salutations to the one whose form is qualities, who is secret, who transcends qualities;
salutations to the creator of qualities and non-qualities, who is rich in qualities and whose very self is the qualities.

Salutations to the creator of existence and non-existence, to the remover of the worldly existence of devotees, to the source of existence, to the secret one, and to the destroyer of worldly existence. ||34||
Salutations again and again to the sacrifice, to the one whose form is the sacrifice, and to the Lord of the sacrifice;
salutations to the one who is intent upon sacrificial acts, and to the bearer of the conch. ||35||
Salutations again and again to the Golden One, salutations to the bearer of the discus;
to the Truthful One, whose nature is truth, and who consists entirely of truth. (36)
Salutations to you who are both the performer of dharma and the performer of adharma, and the performer of all things;
salutations to you whose limbs are dharma, who are the heroic one, and who are the support of dharma. ||37||
Salutations to the Great Soul, the son of Puṇyā and the son of Hyā, who destroys the delusion of Māyā and acts as the creator of all Māyā. ||38||
Salutations again and again to the one who possesses the power of illusion, to the one who is both embodied and unembodied;
salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who indeed assumes every form. ||39||
Salutations to You, the Brahman, whose form is Brahman and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman; salutations to You, the abode of all, and salutations to You, the sustainer of that abode. 40.
Salutations again and again to the illustrious one, the abode of glory, the sustainer of fortune;
salutations to that immortal one who dwells in the ocean of milk. ||41||
Salutations to the Great Medicine, to the Non-Terrible, to the One Supreme in Great Wisdom, to the Non-Cruel, to the Pure, and to the Lord of the Impure. ||42||
Salutations again and again to the protector of all without exception, O sinless one;
salutations to you who are the illumination of space and who take the form of a bird. ||43||
Homage to the one who has offered oblations and who consumes the unoffered, whose form is the sacrificial offering;
homage to the awakened one, whose form is the unawakened, yet who is eternally awakened. ||44||
Salutations to the one who is the utterance of *namas*, the utterance of *svāhā*, and the utterance of *svadhā*;
salutations to the pure, the unmanifest, and the Great Self. 45.
Salutations to Vyāsa, to Vāsava, and to him who possesses the form of Vasu;
salutations to Vāsudeva, to Viśva, and to him who possesses the form of Agni; salutations again and again to Hari, to Kevala, and to Vāmana. ||46||
Salutation to the divine Man-Lion, the protector of living beings; salutation to him. ||47||
Homage to Govinda, to the protector of the earth, and to the one-syllabled;
homage indeed to the one who is all syllables, and to you who possess every form, homage! 48.

Salutations to you who are the path of the three principles; salutations to you who are the path of the five principles; salutations indeed to you who are the path of the twenty-five principles and the support of all principles. ||49||
Salutation to the one who is dark yet possesses a non-dark form, the Lord of Lakṣmī;
salutation to the one with the petals of a lotus, who is intent upon bestowing bliss.
Salutations indeed to the bearer of burdens, salutations to the destroyer of sins;
salutations to the most meritorious and virtuous one, salutations to you who are truth and dharma. ||51||

Homage, repeated homage to the eternal and imperishable one; homage, repeated homage to the Lord of the Sangha who moves through the sky. Homage to the glorious Padmanābha, the Great Lord; homage to the peerless lotus-feet of Keśava. (52)
O Ānanda, O Daka, O Dakanala, O beloved Vāsudeva, O Lord of all, O Īśa, O Madhusūdana, grant me the service of being Your slave;
O Keśava, whose hair is like a peacock’s tail, bowing at Your feet, show me mercy birth after birth and grant me peace, O Śaṅkhapāṇi! 53.

O Lord of the World, whose form is my refuge, O Lotus-navelled One, you have caused the boat of knowledge to float upon the ocean of existence for me, who am distressed, having been scorched by the heat of the terrible fire of worldly existence and by the many sorrows and agonies of the death of sons and other kinsmen. (54)
Having thus heard this hymn from the high-souled Aṅga,
[the Lord] revealed His own form, which was intensely dark and possessed of great majesty.
The great Lord, whose hands hold the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who has a lotus in his hand, was revealed in his own form, mounted upon Vainateya. ||56||

Where a deity, a sacred shrine, a mendicant, or a guru is seen, there compassion is indeed the supreme dharma, and there liberation is clearly perceived. (17)

Pātaka said:

Afterwards, it enveloped the space and the state of a bubble was produced;

It may be seen for a mere moment, yet in the next moment it is no longer seen;
in that same way, the conjunction of the elements is perceived everywhere.
At that time, when the self departs, those five go to the five;
then, deluded by ignorance, those mortals revolve among one another.

O best of kings, where does the deceased reside, and how does he eat? What is his nature? (30)
"Tell me, O voice, what is knowledge, what is its nature, what is the body, and by whom has it been seen?
For even after feeding them with sweet food, the Brahmins depart unsatisfied. (31)

I shall now speak of something else: the cruel ritual action of the Vedas. (32)
O King of kings, when a guest arrives at the house, a twice-born man should cook a great bull or a goat and feed that guest.

the human-sacrifice with a man, and likewise the Vājapeya sacrifice with goats.

listen, O King, to how this is declared across all its various forms. (36)
The slaughter of animals of various distinct species is recorded [in tradition];

That food which is known [to be pure] is made into leavings by the act of eating excessively;
they laugh at that which is faultless and fit for consumption even in a great sacrifice. (38)
In that regard, O King, what dharma is seen there, and what is its fruit, wherein the slaughter of animals is ordained by those learned in the Vedas? (39)
Therefore, a dharma that lacks compassion is devoid of merit and does not bestow liberation; indeed, such a dharma becomes as fruitless as any other dharma.
The protection of living beings wherever it may be is undoubtedly dharma; so too, O best of kings, are the utterances of Svāhā and Svadhā, austerity, and truth. (41)
Therein, there is fickleness devoid of compassion, and no praise for dharma exists;

That brahmin who is merciless and devoted to the slaughter of animals is indeed utterly pitiless, sinful, hard-hearted, and cruel-minded. ||44||
The Veda has been described by Vaṃcaka as that which is devoid of knowledge;

Reservoirs, great silver ponds, and likewise oceans;

The king, the son of Aṅga, was incited by many people of sinful nature toward that entire system of sacrifice— which includes the Vedas, bestows merit, and is the very form of the supreme sacrifice— by that wicked man.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||37||
Chapter Thirty-Eight.

When the wicked have thus gathered together for the destruction of the Mlecchas, the Lord Kalki himself will undoubtedly appear; of this there is no doubt.
Abandon worldly affairs and even the pursuit of merit;

Chapter Thirty-nine.
The sages said:

O highly fortunate lady, by the very power of that king’s fierce austerity, the Lord who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace became truly pleased with that sinless monarch.

once, while Brahmā was absorbed in meditation within the lotus of [Viṣṇu’s] navel.

"O you who are fond of virtue, having spoken thus to your father, 'A noble son shall be born to you who desires to deliver you. (34)

They did not speak so as to make you, who follow the path of dharma, appear in a form devoid of fire;

To a Brahmin who is a worthy recipient, he who gives a great gift with a mind purified by faith, having fixed his devotion upon me; 45.
"I shall give him everything that he desires in his mind.

What can be said of that king who, when that auspicious hour has arrived, is a man performing meritorious deeds, thereby constantly increasing his merit? (52)
Having bathed and worshipped the ancestors and the gods, one should again become a giver of gifts,

Food, milk, fruit, flowers, clothing, betel, ornaments, gold, jewels, and so forth—the merit of these belongs entirely to him. (54)
O King, whoever should behold me at midday or likewise in the afternoon,

Food, drink, and the like; sweet ointments, fragrant saffron, camphor and other such items, as well as garments and ornaments. (56)

The Revā, Yamunā, Tāpī, as well as the river Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, Ghargharā, and Veṇā—all of which destroy every sin. ||88||

O King, wherever one may perform acts such as bathing and giving gifts, one obtains inexhaustible fruit through the grace of the excellent holy places (sutīrtha). ||97||

These are declared to be holy places (tīrthas), as are one's father and mother;

"These sacred fords have been fully described, as well as the royal palace.

Now, therefore, I shall describe the giving of gifts that is fruitful and bestows merit. 123.
Through the conjunction of faith with the right time, the sacred ford, and worthy recipients, merit arises;

One attains that [state] through my grace and shall become happy. ||127||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the Śrī Padma Purāṇa, within the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses. ||39||

As long as Brahmā lives, he remains there as long as existence lasts;

Chapter Forty-one.
Vena said:
"Tell me, how can a son, a wife, a father, and a mother be a sacred ford (tīrtha)?"
And how is the Guru himself a sacred ford (tīrtha)? Tell me that in detail.
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
There is a beautiful great city named Vārāṇasī, joined by the Gaṅgā;
in it dwells a certain vaiśya known by the name Kṛkala. 2.
His wife was a great virtuous woman, devoted to her husband; she was constantly intent on righteous conduct and entirely dedicated to her lord. ||3||
She was of auspicious limbs, possessing the merit of virtuous women; she was a beautiful and auspicious mother of excellent sons.
She always spoke the truth, was pure, pleasant in appearance, and dear to her beloved. (4)
Endowed with such qualities, she was fortunate and graceful in her conduct;
he, moreover, was the most excellent of vaiśyas, knowledgeable in various dharmas, wise, and virtuous.
He was always intent on hearing the Purāṇas and the Śrauta-dharma;
and through the course of his pilgrimages to sacred sites, he performed many acts that bestow great merit.
Out of faith, he set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords that were meritorious and auspicious,
accompanied by that caravan leader and through the company of Brahmins.
But as he had set out upon the path of dharma, his devoted wife, deluded by affection for her husband, spoke these words to her lord: (8)
Sukalā said:
"O beloved, according to dharma, I am your wife, a sharer in your merits;

O best of the twice-born, when shall this proximity of yours never have to be abandoned by me?
Taking refuge in your shadow, I shall perform the highest dharma. (10)

This [account] known as "Devoted to Her Husband" (Pativratā) destroys sins and grants a supreme state to women; in this world, she who is solely devoted to her husband shall be celebrated among virtuous women. 11.
For young women, a separate pilgrimage site is not auspicious without their husband; there is nothing in this world that bestows happiness, nor grants heaven and liberation. (12)
O best of beings, know that the right foot of the Lord is Prayāga, and his left foot is Puṣkara; this is what a woman should assign.
From bathing with the water from his feet, that merit is fully produced;

He is the sustainer consisting of all sacred fords, the Lord composed of all merit;

Indeed, by serving the master alone, one attains that very fruit which would otherwise result from undertaking pilgrimages to excellent sacred sites such as Gayā and others. (16)
One obtains that very fruit through service to one's husband;

For there is no separate duty for these women apart from service to their husbands;

"Relying upon your shadow, I shall come; it shall not be otherwise.

"Having observed your form, character, virtue, devotion, as well as your age," (19)
Having considered his extreme delicacy, Kṛkala spoke thus again and again:

Her beauty would be destroyed by the agitation of cold and heat;

She who occupies my left side is my place of comfort, O fair-faced one;

"I shall surely lead him to that sacred ford, and I alone shall go there as well," having reflected thus for a moment, by the high-souled Kṛkala.

During the auspicious times for divine rites and at holy moments,

Entering the fire is better, and the destruction of the body is better;

"People on the surface of the earth say that she is undoubtedly a woman of loose character; therefore, O noble ones, listen to me regarding her who has been separated from her husband. (81)

The forty-second chapter.
The friends said:

O illustrious one, what has been spoken by you is indeed the truth. ||1||
Sukalā said:
In Ayodhyā there was a great king, an expert in dharma;

O great king, that lord of the earth, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, married her, who was the daughter of the Sudevas, free from defects, and devoted to truthful conduct.

That tiger among kings always sported with his beloved wife;

Having seen that invincible king of kings, who was devoted to hunting,

"O Lord of Men, this one who has arrived is indeed a meritorious king in the form of Keśava, superior to the universe.
O beloved, I shall engage in battle with that great-souled one through my prowess and valor. (23)
If I conquer the king by my own splendor, I shall enjoy incomparable fame upon the earth;
but if slain in battle by that best of heroes, I shall go to the world of Madhusūdana.
"By means of my own flesh and fat, the lord of the earth shall attain supreme satisfaction;
the deities of the auspicious realms shall become satiated, and for this reason, Vajrapāṇi has come here. (25)
Since death shall come from his very hand, and I shall obtain the supreme fame of being beautiful,
therefore I shall go from this earth, the ground of glory, to the world of Madhusūdana in the three worlds.
"I am not afraid in this way, nor am I agitated; I have gone to the mountain peaks.
Fearing sin, I have come here; having seen what dharma, O fair one, do I stand firm? (27)
I do not know what sin was previously accumulated in another birth, by which, through the accumulation of that evil, I have entered the womb of a sow. 28.
I shall wash away my terrible accumulation of past sins with hundreds of most fierce, sharp, and whetted arrows, which are like water. (29)
Taking your sons, grandsons, your daughter-in-law, and the children of your household, go to the mountain and abandon this delusion. (30)
Abandoning my attachment, this Hari has arrived;
from his hand I shall depart for that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Today, by destiny, the door of heaven has been flung open for me; I shall go to that most excellent, great celestial realm.
Sukalā said:
Having heard those words of that high-souled boar, his beloved friends then spoke to her as she was sinking in distress. (33)
The sow said:
"In that herd where you are the lord, adorned by sons and grandsons,
as well as by friends, brothers, and other kinsmen and husbands," (34)
Adorned by you alone, the herd shines;
O illustrious one, what will this herd become without you? (35)
Even by their own strength, the boars roar as they roam the mountain caves, and my children play there. (36)
Now, rendered fearless by your splendor, they will devour roots even in difficult places, in forest thickets, in villages, and in cities. (37)
O mighty-armed one, protected by your splendor, men on this mountain do not feel intense fear even from lions. (38)
Abandoned by you, all these children, boys, and young men will become wretched, distressed, and senseless. (39)
Fools perceive happiness as something that always exists on the path;
yet, like a woman deprived of her husband, it does not truly shine with beauty.
Adorned with divine ornaments of every kind, along with retinues, jeweled garments, and [accompanied by] fathers, mothers, and brothers. ||41||
She appeared to her mother-in-law, father-in-law,
and others like a night deprived of the moon or a family deprived of its son, for she was bereft of her husband.
Just as a house devoid of a lamp never shines at all, so too, O Giver of Joy, this herd does not shine without you. 43.
A mortal devoid of proper conduct is like an animal lacking knowledge; just as a king is not at all splendid when deprived of his mantra, so too is this [person] not at all splendid. 44.
Just as a boat on the vast ocean does not shine without a fisherman,
so too a caravan does not shine without its leader.
O high-minded one, just as an army does not shine without its commander-in-chief, so too this army of boars does not shine without you. (46)
Deprived of the Veda, he will become as wretched as a twice-born man who has lost his sacred knowledge;
for you are departing after having placed the burden of your household upon me. (47)
Knowing that death is easily attained,
yet having made no such vow, O beloved Lord, I am unable to sustain my life-breaths without you.
O high-minded one, whether in heaven, on earth, or even in hell, I shall experience it together with you alone; I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
