Or else, O sonless one, having taken up this excellent herd of grandsons, let us two go to that very place which is difficult for the leader of the herd to reach, yet easy to traverse. (50)
Having abandoned the desire for life, one goes forth into the forest;
what gain is seen there that is not even found at the time of death? (51)
Vārāha said:
You do not know the true dharma of heroes; listen now.
For a hero seeking battle must go before another hero and make his request. (52)
"Give me this wealth; I have come seeking battle in a conflict.
When a man does not grant a challenge for battle that has been requested by another," 53.
O beloved, listen: whether out of lust, greed, fear, or delusion, one shall dwell for a thousand yugas in the hell named Kumbhīpāka.
For Kṣatriyas, battle is the supreme duty; it must be waged, of this there is no doubt.
That battle must indeed be fought by one who has gone to the field of combat.
There he conquered the supreme Lord Tuṣpara, who was endowed with fame and renown;
fighting with great fearlessness and manliness, he struck him down.
O beloved, listen: he attains the world of heroes and enjoys divine pleasures as the lord for twenty-one thousand years.
He shall dwell in the world of heroes and be honored by the conduct of the gods;
this hero has arrived as a son of Manu, of this there is no doubt. (58)
"Requesting battle, he must certainly be granted combat by me;
for this eternal guest of war has arrived, possessing the form of Viṣṇu. (59)
"O auspicious one, you must perform the act of war in the form of hospitality.
The sow said:
"When war must be waged by you against that high-souled king..."
Then, having spoken thus, she hurriedly summoned her beloved sons and asked, "O sons, what kind of asceticism do you see in me? (61)
He said: "O sons, listen to my words!
A guest of war has arrived, the eternal one whose form is Viṣṇu. (62)
I must go forth to that place where he will go;
as long as this protector remains, he shall be the guardian of you all.
Go far away to a distant, inaccessible mountain cave;
live there happily, avoiding these greedy hunters. (64)
I must go to that very place where he intends to go;
this brother of yours, the best among you, shall provide protection for the herd.
"All these paternal uncles are your protectors;
O good sons, all of you depart far away from here into the sky. (66)
The sons said:
"This is indeed the best of mountains, abounding in roots, fruits, and water; for whom could there be fear? Indeed, there is a life of happiness here."
"Indeed, this terrifying thing was spoken by you two quite unexpectedly; therefore, O Mother, tell us the true reason for it right here."
The sow said:
"This most fierce king, who is like the very form of Time (Kāla), has arrived;
hunting for sport, he has killed many deer in the forest. (69)
O dear sons, this invincible and mighty Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu, will seize [the kingdom]; this time has come far advanced. (70)
The sons said:
"He who departs, abandoning his mother and father, is a man of sinful mind; he falls into a most fierce and terrible hell. (71)
Having drunk his mother’s meritorious milk, he becomes nourished yet devoid of compassion;
having abandoned both mother and father, he departs as one utterly weak. (72)
One goes here to the pus-filled hell, crowded with worms and foul odors;
therefore, one should not abandon one's mother or one's guru even in this very place.
Thus, a despondency born of their concern for dharma and artha arose within them;
having formed a battle array, they all stood there, filled with military power and splendor.
Possessed of daring and enthusiasm, they beheld the king’s son;
endowed with manly prowess, they then sported there as if in a forest.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the Legend of Vena, within the Life of Sukalā, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||42||
(43) Chapter Forty-Three.
Sukalā said:
Thus all those boars stood ready for battle;
and the hunters remained positioned in front of the king who stood before them.
Resorting to the peak of the Mahāvarāha mountain, the king of mountains,
he remains there, having formed a military array with a great multitude of followers.
O King, the boar Kapila—possessing thick, stout limbs, large tusks, and a massive mouth; unbearable and roaring most terrifyingly—[advanced]. (3)
Not seeing them, O great king, the powerful son of Aṇu, having heard those words of theirs who were dwelling in the groves of śāla and tāla trees, [acted]. ||4||
"Seize the heroic Varāha! Pierce him who is arrogant in his strength!
Thus spoke the powerful son of Manu, whose body hair stood on end.
Then all those hunters, infatuated by the intoxication of the hunt,
equipped themselves with sharp weapons and set out together with their dogs.
Overcome with great joy, the mighty king of kings mounted his horse,
accompanied by a well-disciplined fourfold army.
He arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā on Meru, the most excellent of great mountains,
which was strewn with jewels and minerals and adorned with various kinds of trees.
Sukalā said:
That king of mountains shines, exceedingly lofty and composed of a mass of rays that are the abode of power;
having reached the very sky itself, it is beautified by the movements of various wild animals.

One who beholds the mountain, whose pure rocky surfaces and plateaus are everywhere washed white by the spray of droplets resembling pearls—emerging from the waves and ripples on the banks of the broad, stainless Ganges flowing for a league—is endowed with great splendor. (10)

Surrounded by gods, *cāraṇas*, and *kinnaras*; by *gandharvas*, *vidyādharas*, *siddhas*, and throngs of *apsarases*; by hosts of sages, lords of *nāgas*, and *vidyādharas*; it shines with sandalwood trees, many *candana* trees, *sarala*, *śāla*, and *tamāla* trees; with mountains, *rudrākṣa* trees, dense clouds that grant excellent *siddhis*, and *kalpa* trees. (11)
It is adorned with celestial palaces variegated by various elements, embellished with diverse jewels, and featuring golden pillars and balconies.
It shines with divine coconut groves and betel-nut trees, adorned with divine punnāga and bakula trees and clusters of plantain trees. (13)
The mountain was likewise adorned with *puṣpaka* flowers, *pāṭala* trees, and *ketaka* blossoms,
as well as with canopies of various flowering creepers and *padmaka* trees.
Adorned with various trees bearing many-colored, beautiful flowers,
it was filled with celestial trees and possessed surfaces of crystalline stone.
The mountain was inhabited by yogis, lords of yogis, and perfected beings (siddhas), and it was made beautiful by delightful waterfalls and many springs.
It is graced by confluences where the river currents meet with joyful splashing,
and by lakes, ponds, and pools bearing pure water.
The king of mountains shines alone, standing with its peaks, adorned as if by śarabhas, tigers, and herds of deer. ||18||
With great elephants, wild buffaloes, and vast uru-beasts, as well as with many divine beings, that king of mountains shines eternally. (19)
The heroic lord of Ayodhyā, Ikṣvāku, the delighter of the Manu lineage,
was accompanied by that noble wife and by a fourfold army.
In front, brave hunters and swift-moving dogs come toward where the powerful and heroic boar dwells together with his wife. (21)
Then, protected by many elders and children,
he took refuge on the ground of Mount Meru and likewise on the level banks of the Gaṅgā.
Sukalā said: The Boar, filled with joy, spoke to that very dear one:
"O beloved, behold, the powerful lord of Kośala has arrived. (23)
"Aiming at me, the highly wise king is engaged in the sport of hunting;
I shall indeed wage a battle that will bring great joy to both gods and asuras. (24)
Then the king, possessed of great splendor, bow in hand and arrow in grasp,
spoke with great joy to Sudevā, whose very body was the embodiment of truth and righteousness.
Behold, my dear, this mighty boar of great strength, roaring and accompanied by its herd, which is unbearable for hunters. (26)
"O beloved, this very day I shall slay him with sharp, excellent arrows;
let the great hero Himavat come to me for battle. (27)
Having spoken thus to his beloved wife, the hunter addressed these words to the hunters:
"O great heroes, just as you are brave, send forth that boar! (28)
Then those heroes, endowed with strength, splendor, and prowess, having been dispatched, rushed forward roaring with their strength, splendor, and prowess. ||29||
Having all returned to the island by the force of the wind,
those forest-dwellers pierced him with nets of sharp arrows.
Then, with various weapons and missiles, [they struck] the Boar-form, who possessed the appearance of a hero. ||31||
Sukalā said:
Just as clouds rain down upon the great mountain, so do arrows and javelins released by hunters fall upon the earth;
likewise, the leader of the herd, along with his followers, having been struck by those who deal firm blows, was utterly defeated and fled from the field of battle. (32)
Carrying his sons, grandsons, and kinsmen, he would take them to the highest state; yet all those greedy hunters, struck by his tusks in battle, fell down.
With their feet and hands, they fell as he stood there, whirling with speed; the boar saw that very hunter approaching while he was roaring. (33)
Struck by the tip of his tusk and destroyed by his own splendor,
that King of the Yakṣas went to the battle with his entire army.
The enraged lord of the boars, possessing great power, having violently terrified the protector of the Ikṣvākus,
engaged in battle with that Ikṣvāku in the forest, filled with the joy of combat.
Furthermore, O King, that boar, skilled in combat, eager for battle,
and agitating the earth in his wrath, strikes with the tip of his snout and his very sharp teeth and claws at that stainless lord of the earth out of pride in his roar.
Having recognized Viṣṇu’s prowess, the son of Manu, his hair standing on end with joy, [spoke]. ||36||
Beholding that boar-like prowess, which was incomparable even to Yama, the lord of the gods (Indra) reflected in his mind upon the enemy of the gods (Viṣṇu) as the supreme boar;

and seeing him possessed of great strength, he quickly dispatched a vast army equipped for the destruction of the enemy. Elephants and chariots were sent forth with great speed, carrying excellent arrows, swords, *bhuśuṇḍis*, and mallets. Let them seize him by force, seizing him again and again! 37.
Hunters with nooses in their hands were devouring [the creatures] here and there; horses and elephants, having fled, stood there unobstructed as they bent down.
In some places he was not seen, and in some places he was clearly seen; in some places he would display fear, and in some places he would trample down horses.
Having crushed the heroic warriors, that one invincible in battle, his eyes red with rage and difficult to withstand, let out a roar.
Seeing him—who was difficult to conquer even in battle, possessed of a massive body, and emitting a roar like a cloud—the heroic lord of Kosala [prepared for combat]. (41)
Roaring through the battle, the fearless hero moves about and sports with his own splendor;
like lightning in the midst of clouds, his curved fang shines as it gleams forth.
Having seen it thus, Manu’s son pierced the boar with sharp arrows,
striking each one individually with celestial weapons.
The lord of men said: "O brave soldiers, why do you not seize him here with your might?
Fight him there with sharp, keen arrows! ||44||
Having heard those words, even though the high-souled one was angry, all those soldiers then advanced for battle. (45)
Surrounded on all sides by many thousands of warriors standing in battle, they pierced the boar in the fray.

Pierced on the vast battlefield by the wheels and by the nets of arrows from those excellent warriors, that great and invincible host was struck down by them—some with blows from the wheels and others with the falling of thunderbolts. ||47||
Then, filled with rage, he set out for battle along with his men and his boars; having completely severed the snares, he advanced together with the great boars, drenched by streams of blood. (48)
The hero struck with his four tusks at the horses of the enemy and cut down the elephants;
with the sharp tips of his own fangs, he brought down the heroic foot-soldiers through his wrathful state.
Enraged, he struck the trunk of that elephant; and being delighted, he [the elephant] trampled with his toe-nails the soldiers who had already been slain.
Then all those boars and hunters, their eyes red with rage, engaged in combat with one another, having made a solemn vow of battle.
Boars were killed by hunters, and hunters too were killed by boars;
they lay fallen upon the ground, drenched in blood and smeared with gore.
Having abandoned their lives, the hunters were killed by the boars and fell upon the battlefield;
the pigs died there, and the dogs likewise gave up their breaths.
Wherever on the ground the hunters of deer lay dead,
there were many boars fallen by the blows of swords, O King.
O best of kings, some were lost or slain, while others remained stationed in difficult terrains, in thickets,
on mountain peaks, and in caves.
And some hunters, their tusks severed by boars, gave up their lives and went to heaven, even as they were being torn to pieces limb by limb. (56)
Snare-traps, nets, snares, and likewise pits and ravines,
as well as channels, lay fallen upon the ground everywhere, level on all sides.
Accompanied by his sole wife, Vārāha stands there,
arrogant in his strength, for the sake of battle with his fifty-seven grandsons.
Then that sow spoke again to her mate:
"Go, my dear, together with these young ones. (59)
The delighted boar spoke thus to his beloved who was distraught:
"Where shall I go? I am broken; there is no place for me upon the surface of the earth."
"O highly fortunate one, if I am lost, the herd of boars will perish;
the hog drinks the water between two lions. (61)
In the midst of two boars, this lion drinks water as if he were alone;
thus, such supreme strength is seen even among those of the boar species.
Therefore, I shall surely destroy it when I depart having broken [it]; for I know, O illustrious one, that dharma bestows manifold blessings. (63)
Why does one who fights perish out of greed or even fear? By abandoning the holy ford of battle, he becomes a sinner; of this there is no doubt. (64)
Having seen the array of sharpened weapons, he experiences joy;
having plunged into the ocean of the immortals, he reaches the further shore of the sacred ford.
He shall eternally go to the world of Viṣṇu and uplift all men;
how then could I, having failed in that vow, go [to hell] like one who has broken his word? ||66||
Having seen a battle crowded with weapons and bringing joy to great heroes, he departs filled with delight; hear now the fruit of his merit.
O beloved, listen: for one who, out of greed, flees from battle and returns home broken, a great bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs at every step.
One born of a woman is said to be "born of a woman" because he reveals the faults of his mother;
here [in this world] are sacrifices, sacred fords, and gods of great majesty. (69)
The sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas behold that wonder:
how this triple world exists through the manifestation of the Hero. (70)
All the inhabitants of the three worlds behold him broken in battle;
they curse that pitiless sinner and laugh again and again.
The King of Dharma will undoubtedly show him the miserable realms;
he shall face him in battle and drink the blood from his own head.
O fair-faced one, when that hero conquers his enemies in battle, he enjoys the fruit of the horse-sacrifice and proceeds to the world of Indra.
Then, without a doubt, he shall obtain mastery, fortune, and various enjoyments;
provided that he gives up his life there, facing forward and without any support. (74)
One should go to the supreme state and obtain a divine maiden as a lord;
such is the Dharma I know—how then can I, being broken, depart? (75)
Without hesitation, he will engage in battle here with no doubt, together with the wise King Ikṣvāku, the son of Manu. (76)
"O fair-faced one, bestow happiness upon me by taking this *ḍimba* [flower] and becoming my husband.
Having heard his words, she said: "I am bound by your fetters. (77)
O beloved, O giver of honor, I shall give up my life before you, together with these sons of mine known as Sneha, Māna, and Rasa, who are my playthings for pleasure. (78)
Thus, having conversed with one another and desiring each other's welfare, these two,
having resolved upon battle, gazed at their enemies.
The heroic lord of Kosala, that Ikṣvāku of great intelligence. ||80||
Just as a cloud thunders in the sky during the pleasant seasons of the rainy season with flashes of lightning,
even so that best of kings roared and challenged him to battle with the tips of his hooves.
The high-souled hero, endowed with manly prowess, beheld that single boar roaring aloud;
then that steadfast warrior, possessed of the speed of a running horse, charged directly toward it. (82)
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||43||
The forty-fourth chapter. Sukalā said:
Having seen her own army, which was difficult to restrain, defeated by that Durdhara;
The king became violently enraged toward the cruel and unbearable boar. ||1||
Taking up his bow with speed, he discharged an arrow resembling the fire of cosmic destruction and rushed toward him on his horse.
The leader of the boar herd beheld the king, the slayer of enemies, endowed with supreme prowess, mounted upon the back of a horse, as he advanced toward him upon the surface of the battlefield. (3)
When he was struck by a sharp arrow and fell at the foot of the king’s horse,
that excellent monkey, his mind intent on speed, leaped over him right there with fierce velocity.

The horse, distressed along with its rider, its movement obstructed by the piercing of the nails and struck by the goad, fell to the ground; the king, his mouth struck, became as light as a blade of grass. ||5||

That leader of the herd, standing in the midst of the forest, was indeed struck with a mace by the king as he pursued him with the speed of horses from Kośala, while the sound of his own species roared like thunder.
Having cast off his own body, it is indeed better that he has come here to the abode of Hari for his own welfare. ||7||
Having fought a battle in the conflict with that king, the king of the boars fell to the ground; and then the best of gods rained down excellent flowers like clouds pouring forth rain.
Above him, a well-formed mass of flowers rises like the fragrance of *saṃtānaka* trees;
and the gods, being highly gratified, shower down sandalwood mixed with saffron. (9)
O King, as he was being reflected upon by the king with a concentrated mind, that four-armed one also appeared;
possessing divine garments, ornaments, and a divine form, he shone with his own splendor like the sun in the sky. ||10||
When he had departed to heaven by means of a divine vehicle, being well-honored by the gods and the king of the gods,
he once again became the king of the gandharvas, having abandoned his own body right here on earth.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," within the Legend of Vena in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
(45) Chapter Forty-Five. Sukalā said:
Then all the hunters set out toward the sow;
they were brave, fierce, and terrifying, arriving with nooses in their hands. ||1||
Then, having made four *toḍis* and remaining in the *śūkarī* posture, she saw her husband killed in that great battle by Kuṭumbena Samaṅka. ||2||
Thinking thus, his father attained him; honored by sages and gods, that great-souled one went to heaven through this heroic deed.
"By this very path you shall go to heaven while your husband remains alive.
Having made this firm resolve, she then reflected upon her sons.
When these four young sons of mine, who are like pillars of the lineage, live on, it will be for the sake of this great-souled hero Kola. ||5||
"By what means can I make my sons endowed with enmity?"— becoming intent on this thought, she beheld the mountain pass.
Having made that path very wide for the purpose of exiting,
she, having become well-resolved, reflected upon her sons.
He spoke to those greatly deluded princes:
"O sons, go quickly while I remain here. (8)
"Among them, I am the eldest son; how could I go [away] abandoning my mother out of a greed for life? Alas, O mother, my life is well-lived! (9)
"I shall avenge my father's enmity and slay my enemies in battle;
having taken you and my three younger brothers, we shall overcome Durgakandara."
That person of sinful intellect who departs after abandoning his father and mother goes directly to hell, which is teeming with millions of worms.
Afflicted by great sorrow, she said to him: "O son, how shall I go on living after abandoning you? O my sons, I am a woman of great sin; come with me."
The three younger ones, however, having reached the mountain forest,
went to the field of battle while those very [others] looked on.
Roaring again and again with their splendor and the strength of their vital breath,
those two then reached the courageous hunters who were waiting below.
O King, even though they were sent by that difficult path, those three remained there,
having blocked the way— those two, the mother and her son.
Then the hunters arrived, bearing swords, arrows, and bows;
they struck [them] with sharp javelins, spears, and pestles.
Placing his mother behind him, the son fought with them;
some were struck down by his fangs, while others were killed by his snout.
The brave ones struck him with the tips of their hooves as they fell from their chariots;
that boar fought in battle when seen by the high-souled king.
Having learned from his father that he was a hero, the son of Anasūyā, possessed of great splendor and majesty, stood facing him with arrows in hand.
Struck by the high-souled king with a sharp arrow resembling a crescent moon,
his chest pierced, he fell to the earth.
The boar, who was capable of enduring a fall from a thousand *mamas* onto the earth, reached a state of supreme delusion regarding his son and went up onto him. (21)
O King, by her, those heroic hunters were struck down upon the earth with blows from her snout; many of those brave men fell, some dead and others nearly dead.
Then that sow, having emerged like a malevolent *kṛtyā* that instills great terror, began to rout that vast army with her tusks. ||23||
Then the queen spoke to him, who resembled the son of the king of gods:
"O King, by this [child] alone was your great army indeed destroyed. (24)
"Why do you disregard her? Tell me the reason for that. The great king said to her, "I will not kill this woman. (25)
The killing of a woman is indeed seen as a great transgression by the gods;
therefore, one should not kill a woman, nor should I send anyone away. (26)
"O beautiful one, I am afraid of sin for the sake of this reason of non-attention.
Having spoken thus, the king, the lord of the earth, then fell silent. (27)
Then a hunter named Ujjharṇa saw a female boar who was causing them unbearable distress, even for great warriors. (28)
Indeed, by a sharp arrow discharged with great force, she was pierced;
and by that arrow which had become stuck [in her], she was drenched in blood.
Attaining a state of radiant haste, she was overwhelmed by the glory of heroism;
moreover, in that battle, the Jhārjhara drum was struck again and again with her beak.
Struck by that falling torrent of spray, she fell down, shattered as if struck by a sharp sword. ||31||
Even while gasping for breath,
overwhelmed by fainting and possessed by great suffering, she remained alive upon the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||45||
Chapter Forty-Six. Sukalā said:
Having seen a sow, devoted to her young, fallen down while breathing her last;
Overcome with compassion for Sudeva, he went toward her who was thus distressed. ||1||
He sprinkled her face with cool water,
and then [he sprinkled] all her limbs as well— she who was suffering and radiant with the marks of battle.
With meritorious cool water, she said, "Be consecrated";
she spoke in a human voice, melodious and pleasing to the king.
O Goddess, may you be well; for by your consecration, my accumulation of sins has been destroyed through contact with and the sight of you. (4)
Having heard those great words endowed with a wondrous appearance, [he said:
"This is marvelous; I have seen this, and you have spoken these words of well-being. (5)
This woman, though belonging to the species of beasts, speaks with great clarity;
she utters for me the most excellent Sanskrit, complete with its vowels and consonants.
Filled with both joy and wonder, having committed a supreme act of daring, that illustrious lady, remaining there, spoke these words to her husband: ||7||
"Behold, O King, this unprecedented and great refined speech she utters;
though she has entered the womb of a beast, she speaks just as a human would."
Then the king, the best among those possessing all knowledge,
heard that which was wonderful and of wondrous form, the like of which had never been seen or heard by him.
Then the king spoke to that Sudeva, his beloved wife; he asked her, "O lady of auspicious limbs, who is this woman who will belong to you? (10)
Having heard the king's words, he then questioned the sow: "Who will you become, O blessed lady? Much that is wondrous is seen in you. (11)
"Though you have entered the womb of an animal, O Vaibhāṣika, you speak human speech; it is eloquent and endowed with wisdom—this must be the result of your former deeds. (12)
And what was this great dharma of my husband, this high-souled warrior, by whose heroic prowess he has gone to heaven? (13)
"Tell me everything concerning yourself and your husband, following from the past.
Having spoken thus, the illustrious beloved of the king fell silent.
The sow said:
"O auspicious one, if you ask me about this great-souled one, I shall tell you all of his life story and his former deeds. (15)
This Gandharva, Eṣa-mahāprājña, is an expert in song;
he is named Raṅgavidyādharas and is proficient in the meaning of all the scriptures. ||16||
Resorting to that Meru, the best of excellent mountains, beautiful with its cascading waterfalls, the highly resplendent Pulastya, the most eminent of sages, [dwelt there]. (17)
The radiant Vidyādhara, having arrived there of his own accord, O Great Lord, performed penance with a heart free from guile. (18)
O lady of beautiful smiles, having taken refuge on that best of mountains, she then practiced singing with excellent tone, endowed with both musical notes and rhythm.
Having heard his song, the sage’s mind was moved from meditation;
while singing, he spoke thus to that Vidyādhara.
O learned one, the gods are enchanted by this divine song of yours, sung with such beautiful melody, great merit, and perfect rhythmic measure; it cannot be otherwise.
O observer of noble vows, my mind has been drawn away from meditation by this song, which is accompanied by a state of absorption and joined with a fainting-like rapture.
"Abandoning this place, go to another place.
The Gītavidyādhara said: "Why should I go to another place, when I am already possessed of the song of self-knowledge?"
He who always bestows happiness upon others never causes suffering to anyone;
by this divine song, all the deities are gratified. (24)
O twice-born one, the sound of singing was also brought there by Śambhu;
singing is said to contain all aesthetic flavors and bestows the bliss of song. (25)
All the aesthetic sentiments (rasas), beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), are established through song;
even the four supreme Vedas attain their full splendor through song. 26.
All the deities attain satisfaction through song and not otherwise;
thus, you who revile song would be causing me to falter. (27)
"O illustrious one, this injustice is clearly seen by you.
Pulastya said:
"What you have spoken today is true; it is the meaning of the Gītā, which bestows great merit. (28)
Listen to my words and abandon pride, O high-minded one! I do not censure what is sung by me; I shall not speak otherwise than this. (29)
These fourteen sciences, when unified, bestow existence upon living beings; they lead to perfection for those whose minds are unwavering.
Austerity, as well as mantras, are successfully accomplished through one-pointed meditation;
likewise, the great multitude of the senses is considered to be overcome by means of *aloma*. (31)
Having agitated the mind from that very meditation, he leads the self forcefully toward all objects of the senses; of this there is no doubt. (32)
Where there is neither sound nor form, and no young woman dwells, there indeed the sages go for the very purpose of accomplishing their asceticism. (33)
This song is sacred and bestows great happiness upon you;
we do not see [any danger], O Hero, as we remain established in the forest. (34)
"Let us go elsewhere; let us not proceed to this place.
Gītavighādhara said:
"By which great-souled one has the entire host of the senses been conquered? (35)
O Great-minded One, having heard a sound or seen a form, that yogi is called a "conqueror" (sajayin), a "hero" (vīra), and an "accomplisher" (sādhaka). 36.
O brave one, you have indeed departed from Ayodhyā through asceticism;
for you are devoid of splendor because your senses have been conquered.
Even in heaven, my song possesses no power to overcome [them];
all those of inferior prowess avoid the forest, of this there is no doubt. (38)
This forest region of the brahmin is common to all, without a doubt;
it belongs to the gods and to all living beings just as much as it does to you. (39)
"How can I go, having abandoned this most excellent forest? You may go; as for me, let it be what must be, and not otherwise. (40)
When the Vidyadhara Gītavidya had thus addressed that Brahmin,
the sage then heard his reply.
The wise one reflected: "What good deed might I perform? Then, having practiced forbearance, that best of the twice-born went to another place. (42)
The righteous-souled one practiced austerity, always remaining in a yogic posture, having completely abandoned desire, anger, delusion, and likewise greed. (43)
Restraining all the senses with an equanimous mind, the yogi Pulastya, the best of sages, remained thus established at that time. (44)
Sukalā said: When that illustrious Pulastya, the bull among sages, had departed, along with that Vidyādhara who was commanded by Kāla, [she remained there]. (45)
He reflected for a very long time: "Because of my fear, he was not seen; where has he gone? Where does he stay? And what is he doing, and how? (46)
Having learned that the son of the Lotus-born One was dwelling alone in penance,
he went to his unsurpassed hermitage in the form of a boar.
O beautiful lady, seeing that high-souled one seated upon his throne, enveloped in a blaze of splendor, she caused no agitation in that brahmin.
If one should surely assault a brahmin with the tip of his snout through wicked behavior, the Great King, recognizing him as a beast, forgives that misdeed. 49.
Having first passed urine, he then voids excrement;
he dances and plays there, falling down and rising up again. (50)
O King, having recognized the beast and abandoned it by that sage, it once again returned in that very form. 51.
Then, with a loud, boisterous laugh, he laughed once more;
yet there, he wept and sang a song in a beautiful voice. (52)
O King, having seen the conduct of that brahmin who had arrived there as a master of the sciences of the *vidyādharas*, it would not have been otherwise for Ghoṇira. (53)
Having known his conduct, he would surely drive me away;
having recognized this beast as one who has not abandoned me, he is wicked and utterly merciless. (54)
Knowing him thus to be the lowest of the Gandharvas, that great-souled one, the tiger among sages, became enraged; and the high-minded one cursed him.
"Since you have caused me to wander even in the form of a pig, therefore you shall go to the most sinful womb of a sow. (56)
Cursed by that brahmin as well, he went to the god Purandara;
O lady of beautiful countenance, having approached that high-souled one, he spoke to him with humility. (57)
"Listen to my words: your task has been accomplished by me.
For that bull among sages was indeed performing a most formidable penance. (58)
Therefore, having been moved and agitated by me through the power of my asceticism, that brahmin cursed me and destroyed my divine form. (59)
Protect Śakra, who has entered the womb of a beast, right now;
having learned the true conduct of him and that Vidyādhara Gīta.
Having gone together with him, Indra addressed that sage:
"O Lord, grant me your favor; you are a knower of the perfections, O best of the twice-born. (61)
"May you forgive me, O best of sages; please grant me release from this curse.
Thus entreated by Mahendra, the Brahmin, his mind filled with joy, replied: ||62||
Pulastya said:
"O Lord of the Gods, you must indeed forgive me for these words;
there shall be a son of Manu, a great king of immense strength."
The righteous-souled Ikṣvāku, the protector of all dharmas, shall be his death;
from his hand, his own death shall come to pass.
Then he will regain his own body; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has the entire account of the boar been related to you.
I shall also declare my own [transgression]; listen indeed along with your husband, as to what terrible sin was committed by me, a sinful woman, in the past. (66)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||46||
The forty-seventh chapter.
Sukalā said:
Then she spoke to that female pig, Sudevā, whose every limb was beautiful.
Since you have entered the womb of an animal, how indeed can you speak in the refined language of Sanskrit? ||1||
"Tell me, from where did such great wisdom arise? O auspicious one, how do you know the life-story of the Lord as if it were your own? (2)
The sow said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I have been robbed of my senses by the delusion of being a beast;
struck by swords and arrows, I have fallen upon the surface of the earth. (3)
O fair-faced one, I am distressed by fainting and deprived of consciousness;
O beautiful lady, I have been consecrated by you with your meritorious hand.
Indeed, when I was sprinkled with the cool, meritorious water held in your hand, my delusion vanished instantly while I remained here.
Just as darkness departs through the splendors of light so that it may never return,
even so, O auspicious one, has my sin vanished through your consecration.
"O lady of beautiful limbs, through your grace I have obtained ancient knowledge;
O auspicious one, I have realized that I shall attain a meritorious state. (7)
Listen, O auspicious lady, as I shall relate my own former history— the many evil deeds that were committed by me, a sinful woman.
In the great land known as Kaliṅga, there was a city named Śrīpura, filled with all perfections and inhabited by people of the four castes. ||9||
There lived a certain twice-born man known as Vasudatta,
who was always devoted to the conduct of a Brahmin and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
A knower of the Vedas, a knower of the unknown, pure, virtuous, and wealthy;
filled with riches and grain, he was adorned with sons and grandsons. ||11||
O auspicious lady with a beautiful face, I was adorned by her with ornaments and decorations, along with her sons, brothers, kinsmen, and husbands.
The one of great intelligence performed this for the Sudevas;
O you of great intelligence, I am also eternally dear to that father of mine.
Born with a form unparalleled and incomparable, such as there has never been, I am a woman of lovely smiles, intoxicated by the pride of my beauty and youth. (14)
Then, seeing me—a maiden of beautiful form adorned with every ornament—all the people and my circle of kinsmen [were struck with wonder]. (15)
O fair-faced one, they were entreating me alone for the sake of marriage;
though I was requested by all the twice-born, my father did not give me away.
And because of affection, O illustrious one, that great-minded man was utterly deluded;
at that time, I was not given away by him, his high-souled father. (17)
"Youth has arrived for me, endowed with the state of childhood;
seeing my form to be such as this, my mother is deeply distressed. (18)
Then he said to my father: "Why is the girl not being given? To which virtuous twice-born man, to which high-souled Brāhmaṇa, shall she be given? (19)
When Dehikanyā had reached her youth, O highly fortunate one,
that best of brahmins, Vasudatta, spoke thus to that most excellent of the twice-born.
O highly fortunate mother, let my words be heard:
O lady of excellent complexion, I have been deluded by great infatuation regarding my daughter. (21)
O auspicious lady, listen: I shall become a householder Brahmin;
I will give my daughter to him as a son-in-law, of this there is no doubt. (22)
"She is as dear to me as my own life, O Sudeva; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did my grandfather speak for my sake, bestowing all his wealth upon me. (23)
Born in the family of Kauśika, he was proficient in all branches of knowledge;
endowed with the virtues of brahmins, he was possessed of good character, merit, and purity.
He was accomplished in the study of the Vedas, reciting them with a beautiful voice;
he had come to the door for alms, being destitute of both father and mother. (25)
Seeing that form approaching, the high-minded father looked at it and said to him: "Who are you, and what will you become? (26)
"What is that? Tell me his name, family, lineage, and conduct.
Having heard these words of his father, he spoke to Vasudatta. (27)
Born into the lineage of Kauśika, I am a master of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
my name is Śivaśarman, and I am bereft of both father and mother. (28)
I have four other brothers who have mastered the Vedas;
thus is my lineage described, for conduct is born of one's family. (29)
Thus everything was related by Śivaśarman to his father,
when he had arrived on an auspicious lunar mansion, a favorable day, and a propitious moment.
"O fortunate one, I have been given by my father; give me to that very Brahmin.
I shall dwell alone in my father's house together with that high-souled man. (31)
At that time, I, a sinner, did not serve my husband at all;
I was utterly deluded by pride and the great wealth of my father and mother. (32)
O auspicious one, when did I ever perform service for him—whether by massaging his limbs, by showing affection, or by speaking kind words—with a sense of pleasure or love? (33)
O inauspicious one, this [child] was always gazed upon by me with a cruel mind and sinful intent; indeed, through association with unchaste women, I have come to possess that very nature. (34)
"Wherever I go, I do not act for the benefit of my mother, father, husband, or brothers. (35)
Having thus seen my misdeed, my husband, the highly intelligent Aśivaśarman, out of affection for his circle of parents-in-law [acted]. //36//
She said nothing at all to me, yet she forgave my misdeed; though I was restrained by my family, I alone am the great sinner.
Having recognized the virtue and goodness of Śivaśarman, my father, mother, and all [the others] were no longer afflicted by sorrow on account of my sin. (38)
Seeing his own misdeed, the husband went out from his house;
having abandoned that region and this village, he departed from there. (39)
"O Father, having heard that my husband has departed from here, he is now filled with anxiety;
his soul is pained by my sorrow, just as one is afflicted by a disease. (40)
My mother said this to her husband, who was oppressed by grief:
"Why do you worry about one thing while my own suffering lies before me? (41)
Vasudatta said to this mother of mine:
"O beloved, listen; the brahmin who was my son-in-law has come here after abandoning his daughter. (42)
"This woman is of evil conduct, merciless, and a doer of wicked deeds;
by her, indeed, the high-minded Śivaśarman has been abandoned. (43)
Out of courtesy toward his entire family, this high-minded and virtuous brahmin does not speak even a single word of reproach against me. (44)
He dwells with a gentle disposition; he neither censures nor reviles Sudevā, even though she is a sinful spy; indeed, he possesses the intellect of a wise man. 45.
"O dweller in the house, this woman will become the destroyer of the wicked and the lineage of the Asuras; therefore, I shall abandon her and depart."
The Brāhmaṇī said:
"O you who desire a son, this defect in your daughter's character is unknown to you; she has been ruined by your delusion and affection. Listen now to her true nature. (47)
One should pamper the son until he is five years old;
thereafter, with the intent of training him, one should always discipline him, and not nourish him with delusion.
With baths, garments, foods to chew, foods to eat, and drinks—without a doubt—one should endow a virtuous son with whatever learning he desires. (49)
For the sake of virtue and training, he is always free from delusion and acts as a father;
yet, in his exclusive concern for protection and nourishment, delusion arises. (50)
One should not speak of his son's virtues; rather, one should disparage him day after day, constantly speaking of his harshness and tormenting him with such words. (51)
Just as one who is devoted to knowledge should constantly accomplish true learning, so too, having abandoned sin even by means of the pretext of pride, one should remain not far from it. 52.
Skillfulness constantly arises in learning and in excellent virtues;
moreover, a mother may strike her daughter, and a mother-in-law may strike her daughter-in-law.
If the guru should strike the disciple, then [the mantras] succeed; not otherwise.
Likewise, if the king should strike his wife or his minister. (54)
O Lord, one should strike a horse afflicted by disease with the proper measure day after day;
through the intent of training, horses succeed by being struck, but not by being merely pampered.
Without a doubt, this [woman] has always been rendered helpless by you, along with the excellent brahmin Śivaśarman. (56)
O Mahāmati, a maiden has been lost by this man who acted without restraint;
listen to my words as to how long she should be kept in the house. 57.
As long as she has not reached the age of eight years and does not possess strength, whatever sin a daughter commits while residing in her father’s house, [she alone bears]. (58)
Both parents, as well as the ancestors, share in that sin;
therefore, a daughter who is capable [of giving birth] should not be kept in her father's house.
To whomever she has been given, she should nourish him in his home;
staying there, she should win over that virtuous man with devotion.
The family gains renown and the father lives in happiness; yet whatever sin she commits while staying there, the husband suffers for that sin. (61)
Remaining there constantly with her sons and grandsons,
she always attains fame through the excellent virtues of her daughter, O beloved.
Therefore, one should not keep a daughter-in-law with her husband in the house;
regarding this matter, there will be a Kāntī-tīthāsa (legend) which shall be heard.
O Great Lord, when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age had arrived,
[this occurred] for the heroic Ugrasena, the eldest of the Yadus.
O twice-born one, listen with a focused mind as I shall proclaim your life story. 65.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||47||
Chapter Forty-Eight.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
O best of kings, in the beautiful region of Mathurā, there was a supreme monarch.
There was a Yādava renowned as Ugrasena, a slayer of enemy heroes.
The king knows the true meaning of all phenomena, is a knower of the Vedas, learned, and powerful;
he is a giver, an enjoyer, a perceiver of virtues, and one who recognizes the qualities of others.
The wise one ruled the kingdom and protected his subjects according to dharma;
thus did that highly resplendent and powerful Ugrasena govern.
In the meritorious region of Vaidarbha lived the powerful Satyaketu;
his daughter was highly fortunate, lotus-eyed, and lotus-faced.
Named Padmāvatī, she was devoted to truth and righteousness;
endowed with the virtues of women, she was like a second Lakṣmī.
O King, the son of Ugrasena of Mathurā married the beautiful-eyed Sulocanā, who was radiant with the virtues of the Vaidarbha lineage and was the cause of his own truthfulness.
Together with her, that illustrious and powerful king enjoyed happiness;
exceedingly delighted by her virtues, he lived happily with her.
Out of affection and love for her, the charming Lord of Mathurā was infatuated;
O highly fortunate one, Padmāvatī became as dear to him as his own life.
Without her he did not eat; with her he would play;
without her he did not enjoy even the highest happiness. (9)
Thus, O best of the twice-born, those two supreme beings, possessing power that brought joy and filled with affection for one another, bestowed happiness and delight upon each other.
And King Satyaketu, O Indra among kings, remembered his daughter Padmāvatī;
the highly fortunate mother of that girl was deeply distressed. (11)
O best of the twice-born, the King of Vidarbha then respectfully dispatched messengers to Ugrasena, the foremost of men and kings, in Mathurā.
The heroic lord of Vidarbha, out of devotion and affection, spoke these words through a messenger to the great king Ugrasena, showing him compassion. (13)
"Satyaketu, O Great King, speaks of his own welfare and inquires after yours; he has thus questioned you. (14)
If you consider it right, O noble one, for the sake of affection, love, and what is beneficial, then send your daughter Padmāvatī to see me. (15)
"O illustrious one, send your beloved wife, who brings you joy;
O great king, she remains filled with longing and intense yearning for you. (16)
Then, having heard those words, Ugrasena, the best of kings,
with affection honored that high-souled Satyaketa as well.
Out of courtesy, O best of Brahmins, the powerful King Ugrasena sent his beloved wife Padmāvatī.
O lord of kings, Padmāvatī, sent by him, has gone to her own former home, filled with great joy because she is virtuous. 19.
Then Satyaparā, auspicious and beautiful, beheld her family led by her father;
she bowed her head at her father’s feet.
O best of the twice-born, when Mahārājā Padmāvatī had arrived,
the king, the lord of Vidarbha, was filled with great joy.
And through the increase in gifts and honors, as well as garments, ornaments, and decorations,
she lived happily even in her father’s house with Padmāvatī.
Accompanied by her friends, she moves about without hesitation;
she rejoices in that very same way as before. (23)
In the house, in the forest, by the ponds, and likewise in the palace, she again became like a young girl; shameless, she engaged in amorous conduct.
Free from fear, that highly fortunate and devoted wife always moved about together with her friends, filled with great joy. (25)
The happiness found in the home of one's father-in-law is difficult to obtain; knowing this, one should dwell with one's own wife, for at some point it will become like that. (26)
At that time, she—whose face was lovely and who was addicted to the sport of this delusive cultivation—was constantly accompanied by her friends in the forests and groves. (27)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Story of Sukalā," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 48 ||
The forty-ninth chapter.
The Brāhmaṇī said:
O highly fortunate one, once she went to that best of mountains.
Having seen the delightful forest adorned with groves of plantain trees. ||1||
With *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, as well as abundant coconut palms;
with betel nuts, citrons, oranges, and beautiful *jaṃbuka* fruits. (2)
It was adorned with various trees, including holy *caṃpaka*, *pāṭala*, and blossoming *kuṭaka* and *vaṭa* trees, as well as *aśoka* and *bakula*. ||3||
That mountain is meritorious, appearing everywhere filled with various minerals and the finest of flowering trees. (4)
A pond, auspicious on all sides and filled with holy water,
[adorned] with blossoming lotuses and other fragrant flowers, such as golden lilies.
It shone with white lotuses and those beautifully blossomed red lotuses,
as well as with blue lotuses, kahlāras, swans, and water-fowls.
Filled with various minerals by birds, aquatic creatures, and others,
the pond was bright on all sides and frequented by flocks of diverse birds.
Adorned with the meritorious and melodious songs of cuckoos,
it likewise resounds with sweet sounds everywhere, becoming entirely sweet.
Resounding with the beautiful humming of bees, it is adorned everywhere;
such was that delightful mountain and that most excellent forest. (9)
Then the daughter of the king of Vidarbha, sporting together with her friends, beheld a pond called Sarvatobhadra.
Having beheld the holy forest, which was everywhere filled with flowers,
[she acted] through her fickleness, her power, her womanhood, and her playful charm.
Then, on the shore of the Padmāvatī lake, she, together with her female companions, was engaged in water-sports; as they sang, she laughed again and again.
And thus, O Brahmin, that beautiful woman, sporting there upon that lake,
should pass the time happily.
Viṣṇu said:
There was a Daitya named Gobhila, a servant of Vaiśravaṇa,
who, though possessing a divine celestial chariot, was overwhelmed by all worldly enjoyments.
Then, as the excellent Daitya Gobhila traveled through the path of the sky,
he beheld the large-eyed princess of Vidarbha there, free from fear.
She was the most excellent of all women, the beloved of Ugrasena;
peerless in beauty in the world, she shone resplendently in every limb. (16)
Is this Rati, the wife of Kāma? Or could she be the beloved of Hari? Or perhaps it is the goddess Pārvatī, or might it be Śacī? (17)
"Such as this woman seen here, the most excellent and supreme among women, there is no other like her, even a second one, upon the circle of the earth. (18)
Just as the moon shines most beautifully when full among the stars, so too did that fair-faced woman shine with her virtues, beauty, and arts. 19.
Just as I am among the Puṣkaras, so too is this sweetly smiling woman;
her beauty and her very being are truly wonderful to behold. (20)
The Daitya Gobhila caressed the lovely-faced Padmāvatī, whose breasts were beautiful, firm, rounded, and shapely like those of a young woman.
Having reflected upon this inopportune moment, he will undoubtedly come to know her as the princess of Vidarbha through his great power of knowledge. (22)
The beloved wife of Ugrasena, devoted to her husband, stood by her own power, being difficult to approach even for other men. (23)
Ugrasena is a great fool, by whom this excellent girl was sent to her father’s house; he is devoid of good fortune. (24)
How could one with a crooked mind ever live without her? Or rather, what king would abandon her, for she is like a queen to a eunuch? (25)
Upon seeing her, his soul instantly became filled with desire;
yet this young woman, devoted to her husband, is difficult to attain even for men.
"How shall I eat, lest my hunger torment me?
If she should come while I have not yet eaten this, it would surely be death for me. (27)
"Since this body lasts for only a single day, desire is exceedingly powerful";
thinking thus, Gobhila became absorbed in reflection and perceived with his mind alone. (28)
Having assumed an illusory form of King Ugrasena,
exactly like the great king Ugrasena himself in every limb and feature.
Gobhila, having become such a person, arrived and spoke in his own dialect, appearing exactly as he was dressed, as he was attired, and according to his age. (30)
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
his limbs adorned with all kinds of ornaments— such was Māthureśvara.
Then, having become such a Daitya consisting of Ugrasena,
he was endowed with supreme illusory power (māyā) and a perfection of beauty and charm.
Resorting to the shade of an aśoka tree on the mountain peak,
the evil-minded Vīraka sat upon a stone slab with his vīṇā-lute.
He sang a song of beautiful melody that utterly deludes the universe, endowed with rhythmic timing, measure, and execution, and adorned with the seven musical notes. ||34||
O Brahmin, that wicked-souled one, deluded by her form,
sang songs on the mountain peak, filled with great joy.
But Padmāvatī, of beautiful countenance, standing in the midst of her friends, heard a sweet song accompanied by rhythm, measure, and tempo. (36)
Who is this righteous-souled one who sings this song, which bestows great happiness, is endowed with virtuous actions, and is permeated by every feeling? (37)
Accompanied by her friends, the princess arrived and, out of eagerness,
took refuge in the shade of an Ashoka tree upon a spotless, beautiful stone slab.
He beheld that lowest of Dānavas, Gobhila, dressed in the guise of a king,
wearing a garland of flowers, clad in fine garments, and anointed with divine unguents.
When will Mathureśa, whose limbs are adorned with all ornaments and who is devoted to righteousness, arrive, along with his chaste wife Padmāvatī? (40)
As soon as my noble lord, having abandoned his sovereignty,
thought of her while she was not far away, she was [seized] by that sinful man.
Having been summoned, she became agitated and approached, saying, "O my beloved! How is it that the husband has arrived, while she was startled and filled with apprehension? (42)
Born of shame and sorrow, I cast my face downward; I am a sinful woman of wicked conduct, having acted without hesitation. (43)
The illustrious one will undoubtedly become angry; for as long as that sinner continues to think in such a way, he will provoke his wrath. (44)
"O my beloved, come, come! Having become distressed at being summoned, O Goddess of lovely countenance, I am unable to sustain my life-breaths without you. (45)
Indeed, I am unable to bear my own life, which is so dear to me;
for I am so captivated by my affection for you that I cannot bring myself to leave you at all.
The Brahmin woman said: Having been addressed thus, she went and beheld Sumukha, filled with shame;
then the Daitya embraced the virtuous Padmāvatī.
Then, at his own will, that daughter of Satyaketu was brought by the Daitya Gobhila and enjoyed by him alone. 48.
Sukalā said:
"O fair-faced one, you have made a secret sign at the place of the scrotum;
having grasped her own garment, she became apprehensive and indeed distressed. (49)
Filled with rage, she spoke these words to Gobhila, the lowest of demons:
"Who are you, a man of sinful conduct, merciless, and possessing the form of a demon? (50)
Desirous of cursing him, she was intensely exerted, her eyes agitated with grief;
trembling then, O King, she was oppressed by a heavy burden of sorrow.
O wicked-souled one, having come here under that very pretext, you have destroyed my supreme dharma, the unsurpassed devotion to my husband. (52)
"Having made a melodious sound, you have brought about my birth;
behold me right here, for I shall pronounce a most terrible curse upon you. (53)
While they were conversing in this manner, [he addressed] Gobhila, who desired to curse him.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Deeds of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The Fifty-fifth Chapter. Sukalā said:
Having heard her words, Gobhila spoke these words.
"O lady, you desire to curse me; tell me the reason why. ||1||
"By what fault am I tainted that you are intent on cursing me? O auspicious lady, I am a Daitya named Gobhila, a soldier of Paulastya. (2)
I conduct myself according to the way of the Daityas; I know the unsurpassed science, I am a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, and furthermore, I am proficient in the arts.
Thus I understand everything; now hear from me the conduct of the Daityas:
they enjoy the property of others and the wives of others by force, and not otherwise.
"O Daityas, having heard this, we shall conduct ourselves according to the conduct of Daityas with a spirit of wisdom;
I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (5)
For day after day we observe the vulnerabilities of the Brahmins;
we undoubtedly cause the destruction of their ascetic merit through obstacles. (6)
"O Goddess, having found a vulnerability, we shall destroy him without a doubt.
O auspicious one, O fair-faced lady, listen, O Brāhmaṇas, to the sacrifice for the gods."
We shall destroy the sacrifices—there is no doubt—but not the sacrifice of Dharma, having abandoned the true Brahmins and the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa. (8)
Having utterly abandoned the highly fortunate Sumati, who was devoted to her husband, we shall remain here; of this there is no doubt. (9)
The Daityas were not capable of withstanding the splendor of the excellent Brahmin, nor that of the high-souled Hari, nor that of the woman devoted to her husband. ||10||
Even by the power of a devoted wife, of Viṣṇu, and of a true brāhmaṇa,
all the dānavas and the foremost of the rākṣasas are destroyed and driven far away.
"I wander the surface of the earth according to the nature of a Dānava;
consider this well—why do you wish to curse me who am without fault? (12)
Padmāvatī said:
"My dharma and my beautiful body have been utterly destroyed by you alone.
I am a virtuous, devoted wife, emaciated by penance and longing for my husband. (13)
Established on your own path, you have not been destroyed by deceitful illusion;
therefore, O wicked one, I shall surely consume you as well—of this there is no doubt. (14)
Gobhila said:
"I shall indeed proclaim the dharma, if you, O Queen, so desire. Listen also, O lady who delights the king, to the case of the Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires. (15)
He who offers oblations to the Divine twice a day and does not abandon this fire for even a single moment becomes an Agnihotrin; he indeed performs sacrifice day after day.
Moreover, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall speak further regarding the duty of a servant: he who is always pure in thought, deed, and speech; (17)
One who always carries out his instructions and stands behind or before him, along with his servants, O God, is said to be a partaker of merit; of this there is no doubt. (18)
That virtuous son who, being wise and auspicious, protects his father and especially his mother with his mind, body, and actions; ||19||
For him, bathing in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day;
for he who acts otherwise is a sinner, without a doubt. (20)
Moreover, O beautiful lady, listen as I shall proclaim this unsurpassed vow of devotion to one's husband, to be observed through speech, mind, and action. (21)
She should perform service to her husband day after day;
when her husband is pleased, she should be joyful herself, and she should never again abandon him even if he is angry.
She does not seize upon his faults; even when struck, she is satisfied once more.
She always stands before her husband for all his tasks. (23)
And that woman was also described as one devoted to her husband, even though her father had fallen from his status and was possessed of many faults by his sons. (24)
Furthermore, one should never abandon a father even if he is afflicted with leprosy or is angry;
thus indeed do sons serve their father and mother. (25)
They go to the supreme world, that highest step of Viṣṇu;
for such indeed do those servants serve their master. ||26||
Then, by the grace of their lord, these women go to the world of their husband;
likewise, a Brahmin who does not abandon the sacred fire goes to the world of Brahmā.
A Brahmin who neglects the fire-sacrifice is called the husband of a *vṛṣalī*;
a servant becomes a traitor to his master by abandoning his master—of this there is no doubt. (28)
O auspicious one, a Brahmin son or servant should never abandon the fire, his father, or his master; I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth. (29)
O Goddess, those who depart after abandoning one who is fallen, diseased, crippled, or likewise afflicted with leprosy, go to the ocean of hell.
If a woman desires her own welfare in this world, she should not abandon her husband even if he is destitute of all means of action and has lost his accumulation of wealth and other possessions. (31)
If a woman abandons her desire for her husband and seeks another purpose here, she is considered unchaste in this world and excluded from all dharma. (32)
When her husband has gone abroad, a woman who, out of fickleness, indulges in luxury, enjoyment, and adornment, is called a "loose woman" by people, even though she is chaste. (33)
Thus I understand the Dharma, which is in agreement with the Vedic scriptures:
that from the very beginning, the Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Pretas were created by the Creator.
In this regard, I shall explain the entire cause without any doubt:
the Brāhmaṇas, Dānavas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas. ||35||
O beautiful one, although they have studied all that was spoken for the sake of the Dharma, those wicked ones do not practice it at all; rather, they act in every way contrary to it. (36)
Deprived of knowledge, these Dānavas perform their rites devoid of prescribed rules;
bereft of the proper method, these men proceed by unjust means.
These [scriptures] were composed for the purpose of their teaching and not otherwise; those lowest of men who perform dharma contrary to the injunctions act improperly. (38)
We indeed punish them with a truly great rod;
for you have committed a most cruel and utterly merciless deed. (39)
"Having abandoned the life of a householder, for what purpose have you come here? Even with your own mouth you say, 'I am indeed one for whom my husband is a deity. (40)
That which was seen by you through your own karma was surely ordained by fate;
for what reason have you come here, having abandoned that husband? (41)
Having adorned yourself with ornaments and dress, you stand there pitilessly;
tell me, O sinful one, for what purpose and on whose account have you done this? 42.
Listen: while you were wandering fearlessly and heedlessly in the mountain forest, you have been subdued by me with a great punishment for your sin. 43.
Having abandoned her husband who was wicked and unrighteous in conduct, you have come here; where is that devotion to your husband? Show it before me! (44)
When a woman gives her own husband—who has not been abandoned by her—to sleep on a separate bed, then she is considered unchaste. 45.
Within a distance of one hundred yojanas, she moves about;
where does that deity presiding over the male organ dwell, practicing the conduct of a man? (46)
O shameless, pitiless, and wicked one, why do you bite me with your face?
Where is your asceticism, where is your disposition, and where indeed is your splendor and strength? 47.
"Show me this very day your strength, heroism, and prowess!
Padmāvatī said: "O lowest of asuras, listen; she was brought here out of affection. (48)
I was sent by my father from my husband’s house to that place; and there, I committed no sin out of desire, nor greed, nor delusion, nor envy. (49)
I have come here having abandoned my husband, remaining established in the state of being his wife; yet even by the pretext of my husband's form, I have been deceived by you alone. (50)
"O lowest of Dānavas, having recognized you as that Māthura, I have come before you; for I know you to be a master of illusion. (51)
"With a single roar of 'huṃ,' I shall reduce them to ashes.
Gobhila said:
"Listen attentively; men who are deprived of sight do not see. (52)
"How can you know me here, being deprived of the guidance of the Dharma?
Listen: when your state arose, it was directed toward your father's house. (53)
At that time, you abandoned the meditation on the husband through the meditation on liberation;
then, the eye of knowledge was clearly lost within your heart. (54)
How do you know me, you whose eye of wisdom has been destroyed on this earth? Whose mother and father are you? Whose brother? And whose are your kinsmen and husband? (55)
"Indeed, he alone is the lord over all her stations; of this there is no doubt," having said this and laughed, Gobhila, the lowest of givers, departed. (56)
No fear exists for me today; listen, O trembling one!
Why do you vainly threaten me with your curse? 57.
"Resorting to my house, enjoy pleasures according to your heart's desire.
Padmāvatī said: "Go away, you of sinful conduct! Why do you speak thus, O merciless one? (58)
Established in the state of a virtuous wife, devoted solely to my husband, I shall burn you, O great sinner, if you speak thus. (59)
Having spoken thus, Gobhila sat down upon the ground before her as she was overcome with great sorrow, and he said to her: 60.
"O auspicious one, you have deposited your own well-performed vigor within your womb;
from that, a son shall be born who will cause agitation in the three worlds."
Having spoken thus, the Dānava Gobhila then departed;
once that evil-doing, wicked-conducted Dānava had gone, [she remained].
Overcome with great sorrow, the princess wept.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the *Sukalā-caritra* within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. || 50 ||
The fifty-first chapter.
The Brāhmaṇī said: When that Durācāra Gobhila, whose mind was filled with sin, had departed...
Then Padmāvatī wept, overcome by great sorrow.
O best of the twice-born, having heard her lamentation,
all those beautiful-faced female friends questioned that princess.
"Why do you weep? May it be well with you; tell me what has happened.
Where has that great king, your lord of Mathurā, gone? (3)
Having said, "By whom indeed have you been summoned?
Speak, O dear one," she, weeping again and again with great sorrow, spoke to them. (4)
She reported everything that had occurred arising from the fault;
trembling and deeply distressed, she was led by them to her father’s house. ||5||
Then those women reported that matter to her mother's presence;
having heard it, the queen went to her husband’s palace.
She informed her husband of that very account concerning her son;
upon hearing it, the king then became deeply distressed.
Having provided her with a vehicle, clothing, and attendants, he sent her to Mathurā; she went there to the presence of her beloved.
O best of the twice-born, having concealed the fault regarding their daughter,
the righteous Ugrasena welcomed Padmāvatī who had arrived.
Having seen her, he rejoiced immediately and spoke these words again:
"O lady with the beautiful face, I am not able to live without you."
They were always delighted by their many splendors, virtues, and moral conduct;
through devotion, truthfulness, and those qualities which have the gods as their presiding deities, they attained supreme bliss.
Having addressed his beloved wife Padmāvatī,
Ugrasena, the best of kings, enjoyed himself with her amidst all his pleasures.
The terrible fetus, which brought fear to all the worlds, grew;
Padmāvatī understood the cause of that fetus.
Thinking day and night about [the child] growing within his own womb, he wondered: "What is the use of this being born, who will surely bring about the destruction of the world?"
By this wicked son, who has committed an offense against his father, she is now being asked everywhere for a medicine that will cause an abortion. (15)
Day after day, she employed many methods, such as consuming potent herbs and snake venom, solely for the purpose of inducing an abortion. (16)
The terrible fetus, which caused fear to all the worlds, grew;
then that fetus spoke to its mother, Padmāvatī.
"O Mother, why do you grieve day after day because of medicinal herbs?
Through merit one's lifespan increases, but through sin, life becomes short. (18)
They live and die according to the ripening of their own karma;
some depart as raw embryos, while others remain uncooked upon the surface of the earth.
Some die as soon as they are born; others pass away while still in their youth; and both children and the elderly fall under the power of death even in their prime. (20)
All herbs, mantras, and deities live and die through the ripening of karma; they are merely signs, of this there is no doubt. (21)
"You consider me to be low-born, yet such as I am—have you not previously seen or heard of the mighty Kālanemi? (22)
Possessing great heroism among the Dānavas and causing fear to the three worlds,
I was formerly slain by Viṣṇu in the great battle between the gods and the asuras.
"I have come to your belly to accomplish that enmity;
O Mother, do not commit such rashness and weariness day after day. (24)
Having spoken thus to the best of the twice-born, he ceased;
O Mother, at that time she abandoned her effort due to great sorrow.
As many as ten years passed, he attained growth;
thereafter, the one of great splendor was born, who was possessed of equal great strength.
By whom the inhabitants of the three worlds were terrified, he who was slain by Vāsudeva has undoubtedly attained liberation. 27.
"Thus have I heard: 'It will not be so; it will indeed be so.
This has been stated with certainty for you in all the Purāṇas. (28)
A maiden who remains in her father's house surely goes to ruin; therefore, one should not allow such a daughter to live alone in the home. 29.
Abandon this wicked woman, a great sinner, and remain steadfast;
for you must experience great sin and indeed terrible suffering. (30)
"Eat this, which brings the highest good in the world, together with me.
The sow said:
"Having heard these most auspicious words, that best of the twice-born [remained] with her. (31)
She then set her mind on renunciation, for she had been summoned at that time;
listen, O auspicious one, to how she gave me all her garments and ornaments.

O wicked woman, it is solely due to your misconduct that the excellent Brahmin Śivaśarman, though wise, has indeed fallen into a state of delusion, O you who act with the depravity of your lineage! 33.
"Go wherever your husband stays; of this there is no doubt. Go to whatever place pleases you, and act exactly as you have been instructed. (34)
Having spoken thus, O illustrious one, I was abandoned by my father, mother, and kinsmen; O lady of beautiful countenance, I have come here quickly, devoid of shame. (35)
O auspicious one, I do not even find a place to rest in comfort; moreover, people revile me, saying, "This unchaste woman has arrived. (36)
Wandering and arriving from various regions, she was free from pride regarding her lineage; she came to the auspicious Gurjara country, to the holy Saurāṣṭra, to the abode of Śiva. (37)
Listen, O Devī: I was then residing in that city known as Vanasthalī, which was teeming with prosperity, yet I was exceedingly afflicted by hunger. (38)
Taking up her alms-bowl, she set out for the sake of alms;
deeply distressed, she entered the doorways of householders. (39)
"O beautiful woman, people see my form and despise me; they say, 'She has come here for alms, she is a sinful woman. (40)
Thus, oppressed by poverty due to the accumulation of suffering, she wandered about until, by chance, she beheld a single, unsurpassed house. (41)
It was surrounded by high walls, equipped with halls for Vedic study, filled with the sound of the Vedas, and crowded with many Brahmins. ||42||
Abounding in wealth and grain, adorned with female and male servants, he entered that delightful house which was filled with the joy of prosperity. (43)
Then Sudevā, afflicted by grief, said, "Give me alms," at the house of that very Śivaśarman, which was auspicious on all sides.
Then Śivaśarman, the best of the twice-born, heard the sound of begging from his wife named Maṅgalā, who was like Lakṣmī in form and possessed a beautiful face. 45.
Smiling, the righteous and highly intelligent Śivaśarman said to her:
"This poor woman has arrived at the door, having come for the sake of alms. (46)
"O auspicious one, having summoned your beloved, give her food;
you are overcome with supreme compassion, knowing that I have arrived. (47)
She spoke to Maṅgalā, "I shall give you a beloved meal.
Having spoken thus to her husband, Maṅgalā was filled with auspiciousness. 48.
He fed me, who was very weak, again with delicious food;
then the great sage Śivaśarman, whose soul is righteous, spoke to me. (49)
"Whence have you come here, or whose wandering through the world are you? For what purpose are you everywhere? Tell me all before me. (50)
Having thus heard those words of her high-souled husband, Kāntā was then recognized by me through her voice: "Alas, what a sinful thing has been done! (51)
When her husband was not seen by me because he had become downcast with shame, Maṅgalā, whose every limb was beautiful, spoke this to her husband: ||52||
"Tell me truly who this woman is; seeing you, she is overcome with shame.
Please, out of your favor, tell me who she will become. (53)
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. || 51 ||
The fifty-second chapter. Śivaśarman said:
O Maṅgala, listen to my words if you wish to hear them.
O lady of beautiful countenance, understand that for which you have asked me.
"O fair-eyed one, this wretched woman who has arrived here in the form of a mendicant is indeed the daughter of the brahmin Vasudatta. (2)
"O auspicious one, this wife of mine is ever dear to the virtuous gods;
for some reason or other, she has come here after leaving her own country. (3)
"O fair-faced one, this [city] is consumed by the fire of grief for me;
knowing that I was here, she has come to your house in the guise of a mendicant. (4)
Knowing this, O auspicious lady, you must perform hospitality with great care;
have no doubt about it, for I desire you as my own beloved.
Having heard these words of her husband, the auspicious Aṅgalā, whose deity was her husband, was herself filled with great joy; she was truly Sumaṅgalā.
O lady with the face of an excellent elephant, the devoted wife provided bathing materials, clothing, and food,
as well as ornaments set with jewels and gold, upon the wheel of the *camasa* vessel.
"O auspicious lady, I was indeed adorned by her alone through her desire for me as a husband;
O Goddess, I was adorned by her with baths, garments, and meals. (8)
O Goddess, because I was insulted by my husband, an immeasurable sorrow has arisen within me—a great and intense pain in my chest that threatens to destroy all my life-force. (9)
In that state, I have perceived the suffering inherent within myself;
such a terrible anxiety has arisen because of which my vital breaths are departing.
Once, an evil and inauspicious word was spoken by me, a sinful woman, while practicing wicked conduct toward this very best of brahmins. (11)
There was no washing of feet, nor indeed any massaging of the limbs;
he offered only a single prostration to that very Great-Souled One. (12)
Having made this sinful resolve, how indeed shall I carry out my conversation with him? And then, during that very night, she fell into an ocean of misery.
Thus, as I was reflecting, my heart burst apart;
O fair-faced one, my life-breaths departed, leaving this body behind. (14)
Then the messengers of Dharmarāja arrived there;
they were heroic, formidable, and cruel, bearing maces, discuses, and swords. ||15||
Bound by those great, firm-chained fetters,
O noble lady, they were led by them to the city of Yama, weeping and deeply distressed.
Being struck with mallets and tormented on a difficult path, and being reviled by those in front of Yama, I was made to enter there. (17)
I was seen by the high-souled King Yama, who was filled with wrath;
I was cast from one heap of glowing coals into another heap of hells.
Having fashioned a man out of iron and heated it with fire, she hurled it at my chest at her husband's command. (19)
Excessively tormented by various afflictions and scorched by the fires of hell,
they are cast into vats of oil and upon sands of burning gravel.
Cut by sword-leaved trees and driven by the wind,
they were cast upon the thorny *kūṭa-śālmalī* trees by that great-souled one.
O King, I have been cast into all the hells, which are filled with worms and teeming with pus, blood, and excrement. (22)
Even by that very same high-souled one, while I was in intense agony,
I was split open with saws and struck violently with spears.
O King, I have been cast into other hells as well;
I have been thrown into the pits of various wombs and fallen into a multitude of miseries. (24)
By that King of Dharma, I was cast into the hells; having reached the womb of a Valguṇī, I experienced most terrible suffering. (25)
I went to the womb of a female osprey, and then again to the womb of a female dog;
I indeed entered the wombs of a hen, a female cat, and a female mouse. (26)
Thus, I have been cast by the King of Dharma into various types of wombs, including those of evil birth, and I have been tormented in every kind of womb. (27)
By that very [act], O King, on the ground where the sow was killed, there are many sacred sites (tīrthas) in your hand, O highly fortunate one. (28)
O lady of excellent complexion, it was by you alone that I was sprinkled with water; O Goddess, O beautiful one, my sin has departed through your grace. (29)
O fair-faced one, this knowledge has arisen from your own merit and splendor;
now deliver me, who have fallen into the peril of hell. (30)
O illustrious one, when you lift me up, I shall again enter that terrible hell;
therefore, protect me, who am a partaker of suffering. (31)
"I have fallen into a state of sin; I am miserable and without refuge. Sudevā said: "O blessed lady, what meritorious deed, born of virtue, was performed by me? (32)
"Tell me that by which I may rescue you; speak this to me quickly.
The sow said:
"This king, O highly fortunate one, is the descendant of Ikṣvāku and the son of Manu. (33)
This Viṣṇu is of great wisdom; otherwise, she would not have become Śrī, the highly fortunate woman devoted to her husband, who is solely dedicated to her husband. 34.

O Satī, you are eternally the sovereign of all auspiciousness; O Goddess, you are the beloved who embodies all sacred fords, you are eternally composed of all things, and you are forever composed of all the gods. (35)
The beloved of the king, who was the sole embodiment of the world of great devoted wives, served her husband day and night. (36)
O lady of beautiful countenance, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, then grant me the merit of even a single day spent in serving my husband. (37)
"You are my mother and father, you are my eternal guru;
I am a sinner of wicked conduct, devoid of truth and knowledge. (38)
"O noble one, deliver me; I am terrified by the beatings of Yama.
Sukalā said:
"Having heard what was spoken by her, she then looked at the king. (39)
"What shall I do, O Great King? What does this animal say?
Ikṣvāku said: "O auspicious lady, [speak to] this wretched, miserable one who has entered this sinful womb. (40)
"By your merits, you shall uplift [others] and great welfare will come to pass.
