Thus addressed, the noble lady Sudeva was auspicious and beautiful. (41)
"O fair-faced one, I have given you the merit of one year," she said.
As soon as these words were spoken by that goddess, at that very moment—
Endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with divine garlands, she possessed a celestial body and was enveloped in a blaze of splendor. ||43||
Richly adorned with the splendor of all ornaments and beautified by various jewels, she was born with a divine form, possessing celestial garments and unguents.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot and gone into the sky,
she [the goddess] then spoke to that queen, who stood with her head bowed low in prostration.
"May it be well with you, O highly fortunate one; by your grace, O beautiful lady, I shall go from this sin to the most meritorious and auspicious heaven. (46)
Having thus paid obeisance and gone to heaven, O Sudevā, best of virtuous ones, all this that was reported by Sukalā has been told to you. 47.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Ascent to Heaven of Sudeva," within the Story of Sukalā in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||52||
The fifty-third chapter. Sukalā said:
"In this manner, I previously heard about Dharma in the Purāṇas at that time."
"Deprived of my husband, how shall I, with my mind fixed on sin, make use of wealth? ||1||
"Without whom shall I sustain this life with this body?
Viṣṇu said:
"Having thus spoken of the supreme dharma, the unsurpassed devotion to one's husband..."
Having heard that supreme and meritorious dharma which grants women their goal, those noble friends were filled with great joy. (3)
O best of men, all the brahmins and gods praise that highly fortunate Sukalā, who is devoted to dharma and is a virtuous woman. (4)
They perform meditation upon him by the power of their desire for a husband;
Indra, the lord of the asuras, having reflected well, [perceives] his extreme firmness.
Having thoroughly considered the supreme disposition of Sukalā, the Lord of the Immortals would undoubtedly cause her fortitude to waver and her affection for her husband to falter.
Hastening, the lord of the gods, whose banner bears the fish, remembered the god Manmatha; taking up his flower-bow, he arrived. ||7||
Joined by his beloved wife and endowed with great power through the sight of Rati, he joined his palms in reverence and spoke to the Thousand-eyed One: ||8||
O Lord, why have you now remembered me, who am without a protector? O bestower of honor, let your command be given to me today with your whole being.
Indra said:
"This highly fortunate daughter of Sukalā is devoted to her husband;
listen, O God of Love, and provide her with your supreme assistance. (10)
"Bring forth the highly fortunate Sukalā, who is meritorious and auspicious.
Having heard those words of Śakra, he then spoke to him: ||11||
"Let it be so; O Lord of the Gods, I shall undoubtedly provide assistance for the sake of your curiosity. (12)
Having spoken thus, the one of great splendor, Kama, who is difficult for sages to conquer, said:
"I am capable of conquering even the gods, along with the sages and the best of ṛṣis. (13)
How much more so, O Lord, the power residing in the limbs of a beautiful woman?
For I, O Lord, dwell within the very limbs of beautiful women. (14)
Always [one should place them] on the forehead, the cheeks, the eyes, and the tips of the hair; likewise on the navel, the hips, the region of the back, the buttocks, and the circle of the yoni.
I dwell indeed in the lower part, in the divisions of the body, and in the armpits; there is no doubt that I reside thus in all the limbs and even in the minor members. 16.
I always dwell there in the house of that woman;
staying there, I kill all men without a doubt. (17)
Seeing her father, mother, other kinsmen, and her husband, she was naturally distressed by the arrows of the god of love. 18.
Struck by the arrows of the god who is beautiful and possessed of qualities, the virtuous woman trembles;
she should not think of her body as being subject to decay.
O Lord of the Gods, the vulva of women throbs and their nipples quiver;
they possess no fortitude, O Lord of the Gods, and I destroy even their good fortune. 20.
Indra said:
"O Mind-born One, I shall become a man, handsome, virtuous, and wealthy; for the sake of curiosity, I shall move this woman. (21)
Neither out of desire for wealth nor out of fear, nor out of greed, nor for any ulterior motive, nor out of delusion, nor out of anger—O lover of truth, this is the truth, the absolute truth. (22)
"How can such a great truth and devotion to her husband be seen in her?
I shall go and extract it from her; this delusion must have a cause. (23)
Having thus directed his desire, the king of the gods himself departed,
having personally manifested a transformation of his own self into one endowed with beauty and virtue.
His limbs were adorned with the splendor of all ornaments; he was endowed with every enjoyment;
he was filled with the play of worldly delights; and he was possessed of all forms of magnanimity. ||25||
O King, where the Goddess, the beloved of Kṛkala, resides, she reveals her own play, her true form, her qualities, and her disposition. (26)
O King, she did not see that man who was endowed with beauty;
wherever he went, she saw him there.
With a longing mind, he gazed upon her alone;
the thousand-eyed Indra displayed amorous gestures before all the beings.
Wherever that goddess goes—whether at a crossroads, on a path, or at a sacred ford—the thousand-eyed one beholds her right there. (29)
A female messenger sent by Indra arrived back from Sukalā and,
laughing, spoke indeed to the highly fortunate Sukalā.

There is no woman with a beautiful face who possesses such greatness of being, such great fortitude, such great loveliness, and such secret forbearance as she does through her form and her essential nature. 31.
"Who are you that you shall become the wife of Bhavaśikalyāṇika? You, whose virtuous wife he is, are a fortunate one who shares in merit upon this earth. (32)
Having heard her words, that high-minded woman said to her:
"He was born of the Vaiśya caste, a righteous soul who was devoted to truth. (33)
I am indeed the beloved wife of that wise Vaiśya Kṛkala, who was truthful and firm in his resolve; I speak this very truth to you. (34)
"My husband, a virtuous soul and wise man, has departed on a pilgrimage to sacred fords;
now that that illustrious one has gone, [I am left] with respect to this husband of mine. (35)
Listen, three years have already passed;
since then, I have become sorrowful, being without that great-souled one.
All this account of my own life has been told to you;
now tell me what you will become when questioned by her.
Having heard the words of Sukalā and what was spoken again by Dūtī, [the king said:
"O auspicious lady, you ask me this very thing; I shall tell you all of it. (38)
"O lady of excellent complexion, I have come into your presence for the sake of a certain task;
listen, for I shall speak, and having heard it, you should take it to heart. (39)
O lady of beautiful countenance, your merciless husband has departed, having abandoned you; what will you do with him, who has committed such a cruel deed against his beloved? (40)
"O sinful woman, what has become of him who left you—who are endowed with virtuous conduct—and went away?
O girl, is he alive there, or indeed is he dead? (41)
"What will she do with that?"—thus you suffer in vain;
why, O dear one, do you destroy this divine body, which possesses a luster like gold? (42)
O highly fortunate one, O auspicious lady, when a human being reaches the age of twenty, he does not possess even a single moment of happiness without childish play. (43)
The onset of the suffering of old age destroys the body;
therefore, O fair-faced one, all enjoyment should be experienced with ease while in youth. 44.
As long as youth remains, so long do human beings enjoy all things such as pleasure and luxury; a person indulges in them according to his own will. (45)
As long as youth remains, one enjoys pleasures; O friend, once that auspicious youth has passed away, what will one do? (46)
When old age has arrived, O Devikā, no purpose whatsoever is accomplished; the elder man constantly broods and does not engage in activities that bring happiness.
Friend, a bridge is constructed when the water has already receded;
such indeed would this body become once auspetic youth has passed away. (48)
Therefore, eat with pleasure and drink the honeyed wine;
O fair-eyed one, I shall abandon this body of mine because of the arrow of desire for you. 49.
This one man has arrived, handsome and virtuous;
for he is a tiger among men, all-knowing, endowed with excellence, and wealthy. (50)
"O woman of excellent complexion, you are eternally bound to me by affection for my sake.
Sukalā said:
"Even childhood does not exist for a living being; youth does not exist within life. (51)
He has no old age; he is self-perfected and the bestower of perfect success.
He is immortal, free from decay, all-pervading, perfectly accomplished, and the supreme knower of all.
Free from desire, he exists in the world of desire in his own true form;
just as the structure of a house is perceived, so too is the body seen.
Just as a carpenter shapes a body with a measuring line, so too [is it done] with many collections of wood and various assemblages of timber. (54)
One should transform even clay and water by means of application;
wood becomes variegated through coatings and by means of pigments.
First, the form that is the abode of illusion is delineated by the thread;
and they themselves nourish it day after day with their own ointment. (56)
A house that is constantly shaken by the wind becomes soiled;
this is described as the intermediate period for a house.
There would be a loss of beauty for him; therefore, the master of the house should apply ointments, and the master of the house may, according to his own will, bring the house to a state of beauty.
O messenger, the youthfulness of that house is said to have passed away long ago through the accumulation of masses of wood and its resulting state of decay. (59)
Falling from their place, they are born; they waver at the root and the tip.
Without a supporting base, they cannot sustain the weight of the plastering.
O messenger, listen to this which has been told regarding the old age of a house:
seeing the house falling into ruin, the master of the house would abandon it. (61)
Just as one hastens indeed to enter another house,
so too do youth, old age, and even decrepitude pass away for men.
Though he may be young, he should manifest the form of a child and display himself as devoid of knowledge;
he should even paint his body with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Through ointments, perfumes, and other things such as betel-leaf preparations,
the body attains youthfulness and becomes exceedingly beautiful.
One should nourish [the body] with all external and internal rasas;
through that state of nourishment, it becomes fully developed.
O King, this supreme and new prosperity arises through the juices; and even the nourished limbs attain expansion.
Indeed, through the dissolution of their respective minor limbs, they each attain their own specific forms:
the teeth, lips, breasts, arms, waist, back, and both thighs.
In the same way, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet attained growth;
indeed, those very [marks] on both [sides] undergo increase.
O messenger, when their limbs are equal in measure and well-formed, a mortal becomes bound by those very forms. (69)
O messenger, by what means can a mortal in this world be called handsome and beloved, when this body is merely a vessel for excrement and urine? (70)
This body is impure and is always flowing with [impurities];
O auspicious one, how can its form be described? It is like a bubble on the water. (71)
It remains firm for as long as fifty years;
thereafter, its deterioration occurs day by day.
Then those [faculties] become slack, and likewise the mouth drools;
one no longer sees with the eyes, nor does one hear with the ears. (73)
O messenger, the body, afflicted by the time of old age, becomes incapable and unable to move about with its hands and feet. (74)
That essence, dried up by the heat of the fire of old age, undergoes desiccation;
it becomes incapable [of functioning], and by what means is the state of being a messenger desired? (75)
Just as an old house goes to ruin without a doubt, so too does this body, like a house on fire, go to its destruction in old age. (76)
My form has come to be thus day by day, like [the fading] of a color;
by what am I endowed with form, and by what is the state of formlessness desired? (77)
Just as a dilapidated house is destroyed by a traveler, so too was that powerful man destroyed; for what purpose did the messenger come, and who is she who speaks of him? (78)
"Tell me, what have you seen on my body that is not present on hers?
For there is nothing lacking in her limbs, nor is there anything additional. (79)
As you are, so is he; as he is, so am I—of this there is no doubt.
Whose form is not found here? There is no one possessing a form upon the surface of the earth.
O auspicious one, just as trees and mountains, despite their height, eventually fall when oppressed by time, so it is with all living beings; it cannot be otherwise.
O messenger, he is formless yet possesses form, divine in nature, all-pervading, and pure; he dwells within all things, both the stationary and the moving.
Just as water that has been contained in many separate jars becomes one again when those jars are destroyed, you do not perceive this oneness. 83.
Due to the destruction of the body and so forth, this self is born with a single form;
while dwelling in saṃsāra, I have always perceived it as having but one form. (84)
Speak thus, having understood for whose sake you have come here; show me that unprecedented thing, if you wish to eat here. (85)
In one who is afflicted by disease and obstructed by phlegm,
the blood moves from its location within the limbs and becomes displaced from its proper site.
When all the constituent parts have perished, the state of being a stone [the body] likewise vanishes from the midst of the waves;
it meets with destruction on one side, for it must abandon its own dual form.
It quickly turns into excrement and indeed becomes infested with worms;
likewise, one should abandon that which causes suffering or is of a repulsive nature. 88.
Listen: thereafter, it becomes filled with worms and foul odors;
there, indeed, either lice or worms are born—of this there is no doubt. (89)
A worm causes eruptions and a most terrible itching;
a louse produces pain and makes the entire body tremble. (90)
Just as the itching of one who is being rubbed with the tips of the nails is pacified, so too is it for those [who practice] sexual union; listen to this, there is no doubt. (91)
When a mortal eats savory foods and drinks well-prepared meals,
they are carried by that vital breath (prāṇa) to the seat of digestion.
Whatever food has been eaten by living beings that has entered the place of digestion, all of that is concealed there; indeed, the wind expels it as waste.
There, the essential sap becomes that very blood;
being stainless and possessing pure potency, it proceeds to the abode of Brahmā.
Drawn along by that equalizing wind, it does not find a stable place;
due to its mobility, it remains in a state of constant motion. (95)
In the skulls of living beings, there are five types of worms;
two of these are at the root of the ears, and then again, those located in the eyes. (96)
O messenger, those with red tails are measured by the size of the little finger;
those with black tails have the color of butter, without a doubt. (97)
O blessed lady, hear from me their names as they are uttered:
Piṅgalī and Śṛṅkhalī are at the two roots of the ears, and Kṛmi is at the root of the ear. (98)
Capala and Pippala—these two are located on the tips of the nostrils;
Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī are situated in the other two eyes. (99)
There are fifty-one types of worms; they exist within the forehead, all of them equal in size to a mustard seed. 100.
All those afflicted by the disease of the skull undergo transformations, there is no doubt;
two hairs are found in his mouth, O messenger—listen! (101)
Know that there is the destruction of living beings at that very moment, without a doubt, even for one established in his own place, when the Prajāpati [planet] is adverse. (102)
That semen falls there in the form of fluid; of this there is no doubt.
He drinks the semen with his mouth, and by that he becomes intoxicated. 103.
In the middle region of the palate, the letter *ca* exists in a moving state;
there also reside the channels known as Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā. (104)
Even for one who is weak, this net of channels causes a fever; indeed, in this world, the itch of desire arises in all living beings.
O messenger, when the male's phallus throbs and the female's vulva [is aroused],
then the man and woman, being intoxicated with passion, proceed to union.
The friction of body against body that constitutes sexual intercourse produces only a momentary pleasure for the body, followed by a corresponding itchiness. (107)
Indeed, this very nature of the messenger (dūtī) is seen everywhere;
go now to your own abode, for there is nothing unprecedented here.
There is nothing unprecedented for me; I simply act, without a doubt. ||109||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||53||
The fifty-fourth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Thus addressed by that messenger, Asukalā, who had arrived at that time...
Having understood this which has been well-proclaimed in brief, the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) [acted]. ||1||
For that purpose, he spoke words endowed with truth and righteousness; having considered her audacity, her fortitude, and her very knowledge, the Destroyer of Cities [Śiva] acted. (2)
For such a speech as this, having become a woman on the surface of the earth, he would speak—speech that is well-refined in the form of yoga and washed by the waters of logic. (3)
This highly fortunate one is the very embodiment of truth, there is no doubt;
she is capable of bearing the burden of the entire three worlds. (4)
Having reflected upon this very matter, Viṣṇu spoke to Kaṃdarpa:
"I shall go with you to see that beloved of Kṛkala. (5)
Proud of his strength, Manmatha replied to the thousand-eyed one:
"O Lord of Gods, go to that place where she who is devoted to her husband resides."
"O Lord of Asuras, how much pride, vigor, strength, and fortitude does her truthful devotion to her husband possess? Having gone there, I shall destroy it. (7)
Having heard the words of the Thousand-eyed One and of Manmatha, [Indra said]:
"O Naṅga, listen! You have spoken excessively and in vain."
This current age is invincible due to its very firm untruthfulness and vigor, and because of the stability of its unrighteous deeds;
therefore, human effort is of no avail here.
Having heard this, Manmatha became enraged and said to Indra:
"The power of both the sages and the gods has been destroyed by me. (10)
I shall tell you only this much by way of ornament:
behold, O Lord of Gods, I shall destroy that woman right now.
Just as butter, upon seeing the heat of fire, melts away, so shall I cause this [ignorance] to melt by means of my own form and splendor. 12.
"Go there; a great task has certainly presented itself before you now.
Why do you revile him who possesses the splendor that brings about the destruction of the three worlds? (13)
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard those words of the mind-born [Kāma], and knowing her to be unattainable by you due to your lust,
he summoned his fortitude and spoke of her who was meritorious in body, pure through merit, and whose conduct was full of virtue.
"Behold their manliness and fierce valor; having gone from here, let us challenge those archers.
With these words, she went forth once more with him, out of both passion and her role as a messenger, toward that devoted wife.
She was alone, highly meritorious, staying in her own home, and absorbed in meditation on the feet of her husband;
just as a skilled yogi, having fixed his mind, remains free from conceptualization and does not form mental constructs. ||16||

Then the Great-Souled One, whose banner bears the fish and who is the destroyer of cities, assumed a most wonderful form, endowed with immeasurable splendor; he appeared dark-hued, adorned with ornaments, and possessed of great majesty, causing Satī to be utterly bewildered.

Having seen that great person of easy grace moving about in such a state of intense passion—the high-souled husband of the Vaiśya woman, who was endowed with beauty, possessed of virtue, and aware of her feelings—[he spoke]. (18)
Oṃ! Just as the fame of a pearl situated upon a lotus petal shines forth, so too did the true nature of that devoted wife shine forth, endowed with perfect truth. 19.
"By this messenger sent previously, tell that young woman who knows his virtues:
'He shall show me all of this—the very essence of his playful nature and his manifold forms. (20)
Having abandoned me, who am powerful and whose time has come, how could that wicked man live, even if joined with pleasure, when he is crushed by the heavy burden of Satī? (21)

Whoever, endowed with excellent intelligence, should live by fully grasping even my own nature—this body of mine is indeed empty, for it is currently devoid of activity and is just like a corpse. (22)

The subjects of the village of the body have perished; having undertaken the task known as "well-transformed," he, desiring it, led that fair one—who was equal even to my superior—to a state of supreme splendor. (23)
When he is immortal, powerful, filled with joy, and himself dancing before my very eyes, then let him speak such a marvel as well—he who desires me and wishes even to consume me. (24)
Having reflected thus, that great chaste woman, whose mind was firmly bound by the rope known as truth, entered her own home at that time in order to ascertain his state with certainty. (25)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Upākhyāna* (Episode) of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. || 54 ||
The fifty-fifth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Having understood her intention, the king of the Asuras spoke to Kāma, who was standing before him.
And there exists no sharp, virtuous bliss of meditation that is false in nature, which can withstand the power of the fire of mindfulness. ||1||
Having taken the bow called Dharma in her own hand and the excellent arrow named Jñāna,
she stands ready in the field of battle to fight.
Like a hero who is full of proud valor. ||2||

Desiring victory, you exert your human effort solely for the sake of your own human goals; yet you are unable to defeat me in battle today—whatever is destined to happen must be considered right here and now.
O Śambhu, you were previously burnt right here by that great-souled one; having entered into conflict with him, the fruit of that evil deed has now arisen for you as Anaṅga—Smara, truly so. ||4||

Just as you previously experienced the intense fruit of the karma you committed, so too shall you certainly attain a most contemptible womb; O virtuous one, you are being addressed right here along with this woman.

Those ignorant men who harbor enmity toward high-souled beings throughout the three worlds consume their own evil deeds; that fruit is indeed accompanied by suffering and the destruction of their physical form.
Having proclaimed this and having abandoned this virtuous woman, we two have indeed gone forth as we pleased;
yet, through our association with Satī in the past, an unbearable fruit consisting of sin was obtained by us. (7)
"You alone know this history: I was cursed by Gautama because of my smile;
ever since then, I have been born with the testicles of a ram. You, however, having abandoned me there, have departed. (8)
The splendor and power of virtuous women are indeed incomparable; even the Creator and the Sun are unable to endure it.
This most despicable form would have been destroyed long ago, for it was cursed by the sage Anasūyā.
He eclipsed the rising sun with his great speed, blazing thus with splendor as he warded off the death of his master, which had been brought about by the curse of Kauṇḍinya Māṇḍavya.

The three gods were reduced to the status of his own sons by Atri’s beloved wife through her devotion to her husband; have you not heard this from the Purāṇas? Truly, virtuous women who are ever-yoked to truth possess great power. (11)
Sāvitrī, the daughter of Dyumatsena, brought back her beloved who had been taken away;
she restored here to Aśvapati his excellent son, and her virtue was thus celebrated throughout the world.

A fool who touches the crest of a flame or attempts to cross the ocean with his arms would surely perish; likewise, one who tries to subdue a virtuous woman who has transcended passion is like one attempting to carry a heavy stone bound to his neck while swimming.
When Indra had spoken these words, endowed with much wisdom, for the purpose of thoroughly instructing Kāma,
the god Makaradhvaja, having heard those words, then spoke thus to that very Indra.
Kāma said:

"By your command I have come here; yet you have abandoned my firmness, my friendship, and even the very purpose of human life. For the sake of that [other goal], you speak thus to me, who am devoid of courage and filled with many fears. (15)

If I go forth with an awakened mind, there will be destruction of my reputation among the world of the lords of the Asuras; everyone will say that I am devoid of manliness and have been conquered by this woman. (16)

Even those hosts of gods and dānavas who were previously conquered by me and who formerly applied themselves to the penances of sages will immediately make even me laugh, for this terrible Manmatha has not yet been subdued by me. (17)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, I shall go forth together with you; thus I shall utterly destroy his feeble pride, as well as his splendor and fortitude.
Why, O Śakra, do you fear this?
Having thus awakened the Lord of the Suras, who held his bow with an arrow and beautiful flowers, he spoke to that illusory form standing before him in play: "Let your ladyship depart. (19)

O dear friend, listen: having gone from here to the wife of a Vaiśya—Sukalā, who is highly meritorious, established in truth, a knower of dharma, and wise in her virtues—you must perform the task that has been described as a form of assistance. 20.

Having thus addressed her with playful words, the Mind-born God (Kāma) then summoned the Love that resided within her: "A supreme task for me must be performed by you; therefore, treat her with great affection. (21)
For upon seeing Indra, this woman of beautiful eyes will surely become filled with affection;
therefore, O dear friend, listen, you must certainly bring him under your control by means of those various powers joined with virtuous words. (22)
"O friend, go quickly and prepare an illusory tree endowed with the form of a mango;
let it be adorned with flowers, preeminent with fruit, and resounded by the cries of cuckoos and bees. (23)
Having summoned the heroic Makara, who is indeed an elixir endowed with the quality of sweetness,
he sent him forth together with Anila and the others, each engaged in their own respective tasks, according to his desire.
Having thus commanded his great army, desiring to cause the delusion of the three worlds,
he set out on his expedition together with the king of the gods for the very purpose of deluding that great virtuous woman.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. || 55 ||
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
For the sake of destroying her truthfulness, Manmatha, together with the lord of the gods, [approached].
Having set out for Sukalā, Satyavat then spoke of the Dharma. ||1||
Behold the activity of the great sage Manmatha, who possesses supreme wisdom—acting for your sake, for his own, and even for the merit of that great-souled one. ||2||
We shall now describe the great site-plan known as Satya, which brings about happiness, as well as the excellent houses named Supriya and Sudeva.
Having gone there, one whose mind is heedless would surely destroy him;
for he is an enemy in the form of a friend, most wicked in nature—of this we have no doubt. (4)
The husband is a Brahmin rich in asceticism; the wife is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband.
The king is truly righteous; there is no doubt that my home is a place of dharma. ||5||
Wherever I have grown and flourished, there my dwelling shall be for my welfare;
there merit arrives and sports together with faith.
Endowed with patience, tranquility, and equanimity, he was free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of pride; likewise, he possessed truthfulness, self-restraint, compassion, and friendliness.
Endowed with wisdom and free from greed, wherever I am established, there my pure nature resides; even these kinsmen of mine are present right there.
Non-stealing, non-violence, forbearance, and the increase of [virtuous] conduct have arrived at my house;
O King of Dharma, hear of this great fortune! (9)
Viṣṇu, surrounded by Lakṣmī, performs service even to his gurus;
and the gods, led by Agni, come to my house.
Endowed with the brilliance of wisdom, he shall illuminate the path to liberation;
together with these virtuous and righteous ones, I shall indeed dwell here.
Among all these virtuous ones who are always in the form of my household, I shall indeed dwell with you, even though you have been spoken of as my family.
O illustrious one, those beings of virtuous form were taken by the Creator as his own;
we wander about with the pure, effortless play of the gods. 13.
And Īśvara, the Lord of the universe, the three-eyed one whose vehicle is the bull, dwells in my house in his own form, united with Śivā. (14)
This very abode of Maheśvara, which is the essence of worldly existence and whose form is like that of a deer, known by the name Śaṅkara’s dwelling, has indeed been destroyed by Manmatha. 15.
In the past, having relied upon Menakā, this one conquered the high-souled Viśvāmitra, who was performing supreme austerity, by means of desire.
Ahalyā, the virtuous and devoted wife of Gautama, who was dear and auspicious to him,
was moved from her great truth by that evil-minded Manmatha.
The sages who know truth and dharma, and these women devoted to their husbands—they were all in my house, yet they have been set ablaze by the fire of passion. (18)
Difficult to restrain, unbearable, pervasive, exceedingly true, and harsh—he who is ever-present and established as the ultimate truth gazes upon me alone. (19)
Knowing me to be alone, that archer with arrows in hand, that sinner, will come and destroy my house by means of the fires known as Vītihotra. (20)
Those who possess even a trace of evil, those who are cruel, and others who take refuge in heresy—
all of them, though harmful in their intellect, indeed enter the abode of truth.
Accomplished by that wicked and deceitful commander of the army through fraud,
the sinner would cause [the enemy] to fall and destroy the house with weapons and evil spirits.
May that sinful Mahābala, born of passion, strike me alone;
for, consumed by his splendor, I shall surely attain emptiness.
We desire a new house called "Woman," with the husband as its sovereign;
for this Śivamaṅgalā is dear even to the merit of Kṛkala. (24)
That wicked one has prepared himself to destroy that house called Sukalā;
here comes the powerful thousand-eyed Indra accompanied by Kāma.
For what reason, on account of desire, do they not remember their previous conduct? It was through the incident with Ahalyā that this organ was produced. (26)
Having witnessed the manly prowess of the sage and the transgression of Satī,
the king of the gods, destroyed by the fault of lust, remained there trembling with fear.
Having endured a terrible curse and being filled with great sorrow,
he [approached] this Sukalā, the beloved wife of Kṛkala, who was of virtuous conduct.
"O thousand-eyed one, I am here, impelled by desire;
act in such a way that this man does not come to Indra. (29)
The King of Dharma, the great wise one, the best among the intelligent, spoke:
"The King of Dharma said:
'I shall diminish the splendor of this Kāma and likewise bring about his death. (30)
May he behold that single means which has not been seen by me right here; and this wisdom of mine, O Great Wise One, moves about in the form of a bird. (31)
The auspicious arrival of her husband was announced by the sound from this side;
it was due both to the power of the omen and to the arrival of her husband himself.
Those who were ruined by the wicked will undoubtedly regain their mental composure;
sent forth by that Wisdom, she has gone to the house of Sukalā.
Making a great sound, she shone with the power of a goddess upon being honored and revered at that time with offerings such as incense, lamps, and food.
Sukalā asked the brahmin, "What did she say to me?
The brahmin said:
"O fortunate one, she spoke of the arrival of your husband; remain steadfast. (35)
He will arrive within seven days; it shall not be otherwise.
Having heard these most auspicious words, she suddenly became filled with great joy;
for that one who knew the Dharma, who was endowed with virtue, had arrived as indicated by the omen.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter in the Story of Sukalā within the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||56||
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Viṣṇu said:

To her who had assumed the form of a playful Satī, who was radiant, whose home was reached [by me], and who was a beautiful, devoted wife; Please note that the provided Sanskrit fragment appears to be incomplete. The translation reflects the portion given. If you have the full verse or passage, please provide it for a complete rendering.
When she had arrived, the virtuous woman, endowed with the nature of truth, spoke these words with reverence: "Blessed one! (1)
Honored by those most meritorious words, she laughed and spoke of her skill in the arts of play;
the virtuous woman gave a reply that followed the ways of illusion, which deludes the entire world, yet was measured by truth.
My husband too—my lord, who knows my virtues, who is steadfast, learned, endowed with greatness, virtuous, and of holy fame—has abandoned me and come here, O most sinful woman; listen! ||3||

Having heard everything spoken by Sukalā through meritorious words, [the king], considering her to be pure in disposition because of her feminine nature, said: "O Sundarī, why has my lord departed today? (4)
O lady who has abandoned all forms, tell me everything truly about your excellent husband;
you, whose nature is like that of a friend to those free from blemish, have come to my home while I am engaged in meditation.
In play she spoke: "Listen to this truth regarding the character and disposition of my husband:
I am always devoted to him as his beloved, and I wish to go back to him along with you. (6)

O Goddess, I shall make the words of my most virtuous husband, who is devoted to meditation, entirely stainless; O Queen, I shall serve him alone here, in accordance with his singular character and virtues.
"This is the ripening of my own past karma that manifests right before me;
for he has abandoned his husband and come to me, an unfortunate woman. (8)
With her husband, she should sustain both her life and her own body;
for how can women who are bereft of their husbands live on without being merciless? (9)
Beauty, charm, and good fortune are experienced as happiness through union with others;
however, in the scriptures, it is proclaimed that for women, a husband of great fortune is their supreme portion. (10)
Having heard everything that was said by her at that time in jest,
and having understood her true intention, he then spoke these words to her.
To those who were trusting, that illustrious lady, the goddess-like wife of Sukalpa,
spoke again all these words concerning her own actions.
In brief, he related his own previous history,
how his husband had gone on a journey intent upon performing meritorious deeds.
"O high-minded lady, your suffering is indeed very real; yet it is like a penance.
Having thus awakened her with these words and comforted her, the devoted wife [spoke]. (14)
Sūta said:
Once, while playing, she spoke thus to Sukalā: "O friend, behold this beautiful Aśvana forest, adorned with divine trees. (15)
There is a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) there that destroys all sins;
it is beautifully adorned with various spreading creepers and exquisite flowers. ||16||
"O fair-faced one, we two must also go for the sake of merit";
having heard this, Sukalā then arrived there with her. (17)
She entered that divine grove, which was like the garden of Nandana,
endowed with flowers of every season and resounding with the songs of hundreds of cuckoos.
It was being sung to by bees with most sweet sounds,
and it was filled with the holy resonance of auspiciously warbling birds.
It was resplendent with fragrant trees such as sandalwood and was perfectly filled with all enjoyments by Mādhava himself during the month of Vaiśākha.
It was created solely for the sake of deluding Sukalā;
she entered that forest, which embodies all things, together with her.
O Lord of Men, beholding that divine forest together with her, he saw that merit-bestowing, bliss-giving state which does not perceive the nature of illusion.
Then Śakra approached there, resplendent in his divine form;
Kāma also arrived there, having come together with that messenger.
Having become the lord of all enjoyments and filled with amorous playfulness, he addressed Kāma with a laugh: "This very woman has come from a noble family. (24)
"O highly fortunate one, having employed an illusion, she was brought by me from before the game and placed in your presence for the sake of play. (25)
"Show your manly prowess this very day; if you have it, do so with certainty.
Kāma said:
"Reveal your own form, which is clever and endowed with grace."
"O thousand-eyed one, with what [strength] do I strike her with five arrows?
Indra said:
"O fool, where is that manliness of yours by which you mock the world? (27)
"Having become my support, you wish to fight this battle.
Kāma said:
"Even by that God of gods, the Great God who wields the trident—" [28]
My form has already been taken away; no sense of "mine-ness" exists for me.
Listen to my response when I wish to strike a woman. (29)
Relying upon the male form, I shall manifest my own nature;
O thousand-eyed one, I shall undertake the task for the sake of the noble lady.
When a man repeatedly contemplates the very form of a woman previously seen, that form of the woman [becomes] the object of his repeated thought. (31)
Relying upon the unseen (adṛṣṭa), I drive men to madness;
likewise, I certainly drive women to madness in this way—of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of the Gods, by remembering you, I have remembered my own unborn nature;
having seen her, I take refuge in that form which is the very essence of such a body.
Through the radiance of her own splendor, she may become both the subduer and the subdued;
assuming the form of a woman, she can utterly delude even a steadfast man. (34)
"O Indra, I shall resort to a man and become a beautiful woman;
for I am devoid of form here, so may he take on my appearance. (35)
"By relying upon your form, may they accomplish their desired goal.
Having spoken thus to the Lord of the Gods, [he entered] the body of that Great-Souled One.
The wielder of the excellent weapon (Kāma) also took refuge with Sakhāsaumādhaveya. ||37||
Even the god whose weapon is the flower, though he is the husband of that very same virtuous and highly auspicious Kṛkalā,
remains full of longing as he gazes with his eyes upon her body, which is the target of Bāṇa’s arrows.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Life Story of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* section of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. ||57||
The fifty-eighth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
"Engaged in play, the slender Sukalā, the wife of the Vaiśya, entered the forest."
She beheld that delightful grove, dense with all its trees, and Satīsā questioned her friend.
"This forest is most excellent, highly meritorious, divine, and delightful to the mind of Śiva;
it is perfected by all the foremost Siddhas who have fulfilled their desires. With joy, he questioned that friend of Sukalā. (2)
Kriḍā said:
Behold this entire forest of Makaradhvaja, endowed with divine qualities through the contemplation of perfected natures, filled with flowers and provided with the fruits of desire.
Having heard these words, she was filled with great joy;
she beheld the great conduct of the wicked-souled Kama.
The wind, carrying that fragrance which was being inhaled, blew forth,
naturally endowed with that very same scent.
His arrow entered their noses with such ease that the fair-faced lady did not even notice the fragrance of the flowers.
Yet that great lady did not relish those delicious flavors;
she was like the god of love himself, conquered while sporting with his companions.
Ashamed, he turned his face away and fell to the ground like a leaf;
for from well-ripened fruits, an old flower has been cast out.

But the son of that king, whose form was like a wave and who had been defeated by the brilliance [of the enemy], being extremely dejected in spirit, gave up the land he had obtained from the fruit [of his efforts] and returned once more. ||9||
Just as a corpse is devoured by flies in battle, so too he,
being devoured by flies, proceeds along in a continuous stream.
"Maṃ daṃ maṃ daṃ"—thus he indeed proceeds, and the birds laugh at him with various cries, fluttering about with hearts full of joy. (11)
There, birds dwelling on trees in the middle of the forest were crying out with joy;
indeed, having been conquered by Sukalā, he had taken to a downward path. ||12||

Accompanied by delight, Rati, the wife of Kāma, approached Sukalā and, smiling, said: "May it be well with you; welcome indeed, O auspicious one! Dwell here with joy, for this place is delightful due to my arrival. (13)
"Even for the high-souled Indra, there is nothing desired that is not pure;
therefore, tell me what you desire, and I shall bring it to you without a doubt. (14)
Sūta said:
Having seen his wife speaking thus, or having heard her well-spoken words, my high-minded husband accepted her affection and departed from there. (15)
"Wherever my husband goes on his journey, there I shall go along with him;
for that is my desire, my pleasure, and that is the source of my longing and my refuge. (16)
Having heard both [the words] spoken, Rati and Prīti, overcome with shame and feeling abashed, departed; there, the exceedingly powerful Kāma remained.
They spoke to that great hero, who was stationed upon Indra’s body, drawing his bow with great strength and making himself a target for their eyes. (18)
This highly fortunate woman, ever devoted to her husband and desiring her husband, has abandoned her own great wisdom, manliness, and self-will, which are otherwise difficult to overcome. (19)
Kāma said:
"O lady, behold the form of this high-souled Indra;
if you do so, then I shall slay him, without a doubt."
Then the god, the lord of the gods, assuming a great form and wearing a disguise,
quickly followed her with supreme grace.
Surrounded by all manner of enjoyments and adorned with every ornament,
he wore divine garlands and garments, and was anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
Accompanied by that Arati, he went to where his wife,
the goddess-like Sukalā, who was of great fortune and a follower of truth, was staying, and spoke to her.
"O auspicious one, previously I sent you to him with affection in the presence of a messenger; why do you not welcome him, now that he has come here to you? (24)
Sukalā said:
"I am protected by my high-souled sons, who are the guardians of my husband; may you be blessed.
Being alone with them as my companions, I have no fear of anyone whatsoever."
Guarded on all sides by brave men who act like heroes,
she was not permitted to speak too much, as he was occupied with his duties.
O Mahāmati, as long as his eye remains fixed upon her, why do you not feel shame while sporting with me for all that time? (27)
"Who are you that have arrived here, fearless even of death?
Indra said:
"I see only you, who have come into the midst of this forest. (28)
"You have described the heroic sons of my husband;
how may I see them? Show them before me. (29)

Sukalā said: Having established me in the sovereignty over his entire circle of attendants, and having entrusted [the kingdom] to those known as Dhṛti, Mati, Gati, and Buddhi while remaining true to his word,
that great-souled one— who was ever devoted to all immovable dharma and whose nature was the dharma of Madana’s son— always protected me.
May this Dharma, which always protects me through its pure virtues, behold me ever present before him, joined with peace and forbearance;

and may Awakening, possessed of great power and vast fame, never fail to protect me—if he does not, I shall surely be bound by firm fetters born of my own qualities, and thus fall into his very presence.
All were made endowed with protection against the calamities of this world through truth and other virtues; all attained the gains of Dharma and the like, possessing wisdom and prowess. (32)
"They protect me alone; why do you seek me by force? Who are you, having become fearless, who has come together with the messenger? (33)
Truth, righteousness, merit, and likewise powerful knowledge and other virtues—
these are the companions of my husband, and they protect him within this dwelling.
I am constantly protected by a thousandfold guard and devoted to self-restraint and tranquility;
even Śacīpati himself would not be able to conquer me. (35)
Or even if the powerful god of love himself should approach me, I am always ready to bite him; this is the truth by my very name Satyakā, and it is not otherwise.
His arrows will be useless, there is no doubt;
for Dharma and the other great warriors will surely slay you alone. (37)
"Go far away! Do not stay here; depart quickly! If you remain even though being forbidden, you shall be reduced to ashes. (38)
When you behold that immortal form without your husband, I shall consume you just as fire burns wood; it shall not be otherwise.
Having heard this, the Thousand-eyed One spoke in the presence of Manmatha:
"Behold his manliness; fight with your own manly prowess! (40)
Just as they had come, so all of them— Indra and the others, O Great King— then departed for their respective abodes, distressed by the fear of the great curse.
When all of them had departed, Sukalā, devoted to her husband and endowed with merit, returned to her own home while meditating upon her husband. ||42||
Then, O King, she whose deity is her husband reached her own home, which was endowed with merit, composed of all sacred fords, and consisting of all sacrifices. 43.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," in the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. 58.
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Having visited all the holy fords (tīrthas), Kṛkala was returning toward his home.
He set out accompanied by the caravan leader and a great multitude of people.
Thinking thus constantly: "My saṃsāra is fruitful;
my ancestors, being satisfied, will go to heaven, and not otherwise. (2)
Having bound his grandfathers in the form of a direct visual manifestation before him, he spoke thus: "This is the supreme merit for your benefit. (3)
Divine in form and of great body, Kṛkala spoke these words: "There is no fruit from your pilgrimage; you have merely exerted yourself in vain. (4)
"You yourself attain contentment, yet you do not perform the highest merit.
Having heard this, the Vaiśya Kṛkala was then afflicted by grief.
Who are you that speaks thus? Why have my grandfathers been bound? By the power of what fault has this occurred? Tell me the reason for this.
Why is there no fruit from visiting sacred fords? Why is my pilgrimage not [fruitful]?
Explain all of this clearly, if you know it for certain. (7)
Dharma said:
"He who departs, abandoning his own wife—who is pure and most meritorious—all the fruit of his merit becomes futile; it is not otherwise. (8)

[He saw] his wife, who was devoted to the practice of dharma, meritorious, dedicated to virtuous vows, intent on devotion to her husband, endowed with excellent qualities, and affectionate toward the righteous.
If one abandons that very [duty] and proceeds to perform religious acts, all his religious practice becomes futile; it is not otherwise.
She was devoted to all proper conduct, intent on the practice of dharma,
constantly dedicated to her husband's vow, and always fond of knowledge.
In the home of that man who possesses such a meritorious and great chaste wife endowed with these qualities, the gods of great majesty always reside. (12)
The ancestors residing within his body desire his welfare;
likewise, the sacred rivers such as the Gaṅgā and the oceans are present there—of this there is no doubt.
In the house of Puṇyāsatī dwells Satyavatī, who is devoted to truth;
there are sacrifices there, cows, and sages—of this there is no doubt.
There, all the sacred fords and various meritorious sites remain through their union with their wives; none of these exist otherwise. (15)
Through the application of a meritorious wife, the state of householdership is fully realized;
there is no dharma higher than the life of a householder on this earth. (16)
The home of a householder is meritorious, endowed with truth and virtue; it indeed contains all sacred fords (tīrthas) and is filled with all the gods, O Vaiśya. ||17||
All living beings subsist by relying upon the householder's stage of life;
we do not see any other stage of life that is so excellent. (18)
In the house of that man, O gods, the Agnihotra sacrifice, all eternal dharmas, and the practices of charity and conduct continue to prevail. (19)
Thus, for one who is deprived of his wife, his home becomes like a forest;
even his sacrifices and various acts of charity do not succeed.
For a man deprived of his wife, even the great vow is not accomplished; nor are all religious duties or various meritorious acts fulfilled. 21.
There is no sacred ford equal to a wife for the purpose of accomplishing dharma;
listen, for there is no other dharma for a householder in the three worlds.
Wherever the wife's house is, there also is the man's; it is not otherwise.
Whether in a village or in the forest, that is the means for accomplishing all dharma.
There is no sacred ford equal to a wife; there is no happiness equal to a wife;
there is no merit equal to a wife for the sake of crossing over and for one's welfare. (24)
O lowest of men, having abandoned your virtuous wife who is devoted to righteousness, and having forsaken your home and duty, where do you dwell? What fruit of dharma have you obtained? (25)
Because you did not perform the *śrāddha* and the giving of gifts at the Ādītīrtha, your ancestors have indeed been bound by that very fault. (26)
"Your honor is indeed a thief, for these very thieves have consumed the food of the *śrāddha* offered by you, which was given without her, they being so exceedingly greedy. (27)
I shall describe the merit of that good son who, endowed with faith, offers the śrāddha gift; even by means of the piṇḍa offered by his wife, I declare his merit. (28)
Just as satisfaction arises for men by drinking nectar, so too does it arise for the ancestors through the śrāddha; I tell you this truth, the absolute truth. (29)
"For the householder's dharma, the wife is the mistress.
This act you have committed—climbing onto the funeral pyre like a foolish thief—is in vain. (30)
These ancestors are thieves by whom food was eaten without her; for even food resembling nectar, when offered with one's own hand, becomes an offense against the wife. (31)
The ancestors, with delighted minds, eat that very food;
by that alone they attain satisfaction and become fully contented.
Therefore, without a wife, dharma cannot be accomplished by a man;
there is no sacred ford equal to a wife for men who bestow a happy rebirth.
Whatever dharma one performs without a wife shall likewise become fruitless. ||34||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixtieth chapter.
Kṛkala said:
How is perfection attained? How is the liberation of the ancestors achieved?
Now, O King of Dharma, explain this to me in detail as well. ||1||
Dharma said:
"Go home, O highly fortunate one; without you, she suffers.
Console your own wife Sukalā, who is a practitioner of dharma. (2)
"Go to his house for the offering of the *śrāddha* and perform it with your own hand;
remembering the sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*), worship the supreme gods. (3)
Furthermore, your success in undertaking pilgrimages will come to pass;
for he who wishes to accomplish dharma in this world without a wife [is like one without a companion]. (4)
Having utterly abandoned the life of a householder, he who wanders alone in the forest becomes fruitless in this world; the gods do not honor him. ||5||
Sacrifices attain success only when there is a housewife in his home;
for he who is alone is incapable of accomplishing the goals of dharma and artha.
Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to that Vaiśya, Dharma departed as he had come; and the righteous-souled Kṛkala also set out for his own home.
Having reached his own home and seen that devoted wife,
the wise and intelligent man, along with that merchant, returned to his own place.
Seeing her husband, who was skilled in the Dharma, reunited with her,
she then performed auspicious and meritorious rites for his arrival.
The virtuous-souled one also related the activities of Dharma;
having heard her husband’s words, which brought great joy, the highly fortunate lady [listened]. (10)
Having praised the words concerning the Dharma, he then approved them accordingly.
Viṣṇu said:
"Then that Vaiśya, Sakalaka, together with her, performed a most meritorious act."
Standing in the temple of the deity, he performed a śrāddha rite with faith;
the ancestors, gods, and gandharvas arrived together in celestial chariots. (12)
The high-souled sages likewise praised that Lord of the Universe; and I, as well as Brahmā, were joined by the Goddess in praising Maheśvara.
All the gods, together with the gandharvas, assembled there in their celestial chariots;
then I myself was Brahmā, and Maheśvara was united with the Goddess.
All the gods, together with the Gandharvas, were gratified by her truthfulness;
they spoke to those two high-souled ones, who were knowers of dharma and experts in truth.
"O you of excellent vows, may it be well with you; choose a boon together with your wife.
Kṛkala said:
"By whose merit and by whose asceticism, O best of gods, [have we been favored]? (16)
"We have come here to grant a boon to you along with your wife.
Indra said:
"This Satī is highly fortunate, virtuous, beautiful, and auspicious. (17)
"Delighted by her truthfulness, we wish to grant you a boon;
that has been stated in brief, as well as her previous history. (18)
Having heard the greatness of her conduct, her righteous husband was filled with joy; his eyes overflowing with delight, he rejoiced together with her. (19)
All the various deities spoke again and again:
"O highly fortunate ones, O three eternal gods, if you are pleased... (20)
And other meritorious sages, having shown compassion toward me, said: "In birth after birth, I shall indeed practice devotion to the gods. (21)
"By your grace, may I find delight in the truth of the Dharma;
thereafter, together with my wife and my ancestors, may I indeed reach the world of Viṣṇu. (22)
"O gods of great majesty, I wish to go, provided you are pleased.
The gods said: "So be it, O highly fortunate one; everything shall come to pass."
Then, O King, they rained down a shower of flowers upon the two of them; thereafter, they sang a most meritorious, charming, and melodious song.
The hosts of Apsaras danced, knowing the true essence of the songs sung by the Gandharvas;
then, O best of kings, the gods along with the Gandharvas returned each to his own abode.
Having granted the boon, they departed while being praised by that devoted wife.
This is celebrated as Nārītīrtha; shall I tell you anything else? 26.
All this, an unsurpassed and meritorious narrative, has been told to you;
O King, the man who hears it is liberated from all sins. (27)
A woman who listens with faith to this supreme narrative of Sukalā shall never be deprived of good fortune, truthfulness, sons, or grandsons. (28)
She shall live happily with her husband, possessing moderate wealth and grain; she shall remain devoted to her husband in birth after birth, and not otherwise. (29)
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of the Vedas, a Kṣatriya shall be victorious,
and there is no doubt that wealth and grain shall indeed abound in the house of a Vaiśya.
O King, one who knows the Dharma and practices virtuous conduct shall always be happy;
even a Śūdra attains happiness and prospers through sons and grandsons. (31)
From this, vast prosperity arises, adorned with wealth and grain. ||32||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Life of Sukalā," in the *Venu-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-one.
Vena said:
The Bhāryātīrtha is proclaimed as the most excellent among all holy places;
the Pitṛtīrtha is declared to be the supreme means for the liberation of sons. (1)
Viṣṇu said:
In the great sacred field of Kurukṣetra, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Kuṇḍala;
the noble-souled Kuṇḍala had a virtuous son named Sukarman. (2)
The two great-souled ones, his preceptors, were very aged, knowers of the Dharma, experts in the scriptures, and afflicted by old age. (3)
Then, possessed of supreme devotion and endowed with a pure disposition, that knower of dharma served the two of them tirelessly, day and night.
Therefore, he studied the Vedas from his father and numerous treatises;
he was devoted to all forms of conduct, skillful, knowledgeable in dharma, and fond of wisdom.
He himself performed the massaging of the limbs, the driving of the carriage,
and the washing of the feet, as well as the bathing, feeding, and service for his two gurus.
Through devotion and by one's own nature, one should become absorbed in that meditation;
O King of kings, one should also perform service toward one's mother and father.
Sūta said:
O best of kings, at that time there was a Brahmin named Pippala, who was a descendant of the high-souled Kaśyapa. (8)
He performed austerities, abstaining from food, with his self controlled and his envy conquered; endowed with compassion, charity, and self-restraint, he had fully subdued desire and anger.
The wise and high-minded one, having gone to the ten forests, being devoted to the peace of knowledge, performed austerities while restraining all his senses. 10.
By the power of his asceticism, those whose bodies move with the speed of thought dwell there in that auspicious age as if they were within a single womb.
Seeing that austerity of his, the sages were filled with wonder;
no one had ever performed such penance as the sage was performing.
And the gods, headed by Indra, were struck with supreme wonder:
"Oh, how intense is his austerity, and how perfect his tranquility, self-control, and restraint! (13)
Free from change and free from agitation, devoid of desire and anger, he remained like the earth, enduring cold, wind, and heat. ||14||
O best of the twice-born, that wise one, whose mind was detached from sense objects and whose hair stood on end with joy, did not hear the sound of anyone approaching. 15.
Having gone to such a place and remained there with a one-pointed mind, he became absorbed in the meditation on Brahman, his lotus-like face serene. ||16||
Having become like stone or wood, motionless and standing like a mountain, he appeared as firm as a pillar, a lover of dharma.
With his body emaciated by austerity, full of supreme faith, and free from malice, one thousand years passed for that wise man in this manner. (18)
A great body of earth had been accumulated by many ants;
upon it was their own natural dwelling, an anthill with a massive form. (19)
Remaining within the interior of an anthill as if rendered inert,
that very Brahmin Pippala thus performed great austerity.
The best of the twice-born was completely encircled by black cobras;
those snakes, fierce with virulent poison, bit that brahmin of formidable splendor. (21)
Even though the poison reached his vital organs, it did not cause him pain;
by the power of that brahmin, the serpents attained peace.
From his body there arose flames of blazing splendor;
they were seen in many forms and in great abundance, each distinct from the others.
O best of men, just as the rays of fire are extremely fierce, so too [is he];
just as the sun, having entered the interior of a cloud, shines with its beams.
Likewise, a brahmin staying within an anthill was bitten by a serpent with great fury and even with its fangs, due to the excessive splendor of the Pippala tree.
O best of kings, having pierced his navel with the tip of his tusk and split open his skin, he thus performed penance for one thousand years. (26)
The time passed for that great-souled sage, the king of kings, as he practiced his ascetic discipline through the three periods of the day, enduring cold, rain, and heat. (27)
The time has passed for the great-souled Pippala, the great king;
likewise, that high-minded one practiced subsisting only on air.
Three thousand years passed while he was performing his austerities;
then, in ancient times, the gods showered a rain of flowers upon his head.
O highly fortunate one, you are a knower of Brahman and a knower of Dharma; of this there is no doubt.
You have become composed of all knowledge through your own past actions. (30)
Whatever you desire to obtain, that you shall obtain; it shall not be otherwise. You yourself shall become one whose every desire is fulfilled. (31)
Having heard these great words, the high-minded Pippalāda bowed to all the deities with devotion, his body bent low.
Overcome with great joy, he replied to those words:
"How may this entire universe come under my control? (33)
"O King, act accordingly so that I may become a vidyādhara.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, the wise one became silent. (34)
"Let it be so," the gods then said to that best of the twice-born;
having granted the boon, O highly fortunate one, they departed from that great-souled being. (35)
When those gods have departed, O best of the twice-born, the Pippala tree should constantly accomplish devotion to Brahman and contemplate the subjugation of the universe. 36.
From that time forward, O Indra among kings, that best of brahmins, Pippala,
having attained the station of a Vidyadhara, was honored as one who travels at will.
Thus the brahmin Sapippala attained the station of a Vidyādhara;
he was born as a lord in the world of the gods, proficient in all the scriptures. (38)
Once, the immensely powerful Pippala reflected:
"Everything shall be subject to my will, for I have been granted this most excellent boon. (39)
To that end, the eminent brahmin prepared to give his word of assurance;
whatever he intended to do, he brought that very thing under his control. (40)
Thus, with a mind full of confidence, he reflected:
"In this world, there is no second person, no supreme being equal to me. (41)
Sūta said:
While the high-souled Pippala was thus reflecting,
the crane, having understood his mental state, spoke to him.
O King, standing on the shore of the lake, he addressed Pippala with a melodious voice, full of meaning and endowed with excellence of diction. 43.
Why do you harbor such pride, thinking yourself to be the Supreme Self? For I certainly do not consider that the power to control all things belongs to you alone.
"This rite, whether it be under one's control or not, is praised as being directed toward this world;
you do not know that which is directed beyond, O Pippala, you of deluded intellect. (45)
"For as many as three thousand years you have practiced austerities;
O twice-born one, why now do you indulge in pride in vain? (46)
The son of Kuṇḍala was wise, virtuous in action, free from disease, and highly intelligent;
the entire world, both those who were submissive and those who were not, was under his control—listen to this in detail. 47.
The wise man understands both that which is near and that which is far;
there is no one in the world with great knowledge equal to him—listen, O Pippala! (48)
You are not equal to Sukarman, the son of Nakuṇḍala;
for he gave no gift, nor did he contemplate the knowledge of the Vedas. (49)
At one time, he did not perform rituals such as burnt offerings (huta) or sacrifices (yajña),
nor did he go on pilgrimages to sacred fords (tīrtha-yātrā), nor did he practice the worship of the sacrificial fire.
He had once performed the supreme service of following the dharma of a brahmin;
he was pure, self-controlled, wise, and always devoted to his father, mother, and friends. (51)
He was accomplished in the study of the Vedas and skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures;
indeed, such was the wisdom of that boy of virtuous deeds.
"Such knowledge as yours does not exist; you carry this vain pride in vain.
Pippala said: "Who are you that, in the form of a bird, would thus revile me?"
Why is this knowledge called *niṃda*? What is its nature, and how does it transcend [the senses]?
Tell me that in detail; how can such knowledge be attained by you? (54)

May he explain in great detail, preceded by knowledge, the entire course of that which is directed toward the transcendent, as it pertains to all those who have turned their course back toward it, O best of the egg-born.
"Or will you become Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Rudra?
The crane replied: "There is no essence to your asceticism, nor is there any fruit from it. (56)
Listen now to the fruit of the penance performed by you without weariness, as well as the qualities of your son Kuṇḍala, though he is but a child. (57)
"Thus, although he possesses consciousness, that state has not been fully realized by him.
O best of the twice-born, go from here and ask me about his form."
"The righteous-souled one will indeed declare all knowledge to you alone.
Viṣṇu said:
"Having thus heard all that was spoken by the King of Sārasa," [he departed].
He went forth with great speed to the great hermitage of Daśārṇa.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within this very narrative. ||61||
The sixty-second chapter.
Viṣṇu said: Having gone to the hermitage of Kuṇḍala, which was filled with truth and righteousness.
Then, seeing him performing good deeds and being devoted to his father and mother.
He was serving that high-souled one, whose valor was true to his preceptors, who possessed a magnificent form, great splendor, and was filled with vast knowledge. ||2||
He saw him seated at the feet of his parents, endowed with great devotion, peaceful, and a vast treasury of all knowledge. ||3||
Having seen the high-minded Pippala arrived at the gateway, the noble-souled Sukarman, the son of Kuṇḍala, [approached him]. (4)
Rising quickly from his seat, he again performed a respectful welcome: "Come, O highly fortunate one, O great-minded Vidyādhara! (5)
The one of great intelligence offered him a seat, water for the feet, and the respectful offering;
"O one of great wisdom, may you proceed without obstacles through your skill. (6)
He questioned that Pippala who had arrived, saying, "I shall tell you everything regarding the reason for your arrival today. (7)
O highly fortunate one, for three thousand years you performed such ascetic penance,
and thus you obtained a boon from the gods.
You have not attained submissiveness, nor likewise the power to act according to your will;
therefore, you do not know me, and you carry your pride in vain.
Having observed all their actions, the high-souled Sārasena spoke my name and my unsurpassed knowledge.
Pippala said: "O Brahmin, that crane on the riverbank who imparted all this knowledge to me—who indeed is the powerful Lord capable of harming him? (11)
Sukarman said: "That crane on the bank of the river whom you have described as Brahmā, know him to be the Supreme Lord of great knowledge. (12)
"Ask whatever else you wish; I shall speak thus.
Viṣṇu said:
"O King Nandana, having been addressed in this way, that righteous-souled one of virtuous deeds—"
Pippala said:
"We have heard on this earth that the entire world is certainly under your control;
therefore, O Brahmin, out of curiosity, show me that through your own effort. (14)
"Behold this very curiosity of mine today, which is the cause of both subduing and not subduing!
Thus spoke the virtuous Sukarman to Pippala.
Then Sukarman called to mind the gods for the sake of providing proof:
Indra and the other world-protectors, and the gods led by Agni.
Then the various Vidyādharas who had been summoned gathered together,
and the gods, led by Agni, spoke to Sukarman.
"Why have you remembered him? Tell me the reason for this purpose. Sukarman said:
"This very Pippala, the Vidyadhara, has indeed arrived here."
He spoke to me alone, the cause of both subjection and liberation; I was summoned for the sake of providing testimony before this very Great Soul. (19)
"Go each to your own respective place," he said to the asuras.
Then the gods spoke to that high-minded one of noble deeds. (20)
Our vision of you, O Brahmin, has become fruitful;
choose a boon—whatever is pleasing to your mind—for it shall be well with you. (21)
Having thus spoken, those best of gods were freed from doubt;
then that most excellent of brahmins, having bowed with devotion to those deities, made this request: ||22||
One should offer unwavering and intense devotion, endowed with true feeling, to one's mother and father; that indeed is the unsurpassed supreme boon.
O Lord of Gods, let my father go to that world which you have granted as this most excellent boon; likewise, O Lord of Gods, I do not ask for any other boon from my mother.
The gods said:
"O best of Brahmins, you are devoted to your father; O twice-born one, by your devotion we are pleased.
O performer of good deeds, listen with affection to our words, which are endowed with divine power. (25)
Having spoken thus, O King Nanda, the gods departed for their own celestial realm;
by him, his entire sovereignty was displayed before her.
But Pippala also witnessed a curious and most wonderful sight;
then that righteous-souled one spoke to Pippala, the son of Kuṇḍalā.
"This form is directed toward us, while that other form is directed away; O best of speakers, tell me of the power of both."
Sukarman said:
I shall describe the very sign of the supreme form, by which the worlds—including Indra and the others, along with all things moving and stationary—attain joy. (29)
This very Lord of the World is the all-pervading Sovereign;
His form has indeed never been seen by any yogi whatsoever.
The Śruti itself speaks thus, as if apprehensive of being questioned:
"He is without hands, feet, or nose; He is without ears and devoid of a mouth. (31)
He perceives all the deeds performed by the inhabitants of the three worlds; he hears what they have spoken without ears, acting as their perfect witness.
Even one devoid of means of locomotion may go forth, for he is seen everywhere;
even one devoid of hands grasps, and one devoid of feet runs swiftly.
O Brahmin, he is seen everywhere as all-pervading, yet devoid of feet;
that Lord whom the sages who perceive reality do not behold.
He beholds them all established in the states of truth and untruth—the pervasive, stainless, perfected one, the bestower of perfection, the leader of all. (35)
That which the great yogi Vyāsa, skilled in the meaning of the Dharma, knows as the embodiment of splendor, the sky, uniform in color and infinite— 36.
This very stainless form has been declared with certainty by the Śruti;
Vyāsa knows this state, as does Mārkaṇḍeya.
I shall proclaim that which is recent; listen with a one-pointed mind:
when the self of all beings has departed, he goes forth alone. (38)
Having established his bed upon the waters, seated upon the throne of all enjoyments,
Janārdana alone rests there for a long time.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, whose soul was absorbed in yoga, became weary of wandering; desiring a place of rest, he went to the Jalāṃdhaka forest. ||40||
While wandering about, he beheld the Lord reclining upon the serpent Śeṣa as his couch,
resembling ten million suns and adorned with divine ornaments.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, the all-pervading Lord,
who had entered into yogic sleep, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
O best of the twice-born, there was a single woman of great fortune, dark as a mass of people, with a terrifying form and a mouth made fearsome by her fangs. 43.
Thus addressed by her, that best of sages, the great muni, said,
"Do not fear," and [offered] a very broad lotus leaf, five yojanas in length.
In that leaf, the great goddess Mārkaṇḍeya was placed;
even while Keśava was asleep, there was no fear for you there. (45)
He said to that yoginī: "O beautiful lady, who are you? Now that he has been conquered, you alone remain here, strengthened by him. (46)
Thus questioned by the sage, O Brahmin, the Goddess respectfully replied:
"Keśava is sleeping upon a couch formed by the coils of a serpent. (47)
I am indeed his Vaiṣṇava power, called here Kālarātri;
know me alone, O best of Brahmins, as being endowed with all illusory powers (māyā). 48.
"In the Mahāmāyā Purāṇas, this is told for the purpose of deluding the world.
Having said this, the goddess departed; indeed, the Pippala tree vanished from sight. 49.
While the Goddess was following after him as Ārkaṇḍeya looked on, a lotus with the luster of gold sprang up from his navel. 50.
From him was born Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, possessed of great splendor;
from him all the worlds, both stationary and moving, were produced.
O King, Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as the gods led by Agni,
have displayed their forms in their current, manifest states through me.
This one whose nature is directed inward is without support when directed outward;
when he manifests a body, they become the very form of that body.
O Ahipippala, all the worlds beginning with Brahmā are indeed transitory;
these worlds that exist within the three realms are transitory. (54)
Yogis clearly perceive this supreme state,
which is the form of liberation and the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, as the self that has become turned away from the world.
The unmanifest, the imperishable, the syllable *Haṃ*, pure and endowed with accomplishment—know that to be the form of the Transcendent One standing before you as a Vidyādhara. (56)
"I have explained everything; I shall speak further as another sage would. Pippala said:
"O you of excellent vows, from where did this great knowledge arise for you?"
Knowing the course that leads hitherward as well as the course that leads away, such supreme knowledge of the three worlds revolves within you alone. (58)
O you of excellent vows, I do not see any higher culmination of austerity than this:
that you have performed sacrifice, officiated at sacrifices, visited sacred fords, and practiced penance through speech. (59)
"Tell me of his power; by what means was all this knowledge attained by you?
Sukarman said:
"I know nothing other than austerity, nor have I performed any emaciation of the body. (60)

Neither performing sacrifices nor officiating at them, nor visiting sacred fords, nor meditation accomplished through prostration, nor even the auspicious time born of virtuous deeds [can equal this]. (61)
I clearly understand that the worship of both one's father and mother is always performed with the hands of both of them. (62)
I myself shall perform the meritorious washing of his feet, as well as the massaging of his limbs, his bathing, and his feeding. (63)
Absorbed in meditation throughout the three periods of the day, I shall perform their service day after day;
likewise, I shall offer the water from washing their feet to my mother and father every single day.
O Pippala, with a spirit of devotion and a pure disposition, I honor and worship you as long as my gurus remain alive.
For that duration, an incomparable snow and sandalwood fragrance is produced;
I worship these two three times a day with a mind of pure devotion. (66)
O Pippala, I am indeed abiding here, pure and engaged in the graceful play of movement;
what is the use of other austerities, or what is the use of withering my body? 67.
O twice-born one, what need have I for pilgrimages to sacred fords or other merits? For that very fruit which is obtained through all sacrifices is attained by her alone. (68)
The fruit of that [merit] is not seen by me even from service to a father;
likewise, service to a mother bestows a supreme state upon sons. (69)
Service to one's mother is the essence of all actions and the very soul of everything in the three worlds; through it, even the world of one's son is attained.
In serving one's father, just as this great merit is produced, there too is the holy site of Gaṅgā-Gayā, and there indeed is Puṣkara as well. (71)
Wherever one's mother and father may reside, that is undoubtedly the son's [true] pilgrimage site; there are other various meritorious tirthas as well. (72)
Indeed, my son, even more than from serving his father, this is the fruit of that father’s service, as well as the fruit of his giving and his asceticism. (73)
O Brahmin, for a virtuous son, any other duty becomes mere labor;
through service to his father, a son attains unsurpassed merit. (74)
One's own actions alone are one's everything, both in this world and in the next;
likewise, while living, these two—one's mother and father—are one's gurus.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who becomes a son and serves him:
even the gods and the sages, who are fond of merit, are pleased with him. (76)
In this world, the three worlds are satisfied by service rendered to one's father; indeed, he who constantly washes the feet of his mother and father [attains great merit]. (77)
For him who provides his father and likewise his mother with meritorious offerings of sweet food and drink, a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day.
I shall describe the merit of him who constantly feeds [them] with devotion:
the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) arises for his son. (79)
They were honored with devotion by their guru with betel-leaves, coverings, drinks, foods, and meritorious meals. (80)
He too shall become omniscient and shall attain glory and fame;
having seen his mother and father, the son shall address them with joy. 81.
The treasures are pleased with him and remain in his house;
cows become friendly toward him, always bestowing happiness upon his son.
