Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Pilgrimage Site of Mother and Father," in the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-third chapter. Sukarman said:
And when those two, his mother and father, the best of the twice-born, had bathed—
For even when a mere fragment falls upon every limb of his son, [he feels it as if it were his own]. ||1||
A bath equal to all sacred fords (tīrthas) is produced even for a son who is fallen, infirm, aged, or incapable of all ritual acts. ||2||
O dear one, I shall describe the merit of that son who attends upon his father afflicted with leprosy, as well as his mother in such a condition. (3)
Viṣṇu becomes pleased in spirit toward him; of this there is no doubt.
He goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is indeed unattainable even by yogis. ||4||
These two parents, his elders and preceptors, are now infirm, wretched, and aged; yet this evil-minded son abandons them when they have fallen into a great illness. (5)
He attains the terrible Putranaraka hell, which is teeming with worms;
and having been summoned here by his two aged elders, he remains in this state.
I shall declare the sin of him who, having become a son of one who has not set out [on pilgrimage], becomes a fool eating excrement; he is born as a village pig, without a doubt. (7)
Furthermore, for as many as a thousand births, one is born again as a dog;
likewise, when the mother and father remain in their old age within the home with their sons.
If a son eats food himself without first having fed those two,
he shall consume urine and excrement for as long as a thousand births.
He who behaves with contempt toward his mother, father, or elders shall become a sinful black serpent for two hundred births. (10)
Even a grasping [mind] becomes corrupted even after hundreds of millions of births;
yet such a son reviles those two [parents] with even bitter words. (11)
Even if a tiger should become sinful, it later becomes a bear;
likewise, a son of evil intellect may come to despise his mother and father. (12)
One shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a thousand yugas;
there is no sacred ford (tīrtha) equal to the mother, nor is there anything equal to the father for sons. 13.
For the sake of crossing over, for welfare, and indeed for benefit both in this world and the next;
therefore, O highly wise one, I worship the Father-God. (14)
I have become one with all the gods through union with the Mother-God;
by the grace of my mother and father, this supreme knowledge has arisen within me. 15.
Know that this entire threefold world has come under the power of me, the servant of this high-souled deity, whose course is directed toward the lower realms. (16)
O high-minded one, all knowledge arose for that very Vāsudeva from the grace of his father and mother. (17)

What wise man truly honors his father and likewise his mother, by means of those [Vedic] studies complete with their limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas), and endowed with the Śrutis and Śāstras? (18)
O Brahmins, for him by whom the preceptor has not been honored even with the Vedas, and for him by whom the mother has not been honored, the Vedas are useless. (19)
O Brahmin, what is the use of sacrifices, austerities, gifts, or acts of worship for one by whom his mother has not been honored? For him, all these go to utter futility.

He by whom the barber is not honored while living and residing in his house—this is a violation of dharma for a son, and likewise it is a failure regarding the sacred sites among men in this world. (21)
This is the liberation for one with a son, as well as the auspicious fruit of birth;
this is indeed the sacrifice and the gift for one with a son—of this there is no doubt.
One should constantly worship one's father with devotion, being intent upon that state;
for him, all that which was previously mentioned indeed comes to pass.
By him the fruit of giving has been obtained, as well as that of the sacred ford; there is no doubt.
By him who has served his mother, the fruit of sacrifice has also been attained. (24)
For him by whom the Father has been constantly worshipped with true devotion, all meritorious rites such as sacrifices and the like become fully perfected. (25)
For this purpose, I have studied this Dharmaśāstra as it was proclaimed;
indeed, O Pippala, a son should always be devoted to his father. 26.
Listen now: in the past, when his father was pleased, Yadu obtained great happiness; and when his father was angry, he incurred great sin. (27)
Even by Ruru, the descendant of Puru, who was cursed by his father to dwell upon the earth, such knowledge was attained because he worshipped these two. (28)
And through the grace of these two, the unsurpassed fruit has been attained. ||29||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Holy Site of Parents," in the *Even-upākhyāna* (Even Narrative) within the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-fourth chapter.
Pippala said: Indeed, by virtue of his father’s grace, Vaiya obtained supreme happiness.
How was it obtained and how was it well-enjoyed? Tell me this in detail.
"O best of the twice-born, son of Kuṇḍalā, why did you drink up the entire power of that sin in its full extent? [2]
Sukarman said:
Listen, for I shall relate the sin-destroying life-story of the highly meritorious Nahuṣa and the great-souled Yayāti. (3)
From Somavaṃśa was born Nahuṣa, the lord of the earth;
he indeed performed many incomparable acts of charity and righteousness.
He performed one hundred supreme horse-sacrifices (aśvamedha),
a hundred vājapeya sacrifices, and many other various kinds of sacrifices.
By virtue of his own merit, he attained the world of Indra;
there, he made his son, endowed with the qualities of righteousness, the protector of his subjects.
To Yayāti, who was true to his promise, possessed of the vigor of dharma, and great in intellect—
the son of King Pūru— [he spoke] regarding his own station.
Yayāti, being established in truth, protected his subjects according to the law;
he himself personally supervised even those various activities of his people.
Having heard the unsurpassed Dharma, that knower of righteousness caused [the king] to perform sacrifices;
he performed all the meritorious acts of giving, such as pilgrimages to sacred fords and other rites.
The wise king Nṛpanandana ruled the kingdom according to truth and dharma for eighty thousand years.
At that time, the great-souled Yayāti passed away;
he had four sons who possessed his own heroism, strength, and prowess.
I shall declare their names; listen with a one-pointed mind.
His eldest son was named Tururu, who possessed great strength.
Puru was the second by name, and Kuru was the third; the fourth son of the king was Yadu, whose nature was righteous. (13)
Thus were the four sons of the great-souled Yayāti, equal to their father in splendor, prowess, and valor. (14)
In this manner, Yāyāti ruled the kingdom with righteousness;
his fame and glory became abundant throughout the three worlds. (15)
Viṣṇu said:
Once, O best of the twice-born, Nārada went from the world of Brahmā to the world of Indra to see the city of the Destroyer of Cities (Indra). 16.
Then the thousand-eyed god beheld that brahmin arriving upon the earth, possessing a radiance equal to fire, omniscient, and a scholar of wisdom.
Having honored him with offerings such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and bowing his neck in devotion,
he seated the bull among sages upon an auspicious seat and questioned him.
Indra said: "O great sage, why have you come today? For what purpose have you arrived here? What very dear thing may I do for you now?"
Nārada said:
O highly wise one, I am well-pleased with everything you have spoken with devotion regarding the deeds of the King of the Gods; I shall now provide the answer to your question. 20.
Having arrived safely from the world of mortals, I have come here quickly;
I have come to search for you and have seen the son of Āhuṣa.
Indra said:
"King Akopa always protects his subjects with truth and righteousness;
he is endowed with all virtues, learned in the scriptures, possessed of wisdom, and full of excellence. (22)

On this earth there was a king of great renown, a knower of the Vedas, beloved of the Brahmins, devoted to the Brahman, learned in the Vedas, heroic, a performer of sacrifices, generous, and full of true devotion. (23)
Nārada said:
Endowed with these very qualities was the powerful son of Nahuṣa, by whose truth and valor all the worlds were established. (24)
For in this world of mortals, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was like you;
and he who exists in heaven is likewise present on earth as you, O increaser of prosperity.
Yayāti, the lord of the earth and the best among his father’s sons, performed a hundred great horse-sacrifices as well as a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices.
By him, various kinds of gifts were offered with devotion:
thousands of lakhs of cows and hundreds of crores of cows. (27)
Then he performed ten million fire-sacrifices (*koṭihoma*) as well as one hundred thousand fire-sacrifices (*lakṣahoma*),
and he bestowed gifts such as land and other offerings upon the Brahmins.
Indeed, by him the true nature of dharma was preserved in its entirety;
such were the qualities with which Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was endowed. (29)
For eighty thousand years,
that best of kings ruled the kingdom with truth, enjoying divine splendors here on earth.
Sukarman said:
Having heard this from the lord of sages, the divine Nārada, the wise one reflected upon it and became apprehensive regarding the protection of dharma.
Indeed, by the power of a hundred sacrifices, the hero Nahuṣa formerly went to my city and became the king of the gods.
By the power of Śacī’s intellect, he was born fallen from his station;
such was this great king, equal in prowess to his father. ||33||
"He will attain the station of Indra; of this there is no doubt, no uncertainty.
By whatever means possible, I shall lead that king to heaven."
Thus he reflected; and from that great fear of King Yayāti, O best of kings, the Lord of the Gods became terrified. (35)
Then the King of the Gods dispatched a messenger to bring him [Indra],
along with Nahuṣa’s celestial chariot, which was endowed with all objects of desire.
Accompanied by his charioteer named Mātali and the celestial chariot,
Mātali went to that place where the son of Nahuṣa was located.
Sent by the king of the gods to bring the one of great intelligence, he shone like Indra when present in the assembly hall. (38)
Likewise, the righteous-souled Yayāti shone in his own assembly;
[Nārada] spoke to that high-souled king, whose ornament was truth. (39)
O King, listen to my words, for I am the charioteer of the king of the gods, sent by the king of the gods to your presence. (40)
"O God, perform all that the King of the Gods has said with a well-disposed mind;
you must come to see me, O Lord, for otherwise the world will perish. (41)
Having renounced the kingdom to his son and performed the most excellent final sacrifice,
the immensely radiant King Ilā, the son of Nahuṣa, departed.
The highly heroic Purūravas, the high-minded Vipracitti, Śibi, and likewise Anu, the lord of the Ikṣvākus, all resided right there. ||43||
Sagara, the wise Medhāvin, and your father Nahuṣa;
also Ṛtavīrya, Kṛtajña, Śaṃtanu, and the high-minded [Bhīṣma]. 44.
Bharata, Yuvanāśva, and Kārtavīrya, the lord of men, having performed various sacrifices, brought you great joy in heaven, O mountain. (45)
Moreover, those four kings who were entirely devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites—all of them rejoice in heaven with Indra by virtue of their own deeds. (46)
Furthermore, you who are the knower of all phenomena and are established in all phenomena, O lord of the earth, rejoice together with Śakra in the heavenly world! 47.
Yayāti said: "What deed have I performed because of which you have made this request of me?
Tell me all that regarding Indra, the king of the gods."
Mātali said:
"O King, when you had completed eighty thousand years by means of acts such as charity and merit, as well as sacrifices, [your time here] was exhausted."
O great king, by virtue of your own royal deeds, go to heaven;
establish friendship with the King of the Gods and depart for the abode of the immortals. (50)
O Mahāmati, abandon this earthly body composed of the five elements;
assuming a divine form, enjoy pleasures that accord with your mind.
O Lord of Men, in whatever manner a person performs sacrifice, charity, and austerity on this earth, in that very same way they shall obtain the enjoyments of heaven by their own prayer. 52.
Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, how can one abandon that body by which good and evil deeds are accomplished on earth, and go to the world one has earned? (53)
Mātali said:
"O King, having abandoned right there this very body composed of the five elements which was acquired, they proceed to that [state] by means of the divine [path]."
All other human beings, who accomplish both sin and merit,
they too, having abandoned the body, indeed go downward or upward.
Yayāti said: "O Mātali,
having produced both good and evil deeds with this body composed of the five elements, men indeed depart from here, both downward and upward."
Indeed, a knower of the Dharma may abandon the body at any specific time;
however, the falling away of the body occurs due to the power of sin or merit. (57)
O Sūta, such a thing is seen directly in the realm of mortals;
indeed, I perceive no distinction whatsoever between sin and merit. (58)
Why would a mortal man abandon that very body by which he accumulates merit such as truth and righteousness? (59)
Both of these—the self and the body—are alike in form as friends;
yet, having abandoned the body which is a friend, the self departs with complete certainty. (60)
Mātali said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; he departs having abandoned the body. For there is no connection whatsoever between that body and the self."
For this body is always worn out by old age; it is constantly afflicted by decay and perpetually corrupted by various diseases.
Broken by the defects of old age, he no longer desires to remain here;
becoming agitated and distraught, life abandons him and departs. (63)
By truth, by the merit of dharma, by gifts, by observances and restraints, by sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice, and likewise by pilgrimages and self-discipline; ||64||
O Great King, even by great merits and other well-performed deeds, old age is not held at bay; rather, through sins as well, this very body simply wastes away.
Yayāti said:
"O best of beings, why does old age, once it has arisen, suddenly afflict the body? You ought to explain this to me in detail."
Mātali said:
O best of kings, I shall describe to you the cause of old age, from which this [condition] has arisen within the body.
The body, composed of the five elements and supported by the five sense objects,
O King, will be completely consumed by fire when the self abandons it.
O King, as the fire blazed up with intense brilliance,
smoke was produced from it, and from that smoke the clouds were born.
From the cloud, water flows forth; from that water, the earth is formed. That water comes forth like a virtuous woman in her menses.

From that, O best of kings, food is produced; from food, the vital essence (rasa) arises; and from the vital essence, food [as bodily tissue] is generated; and from food, semen is produced—of this there is no doubt. (71)
From semen the body is born, and that body is indeed of poor form;
just as the earth produces fragrance and juices through its essence upon the surface of the ground.
In this way, the body should always move about, for it is the support of all tastes;
from that [body] fragrance arises, and from fragrance, taste arises again. (73)
Therefore, O King, behold that Great Fire which has been seen;
just as fire arises from wood and in turn illuminates the wood. (74)
From the impurity in the center of the body, fire is produced in that very same way;
it moves there constantly and nourishes the body, O Lord of the Earth. (75)
As long as there is an abundance of rasa, the jīva attains tranquility;
having experienced such a state, the fire exists in the form of hunger. (76)
One who intensely desires food obtains food accompanied by milk as a gift, and he also drinks water, O Lord of the Earth. (77)
Just as fire consumes blood, so too does it consume semen; of this there is no doubt.
From that, the disease of consumption arises, which destroys the entire body. (78)
O King, there may be an excess of rasa, or else the digestive fire (vahni) becomes extinguished;
being oppressed by rasa, it manifests in the form of fever. ||79||
The fire resides, as it were, having ascended the neck, back, waist, and anus in all the joints; thus the fire functions within the body.
If that [rasa] increases constantly, it nourishes the body in every way;
then the rasa attains firmness, and strength and beauty arise. (81)
By means of that very excess of strength, one should agitate the vital points through vigor;
by that alone, O King, desire is born, and it becomes like a thorn.
O King, this is known as the fire of lust, which destroys one's strength;
through attachment to sexual intercourse, destruction occurs within the body. 83.
A living being, tormented by the fire of desire and emaciated by passion, might resort to a woman, becoming infatuated through attachment to sexual union. (84)
The body becomes devoid of luster and a loss of strength occurs;
when it is devoid of strength, it is rendered weak by the digestive fire. ||85||
Together with the fire, the lord of the body consumes the blood and the semen;
through the destruction of both semen and blood, the body becomes empty.
An exceedingly violent wind arises, fierce and terrible in form;
then one becomes discolored, tormented by suffering, and empty-minded. (87)
One whose mind is distracted by what has been seen, heard, or thought never attains satisfaction;
for one who is greedy, no satiety arises on the path of the mind. 88.
Deformed and handsome alike are born from meditation in the intermediate state;
when one is devoid of strength due to the depletion of blood and semen, one desires this [intermediate state]. (89)
Gray hair arises upon the body through the black fire of desire;
therefore, one becomes a lustful man as he grows older day by day. (90)
O Lord of Men, just as a usurer suffers loss by lending money to a woman who is devoted to her husband,
so too does his own splendor diminish.
From that, the womb-born is produced and attains the form of destruction;
fire is produced again in the form of old age—of this there is no doubt. (92)
A terrible fever arose among living beings in the form of consumption; all things, both stationary and moving, were tormented by that fever. (93)
All of them, though afflicted by many torments, do not meet with destruction.
All this has been told to you; I shall tell you something else besides. 94.
Having been addressed thus, the great king spoke these words to Mātali. ||95||
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Holy Site of Parents," within the narrative of Eṇī in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-fifth chapter. Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, the body is the protector of dharma, together with the self."
I have set out seeking heaven; tell me the cause for that. ||1||
Mātali said:
"O King, there is no association even among the five elements;
they do not attain association with one another, nor indeed with the Self."
Therein, the aggregate of all [elements] proceeds within the village of the body;
afflicted by old age, they all depart to their respective places. (3)
Just as the earth, when prepared by a great king who possesses an abundance of moisture, becomes soft through that moisture spreading across it, O Lord of the Earth. (4)
It is broken by ants and likewise by mice; holes indeed multiply, and anthills with large bellies arise. (5)
In the same way, O best of men, this body is produced with goiters, scabs, and eczema, and it is being torn apart by worms. (6)
Then, tumors arise there, causing immediate pain;
O son of Nahuṣa, this body is thus afflicted by these defects.
O Lord of Men, how does one go to heaven through the union with the vital breath?
This earthly portion of the body is established for the sake of common purpose;
the body does not go to heaven, for it remains just as the earth does.
All this has been told to you regarding the flood of faults belonging to the king.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Holy Site of Mother and Father," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-sixth chapter. Yayāti said:
"O Mātali, listen: this body falls because of sin and rises through dharma."
Nor do we perceive any distinction on this earth, even regarding merit. ||1||
Furthermore, the body is born again just as it fell before;
tell me in detail how that body is produced.
Mātali said: Now,
for those men who belong to hell,
a body arises from the elements in a mere moment solely through their own karma.
In the same way, by means of a single dharma, the divine body of the gods, which arises through spontaneous birth, is produced immediately from the essence of the elements. (4)
The body of great-souled beings, which is unmixed with [unwholesome] karma, should be understood as being of four kinds according to its transformation into that form. (5)
The sprout-born (udbhijja) are to be known as the immobile beings, consisting of grasses, shrubs, and the like;
while worms, insects, moths, and so forth, are the body-less ones born from moisture (svedaja).
O King, all birds, snakes, and crocodiles are born from eggs;
humans and quadrupeds are to be known as those born from a womb.
There, the ground, moistened by waters and ripened by the heat of the blood,
being fanned by the wind, receives the seed in its fields.
Just as seeds that have been sown and moistened with water attain softness and proceed toward the state of becoming roots; ||9||
From that root arises the sprout; from the sprout, the birth of the leaf; from the leaf, the stalk; and from the stalk, there is again the production of the stem. (10)
From *prabhava* milk is produced; from that milk, *tandula* is produced;
and from that *tandula*, when cooked, medicinal herbs likewise come into being.

Beginning with barley and ending with śāli rice, seventeen types of plants are recorded as the most excellent; those rich in fruit and pith are [the aforementioned], while the remainder are proclaimed as minor.
These were crushed by the sages, who had previously prepared them with winnowing baskets,
mortars, vessels, and the like, as well as with cooking pots, water, and fire.
Through the distinction of six kinds of tastes, they undergo transformation; through mutual contact with juices, they attain manifold flavors. (14)
O King, there are the six types of food—those to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, sucked, and tasted—and their six varieties, such as the sweet and the other [five] tastes. (15)
When that food is eaten by embodied beings in morsels and mouthfuls, it gradually establishes all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) within the stomach, which is the root of the body. (16)
The vital air (vāyu),
having entered the midst of the food, divides the uncooked ingested meal into two parts, separating them according to their respective qualities.
Water is placed above the fire, and that food is upon the water;
one's own vital breath (prāṇa), situated below the water, gently fans the fire.
The fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water extremely hot;
that food is then cooked thoroughly through the application of that heat. (19)
When that [food] is digested, it becomes twofold: the *kiṭṭa* (solid waste) separately and the *rasa* (nutrient essence) separately.
The *kiṭṭa*, divided by the twelve impurities (*mala*), goes out from the body. (20)
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, lips, generative organ, and anus—these twelve are known as the excretory orifices from which impurities, tears, sweat, feces, and urine flow. 21.
All the channels are likewise connected to the heart-lotus;
the vital breath (prāṇa) places that subtle essence at their openings.
The vital breath (prāṇa) then fills the channels with its essence;
thereafter, those filled channels completely satisfy the body evenly.
Then, situated within the central channel, the nutrient essence is cooked by the bodily heat;
and as it is being cooked, it undergoes two further stages of digestion.
Skin, flesh, bone, marrow, fat, and blood are produced;
from blood arise body hair and nails, and from flesh arise hair of the head and sinews.
From the sinews, marrow, and bones arise fat, marrow, and bone;
from marrow comes semen, which is the essence of procreation. (26)
Thus, the twelve transformations of the tranquil [self] have been proclaimed.
Semen is its transformation, and from semen arises the birth of the body. (27)
When, during the fertile period, the semen—free from defects—is situated in the womb, it then, impelled by the vital wind, attains unity with the female blood. (28)
At the time of the emission of semen, the individual soul (jīva),
joined with its causal body and constantly constrained by its own past actions, enters the womb.
From the semen together with the blood, the *kalala* (embryonic mass) comes to be in one day;
after five nights, that *kalala* then becomes a *budbuda* (bubble).
Within a month, that being is born again with five parts:
the neck, the head, the shoulders, the backbone, and the belly.
Likewise, the hands, feet, sides, hips, and limbs, as well as the joints, gradually come into being over the course of two months. (32)
In three months, the fetus produces the collection of sprouts such as the limbs;
and in four months, the fingers and so forth are produced in their proper sequence.
The face, nose, two ears, and the anus arise from these five [fingers];
likewise, the row of teeth, the tongue, and the nails are produced. (34)
And within six months, there shall be an opening in the two ears; furthermore, the anus, the penis, the generative organ, and the phallus are produced. 35.
Within seven months, all the limbs are fully formed;
the body becomes complete with its major and minor members, and the head is endowed with hair. (36)
When its parts have become clearly distinct, it shall again exist at the eighth month;
endowed with the fivefold [elements], it remains fully matured.
By the potency of the mother’s food and by the sixfold taste,
it grows day by day, bound to the umbilical cord.
Then the individual soul (jīva) regains its memory within this body;
it perceives pleasure and pain, as well as sleep, dreams, and past deeds. (39)
I have died and been born again; having been born, I have died again.
Thousands of various wombs have been seen by me in manifold ways. (40)
I have only just been born and have already received the purificatory rites;
therefore, I shall perform that which is most beneficial, so that there may be no further birth from a womb.
While staying in the womb, he thinks thus: "Once I have emerged from the womb, I shall study the supreme knowledge that brings about the cessation of saṃsāra. (42)
Necessarily tormented by the great suffering of the womb, the living being remains there under the power of karma; therefore, one should contemplate the means to liberation. 43.
Just as someone oppressed by a great mountain remains in pain, so too does the embodied being, distressed, remain in suffering due to the fetal membrane. (44)
Just as one who has fallen into the ocean remains distressed and agitated, so too does he remain with an agitated soul, his limbs drenched by the fluids of the womb. 45.
Just as something placed in an iron vessel is cooked by fire,
so too that which is cast into the vessel of the womb is cooked by the digestive fire.
The suffering that arises when one's limbs are incessantly pierced by needles the color of fire— that very suffering in the womb is eight times greater than it.
There is no dwelling anywhere more difficult than dwelling in the womb;
for embodied beings, it is incomparable suffering, most terrible and full of peril. (48)
Thus, this suffering of the womb has been fully described for all living beings—both moving and stationary—in accordance with their own respective wombs. 49.
For the embodied being who is about to be born, there arises a pain ten million times greater than that in the womb, due to the compression of the birth canal as he becomes unconscious.
Like sugarcane being crushed by the hammering of the mallet of evil, [the body suffers] as it emerges from the womb due to the powerful winds of labor. (51)
Great suffering arises, yet they find no protection;
being oppressed by the rod, they become as sapless as sugarcanes. (52)
Likewise, this bodiless [embryo], situated in the womb, is cast down due to the pressure of the birth canal;
it possesses bones, is spherical in shape, and is encircled by the binding of sinews.
Smeared with blood, flesh, and fat, a vessel for the substances of feces and urine, covered with hair, body hair, and nails—it is the supreme abode of disease. (54)
Adorned with the single great door of the face and the eight windows of the limbs, it has the two lips as its panels and is provided with the tongue and throat as its bolt. 55.
The flow of sweat from the channels was overflowing with phlegm and bile;
it was overwhelmed by old age and grief, and situated within the fire of the mouth of Time.
Overcome by desire and anger, crushed by the vital breaths, afflicted by thirst for enjoyment, and hidden within, it follows the sway of passion and hatred. (57)
With its major and minor limbs fully formed, yet enveloped by the fetal membrane,
it emerged through the narrow and impure birth canal.
In this body, one should know that there are bones, a collection of decaying flesh, and limbs drenched in feces, urine, and blood, produced from the six sheaths. (59)
It consists of three hundred and one hundred [i.e., four hundred] plus five hundred peśīs;
it is covered by three and a half [hundred] and is even with seven million pores.
The body is composed of these millions of channels, both gross and subtle, visible and invisible, and is pervaded by them.
By means of those [teeth], one should remove the impure sweat situated within;
thirty-two teeth are proclaimed, and twenty nails are recorded.
One *kuḍava* of bile should be known [to be required], and likewise half an *āḍhaka* of phlegm;
five *palas* of muscle fat, and half of that for the fruit.
The *arbuda* should be known as five *palas*, and from this, fat (*medas*) is ten *palas*.
Great blood (*mahā-rakta*) is three *palas*, and marrow (*majjā*) is four times the amount of blood. (64)
Half a *kuḍava* of semen should be known [as the standard]; half of that is the strength of embodied beings.
One *piṇḍa* of grain is said to be one thousand *palas*.
Blood should be known as one hundred palas, while feces and urine are immeasurable;
thus, O King, the self dwells eternally within this house of the body.
And that which is impure belongs to the pure one, produced by the bondage of karma;
a body is born somewhere from the union of semen and blood. (67)
Because it is constantly joined with feces and urine, this body is remembered as impure;
just as a jar filled with excrement is not pure either inside or out. (68)
Even while being purified by ritual cleansing, this body remains impure;
for even the most sacred five products of the cow and sacrificial oblations become defiled upon reaching it. (69)
This body quickly becomes impure; therefore, it is impure. Even delicious foods and fragrant drinks, once they have reached it, [become foul]. (70)
If impurity departs quickly, then another would become impure immediately thereafter;
O people, do you not see that which flows out day after day? (71)
The body is followed by impurity and is foul; how then can its substratum be pure?
Even when that body is being cleansed with the five products of the cow and water infused with kuśa grass, [it remains impure].
Like charcoal being rubbed, it does not attain purity;
its streams flow constantly like those of a mountain. (73)
How can this body, which is impure with phlegm, urine, and so forth, ever be purified?
For there exists no purity in this body, which is a repository of all that is unclean. (74)
Even if one is pure in every single respect, one would not be pure unless the hand is cleansed with earth and water, whether by day or by night. (75)

Nevertheless, people do not become disenchanted with this body even though it possesses a state of purity; for although this body is carefully refined with the finest incense and other such things, [it remains impure]. (76)
For it does not abandon its own nature, just as a dog's tail cannot be bent down;
likewise, from birth itself, black wool does not become white, nor does that which is not born ever come into being.
Even while being thoroughly cleansed, the body would not thereby become pure, for it continues to smell its own foul odor and perceive its own impurities. (78)
This world does not become dispassionate even when its nose is being pinched;
alas, what great power lies in delusion, by which the entire universe is utterly infatuated! (79)
Smelling and seeing the defects of his own body, one does not become dispassionate; that man would not become dispassionate even upon the putrefaction of his own body. (80)
What other cause for detachment can be taught for him?
The entire world is pure; only the body is supremely impure. (81)
Since even one who is pure becomes impure through contact with the parts of filth, purification of the body is prescribed for the removal of odor and stain. (82)
After the departure of duality, one becomes pure through the purification of existence;
not by all the water of the Ganges, nor by loads of clay smeared upon the body. (83)
This mortal body, foul-smelling and corrupted by its very nature, is not purified;
nor is a person of wicked soul purified by bathing at sacred fords or by austerities. (84)
One's own form, though washed in a sacred bathing place, does not attain purity;
for one whose inner disposition is corrupt, even entering the sacrificial fire [does not bring purification]. 85.
Neither heaven nor liberation exists for one whose body is consumed by passion;
purity of intention is the supreme purification and the authority in all actions. (86)
In one way a daughter is embraced, while in another way she is not;
even regarding objects that are not distinct, the mental mode of operation differs. (87)
One should contemplate the son as one thing and the husband as another, exactly as it has been described by the Great Fortunate One regarding the nature of things. (88)
Even when embraced by his wife, he should not engage in it if she is devoid of feeling; nor should he eat various kinds of food, whether they be savory or fragrant.
Therefore, since non-existence is not a person, existence is the cause in all cases;
purify the mind with effort—what is the use of other external purifications? (90)
With a mind pure and cleansed through its true being, he attains heaven and liberation;
he then washes away [the stains of] ignorance with the water of stainless knowledge and with the clay of dispassion.
The stains of ignorance, passion, feces, and urine are removed by means of purifications;
thus, they know this body to be impure by its very nature. (92)
Having understood that the body is thus full of defects, resembling the pithless core of a plantain tree, the wise man should become detached from it. (93)
Having transcended the core [of existence], one remains in firm grasping;
thus is this great misery, the suffering of birth, proclaimed. (94)
Due to the fault of ignorance regarding the male [organ] and by the power of various karmas, the consciousness that existed while in the womb perishes once one is born. (95)
For embodied beings who have fainted due to suffering from the pressure of the womb, there occurs a state of delusion caused by the external wind and by attachment. (96)
As soon as he is touched by the terrible [demon], a fever arises;
by that great fever, a state of great delusion is produced. ||97||
In one who is thus deluded, a loss of memory quickly arises again;
from that loss of memory, he [is further affected] by the power of his previous karma. (98)
Attachment arises for that person right there in that very birth;
this world, being passionate and deluded, engages in what ought not to be done. (99)
He does not know himself, nor another, nor the deity;
he does not hear of the highest good, and though possessing eyes, he does not see. 100.
Walking slowly along the same path, he seems to stumble at every step;
though being enlightened by the wise, he does not understand even when the truth is present. 101.
Driven by the power of greed, that man suffers affliction within saṃsāra;
and when there is an absence of memory of the womb, the scripture was spoken by Śiva. (102)
For the purpose of describing that suffering, [this work] establishes heaven and liberation;
by means of which, when that auspicious [work] is known, one accomplishes virtue, pleasure, and wealth. (103)
That he did not perform what was for his own welfare—this is a great marvel;
furthermore, due to the unmanifested state of his senses and intellect, there was great suffering in childhood. (104)
Even though he desires it, he is unable to speak or act with integrity;
thus, this great suffering of birth arises from his greed, driven like the wind.
Afflicted by various childhood diseases and even by the seizures of infantile spirits, his body overwhelmed by thirst and hunger, he stands or moves about here and there. (106)
Out of delusion, a child may commit acts such as eating feces and urine;
likewise, a youth [suffers] from the piercing of the ears and from the beatings of his parents. (107)

And because of the suffering caused by the study of letters and so forth, by the instructions of teachers and others, by the heedless activity of the senses, and by being tormented by sensual passion; ||108||
For one constantly afflicted by disease, how can there be happiness even in youth?
Through envy arises great suffering, and from delusion, suffering is born. (109)
Remaining there, as if enraged, he experienced nothing but suffering born of passion; exhausted by the fire of desire, he found no sleep at night. (110)
What happiness can there be for one who spends his days worrying about the acquisition of wealth, his body exhausted by women, whose only essence is that drop of semen? (111)
The bodies of those born of sweat, such as worms, and of lepers or common folk who are being tormented by worms, must not be touched even for the sake of pleasure. (112)

The wise know that the pleasure found in women is like the pleasure derived from scratching an itch or from the heat of a fire; it is just as one considers the happiness gained from the anxiety of acquiring wealth.
There is nothing whatsoever superior to such a woman;
for a mortal, there is no peace of mind without her touch. (114)
Therefore, that which was previously unattainable to one another has now become otherwise;
thus, it is seized by old age and pervaded by disease, becoming unpleasant.
Who else is more senseless than he who, seeing himself as never before—now overwhelmed by old age—does not become dispassionate? (116)
Even one who is overcome by old age is humiliated by his wife, sons, and other kinsmen, as well as by servants who, due to their own incapacity, behave with misconduct. (117)
One joined with old age is not able to accomplish dharma, wealth, desire, or liberation; therefore, while young, one should practice dharma.
The imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth is called disease;
this body is proclaimed to be a collection of wind and the other [humors]. (119)
Therefore, this body of the self should be known as consisting of disease, because diseases and old age are not distinct from wind and the other [humors]. (120)
Through various kinds of diseases, the embodied being undergoes manifold sufferings; these are to be known by one's own self—what else shall I say? (121)
One hundred and one deaths are established within this body;
among them, one is joined with Time (Kāla), while the remainder are known as accidental.

However, those [afflictions] previously mentioned that have come here are pacified by medicines, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, and gifts; but death at its appointed time cannot be averted.
Or rather, if there were no untimely death from tasting poison without hesitation, a person would not eat it; therefore, he fears untimely death.
Various diseases, as well as serpents and other such creatures, poisons, and malevolent spells, are the gates of death for embodied beings. (125)
Even Dhanvantari himself is unable to restore to health one who is afflicted by all manner of diseases and the like, for when the time has arrived, it cannot be otherwise.
Neither medicine, nor penance, nor charity, nor mother, nor kinsmen are able to protect a man who is tormented by Time (Death). 127.

Through great-souled ones who have attained perfection in elixirs, austerities, recitation, and yoga, there may be peace from untimely death; yet one shall still encounter death at the appointed time.
Dying again by the power of karma, he is born among the insects of the womb;
yet, through the dissolution of karma, he who perceives the separation [of the self] from the body [is liberated]. (129)
Death is defined as that [state] when one has entered the great darkness while the vital organs are being severed; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not a total destruction.
There is no comparison anywhere in this world for the suffering born of death;
one who is dying, deeply afflicted, cries out, "O father! O mother! Where are you going? (131)
Like a frog swallowed by a serpent, the world is seized by death;
abandoned by one's kinsmen and surrounded by those once dear. (132)
Sighing long and hot breaths through his parched mouth,
he rolled about upon his bed and fainted again and again.
Utterly bewildered, he throws his hands and feet about here and there;
from the bed he falls to the ground, and from the ground back to the bed, and again from the bed to the earth. (134)
Helpless, having cast off all shame, smeared with urine and excrement, he begs for water, his palate and lips parched dry. (135)
Thinking of his own wealth—both what has been spent and what remains—he is led away by the messengers of Yama, dragged along by the noose of Time. (136)
While all are looking on, one dies; the body groans with a deep rattling sound.
Like a leech moving from blade to blade of grass, the living soul enters one body after another in succession. (137)
One attains the subsequent limb while abandoning the previous body;
for the wise, the suffering resulting from the prayer at the time of death is indeed greater than that of dying itself. (138)
The suffering of death is momentary, whereas that caused by making a request is not; thus, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the worlds, assumed the form of a dwarf because of his being entreated [by Bali]. (139)
There is no greater enemy than this; it brings about extreme insignificance. Now I have realized this: that death becomes heavy [with consequences]. (140)
One should not further desire anything more, for craving is the cause of wretchedness;
it is suffering at the beginning, suffering in the middle, and likewise terrible at the end.
By their very nature, all living beings experience a succession of extreme sufferings; these include both those currently occurring and those that have passed. (142)
A person should not cause grief for birth, nor should he become detached from it;
indeed, excessive eating leads to great suffering, while eating too little leads to even greater distress. (143)
There is no happiness in eating too little, nor is there happiness in eating too much;
for hunger is considered the most severe of all diseases. (144)
By the application of this true medicinal herb, even the most intense pain from the affliction of hunger is pacified in a mere moment, completely restoring one's strength. (145)
Overcome by that [taste], a man dies just as he would from other diseases; so what pleasure is there even in that flavor which merely rolls upon the tip of the tongue? (146)
Reaching [the state of] *kaṃ* and *ṭhaṃ* within half that moment, one returns;
thus it is remembered as being like food and medicine for those tormented by the disease of hunger. (147)
This pleasure should not be sought by the wise in the ultimate sense;
for he who lies like a corpse, devoid of all purposeful activity, is as if dead. (148)
Even there, how can there be happiness for one whose self is impelled by darkness? And even upon awakening, how can there be happiness for one whose self is impaired in its duties? (149)
Through the arduous labors of agriculture, commerce, service, cattle-herding, and so forth;
through urine and excrement in the morning; and through hunger and thirst at midday. (150)
Satiated by sensual desires, they are overcome by sleep at night;
there is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the preservation of what has been acquired. (151)
One should destroy suffering and exhaust suffering; for where is there happiness in wealth?
[It comes from] thieves, from waters, from fire, from one's own kin, and even from the king. (152)
There is constant fear for those possessed of wealth, just as there is for embodied beings from death; I am being devoured on this earth by beasts of prey, like a bird by hawks.
Just as fish devour one another in the water, so too does the wealthy man [suffer] everywhere;
they delude him in times of prosperity and abandon him in times of adversity. (154)
The objects acquired at the time of renunciation may bring happiness;
first the master of wealth was anxious, but later he became indifferent to all possessions. (155)
Arthapati, whose mind was detached from others, remained sorrowful in their [the two women's] suffering and joyful in their happiness;
he dwelt there during the terrible heat of summer and the rainy seasons.
Due to wind, heat, and rain—even at improper times—how can there be happiness?
There is suffering in the elaborate preparations for a wedding, and again in carrying that fetus. (157)

There is suffering from the pains of difficult childbirth and from tasks such as cleaning excrement; there is the pain of my son’s toothache and eye disease—alas, what a tragedy! What can I possibly do? (158)
The cows are lost, the cultivation ruined, and my wife has fled;
yet these guests have arrived at my home seeking protection. (159)
"My wife has young children; who will provide for our livelihood? At the time of her marriage, what kind of groom would there be? (160)
For those overcome by these reflections, where is there happiness for householders? (161)
The family, the lineage, the learning, the character, and all the virtues of a man who is agitated by greed—all these perish along with the body, like water poured into an unbaked earthen pot. (162)
Even in a kingdom, where is there happiness when one is constantly anxious about peace and war? Since there is even fear from one's own son, what kind of happiness can there be anywhere? (163)
For almost all embodied beings, there is fear of their own kind, because they desire the same objects, just as dogs do toward one another. (164)
There is no king on earth renowned for not entering the forest of battle;
he alone is truly famous who, having overcome everything, dwells fearless and at ease. (165)
In battle, the powerful son of a sage brought down the thousand arms of the illustrious Kārtavīrya to the surface of the earth. 166.
The son of Daśaratha, Rāma, struck down the incomparable, upward-moving power of the great-souled Rāma, the son of the sage.
The fame of Jarāsandha was destroyed by the splendor of Rāma;
that of Jarāsandha was destroyed by Bhīma, and his [Bhīma’s] in turn by the son of the Wind-god.
Hanumān, too, being struck by the sun, fell to the earth;
[he then encountered] all the Nivātakavacas, the Dānavas who were arrogant in their strength.
Even the illustrious Arjuna was once defeated by cowherd boys;
even the sun, though possessed of great heat, is sometimes obscured by clouds. (170)
The cloud is scattered by the wind, yet the power of the wind is overcome by mountains;
the mountains are consumed by fire, yet the fire along with itself is extinguished by waters. (171)
That water is dried up by the suns, and the suns along with the waters perish together with the entire triple world at the end of Brahmā’s day.
Even Brahmā, together with the thirty-three gods, is withdrawn again at the end of a period of two *parārdhas* by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (173)
Thus, there is nothing whatsoever that possesses such supreme strength as this, except for the one Lord of the World, the immutable Supreme Self. (174)
Having understood this excellence, one should abandon all pride; for in this world being thus constituted, who—be they a god or even a scholar—is superior? (175)
There is no one who knows everything, nor is anyone entirely ignorant;
to the extent that one understands something, to that extent one is a scholar. (176)
The power of one who possesses concentration is considered equal everywhere;
however, the power of some may be superior in certain instances due to the excellence of their wealth. (177)
The gods were conquered by the Dānavas, and then they in turn were conquered by the gods;
thus the world is subject to one another through fortune, victory, and defeat. (178)
In this way, a pair of garments for kings, a meal of only a *prastha* measure, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats—everything else leads only to suffering. (179)
Even in the seventh existence, one’s possession consists of nothing more than a bed;
yet there is an expansion of suffering and exhaustion for the sake of thousands of water-jars.
At dawn, the sound of musical instruments arose simultaneously with the city-dwellers;
yet in my house, this music is played merely out of pride in sovereignty, like frost.
Every ornament is a burden; every ointment is but filth;
every song is mere prattle; and dancing is the behavior of a madman. (182)
Thus, when one reflects upon them, where is there any happiness in the enjoyments of sovereignty for kings? For they are consumed by the anxiety of war and their mutual desire for victory. (183)
Generally, great kings such as Nahuṣa and others, having attained heaven due to the intoxication of pride in their prosperity, fell from it; who, then, can find happiness through prosperity? (184)
Even in heaven, where is there any happiness for one who beholds the blazing splendor of others, which exists in a state of mutual superiority among the gods, rising higher and higher? (185)
In heaven, men enjoy the fruit of their merit by cutting off its very root;
no other karma is performed there, and thus that fault is most terrible. (186)
Just as a tree whose roots have been severed falls to the earth within days, so too do the denizens of heaven fall when their merit is exhausted. 187.
For the inhabitants of heaven, who have reached the culmination of their longing for pleasure through the abundance of enjoying happiness and the like, a painful suffering falls unexpectedly. (188)

Thus, even in heaven, there is no happiness for the gods when one reflects upon it; for there is exhaustion when sense objects fail to be attained, and the enjoyment of pleasures in heaven depends upon one's past actions. (189)
Therein, for embodied beings in the fires of hell, there is great suffering and intense agony, arising from various terrible states produced by speech, mind, and body. (190)
There was the fierce lopping off of bark with axes, the immediate stripping away of rind, and the falling of leaves, branches, and fruits by the violent wind. (191)
In the stationary classes of beings, there is suffering caused by being uprooted, by rivers, by elephants, and by other embodied creatures, as well as by forest fires, frost, and desiccation. (192)
In the same way, the anger of serpents and snakes is terrible suffering;
likewise, the slaying of the wicked in this world and their binding with a noose [is likewise painful]. (193)
There is the sudden birth and death of insects again and again, as well as the manifold sufferings of the various classes of reptiles. 194.
For domestic animals, self-restraint consists of being struck with a staff, as well as the piercing of the nose, the fear [induced by it], and being beaten with a goad. (195)
The binding of limbs with cane, wood, and other fetters, or with a goad;
the tormenting of alms-seekers with harsh words and the like, through one's disposition and mind, [is a transgression]. (196)
And through separation from their own herds, by being forcibly led away, and by the binding of their eyes, cattle undergo manifold sufferings of the body. (197)
For the beasts and birds, there is suffering from rain, cold, and heat; for those with emaciated bodies, there are manifold sufferings arising from affliction and hunger. (198)

The great suffering of dwelling in the womb, as well as the suffering of birth for those who are not free from debt; the suffering of early childhood, ignorance, and the instruction of a teacher during youth. (199)
Furthermore, there is suffering from youth, sensual desire, and envy, as well as from activities such as agriculture, commerce, service, and cattle-herding. (200)
In old age, one is tormented by decay and diseases; at death there is great suffering, and even greater than that is the agony of longing. (201)
There is great fear from kings, fire, floods, calamities, thieves, and enemies; furthermore, there is fear in the acquisition and protection of wealth, as well as in its loss and expenditure. (202)
Miserliness, envy, deceit, great fear arising from an abundance of wealth, and engagement in improper acts—these are the constant sorrows of the wealthy. (203)
Service as a servant, usury, slavery, dependence on others, and the encounter with the desirable and the undesirable—these and thousands of other such conjunctions [occur]. (204)
Famine, misfortune, stupidity, and poverty; the state of being inferior or superior, hellish rebirth, and the prowess of kings. (205)
The suffering of kings consists in mutual subjugation, great fear from one another, and mutual provocation. (206)
For an embodied being who desires what is created, there is impermanence due to the mutual piercing of vital points and the mutual oppression by hands. (207)
Because the world of moving and non-moving beings is terrified by such sufferings as greed, the distinction between the virtuous and the wicked, and devouring one another. (208)
Therefore, a wise person should abandon everything from the hells up to the human realm,
just as one who shifts a burden from one shoulder to the other considers it a rest.
In the same way, all this suffering in the world is extinguished by suffering; for the floods of enjoyment are always characterized by mutual excess. (210)
Due to the exhaustion of merit, suffering remains for the gods in heaven; due to the depletion of their store of virtue, they undergo rebirth among thousands of various wombs. (211)
Various kinds of diseases are recorded even in the world of the gods;
for the head of the Sacrifice, which had been severed, was restored by the Aśvins.
Indeed, due to that fault of the sacrifice, Mārtaṇḍa Bhānu always suffered from headache,
while Varuṇa suffered from leprosy and dropsy.
The loss of teeth for Pūṣan, the withering of the arm for Śacīpati (Indra), and a very great wasting disease for Soma are thus proclaimed. (214)
Even for Dakṣa, the Prajāpati, there was a most great fever;
and in every kalpa, there was the destruction even of the great gods.
The lifespan of that Brahmā is two parārdhas, and even he is impermanent;
furthermore, Brahmā lusted after the granddaughter of Dakṣa, who was his own daughter.
Out of anger, the Lord cursed the goddess Jayā, who was skilled in yoga:
"Wherever desire and anger abide, there the faults consisting of those two shall reside. (217)
All sufferings are undoubtedly present;
birth and death are shattered, and he is the consumer of all oblations.
The killing of a woman, attachment to desire, and acting as a charioteer for the Pāṇḍava host;
by Rudra, Tripura was burnt and the sacrifice of Dakṣa was destroyed. (219)
From the birth of Skanda, [there arose] thousands of sports and other such events;
thus, even the gods are possessed of defects such as passion and the like. (220)
Beyond these is the Lord, peaceful, perfect, and the bestower of liberation;
thus this entire world exists in a state of mutual excellence.
Having recognized that [the world] is agitated by sufferings, one should attain supreme detachment;
from detachment arises dispassion, and from dispassion arises the birth of knowledge. (222)
Through knowledge, one attains that supreme knowledge which is auspicious and leads to liberation;
then, freed from all suffering, with a self established in its own state, one becomes happy.
He is called omniscient, perfected, and liberated.
Mātali said:
"All this that you have asked has been explained to you."
For the discernment of dharma and adharma arises from all-encompassing knowledge;
by the command of the King of the Gods, it must be proclaimed in the world of Indra. (225)
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Tīrthas of the Father and Mother," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-seventh chapter. Yayāti said:
"It is through the influence of our good fortune that I have obtained the sight of you."
This birth is like the mount of Śakra; it is incomparable and superior even to me. ||1||
Those who commit terrible sins in the world of mortals—
describe to me in detail the ripening of their karma upon the surface of the earth.
Mātali said:
Listen, for I shall describe the characteristics of one of sinful conduct;
by hearing them, great knowledge arises here in this world. (3)
Those who make the gift of the Veda and the disparagement of the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya) should be known as committing a great sin (mahāpātaka) by those wise in knowledge. ||4||
He who inflicts pain or injury upon any of the virtuous indeed incurs a great sin; yet, through expiation, he may indeed depart from it.
Abandoning their own family traditions and adopting the customs of others—
this is declared by those who know the sacred duties to be a most terrible sin.
To strike one's mother or father, or to beat one's sisters,
as well as to strike one's father's sister— that is certainly a mortal sin (pātaka).
Even when the time for the śrāddha ceremony had arrived,
he passed by the son-in-law and likewise the daughter’s son who were staying within five krośas.
When one proceeds to feed another out of desire, anger, or fear, having neglected one's own sister or sister's son, [that is a fault]. (9)
Neither do the ancestors eat, nor do the gods eat;
this is a sin for him, equal to the murder of one's father. (10)
Even when the time for giving has arrived and a brahmin has come, alas, after setting aside abundant gifts, how many indeed are they given to? (11)
If a gift is given to one person but not to others,
this is remembered as a terrible sin that causes the failure of the act of giving.
To give a gift while abandoning one's own Brahmins who reside in the service of the sacrificer’s household is indeed not the characteristic of true giving. 13.
O King, one should nurture with every means and many excellent gifts that brahmin who has sought refuge, who is modest, and who is endowed with righteous conduct.
A learned man should not disregard a fool; rather, he should always support the Brahmin, O King, who is endowed with all merits through many excellent gifts. 15.
Having honored him, the wise man should always revere the arrived Brahmin;
for if he were to abandon him and instead give the gift to another Brahmin, [he would incur a fault].
Whatever is given or offered as an oblation by him becomes fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
[This applies to] the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra as the fourth. ||17||
On all auspicious occasions, one should honor a twice-born man, whether he be a fool or even a scholar; hear now the fruit of his merit. (18)
The fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) is produced for him. For what reason, O King, should one not cause it to be performed when it is possible to obtain [the means]? 19.
At that time, during the performance of the śrāddha rite, another Brahmin arrived;
he then honored both of them there with food and clothing. (20)
His ancestors are delighted by the betel leaves and the ritual fees (dakṣiṇā);
for that which is to be given after the Śrāddha meal is indeed a constant gift, namely the dakṣiṇā.
The performer of the śrāddha would incur a sin equal to that of killing a yogin;
therefore, O best of kings, one should worship these two with faith.
O best of kings, due to the power of poverty, one should worship this single non-duality even when the Vyatīpāta or Vaidhṛti yoga has arrived.
Likewise, O King, on the new moon day, on the anniversary of death, and during the dark fortnight,
the Śrāddha ceremony must be performed by those of the three varṇas beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
O great king, one should likewise cause the sacrificial priests to be appointed for the sacrifice;
in the same way, Brahmins should always be engaged for the giving of the śrāddha offerings. 25.
A Brāhmaṇa who does not know [the lineage] must never perform [the rite];
even for one whose lineage and family up to three generations are thus known. (26)
O King, one should honor that Brahmin who possesses such conduct; for the lineage of one whose family is unknown should be ascertained by means of his conduct. (27)
Indeed, when a *śrāddha* offering is to be performed, one who is pure but a fool—even a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas—would be considered ignorant. (28)
Therefore, one should perform the śrāddha offering; for that reason, one should invite a brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, O best of kings, one should practice hospitality that has never been done before.
Otherwise, that sinner will certainly go to hell;
therefore, a Brahmin should be employed for giving gifts, for śrāddha rites, and on festival days.
First, one should examine the Brahmin and then employ him for the giving at a śrāddha;
if he is devoid of Brahminical qualities, the ancestors do not eat in his house.
Having uttered a curse, they depart from that *śrāddha* which is devoid of Brahmins;
even he who performs it becomes a great sinner, even if he were equal to Brahmā himself.
O best of men, he who acts by abandoning the conduct of his ancestors should be known as a great sinner, excluded from all dharma. ||33||
Those who abandon the auspicious conduct of Śiva which bestows enjoyment, and who revile the Brāhmaṇas and the Dharma, should be known as increasers of sin. ||34||
Those sinners who always abandon the conduct of Śiva, hate the devotees of Śiva, revile Hari, and harbor hatred toward Brahmanas; (35)
Those who have committed great sins should cause this Ācārani to be heard;
likewise, they should honor the primordial, supreme knowledge, the meritorious Bhāgavata. ||36||
I shall declare the welfare of those who worship the Vaiṣṇava, the Harivaṃśa, the Mātsya, the Kaurma, and the Pādma Purāṇas. (37)
By that very act, the divine Madhusūdana was worshipped directly;
therefore, one should indeed worship Vaiṣṇava knowledge, which is dear to Viṣṇu. (38)
O King, the Vaiṣṇava book is eternally present in the temple; when it is worshipped, O Brahmin, the Lord of Kamalā is worshipped. (39)

Those who sing of the knowledge of Hari, which is worthy of worship, those who write it down, those who bestow it upon the ignorant, those who hear it, and those who recite it—[they are the ones who truly honor Him]. ||40||
They sport with restless desire and through the discipline of false knowledge;
they establish themselves as they please in unconditioned realms.
One who possesses knowledge of the Lord, which is as secure as direct perception, should proclaim it;
likewise, one who has studied and is capable, yet commits negligence, [should be corrected]. (42)
He who speaks or listens while impure and standing in an impure place—all this, in brief, is remembered as equal to the contempt of knowledge. (43)
He who desires to hear the scripture without first performing worship of the guru, and who does not practice service or who intentionally violates his commands; (44)
He does not accept their words nor provide a reply; furthermore, when a task requiring great effort must be accomplished, he remains indifferent toward it.
A sinful person abandons a guru who is suffering, incapacitated, setting out for a foreign land, or being oppressed by enemies. (46)
I shall declare the ancient sin of one who reviles [the teacher]: he shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as fourteen Indras endure. (47)
That person of evil intellect who disregards even the Guru of the first [initiation] incurs a terrible sin that yields rebirth in hell for a long time. (48)
And whoever shows contempt toward his wife, sons, or friends—this sin should be known as great, equal to the reviling of one's guru. (49)

The killer of a Brahmin, the thief of gold, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is one who associates with them. (50)
One who, out of anger, hatred, fear, or greed—especially toward a Brāhmaṇa—cuts into the vital parts [of another] is proclaimed a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (brahmaghna). ||51||
O King, he who, having summoned a Brahmin who is destitute and begging,
subsequently says "there is nothing," is indeed a slayer of a Brahmin.
But he who, out of pride in his own learning, insults a Brahmin who is neutral in the midst of an assembly, is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin (brahmahā). ||53||
Furthermore, he who exalts himself by means of false qualities and opposes his teacher is considered a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who creates an obstacle for those whose bodies are tormented by hunger and thirst and who desire food and drink, him they call a slayer of a Brahmin.
A slanderer who is intent on seeking out the faults of all people, who causes agitation and is cruel—he is considered a slayer of a Brahmin. (56)
He who takes away land previously given to the gods, the twice-born,
or cows— even if it has been lost over time— is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
The seizure of a Brahmin’s wealth acquired through a trust deposit is to be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin; that is the most grievous sin. (58)
One who abandons the Agnihotra sacrifice and the rites of the five sacrifices, and one who would give false testimony regarding his mother, father, or teachers; ||59||
Doing what is displeasing to the devotees of Śiva, eating things that are forbidden to eat, and the senseless slaughter of innocent living beings in the forest. (60)
Setting fire to a cow-pen, a forest, a fire-sanctuary, a city, or a village—these are terrible sins equal to the drinking of liquor. (61)
The seizure of all one's meager possessions, as well as the abduction of another's wife, elephants, horses, cattle, land, silver, clothing, medicinal herbs, and liquids; 62.
The theft of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and fine garments,
when they have been deposited with another, is recorded as being equal to the theft of gold.
The giving away of a daughter fit for marriage to a suitable groom; and sexual intercourse with one's son, friend, wife, kinsmen, and sisters. 64.
Abandon the terrible practice of violating thousands of virgins and the pursuit of women;
sexual intercourse with a woman of one's own caste is recorded as equal to violating the bed of one's teacher.
Those sins which have been described as equal to the great mortal sins (mahā-pātaka) are known by the name "pātaka" (mortal sin); that which is less than those is an "upapātaka" (minor offense).
Furthermore, he who promises wealth for the sake of a twice-born man but does not give it,
and the brahmin who forgets about it— both commit an equal minor offense (upapātaka).
The seizing of a Brahmin’s property, the transgression of established boundaries, excessive pride and excessive anger, stinginess, and ingratitude; 68.
Attachment to other objects, stinginess, deceit, envy, approaching the wives of others, and defiling virtuous women or maidens; ||69||

The elder brother who remains unmarried while his younger brother marries, and the younger brother who marries before his elder—these two, as well as the gift of a maiden to them and the performance of a sacrifice for them, [are forbidden]. (70)
The abandonment of sons, friends, wives, and likewise masters, as well as the abandonment of wives, and [the abandonment] of holy men and ascetics; 71.
The killing of cows, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, or Śūdras;
and the destruction of trees in a temple of Śiva or the ruin of a sacred grove. (72)
Whoever should inflict even the slightest harm upon those residing in hermitages, or upon their circle of servants, or upon their cattle, grain, and forest produce; ||73||
Stealing grain, cattle, or land; officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice; and the sale of a sacrifice, a grove, a tank, one's wife, or one's children. ||74||
They subsist on the wealth of women from pilgrimages, fasts, vows, and meritorious deeds; their very life is the vulva of women. (75)
That man who sells his own dharma, who describes it as adharma, who speaks of the faults of others, and who looks for the weaknesses of others; ||76||
O King, one who covets the property of others and one who gazes upon the wives of others—these should be known as equal to cow-killers. (77)
He who is the author of all scriptures, the one who seizes cows and sells them, who is exceedingly merciless toward his servants, and who is a tamer of animals; ||78||
He who listens to the speech of others while speaking falsely, he who betrays his master, he who betrays his teacher, the deceitful, the fickle, and the rogue—[these are the ones to avoid]. (79)
He who eats while leaving his wife, children, friends, the young, the elderly, the emaciated, the sick, his servants, guests, and kinsmen hungry, [is a sinner]. (80)

They eat what has been well-prepared, but they do not give even a small portion to others; such a person, who cooks separately for himself alone, should be known as one condemned by those who discourse on Brahman. (81)
Having themselves taken up the restraints, they abandoned the Unborn; those whose senses were cast away, who had entered into the life of renunciation, and likewise those addicted to wine.
Furthermore, those who do not diligently protect cows whose limbs are afflicted by wasting diseases, or who are distressed by thirst and hunger,
are remembered as cow-killers destined for hell.
Those who delight in every kind of sin, those who divide the four-footed livestock or the fields, and those who strike virtuous brahmins, teachers, or cows; ||84||
Yet he strikes that woman who is faultless and established in virtuous conduct;
he whose every limb is bound by laziness sleeps again and again. (85)
They do not nourish the weak, nor do they seek out those who have lost their food;
they oppress them with excessive burdens and force even the wounded to carry loads. ||86||

Those who are devoted to all kinds of evil, those who are addicted [to vice], those who eat [impure food], those with broken limbs, those afflicted by wounds and disease, those with deformed bodies, and those tormented by hunger; ||87||
Those who do not protect these people with effort are remembered as hell-beings;
and those most sinful ones who strike at the testicles of bulls [are likewise so remembered]. (88)
And those men who belong to the great hells torment the calves of cows that have arrived at their shelter, being afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue. (89)
Those who do not honor a guest by name are indeed destined for hell;
as are those who neglect one who is helpless, disabled, miserable, a child, an elder, or severely afflicted. ||90||
Those fools who do not show compassion go to the ocean of hell;
so too does one who owns goats, sheep, or buffaloes, and he who is the husband of a Śūdra woman or a Vṛṣalī. ||91||
A Śūdra who conducts himself according to the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, as well as artisans, craftsmen, physicians, and men who serve as temple-priests (Devalakas); ||92||
Those who perform the work of ministers for wages go to all the hells; likewise, he who collects taxes according to his own will, transgressing what has been ordained. 93.
He who wields punishment in vain shall be cooked in the hells;
he is tormented by bribe-takers, officials, and thieves.
That king in whose kingdom and realm the subjects suffer falls into the hells;
so too do those twice-born who accept gifts from a king who walks the path of sin.
They too go to terrible hells, there is no doubt;
[they incur] whatever sin belongs to adulterers, thieves, and kings. (96)
The royal domain of that king who fails to protect becomes terrible;
for one who is not a thief is treated like a thief, and a thief, moreover, is treated like one who is not a thief. (97)
If a king acts without deliberation, he too shall go to hell;
[for consuming] ghee, oil, food, drink, and the like, as well as honey, meat, liquor, and spirits. (98)
Molasses, sugarcane, milk, vegetables, curd, roots, and fruits;
as well as grass, wood, flowers, leaves, and vessels made of clay. ||99||
Sandals, umbrellas, bracelets, palanquins, soft seats, copper, lead, tin, brass, and other substances originating from water such as conch shells; 100.
Musical instruments, flutes, lutes, and household utensils; as well as wool, cotton, silk, dyes, and those produced from lotuses. 101.
Those who, out of greed, steal cotton, fine garments, and various other such diverse articles; ||102||
One will swiftly go to the hells by stealing even the slightest amount of another's property, or indeed any other's wealth, even if it is only the size of a mustard seed. (103)
Having stolen [the property] of another, even if it be much or little, one goes to hell as a non-human being; of this there is no doubt.
Having committed such acts as stealing, a man goes to hell; of this there is no doubt. Immediately after death, a man [suffers] due to such sins as these. (105)
For the purpose of destroying the body, he assumes his former form;
by his command, these [beings] go to the world of Yama while remaining within the body. (106)
Being led away by the most terrible messengers of Yama, those gods, animals, and humans whose souls were fixed upon unrighteousness are filled with extreme suffering. (107)
The Teacher is remembered as the King of Dharma, who [punishes] those of impure soul through various most terrible executions because of their negligence regarding discipline and conduct. (108)
Through penances, the Guru is the teacher; through fasts, Yama is observed as the judge over adulterers, thieves, and those who act unjustly. (109)
The king is declared to be the punisher, and for secret sins, he is the King of Dharma;
therefore, one should perform expiation for the sin committed. 110.
There is no destruction of an action that has not been experienced, even in hundreds of millions of aeons;
whether one performs the action oneself, causes it to be done, or approves of it. (111)
Through body, mind, or speech, the fruit of that [action] is a downward rebirth.
Thus, the divisions of evil have now been briefly explained as threefold. (112)
The various destinies of men who have committed evil deeds must be told;
thus, O King, this fruit of dharma has been explained to you in great detail. (113)
O best of men, tell me what else I shall speak to you?
I have declared the fruit of unrighteousness; now I shall also give you the fruit of righteousness. (114)
Having spoken thus to the king, who is compassionate toward all beings, Mātali,
the high-souled one, related this [account] there in the course of a discussion on dharma.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places for Ancestors within the Narrative of Yayāti," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The sixty-eighth chapter.
Yayāti said: "O Sūta, O Lord, I have heard all about the fruit of unrighteousness."
Tell me also the fruit of dharma; I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Mātali said:
"Furthermore, these four classes of embodied beings, rendered helpless, go to the world of Yama because of their sins—a place that is terrible and causes great terror. (2)
Therefore, all living beings—whether staying in the womb, being born, or being infants, youths, middle-aged, men, women, eunuchs, or the elderly—must depart from there. (3)
There, the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of embodied beings are scrutinized by Citragupta and all others, who are impartial and all-seeing. (4)
There are no living beings who do not go to the abode of Yama;
for one must inevitably experience the karma that has been performed, as it has been determined. (5)
However, those who have performed auspicious deeds and possess gentle minds and compassion come to the abode of Yama by that gentle path.
He who gives wooden sandals or shoes to Brahmins goes happily to the abode of Yama by means of a great celestial chariot.
By the gift of an umbrella, embodied beings travel along paths free from the clouds [of heat];
by the gift of clothing, those who give garments come attired in divine raiment. (8)
By the gift of a palanquin, one shall travel happily in a celestial chariot;
by the gift of a comfortable seat, one goes happily to the abode of Yama.
The builder of a grove shall go happily in the cool shade;
those who bestow a flower garden travel by means of a celestial flower-chariot (puṣpaka).
He built temples for the gods, hermitages for ascetics,
and pavilions for the helpless, surpassing the finest dwellings of his enemies.
He is a worshiper of the gods, the sacred fire, his teachers, the brahmins, and his mother and father. ||12||

Whatever is given with faith, even if it is very little, to Brahmins who are impoverished yet endowed with virtues, that attains all desires in this world; thus do the wise proclaim the gift made at a śrāddha ceremony.

Even if it were no larger than the tip of a hair, that which is given with faith—whether it be the four requisites beginning with the alms-bowl—is always dear to me among those who possess faith. (14)
Therefore, faith is always to be trusted; from that faith its fruit arises.
One should give even dwellings to the poor who are endowed with virtuous qualities.
O King, that place of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which fulfills all desires,
belongs to that brahmin who, with faith, has given even a mere kākiṇī coin.
A guest from heaven [a divine being] is more worthy than grain; he increases the fame of kings and gods.
Therefore, those endowed with faith should give to him, for the fruit of that action is certain.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Account of Yayāti," within the "Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of the Ancestors" in the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The sixty-ninth chapter.
Mātali said:
