Now, the duties spoken by Śiva, which are the supreme teachings of the Śivadharma Āgama, [are as follows].
These are to be known as manifold, according to the various divisions of the yoga of action. ||1||
For they are free from the faults of violence and the like, devoid of the exhaustion of the afflictions, beneficial to all beings, pure, subtle in their exertion, and yielding great fruit. ||2||
The eternal Śiva-dharmas have their branches spread throughout the Vedas, are rooted solely in Śiva, and are enriched with the beautiful flowers of knowledge and meditation. (3)

Because they maintain auspiciousness and because they are maintained by the words spoken by Śiva, the Śivadharma scriptures are so called; they are remembered as those which enable one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra. ||4||
For thus: non-violence, truthfulness, modesty, faith, self-restraint, sense-control, charity, sacrifice, austerity, and generosity—this tenfold set is the means for accomplishing Dharma. (5)
Now, whether the attributes of Śiva are practiced individually or collectively,
once they have attained complete identity with Śiva, only one single goal is envisioned.
Just as the state of being is considered common to all beings, so too is the City of Śiva considered equal for all devotees of Śiva. (7)
Just as the enjoyments of all beings here are said to be characterized by degrees of excellence,
so too are the enjoyments in the City of Śiva [determined] by the particularity of various merits.
Furthermore, the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds are experienced by all embodied beings;
however, it is there that the fruit of the singular Śivadharma is enjoyed.

Whatever merit one may possess, according to the specific nature of the object of faith and the recipient, one's auspicious enjoyments in the city of Śiva are to be known as being correspondingly superior. (10)
The attainment of a high station is supreme; those who abide in tranquility possess equal enjoyment.
Therefore, one should perform great merit with the desire to attain great enjoyment. (11)
That which is cultivated by the best of gods is indeed the singular state of surpassing all;
it is sovereignty over one's own enjoyments, and Śiva is the lord of the entire world. (12)
Some people there, having been told this, are devoted to the yoga of knowledge; others, however, revolve again, being intent upon the essence of worldly enjoyments.
Therefore, one who desires liberation should abandon attachment to enjoyments;
being dispassionate, with a peaceful mind and self, one shall attain the knowledge of Śiva. 14.
And even those who have generated devotion to Īśa through incidental association, to them too the Lord grants a station in accordance with their disposition. (15)
There, those whose impurities have been once and for all severed worship Rudra;
to them the Lord bestows enjoyments even within the worlds of the Piśācas. (16)
All embodied beings die from the burden of suffering that has been heated within them;
therefore, the giver of food is declared to be the giver of merit, the giver of life, and indeed the giver of everything.
Therefore, by the gift of food, one obtains the fruit of all gifts:
whatever jewels, enjoyments, women, and vehicles exist in the three worlds. (18)
The giver of food shall obtain all the fruits of his merit both in this world and the next, for he whose limbs are nourished by food and drink performs an accumulation of virtue. (19)
Half belongs to the giver of food and half to the doer; of this there is no doubt.
For dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, the body is the supreme means. (20)
Its stability is maintained by food and drink; therefore, these are the means for everything.
Food is Prajāpati himself; food is Viṣṇu; food is Śiva himself. (21)
Therefore, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to food;
water is remembered as the very life of all three worlds.
Divine, pure, and sanctifying water, which is a panacea for all;
as well as food, drink, horses, cows, clothing, beds, thread, and seats. (23)
In the world of the departed (pretaloka), eight types of gifts are especially praised;
by such specific acts of giving, a person reaches the city of Dharmarāja.
Therefore, one should practice the Dharma with great ease;
however, those who perform cruel deeds and are devoid of the taking of what is evil [should act otherwise]. ||25||
O King, those who do not give experience terrible suffering in hell;
likewise, it is only the givers of gifts who enjoy happiness. (26)
But for those whose souls are devoted to the yoga of action, happiness shall arise through divine celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and possess immeasurable qualities. (27)
That city was pervaded by countless beings who bring benefit to all living creatures;
it possessed a divine splendor like a thousand moons and a radiance equal to the brilliance of the sun.
It is declared to be the world of Rudra, endowed with all virtues;
that city is proclaimed as the abode for all devotees of Śiva. (29)

And whoever, with singular devotion, worships Śaṅkara even for a single day on behalf of those who have died in the field of Rudra—whether they be mobile beings or immobile things—[attains the highest state]. (30)
He went to that exceedingly auspicious place while offering many prayers;
there were Vaiṣṇavas, devotees of Viṣṇu, who were entirely devoted to the meditation upon Viṣṇu. ||31||
They go to the vicinity of Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord who wields the discus;
and that righteous soul, a knower of Brahman, proceeds to the world of Brahmā.
The doer of merit goes to the world of merit by means of his great merit;
therefore, one should always cultivate devotion toward the Lord within one's own self by means of the self. 33.
O Great King, even one who is self-disciplined and possessed of knowledge himself may fall;
therefore, through every investigation, one must investigate the defects of mental states. (34)
Thus, even by means of distinguished action through the power of Viṣṇu, a man attains this station in accordance with his disposition toward the land. (35)
This other great Śrīmacchivapura has been described; it is remembered as the place of return for embodied beings devoted to ritual action. (36)
Above the city of Śiva is to be known the supreme world of Viṣṇu;
those devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu go there as divine human beings (mānava). ||37||
The Brahmins of excellent conduct, the best among men, who have performed sacrifices and are proficient in the true principles, all go to that city, the world of Brahmā. (38)
Likewise, Kṣatriyas who are skilled in battle go to the world of the gods;
others who perform meritorious deeds go to the worlds of merit. (39)
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Story of Yayāti at the Pilgrimage Site of the Ancestors," within the *Pitṛ-tīrtha* section of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventieth chapter.
Mātali said:
I shall now describe the suffering of Yama, which is exceedingly intense and most terrible.
All those sinful and cruel slayers of Brahmins eat [the flesh]. ||1||
In some places the sinners are cooked by the fierce fire of iron;
in others, they are tormented by tigers, wolves, leopards, dogs, and dreadful insects.
In some places with great leeches, in others with pythons, in some places with fierce flies, and in others with snakes of virulent poison. ||3||
And by herds of rutting elephants, preeminent in strength and destructive; and by great bulls with sharp horns, scratching the path [before them]. (4)
And with buffaloes possessing great horns that afflict with their wicked bodies, with fierce ḍākinīs, and with terrifying rākṣasas. ||5||
Afflicted by most terrible diseases,
they go toward the great scales, being burned in the fire of hell.
They were violently shaken by a wind of great ferocity,
and were being shattered on all sides by a rain of massive boulders.
Being struck by falling thunderclaps, by terrible falls of meteors,
and by a rain of blazing coals, they go forth [to their destruction].
Those people of sinful deeds who have gone to Yama’s realm, being filled by a great downpour of rain, experience terrible suffering for their evil karma.
Thus, according to the specific nature of their sins, those most wicked evildoers experience hell, which is filled with manifold torments. ||10||
All this has been told to you regarding the distinction between merit and demerit;
I shall now further proclaim the unsurpassed Dharmaśāstra.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Account of Yayāti," within the Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of the Ancestors, in the *Evena* Narrative of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventy-first chapter. Yayāti said:
"All that you have related concerning dharma and adharma is unsurpassed."
Even as I listen, lack of faith arises once again. ||1||
The number of worlds of the gods has been proclaimed as infinite;
by the power of his merit, he attained them all upon the surface of the earth.
Mātali said:
I shall describe that which is attained through yoga and austerity, the station among the worlds of the gods, which bestows the enjoyment of happiness. (3)
I shall explain the nature of dharma, acquired through various efforts, as well as the nature of the worlds above, in their proper sequence. (4)
In that regard, the sovereignty of the flesh-eaters consists of eight qualities; it is taught that for humans who have attained that state immediately, their sovereignty is equal to that.
The power of the Rākṣasas is sixteenfold, and that of the kings is of that same kind; thus, without exception, [he subdued] the remainder of those possessing the splendor of their lineages.
The Vāyavya [weapon] is known to belong to the Gandharvas, and the entire Yākṣa [weapon] is likewise remembered; the Pārthiva belongs to the Bhūtas, and the great Indrāstra possesses forty qualities.
The divine mind of Soma is the Lord of the All (Viśveśa), consisting of the five elements;
it is gentle, belonging to Prajāpati and Īśāna, and is characterized by a predominance of the quality of ego (ahaṅkāra). ||8||
The supreme sovereignty of Baudha is sixty-four times that of Brāhma;
the sovereignty of Viṣṇu is Prādhānika, and that of Brahmā is the station of Brahman.
In the divine Śrīmacchivapura, there is sovereignty that fulfills all desires;
it is the infinite quality of sovereignty, the great inherent attribute of Śiva.
Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, pure, characterized by reality, illuminating all, subtle, incomparable, and higher than the highest. (11)
This world is completely filled with the form of Śiva, who liberates beings from their bonds;
whatever state a person attains, his enjoyment consists of that very nature.
By the grace of the Lord, that celestial chariot shall become equal to it;
these millions of stars of various forms are visible to you. 13.
Thus, twenty-eight [rebirths] are illuminated for those of virtuous nature who offer salutations to the Lord here and there. (14)
They obtain that celestial chariot through association, curiosity, or greed;
or even by the mere incidental chanting of the name of Śiva.
One should perform prostrations; for one who bows, [the obstacle] shall dissolve. These are the great traditional injunctions regarding the rites of Śiva. 16.
Even by means of another action, or through the state of being a master over men, or even incidentally, those men who perform the remembrance of Śaṅkara; (17)
Even by them incomparable happiness is to be attained; how much more so by those who are solely devoted to Him!
With their minds withdrawn through meditation, they practice contemplation upon Viṣṇu. (18)
They go to the supreme abode, that highest step of Viṣṇu;
for the form of Śiva and the form of Viṣṇu are one and the same, O best of men. (19)
There is no difference between these two, who possess a single form and a great self;
to Śiva in the form of Viṣṇu, and to Viṣṇu in the form of Śiva.
Viṣṇu is the heart of Śiva, and Śiva is the heart of Viṣṇu;
the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—are one single form.
There is no distinction between these three; they are proclaimed to be identical in their qualities.
You are indeed a devotee of Śiva, O lord of kings, and you are likewise a devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata).
O King, O observer of excellent vows, because of that very deed of yours, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara became pleased and were well-disposed to grant you boons.
"O Tava-māna, having arrived here by the command of Indra, go now to this place;
afterwards, go to the supreme abode of Brahmā, the Great Lord."
O Vaiṣṇava, you shall attain the state of being unassailable and free from burning or dissolution;
indeed, by means of this divine celestial chariot that travels everywhere.
Therefore, having ascended the Puṣpaka celestial chariot which moves with ease, enjoy divine and delightful pleasures in your divine form.
Sukarmā said:
Having spoken thus to the best of the twice-born, Mātali then became silent before King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, who was a knower of the essence of dharma.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Narrative of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-second chapter.
Pippala said:
Having heard the words of Mātali, King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, [spoke].
What did the one of great wisdom do? Tell me that in detail. ||1||
This narrative, consisting of all merit and destroying sin, is indeed meritorious;
O wise one, I desire to hear it, for I am never satiated. (2)
Sukarman said:
Yayāti, the best among all upholders of dharma and the most excellent of kings, spoke to Mātali, the charioteer of Śakra, who had arrived as a messenger. (3)
Yayāti said: "I shall not abandon this body; I will go again to heaven with this very body, O messenger of the king, there is no doubt."
Although these great defects of the body have thus been proclaimed, you have previously explained all its virtues and faults as well. (5)
"I shall not abandon my body, nor shall I go to heaven again"; having gone there, tell this to the God of gods, the Destroyer of Cities (Purandara).
O Mahāmati, even with this very body, one who lives alone does not attain accomplishment in this world, nor indeed in the hereafter. //7//
The body does not exist without the vital breath, nor indeed does the living soul exist without the body;
O Indra, you shall lead both of them to their destruction through their very friendship.
By whose grace one experiences not only supreme bliss, but also this very life-force of the body and other enjoyments that follow the mind. (9)
O messenger of the gods, knowing thus that the enjoyments of heaven are not to be relished, one realizes that great and most wicked diseases, which cause suffering, arise there. (10)
O Mātali, [this body] arises from sin and the defect of old age;
behold this body of mine, endowed with merit, appearing sixteen years of age.
From birth, a person proceeds with single-minded focus for fifty years;
nevertheless, a renewed state arises even within the body.
The messenger who has gone to my abode is unsurpassed and eternal;
his body shines like that of a man sixteen years of age. ||13||
Likewise, this body shines, endowed with strength and vigor;
there is no exhaustion, no hunger, no fatigue, no diseases, and no old age.
O Mātali, even my body increases through enthusiasm for the Dharma;
it is entirely composed of nectar, a divine medicine, the supreme medicine. (15)
In the past, that which is called Dharma was indeed uttered for the sake of destroying the disease of evil;
by that, the body is purified, and no fault arises.
Meditation upon Hṛṣīkeśa and the supreme utterance of His name—this is the elixir; O messenger, I perform this constantly. (17)
Therefore, those diseases and defects such as sin have gone to their destruction,
for while saṃsāra exists, there is the great medicine named Kṛṣṇa.
Afflicted by the disease of sin, those great fools go from manhood to death; they do not drink the elixir of the name of Kṛṣṇa. (19)
O Mātali, by virtue of that meditation, that knowledge, that spirit of worship,
and through truth and the merit of giving, my womb is free from disease.
From the accumulation of sins, diseases and afflictions arise for embodied beings;
from these afflictions, death is born for living creatures—of this there is no doubt. (21)
Therefore, dharma must be practiced by men who take refuge in merit and truth;
for this body, composed of the five elements, is worn out by its network of veins and joints. (22)
In this way, the mortal who has been thus refined by means of borax and other agents, like a goldsmith with his crucible,
shines there as a great fire, moving eternally as the very essence of the mineral.

O Pippala, that wise man who, through the divine name of Hari and through good fortune, gathers together even that which has been shattered into a hundred pieces— he indeed possesses true intelligence.
Even those five hundred fragments, shattered by a hundred joints, were all held together by him; they became equal to the element of the body (kāyadhātu). ||25||
Through the ritual service of worshiping Hari, through meditation, through observance of vows,
through sincerity, and through giving, a new body is produced.
The defects of the body and its diseases perish; listen, O Mātali!
For when there is both external and internal purity, delusion never arises again. (27)
Then, O Sūta, by the grace of that wielder of the discus, he became pure;
"I shall not go to heaven, for I am making heaven right here. (28)
"By means of austerity, devotion, and my own duty, I shall transform the surface of the earth into heaven itself through the grace of that wielder of the discus."
"Knowing this, drive on and tell Puraṃdara.
Sukarman said: "Then the charioteer heard the command of the king. (30)
Having greeted him with blessings, he approached the great-souled Indra, the lord of the three worlds, and reported everything to him.
Having heard this from the high-souled Yayāti,
the thousand-eyed Indra then reflected upon bringing him back to heaven.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-third chapter.
Pippala said:
After that illustrious one had departed, Dūta again [approached] Indra.
What did that righteous-souled Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, do? (1)
Sukarman said: When that messenger of the best of gods had departed, the prince reflected;
then, having quickly summoned his foremost messengers, he commanded them with words endowed with righteousness and purpose.
Let my excellent messengers go to all the regions, cities, islands, and worlds, carrying out my righteous command; let the people of Vraja likewise follow the auspicious path of Hari.
Through meritorious states that are like nectar,
through meditations, knowledges, sacrifices, and austerities,
and through rituals, offerings, and gifts— [I seek] Madhusūdana alone.
May the worlds worship [him], having abandoned sense-objects. ||4||
Everywhere I saw the sole enemy of the Asuras—
in dry things and in moist ones, in stationary things,
in the clouds, on the earth, and among all things moving and unmoving.
Even within their own bodies, they perceive the form of a living being. ||5||
In honor of that god, let them give gifts with the spirit of hospitality and ancestral devotion;
worship Nārāyaṇa, the best of gods.
You shall soon be liberated from the defilements.
Any man here who, out of greed or even delusion, does not carry out my word,
shall certainly undergo punishment as a pitiless one.
For even my thief is indeed base. ||7||
Having heard the words of the king, all the messengers, filled with joy,
proclaimed throughout the entire earth this royal decree issued by the king to the subjects.
Thus, having brought this most meritorious nectar for mortals beginning with the Brahmins,
let the king drink this merit known as Vaiṣṇava, which is free from defects and results in a desirable transformation.

O people of the world, drink indeed this nectar of the names of the glorious Keśava—the remover of afflictions, the most excellent, the one who subdues pride, whose form is the supreme reality itself, which destroys all faults, and which has been brought forth by the great king. 10.

O people of the world, drink indeed this nectar of the Name—which removes all defects, is brought by the great king, and belongs to that Lord of the gods named Madhusūdana, who dwells in Śrī, possesses all virtues, and holds a sword in his hand. 11.

O people, drink indeed this nectar of the Name—which removes all defects and was brought by the noble king—to the glorious Padmanātha, the lotus-eyed one, the foundational form of the worlds, and the Great Lord. 12.

O people of the world, drink this very nectar of the Name, which destroys evil, bestows honor that takes the form of the destruction of disease, annihilates Dānavas and Daityas, removes all defects, and has been brought by the great king. 13.

O people of the world, drink indeed this nectar of His name, which is brought by the virtuous king; it has the form of the limbs of sacrifice, holds the wheels of a chariot in its hands, is a mine of merit, and is the very embodiment of infinite bliss, removing all defects. (14)

O people of the world, drink indeed this nectar of names—brought by the virtuous king—which is the abode of all, stainless, the ultimate repose, named Rāma, the delighter, the enemy of Mura, which removes all defects. 15.

O people of the world, drink indeed this nectar of the Name, which is like the sun that destroys darkness, which brings about the destruction of bondage, which is the destroyer of the lotuses of ignorance, and which removes all defects—brought forth by the Great King. 16.
Having studied this truly meritorious nectar of names, the high-souled devotee of Viṣṇu who is self-restrained at the time of dawn attains liberation; indeed, there is no other cause for it. (17)

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Account of Yayāti," within the "Description of the Pilgrimage Sites of the Ancestors" in the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventy-fourth chapter. Sukarman said:
"O messengers, they say [this] in all the villages, on all the islands, in all the regions, and likewise in the cities."
O people, hear the command of the king: worship Hari with all your powers! ||1||
Through gifts, numerous sacrifices, austerities, desires for dharma, offerings, and mental rites,
let the worlds meditate upon Madhusūdana.
Thus was the command of that king.
Thus, all that well-proclaimed merit was heard by the people throughout the regions of the earth;
from that time forward, they worshipped Viṣṇu.
Mortals meditate, sing, and recite prayers. ||3||
With their minds fixed upon Him, they [worship] Śrī Keśava with well-composed Vedic mantras and most meritorious hymns that are like nectar.
By means of vows, fasts, observances, and gifts. ||4||
Having abandoned all faults arising from their own body, mind,
and speech, they were all devoted with love to the abode of Lakṣmī, the refuge of the worlds.
They worship Śrī Vāsudeva. ||5||
Thus commanded by the king, all those people on the circle of the earth live according to the Vaiṣṇava disposition; they are victorious.
Those skilled in knowledge worship Viṣṇu by means of His names and deeds;
they are absorbed in meditation upon Him, intent on Him, and devoted solely to the worship of Viṣṇu.
As far as the entire circle of the earth extends, and as far as the sun shines,
so far did all the people of the Himalayas become devotees of the Lord.
Through the power of meditating upon Viṣṇu, by means of worship, hymns of praise, and his names,
those humans then became free from mental and physical afflictions.
Free from sorrow and meritorious, all those rich in asceticism became Vaiṣṇavas through the grace of that discus-wielding Brāhmaṇa.
They were free from diseases and devoid of faults and passions;
they possessed all sovereign powers and were liberated from every ailment. ||11||
Then, through the grace of that god,
all human beings became like immortals, free from decay, and endowed with wealth and grain.
O highly fortunate one, by the grace of Viṣṇu, those mortals who are adorned with sons and grandsons always have [him] at the doors of their very houses.
The wish-fulfilling trees are most meritorious, bestowing the fruits of all desires; likewise, there are cows that yield every wish and cintāmaṇi jewels.
In their homes there are meritorious beings who grant all desires; born of gods and men, they are adorned with sons and grandsons. ||15||
By the grace of Viṣṇu alone, they shall be free from all defects, endowed with every form of prosperity, and possessed of merit and auspiciousness. ||16||
For those endowed with great merit, generosity, and wisdom, and devoted to meditation,
there is no famine, no disease, and no untimely death among men.
While that king, a knower of dharma and a follower of the path of knowledge, was ruling, all the men were devotees of Viṣṇu and dedicated to the observance of Viṣṇu’s vows.
All of them were absorbed in that meditation, intent upon the state of non-existence;
their dwellings, O best of the twice-born, became divine and meritorious. (19)
They were indeed adorned with very white banners and conchs,
and their flags were constantly marked with maces and discs.
Their houses, resembling celestial chariots, were marked with lotuses and decorated on their wall surfaces by skilled painters.
O best of beings, at the doors of every house and in sacred places, there are divine forests, lush with green grass and auspicious. (22)
O best of the twice-born, among those [trees], Keśava always dwells within the Tulasī; by its mere sight, he grants divine and meritorious abodes to living beings.
O friend, everywhere on this earth, auspiciousness pertaining to Viṣṇu is seen in many forms, along with the sounds of conch shells and the mutual crashing of thunderous roars.
O best of brahmins, it is heard that conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses, which destroy faults and sins,
should be placed upon the doors and walls of houses.
O best of the twice-born, these were written by women through devotion to Viṣṇu,
accompanied by songs of melodic passion and beautiful tones with their various modulations (*mūrcchanās*) and expansions (*tānas*).
Devoted to meditation upon Viṣṇu, the worlds sing of Keśava.
Some call him Hari, Murāri, Keśava, and others affectionately call him Ajita and Mādhava; some call him Śrī-Nārasiṃha, Kamalekṣaṇa, Govinda, and the sole Lord of Lakṣmī.
Those who chant the name of Kṛṣṇa, the refuge of all, as their protection; who worship Rāma with prayers;
and who bow down to Viṣṇu with prostrations like a staff—engrossed in meditation upon Him, they are the supreme Vaiṣṇavas. (29)
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The seventy-fifth chapter.
Sukarman said:
[I bow to] Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, Rāma, Mukunda, and Madhusūdana.
Nārāyaṇa, the form of Viṣṇu, the Man-Lion, that infallible one.
Keśava, Padmanābha, Vāsudeva, and Vāmana; the Boar, the Tortoise, the Fish, Hṛṣīkeśa, and the Lord of the Gods.
To Viśveśa, who possesses universal form, the sinless and pure one;
to the Puruṣa with lotus-like eyes, the bearer of Śrī, the Lord of Śrī, Hari. ||3||
"Śrīnivāsa, Pītavāsa, Mādhava, Mokṣada, Prabhu"—thus indeed should men always utter these names together. (4)
All men—children, the elderly, and young girls—as well as women, while constantly engaged in their household duties, sing beautifully of Hari. (5)
While playing on their seats, beds, vehicles, and even while meditating,
those children likewise bow down to Govinda.
Day and night they utter the very sweet name of Hari;
O best of the twice-born, the chanting of Viṣṇu’s name is heard everywhere.
By the power of Viṣṇu, mortals move upon the surface of the earth,
as well as at the tops of temple domes and in the sanctuaries of the deities.
Just as the orbs of the sun shine, so do the wheels [of his chariot] appear;
such is the state perceived in Vaikuṇṭha, and that same state exists upon the surface of the earth.
By that high-souled king, the merit of the Brahmins was performed,
and thus the surface of the earth was brought to a state equal to the world of Viṣṇu.
By Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa and a devotee of Viṣṇu,
the surface of the earth was made one with the state of both worlds.
No distinction whatsoever is seen between the ground and Viṣṇu;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇavas pronounce the name of Viṣṇu as if it were Vaikuṇṭha itself. (12)
O Brahmin, when human beings on the surface of the earth utter such a sound,
a single state of being is perceived in both worlds.
Free from the fear of old age and disease, men lived devoid of death;
and on earth, the power of their generosity and enjoyment was seen to be even greater.
O best of men on earth, human beings attain even greater merit and happiness through their sons than they do through their grandsons; indeed, they reach the Lord with ease. 15.
By the granting of Viṣṇu’s grace and by his instruction,
human beings who are devotees of Viṣṇu are forever liberated from all diseases.
O best of kings, the majesty of the heavenly world was thus established by the king upon the surface of the earth for a duration of twenty-five years.
All men were free from disease, devoted to knowledge and meditation;
all human beings were intent on sacrifice and charity, and possessed a nature of compassion. ||18||
Devoted to helping others, meritorious and fortunate, they were vessels of fame;
all were intent on righteousness and dedicated to meditation upon Viṣṇu. (19)
Instructed by that king, they became Vaiṣṇavas on this earth.
Viṣṇu said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to the life-story of that monarch."
The son of Nahuṣa, a devotee of Viṣṇu who was eternally devoted to all dharmas,
likewise passed a hundred thousand years on this earth.
A body appeared as if twenty-five years old; at that time, he shone with the form and age of one twenty-five years of age.
Having attained maturity and becoming powerful through the grace of that wielder of the discus,
they do not go to Yama even after reaching the human world.
Freed from passion and hatred, liberated from the snares of the afflictions, they are happy through the merit of their generosity and are devoted to all wholesome qualities. ||24||
O King, all those arrows spread out as they fell,
just as blades of dūrvā grass and banyan trees spread across the surface of the earth.
Just as all these men have expanded through their sons and grandsons, so too those people,
free from the defects of death, indeed live for a long time.
With stable bodies and happiness, free from old age and disease, all men on the face of the earth will be seen to live for twenty-five years. (27)
All were devoted to truthful conduct and intent upon meditation on Viṣṇu;
thus all those mortals existed through the grace of that wielder of the discus.
O best of men, among all those born as humans who are solely devoted to giving and enjoyment, not a single mortal is heard of as having died in this world. (29)
They perceive no sorrow whatsoever, nor do they fall into any fault;
for such is the nature of the heavenly realm as it is the nature of the earth.
By the grace of that Cakrin, the best of men, as soon as he was born,
those messengers of Yama fell away, struck down by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
Weeping, they all approached the King of Dharma and recounted to one another all that had been done by the king, as reported by the messengers who praised him.
When the sun was in Dhanistha, the earth became free from death through the enjoyment of gifts;
this was also accomplished by Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
Through the merit of a devotee of Viṣṇu, the form of heaven was revealed;
all this was heard by Dharmarāja at that time.
Then the King of Dharma, having heard the full account from the messengers and having thus heard the conduct of the king, reflected upon the entire matter.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 75 ||
The seventy-sixth chapter. Sukarman said:
Thus, accompanied by all his messengers, the son of Sūrya went to heaven.
To behold the thousand-eyed one there, surrounded by hosts of gods. ||1||
Then the king of the gods beheld that Dharmarāja upon his arrival; rising up with haste, he offered him the most excellent arghya. ||2||
He asked about his arrival: "Tell me [the reason] before me.
Having heard those great words spoken by the King of the Gods, [he replied]. (3)
The King of Dharma related the entire great life-story of Yayāti.
The King of Dharma said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, hear from me the reason for my arrival."
I shall tell you here also why I have come to you—
by the high-souled son of Nahuṣa, who is a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The Vaiṣṇavas, having attained immortality, dwell upon the surface of the earth;
the form of the mortal world has become equal to that of Vaikuṇṭha.
Born neither as gods nor as humans, free from old age and disease,
they commit no evil at all and do not speak untruth.
Free from desire and anger, devoid of greed and delusion, they were high-souled men devoted to charity and virtue, all of whom were dedicated to righteousness. ||8||
By means of all dharmas, men on the surface of the earth worship the stainless Nārāyaṇa through that very Vaiṣṇava dharma. 9.
Free from disease and devoid of sorrow, all of them possessed stable youth and spread across the surface of the earth like dūrvā grass and banyan trees.
In this manner, they attained great expansion through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons;
their sons and great-grandsons caused lineage after lineage to surge like waves.
For in this way, the entire mortal world was rendered free from old age and death by that son of Nahuṣa, a true devotee of Viṣṇu.
"I have fallen from my station and am deprived of my livelihood;
all this has been explained as the destruction of my merit. (13)
Knowing this, O Thousand-eyed One, act for the welfare of this world.
All this has been told to you, exactly as I was questioned by you.
For this reason, O Indra, you have come into my presence.
Indra said:
"Even before this, O messenger, I had already received news of that high-souled one."
Having been sent by the messenger of the Lord of Dharma, he spoke thus:
"I do not seek the happiness of heaven; I shall not return to this world again. (16)
"I shall make this entire circle of the earth take on the form of heaven," thus spoke the protector of the earth, who was engaged in protecting his subjects. (17)
"By the power of his merit, I remain forever fearless.
Dharma said:
"By whatever means possible, bring that virtuous king here."
"O highly fortunate King of the Gods, if you desire this unpleasant thing,"—having heard these words of Dharma, the Lord of the Suras [replied]. (19)
O King, the wise Purandara reflected upon the entire matter as it truly was;
he summoned Kāmadeva and the Gandharvas.
The high-minded one brought Makaranda, Daṇḍa, Rati, and Devānī;
"O you all, act in such a way that the king arrives. (21)
"Go to the world of Bhūrloka as commanded by me; of this there is no doubt.
Kāma said:
"I shall perform what is pleasing and meritorious for you both; of this there is no doubt. (22)
Having seen the king standing there in the midst of the battle,
they all said, "So be it," and went to where King Sāhuṣi was seated.
O twice-born one, all these beings, beginning with Kāma, having assumed the forms of actors through their own karma,
greeted him with blessings and spoke of a beautiful drama.
Having heard those words of theirs, the wise Yayāti, lord of the earth,
constructed an assembly hall of celestial beauty together with highly learned men.
The king himself, an expert in both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, arrived there;
King Nahusha watched their dramatic performance.
[They heard] the life-story of Vāmana, who was born in the form of a brahmin, whose beauty was peerless in the world, and whose excellent song was sung with a beautiful voice. (27)
O King, she who is beyond old age sang this very thing in the form of a noble woman;
by means of her singing, her charm, her laughter, and her graceful movements.
Who could withstand his sweet speech, his pride, or his guile, being deluded by that disposition and his divine conduct? (29)
He assumed the form of Bali exactly as it was before, and likewise the form of Vindhya; he also assumed the form of Vāmana and mounted upon him in that very manner. (30)
The Sūtradhāra himself, having entered the stage, [is joined by] the Pāripārśvaka;
the Naṭī, wearing her costume, has appeared, and their mutual affection is joyful. (31)
O King, during that performance of dance,
the highly wise Taścarī from Nepathya agitated the lord of the earth like a great Makara.

In whatever manner the lord of the earth beheld the supreme dance and listened to the song, in that very same way the noble-minded one deluded the king by means of what was presented by the actress. (33)
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Story of Yayāti and the Sacred Site of Parents," within the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventy-seventh chapter. Sukarman said:
"By means of the singing, dancing, laughter, and graceful movements of Kāma..."
O Pippala, you were deluded by the King of Kings in the form of Droṇa.
Having voided urine and feces, King Nahuṣa’s son sat down on his seat without having performed the purification of his feet.
Then, having reached Tuṣita, he moved toward King Jarā;
even by his own will, O best of kings, he performed this beneficial deed for the sake of Indra's purpose.
When that drama had concluded and those arrows had departed, the king—
virtuous in soul yet overcome by old age and his mind attached to sensual desires— [reflected].
Deluded by the delusion of desire, overwhelmed and with impaired senses,
that virtuous soul was utterly infatuated and carried away by the objects of the senses.
Once, the king, afflicted by his addiction to hunting, went out;
he too sported in the forest, having fallen under the sway of delusion and passion. (6)
While the high-souled king was sporting in the lake,
a single incomparable deer with four horns appeared.
O King, his limbs were beautiful in every part, his body-hair was like gold, and his limbs were wonderfully variegated with the luster of jewels; he was lovely to behold and captivating to the mind.
Holding his bow and with arrows in hand, he rushed forward with great speed;
thus, another intelligent Daitya also arrived.
Drawn far away by the deer even as it fled,
the king went with the speed of his chariot, exhausted by fatigue.
As he was looking on, the deer vanished from his sight;
there he beheld a forest, wonderful and beyond compare.
It was filled with beautiful trees, graced by the five elements,
and adorned with auspicious sandalwood trees and groves of plantain trees.
With *bakula*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, coconut palms, *tiṃduka* trees, betel nuts, dates, water lilies, and *saptaparṇaka* trees; ||13||
With flowering *karṇikāra* trees and various ever-fruiting trees, and with *ketaka* and *pāṭala* flowers endowed with the fragrance of their blossoms; ||14||
Looking about, the great king saw that most excellent lake, filled with holy water and five yojanas in extent. ||15||
It was filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, resounded with the cries of water-birds,
gladdened by lotuses, and adorned with white water-lilies.
It was resplendent with red lotuses, adorned with golden lotuses,
illuminated by blue lotuses, and exceedingly beautified by white water-lilies.
And it was made to resound everywhere by intoxicated bees;
thus he beheld that most excellent [palace], endowed with every excellence. (18)
The lake, extending five yojanas in width and ten yojanas in length,
was auspicious on all sides and adorned with divine qualities.
Exhausted by the speed of the chariot and somewhat oppressed by fatigue,
he sat down in the very cool shade of a mango tree on that bank.
Having bathed and drunk that cool water, scented with lotuses and saugandhika flowers, which pacifies all fatigue and is like nectar itself—[he felt refreshed]. (21)
Then, as the king sat there in the shade of a tree,
he heard the sound of singing being performed in such-and-such a manner.
Just as a divine song is sung by women, so too is this sound heard;
the great king, who is fond of music, has indeed become completely absorbed in that thought.
While that righteous-souled one, agitated by anxiety, was reflecting for a moment,
a certain wretched woman with full hips and breasts appeared.
While the king was watching, she arrived in that forest,
her limbs adorned with all ornaments and endowed with the perfection of virtuous character and auspicious marks.
When she had arrived in that forest and stood before the king, the great monarch said to her: "Whose wife will you become? (26)
"For what purpose have you come? Tell me the reason for that. Thus questioned by him, she then said nothing at all, O Pippala.
Smiling, the fair-faced woman, holding the neck of her lute in her hand, spoke of both the auspicious and the inauspicious to the protector of the earth, and then quickly departed. 28.
O King, even though I was then overwhelmed by great amazement, she did not give me any reply when addressed by me. (29)
Furthermore, King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, again fell into that same state of anxiety regarding that golden bull with four horns which had been seen in the cow-dung.
Therefore, that which has arisen from a woman appears as truth;
this illusory form shall become the truth for the Dānavas. (31)
Having reflected upon this misfortune, King Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa,
was still pondering when, O King, he beheld a woman in the great forest.
In that interval, while the Brahmins were laughing at the disappearance of the king's son, this same song was once again sung in a melodious voice. (33)
He heard a supreme, divine sound, endowed with melodic modulations and rhythmic expansions; the king went quickly to where that great sound of singing arose.
In the midst of the waters was a supreme thousand-petaled lotus;
upon it sat an excellent woman, endowed with virtuous character, beauty, and all good qualities.
Endowed with divine marks and adorned with celestial ornaments,
she alone shines forth with divine qualities, her hand holding the neck of a lute.
Singing a song with beautiful melodies, accompanied by rhythm, measure, and tempo,
I deluded all moving and non-moving beings through the power of that song.
Seeing her—the large-eyed one, resplendent with beauty and splendor—all the gods, hosts of sages, daityas, gandharvas, and kinnaras [were struck with wonder]. ||38||
In this world of the moving and the unmoving, there is indeed no other woman like her;
for she was formerly a dancer afflicted with old age who became the very body of the king. (39)
Then that great desire, having been stirred, became manifest,
just as fire arises when it touches ghee or as the sun appears when its rays emerge.
Upon seeing her, his desire manifested itself from his body;
his mind possessed by the god of love, he gazed upon that woman of beautiful eyes. (41)
Having contemplated for a moment such a maiden, unseen before and enchanting the entire world, the king’s mind became deeply attached to desire.
Even during her absence, the king then became filled with longing;
he was scorched by the fire of desire and tormented by the fever of passion.
"How might this happen to me, and how will my state of being come to pass, when this foolish girl with the lotus-face and lotus-eyes hides her limbs? (44)
"If she is obtained, then my life will have become fruitful.
Thinking thus, the righteous-souled Yati, the lord of the earth, [proceeded]. (45)
He said to her: "O auspicious one, which woman has ever been seen by you first on one lap and then again on another? (46)
The virtuous-souled one asked her: "Who is this woman by your side?
Tell me everything, O auspicious lady; for I am the son of Nahuṣa. (47)
"O auspicious lady, I am born of the Soma dynasty and am the sovereign of the seven continents;
O Queen, my name is Yayāti, and I am renowned throughout the three worlds. (48)
My heart thus desires union with you; O blessed lady, grant me this union and do what is most pleasing. (49)
"Whatever you desire, O blessed lady, I shall grant it to you without a doubt;
yet I have been struck down by Durjaya, O woman of excellent complexion. (50)
Therefore, protect me, who am utterly wretched and have come to you for refuge—granting me my kingdom, the entire earth, and even my own body. (51)
"I shall give you this very triple world as a reward for your union.
Having heard these words of the king, she, whose face resembled a lotus, [spoke]. (52)
She said to her friend Viśālā, "O auspicious one, tell the king that you have arrived, and [tell him] your name, your place of origin, your father, and your mother. (53)
"Tell her my state of mind with one-pointed attention;
then, having ascertained her desire, [inform] the lord of Viśālā."
She spoke with sweet words: "O King, listen.
Viśālā said:
"This Kāma was long ago consumed by the God of gods, Śambhu."
Deprived of her husband, Sāratī wept piteously with a melodious voice out of grief;
at that time, Sāratī was dwelling in this king of lotuses.
Having heard his lamentation, which was filled with piteous and sorrowful tones, the gods were then moved by supreme compassion. (57)
Having been born together, they addressed these words to Śaṅkara, the lord of the kings of kings:
"O Great God, restore the Mind-born one to life once again! (58)
"O highly fortunate one, what will become of this wretched woman, now deprived of her husband?
Out of affection for us, please unite her with Kāma. (59)
Having heard those words, he said: "I shall restore the Mind-born to life;
though deprived even of his body, this five-arrowed Mind-born [Kāma] shall live."
The body of Mādhava’s friend shall not perish;
he will continue to exist even with a divine body, and not otherwise.
"O best of men, by the grace of Mahādeva, Mīnaketu has been restored to life; thus, through the goddess's blessings, his desire has been fulfilled. (62)
"Go, O Kāmapravarta, and always remain with your beloved.
Thus spoke the one of great splendor, the agent of maintenance and dissolution.
Furthermore, O King, Kāma has reached the lake where Duḥkhitā and Arati dwell; this is the lake of Kāma, and Rati is well-established here. (64)
O highly fortunate one, when [the body] was consumed by fire, Manmatha, overcome by the pain [of separation], produced from Rati’s wrath a fire of terrible form. (65)
O best of men, though she was utterly consumed by that fire, Sārati, fainting with delusion and deprived of her husband, then shed a torrent of tears.
From her eyes, drops of tears fell;
from them was born Great Sorrow, the destroyer of all happiness. (67)
O best of kings, after old age had arisen from tears, there was born from them the evil-minded one named Separation, who causes destruction. (68)
Then, both suffering and torment arose, terrible and fierce;
from that, a state of fainting was produced, dreadful and destructive of happiness.
From grief arise great royal distress, the fever of desire, or delusion; as well as lamentation, agitation, insanity, and even death. (70)
From her teardrops were born all the Viśvanāśakas;
they emerged from the side of Rati, and all of them possess oblique glances.
"O King, he who is endowed with the qualities of the true nature of the Great King has arrived in embodied form; this is Kāma," so it was said by someone at that time. (72)
Seeing Mahānaṃdena arrived with longing and joined together, drops of tears fell from his eyes which were filled with tears. (73)
O great king, while in the midst of the waters, the subjects were born through his restlessness;
then, O best of men, there was born affection by the name of Khyāti and Modesty (Lajjā). 74.
O best of kings, from them were born ten sons who subdued other [enemies], and two auspicious daughters who bestow happiness and enjoyment. (75)
O King, through that great union of playful sport and mental disposition, tears indeed flowed from the left eye of Rati in the form of droplets. (76)
From that king who had fallen into the water, a beautiful lotus was born;
from that beautiful lotus, this woman of lovely countenance was born. ||77||
O Best of Men, I am the daughter of Arati, named Aśrubindumatī;
out of affection for her, I have made myself unhappy and constantly remain by her side. (78)
O King, the daughter of Varuṇa, who was always auspicious and delighted by her very nature as a friend, became renowned among the Viśālas. 79.
Out of affection, I shall always remain devoted to her; out of love, I am ever tender toward her.
All this has been told to you—both concerning her and concerning myself. (80)
Desirous of obtaining her husband, the fair-faced woman performed penance, O lord of kings.
The king said:
"Everything has been told by you; it has been understood by me, O auspicious one; listen. (81)
"Let this lovely-faced daughter of Rati choose me alone;
whatever she desires from us out of childishness, I shall grant it all. (82)
"O auspicious lady, act in such a way that she indeed attains the state of Śyāmā.
Viśālā said:
"O King, I shall proclaim her vow; listen to it. (83)
O King, he was a man endowed with youth, omniscient, possessing the marks of a hero, equal to the king of the gods, and fully possessed of righteous conduct.
He was radiant, possessed of great wisdom, a donor, the best among those who perform sacrifices, a knower of virtues and the nature of dharma, and a vessel of merit. ||85||
O King, he was equal to the lord of the world, devoted to righteousness through excellent sacrifices, and endowed with all sovereignty like another Nārāyaṇa. 86.

He was eternally dear to the gods and exceedingly beloved by the Brahmins; he was devoted to the Brahmanas, a knower of the true essence of the Vedas, and his prowess was renowned throughout the three worlds.
Endowed with such qualities and honored by the three worlds,
he desired in his mind that Sumati, who was so very dear to him, as his supreme bridegroom.
Yayāti said:
"Know me to have come here endowed with such qualities;
I am the husband suited to her, ordained by the Creator, of this there is no doubt. (89)
Viśālā said: "O King, know him to be the ancient one, the increaser of merit throughout the three worlds;
all the qualities previously mentioned by me exist in you. (90)
She regards you as having been bitten by even a single snake; O King, this doubt has arisen in her mind that you are not Viṣṇu.
Yayāti said:
"Tell me truly of that great fault for which she does not grant her consent;
O lady of beautiful limbs, become gracious with a pleasant countenance. (92)
Viśālā said:
"O Lord of the Earth, why do you not recognize your own fault?
Your body is pervaded by old age; for this reason, she does not honor you. (93)
Having heard these great and unpleasant words, the lord of the earth,
the king, overcome with great sorrow, spoke to her again.
"O lordly elephant, when and from whom did this defect of old age arise? It has appeared upon my own body; I have not seen it among other people. (95)
"O auspicious lady, whatever you desire that is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds, I wish to grant it to you; choose an excellent boon. (96)
Viśālā said:
"O King, when you are free from old age, she will become very dear to you;
this is certain, O King, I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (97)
O King, the Śruti declares thus: "Upon whomsoever old age is transferred—whether to a son, a brother, or a servant—it shall move about within his own body. (98)
Having taken back his youth from him and given him old age in return, an auspicious conversation regarding mutual affection arose between the two through Suruci. (99)
O King, just as one gives away the merit of self-sacrifice out of compassion, a beneficial fruit arises for that person; of this there is no doubt. (100)
Merit acquired with great difficulty is bestowed here upon another;
it becomes excellent merit for that person, who then enjoys the fruit of that merit. (101)
"O King, let youthfulness itself be given to your son;
O Lord of the Earth, come together with him, having assumed beauty. (102)
"But when you wish to eat, O King, then do so. Having addressed the king in this manner, Viśālā ceased speaking. 103.
Sukarman said:
Having heard this, O Indra among kings, he then spoke to Viśālā.
The king said:
"So be it, O noble one; I shall certainly do this for you. ||104||
Attached to sensual pleasures and utterly deluded, King Yayāti went to his home,
summoned his sons, and spoke these words.
"O Turu, Pūru, Kuru, Yadu, and Capita, you who are devoted to your father:
O sons, by my command, may you all attain happiness. (106)
The sons said:
"The words of our father must be carried out by us, whether they be auspicious or inauspicious.
O father, let it be spoken quickly; know that it shall be done without a doubt. (107)
Having heard these words of his sons, the lord of the earth,
his mind agitated with joy, spoke to them once again.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Story of Yayāti, in the *Evena* Episode of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventy-eighth chapter. Yayāti said:
"O sons, let this old age, which bestows misery, be taken up by one of you."
"Among you who are wise, let youth be granted to me. ||1||
O highly fortunate ones, this supreme nature of yours is now being scorched;
for the mind, attached to women, is fickle and impure. (2)
Just as fire causes the water contained in a vessel to boil,
so too, O sons, does the fire of desire agitate my mind.
"O sons, let one of you take upon himself this old age that brings such suffering;
let him give me his own youth so that I may enjoy myself as I desire. (4)
"My excellent son will effect the removal of old age;
he shall enjoy the kingdom and wield the bow of Śiva. (5)
He shall possess happiness, excellent prosperity, wealth, and grain; he shall have vast satisfaction, as well as fame and renown. (6)
The sons said: "O King, you are devoted to dharma and protect your subjects with truth; why has such a disposition as this arisen in you—one so contrary to your nature? (7)
The king said:
"Formerly, dancers who were performers for the gods arrived at my city; from among them, one woman was chosen, and from that choice, such delusion as this arose. (8)
O best of sons, his body pervaded by old age yet his mind possessed by passion, he became utterly distraught and agitated by desire.
O sons, I saw a certain woman of divine form and beautiful face; I addressed her, yet she did not utter a single word in reply.
And the friend of Viśālā, named Cāruvicakṣaṇā, spoke these auspicious words to me, which bestow happiness upon me. (11)
"When you are free from old age, she will become very dear to you.
Having accepted these words spoken by her, he returned home. (12)
This has been thus proclaimed by me for the purpose of removing old age;
having understood this, O good sons, my happiness must not be disregarded. (13)
Turu said:
"A body is obtained by sons through the grace of their father and mother; and with that body, O King, dharma is performed by the wise man. (14)
O lord of men, service to one's parents must be performed by sons, especially so; this is not the time for the giving away of a daughter in marriage. 15.
O King, human beings must first enjoy the objects of the senses;
now, however, this time for the practice of austerities has arrived for you. (16)
"O father, having bestowed upon your son this great old age, you may afterwards enjoy happiness; otherwise, your life would not endure. (17)
"Therefore, O Great King, you shall not perform [the sacrifice] again.
Thus did Turu, the eldest son, then address the king.
Having heard Turu’s words, that righteous king became enraged;
with eyes reddened by anger, he cursed Turu. (19)
"O evil-minded one, you have violated this command of mine;
therefore, become a sinner, excluded from all dharma. (20)
If you are deprived of your topknot, devoid of the Vedas and the Shastras, and destitute of all proper conduct, you will undoubtedly become so. ||21||
"You are a slayer of Brahmins, a hater of the gods, a drinker of liquor, and devoid of truth;
you are a performer of cruel deeds and shall become the lowest of men. (22)
"You shall be one who is addicted to wine, gluttonous, sinful, and a killer of cows; you shall have bad skin, untied loincloth, be a hater of Brahmins, and be an outcast. (23)
You will always be one who approaches the wives of others, extremely fierce, a rogue, a glutton, and dull-witted. (24)
By sporting with a woman of the same lineage, you, who destroy all dharmas, whose self is devoid of merit and knowledge, shall become afflicted with leprosy. (25)
Your sons and grandsons will undoubtedly become such mlecchas, destroyers of all merit, who have been rendered utterly defiled. (26)
Having thus firmly bound Turu, he then spoke to his son Yadu:
"Accept this old age here, and enjoy the kingdom free from all thorns."
Joining his palms in reverence, Yadu spoke to the king from afar.
Yadu said:
"O father, have mercy; I am unable to bear the burden of old age."
Cold, travel, bad food, women who have passed their youth,
and opposition to one's mind— these are the five causes of old age.
O King, I am unable to ward off the suffering of old age while my youth still remains; for who indeed is capable of turning it back? Therefore, please forgive me now.
O great king, being thus enraged, he cursed the twice-born Danu:
"This one shall never at any time become worthy of the kingdom. (31)
Devoid of strength, majesty, and forbearance, and abandoned by the dharma of the kshatriya, this body shall not exist if it turns its back on my command. (32)
Yadu said:
"O Great King, I am faultless; why have I been cursed by you now?
Have mercy on this wretched man and become gracious with a favorable countenance. (33)
The king said:
"O son, Mahādeva himself will surely effect the procreation within this lineage by means of his own seed; then your family shall be purified."
Yadu said:
"O great king, I am your son, yet I have been cursed by you though I am innocent. If you still have compassion for me, let some favor be granted to me. (35)
The king said:
"He who is the eldest son and the remover of his father's sorrow, he indeed enjoys the inheritance of the kingdom and becomes the bearer of its burden. (36)
No unrighteousness has been committed by you, so there is no doubt that you are blameless;
yet you have been struck down by a great punishment for those who caused harm. (37)
"Therefore, there is no favor [to be granted]; do as you wish.
Yadu said:
"O King, since you have consumed my kingdom, lineage, and beauty," (38)
"Therefore, O King, you shall become corrupt;
and from your lineage shall arise Kṣatriyas of various divergent types. (39)
Those exceedingly fierce and mighty-bodied ones shall indeed enjoy their villages, excellent regions, women, and whatever jewels there may be. 40.
Those who have arisen from my own lineage in the form of Turuṣkas and Mlecchas have all been consumed by you and cursed with most terrible curses. ||41||
Thus did Yadu speak to the king, O best of monarchs;
then the great king, being enraged, cursed him once again in this manner. (42)
Listen indeed to how all these [beings] are born as destroyers of my progeny:
as long as the moon and the sun, the earth, the lunar mansions, and the stars exist. (43)
Then those non-Aryans (mlecchas), having seen Kuru playing there with beautiful marks, fell into the hells of Bhiṣaka and Raurava. ||44||
Knowing him to be a child, the king abandoned that son, Nandana; then Sakra summoned him and spoke as follows. 45.
The Lord of the World summoned that meritorious Pūru, the son of Śarmiṣṭhā, and spoke to him again: "Let this old age be accepted. (46)
"Enjoy the kingdom granted by me, which is highly meritorious and free from enemies.
Pūru said: "The kingdom must be enjoyed by the god-like king, just as it was enjoyed by your father. (47)
"O King, I shall carry out your command; let old age be given to me, so that today, by means of my youth, I may possess a beautiful form and appearance. (48)
O highly fortunate one, enjoy the fruits of your good deeds while your mind is attached to the objects of the senses; sport with her as long as you desire. (49)
"As long as I live, O father, I shall bear this old age.
Thus was the lord of the world addressed by that Pūru.
Overcome with great joy, he spoke to that son:
"Since you have here performed this service for me at my command. (51)
Therefore, I shall bestow that which grants great happiness, since you have given me your own youth, which had been seized by old age. (52)
"Therefore, O high-minded one, enjoy the kingdom bestowed by me.
Thus addressed by that king, O lord of the earth, the noble man [replied]. (53)
O King, he gave youth to him and took old age from him;
thus, an exchange of ages was made between the father and the son.
Therefore, Pūru appeared older in all his limbs,
yet the king appeared as fresh as a sixteen-year-old.
Endowed with a magnificent form like a second Manmatha, he held the bow, the royal umbrella, the fly-whisk, and the elephant-throne. (56)
The great king gave him the treasury, the entire territory, the army, as well as the fly-whisk, the white umbrella, and the chowrie; he likewise gave these to the high-souled Pūru.
Attached to desire and constantly thinking of that woman, the son of Nahuṣa, though righteous in soul, beheld that lake known as Kāma, which resembled the ocean.
With swift strides, he went to the river Aśrubindumatī;
having seen her, the large-eyed woman with beautiful, full breasts, [he approached]. (59)
Whom did the great king Viśāla approach, his mind drawn by pride?
The king said:
"O illustrious one, O Viśālā of beautiful eyes, I have come to you. (60)
"O auspicious one, you have cast off old age and are endowed with youth;
having become young, come now to be present before them. (61)
"Whatever this woman desires, I shall grant it to her, without a doubt.
Viśālā said:
"When you arrived, having abandoned this wicked old age..."
"You are tainted by a single fault, yet you do not recognize it as such.
The king said: "Tell me my fault, if you know it for certain. (63)
One will undoubtedly abandon that fault and assume the form of virtue. ||64||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 78 ||
The seventy-ninth chapter.
Viśālā said:
"Śarmiṣṭhā is his wife, and Devayānī is the fair-faced one."
O King, good fortune is seen only there; otherwise, it does not exist.
Therefore, O illustrious one, how did you come to be under her influence for the sake of her purpose? How have you been established as her husband by means of a feeling born of a rival wife? (2)
Just as there is a great sandalwood tree on the surface of the earth surrounded by serpents, O King, so indeed was the Great Sandalwood Tree itself encircled by snakes.
Enveloped by serpents that do not recognize their own consorts, such is the state of reality;
better indeed is entry into the fire, and better still is falling from the tip of a flame. (4)
He was endowed with physical splendor, beloved, and accompanied by his wife;
yet that very person was filled with such a fear of his wife's poison.
Therefore, he did not consider that one existence to be equal to that ocean of virtues.
The King said:
"O fair-faced one, Devayānī’s desire was for Śarmiṣṭhā."
"Behold this single treasury, endowed with the qualities of sentient beings.
Bindumatī said:
"O King, I am the enjoyer of the kingdom and of your body. (7)
"O King, whatever I say must certainly be carried out by you;
for this purpose, O lover of righteousness, grant me your hand. (8)
"Endowed with many virtues and possessed of beautiful marks," the king said,
"O woman of excellent complexion, I will not accept any other wife except for you."
"O fair-faced one, enjoy the entire kingdom and the whole earth as my body; O lovely-limbed one, it is with treasury included. This hand of yours has been given by me. (10)
"O auspicious one, I shall do exactly as you say.
Aśrubindumatī said: "By this very act, O noble one, I shall become your wife. (11)
Having heard this, O King, the lord of the earth Yayāti, his eyes agitated with joy, married Gāndhārī according to the *dharmya* rite.
O best of men, he married that auspicious daughter of Manmatha;
together with her, the high-souled son of Nṛpanandana lived according to his own will.
On the shores of the ocean, in forests and groves, on delightful mountains, and by rivers, he dwelt together with her.
Thus twenty thousand years passed while that lord of the earth, Rāmatera-jarājendra, remained devotedly engaged in youth.
To that high-souled king of kings, Yayāti, Viṣṇu said:
"In this manner, O great king, Yayāti was then deluded by her. (16)
"O high-minded one, for what purpose was this manifestation of pride on the part of Indra?
Sukarman said: "Thus it was, O King, that Yayāti, the lord of the earth, [was the king of the Pippalas]. (17)
In that [city], the innocent youth, through his longing for union, his passion, and his playful dalliance with the daughter of Kāma, knew not day from night. (18)
Once, the beautiful-eyed Dinī spoke to King Yayāti, who was infatuated with her, bowing low, humble, and submissive to her will.
Aśrubindumatī said:
"O Lord of the Earth, fulfill this longing that has arisen within me; perform for me the Aśvamedha, the most excellent of sacrifices, so that my heart's desire may be realized. (20)
The king said: "So be it, O highly fortunate lady! I shall do what is pleasing to you. Having summoned my eldest son, who is free from desire for the enjoyments of kingship," 21.
Summoned, he arrived, bowing his head with devotion; then, joining his palms in reverence, he offered his salutation.
O King, let an order be given to that servant, whose head is bowed in devotion at her feet, so that he may come when summoned.
"What shall I do, O highly fortunate one? I am your servant, bowing before you.
The King said:
"O son, prepare the materials for the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha)."
Having summoned the meritorious twice-born ones, the officiating priests, and the protectors of the earth,
the immensely radiant and supremely righteous Pūru was thus addressed.
He performed everything in its entirety, exactly as instructed by that Great-Souled One;
together with that daughter of Kāma, he received the excellent initiation.
In the sacrificial enclosure of the horse sacrifice, the great king gave various kinds of gifts to the Brahmins, including abundant food and many other offerings. (27)
And especially toward the poor, King Yayāti,
O great king, spoke those words to that lovely-faced woman.
"O foolish girl, tell me what else is dear to you;
I shall do all of that, whether it be possible or impossible, O lovely-faced goddess. (29)
Sukarmā said:
Having been addressed thus by that king, she spoke to the monarch:
"O King, a great aversion has arisen within me; therefore, O sinless one, do that for me. (30)
O great king, I desire to behold the beloved worlds of Indra, Brahmā, Śiva, and likewise the world of Viṣṇu. (31)
"O illustrious one, show yourself to me, for I am very dear to you.
Having been addressed thus by her, the king spoke to that Supriyā.
"Excellent, excellent, O lady of noble form! You speak only of merit, yet out of feminine nature, fickleness, and curiosity, O fair-faced one. (33)
O highly fortunate one, that which you have described as impossible appears to me;
yet it can be accomplished through the gift of merit, through sacrifice, and also through austerity. (34)
O fair-faced one, that which you have described as achievable would otherwise be unachievable; yet what has been spoken by you is mixed with merit and thus becomes possible. (35)
Even with this very body from the world of mortals,
that man who has heard [this] or seen [it], having performed great merit, has gone to heaven even today.
"Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, that which you have spoken to me is impossible to accomplish. I shall do something else that is dear to you; tell me that, O beloved. (37)
The Goddess said: "O King, there is no doubt that this would be impossible for other men;
O Great King, it is achievable by you—I tell you the truth, the absolute truth. (38)
O Lord of the Earth, through asceticism, fame, Vedic learning, gifts, and sacrifices, there is no other mortal man in the world of mortals who is like you. (39)
The power of the kṣatriya and great splendor—all this is established in you.
Therefore, O son of Nahuṣa, you must act in this way for my sake. 40.

Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Parents," within the narrative of Yayāti, in the *Evenopākhyāna* section of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The eightieth chapter.
Pippala said:
O best of the twice-born, when the king married Kāmakanyā, [he...]
What did those two very virtuous former wives do then?
The highly fortunate Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan—
tell me all of their history before me.
Sukarmā said: When that king brought the maiden Kāmakanyā to his own home,
the high-minded Devayānī vied with her excessively.
When her purpose was thus thwarted, she, her soul agitated by anger, cursed the two sons;
then the illustrious lady summoned Śarmiṣṭhā and raised a cry.
In beauty, splendor, and in their acquisitions, as well as in truth, merit, and vows,
Śarmiṣṭhā used to vie with Devayānī and with me.
She also perceived their wicked disposition born of lust;
at that very moment, she related everything to the king here.
Then, O great king, the enraged monarch summoned Yadu and said:
"Śarmiṣṭhā has incurred the death penalty, yet she is the daughter of Śukra. ||7||
"If you consider Supriyaṅkura alone to be the most excellent, then listen to these words of your father. Thus did Yadu hear his father's speech at that time.
He replied to that lord of kings, his father, who was bestowing honor upon him:
"I shall not cause the death of my mother, who is free from fault. (9)
"The killing of one's mother is said by the scholars of the Vedas to be a great transgression;
therefore, O Great King, I shall not carry out the execution of these two. (10)
O Great King, when she becomes smeared with a thousand faults,
she is likewise [regarded as] a sister and a daughter.
She must never be killed by sons or even by brothers;
knowing this, O Great King, do not cause these mothers to be slain.
Having heard those words of Yadu, King Yayāti, the lord of the earth, became enraged;
he then cursed his son. (13)

Since you have been struck down by my command even now, though you were once a sinner, you must nevertheless resort to the protection of your mother, even though you have been defiled by my curse. 14.
Having spoken thus to his son Yadu, Yayāti, the lord of the earth,
that highly illustrious great king, having cursed his son, [departed] together with her.
Intent on the meditation of Viṣṇu, she enjoyed the pleasures of delight;
and that beautiful-eyed woman, Matī, shed tears along with him.
He enjoyed meritorious pleasures that were agreeable to his mind, with all his limbs beautiful;
in this manner, time passed for that high-souled Yayāti. (17)
All other beings were likewise free from decay and old age;
O highly fortunate one, all the worlds were solely devoted to meditation upon Viṣṇu. (18)
O Pippala, through austerity, truthfulness, and meditation upon Viṣṇu, all the worlds, O highly fortunate one, shall become happy and devoted to the virtuous. (19)
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sacred Site of Parents," within the Narrative of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 80 ||
The eighty-first chapter.
Sukarman said:
"O highly wise one, just as Indra was always afraid of that great-souled one..."
Having observed Yayāti’s prowess, as well as his great generosity, merit, and other virtues.
He dispatched the Apsaras Menakā on a mission as a messenger:
"Go, auspicious and highly fortunate one, and deliver this command of mine. (2)
"Go to Amita, the daughter of Kāma, and speak the words of the king of the gods: 'By whatever means possible, you must bring the king here.'"
Having heard this, Menakā, sent by her out of shame,
arrived and related everything that the king of the gods had said.
Thus addressed, Menakā departed; having been urged by him, the high-minded daughter of Tura went away once Menakā had left. (5)
The illustrious lady addressed King Dharmasaṅketa:
"O King, in the past, I was brought here by you through a false word."
"O King, you have crossed over your own hand and brought your home under control; whatever I say, that indeed must be done by you. (7)
Therefore, O hero, having abandoned this speech uttered by you, I shall leave you and go to the realm of my father. (8)
The king said:
"O auspicious lady, I shall undoubtedly do for you what you have said;
however, O Goddess, having abandoned that which is impossible, tell me that which is possible."
Aśrubindumati said:
"It was for this purpose that you, endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed of all virtues, came here, O Great King. (10)
Knowing that everything is to be accomplished, and [knowing Him] as the sustainer of all, the agent of all dharmas, and the creator of meritorious deeds; ||11||
Knowing him to be the achiever of the three worlds and indeed peerless in the three worlds, I recognize him as a devotee of Viṣṇu, the greatest among the Vaiṣṇavas. (12)
"Because of such an intention, you were not accepted as my husband in the past;
however, he who possesses the grace of Viṣṇu may wander everywhere. (13)

O King of Kings, that which is difficult to obtain does not exist anywhere in the three worlds, including the mobile and immobile; O you of noble vows, it is found within all the worlds belonging to you.
And by the grace of Viṣṇu alone, O lord of the earth, you attained supreme movement through the sky after reaching the world of mortals. 15.
O bull among men, all mortals were rendered free from old age and grey hair, and even devoid of death, at the doors of every house. (16)
You alone have fashioned many wish-fulfilling trees (kalpadruma) for those mortals in whose homes there are sages and wish-cows (kāmadhenu). (17)
O King, it was by you alone that they were sent forth; by you they have been made steadfast and well-established. By you, O Mānava, all men have been rendered happy with every object of desire. (18)
In the midst of a single house, a thousand noble lineages are seen;
in this way, the increase of your own lineage has been brought about by you among men. 19.
O best of men, by opposing even Yama and Indra, you have made the world of mortals free from disease and sin. (20)
By your own splendor and through your ego, you have shown that the surface of the earth is like heaven; O great king, there is no monarch equal to you.
Indeed, no one has ever been born nor will there ever be born like you;
I know you, Bhava, to be the illuminator of all dharmas.
Therefore, you have been made my husband by me; speak thus before me!
Having spoken in jest, O King of Men, speak the truth before me. (23)
O lord of men, if truth exists here and dharma exists here, then let there be for me this supreme movement through the sky among the worlds of the gods. (24)
If you do not go to heaven by abandoning the truth, then your word will undoubtedly become false; of this there is no doubt. (25)
"For that which was previously done will surely turn to ashes, even if it were for one's own welfare.
The King said:
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth; however, I do not possess the power to accomplish what is impossible."
O Lord of the World, by my great grace, everything that is to be accomplished shall become a beautiful world;
hear now the single cause for this, O Goddess, which leads to heaven. 27.
O lady with the beautiful countenance, when the gods in the mortal world have come, then all humans and all creatures shall belong to me. (28)
They will be joined with death, for they are devoid of me; of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, I do not desire to go to heaven; this is the truth I have spoken. (29)
The Goddess said:
"O Great King, having seen the worlds, you shall indeed return again;
fulfill today my very great and intense longing."
The king said:
"I shall do everything exactly as you have said, without a doubt.
Having thus spoken, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, possessed of great splendor, looked upon [him]. (31)
Having spoken thus to his beloved, the king then reflected:
"Even a fish dwelling in the water within the lake is caught by a net."
Even a deer, though possessing a speed equal to the Maruts, falls into captivity;
likewise, a bird spies out its prey even when it lies a thousand yojanas away.
Deluded by fate, one may not perceive the noose already ensnaring one's own neck;
Time makes all things equal or unequal, and Time is that which destroys honor.
Time is a scorner that dwells everywhere;
it makes the giver a beggar, and the beggar, in turn, a giver. (35)
Time calculates all beings, whether stationary or moving, whether in heaven, in the air, or on earth;
for Time alone is this entire world. 36.
The supreme cause of the world is the element (dhātu) without beginning or end;
Time cooks the worlds like fruit placed within a vessel. (37)
O lords of men, even those who are protectors, ascetics, givers, kinsmen, friends, and relatives are unable to rescue a person afflicted by time (death). 38.
There are three snares created by Time that can be overcome by him:
marriage, birth, and death—whenever and wherever they may occur. (39)
Just as clouds in the sky are driven about by the wind, so too is this world driven about by time joined with karma. 40.
Sukarman said:
This time, conjoined with karma, is that which is worshipped by men;
yet it is time that impels karma, and that time is what acts.
Calamities, injuries, defects, serpents, and diseases—all these, being appointed by karma, roam among human beings. (42)
Furthermore, those means which are the causes of happiness and are mixed with merit—all those should be seen as being joined with karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (43)
In this world, the karmas of those who are heirs to their own actions are bound to them;
these very karmas impel the person here toward pleasure and pain. (44)
Just as gold or silver is fashioned into whatever form is determined,
so too is a living being bound by its own karma, following its own destiny.
These five are emitted here for the embodied being while still in the womb:
lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and death itself. (46)
Just as a maker fashions from a lump of clay whatever he desires, so does previously performed karma follow after the doer. //47//
