Divinity, humanity, the state of a beast, likewise that of a bird,
the condition of an animal, and even the state of an immobile being— all these are attained through one's own actions.
He alone experiences that accordingly, as it was always ordained by himself:
the suffering ordained by himself, and the happiness ordained by himself. (49)
From the time they take up their bed in the womb, they experience the results of their previous bodies;
yet on this earth, men never abandon their own karma.
Neither by strength nor even by wisdom are they able to alter [their fate];
they experience the fruits of their good deeds, whether they be suffering or happiness. (51)
Having encountered a cause, a human being is constantly bound by the fetters of karma,
just as a calf seeks out its mother among a thousand cows.
In the same way, it follows the doer of both auspicious and inauspicious karma;
for that which is not subject to experience, there is no destruction whatsoever. (53)
One may indeed alter past karma, which is a bond;
however, that [karma] pursues its ordained course even if one runs very swiftly. (54)
It lies down with him as he lies down, according to his past actions;
it stands near him when he stands, and it follows him when he goes.
As one performs an action, its shadow follows;
just as shadow and sunlight are always closely bound to one another. (56)
In the same way, the doer of karma and the karmic wheel are mutually bound;
likewise are the planets, diseases, poisons, serpents, śākinīs, and rākṣasas.
They afflict a person later on, who has already been afflicted by his past karma;
for wherever one must experience the fruit—whether it be happiness or indeed suffering—it must be experienced there. (58)
Bound by the rope of fate, one is led away by force;
for destiny is the master over all beings in the production of happiness and suffering. (59)
O wise one, an action intended in one way by one who is awake or even asleep may turn out otherwise;
thus does destiny seek to destroy.
That which is to be protected from weapons, fire, poison, and difficult terrains protects itself;
that which is unprotected remains truly so, for it is thus protected by destiny.
But that which is destroyed by fate, no protection is seen for it;
just as seeds sown upon the earth and riches [perish]. (62)
In the same way, actions abide within the self and manifest from it; yet, just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted, [the self is extinguished when karma is spent]. ||63||
Just as one attains the destruction of the body through the exhaustion of karma, so too is death declared by the knowers of reality to result from the exhaustion of karma. (64)
Various living beings, death, and diseases are its causes;
likewise, this ripening of my own [karma] is due to what was done previously, and not otherwise. (65)
"He has arrived; there is no doubt about this. He is in female form, of this there is no uncertainty. Where is the house? O actors, dancers, and performers, why have you come? (66)
Through the consequence of association with them, old age has taken refuge in my body;
I consider it certain that everything performed by me is now rendered futile.
Therefore, karma is primary and expedients are useless;
formerly, for my sake, the best of messengers was sent by the King of the Gods.
Mātali was sent by him; his words have been fulfilled.
This ripening of his karma is now seen clearly before me. (69)
Thinking thus, overcome by great sorrow, he reflected:
"If I do not carry out this serpent's word with affection, it will surely happen in every way. (70)
Both truth and dharma will undoubtedly follow him;
what I have seen through my own experience is consistent with this.
"The body will surely perish, for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having become thus absorbed in reflection, Yayāti, the lord of the earth, [proceeded].
He went for refuge to Lord Hari, the dark-hued god who removes afflictions;
having meditated upon, bowed to, and then praised Madhusūdana with his mind.
Save me, O beloved of Kamalā; I have come to you for refuge.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Story of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||81||
The eighty-second chapter.
Sukarman said:
While the most righteous king was reflecting in this manner, [the following occurred].
Then that goddess, the daughter of Rati, of beautiful countenance, spoke.
"Why do you reflect thus, O King of great intelligence?
Generally, all women are fickle; of this there is no doubt. (2)
"O best of kings, it is not out of fickleness that I am disturbing you; nor do I cause this hiccup today by your side. (3)
O Indra among the kings of kings, just as other women in the world speak out of fickleness, they utter improper words out of greed and delusion, like shifting cloths.
I was born for the very purpose of showing the worlds;
the sight of the gods is meritorious and indeed difficult for mortals to obtain. (5)
O King, tell me to have them brought before you, so that whatever fault or evil deed might arise here from association with me may be addressed. (6)
You should contemplate suffering in this way, just as an ordinary person does:
like one terrified by a great danger, or like one who has fallen into a pit of delusion. (7)
"O great king, abandon that anxiety; you must go to heaven. Whatever causes suffering to arise, that I shall never do. (8)
Thus addressed by the king, he spoke to that fair-faced lady:
"O Goddess, hear that which has been contemplated by me; indeed, it is for your sake. (9)
O beloved, the shattering of my pride was not seen by me;
for when I have gone to heaven, what concern will you have for your subjects and the rest? (10)
"This evil-minded one will terrify the subjects with various diseases;
O fair-faced one, I shall go to the heavenly world together with you."
Having spoken thus, he summoned his eldest son,
Pūru— the knower of all dharma, possessed of great intelligence, and already burdened with old age.
Come, come, O knower of all dharmas; you know the Dharma with certainty.
By my command, O soul of Dharma, the Dharma has been perfectly protected by you. (13)
"O father, let old age be given away and let youth be taken back;
you rule this kingdom of mine, complete with its treasury, army, and vehicles. (14)
"O highly fortunate one, enjoy the earth filled with jewels, extending as far as the ocean, together with its villages, forests, and cities, given by me. (15)
O sinless one, the protection of subjects must always be performed as a meritorious act; there must be constant punishment of the wicked and the thorough protection of the virtuous. (16)
O highly fortunate one, you must perform [this] according to the authority of the sacred scriptures of the True Dharma, and by means of the rites and duties prescribed for Brahmins. (17)
Protection must be performed with devotion, for he is the one to be worshiped in the three worlds;
O wise one, behold the treasury within the fifth and seventh [sections] of the day. 18.
The army must always be honored with gifts, wealth, and food; let your eyes be your spies, and be constantly devoted to giving. (19)
"O son, this existence is unstable; even the most wise Gopas have always trembled before it. Therefore, make yourself self-controlled and do not go hunting. (20)
O you who possess great strength through the power of women, trust should not be placed in anyone;
however, you must gather all the various types of vessels and the digits of the lunar phases. 21.
By performing sacrifices with various *yajñas*, O Hṛṣīkeśa, may you always become a meritorious soul;
day after day, crush all the thorns that afflict the subjects. 22.
Day after day, entrust all the desires of the subjects to you both;
the welfare of the subjects must be ensured, so nourish the people, my son. (23)

One should always act for one's own welfare; do not set your mind on the wives of others, nor ever harbor evil thoughts regarding the property of others, but always follow the path of your ancestors. 24.
Always perform the recitation of the Vedas and likewise that of all the scriptures; O child, remain thus forever devoted to the practice of the sacred texts.
Being content, always remain devoted to your calf, your own bed,
the practice of elephants, horses, and the art of archery.
Having thus greeted his son with blessings,
he placed his own weapon into his hand and set it before him.
Having taken his own old age and given his youth to him,
King Yayāti, desiring to go to heaven, then departed.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Places of Mother and Father" within the Legend of Yayāti, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The eighty-third chapter. Sukarman said:
Having summoned all the subjects from the various continents, the lord of the earth [spoke].
Overcome with great joy, he spoke these words.
The world of Indra, the world of Brahmā, the world of Rudra beyond that, and the world of Viṣṇu which destroys all sins and grants the ultimate goal to living beings. ||2||
"O best of beings, I shall depart; this body will not exist without Anayā.
O Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, she is my progeny. (3)
"You must remain on this earth together with your families even at the cost of some hardship;
this highly fortunate Pūru shall be your protector here."
"The fearless King Alokārāja has been established by me together with his staff.
When this was said, all those subjects, having offered their praise, spoke to the king. (5)
O best of kings, it is heard in all the Vedas and Purāṇas that such was the dharma; for by whom indeed has it ever been seen otherwise in the past?
We have seen this Dharmadaśāṅga, who is dear to the truth,
born in the great house of Nahuṣa within the Lunar dynasty.
Endowed with hands, feet, and a face, he is the practitioner of all proper conduct; perfected in both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom, he is a great treasury of merits. ||8||
He is a mine of virtues, a great king of snow-mountains, and a scholar of truth;
those of great majesty perform the great dharma and possess the power of truth. ||9||
We have seen that Dharma, we have seen that Bhava, who possesses the form of desire;
we have seen that Bhava, the creator of desire, such a speaker of truth. ||10||
We are unable to abandon even these three kinds of actions;
wherever you go, there we shall go, for it will be full of great happiness and merit. (11)
We shall undoubtedly be born in hell elsewhere;
what is the use of wives, wealth, enjoyments, or even life itself? (12)
O great king, there is no reason here for this [state of affairs] without you;
O lord of kings, we shall go together with you alone, and not otherwise. (13)
Having heard these words of those subjects, the lord of the earth,
filled with great joy, spoke these words to the people.
All those highly meritorious people came along with you;
the king, having mounted his chariot, came together with that maiden Vaikā.
I shall go in a chariot of golden hue, resembling the sun,
while being fanned by chowries and fans, free from all distress.
Shining with that banner of merit,
pure and most exalted, he was like the god Indra, the slayer of Pura, the king of the gods.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, was being praised by sages, gods, and celestial bards, as well as by his subjects. ||18||
Then all the subjects, having approached the lord of men with their vehicles— elephants, horses, chariots, and others— set out as if toward heaven.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other common people—all the worlds were indeed Vaiṣṇavas, devoted solely to the meditation upon Viṣṇu. ||20||
But their banners were white, adorned with golden staffs;
all of them were marked with the conch and the discus, equipped with handles, and provided with flags.
Driven by the wind of their desire, they shone with the brilliance of the expansion of progeny;
all of them wore divine garlands and were adorned with tulasī leaves.
Their limbs were smeared with divine sandalwood paste, they were anointed with divine perfumes,
their beauty was enhanced by divine garments, and they were adorned with divine ornaments.
All the worlds, being of beautiful form, approached the king—
hundreds of thousands of subjects, and hundreds of millions and billions as well.
Thousands upon thousands of people followed him;
they were all devotees of Viṣṇu and performers of meritorious deeds, equal to the king himself. 25.
All were intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu and devoted to the practice of recitation and charity.
Sukarman said:
"Thus they all set forth, filled with great joy. (26)
Having consecrated his son Pūru upon the great kingdom, King Yayāti,
the lord of the earth, then departed for the world of the moon.
Then, by virtue of his splendor, merit, righteousness, and austerity,
all those Tejanas set out for the supreme world of Viṣṇu.
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, kinnaras, and cāraṇas,
together with the king of the gods, arrived at his presence.
While that very lord of men was being honored, O best of kings, Indra said:
"Welcome to you, O great king; enter my abode."
"Enjoy here the divine pleasures that follow your heart's desire.
The King said:
"O thousand-eyed one, O highly wise one, [I seek] your pair of lotus feet. (31)
"I pay homage; I am going to the world of Brahmā.
Being praised by the gods, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Then Padmayoni, of great splendor, together with the best of sages,
offered him hospitality with water for the feet, respectful offerings, and excellent seats.
"Indeed, you shall go to the world of Viṣṇu by virtue of your own karma. When the Creator had spoken thus, Śiva arrived at his abode. (34)
And Śaṅkara, together with Umā, performed the rites of hospitality for that very lord of kings, and spoke these words to the king: 35.
"O king of kings, you are a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and are very dear to me as well; therefore, O king of kings, dwell in my mind for a long time, just as Yayāti did. (36)
Enjoy all these pleasures, which are difficult for mortals to attain;
O Indra among kings, there is no difference between me and Viṣṇu, of this there is no doubt. (37)
He who exists in the form of Viṣṇu is undoubtedly Rudra;
O King, he who is known as Rudra is the eternal Viṣṇu. (38)
There is no intermediate state between these two; therefore, I declare this:
I grant a place of merit specifically for the devotee of Viṣṇu. (39)
"Therefore, O great king, you must remain here, O sinless one.
Having been addressed thus by Śiva, Yayāti, the beloved of Hari, departed.
Having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods, the Supporter (Dhara) said:
"O Mahādeva, all this has been spoken by you here in its entirety. (41)
There is no difference between you two; the one form of Kāma has become twofold.
I desire the Vaiṣṇava limb, and I bow at your feet. 42.
"So be it," said the great king; "go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus commanded by Śiva, the lord of the earth set forth. 43.
Then, by those great meritorious Vaiṣṇavas, beloved of Viṣṇu, who were dancing before that king, the lord of the earth [was delighted]. 44.
Honored by excellent bards with the sounds of conchs that destroy great sins and with abundant lion-roars,
the king proceeded amidst those resonant noises.
While being sung to with melodious voices by reciters learned in the scriptures,
the Gandharvas, devoted to song, sing before him.
Being praised by the sages and accompanied by hosts of gods, the son of Duṣyanta was attended by beautiful apsaras. 47.
By Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas of auspicious merit;
by Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, O King, as well as by Maruts and Vasus. ||48||
Then, O Great King, he was praised simultaneously by the Rudras, the hosts of Ādityas, the world-protectors, and the lords of the directions throughout the three worlds.
O King, he beheld the incomparable and painless realm of Viṣṇu,
filled with golden celestial chariots that eclipsed all other splendors.
I see it adorned with swan-like palaces of pure white, shining with celestial chariots, and with hundred-storied mansions resembling the peaks of Mount Meru. ||51||
That most excellent city shines with peaks that scrape the celestial vaults and are adorned with banners,
and with brilliantly blazing finials.
Like the sky illuminated by the hosts of stars, he shines with the splendor of his radiance;
with the blazing flames of his brilliance, he gazes as if with eyes. (53)
The world of Hari, as if with its various jewels that were its smiling teeth,
seemed to call out to those meritorious Vaiṣṇavas who are dear to Viṣṇu.
With their beautiful sprouts—the tips of the banners—moving as if by the pretext of being flags, and with those charming banner-tops swaying in the wind; ||55||
It was adorned everywhere with golden staffs and bells,
and further embellished with gate-towers and watchtowers that radiated the brilliance of the sun.
With windows, lattices, and charming balconies;
with the illumination of main streets and ramparts fashioned of gold.
With gateways adorned with beautiful banners, auspicious sounds of various kinds,
and the tips of jars possessing a radiance like that of the sun and moon.
With excellent palaces having a hundred stories, resembling clouds and free from dust, crowded with staffs and umbrellas, and adorned with water-pots; ||59||
With those jars, adorned with lotuses and filled with wine, the earth shone like the sky graced by the constellations during the rainy season.
With staffs, nets, and banners possessing a luster like that of a constellation of bears,
and with such things having the appearance of crystal, the radiance was like that of a conch or the moon.
Then, with golden palaces crowded together and made of various minerals,
there were celestial chariots numbering in the hundreds of billions and tens of millions.
The city of Hari shines as if endowed with all enjoyments by those who have propitiated the Lord who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
By his grace, those men dwell in his houses,
which are all meritorious, divine, and rich in enjoyments.
The Vaiṣṇavas, performers of meritorious deeds whose every impurity has been washed away,
adorned that temple of Viṣṇu with such auspicious dwellings.
It was filled with various trees and adorned with groves beautified by sandalwood; O King, it was everywhere decorated with trees that bear fruits fulfilling all desires.
It was adorned with step-wells, ponds, and lakes graced by cranes,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and beautified by white water-lilies.
It shines with hundred-petaled great lotuses, adorned with red and blue lotuses,
and with lakes possessing the hue of golden lotuses.
Vaikuṇṭha is enriched with every splendor, adorned with celestial gardens,
filled with divine beauty, and graced by the devotees of Viṣṇu.
O King, Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, beheld Vaikuṇṭha, the unsurpassed abode of liberation,
crowded with hosts of gods.
He entered the beautiful city, which was entirely free from fire;
there he beheld Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of all afflictions and free from disease.
He was graced by celestial chariots, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing yellow garments, the Lord of the World, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and possessed of great splendor.
Mounted upon Vainateya, endowed with Śrī, and higher than the highest,
the Supreme Lord is the means of union for all the worlds of the gods.
Hari shines forth in his supreme form as absolute liberation, being served by great worlds and by most meritorious Vaiṣṇavas. 74.
[They beheld] Hari, the Great-Souled One, who is crowded with hosts of gods, attended by throngs of gandharvas, and surrounded by apsarases; he is the remover of suffering and affliction. (75)
Then the king, together with his queen, bowed down to Nārāyaṇa;
all the human beings there, being devotees of Viṣṇu, prostrated before Madhusūdana.
O high-minded one, as soon as he had departed, all the Vaiṣṇavas bowed with devotion at his pair of lotus feet, O high-minded one.
To that high-souled king of radiant splendor who was bowing down, Hṛṣīkeśa said: "O you of excellent vows, I am pleased with you."
"O great-minded one, you are my devotee; whatever is in your heart, O King of the best of those who grant boons, that I shall give to you without doubt. (79)
The king said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Madhusūdana, if you are pleased with me, then grant me the state of being your eternal servant, O Lord of the universe. (80)
Viṣṇu said: "So be it, O highly fortunate one; you are my devotee, there is no doubt. O great king, you must remain in this world together with her."
Thus addressed, the great king Yayāti, lord of the earth,
by the grace of that god, attained the perfected realm of Viṣṇu.
This king dwells in the supreme realm of Viṣṇu. ||83||

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Ascent of Yayāti to Heaven," within the *Yayāti-carita*, the description of the *Pitṛ-tīrtha* (ancestral pilgrimage site), in the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*. || 83 ||
The eighty-fourth chapter.
Sukarman said:
"I have related all of this to you, a life-story that destroys sin."
It is divine, the savior of sons, and the bestower of great merit. ||1||
In this world, the conduct of Yayāti is seen directly and heard by tradition;
Pūru obtained a great kingdom, while Turu fell into a miserable state.
By the grace of his father and through his own wrath, he restored them to their original state;
it was a meritorious act that saved his sons, bringing him fame and bestowing wealth and grain.
These two words, "śāpa" (curse) and "yukta" (joined), are indeed very difficult to endure;
yet there is nothing equal to father and mother that bestows desired fruits. 4.
If a father should call out to his son with a longing heart, and a mother likewise calls "Son!
Son! to her child, hear now the fruit of that merit.
He who, summoned like a son,
goes toward his mother with a heart filled with great joy, shall obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
O son, that person of great fame who performs the washing of their feet enjoys the fruit of all sacred bathing places (tīrthas) by the grace of those two.
A son who supports his guru with food, clothing, and baths obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) and other benefits beyond the mere carrying of his limbs.
Merit equal to the gift of the earth arises through that son;
likewise, the mother is no different from the Gaṅgā, who embodies all sacred fords—of this there is no doubt. (9)
Just as the ocean, consisting of abundant merit, is established in this world, so too do the ancient poets know the father [the Purāṇa] to be in this world. 10.
Sukarman said:
He who curses or reviles his father or mother, along with his sons, goes to the hell named Raurava; of this there is no doubt. (11)
If a householder, even one who has sons, does not support his mother, father, or elders, he will certainly go to hell and experience intense suffering. ||12||
A son of wicked mind who reviles his preceptor is a doer of evil;
no atonement for such an act has ever been seen by the wise poets of the Purāṇas. (13)
Knowing this, O Brahmin, I worship my mother and father every single day, constantly bowing with devotion while supporting them. (14)
"O Pippala, having summoned me, my guru said, 'Tell me what ought to be done and what ought not to be done'; I perform that without hesitation according to my own power."
By them, that supreme knowledge which bestows the [true] goal has been fully realized;
yet, by the grace of these two, one continues to wander in saṃsāra. ||16||
Whatever men dwelling on earth perform,
I, as a householder, shall know it, and how it proceeds in heaven.
O Pippala, I know the means of treatment even while staying here for the sake of the Nāgas;
and by the grace of these two, the three worlds have come under my control. (18)
The best of the Vidyādharas departed to worship Mādhava.
Viṣṇu said: "Thus urged by him, Pippala performed his own duty. (19)
O King, though he was ashamed, that best of the twice-born went to heaven after being bowed down; and Sukarman, whose nature was righteous, continued to serve his guru.
All this concerning the ancestral pilgrimage sites has been narrated to you by me;
O high-minded one, I shall now speak further regarding the Vadava fire.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Pilgrimage Site of Mother and Father," in the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Eighty-Five.
Vena said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, by your grace toward me..."
The Bhāryātīrtha is proclaimed as the unsurpassed Pitṛtīrtha. ||1||
Mātṛtīrtha bestows great merit upon Hṛṣīkeśa;
having become gracious and well-disposed, please speak of Gurutīrtha.
The Blessed Lord said:
O King, I shall describe the unsurpassed Gurus Tīrtha, which is declared to remove all sins and grant the supreme goal to disciples. (3)
It is the supreme merit for disciples, the eternal embodiment of Dharma, the highest sacred ford, and the supreme knowledge that bestows perceptible fruit. ||4||
O King of kings, by whose grace one enjoys the fruit even in this world, and in the next world enjoys happiness and attains glory and fame. ||5||
O Indra among kings, through the grace of this high-souled Guru,
the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are perceived directly by his disciples.
O King, by understanding the worldly dealings and the conduct of people,
a disciple attains discernment and indeed proceeds toward liberation.
Just as the sun is the illuminator of all the worlds, so too is the Guru the illuminator; he is the supreme refuge for his disciples. (8)
O best of kings, King Soma shines only at night;
by his splendor, he accomplishes all authority over the world of moving and unmoving beings.
O best of kings, a lamp placed in a house illuminates the entire assembly and, by its brilliance, destroys all the dense darkness that obscures it. (10)
O high-minded one, the guru illuminates the disciple who is enveloped by the darkness of ignorance through instructions that shine with the light of the disciple’s own awakening. (11)
The sun is the illuminator by day, the moon is the illuminator by night, and the lamp is always the illuminator of the house and the destroyer of darkness. 12.
Whether by night or by day, the Guru always [removes] that darkness called ignorance from his disciple; indeed, the Guru shall destroy it all. 13.
Therefore, O lord of the earth, the guru is the supreme sacred ford for disciples;
knowing this, the disciple should always worship him. (14)
"Knowing the Guru to be composed of merit, one should serve him through all three kinds of action;
in this regard, O Brahmin, an ancient historical account (itihāsa) is heard. (15)
It is declared to be the remover of all sins, belonging to the high-souled Cyavana;
that best of sages, Cyavana, was born in the lineage of Bhṛgu. 16.
O best of kings, a thought arose in him once:
"When, indeed, shall I become endowed with knowledge upon this earth? (17)
Seeking knowledge, that best of sages reflected thus day and night;
as he was reflecting in this manner, the thought occurred to that high-souled one: ||18||
"I shall set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords that bestows desired fruits, having renounced my home, fields, and so forth, as well as my wife, son, and wealth. (19)
At that time, O King, while wandering the earth on the occasion of a pilgrimage to sacred fords,
he performed a pilgrimage following the course of the Gaṅgā from its source down to its mouth.
The lord of sages [performed this] for the Satadru, the Narmadā, and the Sarasvatī,
as well as for all rivers such as the Godāvarī and for the ocean.
O best of kings, under the pretext of pilgrimage, he wandered to all other holy fords, sacred fields, deities, and meritorious lingas.
As he wandered through those most excellent holy places,
his body became pure, possessing a radiance equal to the splendor of the sun.
Then Cyavana, his soul purified by that deed and shining with splendor,
arrived while wandering at that most excellent of sacred fields.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā, he beheld the great liṅga named Amarakaṇṭaka, which bestows the supreme goal upon all. ||25||
Having bowed to, praised, and fully worshipped the Great Lord Siddhanātha,
he then beheld Jvāleśvara and also beheld Amareśvara.
Having likewise performed the pilgrimage to Brahmeśa, Aṅkapileśa, and the excellent Mārkaṇḍeśvara, he then arrived at Oṃkāra.
Taking refuge in the cool shade of a banyan tree, which dispels fatigue,
the brahmin Cyavana, son of Bhṛgu, sat down comfortably.
There, he then heard a sound uttered by a bird,
endowed with divine speech and possessed of knowledge and discernment.
There lived a certain parrot who had lived for a very long time;
he was a righteous soul named Kuñjala, accompanied by his wife and four sons. (30)
He indeed had four sons who delighted their father; O lord of kings, I shall recount their names before you. (31)
The eldest was named Ujjvala, the second was Samujjvala, the third was named Vijvala, and the fourth was Kapiñjala. ||32||
Thus, O high-minded one, there were four sons of that meritorious Kuñjala, who were devoted to their father and mother. (33)
They wander through mountain bowers and islands, composed in mind, yet agitated for the sake of food and tormented by hunger. (34)
O best of kings, they pacify the hunger within their own bellies with fruits that yield gentle results and are like nectar, using water as sweet as ambrosia.
"O dear sons, having given ripe mangoes for the sake of food, they diligently place these fruits before their husbands. (36)
For the sake of their mother, those highly fortunate ones, endowed with a state of devotion, being satisfied, produce food, eat it, and recite [the scriptures]. ||37||
There, all of them, delighting in play, sport and enjoy themselves; perceiving that it was the time of twilight, they approached their supreme father. (38)
They arrived, bringing food with great effort for the sake of their preceptor,
while that high-souled brahmin Cyavana looked on.
O high-minded one, all the egg-born birds arrived at their father’s beautiful nest and bowed down to both their father and mother. 40.
Having obtained food from those two, all those excellent sons stood before them; they were addressed by their father and honored by him. ||41||
Then, O King, by the compassionate words of his mother, which were full of affection, and by the cool breeze from her wings, the parents felt great joy.
O King, those two birds then performed a nourishing rite for them,
and with blessings they both greeted their two excellent sons.
And they gave them excellent, nourishing food that was like nectar;
O best of the twice-born, those two indeed felt great joy.
Drinking the pure water arising from ten million sacred fords, they remained in their own abode, happy and with contented minds. 45.
They engaged in a divine, highly meritorious, and sin-destroying conversation.
Viṣṇu said:
"O father, even by the mere water sprinkled from your back, a son has been born who is radiant. (46)
"Where have you been today, my son? What unprecedented thing have you seen or heard there that is meritorious? Tell me that in detail."
Having heard the words of his father Kuñjala, that resplendent one,
bowing with devotion, then spoke to his father.
He prostrated with his head and engaged in a charming conversation.
Ujjvala said:
"O highly fortunate one, I go constantly to Plakṣadvīpa."
O Great-minded One, despite great effort for the sake of food, O Great King, there are many lands on the island of Plakṣa. (50)
The mountains, rivers, gardens, forests, and lakes, as well as the villages and other towns, were filled with joy by their prosperous populations. (51)
Those people dwell there, joyful and content with constant happiness;
they are endowed with the merit of giving and recitation, and possessed of a state of faith. (52)
O great king, in Plakṣadvīpa there was always the virtuous Divodāsa, whose soul was devoted to dharma; his daughter was Anūpamā.
Endowed with virtues and beauty, of excellent character, charming and auspicious, she was renowned as the divine goddess Divyādevī, peerless in form upon the earth. (54)
Beheld by her father, she who was auspicious with the beauty of youth and form—
Cārumaṅgalā— turned back at that very first moment.
Then, seeing the divine daughter of the goddess as if she were the very embodiment of the virtuous, [the sage] thought:
"To whom shall this maiden be given—[to one who is] most excellent and a great soul? (56)
Having become intent on this thought, that best of men,
the lord of the earth, looked about and beheld the king of Rūpadeśa.
Having summoned the high-souled Citrasena, that best of men,
the high-souled one, gave his daughter to the wise Citrasena.
O King, when the time for her marriage had arrived,
Citrasena indeed passed away due to the law of time.
Then the righteous King Divodāsa,
the lord of the earth, summoned excellent brāhmaṇas and questioned them regarding Nṛpanandana.
But at the time of her marriage, Citrasena passed away;
tell me, what kind of destiny will befall her? (61)
The Brahmins said:
"O King, the marriage of this maiden appears to be according to the prescribed rites; yet her husband will meet his death, unless he avoids her company. (62)
Seized by a great mental affliction, O King, he departs after having made a renunciation; it is seen in the treatises on dharma that such a person becomes a wandering mendicant.
The wise perform the marriage of an unmarried maiden until she becomes menstruating;
no other husband is ordained for her [after that]. (64)
A father should perform the marriage according to the prescribed rule; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O King, has the Dharmaśāstra been taught by wise men. (65)
"Let her marriage be performed," said those best of the twice-born;
and the righteous Divodāsa, impelled by the words of the brahmins, [acted accordingly].
O great king, O best of the twice-born, King Dattātreya made an effort for the sake of marriage with the divine lady Divyā. (67)
To that great-souled king Rūpasena, a field of merit,
the lord of the earth, the king, having fallen under the power of death, went to take his bride.
Whenever the lord of the earth and the highly fortunate divine queen both die at the time of their destined end, it always occurs at the moment of the lagna. 69.
O father, twenty-one husbands have died one after another in due course;
thereafter, the king of renowned valor became deeply afflicted by great sorrow. (70)
Having deliberated and summoned the three ministers—who were equal to themselves—the lord of the earth himself chose the one of great intelligence as his counselor. (71)
The kings of Plakṣadvīpa were summoned by that high-souled one;
likewise, those devoted to dharma were summoned for the sake of choosing a husband for themselves.
Infatuated by her beauty, the foolish kings, urged on by Death, engaged in battle; they perished upon the field of combat. (73)
Thus, O father, the destruction of the high-souled Kṣatriyas has occurred;
Divyā, afflicted by great sorrow, has come to this forest. (74)
The noble lady, the daughter of the gods, wept piteously like a child;
thus she spoke there to her father regarding this unprecedented and unseen event.
Therefore, O father, tell me that matter in full detail.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Episode of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Bhūmi-khaṇḍa" in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||85||
The eighty-sixth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
O child, I shall describe to you the divine deeds of that goddess.
Listen as I recount everything performed in my previous births.
There is a meritorious city named Vārāṇasī, which destroys all sins;
in it dwells one of great wisdom, known by the name Suvīra.
Born into the Vaiśya caste, he was well-stocked with wealth and grain;
his wife was highly wise and very famous by the name Citrā. (3)
Abandoning the family tradition, she conducts herself with improper behavior; she does not respect her husband and acts according to her own wilful impulses.
Devoid of merit from the Dharma, she would practice only evil; she would constantly revile her husband and always delight in quarreling. (5)
She constantly wanders from house to house, dwelling in the homes of others;
she always observes the faults of others and is ever malicious toward living beings.
Knowing her to be wicked, always laughing at the virtuous,
a demoness of improper conduct and great sin, she was struck down by the Hero.
Having abandoned the virtuous, that man of great wisdom and vast intelligence married the daughter of another Vaiśya; with her, he lived together.
A virtuous soul who always practices the conduct of Dharma and whose mind is fixed on truth and righteousness wanders the earth,
having cast off various and fierce sins.
Then she, whose resolve was fixed on sin, performed the work of a messenger for those wicked men who were always in the company of evildoers.
Then that evildoer caused the ruin of the household of the virtuous;
she summoned a chaste woman and enticed her with wicked words.
Furthermore, he brought about the destruction of the Dharma with words that created conviction;
he would bestow upon another the various wives of virtuous men. (12)
Thus, having ruined a hundred households through her resolve for sin,
that most wicked woman instigated a battle with her husband and sons.
He agitated the minds of wicked men toward women and instigated a war that increased the population of Yama’s realm.
Having thus destroyed a hundred houses, she subsequently met her death;
she was punished with many severe penalties by King Amarāja, O Sudhanvan.
The son of Taraṇi fed the inhabitants of the terrible hells, Raurava and Sunaraka; having cooked them, he displayed various torments in the Raurava hell.
As one performs an action, so does one experience its result;
by Citrā, through her resolve toward evil, a hundred houses were destroyed.
O best of the twice-born, this is the ripening of various past actions that she has experienced;
because a hundred houses were destroyed, therefore she now suffers great misery. (18)
When the time for marriage arrives, fate turns into misfortune;
when the time for marriage has come, the husband meets his death. (19)
Just as a hundred houses may fall into ruin, so too may a hundred dependents die;
yet for oneself, one's son, and one's marriage, twenty-one [generations] are preserved.
I have related to you, O Goddess, all that was asked by you;
thus has been told to you her entire previous history.
Ujjvala said:
"O Divine One, you have previously related the former deeds of the Goddess,
as well as her terrible sin known as the 'Destruction of the House'."
By what power of merit did the daughter of Divodāsa, the king of Plakṣadvīpa, attain such a noble lineage? (23)
O father, tell me this which is my doubt;
explain how it was that the daughter of the king came to have such sinful conduct. (24)
Kuñjala said: I shall relate all the meritorious deeds performed by Citrā;
listen to what was done in former times by Citrā, the mother of Ujjvala. 25.
While wandering about, a certain highly wise Siddha arrived;
he was clad in rags, devoid of fine garments, a renunciant carrying a staff. (26)
Equipped with only a loincloth, using his hands as a bowl, and clad in the directions for clothing, he resorted to the door of a house, taking refuge under the constellation Citrā. ||27||
He was silent, with his head completely shaven, self-conquered, and having mastered his senses;
he was without food, having conquered the need for nourishment, and was a seer of the true meaning of all principles.
Exhausted by the long journey, his mind distressed by the heat, suffering from fatigue and overcome by thirst, O good son. (29)
Taking refuge at the gateway of Citrā and staying there in the shade,
that high-souled one was seen by Citrā and tormented by her.
Out of great wonder, he performed service for that very same Great-Souled One;
having washed his feet, he offered him an excellent seat. (31)
"Please sit upon this very soft seat at your ease;
indeed, let the finest food be eaten for the purpose of dispelling hunger. (32)
"Drink cool water, being content with whatever you desire.
Having spoken thus and acting accordingly, O son, he was honored like a god.
Having made his body his vehicle and being free from fatigue, that great-souled one, addressed by her, O best of the twice-born, ate and drank. (34)
Thus gratified by her, that perfected one who reveals the meaning of reality, being fully satisfied as the soul of all dharmas, remained still for some time. (35)
When that great-souled, highly fortunate perfected one (siddha), a brahmin and great yogi, had departed at his own will according to his destination, [the others followed]. 36.
Having met with a variegated death, she came under the power of her own karma and was punished by Dharmarāja with great torments that cause intense suffering. (37)
Having reached the Sācitra hell, which bestows a multitude of agonizing sensations,
that great king shall experience suffering for a thousand yugas.
Those enjoyments were obtained by that human being upon his rebirth;
for he had previously been honored by her, being a perfected one (siddha) and the best among the meritorious. ||39||
This is the ripening of his karma, which has come upon him in the family of the meritorious, in the house of the great Kṣatriya king Divodāsa. (40)
O best of men, that which was born from her, named Divyādevī, gave food and meritorious drink to that great-souled one. (41)
He enjoys the arising of the great fruit of merit from that gift; he indeed drinks cool water and eats sweet food. (42)
He enjoyed divine pleasures and lived as a lord in the world of the ancestors;
by the power of this perfected being, a princess was born to him.
O lord of the earth, O noble son, due to the influence of her evil karma and the destruction of her home, that divine lady experiences widowhood.
All this, the conduct of Divya and Devī, has been told to you.
What else do you wish me to tell you here that you ask of me? 45.
Ujjvala said:
"Tell me, how is one liberated from sorrow and great suffering?
And what was that young girl like, who was tormented by such great misery? (46)
What kind of happiness is that, and what will its maturation be?
O Father, you ought to sever this doubt of mine immediately. (47)
Tell me how she may obtain liberation and the means for it;
the illustrious lady weeps alone in the great forest. (48)
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard the great words of his son, the highly wise Kuñjala reflected for a moment and replied to his son. 49.
Listen, O highly fortunate one; I shall tell you this truth: having entered that sinful womb arising from past karma, [he remains there]. (50)
O dear son, through contact with this great-souled tree who was striving for liberation, my knowledge as an animal has been destroyed. (51)
By the grace of the Revā and by the grace of Viṣṇu himself, he by whom knowledge is attained returns to the state of liberation. ||52||
I shall proclaim the instruction on the unsurpassed path to liberation,
by which one, freed from impurities, proceeds like gold from fire.
And it becomes pure through association with that child, like the true nature of fire;
so too, O man of great wisdom, [the mind] quickly [becomes pure] through meditation on that Great-Souled Hari. (54)
Through recitation, fire-offerings, and vows, the sin of evildoers goes to destruction;
one should always abandon pride, just as a serpent abandons fear when it encounters the month of Sahas (Kārtika).
By the utterance of Kṛṣṇa’s name, that sin indeed departs,
just as serpents are rendered devoid of poison by the splendor of Vainateya.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin go to destruction, and not otherwise;
by the mere utterance of the name of that wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu), they depart.
When she has become steady and free from desire and anger, she should recite that hundredfold name which is meritorious and destroys heaps of sin. (58)
Having restrained all the senses, one should guard them through self-knowledge;
for her who has entered into meditation, she becomes unified and composed.
She should recite that supreme knowledge; then she goes to liberation when, with her mind fixed on that state, she becomes absorbed in it through the practice of yoga.
Ujjvala said: "O venerable one, speak of the supreme knowledge that is most excellent for me;
afterwards, [speak of] the meritorious vow of meditation and the hundred names right here. (61)
Kuñjala said: I shall proclaim the supreme knowledge which has not been seen by anyone;
listen, my son, to that absolute liberation which is entirely free from impurity.
Sūta said:
O high-minded one, just as a lamp standing in a windless place, motionless and free from air, burns brightly and destroys all darkness; ||63||
In the same way, the self, freed from defects, becomes indeed without support;
like a calf, it is free from desire and stainless—when is it ever an enemy to man? ||64||
There is neither sorrow nor joy, neither greed nor envy;
alone, he is liberated from dejection and exultation, as well as from pleasure and pain.
One should withdraw the senses from all objects;
then, having become solitary, the state of solitude arises.

O King of kings, in connection with the procedure for cauterization (*agnikarma*), one should dry the oil of the lamp by means of a wick-holder, remaining free from attachment and sheltered from the wind. (67)
O Great-minded One, it subsequently vomits soot even from the oil;
O Great-minded One, a black line is seen before the lamp. 68.
Just as oil drawn out by itself becomes pure through its own brilliance,
so too the oil of karma situated within the wick of the body shall be dried up.
Having turned the objects of the senses into collyrium, he should manifest them directly;
having become pure himself, he should illuminate them by his own power.
Completely freed from the winds known as the afflictions, such as anger and the rest,
and having become free from desire and immovable, one shall blaze forth by one's own splendor.
Remaining in his own place, he beholds the entire three worlds by his own splendor;
this one, whose nature is absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), has been described to you by me. (72)
I shall describe his two-fold meditation;
it is perceived by the eye of knowledge in the form of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna). ||73||
That which those great-souled ones, disciplined in yoga and devoted to the supreme truth, behold while free from sleep—that is the austerity which reveals everything. (74)
Though devoid of hands and feet, O son, he moves everywhere;
he grasps the entire triple world, both the stationary and the moving. 75.
O son of the king, though devoid of nose and mouth, he smells;
though without ears, he hears everything—the Lord of the world, the witness of all. (76)
Though formless, he is bound to form; though subject to the power of the fivefold group, he is the life-force of all the world, worshipped by all things moving and stationary.
O son, though tongueless, he spoke everything in accordance with the Vedas and the Shastras; and though skinless, the sensation of touch occurred for all beings. (78)
Always free from the duality of giving and receiving, his soul detached, uniform, and without support; free from decay, devoid of "mine-ness," righteous, possessed of virtues, and stainless. ||79||
He is the inevitable, the self that brings all under control, the giver of all, and the supreme knower of all;
for him there is no creator, and he is the all-pervading Lord who consists of everything.
Thus, he who perceives this meditation consisting of all things belonging to the Great Self goes to the supreme station, which is formless and like unto the immortal.
Now I shall describe the second meditation upon this Great-Souled One, who possesses both form and formlessness, yet is formless and free from all affliction. (82)
The entire incomparable universe is perfumed by His latent impression;
therefore, O Anandana, He is called Vāsudeva by me. 83.
He would have the color of a raining cloud;
he was the Lord of the Gods, possessing four arms and resembling the splendor of the sun. (84)
To the right shines a conch shell adorned with gold and jewels;
the discus has the form of the solar orb and is established upon a lotus. (85)
The Kaumodakī mace, the destroyer of great asuras, shines upon the left hand of that high-souled one, which holds a calf. (86)
The great lotus, fragrant and magnificent, rests in his right hand;
always resplendent and bearing his weapons, he dwells as the beloved of Kamalā.
[He saw] Hṛṣīkeśa, who was shining with teeth resembling jewels, possessing a beautiful neck, a rounded face, and eyes like lotus petals. 88.
O son, he whose hair is like matted locks, whose lower lip has the appearance of coral, and who is adorned with a diadem—Puṇḍarīkākṣa shines resplendently. 89.
Janārdana shone with his vast and most radiant form, O Keśava,
being adorned by the Kaustubha gem itself.
Hari always shines with the auspicious Śrīvatsa mark and with two earrings that radiate light like the splendor of the sun. (91)
With armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and pearls resembling stars, Vijaya, the best among victors, shone resplendently with his body. 92.
That Govinda also shone with a garment of excellent color;
he was resplendent with fingers adorned with jeweled rings. (93)
Hari, the creator of the worlds and lord of the universe, was mounted upon Vainateya and was fully equipped with all divine weapons and celestial ornaments. (94)
Thus, the man who meditates on Him constantly with an undistracted mind is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||95||
All this concerning the meditation on the Lord of the World has been told to you;
now I shall proclaim his vow, which wards off all evil. (96)
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Holy Site of the Guru," within the "Story of Eka" in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
[Verse 86]
(87) The eighty-seventh chapter.
Kuñjala said:
I shall proclaim the various types of vows by which Hari was propitiated;
namely, Jaya, Vijayā, and Jayantī, which destroys sins. (1)
Another was Trispṛśā, and another Julī; likewise there was Atiladagdhā, and the maiden Akhaṇḍācārā, O son of noble mind.
O son, there are many different varieties of Ekādaśī;
others include Aśūnyaśayana and the great vow of Janmāṣṭamī. ||3||
By these vows of great merit, the sin of living beings departs far away; there is no doubt in this matter. I speak the truth, the absolute truth. (4)
Kuñjala said:
I shall proclaim his hymn of praise, which destroys heaps of sin, is known by the name "The Hundred Names of the Good Son," and bestows a supreme goal upon men. (5)
I shall now fully proclaim the supreme hymn consisting of one hundred names of that god Kṛṣṇa; listen to it, O best of sons. (6)
O highly fortunate one, I shall now declare the seer and the meter of this "Hundred Names of Viṣṇu," as well as its deity, which purifies all sins. (7)
For this *Viṣṇu-nāma-śata*, Brahmā is proclaimed as the seer (*ṛṣi*);
Oṃkāra is declared the deity, and likewise the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. (8)
This hymn of one hundred names of Viṣṇu is for application toward the attainment of all desires as well as liberation.
Brahmā-ṛṣi; Viṣṇu is the deity; Anuṣṭubh is the meter.
The application is for the sake of fulfilling all desires and for the sake of the destruction of all evils. ||9||
I bow to Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, Madhusūdana, the destroyer of all the Daityas, Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment. 10.
Victory to Him who brings victory, to Kṛṣṇa, to the Infinite One, and then to Vāmana;
to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, the Meritorious, the Support of the Universe, and the one worshipped by the gods.
The sinless one who destroys sin, the savior, Narasiṃha, the beloved of Śrī;
the Lord of Śrī, the upholder of Śrī, the giver of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the source of great prosperity. ||12||
Śrī Rāma, Mādhava, the one who grants liberation, Kṣamārūpa, Janārdana—the omniscient, the knower of all, the giver of everything, the leader of all. ||13||
Hari, Murāri, Govinda, Padmanābha, Prajāpati;
Ānanda, the one endowed with knowledge, the giver of knowledge, and the leader of knowledge. ||14||

The infallible one, together with Balarāma and Candra, the wielder of the discus, the higher and the lower, the support of the ages, the source of the world, the form of Brahman, the Great Lord. ||15||
To Mukunda, the most excellent, the supreme, the one whose form is singular, the Lord of the universe, the high-souled Vāsudeva, who is devoted to Brahman and dear to the Brāhmaṇas. ||16||

He who is dear to the cows and priyaṅgu plants, the benefactor, the sacrifice itself, the constituent part of sacrifice, the increaser of sacrifice, the excellent enjoyer of the sacrifice, and one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. ||17||
To him who knows the Vedas, whose form is the Veda, the abode of knowledge, the Lord of the gods;
to that unmanifest Great Swan, the ancient one with the conch in his hand. ||18||
To Puruṣa, Puṣkarākṣa, Varāha, Dharaṇīdhara, Pradyumna, Kāmapāla, Vyāsa, Vyāla, and Maheśvara. ||19||
He is all happiness, supreme happiness, liberation, and the Supreme Lord; he is the form of yoga, great wisdom, the beloved who grants grace to yogis. ||20||
To Murāri, the guardian of the world, who holds a lotus in his hand and wields a mace;
who dwells in the cave, who is the abode of all, the dwelling place of merit, and the one of mighty arms. ||21||

I bow to the Lord of the Gopīs, who bestows prosperity, possesses a vast body, is purifying, and destroys all sins; he who has the cowherds as his companions, is the protector of the cows, and is the refuge of the multitude of cattle.
I bow eternally and unwaveringly with my mind, speech, body, and actions to the Supreme Self, the Lord of others, who is beyond the reach of Kapila and other human beings. 23.
Even he who performs great merit and praises Kṛṣṇa with a steady mind by means of even a hundred names,
being purified by his merit, leaves behind these worlds and goes to the realm of Madhusūdana.
One should recite this hundred names, which is of great merit and purifies all sins, with an undistracted mind, while meditating with full concentration. (25)
A person shall always obtain the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā through meritorious deeds; therefore, becoming very steady and with a concentrated mind, one should recite [the mantra]. 26.

If a mortal, remaining self-restrained and established in his observances, recites this at the three times of day, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice arises for him; of this there is no doubt. ||27||
I shall now describe the merit of that mortal who, having fasted on the eleventh day, performs the vigil before Mādhava and recites prayers. (28)
A person who, standing in the presence of Tulasī, recites [the mantra] with a focused mind, obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice. (29)
A person enjoys the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice even within a year where there is a Śālagrāma stone and where there is a Dvārāvatī stone. (30)
One who desires happiness should perform the recitation when both are present;
by doing so, one will enjoy great happiness and indeed a hundred generations of one's lineage.
He who performs the ritual bath during Kārttika and worships Madhusūdana shall, by that single act, deliver even his mortal self along with others.
He who, being self-restrained, recites this hymn attains the supreme goal;
likewise, one who bathes during the month of Māgha and worships Hari, the slayer of Madhu, with devotion [attains the same].
One should meditate upon Hṛṣīkeśa, or recite His name, or even hear it;
thereby, casting off sins such as the drinking of liquor, one attains the supreme state. (34)
A man who, at the time of a śrāddha ceremony, eats before the Brahmins while they are eating, goes to Janārdana without obstacle, accompanied by his sons. (35)
This hymn of one hundred names, which destroys all sins, should be recited;
thereby the ancestors attain satisfaction and, being gratified, reach the supreme goal. (36)
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of the Vedas; a Kṣatriya shall conquer the earth; and a Vaiśya, who always recites [this], shall attain mastery over wealth and prosperity. (37)
The Śūdra enjoys happiness and attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa; having obtained another birth, O child, he masters the knowledge of the Vedas. (38)
This hymn, which bestows happiness and liberation, should be recited without doubt;
by the grace of Keśava, a person shall attain all perfections. (39)

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Description of the Holy Places of the Guru" in the *Evena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The eighty-eighth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
"O good son, [I shall tell you] the vow, the hymn, the great knowledge, and likewise the meditation."
I have thus related before you this account of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins. ||1||
When one thus performs these four meritorious acts with devotion, one indeed goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. ||2||
Having gone there, O Vatsa, awaken the divine goddess;
proclaim to her this king of vows, named Aśūnyaśayana.
I have related to you, as you requested, this merit-bestowing and sin-destroying account of how the illustrious princess was rescued from the great mountain of evil. (4)
"Go, go, O highly fortunate one! Having said this, he became silent.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: "Though thus addressed by his father, Ujjvala was indeed not satisfied with that water. (5)
Having prostrated at the feet of his father and mother, O King, that highly intelligent and radiant one, whose nature was dharma, departed in haste for Plakṣadvīpa.
That mountain was auspicious on all sides and filled with various minerals;
it was adorned with lofty peaks composed of diverse precious gems.
O King, on that best of great mountains there are rivers with clear water, filled with brilliant waters flowing in various currents. (8)
O King, the Kinnaras sing there and the Gandharvas with melodious voices;
it is crowded with Apsarases and surrounded by hosts of gods.
Resounding with the cries of perfected beings and celestial musicians, adorned by throngs of sages,
and made to echo on all sides by the songs of various birds.
Having thus reached the mountain with swift and agile strides,
that girl wept aloud on that mountain with a plaintive voice.
To her who was weeping piteously, he spoke these words with wisdom: "Who are you, O auspicious lady? Why do you weep so bitterly? (12)
O highly fortunate lady, tell me now who has done you this displeasure;
explain to me today the cause of all this suffering.
Divyādevī said: "O illustrious one, this is surely the ripening of my own past actions;
thus I remain here, filled with sorrow and the state of widowhood. (14)
Who are you, O illustrious one, who, out of compassion for me and free from affliction, addresses me with joy while assuming the form of a bird? (15)
Having heard all that spoken by the princess, [he said]:
"O noble lady, I am a bird, distressed by compassion for you. (16)
"Assuming the form of a bird, I am merely a perfected being (siddha) and not a possessor of wisdom;
I beheld you here weeping with loud cries. (17)
Thereupon, O Goddess, I questioned him regarding the sole cause here: what had occurred in my father’s house and indeed my own conduct. (18)
Having heard in brief everything she reported regarding the succession of those who brought misery, I, Ojjvala, became troubled in mind.
The great bird spoke to that divine lady who was deeply distressed:
"Just as at the time of your wedding, your husbands have gone to their death. (20)
On account of the svayaṃvara, those kṣatriyas have met their destruction;
all these deeds of yours have been recounted by me as well. (21)
"O fair-eyed one, my father has compassionately declared before me that this evil karma was committed by you in another birth. (22)
O fair-faced one, she became smeared and nourished by that very fault;
this is the entire reason explained by my father. (23)
"Enjoy, however, the ripening of your past karma, and take heart.
Having heard these words spoken by that radiant youth, she [replied]. (24)
Bowing down with a piteous voice, she replied again to the high-souled bird who was speaking: "O bird of the Kuru race, show me mercy. (25)
Out of your grace, please tell me the expiation for that sin—a most meritorious atonement that purifies even the gravest of transgressions. (26)
O highly fortunate one, by your grace, may I go to that meritorious place where my impurities have been washed away and purified; please grant me this expiation.
Ujjvala said: "O highly fortunate one, for your sake I questioned my father;
therefore, the unsurpassed atonement was explained by my father. (28)
O highly fortunate one, who are like a sprout of reality, meditate upon Hṛṣīkeśa, the purifier of all sins, and recite His hundred names. (29)
The vow of not sleeping on an empty bed is supreme, eternal, and the highest of vows; it is meritorious and the destroyer of sins. (30)
The virtuous-souled one fully explained the knowledge that illuminates all wisdom,
as well as the hymn, the vow, and the meditation upon the great-souled Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu said:
Therefore, she took hold of him while he was staying in the lonely forest;
freed from all duality, she became established in asceticism.
She undertook a vow, abstaining from food, without support, and deeply distressed;
free from desire and anger, she constantly restrained the group of senses.
Having cast off the great delusion of the senses, O Great King, at the arrival of the fourth year, Janārdana became exceedingly gracious toward her. (34)
Desiring to grant him a boon, the Supreme Leader arrived;
the Lord, the bestower of boons, revealed his true form to him. (35)
Sūta said:
[He saw] the Great Lord, dark as a sapphire cloud, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, and holding a lotus in his hand. 36.
With her hands joined in supplication, trembling and without support,
she bowed down and spoke with faltering words to Madhusūdana.
Indeed, I am not able to stand before you due to your divine splendor; become one of divine form—tell me, who are you? Out of compassion for me, appear before me. (38)
"Please tell me out of your grace what the cause here is;
O high-minded one, explain everything to me through your favor. (39)
O Lord of the World, those devoid of knowledge do not recognize You as a god through Your splendor or Your gestures; they know neither Your birth nor Your name. (40)
"Are you indeed Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or perhaps Śaṅkara himself?
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself before him like a staff upon the earth.
To her, who was bowing down, the Lord of the World spoke;
the Blessed One said:
"O beautiful one, there is no difference even among the three gods."
O fair-faced one, by him who has worshipped either Brahmā or Śaṅkara, I am always worshipped; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (43)
This [image] is non-different from me and is also eternal;
for those by whom I am worshipped, these two are likewise well-worshipped. (44)
"I am the god Hṛṣīkeśa; out of compassion for you, I have come here because of this meritorious hymn of praise, as well as your vow and your observance. (45)
O you who are born free from blemish, devoid of inferiority, and possessed of excellent glory!
The divine goddess said:
"Be victorious, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Kṛṣṇa, the remover of afflictions! (46)
I bow to Your two feet; O Lord of the Gods, lift me up!
O Wielder of the Discus and Sword, I desire a boon from You; be gracious to me. 47.
O sinless one, grant devotion even for my pair of feet;
show me, O Lord of the World, the path to liberation that is free from all affliction. 48.

In conjunction with Meghanāda and likewise at the confluence of the Ūru, the Revā is exceedingly meritorious and highly auspicious, being difficult to encounter anywhere. (32)
She is difficult to attain even for the best of gods through human efforts alone at Oṃkāra, Bhṛgukṣetra, the confluence of the Narmadā and Kubjā, and at Māhiṣmatī.
The auspicious Śrīkaṇṭha is at Viṭaṅkāsaṅgama, and Maṅgaleśvara is there;
the Revā, filled with the merit of the gods, is difficult to find everywhere. 34.
The Great Goddess, the Mother of the Tīrtha, who destroys the lower zodiac signs—wherever she is situated between the two banks, there a man is happy. (35)
By a single bath, a human being enjoys the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
All this that was asked by you has been explained to you. (36)
"It removes all sins and bestows merit upon those who hear it.
Having spoken thus, the one of great wisdom addressed his third son. (37)
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the Story of Cyavana in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Ninety-third Chapter.
Kuñjala said: "What unprecedented thing have you seen while wandering the earth, O Vijvala?"
O you of excellent vows, tell me that which is filled with wonder.
"O best of sons, tell me this wonderful thing: why did you, so diligent, come from here to this place of hardship for the sake of food?"
Vijvala said:
On the summit of Mount Meru, there is a forest named Ānanda,
which is always filled with divine trees laden with fruits and flowers.
It was crowded with hosts of gods, accompanied by sages and perfected beings (siddhas),
and filled with beautiful apsaras, gandharvas, kinnaras, and uragas.
With its ponds, wells, and tanks, as well as rivers and springs,
that sacred grove of Ānanda shines with divine splendors.
It resounded with the delightful clamor of songs from tens of millions of celestial palaces, which resembled swans and kumuda lilies, and was filled with the rumbling of clouds.
It resounds everywhere with the humming of bees and is surrounded by sandalwood trees,
mango trees, and flowering campaka trees.
Thus that supreme forest shone with various trees,
filled with the great clamor of the cries of diverse birds.
Thus, O dear one, I beheld that most beautiful lake there;
it was stainless and shone like the ocean. (9)
It was completely filled with meritorious waters, auspicious and fragrant with lotuses;
it was strewn with aquatic flowers and inhabited by swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks.
Thus there was a lake in the very center of that forest,
adorned by throngs of sages and crowded with gods and gandharvas.
Of what avail are humans, nāgas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas?
My father, I cannot describe the wonder that I have seen there. (12)
O best of beings, it is further adorned with a divine celestial chariot, graced by jars,
umbrellas, staffs, and banners.
O observer of excellent vows, he was resplendent as he was being sung to by kinnaras, gandharvas, and apsaras, even while they were overwhelmed by all manner of enjoyments.
Being praised by great siddhas and ṛṣis who know the ultimate reality, he was seen by the world as one whose form was incomparable; such a being had never been seen anywhere before.
His limbs are beautified by the splendor of all ornaments and adorned with divine garlands;
a necklace made of great jewels shines upon his chest. (16)
And standing near him, one woman was seen with a beautiful face, adorned with bracelets and bangles made of gold, pearls, and gems. (17)
Being praised and sung to with divine garments, perfumes, sandalwood, and beautiful ointments, a man arrived there.
She possessed the form of Rati, with broad hips and full breasts;
her limbs were adorned with all ornaments, and she was endowed with such perfection of beauty.
These two, whom I have never seen before, have arrived even by means of a celestial chariot;
they are endowed with beauty, grace, sweetness, and the perfection of all splendor. (20)
Having descended from their celestial chariot,
those two great-souled ones, a man and a woman with lotus-like eyes, approached the edge of the lake and bathed.
Grasping great weapons, they fell upon one another;
both such corpses lay there fallen on the bank of the lake.
Then those two, a man and a woman with beautiful eyes, shone forth;
O highly fortunate one, those two corpses were indeed possessed of such beauty.
Just as a corpse appears like a god to one who is deluded,
so too does that which is beneficial appear in such a form to him there.
Just as was the form of his wife, so too was the second corpse;
having then cut away the flesh from that female corpse with a weapon, he [proceeded]. (25)
The dog devoured those [limbs] of his, drenched in blood;
likewise, the man, overcome with distress, devoured the flesh of that corpse.
Afflicted by hunger, they ate the flesh of those two in that field until they had reached satiety; meanwhile, I was devoured by them.
Having drunk the water of the lake, the two of them became happy and rested;
after staying there for some time, they departed again by means of the celestial chariot.
On another day, he saw two women there who were endowed with beauty and grace,
possessed of auspicious marks, and accompanied by their husbands.
When that flesh has been devoured by those two in the great forest, he will then laugh at them here with loud, boisterous laughter.
And these two constantly devour their own flesh;
for there, while they are performing their ablutions and other rites, they look upon me, who am present there.
O noble one, there was another woman endowed with a fierce form,
her face terrifying with bared fangs, and exceedingly fearsome right there.
Then they both said again and again, "Give it!
Give it! Thus was it seen by me while staying in the vicinity of your forest abode.
One should constantly carve out and consume these two [flesh-masses] and likewise the marrow;
then the bodies of the two corpses will once again become perfectly full and youthful. (34)
"O Nitya and Uttīrṇa, you as well as those others from Pitṛloka perform similar activities as previously described while observing me. (35)
"O father, this wondrous event was seen by me at that time;
O father, you have asked about it, and indeed that wonder has been witnessed by you. (36)
I have explained before you the cause of all doubt; please speak [further] out of your grace, with a pleased mind. (37)
O best of the twice-born, he who has arrived by celestial chariot together with a woman, possessing a divine form and lotus-like eyes—he is Śakra. (38)
A certain woman devours a man of great fortune and great flesh;
then another arrives, O Father, and having approached, he too devours her. (39)
Then he may laugh at them, or they may speak with voices like his own; or they may say to him, "Give! Give! again and again. (40)
"O father, tell me this: who are these two women so exceedingly terrifying?
O you of noble vows, you ought to sever this doubt of mine. (41)
Having spoken thus, the great king, along with the bird, became silent;
he, having been questioned in this manner by his third son, Vijvala.
He related the entire account while Cyavana listened.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the section on the Sacred Site of the Guru, in the *Even-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The ninety-fourth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
"Listen, my son; I shall explain all the reasons for that."
Because they were born with such power that they consumed their own flesh. ||1||
In all cases, wholesome and unwholesome karma is undoubtedly the cause;
through meritorious karma, a man attains happiness and sovereignty over his sons. (2)
One experiences the fruit of evil deeds here through action joined with sin;
thus, one should investigate the subtle path with the eye of knowledge of the scriptures. (3)
Having clearly perceived the gross nature of phenomena and having reflected upon them again and again,
a person should undertake an action with a skillful mind.
Just as a sculptor working with a material might not bring it back to its original state, so too,
by the heat of the fire and subsequently by the flames, the son was not restored.
A metal, when heated gradually by fire, becomes liquefied;
just as the food of a calf, once cooked with oil, is poured [into the mold]. (6)
A calf of such a kind is born, there is no doubt;
for as the action is performed, so it is experienced. (7)
Karma alone is primary, which exists in the form of rain;
it is like the seed that a farmer sows in various fields. (8)
One will surely experience the fruit corresponding exactly to that; there is no doubt.
Whatever kind of action is performed, that very same kind is experienced. (9)
Karma is the cause of destruction for this world; we are all under the power of karma.
Time is the heir to karma, and karma is the kinsman and supporter of all beings. (10)
In this world, karma impels a person toward pleasure and pain,
just as gold or silver is cast into whatever form it takes.
Thus is the embryo infused with heat, following the power of past karma;
these five are perceived here even while the embodied being remains within the womb.
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—
the maker of the body (the Creator) ordains these according to his will, exactly as he desires up until the time of death.
In this way, one encounters the results of one's own actions, whether they lead to divinity, humanity, the state of a beast, or likewise, the state of a bird. (14)
Through his own actions, he indeed undergoes birth as an animal or as an immobile being; thus he constantly experiences that which is ordained for himself by his own karma.
Suffering is not created by oneself, nor is happiness created by oneself;
from the time one takes up residence in the womb, one experiences the results of actions performed in previous bodies. (16)
A certain supreme person, having performed karma in a previous body, is capable of making it otherwise through either power or wisdom. (17)
One experiences only the sufferings and pleasures created by oneself;
one is afflicted by egoism, whether through causes or through conditions. 18.
Just as a calf finds its own mother among a thousand cows, even so do good and evil deeds follow the one who performs them. (19)
For one whose destruction does not exist apart from experience, who else is able to alter the bondage of past karma? (20)
Running very swiftly after him, destiny pursues that person;
it shines forth through the falling out [of results] according to the actions performed in the past.
When he stands, it stands; when he moves, it follows him.
When he performs an action, it conforms to him like a shadow.
Just as shadow and sunlight are eternally and closely bound to one another, so too are the afflictions— the objects of the senses— and the secondary afflictions such as old age and the like.
They afflict a person later on, who has been afflicted by his prior karma;
for wherever one must experience suffering or even happiness, it is determined by that very cause.
There, bound as if by a rope, one is led away by force by destiny;
they say that destiny is the bringer of happiness and suffering for all beings. (25)
One should consider that karma may be otherwise for one who is awake or even asleep; for destiny may arise in one way, yet it binds when one intends to strike down another.
He protects well that which ought to be protected from weapons, fire, poison, and difficult terrains, just as seeds, trees, shrubs, and even grasses are protected upon the earth. (27)
In the same way, actions abide within the self and emerge from it; yet, just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted, [the self is extinguished]. ||28||
Likewise, from the exhaustion of karma, the body born of that [karma] meets its destruction;
likewise, from the exhaustion of karma, death occurs—so it has been declared by those who know reality. (29)
Various diseases of living beings and their causes have been recorded;
therefore, for living beings, karma alone is indeed the primary reality.
Whatever karma was performed in the past is experienced right here; and as for that which you have seen and asked about, O father, it is exactly so.
I have told you its meaning; indeed, these two were born for slaughter. In that forest of bliss, their most dreadful deed was witnessed.
I shall describe the activity of those two; listen as I speak, O dear one:
this is the land of action, while the others are lands for the purpose of enjoyment. (33)
He attained great wisdom and was born as Sugata at the beginning of the creation.
Sūta said:
O highly wise one, in the land of Cāula there was a king named Subāhu. 34.
There was no one on earth like him—possessed of beauty, virtue, and wisdom;
a devotee of Viṣṇu, highly intelligent, and very dear to the Vaiṣṇavas. (35)
O King, by meditating upon Madhusūdana through all three types of action,
one may perform all sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and others.
He had a family priest named Jaimini, a brāhmaṇa;
and having summoned Subāhu, he spoke these words to him: ||37||
O King, give excellent gifts by which you may conquer the lord of happiness;
for by means of gifts, a man who has departed for the next world overcomes even difficult realms. (38)
Through giving, one attains happiness and achieves eternal fame;
through giving, incomparable renown arises within the realm of mortals. (39)
As long as one's fame remains here, for that long the donor shall dwell in heaven;
they say such a gift is difficult to perform, for it is truly not easy to give.
Therefore, men should always give with every effort.
Subāhu said: "Between the two—giving and austerity—which is more difficult to perform? (41)
"Or what is the great fruit after death? Tell me this, O best of the twice-born.
Jaimini said:
"There is nothing on earth more difficult to perform than the giving of food."
O King, this very thing is seen directly before our eyes, witnessed by the world:
that those deluded by greed abandon even their dear lives for the sake of wealth. (43)
Just as men enter the ocean or a forest,
others resort to service, which is established as the way of the horse.
Indeed, in former times, agriculture was characterized by much suffering and toil;
yet that wealth, though acquired through such hardship, was held dearer to him than even his own life. (45)
O tiger among men, it is exceedingly difficult to abandon wealth, especially that which has been acquired through righteous means by a great king. (46)
There is no greater gift than that which is given with faith, according to the rules, to a worthy recipient.
Faith is the daughter of Dharma, a goddess who purifies and delivers the entire world. 47.
She is the progenitor of Sāvitrī and the one who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence; dharma is accomplished through faith, not by heaps of wealth. 48.
O best of kings, there are sages who possess nothing and have attained the dharma of faith; there are also many kinds of gifts with various distinctions. (49)
There is no gift for living beings that brings such a goal as the gift of food;
therefore, food should be given along with milk.
There is no gift superior to food, both in this world and in the next, even when accompanied by sweet and meritorious words. (51)
