For the sake of crossing over, for the sake of welfare, and for the sake of the attainment of happiness, [one should give] with faith, according to the rule, to a worthy recipient, and with a stainless mind. (52)
A man may enjoy the fruit of giving even a single meal;
one should give morsel after morsel, whether it be a handful or a prastha—of this there is no doubt. (53)
For him, that gift shall become inexhaustible and yield great fruit;
indeed, for such a person, there can be no lack of even a prastha or a muṣṭi.
On the occasion of a festival, a person, through the power of avoiding atheism, should feed at least one brāhmaṇa with faith and devotion. (55)
O Lord of Creatures, even for a single primary being, having attained a favorable birth in another life, one eternally consumes food as its master. (56)
Whatever was given with devotion by men to a worthy recipient even once in a previous birth, they enjoy that very thing constantly after attaining a good birth in another life. (57)
They constantly bestow gifts of food upon the Brāhmaṇas;
by that, those kings who give food enjoy sweet food and drink. (58)
The sages who have reached the further shore of the Vedas declare that food alone is indeed the vital breath;
of this there is no doubt, for it has arisen from the immortal.
O Great King, life has indeed been bestowed by him who has offered food; the gift of food diligently bestows the very state of embodied existence. (60)
Having thus heard from the high-souled Jaimini, the son of Vairāja,
he again questioned that brahmin Jaimini, who was learned in wisdom.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-fifth chapter. Subāhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me truly the virtues of heaven."
O best of the twice-born, I shall perform all this according to my own nature.
Jaimini said: There were various delightful and divine gardens, auspicious and endowed with all objects of desire, such as Nandana and others. ||2||
Then, all around, there were beautiful celestial palaces, adorned with trees that bore the fruits of every desire,
and frequented by hosts of apsarases.
Everywhere there were various [ornaments] that moved at will and were subject to one's control,
as well as canopies with lattices of pearls, possessing the color of the rising sun.
They possess golden beds and seats as bright as the orb of the moon;
they have all their desires fulfilled and are entirely free from suffering.
Those men who have performed good deeds wander there just as they do upon the earth;
neither atheists nor those with unconquered senses go there.
They were not cruel, nor slanderous, nor ungrateful, nor arrogant;
they were truthful, established in austerity, heroic, compassionate, and devoted to forbearance.
Those people who perform sacrifices and are of a generous disposition go there; for them there is no disease, no old age, no death, no sorrow, and neither cold nor heat. (8)
There, neither hunger nor thirst exists, nor does any exhaustion;
these and many other such qualities belong to heaven, O King. (9)
Listen now to the defects that exist in that very [realm], as proclaimed by the words [of the sages]:
the entire fruit of auspicious action is experienced in that very place. (10)
Furthermore, no further action is taken here; that great fault is well known:
discontent arises upon seeing the supreme splendor of others. (11)
Likewise, for those whose minds are pervaded by happiness, there is a sudden falling [into the realm];
whatever karmic fruit is performed here, it is experienced right there. (12)
"O King, this is known as the land of action, while that is remembered as the land of results.
Subāhu said: "Great indeed are these defects of heaven that have been described by you. (13)
"O twice-born one, you have declared that these worlds are faultless and lead to eternity.
Jaimini said:
"O King, from the abode of Brahmā downwards, there are indeed faults."
For this very reason, the wise desire the attainment of heaven as inferior; for above the abode of Brahmā lies that supreme station of Viṣṇu. (15)
They know that the auspicious, eternal light is the supreme Brahman;
deluded men, whose nature is bound to sense-objects, do not go there.
Those who are assailed by delusion, bewilderment, fear, malice, anger, and greed—[only] those whose senses are restrained are free from possessiveness, free from egoism, and free from duality. (17)
Furthermore, virtuous people devoted to the yoga of meditation go there.
All this that you asked me has been explained to you. (18)
Having thus heard the qualities of heaven, King Asubahu spoke to that high-souled Jaimini, the best among speakers. (19)
Subāhu said: "O sage, I shall not go to heaven, nor do I even desire it;
for I shall not perform that action which is said to lead to a fall."
O one of great fortune, I shall certainly give a gift at some time;
yet, because of greed for the fruit of that gift, a man surely falls from there. (21)
Having spoken thus, the righteous-souled Subāhu, lord of the earth,
resolved to worship the Lord of Gods, the beloved of Lakṣmī, through the yoga of meditation.
"Free from burning and dissolution, I am going to the world of Viṣṇu.
Jaimini said:
"O lady, you have spoken the truth; it is filled with every form of supreme well-being."
Those kings who are virtuous in character perform great sacrifices;
all kinds of gifts are bestowed by those kings during their sacrifices.
At the beginning of sacrifices, they indeed bestow food, clothing, betel-leaf, gold,
the gift of land, and the gift of cows.
By means of excellent sacrifices, those best of men go to the world of Viṣṇu;
through charity they attain satisfaction, and thus the lords of the earth remain contented.
Those high-souled ascetics always worship him;
having requested alms for their sustenance, they returned to their own abodes. ||27||
O lord of the earth, for the sake of alms, they divide his portions; O high-minded one, they give a single portion to the Brāhmaṇa, while Goga takes a mouthful. (28)
The ascetics bestow one [portion] upon those who dwell at Supārśva;
by the gift of that food, human beings enjoy its fruit. (29)
Deprived of hunger and thirst, they indeed go to the world of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O king of kings, you too [should give] wealth acquired by the body through righteous means.
From giving comes knowledge, and from that attained knowledge one shall attain perfection;
so too shall that mortal who hears this unsurpassed, meritorious narrative. (31)
For him, all goals shall be accomplished and all evil shall dissolve;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||32||
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the narrative of the Earth (Bhūmikhaṇḍa) in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-sixth chapter.
Subāhu said: By what kinds of actions do men go to hell after death?
But by what kind of people is heaven attained after death? You ought to tell me this. ||1||
Jaimini said:
Those twice-born ones who, deluded by greed, abandon their meritorious Brahminhood and subsist on evil deeds, they indeed go to hell. (2)
Those who have no sense of boundaries, who are like atheists, who are intent upon the objects of pride, who are beggars for alms, and who are ungrateful—they indeed go to hell. (3)
Those men who, having promised wealth to Brahmins, do not give it,
and those who seize the property of Brahmins, go to hell.
Men who are backbiters, conceited, speakers of falsehood, and those whose speech is incoherent—these indeed go to hell. ||5||
Those who steal the property of others, those who find fault with and inform on others,
and those who go to the wives of others— they indeed go to hell.
Those who are always devoted to the injury of the lives of living beings,
and likewise to the violation of the wives of others, these indeed go to hell.
Furthermore, those men who destroy wells, tanks, water-stations, and lakes are destined for hell. (8)
Those who treat their wives, children, servants, and guests with contempt,
and who have abandoned the worship of the ancestors and the gods, go to hell.
Those who defile the state of renunciation, those who harm the king, those who corrupt the stages of life (āśramas),
and those who violate their female friends— these indeed go to hell.
Those who do not meditate upon Viṣṇu—the primordial Person, the Sovereign, the Great Lord of all the worlds—they indeed go to hell. ||11||
Those who revile the *prayāja* sacrifices, the gods, kinsmen, friends, the virtuous, and their gurus, go to hell. (12)
Those who obstruct the paths with logs, or even with stakes, or indeed with empty stones, they are destined for hell. 13.
Those who have no trust in any living beings, those likewise afflicted by lust,
and those who are deceitful toward all beings— they indeed go to hell.
Those who refuse Brahmins who have arrived seeking food and are emaciated by lack of livelihood are destined for hell. 15.
Those men who destroy fields, livelihoods, and homes, who destroy joy, and who destroy hope, are indeed destined for hell. ||16||
O King of kings, those who manufacture weapons, arrows, and bows, as well as those who sell them, go to hell. (17)
Those fools who do not show compassion for one who is helpless, distressed, miserable, afflicted by disease, or even aged, go to hell. (18)
Those who, having first undertaken the restraints, later transgress them due to their lack of self-control because their senses are unsubdued, go to hell. (19)
Thus, O King, have been described those men who go to hell; now learn from me about those people who are destined for the heavenly world. 20.
Those men who follow dharma through truth, austerity, self-restraint, generosity, and study go to heaven. (21)
Those high-souled men who are devoted to burnt offerings, study, and the worship of deities, and who take [only what is rightfully theirs], go to heaven. (22)
Pure and dwelling in pure places, devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
those men who recite and sing the praises of Viṣṇu go to heaven.
Those men who always respectfully perform service to their mother and father and avoid sleeping during the day go to heaven. (24)
Those men who have turned away from all sins, who associate with the virtuous, and who are intent upon the welfare of all, go to heaven. (25)
Those men who have desisted from all greed, who are helpers to all,
and who have become a refuge for all, go to heaven.
Those men who serve their gurus with austerities, who bestow honor upon them, and who refrain from accepting gifts, go to heaven; they are true *nārāḥ*. ||27||
Likewise, those who provide for thousands, those who give thousands, and those who are protectors of thousands—such men go to heaven. (28)
Those thieves who release those who are emaciated by fear, sin, penance, grief, poverty, and disease go to heaven. (29)
O Bhārata, those who possess knowledge of the true nature of the self, who are established in youth, and who have conquered their senses—those wise men go to heaven. (30)
O Bhārata, those men who give gold, cows, land, food, and clothing go to heaven. (31)
Those who rejoice when asked for something, speak kindly after giving what is dear, and have abandoned the desire for the fruits of their giving—such people go to heaven. (32)
O ascetic, those men who, having produced for themselves, give away dwellings, grain, and other things, go to heaven. (33)
Those men who never speak of the faults of even their enemies, but rather proclaim their virtues alone, are destined for heaven. 34.
Those who, upon seeing the prosperity of others, do not burn with envy, but instead rejoice and offer their congratulations, those people go to heaven. (35)
In both worldly engagement and renunciation, these high-souled men practice exactly what is declared in the Vedas and the scriptures; therefore, they go to heaven.
Those men who do not know how to speak unpleasant words to others,
but are experts solely in pleasant speech, go to heaven.
Those men who, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, divide their portions [of food] with others, go to heaven as those who have performed the act of "haṃ" (the sound of giving). ||38||
Those men who are the makers of step-wells, wells, ponds, water-stations, dwellings, and groves go to heaven. (39)
Those men who are truthful even toward the untruthful, upright even toward the crooked, and well-disposed even toward their enemies, go to heaven. (40)
Born into whatever family they may be, those men who have many sons, live for a hundred years, are compassionate, and follow right conduct, go to heaven. 41.
Those men who always spend their day thus with single-minded devotion to dharma and constantly undertake such vows go to heaven.
Those people who regard abuse and praise as equal, whose minds are peaceful and who have conquered pride, go to heaven. (43)
Furthermore, those men who protect Brāhmaṇas, as well as women, caravans, or others who are terrified by fear, go to heaven.
Those men who offer funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to their ancestors at the Gaṅgā, at the Puṣkara tīrtha, and especially at Gayā, go to heaven.
Those men who, having restrained the nine gates of the senses, remain established in self-control, and who have abandoned greed, fear, and anger—they are the ones who go to heaven. 46.
Those men who protect the bodies of lice, bugs, gadflies, and other such creatures as if they were their own children go to heaven. 47.
Even those who, through ignorance, accumulate [merit] according to the prescribed method, go to heaven; for in this world, all dualities are overcome by such people. 48.
Those pure men who, established in goodness, do not take pleasure in the wives of others through action, thought, or speech, go to heaven. 49.
They do not perform forbidden acts, they perform those that are prescribed, and they understand their own capacity; therefore, such men go to heaven. (50)
Thus, O King, everything has been told by me according to reality:
how both an evil destiny and a good destiny are attained through one's actions. (51)
A man who acts in opposition to others goes to a most terrible and dreadful hell;
for a man who always lives in accordance with others, liberation that brings happiness stands not far away. (52)
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The ninety-seventh chapter.
Kuñjala said: Having thus heard what was spoken by the sage at that time, the king [listened].
He spoke to that Sage concerning the entire course of dharma and adharma. ||1||
Subāhu said:
"O best of the twice-born, O sage, I shall perform dharma; I shall perform merit. I shall worship Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, with the utmost devotion."
One should worship Madhusūdana through oblations and even through recitation alone;
having performed sacrifice and practiced austerity, that lord of the earth [attains] the world of Viṣṇu.
Honored with all his desires, he quickly attained joy;
yet, having gone to that great world, he did not see the God of gods. ||4||
From hunger arises great and intense thirst, and these two, O wise one, cause much suffering for living beings. (5)
The king also, together with his beloved wife, was tormented by hunger and thirst;
overcome by great suffering, he did not see Hṛṣīkeśa.
Sūta said: Thus, O best of men, the king, together with his beloved wife, became deeply distressed and utterly overwhelmed, being severely tormented by hunger.
The lord of the earth ran here and there with great speed,
his limbs adorned with all kinds of ornaments and decorated with garments and sandalwood paste.
With his limbs beautifully adorned with flower garlands, necklaces, earrings, and bracelets,
and his body radiant with the luster of jewels, that lord of the earth proceeded forth.
Thus, though his conduct was one of suffering and he was being praised by those reciting [his deeds], he, overwhelmed by pain and grief, spoke these words to his beloved: (10)
O beautiful one, I have reached the world of Viṣṇu together with you,
O radiant lady, while being praised by sages and traveling in a celestial chariot.
By this very action, his hunger increased exceedingly;
and having reached the world of Viṣṇu, he did not see Madhusūdana.
O noble lady, for what reason do we not enjoy great fruit?
For even by one's own past actions, this suffering is brought about. (13)
Having heard those words, she spoke thus to the king: ||14||
The wife said:
"O King, you have spoken the truth; there is no fruitlessness in dharma.
Those brāhmaṇas who study the Vedas, the Śāstras, and the Purāṇas [attain their goals]. (15)
Having shaken off suffering and grief here, one is liberated from all defects by the mere utterance of the name of the divine Viṣṇu, the wielder of the beautiful discus.
"O meritorious and highly fortunate ones, you are meditating upon Janārdana;
by you alone has the Lord who bears the conch, discus, and mace been propitiated. (17)
I do not know the fruit of that gift of food and other offerings which was not bestowed upon the Brahmins as prescribed by the twice-born; Madhusūdana has not been seen by me. (18)
"O King, hunger oppresses me and thirst indeed dries me up. Kuñjala said:
Thus addressed by his beloved, the king's senses became agitated with anxiety. 19.
Then he beheld that most meritorious hermitage, which dispels fatigue, filled with divine trees and adorned with ponds. ||20||
It was adorned with step-wells, ponds, and lakes filled with holy water,
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and beautified by *kahlāra* lilies.
The hermitage shines with sons who are sages knowing the truth;
it is filled with divine trees and graced by herds of deer.
It was strewn with various flowers, filled with delightful fragrances,
crowded with twice-born ones and siddhas, and thronged by the disciples of the ṛṣis.
Resounding with the assemblies of yogis and lords of yogis, adorned by hosts of gods, and graced by dense groves of plantain trees laden with excellent fruit. (24)
It was filled with various kinds of trees, endowed with everything that fulfills every desire, and always adorned with sandalwood trees of lovely fragrance and excellent fruits. (25)
Thus, filled with merit and endowed with the marks of a Brahmin,
King Sasubāhu then [departed] together with that very dear wife.
He entered that great, merit-bestowing forest which grants all desires,
where he shone like the sun, illuminating all directions.
Shining with great splendor, he was like a second sun;
he was seated upon a yogic posture and encircled by a yogic belt.
Vāmadeva, the best of sages and the foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, meditated upon Hṛṣīkeśa, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (29)
Having seen that high-souled Vāmadeva, the best of sages,
the king, together with his beloved wife, went quickly and bowed down to him.
Then Vāmadeva, seeing that best of kings bowed down together with his beloved wife, greeted the king with blessings.
Having seated Subāhu, that best of kings, upon auspicious seats,
he then honored him with offerings such as water for the feet, water for the guest-offering (arghya), and other rites of worship.
The king, who had not been honored by the Sage, arrived together with his beloved wife;
then he questioned the king, the most excellent among the great devotees of the Lord.
Vāmadeva said:
"O king of kings, through divine knowledge I recognize you as a knower of the dharma of Viṣṇu, a devotee of Viṣṇu, the best among men, and a ruler of the earth. (34)
"And you have arrived free from ailment, together with your wife, the daughter of Tarkṣya.
The king said:
"I have arrived free from ailment; I have attained the supreme state of Viṣṇu. (35)
By me, with supreme devotion, Janārdana, the God of gods and Lord of the world, was propitiated;
pleased by my devotion, he [granted] the sovereignty of the gods.
"O father, why do I see that lotus-eyed Lord? O father, hunger afflicts me, and my thirst is exceedingly terrible. (37)
"O best of sages, because of those two, we find neither peace nor happiness; this is the cause of the suffering that has arisen for me. (38)
"Therefore, tell me the reason for this; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance.
Vāmadeva said:
"O King of kings, you have indeed always been a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (39)
Madhusūdana was propitiated by you with supreme devotion, through acts of service such as bathing and the like, as well as with offerings of fragrances, flowers, and so forth. (40)
The Lord of the worlds was not worshipped with offerings and fruits;
having reached the tenth day, O King of kings, you have always acted thus.
You did not give even a single meal of fine food to a brāhmaṇa;
moreover, having reached the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight], you did not observe a fast. ||42||
Food was not offered by you to a Brahmin with Viṣṇu in mind;
yet food, existing eternally upon the earth, is of the nature of nectar. 43.
O great king, you have not specifically given the gift of food; however, various kinds of medicinal herbs have been praised—listen to them. 44.
O King, there are pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, sour, and alkaline substances; all these various kinds of condiments, such as asafoetida and others, [are present]. 45.
From the nectar were born all medicinal herbs that cause nourishment;
and by properly preparing food itself, one becomes endowed with the power of these herbs.
Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), it is offered to the gods who are forms of Viṣṇu;
indeed, it is placed in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa for the ancestors who are forms of Viṣṇu.
Having first given that [food] to the guests, one should feed one's dependents;
thereafter, one should eat that food, which is like nectar, oneself. 48.
O King, there is no suffering after death for him, nor is there any lack of happiness;
for the Brahmins, the ancestors, and the gods, O King, take the form of Kṣatriyas. 49.
Just as a certain farmer always practices good cultivation, so too, O King, should a mortal perform his cultivation in the field that is the mouth of a Brahmin. 50.
One should constantly break apart the bull of the menstrual period with the plow of intrinsic nature and the sword of faith; likewise, one should employ both wisdom and austerity. 51.
The Lord, who experiences truth and knowledge and whose self is pure, should be dismissed with salutations in the great field known as Vipra. ||52||
O King, just as a farmer constantly breaks up the impurities of the field by applying effort, so should one who desires Viṣṇu propitiate Him.
In the same way, one should propitiate the Brahmins with auspicious and meritorious words;
for the time of reaching a mountain pilgrimage site is like a cloud raining down.
Just as one who desires to sow would sow in a field,
so too, O King, [this gift] is bestowed upon a Brahmin who is well-pleased.
Just as the owner of a field reaps the fruit from the seed sown in that field, O Great King, so too does the giver enjoy the very fruit. //56//
And having passed away, one becomes eternally satisfied right here and not otherwise;
for the Brāhmaṇas, the ancestors, and the gods are the very form of the sacred field—of this there is no doubt. (57)
And those [trees] planted by great kings among men certainly yield fruit; whatever kind of body one has, such fruit it will surely give. (58)
O King, from that which is called pungent, the sweet indeed arises;
likewise, from that which is called sweet, the pungent arises again.
Whatever kind of seed one sows, such is the fruit one reaps; he who does not sow in the field does not enjoy its fruit. (60)
In the same way, O King, the Brahmins, the gods, and the ancestors in the form of the field manifest the fruit of what has been given; of this there is no doubt. (61)
O King, whatever kind of action—whether auspicious or inauspicious—you yourself have performed, such you shall experience; otherwise, it does not come to pass.
At that time, with a devout mind, she also gave delicious food and drink to the gods, the Brahmins, and the ancestors.
Exquisite foods, refined and sweet, along with things to be chewed and drunk, and excellent delicacies—you yourself have eaten them, yet you have given nothing to anyone else. (64)
"O Great King, since your own body has been nourished by you with foods resembling nectar, therefore hunger arises. (65)
O King, O highly fortunate one, karma alone is the cause of happiness and suffering for men, as well as of birth and death; therefore, enjoy this fruit of your own karma.
In the past, even those great-souled ones who attained heaven through their own karma returned again to the world of mortals when the time for the exhaustion of that karma arrived. (67)
O King, Nala, Bhagiratha, Viśvāmitra, and Yudhiṣṭhira likewise attained heaven through their actions alone at the appropriate time.
For one obtains this suffering or happiness as a result of previously performed karma;
O King, who is capable of transgressing that, even if he were the Lord himself? (69)
Therefore, O best of kings, even though you have gone to heaven, the force of hunger and thirst has arisen within you; consequently, your karma is wicked. (70)
"O best of kings, since you desire a remedy that resembles sugarcane, then go and enjoy your own body as it stands in the forest. (71)
"And this great queen of yours appears exceedingly emaciated by hunger.
Subāhu said: "For how long must this task be performed together with my beloved? (72)
Tell me that, O highly fortunate one; when is such grace seen? By the gift of what substance is what merit obtained, O best of sages? (73)
Therefore, O one of great wisdom, speak of that by which you may be satisfied; for this is my desire.
Vāmadeva said:
"O high-minded one, from the gift of food comes great happiness, as does the gift of water. (74)
Mortals enjoy heaven even through those very sins, provided that what was taken by them has not been given back by those men. (75)
Even when the time of death has arrived, people give all their gifts;
however, food along with water should be given right at the very beginning.
One should give a fine umbrella and sandals, a very beautiful water-vessel, excellent land, a goat, a cow, and gold— these are the eight gifts that one should bestow.
For him who is born in heaven, there arises no occurrence of hunger, thirst, or the like;
O King, by the gift of food, he is not afflicted by hunger and remains fully satisfied.
O King, by the gift of sandals and the gift of an umbrella, one who is intensely thirsty shall never again remain unsatiated. 79.
O best of kings, a giver indeed obtains shade, as does one who provides a marriage dowry;
by the gift of sandals, I shall tell you yet another thing. (80)
O highly fortunate one, through the gift of land one shall obtain all desires;
O great king, through the gift of a cow, one shall always be nourished by the [six] flavors.
Knowing himself to be the master of all enjoyments, a man shall dwell in the heavenly world;
the giver indeed becomes satisfied by the gift of a cow—of this there is no doubt.
Free from disease, endowed with happiness, contented, and possessed of wealth, he is born with gold that is free from blemish; of this there is no doubt. (83)
That man becomes illustrious, handsome in form, generous, and an enjoyer of jewels;
moreover, when the time of death has arrived, he who bestows the gift of sesame seeds [attains these fruits]. (84)
Having become the lord of all enjoyments, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
thus, through this specific kind of gift, supreme happiness is attained. (85)
O Indra among kings, while you were still living, you did not indeed bestow upon a brahmin the gift of a cow, the gift of land, or even food and water. (86)
Even at the time of death, nothing was given; therefore, hunger arises.
This cause has been declared to you, which has come into being through the power of past actions (karma). 87.
"Whatever kind of karma has been performed, that is the kind one experiences.
Subāhu said: "O best of sages, how may my hunger be pacified? (88)
"O best of the twice-born, this body, withered by this [fasting], is indeed suffering greatly; O boat, tell me the atonement for hunger. (89)
"And how may there be peace for me regarding this terrible karma?
Vāmadeva said:
"O best of kings, there is no atonement for this except through experiencing its results."
"O King, you shall enjoy the entire fruit of this deed while remaining in good health, as well as that of your beloved wife, wherever this body falls. (91)
"You two must certainly depart from here, there is no doubt;
both of you must enjoy that which is indeed imperishable. (92)
"O King, there is no doubt that each [of us] shall enjoy [our respective realms] together with our beloved.
The king said: "For how long a time must I enjoy it in this way with my beloved? (93)
"O highly fortunate one, my words are of that same measure.
Vāmadeva said:
"This great hymn to Vāsudeva is the destroyer of great sins. (94)
When you hear this merit, then you shall attain liberation.
All this has been told to you; go now, O King, and enjoy [the fruits].
Having heard this, the king then, together with his wife,
once again began to consume the flesh of his own body along with his beloved.
O King, O Prince, the body of one who eats this [medicine] shall always be possessed of great wisdom and remain full; it shall always be radiant. 97.
Just as the king eats and the body decays, the ignoble one always laughs; I shall describe the nature of those two. (98)
Together with Prajñā, that great virtuous woman constantly mocked the conduct of that king, her faith in him never wavering. (99)
Impelled by wisdom, having made a firm resolve, one should offer food endowed with faith to the Brāhmaṇas, dedicated specifically to Viṣṇu.
In this way, she constantly devours her own body, just as a woman consumes her own body with foods that are like nectar. (101)
Then, after a hundred years had passed, he remembered the great sage Vāmadeva and, O you of excellent vows, reproached himself.
Never have I given anything to the ancestors, the gods, or the Brahmins; nor indeed have I given to guests, especially not to the elderly. (103)
Out of compassion, he gave food to the destitute and to the sick;
thus he enjoys his own wealth while censuring me and his own past actions. (104)
Thus, knowing Subāhu—who was his own self—to be Śambhu together with his beloved, he would laugh upon seeing those two women, Prajñā and Śraddhā. (105)

O King, due to that ripening of karma, because of my association with you who are pure by nature, yet through attachment to me, you have become one of sinful intent regarding what was not given. (106)
With those words of wisdom, they laughed at the king once more:
"O King, where has that great delusion gone, by which you were so deluded? (107)
One is cast into the pit of darkness by greed joined with delusion;
having not fallen there myself, I have nevertheless fallen into this narrow strait of suffering. (108)
"O King, having abandoned the path of generosity and entered the path of greed, you are now consumed by intense hunger; enjoy this together with your wife. (109)
Thus they both laugh, Prajñā and Subāhu, accompanied by their beloved; this, my son, is the entire reason for their laughter.
Then, while the king was being devoured, his own body became distressed; he was constantly entreated, "Give! Give! as they begged for it. (111)
In that place, terrifying with its great and fearsome forms of hunger and thirst, one should beg the lord of kings for food mixed with milk. 112.
All this that was asked by you has been explained to you. O Mahāmati, speak whatever else you wish to ask. 113.
Vijvala said: "Being thus impelled, tell me that hymn named Vāsudeva, by which the king may attain liberation—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (114)
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the *Evena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The Ninety-eighth Chapter.
Sūta said:
When these auspicious words had been spoken by the high-souled Vijvala, [the following occurred].
The best among those speaking in the Kuñjala style uttered this meritorious hymn. ||1||
Having meditated upon and bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of all afflictions and the bestower of all that is auspicious, this hymn to Hari is proclaimed. (2)
That which is named Vāsudeva bestows all that is most auspicious;
it is the gateway to liberation, endowed with happiness, the giver of peace, and the increaser of nourishment. (3)
This hymn of Vāsudeva, which bestows all desires, grants knowledge, and increases wisdom, was revealed by Vijvala.
And having understood everything concerning that one named Vāsudeva— who is immeasurable and increases merit— from his father, Vijvala, the best of birds, [acted accordingly].
Then, O King, he set out to go there, having been questioned by his father;
thus did he depart, his mind resolved, radiant and having reached the further shore of knowledge.
The righteous-souled one spoke to his son, who was intent on performing a service.
Kuñjala said: "O son, hear of the great sin committed by that king;
for you went there and recited it while Subāhu was listening."
To the extent that one shall hear this supreme hymn, to that same extent one will become composed of knowledge;
there is no doubt regarding Śrī Vāsudeva. By His grace, what I have spoken is most auspicious. 9.
Then Vijvala, moving with the swift stride of a flying insect, reached the holy Ānanda-dakānana, which was situated beyond the Tryasaguru mountain.
Seated and filled with joy, having taken refuge in the shade of a tree,
he beheld the king once again arriving by means of a celestial chariot.
This King Asubāhu will come here with his beloved wife;
we shall liberate him from his sin by means of this hymn of praise at some point. (12)
Just then, that celestial chariot arrived, adorned with a network of tinkling bells,
filled with the sound of gongs, and accompanied by the music of lutes and flutes.
Resounding with the voices of Gandharvas and accompanied by Apsarases, it is enriched with all objects of desire, yet devoid of food and water. ||14||
King Subāhu, seated in that vehicle together with his beloved,
descended from the celestial chariot along with his son, Tārkṣya, and his wife.
As soon as he took up a sharp weapon and began to cut that corpse, Vijvala then issued a challenge.
"O tiger among men, O you who resemble a god! This cruel deed is being committed by ruthless people, and it cannot be stopped. (17)
O tiger among men, this reversal of destiny has been brought about so that he may commit an evil deed, a rash act, and a contemptible action that is always censured in the worlds. (18)
Why have you begun this work here, devoid of Vedic conduct?
Tell me the entire reason for that exactly as it is.
Having heard these words spoken by that high-souled Vijvala,
the great king spoke these words to his beloved wife.
"O beloved, for a hundred years this evil deed was committed by me; when and by whom was it spoken that he should thus revile me? (21)
O beloved, as my heart was thus being tormented by hunger, it went out toward you; yet, longing for you, peace does not prevail within my mind. (22)
O lady of lovely smiles, as long as his words— which grant peace from all suffering— are heard, so long does delight persist within the mind.
"Who is this god who will become a thousand-eyed one?
Will the words spoken by the sage in the past come true for the sages? (24)
Having heard these words spoken by her beloved,
his wife, who was devoted solely to her husband, then replied to the king immediately thereafter.
O Lord, you have spoken this most wonderful truth; for just as it exists within your mind, so too does it exist in mine. (26)
"Who is this wearing the form of a bird that asks [this] like one wishing me well?
Having heard these words spoken by his beloved, the lord of the earth [replied]. (27)
Having joined his palms in reverence, he addressed the bird with these words.
Subāhu said:
"Welcome to you, O highly wise Lord who has assumed the form of a bird! (28)
With my head, together with my wife, I bow to the pair of your lotus feet; by your grace, may there be merit for us both. (29)
Who are you that, in the form of a bird, speaks only of merit? O best of beings, such is the karma as it was performed by your previous body.
Whatever good or evil has been sown is experienced right here;
then, he reported his own conduct before him. (31)
"Just as it was previously heard by my father Kuñjala, relate your own history; who are you that speaks to me? (32)
Then the best of birds spoke these words to Subāhu;
Vijvala said:
"Born of the parrot species, my father was named Kuñjala."
Among his sons, I am the third, named Vijvala;
O mighty-armed one, I am neither a god, nor a Gandharva, nor a Siddha.
I behold this most dreadful karma as ever-present; for how much longer must it endure, joined with such great acts of reckless violence? (35)
"O Great King, tell us that which we shall perform.
Subāhu said:
"That which was previously mentioned by the Brāhmaṇas as being designated by the name Vāsudeva. (36)
"When I attain my own auspicious state, I shall hear that which was spoken by the meritorious sage, who was self-restrained and free from passion. (37)
"Then I shall be liberated from my sin, there is no doubt.
Vijvala said:
"O father, I was questioned for your sake, and that which was told by him has been related."
Therefore, O best of beings, listen as I proclaim that which is eternal. 39.

Oṃ. Of this hymn named *Śrī-Vāsudeva*, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Oṃ-kāra is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of destroying all sins and for the attainment of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) during recitation. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—this is the mantra.
I bow to the Praṇava, the supreme purifier, the highest merit, the knower of the Vedas, the essence of the Vedas, the support of knowledge, and the support of existence. (40)
I bow to the supreme Praṇava, which is without abode, without form, perfectly luminous, and of great exaltation; it is devoid of qualities, yet connected with all qualities. 41.
I bow to Him who is of great splendor, of great energy, and the destroyer of great delusion; to Him who pervades the entire world and transcends all qualities. 42.
Having become the source of all prosperity for all beings, increasing their well-being, I bow to the auspicious Praṇava, which is the fearless mendicant and the ultimate bond. 43.
I bow down to that Praṇava, the singer of the Gāyatrī Sāman, whose song is auspicious and beloved by singers, and who is the enjoyer of the songs of the Gandharvas. 44.
I bow down to that Oṃkāra, who is the form of the Vedas, who resides in the sacrifice, who is compassionate toward his devotees, and who is the source of the entire world. 45.
I bow to the Praṇava, who is Hari, the savior of all beings, manifesting in the form of a boat for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. 46.
I bow to the auspicious Praṇava, who dwells in all worlds in a single form and not in many ways, whose nature is the abode of absolute liberation (kaivalya). 47.
Subtle, subtler than the subtle, pure, devoid of qualities yet the leader of qualities, free from all material states, I bow to that which is the locus of the Vedas. 48.
I bow to that Oṃkāra, which is forever free from the separations of gods and demons, always accompanied by contentment, and is to be meditated upon by the gods and yogis. 49.
I bow to the pervasive Lord, the knower of the universe, supreme consciousness, most auspicious,
Śiva, possessing the qualities of Śiva, peaceful, the syllable *vaṃ*, and the Praṇava.
I bow to Him whose illusion even Brahmā and the other gods and demons have entered, yet do not perceive that supreme, pure gateway to liberation. 51.

Salutations to Him, the leader of the hosts, the illustrious Vāsudeva of great splendor, who is pure, whose intellect is purified by the gift of the waters of life, and who is both transcendent and immanent. 52.
I perpetually take refuge in that Lord who shines with the Śrīvatsa mark, with the Sudarśana discus possessing the splendor of the sun, and who also shines with the mace and the lotus. (53)
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the secret of the Vedas, who possesses all qualities and is the support of all things moving and unmoving, whose splendor is equal to the sun and the fire. ||54||

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the treasure-house of compassion, who is stainless, possessed of beautiful form, and resplendent with self-restraint; having attained him, the worlds beginning with the gods continue to live. ||55||

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who, shining with the radiant splendor of the sun, is the constant cause of purification, bringing about the destruction of the masses of darkness by his own hands. 56.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who, as the wind moving within all living beings, causes dryness through his pervasive power everywhere and bestows the subtle element of moisture. 57.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who, like a boat for the purpose of crossing over, sustains all the worlds and their protectors according to his own will. (58)

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is composed of the worlds within, who eternally consumes all things both stationary and moving, and who is the cause of the Svāhā-utterance for the host of gods. 59.
He who nourishes all beings in this world with all the most meritorious flavors and gentle qualities, and who is the source of food through his pure splendor—to that Vāsudeva I go for refuge. 60.
There truly exists everywhere the cause of destruction, which is the support of all, composed of all, and all itself;
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva who enjoys the objects of the senses even without the sense organs. 61.
He sustains the worlds in the form of the individual soul (jīva), and from Him proceed all things, moving and unmoving, as His own manifestations;
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is absolute, consisting of pure knowledge, and perfectly stainless. (62)

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, the destroyer of the Daityas, the root of the destruction of suffering, the supreme peace, consisting of power, and vast; by attaining whom the gods attain freedom from pride.

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is bliss, the giver of bliss, the Lord of the gods, the ocean of knowledge, the sage among sages, the Lord of the gods, the refuge of truth, and who is established in the quality of truth. 64.

I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is the form of the limbs of sacrifice, the form of the ultimate reality, endowed with *māyā*, the Lord of the earth, possessed of fierce merit, the singular consciousness, and the abode of the worlds. (65)
I perpetually bow to the two lotus feet of that Vāsudeva, whose bed in the midst of the ocean is the vast coils of the body of the serpent Śeṣa, and who is the source of all benefit. 66.
That very pair of lotus feet of Śrī Vāsudeva— ever endowed with merit, auspicious, and served by many sacred fords— is the destroyer of all sins.
I perpetually bow to the lotus feet of Śrī Vāsudeva, which resemble great red lotuses, which serve as a mountain for the elephant of my mind, and which are adorned with anklets and rings. 68.

I perpetually bow down to that very meritorious lotus-foot of Śrī Vāsudeva, which is always praised with great devotion by the gods, the perfected ones (siddhas), the sages, and the lords of the serpents. 69.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, at whose feet even those sages who were sinking in the mud attain heaven, purified and freed from sin, and who, being well-pleased, grant them liberation.
Wherever the water from Viṣṇu’s feet remains, there the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords (tīrthas) along with their presiding deities are always present.
Even those who drink it while still possessing bodies of sin go purified to the beautiful abode of Murāri.
Even those whose bodies are smeared with terrible sins attain liberation by being sprinkled with the water from the feet of the Supreme Lord; I perpetually bow at His very feet. (72)

By merely consuming the food offering of that noble-souled wielder of the beautiful discus, one obtains the fruit of the Śrī-Vājapeya sacrifice; moreover, such men become endowed with all their goals fulfilled.
I take refuge in that Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of the hells, who is free from illusion and the knower of all qualities; meditating upon whom, people attain a happy state. 74.
He who is thus always worshipped by hosts of ṛṣis, siddhas, cāraṇas, and gods;
he who is the Lord of the gods beginning with Brahmā, acting as the cause of the creation of the universe;
he who is compassionate, the one who delivers those fallen into the great ocean of saṃsāra.
With devotion, I bow to his very feet, which are beautiful, excellent, and purifying. ||75||

The illustrious Vāmana, the sole Lord of the three worlds, who was accompanied by the Sāma-singers and whose singing was joyfully celebrated with curiosity by the hosts of gods, was seen by the throngs of deities in the sacrificial pavilion;
as he performed that rite which brings auspiciousness, he rendered his army free from sin through his pure glances.
I bow to his pair of lotus feet, which are the supreme purifier. ||76||
O King, that jewel among the twice-born, who at the commencement of the sacrifice was resplendent with the glory of Brahman,
who was like a mass of light with divine brilliance resembling a sapphire,
and who was born as the son of Virocana out of a desire for the welfare of the gods— [he has been brought here].
I beg you: let that three-strided Vāmana, the Lord of Vaṃ, be given to me. ||77||

To behold him, the hosts of sages reached the solar orb and the heavens; and at that time, between the setting of the moon and the sun, they covered the sky with their single steps. Then, the hosts of gods attained dissolution into that very Lord who wields the beautiful discus.
I bow to the incomparable prowess of the Lord, whose body is like a banner with its sheath opened wide. ||78||
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 98 ||
The ninety-ninth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
This hymn is supremely purifying, ancient, a destroyer of sins, full of merit, and auspicious.
Having heard this auspicious, well-spoken, supreme, and most excellent recitation, the king became sorrowful. ||1||
The lord of the earth became like a god, free from thirst for worldly existence and devoid of hunger;
his wife as well was endowed with radiant beauty, and they both attained the bond of merit.
The Lord, surrounded by noble gods, sages, and perfected beings endowed with devotion to Hari, arrived there;
He who bears the glorious conch, discus, lotus, mace, and sword, came to that king whose sins had been destroyed.
Śrī Nārada, Bhārgava, Vyāsa, and the meritorious son of Ṛkaṇḍa arrived there;
likewise, the sage named Vālmīki, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, arrived. ||4||
The high-souled Garga, endowed with devotion to Hari, as well as Jābāli, Raibhya, and Kaśyapa—these foremost of Bhāgavatas, beloved by Viṣṇu, arrived together with Hari. ||5||
Meritorious, most fortunate, and cleansed of all taints, they were devoted to the lotus feet of Hari;
surrounding Śrī Vāsudeva, they stood there and praised the King in various ways. (6)
All the gods, headed by the fire-eaters (Agni), as well as Brahmā, Hari, and the most divine goddesses,
along with the Gandharva kings and other excellent singers, sing a divine, sweet, and captivating song.
The sages praise him with hymns that are well-composed, consistent with the ultimate truth, and highly meritorious;
and seeing the Lord who is like a sovereign, Hari spoke these enchanting words.
"O King, choose whatever boon you desire; since I am well-pleased, I shall grant it to you.
Having heard these words of Hari and seeing the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) speaking before him, the king—
I bow to that Lord, the slayer of Mura, who has the luster of a blue lotus; who bears the conch, discus, sword, and mace as his primary weapons;
who is endowed with Śrī; who is the Supreme Sovereign; and who is adorned with armlets and necklaces blazing with jewels. (10)

The king, prostrating himself upon the earth with sentiments of deep devotion, beheld Hari— who possesses the splendor of the sun, who is well-served by hosts of gods, who is beautifully adorned with costly necklaces and ornaments, and who is anointed with excellent divine perfumes and unguents.
Then the great king, with prostrations like a staff and with the words "I bow to you," said:
"I am your slave, I am your servant; I always offer devotion before you and possess the highest state of being. (12)
O Hari, protect me who have come here accompanied by my wife, having sought refuge in you;
blessed indeed are those twice-born men of the Mādhava lineage who, with their minds dissolved in meditation, always meditate upon you along with the gods. (13)
Those who utter "Obeisance to Mādhava" depart from here for Vaikuṇṭha, becoming perfectly pure;
likewise, those who bear upon their heads the holy water flowing from your very lotus feet.
Those men who have bathed in the waters arising from all the sacred fords go to the abode of Hari. ||15||
I have no yoga, nor devotion to you; I have no knowledge, nor do I perform any ritual action. By the grace of what merit do you bestow this boon upon me? (16)
Hari said:
"O King, you have heard from the meritorious Avijvala that which is named Vāsudeva, the destroyer of great sins; thus you are cleansed of all taint."
Therefore, you have become a partaker of liberation; there is no doubt in this. In my world, enjoy divine pleasures that accord with your heart.
The king said:
"If indeed this boon is to be granted by you to me, who am not in distress, then grant first this most excellent boon to Vijvalā. (19)
Hari said:
"O King, Vijvala’s father was the meritorious Kuñjala, adorned with knowledge;
he constantly recites the great hymn to Vāsudeva. (20)
Accompanied by his beloved and his sons, he will go to my abode;
I shall always grant this fruit to the reciter of this hymn.
When these auspicious words had been spoken, the king said to Keśava:
"O Keśava, may this hymn of great merit bear fruit. (22)
Hari said:
O great king, when men shall satisfy me in the Kṛta Yuga, they will attain liberation at that very moment; of this there is no doubt. (23)
In the Tretā age they [attain the goal] in just one month; in the Dvāpara, in six months;
and in the Kali age, men attain it by means of recitation in a single year.
O Indra among kings, a Brāhmaṇa who bathes and recites [the mantra] three times a day or even once, attains heaven and the goal granted by Vaiṣṇava.
Whatever desire you may have for this living being, that Kṣatriya shall attain it, adorned with wealth and grain. (26)
A Vaiśya shall become prosperous and happy, and a Śūdra shall likewise become happy. Whoever recites or causes others to hear this [text] beginning with "aṃ" shall be liberated from sin. ||27||
A disciple shall never behold the terrors of hell;
by the grace of this hymn of praise to me, he shall attain all siddhis. ||28||
O King, while the Brahmins are being fed, he shall recite [this] at the time of the Śrāddha;
thus satisfied, the ancestors will go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, one should perform the *tarpaṇa* libation with *teja-paṅku*;
his ancestors, their minds filled with joy, drink that nectar (*amṛta*). (30)
If a person recites this with devotion within their home or during the course of a sacrifice, no obstacles shall arise there; all success shall be attained. (31)
In places difficult and inaccessible due to poison, in the presence of wild tigers, or when one has encountered the peril of thieves, one should recite this hymn. (32)
In that regard, O Great King, there will be peace without a doubt;
even for other fortunate men who have gone to the king's gate. (33)
A person who has bathed while observing celibacy, free from anger and greed, should recite ten thousand times the name of Vāsudeva. (34)
Having worshipped Vāsudeva with a focused mind, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) of ten parts consisting of sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with clarified butter, and then offer it. 35.
For those who offer a verse, a gift, a fire-oblation, or meditation, I shall never abandon their side, remaining ever by them like a devoted servant. (36)
When the Kali age has fully arrived, he will become a servant through the chanting of hymns;
to anyone at all, he shall be given on the occasion of breaking the Veda.
And he shall indeed have all his desires fulfilled;
listen, O King, to this hymn of praise which I have composed that yields such fruit. (38)
In ancient times, it was fashioned by Brahmā and recited by Rudra;
by it, Indra was liberated from the sin of Brahman-slaughter and freed from his transgression.
The gods, the ṛṣis, the secret ones, the siddhas, the vidyādharas, and the immortals—
when this hymn was worshipped by the nāgas, they attained the desired perfection.
He shall become rich in merit, wealthy, a donor, and possessed of sons; he who recites this hymn of mine—of this there is no need for doubt. (41)
"Come with your wife to my abode, O best of kings;
the hand of support has been granted by Hari to that monarch. (42)
The two drums resounded there, the Gandharvas sang charmingly, the foremost Apsarases danced, and they let fall a rain of flowers. 43.
All the gods and sages praised him with Vedic hymns;
then the king went to Hari together with his beloved.
While he was being praised by hosts of gods and siddhas, the blazing one, with a joyful mind, beheld him;
and having arrived, that one of great power stood right there with speed. 45.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana at the Sacred Site of the Guru," within the *Guru-tīrtha* section of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The hundredth chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
On the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, there stands a banyan tree known as Vaṭa.
Vijvala also arrived and, having prostrated before his father, [he spoke].
The high-minded and virtuous-souled one also described the greatness of the hymn named Vāsudeva before his father. (2)
Just as Viṣṇu, having arrived, granted him an auspicious boon,
he related all of that with a very gracious mind.
Having heard that account from the king, he was filled with great joy; embracing his son Vijvala, he [spoke].
He said: "O child, great merit has been earned by you, a high-souled king, through this most meritorious service rendered by chanting the praises of Vāsudeva. (5)
Having thus addressed his son with blessings and having praised him, who was endowed with divine qualities, again and again, [he spoke].
Standing on the delightful bank of the river while Cyavana looked on—all this conduct of those great-souled ones has been related to you. (7)
"O great king, I shall tell you something that is not even told to Vaiṣṇavas.
Vena said:
"The nectar was offered to me for the purpose of drinking from a conch vessel. (8)
Therefore, what mortal on earth would not have faith to drink this supreme Vaiṣṇava knowledge, which is always the best among all drinks? 9.
As you speak in this manner, no satiety arises in me for drinking [your words];
indeed, my faith increases further to hear of the Lord of the Gods of gods. (10)
Out of your grace, please tell me also of the conduct of Mekuñjala;
and what was said by that great-souled one regarding his fourth son? (11)
"Please tell me the truth in great detail out of your compassion.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Listen, I shall relate the life-story of Kuñjala."
The life story of Cyavana is endowed with much that is auspicious;
O best of men, this meritorious narrative destroys all evil. (13)
The man who listens with devotion shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the *Even-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and first chapter.
Sūta said:
Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, [spoke to] the son of Aṅga, that best of kings.
He narrated the account called Mahā-śreya, which destroys all evil. ||1||
Listen, for I shall relate the life-story that bestows spiritual welfare— the account of the high-souled twice-born Kujjala.
Viṣṇu said:
Then the righteous Kuñjala, having summoned his fourth son, spoke these words to him with great joy: "O monkey, [enter] the water."
"My son, what unprecedented thing have you seen? Tell me!
Why have you come here for the sake of food, O best of sons? (4)
"O highly fortunate one, tell me that which was seen, which bestows great merit.
Kapiñjala said: "O dear one, I shall relate to you that unprecedented [account] about which you have asked. (5)
"That which has not been seen or heard by anyone, and which has never before been heard by me—this very thing I shall now proclaim; let it be heard even at this moment. (6)
"Listen, all you brothers; O mother, listen to this with attention:
Kailāsa is the best of mountains, white and resembling the moon. (7)
O Father, it is strewn with various minerals, adorned with diverse trees,
and washed on all sides by the auspicious and meritorious waters of the Gaṅgā.
Thousands of various divine rivers also [flowed forth],
because from him, O Father, diverse waters were produced.
On the great mountain there are thousands of water-filled reservoirs, and there are vast rivers frequented by cranes and saras birds. (10)
On that best of peaks, there were merit-bestowing and sin-destroying groves of various kinds, both in flower and in fruit. (11)
It was filled with the lush and auspicious foliage of various trees,
frequented by the courtyards of the Kinnaras, and crowded with Apsarases.
It was beautifully adorned by Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and hosts of gods;
it was endowed with divine groves of trees and filled with celestial splendors. ||13||
Abundantly adorned with divine fragrances and endowed with various jewels,
it was exceedingly beautiful with white slabs of crystal.
O King, it was filled with splendors like the radiance of the sun,
and with sandalwood of lovely fragrance, as well as *bakula* trees bearing blue blossoms.
It is adorned everywhere with trees made of various flowers, and it resounds sweetly with the beautiful songs of divine birds. (16)
With the humming of bees and the swarms of trees, the mountain is made sweet;
and with the songs of cuckoos, that forested peak is truly beautiful.
There stands the auspicious temple of Śiva, crowded with tens of millions of attendants;
it is white with splendors, meritorious, and a mountain-like heap of virtue. (18)
Then, with lions roaring and with bellowing buffaloes and elephants, the quarters resounded simultaneously with the deep cries of the world-elephants.
It was crowded with various wild beasts, teeming with troops of monkeys,
and resounded with the cries of peacocks and the echoes from its caves.
It was resplendent with caves, slopes, peaks, and ridges;
it was endowed with various waterfalls and adorned with medicinal herbs.
The divine mountain, possessing divine qualities, meritorious, filled with the abodes of merit, frequented by those from the worlds of merit, and a mass of virtue. (22)
Frequented by tigers, wild dogs, and boars, that best of mountains,
the king of mountains, shines forth with its formidable peaks and summits.
With various other merits, auspicious ceremonies, and propitious rites, as well as with the flow of the waters of the Gaṅgā, a great sound resounded. ||24||
I went there to the house of Śaṅkara on Kailāsa;
there I beheld a marvel such as had never been seen or heard before. (25)
Listen, for I shall now declare everything that has been spoken by me from the auspicious and greatly exalted peak of Meru, the king of mountains.
A great stream of snow, milk, and gold falls upon the earth from the Gaṅgā, O highly fortunate one, adorned with the cries of swans. (27)
Having reached the summit of Kailāsa, it spread out there;
measuring ten yojanas in extent, the great lake of the Gaṅgā is situated there.
He shines with great water-like merit that is stainless;
having attained auspiciousness in every respect, he is resplendent with great swans. ||29||
By the merit of chanting the Sāman hymns, which is divine and sweet,
the swans there warble melodiously, and that lake shines with splendor.
On its bank, O Mahāmati, there was a daughter of the Himavat seated upon a stone, her hair disheveled, and endowed with the wealth of celestial beauty. (31)
Endowed with a divine form and possessing the fifty divine marks and qualities,
she shines upon its bank, adorned with celestial ornaments.
I do not know whether she is the daughter of the King of Mountains or of the great ocean; nor do I know if she is the wife of Brahmā, or if she will become Svāhā.
She will be like the highly fortunate Indrāṇī, or like Rohiṇī;
such perfection of beauty as this is not seen among young women. (34)
And, dear father, whatever kind of beauty, majesty, virtue, and character is seen in other celestial women, [it is all found in her]. (35)
O limb, such is the characteristic of the beauty of the apsarases that no such form has ever been seen by me; it is the enchantment of the entire universe.
Sitting upon a stone slab, agitated even by suffering, the young girl wept with melodious voices, deprived of her many kinsmen. (37)
O high-minded one, as they shed many tears that possessed the luster of pearls and were as pure as the waters of a lake, they seemed to feel ashamed. 38.
From those [jewels], pearls with the luster of the moon fall into the great waters;
from them arise lotuses that are heart-pleasing and fragrant. (39)
O high-minded one, from these tears from his eyes, lotuses were born;
they were as innumerable as the sands of the Ganges. (40)
Those who have fallen from their friends and those who are devoid of joy—
let them all be cast into the midst of the Ganges' current, which is well-served by flocks of swans.
The current of the Bhāgīrathī issued forth from that place and,
reaching the beautiful peak of Kailāsa known as Ratna, it flowed gently.
It was filled with water, extending for two yojanas,
crowded with swans and cranes, and teeming with aquatic birds.
And there, in that place frequented by the assembly of sages, there are lotuses of various distinct colors,
pure due to their constant flow.
Those lotuses which were born from her tears became, at dawn,
as if drenched in the waters of the Gaṅgā— fragrant and magnificent.
They cross over by boat upon rivers filled with pure water, which resound with the cries of aquatic birds and are pleasant at every turn. (46)
Sūta said:
O dear one, on that mountain named Ratnākhyatu, the Great Lord Maheśvara, known as Ratneśvara, who is highly worshiped by gods and daityas, resides forever. 47.
There, a certain sage consisting of merit was seen by me;
he was burdened by a mass of matted hair, naked, and carrying a staff. ||48||
Without support and without food, he was exceedingly weakened by his asceticism; though his body was emaciated, it was a mere collection of bones wrapped only in skin. ||49||
All the limbs of that great-souled one were merely smeared with ashes;
he would eat only dry leaves that had withered and fallen.
Seated in profound devotion to Śiva, he was a great ascetic of formidable splendor;
from his tears there arose fragrant lotuses.
Having brought water from the Gaṅgā, the highly fortunate one, skilled in song and dance, should worship Ratneśvara, the God of gods. (52)
The righteous-souled one, having come to the monastery of that enemy of Tripura who was singing and dancing at his gate, laughed with loud sounds.
"O Father, best among speakers, this unprecedented thing has been seen by me;
tell it to me out of your grace, if you know the cause. (54)
"O noble lady, why does my father weep all of a sudden? Why do these gods and men worship the Great Lord (Maheśvara)? (55)
"Therefore, explain that to me in detail, for it is the cause of all my doubts.
Thus addressed by his son, the highly wise Kuñjalo replied:
He spoke at length to the monkey in the water, while the sage listened.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Deeds of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 101 ||
The one hundred and second chapter.
Kuñjala said:
"O child, I shall explain everything that you have just told me."
O best of the twice-born, that which arose from the gambling of both [parties]—[that is what I shall tell you]. ||1||
Once, the great goddess Pārvatī, the most excellent of women,
while sporting with the high-souled Īśvara, spoke these words.
O Great God, born of Māmorasi, you who possess a great desire to bestow [boons], show yourself before me—you, the one whose face is like a forest, the most excellent among those with faces. 3.
The illustrious Mahādeva said: "So be it, O Great God! I shall show you this meritorious place, crowded with gods and frequented by the twice-born and the perfected ones."
Having thus addressed the goddess along with her attendants, the god,
eager for combat, then went toward the forest of the Nandana grove.
All-pervading, beautiful, with a divine back adorned with ornaments, joined by garlands of bells and encircled by a network of tinkling bells. ||6||
Adorned with chowries, silk threads, and beautifully decorated pearl necklaces,
the bull possessed auspicious marks and resembled a white cloud.
The Great God has ascended, surrounded by ten million attendants;
[he is accompanied by] Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Manohara.
Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Puṣpadaṃta, Maṇīśvara, Atibala, Subala by name, Meghanāda, and Ghaṭāvaha; ||9||
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Cakrākṣin, Daḥ, Pulinda, Vīrabāhuka, Keśarin, Kiṅkara, Caṇḍahāsa, and Prajāpati. ||10||
These and many others, such as Sanaka and the rest, possessed the power of asceticism;
and Śiva was surrounded by hosts numbering in the tens of millions.
The Great God, accompanied by his hosts and the Goddess, entered that very forest of Nanda, which was frequented by gods and kinnaras. ||12||
The Lord of Gods showed to Girijā that most beautiful place,
filled with various trees and abounding in many flowers.
It was filled with divine splendor and abounding in blossoming flowers—
exquisite *mallikā* blooms and thickets of *mālatī* vines.
It was ever resplendent with the finest groves of *pāṭala* trees whose branches were perpetually in bloom, and with great *candana* trees of beautiful appearance. ||15||
It was frequented by forests of *devadāru* trees and crowded with tall trees, as well as with *sarala*, coconut, and betel-nut trees. (16)
It was filled with divine dates and jackfruits, bending under the weight of their fruit,
and crowded with sandalwood trees exuding a rich, pervasive fragrance.
It was beautifully adorned with seven-leaved trees that shone like the brilliance of fire,
and it was always endowed with the splendor of flowers from royal trees and kadamba trees.
It was filled with jambū trees, great banyan trees, and mātuliṅgas, as well as nāraṅgas, sindhuvāras, priyālas, śālas, and tindukas. ||19||
It was adorned with *udumbara*, *kapittha*, and *jaṃbū* trees;
it was crowded with *lakuca* trees fragrant with blossoms and with blooming *nāga* flowers. (20)
Then there were mango trees, the kings of fruits, resembling dark clouds, along with divine groves of blue *śāla* trees and thickets of *jāla* creepers.
It was frequented by vast tamāla trees resembling the sun,
and the meritorious Nandana grove was graced by Śiva’s presence.
It was adorned with other trees resembling dark blue forests, which were endowed with fruits that grant all desires and bestow auspicious results. ||23||
The Nandana grove was adorned with wish-fulfilling trees of great merit, and it resounded with the various warblings of birds singing in sweet tones. (24)
It resounded with the meritorious warbling of cuckoos and honey-bees,
and was made to ring out by the cries of birds eager for the baited hook.
It was filled with various trees and teeming with diverse herds of deer;
from the trees, various fragrant flowers had fallen upon the ground.
And that city shines like a woman adorned with fragrant perfumes when honored by her sons;
there, moreover, are great and meritorious ponds, pure with the fragrance of lotuses. (27)
The ponds were filled with water, frequented by swans and water-fowl, resembling oceans, and honored by the fragrance of their waters. (28)
That great gift of his was accompanied by hosts of brothers and celestial nymphs,
with aerial chariots, auspicious jars, and beautiful golden staffs.
There, the rows of Naṃdana and Nandana forests, together with palaces plastered with white lime, shine everywhere due to the great throngs of kinnaras.
O best of the twice-born, [it was filled] with Gandharvas and Apsarases of beautiful form,
with the diversions of the gods, and with throngs of sages who were excellent yogis.
Everywhere, the abode of Nandana shone with merit. ||32||
Thus having observed, the great-souled Bhava, accompanied by Sudevi, [approached] Śrī-Nandana, the abode of the meritorious, a source of happiness, endowed with the quality of peace. ||33||

With its courtyards possessing a splendor equal to the radiance of the sun, with rays of light shining at dawn, and consisting of gold, it was endowed with flowers and fruits that provided all objects of desire—even like the wish-fulfilling tree in the Nandana grove. (34)
Having beheld such a king of trees, the Goddess spoke to Śiva:
"O Lord, tell me the name of this most meritorious mountain, which is itself a source of all merit. (35)
Śiva spoke equally to the illustrious Sūryavara and to the divine goddess:
Śiva said— "The installation of this [image] shall be called 'Greatly Auspicious' (Mahāśubhā), and Madhusūdana shall be the foremost among the gods. (36)

Just as the creator is the one who releases the principal rivers, the Asuras, and the streams; just as the sun brings happiness to all things; and just as the earth is the foremost among all beings; [so too is he]. (37)

Just as the king of serpents is among snakes, just as the ocean is among reservoirs of water, just as food is among great medicinal herbs, O Queen, and just as the Himavat is among mountains; (so is he among men). 38.

Just as true knowledge is foremost among all branches of learning, and just as a sovereign is preeminent among all people in the worlds, so too is this king of trees the most eminent; it is a guest to all and beloved by the Lord of the Gods. (39)
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"Now, O Bhoma, proclaim the auspicious and most meritorious virtues of this lord of trees.
Having heard the words of the goddess, the god spoke everything concerning the benefit of that excellent tree.

Whatever those most meritorious gods, resembling gods and foremost among gods, may imagine, that very thing this tree named Kalpadruma, the most excellent, bestows upon those seeking their welfare. (41)
From this merit all things arise; it is difficult to attain even here for those superior in austerity.
The great lords among the gods enjoy that which is superior to life itself, divine, and composed of jewels. (42)
He heard the words of the goddess concerning Śiva, which were marvelous and contemplated by his mind;
and with her approval, he prepared a single jewel among women, endowed with excellent qualities and beautiful form.
From that excellent tree, the Daughter of the Mountain obtained one who possessed all limbs, endowed with virtues, and beautiful in form;
she was like an assistant to the god of love for the purpose of deluding the universe, seated as she was.
She is a treasury of play, the very form of the accomplishment of happiness, with eyes as broad as lotuses and endowed with every excellence;
her face is like a lotus, her hands are like lotuses, she is a beautiful lotus herself, and her form is like that of refined gold. (45)
They possess abundant, pure, and beautiful splendor, and their hair is long, very fine, well-bound, and anointed with fragrant flowers. (46)
With her hair bound by such firm locks, that young woman shines with supreme beauty;
on the parting of her hair, she appears like a garland of pearls upon the path of the trees.
Just as the radiant preceptor of the Daityas (Śukrācārya) rose over the Tilaka tree at the root of the Sīmantinī,
so too does the splendor arising from the lotus of musk shine upon the foreheads of these noble ladies like lotuses.
The brilliance of the tilaka at the root of her hair reveals the beauty of her form in this auspicious world;
it constantly enhances her great splendor upon her hair, her pearl-ornaments, and her forehead. (49)
Just as the moon shines with its splendor according to its own nature, so does he shine through his noble conduct;
he appears like the full moon, enveloped in a canopy of moonlight and a mass of cool rays.
Her face shone forth, creating splendor and renowned throughout the world;
yet even the moon, though possessed of cool rays, is diminished and eternally deprived of its full digits because it bears a dark spot. ||51||
Her face was always full and ever-joyful, perfectly stainless;
yet, upon seeing its own reflection in the blooming lotus, it found no pleasure. (52)
This lotus-faced woman, endowed with all virtues, was fashioned from my own states of being;
O Vipashyin, the wind from her mouth wafts the fragrance of her own lotus throughout the world. (53)
Overcome by shame, he suddenly took refuge in the water and remains there forever;
with minds of extreme certainty, the wise describe this as the treasury of King Cupid, filled with the arts of the ocean. (54)
His face was radiant with a row of beautiful teeth like jewels, joined with playful smiles, and his crimson bimba-like lips were shining. ||55||
Her eyebrows were beautiful, as was her nose; her ears were adorned with jewels, and her cheeks, possessing the luster of gold, were endowed with radiance. (56)
Three lines, beautifully situated upon the neck, shine forth;
indeed, these three lines here signify good fortune, virtuous character, and amorous charm.
Her breasts, firm, full, and resembling globular forms,
were like two jars of pride prepared for her consecration.
Their arms were beautiful, symmetrical, endowed with even proportions, well-rounded, smooth, golden-hued, and possessed of auspicious marks. (59)
Their hands and feet were perfectly symmetrical and lotus-colored, exceedingly cool to the touch;
they were endowed with divine marks and possessed the auspicious svastika sign upon their palms and soles. ||60||
The fingers are straight, joined like lotuses, and endowed with nails;
the nails are not too sharp and resemble drops of water.
Her complexion, born from that limb, resembles the interior of a lotus;
O beautiful woman, with a lotus on every limb, she shines like a lotus itself.
She was beautifully adorned with all the auspicious marks, like a celestial maiden;
her feet, resembling red lotuses, were smooth and exceedingly beautiful. (63)
The nails, arising from the tips of the feet, possess a form like the radiance of jewels;
and just as it is described in the treatises, so too is it seen in the limbs.
Her limbs are beautified by all kinds of ornaments— necklaces, bracelets,
and anklets— and she shines with a girdle and a waist-cord made of fine Chinese silk.
She attained supreme beauty with a blue silk garment;
she was endowed with excellent qualities through a divine, deep-red upper cloth.
Having obtained the great excellence resulting from the disposition fashioned by Pārvatī, she received joy from the wish-fulfilling tree and spoke these words to Śaṅkara: ||67||
"Just as you have described it, O deity, so has the tree been seen by me.
Whatever nature a thing is conceived to be, such it is perceived. (68)
Sūta said:
Then she, whose every limb was beautiful, approached the side of the two of them and bowed at their lotus-feet with devotion. (69)
Then he spoke these words, affectionate, heart-pleasing, and captivating:
"O Mother, tell me the reason why you have created this helpless one."
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O auspicious one, out of curiosity regarding the tree, I have indeed put it to the test;
and immediately, O lady of excellent form, the fruit has been obtained."
"You shall attain renown in the world by the name Aśokasundarī;
there is no doubt that you will be endowed with all auspicious fortune and remain childless. (72)
Soma will be renowned as Śeṣu, like the god Purandara; he will become the lord of that [lineage], a king of kings named Nahuṣa. (73)
Having thus granted that boon to him,
the daughter of the mountain (Pārvatī) went with Śaṅkara to Mount Kailāsa, filled with supreme joy.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 102 ||
The one hundred and third chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Then Aśokasundarī was born from the best of all women.
In this boat, which is endowed with the excellence of all desirable qualities through the merit of giving, [cross over].
Possessing beautiful forms and lovely daughters, she was the sweet-smiling one of the gods;
skilled in song and dance, she knew how to provide all enjoyments for her lord.
Vipracitti’s son, Huṇḍa, who was always fierce and violent,
acting according to his own will and possessed of great lust, entered Nandana.
Upon seeing Aśokasundarī adorned with every ornament,
the Daitya was pierced by the arrows of Kāma at the mere sight of her.
The great-bodied one said to her: "O inauspicious woman, whose daughter are you? For what reason have you come here to this most excellent mountain? (5)
Aśokasundarī said: "Listen well; I am the daughter of the most meritorious Śiva. I am the sister of Kārttikeya, and my mother is his own kinswoman."
"Having reached this forest of Nandana by chance in my childhood state, who are you, and for what purpose do you question me thus? (7)
Huṇḍa said:
"I am the son of Vipracitti, endowed with the characteristics of the quality of passion (rajas);
I am renowned by the name Huṇḍa, arrogant with strength, heroism, and pride."
I am the foremost even among the Daityas; there is no Rākṣasa equal to me, whether among the gods or in the worlds of mortals, in terms of ascetic power or fame. (9)

O fair-faced one, O large-eyed lady, what pride can be destroyed by the arrows of my own wealth and enjoyments in other worlds of the nāgas when it has already been struck down by the sight of you? (10)
I have come to you for refuge; be gracious and look upon me with a favorable countenance. Be my beloved wife, dearer to me than life itself. (11)
Aśokasundarī said:
"Listen, I shall explain the cause of all these connections; for in this world, it is destined for every man and woman to be born. (12)
