A husband must likewise be one who is equal to his wife in qualities; this is the path of the world in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). Listen, O Guṇḍa, according to the rule. 13.
O King of the Daityas, there is indeed a reason for this as to how I have become so; O lord of excellent wives, listen with a focused mind. (14)
O high-minded one, when I was born from the king of trees at the proper time,
I was fashioned by Pārvatī after she had carefully grasped the essence of Śambhu.
"By the will of the divine Anumati, this son shall indeed be my husband;
he will be of the Lunar dynasty, highly wise, and a soul devoted to righteousness. (16)
Victorious, equal to the Victorious One in heroism, and like fire in brilliance;
omniscient and true to his promise, he was like Vaiśravaṇa in generosity. (17)
He too was a performer of sacrifices and a lord of charity; in form he was like the god of love, a righteous soul named Nahuṣa, a great treasury of virtues and good character. (18)
"The god has granted me a husband who will be renowned;
therefore, I shall obtain a beautiful son endowed with all virtues. (19)
O Lord, by Your grace, may I obtain in battle that steadfast Yayāti, who is dear to the people and equal to Indra and Upendra in this world. (20)
"I am the wife of a hero and especially the wife of one devoted to his spouse;
therefore, you must by all means abandon this delusion, Huṇḍa, and go hence. (21)
Laughing, he spoke these words to Aśokasundarī.
Huṇḍa said:
"What you have said is certainly not proper, nor indeed was it spoken by the Goddess or by the God."
In the lineage of Soma, there will be a righteous-souled one named Nahuṣa;
though you are superior in age, he shall not be joined with the status of being the youngest. (23)
"A younger woman is praiseworthy, but a man is not praised;
when, O auspicious one, will that man become your husband? (24)
Both childhood and youth will surely pass away into destruction;
even beautiful women are always dependent on the power of youth. (25)
O woman of excellent complexion, they become beloved by men;
for youth, O fair-faced one, is the great root of young women. (26)
"By means of him, they enjoy pleasures and desires that follow their heart's wish. O blessed lady, listen to me: when will this son of Āyu come here? (27)
Youth exists only today, yet it will surely become useless;
consider also the states of being in the womb, childhood, and adolescence. (28)
"When will he, endowed with youth, become a suitable match for you?
By the power of his youth, drink the honeyed wine of spring. (29)
Having heard the words of Huṇḍa, the daughter of Śiva spoke again to me, the large-eyed one, "May you indeed sport with me in happiness. (30)
Then, filled with trepidation, she spoke to that lord of the Dānavas when the twenty-eighth age known as Dvāpara had arrived.
The remaining incarnation, the righteous-souled Balarāma, son of Vasudeva,
will take as his wife the divine daughter of Revata.
She too was born in the best of ages (the Kṛta-yuga) as Mahābhāgā; by the measure of three ages, she was indeed Jyeṣṭhā even by virtue of her power.
Born as the beloved of Bala, Revatī is equal to his very life-breath;
when the Vāpara age arrives, she shall indeed exist here.
The best of the Dānavas, having carried off the excellent daughter of the Gandharva born in the city of Māyāvatī, bound her by force. 35.
His husband is declared to be the powerful Pradyumna, the son of Mādhava,
the lord of heroes, and the grandson of the Lord of the Yādavas.
In that age, this which was to come to pass was foreseen by the ancient ones—by the highly fortunate, wise, and great-souled Vyāsa and others. ||37||
Thus indeed was the speech of the Daitya seen as it was uttered by the Goddess, the mother of the world, who was then the daughter of Himavat. (38)
Free from greed despite your desire for gain, you speak of evil deeds—those things possessed by sin and devoid of the Vedic scriptures. (39)
Whatever is firmly ordained for one, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that comes to pass for him in accordance with his prior karma. (40)
Whatever well-spoken word issues from the gods and the Brahmins—if it be true, it can never be otherwise. (41)
"By my good fortune, this has been learned; having thus considered the union of Nahuṣa and Āpīta, it was spoken by the Goddess and by Śiva. (42)
Knowing this, let your mind attain tranquility and remain free from delusion;
you are certainly not able to move my mind, O Daitya.
"O great Asura, since your mind is firm in devotion to your wife and cannot be shaken even by me, I shall consume you with a great curse; go from here! (44)
Having heard those words, the powerful Dānava Huṇḍa thought in his mind: "How might this woman become my wife? (45)
Having reflected thus, the illusory Ahiṇḍu arrived at that place of concealment;
then, leaving that spot with speed, he departed.
When another day had arrived, she created an illusion consisting of darkness.
Then those ignoble Dānavas, having assumed a divine form composed of illusion,
appeared through their magical power in the form of young maidens, O descendant of Manu.
Then, from that place, Māyā came in the form of a woman of beautiful hips, endowed with laughter and playful charm, where the abode of the Lord was located. 48.
He spoke these words affectionately to Aśokasundarī: "O beautiful one, who are you? Why do you stay here in this forest of asceticism? (49)
"O young girl, for what purpose do you perform this asceticism that withers desire? Tell me, O fortunate one, what is the cause of this most difficult practice? (50)
Having heard those auspicious words spoken by the Dānava—who was disguised in a deceptive form and filled with longing—he quickly [responded]. (51)
Deeply distressed, she related to him— just as before he had engaged in his own creation— the entire reason for his asceticism and how it had proceeded.
But she did not recognize that this was a deceptive form used by that evil-minded Dānava, for it had been described to her out of friendship. (53)
Huṇḍa said:
"O Goddess, you are devoted to your husband, intent upon excellent vows,
possessed of virtuous character and conduct, and a great, noble satī."
"O auspicious lady, I am a devoted wife, dedicated to my husband; O fortunate one, I, a great satī, perform penance for the sake of my husband. (55)
"My husband has been slain by that evil-minded Huṇḍa;
for his destruction, I am performing this most terrible and great penance. (56)
"I shall dwell in this holy hermitage on the bank of the Gaṅgā," she was told with other charming words that were intended to inspire confidence. (57)
Deluded by her friendship with Huṇḍa,
the daughter of Śiva was violently dragged away, stupefied by great infatuation.
He brought him to his own divine, incomparable, and most beautiful home—
the supreme city called Vaiḍūrya, located upon the peak of Mount Meru.
There was the great Śiva named Kāñcanākhyā, endowed with all virtues, crowded with lofty palaces, [decorated with] finials, staffs, and chowries. ||60||
It was endowed with forests filled with various trees, dark as dense clouds,
and possessed ponds, wells, lakes, rivers, and other reservoirs of water.
It was resplendent with great jewels and surrounded by walls made of refined gold;
indeed, it was filled with every object that fulfills all desires for the Dānava.
Then that beautiful Aśoka-sundarī beheld a delightful city; "O friend, tell me, whose abode is this? she asked. (63)
She said: "O highly fortunate one, that place of the lord of the Dānavas, whom you have seen before, is his; I am that preeminent among the Dānavas. (64)
"O woman of excellent complexion, you have been brought here by me through my illusory power.
Having addressed her thus, he led her to his home, which was as beautiful as the celestial realm of Śatakratu.
Having settled Sundarī there in a dwelling adorned with various chambers and resembling a peak of Mount Kailāsa, he, free from all anxiety, placed her upon a swing.
Then the lord of the Daityas, having returned to his own form and being tormented by the arrows of desire,
joined his palms together and spoke these words.
"Whatever you desire, O lady of beautiful hips, I shall grant that to you without a doubt. Worship me, O large-eyed one; worship me, who am afflicted by love for you. (68)
The illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord of the Dānavas, you are not able to move me even with your mind; nor can the delusion that has come upon me be sustained by you. (69)
"By gods like you, who are great sinners and the lowest of dānavas, this body of mine is difficult to obtain; do not speak thus again and again! (70)
Joined with the intense heat of her ascetic penance and blazing with great wrath, she,
desiring to destroy that entire host of Dānavas, quivered like the very tongue of Time.
Then that goddess spoke again to that lowest of Dānavas, who had committed such a terrible deed, for the sake of destroying his own sinful self: ||72||
By you, the destruction of your own self and of these kinsmen was brought about when the blazing fires of the black-pathed one were led into your own home. (73)
Just as an inauspicious cuckoo that has emerged from all its sorrows enters a house, it brings about the destruction of that [house]. (74)
One should desire the destruction of one's own people, of all one's possessions, and of one's family, when death enters the house. (75)
Thus, having reached your home, she strives for the destruction of you, [seeking] the loss of your sons, wealth, grain, and your very crops. (76)
Having caused you to lose your life, family, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and everything else, I shall depart; of this there is no doubt. (77)
Just as I was brought by you, I performed supreme austerity, desiring a husband—Nahuṣa, Āyu, and Danu. (78)
"O Dānava, my husband will likewise destroy you;
indeed, this means for your destruction on my account was perceived by the Lord long ago. (79)
This worldly verse is true, which wise people sing:
"The world perceives directly; those of evil intellect deny it. (80)
From whatever [cause] and by whatever means pleasure, pain, and so forth are to be experienced here, that very [cause] experiences them there; of this there is no doubt. (81)
"Enjoy the fruit of this, your own karma, upon the surface of the earth;
you shall go to the place of hell for having violated another's wife. (82)
For he brandishes a very sharp, well-edged sword with ease, yet pierces me with the tip of his finger; know me thus to be one who is easily subdued. (83)
Having approached the face of the enraged lion as it roared, he,
endowed with a courageous demeanor, seized its hair from the tip of its mouth by force.
She who is truthful in conduct, endowed with self-control, disciplined, and established in austerity—he who desires to enjoy her indeed seeks his own destruction. (85)
He desired to seize that very life-breath of the black serpent while it was still living, just as he had been sent forth at the proper time.
You were sent by that deluded Time, who is himself bewildered by time; do you not see how such a wicked intellect has arisen within you? 87.
Who else in this world can behold him, the son of Ṛtayu, except for one who attains death after having beheld his immortal form? (88)
Having spoken thus, she went to the bank of the Gaṅgā, filled with grief, distressed by suffering, and constrained by both her resolve and the lack of one. (89)
Having previously performed a terrible penance out of a desire for my husband,
I shall now again perform a harsh and dreadful penance with the intent of destroying you.
But when you, the wicked one, were slain by the high-souled Nahuṣa with sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts and like venomous serpents, [then... (91)
When I see my husband fallen on the battlefield—his hair disheveled, covered in blood, and lifeless—then indeed shall I come to him. 92.
Having thus made a firm resolve, she remained on the unsurpassed bank of the Gaṅgā, intent on the destruction of her own body, motionless and devoted to Śiva.

Just as a blazing crest of fire, radiant with its flames and endowed with brilliance, might consume the worlds, so did the daughter of the Lord of the Gods, inflamed with anger, perform difficult penance on the banks of the Gaṅgā. 94.
Kuñjala said:
Having been addressed thus, the illustrious daughter of Śiva went to the Gaṅgā; having bathed there with ashes, she called out to someone in her own city. 95.
For the sake of slaying Huṇḍa, the slender-limbed maiden Aśokasundarī performed austerities, endowed with truth and self-restraint. (96)
Huṇḍa also became distressed, his mind scorched by the curse;
burning intensely with the fires of those words, he reflected.
Then, having summoned the minister named Panaka, he spoke to him,
recounting the entire great account of how that curse had arisen for her.
"I have been cursed by Aśokasundarī, the daughter of Aśiva:
'You shall die at the hands of my husband, Nahuṣa. (99)
"Neither has he been born, nor is the womb of his mother pregnant; yet you have praised him falsely as if he were real. Act so that her curse may come to pass accordingly."
And what did he say?—"Abduct his beloved and bring her here;
in this way, your enemy will not come into being. (101)
By terrifying her with these formidable [mantras], you shall cause her to miscarry her fetus;
by this means as well, your enemy shall not come into being.
Wait for the time of birth of the evil-minded Nahuṣa; having seized him, bring him here and abandon that sinful-minded one. 103.
Thus, even though he was restrained by the three gods, that Dānava did not desist; rather, Nahuṣa became possessed of the resolve to bring about his own destruction.
Viṣṇu said:
"O highly fortunate one, there was a lord of the earth named Āyu, the son of Vīra;
he was a sovereign ruler of the whole world, righteous in soul, and devoted to the vow of truth. (105)
The king was equal to Indra and Upendra in asceticism, fame, and strength, as well as in most meritorious acts of charity and sacrifice, truthfulness, and self-restraint. (106)
Under a single umbrella, that best of kings exercised sovereign rule; he was a knower of all dharmas and an ornament to the Lunar dynasty. 107.
The king was born sorrowful because he had no son;
that righteous-souled one reflected, "How may a son be born to me? (108)
Having reached this conclusion, the lord of the earth reflected upon his lifespan;
with a highly concentrated mind, he made a supreme effort for the sake of a son.
There was the high-souled son of Atri, the great sage Dattātreya, sporting with a woman, his eyes reddened by wine. ||110||
In the western quarter, he whose nature was intoxicated with dharma was surrounded by throngs of women;
placing upon his lap a young woman, the most auspicious and excellent of all womankind.
The Brahmin, the supreme lord of great yogis, sang, danced, and drank wine profusely without his sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta). ||112||
With divine flower garlands, pearl necklaces, and fine raiment,
the lord of sages shone, his limbs anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
Having gone to his hermitage and beheld that best of the twice-born, the king, with a deeply concentrated mind, prostrated himself before him like a staff, bowing his head. (114)
The son of Atri, whose soul was devoted to righteousness, beheld the best of kings who had arrived before him with devotion; he then established himself in meditation. (115)
O best of men, for a hundred years that king remained thus:
steadfast, having attained peace, and devoted to honor and devotion.
Having summoned him, he said this: "O King Ikṣvāku, for what reason am I devoid of the conduct of a Brahmin? At one time, my status as a Brahmin did not exist. (117)
In this world, he was always greedy for liquor and meat and ever attached to women;
by virtue of the boon granted to him, he had the power to command another Brāhmaṇa to serve him.
Āyu said: "O highly fortunate one, there is no best of Brahmins like you;
you are the supreme lord in the three worlds, the granter of all desires. (119)
In this very way, O highly fortunate one, the supreme lord Govinda, whose banner is Garuḍa, has become you in the form of a brāhmaṇa. 120.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord!
I have come to you for refuge, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek your protection. 121.
Having made Hṛṣīkeśa your own, you stand as the one who upholds;
indeed, you are the wise leader of all beings established in the universe. 122.
I know you, O Lord of the World, to be Bhava, that Madhusūdana;
protect me alone, O Govinda—salutations be unto you in your universal form! 123.
Kuñjala said:
After a long time had passed, Dattātreya, assuming an intoxicated form, spoke to the best of kings: "Carry out my word. (124)
"Give me a skull-cup filled with wine and cooked meat as my meal.
Having heard these words, King Āyu [acted accordingly].
Eager and impetuous, he brought the surā liquor with a skull-cup, and having quickly cut off a well-cooked piece of meat with his hand, [he offered it]. 126.
The king of men also gave [these] to Dattātreya, the most excellent;
then that bull among sages became one whose mind was full of grace.
Having observed his devotion, his power, and his supreme service toward his guru,
he spoke to that lord of men, Āyu, whose mind was intent on making a vow.
"O King, choose a boon that is difficult to obtain on this earth;
I shall grant you everything, whatever you desire. (129)
The king said:
"O best of sages, you are the giver of boons; out of compassion, grant me a son endowed with virtues, omniscient, and possessed of all good qualities. (130)
He possessed divine vigor and great splendor, and was unconquerable by gods and dānavas, as well as by kṣatriyas, terrible rākṣasas, dānavas, and kinnaras. (131)
He was devoted to the gods and the Brahmins, especially a protector of his subjects;
he was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, a hero, and compassionate toward those who sought refuge. ||132||
He was a donor, a non-possessor of wealth, and a great soul; he was learned in the Vedas and the Shastras, skilled in the science of archery, and devoted to the sacred scriptures. ||133||
One whose intellect is unstruck [innate], who is steadfast, and undefeated in battles—one endowed with such qualities and handsome form is the one from whom a lineage is produced. (134)
O Lord, please protect this illustrious son of yours, the upholder of the Avataṃsaka;
or else, O All-pervading One, out of compassion, you should grant him a boon. (135)
Dattātreya said:
"So be it, O illustrious one; you shall have a son who will be a virtuous protector of the earth, a benefactor of all living beings, and a performer of meritorious deeds. (136)
Endowed with these qualities and possessed of devotion to Viṣṇu, he becomes a sovereign emperor, a lord of men equal to Indra. ||137||
Having thus granted the boon, the great yogin gave this unsurpassed fruit: "Let me be given as a husband to that virtuous wife. (138)
Having spoken thus and dismissed Āyu, who stood bowed before him, he honored him with blessings and then vanished from sight.
Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Deeds of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Story of Eno" in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fourth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
When that illustrious and great sage Dattātreya had departed, [the following occurred].
O great king, he returned to his own city with his life. ||1||
Joyfully, he entered the palace of Indumati, which was endowed with splendor, filled with all desired objects, and resembled the abode of Indra. ||2||
O best of the twice-born, that wise king ruled his kingdom together with Indumati, the daughter of Svarbhānu, just as Indra rules in heaven.
And that Queen Dumatī, by eating fruits from the womb [of the tree],
gave birth to one endowed with divine splendor, according to the word of Dattātreya.
O noble father, this night has been joined with day for me as I have seen an unsurpassed dream, which bestows many auspicious blessings. (5)
He entered that house and saw a man resembling the sun,
a brahmin adorned with a necklace of pearls and graced by white garments.
A garland made of white flowers shines upon his neck;
his limbs are adorned with all manner of ornaments and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents.
He had four arms, holding a conch, a mace, a discus, and a sword; and an umbrella was being held over him, resembling the orb of the moon.
Shining with great splendor, adorned with divine ornaments, he was resplendent with necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and anklets. ||9||
Adorned with two earrings that resembled the moon and the sun, such a man of great wisdom arrived. (10)
Then, having summoned Indumatī, that beautiful woman was bathed with milk from a conch shell filled with milk, which was as white as the moon.
Again and again, he [was seen] with a white elephant, beautiful in form, possessing a thousand excellent heads, and bound by a golden chain set with jewels.
A blazing great jewel, filled with a mass of radiant flames, was hurled by him from the tip of his mouth; yet once again, it became a pearl. 13.
"What can be done for this wicked-minded woman, even by the lords of the gods?
Having said this, the one of great fame placed his lotus-hand upon her head and returned to his own abode. ||14||
Having seen such a great dream portending an excellent son, that highly fortunate woman related it to the long-lived lord of the earth.
Having heard this, the great king reflected once more;
he then summoned his preceptor and related his excellent dream.
The king said to the highly fortunate Śaunaka, the omniscient one and the best among the wise:
"O best of the twice-born, this very night my wife gave birth to a highly fortunate son."
Entering the house at dawn, he was seen [by his wife] and asked, "What is this cause of my dream?
Śaunaka said: "A boon had been granted to you previously by the wise Dattātreya. (18)
O King, that auspicious fruit which was ordained for the sake of a son has been rendered futile; why was it not communicated by you? 19.
Having heard these words spoken by the king, "I have given her to a worthy wife," Śaunaka, the most excellent of the twice-born and possessed of great wisdom, spoke.
By the grace of Dattātreya, an excellent son endowed with a portion of Viṣṇu shall be born in your house; of this there is no doubt.
O King, I have thus explained to you the cause of this dream;
a son equal to Indra and Upendra, endowed with divine prowess, shall be born to you.
Your son shall be the soul of all dharmas, the enhancer of the Lunar dynasty; he will be virtuous in both the science of archery and the Vedas. (23)
Having spoken thus to the king, Śaunaka went home;
the king, filled with great joy, remained together with his beloved.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Story of Eno," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||104||
And so ends the one hundred and fifth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
The daughter of Danu went with her companions to play in the forest.
There, he then heard those great words of his father, which were unpleasant to hear.
While the perfected celestial bards were speaking with great joy, he was born with immense vigor, possessing great heroism and prowess equal to that of Viṣṇu. ||2||
"O Huṇḍa, this best of sons will come into being and he will do that;
such was the great speech, unpleasant and bringing sorrow. (3)
Having heard what was reported by the messenger who had arrived before his father,
he briefly related that which was so distressing in the presence of the king.
Then, in the presence of his father, he spoke; having heard it, the father was struck with wonder and recalled the curse of Aśokasundarī and what had been done in the past.
For this purpose, this Aśokasundarī performed penance,
while that wicked Dūnamatī constantly practiced austerities for the very sake of destroying the fetus.
The wicked and evil-minded one, drawn by Time, exerted his efforts;
having become a constant seeker of flaws, he [watched] her who was possessed of poor intellect.
When he saw that queen, endowed with the qualities of beauty and nobility, possessed of divine splendor, and protected by the power of Viṣṇu; ||8||
Endowed with divine splendor and resembling the orb of the sun, she was praised;
by her side, O highly fortunate one, he stood ever ready for her protection. (9)
From afar, that wicked demon, displaying many things to her,
manifested various kinds of fierce spells and terrifying threats.
Protected by the splendor of the embryo and by the splendor of Viṣṇu,
no fear shall ever arise for her, just as there is none for the wind.
The effort exerted by the wicked-souled Huṇḍa in sowing the seeds of charity was fruitless and useless; not even the slightest thing he desired came to pass.
Thus, as he gazed for a full hundred years,
the son of Svarbhānu then brought forth a son for the daughter of the Nāga king.
During the night itself, the best of sons was born to her;
by his splendor he shone intensely, like the sun in the vault of heaven.
Sūta said:
Now, a certain very wicked maidservant came to the lying-in chamber;
she was engaged in impure practices yet spoke words of great auspiciousness. (15)
Having learned all of this, Guṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas,
entered the body of a maidservant and thus entered the palace of Āyu.
While the great multitude was fast asleep, utterly deluded by sleep,
he took that son, who shone like the offspring of a god, and went outside.
Having arrived at the city named Kāñcanākhyapura,
that lowest of Dānavas summoned his beloved wife Vipulā and spoke these words.
"Slay this great sinner, my enemy in the form of a child;
afterwards, let him be delivered into the hands of the cook for his meal. (19)
"O highly fortunate one, cook [him] mercilessly with various methods and diverse means from the hands of the cooks;
afterwards I shall eat him, of this there is no doubt. (20)
Hearing those words of her husband, Vipulā was struck with great astonishment:
"Why does my husband, so exceedingly cruel, resort to such heartlessness? (21)
Whose son, endowed with all auspicious marks and resembling a divine infant, would a man devoid of patience and utterly merciless dare to devour, and for what reason? (22)
Thinking thus, filled with compassion, she questioned her husband again: "Why do you devour the child? (23)
"Why are you so enraged, O lord of the Asuras, utterly devoid of shame? Tell me the entire reason for this in truth."
And he briefly related his own fault as it had occurred,
as well as the curse pronounced by Aśokasundarī and by the evil-minded Huṇḍa.
She understood all that to be the reason for the Dānava's [action]:
"This child must truly be slain; otherwise, he will cause the destruction of us both. (26)
Having reflected thus, she, overcome by intense anger, summoned Mekhalā and spoke these words: "Sairandhrī! (27)
"Kill this wicked child today in this solitary great kitchen;
place him in the hands of the cook for the sake of Huṇḍa's meal. (28)
Taking the boy Ekalavya, he summoned his cook and said: "Carry out the king's command today; cook this boy. (29)
Having heard this,
that noble-minded cook took the boy from his hand, raised a weapon, and prepared himself for action.
Protected by the splendor of Dattātreya, the god of gods, this son of Āyu laughed again and again. (31)
Beholding him again and again, the cook was filled with compassion;
moved by pity, Sairandhrī addressed that cook. (32)
"O Sūda of great intelligence, this child is not to be killed by you; he is endowed with divine marks. Whose son is he, born into such a noble family? (33)
The cook said:
"O auspicious lady, you have spoken the truth with compassion.
To whom does this beautiful boy belong, endowed as he is with the marks of royalty?"
"Why will this evil-souled Huṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas, enjoy [the fruits of his deeds], since our lineage was previously protected by him through his own virtuous actions? (35)
Even in calamities, one may live through these hardships, but not otherwise;
whether carried away by the force of the ocean or entered into the midst of fire. (36)
In this world, that body which possesses action as its companion truly lives;
therefore, action endowed with dharma and merit is highly esteemed.
O venerable Tona, they proclaim happiness from that;
for it protects the one who crosses over, the protector, the worker, and the one who is vigilant for his own welfare. (38)
It constantly bestows liberation and grants the state of loving-kindness;
it is endowed with the merit of giving and characterized by actions accompanied by pleasant speech. (39)
When one who performs virtuous deeds acts with helpfulness, karma certainly protects that very person at all times; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Driven by one's own karma, one goes to another womb; what can the father, mother, or other kinsmen and relatives do? (41)
"But for one who is struck down by his own karma, there is no protection.
Sūta said:
"By that very same karma, however, the son of Nanda was protected."
Therefore, moved by compassion, the cook became subject to the power of his karma;
likewise, Sairandhrī was born as a result of being impelled by her own past actions.
By those two alone was Suta, who possessed beautiful marks, protected;
he was brought from that house to the great hermitage during the very night.
In that very great hermitage, at the auspicious door of a leaf-hut, Sairaṃdhri, by virtue of her meritorious deeds, was staying in the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha. (45)
After setting down that most excellent child in his own home, he had the deer killed by a cook and ate its meat right there with me. 46.
Having fed the lord of the Daityas, Druhiṇa then became overjoyed;
the Asura then considered the curse upon Aśokasundarī to be infallible.
Filled with great joy, that lord of the Guṇḍas, Kuñjala, spoke;
and when the clear dawn had arrived, the most excellent sage Vasiṣṭha said: 48.
The righteous-souled one, having gone outside, looked from the door of the hut;
seeing the boy there, complete and endowed with divine marks. (49)
He was perfectly full, resembling [the moon], beautiful, and with lovely eyes.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O sages, all of you come and behold this boy. (50)
"By whom and by what means was this brought to the courtyard of my gate at night—this object, which possesses the marks of royalty and has the luster of the offspring of gods and gandharvas? (51)
Then the sages, the best of the twice-born, filled with great wonder and joy, beheld that stainless one who resembled ten million suns. 52.
Then Vasiṣṭha, that righteous-souled one, beheld the son of those two high-souled ones; having perceived the boy through his spiritual knowledge, he [recognized him].
He related the life-story of that wicked and evil-minded Huṇḍa, as well as the account of Āyuputra, who was renowned and endowed with virtuous conduct.
Out of compassion, the son of Brahmā rose up and seized Subālaka with both hands, as soon as that most excellent of the twice-born did so.
Then the gods rained down a shower of flowers upon their son;
the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang a charming song with beautiful voices. (56)
The sages praised the king with Vedic hymns;
then, having gazed upon him, Vasiṣṭha granted him a boon.
"O lord of men, he shall be known in the world by the name Nahuṣa; for even in his childhood, he was never corrupted. (58)
"Therefore, by the name Nahuṣa, you shall become one worthy of worship by the gods.
Then that best of the twice-born performed for him the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
The undertaking and relinquishing of vows, the characteristics of the guru, the disciple, and so forth;
and having studied the Veda in its entirety, along with its six limbs and the padapāṭha and kramapāṭha.
And having studied all the sciences from Vasiṣṭha, the best of the twice-born,
that highly intelligent one mastered the science of archery along with its secret doctrines.
He [bestowed] divine weapons and missiles, along with the methods for seizing and releasing them;
as well as the sciences of knowledge, logic, royal polity, and the various virtues.
And the son of Āyu, born from Vasiṣṭha, was devoted as a disciple;
thus the exceedingly handsome son of Nahuṣa was fully accomplished in every way. 63.
By the grace of Vasiṣṭha, he became a wielder of the bow and arrows.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 105 ||
The one hundred and sixth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
O highly fortunate ones, [this is] the son of Svarbhānu’s daughter, Āyu’s wife.
I beheld that Tīsubāla, who was like a god and beyond compare. ||1||
Raising a great cry of lamentation, the woman of excellent complexion ascended [the palace], asking:
"By whom has this boy, endowed with auspicious marks and possessing beautiful characteristics, been carried away? (2)
O son, he has been attained through austerities, gifts, sacrifices, and difficult observances,
as well as through repeated hardships and terrible trials.
Filled with compassion for Ruru, she said: "By the meritorious and high-souled Dattātreya, who was well-pleased, a son was granted; by whom has he been taken away? (4)
"Alas, you who were like a son to me! Alas, you who were a treasure-house of the virtues of a youth! Where have you been taken away by that wretch? Let my voice be returned to me! (5)
"You are undoubtedly the ornament of all that is praiseworthy;
by whom have you been stripped of your life while still endowed with this [splendor]? (6)
"Endowed with divine and auspicious marks of a king, that lotus-eyed child—by whom has he been abducted today? What shall I do, and where shall I go? (7)
I clearly know what was done by me in another birth;
for whom was a deposit destroyed? Therefore, my son has been taken away from me. (8)
Or rather, by whom was it adorned with deceit in a previous birth? Otherwise, how could one experience the suffering resulting from that evil deed? (9)
A thief of jewels has been born; my jewel-like son has been stolen from me. Therefore, by fate, this one of incomparable qualities has been taken away. (10)
Or rather, what unconsidered fault of mine has led to this fruitlessness of that deed? Without a doubt, I have now attained this state, intensely filled with grief for my son. (11)
Or what hostility toward infants was committed by me in another birth, that such is the fruit of that sinful deed of eating [the flesh] of a child? (12)
And for one who is begging before the Vaiśvadeva rite, what is the difference between food that has not been offered and that which has been offered by the twice-born with the Vyāhṛtis? (13)
Thus, at that time, the highly fortunate Indumatī, overwhelmed with compassion by grief, [spoke] to Sudeva because of his son Svarbhānu.
Having fallen and fainted from grief, she became utterly distraught;
sighing deeply, she was like a cow separated from her calf.
King Āyus, overcome by great grief and sorrow upon hearing that his son had been carried off, abandoned his fortitude. (16)
There is no fruit of austerity, and there is no fruitlessness of giving;
since my son has been taken away in this manner, therefore it is so, without a doubt. (17)
In the past, Dattātreya, out of his grace, granted me a boon:
a son who was invincible, endowed with victory, and possessed of all virtues. (18)
"How indeed did an obstacle arise for that granting of the boon?"—pondering thus, the king, overcome with grief, wept bitterly. (19)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana within the Account of Nahuṣa," in the *Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya* of the *Evenopākhyāna* section of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and seventh chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Then that Nārada, having come from heaven, approached King Āyu.
Having arrived, he said: "O King, why do you grieve so suddenly?"
"O high-minded one, O great king, the abduction of your son today has brought misfortune even to the gods and others; knowing this, do not grieve for yourself. (2)
Your son will come, having become omniscient and endowed with all virtues, possessed of all specialized knowledge, and perfected in all arts.
He by whom this boy, who resembles a god in his qualities, was carried away today—without a doubt, he has brought him to his own home as a great king would take a captive. (4)
Then that king, possessed of great heroism and great strength,
will come to you along with the daughter of Śiva.
A son equal to Indra and Upendra shall be born by his own splendor;
he too shall enjoy the status of Indra through his own meritorious deeds.
Having thus addressed the king, the best of divine sages departed suddenly while he and his followers were looking on.
When that illustrious Narada, who was like a god, had departed,
Ayus approached the queen and reported all of that to her.
The son bestowed by Dattātreya, the most excellent among the best of gods—he and all those kings are well through the grace of Viṣṇu alone. (9)
O Queen, even if your son is unfriendly, provided he is indeed virtuous,
he will return once more after taking his head with him.
Thus spoke Nārada, "O auspicious lady, do not grieve;
abandon this great delusion which destroys one's duty and dharma. (11)
Having heard these words of her husband,
Queen Sudarśanā was then filled with joy regarding the arrival of her son.
As it was spoken by the divine seer, so shall it come to pass;
having been granted by Dattātreya, this body of mine shall be free from old age and death.
"There will be no doubt; indeed, this very thing appears to him.
Having thought thus, he bowed down to that bull among the twice-born. 14.
Salutations to that great-souled one, the bestower of success upon Atri, who is the excellent son [of Brahmā];
by whose grace I have obtained this wise, very steadfast, virtuous, and highly meritorious excellent son. (15)
Having spoken thus, the queen Aditi, distressed with grief, became silent, awaiting her son Nahuṣa’s return. (16)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana," within the "Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha" section of the "Story of Nahuṣa" in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and eighth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, possessed of great splendor, was the best among those who perform austerities.
Having summoned that Nahuṣa, she spoke these words.
"Go quickly to the forest and bring abundant wild flowers.
Having heard the sage's words, Nahuṣa went to the forest. ||2||
There, the powerful Nahuṣa heard of someone of excellent conduct: "This is that virtuous-souled and heroic one named Nahuṣa. (3)
The son of Āyu, who was possessed of great wisdom, was separated from his mother while still a child;
due to this very separation, Āyu’s wife wept bitterly. (4)
Aśokasundarī has also performed most difficult austerities;
when will that auspicious queen Indumatī see her son? (5)
The daughter of Śiva, who was without support, performed penance for the sake of the son of Nahuṣa, the knower of dharma, who had previously been abducted by the Dānavas.
For the sake of the young girl Aśokasundarī, who is the daughter of Āyu, he too will come into contact with Kadāsāhi. (7)
Thus the righteous-souled Nahuṣa, overcome by delusion, heard those words concerning the assembly hall, spoken by the divine deliberators.
Having gone there and taken forest produce,
that righteous-souled one presented the forest offerings to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha at his hermitage.
With palms joined in reverence, the Supporter of the Earth, bowing with devotion, spoke to that highly wise Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity. (10)
"O Blessed One, listen to these unprecedented words uttered by the Cāraṇa:
'This one named Venaḍhuṣa, the son of Āyu, has been separated [from his life]. (11)
Enduring thousands of hardships caused by the wicked-minded Dānavas, that young girl performed extremely difficult penance for the sake of Śiva. 12.
"O Preceptor, such was the sign of this wise Nahuṣa;
all that was spoken by them has indeed been heard by me. (13)
Who was that Āyu, that righteous soul? Who was the auspicious Vadumatī? Who was that Aśokasundarī, and who is called Nahuṣa? (14)
This doubt has arisen within me; may you, sir, please dispel it:
who else is this other person of great wisdom, and where is that Nahuṣa? (15)
"O dear one, tell me all of that, for there must indeed be another underlying cause.
Vasiṣṭha said: "Āyu was a king of righteous soul, powerful and the sovereign of the seven continents. (16)
The wife of Dumatī was Satyarūpā, renowned for her fame;
in her you were born as a son, Vaiguṇamaṇḍira. (17)
By King Āyus, the ornament of the Lunar dynasty, [she was married];
she, a daughter of Hara, was adorned with beautiful hips, virtues, and beauty. (18)
Named Aśokasundarī, she was fortunate and possessed a beautiful smile; for his sake, she performed penance in a forest of asceticism, remaining without support. (19)
The Creator, having determined it through his power of yoga, ordained you as her husband;
she, taking refuge on the bank of the Gaṅgā, was fully absorbed in the yoga of meditation.
Then Huṇḍa, the lord of the Dānavas, seeing that virtuous woman alone—blazing with ascetic fervor, auspicious, and possessing lotus-like eyes—[approached her]. (21)
Afflicted by the arrows of desire, he approached her who was endowed with the virtue of magnificent beauty and said to her, "Become my wife."
Having heard these words of Sātā, the ascetic woman said to him: "Do not commit such a rash act; do not speak thus again and again. (23)
"O hero, you have not attained me, especially since I am the wife of another;
it was by fate that the son of Āyu, possessed of great strength, was created for me long ago."
One named Nahuṣa will become wise, of this there is no doubt;
Devadatta, possessed of great splendor, you shall cause to change otherwise.
"Therefore, I shall cast a curse by which you will be reduced to ashes.
Having heard these words, he was tormented by the arrows of desire.
Having been deceived by him through a pretext and led into his own abode, that illustrious one recognized her and cursed that lowest of Dānavas.
Your death shall come at the very hand of Nahuṣa;
it will happen while you are still unborn, just as it happened while Aśvatthāman was already born.
Satvāmāyu’s son, Vīra, was abducted by the sinful Huṇḍa;
he was rescued by Sūda and sent as a messenger to my hermitage by the maidservant. (29)
O child, that which was proclaimed by the Cāraṇas and Kinnaras upon seeing you there in the midst of the forest has now been related to me by you once again.
Wipe away the tears from your eyes for that lowest of dānavas named Huṇḍa, the doer of evil, who has been abandoned by you. (31)
"Go, O mighty one, and having gone there, behold the bank of the Gaṅgā;
having struck down that lord of the Dānavas, bring him from his palace. (32)
"You indeed became the husband of her who was named Aśokasundarī.
All this has been told to you as the reason for this question. (33)
Having addressed Nahuṣa, the wise brahmin ceased speaking.
Having heard everything uttered by the sage—which was truly marvelous—and reflecting upon it, one son of Āyu, desiring to cut him down, then gave way to anger. (35)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 108.
The one hundred and ninth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Having prostrated and propitiated Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity, [he spoke].
Then the archer, bow in hand and arrows in his grasp, went forth toward Āma. ||1||

That son of Āyu—well-cooked with the meat of the ena deer, eaten by me while he was still a child and unguarded by his own intellect—was virtuous, handsome, god-like, and endowed with divine qualities. (2)
Then,
having thus addressed that wicked Daitya, the cook, with great joy, fed him that very meat which had been well-prepared, seasoned, roasted, and made savory.
The Dānava ate that meat, which was endowed with delicious flavor;
filled with joy, he went to Aśokasundarī.
Then, his mind overcome by passion, the son of Āyu quickly said to her: "O auspicious lady, your husband has been devoured by me."
Devote yourself to me alone, O fair-limbed one, and enjoy pleasures that are agreeable to your heart;
what will you do with this mortal man whose life has come to its end?
Having heard this, the ascetic daughter of Śiva replied:
"The gods have granted me a husband who is free from old age and devoid of faults. (7)
"His death has not been seen even by the gods or by the high-souled ones.
Having heard these words, the Dānava of wicked conduct [spoke].
Laughing again and again, he said to that large-eyed woman:
"O beautiful one, today my life and my son have been consumed by me."
Having heard these words regarding the wicked-souled Nahuṣa as soon as he was born, he became filled with a most dreadful anger.
She, who was established in truth and purified by austerity, spoke again:
"Indeed, this very austerity has been practiced by me with my mind and with self-restraint."
Āyusuta and Cirāyu will indeed come to be through truth alone. ||11||
Go away, you of evil conduct, if you wish to live;
otherwise, I shall curse you once again, without a doubt. (12)
Having heard this from her, the cook said to the king:
"O Great King, abandon her and take refuge with another. (13)
Sent by the cook, that evil-minded Daitya, Sahuṇḍa,
went out in great haste toward his own beloved wife.
She did not know at all the actions performed by her maidservant and cook;
she reported everything that had occurred to her beloved. (15)
Sūta said:
Indeed, by means of great austerity, Aśokasundarī—who was tormented by suffering and grief and had become emaciated through her asceticism—[attained her goal]. 16.
Thinking of that Priyaṅkā, he meditated upon her again and again:
"What will the Daityas not do, even by means of various stratagems? (17)
Those who possess knowledge of skillful means always proceed with constant wisdom and exertion,
and they always engage with various states of being.
Formerly, I was carried off by that sinner through the employment of illusory means;
likewise, my son will be slain, and so too will Ayo. (19)
Having seen one who is destined to be free from affliction through the power of destiny, what would one see even with effort, or what indeed would not perish?
Or rather, would it not [perish]? 20.
Is this effort supreme, or is it the fruit born of that action?
How might future existence be destroyed? Only from that [knowledge] does the Veda stand firm.
"How could that which has been cultivated with distinction by the gods be otherwise?
Thus did I, O highly fortunate one, reflect again and again. (22)
There was a great-bodied Kinnara named Vidvaras, possessing a massive frame; his body was human from the navel upward, yet it was entirely devoid of wings. (23)
Having two arms, with his hand holding a conch and adorned with bracelets,
his limbs smeared with divine sandalwood paste, he arrived together with his wife.
He spoke to that daughter of Śaṅkara, who was distressed along with her son: "For what reason do you grieve? Know that this best of gods has arrived. (25)
"I am a Kinnara devoted to Viṣṇu, sent by the best of the gods; you must not feel any sorrow on account of Nahuṣa. (26)
O auspicious lady, for the sake of killing that wise one, Huṇḍa committed every possible evil deed; his life-span was taken away.
O gods, though protected by Satu and Vaira and despite various means employed, Huṇḍa alone understands this: "The son of Āyu has been carried off by me. (28)
O lady of very large eyes, O auspicious one, having caused you all to hear [this], that lowest of Dānavas has indeed departed after devouring the offspring of the Earth. (29)
O highly renowned lady, even for one who is not virtuous, your husband lives on solely by the ripening of his own karma acquired in a previous birth. (30)
Even by the power of merit alone, the lifespan of those who have earned it for themselves has been fashioned; yet the slayers desire its destruction despite their great fortune. (31)
Evil-minded and greatly sinful, they are detractors of the splendor of others; for the sake of destroying their fame, they spread [falsehoods] day after day. (32)
Then, by various means such as poisons, weapons, and the like,
they seek to kill that meritorious person who is protected by his own virtuous deeds.

And the wicked ones, such as Huṇḍa and others, afflict those great sinners with various kinds of delusions, such as the destruction of their intellect, by means of powerful and unrestrained stratagems. (34)
O highly fortunate one, through the application of well-performed deeds earned in previous births, even merit is well-protected by that which possesses merit. (35)
O auspicious lady, the expedients of those sinners indeed go to futility—those very vows, protections, refuges, weapons, fires, poisons, and bonds. (36)
They protect the Great-Souled One, who is well-guarded by the merits of the gods;
those who attempt to harm him are reduced to ashes, while he alone remains, possessing all merit.
O auspicious one, the protective deities of the heroic Āyuputra [regard him] as a heap of merit and indeed a treasury of all ascetic powers.
Therefore, the hero Nahuṣa, the best among the strong,
was protected by truth, austerity, merit, self-restraint, and self-control.
Do not inflict terrible suffering upon yourself, and abandon this groundless grief; that righteous-souled one lives happily even without mother and father. (40)
He dwells alone in a penance grove, protected by ascetics;
he is a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and has reached the further shore of the science of archery.
O slender-waisted one, just as the moon shines with its own digits by means of its own luster,
so too does he shine with his own digits.
Through his sciences, great merits, ascetic penances, and likewise through his fame, that slayer of enemy heroes, the destroyer of foes and beloved of the gods, shines resplendent. (43)
Having slain the lord of the Daityas, Huṇḍa, he shall obtain you alone;
together with you and the woman, he shall be the sole sovereign on earth. ||44||
"O auspicious lady, you shall obtain a noble son comparable to Vāsava, just as the great yogi Vāsava [Indra] dwells in heaven. (45)
[He saw] Yayāti, a knower of dharma devoted to the protection of his subjects,
as well as a hundred daughters endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtuous qualities.
By their merits, O Great King, you shall go to the world of Indra;
and by those merits, the divine Nahuṣa, whose prowess is meritorious, shall enjoy the sovereignty of Indra.
A son named Yayāti shall be born to you, a righteous soul, a great king who protects his subjects and is devoted to compassion for all living beings. (48)
He will have four sons of great majesty,
endowed with strength and heroism, who will reach the further shore of the science of archery.
The first was named Caturu, the second was named Puru, the third was named Uru, and the fourth was the powerful Yadu. (50)
Thus, these sons will be of great heroism, radiant, and possessed of great strength; they will be high-souled and endowed with all splendor. ||51||
The sons of Yadu were indeed heroes, possessing prowess equal to that of lions;
hear from me now their names, O Bhadra, with full attention. (52)
Bhoja, Bhīmaka, Aṃdhaka, and Kuñjara,
as well as the one named Vṛṣṇi, who is virtuous in soul, shall be Satyādhāra.
The sixth was Śrutasena, and the seventh was Śrutādhāra; the eighth was the mighty Kāladaṃṣṭra, who was powerful and victorious over Time in battle.
O fair-faced one, the sons of Yadu shall be known as the Yādavas and will possess great heroism;
their sons and grandsons, in turn, will become thousands in number.
In this way, O Nahuṣa, your lineage will become like that of Uśanas;
having completely abandoned suffering, proceed with happiness.
O lady of auspicious countenance, your husband, possessed of great wisdom, will come to you after slaying the Dānava Huṇḍa; he shall marry none other than you.
And from her eyes, which are born of suffering, parched, and hot, tears fall; he who bestows honor wipes away those tears of the woman of poor intellect. 58.
Having uprooted the suffering of his kin, he will deliver his own family;
having made his father happy, he will become a protector of his subjects. ||59||
All this discourse of the gods has been told to you, O auspicious lady;
casting aside sorrow and grief, conduct yourself with happiness.
Aśokasundarī said:
"O knower of dharma, if my husband is indeed destined for me by the gods, tell me the truth; do not increase my misery. (61)
Vidvara said:
"O beautiful one, listen; you yourself shall soon behold your husband.
Having spoken thus, the Gandharva then departed for the abode of the gods.
There, Aśokasundarī,
the daughter of Śiva, indeed performed penance, having completely renounced desire, anger, and greed.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha," in the *Upākhyāna* of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and tenth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
He addressed all the sages, beginning with Āma, and Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who practice austerity.
Nahuṣa was filled with longing and desired to go toward the Dānava.
Then all those sages, Vasiṣṭha and the others, whose wealth was their asceticism,
greeted that mighty son of Āyu with blessings and salutations.
All the deities in the sky joyfully struck their vīṇās and rained down a shower of flowers upon the head of that army of Huṣa.
Then the thousand-eyed god Indra arrived together with the deities and bestowed upon him weapons and missiles that were like the splendor of the sun.
O best of the twice-born, that tiger among kings received those divine weapons from the gods,
and he became like one possessing a celestial form.
Then all those deities spoke to the thousand-eyed one:
"O Lord of the Asuras, let this [position] be given to this Nahuṣa."
O twice-born one, having understood the will of the gods, Vajrapāṇi summoned his charioteer Mātali and commanded him.
"Go now to that high-souled one, the greatly wise Āyudha, who is prepared for battle, together with Syandana, his banner, and his chariot. (8)
Saci said to the thousand-eyed one, "You shall carry out your command.
Having spoken thus, she quickly went to the son of Āyu, who was prepared for battle.
He spoke thus to the king regarding the words of the King of the Gods:
"O Knower of Dharma, may you be victorious in battle with this chariot."
Thus spoke the Thousand-eyed One: "O Lord of Kings, abandon this evil-minded Dānava Huṇḍa in battle! (11)
Having heard this, the king, along with his queen, experienced horripilation born of joy,
due to the grace of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, the god of gods.
I shall slay in battle that evil-minded Dānava, who has especially practiced deceit against the gods and me. (13)
When these great words had been spoken by the high-souled Huṣa, the Lord himself, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace, arrived there. 14.
Having uprooted one wheel after another—each as vast as the orb of the sun, blazing with radiant splendor, perfectly circular, and bringing auspiciousness—[he advanced]. (15)
Indeed, with great joy, the god gave it to Nahuṣa;
Śambhu gave him a trident that was exceedingly sharp and endowed with splendor.
With that excellent spear, he shone as he prepared for battle;
he was like a second Śaṅkara, the Lord who destroyed Tripura.
Brahmā gave him the Brahmāstra, Varuṇa the supreme noose, and Candra the auspicious conch that resembles the brilliance of fire. ||18||
Indra gave him the thunderbolt, as did Śakti; Vāyu gave him the bow along with arrows;
and likewise Agni gave that high-souled one the fiery weapon.
The high-souled gods gave many various divine weapons and missiles to that king of great prowess. (20)
Kuñjala said: Then the son of Āyu,
honored by the gods and saluted with blessings by the sages who know the truth, [departed].
He ascended a divine chariot, radiant and garlanded with jewels,
resounding with the cries of "ghaṃ" and "ṭā," and filled with the tinkling of small bells.
O King, shine with this divine and beautiful chariot upon the path of heaven,
just as the sun indeed shines with its own splendor.
In the same way, he swiftly went with great speed upon the heads of the Daityas through his splendor, like the ever-moving wind.
Where that wicked Dānava stood, accompanied by his own forces,
there [he went] together with Mātali, the high-souled charioteer.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, in the Greatness of the Guru-Tīrtha, in the Episode of Eka, in the Bhūmi-Khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 110 ||
The one hundred and eleventh chapter.
Kuñjala said:
While that hero Nahuṣa, who was equal to the king of the gods, was setting out for battle...
All the women there followed along, accompanied by curious and auspicious songs. ||1||
Then the gods, the excellent Āryās, the foremost Apsarases, and the Kinnarīs, eager with curiosity, sang with their voices, O best of beings. (2)
Likewise, Gandharvas and noble women, adorned with beautiful ornaments, went there out of curiosity to where the king was staying. ||3||
There was a city named Mahodaya belonging even to the evil-minded Huṇḍa;
it was adorned everywhere with divine groves and pleasure gardens.
That best of cities was adorned with houses possessing seven stories, beautified by water-jars,
and shining with great flagstaffs bearing banners.
That supreme city was resplendent with divine mansions that resembled the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, lofty and reaching toward the heavens, endowed with every splendor.
With divine forests and groves, and with lakes resembling oceans,
filled with water and beautifully adorned with lotuses and red water-lilies.
It was adorned with walls made of great jewels, hundreds of watchtowers,
and moats filled to the brim with clear water.
It was resplendent with various other great jewels, elephants, and horses; it was crowded with beautiful women and men of great luster. (9)
The best of kings, the great hero Nahuṣa, beheld that city of great prosperity, which was resplendent with various divine powers.
The great hero entered that divine forest on the edge of the city, adorned with celestial trees, just as an immortal enters Nandana.
Then that righteous-souled one, together with Mātali, entered the middle of the forest on the bank of the river in a chariot, O King.
There, noble celestial beings endowed with beautiful forms gathered together;
the Gandharvas, who knew the true essence of song, sang songs for the best of kings.
All the charioteers and bards praised that best of kings, the son of Āyu, who was resplendent like the sun. (14)
Nahuṣa heard a sweet song sung by a kinnara.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa within the Life of Cyavana," in the *Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya* section of the *Evenopākhyāna* within the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and twelfth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Having heard that very song sung by the celestial damsels with fixed musical cadences, he [listened].
And there, the daughter of the king became agitated with anxiety as she reflected upon him. ||1||
Rising quickly from her seat with great enthusiasm, that woman of beautiful limbs, endowed with a spirit of austerity,
departed swiftly.
Having seen him, who resembled a god, possessing a divine form and radiance, with limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with celestial garlands; ||3||
The king’s son was adorned with divine ornaments and garments, radiant like the sun, and endowed with divine marks. ||4||
Or could he be a great wise god, or perhaps a gandharva? Or might he be the son of Naga, or even a vidyadhara? (5)
I do not see him among the gods, nor how he is born among the yakṣas;
by this very play, even the thousand-eyed Indra is born as a hero.
"Is this the mind-born god of love?
Or could it be the friend of his father, this lord of wealth, the descendant of Pulastya? (7)

While she was reflecting thus, the goddess Rūpaguṇādhipā, accompanied by her radiant great female companions, quickly approached and, laughing, spoke these auspicious words to the daughter of Bhuśuṇḍa. (8)

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa within the Life of Cyavana," in the *Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya* section of the *Evena-upākhyāna* within the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and thirteenth chapter.
Bhava said:
"O auspicious lady, having abandoned this asceticism, what else do you behold?"
There would be a depletion of ascetic merit even from thinking about a person. ||1||
Aśokasundarī said: "Even the gods, asuras, and great serpents are not capable of moving me, whose mind is absorbed in penance and who is desired even by Nahuṣa."
"O highly fortunate one, seeing him, my mind wavers greatly; having become thus filled with longing, I wish to go there to see him. (3)
Thus there was this perversion of the mind alone toward Rāvaṇa;
therefore, tell me the cause of that, if you possess supreme knowledge.
"I am the wife of Āyuputra, created by the high-souled gods; why does my mind feel such longing, even though I desire only to sport? (5)
Raṃbhā said:
"O noble lady, in all these forms of bodies, the eternal Self, whose nature is knowledge, dwells as Brahman itself. (6)
Although bound by the sense organs which are bound by their functional processes and serve as instruments of utility— and which consist of the snares of delusion— he remains forever liberated.
O beautiful one, he who does not know *prakṛti*—which consists of the sequence of knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*)—is not a knower of the Dharma, even though this self is pure. (8)
Even while going along, having seen this great-minded one, he abandons this mental anguish and, casting aside sin itself, runs toward truth alone. //9//
"This husband of yours is indeed the son of Āyu; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Having seen another man marked by sinful characteristics, you became suspicious. (10)
Thus was the rite performed by the gods, bound by the noose of truth,
so that even her son shall attain the status of husband to her.
"O auspicious one, O beautiful lady, having heard this which was spoken by yourself, I have remained here myself, accepting that relationship as being true in its essence. (12)
She does not know any other state of being, yet she gives birth to the Son of Life;
O Goddess, Prakṛti does not even know her own husband when he has arrived. 13.
Knowing this, the Self, who is not subordinate to anything else, hastens [to liberation] this very day;
the Self knows all, for the Self is the eternal God. (14)
This is that very one, the powerful hero named Dronahusha;
if it is your desire, he truly wishes to establish a relationship with you. (15)
"O blessed lady, having known the son of Ācārya, he does not go to another;
all this eternal truth that was in your mind has been told to you. (16)
Having slain the most terrible Huṇḍa, that lowest of Dānavas in battle,
he will lead you to your own abode, the supreme home of Āyī.
O hero, having been carried away by the Daitya and left behind due to the merit of Droṇa’s son,
you have indeed been separated from your own kinsmen since childhood, O hero.
Deprived of both father and mother, he will surely go to his father’s house after growing up in the great forest; you yourself must go there immediately.
Having heard these words spoken by Śiva,
the daughter of the ocean was filled with great joy and spoke to him.
This very husband of mine, truthful and possessed of great heroism, is excessively distressed in mind, overwhelmed and agitated by grief. (21)
O lady of beautiful smiles, the god knows with perfect certainty that there is no such thing as a mind; this truth has been seen by me in its wonderful variety. (22)
"O friend, having seen this man who possesses divine marks and is equal to the God of Love himself, why does your great heart not run toward him? (23)
Likewise, O blessed lady, he does not consider himself equal to any other man;
therefore, this matter must be kept secret by us two along with our friends, right here in the house. (24)
Having spoken thus, he prepared to depart;
perceiving that she was eager to go toward the presence of Nahuṣa, he set out on his journey.
She said to him at that time: "O Lord, why are you not going?
Sūta said:
"Out of fear, I was moving along with my friend toward Nahuṣa, who possesses the marks of a hero. (26)
Having approached him with great joy, she sent her friend [to him], saying: "O noble lady, go to Huṣa, who possesses divine beauty."
"Tell this story, for you have come here for my sake.
He said, "O friend, O lady of excellent vows, I shall do this very pleasing service for you."
Having spoken thus, he approached King Danu, the son of Bhanu,
that hero bearing bow and arrows, who was like a second Indra.
She replied with these excellent words, her voice trembling: "O illustrious son of Āyu, I have come here seeking you. (30)
I have been sent by Vīratā, the daughter of Śiva;
long ago, for your sake, she was sent by the God of gods and the Goddess.

A wife of excellent form, most sublime and difficult to find in the worlds, is hard to attain even for the best of men, for the gods led by Indra, or for those whose wealth is their asceticism. ||32||
It has come here of its own accord for your sake, accompanied by Gandharvas, Pannagas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas endowed with meritorious marks; listen now to this.
That jewel among women, full of great wisdom and fashioned by merit, remained engaged in ascetic penance for the sake of one named Aśokasundarī. (34)
O Bhava, you have performed most intense austerities because you always desire her;
knowing this, O highly fortunate one, please accept me who am devoted to you. (35)
"Except for you, O noble lady, she does not ask for any other man.
Having heard what was said by Nahuṣa, that speech was duly considered.
Then Bhīma gave this reply: "O Rāma, let my words be heard;
I understand everything that has been spoken by you before me. (37)
"Everything that was previously told to me by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, I know it all; her penance is indeed supreme. (38)
"Listen, O blessed lady, to the reason why we do not go to that excellent woman, so that there may be happiness for you: because we have not killed the demon Huṇḍa. (39)
I know all this to be perfectly true;
indeed, your birth was for my sake, and penance was practiced by you.
"This body has been made by you, O lady, as my wife according to sacred ordinance;
having made a firm resolve for my sake, you have performed penance. (41)
From that place, I was carried away by that most wicked one who is devoid of all restraints;
indeed, I was taken from the birth-chamber by that vile Dānava.
"O Goddess, he remains in the state of childhood, deprived of father and mother;
therefore, I shall slay that Hunda, the lowest of the Dānavas."
"Afterwards, I shall lead you to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having spoken thus to her, who was dear to him and wished him well, he [departed].
Thus dismissed by him, she returned quickly and spoke to Queen Aśokasundarī concerning him.
"In brief, O best of the twice-born, everything was thus [expressed] by Raṃbhā.
Having heard these well-spoken words, Aśokasundarī—
Filled with joy at the sight of the heroic Nahuṣa,
she remained there with her dear friend, free from fear.
"I shall always observe what kind of prowess my husband possesses. (48)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the *Evenopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and fourteenth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Now, all these Dānavas were the attendants of Huṇḍa.
I shall also relate the conversation of Nahuṣa exactly as it was heard from him out of fear. ||1||
They related everything that had been well-spoken to Huṇḍa, the lord of the Daityas;
having heard it, he became enraged and then spoke these words to his messenger.
"Go, O hero, at my command and learn of the man's welfare;
let that man converse with her, the daughter of Śiva. (3)
Having heard the command of his master,
the swift Dānava went to the secluded Vīra Nahuṣa and spoke these words to him.
He stands ready with a divine chariot drawn by horses and a charioteer;
indeed, he is terrifying within the assembly hall with his bow and celestial arrows.
By whom and for what purpose have you been sent?
And by whom were you dispatched here today, O Lord, by this daughter of Śiva or by another?
Tell me clearly and in its entirety everything that was said;
O Lord, how is it that you do not fear Huṇḍa, the crusher of gods? (7)
Tell me all this if you wish to live;
go quickly and stand before the unbearable lord of the Dānavas.
Nahuṣa said:
"Know me to be the son of that powerful King Āyu, the lord of the seven islands and the destroyer of all the Daityas."
O Lord, the one renowned by the name Nahuṣa, who was a worshiper of the gods and Brahmins,
was carried off by Huṇḍa in his childhood and killed by that Dānava.
This very daughter of Śiva was also abducted by the Daitya in the past;
she now performs severe penance for the sake of slaying Huṇḍa as well.
I, that child who was brought from the lying-in chamber by you, was given into the hands of a wicked-souled servant, even by a maidservant. (12)
Listen, for the purpose of his execution, I have arrived today as the destroyer of this wicked Huṇḍa Daitya, a man of evil deeds. (13)
"O most sinful one, know me to be that very [goddess] who shall lead other terrible Dānavas to their destruction as well"— thus she spoke to the Dānava.
Having heard all this from the high-souled Nahuṣa,
that wicked-minded one went to Guṇḍa and reported his speech.
Hearing that from his mouth, the lord of the Daityas immediately became enraged:
"Why has that sinful cook struck her with the weapon while she was innocent? (16)
"This disease, which I have neglected, has now reached full growth;
therefore, I shall destroy it with this inauspicious maiden. (17)
"O son of Āyu, with these arrows sharpened on stone, break his arm-armor in battle.
Having reflected thus, he spoke these words to his charioteer. (18)
Having summoned the commander-in-chief, he, being deeply distressed, spoke thus: "Harness this chariot with excellent and auspicious horses. (19)
"Prepare my army; array the heroic elephants with their riders, and the warriors on horseback with banners, parasols, and chowries. (20)
"Quickly mobilize my fourfold army today!
Having heard this from Huṇḍa, that [minister] was swift to act.
The highly wise commander-in-chief performed everything according to the prescribed rites;
he was surrounded by that great fourfold army.
They approached the heroic Nahuṣa in battle, who bore a bow and arrows,
was yoked to Indra’s own chariot, and was the best among all wielders of weapons.
The gods of great majesty, stationed in their celestial chariots in the sky, behold that hero of immense power rising in battle, who is difficult even for the gods and dānavas to overcome.
It was enveloped in flames of splendor, like a second sun.
Sūta said:
Then all those Dānavas showered him with excellent arrows.
They fought in that battle with that high-souled Nahuṣa using swords, nooses, great spears, javelins, and axes.
Like clouds thundering upon a mountain, they rushed forward;
and beholding that prowess, the powerful son of Āyu [reflected].
Drawing his bow, which was like the rainbow of Indra, he produced a sound from the string;
the sound of that great-souled one’s bow was like the crash of a thunderbolt. (28)
Caused by Nahuṣa, that which brought fear to the brahmins and the dānavas resounded with a great roar, and because of that sound, the dānavas trembled.
In this great battle, her heart was overcome by dejection and her courage was broken. //30//

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Story of Eno, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and fifteenth chapter. Kuñjala said:
Then that high-souled one, honored as the king of ascetics, stood ready, bearing his bow.
Just as Time, when enraged, desires to destroy all the worlds, so too did he [desire] to destroy the Dānavas. ||1||
With great nets of arrows equal to thunderbolts and exceedingly radiant, he struck down the Dānavas;
just as the wind uproots trees here on earth, so did the king strike down the Dānavas. ||2||
Just as the wind, by its own strength and power, disperses a mass of celestial clouds,
so did the king destroy the asuras, who were intoxicated with pride, with his most excellent and exceedingly sharp arrows.
All the dānavas were unable [to withstand] the shower of arrows from the high-souled one;
some died, some fled, and some perished in that great battle. ||4||
Sūta said:
Seeing that son of Danu, who possessed great luster and great wisdom and was the destroyer of the great Dānavas, the evil-minded Huṇḍa became enraged. (5)
Having approached him who was standing there, he addressed him in the midst of the battle, saying, "Stay! Stay!
Today I shall lead you before Yama, the son of Āyu."
Nahuṣa said:
"I stand here in battle; I have come to slay you.
I shall now kill you, O Dānava of sinful mind."
Having spoken thus, he took up his bow and arrows resembling tongues of fire;
with a parasol being held over him, he shone like Śaṅkara himself in the Kṛta Yuga.
He spoke these words to Mātali, the divine charioteer of Indra:
"Drive my chariot today into the presence of Huṇḍa. (9)
Thus addressed by that hero,
Mātali, who is swift in prowess, urged on the horses whose speed was like that of a great wind.
Then those steeds leapt up, and I too rose into the sky upon that excellent chariot, which was of dark hue and adorned with banners, while the umbrella was held aloft.
Just as the sun shines brilliantly upon reaching the vault of the sky,
so did Āyuputra shine with his immeasurable splendor and prowess.
Then Huṇḍa, though mounted on a chariot, shone with his own splendor;
he was equipped with all weapons and likewise remained steadfast in the vow of a hero.
Then the battle between those two heroes was astonishing to the gods; it was exceedingly great, terrible, and inspiring of fear. 14.
Then King Subāhu was struck by Huṇḍa with sharp, whetted arrows, fletched with heron feathers and having stone-tipped shafts, between his two arms.
Pierced by Subhāla’s five arrows, he then became enraged;
yet, pierced by those arrows, the king shone even more brilliantly. (16)
The sun, rising with its garlands of rays, appeared as if reddened by blood,
its body smeared with gore from the golden arrows lodged within it.
The king shone like the sun at the beginning of the day;
having witnessed his prowess, he spoke these words to the Dānava.
"Stay, stay for a moment, O Daitya! Behold once more my agility!
Having said this, he rushed at the Daitya and struck him with ten arrows. (19)
Struck by Mukhebhāla, he fell down unconscious;
meanwhile, the gods of divine vision beheld that one of great strength from above.
The gods, the cāraṇas, and the siddhas raised a cry born of great joy; "Victory! Victory! they cried, O Indra among kings, and blew their conchs again and again.
Accompanied by a tumultuous sound and the cries of the gods, that noise entered the ears of the unconscious Huṇḍa.
Having heard this, he took up his bow and an arrow resembling a venomous serpent and cried out: "Stay! Stay! I am not dead; I have been struck by you! (23)
Having spoken thus, rising once more and endowed with agility,
he struck Nahuṣa again with twenty-one arrows.
With one [hand] he held the middle of his fist, with four the middle of his arms,
with four the great horses, and with the ninth indeed the parasol.
Having pierced Mātali with five arrows and the interior of the chariot with seven,
the Dānava struck the flagpole with three sharp shafts feathered with peacock plumes.
Seeing the grasping, the cause, the weighing, and the liberation of that evil-souled one, as well as his lightness, the deities were filled with wonder. (27)
The king beheld his manly prowess, that best of Dānavas: "You are a hero, you are one accomplished in learning; you are courageous and skilled in the art of battle. (28)
Having spoken thus, the king, displaying swift prowess, drew his bow and pierced that Dānava with ten arrows.
With three arrows he cut down his standard, which fell to the surface of the earth;
with four more shafts, he struck down his horses.
With a single [arrow], he of swift prowess cut off his umbrella;
with ten [arrows], he dispatched his charioteer to the abode of Yama.
Having cut that bow with ten arrows and shattered it,
he pierced the lord of the Asuras in all his limbs with thirty shafts.
Deprived of his horses and chariot, the wielder of the bow, with arrows in hand,
rushed forward with great speed, raining down sharpened shafts.
Bearing a sword and shield, the Daitya rushed toward that king;
as Huṇḍa was charging, the monarch cut off his sword.
The king cut through his armor with sharp razor-headed arrows;
then the wicked-souled Huṇḍa, having observed him, immediately [attacked].
He of swift prowess quickly seized a mallet and hurled it;
the king then beheld him approaching with the speed of a thunderbolt.
Then,
by his own prowess, he struck down that resounding mallet with ten sharp, razor-edged arrows.
Seeing the mallet fallen on the ground in ten pieces,
he raised his club with great force and rushed toward the king.
With a sharp-edged sword, he severed his arm, which, along with its mace,
fell to the ground together with its bracelets and armlets.
Then, letting out a great roar equal to the crash of a thunderbolt,
with his limbs smeared with blood, he rushed forward into the great battle.
Possessed by great anger and desiring to devour the king,
he approached the side of that monarch, being difficult to restrain.
Struck in the heart by Nahuṣa with a great spear, that Dānava suddenly fell to the earth like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt. 42.
When that Daitya had gone to the earth, the other Dānavas arrived;
some entered various difficult terrains, while others took refuge in the netherworld.
When that great sinner Huṣa had been slain by the high-souled [Kaca], the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas attained great joy.
When that foremost of Daityas was slain in the great sacrifice, all the gods attained supreme joy;
and Āyu’s son, having obtained her who possessed a divine form and had been nurtured by ascetic penance, was filled with delight. (45)
