Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa," within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Episode of Eno, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 115 ||
The one hundred and sixteenth chapter. Kuñjala said:
Aśokasundarī, filled with fear yet thrilled by the merit [of her deeds], spoke.
Having approached the powerful Nahuṣa, that ascetic woman spoke to him.
"I am your wife by dharma, ordained for you by the gods, though I am but an ascetic woman.
Marry me, O hero, if you desire this dharma here."
"O best of kings, while remaining engaged in asceticism, I have always been meditating upon you; it is by the grace of Dharma that you have been obtained by me."
Nahuṣa said: "O noble lady, if you remain steadfast in penance for my sake,
by the word of my preceptor, I shall become your husband in a mere moment."
"O beautiful lady, let us go together with Aṅgāra;
having mounted her upon this delightful chariot. (5)
With that very same excellent chariot, the one of great renown proceeded with great speed toward the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha along with those two.
Having seen that brahmin who had come to the hermitage and having bowed down to him,
he of great splendor was filled with immense joy along with her.
Just as the battle had unfolded in the fray and the lowest of the Dānavas was slain,
he reported everything to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha, having heard of Nahuṣa’s conduct,
was filled with great joy and honored him with blessings.
When an auspicious lunar day and the lord of the ascendant had arrived,
that bull among sages caused their marriage to be performed in the presence of the sacred fire and Brahmins.
O high-minded one, having been thus sent back by the couple with blessings, he went quickly and beheld his mother and father.
And upon seeing you, O observer of noble vows, let your mother and father attain an increase of joy, like the ocean on a festival day. (12)
Thus dispatched by that heroic sage, the son of Brahmā,
he proceeded with swift strides in that very same excellent chariot.
Having then paid homage to that lord of the twice-born,
Mātali departed for his own city to see his father and likewise his mother.
Sūta said:
Then, sent by the gods from among the hosts of Apsarases,
Menakā, with great sorrow, fell into an ocean of grief for the sake of Āyu’s wife.
She spoke to that illustrious lady, Queen Indumatī, regarding Śoka: "O illustrious one, abandon your grief; behold your son together with his daughter-in-law. (16)
Having slain the wicked Dānava who had abducted your son,
he has returned to that assembly hall, endowed with the splendor of a hero.
Camenikā, being of evil intellect, reported to him how Nahuṣa had committed that misconduct with her.
Having heard the words of Menakā, she was filled with great joy and said in a faltering voice, "Friend, you speak the truth. (19)
It is said to be nectar-like, very dear, and that which inspires the mind;
indeed, my very life and all my possessions are to be given by me unto you. (20)
Having been addressed thus, the queen spoke these words to the king:
"Your mighty-armed son has indeed arrived at this very moment. (21)
O great king, this foremost of Apsarases, having addressed her husband alone, ceased speaking, filled with great joy. (22)
Having heard that praise of the king of men, he spoke to his beloved:
"O highly fortunate one, this was indeed spoken of old by the sage Nārada. (23)
"O King, you must never again experience such sorrow regarding your son;
for having slain that Dānava with his great heroism, your son shall return. (24)
"O Goddess, that which was spoken by the Sage of the Lotus Navel at the very moment of his birth was indeed the truth;
how could his word ever be otherwise? (25)
Dattātreya, the best of sages, will become a god manifest before you; O Goddess, he was served by me through penance in the past. (26)
By him, that jewel of a son, a wearer of the Vaiṣṇava mark, was given;
he shall always slay the supreme Dānava of sinful mind.
The slayer of all Daityas, the protector of subjects, and possessed of great strength—this most excellent son was granted to me by Dattātreya as a portion of Viṣṇu. (28)
Having thus addressed Queen Cenumatī,
the king then celebrated a great festival in anticipation of his son's arrival.
Filled with great joy, he then remembered Viṣṇu once again.
This supreme reality, endowed with all perfections and possessed of a form like that of the host of gods, is the singular ultimate truth;
it removes the afflictions of men and bestows happiness, granting the highest liberation to true Vaiṣṇavas. (31)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa" within the Life of Cyavana, in the Section on the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Story of Eno, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||116||
The one hundred and seventeenth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
Nahuṣa, together with his beloved wife, spent his time in joy.
By means of that divine [vision], by his birth, and by his boon. ||1||
He arrived at the city named Nāga, which was endowed with every kind of beauty,
filled with divine auspicious objects, and adorned with magnificent mansions.
It was provided with golden archways, adorned with banners,
resounded with the sounds of various musical instruments, and graced by celestial bards from all directions.
It was adorned with men whose merit made them resemble gods,
as well as women of celestial beauty, along with elephants, horses, and chariots.
It was filled with various auspicious sounds and the resonance of Vedic chants,
as well as the sounds of singing and musical instruments, and the tones of lutes and flutes.
He entered that most excellent city, which was filled with every kind of splendor,
being honored by the chanting of Vedic auspicious hymns and by the brahmins themselves.
The hero beheld his father and his mother, who was full of merit;
filled with great joy, he bowed at the feet of his father.
With a face full of longing, she bowed again and again with devotion at the feet of both Aśoka and Sundarī.
Having prostrated and addressed his own guru, Nṛpanandana also displayed affection for the one named Bhācasāna.
He inquired after the health of his mother and father;
thus addressed, the illustrious one, with tears and bristling hair, [replied]. (10)
Āyu said:
"This very day diseases have perished, and both suffering and grief have departed;
O son, by the sight of you, the entire world rejoices in supreme satisfaction."
I have achieved my purpose and been truly born upon the birth of you, O one of great majesty;
having performed the upliftment of my own lineage, I myself have been delivered.
Indumati said:
"O highly fortunate one, just as the great ocean attains increase upon reaching the full moon and beholding its splendor,
so do I [attain increase] from the sight of you."
I have grown strong, I am greatly delighted, and I am filled with joy; O wise one, bestower of honor, by the sight of you, I have become blessed. 14.
Having thus addressed his son, that best of offspring,
he embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, just as a cow licks her own calf.
Then Queen Puṇyā, with auspicious blessings, honored Nahuṣa, who was of divine form, as he arrived at Abhinandya, the son of Dyutimat.
Sūta said:
Then the son spoke to his meritorious mother, Queen Indumatī,
concerning the account of how he had been carried away.
The one of great fame likewise [described] the birth and attainment of his own wife, as well as the battle with Huṇḍa and the slaying of Huṇḍa. (18)
In brief, he himself related that entire account of his parents exactly as it had occurred, which brought them great joy. (19)
Having heard of their son’s heroic endeavor, his parents were filled with great joy; their hearts became completely fulfilled. (20)
Nahuṣa, having taken up the bow of Indra with its arrow,
conquered the entire earth with its seven islands and its cities.
He offered the earth, filled with wealth, to his father,
constantly gladdening his father through the performance of good deeds consisting of charity and righteousness.
At that time, they caused their father to perform sacrifices such as the Rājasūya,
along with great sacrifices, gifts, vows, observances, and restraints.
The two parents were fully gratified by the son of Āyu through liberal gifts, fame, merit, and sacrifices that result in great religious merit.
Then the gods, having assembled at the supreme city called Nāga,
consecrated the high-souled Nahuṣa, the subduer of heroes.
Then, by that king Āyu, together with sages and perfected beings (siddhas), he was consecrated in his own kingdom along with the daughter of Śiva.
Accompanied by his wife and his own body, the righteous King Āyurāja, possessed of great fame, went to heaven, highly honored by gods and siddhas. ||27||
Having abandoned that very spot and gone again to the world of Brahmā, he then proceeded to the world of Hara, honored by sages and gods. ||28||
By his own deeds and by the great splendor of his son, this king, having gone to the world of Hari through his merits, dwells there, O Great King.
O highly fortunate one, such supreme merit as this must be produced by men known for their meritorious deeds; what is the use of others who only cause grief? (30)
Nahuṣa, whose nature was consistent with his birth, was a savior of his ancestors; he was the upholder of his entire lineage and a scholar of wisdom. ||31||
All this conduct of that king has been related to you; I shall now speak of another, O son of Vadapu, tell me, what more do you wish to hear? 32.
A mortal who hears this meritorious, purifying, and glorious life-story of the son of Āyu likewise enjoys all pleasures and attains the abode of Murāri. (33)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Nahuṣa within the Life of Cyavana, in the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Episode of Eka, in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa."
The one hundred and eighteenth chapter.
Kapiñjala said: At the mouth of the Gaṅgā, a noble woman was weeping before the city-gate.
And from his two eyes, drops of tears fell into the great water. ||1||
In the midst of the Gaṅgā, lotuses emerge, possessing divine forms, fragrant and magnificent. (2)
O noble one, for what reason do these pure drops of tears fall from her beautiful eyes like the waters of the Ganges? (3)
Reduced to nothing but skin and bone, yet wearing matted hair and bark garments,
he again searches for those fragrant lotuses.
Having brought divine golden-colored [flowers], one should worship Śiva;
tell me, O great-minded one, what is that woman like? ||5||
Having worshipped Śiva, he then suddenly reviles him;
tell me all of this, if I am dear to you. (6)
Kuñjala said:
Listen, O child, I shall relate the account fashioned by the gods—the life-story of the high-souled Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins. (7)
That Huṇḍa, possessed of great heroism, was slain by Nahuṣeṇa at the gateway;
his son, the renowned Vihaṇḍa, has now undertaken ascetic penance.
Having heard that his father, along with his ministers and retinue, had been slain by the heroic and powerful Nahuṣa, the son of Āyu, [he was overcome with grief].
Out of anger, I am prepared to consume the gods with my ascetic power;
such is the prowess of that wicked one, who has been strengthened by his own penance.
All the deities know that Huṇḍa’s son, Vihuṇḍa, is intent on destroying the three worlds; he is indeed unbearable on the field of battle. ||11||
"I shall avenge my father's enmity; I will slay these gods and men.
Thus did the wicked Kaṃṭaka prepare himself for the slaughter of gods and brahmins.
He began to cause calamity and oppressed the subjects;
scorched by his very splendor, the gods, led by Indra, [sought refuge]. ||13||
They went for refuge to Viṣṇu, the high-souled God of gods, the Lord of the world, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace. (14)
And they spoke, seeking protection constantly from the great fear of Vihuṇḍa.
Śrī Viṣṇu said: "O all you gods, O Maheśvaras, may you prosper with great happiness. (15)
"I shall destroy Vihuṇḍa, the most wicked Devakaṭaka.
Having spoken thus to the gods, Janārdana assumed his illusory form (māyā).
Then the one of great fame, remaining there himself,
assumed a form consisting of illusion, endowed with the five qualities, in the likeness of a woman.
The highly fortunate Viṣṇu-māyā, who deludes the entire universe, assumed an incomparable form; she is the Māyā that utterly bewilders even Viṣṇu. 18.
Kuñjala said: For the sake of slaying Vihuṇḍa, she who was endowed with incomparable beauty and charm went by the divine path for the purpose of killing the gods. 19.
Then the lord of the Daityas beheld that illusion created by Tārā;
deluded by her, the demon was overwhelmed by the arrows of desire.
He did not realize his own destruction, seeing that excellent woman who was like the very form of Death, possessing a luster like refined gold and endowed with the wealth of beauty. (21)
The greedy and wicked-souled Vihuṇḍa spoke to that excellent woman:
"Who are you, O lady of beautiful hips, who agitates my mind? (22)
Grant me union with these auspicious ones; protect, protect me, O lady of beautiful countenance! Through union with you, O Mistress of the Gods, whatever I desire shall be accomplished. (23)
"O highly fortunate one, this is difficult to obtain even for gods and dānavas.
Māyā said:
"O Dānava, if you desire to enjoy me alone, then give me my dowry. (24)
And he worshipped Śaṅkara with as many as seventy million divine flowers, produced from the Kāmoda tree, fragrant and difficult even for the gods to obtain. ||25||
O great-souled one, place this garland made of flowers upon my head; O Danava, give this gift to me.
"Then I shall become your beloved wife, of this there is no doubt. Vihuṇḍa said: "O Goddess, I shall do exactly as you say; I grant the boon you have requested."
Overcome by passion, the lord of the gods roamed through those divine and auspicious forests, yet he did not see that tree.
Wherever he went, he himself asked about the tree called Kāmodaka; people replied, "The tree named Kāmodaka does not exist. (29)
Being thus questioned, the wicked-minded one, tormented by the arrows of desire,
went to Bhārgava and, bowing with devotion, asked him.
[He saw] a desire-yielding tree (*kāmodaka*) and a *brūhikā* plant covered in flowers.
Śukra said:
"O Dānava, there is no such tree as the *kāmoda*; there is only a woman. (31)
When she laughed out of excessive joy due to that impulsive encounter, even the most excellent intellects of the Daityas and the gods were bewildered by that laughter.
These divine flowers are undoubtedly for the sake of fragrance; they are heart-pleasing, yellow-hued, and endowed with a sweet scent. (33)
Even for one who worships Śaṅkara with only a single flower,
Śaṅkara fulfills his desired great wish.
From her weeping, the Daityas arise without a doubt;
likewise, there are great red flowers of that very same nature. (35)
"One should not allow them to touch [the cow] without Saurabheyī.
Thus he heard those words spoken by Śukra.
She asked: "O son of Bhṛgu, where is that place of great joy?
Śukra said: "At Gaṅgādvāra, which is immensely meritorious and the destroyer of great sins. (37)
There, the city named Kāmoda was constructed by Viśvakarman;
by means of that city of Kāmoda, women were adorned with divine enjoyments.
Likewise, she shines with ornaments and is well-worshipped by all the gods;
you must go there yourself and worship that most excellent Apsaras.
O Asura, even by means of merit and skillful methods, one should cause her to laugh;
having spoken thus to the Yoginī, he became enraged toward the Asura.
The one of great splendor ceased and became intent upon his own task. ||41||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmā," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the Story of Eka, in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. || 118 ||
The one hundred and nineteenth chapter.
Kapiñjala said:
"O dear one, from whose laughter indeed do friends become enemies?"
Flowers of divine fragrance, difficult even for gods and asuras to obtain. ||1||
O Mahāmati, why do all the deities desire [him]?
Śaṅkara comes joyfully when he is well-worshipped with flowers that cause laughter. (2)
Tell me in detail all the qualities of that flower, so that Kāmakandalā, the daughter of Kautuka and an excellent woman, may become his wife. (3)
From laughter, excellent flowers appear in that [lotus] every day;
tell me, what is the merit [of this], and explain it all in detail. (4)
Kuñjala said:
In ancient times, having established the highest friendship with the gods and the great daityas,
they churned the ocean of milk, being intent upon obtaining the nectar of immortality.
From the churning of the gods and demons, four jewels among maidens were first revealed by Varuṇa, and likewise again by Soma.
Afterwards, merit was revealed as the nectar situated within the jar;
previously, the four maidens desired the welfare of the gods. ||7||
One was named Sulakṣmī, and she alone was the peerless Vāruṇī; another was celebrated by the name Jyeṣṭhā, while yet another they call Kāmodā.
O Mahāmati, among them, she who was born first was the most excellent;
therefore, she is renowned in the world as Jyeṣṭhā and is always worshipped. (9)
And that which had the form of drinking wine (vāruṇī), arising from the foam of milk, became known as Kāmodā, produced from a wave of nectar. ||10||
From Soma, Lakṣmī was likewise born, as was [the goddess] from the nectar;
Soma, the ornament of the three worlds and the beloved of Śaṅkara, was thus born. 11.
Vāruṇī was born from Mṛtyurogahara, as were the Asuras;
Jyeṣṭhā, who bestows great merit, was born for those who desire the welfare of the worlds. 12.
The goddess named Kāmodā, who bestows merit, shall arise from the nectar;
for the pleasure of Viṣṇu, she will assume the form of a tree.
It shall always indeed bring delight to Viṣṇu;
there is no doubt that the name of Tulasī will be meritorious. (14)
If she were to offer even a single leaf of Tulasī to Kṛṣṇa after having first placed it upon her head, the Lord of the World would undoubtedly take pleasure in her; of this there is no doubt. (15)
"I shall always give him assistance as he goes on his way"—one who thinks thus will become a source of joy to him. (16)
Thus was she formerly born from the ocean, named Kāmodā;
when that goddess laughs, she speaks with a voice faltering with joy. (17)
Indeed, fragrant flowers of friendship fall from her mouth; he, being diligent, gathers those unfading, beautiful blossoms.
One should worship the god Śaṅkara, as well as Brahmā and Mādhava;
the gods are well-pleased with him and grant whatever he desires.
When she weeps, afflicted by sorrow, tears flow forth from her eyes and fall. (20)
Those very flowers are highly auspicious, pleasing to the heart, and exceedingly large; yet he who worships Śaṅkara without them [is deficient]. (21)
For him, suffering and torment arise; of this there is no doubt.
Yet, with such flowers, the evil-minded one worships the gods even once. (22)
The gods cause him suffering there; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has this entire, supreme narrative called Kāmoda been recounted to you.
Then Kṛṣṇa, having reflected and observed the valorous audacity of the wicked Vihuṇḍa, as well as his exertion and that rashness at that time, [acted].
"I shall send Nārada; he will delude this one who is difficult to overcome.
Then Nārada, having heard these words of the high-souled Viṣṇu, [set out].
As the evil-minded lord of the Daityas was departing toward Kāmodā, Nārada went up to him and spoke to that king of the Daityas as if laughing: 26.
"O Lord of Daityas, where have you been? Why are you so hurried and distressed? For what purpose, for whose sake, and by whom were you sent? (27)
Having paid homage to the son of Brahmā with palms joined in reverence, he replied:
"O best of the twice-born, I have set out for the sake of kāmoda flowers. (28)
The righteous-souled one said to him, "What need have you for flowers? To which the best of brahmins spoke again, explaining his own purpose.
In a certain grove of Naḍana, a woman with a beautiful face [appeared];
by the mere sight of her, I fell under the sway of desire. (30)
O best of Brahmins, I was told by her: "Worship the Great God with seven crores of flowers produced from the Kāmada tree."
"Therefore, I shall undoubtedly become their beloved wife;
for that purpose, I have set out today toward the city named Kāmoda."
I shall desire that woman; listen to my vow:
I shall make her laugh again with the delight of my mind and with great laughter. (33)
Being pleased, the highly fortunate lady blessed him again and again; that laughter of hers was faltering, O Brahmin, and increased my sense of unworthiness. (34)
Therefore, divine flowers will fall from his laughter;
with them, I shall worship that god, the beloved of Umā, this very day. (35)
"By this offering of worship, may the Lord Śaṅkara, the master of all beings and the creator of the worlds, be pleased and grant me its fruit. (36)
Nārada said: There,
in that supreme city called Kāmodā,
there was a very intelligent Daitya named Viṣṇu, who brought about the destruction of all the Daityas.
O Dānava, I shall tell you the means by which these flowers called Kāmoda will come into your hand. (38)
Divine [objects] will undoubtedly fall into the waters of the Gaṅgā;
carried along by the divine waters, they will return to that very place immediately. (39)
Therefore, please accept these flowers which are both beautiful and large;
having taken them, accomplish that which you desire.
Then, having again deluded that best of Dānavas, Nārada,
that righteous-souled one reflected once more.
"How can she, being so distressed, shed tears for him?"—
as he was thus reflecting, a moment passed for Vaināradā.
Then, having gone to the city named Kāmoda, the thought arose within him. ||43||

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmā," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the *Venopākhyāna* of the *Bhūmikhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and twentieth chapter.
Kuñjala said:
There is a divine city named Kāmoda, crowded with all the gods.
Then, for the sake of fulfilling all desires, Nārada perceived [this].
Having reached the house of Kāmodā, that best of the twice-born entered;
then, having seen Kāmodā, who was filled with all desirable things, [he was amazed]. ||2||
Having been honored by her with auspicious words such as "Welcome," that best of brahmins,
seated upon a divine throne, questioned her.
"O blessed one, born from the splendor of Viṣṇu, you dwell in happiness;
may you be free from ailment," he said, greeting her with blessings. ||4||
Kāmodā said:
"By the grace of you and Viṣṇu, I am living in happiness.
O highly wise one, please tell me the reason for this answer to my question. (5)
O bull among sages, a great delusion has arisen within my body;
it pervades all the worlds and destroys my intellect. (6)
Therefore, O Sage, this terrible dream which arose from sleep occurred just as it does among mortals; having been seen while asleep, it was perceived by me as if it were real.
O best of the twice-born, someone approached him and said right before him:
"This Hṛṣīkeśa is unmanifest; he will go to the state of worldly existence. (8)
"From that time forward, O Mahāmati, I have been pervaded by suffering;
therefore, you who are the best among the wise, tell me the cause of that. (9)
Nārada said:
O auspicious one, dreams arise among human beings as being born of wind (vātika), bile (paittika), phlegm (kaphaja), or from the combination of all three (sānnipātika); of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, neither sleep nor dreaming occurs among the gods;
however, at the time of sunrise, an excellent dream is seen.
Indeed, for human beings, a dream of a living being bestows the fruit of merit;
O auspicious lady, I shall now explain another cause of dreams.
O lady with the face of a doe, by the swaying of great winds, that [water] becomes mobile;
from that accumulation of water, subtle droplets break away. (13)
O auspicious one, these stainless drops of water fall outside;
having fallen, they once again go to dissolution and indeed become visible and invisible.
In the same way, O beautiful lady, listen as the nature of the dream state is described:
the self is pure, dispassionate, and free from attachment and aversion. (15)
Having transcended the nature of the five elements, he is perfectly immovable;
he shines resplendent in the midst of the twenty-six fundamental principles (tattvas). ||16||
The pure self is eternal and solitary, yet having come into contact with primordial nature (prakṛti),
it moves through its various states— like the wind— just as water moves from one place to another.
From your own self and from splendor, a corresponding splendor is produced;
that which is within is called his "Aśubha" (the inauspicious). ||18||
Just as the various grains of rice within a mass of milk-porridge are indistinguishable from it, O auspicious one,
so too is the individual self proclaimed to be non-different from the supreme Self through its own splendor.
Indeed, it consists of earth, water, fire, air, and space; it contains all water and all light—these five were created in the beginning. (20)
Having attained union with that Great-Souled One, who has become the pure form of your own spiritual luster,
they indeed reach oneness with him.
O fair-faced one, by defiling their own self-nature they destroy it;
yet again and again, O fair-faced one, they desire another state of being.
This creation is their playground and place of recreation, the cause of their mutual connection;
just as a wave arises from water and dissolves back into it. //23//
The repeated arising and repeated destruction of such a being is seen to be just like that of the form of water; of these [beings], there is no doubt it is the same. (24)
O Goddess, the self perishes, yet fire and wind do not perish;
earth and space do not perish, nor indeed do the waters.
These five, together with the self, arise and pass away;
for these, beginning with the self, O blessed one, are of eternal nature, without a doubt. (26)
Their very essence perishes as soon as they are born, struck down by the great defects of the sense-objects, such as passion, hatred, and the like. (27)
O twice-born one, the vital breaths depart from the body, which consists of the five elements;
and his soul, which is its counterpart, likewise enters into those very elements.
Just as a spark from a fire shines forth, so does the inner self shine; though it is both visible and invisible, it manifests itself. 29.
The pure Self is the Supreme Brahman and is eternally awake;
the inner self, however, is bound by the great qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Nourished by food as its sustenance, the inner self attains happiness;
from great happiness arises delusion, and because of that, the mind becomes bewildered. (31)
Afterwards, sleep arises, which increases the quality of tamas;
it is that by means of which the sun, having ascended Mount Meru, proceeds through the path of the channels (nāḍīs). //32//
Then that night gives birth until the sun rises;
freed from the darkness of sense-objects, the inner self shines forth.
The inner self is grasped by means of the states consisting of the principles, which are nourished by the five elements and exist as the aggregates from previous births. (34)
O Mahāmati, the self, bound by the defects of saṃsāra, is led through various high and low states of existence. (35)
The individual soul protects the body and subsequently remains situated within its midst;
the udāna breath vibrates intensely, and from that, sound is produced.
Just as a dry leather bellows, when filled with air, produces a sound,
so too does the udāna breath forcibly produce a sound by means of the breath.
But by the power of the self (ātman), the udāna becomes strong;
thus the body becomes utterly stupefied and is rendered as if dead. (38)
Then that Great Illusion of sleep enters his limbs; it goes to the heart, the palate, and likewise establishes itself at the tip of the nose. (39)
With the arms drawn back, one should remain with the breath directed from the heart toward the navel region;
by the power of the self, the vital air named udāna [arises]. (40)
He produces an exceedingly intense and powerful obstruction, just as one who holds a wooden wedge remains bound by a rope. (41)
Thus, O fair-faced one, there is no doubt that the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) is firmly attached to the self;
indeed, the vital breath is connected to the inner self.
Driven by the intellect and bound by its own nature, the self runs forward;
remembering the latent impressions (vāsanās) acquired in previous births, it rushes toward them. (43)
There, that highly wise one again sports according to his own will;
thus does the inner self perceive various kinds of dreams. (44)
He beholds excellent, unobstructed paths joined with works;
likewise, he beholds mountains that are very difficult to traverse and both high and low. ||45||
Know that this same [state] is characterized by wind; likewise, I shall describe that which is characterized by phlegm:
one perceives water, rivers, ponds, and reservoirs. (46)
O Goddess, know that when one perceives fire as exceedingly great and most excellent, that indeed is the pitta-type [vision]; and I shall now describe what is to be contemplated.
O lady of excellent hips, at dawn a dream is seen that is either auspicious or indeed inauspicious;
joined with karma, it reveals gain and loss. 48.
O woman of excellent complexion, even the state of dream has been declared;
O lady of beautiful hips, that which is to be realized shall indeed belong to Viṣṇu.
For that reason, you saw that evil dream; indeed, it was perceived by you. ||50||

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter in the *Cyavana-caritra*, within the *Kāmodya* narrative, in the *Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya* section of the *Vena-upākhyāna* in the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma-purāṇa*.
(121) The one hundred and twenty-first chapter. Kāmado said:
All the deities do not know her, nor even her form;
that in which all this is dissolved is proclaimed as the one Self.
O Nārada, listen to the essential summary of that which is the expansion of Māyā:
why does my Lord, the Master of the World, proceed toward dissolution? (2)
A man is bound by both evil and very meritorious actions; he wanders through saṃsāra, O Brahmin.
Tell me, why would Hari go [there]? ||3||
Nārada said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall tell you what was done by that wielder of the discus;
having made a promise before Bhṛgu, he said, "I shall perform the protection of the sacrifice."
At the word of Indra, Sadyoga departed from that excellent sacrifice of Bhṛgu along with the Dānavas to fight Viṣṇu, the wielder of the discus.
When the god had departed after abandoning the sacrifice, those foremost of dānavas,
possessed of sinful intentions, arrived and completely desecrated that entire sacrifice.
Enraged at Hari, the ascetic Bhṛgu cursed Revata:
"Corrupted by my curse, may you undergo ten births. (7)
O Goddess, Janārdana will experience the enjoyment of his own karma;
it is for that reason, O Goddess, that you have beheld this evil dream.
Having spoken thus, that Brahmin Nārada departed for the world of Brahmā;
and she, too, became distressed at that time by the profound sorrow of Kṛṣṇa.
The young woman wept piteously, crying out "Alas!
Alas! repeatedly; O Nandana, hear from me as she sat upon the bank of the Gaṅgā with her hands in water.
Likewise, from his beautiful eyes, he shed tears out of sorrow;
those shed tears also fell into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
And her teardrops sink indeed into the water;
they arise once more, O Father, in the form of lotuses. (12)
The best of Dānavas, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, beheld them indeed proceeding like full-blown lotuses carried along in the waters of the Gaṅgā. (13)
Although these were spoken by the Sage who knows the origin of suffering,
that asura, filled with great joy, accepted them.
O Lord of Daityas, deluded by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, he too worshipped the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain with blossoming lotuses numbering seventy million. 15.
Then, filled with rage, the Mother of the World spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
"Behold, O high-minded one, the wicked deed of this Dānava! (16)
"These lotuses born of grief that have fallen into the waters of the Gaṅgā—here he is, his mind agitated by desire, seizing them. (17)
How could there be any great welfare for one of wicked soul who worships with flowers born of suffering and grief, which cause sorrow and torment? (18)
With whatever disposition one should worship me alone, with that very same disposition his accomplishment will come to pass. (19)
Deprived of truth and meditation, his mind intent on sensual pleasures, he was born with sinful conduct; O Goddess, abandon him by your own splendor.
Having thus heard those words of the high-souled Śambhu, [he said]:
"By your command, I shall bring about the destruction of this very [demon]. (21)
Having spoken thus, the goddess then, desiring his death as well,
remained there and reflected upon the means for the slaying of Vihuṇḍa.
Having assumed the illusory form of a high-souled Brāhmaṇa,
one should worship the Lord Śaṅkara with excellent flowers born of the Pārijāta tree.
Then the sinful Dānava, agitated by lust, afflicted by great suffering, and absorbed in that state with his mind intent upon it, destroyed the divine worship. ||24||
And thus, the wicked Dānava, tormented by the arrows of desire, remembered that great Māyā of Viṣṇu which he had previously witnessed. (25)
Merely by remembering her, he, afflicted by the pain of separation and overwhelmed by powerful pride, weeps again and again.
Drawn by Time, that wicked-souled one, having gathered those [flowers] born from the *aśoka* tree, arrived seeking to worship Maheśvara. ||27||
Having destroyed the worship performed by the Goddess with excellent flowers born of the Pārijāta tree, he, out of great greed, should worship her instead with flowers born of the Śoka tree.
From the eyes of that wicked man, drops born of tears fell incessantly upon the head of the Liṅga. ||29||
Then, in the form of a divine brahmin, he said to him: "O high-minded one, who are you that always worships the Lord with a mind overwhelmed by grief? (30)
"O Goddess, these tears born of grief have fallen upon the head of the Lord;
tell me, before me, that this is indeed impure. (31)
Vihuṇḍa said:
"Previously, I beheld this woman, who possesses every perfection of beauty,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and a great abode of desire."
In that state, scorched by passion and his body overcome with agitation, he was told by her: "Indeed, during our union, give me this excellent garment. (33)
Worship Maheśvara with flowers born of desire;
place a garland made of those flowers around my neck. (34)
"Worship Maheśvara with seven crores [of offerings];
for that purpose, I myself worship the Lord who bestows the fruit. (35)

With flowers born of desire, which are difficult even for gods and demons to obtain, Śrī-Devī said: "Where is the devotion of this evil-minded one? Where is his meditation? Where is his knowledge? (36)
Even for Īśvara, there is indeed some connection with you;
tell me, what kind of excellent form did he assume to manifest his desire? (37)
"Excellent flowers have been obtained, and they have arisen from her laughter.
Vihuṇḍa said:
"I do not know her disposition or her meditation; she has never been seen by me at any time. (38)
I constantly take up only those [flowers] that have fallen into the waters of the Gaṅgā; with them, I worship the one Śaṅkara—this I declare. (39)
O Brahmin, this was also told to me by the high-souled Śukra;
at his word, I worship the Lord of Gods day after day.
"All this that I was asked by you has been told to you, O lady.
Śrī-Devī said: "By those flowers born from the weeping of Kāmā, which arose from sorrow... (41)
You should worship the *liṅga* every single morning, with whatever disposition and with whatever flowers you have. (42)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, having worshipped him, obtain such a fruit as that!
Having thus destroyed the divine worship, you now worship with flowers of grief. (43)
This most terrible fault of yours has arisen for the first time today;
therefore, I shall inflict punishment upon you—reap the fruit born of your own karma! 44.
Having heard his speech, Kāla spoke: "Ho there, you wicked one of evil conduct, you defiler of my work! (45)
"I shall kill you here with this sword; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus to that brahmin, he took up his sharpened sword.
Then that Dānava, evil-minded and desirous of seizing her, rushed forward;
the Supreme Goddess, enraged, appeared in the form of a Brahmin woman.
"I shall surely slay you here with this sword; of this there is no doubt.
Seeing that he had returned to his own place, she uttered the sound "Huṃ!
At the roar of that "Huṃ," the lowest of Dānavas fell down.
Motionless, though possessing the power to assume any form at will, he remained as immovable as if struck by a vajra; when that destroyer of all worlds, the Dānava, had fallen. 49.
All the worlds have attained well-being and are freed from the heat of suffering;
for this reason, my child, the woman laments like a cow.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, that woman of excellent form, her mind agitated by grief—this which you asked has all been told to you. (51)
Viṣṇu said:
Having spoken thus to that excellent son, O King, the Lord of the Egg-born, possessed of great wisdom, ceased speaking and said nothing further. 52.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmā," within the Life of Cyavana, concerning the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the *Evena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and twenty-second chapter.
Viṣṇu said:
Having thus spoken to those sons, [the Lord] who is the bird of the wing of dharma in the water of the world...
The one of great wisdom ceased speaking and said nothing further to them.
Standing beneath the banyan tree, that best of the twice-born spoke to the great parrot: "Who are you, a speaker of dharma, who exists here in the form of a bird? (2)
"Are you a god, or perhaps a gandharva, or are you an vidyādhara?
By whose curse have you come to this sinful birth? (3)
O Śuka, why does such knowledge exist within you, which transcends the senses? Is it the fruit of great merit, or of some ascetic practice? (4)
"O Great-minded one, what is the use of this disguised form?
Are you a perfected being (siddha) or a god? Tell me the reason for that. (5)
Kuñjala said:
"O Siddha, I know your lineage and that most excellent clan; I know your learning, your austerity, and your power, by which you wander the earth."
"I shall explain everything in detail; welcome to you, O observer of noble vows! Sit upon this auspicious seat and take refuge in the coolness of its shade. (7)
From Brahman, whose origin is unmanifest, Prajāpati was born;
and from him was born the twice-born Bhṛgu, a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues and equal to Brahmā himself.
There was one named Bhārgava, who knew the true meaning and essence of all dharmas; in his lineage, O Brahmin, you were born as the renowned Cyavana on this earth.
I am neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor again a vidyādhara;
listen as I speak to you, O brahmin, that which I shall declare. (10)
In the lineage of Kaśyapa was born a certain most excellent brāhmaṇa, who knew the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and who illuminated all ritual actions. ||11||
Renowned as a Vidyādhara, endowed with noble lineage, character, and virtues,
that brahmin then shone with splendor through his conduct and asceticism.
Three sons were born to that Vidyādhara:
Vasuśarman, Aśarman, and Dharmaśarman—these three. (13)
Among them, I am Dharmaśarman, devoid of excellent qualities and born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
my brother is Vasuśarman, who is proficient in the meaning of the Vedas and the Śāstras. (14)
Furthermore, Nāmaśarman was well-established in right conduct and possessed of excellent qualities such as learning; he was highly wise and likewise pre-eminent in virtues. (15)
O best of beings, listen: I alone have become a great fool;
[yet] the power of knowledge, O Brahmin, is the supreme wealth that brings about auspiciousness. (16)
I do not hear the unsurpassed house of my father, Vaiyāghrapadya;
therefore, my father will surely think that I have departed. (17)
"The name of this son, Dharmaśarman, is indeed meaningless; for though born in the midst of the earth, he is unlearned in the Vedas and a mine of vices. (18)
Having reflected thus, the righteous-souled one, deeply distressed, said to me:
"O son of Vraja, go to the house of your preceptor and accomplish your studies. (19)
Having heard those inauspicious words of my father, I said:
"O father, I will not go to the home of the guru, which brings such great suffering. (20)

O best of beings, listen to what happens there by the power of karma: where there is constant beating, crying out with contortions of the eyebrows and other gestures, and where food is not to be seen. (21)
Day and night there is no sleep; there is no means for attaining happiness.
Therefore, O Father, this [world] consists of suffering; one should go to the great mountain. 22.
"I shall perform the work of knowledge; I am eager for play. By your grace, O Father, I shall eat, sleep, and engage in sport. (23)
Together with Ḍimbhaka, he remained there happily day and night for an immeasurable time;
then, perceiving me to be deluded, that righteous-souled one, deeply distressed, spoke to me. (24)
The Vidyādhara said:
"O son, do not commit such a rash act; exert yourself for the sake of knowledge.
Through knowledge, happiness is attained, as well as fame and incomparable renown. (25)
Knowledge leads to both heaven and liberation; therefore, strive for learning.
It first uproots the cause of great suffering and subsequently bestows the happiness of knowledge. (26)
Therefore, establish your status as a son and go to the teacher’s house for learning;
by not following my father’s word, I myself am [dying] day by day.
Wherever I remained, I constantly caused the loss of wealth;
I was ridiculed by the people and censured by the brahmins. (28)
At that time, when my livelihood was destroyed by the arising of shamelessness, I, striving for the sake of knowledge, O Brahmin, entreated a certain teacher. (29)
Thus, born from the fever of thought, he was overwhelmed by suffering and grief: "How shall I know the Jina? How shall I understand his qualities? (30)
"How is heaven attained? How do I go to liberation?"—thinking thus, O Brahmin, I again reached old age. (31)
Once, while I was sitting dejectedly in a temple, a certain Siddha, impelled by my good fortune, arrived there. (32)
Without support, taking only prescribed food, always free from desire for material things, dwelling in solitude, devoted to dispassion, and having conquered the senses; ||33||
I have taken refuge in that one of great intelligence, whose form is wisdom, who is absorbed in the Supreme Brahman, and who possesses knowledge, meditation, and samādhi. (34)
With a pure disposition and devotion, I, bearing the bow named Nāmitaka, bowed to that Great-Souled One and stood before him. (35)
"Indeed, I was born as a gold coin (dīna), yet I have become unfortunate once again;
therefore, O Brahmin, I asked you: 'Why are you grieving? (36)
"O best of Brahmins, I was then asked by that wise yogi: 'With what intention does one indeed experience only suffering? (37)
Indeed, how could that very same person, having been made to hear all of that very same former history by one who is utterly deluded and not a [true] teacher, attain omniscience? (38)
"For this reason, my state has always been one of great suffering.
Then that Great-Souled One told me everything regarding the cause of knowledge. (39)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Life of Cyavana," within the "Guru-tīrtha-māhātmya" section of the "Even-upākhyāna" in the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The one hundred and twenty-third chapter.
The Siddha said:
Listen; I shall describe the nature of knowledge before you.
Knowledge has no body, nor hands, feet, or eyes. (1)
In the knowledge of the nose and ears, there is no collection of bones at all;
by whom, then, has that knowledge been seen, and what are its signs?
You, the All-Knowing One, eternally know everything devoid of mental constructs;
as the sun illuminates by day, so does the moon illuminate by night.
A lamp illuminates a house, yet those situated in the midst of light do not see that very place; hear this, O best of beings. (4)
Those deluded ones, enchanted by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, do not perceive the incomparable knowledge situated within the body, which is illuminated by meditation. ||5||
That state cannot be seen by the moon, the sun, or other such luminaries;
it is devoid of hands and feet, and is without knowledge, eyes, or ears.
O best of Brahmins, its movement is universal; it grasps everything, sees everything, smells everything, and hears everything—of this there is no doubt.
There exists no lamp equal to knowledge for the destruction of all darkness;
it is seen in heaven, on earth, in the underworld (pātāla), and in every place.
The foolish do not perceive the gnosis situated in the center of the body;
I shall explain the locus of gnosis from which gnosis is produced. (9)
O twice-born one, it is always and eternally situated within the hearts of living beings, [producing] great enjoyments such as desire and the like, as well as great delusions and so forth. (10)
He who always desires to burn away all [defilements] with the fire of discernment should crush the objects of the senses, having become composed of universal peace. ||11||
From that, knowledge arises which reveals the meaning of all principles;
this knowledge is rooted in reality, stainless, and all-seeing. (12)
Therefore, practice peace, which increases all happiness;
be impartial toward enemy, friend, and stranger alike, just as you are toward yourself.
Always remaining steadfast in existence, with food conquered and senses subdued, one should not practice even ordinary friendliness; one must utterly abandon enmity.
Becoming free from attachment and free from longing, and resorting to a solitary place, you will become an illuminator of all things, possessing knowledge and seeing all. ||15||
Remaining in one place, O Vatsa, you will know through my grace everything that will happen in the three worlds; of this there is no doubt.
Kuñjala said:
By that perfected one (siddha), the nature of supreme wisdom was revealed to me;
I remain eternally established in his words and am likewise permeated by his being. ||17||
Whatever exists throughout the three worlds, even though I remain in a single place, all that I perceive through the grace of that true guru. (18)
All this account of my own life has indeed been told to you;
I shall now speak of something else—tell me, O best of the twice-born. (19)
Cyavana said:
"O best among the wise, how did you come to be born from the womb of a bird?
Tell me the reason for that, which shall destroy all my doubts. (20)
Kuñjala said:
"From association indeed arises sin, and from association arises merit as well.
Therefore, one who is pure and worthy should avoid both that which is contrary [to dharma] and even that which is otherwise."
A certain wicked hunter had captured a young parrot and brought it along, intent on selling it. ||22||
Having observed that he was flattering, handsome, and eloquent in speech, he was seized by a certain Brāhmaṇa and handed over to me out of affection for me. (23)
O best of the twice-born, I myself am eternally established in knowledge and meditation;
yet, out of curiosity, I abide in the hand with the nature of a child.
O best of the twice-born, I was not deluded by his curious words;
rather, my mind was constantly fixed upon that parrot who had taken the form of a son. (25)
"He says to me, 'O father, stay here;
go and bathe, O noble one, and worship the Lord immediately. (26)
With such flattering words as these, he would have addressed me alone;
through the diversion of his speech, his supreme knowledge was forgotten. (27)
"I had gone to the forest for the sake of flowers and for the enjoyment of fruits; yet the parrot was led away by a cat, becoming the cause of my sorrow. (28)
Though surrounded by all my companions, who were well-behaved and like brothers to me, that bird was killed by a cat and indeed devoured by it. (29)
Having heard that the brahmin parrot, who used to speak so sweetly, had passed away,
he was exceedingly distressed by a state of great sorrow and unhappiness.
O best of the twice-born, though I am deluded by that suffering and severely tormented by intense agony, I am bound by the great net of delusion.
With my mind agitated by delusion, O learned one, I prattled to Rāmacandra, calling him "King of Parrots" and "King of Verses. (32)
Then, O best of Brahmins, I became tormented by suffering due to my own karma;
listen now to this account of the separation from Śuka. (33)
"That ignorance of mine has been forgotten, even though it was revealed by the Siddha.
Tormented by grief, I shall now remember that Śuka, who used to speak so sweetly. (34)
O Bhārgava, listen constantly to this discourse of Vatsavatsa, composed of sentences in both prose and verse, joined with refined Sanskrit syllables. (35)
"Without you, who else will awaken this dear child tomorrow with most wonderful stories, while she is being propitiated by the king of birds? (36)
"Having abandoned this secluded garden, where have you gone? Tainted by what fault are you? Tell me that immediately. (37)
Thus deluded by those compassionate words of his, and likewise tormented by grief, I lamented as follows: (38)
I died through that delusion, and even after death, I was deluded by that same state; whatever my condition was at the time of death, such was my state of mind. (39)
O best of the twice-born, even with such a disposition, I was born;
I have entered the womb, which brings about knowledge and memory. (40)
I remember the karma performed by me in the past, which I myself brought about; what indeed have I done, being sinful, deluded, and of undisciplined soul? (41)
Having ascended the yoga of the womb, I again contemplated that [object];
by that means, this stainless knowledge was born, which perceives everything. (42)
By the grace of that guru, indeed, the supreme knowledge was attained; and by the pure waters of his words, the impurity of my body was washed away. (43)
Having been thoroughly cleansed both internally and externally, and rendered stainless and purified, I attained the state of an animal, born into the species of a parrot. (44)
When death was imminent due to Śuka’s state of meditative absorption,
at that time the Brahmin died, having been permeated by that very same state.
I have been born again on this earth in the form of a boar;
such is the state that arises for living beings at the time of death.

Those virtuous beings indeed become such as He is; they take that form, have that as their ultimate goal, possess those qualities, and have that very nature, for they truly become one with His being. 47.
O best of Brahmins, there is no doubt that even through the state of death, I have attained incomparable knowledge here, O high-minded one. (48)
Therefore, O Great-Minded One, by means of my great wisdom, I perceive everything that has been, that will be, and that which is present. (49)
For I know everything here, even while remaining stationed [here], without a doubt,
for the sake of delivering those human beings who wander through cyclic existence.
O twice-born one, there is no teacher equal to a Tīrthaṅkara for cutting the bonds;
all this has been told to you, so listen, O descendant of Bhṛgu. (51)
O Brahmin, all that you have asked has been explained to you.
All external impurity is destroyed by both land-born and water-born [substances]. (52)
The pilgrimage site of the Guru destroys the sins committed throughout previous births;
it is the supreme moving pilgrimage site for the very purpose of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
Viṣṇu said:
O best of kings, having thus revealed the truth to the high-souled Cyavana, the exceedingly wise Śuka became silent.
All this has been told to you regarding this supreme, moving tirtha;
choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells within your mind.
Vena said:
"I do not desire the kingdom for the sake of pleasure, nor do I crave anything else; O Janārdana, I wish to enter your body along with my own."
"I would consider even this a boon, whatever you wish to grant here.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord of the Earth, perform the Aśvamedha and the Rājasūya sacrifices. (57)
O Mahāmati, the gift of cows, land, gold, water, grain, and roots destroys even the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils through the act of giving. (58)
The fourfold set of goals is indeed accomplished through giving; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O King, you should practice giving, dedicating it to me. (59)
With whatever disposition anyone gives to me, I truly bring about a corresponding state of being for them. (60)
By the sight and touch of the sages, your accumulation of sins has been destroyed;
you shall come to this sacrifice of mine in an incorporeal state, without a doubt.
Having been addressed in this manner by Vena, Hari vanished from that place.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Life Story of Cyavana," within the Description of the Completion of the Greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, in the *Evena-upākhyāna* of the *Bhūmi-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter.
Sūta said:
When Viṣṇu had vanished from sight, the highly intelligent King Vena [reigned].
"O Lord of the lords of gods, where have you gone?"—thus he became absorbed in anxious thought.
Overcome with great joy and having reflected, that best of kings summoned Pṛthu,
the most excellent of monarchs, with sweet words.
Then, with great joy, he spoke to that high-souled one:
"By you as my son, I have been delivered from a great sin in the world of mortals."
O Vatsavaṃśaśoma, this lineage of yours has been brought to brilliance by me;
its faults have been destroyed by me, while it has been illuminated by you with virtues. 4.
I shall perform the horse sacrifice and give gifts manifold;
today, by your grace, I go to the world of Viṣṇu with my body.
O illustrious one, O best of kings, you have gathered the necessary provisions;
O illustrious one, summon three Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
Thus instructed by that high-souled one,
the great-souled Pṛthu replied with reverence to his father.
O great king, enjoy the kingdom of the Kurus and the pleasures that accord with your heart;
perform meritorious sacrifices with divine and human offerings to Janārdana.
Having spoken thus and bowed to his father, who was intent upon knowledge,
the lord of the earth took up his bow along with an arrow with great care.
He commanded all his soldiers: "Proclaim throughout this earth that no sin whatsoever must be committed by means of the threefold action."
And whatever sin they shall commit by transgressing the command of King Vena—by violating his authority to execute—they shall go there [to hell], of this there is no doubt. (11)
One should indeed give gifts and worship Janārdana with sacrifices; all you men, being single-minded and free from envy, perform sacrifice to me. 12.
O Brahmins, having thus imparted instruction regarding the kingdom to his servants, the son of Vena cast it aside and departed for the forest of asceticism for the sake of penance.
Having abandoned all faults and restrained his senses from their objects,
he remained without food for a period of one hundred years.
Pleased by his asceticism, Brahmā said to Pṛthu:
"O ascetic, why do you perform penance? Tell me the reason for that. (15)
Pṛthu said:
"O highly wise one, this father of mine, Vena, was a promoter of my fame;
yet that lowest of men, who commits sin while ruling his kingdom, [is now dead]. (16)
The Lord Janārdana became the one who would sever his head;
and Hari himself, with invisible great discuses, became his punisher.
Whoever commits a heinous sin against you through mind, deed, or speech—
their heads shall shatter like a ripe fruit from a tree.
O Lord of the Gods, listen to this which I consider the best boon from you:
that my father shall not be tainted by the fault of his subjects. (19)
O Lord of Gods, act accordingly if you wish to grant a boon; O Four-faced One, grant this supreme desire, salutations be unto you. (20)
Brahmā said: "So be it, O highly fortunate one! Your father has attained purification through Viṣṇu; he has been instructed by you, his son, O Pṛthu."
Having thus granted a boon to Pṛthu, the All-pervading Lord departed; Pṛthu himself returned and remained established in the duties of kingship. ||22||
O best of Brahmins, no one should commit even the slightest sin during the reign of Vainya;
yet, some might contemplate evil through all three types of action. (23)
His head would have been severed as if cut by discuses;
from that time forward, no one at all would commit such a sin.
Thus, by the command of that high-souled son of Vena,
all the worlds perpetually revolve according to their proper conducts.
Devoted solely to all dharmas, they flourished through acts of giving and enjoyment;
by the grace of that king, they increased in every form of happiness. (26)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within this very narrative. || 124 ||
The one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter.
Sūta said: Having received the command of Vena, the supremely righteous Pṛthu [acted].
The prince arose from all the various accumulations of merit. ||1||
Then that king invited all those Brāhmaṇas from various lands,
or else he had them brought by means of messengers for the sake of the horse sacrifice.
Having bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the brahmins many times over,
that lord of the earth went to the realm of Viṣṇu in his physical body.
Together with Viṣṇu, that righteous soul constantly engaged in his duties;
thus has this entire life-story of that king been narrated to you. 4.
It pacifies all evils and destroys all sufferings;
King Pṛthu, whose nature is true dharma, rules the earth. (5)
That best of kings milked the earth, which was equal to the three worlds;
by his meritorious deeds and acts of righteousness, he conquered the subjects.
All this has been narrated to you, the unsurpassed Bhūmikhaṇḍa;
first was the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and second is this Bhūmikhaṇḍa. ||7||
I shall again recount the majesty of the Bhūmikhaṇḍa;
that best of men who hears even a single verse of this section [attains great merit]. ||8||
The sin of that very day is destroyed for that wise person who, endowed with devotion, listens to this chapter. (9)
O best of the twice-born, listen as I declare the merit of one who has given a thousand cows to Brahmins on a sacred festival day.
Whatever fruit may arise from this, Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly recites this Padma Purāṇa. (11)
"But in the Kali age, O Lotus-born One, obstacles do not arise for a man who listens [to this].
Vyāsa said: "Why is it that in the Kali age they do not arise for one who listens? Please tell me. Padmaja replied: "Listen. 12.
For a man endowed with merit, there are various most terrible obstacles.
Brahmā said: "That fruit which is proclaimed for the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha)... (13)
The fruit of that is seen in the Padma Purāṇa, O dear one;
the meritorious horse-sacrifice does not take place at all in the Kali age. (14)
Tell me also that which is ancient and indeed equal to the Aśvamedha;
whatever merit belongs to the Aśvamedha, which bestows the fruits of heaven and liberation. (15)
O best of beings, sinful men established upon evil paths go to hell,
[but those who follow] this meritorious Purāṇa known as Padmasaṃjña.
In the Kali age, men do not obtain merit equal to that of the horse sacrifice; rather, sinful men in the Kali yuga must go to the ocean of hell.
Why shall they not hear that merit which accomplishes the fourfold aims of life, by means of which this meritorious *Padma Purāṇa* was heard in the past? (18)
For by him all the means for accomplishing the four aims of life have been accomplished;
therefore, O high-minded one, sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha have become obsolete.
In the Kali age, all the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and accents, have gone to heaven;
yet whoever is endowed with goodness, possessed of faith, and devoted to the Blessed One [remains].
That righteous son, together with his wife, desires to hear;
for the sake of hearing, great faith arises within him. (21)
Even for a man who merely hears it, no great obstacle shall arise;
yet first, lack of faith arises in the person who recites it. (22)
O best of the twice-born, as he listens, greed arises within him;
the most terrible great delusion has been sent by Lord Viṣṇu. (23)
While he was constantly listening to this, he brought about its destruction;
for day after day, corrupters, revilers, and sinners came into being. (24)
But it must be understood by the wise one that an obstacle has now arisen for me;
since it is seen to have come about, O Vyāsa, one should perform the fire sacrifice accordingly. (25)
And with Vaiṣṇava great mantras, with the Viṣṇu-sūktas that bestow great merit, with the "Viṣṇorarāṭam" mantra, and with the "Sahasra-śīrṣaka" [Puruṣa-sūkta]. ||26||
One should perform the oblation repeatedly with the "idaṃ viṣṇu" mantra, the "tryambaka" mantra, and the "tryaṃbaka" mantra. ||27||
One should perform the oblation with the Bṛhat Sāman mantra and the twelve-syllable mantra; whichever deity’s oblation it may be, one should offer it with that deity's specific mantra.

O twice-born one, the installation and worship of the planets should also be performed with one hundred and eight offerings of sesame seeds and clarified butter, as well as fuel-sticks of the palāśa tree.
There one should worship Vighneśa, Śāradā, Sureśvarī,
Jātavedas, Mahāmāyā, Caṇḍikā, and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetranāyaka).

With sesame seeds, durva grass, and clarified butter, while those mantras are being recited, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in this manner; one should then bestow wealth upon the brahmins.
Just as one gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to one's father consisting of a cow together with its calf, so too do obstacles perish and one attains ancient perfection. ||32||
I declare that for one who does not act in this way, an obstacle arises;
a disease will be born in his body, bestowing much suffering. (33)
Grief for a wife, grief for a son, and loss of wealth arise;
one suffers from various kinds of great diseases—of this there is no doubt. (34)
He who possesses no wealth in his home should observe a fast;
having reached the auspicious Ekādaśī, he should worship Madhusūdana.
And with a mind imbued with devotion, one should afterwards feed the Brahmins with the sixteen types of offerings, according to the extent of one's wealth. (36)
Having offered a vow accompanied by an oblation to Keśava,
the wise man should then himself partake of a meal together with his kinsmen.
Then, joined by his sons and wife, he shall attain perfection;
those devoted to righteousness should listen to the complete Purāṇa-saṃhitās.
The accomplishment of the fourfold aims arises for him, and not otherwise.
Now hear about the single hundred thousand [verses] with a quarter more, known as the Brahma-Puṣkara. 39.
O twice-born one, in the Kṛta Yuga, men are free from sin;
they hear half of the hundred thousand [verses], and thereafter the entire Purāṇa known as Padma.
When two thousand and more verses have been reached, and the Tretā Yuga has arrived, human beings shall hear them. (41)
Having enjoyed the fruits of the four aims of life, they shall go again to Hari;
twenty-two thousand [beings] will dwell together in the Saṃhita-padmaka world-system.
In the Dvāpara age, the supreme Brahman himself proclaimed the collection known as the Padma-saṃhitā, consisting of twelve thousand verses. 43.
In the Kali age, those men devoted to Viṣṇu who shall recite this will find that a single purpose and a single state of being are manifested throughout all four [ages].
O best of beings, O lord of brahmins, the extensive narrative known as the Śeṣa within the Saṃhitās itself shall go to destruction after twelve thousand [verses].
When the Kali age has arrived, this Bhūmikhaṇḍa will indeed appear first; by hearing it, a man is liberated from all sins. ||46||
One is liberated from all sufferings and is freed from all diseases;
having abandoned everything else—be it recitation, charity, or sacred learning—one attains this. (47)
Indeed, one should listen with diligence to this work called Padma, which destroys sin;
first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa.
The third is the Svargakhaṇḍa, and the fourth is Pātāla;
the fifth is the Uttarakhaṇḍa, which destroys all sins. ||49||
The man who listens with devotion to the five sections in their proper sequence obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

O gods, these five sections, which are difficult to obtain even through great fortune and which grant liberation when heard, truly bestow such results; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (51)
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Vena," in the Bhūmikhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, consisting of fifty-five thousand verses. 125.
This second section, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, is completed. ||2||
Thus ends the second section, the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the third section, the Svarga-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Oṃ, salutations to the remover of obstacles; Oṃ, salutations to the one possessed of glory.
(1) First Chapter:
I bow to the lotus-feet of Govinda.
Worshipped by the virtuous, most excellent and wealthy,
dwelling in the hearts of the people of the world, the sole refuge for the great multitude, and the highest of the high. ||1||
Once, all the sages who dwelt in the Himalayas—sages who had mastered the Vedas and were like blazing fires—all gathered together. (2)
Those great-souled ones who know the three periods of time, who are the refuge of various merits;
those who delight on Mount Mahendra and those who dwell in the Vindhyas; (3)
Those who are devoted to Arbuda-araṇya, those who dwell in Puṣkara-araṇya, those who are devoted to Śrī-śaila, and those who reside in Kurukṣetra; ||4||
And those who delight in the Forest of Dharma, those who dwell in the Daṇḍaka Forest, those who delight in the path of Jambū, and those who dwell in Satyanivāsa; ||5||
These and many other stainless sages, accompanied by their disciples,
arrived at Naimiṣa, eager to see Śaunaka.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, they too were well-honored,
seated in due order upon various seats such as grass mats (bṛsī) and the like.
Seated upon the seats provided by Śaunaka, those ascetics,
devoted to Kṛṣṇa, then spoke to one another of meritorious stories concerning him.
Then, while those sages of purified souls were engaged in conversation,
the Sūta of great splendor and immense luster arrived there.
The disciple of Vyāsa, known as Romaharṣaṇa and well-versed in the Purāṇas,
having prostrated before them in the prescribed manner, was honored by those sages as if he were their own son.
The great sages, headed by Śaunaka,
approached Sūta Vairomaharṣaṇa, the disciple of Vyāsa, as he sat comfortably according to the proper custom.
The highly fortunate ascetics, headed by Śaunaka, questioned him.
The sages said: "O knower of the Purāṇas, O one of great intelligence, O Romaharṣaṇa of noble vows! (12)
In the past, I have heard from you the highly meritorious ancient stories of the Purāṇas, as well as those concerning the present activities of Hari, for which I am now eager to listen.
Indeed, the supreme duty of men is that which consists of devotion to Adhokṣaja;
therefore, relate once more the Purāṇa, which is filled with accounts of Hari.
Conversation concerning anything other than Hari is considered by the wise to be like a cremation ground;
it is heard that Hari himself dwells there in the form of sacred pilgrimage sites.
"Pray, proclaim the names of the holy fords that bestow merit;
from where did they originate, and by whom are they protected? (16)
In what does this world, with its moving and unmoving beings, find its dissolution?
What are the meritorious fields, and which mountains are worthy of worship? (17)
And which rivers are supreme, meritorious, auspicious, and removers of the sins of men? O highly fortunate one, tell all of this to me in due order. (18)
Sūta said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate ones! Well asked, O you whose wealth is austerity!
Having bowed down to Him, I shall proclaim that Purāṇa which is born from the lotus."

To the son of Parāśara, the Supreme Person, the sole source of all that is to be known in the universe, the repository of knowledge, the bestower of vast intelligence, who is to be realized through the Vedas and Vedānta;
who is eternally peaceful, the object of one's own intellect, and expansive with pure splendor.
I bow to Veda-Vyāsa, whose fame is far-reaching and who burns away all [ignorance]. ||20||
Homage to that Blessed One, Vyāsa, of immeasurable splendor, by whose grace I shall recount this narrative of Nārāyaṇa. (21)
I shall proclaim this highly meritorious Purāṇa known as Padma,
consisting of one thousand and fifty-five [verses] and endowed with six sections.
Therein, first there shall be the Ādi-khaṇḍa; after that, the Bhūmi-khaṇḍa;
then, after that, the Brahma-khaṇḍa; and following that, the Pātāla-khaṇḍa.
Then the Kriyākhaṇḍa is proclaimed, and finally the Uttarakhaṇḍa;
this very thing is the great, wondrous Mahāpadma, of which the entire world is composed.
Therefore, because it has that as its subject matter and that as its basis, it is called the Pādma by the wise;
this Purāṇa is stainless and the supreme glorification of Viṣṇu. (25)
That which Hari, the God of gods, formerly declared to Brahmā,
Brahmā told that to Nārada, and Nārada [recounted it] before our guru.
Vyāsa repeatedly taught me all the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas and the Saṃhitās, for he was exceedingly dear to me.
I shall fully declare to you that Purāṇa which is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
by hearing which, a person is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin. 28.
Whoever hears this with supreme faith and devotion obtains the merit of bathing at all sacred fords; merely by hearing it, it bestows liberation. (29)
Even one who listens without faith acquires a store of merit;
therefore, with every effort, make the Lotus the guest of your ears. 30.
Therein I shall proclaim the first section, which is meritorious and destructive of sin;
let all you sages, together with your disciples, who are gathered here, listen. (31)
Thus ends the first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
(2) Second Chapter.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall first describe the primordial creation, by which the Lord, the eternal Supreme Self, is known. (1)
O best of the twice-born, after the dissolution of the created world, nothing at all existed;
there was only the single light of Brahman-consciousness, which is the cause of all.
Eternal, stainless, peaceful, pure, and eternally immaculate—an ocean of bliss and clarity—this is what those seeking liberation desire. ||3||
It is omniscient because its nature is knowledge; it is infinite, unborn, and undecaying; indestructible, eternally pure, infallible, all-pervading, and great.
But when the time for creation arrived, having recognized that modification— which was of the nature of knowledge and dissolved within the Self— he began to bring it forth.
From that, the Pradhāna manifested, and from that, moreover, the Mahat arose;
the Mahat is threefold: indeed, Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa.
Indeed, this very [intellect] is enveloped by the Pradhāna, just as a seed is covered by its skin;
it is threefold: the Vaikārika (the lucid), the Taijasa (the passionate), and the Bhūtādi (the source of elements), which is Tāmasa (dark).
This threefold ego-sense was born from the principle of Mahat; just as Mahat is enveloped by the Pradhāna, so too is it enveloped by the Great One (Mahat). ||8||
Then the primordial element (bhūtādi), undergoing transformation, created the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra);
from that subtle element of sound, it produced space, which is characterized by sound.
The subtle element of sound likewise enveloped the ether equally;
then the subtle element of sound likewise produced the ether, which in turn produced the subtle element of touch.
The wind became powerful, and touch is considered its quality;
space, which consists of sound alone, then enveloped the subtle element of touch alone.
Then, undergoing transformation, the wind produced the subtle element of form;
light arose from the wind, and that is said to have the quality of form.
The subtle element of air (vāyu), consisting of the quality of touch alone, enveloped the subtle element of form;
and light (jyotis), undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of taste.
From that, portions equal to a head arose;
and portions equal to a taste completely covered what was equal to a form. ||14||
And as they were undergoing transformations, they emitted only fragrance;
from that, this earth was born, preeminent with the qualities of all elements. ||15||

Therefore, because it is accompanied by its corresponding aggregate, that fragrance is considered its quality. Furthermore, because [the subtle element] exists within each respective [gross element] through that subtle essence (tanmātra), it is known as "subtle essence" (tanmātratā). ||16||
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are non-specific (aviśeṣa), while the others are specific (viśeṣa) in their respective order;
this creation of the gross elements and subtle elements proceeds from the tamasic ego.
Thus, O best of sages, those whose wealth is austerity have briefly described the ten deities born of the vaikārika [ego], whom they call the organs of sense. (18)
The eleventh is the mind (manas), proclaimed here by the contemplators of reality; furthermore, there are the five organs of knowledge (jñānendriya) and the five organs of action (karmendriya). 19.
I shall describe them to you, O purifiers of the lineage, as well as their functions:
hearing, touch, sight, taste, and the nose as the fifth.
Indeed, for the sake of accomplishing the cognition of sound and the other [objects], there are five organs endowed with intellect:
the anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and speech is declared the fifth. (21)
The emission, bliss, the movement of nāda, speech, action, and the recollection thereof—these are known as ether, air, fire, water, and earth. 22.

O Brahmins, endowed with the qualities beginning with sound, each succeeding one possessing greater power, they were separate and possessed diverse potencies; therefore, without their union, [they could not produce a body]. (23)
Being unable to create living beings without coming together as a whole,
they then met one another and took refuge in mutual union.
And having attained complete unity with the single Saṅgha as their common objective, [they act] both because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of Pradhāna. ||25||
The principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣas) produce that egg;
it grows gradually, like a bubble upon water, at all times.
From the elements arose the egg, vast and increased by great wisdom, resting upon the water;
it was the primordial, unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu in the form of Brahmā. ||27||
There, that Lord Viṣṇu, the Sovereign of the Universe, remaining himself in his unmanifest form, established himself by assuming the form of Brahmā. ||28||
From that Great Self, the mountains became his fetal membrane and his eggshell;
the oceans became his amniotic fluid. (29)
Within that egg, everything came into being—the mountains, islands, and oceans, along with the collection of worlds including the luminaries, together with the gods, asuras, and humans. (30)
By the will of Śrīkeśava, that lotus which had arisen from the navel of Viṣṇu himself— who is indeed without beginning or end— became the golden cosmic egg (Haimaṇḍa).
The Lord, who possesses the quality of rajas, being himself devoted to Hari,
assumes the form of Brahmā and proceeds to create the world.
He emits [the universe] at every age until the end of the kalpa-cycle; and in forms such as the Man-Lion (Narasimha) and others, he withdraws it in the form of Rudra.
The Great-Souled One, desiring to protect the entire world, emitted his form as Brahmā;
then, assuming the forms of Rāma and others, he became Rudra to devour this universe. (34)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||2||
The Third Chapter.
The Sages said: [Tell us] all the names of the rivers and the mountains.
Likewise, those who belong to the various regions and others who have taken refuge in this land. ||1||
O best of beings, please describe in its entirety the extent of the earth known by those who understand the means of valid cognition, as well as all its forests on every side.
Sūta said:
O highly wise one, the learned declare that these five great elements, which comprise everything existing in the world, are all equal. (3)
Earth, water, air, fire, and space—each of these possesses an increasing number of qualities; among them, earth is preeminent.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these are declared by the seers who know reality to be the qualities of earth. (5)
Water has four qualities, O Brahmin; smell is not found therein.
Sound, touch, and form—these are the three qualities of fire.
Sound and touch belong to air, while sound alone belongs to space;
these, O Brahmins, are the five qualities within the five great elements.
In all those worlds where beings are established, they do not transcend one another; this indeed constitutes their state of equality. ||8||
When they enter into mutual disharmony, then those embodied beings obscure one another; it is not otherwise.
They perish in succession and are born in succession;
all of them are immeasurable, and that is their divine nature. (10)
Wherever the objects of perception are seen, the elemental beings run toward them;
regarding these, humans declare their authorities based on reasoning.
Indeed, those entities which are inconceivable cannot be established through logical reasoning.
O best of sages, I shall now describe the island of Sudarśana.
The continent Mahābhāga is circular in shape and situated like a wheel;
it is divided by river waters and by mountains resembling oceans. ||13||
It was filled with cities of various beautiful forms as well as delightful provinces,
