and it abounded in trees endowed with flowers and fruits, and was rich in wealth and grain.
It was surrounded by the salt ocean as if by a wall, just as a man might see his own face in a mirror. ||15||
In this way, the island of Sudarśana appears as a circular mandala;
its extent is twice that of Aṃśa, and its circumference is twice that of Śaśa.
Having gathered all medicinal herbs and being surrounded on all sides, the waters are then to be known as "nyāvijñeya"; this is stated as the summary of the remainder.
The sages said: O wise Sūta, you have duly related the summary of that [Purāṇa] which you know; since you are a knower of the truth of everything, tell us its detailed account.
"Tell me the measure of this extent of ground that is visible upon the moon marked with the hare; from that, you shall speak of the pippala fruit."
Thus questioned by them, the charioteer then spoke these words.
The charioteer said: "O highly wise ones, there are six great jewel-mountains extending from the east."
For it is deeply immersed on both sides in the eastern and western oceans;
and there are Himavat, Himakūṭa, and Niṣadha, the best of mountains.
There is also the mountain named Śṛṅgavān, which is blue and made of lapis lazuli, white and resembling the moon, and encrusted with all kinds of minerals.
These very mountains, O Brahmins, are frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
the distance between them is thousands of yojanas.
There, O noble ones, are the meritorious provinces and those rainless years;
therein dwell beings of various kinds in every way. (24)
This, however, is Bhāratavarṣa; beyond that is Haimavatam;
and beyond Hemakūṭa, they declare Hari-varṣa.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha,
there is a great and fortunate mountain named Mālyavat, extending toward the east.
Beyond that is Mount Mālyavat, and [beyond that] Gandhamādana;
between those two is the circular Meru, the mountain of gold. ||27||
With a radiance like that of the young sun and resembling a smokeless fire, he is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height. ||28||
O best of the twice-born, it stands eighty-four yojanas below,
encompassing the worlds above, below, and across.
On its sides, O twice-born ones, these four continents are situated:
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and Jambūdvīpa, O most excellent ones. (30)
And the Northern Kurus are the refuge for those who have performed meritorious deeds;
he who was indeed the son of Supārśva was Vihaga-sumukha.
Seeing those golden crows, he indeed reflected upon Mount Meru as the abode of the best, the middling, and the lowest of birds. (32)
Since it makes no distinction, therefore I know this [Self] as infinite;
the Sun, the best among luminaries, constantly revolves around it. (33)
The moon together with the constellations, the wind blowing favorably, and the great mountain adorned with divine flowers—O wise one, [all these appeared]. (34)
O Brahmins, there the hosts of gods, gandharvas, asuras, and rākṣasas dwell in all their auspicious palaces made of Jāmbūnada gold, which are unobstructed by worldly existence.
Accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, they sport there on the mountain at all times;
and there Brahmā, Rudra, Śakra, and Āpsu, the lord of the Asuras, [dwell].
Having assembled, they performed various sacrifices with manifold sacrificial fees;
Tumburu, Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū were there as well. (37)
Having approached the best of the immortals, the high-souled seven seers and Kaśyapa, the lord of progeny, praise him with various hymns.
They go there—may you have prosperity—on every auspicious festival day;
there, Uśanas Kāvya is honored upon his very head by the Daityas. (39)
Its gold, gems, and jewels belong to him; the other jewel-mountains likewise belong to him.
Therefore, the blessed Lord Kubera enjoys a fourth part of it.
Then he bestows upon men a portion of his wealth;
there is a divine mountain peak, strewn with flowers of every season. (41)
There was a beautiful grove of Karṇikāra trees, elevated by a multitude of rocks;
there Paśupati himself was present, surrounded by divine beings. 42.
Accompanied by Umā, the Blessed Lord, the creator of all beings,
sports while wearing a garland made of karṇikāra flowers that reaches down to his feet.
Illumined by three eyes like three risen suns,
he was gazed upon by perfected beings of fierce penance, who were firm in their vows and speakers of truth.
O best of the twice-born, Maheśvara cannot be seen by those of evil conduct;
from the peak of that mountain, a stream of milk [flowed]. 45.
Possessing manifold forms, with a terrifying roar that destroys all calamities, and frequented by those of both merit and great demerit, she is as auspicious as the Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī. 46.
With the swift force of her leap, she created that meritorious lake, resembling the ocean, in the auspicious pool of the Moon. ||47||
Then the wielder of the Pināka bow bore her— who was difficult even for mountains to support—
upon his head for a hundred thousand years.
O best of the twice-born, on the western side of Meru is Ketumāla;
O twice-born ones, there, within that very region of Jambūdvīpa, lies a great country.
The lifespan of the best of beings there is ten thousand years;
the men are golden-colored, and the women are equal to the Apsarases.
There, human beings are born free from disease and sorrow, with minds eternally joyful, possessing the luster of refined gold. (51)
On the peaks of Gandhamādana, Kubera, the lord of the Guhyakas, rejoices together with the Rākṣasas and surrounded by throngs of Apsarases.
On the side of Gandhamādana, however, others are free from sin;
their maximum lifespan is eleven thousand years.
There, the men and brahmins were dark-complexioned, endowed with splendor, and possessed of great strength;
and all the women had the luster of lotus petals and were exceedingly beautiful to behold. (54)
The white region holds blue lotuses; superior to the Śveta region is Hairaṇyaka;
and the Airāvata region, O Brahmins, is filled with various inhabited lands.
To the north of the great and illustrious Dhanuṣkhaṇḍa lies Ilāvṛta in the center, and indeed the five [surrounding] regions as well. 56.
Each successive region beyond these excels the preceding one in its qualities—namely, in lifespan, health, righteousness, pleasure, and wealth. (57)
O best of beings, all these elements are endowed with them;
thus, O highly fortunate ones, this earth is covered by mountains.
Hemakūṭa is indeed a very great mountain named Kailāsa;
there the god Vaiśravaṇa rejoices together with the Guhyakas. (59)
To the north of Kailāsa, toward Mount Maināka,
there is a very great mountain with golden peaks, composed of divine jewels.
Beside it was a great, divine, and beautiful lake called Viṣṇusaras, with pure golden sands, where King Bhagīratha resided.
Having seen the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā, he dwelt there for many years;
there the sacrificial posts were made of jewels, and the altars were made of gold.
Having performed sacrifices there, the thousand-eyed one of great fame attained perfection;
there resides the eternal Creator, the Lord of Prosperity, who is honored by all the worlds. (63)
Then, from that [state], he was born as the fierce Jāyatrabhu, who is to be meditated upon;
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Manu, and Sthāṇu as the fifth.
There, the divine river that flows through the three paths was first established;
having descended from the world of Brahmā, it proceeds in seven streams.
The Vaṭodaka, Āsā, Nalinī, Pārvatī, Sarasvatī, the Jaṃbūnadī, the Sītā, and the Gaṅgā as the seventh, along with the Sindhu—[these are the rivers]. 66.
Endowed with the power of the knowledge of the supreme,
immutable Brahman, he is worshipped there during the sacrificial session at the completion of a thousand yugas.
In various places there, Sarasvatī becomes visible and invisible;
these are the seven divine Gaṅgās, renowned throughout the three worlds. (68)
May the Guhyakas provide protection on Himavat and Hemakūṭa; may the Sarpas and Nāgas protect Niṣadha, Gokarṇa, and the penance grove.
The Śveta mountain is said to belong to all the gods and asuras;
the Gandharvas dwell eternally on Niṣadha, and likewise the Brahmarṣis on Nīla.
Śṛṅgavān is the highly fortunate one who moves among the gods;
thus, O highly fortunate ones, these are the seven regions divided by their parts. 71.
Beings are established as both moving and stationary;
among them, various kinds of transformations are seen, whether divine or human. (72)
It is impossible to enumerate [them all], adorned as they are by faith;
O Brahmins, you ask about this divine one who possesses the form of a hare. (73)
The two islands of Pārśveśa and Śasya are said to be in the south and north;
while Karṇa and Nāgadvīpa, as well as Kāśyapadvīpa, are likewise situated there.
The island of Karṇa, the Śila brāhmaṇas, and the glorious Malaya mountain—this second [region] of the island appears situated like the moon. (75)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
The Sages said: O Sūta, please describe now what lies to the north, west, and east of Meru.
And that entire mountain Mālyavat, belonging to the Great Buddha. ||1||
Sūta said:
To the south of Nīla and likewise on the northern side of Meru,
O brahmins, are the meritorious Uttarakurus, frequented by the Siddhas.
There, the trees were laden with honey-sweet fruits and were perpetually endowed with flowers and fruit;
the flowers were fragrant and the fruits were full of flavor. (3)
O best of the twice-born, some trees there yield the fruit of all desires as their sustenance; others, O best of the twice-born, are known as milk-yielding trees.
There, they all constantly yield milk that is like nectar;
and from their fruits, they produce garments and ornaments.
The entire ground is composed of jewels with fine golden sand;
its touch is pleasant in all seasons, O you whose wealth is asceticism, and it is free from fruit-bearing trees.
All those who have fallen from the world of the gods are born there as humans, endowed with pure lineage and all very pleasing to behold. ||7||
Couples are born there, and the women are like celestial nymphs;
they drink the milk of those milk-yielding trees, which is like nectar.
A pair is born at the proper time, and they grow together,
endowed with equal form and qualities, and likewise possessing a harmonious union.
O twice-born ones, they were exclusively of corresponding form, like ruddy geese;
free from disease, they always dwelt in the three worlds with joyful minds.
Those highly fortunate ones live for ten thousand and ten hundred years, and they do not abandon one another.
There are birds called Bhāruṇḍas, with sharp beaks and great strength;
they carry off those who have died here and cast them into caves.
O Brahmins, the Uttarakurus have thus been described to you in brief;
now I shall describe the region on the eastern side of Meru exactly as it is.
O ascetics, his coronation took place at Bhadrāśva,
where there was the Bhadraśāla grove and great trees that were kālāmra mangoes.
The highly fortunate *kālāmra* trees are always auspicious with flowers and fruit;
these trees, a *yojana* in height, are frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*. ||15||
There, those men are white, endowed with splendor and great strength; the women have the color of the kumuda lily, beautiful and pleasing to behold. (16)
And those of the four castes were moon-colored, with faces resembling the full moon;
their limbs were as cool as the moon, and they were experts in dance and song. ||17||
O best of the twice-born, the lifespan there is ten thousand years;
having drunk the juice of the eternal mango, they remain eternally youthful.
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha,
there is the eternal great jambū tree named Sudarśana.
Yielding the fruits of all desires, meritorious, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, that eternal land is known by the name Jaṃbūdvīpa. (20)
O best of the twice-born, on the eastern peak of Mālyavat, there are one thousand and one hundred yojanas of peaks that follow one after the other from east to east.
O twice-born ones, Mālyavat extends for fifty thousand yojanas;
the humans born there resemble great silver in appearance. (22)
Having descended from the world of Brahmā, they are all expounders of Brahman;
they perform divine austerity and become those whose vital energy is drawn upward. ||23||
For the sake of protecting all beings, sixty thousand and sixty more enter the sun. (24)
Surrounding the sun, they proceed ahead of Aruṇa for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
Scorched by the heat of the sun, they enter the lunar orb.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter.
The Sages said:
O best of beings, [tell us] the names of the regions and the mountains.
Tell me truly who those are that dwell upon the mountains.
Sūta said:
To the south of Śveta and to the north of Niṣadha is the region named Ramaṇaka;
there, human beings are born.
All those men born there are endowed with pure lineage, are pleasing to behold,
and are all without rivals.
Those highly fortunate ones, with minds ever joyful, live for fifteen thousand one hundred years. ||4||
To the south of Nīla and to the north of Niṣadha is the region named Hiraṇmaya, where the river Hairaṇvatī flows.
And where, O wise ones, this king of birds, the best of winged creatures, dwells, along with excellent brahmins who follow the sacrifices, skilled archers, and those of pleasing appearance. (6)
There, the people were of great strength, with minds gladdened by the Brahmins;
those whose wealth was their asceticism lived for eleven thousand years.
O best of the twice-born, they live for a lifespan of fifteen hundred years;
moreover, there are three pure peaks.
One there was made of jewels, another likewise of gold and wonderful,
and one was composed of all kinds of gems, adorned with palatial dwellings.
There, O best of the twice-born, the goddess Svayamprabhā, who is ever-shining, dwells; and to the north of that peak is the Samudrāntā [mountain].
Beyond that Śṛṅgavat mountain is the region named Airāvata;
however, the sun does not travel there, and because of that, human beings do not age.
And the moon, together with the constellations, was enveloped in light;
they possessed the luster of lotuses, the color of lotuses, and eyes resembling lotus petals.
And the humans born there possess the fragrance of lotus petals;
they are not produced by sexual union, their scent does not fade, they require no food, and their senses are unsubdued. (13)
Having all descended from the world of the gods, those twice-born ones were likewise free from passion;
they, O best of the twice-born, lived for thirteen thousand years.
The foremost of unrighteous men live for the full measure of their lifespan;
likewise, the Lord is situated to the north of the Ocean of Milk.
Hari Vaikuṇṭha was standing upon a golden chariot;
that excellent vehicle had eight wheels, was yoked with living beings, and possessed the speed of thought. 16.
O best of the twice-born, he was fire-colored, possessed of great splendor, and adorned with gold; he was the lord and the all-pervading master of all beings.
O best of beings, [he is the cause] both in brief and in detail, as well as the agent and the instigator;
likewise, he is earth, water, space, wind, and fire.
Sacrifice is the mouth of all beings, and the consumer of oblations (Agni) is its mouth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||5||
The Sixth Chapter.
The Sages said:
"This land of Bhārata is meritorious and the bestower of merit."
Explain all of that to us, for you are considered by us to be wise. ||1||
Sūta said:
Here I shall proclaim to you the most excellent Bhārata-varṣa,
belonging to Priyavrata, to Deva, and to Manu Vaivasvata.
And [the lineage] of Pṛthu, the wise son of Vainya; likewise that of the high-souled Ikṣvāku;
of Yayāti, Ambarīṣa, Māndhātṛ, and Nahuṣa.
In the same way, [the story] of Ucukunda, of Kubera, and of Uśīnara;
likewise that of Ṛṣabha, of Aila, and of King Nṛga.
Of the royal sage Kuśika and the high-souled Gādhi, as well as of the royal sage Soma and likewise Dilīpa. ||5||
O highly fortunate ones, this supreme Bhārata is dear to all other powerful kṣatriyas and indeed to all living beings.
Thereafter, O great twice-born ones, I shall describe the region as I have heard it:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣavat. (7)
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
O Brahmins, thousands of other mountains are situated in their vicinity.
Some mountains are unknown, possessing substance, vast, and with variegated peaks;
others, however, which are well-known, are short and inhabited by those who live in lowliness.
O twice-born ones, men of mixed descent who share the same dharma as both the Aryans and the Mlecchas drink from the pure rivers— the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the Sarasvatī.
The Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river Bahūdā;
the Śatadrū, the Candrabhāgā, and the great river Yamunā. ||11||
The Dṛṣadvatī, the Vitastā, the Vipāpā with its clear sands, the river Vetravatī, and the river Kṛṣṇāveṇī; ||12||
The Irāvatī, the Vitastā, the Capi, the Uṣṇī, the Devikā,
the Vedasmṛti, the Vedaśirā, the Tridivā, the Sindhu, and the Lākṛmi.
The Karīṣiṇī, the Citravahā, and the river Trisenā;
the Gomatī, the Dhūtapāpā, and the great river Candanā. ||14||
O best of the twice-born, [he visited] the Kauśikī, the Tridivā, the heart-pleasing Nācitā, the Rohitāraṇī, the Rahasyā, the Śatakuṃbhā, and the Sarayū. ||15||
The Carmaṇvatī, the Vetravatī, the Hastisomā, the Diśā, as well as the Śarāvatī, the Payoṣṇī, the Bhīmā, and also the Bhīmarathī. ||16||
[He saw] the Kāverī, the Cūlikā, the Cāpitāpī, the Śatamalā, the Nīvārā, the Mahitā, and likewise the river Suprayogā. (17)
The Pavitrā, Kṛṣṇalā, Sindhu, Vājinī, Puramālinī, Pūrvābhirāmā, Vīrā, Bhīmā, and likewise Mālāvatī. ||18||
[He crossed] the Palāśinī, the Pāpaharā, the Mahendrā, the Paṭalāvatī, the Karīṣiṇī, the Asiknī, the Cakuśacīrī, and the great river [Mahānadī]. ||19||
O best of beings, [they gave] Menā, the foremost of the Maruts, as well as Hemā, Ghṛtavatī, Anāvatī, Anuṣṇā, Sevyā, and Aṅkapi.
The great river Sadāvīrā, which is unassailable, clad in bark garments,
variegated with chariots, possessing celestial vehicles as its light, and having Viśvāmitra as its source and the Aṅgapi as its water.
The Candravahā, the Phalī, the Kucīrā, the Ambuvāhinī, the Vainadī, the Piṅgalā, the Veṇā, and the great river Tuṅgavegā; ||22||
[He saw] the Vidiśā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇā, the Tāmrā, and also the Kapilā; [he saw] a cow that was willing, one that knew the Vedas, one that flowed with sacrificial oblation, and the Mahāpathā. ||23||
The Śiprā, the Capicchala, the river Bhāradvājī,
the river Kaurṇikī, the Śoṇā, the Bāhudā, and the Candrabhāgā.
Durgāmā, Taḥśilā, Brahmamedhyā, Dṛṣadvatī, Parokṣā, Atharohī, and likewise Aja-būnadī. ||25||
The Sunāsā, the Tamasā, the Dāsī, the Sāmānyā, the Varaṇā, the Asiknī, the Nīlā, the Dhṛtikarī, and the great river Parṇāśā. ||26||
The Mānavī, Vṛṣabhā, Bhāsā, Brahmamedhyā, and Dṛṣadvatī—these and many other great rivers, O bulls among the twice-born. (27)
O best of beings, [worship] Kṛṣṇā, who is eternally free from affliction; Maṅgā, the river of grace; Brāhmaṇī, the great Gaurī; and Durgā as well. ||28||
Citrotpalā, Citrarathā, Atulā, and likewise Rohiṇī; Mandākinī, Vaitaraṇī, Kokā, and also the Mahānadī. (29)
[He saw] Śuktimatī, Anaṅgā, and likewise Vṛṣasāhvayā;
Lohityā, Aṅkaratoyā, and likewise Vṛṣakātvayā. ||30||
O most excellent ones, [I praise] Kumārī who is equal to the sages, Camāriṣā, Sarasvatī, the highly meritorious Māṃdākinī, and Sarvāṅgā. ||31||
All of them are mothers of the universe and all indeed yield great fruit;
likewise, there are rivers of brilliant splendor by the hundreds and thousands.
Thus, O brahmins, these rivers have been fully described according to tradition; hereafter, learn from me as I speak of the regions. 33.
Therein were the Ekapādas, the Cālas, the Śālvas, the Mātreyas, the Jāṅgalas, the Śūrasenas, the Pulindas, the Audhas, and likewise the Mālavas. (34)
The Matsyas, Kuśaṭṭas, Saugandhyas, Kutsapas, Kāśikas, Kośalas, Cedis, Matsyas, Karuṣas, Bhojas, Sindhupulinakas, and [others]. (35)
The Uttamas, the Daśārṇas, and the Mekalas together with the Utkalas; the Pañcālas, the Kośalas, and the Naikapṛṣṭhas and Yugandharas. ||36||
The Bodhāmadras, the Kaliṅgas, the Kāśayas and the Upakāśayas, the Jaṭharas, the Kukuras, the Sudaśārṇas, and the Susattamas; ||37||
The Kuṇṭayas, the Avantyas, and likewise the Aparakuṇṭayas;
the Gomas, the Tāmallakas, the Puṇḍras, the Vidarbhas, and the Nṛpavāhikas. ||38||
The Aśmakas and the Sottaras, the Goparāṣṭras and the Kanīyasas, the Adhirājyas, Kuśaṭṭas, Mallarāṣṭras, and the Keralas. ||39||
The Mālavas, the Upavāsyas, the Cakrāvakrālayas, and the Śakas;
the Videhas, the Magadhas, the Sadmās, the Malajas, and likewise the Vijayas;
the Aṅgas, the Vaṅgas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Yakṛllomas.
The Mallas, the Sudeṣṇas, the Prahlādas, the Mahiṣas, and likewise the Śaśakas. ||41||
The Bāhlikas, the Āvāṭadhānas, the Ābhīras, the Kālatoyakas, the Aparāntas, the Tāparāntas, the Paṅkalas, and the Rmacaṇḍikas. ||42||
The Aṭavīśekharas, the excellent Merubhūtas,
the Upāvṛtas, the Anupāvṛtas, the Surāṣṭras, and likewise the Kekayas.
The Āheya regions beyond Kuṭṭāpa, the Sāmudra parks, many Aṃdhās, O Brahmin, and likewise the mountains within them; 44.
The Bahirgiryas, Aṅgas, Maladas, Magadhas, Mālavas, and Arghaṭas; the Sattvataras, Prāvṛṣeyas, and the Bhārgavas, O best of the twice-born. ||45||
The Puṇḍras, Ābhīras, Kirātas, Sudeṣṇas, Bhāsurakas, Śakas, Niṣādas, Niṣadhas, as well as the Ānartas and Nairṛtas; ||46||
The Pūrṇalās, the Pūtimatsyas, the Kuṃtalas, and the Kuśakas;
the Tarigrahas, the Śūrasenas, the Āījikās, and the Kalpakāraṇas. (47)
The Tilabhāgas, the Asāras, the Madhumattas, the Kakundas, the Kāśmīras, the Sindhusauvīras, and likewise the Gāndhārās and Dhārādarśakas; 48.
The Abhīsāras, Kudrutas, Saurilās, and Bāhlikas, as well as the Darvīcams, Mālavas, Darvās, Vātajāmaras, and Uragas. ||49||
Likewise the Balaraṭṭas, the Vipras, the Sudāmanas, the Mummallikas, the Bandhākarīkas, the Kaṣās, the Kuliṅgas, and the Dāgandhikas. ||50||
The Vanāyus, Udaśas, Pārśvaromas, Kuśabindus, Kācchas, Gopālakacchas, Jāṅgalas, and Kuruvārṇakas [are the tribes]. ||51||
The Kirātas, Barbaras, Siddhas, Vaidehas, Tāmraliptikas, Auḍras, Mlecchas along with the Sairindras, and the excellent mountain-dwellers. ||52||
Furthermore, there were other preeminent sages from the southern regions:
the Dravidas, the Keralas, the Prācyas, the Mūṣikas, and the Bālamūṣikas. ||53||
The Karṇāṭakas, Māhiṣakas, Vikandhas, and likewise the Mūṣikas; the Jhallikas, Kuntalas, Sauhṛdas, and the Nalakānanas. ||54||
The Kaukkuṭakas, Bolas, Kokaṇas, Maṇivālakas, Samaṅgas, Kanakas, Kuṅkuras, Aṅgāras, and Māriṣas; ||55||
The *dhvajinī*, *utsavasaṅketā*, *astrivargā*, *mālyasenayaḥ*, *vyūḍhakāḥ*, *korakāḥ*, *proṣṭāḥ*, and likewise the *saṅgavegadharāḥ*. (56)
Likewise, the Vindhyarulikās, together with the Pulindas and Ābalvalas, as well as the Mālavas, Amlaras, and the Aparavartakas. ||57||
The Kulis, Dāḥkālas, Caṇḍakas, and likewise the Kuraṭas; the Muśalas, Tanuvālas, Satīrthas, Apūtisṛks, and Jayas. ||58||
The Anidāyas, Śivāṭas, Tapanas, Sūtapas, as well as the Ṛṣikas, Vidarbhakas, Staṅganakas, and Aparataṅgakas. ||59||
Furthermore, O eminent sages, there are other Mleccha peoples to the north:
the Javanas, along with the Kāmbōjas and the fierce Dāruṇa Mleccha tribes.
The Sakṛdgrahas and Kulaṭīs, together with the Hūṇas and Pārasīkas, as well as the Ramaṇas and others, and likewise the Daśamālikās. ||61||
And the settlements of Kṣatriyas, as well as the families of Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
the Śūras, Ābhīras, Daradas, and Kaśmīras, together with their cattle.
The Khāṇḍīkas, the Tuṣāras, the Padmagas, the Girigahvaras, the Ādreyas along with the Bhirādājas, and likewise the Astanapoṣakas. ||63||
The Droṣakas, the Kaliṅgas, and the tribes of Kirātas,
as well as the Tomaras and Karabhajakas, were being struck down.
O twice-born ones, these and other regions of the east and the north have been described by me merely as a brief enumeration.
And according to the strength of their respective virtues, the four classes [of beings] also obtain great fruit. //65//
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||6||
The Seventh Chapter.
The Sages said: [Tell us] of this Varṣa of Bhārata as well as of Haimavata.
The duration of life, the strength of the vital seed, and its auspicious or inauspicious nature [are determined]. ||1||
O best of beings, tell me in detail about the future, the past, and the present, as well as the sun and the rain.
Sūta said: O best of sages, O excellent among the twice-born, there are four ages in Bhārata-varṣa: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali.
O twice-born ones, first was the age named Kṛtayuga, then the Tretāyuga;
after that the Dvāpara, and thereafter the Tiṣya (Kali) age proceeds.
O best of sages, in the Kṛta Yuga, the lifespan is reckoned at four thousand years for those whose wealth is their asceticism. (5)
Likewise, they know that in the Tretā age the lifespan is three thousand years;
and in the Dvāpara age, two thousand remain on earth at present.
O bulls among sages, during the Kali age (Tiṣya), the duration of life will indeed be that [measure];
moreover, beings die while still in the womb, and likewise they die as soon as they are born.
Possessing great strength and great being, and endowed with the qualities of wisdom, they are born and continue to be born by the hundreds and thousands. ||8||
In the Kṛta Yuga, O twice-born ones, the Brahmins were powerful and pleasing to behold;
they were born as sages whose wealth was their asceticism.
They were possessed of great energy and noble souls, righteous and truthful in speech;
they were pleasant to behold, handsome in form, endowed with great heroism, and skilled archers. ||10||
From the Vīra women were born Kṣatriyas who were esteemed as heroes;
during the Tretā age, all those Kṣatriyas were indeed universal emperors (cakravartins). ||11||
And in the Dvāpara age, all castes are born always with great energy and heroism, yet desiring to slay one another.
O twice-born ones, it is said that in the Tiṣya age men are born endowed with brilliance and wealth, yet they are prone to anger, greedy, and indeed untruthful. (13)
Likewise, O best of beings, envy, pride, anger, deceit, and malice, as well as passion and greed, arise among living beings during the Tiṣya age.
O Brahmins, the Saṃkṣepa region exists in the middle of the Dvāpara Yuga;
beyond that is the Haimavata region, which possesses superior qualities, and after that is the Harivarṣa region.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||7||
The Eighth Chapter.
The Sages said:
"O best of beings, you have described the land of Jambūdvīpa exactly as it is."
Tell me truly the extent of the Viṣkambha and Bhasya [yogas] according to their actual nature. ||1||
He who perceives without flaw [the truth] correctly described the measurement of the ocean,
as well as Śākadvīpa, Cuñcu, Śālmalidvīpa, and the righteous Kuśadvīpa.
[He described] Śālmala and likewise Krauñca island in their true nature.
Sūta said:
O Brahmins, there are very many islands by which this entire world is pervaded.
I shall describe the seven continents; listen, O best of the twice-born!
O best of the twice-born, the Jambu mountain has a width of eighteen thousand and six hundred full yojanas.
The width of the salt ocean is recorded as being twice that [of Jambūdvīpa];
it is filled with various inhabited regions and adorned with jewels and coral.
The circular ocean is adorned with mountains variegated by many minerals, and is crowded with *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*.
O most virtuous ones, listen now as I speak according to the truth about Śākadvīpa, just as it was told by those best of beings. O righteous ones, hear it from me as I explain it in due order.
O bulls among the twice-born, O highly fortunate ones, the ocean also has a diameter that is double the measure of Jambūdvīpa, divided into its respective sections.
Surrounded by that tiger among sages, Kṣīroda, the regions there are meritorious; no person dies there.
How much less, O best of sages, could there be famine in Śākadvīpa, which is endowed with patience and splendor? Its brief description is as follows.
O highly fortunate ones, this has been told; what else shall I relate to you? ||10||
The sages said:
"O righteous one, O highly wise one, you have already related the summary of Śākadvīpa; now tell us its detailed description according to the truth. (11)
Sūta said:
In that same manner, O brahmins, there are seven mountain ranges made of jewels, as well as oceans and rivers; I shall describe their names.
"O righteous ones, ask about every reality that possesses supreme qualities.
Meru is said to be the first, joined by gods, sages, and gandharvas. (13)
To the east lies the highly fortunate mountain named Malaya;
from there the clouds arise and they originate from it in every direction.
Beyond that, O sages, is the great mountain Jaladhāra;
from there, Indra constantly takes up the supreme water. 15.
Thereafter, O best of the twice-born, the year Prabhava begins during the rainy season,
where Mount Raivataka is eternally established on high.
O best of Brahmins, under the constellation Revatī, there is the rite established by Pitāmaha;
and to the north of that is the great mountain named Śyāma.
The noble one, possessing the luster of nine clouds, was tall and possessed a glorious, radiant body;
by him, the subjects attained a dark complexion and became joyful in mind. (18)
The sages said:
"O Sūta, a very great calamity has been brought upon us by you.
O Sūta, how is it that the progeny have here properly attained this state of blackness? (19)
Sūta said:
O best of sages, O twice-born ones, in all these great islands,
there are fair-complexioned, dark-complexioned, and bird-like beings, as well as those of intermediate colors between them.
Because Śyāma originated from this [place], it is known as Śyāmagiri;
beyond that, O best of sages, is the most exalted Durgaśaila.
From where the wind proceeds, it is joined with the Keśarī and Keśara [mountains];
their extent in yojanas is double for each respective division.
O best of Brahmins, among these years, the wise have declared Mahā-meru, Mahā-kāśa, Jalada, and Kumudottara. (23)
Jaladhāra, Mahāprājña, and Sukumāra are remembered as his [sons];
likewise, Reva, Kaumāra, Śyāma, and Maṇikāñcana. ||24||
Then, beyond the Audākī river, there is a great man named Keśara;
he surrounds the lords of the brahmins, both in length and in breadth.
O wise ones, in the center of that continent which is reckoned as Jambūdvīpa, there is a great tree named Śāka; its inhabitants, along with their followers, are known as the Śākas.
There the meritorious regions are located; there Śaṅkara is worshipped;
there the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and deities go.
All the subjects were righteous, free from the four vices and devoid of envy; the social classes were devoted to their own duties, and no thief was seen there.
There, the people— long-lived, highly wise, and free from old age and death—
increased like the rivers flowing toward the ocean during the rainy seasons.
There, rivers with holy waters flow in many ways, such as the Gaṅgā, the Sukumārī, the Kumārī, the Śītā, and the Śītodakā. (30)
O best of brahmins, the Mahānadī, the Maṇijalānadī, and the Ikṣuvarddhanikā are likewise remembered as rivers by the foremost sages. ||31||
Then hundreds of thousands of most beautiful rivers of meritorious gifts flowed forth, as much as Vāsava poured down in rain.
It is not possible to remember their names, nor is it possible to enumerate those meritorious and excellent rivers. (33)
Then there were four meritorious provinces, world-renowned:
the Mṛgas, the Maśakas, the Mānasas, and likewise the Mallakas. (34)
In the Mṛgas, the twice-born are mostly devoted to Brahman and intent on their own duties;
among the Maśakas, the Kṣatriyas are unrighteous yet granters of all desires.
And the high-souled Mānasas, who subsist by the dharma of Vaiśyas, are endowed with all objects of desire; they are heroic and resolute in matters of dharma and worldly purpose. ||36||
In that place, there were always Śūdras who were wrestlers and men of unrighteous character; O best of Brahmins, there was neither king nor punishment, nor were there any who inflicted punishment.
O knower of dharma, they protect one another solely by means of their own duty;
this much alone can be said regarding that continent.
And this very thing is to be heard in Śākadvīpa, which possesses great majesty.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||8||
The Ninth Chapter.
Sūta said: O Brahmins, a story is heard concerning the northern continents.
Thus, listen to that which was spoken there by the highly fortunate one. ||1||
Then there is the ocean of clarified butter, and beyond that the ocean of whey;
indeed, there is the ocean of wine, as well as the ocean of fresh milk.
O best of the twice-born, all the islands, O highly wise ones, as well as the mountains, are each double the size of the preceding one and are surrounded by oceans. (3)
O twice-born ones, on the island of Tumuda there is the great mountain Gaura, made of realgar;
and on the western side is the black mountain Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nārāyaṇa.
There Keśava himself guarded the divine jewels;
being well-pleased, he bestowed happiness upon the subjects.
O twice-born ones, in the middle of the country on Śaradvīpa, there is a *kuśa* tree which is worshipped; and on Śālmalidvīpa, there is a *śālmali* tree, O brahmins, which is likewise honored.
O best of Brahmins, on Krauñcadvīpa there is the great mountain Mahākrauñca, a source of heaps of jewels;
it is constantly worshipped by the four castes.
O Brahmins, there is a very great mountain named Gomanta, consisting of all kinds of minerals, where the glorious, lotus-eyed Lord dwells eternally. ||8||
O best of Brahmins, Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is eternally associated with those seeking liberation;
moreover, in Kuśadvīpa, there is a mountain covered with coral.
O best of Brahmins, Sunāman, who is very difficult to overcome, is the second golden mountain;
Dyutimān is the third, the mountain Kumuda.
The fourth is named Puṣpavat, the fifth is Kuśeśaya, and the sixth is Harigiri; these six are the most excellent of mountains. 11.
The interval between them is twice as great for each successive division:
the first layer is the earth, and the second is the circle of dust. (12)
The third is named Suratha, the fourth is known as Lambana;
Dhṛtimat is the fifth region, and Prabhākara is the sixth region. (13)
The seventh region is Kāpila; these seven regions are inhabited by the Varṣa-bakas.
In these regions, O twice-born ones, the gods, Gandharvas, and subjects dwell in joy.
And they dwell happily; among them, no person dies. ||14||
O best of men, among the Natas there are no bandits, nor even those of Mleccha or Dvija castes;
rather, O most excellent ones, all the people are predominantly fair-skinned and delicate.
O best of the twice-born, I shall speak concerning all that remains;
O wise brahmins, listen as it is described just as I have heard it. (16)
In Krauñcadvīpa, O highly fortunate ones, is the great mountain named Krauñca;
beyond Krauñca is Vāmana, and beyond Vāmana is Aṃdhakāraka. ||17||
O Brahmins, beyond the letter *dhakāra* is Maināka, the best of mountains;
and beyond Maināka, O Brahmins, is Govinda, the supreme mountain. (18)
Beyond Govinda is the great mountain Puṇḍarīka;
beyond Puṇḍarīka, moreover, is proclaimed Duṃdubhisvana.
O best of sages, their diameter is twice as much as that;
I shall describe the regions there—listen to me as I speak.
O you whose wealth is asceticism, the region of Krauñca is auspicious; beyond Vāmana is Manonuga;
and beyond Manonuga is the region named Uṣṇa.
After *uṣṇa* comes *prāvaraka*; after *prāvara* comes *aṃ dhakāraka*;
and after the region of *aṃ dhakāraka*, the region of *tumuni* is traditionally taught to follow. ||22||
Beyond the region of the Munis is said to be Duṃdubhisvana;
it is crowded with Siddhas and Cāraṇas and is known as Gaura, extending for one yojana.
These regions have been fully described as frequented by gods and gandharvas;
in Puṣkara, there is a mountain named Puṣkara, abounding in jewels and gems.
There the divine Lord Prajāpati himself constantly dwells;
all the gods and great seers perpetually attend upon him. ||25||
The best of the twice-born honor him with words pleasing to the mind,
and various kinds of jewels proceed from Jambūdvīpa.
O best of sages, throughout all those continents, the welfare of the people was secured by the Brahmins through their celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint.
O best of Brahmins, in those continents, the inhabitants possess health and a lifespan that double progressively from one to the next.
It has been said that among those who do not follow the laws of their respective regions, the Lord Prajāpati himself wields the rod of punishment. (29)
O best of sages, he always remains protecting these continents, together with the king, Śiva, the Brahmins, his father, and his grandfather. (30)
O best of the twice-born, he protects his subjects along with the virtuous brahmin scholars;
and here, O lords of brahmins, food is presented to him by the subjects themselves. (31)
Thus it is established that this highly fortunate one eats it eternally;
beyond that, the great mountain is seen as the support of the world. ||32||
O great wise one, it is four-cornered and perfectly circular on all sides; there dwell the four lords of brahmins, who are esteemed by the world. ||33||
O Brahmins, the people saw the best of sages, the world-elephants— Vāmana and Airāvata— as well as Supratīka, with their temples and trunks flowing with rut.
I am not able to calculate its measure here;
it is eternally incalculable in all directions—across, upwards, and downwards as well. (35)
There, O best of sages, those twice-born ones seize from all directions, including the intermediate points, those who are unrelated to them. (36)
With lotuses resembling full-blown lotuses and possessing great radiance, they repeatedly draw them in, and then they constantly release them again a hundredfold with great speed.
O best of the twice-born, winds come from there like the breaths from the mouths and trunks of the elephants of the quarters; there the sons of Viśvakarman reside.
Having heard this measurement of the earth as it was declared by me, along with its manifestations—this world which bestows merit and delights the mind—[one attains liberation]. (39)
O best of Brahmins, he becomes illustrious, successful in his aims, and esteemed by the virtuous;
his lifespan, strength, fame, and splendor increase. (40)
For him who, firm in his vows, listens to this section being recited on a sacred festival day, his ancestors and likewise his grandfathers are gratified. 41.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
The Sages said:
[Tell us] the dimensions of the earth, its configuration, and likewise its rivers.
Having heard this from you, O illustrious one, it is as if nectar itself has been drunk.
In this regard, we have heard that there are sacred fords (*tīrtha*) on earth that purify those who bathe there.
O highly wise one, we wish to hear about all of them in detail, as well as how they grant their respective fruits. (2)
Sūta said:
O you whose wealth is austerity, you have asked about this blessed, meritorious, and highly renowned narrative;
I shall relate it according to my understanding, in accordance with its connection, and as I have heard it.
I shall proclaim an ancient dialogue concerning the divine sage Nārada;
listen, O best of the twice-born, to this conversation with Yudhiṣṭhira. (4)
Having been deprived of their kingdom, those great chariot-warriors, the sons of Pāṇḍu,
the highly fortunate Pāṇḍavas together with Draupadī, dwell in that forest.
Then they beheld there the high-souled celestial sage Nārada,
blazing with Brahmanic splendor and possessing a brilliance equal to a kindled fire.
Surrounded by his brothers, the illustrious joy of the Kurus shone with radiant splendor,
like Indra among the gods in heaven.
Just as Sāvitrī did not abandon the gods, nor Yājñasenī her husbands, so she did not,
in accordance with dharma, forsake the sons of Pṛthā, any more than the radiance of the sun leaves Mount Meru.
Then, having accepted the worship, the venerable sage Nārada comforted the son of Dharma with words that were both appropriate and pleasing.
He said to the high-souled Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O best among the upholders of dharma, tell me what you desire; what shall I give to you? (10)
Then King Dharmasūta, together with his brothers, bowed down and spoke these words to Nārada, who was like a divine being, with palms joined in reverence: 11. [He spoke] a measured speech to Nārada.
"O illustrious one, honored by all the worlds, since you are pleased with me, everything has already been accomplished through your grace, O observer of excellent vows. (12)
O sinless one, if I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your favor, then you ought to sever this doubt residing in my heart, O best of sages. (13)
O Brahmin, you ought to tell me in its entirety what the fruit is for one who, devoted to sacred fords, circumambulates the earth.
Nārada said: Listen attentively, O King, to how all of this was formerly heard by Dilīpa from the presence of Vasiṣṭha.
Formerly, on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī, Dilīpa, the best of kings,
dwelt like a sage, having undertaken a righteous vow.
O great king, in that auspicious and meritorious place, worshipped by gods and sages, at Gaṅgādvāra, which is possessed of great splendor and frequented by gods and gandharvas. ||17||
The one of supreme splendor gratified the gods along with the ancestors,
and he gratified the sages by means of rites prescribed by the rules.
After some time, while he was thus engaged in silent recitation, that high-minded one beheld the supreme seer Vasiṣṭha, who appeared like a celestial being.
Seeing the family priest, who was as if blazing with splendor, he experienced incomparable joy and attained the highest wonder. (20)
O Bhārata, that best of the upholders of dharma honored the arrived great king with worship according to the rites prescribed by the sacred law.
Taking the water-offering (arghya) with his head bowed, pure and with a restrained mind,
he proclaimed the names of that most excellent of Brahman-sages.
"I am Dilīpa; may it be well with you, O observer of excellent vows! I am your servant.
By the mere sight of you, I have been liberated from all sins. (23)
Having spoken thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the great king Dilīpa, the best among men, became silent with restrained speech and joined palms in reverence.
Seeing that Dilīpa, the best of kings, who was emaciated by his constant practice of Vedic study, the sage became pleased in mind. (25)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||10||
The eleventh chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
By this humility and self-restraint of yours, O knower of dharma...
O highly fortunate one, I am entirely satisfied with your truthfulness. ||1||
O sinless one, since you possess such dharma as this by which your fathers have been delivered, behold me, O son; you are worthy of my sacrifice.
"My joy increases today; tell me, what may I do for you?
O best of men, O sinless one, I shall grant whatever you say. (3)
Dilīpa said:
"O knower of the true essence of the Vedas and their branches, honored by all the worlds!
I have seen the Lord, and thus [my purpose] is accomplished. (4)
But if I am worthy of your favor, O best among the upholders of dharma, I shall ask about a doubt residing in my heart; you ought to explain that to me. (5)
O Blessed One, there is no doubt regarding the Dharma in my mind that I have not yet crossed over;
therefore, I wish to hear its detailed exposition from you.
O best of the twice-born, O brahmin-sage, O one whose wealth is asceticism, tell me this: what is the fruit for him who circumambulates the entire earth? (7)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I shall relate that which is the supreme refuge of the sages;
listen with a one-pointed mind, my dear, to what the fruit is in sacred fords."
He whose hands, feet, and speech are well-restrained, and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of a true pilgrimage site. (9)
One who has desisted from accepting gifts, who is contented, self-controlled, pure,
and free from the sense of "I," enjoys the fruit of a true sacred ford.
Free from guile, abstaining from food, not obtaining food [yet remaining steadfast], with senses conquered, and liberated from all defects—he enjoys the fruit of the true sacred ford. ||11||
O king of kings, one who is free from anger, truthful, firm in his vows,
and who regards all beings as himself, enjoys the fruit of visiting sacred fords.
The seers have proclaimed the sacrifices among the gods in their proper order,
as well as the fruit thereof in its true nature, both after death and in this world, in every respect.
O lord of the earth, sacrifices cannot be attained by one who is poor;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of materials.
That goal is attainable by these prosperous kings and monkeys;
it is not for destitute groups of men who are solitary and lack means.
O lord of men, that rite which even the poor are able to perform—know, O king, that it is equal in merit to the fruits of sacrifices. (16)
O best among the upholders of dharma, this sacred visiting of holy fords (tīrthas), which is the supreme secret of the sages, is even superior to sacrifices. (17)
By failing to observe the three-night fasts, by not visiting sacred fords,
and by not giving gold and cows, one is born as a pauper.
By performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which is obtained by visiting sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having reached Puṣkara, the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds as the gateway from the world of men to the world of gods, one becomes equal to the God of gods. (20)
O Lord of the Earth, descendant of the Solar Lineage, ten thousand crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) are present at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day.
O Lord, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas along with the hosts of Maruts,
as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, were all present there.

O great king, O twice-born ones, it is there that the gods, the Daityas, and likewise the brahminical sages, having performed austerities through great merit and divine yoga, [attained their goals]. (23)
Even for the wise man who merely desires the lotuses with his mind,
all his sins are purified and he is honored upon the back of the celestial vault.
O highly fortunate one, at the Maṣṭīrtha, the Grandfather (Brahmā), who is honored by both gods and dānavas, always dwelt with supreme delight. ||25||
At Puṣkara, the gods of great fortune, led by the sages, attained supreme perfection, endowed as they were with great merit. ||26||
The wise declare that for one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods who performs an ablution there, the merit is ten times that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Even if one residing in the Puṣkara forest feeds but a single Brahmin, by that act he attains the worlds honored by the gods, situated in the abode of Brahmā. (28)
O King, whoever remembers Puṣkara with palms joined in reverence in the morning and evening has effectively performed ablutions at all sacred fords.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth, it all perishes as soon as one has gone to Puṣkara. (30)
Just as Madhusūdana is said to be the first of all the gods, even so Puṣkara is declared to be the foremost of sacred fords (tīrthas). ||31||
Having fasted for twelve years at Puṣkara, self-controlled and pure,
one obtains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Brahmā.
He who maintains the Agnihotra sacrifice for a full hundred years gains exactly the same merit as he who dwells for a single Kārttikī night at Puṣkara.
Difficult is it to dwell at Puṣkara; difficult is the asceticism at Puṣkara;
difficult is the giving at Puṣkara, and to dwell there is indeed most difficult. (34)
There are three white peaks and three springs;
we do not know the reason why the Puṣkara tirthas are located there at the very beginning. ||35||
Having fasted for twelve years, self-restrained and restricted in diet, one is liberated from all sins and obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. ||36||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Puṣkara Tīrtha," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
(12) The Twelfth Chapter.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having performed a circumambulation, one should enter the path of the jambu tree;
having entered the path of the jambu tree, which is honored by the ancestors, gods, and sages. ||1||
He obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu; having stayed there for five nights, the man partakes of food at the sixth mealtime. ||2||
He does not fall into an evil rebirth and attains unsurpassed perfection;
having turned back from Jambumārga, he should go to the Tululikā hermitage.
He does not fall into an evil rebirth, but is honored in the heavenly world;
having reached the hermitage of Agastya, he becomes devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods. ||4||
O King, having fasted for three nights, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
subsisting on vegetables or fruits, one attains the supreme state of Kumāra.
O bull among kings, having reached Kanyāśrama— which is prosperous, nourishing, honored by the worlds,
the sacred Dharmāraṇya, beneficial, and primordial— [one attains merit].
Merely upon entering it, one is indeed liberated from all sins;
having honored the ancestors and the gods, being self-restrained and restricted in diet. ||7||
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled;
then, having performed a circumambulation, he should proceed to Yayāti’s fall.
One obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) sacrifice there;
therefore, one should go to Mahākāla with self-restraint and a regulated diet. 9.
Having touched the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
from there, the knower of dharma should go to the sacred site of Umāpati.
There is a place named Abhadravaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having gone there and approached Īśāna, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Through the great grace of the God,
O best of men, one shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya), which is prosperous, free from rivals, and endowed with glory.
Having reached the river Narmadā, renowned throughout the three worlds, and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. ||13||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||12||
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) was described by Vasiṣṭha to Dilīpa."
And it is renowned as Narmadeti, which shatters the mountain of sins. ||1||
Furthermore, O Nārada, best of the twice-born, I wish to hear again from you the majesty of the Narmadā as it was described by Vasiṣṭha.
O Nārada, tell me how this river of great merit, renowned everywhere and celebrated by the name Narmadā, became so famous. 3.
Nārada said: Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins;
she delivers all beings, both the stationary and the moving. (4)
O great king, I have heard the majesty of the Narmadā as spoken by Vasiṣṭha; all of that, indeed, I shall relate to you. (5)
The Gaṅgā is sacred at Puṣkara and Nakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
yet the Narmadā is sacred everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest.
The Sarasvatī purifies with three [days], the Yamunā with seven; the Gāṅgeya purifies instantly, and the Nārmada by the mere sight [of its water]. (7)
In the western half of the Kaliṅga country, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
there is a sacred place, auspicious in the three worlds, delightful and enchanting.
O great king, the gods, asuras, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism,
having performed penance, have attained supreme perfection.
Having bathed there, remaining under the great royal vow with senses subdued,
and fasting for one night, one shall deliver a hundred of one's lineages.
O Lord of Men, having bathed and offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule,
his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
On that parvan day, ten million Rudras are established there;
whoever performs a ritual bath at that place, offering perfumes, garlands, and unguents— ||12||
The entire multitude of ten million Rudras will be pleased with him, without a doubt;
for on the western edge of the mountain, the Lord Maheśvara himself resides. (13)
Having bathed there, become pure, observing celibacy and with senses subdued, one should perform the ancestral rites according to the procedure prescribed by the rules. ||14||
There, O Pāṇḍava, one should satisfy the ancestral deities with water mixed with sesame seeds; his lineage shall remain in heaven for seven generations.
For sixty thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world,
surrounded by throngs of Apsarases and attended by celestial women.
Anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments, he then, having fallen from heaven, is born into a great family. (17)
One is born wealthy, charitable, and indeed righteous;
one remembers that sacred ford again and makes a journey there. (18)
Having delivered hundreds of families, one goes to the world of Rudra;
this most excellent river is heard to extend for more than a hundred yojanas.
But in its extent, O Lord of Kings, it is two yojanas across;
likewise, there are sixty thousand and sixty million sacred fords (tīrtha). ||20||
Having become pure through celibacy, with anger conquered and the senses subdued, one should stand upon the Amarakantaka peak for as long as that [period] lasts. 21.
Having desisted from all violence and being devoted to the welfare of all beings, one who conducts oneself in this manner should wander among the guardians of the field. 22.
O King, listen with focused attention to the fruit of his merit:
O Pāṇḍava, he shall rejoice in heaven for a hundred thousand years.
Surrounded by throngs of Apsarases and attended by celestial women,
he was anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine ornaments.
He sports in the world of the gods and rejoices together with the deities;
then, having descended from heaven, he becomes a powerful king.
And he obtains a house adorned with various jewels, with pillars made of divine gems, embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli. (26)
Divine, accompanied by paintings, provided with male and female servants, and filled with the sounds of rutting elephants and the neighing of horses. (27)
His gateway trembles like the palace of Indra;
he is the glorious lord of the kings of kings, beloved by all women. (28)
Having dwelt in that house, endowed with the enjoyment of play and pleasures, he shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases. ||29||
In this way, he who dies by falling from a cliff, by entering fire or water, or likewise by fasting unto death, shall possess such enjoyment.
O lord of men, for that man who falls from the summit of that mountain, there is no returning; his course is irreversible. 31.
There are three thousand maidens, and for each one there are others as well;
they dwell in his palace and offer their services.
Having arisen with divine enjoyments, he sports for an inexhaustible time;
such a person as this is not born anywhere upon the earth, as far as the oceans.
O best of men, just as this [place] is on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, so too should Koṭitīrtha be known; its festival occurs on the western side of that mountain.
There is one named Rudrojaḷeśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to him and by performing the rite of twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), [one attains the highest goal]. ||35||
Those ancestors for whom libations are offered remain satisfied for ten years.
To the south of the Narmadā is the great river named Kapilā.
Not far away stands the sacred and highly blessed river, renowned throughout the three worlds, covered with *sarala* and *arjuna* trees. (37)
In that regard, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, more than a hundred crores of sacred fords are heard of in the Purāṇas; O King, all of them become ten-million-fold [meritorious] there.
Furthermore, whatever trees on her banks have fallen due to the passage of time, they too attain the supreme goal when joined with the waters of the Narmadā. (39)
The second is the highly auspicious Viśalyakaraṇā;
by bathing there on its bank, a person becomes free from all thorns [of affliction] in an instant. (40)
There, all the hosts of gods, along with the kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism, [were present]. (41)
They all assembled there on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
together with all those sages whose wealth is their austerity.
Taking refuge in the Narmadā, she became known by the name Viśalyā;
highly fortunate, she was born as the destroyer of all sins. 43.
Having bathed there, O King, a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses,
by fasting for a single night, shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
O best of kings, it is heard that Kapilā and Viśalyā were formerly proclaimed by the Lord out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. 45.
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
and he who performs a fast at that sacred ford, O lord of men, [obtains the same]. (46)
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Indra;
this was heard by me, O lord of kings, in the Purāṇa concerning the Narmadā. ||47||
Having bathed in each of those places, a person shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
they dwell in the world of Indra on the northern bank of the Yavakī. 48.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Śaṅkara has told me that giving gifts and bathing are equal at the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, and the Narmadā.
He who gives up his life on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka is honored in the world of Indra for more than a hundred crores of years. ||50||
The meritorious water of the Narmadā, rendered beautiful by foam and waves, is pure and worthy of being borne upon the head; by it, one is liberated from all sins. (51)
The Narmadā is meritorious in every way and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by fasting for a day and night, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin. 52.
Thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, this great river purifies even the three worlds through its meritorious course and its waters. (53)
At the highly meritorious Vaṭeśvara, at Gaṅgādvāra, and in the penance grove—
at all these places, those who have died while firm in their vows [attain liberation].
It is heard that at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Udvasā, the merit is tenfold.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||13||
Chapter Fourteen. Nārada said:
Among the three worlds, there is no river more excellent than the Narmadā, more meritorious, and most holy.
It has been analyzed by the highly fortunate sages who were seekers of Dharma. ||1||
O Pāṇḍava, O Indra among kings, there are sacrificial threads (yajñopavīta) divided into specific measures;
by bathing in them, one is liberated from all sins. ||2||
O delighter of the Pāṇḍavas, listen as I describe the origin of that holy ford known as Jaleśvara, which is renowned throughout the three worlds. 3.
In former times, all the hosts of sages, along with Indra and the hosts of Maruts, praised that Great-Souled One, Maheśvara, the God of gods. ||4||
Praising him, they arrived where the god Maheśvara was;
together with Indra and the hosts of Maruts, they made their report to the Lord of Gods:
"O Lord, O Virūpākṣa, protect us who are agitated by fear! ||5||
Īśvara said:
Welcome, O best of sages! For what purpose have you come here?
What is your sorrow, what is your distress, or from where has fear come upon you?
"Tell me, O highly fortunate ones; I desire to know this.
Thus addressed by Rudra, those of immeasurable vows spoke.
The sages said:
"Furthermore, there was a Dānava named Bāṇa, who was terrible, possessed of great heroism, and arrogant because of his strength; he was very famous, and Tripura was his city. (8)
A divine darkness roams the sky by his splendor;
terrified of that, O Virūpākṣa, we have come to you alone for refuge. (9)
"Save us from this great suffering, for divinity is indeed the supreme goal.
O Lord of Gods, it behoves you to show such grace toward all. (10)
O Śaṅkara, you ought to act so that the gods, being well-pleased, may prosper in happiness and attain supreme bliss. (11)
The god said:
"I shall do all this; you must not despair. In a very short time, I will bring about that which brings you happiness."
Having comforted them all, the Lord of All remained on the bank of the Narmadā and,
O Pāṇḍava, reflected upon their slaughter.
"How, by what means, shall I abandon her?"—
thinking thus, the Blessed One then remembered Nārada.
By that very act of remembrance, Nārada arrived and stood before him.
Nārada said:
"O Great God, command me; for what purpose have I been remembered? O Lord, tell me what task must be performed by me. (15)
The Lord said:
"Go, Nārada, to that very place where the city of Tripura is located;
go quickly to the city of Bāṇa, the lord of the Dānavas, and perform that task."
Their husbands were like deities and their wives resembled apsarases;
by their splendor, that triple city shone brilliantly in the sky.
Having gone there, urge another mantra upon the supreme lord of sages;
having heard the word of the god, the sage, swift in his prowess, [acted]. (18)
Having entered that city for the purpose of destroying the hearts of women, that divine city, adorned with various jewels, shone brilliantly. 19.
It was a hundred yojanas wide and twice that in length;
there he saw Indrajit, who was arrogant in his strength.
He was resplendent with garlands, earrings, and armlets, adorned with a crown,
covered with necklaces and jewels, and embellished by the luster of the moon.
His women were rich in jewels and his men were adorned with gold;
seeing Nārada standing there, the exceedingly powerful lord of the Dānavas rose up.
Bāṇa said:

"O best of the twice-born, since you have now arrived at my home along with the gods and sages, let the guest-offering (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya) be provided according to the prescribed rule."
"A brahmin has arrived after a long time; please be seated on this seat. Having thus honored Nārada who had approached him, [he spoke]. (24)
His chief queen was named Anaupamyā. ||25||
Anaupamya said:
"O Blessed One, by what indeed do the gods become pleased in the world of humans—by a vow, or by a religious observance, or by a gift, or even by austerity? (26)
Nārada said:
Whoever should give a sesame-cow to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, it is as if the entire earth,
with its oceans and seven islands, has been given.
In celestial palaces resembling ten million suns and fulfilling all desires,
he rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time, having long performed his duties.
There were mangoes, wood-apples, plantains, and groves of kadamba, bakula, pāṭala, and aśoka trees, as well as many other various kinds of trees. (29)
The eighth, the fourth, and likewise both twelfth [lunar days], as well as the solstices, the equinoxes, and the beginnings of the day-intervals (dinacchidramukha). ||30||
For those women who observe all these meritorious fasts and are endowed with righteousness, there is no doubt that their dwelling shall be in heaven. (31)
Freed from the Kali age and devoid of all sins,
those ascetics, devoted to fasting, do not approach noble women.
"Having heard this, O lady of beautiful hips, you should do as you wish.
Having heard the words of Nārada, the queen spoke these words: [33]
"O best of Brahmins, show favor; accept as you desire gifts such as gold, gems, jewels, garments, and ornaments. (34)
"O Brahmin, I shall give you this, as well as whatever else is difficult to obtain;
please accept it, O best of the twice-born, so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased. (35)
Nārada said:
"O blessed one, let this be given to another brahmin whose livelihood is exhausted;
as for us, we are endowed with good character, yet devotion is what is practiced by me. (36)
Having thus captivated the minds of all those women and instructed them, O best of the Bharatas, he returned once more to his own abode. (37)
With their minds drawn away and their hearts gone elsewhere,
a vulnerability arose in the great-souled Bāṇa.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
(15) The Fifteenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O son of Kuntī, listen and understand that which you ask me;
in this very interval, Rudra was stationed on the bank of the Narmadā. ||1||
There is a place named Hareśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds;
in that place, the Great God meditated upon the destruction of Tripura.
Having made the Gāṇḍīva his bow, Vāsuki his string,
Vaiśākha his stance, and Viṣṇu his excellent arrow— ||3||
Having established the fire at the front, the wind was placed in the mouth;
the four Vedas were the horses, and the chariot consisted of all the gods.
The two Aśvin deities were the purity of his arms, the wielder of the discus himself was the chest, Indra himself was the bow, and Vaiśravaṇa stood as his arrows. (5)
Yama was placed on his right hand and the terrible Kāla on his left;
the world-renowned Gandharvas were stationed upon the spokes of the wheels.
Prajāpati was the best chariot, and Brahmā himself was the charioteer;
having thus fashioned the chariot consisting of all the gods, the Lord of Devas [mounted it].
He stood like a pillar for a thousand years, until the three [fires] that move through the atmosphere had come together. (8)
Then, impelled by Rudra toward Tripura, that arrow pierced those three cities with its triple-pointed shaft.
Their splendor was lost, their women were born [prematurely], and their strength shattered;
moreover, thousands of portents appeared in that city.
Then, for the destruction of Tripura, he assumed the form of Time (Kāla);
likewise, the wooden figures let out a loud, mocking laugh.
They even perform the act of opening and closing their eyes through the power of painting;
and in dreams, they see themselves adorned with red garments and ornaments. (12)
And those people who are situated in that place see these very same portents in their dreams, though they appear as inverted.
Their strength and their intellect were destroyed by the wrath of Hara; and there arose a great wind named Saṃvartaka, resembling the wind at the end of an eon. ||14||
The best of fires, being fanned by the wind, afflicts the highest peaks;
there the trees blaze and the mountain summits fall down. (15)
All that became utterly chaotic, filled with cries of "Alas! and devoid of consciousness;
all the gardens were shattered and quickly burst into flames. ||16||
By that very [fire], everything was set ablaze with its flaming crests; the trees, the clusters of groves, and various kinds of houses were consumed. (17)
This kindled bearer of oblations has spread forth in the ten directions;
consequently, stones are being discharged from each of the ten quarters. (18)
With thousands of extremely fierce crests of blazing fire, why does the entire city appear as if ablaze, resembling a parrot? (19)
It was possible to go from house to house by means of the smoke [to find him],
as he was being consumed by the fire of Hara’s wrath, crying out and deeply distressed.
The city of Tripura was burning, consumed on all sides by fire;
the peaks of its palace turrets were shattered by the thousands. (21)
Furthermore, celestial palaces variegated with various jewels and many kinds of delightful mansions were being consumed by the blazing fire.
Indeed, there was a great burning in the groves of trees and likewise in Janasthāna;
it blazed and continued to blaze within all the temples of the gods.
Touched by fire, they sink down and cry out with various sounds;
there, heaps of embers resembling mountain peaks are seen.
Oppressed by the fire, they embraced one another and praised the Lord of the gods, saying, "O Lord, protect us! (25)
There, hundreds and thousands of Dānavas were being consumed by fire,
while lotus ponds abounded with haṃsas, kāraṇḍavas, and lotuses.
By that fire, the cities, gardens, and oblong ponds were consumed;
yet they remained covered with unfading lotuses spread over hundreds of yojanas.
There, palaces resembling mountain peaks and adorned with jewels fall down like water-bearing clouds consumed by fire.
Driven by the wrath of Hara, the merciless fire seemed to burn everything— cows, birds, horses, children, women, and the elderly.
Many people, including their wives, were fast asleep;
while embracing their sons tightly, they were being consumed by the Enemy of Tripura.
Then, in that blazing city, women resembling apsarases,
struck by the flames of fire, fall there upon the surface of the earth.
A certain young woman, large-eyed and adorned with a string of pearls, was distressed by the smoke; she awoke from her sleep, tormented by the flames.
As she was reflecting, it was heard that a certain woman of golden complexion, adorned with blue jewels, had fallen upon the surface of the earth. (33)
Distressed by the smoke and fallen to the surface of the earth,
another young girl, her hand not grasped by her friend, is being burned by the children.

Having seen this divine form, she, deluded by intoxication, joined her palms to her head and addressed the Fire-god: 35. Having seen this divine form, she, deluded by intoxication, joined her palms to her head and addressed the Fire-god.
If you desire enmity toward men who have done you harm, what offense have these women committed against you—these aged housewives, like female cuckoos? (36)
Your anger toward women is sinful, merciless, and shameless;
it possesses neither courtesy nor modesty, and is devoid of truth and purity.
"Behold these women, rich in many forms and colors; tell us, have you not heard in the world that all women are inviolable? (38)
But what do these virtues of yours avail against this burner of the three worlds? For you have neither compassion, nor mercy, nor even courtesy toward a woman. (39)
Even Mlecchas show compassion toward women when they see them being burned;
yet for Mlecchas, this [passion] is painful, difficult to restrain, and indeed devoid of consciousness. 40.
These very qualities of yours are intended for the burning and destruction of these women of wicked conduct; why then do you fall [into despair]? 41.
O you who are wicked, merciless, and shameless, a fire that consumes the unfortunate;
you are hopeless, yet you mercilessly burn these children of evil conduct. 42.
Thus lamenting and speaking with many voices, others cried out in great anger, deluded by grief for their child. (43)
The merciless fire, enraged like a universal enemy, burns within the lotus pond, as well as within the flames of the wells. 44.
"Having burned us, to what destination will you lead us, O Mleccha?
To those who were thus lamenting, the Fire spoke these words: 45.
Vaiśvānara said:
"I shall certainly not bring about your destruction of my own accord;
I am merely the executor of orders, and it is He who will bestow grace."
"Overcome by anger here, I am wandering at will.
Then Bāṇa, of great splendor, beheld Tripura set ablaze.
Seated upon his throne, he spoke thus: "I have been destroyed by the gods—those of little strength and wicked conduct—who have reported me to the Lord. (48)
Indeed, I have been consumed by the high-souled Śaṅkara without being examined;
there is no other enemy capable of slaying me except for Maheśvara. (49)
Having risen and placed his head at the feet of the Lord of the Three Worlds in embrace,
he departed from the city gate himself, leaving behind his friends.
Taking various and most wonderful jewels as well as women of many kinds, he placed them upon his head and set down the Linga within the circle of the city. 51.
I praise Śiva, the Lord of the gods and sovereign of the three worlds:
"O Śaṅkara, since you have burnt me with your fire, you are as good as slain by me. (52)
By your grace, O Great God, may this great liṅga of mine perish, which has always been worshipped with supreme devotion to the Great God. (53)
Even if I am to be slain by you, let my body perish;
for me, O Mahādeva, this attainment of grasping your feet is what must be reached.
"O Great God, throughout birth after birth, I have been devoted to your feet;
having thus praised the Supreme Lord with these *toṭaka* verses, [I am now at your service]. (55)

Oṃ! Salutation to Śiva-Śaṅkara, the benefactor of all; salutation to the Great Lord, the auspicious one, who is both terrifying and the source of existence. O you who destroyed the body of the flower-armed god (Kāmadeva), the destroyer of Tripura, and the reducer to ash! 56.
He who delights women and dispels the delusion of those desiring sensual pleasures, who is saluted by hosts of gods and Siddhas,
and who is surrounded by Gaṇas with faces like horses, monkeys, lions, and lordly elephants, as well as those with extremely short and very long faces.

Distressed by many hundreds of bodies of asuras who were exceedingly difficult to perceive, he bowed down with great devotion, O Blessed One; salutations to the god who bears the digit of the moon upon his crest! 58.
May you always grant me victory along with my sons, wife, retinue, and wealth; remember me,
for I am tormented by hundreds of bodies.
Today, the path to the great hell has been traversed.
That which does not turn back is my evil destiny; though it be purified by pure deeds, it abandons me.
Compassionate, it wanders in all directions, it wanders on and on.
This delusion, born of evil intellect, obstructs [the path]. ||60||
Whoever, being self-restrained and pure in mind, recites this divine Toṭaka, Rudra will become a granter of boons to him, just as he was to Bāṇa. (61)
Having heard this great and divine hymn of praise, the god Maheśvara then became pleased with him; indeed, the god Maheśvara himself was gratified.
Īśvara said:
"O son of Suvarṇā, you must not fear, O Dānava, along with your sons, grandsons, wives, and your circle of servants. (63)
"From this day forward, O Pāṇḍava, Bāṇa shall be invulnerable even to the gods; furthermore, a boon was granted to him by the God of Gods."
Inexhaustible and undecaying, Hanu wandered through the world fearlessly;
then Rudra likewise restrained the seven-flamed fire.
The third was protected by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
it constantly wanders through the sky by the power of Rudra’s splendor.
Thus was Tripura burnt by the high-souled Śaṅkara;
blazing with garlands of flames, it fell upon the surface of the earth.
One of them was struck down by him at Śrīśaila, the destroyer of Tripura;
the second was struck down there on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
O King of Tripura, when [the city] was burnt, ten million Rudras were established there;
because that blazing [fire] was cast down there, it is known as Jvāleśvara. (69)
The divine flame that had set out from him ascended to heaven;
at that moment, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the gods, asuras, and humans.
One should bow before that Śara-stambha in the supreme city of Rudra-Māheśvara;
thus one should proceed to that mountain, Amarakaṇṭaka.
O son of Pāṇḍu, having fully enjoyed the fourteen worlds for thirty-three thousand million years and further [thirty-three] million years, (72)
Then, having reached the surface of the earth, he becomes a righteous king;
he enjoys the earth under a single umbrella—of this there is no doubt. (73)
O Great King, this Amarakaṇṭaka is meritorious in every respect;
he who goes to Amarakaṇṭaka during lunar or solar eclipses [attains great merit]. ||74||
The wise declare that it is ten times more meritorious than the horse sacrifice;
by beholding Maheśvara there, one attains the heavenly world.
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, they will come together;
all that merit which exists on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka shall be attained [there]. //76//
A person obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice there on the mountain named Jvāleśvara in Amarakaṇṭaka. (77)
Having bathed there, those who have died go to heaven and are not subject to rebirth;
O Great King, one should likewise renounce one's life at Jvāleśvara.
Listen now to the fruit [obtained] even through devotion during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
There are gods named Amarāḥ on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka. (79)
One attains the world of Rudra until the dissolution of all beings, by [bathing] in the water on the bank of that mountain of the god Amareśvara. ||80||
O King, ten million preeminent sages of excellent vows perform austerities there;
that sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka extends for ten yojanas in every direction.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, having bathed in the auspicious waters of the Narmadā,
one is released from sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||15||
Chapter Sixteen.
The Sage said:
Those great-souled ones, the people of Himavat, questioned Nārada.
All the sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, were devoted to Yudhiṣṭhira. ||1||
O Blessed One, tell us truly of the greatness of the confluence of the Kāverī,
for the benefit of the worlds and for our own increase.
But those who are always devoted to non-evil and do not commit wicked deeds are liberated from all sins and go to the supreme state.
O Blessed One, I wish to understand this; you should deign to explain it.
Nārada said:
"Listen all together, led by Yudhiṣṭhira;
here Kubera, whose valor is truth, performed a great sacrifice."
Having reached this sacred ford, he became superior even to universal sovereignty. ||4||
Having attained success, O great king, listen as I speak of that place where the world-renowned Kāverī and Narmadā rivers meet. (5)
Having bathed there and become pure, Kubera, the lord of the yakṣas whose valor is truth,
performed great divine austerity for a hundred years.
The Great God, being pleased with him, shall grant an excellent boon:
"O Yakṣa of great courage, choose whatever boon you desire!"
But you may perform the work of increasing [the body] as you wish, according to what is in your mind. ||7||
Kubera said: "O Lord of the Gods, if you are pleased, and if a boon is to be granted to me,
let me be the first creator and the sovereign lord of all the Yakṣas."
Having heard the words of Kubera, the Lord Maheśvara was pleased;
having said, "So be it," he then vanished right there.
Having obtained the boon, that Yakṣa went quickly to the Yakṣa clan;
he was honored by all the lords of the Yakṣas and consecrated as their king.
The confluence of the Kāverī there destroys all sins;
