those men who do not recognize it are undoubtedly deceived. 11.
Therefore, with every effort, a person should bathe there in the highly meritorious Kāverī and the great river Narmadā. 12.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, one should worship the bull-bannered god;
having obtained the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||13||
For one who enters the fire and for one who practices fasting unto death, there is the state of non-return; thus has Maheśvara declared to me. (14)
Served by excellent women, he rejoices in heaven like Rudra for sixty thousand years and another sixty crores of years. (15)
Dwelling in the world of Rudra, wherever he may go, upon falling away due to the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king. (16)
One who possesses enjoyments, is virtuous in character, and is born of a noble family—by drinking water there properly, he obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa fast. ||17||
Those mortals who drink that auspicious water go to heaven;
they attain the same fruit as those men who dwell between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. (18)
By bathing at the confluence of the Kāverī, that very fruit is produced for him;
thus, O lord of kings, is the greatness of that confluence of the Kāverī.
It is renowned as Patreśvara, the supreme remover of all sins. ||19||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||16||
The seventeenth chapter.
Nārada said: On the northern bank of the Narmadā, there is a sacred site (tīrtha) extending for one yojana.
It is supremely renowned as Patreśvara, the remover of all sins. ||1||
Having bathed there, O King, a man rejoices together with the deities;
assuming a form at will, he sports for five thousand years.
From there, one should go to Garjana, where Megha is situated;
by the power of that sacred ford, he attained the name Indrajit.
From there, one should go to Megharāva, where the clouds thunder;
there, the host of Meghanāda attained excellence. ||4||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the place known as Brahmāvarta;
for there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Brahmā is eternally present.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
thereafter, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, one should go to the Aṅgāreśvara Tīrtha.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Rudra;
from there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilātīrtha.
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a cow;
from there he should go to Kāñcītīrtha, which is frequented by hosts of celestial sages.
Having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain Goloka;
from there, O lord of kings, he should proceed to the supreme Kuṇḍaleśvara.
There Rudra dwells together with Umā;
having bathed there, O king of kings, one becomes invulnerable even to the gods.
Thereafter, one should go to Pippaleśvara, which destroys all sins;
having gone there, O lord of kings, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to Vimala Vimaleśvara;
there, a beautiful crest of the god was cast down by Īśvara.
There, having renounced my life-breaths, may I attain the world of Rudra;
from there, one should go to Puṣkariṇī and perform a ritual bath there. (13)
Merely by bathing there, a person shall obtain half of Indra’s throne;
the Narmadā is the best of rivers, having issued forth from the body of Rudra. 14.
May he, the Great-Souled Lord, who transcends all gods, deliver all beings, both the immobile and the mobile. 15.
Indeed, this most excellent river Narmadā has been described to the hosts of sages, and especially to us; she is truly praised by the seers. 16.
She emerged from the body of Rudra out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
she is the eternal remover of all sins and is saluted by all living beings. (17)
She was praised by the gods, the gandharvas, and likewise by the apsarases: "Homage to you whose waters are meritorious; homage to you who flow to the ocean! (18)
Salutations to you, who were emitted from the body of Śaṅkara by the hosts of ṛṣis;
salutations to you, who are encompassed by dharma, O fair-faced one; salutations to you, the sole source of delight for the hosts of gods. (19)
Homage to you, the purifier of all that is pure; homage to you, who are well-worshipped by the entire world.
That person who, with a pure mind, recites this hymn daily— (20)
A Brāhmaṇa obtains the Veda, a Kṣatriya becomes victorious, a Vaiśya attains profit, and a Śūdra indeed attains an auspicious state. 21.
Indeed, one seeking food obtains food simply by constant remembrance;
the Lord Maheśvara himself constantly resorts to the Narmadā.
This river of merit should be known as the remover of even the sin of killing a Brahmin. ||22||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||17||
(18) Chapter Eighteen.
Nārada said:
From that time forward, O King, Brahmā and the other sages whose wealth is penance, free from desire and anger, have served the Narmadā.
Seeing that trident fallen upon the earth of the God, its merit was proclaimed by the high-souled Śaṅkara. ||2||
There is a great and most meritorious holy place (tīrtha) renowned as Śūlabheda;
having bathed there and worshipped the God, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||3||
O lord of men, for one who performs [this rite] for three nights at that sacred ford after worshipping Mahādeva, there is no further rebirth. ||4||
Then one should go to Bhīmeśvara and the excellent Narmadeśvara;
likewise, one should visit the greatly meritorious Ādityeśvara with clarified butter and honey. (5)
Having worshipped Mallikeśvara, the fruit of one's birth is fully realized;
thereafter, one should behold Varuṇeśvara and the excellent Nīrājeśvara.
The fruit of all sacred fords is obtained by him from the sight of the Five Abodes;
thence, O King of kings, one should go to where the battle was indeed won.
Koṭitīrtha is indeed renowned as the place where the Asuras were fought;
there, O King, those Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, were slain. ||8||
Having seized their heads, those who had been slain came together;
by them, the god Maheśvara, the wielder of the trident, was installed.
Ten million multiplied by that [ten million] is known there as a *koṭīśvara*;
by the mere sight of that sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one shall attain heaven in an embodied state.
Then, because of his extreme meanness, he was pinned down by a vajra-stake;
from that time forward, the attainment of heaven by people was forbidden. (11)
Having offered a bilva fruit with ghee and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and circumambulation,
one should take it up from all sides with the *sahadeva* mantra and hold it to the head.
O Pāṇḍava, the king becomes fully endowed with all his desires.
Upon death, he attains the state of Rudra and is not born again in this world;
having gone to heaven and ruled there, he then returns to the celestial realm.
Likewise, when a man from the snowy regions worships Mahādeva there on the thirteenth lunar day, he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices upon merely bathing there. ||14||
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the most beautiful sacred site, the supreme Agastyeśvara, for the destruction of the sins of men. 15.
O King, having bathed there, a person is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
this occurs on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika. (16)
Established in meditative absorption and with senses subdued, one should bathe the deity with ghee;
endowed with twenty-one oblations, one shall not fall from the state of the Lord.
One should likewise give cows, sandals, an umbrella, and a woolen blanket;
and by providing food for the Brahmins, all of it becomes multiplied ten millionfold. ||18||
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Ravistava;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the state of sitting upon a lion-throne.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the famous shrine of Śakra;
having fasted for one night, one should perform a bath there. (20)
Having bathed according to the rule, one should worship Janārdana;
he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||21||
From there, one should go to the Ṛṣitīrtha, which removes all sins of men;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Śiva. ||22||
And there is the most beautiful Tīrtha of Nārada;
merely by bathing there, a person obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows. ||23||
From there, one should go to Devatīrtha, which was created by Brahmā in ancient times;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Brahmā. 24.
From there, one should go to Amarakaṇṭaka, which was established by the immortals in ancient times;
merely by bathing there, a person obtains the merit of [giving] a thousand cows. ||25||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Vāmaneśvara;
having beheld Vāmanaka there, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
From there, a man should certainly go to Ṛṣitīrtha and then to Īśāneśa;
having seen Vaṭeśvara thereafter, the fruit of his birth is fully realized. (27)
Thereafter, one should go to Bhīmeśvara, which destroys all diseases;
merely by bathing there, O King, a man is liberated from all suffering. (28)
From there, O lord of kings, one should go to the supreme Vāraṇeśvara;
having bathed there, O King, a person is liberated from all suffering. ||29||
From there, one should go to Soma-tīrtha and behold the unsurpassed Moon;
having bathed there, O King, a man endowed with supreme devotion—
At that very moment, established in a divine body, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva;
for sixty thousand years, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thence, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Piṅgaleśvara;
by fasting for a day and night, one obtains the fruit of a three-night fast. ||32||
Whoever offers a Kapila cow at that sacred ford,
as many hairs as there are on her body and on the bodies of her offspring, [for so many years shall he dwell in heaven].
O lord of men, he who performs the sacrifice of his life there is honored in the world of Rudra for as many thousands of years.
Those men who dwell taking refuge on the banks of the Narmadā rejoice for an inexhaustible period of time, as long as the moon and sun endure. (35)
Just as those who have performed meritorious deeds go to heaven after death, so too do they go to Surabhikeśvara; whereas those who have committed evil go to Nāraka-koṭikeśvara. (36)
On that day at Gaṅgāvataraṇa, there is no doubt that it is meritorious;
one should then go to Naṃditīrtha and perform a ritual bath there. (37)
He shall be pleased with him, and he shall be honored in the world of Soma.
Thence one should go to Vyāsatīrtha, the penance grove of the Lord of the Island.
Formerly, the great river, having turned back there out of fear of Vyāsa, was made to flow toward the south by Vyāsa with the utterance of "Huṃ. (39)
O lord of men, he who performs a circumambulation at that sacred ford (tīrtha) will find Vyāsa pleased with him and shall obtain the fruit of his desire.
He who wraps with thread that blazing deity together with its altar shall indeed sport for an imperishable time, just like Rudra himself. (41)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Eraṇḍī-tīrtha;
by bathing at the confluence of the Nara, one is liberated from all sins. 42.
The Eraṇḍī is renowned throughout the three worlds as the destroyer of sins;
or else, it is the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
Having become pure by bathing, the man should be devoted to fasting. ||44||
Having bathed at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī with a heart overflowing with devotion, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa; it is as if ten million have been fed. (45)
Having placed a piece of mother-of-pearl on one's head and immersed oneself in water mixed with the waters of the Narmadā, one is liberated from all sins. ||46||
O lord of men, he who performs a circumambulation at that sacred ford has,
by that act, circumambulated the earth with its seven islands.
Then, having bathed at Suvarṇatilaka and given gold,
one is glorified in the world of Rudra by means of a golden celestial chariot.
Then, having fallen from heaven at the appointed time, he became a powerful king;
from there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the confluence of the Ikṣu river.
The divine Śiva is established there, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
Thence one should go to Skanda-tīrtha, which destroys all sins;
it removes the sin committed since birth by merely bathing there. (51)
Thence one should go to Āṅgiras and perform a ritual bath there;
he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||52||
From there, one should go to Lāṅgalatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
having gone there, O king of kings, one should perform a ritual bath.
One is liberated from the sins committed over seven lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, one should go to Vaṭeśvara, the unsurpassed of all holy places (tīrthas). (54)
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
from there he should go to Saṅgameśvara, the supreme remover of all sins.
Having bathed there, a man obtains a kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, that man who, having reached Bhadratīrtha, gives a gift, [attains great merit]. (56)
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), everything becomes ten millionfold.
Now, if any woman should perform a ritual bath there, [the merit is likewise multiplied]. ||57||
She becomes equal to Gaurī and goes to Indra without a doubt;
from there, one should go to Aṅgāreśvara and perform a ritual bath there.
A man who has merely bathed there is glorified in the world of Rudra;
one should perform a bath there on the fourth lunar day falling on a Tuesday. (59)
One who has received the instruction of Murāri rejoices for an inexhaustible time;
having bathed at Ayonisangama, one shall not behold the abode of the womb again.
Having gone to Pāṇḍaveśvaraka, one should perform a ritual bath there;
such a person rejoices for an inexhaustible period of time and is invulnerable to gods and asuras. ||61||
Then, having gone to the world of Viṣṇu, endowed with the enjoyment of divine play,
and having experienced great pleasures there, he is born as a king in the mortal realm.
One should go to Kambotikeśvara and perform a ritual bath there;
when the northern solstice has arrived, whatever one desires shall come to pass for that person.
From there, one should go to Candra-bhāgā and perform a ritual bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man is glorified in the world of Soma. ||64||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the famous tīrtha of Śakra, which is honored by the king of gods and saluted even by the deities. ||65||
Having bathed there, O King, and having given a gift of gold, or else one who should release a bull possessing a blue-black hue; 66.
As many hairs as there are on the bull and on its offspring,
for that many thousands of years shall a man dwell in the city of Hara.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a powerful king,
O lord of men, amidst thousands of white-colored horses.
By the power of that sacred ford, he becomes a lord among mortals;
from there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Brahmāvarta.
Having bathed there, O King, a man should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods,
having fasted for one night and offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule.
When the sun has entered Virgo, whatever is accumulated becomes inexhaustible;
from there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilātīrtha.
O King, that man who bathes there and bestows a Kapila cow shall obtain the same fruit as one who has given away the entire earth. ||72||
Narmadeśvara is a supreme sacred ford that has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
There, the king Sarvagata is born upon the earth, fully endowed with all the marks and free from all diseases. ||74||
On the northern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful holy site,
a delightful temple of Āditya, consecrated by Īśvara.
Having bathed there, O lord of kings, and having given a gift according to one's capacity,
that which is given becomes inexhaustible through the power of that sacred ford.
But those who are poor, afflicted by disease, or who have performed evil deeds—may they be liberated from all sins and go to the world of the Sun. ||77||
When the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha has arrived, he who dwells in the sanctuary, selfless and with his senses restrained, [attains the fruit]. (78)
He is not born diseased, nor is he blind or deaf at any time;
endowed with good fortune and beauty, he becomes beloved by women. (79)
This sacred ford is of great merit, as proclaimed by Mārkaṇḍeya; those men who go there, O king of men, are undoubtedly deceived by sin. (80)
Then one should go to Māseśvara and perform a bath there;
as soon as a man has bathed there, he shall attain the world of heaven. ||81||
All the inhabitants of the world rejoice as long as these fourteen Indras endure;
thereafter, having approached the Tāpovana grove belonging to the Lord of the Nāgas, [they dwell there]. (82)
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, and having become pure and composed,
one sports for imperishable time with many daughters of the nāgas.
One should go to the abode of Kubera, where Kubera resides;
[and to] Kāleśvara, the supreme holy site, where Kubera was gratified. ||84||
O King of kings, having bathed there, one shall obtain all prosperity;
from there, one should go to the west to the supreme abode of Marut.
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, and having become pure and composed,
the wise man should then give gold according to his capacity for food.
By means of the Puṣpaka chariot, he goes to the world of Vāyu;
from there, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he should go to my tīrtha during the month of Māgha.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a ritual bath there;
thereafter, one should eat only at night and must not enter the miserable pit of rebirth in a womb.
From there, one should go to Ahalyātīrtha and perform a bath there;
merely by bathing there, a man rejoices with the Apsarases. (89)
Having performed penance for the sake of the Supreme Lord, he attained liberation from Ahalyā when the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight arrived in the month of Caitra. (90)
On that day of Kāmadeva, one should worship Nāhalī with sesame seeds;
wherever a man may be born, he shall become beloved there.
Having reached Ayodhyā, the renowned sacred site of Śakra, one becomes beloved by women, endowed with fortune, like another Kāmadeva. (92)
A man who has merely bathed there obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand cows;
he should then go to Soma-tīrtha and perform the mere act of bathing. ||93||
A man who has merely bathed there is liberated from all sins;
O King of kings, during a lunar eclipse, it brings about the destruction of evil. (94)
O King, there is the Soma-tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds and yielding great fruit;
O lord of men, whoever should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at that sacred ford—95.
With his soul purified of all evil, he goes to the world of Soma, whether by entering fire, or likewise into water, or even by fasting unto death. ||96||
He who dies at Soma-tīrtha is not born again in the mortal world;
from there, one should go to Stambha-tīrtha and perform a ritual bath there.
Having merely bathed there, a man is glorified in the world of Soma;
from there, O king of kings, he should proceed to the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha. 98.
There is the unsurpassed Viṣṇutīrtha, renowned as Yodhanīpura;
there, crores of Asuras were fought by Vāsudeva. 99.
A sacred ford has arisen there, where Viṣṇu becomes pleased;
by fasting for a day and night, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Thence, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Tāpaseśvara, known as Amohaka; he who offers libations to the ancestors there [attains great merit]. 101.
One should perform the Śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules on the full moon day and the new moon day;
having bathed there, O King, a man should cause the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to be offered to the ancestors. 102.
There, stones in the form of elephants are established in the midst of the water; one should indeed cause the *ṣaḍaṅga* [offering] to be given there, especially during the month of Vaiśākha. (103)
The ancestors remain satisfied for as long as the earth endures;
thereafter, O lord of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Siddheśvara. 104.
Having gone there, one should proceed to the presence of Gaṇapati, the lord of kings;
from there, one should go to where Janārdana exists as the Liṅga of the lord of kings.
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
on the southern bank of the Narmadā is a most beautiful sacred site (tīrtha). (106)
There, that great Kāmadeva himself performs austerities;
for a thousand divine years, he attends upon Śaṅkara.
But on the white lunar day (śukla-parvan), the fire, resembling Mount Śveta, was consumed by the high-souled Śaṅkara during the Samādhi-parvan. 108.
All of them, stationed at Kusumeśvara, were thus consumed;
after a thousand divine years, Maheśvara was pleased with them. (109)
Rudra, accompanied by Umā, being pleased with them and ready to grant boons, liberated all those who were stationed on the bank of the Narmadā. ||110||
By the power of that sacred ford, he has returned once more to the state of a god;
and by your grace, O Great God, let this sacred ford become supreme. (111)
The sacred ford extends for half a yojana in every direction;
having bathed in that sacred ford, a man should be devoted to fasting. ||112||
In the form of the Flower-Armed One (Kusumāyudha), he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
likewise in Vaiśvānara, Yama, Kāmadeva, and Vāyu. ||113||
O king of kings, having performed austerities there in ancient times,
[they remained] indeed not very far from that Andhona.
Bathing, giving gifts, eating, and offering funeral cakes (piṇḍapāta) should be performed right there—whether by entering the fire, or in water, or even by fasting. ||115||
Even for one who has died half a yojana away, his state of non-retrogression remains;
a preeminent man should bathe him with water consecrated by Tryambaka. 116.
Having offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at the root of the Andhona tree according to the prescribed rule, his ancestors remain satisfied as long as the moon and sun endure. (117)
When the northern course of the sun has arrived, whatever man or woman performs a bath there and dwells in the sanctuary pure, ||118||
By worshipping the god Siddheśvara at dawn, a person attains the goal of the virtuous, which cannot be reached by all the great sacrifices. (119)
And when, at the time of his passing from the world, he becomes handsome and fortunate, he becomes a king among mortals, with his domain extending as far as the edge of the ocean. (120)
If one does not see the field-guardian nor the mighty staff-guardian, his journey will be in vain, for he has not seen Karna-kundala. 121.
Having recognized this fruit of the sacred ford, all the gods assembled;
they released a rain of flowers and offered praise to Kusumeśvara. (122)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||18||
(19) The Nineteenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then one should go with devotion to Bhārgaveśa, where the Dānavas were sent to their destruction by the Lord Viṣṇu with a roar of "Huṃ. ||1||
Having bathed there, O Indra among kings, one is liberated from all sins;
now hear, O son of Pāṇḍu, the origin of Śuklatīrtha. 2.
On a delightful peak of the Himavat mountain, variegated with various minerals, resembling the rising sun and like molten gold. ||3||
Upon a divine staircase of diamond and crystal, with surfaces of variegated silk and stone, made of Jāmbūnada gold and adorned with various lotuses. ||4||
There he beheld the Great God, the omniscient Lord, the imperishable one,
who bestows grace upon the worlds, who is peaceful, and who is surrounded by hosts of attendants.
Markandeya questioned the God, who was accompanied by Uma and surrounded by Skanda, Nandi, Mahakala, Virabhadra, Ganapati, and others. (6)
O God of gods, Great God, praised by Indra, Kāma, and others;
I am terrified of the existence of saṃsāra—tell me the means to happiness. (7)
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, O Maheśvara, tell me of that supreme among holy places, which destroys all sins. (8)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O illustrious brāhmaṇa, you who are learned in all the scriptures!
Perform your ablutions and other rites, and go forth surrounded by hosts of sages. (9)
Manu, Atri, Yājñavalkya, and Kāśyapa, as well as Aṅgiras;
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati. ||10||
Nārada and Gautama, desiring to know the Dharma, ask: "Is Gaṅgā meritorious at Kanakhala? Are Prayāga, Puṣkara, and Gayā [meritorious]? (11)
Kurukṣetra is indeed meritorious when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu;
whether by day or by night, the Śukla-tīrtha yields great fruit.
From seeing, from touching, from bathing, from meditating, from performing austerities,
from offering oblations, and from fasting, one obtains the great fruit of the Śuklatīrtha.
The Śukla-tīrtha, a place of great merit, is situated upon the river;
there the royal sage named Cāṇikya attained perfection. ||14||
This sacred field has arisen, established as a circle extending for one yojana;
it is the Śuklatīrtha, of great merit, which destroys all sins. ||15||
By seeing the tip of my foot, one dispels the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O best of sages, I dwell here together with Umā. (16)
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the pure month of Vaiśākha, having emerged from Kailāsa, I am indeed present there. (17)
The gods, kinnaras, and gandharvas, as well as the siddhas and vidyādharas;
the hosts, apsarases, and nāgas—all the gods have assembled. ||18||
But those who dwell in the sky remain in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires;
O Indra among kings, they have come to Śuklatīrtha seeking the Dharma. (19)
Just as a washerman makes a garment white with water, so too does one cast off the sins accumulated since birth at Śuklatīrtha. 20.
O Mārkaṇḍeya, best of sages, bathing and giving gifts here yield great merit;
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy site superior to Śuklatīrtha. (21)
Having committed sinful deeds in the earlier stage of life, a person removes them by fasting for a day and night at Śuklatīrtha. ||22||
The nourishment that comes from austerity, celibacy, sacrifices, or again from giving, even through gifts to the gods— that cannot be attained even by hundreds of rituals.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, having fasted, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with clarified butter. (24)
Endowed with twenty-one lineages, he shall not fall from his sovereign station;
this supreme sacred ford, white and pure, is frequented by sages and perfected beings. ||25||
Having bathed there, O King, one is not subject to rebirth;
having bathed at Śuklatīrtha as well, one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva).
One should keep a vigil there with auspicious acts such as dancing and singing;
at dawn, one should indeed perform a bath in the Śuklatīrtha and the worship of the deities. 27.
Then, being pure and devoted to the vow of Śiva, one should feed the teacher;
and as for the meal, it should be according to one's ability, without practicing stinginess regarding wealth. (28)
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should slowly approach the presence of the deity.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for him who acts in this manner. ||29||
Mounted upon a divine vehicle and being praised by hosts of apsarases, endowed with strength equal to Śiva, he remains until the dissolution of all beings. (30)
But a woman who gives auspicious gold at Śuklatīrtha should bathe the God with ghee and worship Kumāra. ||31||
Listen now to the fruit of merit for her who performs [this] with devotion:
she rejoices dwelling in the world of the gods for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. (32)
On the day of the solstice, on the fourteenth lunar day, at the sun's passage into a new sign, or likewise at the equinox,
having bathed and observed a fast, he— having conquered his self and being composed in mind— [should proceed].
One should give gifts according to one's ability so that Hari and Śaṅkara may be pleased;
by the power of Śuklatīrtha, everything becomes inexhaustible. (34)
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who marries off a Brahmin who is destitute or in distress, whether he has no protector or indeed has one, at a sacred ford. ||35||
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on that person, he is honored in the world of Śiva within the families of his descendants. ||36||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||19||
(20) The Twentieth Chapter.
Nārada said:
Then one should go to Naraka and perform a ritual bath there;
as soon as a man has bathed there, he beholds Naraka. ||1||
Listen, O son of Pāṇḍu, to the majesty of this sacred ford;
for, O king of kings, whatever bones one should cast into that ford—
All [sins] go to dissolution, and the man is born endowed with beauty.
Then one should go to Go-tīrtha; having seen it, one is liberated from sin. ||3||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kapilā-tīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||4||
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, especially on the fourteenth day,
that man who, having fasted there with devotion, bestows a tawny cow (kapilā), ||5||
Having lit a lamp with ghee, one should bathe Śiva with ghee;
having offered a bilva fruit with ghee and performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth, one should circumambulate [the deity]. (6)
The man who gives away a tawny cow adorned with bells and ornaments becomes equal to Śiva and is not born again in this world. ||7||
When the day of Aṅgāraka (Tuesday) arrives, especially on the fourth lunar day,
one should bathe Śiva with devotion and provide a meal for the Brāhmaṇas.
On the ninth day of Aṅgāraka and likewise on the new moon day, one should bathe [the deity] there with care; thus one will become handsome and fortunate. 9.
One should bathe the deity with ghee and worship the twice-born with devotion;
[the devotee] shall then travel by means of the Puṣpaka chariot, surrounded by thousands [of attendants].
One attains the state of Śiva; there shall be no returning from it. One rejoices for an inexhaustible time, just as Rudra does.
But when, through the conjunction of his past actions, he returns to the world of mortals, he becomes a most righteous king, born handsome and powerful. (12)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Rishi-tīrtha, where the sage named Tṛṇabindu remained after being consumed by a curse. (13)
By the power of that sacred ford, the twice-born man was liberated from his sins.
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Gaṇeśvara.
When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, a man who has merely bathed there is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||15||
Having performed the libation for the ancestors, one is released from the three debts;
near Gaṇeśvara is the excellent Gaṅgāvadana. (16)
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, a person who bathes there is liberated from the sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt. ||17||
One should always perform a ritual bath there on festival days;
by performing the libation for the ancestors, one is released from the three debts. ||18||
Whatever merit was seen by the high-souled Śaṅkara at Prayāga, that same entire merit is found at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, the Rāhu-tīrtha, and the Arka-tīrtha. 19.
In that very place, nearby and not far away, is the site renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Daśāśvamedhika. (20)
Having likewise observed a fast for one night on the new moon day in the month of Bhādrapada,
a man who bathes shall indeed go to where Śaṅkara resides.
One should always perform a ritual bath there on festival days;
by performing the libation for the ancestors, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. ||22||
To the west of Daśāśvamedha, Bhṛgu, the best of Brahmins,
attended upon the Lord for a thousand divine years.
And as he remained within the anthill,
a great wonder arose regarding the southern abode of both Umā and Śaṅkara.
Gaurī then asked the God: "Who is this stationed here?
Is he a god or a dānava? Tell me, O Maheśvara. (25)
Īśvara said:
O beloved, there is a sage named Bhṛgu, the best of the twice-born and the foremost among the ṛṣis; established in meditative absorption, he contemplates me and prays for a boon.
Thereupon the goddess Prahasitā replied to Īśvara:
"Even now, after the emergence of the smoke-whirlwind and the crest of flame, you are not yet satisfied;
therefore, you are difficult to propitiate—of this there is no need for deliberation. (27)
The god said:
"O great goddess, you do not understand that this one has been moved by anger.
I shall show you the truth as it is, and I shall do what is pleasing to you. (28)
Then the bull, the embodiment of Dharma, was reminded by the God of Gods;
through that very remembrance of the God, the bull appeared swiftly. (29)
He spoke these human words: "O Lord, let an instruction be given!
This brahmin is covered by anthills; strike him down to the ground. (30)
But while he was established in yoga and meditating, he was struck down by him; instantly incensed with anger, he raised up his hand against the bull. (31)
Speaking thus, he said: "O bull, where are you going?
Today, O bull, I shall slay you, a sinner, right before my eyes. (32)
But then the brahmin, having been insulted, beheld the bull that had gone into the intermediate space;
he gazed again at this supreme wonder in the sky. (33)
Then, as Rudra laughed, the rishi stood before him;
upon seeing the third eye, he fell to the ground out of embarrassment.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, he praises the Supreme Lord:
"Having bowed down before you, the Lord of Beings, the source of existence, who possesses a divine form."
O Lord of the World, one who is afraid of worldly existence makes this representation to you. ||35||
O Lord, what human being is capable of describing the multitude of Your virtues?
For even Vāsuki would have to possess a thousand mouths to do so. (36)
O Śaṅkara, Lord of the World, even though I am made speechless by devotion while offering praise to You, be gracious to me who have fallen at Your feet. 37.
O Lord of the universe, O Sovereign of the world, you are indeed sattva, rajas, and tamas in the maintenance, creation, and destruction [of the world]; apart from you, there is no deity whatsoever.
Through restraints, observances, sacrifices, and gifts, and through the diligent mastery of Vedic study—none of this is worth even a thousandth part of a fraction of devotion to You. (39)
Or else, there may be the attainment of the most excellent elixirs, rasāyana, the sword, or the power of sandals and so forth;
these signs shall be manifest in this very life for those who bow down to you. (40)
O Lord, although one may bow with hypocrisy toward those who desire dharma, devotion that severs worldly existence has been fashioned for the sake of liberation, O Protector. (41)
O Supreme Lord, protect me—who am devoted to the wives and wealth of others, scorched by humiliation, intense suffering, and grief, and intent on gazing upon the faces of others. 42.
O Lord of Gods, save me, who am consumed by false pride, whose wealth and splendor perish in an instant, who am cruel, and who have fallen upon a wicked path! 43.
The quarters of the sky are filled with caravans of kinsmen whose faculties are dejected;
yet you, O Piśaṅgaraki, mock me, a fool, even though I am so insignificant. 44.
Quickly take away my craving and grant me the eternal Lakṣmī dwelling within my heart;
O Mahādeva, sever the bonds of pride and delusion and deliver me across [the ocean of existence]. 45.
This divine hymn of praise named *Karuṇābhyudaya*, which bestows spiritual accomplishments, shall please Śiva just as he was pleased by Bhṛgu, for whoever recites it with devotion. 46.
Īśvara said: "I am pleased with you; O best of brahmins, request whatever you desire. Together with Umā, the Lord shall indeed grant him a boon. (47)
Bhṛgu said:
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased with me, and if a boon is to be granted to me, O God, let there be an altar for Rudra; please accomplish this."
The Lord said:
"O best of Brahmins, let it be so; this shall become a place of wrath, and there shall be a single voice between father and son. (49)
From that time forward, all the gods beginning with Brahmā, along with the kinnaras,
have been worshipping at Bhṛgu’s tīrtha, where Maheśvara was pleased.
By the mere sight of that sacred ford, one is instantly liberated from sin;
living beings die there, whether against their will or under their own control.
For those whose goal is the secret beyond secrets, there shall be no doubt;
this field is exceedingly vast and destroys all sins. 52.
Having bathed there, those who have died go to heaven and are not born again.
At that time, sandals, an umbrella, food, and gold should be given.
And food for the eyes should be given according to one's ability;
likewise, one should give whatever gift one desires during a solar eclipse.
Whatever gift is given at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) becomes inexhaustible for him;
likewise, during lunar and solar eclipses, the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) is unsurpassed.
O lord of men, deluded men, bewildered by the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, do not know the divine Vṛṣatīrtha situated on the Narmadā. ||56||
The man who hears the majesty of Bhṛgutīrtha even once, being liberated from all sins, goes to the world of Rudra. ||57||
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Gautameśvara;
having bathed there, O king, a man who is devoted to fasting [attains the fruit]. (58)
By means of this new celestial vehicle (vimāna), one is honored in the world of Brahmā;
from there, one should go to Dhautapāpa, where Vṛṣa has washed away [his sins].
O King, situated on the Narmadā is that which destroys all sins;
having bathed at that tīrtha, a man casts off even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (60)
O great king, whoever gives up their life at that sacred ford shall become four-armed, three-eyed, and equal in strength to Rudra.
He shall dwell for more than ten thousand kalpas with prowess equal to Rudra;
after a long time, he will become the sole sovereign of the earth.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the excellent Eraṇḍī-tīrtha;
whatever fruit is seen at Prayāga has been described by Mārkaṇḍeya.
O King, merely by bathing on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, a person obtains that very fruit.
Having observed a fast for one night, one should perform a ritual bath there;
one will not be tormented by the messengers of Yama and shall go to the world of Indra.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to where Janārdana is perfected,
the place renowned as Hiraṇyadvīpa, which destroys all sins.
Having bathed there, O King, a man shall become wealthy and handsome.
Thereafter, O Indra among kings, one should proceed to the great sacred site of Kanakhala.
O lord of men, Garuḍa performed austerities at that sacred ford (tīrtha), which is renowned throughout all the worlds; a Yoginī resides there.
She sports with the yogins and dances together with Śiva;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra. (69)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Īśatīrtha;
there Īśa was liberated and ascended upwards, without a doubt.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to where Janārdana,
the inconceivable Supreme Lord, has become perfected, having assumed the form of a boar.
Having bathed at Varāha-tīrtha, especially on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī),
a person attains the world of Viṣṇu and does not go to hell.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Soma-tīrtha;
especially on the full moon day, one should perform a ritual bath there.
Having prostrated before Īśāna, Bali was pleased with him;
and the divine city of Hariścandra was seen in the intermediate space.
It was surrounded by the banner of the wheel, with the houses of its inhabitants asleep,
and it was frequented by the banks of the Ruru-kaccha, which were swept by the force of the Narmadā’s waters.
Regarding that place, Viṣṇu said to Śaṅkara:
"A man who bathes in Dvīpeśvara shall obtain much gold. (76)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Rudrakanyā;
merely by bathing there, a man shall attain the abode of the Goddess. ||77||
From there, one should go to Devatīrtha, which is saluted by all the gods;
having bathed there, one rejoices together with the deities, including the lords of kings. 78.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Śikhitīrtha;
whatever gift is given there becomes multiplied ten millionfold.
On the new moon day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a ritual bath there;
by feeding a single Brāhmaṇa, it is as if ten million have been fed.
At Bhṛgutīrtha, ten million Rājendra-tīrthas are situated;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, any human being who bathes there [obtains the fruit]. (81)
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and rejoices together with the deities;
there, Bhṛgutuṇḍa, the preeminent among sages, attained perfection.
An incarnation was thus assumed by that high-souled Śaṅkara. ||82||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-one. Nārada said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Vihageśvara.
By the sight of him, O lord of kings, one is liberated from all sins. ||1||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Narmadeśvara;
having bathed there, O king, a man is glorified in the heavenly world. ||2||
From there, one should go to Aśvatīrtha and perform a ritual bath there;
such a man becomes fortunate, handsome, and possessed of enjoyments. ||3||
Then one should go to Pitāmaha, which was created by Brahmā in ancient times;
having bathed there with devotion, a person should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the ancestors.
One should cause water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass to be offered;
by the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), everything becomes inexhaustible. ||5||
Having reached the Sāvitrī-tīrtha, whoever performs an ablution there, having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||6||
And there is a most beautiful sacred ford (tīrtha) named Manohara;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme holy site of Mānasa;
having bathed there, O King, a man is glorified in the world of Rudra.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Kratutīrtha, which is renowned throughout all the worlds and destroys all sins. ||9||
O lord of men, whatever desires one prays for— be they cattle, sons, or wealth—
one shall obtain them all by bathing there.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the place renowned as Tridaśadyotin;
there, daughters of sages, firm in their vows, perform arduous penance.
May the imperishable Lord and Master be the protector of them all;
and may Mahādeva Hara, assuming a fierce form, be pleased with them. (12)
Having approached that sacred ford, which was hideous with deformed faces, the Supreme Lord there [bestowed] the great kingdom upon the bridegroom. (13)
He who enjoys the prosperity of a maiden and bestows the gift of a maiden in marriage—there, O Great King, is the famous sacred ford known as Daśakanyā. ||14||
Having bathed there, one should worship the God; one is liberated from all sins.
Thence, O king of kings, one should go to the place known as Svargabindu. ||15||
Having bathed there, O King, a man does not see an evil destiny;
from there he should go to Apsareśa and perform his ablutions there.
Dwelling in the world of the Nagas, he sports and rejoices together with Apsarases;
from there, O Indra among kings, one should proceed to the supreme sacred site (tīrtha) of Naraka.
Having bathed there, one should worship the God; he does not go to hell.
Then, devoted to fasting, he should go to Bhārabhūta. ||18||
Having reached this sacred ford and having worshipped Śambhu in his incarnation as Virūpākṣa, one is glorified in the world of Rudra. ||19||
Having bathed at that sacred ford of the high-souled Bhārabhūta,
a man attains the state of Gāṇeśvara for certain, even if he dies anywhere else.
The wise declare that by worshipping Maheśvara during the month of Kārttika, one obtains a hundred times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having prepared a hundred lamps filled with ghee, one should cause them to be offered;
[the donor] goes by means of celestial chariots as radiant as the sun to where Śaṅkara dwells.
He who gives a bull resembling a white cloud shall go to the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with bulls. ||23||
O lord of men, one should offer a single oblation at that sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
consisting of milk-rice mixed with honey and various kinds of edible foods.
One should feed as many kings as one’s ability permits, along with sacrificial fees;
by the power of that sacred ford, everything shall become ten millionfold. ||25||
Having sprinkled the water of the Narmadā and having worshipped the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
they do not see misfortune or poverty, by the power of that sacred ford.
Whoever reaches this sacred ford and gives up their life there goes,
with a soul purified of all sins, to where Śaṅkara dwells.
O lord of men, he who performs the ritual immersion in water at that sacred ford (tīrtha) goes to the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with swans. ||28||
As long as the moon and the sun endure, as long as the Himavat and the great ocean remain,
and as long as the Gaṅgā and other rivers flow, so long shall he be honored in heaven.
O lord of men, O king of kings, the man who observes a fast at that sacred ford (tīrtha) is never again born to dwell in a womb.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Aṭavītīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man shall obtain half of Indra’s throne.
From there, one should go to Śṛṅgatīrtha, which destroys all sins;
by merely bathing there, the state of being a Gaṇeśvara is certain. (32)
The confluence of the Eraṇḍī and the Narmadā is world-renowned;
there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) of great merit that destroys all sins. ||33||
Being devoted to fasting and constantly intent upon Brahman,
one who bathes there, O lord of kings, is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean,
known as Jamadagni, where Janārdana attained perfection.
O King, having bathed there at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, a man goes to that place where Indra, having sacrificed with many sacrifices, became the lord of the gods. (36)
A person obtains the fruit of three horse-sacrifices,
as well as union with the Western Ocean and the opening of the gate to liberation.
There, the gods along with the gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas,
and cāraṇas worship Vimaleśvara, the Lord of Gods, at the three junctions of the day.
With his soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a holy place (tīrtha) superior to Vimaleśvara. ||39||
Those who, having observed a fast there, behold Vimaleśvara, their souls purified of all sins, go to the world of Rudra. ||40||
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to the supreme Keśinī-tīrtha;
having bathed there, O King, a man devoted to fasting [attains great merit]. (41)
Having observed a fast for one night, being self-restrained and restricted in diet,
one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin there by the power of the sacred ford.
Whoever beholds Sāgareśvara obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords;
Śiva is stationed within a distance of one yojana, established in the whirlpool.
Having seen that, all other sacred fords (tīrthas) would undoubtedly be as if unseen;
for it is there that Rudra goes, liberated from all sins. 44.
O Great King, between the confluence of the Narmadā and Amarakaṇṭaka, ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) are situated within that interval. 45.
Wandering from sacred ford to sacred ford is the practice frequented by tens of millions of sages;
it is performed with fire-sacrifices and divine oblations by all those who are devoted to supreme knowledge. ||46||
O Indra among kings, these [mantras], when practiced by him, grant all desired objects;
and whoever should constantly recite this or listen to it with devotion, [attains the same]. (47)
O Pāṇḍava, all the holy fords (tīrthas) consecrate him;
moreover, the Narmadā shall always be pleased with him—of this there is no doubt.
Rudra and the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya become pleased with him;
he obtains sons who are steadfast in meditation, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate. (49)
The husband obtains a maiden, and whatever fruit he desires, he obtains all that; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (50)
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya becomes victorious;
a Vaiśya obtains grain; and a Śūdra attains a good state. ||51||
Even a fool acquires knowledge if he recites it at the three junctions of the day;
such a man shall not behold hell, nor shall he go to a base womb. 52.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||21||
The twenty-second chapter.
Nārada said: Thus, O King, has this supreme sacred site of the Narmadā been described to you.
In former times, there was a terrible fear born of the curse of the Gandharva maidens. ||1||
That [sin] was destroyed by the fire of the droplets of the Revā’s water;
by the touch of the droplets of the Revā’s water, a human being becomes liberated. ||2||
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, how and why was this curse incurred by so many maidens?
Whose offspring were they, what were their names, and what was their age? (3)
O Lord, tell me everything: how were they liberated from the ripening of the curse through contact with the waters of the Revā, and where did they bathe?
The majesty of the Narmadā tīrtha is wondrous;
it is said that even by hearing of it, the impurity of sins is destroyed. (5)
Whoever utters the word "Narmadā" or "Anarmadā," for that person there shall be eternal liberation as long as the moon and stars endure.
The supreme majesty of the Revā was previously described by you;
likewise, let that virtuous account of her deeds be narrated. (7)
Moreover, since this supreme narrative is to be cultivated by the wise,
I therefore ask you, O best of Brahmins, about the most excellent majesty of Revā.
Tell the history, radiant with the deeds of the daughters of Vibhu.
Nārada said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to another story pregnant with dharma, wherein Raṇi was as the womb of fire, while Dharma was like the progenitor Brahmā. (9)
The Gandharva was Śukasaṅgīti; his daughter was Pramohinī.
Suśīla’s [daughter] was Suśīlā, and Svaravedin’s was Susvarā. (10)
O King, these are the names of those apsarases belonging to him, the one of beautiful radiance, who possesses the splendor of the moon and stars: Sutarā, Candrakā, and Dṛkāsuprabhā. 11.
Furthermore, all those maidens were equally beautiful in their youth, and they always addressed one another as sisters. (12)
They emerged like rays from the moon, as radiant as the moonbeams;
they had faces like the moon, beautiful hair, and were as brilliant as the luster of the moon. ||13||
Among the gods, these playful women are like moonlight among white water-lilies; they are enchanting with divine forms, as if they were the very essence of beauty incarnate.
In this month of Āṣāḍha, how much more so do the ketakī plants—with their lotus-like breasts now blossoming—resemble the forest creepers whose sprouts have reached maturity? 15.
Golden-hued and radiant as gold, adorned with golden ornaments, wearing garlands of golden campaka flowers, they were possessed of a golden luster and fine garments. ||16||
In the various melodies of the scales and modes, in the playful diversions of rhythm and percussion, and in the playing of the flute and lute; (17)
They were experts in clay modeling, in the various rhythms of the *lāsya* dance where the beats are neither too fast nor too slow, and in diverse amusements such as painting and other fine arts.
Thus transformed, they all, cherished by their fathers, wandered about in the abode of Kubera, delighting with excellent diversions.
Once, in the month of Mādhava, out of curiosity, five of them gathered together and went from the courtyard to the grove,
gathering flowers for the daughter's marriage ceremony.
Once, in order to worship Gaurī, the celestial nymphs went to the Acchoda lake,
bringing with them excellent golden lotuses along with choice blue water-lilies.

Having bathed in the *tughaṭṭa* where the floors were paved with pure *vaiḍūrya* and crystal, and having put on fine garments, they stood in silence upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and fashioned an image made of *piṇḍikā* clay, adorned with gold and pearls.

Having worshipped Gaurī with sandalwood paste, saffron, and other offerings, as well as excellent lotuses and the like, the young maidens—inspired by pure devotion—performed dances accompanied by various ritual offerings. (23)
Then those fawn-eyed women sang with modulations of their natural voices, relying on the supreme *gāndhāra* note;
they sang with sweet tones, using measured syllables, rising to a high pitch, and with graceful movements.

Then, while the maidens— whose mental dispositions were overflowing with the joy of raining down the essence of pure affection— were fully engaged, the elder son of that sage, the treasury of the Vedas, arrived at the excellent Acchoda-tīrtha to bathe.
In form he was most boundless, with a beautiful face and long eyes like full-blown lotuses;
a youth with a broad chest, fine arms, and exceedingly handsome, with a dark complexion, he was indeed like another Kāma. (26)
Indeed, Suśikha shines among his fellow religious students like the god of love equipped with his bow;
clad in a deerskin, wearing a golden-colored girdle at his waist, he is supreme, upholding the ocean.
Seeing that brahmin there on the shore of the lake, those young women rejoiced, overcome with curiosity, thinking, "He shall be our guest. (28)
There were women who had abandoned singing and dancing, longing to behold her;
they were pierced by the arrows of Kāma, like female deer struck by a hunter. 29.
"Look! Look! they cried out, utterly bewildered and agitated with excitement; toward that best of brahmins, they fell into the delusion that he was the god Kāmadeva. (30)
Having worshipped him again and again with their eyes as if with lotuses,
the apsarases thereafter began to deliberate among themselves.
If this were Kāmadeva, how could he be devoid of Rati? Or perhaps it is both the Aśvin deities, who move as a pair. (32)
Whether he was a Gandharva, a Kinnara, or a Siddha capable of assuming any form at will;
or perhaps the son of a seer, or some other eminent among men. (33)
Surely this man was created by the Creator for our sake, just as a treasure is deposited by previous karmas for the benefit of those who are fortunate. (34)
Likewise, for us maidens, this most excellent bridegroom was brought by Gaurī, whose heart was moistened by the surging waves of the water of compassion. (35)
"O best of kings, this [world] is covered by me, and likewise it is covered by you and by her; thus did he speak to the five beautiful maidens, O Tīṣu."
Having heard those words there, the wise one, having performed his midday rites, reflected:
"What should be done so that it may become a meritorious deed? (37)

Even those twice-born ones such as Gādhi’s son Viśvāmitra and Parāśara, as well as Kaṇḍu, Devala, and others—though they possessed the power of yogis—were wonderfully deluded by the mere playfulness of his women. (38)
Whose deer-like mind does the archer Makaraketu (the Love-god) not strike down with his sharp arrows of glances, discharged from the very firm bow of the creeper-like eyebrows of women? (39)
Only so long does the intellect of logic shine; only so long does fear exist for the people;
only so long is there intense stability of mind; and only so long does the multitude remain agitated by calculation. (40)
So long does men possess the boldness for austerity and so long do they practice tranquility, as long as they are not intoxicated by the swift-acting liquors of the glances of beautiful women. (41)
Women delude and intoxicate the passionate with their charming and captivating graces;
but these [women] delight and intoxicate me, who am devoted to the protection of righteousness, with their own virtues. (42)
Desirous men, their minds utterly deluded, imagine beauty and enter into the bodies of women—which are devoid of merit, impure, and composed of blood, filth, excrement, and urine. (43)
As long as these [creatures] remain near the divine tree, so long shall I go to the abode of the gods— [an abode] proclaimed by dreadful serpents and by pure-minded, wise sages.
Before those excellent women could reach his presence, the twice-born man vanished through the power of Viṣṇu. ||45||
Then, seeing that miraculous feat of the Vaiṣṇava brahmacārin, the king’s disappearance while he was seated upon his throne through the power of yoga, [he was amazed]. (46)
With eyes trembling with terror, their brows knit in distress, they cast their vacant glances toward the ten directions. (47)
The maidens said:
"He clearly knows sorcery, or perhaps he understands illusion; though seen, he has become one whose form is unseen"—thus they spoke to one another. (48)
And at that very moment, their hearts were pervaded by the fire of separation from him, just as a lush, verdant forest is pervaded by a blazing wildfire. 49.
Abandon this illusory art; show yourself to your beloved quickly.
It is not fitting for you to offer yourself as food, like a fly at the tip of a blade of grass.
Alas! Why have you been shown by the Creator? And from where were you fashioned? It is now known that you, our own self, were created as the cause of our great and continuous torment. (51)
Is your heart merciless? Do you have no regard for us? Are you cruel here? Have you utterly stolen away our minds? (52)
I hope you have no lack of confidence in us; I hope you examine us [with care]. I hope you are free from the habit of possessiveness, and I hope you are skilled in discerning deceit. (53)
I wonder if you possess the agility of consciousness to enter the mind;
and do you not know the means of exit, and from where it occurs again? (54)
Are you perhaps angry with us for no fault of ours? Do you not know the suffering that comes from the ruin of others? (55)
Without the sight of you, our lords of the heart have now perished;
we do not live, yet we live again through the hope of beholding you.
May we also quickly go to that place where you have gone—that Creator, who has stolen the joy of seeing you, has inflicted a wound upon our hearts. (57)
Always practice compassion for all embodied beings;
the virtuous do not look upon the end of anyone at all. (58)
Having lamented in this manner and waited for many moments, the maidens then began to go home quickly out of fear of their father.
Bound fast by the fetters of love for him and deeply distressed by separation, they somehow summoned their courage and returned each to her own home. (60)
Having arrived, they all fell down near their mothers;
questioned by the mothers, "What is this? Why has there been such a delay? (61)
When she was staying there at Lake Acchoda, engaged in dalliance together with the Kinnarīs, she did not realize that the day had passed.
O Mother, we are weary from the road; our bodies are exhausted by that heat.
Because of this great delusion, we do not have the strength to say anything at all. (63)
Having spoken thus, the young maidens rolled there upon the jeweled floor;
concealing their true intentions, they spoke charmingly with their mothers.
At that time, out of curiosity, one woman was dancing with her toy peacock,
while another was teaching her parrot the word "Pañjara."
She fondles the mongoose and does not coo to other birds;
she is utterly infatuated with her rival and never sports with the cranes.
They took their pleasure with him alone; they crossed over [the ocean] in his very palace;
they spoke enough with their husbands, yet they did not play the lute.
Whatever flower is produced by the wish-fulfilling tree, all that is like fire;
yet the honey from it is sweet, possessing the fragrance of jasmine blossoms.
These maidens were indeed yoginīs, with their eyes fixed on the tips of their noses;
their meditation was imperceptible, and their minds were intent upon Puruṣottama.
For a moment she stood at the window, gazing for a while at the water-house where water was trickling, concealed by moonstones.
They prepare a long bed for a moment with the leaves of the *bhojinī* plant,
while being fanned by their friends with cool lotus petals.
Thus I spent that night, which was equal to an entire Yuga,
supporting my life somehow with great difficulty, like a woman of the immobile world, trembling and as if consumed by fever.
Having seen the jewel of the sky at dawn and considering it to be their own life,
they informed their respective mothers and went to worship Gaurī.
Having bathed according to that ritual procedure, and having again performed the worship of the Goddess with flowers and incense, they remained there singing.
Then, at that very moment, a certain Brahmin also arrived from his father's hermitage to bathe here in this Acchoda lake. (75)
Upon seeing their friend, those lotus-maidens were as if night had passed;
having seen that celibate student, their eyes blossomed like lotuses.
Having gone there, those celibate youths approached the maidens and formed a noose of their arms by binding them in a left-and-right (savyāpasavya) fashion.
"O beloved, you went away yesterday; today you are not to be found. You have surely been chosen by us; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (78)
Thus addressed, the Brahmin, held by the noose of his arms, laughed and said:
"Auspicious, favorable, and pleasing words are being spoken by you. (79)
However, for one devoted to the first stage of life who is habituated to the practice of learning, there was no end to his studies within the family of his guru. (80)
"In this hermitage, whatever dharma is to be protected by the most wise, I consider this marriage to be that very dharma, O daughters. (81)
Having heard the words of the brahmin, the excellent women spoke to him,
just as cuckoos, longing for the sound of all [other] voices, speak to Mādhava in the spring.
"From dharma comes artha; from artha comes kāma; and from kāma arises the fruit of happiness"—thus do the wise definitively describe these [goals]. (83)
"Because of the abundance of dharmas that accord with your desires, he has arisen before you; therefore, let this pure land be enjoyed with various pleasures. (84)
Having heard those words of theirs, he spoke with a timid voice:
"Your words are indeed true; however, even for me, this vow is obligatory. (85)
"Having obtained the permission of my guru, I shall perform the marriage rites according to the rules.
When he had spoken thus, they replied clearly, "O handsome one, you are a fool! (86)

The perfected medicine, the elixir through the intellect of Brahman, success, the treasure, the women of the noble lineage, the mantra, and likewise the perfected elixir—all these, when encountered, should be pursued with a righteous mind by the wise sage. (87)
If a task has reached the point of success through destiny or other means, those who follow the path of policy do not neglect it;
because neglect does not yield fruit again, procrastination is therefore not praised. (88)
Nectar should be taken even from poison, gold even from filth, the highest knowledge even from a low person, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family. (89)

Those men here who possess women with mutual passion, born of noble lineage and stainless, whose hearts are moist with affection, whose speech is sweet, who choose their own husbands, who are beautiful in form, truly blessed in their youth—let them be such, and no others. (90)
Where are we, the beauties of the gods, and where are you, a young ascetic?
By arranging such an incongruity, Fate alone is truly wise. (91)
Therefore, you should now accept us as auspicious;
let us not live like a cow wedded by the *dharva* rite.
Having heard these words, the brāhmaṇa, the best among those who know the dharma, then said:
"O deer-eyed one, how can there be dharma for those who do not offer clarified butter, when dharma belongs to men whose wealth is dharma? (93)
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—this fourfold set should be known to yield fruit when practiced as prescribed; otherwise, it is fruitless. (94)
Therefore, I, being under a vow, shall not take a noble wife at an improper time;
for he who does not know the proper time for an action does not obtain the fruit of that action.
Since my mind has become intent upon this inquiry into dharma, therefore listen, O maiden, to that which I myself do not desire as a boon. (96)
Having thus understood his intention and observed one another, Pramohinī then released her hand from his and seized Aṅghripra by the hand.
Suśīlā and Susvarā both seized his arms;
Sutarā embraced him, and Candrā kissed his face. (98)
Likewise, though he was changeless and resembled the fire of universal dissolution, that celibate student, utterly overcome by rage, cursed them. 99.
"By clinging to me in this way, you shall become *piśācīs*," he said;
thus cursed by him, they abandoned him and stood before him. (100)
Why indeed have you committed this sinful act by mistreating one who is innocent? Having done what is unpleasant to one who has done you a kindness, you are truly a destroyer of dharma. ||101||
It has been heard by us that for a man who commits treachery against those who are devoted, loyal, and friendly, happiness perishes in both this world and the next. (102)
"Therefore, you too shall quickly become a piśāca due to our curse.
Having spoken thus, those young women sighed, agitated by anger.
O King, while that very lake was shimmering with mutual radiance, those maidens and the celibate student all attained the state of Piśācas. (104)
Together with those Piśācas and Piśācīs, crying out most piteously, they exhaust the ripening of that previously committed karma. (105)
O King, the auspicious or inauspicious karma previously acquired necessarily bears fruit in its own time; it is as unavoidable as one's own shadow, even for the gods.
The fathers devour them, and their mothers likewise here and there;
even the brothers of the children [devour them], for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.
From that point upward, those Piśācas, extremely distressed for the sake of food, dwell on the shore of the lake, running hither and thither. (108)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||22||
Chapter Twenty-Three. Nārada said:
Thus, after a long period of time had passed, Lomaśa, the best of sages, [spoke].
And there arrived by chance a highly fortunate sage. ||1||
Seeing that brahmin, all the piśācas, agitated by hunger, ran toward him, desiring to devour him, and gathered together in a herd.
Scorched by the intense splendor of Lomaśa, they were all unable to stand before him and remained at a distance. ||3||
There, O King, by the power of his past karma, the Piśāca, together with the twice-born man, beheld Lomaśa and prostrated before him with all eight limbs touching the ground.
Having bound his hands in *añjali* at his head, he spoke these truthful words:
"The meeting with holy men occurs only through the dawning of great fortune. (5)
Whether a man bathes in all the sacred pilgrimage sites such as the Gaṅgā, or whether he cultivates the company of the virtuous—the association with the good is superior to both. (6)
O Brahmin, association with gurus on this earth yields both seen and unseen fruits;
it bestows heaven, removes disease—how could it not be considered a dispeller of darkness? (7)
Having said this, he related the wonderful previous account:
"O Sage, these are those very Gandharva maidens; and I am that son of a twice-born. (8)
"O best of sages, all of us, deluded by mutual curses, have taken the form of piśācas; with dejected faces, we remain here before you. (9)
Through the sight of you, our deliverance from ignorance shall come to pass;
for when the sun rises, would the mass of darkness not indeed dissolve within the lotus? (10)
Having heard these words, Lomaśa, his heart softened with compassion, replied to that son of the sage who was distressed, O one of great splendor: 11.
"By my grace, let memory suddenly arise in all of them, and let them abide in righteousness (dharma), so that their mutual curse may come to an end. (12)
The Piśāca said:
"O Great Sage, let dharma be told so that I may be released from this sin;
for this is no time for delay, since the fire of the curse is terrible."
Lomaśa said:
"Perform the ritual bath in the Revā together with me according to the prescribed rules;
the Revā will release you from the curse, for there can be no other atonement. (14)
Listen attentively, O Brahmin: the destruction of the sins of men is certain to arise through bathing in the Revā; such is my settled conviction. (15)
Sin committed in previous births and present transgressions—the bath in the Revā consumes them all, just as fire consumes a heap of cotton. (16)
O Piśācaka, whatever sin they do not see a penance for, all of that is destroyed merely by bathing in the waters of the Narmadā. ||17||
The bathing in the Narmadā produces knowledge; therefore, it indeed yields the fruit of liberation. Truly, the holy fords of the Himavat remove all sins. (18)
Indeed, this [place] was fashioned by the exponents of Brahman as the bestower of the world of Indra;
the Revā is celebrated as the fulfiller of all desires and the giver of liberation. ||19||
The destroyer of sin, the remover of evil, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
the flood of the Viṣṇuloka, the Narmadā river, which annihilates sin. ||20||
The Yamunā is the supreme for leading one to the world of the Sun;
the Sarasvatī destroys all sins and bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā. ||21||
Viśālā is said to bestow large fruits; Ahipīśācaka is malefic; Dhanada brings about fire; and Vāgni destroys the activities related to conception and pregnancy. (22)
The Narmadā is proclaimed as leading to the world of Viṣṇu and to liberation; likewise the Sarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, and Kauśikī. (23)
The Tāpī, Godāvarī, Bhīmā, Payoṣṇī, Kṛṣṇaveṇikā, Kāverī, Tuṅgabhadrā, and other rivers that flow to the ocean. ||24||
The other [river] is said to be the Tāsurī, which bestows the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, the Revā is attained only through merits performed in previous births. O son of a sage, immersion there grants freedom from rebirth. (25)
The gods dwelling in heaven constantly sing: "From whom could there be the fear of serpents whose very sight is deadly?
Where men, having bathed, behold no more the pain of the womb, they remain in the presence of Viṣṇu. (26)
Those men who, being full of many sins, bathe every day in this river as if it were water;
by that [false bath], they sink into hells according to the law of karma, whereas those of beautiful conduct roam like gods in heaven.
In former times, the Creator weighed both Revā and Piśāca on an equal scale using intense vows, gifts, austerities, and sacrifices;
yet between those two, Revā proved superior and was the one who brought about liberation.
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of Lomaśa, the piśācas went quickly with him for the purpose of bathing in the Revā.
Then, by chance, a breeze arose from the bank of the Revā,
bestowing drops of water upon their limbs as they were touched by its current.
By the touch of a drop of Revā’s water, they were instantly liberated from their state as Piśācas; possessing divine bodies, they praised the Narmadā.
Then, according to the words of Lomaśa, those Gandharva maidens were married by that brahmin and lived happily on the bank of the Narmadā.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, and having worshipped the Narmadā through bathing, drinking, and immersion, they went to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O King, has been told to you this highly meritorious history concerning the virtues of the Narmadā, which destroys sin through its mere hearing. (34)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||23||
Chapter Twenty-four.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Now, please tell me of other sacred fords (tīrthas) spoken of by Vasiṣṭha.
O Nārada, having heard [this], whatever sins have been committed go to destruction.
Nārada said:
Listen, O King, to the holy places described by Vasiṣṭha. Having reached the southern ocean, one should remain celibate and have his senses subdued.
Having reached the Carmaṇvatī river, whether self-restrained or eating at regular intervals, he attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and ascends to Vimāna.
Having performed the Ranti sacrifice and being authorized by the gods, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma;
from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to Arbuda, the son of Himavat.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, where there was formerly a fissure in the earth,
there stands the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having stayed there for one night, O lord of men, a man who observes celibacy and touches the waters at Piṅgātīrtha obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
O tiger among men, one shall obtain that fruit;
from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to Prabhāsa, which is world-renowned.
O hero, where the fire-god himself—the mouth of the deities, whose charioteer is the wind—is eternally present. (8)
Having bathed in that best of holy fords, pure and with a restrained mind, a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. ||9||
Then, having gone to the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and is glorified in the heavenly world. ||10||
O bull among the Bharatas, having bathed with a restrained mind at the sacred ford of the Lord of Waters, he shines eternally with splendor like a blazing fire. (11)
Having stayed there for three nights, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
one shines like the moon and attains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
From there, O best of the Bharatas, one should go to the tirtha called Varadāna,
where Viṣṇu was granted a boon by Durvāsas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having bathed at Varadāna, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
thereafter, self-restrained and restricted in diet, he should proceed to Dvāravatī. ||14||
Having bathed at Piṇḍāraka, a man shall obtain much gold.
At that sacred ford, O subduer of enemies, even today those footprints marked with the signs of a great king’s lotus can still be seen; it is truly wonderful.
O joy of the Kurus, tridents and lotuses are seen there;
O bull of the Bharatas, it is as if the presence of Mahādeva himself is there.
O descendant of Bharata, having reached the confluence of the Sāgara and the Sindhu,
one who is restrained in mind should bathe in that sacred ford of the lord of waters.
O bull of the Bharata race, having gratified the ancestors, the gods, and the sages,
one attains the world of Varuṇa, shining with one's own splendor.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the wise declare that after worshipping the god Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, one obtains ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having circumambulated it, O bull of the Bharatas, one should proceed to the sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds, O best of the Kurus. (21)
It is renowned by the name Timiṭiṅga, which liberates one from all sins;
there the gods, headed by Śakra, worship Maheśvara. (22)
Having bathed there and worshipped Rudra, who is surrounded by hosts of gods, a person destroys all sins committed since birth. (23)
O best of men, Timirāraṇya is praised by all the gods;
having bathed there, O best of men, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice. (24)
O King, having there defeated the son of Aditi, the highly wise Viṣṇu performed his purification after slaying the Daityas and Dānavas.
From there, one should go to the celebrated Vasudhārā, praised by the knowers of Dharma;
by merely going there, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice.
O best of the Kurus, having bathed with a self-restrained mind and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, a person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||27||
And there, O bull of the Bharatas, is also the supreme tīrtha of the Vasus;
having bathed and drunk there, one becomes esteemed by the Vasus. (28)
O best of men, by bathing there at the place renowned as Sindhutama, which destroys all sins, one shall obtain much gold.
Having reached Brahmātuṅga, pure and with a restrained mind, that virtuous man, free from passion, attains the world of Brahmā. (30)
There is the Śakra-tīrtha, frequented by the Siddhas, belonging to the virgins;
having bathed there, O best of men, one shall attain the world of Śakra. ||31||
And there is the tirtha of Reṇukā, frequented by the gods;
having bathed there, a brahmin becomes stainless like the moon.
Then, having gone to Pañcanada, one who is self-restrained and moderate in diet attains the five sacrifices which have been described in due order. ||33||
From there, O best of the Bharatas, a man should go to the supreme abode of Bhīmā, who knows the Dharma; having bathed there in the Nayonī, he is purified.
O King, there a son of the Goddess shall be born, whose form is adorned with earrings;
he shall indeed obtain the great fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows. 35.
Having reached Girikuñja, which is renowned throughout the three worlds, and having paid homage to the Grandfather (Brahmā), one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. ||36||
From there, one should go to the supreme sacred ford known as Dharmajña-vimala,
where even today golden and silver fish are seen.
Having bathed there, O best of men, one obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
with one's self purified of all sins, one shall go to the supreme goal. ||38||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||24||
Chapter Twenty-five.
Nārada said:
Having reached the Vitastā and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, [one attains merit].
A man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, O Bhārata.
