In Kaśmīra itself is the abode of Anāgata and Takṣaka, renowned by the name Vitastā, which liberates one from all sins. ||2||
Having bathed there, a person will surely obtain the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
with his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the supreme goal. ||3||
From there, one should go to Malada, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having performed ritual ablutions according to the rules during the evening twilight.
O King, the wise declare that offering a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to the seven-flamed fire according to one's ability is an inexhaustible gift to the ancestors.
A hundred thousand cows, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices,
and a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices are not equal to the merit of a single spark of fire.
Then, having turned back from there, one should enter the abode of Rudra, O lord of kings;
by approaching the Great God, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
O King, having reached Maṇimat, a self-controlled celibate who stays for one night obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Then, O Indra among kings, one should go to Devikā, world-renowned,
where, O bull of the Bharatas, the origin of the Brahmins is heard of.
Having bathed in the Devikā and having worshipped Maheśvara, a man [attains that] place of the Trident-bearer which is renowned throughout the three worlds. (10)
O bull of the Bharatas, by offering even a blade of grass there, one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. (11)
There is the sacred ford (tīrtha) of Rudra known as Kāmākhya, which is esteemed by gods and sages;
having bathed there, O Bhārata, a man quickly attains perfection.
Having gone to a sacrifice, a place where sacrifices are performed, or likewise to a sacred pool,
and having touched water after offering flowers, one does not grieve over death thereafter.
They say that the holy Devikā, esteemed by gods and sages, is half a yojana in width and five yojanas in length.
Then, O knower of dharma, one should proceed in due order to Dīrghasattra,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the Siddhas and supreme ṛṣis [reside].
O subduer of enemies, O lord of the gods, because of your departure, those initiated into the long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) have become observers of fixed vows. 16.
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices; thereafter, one should go to Vināśana, self-restrained and restricted in diet. (17)
The Sarasvatī flows invisibly wherever she goes on the back of Mount Meru;
she is seen at Camasa, at Śivodbheda, and at Āgodbheda.
Having bathed at Tucamasodbheda, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
having bathed at Śivodbheda, a person obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||19||
Having bathed at Nāgodbheda, a man shall attain the world of the Nāgas;
and having reached the rare Śaśayāna, O king of kings, he shall likewise attain that tīrtha.
O highly fortunate one, O Bhārata, there on the Sarasvatī, for the welfare [of all], lotuses are concealed by the forms of rabbits throughout the year.
O best of the Bharatas, they always bathe there on the full moon day of Kārttika according to the prescribed rite;
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one shines forever like Śiva.
O bull of the Bharatas, one shall obtain the merit of giving a thousand cows;
O joy of the Kurus, having reached Kumārakoṭi, one should remain self-restrained.
There, one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution; he obtains ten thousand cows and uplifts his entire lineage. (24)
Thence, with a concentrated mind, one should go to Rudrakoṭi, the reservoir of Dharma,
where in ancient times ten million great royal sages were concentrated in meditation.
Overwhelmed by the rain and longing for the sight of the God, [the women cried] out of a desire to see him:
"I first! I first! I shall see the one whose banner is the bull! (26)
O King, descendant of Bharata, it is said that the sages set out in this manner;
then, O Lord of the Earth, even the Lord of Yogis, having established himself in yoga, [proceeded].
To pacify the anger of those seers of purified souls,
ten million Rudras were created and stood before the seers.
"Haras was seen by me before"—thus they each thought individually.
The Great God was pleased with those sages of fierce splendor. (29)
O King, out of supreme devotion, he granted them a boon:
"From this day forward, there shall be an increase in your righteousness. (30)
Having bathed there at Rudrakoṭī, O tiger among men, a pure man obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and uplifts his entire lineage. (31)
Thence, O king of kings, one should go to the world-renowned confluence at Sarasvatī,
which is of great merit, and there worship Janārdana.
O Indra among kings, it is there that the gods beginning with Brahmā, the ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas go on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one obtains much gold; with one's self purified of all sins, one goes to the world of Śiva. ||34||
O lord of men, by reaching the place where the sacrificial sessions (satras) of the sages were completed, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||35||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||25||
Chapter Twenty-six.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the highly praised Kurukṣetra.
Those who have gone to it are completely liberated from all evils born of their own actions. ||1||
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra"—whoever should speak thus constantly is liberated from all sins. (2)
There, O lord of men, the wise man should dwell for a month on the Sarasvatī,
where the gods headed by Brahmā reside, and where the celestial sages and Cāraṇas dwell.
O lord of the earth, O descendant of Bharata, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, and Pannagas resort to this most meritorious field of Brahmā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even for one who merely desires [to go] to Kurukṣetra in their mind, sins are utterly destroyed and they go to the world of Brahmā. ||5||
O best of the Kurus, having gone to Kurukṣetra endowed with faith,
a person obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Then, O King, [he saw] the very powerful gatekeeper Taramaka;
by merely saluting him, one would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows. ||7||
From there, O King of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed abode of Viṣṇu, the knower of dharma,
where Hari is eternally present.
Having bathed there and beheld Hari, the source of the three worlds, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||9||
Thence one should go to the tirtha known as Pāriplava, renowned throughout the three worlds;
there a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. ||10||
Having reached a sacred ford on earth, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
then, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Śāilvakinī.
Having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika, one obtains that very same fruit;
likewise, having reached Sarpanīvi, the supreme sacred site of the Nāgas.
One obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Nāgas;
from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to Dvārapāla Mātaraṇaka.
Having stayed there for one night, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
then, having gone to Pañcanada, being self-restrained and restricted in diet, [one should stay]. (14)
By touching the waters at Koṭitīrtha, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
by coming to Aśvinītīrtha, one is born endowed with beauty.
From there, one should go to the supreme sacred site of Vārāha, known to the knowers of dharma,
where in ancient times Viṣṇu remained in the form of a boar.
Staying there, O tiger among men, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
thereafter, O lord of kings, one should enter the Soma-tīrtha at Jayantī. ||17||
By bathing there, a person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
by bathing for even a single day, a man shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
O best of the Kurus, having approached Kṛtaśauca, the frequenter of sacred fords attains Puṇḍarīka, and he becomes purified by that act of purification. 19.
Then, having stayed there for one night at the great shrine named Jāvaṭa belonging to the wise Mahādeva, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati. ||20||
O Indra among kings, having bathed there at the world-renowned Jayā of the great king Iḍavatsa and approached her, one shall obtain all desires. ||21||
O bull among the Bharatas, that gate of Kurukṣetra is renowned;
having performed a circumambulation, the pilgrim should return.
Having bathed in the Puṣkara lakes and worshipped the ancestors and the gods,
he was summoned by the high-souled Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
O King, he becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done and obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
thereafter, O lord of men, the pilgrim should go to Rāmahrada.
O Indra among kings, it was there that Rāma, possessing blazing splendor,
by his prowess and speed, cleared away the kṣatriyas and created five lakes frequented by sages.
It has been heard that he filled it with the blood of this tiger among men.
All the ancestors as well as the great-grandfathers were thus gratified;
then those ancestors, being pleased, spoke to Rāma, O lord of the earth. (26)
"O Bhārgava, we are pleased with you, O highly fortunate Rāma, because of this devotion to your father and because of your prowess, O sinless one. (27)
"Choose a boon; what do you desire, O high-minded one? May all be well with you.
Thus addressed, Rāma, the best among speakers and the lord of kings, [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the ancestors stationed in the sky:
"If you are pleased with me, and if I am worthy of your favor..."
"By the grace of my father, I desire once again to nourish myself through asceticism;
for, overcome by anger, I have destroyed a constellation. (30)
And then, by your power, may I be released from this sin;
and may these lakes become sacred fords (tīrtha), renowned throughout the earth. (31)
Having heard these auspicious words of Rāma, his parents then replied,
filled with supreme joy and accompanied by great satisfaction.
May your ascetic power increase even further, especially through your devotion to your father;
for you have destroyed that constellation while overcome by anger.

Therefore, you shall be liberated from that sin, and those [beings] shall be slain by their own karma; moreover, these lakes will undoubtedly attain the status of sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha). ||34||
Whoever bathes in these lakes and offers libations to the ancestors, his ancestors, being well-pleased, will grant him that which is difficult to obtain on earth. (35)
O King, having thus granted this boon— the eternal heavenly world, the desire cherished by his heart— Rāma’s ancestors then [departed].
Having addressed Bhārgava, they then vanished right there, filled with joy.
Thus are the holy lakes of Rāma, belonging to the high-souled Bhārgava; having bathed in these lakes of Rāma, one who observes celibacy and auspicious vows [attains merit].
O best of kings, by worshipping Rāma, one obtains much gold;
O descendant of Kuru, the pilgrim reaches the root of the Vaṃśa tree. (38)
O King, O best of the Bharatas, having bathed at Vaitaraṇīmūlaka, one should reach the holy ford of Kāyaśodhana and uplift one's own lineage.
Having bathed therein, one undoubtedly attains purification of the body;
with a purified body, one goes to auspicious and unsurpassed worlds. (40)
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the sacred ford that is difficult to find even in the three worlds, where in former times the worlds were uplifted by the all-powerful Viṣṇu. (41)
O King, having reached the world-saving Tīrtha, renowned throughout the three worlds, one who bathes in this best of holy sites delivers his own people. 42.
Having reached Śrītīrtha, one obtains supreme prosperity;
and having reached Kapilātīrtha, being self-controlled and practicing celibacy, [one attains the same]. ||43||
Having bathed there and likewise worshipped the gods and the ancestors,
a person obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand Kapila cows.
Having reached Sūryatīrtha and bathed with a restrained mind, one should worship the ancestors and the gods, being devoted to fasting. ||45||
The visitor of sacred fords, proceeding in due order, attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun, reaching the abode of cows.
O lord of men, a pilgrim who reaches the Gaṅgā-tīrtha and performs an ablution there obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. 47.
Having bathed at the Kevya-tīrtha, a man obtains supreme vigor;
from there, O king of kings, he should proceed to the gatekeeper Lavarṇaka.
At his sacred ford on the Sarasvatī, which belongs to the high-souled Indra—
by bathing there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O lord of men, one should go to Brahmāvarta, known to the knowers of dharma;
having bathed in Brahmāvarta, a man shall attain the world of Brahmā. ||50||
From there, one who knows the Dharma should go to the unsurpassed Sutīrthaka, where the ancestors are eternally present together with the deities. (51)
One devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution there;
he obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of the ancestors. ||52||
Then, O best of the Bharatas, having reached another sacred ford in due order, he bathed in the tirthas of the Lord of Kāśī.
Freed from all diseases, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
and there, O King, is the Mātṛtīrtha, where one who bathes [attains this].
O King, by increasing his progeny, one attains the path to heaven;
thereafter, self-restrained and restricted in diet, he should go to Śītavana.
O great king, there is a great and vast sacred ford (tīrtha) which is difficult to attain;
it purifies even a single person by its mere sight, O lord of men. 56.
O Bhārata, by immersing one's hair in that very place, one becomes purified;
there is another excellent tīrtha there, known as Snātalokārtihan.
There, O best of the Bharatas, learned brahmins and tigers among men who are devoted to that place attain the supreme goal after bathing. 58.
O best of the Bharatas, at the tirtha called Svarṇalomāpanayana,
the most excellent of the twice-born remove their own body hair by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
And those of purified souls, O lord of kings, attain the supreme goal at that very tirtha known as Daśāśvamedhika, O ruler of the earth.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, people go to the supreme goal.
From there, O lord of kings, one should proceed to Mānuṣa, which is world-renowned.
There, O King, black deer, afflicted by the hunter's arrows,
plunged into that lake and attained human form.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a man who is celibate and composed, his soul purified of all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world. ||63||
O Lord of the Earth, one krośa to the east of Mānuṣa is an unrenowned river among streams, frequented by the Siddhas. (64)
The man who offers food of śyāmāka grain there, dedicated to the gods and the ancestors, gains great merit as the fruit of his dharma. (65)
And when one Brahmin has been fed there, it is as if ten million have been fed;
having bathed there and likewise worshipped the deities and the ancestors.
Having stayed for one night, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā.
O Bhārata, this is known on earth as Brahmānusvara;
O bull of the Bharatas, one should bathe there in the pools of the Seven Sages.
And at Kedāra, as well as at the [shrine] of the high-souled Kapila, O Indra among kings, one should approach Brahmā, being pure and with a restrained mind. 69.
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the world of Brahmā after reaching Kapiṣṭhala’s Kedāra, which is very difficult to find. (70)
Having burned away his sins through austerity, he attains the power of invisibility;
from there, O king of kings, he should go to Sarvaka, which is world-renowned.
By approaching the Bull-bannered Lord on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one indeed obtains all desires and goes to the heavenly world.
And there are thirty million sacred fords, O joy of the Kurus; it is the most excellent among them.
Likewise, O best of the Bharatas, ten million Rudras are present equally at the wells and lakes; and there, indeed, is the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Ilāspada.
Having bathed there and having worshipped both the deities and the ancestors, one does not meet with an evil fate and obtains the merit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. ||74||
O Lord of the Earth, what gift should a man give after bathing here, and what mantra should he recite,
so that he may obtain immeasurable merit from both charity and sacrifice?
Having sipped water from a jar, one who is full of faith and has conquered his senses [attains this]. ||75||
A person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice by staying to the east of Lake Nārada, belonging to the high-souled Nārada. (76)
O best of the Kurus, there is the auspicious holy site renowned as Rāmajanma;
having bathed at that holy site and cast off his life-breaths there, O Bhārata, a man [attains liberation].
Permitted by Nārada, he attains worlds that are difficult to reach;
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, he should enter Puṇḍarīka.
Having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the *puṇḍarīka* sacrifice;
from there he should go to Triviṣṭapa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds. (79)
There lies the sacred river Vaitaraṇī, which liberates one from sin;
having bathed there and worshipped the trident-bearing Lord whose banner is the bull, [one attains liberation].
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the supreme goal;
from there, O Indra among kings, he should proceed to the excellent Phalaki forest.
There, O King, the gods have taken refuge in the Phalaki forest;
they perform extensive austerities for many thousands of years.
Having bathed at Dṛṣatpāna and having offered libations to the deities, a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. ||83||
O best of the Bharatas, having bathed at the sacred ford of all the gods, a man obtains, O king of kings, the merit of giving a thousand cows. ||84||
Having bathed at Pāṇikhya and offered libations to the deities, a man obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and goes to the world of the Ṛṣis. ||85||
From there, one should go to Miśraka, renowned throughout the world as a knower of Dharma;
there, the great-souled one [performed] the confluence of the kings of sacred fords (tīrtharājendra). 86.
O tiger among kings, we have heard from Vyāsa that a man who bathes in all the holy fords does not equal one who bathes in the Miśraka. (87)
Then, self-restrained and restricted in diet, a man should go to Vyāsavana;
having bathed there with mental speed, he obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Having gone to Madhuvana, the abode of the Goddess, a pure man, having bathed there, should worship the gods and the ancestors, being self-controlled and pure. (89)
O descendant of Bharata, one who bathes at the confluence of the Kauśikī and the Ṛṣadvatī obtains the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices, along with the gods and men.
Having bathed there with one's diet restrained, one is liberated from all sins.
Beyond that is the place named Vyāsasthalī, where by the wise Vyāsa—
O king of kings, when he was intent on abandoning his body, tormented by grief for his son,
he was likewise raised back to life by the gods.
By visiting his sacred site (abhigamyasthalī), one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
and by reaching the well Ṛṇānta and offering a prastha of sesame seeds, [one is likewise purified]. ||93||
O lord of men, one who is freed from debts shall attain supreme perfection;
by bathing at the Vedī-tīrtha, a man obtains the merit of [giving] a thousand cows. 94.
Ahaḥ and Sudina are two tīrthas difficult for kings to attain;
by bathing in them, an excellent man shall reach the world of the Sun. 95.
Then one should go to Mṛgadhūma, renowned throughout the three worlds; having bathed there at Rudrapada and worshipped [the deity], a person becomes tranquil. (96)
By beholding the high-souled Śūlapāṇi, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
by bathing at Koṭitīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||97||
Or else, having gone to Vāmana, which is renowned throughout the three worlds,
one should bathe there at Viṣṇupada and worship Vāmana.
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall attain the world of Viṣṇu;
by bathing, a man purifies his lineage, and that man purifies his own family. 99.
Having gone to Pavanahradam, the supreme sacred ford of the Maruts,
and having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
Having bathed in the lake of the immortals and having duly worshipped the Lord of the Immortals, one is glorified in the heavenly world through the power of the immortals. (101)
O Indra among kings, having bathed according to the prescribed rite at Śālisūrya, the sacred site of Śālihotra, one obtains the merit of gifting a thousand cows, O best of men. (102)
O best of the Bharatas, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) called Śrīkuñja on the Sarasvatī;
having bathed there, O King, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. (103)
Then, O king of kings, having reached the very difficult-to-attain Naimiṣa forest, the sages of Naimiṣa, whose wealth is their austerity, [gathered there]. 104.
In ancient times, having set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, they went to Kurukṣetra;
thereupon, O best of the Bharatas, Kuñja was established upon the Sarasvatī.
O Great One, so that it may be a source of satisfaction for the sages, a man who bathes there in that Kuñja obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. ||106||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||26||
Chapter Seven.
Nārada said:
From there, one should go to the unsurpassed Kanyātīrtha, known to the knowers of dharma.
Having bathed at Kanyātīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
From there, O tiger among men, one should go to the supreme abode of Brahmā;
having bathed there, even a man of inferior caste attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa of most purified soul shall attain the supreme goal;
thereafter, O tiger among men, he should go to the unsurpassed Soma-tīrtha.
Having bathed there, O King, a man shall attain the world of Soma;
from there, O lord of men, he should proceed to the Saptasārasvata tīrtha.

O King, it was there that in ancient times the world-renowned Brahman-sage Kaṇaka attained perfection; it is famously known as Maṅkaṇaka, so called because of Kaṇaka’s [act] with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass.
O King, when he was wounded by the stake, vegetable juice flowed from him;
seeing that vegetable juice, the great ascetic was overcome with joy. (6)
The sage Kila, a brahmin seer, danced with eyes wide open in wonder;
then, as he danced, everything both moving and unmoving began to dance.
Both [the gods and the demons] were made to dance and were bewildered by his heroic splendor;
then [he was addressed] by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, and by the ṛṣis whose wealth is their asceticism.
O Great God, O Lord of Men, for the sake of the sage's instruction, you ought to act, O God, so that this man shall not dance. (9)
Then, having seen the divine sage, with a heart overcome by joy,
Nṛtya spoke to him out of a desire for the welfare of the steadfast ones.
O knower of dharma, for what reason do you dance with such great joy? O bull among sages, why is there such a cause for celebration, or why are you playing the lute? (11)
The sage said:
"O best of the twice-born, O Brahmin, do you not see that vegetable juice has flowed from the wound of this ascetic who stands upon the path of dharma? (12)
Seeing him, I began to dance, overcome by great joy;
then the god laughed and spoke to that ṛṣi who was deluded by passion.
"But I, O Brahmin, do not experience any wonder here, as I behold this.
Having spoken thus to the best of men, Mahādeva said this: 14.
O sinless lord of kings, as his thumb was struck by the tip of [the other] finger,
O King, something resembling snow issued forth from the wound caused by the ash.
Seeing this, O King, the sage was filled with shame and fell at his feet, saying:
"I consider no other deity to be greater or more supreme than Rudra."
O wielder of the trident, you are the destination of this world of gods and demons;
by you was this entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving, created. (17)
O Blessed One, at the end of the eon, everyone enters into you alone;
you cannot be fully known even by the gods, so how could you be known by me? 18.
O sinless one, all the gods, beginning with Śakra, are seen within you;
you are the creator and the instigator of all these worlds day after day.
"By your grace, O Great God, all the gods rejoice here, free from fear from any quarter.
Having thus praised the Great God, the sage bowed down and said:
"O Great God, by your grace, may this sacrifice of mine not come to ruin."
Then the god, with a joyful soul, spoke this to the brahmin seer: ||21||
O Brahmin, by my grace may your ascetic power increase a thousandfold;
O great sage, I shall dwell here in this hermitage together with you.
Those who, having bathed at Saptasarasvatī, shall worship me—for them nothing whatsoever will be difficult to attain, either in this world or in the next. (23)
"He shall go to the world of Sarasvatī; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, the Great God vanished right there.
Then one should go to Auśanasa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the sages whose wealth is asceticism, reside.
And the blessed Kārttikeya, O Bhārata, indeed made his presence there at the three junctions of the day out of a desire to do what was pleasing to Bhārgava.
The Kapālamocana tīrtha is the destroyer of all sins;
having bathed there, O tiger among men, one is liberated from all evils. (27)
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, one should go to Agnitīrtha;
having bathed there, one attains the world of Agni and uplifts one's entire lineage. ||28||
O best of the Bharatas, there is the tīrtha of Viśvāmitra;
having bathed there, O great king, one attains the status of a brāhmaṇa. (29)
Having reached Brahmayoni, pure and with a restrained mind,
one who bathes there, O tiger among men, attains the world of Brahmā.
It purifies one's lineage even unto the seventh generation; there is no doubt about this.
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds.
O King, one who is devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform an ablution at that place known as Pṛthūdaka during the month of Kārttika.
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, whether by a woman or by a man, whatever inauspicious deed has been committed by one with a human intellect toward any ascetic— [33]
O Bhārata, all that perishes for one who has merely bathed there;
moreover, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and even attains heaven.
They say Kurukṣetra is meritorious; from Kurukṣetra, the Sarasvatī is more so;
the holy fords of the Sarasvatī are more meritorious than that, and Pṛthūdaka is more meritorious than those holy fords.
He who casts off his body at Pṛthūdaka, the most excellent of all sacred fords, while intent on silent recitation, shall never again undergo rebirth.
O King, this was sung by Sanatkumāra and by the high-souled Vyāsa;
it is ordained in the Vedas that one should go to Pṛthūdaka.
O best of men, there is no other sacred ford more meritorious than Pṛthūdaka;
this place is undoubtedly pure, holy, and purifying. (38)
Having bathed there, even people who have committed sins go to heaven;
thus do the wise say that Pṛthūdaka is the best of waters. (39)
And there, O best of the Bharatas, is the Madhusrava tīrtha;
by bathing there, a man obtains the fruit of ten thousand cows. ||40||
Then, O best of men, one should proceed in due order to the tīrtha of the Goddess, the world-renowned confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā. 41.
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin and obtains the fruit equal to that of the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices.
It purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation; there is no doubt about this.
And there, O scion of the Kuru family, is the sacred ford known as Avakīrṇa.
O Pārtha, in ancient times, a twice-born man was made compassionate toward Brahmins by means of the Darbha grass,
as well as through vows, the initiation ceremony (upanayana), and fasting.
One who is endowed with ritual actions and mantras would undoubtedly be a Brāhmaṇa;
yet even one devoid of ritual actions and mantras, O bull among men, becomes so by bathing there. 45.
The Brahmin shall have fulfilled his vow; this was seen in ancient times.
Furthermore, even the four oceans were brought together by Darbhin.
Having bathed there, O tiger among men, one shall not fall into an evil state;
he obtains the fruit of four thousand cows.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the tīrtha Śatasahasraka and the Sahasraka; both of these tīrthas are world-renowned. 48.
For by bathing at both, a man obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows;
likewise, whether it be a gift or a fast, its merit becomes multiplied a thousandfold. ||49||
From there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Reṇukātīrtha;
there, devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods, one should perform an ablution.
With his soul purified of all sins, having bathed at Vimocana, he— having conquered anger and mastered his senses— shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One is completely liberated from all sins committed through receiving gifts;
then, having gone to Pañcavaṭa, one should remain celibate with senses subdued. ||52||
Endowed with great merit, he is glorified in the heavenly world,
where the Lord of Yogins, Sthāṇu himself, whose banner is the bull, resides.
Having worshipped that Lord of Gods, one attains success simply by departing;
the Taijasa and Vāruṇa tīrthas shine with their own splendor.
There, Guha was then consecrated to the generalship of the gods by Brahmā and the other deities, as well as by the sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
O best of the Kurus, to the east of Taijasa is Kurutīrtha;
having bathed at Kurutīrtha, a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses [attains merit]. (56)
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the world of Rudra;
from there, self-restrained and with regulated food, he should proceed to the gateway of heaven.
O lord of men, the one who frequents sacred fords attains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, goes to the world of Brahmā,
and thereafter proceeds to Anaraṇya.
Having bathed there, O King, a man shall not meet with an evil fate;
for there Brahmā himself is eternally honored together with the gods. (59)
O bull of the Kuru lineage, O best of kings, there is also the presence of those tigers among men who have attained the supreme state of Nārāyaṇa, upon the sacrificial altar of Rudra.
Having approached that goddess, one shall not meet with an evil fate;
and there, O Great King, [one should worship] Viśveśvara, the Lord of Umā.
By approaching the Great God, one is released from all sins;
and by approaching Nārāyaṇa, the lotus-navelled subduer of enemies.
O lord of men, merely by bathing in the sacred fords (tīrthas) of all the gods, one shines gloriously and attains the world of Viṣṇu, the great king.
Having abandoned all suffering, one shines forever like Śiva;
therefore, O lord of men, the pilgrim should then proceed to Asthipura.
Having reached a purifying sacred ford (tīrtha), one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
O Bhārata, one thereby obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O bull of the Bharatas, there is the Gaṅgāhrada and the Iḍakūpa;
three crores of sacred fords are contained within that well.
Having bathed there, O King, a man attains the world of Brahmā;
having bathed in the Āpagā and worshipped Maheśvara, a man [attains the same]. (67)
One attains the supreme goal and uplifts one's own lineage;
thereafter, one should go to Sthāṇuvaṭa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there and stayed for a night, one shall attain the world of Rudra;
from there, one should go to the grove of jujube trees and then to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Where a man who has fasted for three nights eats jujube fruits (badarī), he would indeed eat jujube fruits for twelve full years. ||70||
O lord of men, having reached Indramārga, the pilgrim should fast for three nights; O lord of men, he thereby becomes equal [to Indra].
By fasting for a day and night, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
having reached [this place], a man who has fasted for a single night [attains that same merit]. ||72||
One who is self-restrained and truthful is honored in the world of Brahmā;
likewise, O king of kings, one should go to the Tīrtha renowned throughout the three worlds. 73.
Where the hermitage of the high-souled Āditya, that mass of splendor, is located—
at that sacred ford, having bathed and having worshipped the Sun-god— 74.
O best of the Kurus, having bathed at the Soma-tīrtha, a man who frequents sacred sites goes to the world of the Sun and uplifts his entire lineage.
A man attains the world of Soma; there is no doubt about this.
Thence, O knower of dharma, O lord of men, one should go to the place of Dadhīca.
O King, there is a most meritorious tīrtha, purifying and world-renowned,
where the storehouse of asceticism attained perfection upon reaching the Sarasvatī.
Having bathed at that sacred ford, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and gains Sarasvatī-like intelligence; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O King, having gone to Kanyāśrama, he dwelt there for three nights, observing celibacy without fixed rules and devoted to fasting.
One obtains a hundred divine maidens and goes to the world of Brahmā;
from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the sacred ford of Saṃnihitī as well. ||80||
There, the gods headed by Brahmā and the sages whose wealth is their asceticism, endowed with great merit, shall assemble month after month. (81)
Having touched the waters at Sannihitī when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one has eternally performed a hundred horse-sacrifices. ||82||
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth, those that move through the atmosphere, as well as wells, brahmins, and holy shrines—[all these are surpassed by this]. (83)
Without doubt, O lord of men, they will assemble on the new moon day every month, O tiger among men, at Sannihitī, O ruler of people. (84)
Renowned on earth as being in close proximity to the gods due to the confluence of sacred fords (tīrthas), one who bathes and drinks there is glorified in the heavenly world. ||85||
Likewise, on the new moon day, or when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, listen to the fruit of merit for that mortal who performs a śrāddha. ||86||
Whatever fruit is obtained from a thousand horse-sacrifices properly performed,
a man obtains that very same fruit simply by bathing and performing the śrāddha rite.
Whatever evil deed has been committed by a woman or a man, all of that perishes as soon as he has bathed; there is no doubt in this matter. (88)
By means of a lotus-colored vehicle, he goes to the world of Brahmā;
then, having saluted the gatekeeper Macakruka by name, [he proceeds]. (89)
And there, O best of the Bharatas, is the Gaṅgāhrada tirtha;
there one who knows dharma, being celibate and composed, should bathe. (90)
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
Naimiṣa is sacred on earth, and Puṣkara is sacred in the intermediate space.
Kurukṣetra is superior even to the three worlds;
for even the dust of Kurukṣetra, when stirred up by the wind, [attains the highest state]. 92.
Moreover, they lead even one who has performed evil deeds to the supreme goal—[the region] south of the Sarasvatī and north of the Sarasvatī. (93)
Those who dwell in Kurukṣetra dwell in Triviṣṭapa; "I shall go to Kurukṣetra," "I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra. (94)
Even by uttering but a single word [of praise], one is glorified in the heavenly world;
for Kurukṣetra at the altar of Brahman is holy and frequented by the Brahman-sages.
O King, those who dwell within that space— between Taraṇḍaka and Karaṇḍaka, between Rāma-hrada and Camacakruka— are by no means to be pitied in any way.
This group of five ascetic groves, equal to Kurukṣetra, is called the northern altar of the Grandfather. ||96||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||27||
The Twenty-eighth Chapter.
Nārada said:
From there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the ancient Dharmatīrtha,
where the highly fortunate Dharma performed supreme austerity.
That meritorious holy site was established by him and marked with his own name;
having bathed there, O King, a man who is virtuous and composed [attains great merit]. (2)
By this, one purifies even one's lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
Thence, O knower of dharma, one should go to the supreme Kalāpavana forest.
Having traveled there with great difficulty and bathed with a concentrated mind, one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||4||
From there, O King, a person should go to the Saugandhika forest,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the ṛṣis whose wealth is their asceticism, reside.
Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, along with Mahoragas—merely by entering that forest, one is liberated from all sins. ||6||
Then, O King, there is the Sarasvatī, the best of rivers and the most excellent of streams, known as Plakṣādevī, which is of great merit. (7)
One should perform an ablution there with water flowing from an anthill;
having worshipped the ancestors and the gods, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||8||
There is a very rare sacred ford (tīrtha) there named Īśānādhyuṣita;
it possesses sixfold merit at its confluences, as does the Tiniśa tree growing upon an anthill.
O tiger among men, by bathing there one obtains the merit of a thousand tawny cows and an Ashvamedha sacrifice; this was seen by the ancients.
O descendant of Bharata, by visiting Sugandhā, Śatakuṃbhā,
and Capapṛṣṭhayajña, the best of men is glorified in the heavenly world.
Having reached that rare sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Triśūlapātra,
one should perform an ablution there, being devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods.
One undoubtedly attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas by abandoning deceit;
thereafter, one should go to Rājagṛha, the exceedingly rare abode of the Goddess. ||13||
Renowned as Śākambharī, she is famous throughout the three worlds;
for a thousand divine years, O Bhārata, she indeed subsisted on vegetables alone.
O King, the sages who were devoted to the Queen and whose wealth was their asceticism arrived there at her mealtime, month after month. (15)
O Bhārata, they performed hospitality for them with vegetables alone;
therefore, the name of that [city] became established as Śākambharī. ||16||
Having reached Śākambharī, a self-controlled and concentrated celibate student, having stayed there for three nights, should eat vegetables while remaining restrained and pure. ||17||
O descendant of Bharata, that fruit which belongs to one who subsists on a diet of vegetables for twelve years perfectly—that same fruit shall belong to him through the grace of the Goddess. (18)
From there, one should go to the place called Suvarṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds,
where in ancient times Kṛṣṇa propitiated Rudra for the sake of obtaining his grace.
And he obtained very many excellent boons, difficult even for the gods to attain;
and he was addressed by the gratified Destroyer of Tripura, O Bhārata: (20)
Moreover, O Kṛṣṇa, you will become the most beloved in the world;
there is no doubt that the entire universe will have you as its face. 21.

Having gone there and worshipped the bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), who is the king of kings to be approached, one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas. ||22||
Then a person should go to Dhūmāvatī and stay there for three nights;
he obtains the desires prayed for in his mind—of this there is no doubt. (23)
O lord of men, to the south of the goddess is Rathāvarta;
having gone there, one who knows the Dharma, is endowed with faith, and has conquered his senses [attains merit]. (24)
By the grace of Mahādeva, one shall go to the supreme goal;
having performed a circumambulation, O bull of the Bharatas, one should depart. 25.
O wise one, O tiger among men, O lord of men, having bathed there at the place named Dhārā, which destroys all sins, you shall no longer grieve. (26)
Then, having paid homage to the Great Mountain, one should go to Gaṅgādvāra, which is equal to Svargadvāra; of this there is no doubt. (27)
There, being composed, one should perform the consecration at Koṭitīrtha; one obtains the Puṇḍarīka [merit] and indeed uplifts one's entire lineage. ||28||
Having stayed there for a single night, one obtains the merit of [giving] a thousand cows;
and at Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Śakrāvarta, one should offer libations.
Having duly honored the gods and the ancestors, he is glorified in the world of merit; then, having bathed at Kanakhala and fasted for three nights, a man [attains the same]. (30)
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world;
O lord of men, the pilgrim should then go to Kapilāvaṭa.
Having stayed there for one night, one obtains the merit of a thousand cows at the abode of the great-souled Kapila, the king of Naga kings and lord of kings. (32)
O best of the Kurus, there is a sacred ford renowned throughout all the worlds;
O lord of men, one should perform an ablution there at the Nāga-tīrtha.
A human being obtains the fruit of a thousand tawny cows. ||33||
From there, O King, one should go to Lalitaka, the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) of Śaṅkara;
having bathed there, a man shall not meet with misfortune. ||34||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||28||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
Nārada said:
Thereafter, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme Kālindī-tīrtha.
Having bathed there, O King, a person shall not meet with an unfortunate rebirth. ||1||
A person obtains that same fruit at Puṣkara, Eka-tīrtha, Kurukṣetra, Brahmāvarta, Pṛthūdaka, Avimukta, and the place called Suvarṇa. ||2||
O best of men, he obtains that fruit at the Yamunā who has an intense longing for the enjoyments of heaven; such is the case for those whose minds are so disposed.
O best of men, by means of bathing and giving gifts especially at the Yamunā,
one attains longevity, health, prosperity, beauty, youthfulness, and virtuous qualities.
Those who possess such aspirations must not abandon the waters of the Yamunā—
those who fear hell and other such realms, and those who dread poverty.
One should immerse oneself there with every possible effort,
for the purpose of washing away the mud of poverty, sin, and misfortune.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is indeed no end to the power of Truth, nor is there anything else equal to it;
for rituals performed without faith are indeed considered to yield only half their fruit.
It bestows the complete fruit merely by bathing in the Yamunā. ||7||
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, O King, one who is purified by the waters of the sage does not see any sufferings in this world or the next. ||8||
Just as the moon wanes and waxes during the two fortnights, so too does sin perish and merit increase through bathing there. (9)
Just as various kinds of jewels emerge from the ocean, so too do longevity, wealth, spouses, and prosperity come into being. (10)
Just as the wish-fulfilling cow grants every desire and the thought-gem grants whatever is conceived, so too does bathing in the Yamunā fulfill every heart's longing. 11.
In the Kṛta age, supreme knowledge was the highest; likewise, sacrifice in the Tretā;
charity in the Dvāpara; but in the Kali age, O Kālindī, devotion is always auspicious.
O Lord of the Earth, bathing in the Yamunā indeed rains down the Dharma through its streams for all people of every caste and for all stages of life. 13.
In this land of Bhārata, and especially in this land of action (karmabhūmi),
the birth of those men who do not bathe in the Kālindī is declared to be fruitless.
Just as there is no sovereignty in the sky, nor in the earth, nor in the orb of the moon, even so, virtuous action does not shine without immersion in the Yamunā. 15.
Hari is not so pleased by vows, gifts, and austerities as Keśava is gratified by merely bathing there. 16.
There exists no splendor whatsoever equal to the splendor of the sun;
likewise, there are no ritual acts born of sacrifices equal to bathing in the Yamunā. 17.
For the pleasure of Vāsudeva, for the removal of all sins, and for the attainment of heaven, a human being should perform an immersion in the Kālindī. ||18||
What is the use of protecting this body, though well-nourished and powerful, if it is unstable and lacks immersion in the Yamunā? (19)
It has pillars of bone, bonds of sinew, and a plastering of flesh and blood;
it is covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement. (20)
Pervaded by old age, sorrow, and calamity, it is a sickly abode of disease;
rooted in passion, impermanent, and the refuge of all defects. (21)
One who helps others, one afflicted by evil, one who harms others, one who envies others, the greedy, the slanderous, the cruel, the ungrateful, and likewise the fickle; ||22||
It is harsh, difficult to restrain, and wicked, corrupted by the three defects;
it is impure, foul-smelling, and deluded by the three types of suffering. (23)
By its very nature, it delights in unrighteousness and is agitated by hundreds of cravings;
it stands at the gateway to hell through desire, anger, and great greed. ||24||
This body, which results in qualities such as excrement, worms, and ashes, is indeed useless without bathing in the Yamunā. (25)
Like bubbles in water or like eggs in birds, those who have avoided bathing in the Yamunā are born only for death. (26)
A Brahmin who is not a Vaiṣṇava is destroyed; a Śrāddha ceremony without the Piṇḍa offerings is destroyed;
a Kṣatriya who is not devoted to the Brāhmaṇas is destroyed; and a family ruined by lack of proper conduct is destroyed.
Dharma is destroyed by pride and greed; austerity is destroyed by anger alone; knowledge is destroyed by lack of firmness; and sacred learning is destroyed by negligence. (28)
A woman struck by devotion to another, a celibate student struck by a woman, an oblation offered into an unkindled fire, and equanimity devoid of devotion—these are all ruined. (29)
A livelihood dependent on others is ruined; the performance of cooking for one's own sake is ruined;
union with a Śūdra woman is ruined; and the wealth of a miser is ruined. (30)
Ignorance destroyed by lack of practice destroys awakening;
a sacred ford destroyed for the sake of livelihood, and a vow destroyed for the sake of living. (31)
Speech that is untrue or harsh, as well as speech that is slanderous; a mantra heard by six ears is lost, and a recitation performed with a distracted mind is lost. (32)
A gift given to one who has not mastered the Vedas is destroyed; the world of the nihilist is destroyed;
and everything performed for the sake of the next world that is done without faith is destroyed. (33)
O King, just as this world is lost for men who are destitute, so too is the birth of human beings lost if they do not perform meritorious deeds. (34)
O King, all minor offenses, all major sins, and even the great transgressions—
all these are reduced to ashes by immersion in the Yamunā.
All evils tremble when a man has gone to the Yamunā;
indeed, if he shall bathe in its waters, which are the destroyers of all sins. (36)
Like fires blazing on the Yamunā, those best of men shine forth, liberated from all sins like the moon from the clouds. (37)
Whether moist, dry, light, or heavy, [the sin] committed through speech, mind, and actions—therein, bathing burns away that evil just as fire consumes sacrificial fuel. (38)
O best of kings, whatever sin has been committed through negligence, whether done knowingly or unknowingly,
is destroyed merely by bathing in the Yamunā.
Those free from sin go to heaven, while the most sinful attain purity;
no doubt should be entertained in this regard concerning bathing in the waters of the Yamunā. (40)
O King, just as all are qualified for devotion to Viṣṇu, so too is the goddess Yamunā, the destroyer of sins, always accessible to everyone. (41)
This alone is the supreme mantra, and this is the highest austerity;
bathing in the Yamunā is indeed the ultimate and supreme expiation. (42)

O King, through the practice of previous births, the minds of men [attain] faith in the Kali age; and proficiency in the knowledge of the supreme self arises from the practice of that very birth, just as it does for others. 43.
The supreme bath in the Yamunā is skilled at washing away the smearing of the mud of saṃsāra; it is the purifier of purifiers. 44.
Having bathed there, O King, which bestows the fruits of all desires, they enjoy auspicious pleasures resembling the moon, the sun, and the planets. (45)
The Yamunā is said to bestow liberation when she is joined with Mathurā;
in Mathurā, she increases one's merit manifold at every moment. (46)
And where the holy Yamunā, the goddess who removes great sins and bestows devotion to Viṣṇu, becomes united with Mathurā; (47)
If one should immerse the Kali age in heaven with a spirit of devotion,
they shall dwell in the presence of Hari for thousands of crores of kalpas.
Men indeed attain liberation even when devoid of Sāṃkhya;
his ancestors remain satisfied in heaven for hundreds of kalpas.
O King, for those men who drink the auspicious water of the Yamunā, what need is there for the consumption of thousands of *pañcagavya*? (50)
What need is there for millions of sacred bathing places that have been frequented?
There, every gift and every burnt offering becomes ten millionfold in merit. ||51||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
(30) Chapter Thirty. Nārada said:
In this regard, O King, I shall describe to you an ancient history from the former Kṛta Yuga, which took place in the excellent city of Niṣadha.
There was a Vaiśya named Kuberābha, also known as Hemakuṇḍala;
he was of noble birth, virtuous in conduct, and a worshiper of the gods, the twice-born, and the sacred fire. ||2||
He was engaged in agriculture and trade, a dealer in various kinds of buying and selling, and devoted to the rearing of cattle, horses, buffaloes, and other livestock. ||3||
Milk, curd, buttermilk, cow dung, grass, wood, fruits, roots, salt, fresh ginger, and long pepper; (4)
He always sells grains, vegetables, oils, various kinds of garments, minerals, and products of sugarcane. (5)
In this manner, by various means and other such methods,
he constantly acquired eight crores of gold coins.
Thus that man of great wealth became grey-haired at his ears;
afterwards, he reflected within his own mind upon the momentariness of saṃsāra.
He spent one-sixth of that wealth on religious works;
he built a temple for Viṣṇu and a house for Śiva.
They caused a vast reservoir to be dug, resembling the ocean;
and many ponds and lotus-pools were constructed by them in various ways.
He then created a forest of banyan, pipal, mango, jujube, and *būni* trees,
as well as a beautiful grove of flowers, according to their own nature.
From sunrise until sunset, he provided food and drink;
outside the city, he established four most beautiful water-stations in the four directions.
O King, that righteous soul, ever devoted to giving, then bestowed those gifts which are well-known in the Purāṇas.
He performed penance for the sins committed throughout his life;
he was constantly devoted to the worship of the gods and always honored his guests. ||13||
O King, while he was living in this manner, two sons were born to him;
they were well-known by the names Śrīkuṇḍala and Vikuṇḍala.
Having anointed their heads with it, she departed for the forest to perform austerities;
there, she propitiated the supreme god Govinda, the lord who bestows boons. (15)
With his body emaciated by asceticism and his mind always fixed on Vāsudeva, he attained the world of Viṣṇu, having gone to which one does not grieve. (16)
Then, O King, his two sons were possessed of great pride;
they were young, endowed with beauty, and arrogant with the conceit of wealth. (17)
Those who are immoral, addicted to vices, and indifferent to the practice of Dharma and other duties;
likewise, the words of the sick and the elderly when they have arrived with new news. (18)
Following evil paths, wicked-souled, they were obstructers of their father and friend; devoted to unrighteousness, they were corrupt and adulterers with the wives of others. (19)
Devoted to song and instrumental music, delighting in the lute and the flute,
and accompanied by hundreds of courtesans, the two of them then lived there singing.
Accompanied by sycophants, they were experts in the art of kissing;
well-attired in beautiful garments and anointed with exquisite sandalwood paste.
Likewise, they were rich with fragrant garlands, marked by the beauty of musk spots, adorned with the splendor of various ornaments, and captivating with pearl necklaces. ||22||
Then those two, intoxicated by drinking wine and infatuated with pleasure with the wives of others, sported here and there with a multitude of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having destroyed that paternal wealth, they gave away a thousand and a hundred [coins];
devoted to constant enjoyment, they remained in their own delightful homes.
In this way, however, that wealth was squandered by the two of them on improper expenses among courtesans, libertines, actors, wrestlers, bards, and the like. (25)
This wealth given to one who is not a worthy recipient is like seed sown in saline soil;
it is neither truly given to a worthy recipient nor offered into the mouth of a Brahmin.
Viṣṇu, the sustainer of beings and the destroyer of all sins, was not worshipped;
consequently, the wealth belonging to both of them soon came to ruin.
Then, having fallen into suffering and reached a state of extreme wretchedness, they both lamented and fainted, tormented by the pain of hunger and distress. (28)
While those two remained standing there, everything that was eaten by their kinsmen, relatives, all their servants, and dependents [was provided]. (29)
O King, when their wealth was exhausted and they were being disregarded in the city, those two subsequently began to commit theft in the town.
Then, terrified by the world and oppressed by everyone, those two kings departed from their own city and took up residence in the forest.
The two fools constantly struck various birds, boars, deer, and rohit deer with sharp arrows smeared with poison.
They constantly hunted rabbits, porcupines, monitor lizards, and many other beasts of prey,
their great strength always devoted to the sport of the hunt.
Thus, while I was engaged in supreme austerity, subsisting on neither ritual food nor impure food, one of us reached the mountain at one time, while the other went to the forest. (34)
The eldest was killed by a tiger and the youngest was bitten by a snake;
O King, on a single day those most wicked ones met their end.
Then, having been bound by the messengers of Yama on account of their sins, they were led to the abode of Yama;
having arrived there, all those messengers reported both sinners.
"These two, Dharmarāja and Nara, have been brought here by your command; grant us an order toward your servants, be gracious, and tell us what we should do. (37)
Having observed this, Citragupta spoke to the messengers:
"O heroes, let one of them be led to the hell of intense suffering. (38)
"Let another be established in heaven, where enjoyments are unsurpassed. Having heard this command from the swift-acting messengers, he then acted accordingly. (39)
O King, when their eldest brother had been cast into the terrible Raurava hell, a certain excellent messenger spoke these sweet words to them: (40)
"Come with Vikuṇḍala and Maya; I grant you heaven.
Enjoy the most divine pleasures, which you have earned through your own karma."
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||30||
(31) Chapter Thirty-one.
Nārada said:
Then, with a joyful mind, he questioned that messenger on the road;
having harbored a doubt in his heart, he was filled with the utmost wonder.
Reflecting in my heart: "For what reason is heaven the fruit for me? (1)
Vikuṇḍala said:
O best of messengers, I ask you about a great doubt;
we two were born in equal families and have performed similar deeds. (2)
Even a miserable death was the same for him; likewise, Yama was seen as equal [to others].
How then was my elder brother, whose karma was the same as mine, cast into hell? (3)
The thought occurred to me, "How [can there be] heaven? O divine messenger, sever this doubt of mine;
I do not see any cause for my own ascent to heaven. (4)
The divine messenger said:
"O Vikuṇḍala, mother, father, son, wife, sister, and brother—this is known as the cause of birth for a living being, for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of one's karma. (5)
And at which tree does the gathering of birds take place?
Whatever action one who is conditioned by past impressions performs according to his desire, [that is the result]. (6)
A person always experiences the fruit of each respective action; I tell you this truth out of affection—that for men, there is both auspicious and inauspicious karma. (7)
O Vaiśya, one's own deeds are indeed experienced again and again throughout time;
one person performs the actions, and another alone reaps their fruit.
No one is ever smeared by another's actions;
your brother fell into hell because of his own most terrible sins.
O knower of dharma, by practicing dharma you shall attain eternal heaven. ||9||
Vikuṇḍala said:
"Since childhood, my mind has been devoted to sinful and unvirtuous acts;
indeed, in this very birth, such evil deeds have been committed by me."
O messenger of the gods, I recognize my own well-performed deeds;
if you know of my merit, then please tell it to me out of compassion. (11)
The divine messenger said:
"Listen, O Vaiśya, I shall declare how much merit has been earned by you;
I know all of that, whereas you certainly do not. (12)
There was a brahmin named Sumitra, the son of Harimitra, who had mastered the Vedas; his sacred hermitage was situated on the southern bank of the Yamunā. (13)
O best of people, your friendship with him was born in this forest;
likewise, through association with him, you bathed for two months of the month of Māgha.
At Kālindī, the supreme purifying water that removes all sins, renowned in the world by the name of that sacred ford (tīrtha) which destroys evil. ||15||
O lord of people, by one [fast] you were liberated from all sins;
O sinless one, by the merit of the second Āgha fast, heaven has been attained by you.
By the power of that merit, may you rejoice eternally in heaven;
meanwhile, your brother undergoes great torment for his sins in the hells.
Being cut by sword-leaves, pierced by mallets, ground to powder on the surface of rocks, and roasted in glowing embers; ||18||
Having heard these words of the messenger, he was pained by grief for his brother;
with his entire body covered in horripilation, he was humble and full of modesty. (19)
He spoke these sweet and skillful words to that divine messenger:
"The practice of the seven steps of friendship bears excellent fruit for those who are virtuous. (20)
Having reflected upon our state of friendship, you ought to assist me;
therefore, I wish to hear [your advice], for in my view, you are all-knowing. (21)
By what action do human beings not see the world of Yama, and by what do they go to hell? Out of compassion, please tell me that. (22)
The divine messenger said:
"O Vaiśya, you have asked well; you are now freed from sin.
In the pure heart of men, the intellect for what is most beneficial arises. (23)
Although there is no opportunity for me, as I am devoted to another's service, nevertheless,
out of affection for you, I shall speak according to my understanding.
Those who never inflict pain upon others through action, mind, or speech, and at all times and in every situation, do not go to the abode of Yama.
Men who cause injury to living beings do not attain the path to heaven by any means—neither through oblations, nor through gifts, nor through austerities, nor through sacrifices. (26)
Non-violence is indeed the supreme dharma; non-violence is indeed the supreme austerity;
non-violence is the supreme gift—thus the sages have always declared. (27)
Compassionate men regard mosquitoes, reptiles, biting flies, lice, and other such creatures, as well as human beings, by comparing them with themselves. (28)
Those people who have performed this for him do not go to a miserable state, even one consisting of molten lead, iron spikes, madness, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Whatever beings exist here, whether moving in water or on land, for the sake of their livelihood they go to the miserable state of Kālasūtra.
There they eat the flesh of dogs, drinking pus and blood;
they consume marrow and fat, bitten by downward-facing insects. (31)
Devouring one another and striking each other down,
they dwell for many eons, uttering a terrible cry.
Having entered a hundred births as worms, they remain immobile beings for a long time; thereafter, those cruel ones fall into hundreds of animal wombs.
Thereafter, they are born as those who are blind, one-eyed, hunchbacked, or lame; as poor men, or those deprived of limbs, who cause harm to living beings. (34)
Therefore, a knower of dharma who desires happiness in both worlds should not perform such actions with body, mind, or speech, whether in this world or the next, as those characteristic of a Vaiśya.
Those who harm living beings do not find happiness in either of the two worlds; for by harming beings, they are afraid of nothing whatsoever. (36)
Just as rivers, whether flowing straight or winding, enter the ocean, so too do all dharmas firmly enter into non-violence. 37.
O best of people, he by whom fearlessness has been granted to all beings has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated in all sacrifices. (38)
Those who do not fulfill the duties prescribed in the scriptures, which are a mixture of dharma and adharma, go to the abode of Yama like horses that have lost their reins. (39)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
all those who are devoted to their own respective duties dwell upon the back of the celestial realm.
All those belonging to any caste or stage of life who practice as prescribed, having conquered their senses, go to the eternal world of Brahmā. ||41||
Those who are devoted to sacrifices and charitable works, those who are intent on the five great sacrifices,
and those who are always endowed with compassion— they do not behold this abode of Yama.

Those who have withdrawn from the objects of the senses, who are incapable of [worldly] speech, who are devoted to the Vedic injunctions, and who are constantly engaged in the worship of fire—those Brahmins go to heaven. 43.
Brave men with dejected faces, surrounded by enemies, meet their end in battles; for them, the Sun is the path to heaven.
Those Vaiśyas who give up their lives for the sake of a helpless woman or a Brahmin, or for the protection of one who has come for refuge, do not fall from heaven. ||45||
Those Vaiśyas who always nourish the young, the old, the sick, the protectorless, and the poor, always rejoice in heaven. (46)
Those men who, upon seeing a cow stuck in the mud or a twice-born man afflicted by disease,
rescue them, attain the world of those who perform the horse sacrifice.
Those who provide a morsel of food to cows, those who always serve cows, and those who mount upon the backs of cows, dwell in the heavenly world. 48.
But those men who make even a mere pit where a cow might quench its thirst go to the heavenly realm without beholding the world of Yama. ||49||
Those who are devoted to the worship of fire, the worship of deities, and the worship of gurus, and who are constantly devoted to the worship of the twice-born—those Brahmins go to heaven. (50)
At that time, no religious merit exists in the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like;
for there, the creatures of water and land drink according to their own will. (51)
He is described even by the gods as one who is eternally devoted to giving; for in whatever measure living beings drink that water most abundantly, [so much merit does he gain]. (52)
In that same way, O best of the twice-born, heaven becomes inexhaustible through the thought that it is dharma;
for water is the life of living beings, and they are established within the water as their very breath. (53)
Even those men who are great sinners are purified by daily bathing;
O Vaiśya, morning bathing removes both external and internal impurity. (54)
By bathing at dawn, a man becomes free from sin and shall not go to hell;
however, that man who eats without having bathed is always an eater of impurity.
The ancestors and deities turn their faces away from that man who does not bathe;
a man devoid of bathing is sinful, and a man devoid of bathing is impure. //56//
One who does not bathe experiences hell and is born among male insects and the like;
however, those who perform their ablutions here in the stream on the sacred festival days [attain a different fate]. (57)
By that very [practice], they go to hell; they are not born in evil wombs;
bad dreams and wicked thoughts always become barren. //58//
O best of men, for those persons who have become pure through their morning bath, [offer] sesame seeds, vessels of sesame, and a prastha of sesame according to the prescribed rite. (59)
Having given [these] on the ground to the Lord of the Departed (Yama), men never go anywhere [to a lower state];
likewise by giving land, gold, and a cow, as well as the sixteen types of gifts.
Having gone there, O Vikuṇḍala, they do not return from the heavenly world;
on auspicious lunar days, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and at the transit of the sun, the wise man [should perform these rites].
Having bathed and given something, one does not sink into an evil rebirth at all;
nor do givers ever tread upon the terrible and cruel path of Raurava.
In this world, they are not born into a family destitute of wealth. ||62||
That man who is truthful, always silent [in restraint], pleasant in speech, free from anger, of proper conduct, not given to excessive talk, and free from malice; ||63||
Always endowed with courtesy, always possessed of compassion for all beings, he was a protector of others' secrets and a proclaimer of others' virtues. (64)
O best of men, one should not even mentally covet another's property, however small it may be, such as a mere blade of grass; for these people do not see the torments of hell.
One who slanders others and is a heretic is considered even worse than evildoers; he is cooked in hell for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
O best of men, one who speaks harsh words should be considered as having come from hell; such a person, filled with doubt, goes once again to a miserable rebirth.
There is no atonement for an ungrateful person through pilgrimages or austerities;
that man suffers terrible torment in hell for a long time. 68.
That man who bathes in all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth,
having conquered his senses and restrained his diet, does not go to the abode of Yama.
One should not commit a sin at a sacred ford (tīrtha), nor should one make a living from a sacred ford. Accepting gifts at a sacred ford must be abandoned, as must the sale of dharma.
A sin committed at a sacred ford is difficult to digest; the acceptance of gifts at a sacred ford is also difficult to digest;
indeed, everything done at a sacred ford is difficult to digest, and such a person shall go to hell.
Having bathed even once in the waters of the Gaṅgā, purified by the water of the Gaṅgā, a man does not go to hell, even if he has committed a multitude of sins. (72)
It is heard that vows, gifts, austerities, sacrifices, and other purifying acts are not equal to even a single drop sprinkled from the Ganges for one who has bathed there. (73)
That lowest of men who says that the Gaṅgā is equal to any other sacred ford shall go to the great and terrible Raurava hell, O Vaiśya. (74)
For the pure water that flows from the feet of Vaikuṇṭha is indeed the seed of the waters of the Dharma; it is that very water which Maheśa bore upon his head and released upon the earth. (75)
That Brahman alone is beyond doubt, devoid of qualities, and transcendent of primordial nature (prakṛti).
Within the entire scope of the cosmic egg, who could possibly attain equality with it? ||76||
Even if one were to say "Ganga, Ganga" for hundreds of yojanas, a person would not go to hell; what could possibly be equal to that?
This action, which yields hellish rebirth, is not burned away by anything else immediately.
Human beings should bathe in the Gaṅgā with diligent effort;
he who has desisted from accepting gifts is one who, even though capable of receiving them, remains free from their taint.
The virtuous twice-born shines in the form of the star Vaiśyā for a long time in the sky. ||78||
Those who rescue cows, those who protect the sick,
and those who die within the cow-pen— for them, there are stars in the sky.
Those devoted to the practice of breath control do not see the realm of Yama. ||79||
O Vaiśya, even those who have committed evil deeds, having their sins destroyed by those very [practices],
[are purified] by sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed day after day.
Even those committed by one who has directly slain a Brahmin purify day after day when they are performed. ||80||
Whatever austerities are performed, whatever vows and observances there are, and even the gift of a thousand cows—prāṇāyāma is equal to all of them. (81)
A man who might drink a drop of water from the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month for a full hundred years—prāṇāyāma is equal to that. (82)
Whatever great sin there may be, as well as minor and secondary sins, a person reduces it all to ashes in an instant through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma). ||83||
Those best among men who indeed regard the wives of others as their own mothers, O foremost of men, never go to the torments of Yama. (84)
He who, even in his mind, does not serve the wives of others, exists with both worlds; by him, O Vaiśya, the earth is truly supported.
Therefore, those endowed with righteousness must abandon the pursuit of another's wife;
for another's wife leads one through twenty-one hells. (86)
O best of Vaiśyas, those whose minds harbor no greed for the wives of others go to the world of the gods, and not to Yama.
That man on earth who, amidst constant causes for anger, is not overcome by wrath, has conquered heaven; he is equal to one who has already attained it. 88.
He honors his mother and father like gods; before old age arrives, he passes away to his abode in the course of time. (89)
O best of the Vaiśyas, those men who honor their teacher with even greater devotion than they do their father become guests of Brahmā in this world.
And in this very world, women are fortunate through the preservation of their virtue;
for women who violate their virtue, the world of Yama is most dreadful. (91)
Virtue must always be guarded by women through the avoidance of association with the wicked; for by virtue alone, O women, is the supreme heaven attained—of this there is no doubt. (92)
O Vaiśya, for a Śūdra who performs cooked sacrifices and engages in prohibited conduct, a miserable state is ordained; his destiny is that of hell. (93)
Those who investigate the scriptures, those who are devoted to the study of the Vedas, and those who cause the Purāṇas and Saṃhitās to be heard and read; ||94||
Those who expound the Smṛtis, those who awaken others to the Dharma, and those who are established in the Vedāntas—it is by them that this world is sustained. (95)
Through the greatness of their respective practices, all those whose sins have been destroyed go to the world of Brahmā, where delusion is not found. 96.
Even the gods worship him who bestows the knowledge arising from the Vedas and Shastras, which tears asunder the bond of worldly existence. 97.
Listen, O best of Vaiśyas, to this wonderful secret, which is approved by Dharmarāja and bestows immortality upon all the worlds. (98)
Devotees of Viṣṇu certainly do not see this realm of Yama, nor the beings of terrible appearance; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. 99.
Our brother Yamunā has indeed told us again and again:
"The Vaiṣṇavas must certainly be avoided by you; they should not come within my range. (100)
Those beings who remember Keśava even once, even by chance,
go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, with the entire flood of their sins destroyed.
Even if he is of bad conduct and a doer of evil deeds, that man who is devoted to Viṣṇu and delights in good conduct must always be avoided by you. (102)
Those in whose house a Vaiṣṇava eats, and those who have the company of a Vaiṣṇava—they too should be surrounded by you, for their sins have been destroyed by that association. (103)
"Thus indeed does the Lord who wields the staff always instruct us Vaiśyas;
therefore, we Vaiṣṇavas go to the capital city of Yama. (104)
O best of the Vaiśyas, for sinful men there is no other means, nor any other way, to cross the ocean of hell except through devotion to Viṣṇu. (105)
O Vaiśya, one should not even look upon a dog-eater (outcaste) who is a devotee of Viṣṇu and beloved by the world;
for a Vaiṣṇava, even if outside the [four] castes, purifies the three worlds. 106.
To this extent is the chanting of the qualities, deeds, and names of the Blessed One sufficient for the removal of the sins of men;
for even the sinful Ajāmila, by crying out for his son, [attained liberation].
Uttering "Nārāyaṇa," he attained liberation as he was dying.
Those who were long submerged in hell, both in their own lineage and in the lineages of others, go to heaven at that very moment when they worship Hari with joy. (108)
O Vaiśya, those who are servants of a devotee of Viṣṇu and those who eat the food of Vaiṣṇavas attain, free from agitation, the same destination as the enjoyers of the sacrificial offerings. 109.
A wise person should diligently seek the food of a Vaiṣṇava for the sake of purification from all sins; in its absence, one should drink water.
If a person dies anywhere while chanting the mantra "Govinda," that man shall not see Yama; nor do we ourselves behold him.
Having meditated upon the ocean, that sage [should contemplate] the meter and the deity;
having been duly initiated, he should indeed recite the twelve-syllable mantra according to the prescribed rule.
Those best of men who recite this eight-syllable lord of mantras—by seeing them, even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified and shines forth like Viṣṇu himself. (113)
Having become free from sorrow and devoid of the sense of possession, those men who enter into Brahman dwell indeed in the world of Viṣṇu in the form of Viṣṇu. 114.
Having worshipped Hari in the heart, in the sun, in water, or even upon an image or a sacrificial mound, men go to that state of Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, Vāsudeva should always be worshipped by those seeking liberation in a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, or a discus fashioned by the *vajra-kiṭa* insect. (116)
For that is the abode of Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins, bestows all merit, O Vaiśya, and grants liberation to everyone. (117)
Whoever worships Hari in the discus-marked stone originating from the Śālagrāma rock has, on that very day, performed the merit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. (118)
The Vedāntas always proclaim that the imperishable Nirvāṇa is Brahman;
grace from that [Brahman] comes to men through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (119)
Just as fire situated in a great log shines forth in the sacrificial ground, so too does the all-pervading Hari manifest in the Śālagrāma. 120.
O Vaiśya, even those of sinful conduct who are ineligible for ritual action do not go to the abode of Yama if they are worshippers of the Śālagrāma. (121)
Hari does not delight in such a way in his own city nor in such a way in Lakṣmī as he always delights in the circle of the Śālagrāma stone. 122.
By him the Agnihotra sacrifice has been performed, and the earth together with its oceans has been given as a gift, by whom Hari was worshipped in the form of the Śālagrāma stone. (123)
O Vaiśya, I shall describe to you the merit of one who has duly worshipped twelve Śālagrāma stones according to the prescribed rites. (124)
Whatever merit would result from worshipping twelve million liṅgas with golden lotuses at twelve different times [over a long period], that same merit shall be obtained in a single day. 125.
Furthermore, he who worships with devotion a hundred Śālagrāma stones shall dwell in the world of Hari and be born here as a universal monarch (cakravartin). ||126||
Even that lowest of men, who is pervaded by lusts, anger, and delusions, goes to the world of Hari through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. (127)
And the man who joyfully worships Govinda at Śālagrāma shall not fall from heaven until the dissolution of all beings. 128.
O Vaiśya, without visiting sacred fords, without gifts, without sacrifices, and even without spiritual wisdom, men attain liberation through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. 129.
O Vaiśya, even a sinner who worships the Śālagrāma stone does not go to hell, nor to dwelling in a womb, nor to the state of an animal, nor to birth as a worm. (130)
He who, knowing the mantras for the rite of initiation, performs the bali offering, [purifies] the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, and those rivers which bestow liberation. 131.
All the beneficial goddesses dwell in the water of the Śālagrāma stone;
[they are pleased] with various food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments. (132)
That man who, being devoted to bhakti, performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone in the Kali age with songs, instrumental music, hymns, and so forth— 133.
One rejoices in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas;
indeed, that same fruit which is obtained by seeing ten million lingas and by worshipping them is attained [here]. (134)
Indeed, by worshipping even once a linga produced from a Śālagrāma stone, one obtains that same fruit which is gained [by other means] in a single day. (135)
Human beings undoubtedly attain liberation even if they are devoid of Sāṃkhya philosophy, wherever Keśava resides in the form of the Śālagrāma stone. ||136||
Therein reside the gods, the *surās*, the *yakṣas*, and the fourteen worlds;
