He becomes wealthy, handsome, skillful, generous, and righteous;

In this [age], dharma arises simply from bathing;

Where the Sindhu joins [the Ganges], it is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra;

This should be known as a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra); no doubt should be entertained here.
It delivers mortals from the earth and likewise delivers even the nāgas from below.
The path leading to the gods is known as the threefold path;
it remains for that embodied soul as long as his bones remain in the Gaṅgā.
For so many thousands of years one is glorified in the heavenly world;
it is the supreme among holy places and the most excellent river among rivers. (53)
The Gaṅgā grants liberation to all beings, even to those who have committed great sins;
she is easily accessible everywhere, yet difficult to attain at the three sacred sites. (54)
At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean—
having bathed there, those who die go to heaven and are not born again.
For all beings whose minds are afflicted by evil and who are searching for a refuge, there is no destination equal to the Ganges.
The most sacred of purifiers, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, fallen from the head of Maheśvara, she is the remover of all sins and inauspiciousness. (57)
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
And the forty-fourth chapter.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga.
Having heard this, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter. ||1||
There is a sacred ford named Mānasa on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā;
having fasted there for three nights, one shall obtain all desires.
Whatever fruit a man may obtain by the gift of cows, land, and gold, he obtains that same fruit simply by remembering that sacred ford (tīrtha). ||3||
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, whoever dies in the Gaṅgā becomes one who dwells in heaven after death; he does not behold hell. ||4||
Awakened by the musical performances of hosts of apsarases,
he goes forth in a celestial chariot drawn by swans and cranes.
O Indra among kings, he enjoys [the fruits of his merit] for many years—six thousand in total.
Then, his karma exhausted, he falls from heaven and descends due to the force of that [remaining] destiny.
One is born into a great family, enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls;
there are sixty thousand and sixty hundred sacred fords [therein]. (7)
In the month of Māgha, they shall go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
the fruit that belongs to one who has duly given a hundred thousand cows [shall be theirs].
The fruit of bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha is equal to that of one who practices the five-fire penance between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
He is free from the diseases of serpents and is endowed with the five sense faculties;
as many as are the pores on the body of that embodied being, [so many hairs does he possess]. (10)
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world;
then, having descended from heaven, he becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, that man who resorts to that sacred ford and enters the water at the world-renowned Sangama shall [attain liberation].12
Just as the moon when seized by Rāhu is liberated from all sins, he attains the world of Soma and rejoices together with Soma. ||13||
For sixty thousand and sixty hundred years,
he attains the heavenly world, served by sages and gandharvas.
But having fallen from that state, O lord of kings, he is born into a prosperous family;
with his head downward and his feet upward, the man must drink the flames. 15.
He is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years;
then, having descended from there, O Indra among kings, that man shall become a performer of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
That man who, having enjoyed vast pleasures, resorts to that sacred ford and, having cut his own body, offers it to the birds; ||17||
Listen also to the fruit for one who has consumed it in the air:
he is honored in the world of Soma for a hundred thousand years.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a righteous king—virtuous, endowed with beauty, learned, and possessing a very pleasing body. (19)
Having enjoyed vast pleasures, he again resorts to that holy place on the northern bank of the Yamunā and to the south of Prayāga.
That supreme sacred ford named Ṛṇapramocana is remembered;
having stayed there for a single night, one is liberated from all debts. (21)
One attains the world of the Sun and shall always remain free from debt. ||22||
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Chapter Forty-Five.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Having heard this account of Prayāga which has been narrated by you, [I am filled with wonder].
This heart becomes purified by the chanting of the name of Prayāgaga.
O Blessed One, tell me: what is the fruit of fasting unto death like in that case? (1)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, O Lord, to the kind of fruit that a wise and faithful man obtains at Prayāga by fasting unto death. ||2||
Free from fear of snakes and free from disease, endowed with the five senses, he obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step as he goes. (3)
O King, he shall deliver ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants;
liberated from all sins, he shall go to the supreme state. ||4||
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O illustrious one, you are a knower of dharma; tell me, O Lord, of that gift by which one may attain many merits through even a small and primary offering. (5)
"The horse sacrifice is attained here through many meritorious deeds;
explain this doubt of mine to me, for my curiosity is great. (6)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to what was spoken by the Lotus-born One in the presence of the sages, which was heard by me as it was being told previously. (7)
Entering that region of Prayāga, five yojanas in extent,
he performed an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step upon its ground.
A man who gives up his life saves all seven ancestors who have passed away and fourteen future descendants.
Knowing this, O lord of kings, one should always be devoted to faith;
for those men who lack faith have their minds struck down by sin.
They do not attain that place, Prayāga, which was created by the gods. ||10||
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
But for those who have fallen under the sway of desire, whether out of affection or greed for wealth, how can they obtain the fruit of the holy ford? How may they attain merit? (11)
For one who sells all kinds of goods without knowing what should or should not be done, Prayāga is his only refuge; speak thus, O great sage. (12)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, to this great secret that destroys all sins:
having resided for one month at Prayāga with your senses restrained, O lord of kings. (13)
Having become pure, restrained, non-violent, and endowed with faith, one is liberated from all sins, just as it was ordained by the Self-born One himself. (14)
One is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state;
now hear the fruit for those who slay birds at Prayāga. ||15||
One should bathe at the three periods of the day and subsist on alms;
by three months, one will undoubtedly be liberated from Prayāga. ||16||
But he who, through wisdom, undertakes such things as pilgrimages here [in this world], being fulfilled in all his desires, is glorified in the heavenly world. ||17||
He shall always obtain a dwelling-place filled with wealth and grain;
thus, being perfected through knowledge, he becomes forever possessed of enjoyments. 18.
By him, his fathers and great-grandfathers were delivered from hell,
as he was questioned again and again by that knower of reality who followed the Dharma.
This eternal secret has been fully declared for the sake of your pleasure. ||19||
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Today my birth has borne fruit; today my lineage has borne fruit. O deity, by the very sight of you today, I am delighted and I am graced.
O virtuous-souled one, by the sight of you, I am liberated from all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"By good fortune your birth has become fruitful; by good fortune your lineage has been delivered.
By reciting this, merit increases; by hearing it, sins are destroyed. (21)
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O great sage, what is the merit of the Yamunā, and what is its fruit?
Tell me all this exactly as it was seen and exactly as it was heard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The goddess Yamunā, the daughter of Tapa, renowned throughout the three worlds, arrived at that place where the highly fortunate river flows. 23.
The Yamunā flows by the very same path as which the Gaṅgā has issued forth;
she destroys sins through her glorification even from thousands of yojanas away. (24)
Having bathed and drunk there at the Yamunā, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
one obtains merit through its glorification and beholds auspicious things upon seeing it.
One who bathes there and drinks its water purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation;
he who gives up his life there attains the supreme goal.
The place known as Agni-tīrtha is on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
to the west of Dharmarāja is the tīrtha remembered as Haravara.
Having bathed there, those who have died go to heaven and are not born again;
such are the thousands of sacred fords on the southern bank of the Yamunā. (28)
I shall describe further the origin of that great-souled one;
there is a sacred ford named Viraja, where the gods together with Vāsava [Indra] reside.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, they worship that sacred ford at the time of the two twilights regularly;
there the gods and other wise people resort.
Becoming devoted to faith, perform ablutions at Kurukṣetra;
there are many other auspicious tīrthas as well that remove all sins. (31)
Having bathed in them, those who have died go to heaven and are not born again;
both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are remembered as yielding equal fruits.
The Gaṅgā is honored everywhere solely because of her supreme nature;
in this same way, O son of Kuntī, perform your ablutions at the heavenly tīrtha.
The sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment for whoever, having risen at dawn, recites or hears this. (34)
One is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world. ||35||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Yamunā," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||45||
(46) Chapter Forty-Six.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have heard what was proclaimed by Brahmā in the Purāṇas, which is equal to merit:
there are thousands, hundreds, and millions of sacred fords (tīrthas). ||1||
All are meritorious and pure, and their destination is declared to be supreme;
Naimiṣa is meritorious on earth, and Puṣkara is so in the atmosphere.
Even compared to Prayāga, Kurukṣetra is superior for people;
why do you praise this one alone, having abandoned everything else? (3)
This supreme, unsurpassed teaching has been proclaimed as immeasurable and beyond belief;
it grants the highest divine state and all enjoyments according to one's desires.
"For what purpose do you praise so many dharmas through such a brief yoga?
Explain this doubt of mine exactly as it has been seen and heard. (5)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Even that which is directly perceived may become unbelievable and should not be spoken of to a man who lacks faith and whose mind is afflicted by sin.
For one who lacks faith, is impure, is evil-minded, and has abandoned auspiciousness—all these are sinners; it is for this reason that I have spoken this.
Listen to the majesty of Prayāga as it has been seen and as it has been heard—both directly perceived and indirectly known, as well as whatever else may come to pass. (8)
O King, just as I have previously seen and heard from others, so too,
taking the scripture as authority, one honors one's own yoga.
And another who is indolent there will never attain yoga;
for men, yoga may be obtained only after thousands of other births. ||10||
Just as a yogin may be attained by men through a thousand yogas,
so too is he who bestows all jewels upon the Brahmins.
By that gift given, this yoga may be attained by human beings;
for one who has died at Prayāga, all this comes to pass as described. ||12||
O Bhārata, listen with faith as I shall explain the primary cause, by which it is seen everywhere among all beings. 13.
There is nothing else whatsoever that exists as a Brahmin; rather, it is said that just as Brahman is everywhere worshipped within all beings, so too is this [Brahmin]. 14.
Thus, in all the worlds, Prayāga is honored by the wise;
it is honored as the king of holy places—this is the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira. (15)
Even Brahmā constantly remembers Prayāga, the supreme sacred site;
having reached the king of holy places, he desires nothing else whatsoever.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, by this very inference you shall know that he, having attained the state of a god, desires to assume human form. (17)
"Just as merit or demerit exists, so indeed have they been described by me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard that which was spoken by you; I am struck with wonder again and again. (18)
How is that attained through yoga? But the heavenly world is attained through ritual action (karman). Then one enjoys pleasures; and the earth is the fruit of those actions. 19.
"Tell us again those deeds by which the earth is obtained.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O mighty-armed King, to how the earth is attained through the performance of prescribed deeds."
O lord of men, one should not point out a cow, fire, a Brahmin, a sacred scripture, gold, water, women, one's mother, one's father, or even one's own birthplace. (21)
Prajāpati has not declared that these [beings] go upwards;
such is the attainment of yoga, a station most difficult to reach.
By [stealing] elephants, horses, cows, oxen, jewels, pearls, gold, and so forth, those people who commit evil deeds go to a terrible hell. (23)
Those who take away [the wealth] in secret and later offer a gift as a mere pretext do not go to the heavenly realm where the donors enjoy their rewards. (24)
Engaged in such actions, those base ones are cooked in hell;
likewise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [they suffer for] their practice, their dharma, and their giving.
Whether it be true or false, whatever fruit exists or does not exist—its etymological explanation I shall now declare, so that one may attain it for oneself. (26)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||46||
Chapter Forty-Seven.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga.
Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gotīrtha, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean. ||1||
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā with the ocean—these and many other sacred mountains as well. ||2||
Ten thousand holy places (tīrthas) and thirty crores, as well as others, are eternally situated at Prayāga; thus say the wise. (3)
There were also three fire-pits, in the midst of which the Ganges,
preceded by all sacred fords, emerged from Prayāga.
The goddess, daughter of Tapaṇa, renowned throughout the three worlds, stands together with Gaṅgā and Yamunā, bringing light to the world. (5)
The region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is known as the hips of the Earth;
O tiger among kings, Prayāga is not worth even a sixteenth part of it.
Vāyu declared that three and a half crores of sacred fords—
whether in heaven, on earth, or in the intermediate space— all become remembered as being within the Ganges.
Prayāga is the central seat, as are both Kambala and Aśvatara;
and this sacrificial altar belongs to Prajāpati.
There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the gods and the sacrifices, having taken embodied form, as well as the ṛṣis whose wealth is their asceticism, worship Prayāga.
O descendant of Bharata, those kings who thus worshipped the gods with sacrifices and rituals possessed great wealth; indeed, there was none more meritorious than them in the three worlds.
O Lord, by its power it excels all other holy places;
it is said that ten thousand, three crores, and further [innumerable] holy sites [are present there]. (11)
Where the highly blessed Gaṅgā flows, that is the forest of asceticism;
it should be known as a field of the perfected ones (siddhakṣetra), situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā. ||12||
This is true: one should whisper [this] into the ear of the twice-born, the virtuous, one's own son, friends, a disciple, or a follower. (13)
This is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is to be cultivated, this is pure;
this is meritorious, this is delightful, this is purifying—the supreme Dharma. ||14||
This secret of the great seers destroys all sins; by studying and reflecting upon it, a twice-born man shall attain purity. (15)
Whoever should constantly hear of this meritorious and eternally pure sacred site (tīrtha) shall attain the memory of past births and rejoice upon the heights of heaven.
These sacred fords (tīrthas) are to be reached by the virtuous who perceive the true goal;
bathe in these tīrthas, O Kauravya, and do not be of crooked mind.
O Lord, because you were questioned correctly, it has been told by me;
all your ancestors have been delivered, and your grandfathers have also been delivered. (18)
Indeed, O Yudhiṣṭhira, all these— knowledge, yoga, and even sacred fords— do not equal even a sixteenth part of Prayāga.
By being joined with much spiritual effort, they therefore attain the supreme goal;
by the mere remembrance of Prayāga, a person goes to the heavenly world. ||20||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The forty-eighth chapter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O great sage, this entire narrative concerning Prayāga has been told by you.
Tell me all this in such a way that it may cause me to cross over my delusion. ||1||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim this entire world as it has been described:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśāna, the imperishable Lord of the deities. (2)
Brahmā created all beings, both the stationary and the moving;
Viṣṇu protects these very creatures in the world beyond.
At the end of the kalpa, Rudra withdraws this entire world;
he neither gives it away nor bestows it upon another, and he never perishes.
He who sees the Lord as the ruler of all beings truly sees;
from the northern foundation, Brahman now stands firm. ||5||
The Great Lord, the Supreme Sovereign, remains there having become a banyan tree;
from there, the gods, along with the gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme rishis [depart].
Those who always protect [the Dharma] from those intent on evil deeds, as well as others who remain steadfast, go to the supreme destination. //7//
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
You have indeed told me the truth regarding how this tradition stands as it has been heard;
but for what reason do those things esteemed by the world not remain so? (8)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara dwell here at Prayāga.
I shall tell you the reason; listen to the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira. (9)
The sacred precinct of Prayāga extends five yojanas;
there they remain for the purpose of protection and to ward off evil deeds.
In that regard, even a very small sin will cause one to fall into hell;
likewise for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) at Prayāga. ||11||
The seven continents, the oceans, and the mountains on the surface of the earth remain supported as long as the dissolution of all beings.
And all those others, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who exist in great numbers,
have been created by the three gods beginning from the region of the earth.
This field of Prajāpati is renowned as Prayāga;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this Prayāga is meritorious and purifying.
O King of the Kurus, together with your brothers, regain your own kingdom. ||15||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||48||
The forty-ninth chapter.
Sūta said:
All the Pāṇḍavas, together with their brothers, and those who were devoted to dharma, [set out].
Having paid homage to the Brahmins, he gratified his gurus and the gods.
Then Vāsudeva, accompanied by Mādhava, arrived there in an instant,
being honored by all the Pāṇḍavas together.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was consecrated once again in his own kingdom by all those high-souled ones together with Kṛṣṇa. ||3||
Immediately after that, the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, having said "May it be well," arrived at the hermitage from the sky. ||4||
Then the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, together with his brothers,
bestowed great gifts.
But whoever, having risen at dawn, recites or hears this, is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||6||
Vāsudeva said:
Out of affection for you, I speak these words which must be carried out by you:
always remaining devoted to sacrifice at Prayāga, be free from all anxiety.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, O lord of kings, by constantly remembering Prayāga along with us,
you shall yourself attain the eternal world of heaven.
The man who either follows after Prayāga or even dwells there, his soul purified of all sins, goes to the heavenly world. ||9||
He has desisted from accepting gifts, is contented, self-restrained, and pure. ||10||
Having turned away from the sense of "I," O king of kings, I enjoy the fruit of true spiritual companionship; I am free from anger, truthful, and firm in my vows.
And by treating other beings as one treats oneself, one enjoys the fruit of the true ford. ||11||
Sacrifices have been proclaimed by the seers and also by the gods in their proper order;
for sacrifices cannot be attained by one who is poor, O lord of the earth. (12)
A sacrifice requiring many implements and a flurry of various materials was performed somewhere by wealthy monkeys seeking diverse objects of value.
O Lord of Men, that which can be attained even by poor men who are wise—listen now, O Ruler of People, to that merit which results from the fruits of sacrifice. (14)
O best of the Bharatas, this sacred pilgrimage to the holy fords is the supreme secret of the seers; it is even superior to sacrifices. (15)
Ten thousand crores and thirty other crores,
O bull among men, will go to the Gaṅgā in the month of Māgha.
O great king, having become healthy and enjoyed the kingdom for one year,
you shall again behold the Lord of Kings, especially while he is performing a sacrifice.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Prayāga," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||49||
[50] The Fiftieth Chapter.
The Sages said:
Everything you have been asked has been told by you;
now, O one of great intellect, please speak on this one thing which we still ask.
Indeed, whatever fruit one might obtain from visiting all these sacred fords, that same fruit is obtained by performing a single rite once. (2)
"Tell us this: how does the very activity of the omniscient one proceed?
Sūta said:
"Indeed, the yoga of action (karmayoga) has been proclaimed for the social classes, beginning with the twice-born."
O highly fortunate ones, among these various kinds [of merit], one is preeminent:
devotion to Hari performed by him with mind, deed, and speech. (4)
By him it is won, by him it is won—of this there is no doubt;
Hari alone is to be propitiated, the Lord of the lords of all gods. ||5||
The demon of sin is destroyed by the great mantras of Hari’s names;
those of pure heart, having performed circumambulation of Hari even many times, [attain purity]. (6)
One undoubtedly obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords by seeing the image of Hari; indeed, one attains the fruit of all sacred fords.
O best of the twice-born, by chanting the name of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of all mantras;
and by smelling the Tulasī offered as the grace of Viṣṇu.
One who has offered even a single prostration to Kṛṣṇa does not behold that fierce and terrifying mouth of Yama, nor shall he ever drink his mother’s milk again.
Salutations again and again forever to those whose minds are fixed on the feet of Hari;
even if they be Pulkasas, Śvapacas, or any other outcaste tribes (mleccha-jātayaḥ).
Even they, those highly fortunate ones who were the sole servants at the feet of Hari, drank [the nectar];
how much more so then the meritorious Brahmins, the devotees, and likewise the royal sages? (11)
By practicing devotion to Hari alone, a person does not experience dwelling in a womb;
such a person dances with loud voices before Hari while chanting His names.

He purifies the world through sight, touch, conversation, and even by drinking [the nectar of his name] with devotion, just as the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers purify the earth, O Brāhmaṇas. (13)
A man who performs circumambulation of Hari while loudly chanting His name is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt. (14)
The clapping of hands and so forth, performed with a beautiful tone and a soft sound, purifies even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin by that very act of hand-clapping. 15.
Whoever, having spoken of the story of devotion to Hari, listens to this narrative, that person becomes purified by the mere sight of him. 16.
O bulls among sages, how could there be any fear of sins for him?
O great seers, the name of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme holy ford among all holy fords. (17)
Those by whom the name of Kṛṣṇa has been grasped make the entire world a sacred ford;
therefore, O best of sages, they know no merit greater than this. 18.
Having consumed and worn upon his head the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) of Viṣṇu’s grace, a mortal becomes Viṣṇu himself, the destroyer of Yama and sorrow. 19.
Hari alone is undoubtedly worthy of worship and salutation—whether it be the great Viṣṇu, the unmanifest, or even the god Maheśvara. (20)
Those who perceive [the Self] through oneness do not undergo rebirth;
therefore, Viṣṇu is the self, beginningless, endless, and imperishable. (21)
Behold Hari alone, and likewise worship him;
for those who behold Hari as equal to another deity [do not truly see him].
They go to terrible hells; therefore, a wise man should not hold them in contempt—whether they be fools or scholars, or even a Brāhmaṇa who is dear to Keśava. ||23||
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself liberates even the dog-cooker (outcaste);
there is none higher than Nārāyaṇa, who is like a forest fire to the heap of sins. 24.
Even after committing a terrible sin, one is liberated by the name of Kṛṣṇa;
for the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the teacher of the worlds, is present in his own name. (25)
Those of firm vows established their own superior power;
indeed, they disputed with Atri because of his appearance of being easily overcome.
Moreover, due to the weight of their fruits, they go to many hells;
therefore, one should possess devotion to Hara and be devoted solely to the name of Hari. (27)
The Lord should protect the worshipper from behind and Nāmin from the chest;
the great vajra of Hari’s name is for shattering the mountain of evil. (28)
His two feet are truly fruitful, for they possess the power of movement;
those two hands alone are called blessed, which perform acts of worship. (29)
She went to the supreme goal, the supreme goal; she exerted herself solely for the sake of bearing that.
With her tongue she praised Hari, and her mind followed after His footstep. 30.
Having uttered those names, which are in accordance with reality and have arisen from those very names, they shed tears for that [Lord] because of their association with Acyuta. //31//
Alas! People are utterly deceived by the fault of fate;
they do not indeed worship Him who grants liberation by the mere utterance of His name. 32.
Those impure ones are deceived by their addiction to the company of women; they stand with wavering minds, for the word "black" does not appeal to them.
Those fools of unrefined minds, overwhelmed by grief for their sons and the like,
weep with many lamentations, yet they do not utter even a single syllable in praise of Kṛṣṇa.
Even having obtained a tongue in this world, those who do not chant the name of Kṛṣṇa fall away with ease,
even after having attained the very ladder to liberation.
Therefore, with effort, a human being should worship Viṣṇu through the yoga of action;
for Viṣṇu, when worshipped by the yoga of action, becomes truly pleased with that person.
Worship of Viṣṇu is said to be a sacred site even greater than any other sacred site; for it surpasses all other sacred sites through bathing, drinking, and immersion [in its waters]. (37)
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains through other means, that same fruit is gained from service to Kṛṣṇa; blessed indeed are those men who worship Hari through the yoga of action.
Therefore, O sages, worship Kṛṣṇa, the supreme auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Praise of Devotion to Viṣṇu," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||50||
[51] The fifty-first chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, how was Karmayoga practiced, and how was Hari propitiated? O most fortunate one, best among speakers, please tell me how He becomes pleased. (1)
Tell me how that Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, was propitiated by those seeking liberation,
and likewise describe the protection of all the worlds and the compendium of Dharma.
Speaking that yoga of action while assuming the form of a charioteer,
he stood before the Brahmins who were eager to hear him.
Sūta said:
In this very manner, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, was formerly questioned by the sages who were resplendent like fire; listen as Vyāsa spoke to them. 4.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, all you sages, to that which is about to be declared—the eternal Karma-yoga of the Brāhmaṇas, which bestows the ultimate fruit. (5)
Having previously demonstrated the entirety of what is established by tradition for the benefit of the Brahmins while the sages were listening, Manu, the Lord of Creatures, spoke.
It removes all diseases, is meritorious, and is practiced by the assembly of sages;
with concentrated minds, you all listen to me as I speak. (7)

Having undergone the initiation ceremony (upanayana), the best of the twice-born should study the Vedas in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [from birth], according to the procedure prescribed in his own Sūtra.
The sage, carrying a staff, a girdle, and a sacred thread, wearing a black antelope skin, subsisting on alms, devoted to his teacher, and gazing at the face of his guru. (9)
In ancient times, Brahmā fashioned from cotton the sacred thread (upavīta) for Brāhmaṇas;
it should consist of three strands and be made either of kuśa grass or of cloth.
A twice-born man should always wear the sacred thread and always keep his topknot tied;
otherwise, whatever rite he performs becomes as if unperformed.
One should wear an unadorned garment made of cotton or bark-ash; that very same lower garment should be white and made of excellent woven threads. 12.
Furthermore, the sacred tradition prescribes a garment of black antelope skin as auspicious;
in its absence, however, even a garment made of goat hair or the skin of a Ruru deer is ordained.
Having lifted the right arm and placed the sacred thread upon the left shoulder, it is always the *upavīta*; when it is suspended from the neck, it is the *nivīta*.
O twice-born ones, having raised the left arm and holding [the sacred thread] over the right shoulder, this is called *prācīnāvīta*; one should employ it in rites for the ancestors.
In the fire-sanctuary, in a cow-pen, during a fire-oblation, likewise while studying the Vedas, at meals, and always in the presence of Brahmins. (16)
One should always wear the sacred thread (upavīta) during the service of one's gurus, at the two twilights, and in the company of the virtuous; this is the eternal rule.
One should make the girdle of a Brahmin from a triple-strand of muñja grass, equal in thickness and tightly woven;
in the absence of muñja, they say it may be made of kuśa grass, with one or three knots.

A twice-born man should carry a staff made of bamboo or palāśa wood reaching to the hairline, or else one made from a tree suitable for sacrifice, which is gentle in appearance and free from blemishes. (19)
A twice-born man should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) with a concentrated mind both morning and evening;
by abandoning it out of desire, greed, fear, or delusion, he becomes fallen.
Then, with a serene mind, one should perform the fire-ritual in the evening and in the morning;
having bathed, one should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and the hosts of ancestors.
One should perform the worship of the deities with flowers, leaves, barley, and water;
one should always be habituated to saluting elders in accordance with dharma.

Having first performed a perfect prostration, saying "I am so-and-so, sir," he should offer [the gift] for the sake of attaining long life and health, while remaining free from pride and other such faults. (23)
In greeting, a Brahmin should say, "May you live long, O gentle one" (āyuṣmān bhavatu saumya).
Furthermore, the initial syllable of his name should be uttered with a protracted vowel. (24)
A learned man who does not know how to return a greeting should not be greeted by one who knows; he is just like a Śūdra. (25)
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot should be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand. (26)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, having acquired such knowledge, one should first offer salutation to that [teacher]. (27)
One should not carry water, alms-food, flowers, or sacrificial fuel, nor other such items, for purposes other than those related to the gods. (28)
Upon meeting a Brāhmaṇa, one should ask about his welfare; a Kṣatriya, regarding his freedom from illness; a Vaiśya, regarding his prosperity; and a Śūdra, regarding his health.
The preceptor, the father, the elder brother, and the protector from fear;
the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the maternal grandfather, and the paternal grandfather;
the man of the highest caste, and the paternal uncle—these are remembered as the male gurus in this context. (30)
The mother, the maternal grandmother, the paternal grandmother, and the uterine siblings of both the father and the mother. ||31||

O twice-born ones, the mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, an elder sister, and a nurse are to be known as female gurus; this group of gurus is to be understood as beginning with the mother and the father. (32)
One should follow these [preceptors] with actions of mind, speech, and body;
upon seeing one's gurus, one should rise and offer salutation with palms joined. (33)
One should not sit together with these, nor dispute with them for one's own sake;
nor should one engage in conversation with one's gurus out of hatred, even for the sake of one's life.
Even one who excels in other virtues falls low if he harbors hatred toward his gurus;
for among all gurus, these five are especially worthy of worship. (35)

Among them, the first three are the most excellent; among those, the mother is most highly honored—she who nourishes him, she who gives birth to him, and she by whom he is instructed in knowledge. (36)
The eldest brother and the husband—these five are remembered as gurus;
[one should serve them] with every effort, or even at the cost of one's own life. (37)
These five should be especially honored by one desiring prosperity, as long as both the father and the mother remain free from change. (38)
Therefore, having renounced everything else, one should become a son devoted solely to that [the Guru];
for only if he possesses such qualities will both father and mother be well-pleased. (39)
By that deed, he shall attain the entirety of the Dharma along with his sons;
there is no deity equal to a mother, and there is no teacher equal to a father. (40)
No recompense whatsoever exists for those two;
one should always do what is pleasing to them through action, mind, and speech. (41)
Without being permitted by his teachers, he should not perform any other religious duty,
with the exception of those rites that are obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika), which bear liberation as their fruit.

The essence of the Dharma has been fully declared; it bestows the fruit of liberation after death, once the teacher has been properly propitiated and [the teaching] has been released by his permission. (43)
The fool who disregards his eldest brother, who is equal to a father, reaps the fruit of that knowledge as a disciple after death and falls into hell. (44)
Having gone there, one encounters a terrible hell due to that fault;
however, a husband who has been bestowed upon women's path is always to be honored.
Indeed, in this world, respect arises from service;
[one should likewise honor] maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers. (46)
One should rise and greet [the teacher] saying, "I am so-and-so.
An initiated person (dīkṣita) must not be addressed by name, even if he is younger.
One who knows the Dharma should address him by using "bhoḥ" or "bhavat" as prefixes;
he should be saluted, honored, and even bowed to with the head. 48.
Brahmins desiring prosperity should always respectfully [pay homage] to Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others;
however, Brahmins should never, under any circumstances, pay homage to Kṣatriyas and the like.

Even though these [others] may be endowed with knowledge, ritual action, and virtues, and be highly learned, the Vedic revelation states that the Brāhmaṇa alone should bestow well-being upon all the social classes. (50)
One of the same caste must perform the salutation for those of the same caste;
among the twice-born, fire is the preceptor, and among the castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor. (51)
For women, the husband is the preceptor; everywhere, the guest is the preceptor; learning, occupation, age, kinship, and wealth is the fifth.
They say there are five bases of respect, each preceding one being more venerable than the following; among these five, they are more numerous and stronger when found within the three higher castes.
Wherever such a person may be—even if he is a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade—he is worthy of honor;
he is like a path that should be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, or like a king to one with sight.
Having collected alms daily from the houses of virtuous people, he should offer them to those who are elderly, burdened by heavy loads, diseased, and weak, while remaining self-restrained.
Having offered [the food] to the Guru, he should eat with his speech restrained by the Guru's permission;
the best of the twice-born, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, should go for alms, beginning with the word "bhavat" (sir).
The Kṣatriya was in the middle of you, while the Vaiśya was above you;
[he approached] his mother, or a sister, or the sister of his mother, or his own sister. (57)
He should beg for alms, first requesting it from one who does not treat him with contempt; he may seek it only in the houses of those of his own caste, or among all castes.
The practice of begging for alms is prescribed for those who have avoided outcasts and the like, and who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifice, being praiseworthy in their own duties. (59)
The student, being self-restrained, should collect alms daily from the houses of those who are not members of his teacher's family, nor from his own paternal kin, nor from his maternal relatives.
If houses belonging to others are not available, one should avoid each preceding one in turn;
or, if none of those previously mentioned are possible, one may wander through the entire village.
Restraining his speech and not looking toward the directions,
he collected as much alms-food as required with sincerity, having withdrawn his senses.
He should always eat with self-restraint, controlling his speech and keeping his mind focused on nothing else;
he should subsist constantly on alms, and as one observing the vow, he should never rely on food from a single source.
The livelihood of one who subsists on alms is declared to be equal to fasting;
he should always honor his food and eat it without disparaging it.
Upon seeing this, one should rejoice, become serene, and give everything in every way;
for overeating is detrimental to health, detrimental to longevity, and detrimental to rebirth in heaven. (65)
It is demeritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
One should eat food facing either the east or directly toward the sun.
One should always eat facing north; this is the eternal rule.
Having washed one's hands and feet, while eating, one should sip water for purification twice.
Seated in a clean place and having eaten, one should sip water twice.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||51||
The fifty-second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having eaten, having drunk, having slept, having bathed, or upon entering a carriage road;
Having touched his lips, which are hairless, and having put on his garment, [he should perform the purification]. ||1||

Upon the voiding of feces, urine, or excrement; upon speaking untruths; after spitting; at the commencement of Vedic study; and likewise upon the occurrence of belching, coughing, or labored breathing. (2)
Having approached a crossroads or a cremation ground, the best of the twice-born,
as well as when at both twilights, should likewise perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once again.
In conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas, in speaking with a woman or a Śūdra while one is impure from food,
or upon seeing a person who is impure from food, as well as food that is likewise [impure], [one must perform purification].

One should perform *ācamana* upon the falling of tears, as well as when blood is shed; likewise after eating, during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), after bathing, after drinking, and after voiding urine or excrement. (5)
Having slept, one should utter speech only once or repeatedly from another source;
likewise, it is sufficient to touch fire, cows, or even something impure.
Furthermore, after touching women or oneself, or having put on indigo-dyed clothing,
one should touch water, the wind, grass, or even the earth.
According to the Dharma, one may touch one's own hair, one's clothes, or a garment that has slipped off,
provided the water is not warm, contains no hair, and is free from impurities.
For purification, one should always sip water while seated, facing either the east or the north;
having covered the head, with the mouth closed, and neither with hair nor the topknot loosened. (9)

Without having performed the purification of his feet, one does not become impure while walking on the road; likewise, a wise man should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, standing upon a footstool, or wearing a turban.
Nor [should one bathe] while standing under streams of rain, nor with water drawn up [from a well],
nor with water poured by only one hand, nor again without [the use of] a cord.
Nor while standing on a footstool or a seat, nor with the knees outside [the feet], nor while talking, laughing, looking about, or lying down upon a bed. (12)
Nor with water that has not been looked over, nor with water containing foam and the like,
nor even with water released from the hands of a Śūdra or an impure person, nor likewise with alkaline water.
One should not make a sound with one's fingers, nor with a distracted mind;
nor [should one bathe] with water tainted by color or taste, nor with water from a fissure in the ground. 14.
A Brahmin is purified by [the waters] that reach the heart and are not agitated by the hands, nor by the mere scent of the water outside; a Kṣatriya becomes pure by [the waters] reaching the throat.
Likewise, a Vaiśya [is purified] by consuming [the remnants], while a woman and a Śūdra [are purified] by touching [the hand] thereafter.
That area between the root of the thumb and the line is called the Brahma-tīrtha. (16)
The space between the thumb and the forefinger is called the *tīrtha* for the ancestors (*pitṛs*); behind the base of the little finger, they declare the *prājāpatya* [tīrtha] to be located.
The tip of the finger is known as *daiva*, and that same [region] is proclaimed as *ārṣa*;
with the base [of the finger], it would be *daiva* and *ārṣa*, while the middle is remembered as *āgneya*.
Knowing this very same *tīrtha* to be that of the Soma sacrifice, one is not deluded;
however, a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) using the *tīrtha* of Brahmā alone.
Or rather, O twice-born ones, he should perform the oblation according to the divine rite and not the ancestral one;
first, being self-restrained, he should sip water three times with the Brāhma mantra.
One should touch the face with the base of the thumb;
then, one should touch both eyes with the thumb and the ring finger.
One should touch the two nostrils with the union of the index fingers and the thumbs;
one should touch the ears with the union of the little fingers and the thumbs.
One should touch the heart of all [deities] with the yoga of their respective [mantras]; likewise, one should touch the head with the thumb and the two eyes once.
One should eat three morsels; by that, the deities of the mouth are pleased.
We have heard that these are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa—thus they come to be. (24)
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased by the cleansing of you;
the Moon and the Sun are pleased when your two eyes are touched. (25)
If one touches the two nostrils, the Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased;
likewise, when the two ears are touched, Vāyu and Agni are pleased.
When his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased;
by touching his head, that one person alone becomes truly satisfied.
One does not make oneself impure by the drops that fall from the mouth;
one becomes pure upon touching the teeth or what is stuck to the teeth, even if touched by the tongue.
The drops that touch the feet of those who are performing the ritual rinsing (ācamana) for others should be known as pure by kings;
there is no impurity from them. ||29||
Manu has declared that there is no fault in consuming madhuparka, soma, betel,
fruits, roots, or sugarcane.
If a man, while moving among food and drink, should have an object in his hand,
he should place that object on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then sprinkle it with water.
If a twice-born man should become impure while holding a metallic vessel,
he should place that object on the ground, sip water for purification, and then sprinkle it with water.
Whatever substance one has taken up and with which one becomes possessed of leavings, if that substance is not placed on the ground, one incurs impurity. 33.
In this world, there may arise a doubt regarding garments and such; one should touch them here [only] after having purified them.
This applies on a path in the forest, in a desolate place, at night, or on a road infested with thieves and tigers.
Having voided urine or feces, one does not incur fault if the hands are not empty of substances,
provided that one has placed the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) on the right ear and is facing north.
One should void excrement and urine facing south at night;
having covered the ground with wood, leaves, clods of earth, or grass.
One should cover one's head while voiding excrement or urine;
nor should one do so in the shade, in a well, by a river, in a cow-pen, at a sacred shrine, on a path, or on ashes.
One should not discharge feces or urine into fire, nor in a cremation ground;
nor on cow-dung, nor on wood, nor at a large tree, nor on a grassy meadow.
He should never remain standing, nor without clothing, nor on a mountain range,
nor in a dilapidated temple, nor ever upon an anthill.
One should not walk upon living beings, in pits, or on uneven ground;
likewise, one should not walk upon husks, potsherds, or the royal highway.
Neither on a field, nor in a pit, nor at a sacred bathing place, nor at a crossroads; nor in a garden, nor near water, nor on barren soil, nor in a city settlement. (41)
Nor [should one study] while wearing shoes or sandals, nor while wearing wooden clogs, nor while holding an umbrella; nor indeed should one face women, teachers, Brahmins, or cows.
One should never look at a river, a temple, or even water; nor should one look at the celestial bodies, nor face away from them.
Having likewise brought earth from a riverbank—earth that removes stains and odors—from the direction of the sun, from the direction of fire, and from the direction of the moon; ||44||
One should perform purification with alertness using pure water drawn from a source;
a Brahmin should not fetch earth that is dusty or mixed with mud. (45)

Nor from a path, nor from saline ground, nor from what is left over after purification, nor from another person's [water], nor from a temple, nor from a well, nor from stagnant water, nor likewise from flowing water. ||46||
Then one should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) according to the previously stated procedure. ||47||
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The fifty-third chapter. Vyāsa said:
Thus, endowed with the staff and other [emblems], and possessed of purity and right conduct, [he should proceed].
Having been summoned, he should perform the teaching while gazing at the face of the guru. ||1||
One should always have one's hand ready for service, maintain virtuous conduct, and be well-restrained;
when told, "Be seated," one should sit facing the teacher.

One should not engage in conversation while standing when the other is sitting, nor while walking when the other is walking; one should not speak while sitting to one who is standing, nor while eating to one who is not eating; one should not stand before one who is seated, nor face away from them.
In the presence of the teacher, his bed and seat must always be low;
moreover, within the range of the teacher's vision, he should not sit as he pleases.
One should not utter his name alone, even when referring to someone else;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. (5)
Wherever slander or censure of the guru arises, one should cover one's ears there or depart from that place to another.
One should not worship him while standing at a distance, nor when angry, nor in the presence of women; one should not speak back to him, nor remain standing when he is seated in his proximity.
He should always fetch water, clods of earth, kusha grass, flowers, and sacrificial fuel; he should perform the daily sprinkling and smearing of the limbs [of the deity]. (8)
One should never step upon his discarded flower offerings, his bed, his wooden sandals, or his shoes; nor should one ever step upon his seat or his shadow.
One should prepare items such as tooth-sticks and the like, and whatever is obtained, one should offer it to him.
Without taking leave, one should not go away; rather, one should remain devoted to his pleasure and welfare. 10.
One should never, in his presence, emit wind, nor laugh excessively, nor likewise expose one's neck or upper body. (11)
One should always avoid staying in his presence and likewise avoid snapping one's fingers; one should study at the proper time as long as the teacher is not distracted.
Seated at the side of the teacher, he should serve him with full concentration;
he should never stand while the teacher is sitting, lying down, or traveling in a vehicle.
When he runs, it runs after him; when he goes, it follows him—whether on a cow, a horse, a camel, a vehicle, a palace, or likewise on a cushioned seat.
He should sit together with his teacher on a stone slab, a wooden plank, or a boat;
he should always be one who has conquered his senses, self-controlled, free from anger, and pure. (15)
One should always employ speech that is sweet and beneficial, as well as fragrance, garlands, flavors, and appropriate conduct, while avoiding the injury of living beings. (16)
One should avoid massaging people, holding a parasol for others, as well as desire, greed, fear, sleep, singing, instrumental music, and dancing. (17)
One should diligently avoid threatening others, speaking ill of them, gazing at women, breaking things, harming others, and backbiting. ||18||
He should fetch water, clay, *sumana* flowers, cow dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass;
and he should bring alms-food every day until his meal is obtained. (19)
All ghee and salt, as well as anything that has become stale, should be avoided; he should constantly refrain from watching dances and remain indifferent to songs and the like. (20)
One should not gaze at the sun, nor should one practice running while eating;
nor should one converse in private with impure women or with Śūdras and others. 21.
One who employs the remnants of the Guru’s food and medicine with the desire for success should never perform a bath intended merely for the removal of physical impurities.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, entertain the thought of abandoning his guru;
for if he abandons him out of delusion or greed, he becomes an outcaste.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should accept it from whomever it comes and never harbor malice toward that person. (24)
He declared that even a guru—one who is devoid of virtue, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, and who has set out upon a wrong path—should be abandoned. ||25||
When the teacher's teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher. Having bowed and being permitted by the teacher, one should salute one's own teachers. (26)

This same [respect] is due toward teachers of knowledge, toward yogis who are constantly engaged in practice, and toward those who restrain one from unrighteousness and instruct one in what is beneficial. (27)
One should always practice conduct toward the son of the guru, the wife of the guru, and the guru’s own kinsmen exactly as one does toward one's own guru; this is the highest good. (28)
A child should honor those worthy of honor, whether they be elders or even those engaged in ritual acts; likewise, one who teaches the son of a guru deserves honor just like the guru himself.
One should not perform the massaging of the limbs, the bathing,
or the eating of the leftovers for the teacher’s son, nor should one perform the washing of his feet.
The wives of one's teachers of the same caste are to be honored like the teachers themselves;
those of a different caste are also to be honored by rising from one's seat and by salutation. (31)
One should not perform the bathing of this person, nor the massaging of their limbs, nor the dressing of the hair for the teacher’s wife. (32)
One should salute the feet of the young wives of the guru by performing a prostration on the ground while saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should perform a salutation preceded by grasping the feet;
thus should one act toward the wives of the guru, keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous. (34)
A mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother-in-law, and a father’s sister are to be honored like the wife of one's guru; they are equal to the wife of one's guru.
One may clasp the wives of one's brothers every single day if they are of the same caste;
however, upon returning from a journey, one should clasp the women who are kinswomen or related by marriage.
Toward his father’s sister, his mother’s sister, and his wife’s sister, he should maintain the same conduct as toward his mother; yet among them all, his own mother is the most venerable.
One should constantly teach the Veda, the Dharma, and the Purāṇas to one who is thus perfected in conduct, self-controlled, generous, and free from fear. ||38||
If a teacher does not impart knowledge to a disciple who has resided with him for a year, he takes upon himself the evil deeds of that disciple while living with him. (39)

The son of the teacher who is obedient, a bestower of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, generous with food like a cloud, and virtuous—such a person should be taught according to the tenfold dharma. 40.

One who has performed his duties, is steadfast, non-malicious, intelligent, respectful toward his teacher, trustworthy, beloved, and proficient in the ritual rules—these six types of twice-born men are to be taught. 41.
One should give gifts to these Brāhmaṇas as is appropriate;
having sipped water and composed oneself, one should always study facing north.
Having clasped the feet of the teacher and gazing at the teacher’s face, he should say, "Recite, sir! and he may begin when told, "Let there be a pause. (43)
Purified by the sacred blades of grass and by the three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), the purifier should sit facing eastward; thus purified, he is worthy of uttering the syllable Om.
O twice-born ones, a Brāhmaṇa should utter the Praṇava at the end according to the rule;
he should always perform the teaching preceded by the Brahmāñjali. 45.
The Veda is the eternal eye for all beings;
one should study it constantly, otherwise one falls from the status of a Brāhmaṇa. (46)
By constantly studying the Ṛgveda, one satisfies the deities with an oblation of milk;
thus, at all times, the deities, being invoked by their desires, are gratified and nourished. (47)
By studying the Yajus-mantras, one constantly gratifies the deities with offerings of curd; by studying the Sāmans, one gratifies them daily with oblations of clarified butter.
He constantly gratifies the deities with the Atharva-Angiras hymns as if with honey; he satisfies the gods with the Purāṇas and the ancient sacred laws (dharmas). 49.
In the morning and in the evening, having gone to the forest with a concentrated mind and being intent on the daily obligatory rite, he should study the Gāyatrī.
One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, which has a maximum of one thousand, a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten; this is proclaimed as the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña). //51//
The Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a scale;
he placed the four Vedas on one side and the Gāyatrī on the other.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and immediately thereafter the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then recite the *Sāvitrī* with one-pointed concentration and endowed with faith. (53)
In ancient times, the three eternal Great Utterances (mahā-vyāhṛtis)—Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ—arose; they are the destroyers of all that is inauspicious.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Kāla; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara; and Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—these are remembered as the three Vyāhṛtis in their respective order. ||55||
The syllable *Oṃ* is the supreme Brahman, and following that is the Sāvitrī;
this mantra is the Great Yoga, declared as the essence of essences. (56)
The student who, having understood its meaning, recites this Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, day after day,
attains the supreme goal.
Gāyatrī is the mother of the Vedas and the purifier of the world; having understood this, it is said that there is no prayer higher than Gāyatrī to be recited. (58)
O best of the twice-born, the commencement of Vedic study (upākaraṇa) is prescribed for the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
or on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha or Bhādrapada.
For five months after the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, a student, being pure and concentrated, should study during the bright fortnights while the sun moves toward the south.
On the Puṣya day, the twice-born should perform the external dismissal of the sacrificial grass (chandasām utsarjanam),
or when the first day of the bright fortnight of the month has arrived, he should do so in the forenoon.
A twice-born man should practice the Vedas during the bright fortnight,
while a human being should study the Vedāṅgas and Purāṇas during the dark fortnights.
One who is studying should always avoid these days of suspension from study,
and one who is teaching should also diligently avoid them.
When the wind is audible to the ear at night, when there is a great accumulation of water during the day, during lightning, thunder, and rain, and during the falling of great meteors; ||64||
Prajāpati has declared that these [days] are without fixed time and without the suspension of study;
one should know them as "risen" when the fires have been made manifest.

At that time, there is no study due to ignorance, nor during the non-study periods, nor when untruth is seen, nor upon the appearance of clouds, nor during a thunderclap, nor during an earthquake, nor during the eclipses of the luminaries.
One should know these to be times unfit for study at all seasons, even during the rainy period:
when the sacred fires have been kindled, and when there is the sound of lightning and thunder.
The suspension of study (anadhyāya) should last as long as the light [of the sun or moon] remains; for the remaining [periods], it is as at night, so too by day.
There should be a constant suspension of study in villages and in cities.

For those who desire proficiency in the Dharma, [study] must never take place in the presence of a foul odor, nor in a village where a corpse lies within, nor in the vicinity of a low-caste person (vṛṣala). ||69||
When there is no study, when the sun has risen, during the twilight hours,
when there is thunder, when there is rain, and at midnight, one should void feces and urine.
A learned twice-born man who has eaten at a śrāddha or is still impure from food remains should not even mentally contemplate the fee for an ekoddiṣṭa rite after having accepted it.

One should not perform [Vedic recitation] for three days during the impurity caused by the death of a Brahmin or a king, nor during the birth-impurity of Rāhu (an eclipse), as long as one continues to eat from the same vessel and as long as the oily residue remains.
O Brahmin, one should not recite even this much of the Veda for an ignorant Brahmin;
nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed the knees upon the thighs. (73)
One should not study after eating meat, nor after food offered at a śrāddha by a Śūdra, nor during mist, nor when the sound of an arrow is heard, nor during either of the two twilights.
On the new moon and the fourteenth days, as well as on the full moon and the eighth days,
and during the commencement (upākarma) and the conclusion (utsarga) of Vedic study, a three-night suspension is prescribed.
On the Aṣṭakā days there is a fast of one day and night;
likewise on the nights following those [Aṣṭakās], as well as in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, and Māgha.
The wise have declared that there are three Aṣṭakās in the dark fortnights;
one should avoid [these] under the shade of the Śleṣmātaka, the Śālmali, and the Madhuka trees. (77)
One should never study under the Kovidāra or the Kapittha trees, nor from one of equal learning, except in the case of a fellow student (sabrahmacārin). ||78||
Even when the teacher is present, a fast for three nights is prescribed;
these are proclaimed as the vulnerabilities of Brahmins, known as periods unfit for study.
For there are Rākṣasas among them; therefore, one should avoid these [days].
There is no suspension of study on account of the daily rites, nor on account of the twilight worship itself. (80)
Likewise, during the Upākarma and the homas between the Tejas and Āditya rites,
one should recite either a single Ṛg-verse, a single Yajus formula, or a Sāman chant again and again.
One should not study on the Aṣṭakā days and the like, nor when the wind blows violently; however, there is no prohibition against studying the Itihāsas and Purāṇas during those times unfit for study.
One should avoid all these [prohibited acts] in other dharmaśāstras as well.
This dharma of the student (brahmacārin) has been proclaimed in brief. 83.
It was previously declared by Brahmā regarding the sages of purified souls:
"That twice-born man who exerts effort in this world without having studied the Śruti [is as one who has failed]. (84)
A fool who does not converse with the twice-born is outside the Veda;
indeed, a twice-born man should not be satisfied merely by the recitation of the Vedas. (85)
He who, having studied the Veda according to the prescribed rules, does not reflect upon the meaning of the Veda, perishes like a cow sinking in deep mud at the edge of a mere puddle. (86)
Being thus deluded, he is like a Śūdra and does not attain the status of a worthy recipient;
yet, if he indeed desires to dwell with his teacher for the rest of his life, [he may remain]. (87)
One should attend upon him with devotion until liberation from the body;
and having gone to the forest, one should duly offer oblations into the fire.
Likewise, being established in Brahman and composed in mind, he should study daily the Sāvitrī,
the Śatarudrīya, and especially those Vedas.
One should practice constantly, disciplined and devoted to subsisting on alms-food. ||89||
This supreme and ancient ordinance,
which was formerly requested by the most eminent of great sages, has been correctly declared here to you from the Vedic tradition.
This is what Svāyambhuva Manu, the god, has said. ||90||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Karma-yoga," in the Svarga-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
(54) The fifty-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born ones, having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or likewise all the Vedas, and having understood their meaning, the best of the twice-born should then perform the ceremonial bath (snāna).

Having given the teacher his fee, he should bathe with his permission; or, having fulfilled his vow and being self-disciplined, one who is incapable [of the full rite] may also deserve to bathe. ||2||
He should carry a bamboo staff, an inner garment, and likewise an upper garment;
two sacred threads, a water-pot containing water, and a water-jar. ||3||
He should carry an umbrella and a stainless turban, as well as sandals and shoes;
he should wear golden earrings, keep his hair and nails clipped, and remain pure.
A Brahmin should never wear a garland that is not red;
he should always wear white garments, be fragrant, and be pleasant to behold.

One should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes when wealth is available; nor should one wear garments that are dyed red, excessively gaudy, or previously worn by another, nor earrings of the same kind.
One should not use sandals, a flower garland, or wooden shoes; nor should one display the sacred thread, ornaments, or the black antelope skin.
He should not wear his garment over the right shoulder, nor should he wear one that is discolored;
he should take a wife according to the prescribed rule—one who is suitable for himself and auspicious.
Those endowed with the characteristics of beauty and free from defects of birth—whether born of the three castes or of another human lineage—[should be accepted]. (9)
A Brāhmaṇa should take as his wife one endowed with good character and purity;
he should approach her during the proper season until a son is born.
One should diligently avoid the prohibited days:
the sixth, the eighth, the fifteenth, the twelfth, and the fourteenth.
One should always remain a celibate student for three days after birth;
likewise, one should establish the marriage fire and offer oblations into the Jātavedas fire.
A Snātaka should always cause these purifying acts to be performed;
he should constantly perform his own duties as ordained by the Veda without indolence. ||13||
One who fails to do so quickly falls into most terrifying hells;
therefore, one should diligently study the Veda and not neglect the great sacrifices.

One should perform domestic duties, as well as the worship of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana); one should cultivate friendship with those who are equal or superior, and one should always approach the Lord.
He should approach the deities, provide for the maintenance of his wife,
proclaim righteousness when he is wise, and likewise conceal no sin.
One who is compassionate toward all living beings should always perform what is beneficial for oneself, in accordance with one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. (17)
One should always conduct oneself by practicing conformity in locality, speech, and intellect;
that which is properly declared in the Śruti and Smṛti and practiced by the virtuous. ||18||
One should practice that conduct which one's ancestors never abandoned, by which one's fathers went, and by which one's grandfathers went. ||19||

By that [path] one should go along the way of the virtuous; by going by that path, one does not incur fault. One should be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) and always wear the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta).
A householder who speaks the truth, has conquered anger, is free from greed and delusion, is devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī, and performs ancestral rites (śrāddha), is liberated. 21.

One who is intent on the welfare of his mother and father, devoted to the welfare of a brāhmaṇa, a giver, a performer of sacrifices, and a devotee of the gods, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||22||
One should constantly pursue the three aims of life and perform the worship of the gods;
one should daily and perpetually pay homage to the deities with a disciplined mind.
One who is constantly disposed toward generosity, endowed with patience, and full of compassion is declared a true householder;
one does not become a householder merely by living in a house. ||24||
Forbearance, compassion, wisdom, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility, and knowledge of the eternal nature of the inner self—this is the characteristic of a brāhmaṇa. ||25||
Therefore, the best of the twice-born should not be negligent, especially regarding this; practicing dharma according to his capacity, he should avoid those things that are censured. 26.
Having attained the unsurpassed yoga and shaken off the turbidity of delusion, even a householder is liberated from bondage; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Forgiveness is the endurance of faults arising from mutual anger—such as censuring, victory, throwing [insults], binding, killing, and so forth. (28)
"Compassion toward one's own sufferings and friendliness toward the sufferings of others—the sages declare this to be 'dayā' (compassion), the direct means for accomplishing Dharma. (29)
The retention of the fourteen branches of knowledge for the sake of others is called "higher knowledge" (vijñāna); that is true knowledge by which the Dharma increases. //30//
Having studied the sciences according to the prescribed rule and having understood their meaning, one should perform the duties of dharma; this indeed is called true knowledge. ||31||
One conquers the world through truth; truth is that supreme state.
The wise declare that truth is non-negligence regarding things as they truly are. (32)
Self-restraint is the cessation of bodily activity; tranquility arises from the clarity of wisdom. One should know the imperishable supreme self, having attained which one does not grieve. (33)
That knowledge by which the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Hṛṣīkeśa, who is beyond ignorance, is perceived directly—that is celebrated as true knowledge. (34)
The learned Brahmin who is devoted to that, intent on that, ever free from anger, pure,
and dedicated to the great sacrifice, attains that which is unsurpassed.
One should diligently protect the body, for it is the abode of Dharma;
indeed, without the body, the Supreme Viṣṇu cannot be realized by men. (36)
A twice-born man should constantly apply himself to dharma, artha, and kāma with discipline;
he should not, even in his mind, contemplate desire or wealth devoid of dharma.
Even when suffering, one should not practice unrighteousness according to the Dharma;
for the Blessed One, the Lord, is the Dharma, the refuge for all living beings. (38)
One should act for the benefit of living beings and not have a mind intent on harming others; one should not revile the Vedas or the deities, nor should one dwell with those who do so.
But that mortal who, being self-restrained and pure, recites this chapter on Dharma, or teaches it, or causes it to be heard, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||40||
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||54||
Fifty-fifth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
One should not harm any living beings, nor should one ever speak untruth.
One should never speak what is unbeneficial or unpleasant; otherwise, one would become a thief of words. ||1||
Whether it be grass, or even a leaf, or earth, or water itself—by stealing these from another, a living being falls into hell. (2)

A wise man should not accept gifts from a king, nor from a Śūdra, nor even from one who is outcast; nor from anyone else unless he is unable to do otherwise, for he should avoid those who are censured.
One should never become a beggar, nor should one ever beg from such a person;
for the beggar thus robs that evil-minded man of his very life-force. (4)
One should not steal the property of the gods, especially if one is the best of the twice-born;
nor should one ever seize the property of a Brahmin, even in times of distress.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Therefore, one should always take great care to avoid the property of a deity as well.
"Flowers, vegetables, water, wood, as well as roots, fruits, and grass—Manu Prajāpati has declared that taking these when they are not given constitutes theft. (7)
A twice-born man, when performing the rite of worshipping the gods, should gather flowers from more than one source,
provided they are not restricted and he has not received permission for them alone.
A wise person should indeed wander about carrying grass, wood, fruit, flowers, and a lamp, solely for the sake of the Dharma, so that he does not become a burden to others. (9)

O Brahmins, it is the established rule that those standing on the road who are hungry may take a handful of sesame seeds from those crying out "Give!", just as one might take from those who are unrighteous and so forth. 10.
One should not perform a vow after having committed a sin under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing a sin with a vow, one commits an act that brings ruin upon women and Śūdras.
If such a brahmin is censured by those who discourse on Brahman after death, it is because the vow he practiced through deceit goes to the Rākṣasas.

He who maintains his livelihood by assuming the dress of one who does not possess the marks [of an ascetic] while being such a person, or assumes the dress of one who possesses the marks while not being such a person,
incurs the sin of that [deceiver] and is born into the womb of an animal.
One who constantly engages in begging, forming family ties, living together, or conversing [with such persons] falls [from his state]; therefore, one should avoid them with great effort. (14)
One should not commit an offense against the gods, nor likewise an offense against the guru;
for an offense against the guru is many millions of times more grievous than an offense against the gods. ||15||
Public scandal and atheism are ten million times more severe than that;
likewise [the sins] of [causing harm to] cows, deities, and Brahmins, and of agriculture and service to kings. (16)
Families that are deficient in righteousness through improper reflections, the omission of prescribed rites, and the failure to study the Vedas descend to the status of non-families.
O Brāhmaṇa, families fall into a state of ignobility through the transgression against Brāhmaṇas, as well as through falsehood, adultery, and the eating of forbidden food. (18)

A family perishes quickly by practicing a dharma that lacks the true lineage, as well as by giving gifts to those who are not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) and likewise to those who are outcaste (vṛṣala). (19)
In a village devoid of those who follow prescribed conduct, the family quickly perishes;
one should dwell in a village surrounded by unrighteous people that is full of many diseases.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by Śūdras, nor in one filled with heretics;
the region between the Himālaya and Vindhya mountains, extending from east to west, is auspicious. (21)
A twice-born man should not dwell in a region that lacks both a sea and a river,
nor where black antelopes constantly roam by their very nature.
A twice-born man, the best of the twice-born, should not dwell there near famous sacred ponds or rivers,
having avoided a distance of half a krośa from the riverbank.

One should dwell in a holy place where people reside, but one should not abandon the vicinity of a village; nor should one live with those who have fallen from their caste, nor with Cāṇḍālas, nor with Pulkasas.
One should not share a bed or a seat with fools, the arrogant, or others who seek only their own wives; nor should one mix one's vessels or cooked food with theirs. (25)
Sacrificing for them, teaching them, marriage alliance, as well as eating together, studying together—this is the tenth—and likewise sacrificing together. (26)
The eleven faults that have been specified exist in a state of mutual confusion;
through their proximity, sin is transmitted among men. (27)
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid performing actions together;
for those seated in a single row touch one another. 28.
For those whose boundaries have been established with ashes, there shall be a confluence [of purification] through fire, ashes, water, and by means of scraping. ||29||
Through the gate and along the path of the whirlwind, the row is divided by six;
one should not engage in dry enmities, nor disputes, nor backbiting. (30)
One should never report a cow grazing in another's field; one should not live with a slanderer, nor should one strike at the vital points of others.
A wise person should not describe to another a solar halo, a rainbow appearing in the afternoon, the moon, or gold. (32)
One should not engage in conflict with many people, nor likewise with kinsmen;
one should not do toward others that which is disagreeable to oneself.
An excellent twice-born man should not mention the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should he point out the constellations; he should not speak to a woman in her courses, nor to one who is impure.
One should not obstruct what is being given to the gods, gurus, or brahmins;
one should not praise oneself, nor should one avoid censuring others. (35)

One should diligently avoid giving a cow that is difficult to milk or one that is barren; for that twice-born man who gives to the gods or the sages a cow that is barren or incapable of bearing calves. (36)
O lords of sages, no atonement for such a person is seen in the scriptures here: he who would revile his guru, a deity, the Veda, or even a supplementary text. (37)
For more than a hundred million eons, that man shall be cooked in the Raurava hell—
he who remained silent when censured and did not offer any reply.
One should go covering one's ears and should not look at him;
a wise person should avoid the secrets of enmity and the censuring of others.
A superior among the twice-born should never at any time engage in dispute with his own kinsmen;
nor should he speak of sin to the sinful, or of sinlessness to them, O best of the twice-born. (40)
