The fault of those falsely accused among men would be equal to that of truth, yet they become possessed of fault through untruth; for tears fall from their weeping. (41)
Those who falsely accuse others of killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, or violating the teacher's bed, will themselves be slain along with their sons and cattle.
The elders have indeed declared that purification is seen [to follow] from not making false accusations;
one should not look at the rising sun or moon without a specific reason. (43)

One should not look at the sun when it is setting, nor when it is reflected in fresh water, nor when it is touched by clouds, nor when it is in the meridian, nor when it is obscured, nor when it is reflected in mirrors and the like.
One should never look at a naked woman or a naked man,
nor at an army arrayed for battle, nor at excrement or urine, nor at those engaged in sexual intercourse.
A wise man, while impure, should not look at the planets such as the sun and the moon;
nor should he speak to another, nor remain with his mouth covered while still having food remnants.
One should not look at a hungry ghost, nor at the face of an angry teacher, nor at the reflection of oil or water, nor at one's own reflection while eating. 47.
One should not look at a woman whose bonds have not been released, nor like a mad elephant; one should not eat together with one's wife, nor look at her while she is eating.

One should not look at one's own reflection in water while sneezing, yawning, or seated on a seat other than one's own, nor should one look at it for the sake of determining whether it is auspicious or inauspicious.
A wise man should never eat at night, nor should he ever preside over a meal; he should not direct his mind toward a Śūdra, nor [should he give] kṛsara, milk-rice, or curd [to one]. (50)

A wise man should not mention to us that food which is leavings, nor honey, nor clarified butter, nor a black antelope skin, nor an oblation; nor should he speak of our vow, nor should he speak of dharma.
One should not fall under the sway of anger; one should avoid hatred and passion, as well as greed, pride, deceit, malice, and the disparagement of knowledge. (52)
One should avoid envy, intoxication, as well as grief and delusion;
one should not cause pain to anyone, yet one may strike one's own son or disciple.
One should not associate with the base, nor should one ever have a mind of craving;
one should not despise oneself, and one should strive to avoid dejection.
A wise person should not treat another who is not superior with contempt, nor should he disparage himself due to his latent impressions (vāsanā).
Indeed, one should not scratch the earth with one's nails, nor should one drive away a cow.
One should speak of rivers as non-rivers and of mountains as non-mountains;
furthermore, one must never abandon a traveling companion during a stay or at a meal.
One should not plunge into water while naked, nor should one cross fire; likewise, one should not anoint the body with oil that remains after it has been used on the head. 57.
One may play with snakes and weapons, touch one's own teeth, pull out the hair of the private parts, and walk together with an unrefined person. (58)
One should not resort to the fickleness of hands, feet, speech, or eyes;
nor the fickleness of the genitals or the belly, nor ever that of the ears.
One should not make noise with the mouth or play musical instruments; one should not drink water with joined palms; nor should one ever strike water with the feet or with the hands.
One should not destroy roots or fruits with bricks; one should not learn the language of the Mlecchas, nor should one drag a seat along with the feet.
A wise person should not, without cause and to no purpose, practice the breaking of nails, slapping the arms, cutting, scratching, or massaging.
One should not eat food from one's lap, nor should one engage in useless activities;
one should not dance, nor sing, nor play musical instruments.
One should not scratch one's own head with hands that have been struck;
nor should one praise the gods, even those of the Lord of Speech, with worldly hymns.
One should not play with dice, nor run about, nor void excrement or urine in water;
one should never enter a dwelling while still impure from food, nor perform a bath while naked.
One should not go to a stūpa, nor should one touch one's own head;
one should not bathe with nails or hair, nor should one awaken a sleeping person. (66)
One should not expose oneself to the morning sun, one should avoid the smoke from a funeral pyre,
one should not sleep in empty houses, and one should not remove one's own sandals.
One should not spit without a reason, nor should one cross a river with one's arms;
one should never perform the washing of the feet with the very foot used for washing.
A wise man should not warm his feet over a fire, nor should he run while wearing sandals;
he should not stretch out his legs toward a deity, a Brāhmaṇa, or even a cow.
While impure, one should not lie down, drink, study the Vedas, bathe, or eat while facing the wind, fire, a king, a Brahmin, the sun, or the moon. (70)
One should never go outside [for these activities]:
sleeping, studying, bathing, anointing the body, eating, or walking. (71)
One should always avoid [these acts] during the two twilights and at midday.
A Brahmin who is impure from eating should not touch with his hand a cow, a Brahmin, or fire.
One should not move a deity’s image from its place, nor touch it with one's feet;
one who is impure should not tend the sacred fire, nor should one invoke the gods or the sages.
One should not plunge into a bottomless ocean, nor should one drink water from an improper source;
nor should one lift it up with the left hand and drink it directly from the mouth.
One should not cross a river without touching water, nor should one discharge semen; nor should one touch anything smeared with impurity, or an object fit for sacrifice, or blood, or a horned animal.
One should not cross a river by swimming, nor should one engage in sexual intercourse in the water; one should not cut down a sacred tree, nor should one discharge phlegm into the water. (76)
One should never step upon bones, ashes, potsherds, hair, or skeletons, nor upon husks, charcoal, or dried cow-dung.
The wise man should not leap over the fire, nor should he ever place it beneath anything; he should not step upon it with his feet, nor should the learned man burn with it using a winnowing basket.
One should not descend from a tree, nor should one ever look at anything impure; one should not throw fire into the sacred fires, nor should one extinguish them with water.
He should not himself report the death of a friend to others; he should not sell what is not for sale, nor should he employ fraudulent merchandise for sale. (80)
A wise person, being impure, should not fan a fire with breaths from the mouth for nine days;
nor should he carry it across a sacred site, a body of water, or a boundary line.
One should never strike at the navel or at a previously agreed-upon spot;
nor should one cause animals, tigers, or birds to fight with one another.
One should not cause distress to others by means of water, wind, heat, and so forth; nor, having caused one's teachers to perform difficult tasks, should one subsequently deceive them. (83)
In the evening and in the morning, he should bolt the doors of the house for the sake of protection;
he should avoid wearing garlands or using perfumes outside, and avoid eating together with his wife.
Having engaged in a dispute, one should avoid entering [the house];
a wise Brāhmaṇa should not stand eating from his fingernails, nor should he speak or laugh. 85.
One should not touch one's own fire with the hand, nor stay for long in water; one should not blow on the fire with the mouth, nor with a winnowing basket, nor with the hand.
Fire was kindled by his mouth; from his mouth fire was born.
A wise man should not speak of another's wife, nor should he officiate at a sacrifice for one unworthy of sacrificing. 87.
A learned man should never discharge semen, nor should he ever avoid a gathering; he should never go to a temple without circumambulating it clockwise.
One should not wear wet clothes, nor should one sleep in a temple.
One should not set out on a journey alone, nor with unrighteous people. (89)
Nor by those afflicted with a new disease, nor by Śūdras, nor by the fallen;
nor one who is without shoes, nor likewise one who is deprived of water and so forth. (90)
A twice-born man should never step over the path of a corpse,
nor should he step over a yogin, a perfected being (siddha), or those observing a vow, even if they are walking toward him.
One should not intentionally step upon the shadow of a temple, of wise deities, of those performing a sacrificial session, of Brahmins, or even of a cow. (92)
A man should not step on his own shadow when it is defiled by outcasts and other such persons;
nor should he ever stand upon charcoal, ashes, hair, or similar things.
A twice-born man should avoid the dust raised by a broom, as well as the water from a jar used for bathing clothes;
he should not eat what is unfit to be eaten, nor drink what is unfit to be drunk. (94)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||55||
The fifty-sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
A Brāhmaṇa should not eat the food of a Śūdra, whether out of delusion or through desire.
He who eats [the food of others] when there is no distress enters a womb of a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man eats the censured food of a Śūdra for six months, he becomes a Śūdra while still alive;
after death, he is born as a dog.
O lords of sages, he whose food remains in the stomach of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, shall, upon death, enter that very womb.

One should avoid the food of kings, the food of commoners (vartaka), the food of eunuchs, the food of leather-workers, the food of groups, the food of courtesans, and the food of those who live by the six [lowly] arts.
One should likewise avoid the food of those who live by the wheel, of washermen, of thieves, and of those who carry banners; as well as the food of cowherds, of goldsmiths, and the food of the dead.
One should avoid the food of a potter, a painter, a usurer, and his wife;
as well as that of the son of a remarried woman, a seller of umbrellas, and one who has been cursed.
The food of a goldsmith, an actor, a hunter,
a fisherman, a physician, a harlot, and a staff-bearer [is forbidden].
The food of a thief, an atheist, one who reviles the deities,
a seller of Soma, and especially that of a dog-cooker (outcaste), [should not be eaten].

The food of one who lives by his wife, of him in whose house there is a paramour, of one who is miserly toward those who have renounced the world, and likewise of one who eats the leavings of others; ||9||
Indeed, one should avoid the food of a wicked person, the food of the Saṅgha, and the food of one who lives by the sword;
as well as the food of one who is afraid, the food of one who weeps, food that is "ava-kruṣṭa" (contemptible), and food from a place where a wound has been inflicted.
The food of one who hates Brahmins, of one who delights in sin, of a corpse, of one who cooks in vain, of one in a state of impurity due to death, and of one who is ill; ||11||
The food of childless women, as well as that of the ungrateful, and especially the food of artisans and of those who sell weapons, [should be avoided]. (12)
The food of a drunkard, the food of a professional wrestler, the food of physicians, the food of the offspring of a learned man, and the food of one who marries before his elder brother; ||13||
Furthermore, due to the specific nature of their rebirth, as well as that of the husband of a Didhiṣū,
it was perceived with contempt, as if cast away, filled with wrath, and accompanied by wonder.
One should not eat even the food of a guru if it is devoid of the proper consecratory rites; for all the evil deeds of a person reside within their food. 15.
Whoever eats the food of another partakes of that person's sin; likewise, a half-brother, a friend, a cowherd, a charioteer, and a barber [are those whose food one should not eat]. 16.
Among these Śūdras, one may eat their food and offer oneself [as a servant] to those who are actors, potters, and those engaged in agricultural work. (17)
Among these Śūdras, the wise have observed that their food is fit to be eaten when it possesses even slight merit;
specifically, milk-rice cooked with ghee, cow's milk, and barley-meal flour.
Oil-cake and oil may indeed be accepted from a Śūdra by the twice-born, as well as potherbs of vṛntāka, nālikā, kusumbha, and likewise bhasmaka. (19)
One should avoid onions, garlic, fermented gruel, and resinous exudations; as well as mushrooms, village pigs, boiled milk, and colostrum. (20)
One should avoid those that are withered or turned away, as well as buds; likewise, one should avoid the *gṛñjana*, the *kiṃśuka*, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa*.
Having eaten a gourd, a bottle-gourd, or a cucumber, a twice-born man falls [from his caste];
likewise for eating *kṛsara*, barley-meal, milk-rice, or cakes.
O gods, do not consume these offerings of food;
do not eat rice-gruel, citron, or even fish that have not been consecrated with the ritual invocation.
One should diligently avoid the nīpa, the kapittha, and the plakṣa;
likewise, one should avoid oil-cake from which the oil has been extracted, as well as grains dedicated to the gods.
At night, one should carefully avoid any connection with sesame seeds;
one should not eat milk or buttermilk, nor should one consume anything that is unfit for consumption.

One should always avoid clay that is infested with worms, contaminated by its nature, or mixed with earth from a burial ground; likewise, one should constantly avoid clay containing insects or worms, or that which is damp with the moisture of a corpse.

Furthermore, food that has been sniffed by a dog, or prepared by a Caṇḍāla, or likewise looked upon by a Caṇḍāla, or smelled by a woman in her courses, by outcasts, or even by a cow— [is unfit to be eaten].
Food that is unwholesome, stale, or constantly overturned;
food touched by crows or cocks, or even infested with worms—[these are forbidden]. (28)
It must not have been smelled by humans, nor touched by one afflicted with leprosy;
it must not have been offered by a woman in her menses, nor by a eunuch, nor by one who is diseased. (29)

One should also avoid the food of a woman with soiled garments or one dressed in another's clothes; likewise, the milk of a cow whose calf has died, and the milk of a sheep within ten days of giving birth.
Manu has declared that the milk of a ewe and the milk of a cow in heat are undrinkable;
likewise, [the meat of] the crane, the swan, the sārasa crane, the sparrow, and the parrot [are forbidden]. (31)
The kurara, the cakra, the cakora, the jālapāda, the cuckoo, the crows, the khañjarīṭas, the hawk, and likewise the vulture; ||32||
The owl, the ruddy goose, the pigeon, the dove, the lapwing, and likewise the village cock. ||33||
One should not eat the lion, the tiger, the leopard, the cat, the dog, the boar, the jackal, the monkey, or even the donkey. ||34||
One should not eat snakes, wild animals, peacocks, other forest-dwellers, or living beings that move in water or on land; such is the established rule. (35)
The iguana, the tortoise, the hare, the rhinoceros, and the porcupine—these five-clawed animals, O best of men, Manu Prajāpati has declared to be always fit for consumption. (36)
One should eat fish with scales and meat from the Ruru deer,
having first offered them to the deities and to the Brahmins according to the rules.
The peacock, the partridge, the pigeon, the cakora, the water-fowl, the vārdhrīṇasa crane, and the fish known as haṃsa-parājita are fit for consumption. (38)
The śapharī, the siṃhatuṇḍa, as well as the pāṭhīna and rohita—
these fish, O best of the twice-born, are declared to be unfit for consumption.

One may eat the meat of these [animals] when it has been consecrated by sprinkling, if for the sake of a Brahmin, or when it is prepared according to the prescribed rule, or even when there is a danger to one's life. (40)

One who eats meat in this manner is not defiled if he eats it without leaving any remainder, provided it is for the sake of medicine, for one who is incapable, by command, or for the purpose of a sacrifice. (41)
And if one who has been invited to a śrāddha for the gods should discard meat, he falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body. (42)
Whether it be unfit to be given, unfit to be drunk, or likewise unfit to be touched, or even unfit to be looked upon by the twice-born—liquor is always thus defined. (43)
Therefore, with every effort, one should always avoid intoxicants;
for by drinking them, a twice-born man falls from his duties and becomes unfit for conversation.
Even after consuming what is unfit for consumption and drinking what is unfit for drinking,
a twice-born man does not become eligible [for ritual acts] so long as he has not expelled that [impurity] downward.
Therefore, a Brahmin should always diligently avoid things that ought not to be eaten and things that ought not to be drunk;
for if he does so, he goes to the Raurava hell.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Rules Regarding Edible and Non-Edible Foods," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The fifty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the unsurpassed dharma of giving.
This was previously declared by Brahmā to the sages who were exponents of the Veda.
The faithful bestowal of appropriate objects upon a worthy recipient is designated as "giving" (dāna), which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||2||
I consider that gift which one gives with supreme faith to those who are most distinguished; everything else belongs to someone else's protection. (3)
Giving is said to be of three kinds: constant, occasional, and for the sake of a desired object;
the fourth is declared to be the stainless, which is the most excellent of all at all times. (4)
Day after day, something is given to some non-benefactor; therefore, one should constantly give to a Brāhmaṇa without aiming for any fruit.
That which is placed into the hands of the learned for the sake of pacifying evil is designated by the virtuous as the unsurpassed *naimittika* gift.
That gift which is given for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty,
or pleasure is declared as *kāmya* (desire-based) by the sages who contemplate dharma.
If that which is known by the knowers of Brahman is well-bestowed for the sake of pleasing Īśvara with a mind endowed with righteousness, that gift is stainless and auspicious. (8)
Having found a worthy recipient, one should practice the duty of giving according to one's ability;
for that recipient is to be honored who delivers one from all [suffering]. (9)
That which remains after providing for one's family and clothing should be given;
otherwise, that which is given in any other way does not yield fruit. 10.
It should be given with devotion to one who is learned in the Vedas, of noble birth, disciplined, ascetic, observant of vows, and poor. (11)
But he who would give land with devotion to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires goes to the supreme abode, having reached which he does not grieve. (12)
He who gives land endowed with sugarcane, barley, wheat,
and rice to one well-versed in the Vedas is not born again into this world.
He who bestows even a piece of ground the size of a cow's hide upon a poor Brāhmaṇa is liberated from all sins. ||14||
There is no gift whatsoever found here superior to the gift of land;
the gift of food is equal to that, while the gift of knowledge is greater than that. (15)
He who bestows knowledge according to the prescribed rite upon a Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled, pure, and virtuous in character, is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||16||
One should give gold every day with faith to a celibate student;
liberated from all sins, he shall attain the abode of Brahman. ||17||
A person obtains the fruit of giving food to a householder;
indeed, food alone should be given to him, for by giving it, one attains the supreme goal. 18.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having fasted according to the prescribed rite, being peaceful, pure, and self-controlled in mind, he should feed seven or five Brahmins. (19)
Having performed worship with black sesame seeds and especially with honey, one should say,
"May Dharmarāja be pleased," whenever it is so intended in the mind.
Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes in that very instant by placing sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, along with gold, honey, and clarified butter. (21)
He who gives ghee, food, and a water-pot to a learned Brahmin on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, especially when it occurs within the month, transcends all evil deeds. ||22||
By reciting this to the King of Dharma and to Brahmins, one is liberated from fear;
furthermore, by offering gold and sesame seeds to seven or five Brahmins. (23)
By offering libations with vessels of water, he removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having fasted on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, [he attains this].
Wearing white garments, having offered black sesame seeds into the fire,
one should, with a concentrated mind, give those very sesame seeds as gifts to the Brahmins.
Whatever sin a twice-born man has committed since birth, all that he destroys by approaching a self-controlled Brahmin on the new moon day and offering it to him. (26)
One should offer a *yati* to some lord of the gods, dedicating it to Keśava, [saying]:
"May the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, be pleased. (27)
The sin committed over seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment for one who,
having bathed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, [worships] the god Pinākin.
One should propitiate him through the mouth of a brahmin; for such a person, there is rebirth again, especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, by means of a righteous brahmin.
Having bathed and worshipped according to the rule with the washing of the feet and other rites, [one should say]:
"May the Great God be pleased with me; may He grant His own wealth. (30)

Completely liberated from all sins, he attains the supreme goal, especially by the twice-born on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and particularly on the eighth day of the dark fortnight. ||31||
Likewise, Trivikrama should be worshipped by devotees on the new moon day;
having fasted on the eleventh day, one should worship Puruṣottama on the twelfth day.
One who worships through the mouth of a brāhmaṇa shall go to the supreme state;
this Vaiṣṇava guest is indeed the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight.
In that [place], one should diligently worship the god Janārdana;
or, for some, the god Īśāna, directed toward a pure Brāhmaṇa ascetic.
Whatever [gift] is given to Viṣṇu alone, that is remembered as yielding the fruit of that [gift].
For whatever deity a man may wish to propitiate, [he should give to Viṣṇu]. (35)
One should diligently honor the Brahmins and satisfy them with wealth;
for the deities always reside within the bodies of the twice-born. 36.
In the absence of a Brahmin, they [the offerings] may sometimes be made to images and the like;
therefore, one who desires the fruit [of the rite] should strive to perform it toward images and such. 37.
Among the twice-born, the deities are always to be honored especially;
one who desires prosperity should constantly worship the destroyer of Tripura.
One desiring spiritual luster should worship Brahmā; one desiring knowledge, [Brahmā];
one desiring health, [the Sun]; and one desiring fuel for the fire, the Fire-god. (39)
One who desires the success of one's actions should indeed worship Vināyaka;
one who desires enjoyment should worship the Moon, and one who desires strength should worship the Wind.
One who desires liberation from all worldly existence should worship Hari with diligent effort;
likewise, one who seeks yoga, liberation, and divine knowledge [should do so]. 41.
Those who desire great enjoyments and various forms of knowledge should worship Virūpākṣa, the Lord of the Gods, with diligent effort. (42)
Those who enjoy worldly pleasures worship Bhūteśa and Keśava;
however, the giver of water attains satisfaction, and the gift of water is superior to that.
The giver of oil obtains desired offspring; the giver of a lamp, supreme vision;
the giver of land attains everything; and the giver of gold, long life. (44)
The giver of a house attains an excellent form with beautiful arms;
the giver of clothing attains residence in the same world as the Moon; and the giver of a horse attains the most excellent vehicle.
The giver of food obtains the prosperity desired by himself; the giver of a cow, a bull, or a Brahmin attains the celestial realm;
the giver of a vehicle or a bed obtains a wife; and the giver of fearlessness obtains sovereignty.
The giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; the giver of the Veda obtains the eternity of Brahman. One should bestow grains upon Brahmins according to one's ability. (47)
By bestowing [gifts] upon those distinguished by Vedic learning, one enjoys heaven after death;
and by the gift of food to cows, one is liberated from all sins. ||48||
By the gift of wealth, a man becomes one whose digestive fire is kindled;
likewise by giving fruits, roots, drinks, and various kinds of vegetables. (49)
One should give medicine, oil, and food to the sick for the sake of alleviating their disease, and one should always remain intent upon [the welfare of] Brahmins.
The giver becomes free from disease, happy, and long-lived;
[he avoids] the path of the forest of sword-leaves, which is lined with razor edges. (51)
A man who gives sharp weapons, shade from a parasol, sandals, and whatever else is most dear to him in the world, as well as whatever he requires in his home; ||52||
One who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible should give it to those possessing such-and-such qualities on the solstices,
the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
What is given during the times of the solstices and so forth becomes inexhaustible, as does that given at holy places such as Prayāga, and in sacred sanctuaries. (54)
Having given [gifts] at rivers and springs, one obtains that which is inexhaustible.
Among all beings in this world, there exists no dharma higher than the dharma of giving.
Therefore, those of the twice-born who desire heaven, prosperity, and likewise the pacification of sin, must give to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas.
One who desires liberation should give [gifts] to Brahmins every day;
however, that which is given out of delusion to cows, Brahmins, fire, or gods [is not so].
One who is unrighteous in soul is restrained [from higher realms] and shall go to the womb of an animal;
he who, having acquired wealth, does not honor the Brahmins and the gods. (58)
The king should confiscate all the property of that man who does not provide food and provisions during a time of famine and banish him from the kingdom. (59)
When Brahmins are dying, a Brāhmaṇa who is censured by the virtuous should not accept gifts from them, nor should he even dwell with them. (60)
Having summoned him from his own kingdom, the king should banish him;
thereafter, he bestows upon the virtuous here in this world his own wealth, which is the means for practicing dharma.
A man who is more sinful than those previously mentioned is cooked in hell;
whereas those Brahmins who possess sacred study, who are learned, and who have conquered their senses [attain the highest state].
One should give to those best of the twice-born who are endowed with truthfulness and self-restraint;
even if he has already eaten, a wise man should feed a righteous brahmin.
He who, bypassing a nearby *śrotriya*, gives [a gift] to one who is ignorant, not established in good conduct, and has fasted for ten nights; ||64||
By this sinful act, he destroys his family unto the seventh generation,
unless he himself be a Brahmin superior in character, learning, and other such qualities.
One should bestow [the gift] upon him with effort, even bypassing those who are nearby;
one should accept what has been honored and likewise give only that which has been honored.
Both of them go to heaven, but in the opposite case, they go to hell; one should not offer [instruction] even to a noble person who is an atheist or a rationalist.
Among all heretics, there is no one who knows the Dharma without knowing the Vedas; nor [should one give] silver, gold, a cow, a horse, land, or sesame seeds [to such]. 68.
An ignorant man who accepts [gifts] is reduced to ashes like wood;
therefore, the best of the twice-born should seek wealth from commendable members of the twice-born.
This may be done by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, but never by a Śūdra under any circumstances; he should seek a restriction of his livelihood rather than the expansion of wealth.
But one who is excessively attached to greed for wealth falls away from his very status as a Brahmin, even after having studied all the Vedas and performed all the sacrifices in their entirety. (71)
He attains the state of those who have bowed down; he should attain contentment and should not take pleasure in accepting gifts, nor should he consume the food of a Śūdra.
A Brāhmaṇa who takes more than what is necessary for his maintenance goes to a low state;
but he who is satisfied with what he receives becomes a partaker of heaven.
He causes living beings to tremble just as a thief does;
yet he desires to uplift his teacher and servants, while satisfying the gods and guests. (74)
He should accept from all quarters, yet he himself should not be satisfied by that;
thus the householder, with a disciplined mind, becomes a worshiper of the deities and guests. (75)
Remaining self-restrained in the present world, having entrusted his wife to his sons and gone to the forest, that knower of reality attained the supreme state.
One should always wander alone, indifferent and composed;
this, O best of the twice-born, has been declared as the dharma for householders.
Having understood this, one should remain steadfastly disciplined and likewise cause the twice-born to practice accordingly.
Thus, one should constantly worship this one, beginningless Lord with the duty of a householder;
having transcended all this, he goes to the Supreme Nature, the source of all beings, and does not undergo birth again. //78//
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Duties of the Householder," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The fifty-eighth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus remained in the householder stage of life for the second portion of one's lifespan,
One should go to the forest-dweller stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama) together with one's wife and the sacred fire. ||1||
Or, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go to the forest;
or else, seeing his wife’s offspring with their bodies worn out by old age, [he may go].
In the forenoon of the bright fortnight and during the auspicious northern course of the sun,
one who is self-restrained and composed should go to the forest and perform penance.
One should constantly take as food only pure fruits and roots;
with whatever food one may have, one should worship the ancestors and the deities. (4)
One should worship the Lord of the Earth daily; having bathed, one should honor the gods;
and taking [food] from the house, one should eat eight morsels with a concentrated mind.
He should always wear matted locks and not have his nails or hair cut;
he should perform the private recitation of the Veda in every way and restrain his speech from other matters.
One should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice and carry out the five great sacrifices with various kinds of pure offerings,
or with vegetables, roots, and fruits.
He should always wear garments of bark, bathe three times a day with purity, be compassionate toward all beings, and avoid accepting gifts. (8)
A twice-born man should regularly perform the Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices;
he should also have the Ṛtu-iṣṭi, the Āgrayaṇa, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices performed.
He performed the northern course and likewise the southern course,
dwelling there on food produced by the autumnal rains, obtained through his own efforts.
One should duly offer the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the animal oblations (paśu) separately;
having presented the most pure sacrificial offering to the deities and the ancestors, [one should proceed].
One should consume only the remnants of food and salt prepared by oneself;
one should avoid liquor, meat, underground vegetables, and mushrooms. 12.
One may eat bhūstṛṇa grass, young shoots, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka tree,
provided they have not been ploughed by a furrow and have been discarded by someone else.
Even when distressed, one should never offer flowers or fruits not grown in a village;
one should always attend upon the fire according to this very procedure prescribed for the month of Śrāvaṇa.
One should not harm any living beings; being free from duality, one should be fearless.
One should not eat anything at night, and during the night, one should be devoted to meditation. 15.
Having conquered the senses and subdued anger, reflecting upon the knowledge of reality, he should always remain a celibate student; he should not even resort to a wife.
But he who, having gone to his wife's side, intentionally emits semen through sexual intercourse, his vow is violated; that twice-born man must perform an expiation.
In that regard, the child who is born there [from such a union] is not to be touched by the twice-born;
indeed, he has no entitlement to the Veda, and it is exactly the same for his progeny as well. (18)
He should always sleep on the ground, remain intent upon the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra, be a refuge for all beings, and always be devoted to the distribution of gifts to the virtuous. 19.
One should avoid slander, false speech, sleep, and laziness;
one should maintain the sacred fire alone, remain homeless, and take refuge on ground that has been consecrated by sprinkling.
Self-controlled, he should move about with the deer and dwell together with them;
he should sleep on a stone or upon gravel, remaining perfectly composed.
He may be one who washes his bowl immediately after eating, or one who stores food for a month;
or he may store it for six months, or even for a year. (22)
One should eat food at night after having collected it during the day according to one's ability; or one may observe the fourth-meal rule, or even the eighth-meal rule.
Or, by means of the rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa fast, one should avoid [food] during both the bright and dark fortnights;
instead, one should eat boiled barley gruel only once every fortnight.
Abiding by the doctrine of the Vaikhānasa, he should always subsist solely on flowers, roots, and fruits that are naturally produced and have fallen of their own accord.
One should move about on the ground like a serpent, or stand on one's tiptoes for a day; one should pass the time by alternating between standing and sitting, never relinquishing fortitude.
In the summer he should practice the austerity of exposure to the five fires; during the rains, he should live under the open sky;
and in the winter, he should wear wet clothes; thus he should gradually increase his ascetic penance.
He should perform ablutions at the three periods of the day and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
he should stand on one foot and constantly drink the rays of the sun.

Having practiced the penance of the five fires, the smoke-vow, the cow-hair garment, or the heat-vow, or having drunk soma, one should drink milk during the bright fortnight and cow-dung during the dark fortnight. 29.
He should subsist on withered leaves or constantly pass his time through austerities; he should be devoted to the practice of yoga and always recite the Rudrādhyāya.
One who studies the Atharvaśiras, is devoted to the constant practice of the Vedas,
should always observe the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas) without weariness.
Or else, having consigned the sacred fires into oneself, one should be intent upon meditation.
Without fire and without a fixed dwelling, the ascetic should be intent on liberation; he should obtain alms for his sustenance from brahmins who are themselves ascetics.
While living in the forest, he should eat eight morsels of food brought from the village from other householders who are twice-born and dwellers of the forest.
Having accepted [the offerings] with a hollowed palm, with the hand, or with a fragment of a leaf,
one should mutter the various Upaniṣads for the sake of self-realization.
He should perform specific Vedic recitations, the Sāvitrī, and likewise the Rudrādhyāya;
he may also undertake the Great Departure or observe a fast unto death.
Or else, remaining established in the rite of offering to Brahman, one may enter the fire or perform another [such act]. ||36||
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Duties and Conduct of the Vanaprastha Stage of Life," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||58||
The fifty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having thus remained in the forest hermitage for the third part of one's life,
And he should spend the fourth part of his life in succession through renunciation. ||1||
Having established the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born should become a wandering mendicant;
devoted to the practice of yoga, peaceful, and dedicated to the knowledge of Brahman. ||2||
When dispassion toward all things has become perfected within the mind, then one should desire renunciation;
otherwise, one would fall into error. //3//
Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, or alternatively the Āgneyī,
being self-controlled and wearing white or saffron robes, he should enter the Brahmāśrama.
Some are renunciants of knowledge, others are renunciants of the Vedas, and still others are renunciants of action; thus they are proclaimed to be of three kinds.
He who is completely liberated from everything, free from duality, and fearless,
is called one who has attained the renunciation of knowledge (jñāna-saṃnyāsī), being firmly established in the Self alone.
One who is free from desire and devoid of possessions should constantly study the Veda alone;
such a person, having conquered the senses and seeking liberation, is called a renouncer of the Veda (vedasaṃnyāsī).
But that twice-born man who, making the fire his own self, is intent on offering everything to Brahman—he should be known as one who has renounced action, being devoted to the great sacrifice. (8)
Among these three as well, the man of knowledge is considered superior;
for that wise one, there is no duty to be performed, nor does he possess any outward mark.
Free from possessiveness and fear, peaceful, beyond dualities, subsisting on leaves,
he should wear a worn-out loincloth or remain naked, being solely intent upon meditation.
A celibate student, having conquered his appetite for food, should collect alms from a village;
he should dwell delighting in the inner self, indifferent to worldly things and free from desire.
One should wander here with oneself alone as one's companion for the sake of happiness;
one should neither welcome death nor welcome life. (12)
One should simply await the [proper] time, just as a hired servant awaits his instructions;
one must never study, recite, or listen [to the Veda]. (13)
Thus, the yogi who is devoted to knowledge becomes fit for becoming Brahman—whether he is clothed in a single garment or even one who wears only a loincloth as his covering. (14)
He may have a shaven head or a topknot, carry a triple staff, and remain without possessions; clad in saffron robes, he should be constantly devoted to meditation and yoga. ||15||
He should dwell in a village, at the foot of a tree, or even in a temple;
he should be impartial toward enemy and friend alike, as well as toward honor and dishonor. (16)

He should always subsist on alms and never, under any circumstances, eat the food of a single person. If, however, out of delusion or for some other reason, an ascetic should eat the food of a single person, [he incurs a fault]. (17)
No atonement whatsoever for that is seen in the treatises on Dharma, [except for one] whose self is free from passion and hatred, and who regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal. (18)
Abstaining from harming living beings, he should remain silent and free from all desire;
he should place his foot purified by sight and drink water purified by a cloth. (19)
One should speak words purified by truth and practice a mind that is pure.
A mendicant should not dwell in a single place for more than a year.
Having bathed daily with a sense of purity, pure and holding a water-pot in his hand, he should remain constantly devoted to celibacy and intent on dwelling in the forest. (21)
Devoted to the treatises on liberation, wearing the sacred thread, with senses conquered, free from the notions of "I" and "mine," and devoid of envy and slander; ||22||
If one endowed with the qualities of self-knowledge should attain liberation, one should constantly practice the eternal God known as the Praṇava. 23.

Having bathed and sipped water according to the prescribed rules, being pure in temples and other sacred places, wearing the sacrificial thread, with a self-controlled mind, holding *kuśa* grass in his hand, and being fully composed; ||24||
Clad in washed saffron robes, with his body hair covered, he should mutter the Brahman pertaining to the sacrifice (adhiyajña) as well as that pertaining to the divine (ādhidaivika). 25.
And he should constantly contemplate that which is internal and declared in the Vedānta;
moreover, the sage-yati should dwell among his sons as one practicing celibacy (brahmacārī). ||26||
One should constantly study the Veda alone; by doing so, one attains the supreme goal.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and supreme austerity—these are the means. (27)
He was especially devoted to the vows of patience, compassion, and truth;
he was established in the knowledge of Vedānta and, with a concentrated mind, performed the five sacrifices.
Having bathed day after day, he should indeed perform his duties solely for the sake of alms;
he should constantly recite the fire-offering mantras at the proper times with a concentrated mind.
One should perform one's daily recitation every day and chant the Sāvitrī at the two junctions of the day;
one should constantly meditate upon the God, the Supreme Lord, in solitude.

One should always avoid eating alone, as well as desire, anger, and possessiveness; one may wear either a single garment or two garments, and should remain unshaven-headed while wearing the sacrificial thread.
The wise one, holding a water-pot in his hand, was intent upon the practice of the triple staff.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Ascetics," in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sixtieth Chapter. Vyāsa said:
Thus, for those ascetics established in the stages of life who have restrained their selves...
It is taught that one should subsist on alms, or else on fruits and roots. ||1||
One should go for alms only once a day and should not become attached to abundance;
for an ascetic who is attached to alms becomes attached to sense objects as well. ||2||
He should go for alms at seven houses, and if he receives nothing, he should not go again.
A mendicant should stand with his face turned downward for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow.
Having said "Alms, please," he should receive [the food] repeatedly while remaining silent, restrained in speech, and pure;
then, having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule.
Having looked at the sun, a man should eat his food facing the east;
having offered the five oblations to the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis), he should consume eight mouthfuls with a concentrated mind.
Having sipped water (ācamana) in this manner, one should meditate upon Brahmā as the Supreme Lord;
[using] a vessel made of gourd, wood, clay, or likewise bamboo.
Prajāpati has prescribed four times for the consumption of the vessel [of food]:
at the first watch of the night, at the middle watch, and likewise at the last watch.

At the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā), one should constantly meditate upon the Lord with specific hymns, having placed within the lotus-abode of the heart Him who is called the Universe and from whom the universe originates. 8.
The Self, which stands beyond the darkness of all beings, the unmanifest support of everything—know this to be the imperishable light. (9)
Beyond both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, he is the ether, the fire, the auspicious one;
he is that very Lord of all states of being, whose form is Brahman. ||10||
Having dissolved the self, which consists of the syllable *oṃ*, into the Supreme Self, one should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna, situated in the midst of space, within that very space. 11.
By meditating upon Viṣṇu—the ancient Puruṣa, the cause of all beings, and the sole refuge of the soul—one shall be liberated from bondage. 12.
Or else, having meditated upon the supreme ether—the sole cause of all beings—within the cave of the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the abode that deludes the world; ||13||
It is the life-force of all beings wherein the world dissolves;
it is the blissful, subtle Brahman which those seeking liberation behold. ||14||

In the midst of that, one should meditate with restrained speech upon the absolute Brahman, which is established as the infinite, the true, and the sovereign Lord, characterized by pure knowledge. 15.
This knowledge, the most secret of secrets, has been declared for the sake of ascetics; he who always abides in this attains the supreme yoga of the Lord. 16.
Therefore, one who delights always in knowledge and is devoted to the science of the Self should practice that knowledge; by this, he shall be liberated from bondage. 17.
Having realized the Self as distinct from everything else, as the one and only, as bliss, the imperishable, and pure consciousness—one should then meditate upon that which is beyond this. 18.
Because, having known that from which all beings arise, one is not born again in this world,
therefore He is the Lord, the God who presides over everything beyond.
He who knows this eternal, auspicious, and immutable state that lies within—this very one, though beyond the perception of self and others, is indeed the god Maheśvara. ||20||
These are the vows for monks, and likewise these are the vows;
the expiation is prescribed for the transgression of each one individually. (21)
Having approached a woman out of lust, one who is composed and pure should perform the Sāntapana penance,
accompanied by breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Then, having restrained his semen and exerting himself with a controlled mind,
the mendicant should return to the hermitage and practice there without sloth.
The wise say that untruth joined with righteousness does not cause harm;
nevertheless, one should not indulge in such [untruth], for this addiction is indeed terrible.
Having spoken a falsehood, an ascetic who desires to avoid unrighteousness must perform a fast for one night as well as one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Even when fallen into the greatest distress, one must not commit theft from another;
for there is no unrighteousness greater than theft—so says the Smṛti.
Indeed, this other thirst for wealth is the destroyer of self-knowledge;
for that which is called "wealth" is nothing but these very vital breaths (prāṇas) existing externally. (27)
He who takes away another's wealth robs him of his very life;
having acted thus, that evil-souled man is of corrupt conduct and fallen from his vow.
And having attained even greater world-weariness, that diligent monk should indeed practice this [meditation] suddenly, as it were. (29)
If an ascetic,
due to weakness of the senses, should emit semen upon seeing a woman, he should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or alternatively the Prājāpatya.
Therefore, sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be maintained;
for a wise person, one hundred breath-restraints performed during the day would equal [the merit of] three nights spent in the presence of the Sun.
For eating food from a single source, honey, meat, oil, or clarified butter, as well as for a Śrāddha meal,
and for the consumption of visible salt, the Prājāpatya penance is declared as the means of purification.
All sin is constantly destroyed for one who is steadfast in meditation;
therefore, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, one should remain devoted to his meditation. ||33||
That which is the supreme light of Brahman, having entered the imperishable and immutable;
that which is the inner self, the supreme Brahman—he is to be known as Maheśvara. ||34||
This God is the Great God, absolute and supremely auspicious;
that alone is the imperishable non-dual, that is the eternal, supreme state. (35)

Therefore, he is glorified among the gods in his own abode known as Jñāna; because of his union with the Self, he is remembered as Mahādeva, the Great God, who has transcended to the state beyond. ||36||
He perceives no other god as distinct from Mahādeva;
he who follows that very Self attains the supreme state. ||37||
Those who consider themselves separate from the Supreme Lord do not behold that God;
their exertion is in vain. (38)
The one alone is the supreme Brahman, the reality to be known, the imperishable.
He is the existent God, the Great God; by knowing this, one is not bound. (39)
Therefore, the ascetic, with a restrained mind and striving for self-control, should constantly exert himself; devoted to the yoga of knowledge, peaceful, and solely intent upon the Great God. ||40||
O Brahmins, this auspicious stage of life for the ascetics has been described to you; it was previously proclaimed by the all-pervading Sage, the Grandfather. 41.
One should not bestow this unsurpassed knowledge—declared by Svayambhū, auspicious, and based on the duties of ascetics—upon anyone who is not a son, a disciple, or a yogin. (42)
Thus has this rule been declared for these observances, which serves as the sole cause for the gratification of the best of gods;
yet there is neither arising nor destruction for them, for those of steadfast mind practice them eternally. (43)
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||60||
(61) The sixty-first chapter.
Sūta said:
Thus were the brahmins addressed in the past by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor;
having said this much, the blessed Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, [ceased]. ||1||
Having consoled all the sages, he departed as he had come;
and I have now declared to you the ordinances for the castes and stages of life.
By acting thus, one indeed becomes dear to Viṣṇu and not otherwise.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall speak the secret concerning this matter. (3)
And those duties prescribed here, O twice-born ones, which are bound by the system of social classes and stages of life, are not equal even to a minute fraction of a fraction of devotion to Hari. (4)
Indeed, for some men in the Kali age, devotion to Hari alone is to be accomplished;
for in other ages, various religious duties must be practiced by a person. (5)
In the Kali age, he who worships the divine Nārāyaṇa— who is Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puruhūta, and the Eternal— is a partaker of dharma.
Having taken refuge in the Supreme Peace within his heart, he has indeed conquered the three worlds from the venomous serpent of the Kali age, from sin, and from the Kālakūṭa poison.
Having drunk the nectar of devotion to Hari, a twice-born becomes transcendent;
what need is there for other chants if men have taken up the name of Śrī Hari? (8)
What is the use of ritual baths for one who bears the water from Viṣṇu’s feet upon his head? What is the use of sacrifice for one who holds Hari’s lotus feet within his heart? (9)
What is the use of giving gifts? Hari’s deeds have indeed been made manifest in the assembly hall;
one who hears the multitude of Hari’s qualities would rejoice again and again. (10)
For one who is delighted by meditative concentration (samādhi), that is the state of one whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa;
in that regard, it is said that those skilled in conversation with heretics are creators of obstacles. 11.
Women and those who associate with them are obstructors of devotion to Hari;
the command of women's eyes is difficult to conquer even for the gods. (12)
He who has conquered this world is called a devotee of Hari;
even sages become intoxicated here when they are lusting after the conduct of women. 13.

O twice-born ones, how can there be devotion to Hari for those men who indulge in devotion to women? O twice-born ones, these are Rākṣasīs in the guise of beautiful women who take delight in the world.
Those who are truly beneficial constantly provide the nourishment of wisdom for human beings. ||14||
So long does learning prevail, so long does wisdom function, and so long is the intellect perfectly pure, capable of upholding all the scriptures. (15)

So long is there recitation of mantras, so long is there austerity, so long is there resorting to sacred fords, so long is there service to the guru, and so long is there the mind intent on the battle for one's welfare. ||16||
Awakening occurs only so long, for discernment lasts only that long;
the desire for the company of the virtuous lasts only so long, as does the longing for the ancient [truth]. (17)
O Brahmins, as long as the swinging of the swing does not fall upon the people— those with eyes as restless as those of a woman in passion— there shall be no destruction of all dharma.
In that regard, for those who have been graced by even a drop of the honey from the lotus feet of Hari, the flickering glances of women's restless eyes shall indeed have no power over them. (19)
O twice-born ones, those by whom service to Hṛṣīkeśa was performed birth after birth, have indeed offered gifts to the twice-born and made oblations into the fire in various places. (20)
What indeed do they call the beauty of women? It is said to be merely the glitter of their ornaments and garments. (21)

How can the female form, which is devoid of knowledge of its own nature as consisting of affection, be remembered [as anything else], when it is filled with pus, urine, feces, blood, skin, fat, bone, and marrow? (22)
For that thing is indeed called a corpse; how could there be beauty in it?
Thus, having reflected on them as distinct [from the self], one should become pure by touching and bathing. (23)
Indeed, their body, joined together by those [limbs], is seen as beautiful by people;
yet, O twice-born ones, alas, the extreme misfortune of men is fashioned by cruel destiny! (24)
When the body is covered by breasts, a man perceives it as a woman and proceeds [to act];
yet upon investigation, what woman is there, or what man? There is nothing at all. (25)
Therefore, a virtuous man should avoid association with women in every way;
for who, having encountered a woman, attains perfection on this earth? (26)
One should abandon even the company of those who associate with women;
for it is directly perceived that from such association one goes to the Raurava hell. ||27||
Out of ignorance, people are greedy and deceived by fate;
in this very hell-pot, the womb of a woman, a man is cooked. (28)
One should again take delight in that very place from which one came to this earth;
for it is from there that urine, arising from the impurities of semen, constantly flows forth. (29)
In that very place the world finds delight; who then could be more impure than it?
Alas, what a mockery of fate this is in this world, where such extreme suffering exists! (30)
One might take pleasure there again and again; alas, what shamelessness in men!
Therefore, a wise person should reflect upon the many multitudes of faults inherent in women. (31)
From sexual intercourse there is a loss of strength; from sleep one becomes excessively youthful [in lethargy].
A man whose knowledge is stolen by sleep becomes short-lived. (32)
Therefore, a wise and intelligent person should view a woman with great effort as if she were his own death; he should bring his mind to enmity toward her. 33.
For that service of Govinda’s feet brings happiness both in this world and the next; yet, abandoning it, the small-minded fool serves the feet of a woman. (34)
Indeed, service to the feet of Janārdana bestows freedom from rebirth;
whereas service to the womb of women indeed causes the misery of the womb. (35)
Just as one cast from a mold might fall again and again into the womb, so too would he desire that very same [existence]; one should recognize this as his mockery. (36)
With my arms raised, I speak; listen to my supreme word:
fix your heart upon Govinda, not upon the womb that is subject to torment.
That man who, having abandoned association with women, turns back [from them], obtains at every step the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||38||
If a virtuous woman of noble family, by the turn of fate, should become a widow on her wedding day,
she should give birth to a son there and then avoid contact with him as if he were a stranger.
The Lord of the World becomes pleased with him; of this there is no doubt.
For the association with women is proclaimed by the knowers of Dharma to be association with the wicked. (40)
As long as that [worldly attachment] exists, very firm devotion to Hara does not arise at all;
having abandoned all attachments, one should practice devotion to Hara. ||41||
And devotion to Hari is very difficult for those of dull intellect to obtain in this world;
he who possesses devotion to Hari has achieved his life's purpose, without a doubt. (42)
One should perform whatever action by which Hari is pleased;
for when He is satisfied, the world is satisfied, and when He is gratified, the world is gratified. (43)
The birth of those men who lack devotion to Hari is proclaimed to be in vain;
even Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods worship him for the sake of his pleasure. (44)
Who would not serve that person who bows to Nārāyaṇa, the unmanifest?
Blessed is his maternal grandfather, and his father is a man of great merit. (45)
O Janārdana, whose feet are a pair of lotuses;
O Janārdana, who are the refuge of the world; O You who are compassionate toward those who have come for shelter! 46.
Thus they speak; for those mortals who revile them, their destination is hell—especially in the case of Brahmins, who are the visible forms of Hari himself.
If they should worship Him according to the proper method, Hari becomes pleased with them;
Viṣṇu wanders this earth in the form of a Brāhmaṇa.
Indeed, without a Brāhmaṇa, one never attains the accomplishment of one's actions;
having drunk with devotion the water from the feet of the twice-born and applied it to one's head. (49)
By him the ancestors have been gratified, and his own self has indeed been uplifted, by whom sweet and honored food was given into the mouths of Brahmins. 50.
Hari himself partakes of that which was directly offered from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa;
oh, how difficult it is for people in this world to perceive such a Brāhmaṇa who is none other than Keśava! 51.

In the absence of those [images and so forth], the performance of that [rite] is accomplished through the presiding presence of Brāhmaṇas; thus the earth is celebrated as "the blessed one" (dhanyā). //52//
Whatever was given into their hands was offered into the hand of Hari;
for those who have performed obeisance to them, there is indeed a rejection of all sin.
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and from the offense of insulting a Brahmin;
therefore, a Brahmin should be propitiated by the virtuous with the understanding that he is Viṣṇu.
If anyone gives even a little to this hungry brahmin,
he shall be sprinkled with streams of nectar for ten million kalpas after death.
The beak of a twice-born is a great field, free from salt and barrenness; if anything is sown there, one obtains a fruit of millions upon millions. (56)
Having given food with ghee to us, he rejoices for an entire kalpa;
he who gives various kinds of most delicious food for the satisfaction of the twice-born [enjoys the same]. (57)
For him, there are worlds of great enjoyments that grant liberation until the end of ten million kalpas; this was proclaimed by a non-Brahmin, having placed a Brahmin at the forefront. (58)
One should listen to the Purāṇa daily; it is a forest fire for great sins. Among all sacred fords, the Purāṇa is said to be the most excellent ford. (59)
By hearing even a single word from him, Hari himself becomes pleased;
just as Hari, having assumed the form of the sun, moves about for the sake of illumination.
Just as Hari is the cause of light for all the worlds,
so too is Hari, the ancient one, the constituent part that provides internal illumination.
One should contemplate here among living beings that which is ancient, purifying, and supreme;
therefore, if the mind is applied to generating delight for Hari.
This Purāṇa, which is the very form of Kṛṣṇa, should be heard incessantly by men;
it should be heard by one who is peaceful and devoted to Viṣṇu, for such an opportunity is indeed difficult to obtain.
The Purāṇa is a stainless narrative, the supreme means of purification, in which the meaning of the Vedas was extracted by Hari, who assumed the form of Vyāsa. (64)
O Brahmin, the Purāṇa was created in ancient times; therefore, one should hold it in the highest regard.
In the Purāṇa, dharma is definitively established, and dharma is Keśava himself.
Therefore, when the Purāṇa has been composed and heard, Viṣṇu himself becomes manifest;
O Brahmin, both Hari and such a Purāṇa are directly present.
Having attained the union of these two, a man indeed becomes Hari himself;
likewise, by sprinkling the water of the Gaṅgā, he shall destroy his own sin.
Keśava, in the form of water, delivers the earth from sin;
and the Vaiṣṇava, desiring the worship of Viṣṇu, proceeds along his path.
One should perform the pure sprinkling of Gaṅgā water, which is a means of purification;
for Gaṅgā is celebrated on earth as the goddess who bestows devotion to Viṣṇu. (69)
Indeed, this Gaṅgā has the form of Viṣṇu and causes the expansion of the worlds. ||70||
Toward ancient Brahmins, the Gaṅgā, cows, and the Pippala tree, men should practice causeless devotion with the thought that they are Nārāyaṇa. (71)
These [deities] have been ascertained by those who know the truth as being the very forms of Viṣṇu manifest before one's eyes;
therefore, they should be constantly worshipped by one who desires devotion to Viṣṇu. (72)
The birth of men is said to be fruitless without devotion to Viṣṇu,
[especially when living] in the ocean of the Kali age, which is teeming with the crocodiles of sin.
It has the whirlpools of immersion in sense objects, the foam of difficult-to-comprehend [misconceptions], and is most supreme;
it is terrifying, filled with the great and fearsome serpents of wicked people. ||74||
Those who have boarded the boat of devotion to Hari surely cross over even that which is difficult to cross;
therefore, people should indeed strive for the accomplishment of devotion to Viṣṇu. (75)
What happiness does a living being obtain by attending to false news?
One finds joy through the narration of the wonderful pastimes of Hari. (76)
Therefore, if the minds of men are indeed attached to sense objects, they should listen to this work mixed with various worldly narratives for the sake of the world. (77)
Or if the mind is set upon nirvāṇa, that too should be heard, O twice-born ones;
for Hari becomes pleased even by hearing it with indifference. (78)
Although Hṛṣīkeśa is beyond all purchase, he performed various deeds for the benefit of those who desire to hear them;
he is affectionate toward his devotees for the sake of the welfare of his devotees.
That which cannot be obtained even by a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, nor even by ten thousand Rājasūyas, is obtained through devotion. (80)
That state which is to be cultivated by the mind and repeatedly practiced by the virtuous—take refuge in that essential foot of Hari for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. (81)
O base and cruel men, greedy for the objects of the senses, why will you, by your own actions, cast yourselves into the Raurava hell? 82.
Without serving Govinda, who is as gentle as the moon, you will not attain [liberation];
for if you desire the crossing over of sufferings without effort, [you must serve him]. 83.
Worship the feet of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of attaining the state beyond rebirth;
from where indeed has a mortal come, and to where indeed shall he go again? (84)
A wise person, having reflected on this, should resort to the accumulation of merit;
for even if a man has risen from falling into various hells, [he must still strive]. (85)
Having attained a body such as that of an immobile being and so forth, if by the power of fortune one subsequently obtains human birth, therein dwelling in the womb is exceedingly painful. (86)
Then, O twice-born ones, by the power of karma, if a living being is born on earth, he becomes afflicted by many defects such as childhood and the like. (87)
Furthermore, even upon attaining youth, one is tormented by poverty, or likewise by severe illness, drought, and so forth. (88)
Through old age, one may suffer indescribable affliction here and there;
and from the decline of the mind and from disease, one shall then meet with death. (89)
No suffering greater than this is experienced even within saṃsāra;
therefore, by the power of karma, a living being is tormented in the realm of Yama. (90)
Having experienced extreme torment there, one is born once again;
the living being is born and dies, and dies and is born again. (91)
But for one who has not propitiated the feet of Govinda, such is the condition:
death without effort, and life without exertion. (92)
For one who has not propitiated the feet of Govinda, wealth does not arise;
even if there were wealth in the house, what would be the fruit of its protection? (93)
When he is dragged away by the messengers of Yama, what wealth can he take with him?
Therefore, one should honor the twice-born; for wealth [given to them] bestows all happiness. (94)
Charity is the staircase to heaven; charity is the destroyer of sin;
and the practice of devotion to Govinda increases great merit. (95)
If one possesses strength while in the mortal world, one should not expend it in vain;
rather, one should perform dance and song before Hari, remaining thus unwearied. (96)
Whatever little belongs to men, that one should offer unto Kṛṣṇa;
what is offered to Kṛṣṇa bestows well-being, while what is offered to another brings unhappiness. (97)
With one's two eyes, one should behold only the images and other representations of Śrī Hari;
with one's two ears, one should contemplate the qualities and names of Kṛṣṇa day and night. 98.
The wise should taste the water from the lotus feet of Hari with their tongue, and having smelled the tulasī leaf from the lotus feet of Govinda with their sense of smell. 99.

Having touched a devotee of Hari with one's skin and meditated upon His feet with the mind, a living being becomes one who has achieved his life's purpose; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (100)

For the wise man should become one whose mind is fixed on that; thus he should have his disposition directed toward that alone. In the end, the world reaches that very state—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
What person would not serve Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, who bestows his own state upon one who meditates upon him with the mind? (102)
With a mind constantly fixed upon the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, one should perform acts of giving for the sake of attaining His love according to one's capacity;
one should direct one’s prostration, devotion, and delight toward His two feet.
For he, indeed, shall attain a state of being worthy of worship in the world of men. ||103||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||61||
(62) The sixty-second chapter.
Sūta said:
Thus, [I praise] that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord who assumes various forms, whose majesty is the light by which the world is illuminated and by which the world is delivered. ||1||
Therein is indeed one ancient form, the supreme and great Pādma;
it is the head of Hari, known as the Brāhma, and the heart is marked by the lotus.
The right arm belongs to Viṣṇu, and the left arm to Śiva, the Great Lord;
the thighs are said to belong to the Bhāgavata, and the navel to the Nāradīya.
The right foot of the high-souled Viṣṇu is said to be Mārkaṇḍeya, while the left is Āgneya; the right knee is Bhaviṣya. ||4||
The *Brahmavaivarta* is said to be the left knee;
the *Laiṅga* is indeed the right ankle, and the *Vārāha* is the left ankle. (5)
The Skanda Purāṇa is his body hair; the Vāmana is remembered as his skin;
the Kūrma is declared to be his back; and the Mātsya is proclaimed to be his fat.
The marrow is said to be Gāruḍa, and the bone is sung as Brahmāṇḍa;
in this very way, Hari Viṣṇu became the ancient embodiment of the limbs [of the universe]. (7)
The heart there is indeed the lotus, by hearing which one partakes of the nectar;
this Purāṇa is the lotus, for the Lord Hari himself became it.
By teaching even a single chapter of which one is liberated from all sins—this first [chapter], "Svarga," bestows the fruit of all the *Padmas*. (9)
Having heard this section on heaven,
even those who are great sinners are liberated from their sins, just as snakes are freed from their sloughed-off skins.
Moreover, even one of very wicked conduct, excluded from all religious duties, may attain that fruit which is heard to belong to the primary heaven. ||11||
Having heard this regarding the primary heaven, a person obtains that fruit;
indeed, by bathing every day at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, a person [attains it]. (12)
For by hearing [this], one is indeed liberated from evil just as one is;
it is equal to the gift of gold weighed on a scale and the gift of the entire earth. 13.
By him charity was bestowed, by him debt was cleared,
and indeed the thousand names of Hari were recited incessantly.
All the Vedas were likewise committed to memory, and various ritual acts were performed;
furthermore, many teachers were established by the provision of their livelihoods. (15)
O twice-born ones, he likewise bestowed fearlessness upon those in a world of fear; he honored those who were virtuous, wise, and righteous. (16)
Between the signs of Aries and Cancer, he offered very cool water;
indeed, for the sake of Brahmins and cows, he even gave up his life. (17)
And other virtuous deeds were performed by that wise one,
by whom this Ādikhaṇḍa was heard in the assembly and likewise caused to be recited.
Having thoroughly studied the Svargakhaṇḍa, he enjoys effortless pleasures;
sleeping happily within the inner apartments of the women, he awakens. (19)
By means of the sounds of tinkling ornaments and likewise by sweet speech,
one enjoys half of Indra’s throne and dwells for a long time in the world of Indra.
From there, one goes to the abode of the Sun, and from there to the world of the Moon;
having enjoyed the pleasures in the abode of the Seven Sages, one then proceeds to the Pole Star (Dhruva).
Then, having reached the world of Brahmā with a body consisting of light, and having attained primordial wisdom there, he attains supreme nirvāṇa. ||22||
A wise man should dwell with the virtuous, perform his ablutions at sacred bathing places, always engage in conversation with the good, and listen to the true scriptures. (23)
In that regard, the Pādma Mahā-śāstra bestows the fruit of all sacred traditions (āmnāyas);
within it, the Svargakhaṇḍa specifically grants the fruit of great merit.
Worship Govinda, bow down to Hari, the one supreme among gods;
you shall go to worlds of exceedingly pure enjoyments.
Listen, O people! Speak the incomparable name of Hari alone.
If one desires the easy crossing of the waves of desire, one should obtain the favorable wind. ||25||
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Svargakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
This first section, also known by the name Ādikhaṇḍa—or alternatively called Svargakhaṇḍa—is complete.
May there be auspiciousness! May there be prosperity!
Thus ends the third section, the Svargakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fourth section, the Brahma-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
Salutations to the illustrious Veda-vyāsa.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, when the Kali age has arrived, by what action can the upliftment of living beings indeed occur? Therefore, please tell me this in my presence. (1)
Sūta said: Excellent, excellent, O best of sages! You are the foremost among the meritorious souls, and you are constantly a speaker of auspicious words for all people. (2)
O Vaiṣṇava, listen to that which the all-knowing Vyāsa, honored by all, spoke in former times when questioned by the brahmin Jaimini.
Prostrating himself like a staff before Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, who has reached the further shore of all knowledge, that bull among sages questioned his guru. (4)
Jaimini said:
Tell me, by what means can liberation be attained by men in the Kali age? For mortals possess but short lifespans and even the slightest merit. (5)
Vyāsa said: O brāhmaṇa, O lord, from the association with the saintly comes the hearing of the scriptures;
from that arises devotion to Hari, from that comes knowledge, and from that, the final goal. (6)
Indeed, the discourse on the earth does not please the most wicked person;
that twice-born man should be known as the foremost among the wicked who is a Vaiṣṇava. ||7||
Upon hearing the stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, a Vaiṣṇava indeed becomes filled with bliss; but he who speaks of them when they are not true should be known as the teacher of sinners. (8)
O Brahmin, wherever a discourse concerning Kṛṣṇa takes place, the Lord of the World never departs from that very spot to go elsewhere. 9.
That lowest of men who creates an obstacle at the commencement of a discourse on Kṛṣṇa shall have no liberation from hell for the duration of a hundred manvantaras.
Those who, having heard the ancient stories, indeed revile and mock them—for them, hells that cause manifold suffering are always held in the palm of their hand. (11)
Even the sin accumulated over previous births perishes at that very moment for one who forms even the desire to hear the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 12.
If a person should indeed perform the life-story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with devotion, I do not know what state he will attain upon hearing it. (13)
The sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils, as well as untimely death, the drinking of liquor, and theft—all these perish for the sinner. (14)
But that mortal who, having committed an evil deed, later turns away from evil—his sin shall go to destruction like a heap of cotton in a fire. (15)
O brāhmaṇa, if the book of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes remains in one's house, the messengers of Yama do not approach that home. (16)
Jaimini said:
"O Guru, please tell me which Vaiṣṇavas they speak of;
I now wish to know them and their supreme greatness. (17)
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, for that sinful man who with devotion sprinkles the water from the feet of a Vaiṣṇava upon his head, what need is there for bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites?
O twice-born one, whoever should associate with the virtuous for even a moment or half a moment, his sins, including those such as the killing of a Brahmin, are destroyed. (19)
In whatever family there may be even a single Vaiṣṇava, that family, even if it be joined with sins, shall indeed attain liberation. ||20||
O twice-born one, those men who are free from greed and anger, devoid of desire and wrath, and abandoned by attachment and delusion—they indeed should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. (21)

Those who are devoted to their parents, endowed with compassion, dedicated to the welfare of all living beings, free from envy, followers of Viṣṇu, and speakers of truth—these are to be known as such. ||22||
Those who are devoted to the worship of Brahmins, who are like eunuchs toward the wives of others, and who are intent upon the vow of Ekādaśī—these indeed should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. ||23||
Those who wear garlands of tulasī and sing the names of Hari, and who have been sprinkled with the water used for washing the feet of Hari, are indeed to be known as Vaiṣṇavas. 24.
O Brahmin, those on whose ears and heads the most excellent leaf of Tulasī is ever seen should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. 25.
Those who avoid association with heretics, who are free from hatred toward brāhmaṇas, and who cultivate tulasī—those men should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. 26.
Those who worship Hari, those who honor Tulasī, those who are devoted to the gift of a maiden, and those who indeed honor guests; ||27||
Those men who listen to the deeds of Viṣṇu should be known as Vaiṣṇavas, even in whose house a Śālagrāma stone is well-established. (28)

Those who purify the abode of Hari, who initiate the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), and who are endowed with compassion for the miserable and the poor—these indeed are to be known as Vaiṣṇavas. 29.
Those who view the property of others and the wealth of Brahmins as poison at the time of its end, and who do not eat the food offered to Hari—they are to be known as Vaiṣṇava people. ||30||
Those who are devoted to the Vedas and the scriptures, who protect groves of tulasī, and who are intent on the vow of Rādhāṣṭamī—they indeed should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. ||31||
Those who offer a lamp with faith at the waters of Śrīkṛṣṇapura and do not speak ill of others should indeed be known as Vaiṣṇavas. ||32||
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, as Vyāsa was questioned by Jaimini and spoke accordingly, so shall this be told by me, which I heard from my preceptor in the course of conversation.
Those best of men who listen with faith to this chapter, being liberated from all sins, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (34)
Thus ends the first chapter in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini. ||1||
The Second Chapter.
Sūta said:
Listen, O Śaunaka, I shall describe another ancient dharma.
The dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini, which destroys the sins of those who hear it. ||1||
Jaimini said:
"O Guru, tell me now how that sinful man reached the palace of the Lord of the World through his action; O Lord, I desire to hear this. (2)
Vyāsa said:
That man who indeed applies plaster in the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is liberated from all sins; having bathed, he goes to the abode of Hari. (3)
O Jaimini, listen as I describe the merit of one who applies water and unguents to the temple of the Lord of the World through even a single offering. (4)
O best of the twice-born, for as many particles of dust as they see there,
for that many thousands of kalpas shall he dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
