In the Dvāpara Yuga, there was formerly a thief named Daṇḍaka who struck fear into the world; he was a stealer of Brahmins' property and a slayer of friends.
He was a speaker of untruths, cruel, and devoted to approaching the wives of others;
he ate beef, drank liquor, and associated with heretics.

One who cuts off the livelihood of the twice-born, one who misappropriates a deposit, one who kills those who have sought refuge, and one who is lustful for the amorous dalliances of a courtesan; ||8||
Once, O best of the twice-born, that man of deluded intellect went to the temple of Viṣṇu belonging to someone else for the purpose of stealing Viṣṇu’s wealth. (9)
Then, having entered through the door, he, whose feet were covered in mud,
wiped off all the [mud] upon the low ground of the temple.
By that very deed, the ground became sunken and hollow;
and with joy, he quickly opened it with two iron rods.
He entered the abode of Hari, which was adorned with excellent canopies,
enriched by lamps made of radiant jewels, and where the great darkness had been dispelled.
Abounding with the fragrance of various flowers, filled with various vessels, well-perfumed, and overflowing with fragrant oil, it was completely full of cows. ||13||
On this bed, delightful with various flowers,
Acyuta was seen lying together with Rādhā, wearing yellow garments.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Rādhikā, he then became free from sin;
he thought, "Shall I take him away, or shall I not take him away? What would happen to me by this? (15)
Since I am always unable to perform service because of my chest, I have set my mind on taking wealth, thinking that there is business to be done with it. (16)
Having caused Śuka to fall to the ground, he took the silken garment of the Lord of Kamalā and all his other possessions into his hand, O Father.
O Jaimini, having made a most terrible sound, all those [weapons] belonging to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Māyā, indeed fell down.
Abandoning deep sleep, run quickly! Alas! Many people have arrived, and a thief has swiftly taken the wealth. (19)
Having abandoned his wealth, even the thief fled in fear;
however, bitten by a black serpent, he died, having cast off his sin.
By Yama’s command, his messengers— fanged and clad in skins, with nooses and mallets in their hands— arrived to lead him away.
They led Bāṇa along a difficult path with a noose of dried hide;
seeing him, Śamana became enraged and questioned his minister.
Yama said: "O wise one, declare before me and Citragupta what karma this man has performed— whether it be sinful or meritorious— and tell it with its very root."
Citragupta said:
"Whatever sins have been created upon the surface of the earth by the Creator, these have all been committed by this fool; what I have spoken is the truth. (24)
But what merit of yours, O Lord of the World, is being heard [by me], which exists here?
I believe, O brother, that it is the Yamunā, which destroys all sins. (25)
The King of Dharma said:
"O minister, what merit exists here that is so worthless in my presence? Having heard this, I shall act accordingly so that he may become worthy. (26)
Having heard the words of Yama, Citragupta, free from fear, joined his palms in reverence and said to his own master, O twice-born one: [27]
Citragupta said:
"O King, this foremost of sinners went for the purpose of seizing Hari’s property; he was cast away by Kardama at the threshold of Hari’s feet."
That ground became free from impurities and devoid of holes, cracks, or cavities;
by the power of that merit, his great sin was expelled.
This worthy one has departed from your staff toward Vaikuṇṭha. ||29||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard his words, Pīṭha gave him a seat made of gold; having been honored by Yama, he sat down there.
He bowed his head to him, and the sage, filled with humility, spoke.
Yama said:
"Today my sanctuary has been purified by the dust of your feet."
I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose; of this there is no doubt.
Now go, O holy man, to the supreme abode of Hari.
"Endowed with various enjoyments and warding off birth and death.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, that Dharmarāja sat upon a throne made of gold.
Having placed the sinless one upon a divine royal swan-yoked chariot,
he sent him to the abode of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), which bestows all happiness.
Having thus entered Vaikuṇṭha, he remained there happily for a long time;
those who perform the smearing of the temple of Hari with devotion [attain this]. (35)
O best of the twice-born, I do not know what will become of those who hear this with devotion or who recite it with a concentrated mind. (36)
The sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed without a doubt. ||37||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Smearing the Temple of Hari," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||2||
The Third Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, tell me in my presence the greatness of the month of Kārttika.
What is the fruit of that action, or what is the fault for one who does not perform it? ||1||
Sūta said: O best of sages, in former times Jaimini questioned Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī; the sage then began to relate this which has been told. (2)
Vyāsa said:
He who abandons sesame oil and sexual intercourse during the auspicious month of Kārttika is liberated from the sins committed over many births and goes to the abode of Hari.
That fool who does not renounce fish and sexual intercourse during the month of Kārttika will certainly become a pig in every birth. 4.
In the month of Kārttika, one should worship Vaijanārdaṇa with tulasī leaves;
for every leaf, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. ||5||
He who worships Madhusūdana with the flowers of the Kārttika season obtains liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to attain, through the grace of Hari. (6)
In the month of Kārttika, that best of men ate only leafy vegetables;
by that single meal of greens, the sins committed throughout the year were destroyed.
O Brahmin, a person who has offered fruit to Hari, O beloved of Hari, enjoys the fruit thereof and indeed destroys the sins accumulated over ten million births.
One should offer delicious food mixed with clarified butter to the remover of sins;
liberated from all evils, he shall go to the abode of Hari.
If a person offers even a single lotus to Hara on the Kārtikeya day, he shall go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, freed from all sins. (10)
O beloved of Śrī Hari, whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in all the sacred fords, he indeed attains that same fruit by performing the morning bath during the month of Kārtika. ||11||
O twice-born one, a man who is a devotee of Kārttikeya should offer a lamp in the sky;
liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, he shall go to the abode of Hari.

O best of Brahmins, Hari is always pleased with one who gives a lamp for the pleasure of Hari for even a moment in the month of Kārttika, or during the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), or at the time of the Tāraka constellation.
O twice-born one, if one should offer a lamp with ghee in the house of Kṛṣṇa during the month of Kārtika, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice day after day.
O best of the twice-born, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe the greatness and the specific excellence of the lamp, along with its ancient history. 15.
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a pure Brahmin named Vaikuṇṭha, by the power of whose association even a sinner becomes liberated. (16)
Once, O best of the twice-born, that brahmin Kārtikeya, having offered a lamp filled with ghee before Hari, went home.
Having tasted that ghee, the mouse also approached the lamp;
as soon as he began to eat it, he was awakened by that very lamp. (18)
The mouse fled from there with great speed out of fear of the fire;
by the grace of Hari, all the sins of the mouse were destroyed. (19)
Bitten by a snake, the mouse gave up its life;
then, by the command of Yama, messengers with nooses and mallets in their hands [arrived]. (20)
The wielders of the conch, discus, and mace arrived to bring him back, binding him with ropes of hide as they sought to lead away his mind. (21)
The four-armed messengers of Viṣṇu, mounted upon Garuḍas, arrived;
and in the sky, there was an auspicious celestial chariot accompanied by royal swans.
Out of compassion for Hari, he fashioned a golden, wish-fulfilling noose;
having severed that noose, the messengers then spoke to those thieves.
"Even though you are devotees of Viṣṇu, you fools have rendered this wealth of yours useless;
go now, like messengers of Yama, to the world of the dead to live there! (24)
Having heard this, their father, as if struck by a thunderbolt, questioned them with humility: "By the power of what merit are you being led to the city? (25)
"O you great sinners, you ought to tell me who he is.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "A lamp was lit before Vāsudeva. (26)
By that very same deed, we have been sent as messengers to the abode of Viṣṇu;
for even one who performs the lighting of a lamp for Viṣṇu without desire [for reward] attains this. (27)
Having abandoned the sins accumulated over ten million births, he who offers a lamp with devotion during the days of Kārtika, the festival of Hari, shall go to the abode of Hari. (28)
No one, except for Hari himself, is able to fully describe the merit of that person who, with devotion, offers a lamp filled with ghee in the abode of Hari. (29)
What need has he for a thousand horse-sacrifices?
He who performs a horse-sacrifice on the day of Hari goes to heaven.
"And the giver of a lamp during Kārttika shall go to the abode of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, those messengers then departed just as they had come.
The messengers of Viṣṇu, having placed him upon their chariot, went to that abode of Viṣṇu;
indeed, his stay in the presence of Viṣṇu lasted for a hundred manvantaras.
Then, by the grace of Hari, she became the daughter of a mortal king;
endowed with sons and grandsons, she enjoyed worldly pleasures for a long time.
From here, having departed, they go to Goloka by means of service to Hari.
Sūta said:
"The mortal who listens with devotion to this supreme majesty of Dīpa [attains that state]. (34)
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu. ||35||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gift of Lamps," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||3||
The Fourth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, when is the greatness of this [work] celebrated by people?
Speak of your own nature as a boatman upon the ocean of worldly existence.
Sūta said:
Listen, O best of sages, for I shall explain that which you have asked;
formerly, this was asked by Nārada from Brahmā in the abode of the gods.
Nārada said:
O Grandfather, tell me the greatness of this victory so that, having heard it, I may go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (3)
Brahmā said: Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall speak before you.
By fasting on this day, one attains victory and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Sage, by remembering or chanting [this], the sin accumulated over seven lifetimes is destroyed;
how much more so for one who performs it while observing a fast? (5)
The Janmāṣṭamī and Navamī in the month of Caitra are auspicious when bright;
the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Kumbha and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in Meṣa [are likewise auspicious]. (6)
The Durgāṣṭamī in the bright fortnight of Āśvina, and the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the Śravaṇā asterism—
these six are proclaimed as being of great merit and bestowing auspicious victory.

The Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī occurring on the preceding day (the seventh lunar tithi) is renowned as the destroyer of sins; it is equal to ten million sacrifices and equal to tens of thousands of sacred pilgrimage sites.
One who fasts on this day attains the same fruit as one who gives a thousand cows as a gift every single day. ||9||
The fruit that one obtains by giving a thousand loads of gold at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse,
that same fruit one attains by fasting on the day of Jayantī.
One obtains that same fruit by fasting on the day of Jayantī as one does from [giving] thousands of black antelope skins and hundreds of sesame-cow gifts. 11.
Whatever fruit results from the gift of thousands of millions of maidens, that same fruit one obtains by fasting on the day of Jayantī. ||12||
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving away this entire earth together with its oceans, that same fruit one attains by fasting on the day of Jayantī. (13)
The merit that one obtains from constructing ponds, wells, tanks, and the like at a temple, one attains that same fruit by fasting on this [Jayantī] day. 14.
He who, endowed with devotion, performs service toward his mother, father, and teachers, obtains that same fruit by fasting on this Jayantī day. (15)

O Jaya, the merit that belongs to those who have devoted themselves to visiting sacred fords for the sake of removing calamities, and who are firm in their vow of truth, is attained by you through this fast.
Whatever merit is found in the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, or the waters of the Sarasvatī,
one obtains that same merit by bathing in you, O Jayantī, when fasting on this day.
Whatever merit belongs to those who perform the *śrāddha* for their ancestors at the end of an *iṃdu* [lunar month], one obtains that same fruit by fasting on this *Jaya* day. (18)
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather, tell me who has performed what unprecedented deed.
Brahmā said:
By Kārtavīrya, Karṇa, and the wise Kumāra. ||19||
It was performed in ancient times by Sagara,
Dilīpa, and Kākutstha, as well as by Gautama, Gārgya, and the wise Jāmadagnya.

On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the virtuous son of Draupadī, who was created by Vālmīki as an unprecedented being, grants the desires of those who have cut [the hair] on that day.
The eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) specifically conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism (Prājāpatya-ṛkṣa) should be observed every year for the sake of pleasing the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi). //22//
The sin accumulated over ten million births is dissolved in a single moment by one who,
having mastered the senses, performs a night vigil with unwavering devotion.
He should be worshipped individually with incense, flowers, food offerings, and other gifts; O Brahmin, he who performs this Jayantī fast in such a manner [attains victory]. ||24||
The sin accumulated over ten million births, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly, [is destroyed]. ||25||
By the grace of the son of Devakī, that [sin] which is dissolved by half a watch (yāma) is consumed by those lowest of men who eat upon the arrival of this lunar day (tithi).
The sin arising from the three worlds is undoubtedly consumed by this [penance];
likewise, all the sacred fords beginning with the ocean and all places of liberation [are attained]. (27)
All the Geyas, those who perform rigorous vows, reside in his house;
all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the deities reside in his abode. ||28||
O great sage, a man who, through devotion, conquers these [senses] and worships her who is dear to Kṛṣṇa, beholds her as she is perceived in the Vedas and Purāṇas. (29)
If a man does not perform the Kṛṣṇa-Rādhā Aṣṭamī vow with devotion— neither equal to nor exceeding it—
he shall become a cruel rākṣasa.
O twice-born one, that man who, being exceedingly deluded in soul,
indulges in sexual intercourse on the day of Hari, eats of the great hell as if it were a meal.
One hundred and one generations of one's family, both past and future, would surely fall into the most terrible hell because of providing you with food. (32)
O tiger among sages, when the moon is in conjunction with Rohiṇī on a Wednesday, it is equal to ten million vows performed by those who have conquered their senses.
In the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages,
she who destroys sins brings victory when performed according to the correct ritual procedure.
Whoever causes the Purāṇa of Padmanābha to be recited during the vigil burns away the sins accumulated since birth like a heap of cotton. (35)
The man who listens with devotion to the Purāṇa on the day of Hari [Ekādaśī], his sin accumulated over ten million births perishes at that very moment. (36)
O Sage, on the day of Padmanābha, one should worship the reciter;
having uplifted ten million members of his lineage, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.
The man who, turning his back on this [teaching], observes a fast here for the sake of victory, being devoid of all true dharma, will certainly go to hell. ||38||
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps filled with ghee, and with feelings of devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa. ||39||
The man who, by means of this rite, attains victory over his enemies,
shall, through devotion, deliver twenty-one generations of men.
There shall be no misfortune, no widowhood, and no quarreling in the home;
he shall experience no opposition and shall never witness the loss of wealth. 41.
Whatever desires one who observes this fast seeks to accomplish,
he attains them all in their entirety and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Those who are eternally devoted to Viṣṇu with most intense minds are victorious;
they are blessed, they are of noble lineage, they are lords, and they are wise scholars.
Whatever vehicles, sacred fords, vows, and observances there may be, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of this day. 44.
O child, he who, together with his wife, observes the eighth day of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa during both fortnights of the month of Bhādrapada, attains the presence of Hari.
He who always performs a vow that produces merit for Hari, and who observes the fast of Jayantī, goes to Viṣṇu’s Vaikuṇṭha. (46)
The beloved of Hari quickly destroys the sin of one who is devoid of right conduct, fallen from his lineage, bereft of fame, or born of a base womb—just as fire destroys a heap of cotton. 47.
One who observes the Jaya-vow completely consumes all sins, even those equal to Mount Meru, such as the killing of a Brahmin. 48.
One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires wealth obtains wealth;
one who desires liberation obtains liberation; and one who fasts on this day attains victory. (49)
Those whose minds are supremely intent on performing the Jaya-tīrtha rite reach the supreme goal, even if they have committed sins as grave as Yama himself. (50)
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to Nārada, he departed just as he had come.
O Brahmin, O Sage, I have also related that which I was asked by you.
And those who hear of this majesty and victory with a spirit of devotion, they too, liberated from all sins, go to the supreme abode. (52)
O Brahmin, those sinful men who behold a reciter of the Purāṇas, as well as one who is victorious and intensely devoted, go to the supreme state.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Jayantī," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada within the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa. ||4||
The Fifth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O one of great wisdom, tell me how a person may become bereft of sons.
By what action did he become the son of a charioteer, and by what [action]? ||1||
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen to that which was previously asked by the high-souled Nārada and what Brahmā then told him.
Nārada said:
O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all principles!
By what action, O Lotus-born One, does a mortal become childless? (3)
O you who are devoted to the welfare of all living beings, tell me—while I am listening—who could possibly have acted with such wickedness in my presence? (4)
By what karma is a daughter born, or how does one become a eunuch?
By what cause does one have stillborn children, or become a woman who has lost her children and is thus exceedingly distressed?
O Brahmin, tell me: by what merit might a son be born again? (5)
Brahmā said: I shall relate it in brief; listen to that with attention.
You ask for a narrative that indeed produces wonder in those who hear it.
The conduct of a mortal and that of a Brāhmaṇa in a previous birth—whether one takes away or causes to be taken away [the property of others] in this life—one will indeed become childless. (7)
In this very life, that mortal who, endowed with faith, listens to the Purāṇas and indeed makes a gift of land with its crops, [attains the supreme goal]. (8)
By giving a golden cow of many virtues, yielding much milk, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
and likewise a golden image, his son will certainly be born.
In a previous birth, she who kills another's child through sheer deceit will certainly become deprived of her own children. 10.
A woman endowed with faith should perform the gift of a golden image;
she should drink the water from the feet of a Brahmin with devotion.
One should listen to the Purāṇas and give abundant sacrificial fees;
she will have many children and live with her sons, of this there is no doubt. (12)
He who, upon seeing a child submerged in water, rescues him with a vehicle, will certainly remain childless in this life, whether he be a man without sons or a woman without daughters. (13)
One should give a bull and a pumpkin gourd, along with gold and cloth,
as a gift to a Brāhmaṇa, and perform the auspicious Bālavratam.
One should likewise cause a fair-complexioned maiden to hear the Purāṇas;
indeed, a son who destroys all his sins will be born to him. (15)
O twice-born one, that mortal who, out of anger, treats a guest who is free from desire as if he were a punishment, will certainly become childless in his next birth.
One should perform worship with devotion toward a Brāhmaṇa and a guest; likewise, one should provide gifts of food and water, as well as a beautiful temple for the gods. 17.
Whatever woman a man may have killed as an embryo in a previous birth, he will certainly become one whose children die at birth, even if she was not yet delivered. 18.
That woman who observes the day of Hari (Ekādaśī) together with her husband shall possess good sons and be fortunate with her husband in every birth. (19)
Whatever man, even a Śūdra deluded by ignorance, might commit the theft of a cow's wealth,
or the abduction of a Brāhmaṇa woman, he becomes a eunuch as a result of that deed.
O twice-born one, he who, having committed this transgression, subsequently performs meritorious deeds,
will, by the power of that merit, have a daughter born to him in this world.
O twice-born one, in the Tretā Yuga there was a king named Śrīdhara;
he was wealthy but childless, and his wife was Hemaprabhāvatī.
He questioned Vyāsa—who was learned in all the scriptures and desired the welfare of the entire world—once he had arrived: "O twice-born one, how is it that I am childless? (23)
Having heard the king’s words full of humility,
he spoke [to him] as he sat upon a throne fashioned from gold and other precious materials.
The king and queen, having washed his feet with great joy, both drank that water from his feet which destroys all sins. (25)
Vyāsa said:
O King, listen to that which you have asked—by what karma this queen of yours became childless, despite being devoted to her husband. (26)
In a previous birth, you were known by the name Candravaratnu,
and your wife was known as Vaiśaṅkarī, whose name was Śubhrāṅgī.
Once, seeing their low-born son submerged in water on the road, they both went away with indifference; he then met his death.
"O King and Queen, you two have come here by the power of much merit;
yet, due to the ripening of that very karma, no son shall be born to you two. (29)
The king said: "O Lord, by what merit now is a son born?
For the life of men who are childless is indeed meaningless. (30)
Vyāsa said:
Give a pumpkin gourd with its skin, a bull together with gold;
likewise, perform the gift-giving for a Brāhmaṇa and the Kuru-bāla-vrata.
Likewise, listen to the Dehīpurāṇa while offering a fair-complexioned maiden;
there a son shall indeed be born, who destroys all sins. ||32||
Brahmā said:
Having heard this supreme gift spoken by Vyāsa, as well as the hearing of the Purāṇas, the king, his sins having been removed, performed them accordingly. (33)
Then, in the middle of his reign, the son became honored by all;
he became a sovereign emperor, handsome, and the leader of his lineage. ||34||
Sūta said:
He who hears this with devotion performs an excellent gift;
one who is childless obtains a son. This has been told by me in brief. (35)

O twice-born one, that woman who, having heard this with devotion, performs the worship of a Brāhmaṇa according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, shall always possess excellent sons. (36)
Whoever should devotedly offer gold, silver, clothing, flowers, garlands, sandalwood, and camphor to the book, it shall destroy all sins. (37)
O twice-born one, he who was a fool in a previous birth and a slayer of Brahmins and children will have a cruel son for seven successive births.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Ripening of Karma," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada within the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Sixth Chapter.
Śaunaka said: "O Sūta, by what merit is Vaikuṇṭha attained?"
In the same way, tell that to me who am not hearing it, so that I may cross over the ocean of existence. ||1||
Sūta said:
Excellent, excellent, O best of sages, you who bring about all auspiciousness!
I shall relate in brief that which destroys the sins of those who hear it. 2.
O best of the twice-born, listen to the merit of him who indeed gives such a house constructed of clay to a Brāhmaṇa devoted to Viṣṇu. ||3||
And that brahmin, freed from all sins, shall dwell eternally in a celestial mansion in the world of Viṣṇu and be honored there. ||4||
Whoever gives a palatial mansion to Viṣṇu or to a Brāhmaṇa, having reached the abode of Hari, shall certainly become a dweller in heaven. (5)
O twice-born one, having gone to the city of Viṣṇu accompanied by ten million kinsmen,
you shall dwell in a golden mansion and enjoy pleasures at your ease.
O Sage, even Brahmā, the creator of all things, is unable to calculate the extent of the merit that arises from the establishment of a Brāhmaṇa. //7//

The merit of those who count [the beads] is like that of the *terena* grass; the merit of those who do not count them is like the raindrops from a storm; and the merit of those who do not even count them, yet establish themselves in Brahman, is beyond calculation by the Creator. ||8||
In ancient times, Brahmā was questioned by Nārada regarding the origin of worldly existence;
the Creator explained it to him—listen to that, O great sage. (9)
O Brahmin, formerly in the Dvāpara age, there was a most beautiful woman named Vāranārī,
who had lovely hair, eyes like a doe’s, a slender waist, and a charming smile.
When will those with tremulous eyes, who are joined with all sins, cause others to fall into hell by singing [the name] of another region? (11)
Shaking off her fatigue, she went to the temple with her attendants;
having sat there for a moment, she partook of betel-leaf. ||12||
Out of curiosity, she applied the remaining powder to the wall of the palace; then, for the sake of obtaining wealth, she departed for the city to become a procuress.
She had suddenly made an appointment with a certain lover;
however, having been deluded at night, she went instead to the brothel.
The Vaiśya did not come to the appointment; he was seen by the hunter, distressed.
"How is it that my beloved has not come? Has she been devoured by snakes and tigers? (15)
How could he have come here, abandoning his home and agitated by desire?
Could he truly have become so lustful as to desire another man's wife? (16)
Reflecting thus within his heart, O twice-born one, he did not enter the city out of fear of the city guards,
as the public thoroughfares were blocked by those fierce men.
Then, in that very interval, a hungry tiger capable of assuming any form at will was dispatched by Kāla-deva; it arrived and devoured that brahmin. (18)
Then those messengers of his brother, who rained down terrors, arrived at Girikūṭā to bring Yamunā there by means of that evil deed.

O twice-born one, having seized leathern thongs, ropes, and mallets, they— whose feet were crooked, whose mouths were gaping, and whose noses were prominent— possessed many fangs and went toward the water.
They bound the intoxicated courtesan with leather thongs, while [the gods] bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and wore forest garlands. 21.
Sent by the God of gods, who is affectionate toward his devotees, they resembled dark clouds and possessed lotus-like faces that were radiant. 22.
Wearing turbans, possessing beautiful noses, and adorned with divine earrings,
the messengers of the high-souled Viṣṇu saw them as they traveled along the path.
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: "Who are you, of such deformed appearance, looking as if you were variegated and hideous?
Having abducted this most excellent woman, the beloved of Viṣṇu, where are you going?"
Having heard these words, they departed swiftly.
Then those messengers of Viṣṇu, endowed with wrath and possessed of great strength,
struck down the messengers of Yama, the lord of the world.
And by all his soldiers, who were armed with multitudes of weapons such as discuses and possessed a radiance equal to ten million suns, he was overwhelmed; they all fled, crying out in distress.
O twice-born one, terrified, they related the entire account to Yama;
and Yama, having heard that story, spoke to Citragupta: "Ha! (27)
Dharma said:
"By what merit did this woman, having been born on earth, attain liberation?
Tell me all of this as you see fit, for we are asking you. (28)
Citragupta said: "O Lord of the World, listen to what she has accumulated from birth: though her sins are very many, if there be any merit, let that be heard. (29)
Once, a courtesan, adorned with all her royal ornaments, went swiftly to a certain city named Jārakā, seeking wealth and grain. (30)
Staying there in that temple, he ate the root;
out of curiosity, he then applied the remaining powder to the wall.
By the power of that merit, the courtesan, freed from her sin, has departed from your punishment and gone toward Vaikuṇṭha. (32)
Sūta said:
O twice-born one, having heard these words, Yama then directed his mind elsewhere, as did the female messenger along with her attendants.
Having ascended his face, which was joined with the divine royal swan of Danda,
she went to the world of Viṣṇu, surrounded by the hands of Viṣṇu’s attendants.
By the command of Śrī Viṣṇu, she remained in a palatial mansion together with ten million members of her family, and indeed, O Brahmin, she enjoyed various pleasures there.
O best of the twice-born, who can know what merit would accrue to one who, out of devotion, diligently offers powder at the temple of Hari? (36)
Whoever indeed reads this chapter with devotion or listens to it with reverence, being liberated from all sins, goes to the abode of Hari. (37)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Seventh Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O one of great wisdom, tell me by what action one goes to Goloka.
By what means can a person cross over this ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to traverse?
And on that eighth lunar day, the supreme majesty of Rādhā’s charioteer [is proclaimed]. ||1||
Sūta said:
O great sage, in former times Nārada questioned Brahmā regarding this;
listen to that in brief, O twice-born one, as he asked it.
Nārada said: O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O best among those who know all the scriptures,
please describe before me the account of Rādhājanmāṣṭamī.
O Lord, what is the fruit of her merit, and by whom was it performed in the past?
O twice-born one, what sin would accrue to those people who do not perform it? (4)
By what procedure should that vow be performed, and when?
From whom was Sārādhā born? Tell me this from the very beginning.
Brahmā said:
O child, listen with great concentration to the Rādhā-janmāṣṭamī; I shall describe it to you in brief, though it is complete only in the presence of Hari.
O Nārada, one is not even able to describe that meritorious fruit;
[by it], great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, accumulated over ten million births, are destroyed. ||7||
For those who perform [this] even once with devotion, that [sin] perishes instantly;
a man obtains that fruit which is gained by a thousand Ekādaśīs. ||8||
The merit of Rādhājanmāṣṭamī is a hundred times greater than that;
it yields the same fruit as is obtained by giving away gold equal in weight to Mount Meru.
By performing the Rādhāṣṭamī vow even once,
one obtains a merit a hundred times greater than that which is acquired by people through the gift of a thousand maidens.
The fruit that people obtain by bathing in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā is attained on the eighth day of the month of Vṛṣabhānu. (11)
A person obtains the fruit of the Kṛṣṇaprāṇapriyā-aṣṭamī; even if a sinner performs this vow with negligence or even without faith. ||12||
One who goes to Viṣṇu’s abode shall be accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
O child, in a former Kṛta Yuga, there was a most beautiful and excellent woman. (13)
With a slender waist, eyes like those of a doe, beautiful in voice, and possessing a lovely smile;
with fine hair and charming ears—she was known by the name Līlāvatī. (14)
By her, many very firm sins were committed;
once, desiring wealth, she went out from before herself.
Having gone to another city, he saw there many virtuous people in the temple of the Sun-god,
devoted to the Rādhāṣṭamī vow.
They worship the supreme form of Rādhā with devotion, using incense, flowers, lamps, various garments, and diverse kinds of fruits. (17)
Some sang, some danced, and some recited the supreme hymn; others joyfully played cymbals, flutes, drums, and cow-horns. ||18||
Seeing them in such a state, she was filled with curiosity; she approached them and, full of humility, questioned them. (19)
"O virtuous ones, what are you doing to be so filled with joy? O meritorious ones, tell me, for I am full of humility. (20)
Having heard her words, those devoted to the welfare of others' affairs and intent upon the vows of Viṣṇu began to speak as follows.

The observers of the Rādhā-vow said: "Since Śrī Rādhikā was born from her body on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, we shall diligently observe that Aṣṭamī vow from its very commencement. (22)
The sin produced by killing a cow, that born of theft, that born of killing a Brahmin, as well as that from abducting another's wife and that born of violating the Guru’s bed. (23)
It quickly destroys for men the sin born of betraying trust as well as that produced by the killing of a woman; thus the Aṣṭamī performed on the eighth day [destroys] these sins.
And having heard their words, which destroy all sins, he reflected again and again, "I shall do this. (25)
There, having observed the highest vow together with those who were likewise observing vows,
she, being pure, met her end by the bite of a serpent through the power of fate.
Then, by his command, messengers with nooses and mallets in their hands arrived to bring her back; they bound her with great difficulty. (27)
When his mind became intent on bringing [them] back to his own abode,
then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing conchs, discs, and maces.
They quickly fashioned a beautiful golden celestial chariot yoked with royal swans,
using the edges of their discuses as shears and making the noose itself the binding cord.
They placed that woman, freed from all sin,
upon a chariot and led her to the enchanting city of Viṣṇu known as Goloka.
O dear one, by the grace of that vow, Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā reside there;
therefore, a person of deluded intellect should not fail to perform the Rādhāṣṭamī vow.
There is no deliverance from hell even in hundreds of millions of kalpas for those women who do not observe this auspicious vow. 32.
It brings joy to Rādhā and Viṣṇu and destroys all sins;
those who go to this city of Aṅga fall into hell for a long time. (33)
Once, having attained birth on this earth, she was certainly a widow;
at another time, she was struck by wicked crowds upon the earth like a calf.
Having become a cow, she, being exceedingly distressed, approached Sāma Māṃtika;
weeping again and again, she made known her suffering. (35)
Having heard those words, I went to the presence of Viṣṇu; and Kṛṣṇa was quickly informed of the entire mass of suffering upon the earth.
He said: "Go, O Brahmin, to the surface of the earth along with the gods;
I too shall go there afterwards together with my hosts. (37)
Having heard that, accompanied by the gods, he came to the surface of the earth;
then Kṛṣṇa summoned Rādhā, who was dearer to him than life itself.
He spoke these words: "O Goddess, I shall go to the surface of the earth;
you, for the sake of destroying the burden of the earth, must go to the mortal realm. (39)
Having heard this, Sārādhā then returned to the earth on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada. ||40||
She who was born on the sacrificial ground of Vṛṣabhānu as one even more excellent than Aditi,
was seen in her divine form when the ground had been purified for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having subdued the king and brought him to his own palace, he took the queen and, having led her there, protected her. ||42||
Thus has been told by you, O child, that which was asked;
it must be guarded, guarded, guarded with great effort.
Sūta said: Whoever hears this with devotion— which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human existence—
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the abode of Hari at the end.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of Śrī Rādhāṣṭamī," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada. ||7||
The Eighth Chapter.
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O Teacher, why was the churning of the ocean performed in ancient times?
A curiosity has arisen in my heart to hear [this] from you, O wielder of the fly-whisk. ||1||
Sūta said:
O Brahmin, I shall tell you in brief the cause of the churning of the ocean;
listen to this history of the dispute between Durvāsas and Indra.
Once, the great ascetic Durvāsas, possessed of great luster, a Brahmarṣi born of the Lord, set out for heaven to see Indra.
At that time, he saw the Lord of Śacī mounted upon his elephant;
having seen him, the great sage gave him the Pārijāta garland.
Having taken that garland and placed it upon the head of Indra’s elephant,
the king of the gods, Brahmā, set out toward the Nandana grove accompanied by his army.
Having cut the long garland from the elephant's trunk and cast it upon the surface of the earth,
the great sage, filled with great wrath, spoke to him as follows.
Since you, though endowed with the sole glory of the three worlds, treat [others] with contempt, your glory over the three worlds has surely perished; of this there is no doubt. (7)
Then Śakra departed quickly, and having returned once more to his own city,
he saw that the Mother of the Worlds had herself vanished from sight.
When the three worlds had vanished within that city of Antarddhānavatī,
everyone, overcome by hunger and thirst, cried out incessantly.
The clouds no longer rain, the reservoirs of water have dried up, and all these trees are withered, devoid of both fruit and flowers. (10)
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they all went into the presence of Brahmā;
they all related their suffering and grief to the Grandfather.
Having heard the words of the gods, Dhātṛ, together with the hosts of deities and the sages headed by Bhṛgu, set out for the Ocean of Milk.
He worshipped Viṣṇu on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk,
while the Creator (Brahmā) chanted the eight-syllabled mantra, meditating upon the Lord of the Universe.
Then the gracious Lord, having mounted Vainateya, arrived with compassion for all the inhabitants of heaven. ||14||
Having seen that Lord of the worlds, who wears yellow garments, has four arms, holds the conch, discus, and mace, and possesses eyes like lotuses; ||15||

With eyes overflowing with tears of joy, they praised Viṣṇu—the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence, adorned with a forest garland, his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem. (16)
They praised him with shouts of "Victory! and offered obeisances without ceasing.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O gods, choose a boon; for what purpose have you come here?"
"I am the giver of boons; I shall grant whatever you ask. ||17||
The gods said: "O Lord, the three worlds—along with the gods, asuras, and humans—are bereft of prosperity due to the curse of Brahmā born of compassion, and are afflicted by hunger and thirst. (18)
"Protect all these worlds; we have come to you for refuge.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The asuras have vanished due to the curse of Brahmā and Indrāṇī."
By whose mere sidelong glance the world is endowed with sovereignty—therefore, O all you gods, uproot the Golden Mountain (Sumeru). ||20||
"O gods, together with the Daityas, make the ocean of milk churn, having made it resonant with the sound 'maṃ daraṃ ghargharaṃ' and having encircled it with the king of serpents. (21)
Therefore, O gods, Lakṣmī, the mother of the world, will arise;
gladdened by her, you shall become highly fortunate, of this there is no doubt. (22)
"I myself shall support the mountain from all sides in the form of a tortoise.
Having said this, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu vanished.
O twice-born one, all the gods and asuras went to the churning of the ocean.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Effort for the Churning of the Ocean," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Ninth Chapter.
Sūta said:
Then the hosts of immortals, along with the Gandharvas and the Dānavas, [approached].
Having uprooted Mount Mandara, they cast it into the ocean of waters.
Then the eternal, glorious, and compassionate Lord of the Universe supported the base of the mountain upon his back in the form of a tortoise.
O twice-born one, they then thoroughly churned that ocean of milk; as it was being churned on the eleventh day, first there emerged [the Kaustubha gem].
But seeing that kālakūṭa poison, they all fled;
then, seeing them fleeing, Śaṅkara spoke this: ||4||
O hosts of immortals, do not show any concern;
I shall quickly ward off the great poison Kālakūṭa. (5)
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Pārvatī, meditating on Nārāyaṇa within his heart,
recited the great mantra that removes danger from poison.
By the power of the Great Mantra, the great poison was digested and vanished;
it was the three names of Hari, the slayer of the Daityas, beginning with "Acyuta. (7)

One who, being diligent and devoted, causes [the mantra] beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ* to be recited [for another], for that person there is no fear of poison, consumption, fire, or likewise death. (8)
Then, with delighted minds, the gods churned the ocean of milk;
from that, Alakṣmī arose, black-faced and red-eyed.
Bearing a body with rough, matted hair and wrinkles,
that eldest sister indeed said to the gods, "What must be done by me?"
O gods, speak thus to that goddess who is a vessel of sorrow: "In the houses of those men where quarreling with the goddess prevails... (11)
There we shall grant them a place of residence, O auspicious one, for those men who speak harsh words and those who speak falsehoods. (12)
Those who eat during the twilight hours cause suffering to abide in that house;
for there, indeed, are potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, husks, and charcoal.
There is no doubt that the highest place shall be yours there;
[but as for] those lowest of men who eat without having washed their feet— (14)
In that house, everything remained as it was, bestowing suffering and poverty; they made the washing of that [vessel] with sand, salt, and charcoal. (15)
In their houses, Duhkhada remained together with Kali;
those lowest of men who eat mushrooms and bilva fruits are the ones left behind. (16)
Their dwelling is in houses that bestow impurity upon the eldest [son]: sesame paste, bitter gourd, and the people who eat the leaves of the *potikā* plant. (17)
There is no doubt that you shall dwell in the houses of those evil-minded ones who eat the meat of the black monkey (kalaṃ bukaṃ) and the palāṇḍu (onion). ||18||
O inauspicious one, you always dwell there where there are no teachers, gods, or guests, which is devoid of sacrifice and charity, and where the sound of the Vedas does not exist. 19.
O inauspicious one, you always reside where there is quarreling between husband and wife, where the worship of ancestors and gods is absent, and where people are addicted to gambling.
Where people take pleasure in the wives of others, where they seize the property of others,
and where there is no honor shown to Brahmins, virtuous men, or the elderly;
In that place, she dwells exceedingly, bestowing sin and poverty.
Having thus instructed the eldest of the Asuras, who was beloved by all in the Kali age,
they once again, with great composure, performed the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Churning of the Ocean," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. ||9||
The Tenth Chapter.
Sūta said:
From him [Kaśyapa] were then born Airāvata and likewise the horse Uccaiḥśravas.
Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, Surabhi, and the origin of the Apsarases. ||1||
Then, at the time of dawn on the twelfth day, when the sun had risen,
the Great Lakṣmī, Śrī, appeared, adorned with all auspicious marks.
The deities of Dharma beheld that Great Goddess, their mother, the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s heart, who is the delight of all living beings. ||3||
The cool-rayed moon was born as the brother of Lakṣmī, and from that [nectar] the nectar itself was produced;
then Tulasī, the wife of Hari and the purifier of the world, came into being. 4.
Having restored that mountain as it was before, their desires being now fulfilled,
they gathered together, praised their mother, and recited the supreme Śrīsūkta.
Then the goddess Prasannāsā said to all the gods: "O best of gods, choose a boon; I am a granter of boons; may it be well with you."
The gods said:
Be gracious, O Goddess Kamalā, O Mother, beloved of Hari!
Without you, the world is empty; protect our lives. (7)
Thus addressed, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, replied:
"Now I shall effect the protection of the life-breath of all living beings. (8)
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa, the compassionate Lord of the World, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, suddenly manifested himself. 9.
Then those gods, having prostrated before the Lord of the worlds, offered praise; with palms joined in reverence, they spoke, their voices faltering with joy. (10)
Take Lakṣmī, the mother of Viṣṇu, your beloved queen,
who never departs from you, for the sake of protecting the cycle of worldly existence.
As long as he did not make a formal vow, Indra continued to carry him away repeatedly.
Lakṣmī said:
O Madhusūdana, how is it that you wish to marry me, the younger sister, as your wife, without first marrying the elder sister, Alakṣmī?
Or, while the eldest sister remains unmarried, the youngest is married off. ||12||
Sūta said:

"O gods, why have you all arrived with such distressed faces?"
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Lord of the World, for this reason we have come;
O best of gods, O creator of the worlds, I shall tell you that.
Intoxicated by the boon granted by Śūlin, that unassailable king [Kamsa] struck the Earth;
she was tormented by his blow from his hand. 23.
Having previously granted a boon, he was overcome by delusion and spoke thus:
"Except for my sister's son, death shall come to you all. (24)
Therefore, go yourself to subdue that invincible Devaka;
having taken birth in the womb of Devakī, you shall then go to Gokula.
Urged by Brahmā, the Lord replied to the wielder of the trident:
"O Lord of Gods, give Pārvatī; she will return after staying for one year."
Accompanied by Umā and Arakṣā, the lotus-seated Lord, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
then set out on his journey toward Mathurā.
There, the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara) took birth in the womb of Devakī;
meanwhile, the deer-eyed Śarvāṇī resided within the belly of Yaśodā.
Having rested for nine months within her womb for a period ending on the ninth day,
[he was born] on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
On that night, which resounded deeply with the cries of jackals and was joined by the star Rohiṇī,
the Lord of the World was born as Kaṃsa’s enemy from Vasudeva.
Yaśodā gave birth to a daughter, Vairāṭī, and a son named Padmanābha, who had lotus-like hands and eyes like lotus petals. ||31||
Then, seeing that [the chariot] had been brought, Ānakadundubhi began to rejoice;
and at that moment, Kuntī spoke to Devakī, who was standing there with the Asuras.
"Go to Vairāṭī; it is said that her son has been restored.
Having given your own son to Yaśodā, bring back her daughter. (33)
Having heard his words, Vasudeva also became sorrowful;
taking the child Aṅkeka, he set out toward Vairāṭī.
On that path, along the middle way, there was the Yamunā river, filled with water—terrible, very long, and possessing a deep flood of water. (35)
Having seen this and standing on the bank while gazing at the Yamunā,
Vasudeva, afflicted by grief, lamented with intense anxiety.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? For I have been utterly deceived by fate.
How shall I go from here to Vairāṭī, to the palace of Nanda? (37)
There, his father was joyfully deceived by Hari through his illusory power;
standing on the bank for a mere moment, he gazed upon the Yamunā. ||38||
Then, upon seeing her again, she too became knee-deep in water in an instant;
seeing her, he rose up in joy and set out as before. (39)
Having created an illusion, the Lord of the World fell from his father's lap into the water.
Seeing that son fallen, he cried out "Alas! Alas! and was deeply distressed. (40)
Furthermore, having resolved to employ a great stratagem according to that very method, he said:
"O Lord of the worlds, O best of gods, protect me and your son! (41)
Seeing his father torn apart by the wheel, Kṛṣṇa was moved with compassion;
having finished his water-sports, he went once more to his father's lap. (42)
Just as that best of the Yadus went to the house of Nanda,
having given his son to Yaśodā, he brought back her daughter.
Then, having reached his own palace, he handed over his daughter to his wife; meanwhile, the enemy of the demons (Kṛṣṇa) received news that Devakī had given birth.
Then messengers set out to bring the son and the daughter;
having arrived at Ānakadundubhi’s [Nanda’s] house, those messengers proceeded to lead the daughter away.
Having forcibly dragged her away from Devakī and Vasudeva,
she seized Kaṃsa by his messengers and delivered him to the enemy of the gods (Viṣṇu).
O Great King, because of her virtuous conduct, he became difficult to overcome and filled with fear;
she possessed the luster of pure gold and a face like the full moon. 47.
Seeing her with eyes flashing like lightning, that best of asuras laughed and commanded: "Take her and throw her upon a stone!"
Having received the command, those asuras set out to crush her;
however, Gaurī, with the speed of lightning, went to Mount Śaṅkarātika.
Gaurī said:
"Listen, O King, I shall tell you where your supreme enemy resides; he is hidden in the abode of the Dasyus, O best of Asuras. (50)
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the queen, he departed for his own palace;
and having heard those words of the goddess, King Kaṃsa became deeply distressed.
He said to his sister Pūtanā: "Go to that man's home;
having killed that son by means of a stratagem, return with much of what you desire. (52)
“O auspicious one, I shall kill my enemy; come, let us go very quickly!
Having received this command, that rākṣasī set out toward Gokula.
By means of my illusory power (māyā), I entered that cave in the form of a mountain; having taken up a great burden within the clouds, I have come here to this Gokula.
Thinking she had entered unnoticed at the door of a cowherd's house, she went inside, lifted up a child, gave him her breast, and attained the state of an outcaste. (55)
Then, having cast down the cart, crushed Tṛṇāvarta and the others,
and subdued Kālīya, he subsequently arrived at Mathurā.
Having gone from Akaṃsā, whom did the cruel one defeat in battle?
This, O King, has been told to you: the vow for the birthday of Viṣṇu. (57)

Having heard this, those who have committed sins are liberated; what more could possibly remain to be done? Whatever mortal man or woman performs this vow of Hari, [they shall attain their goal]. (58)
Having attained incomparable sovereignty in that birth where one's every desire is fulfilled,
the third lunar day joined with the second (pūrvaviddhā) and the sixth must not be observed.
One should diligently avoid the eighth lunar day when it coincides with the seventh, as well as the eighth, eleventh, fourteenth, and new moon days, for those desiring merit, pleasure, or wealth.
Even if it falls on a day other than the Arka-nakṣatra (the Sun's asterism), the eighth lunar day joined with the ninth should be observed;
provided that at sunrise there is at least a trace of the eighth, and the ninth is complete.
If the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) is joined with Rohiṇī for even a single Muhūrta, it becomes complete;
likewise, if the eighth day falls on a Wednesday and is accompanied by Rohiṇī.
O King, what is the use of ten million vows?
It is as if one has performed the Soma sacrifice when the Moon is in conjunction with the ninth lunar day (Navamī), even if it occurs on a Monday or a Wednesday. 63.
Even in a hundred years, it may be found or it may not be found:
the eighth lunar day conjoined with the ninth should never be observed without the presence of the constellation [Revatī].
Even if the seventh lunar day is pierced by the eighth, when the eighth of the dark fortnight is joined with Rohiṇī for even a moment, a fraction, or a muhūrta; ||65||
That very [day] joined with the seventh lunar day (saptamī) is certainly not to be taken on a Friday;
how much less so on a Wednesday, and especially on a Monday? ||66||
How much more so, O King of Men, when the ninth lunar day is joined with [the asterism] Ākula-koti, which bestows liberation;
one should abandon the eighth lunar day by piercing it with the seventh.
"Like the Ganges, the source of the jar untouched by wine,
Dilīpa said:
'By whom was this first composed, and by whom was it revealed?'"
O Great Sage, tell me, what is the merit and what is the fruit? ||68||
Vasiṣṭha said:
The great king Citrasena was exceedingly sinful and very wicked;
having committed incest with a woman who should not be approached, he also stole the gold of a twice-born man.
Always insatiable for liquor, constantly devoted to meat obtained through improper means,
and thus joined with such sins, he was perpetually intent on the slaughter of living beings.
He always held conversation with the fallen cāṇḍālas;
thus did the king set his mind upon hunting. (71)
Having recognized a tiger in the forest and having surrounded it on all sides, he spoke these words to all his soldiers with great attention: ||72||
"I alone shall slay him; whoever else shall strike at him, he is to be killed—of this there is no doubt. Having said this, the tiger went along the king's path. (73)
Even though he was ashamed, the king followed after the tiger;
with great concentration, he pursued the tiger despite many hardships and sufferings.
Afflicted by the distress of hunger and thirst on the bank of the Yamunā at twilight, that day—conjoined with the eighth lunar tithi and the Rohiṇī asterism—was his birthday. (75)
O lord of men, on the following day, the maidens indeed performed a vow at the Yamunā with various offerings,
materials, and most beautiful incense and lamps.
Seeing fragrant flowers, beautiful substances such as saffron and the like, and food of many excellent qualities, his mind was inclined toward eating them. (77)
The king said:
"Due to the lack of food, my life-breaths will surely depart this very day.
The women said:
O sinless King, on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight of Janmashtami, you must not eat.
He who eats at the birth of Kṛṣṇa has undoubtedly eaten vulture flesh, dog meat, crow meat, and even beef. (79)
O King, what defect has arisen among those men dwelling in the world that, while the vital breath remains within the body, they have not conquered their enemies? (80)
In that regard, for one who has not observed the fast, the instruction is that the abode of Yama awaits;
whatever is offered to the ancestors daily will not be accepted by them according to the prescribed rule. (81)
"O King, all our ancestors have been cast down because of you for the sake of food.
Having heard this, O lord of men, the king then undertook a vow.
Joyfully bringing some flowers, a little incense, and a cloth,
one who is engaged in this vow performs the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) with these offerings.
By the power of this vow, Citrasena went to the abode of Hari. ||83||
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he went along with his ancestors;
yet the fruit obtained by going to Mathurā and beholding the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa is superior to that. 84.
That fruit which is obtained by going to Dvārakā and beholding Hari, the Lord of the Universe, is attained by a person through the vow of Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī.
That fruit is attained by the destitute by performing the Janmāṣṭamī vow. ||85||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Harijanmāṣṭamī Vow," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O one of great wisdom, ocean of compassion, please tell me [the story] of the brāhmaṇa.
Out of compassion, tell me the greatness of all the castes and that of the most excellent one. ||1||
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the preceptor of all social orders;
he should be known as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, the refuge of all the immortals. (2)
O best of the twice-born, for that person who performs prostration with devotion toward a brāhmaṇa, perceiving him as Hari, his wealth and other blessings shall increase.
Seeing the Brahmin approach, Hari, though proud, did not even acknowledge him with contempt;
rather, he always desired to cut off his head.
Those of sinful intellect who hate a brahmin who has committed an offense,
and those who hate Hari— they should be known as destined for a terrible hell.
If one should look with anger upon a brahmin who has arrived seeking a favor,
Kṛtānta (the God of Death) indeed drives a heated needle into that person's foot.
That lowest of men, the fool, who utters threats against a Brahmin,
they place heated iron in his mouth at the presence of Yama’s messengers.
In whosever home the ascetic Bhumkteksmasura eats,
in that very home Kṛṣṇa himself eats along with the gods.
All sins, including the killing of a twice-born, perish for that man who partakes of even a single drop of the water from a brāhmaṇa’s nose. (9)
And if a man should devoutly wipe with his hand the ground washed by the battle, O twice-born one, I tell you the truth: he is liberated from all sins. (10)
By serving the lotus-like feet of a twice-born woman who is childless, whose children have died, or who has lost her husband, one obtains sons who live long lives. 11.
Whatever holy places exist within the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), whatever holy places exist in the ocean,
and whatever holy places exist in the sea— all of them reside at the feet of the twice-born.
Whose head is constantly sprinkled with the water from the mouths of the twice-born. ||12||
Having bathed in all sacred fords, he is liberated from all sins;
listen, O Śaunaka, as I shall describe this greatness that destroys evil. (13)
O ascetic, I shall relate to you an ancient history concerning the water from the feet of Brahmins.
Long ago, O best of the twice-born, there was a man who was devoted to the livelihood of a Vaiśya. (14)
In the Dvāpara age, there was a Śūdra named Bhīma who had committed a thousand Brahman-murders;
he was cruel and delighted in giving to everyone, and he later married a Vaiśya woman.
This Bhīma has fallen away from the conduct of a Śūdra and has violated the bed of his guru;
what more need I say of that robber one by one? His transgressions are beyond counting.
Once, O tiger among sages, a certain man of evil mind and wicked intent entered the residence of a brāhmaṇa.
Having gone there, he set his mind on taking wealth from that man's house;
he stayed there, near the outer gate of the brāhmaṇa. (18)
He spoke these words full of humility to the earth-dweller who was rich in asceticism:
"O Lord, please listen to my speech; may you look upon me with compassion. (19)
"I am afflicted by hunger; give me food, for my life-breaths will depart very soon. (20)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I am afflicted by hunger; I do not have the strength to speak even a single word.
Take this cooked rice, O Ḍulāni, and eat it as you please. (21)
"There is no father, no mother, no son, no uterine brother;
there is no wife, no maternal kin—all have died and departed from here. (22)
"I remain alone in this house, inactive, devoid of fortune, and without a guest; I am truly unable to endure dwelling here all by myself. (23)
Bhīma said:
"O best of the twice-born, I have no one else to serve, nor do I have anyone to depend upon.
I am a Śūdra by birth; having made my home here, I shall remain with you forever. (24)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his,
that lord of the earth then quickly prepared the cooking and gave him food, O ascetic.
Filled with joy, he remained there in the house of the twice-born, performing charming service full of affection for the Brahmin. (26)
"Today or tomorrow I shall bring back his wealth and my own as well;
when I have resolved to take it, I will not fail to bring it—of this there is no doubt. (27)

Having touched [him] and placed him within his heart, he should describe the ritual for him; and he, having washed the feet and so forth, with the sins [of the disciple] departed from his head, [should proceed]. (28)
Every day, the twice-born man would deceitfully hold water in his hand after sipping it.
Once, a certain food-gatherer arrived to take some goods. (29)
Having torn open the innermost door of the night, he entered that interior of the house;
seeing Bhīma, he approached with a staff in his hand for the purpose of striking him.
Having severed his head along with the necklace, he quickly fled;
then Viṣṇu’s soldiers, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, [pursued him].
O twice-born one, they arrived there to lead away that Bhīma who was free from sin,
as well as the divine Syandana chariot accompanied by Rājahaṃsa.
Having ascended that [vehicle], he went to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is indeed difficult to attain.
Thus has this majesty of the Brahmins been proclaimed by me.
The man who listens with devotion shall have his sins destroyed. ||33||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Brāhmaṇas," in the Brahmakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. ||14||
Fifteenth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
O highly fortunate one, tell me the sin-destroying majesty [of Ekādaśī];
what is the fruit of Ekādaśī, and what is the transgression for one who does not observe it? (1)
Sūta said:
What shall I now speak regarding the greatness of Ekādaśī?
Upon hearing about the Ekādaśīs, even the messengers of Yama become terrified.
There is no doubt that they cause fear to all living beings; yet the auspicious Ekādaśī is the most excellent of all religious observances. (3)
One should observe the fast and remain awake for Viṣṇu, and perform a grand adornment;
indeed, that mortal who performs the worship of Hari with Tulasī leaves [attains great merit]. (4)
O twice-born one, by giving even a single leaf, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
likewise, whatever sin is declared to arise from approaching those who should not be approached, [it is all removed]. (5)
O twice-born one, that sin goes to utter destruction by fasting on the eleventh day;
he who offers a lamp filled with ghee on the day of Viṣṇu [attains the same].
Having destroyed all darkness by his own splendor, he has gone to the city of Viṣṇu;
blessed are those regions, and blessed is that great lord of the earth.
On the day of Hari, during his reign, there was a great festival on the Ekādaśī;
likewise on the occasion of Nārāyaṇa’s reclining and his turning upon his side.
"Especially on Prabodhinī, those who remain without food—what living being, partaker of merit, do you not delight? (9)
Day and night, the Lord of the Ancestors commanded his messengers:
"The eleventh day is dear to the Lord of the World; it increases merit. (10)
Viṣṇu indeed burns their very bodies upon the consumption of that food; fie on their livelihood, fie on their prosperity, fie on their pride, and fie on their conduct! 11.
O best of the twice-born, those most sinful ones who eat food on the Ekādaśī day, and those who consume garlic and onions on the Ekādaśī, do so solely out of attachment to worldly enjoyment.
Many and various evils indeed persist, just as on the new moon day there is great impurity in the union of women. ||13||
Likewise, by eating food on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), one incurs sin; for the sick, it results in asthma, consumption, leprosy, and skin diseases.
Living beings who eat this food indeed become village pigs and fall into poverty. (15)
O best of the twice-born, whatever sins are incurred by eating that food which is bound by the king, all those are destroyed on the day of Hari, O Brahmin. (16)
They remain subsisting on water by command;
for those who perform this, there shall be liberation from hell for all their sins. (17)
There is no atonement for men who eat on the day of Hari; and as many grains of rice as a man eats on the day of Hari [as an offering], [so many sins does he incur].
For every morsel of food [eaten], there shall be the sin arising from ten million acts of Brahmin-slaughter.
I say it again, I say it once more: listen, listen, O men! (19)
One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari;
whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords [is attained by this]. (20)
Having fasted on the eleventh day during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should worship the Lord of Kamalā with garlands of blue lotuses on that very day.
Having performed the ritual breaking of the fast according to the rules, O twice-born one, he decorates the house of Hari on the eleventh day for the sake of his mother’s womb.
Having attained the supreme goal, they shall abide in the abode of Viṣṇu;
those who, having observed Ekādaśī, remain without food, [attain this state].
There is no doubt that those whose minds shine, being completely absorbed in devotion to Tulasī, shall dwell even in the city of Viṣṇu.
Those for whom no desire whatsoever exists for the property of others go, without a doubt, to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Even those whose minds were satisfied with these [offerings] certainly attain the city of Viṣṇu;
for by this, O best of men, they provided sustenance to living beings when a time of famine arrived.
They give food to the abodes of Hari; of this there is no doubt. They provide protection for cows, for the twice-born, and likewise for their masters and wives.

Those mortals who give up their lives [on this day] will certainly attain the city of Viṣṇu; therefore, the tenth lunar day (daśamī) should never be observed as a fast by living beings when it is pierced [by the eleventh]. 28.
O best of the twice-born, one should avoid the proximity of a wicked person just as one avoids the time of dawn if it is joined with the tenth lunar day. (29)
One should fast there on the twelfth day, and the breaking of the fast should take place on the thirteenth day,
provided that the dawn of the thirteenth is not joined with the remnant of the tenth day.
A Vaiṣṇava must observe the Ekādaśī vow on that day;
the four ghaṭikās in the morning are called Aruṇodaya.
This time of sunrise is considered by ascetics to be equal to the Ganges;
however, if the tenth lunar day is seen at the time of dawn, [it is not so]. (32)
In that case, Ekādaśī should not be observed, for it destroys virtue, desire, and wealth;
a wise man should avoid even a very small portion of Ekādaśī that is pierced by Daśamī.
Just as one should abandon a jar of ghee that has come into contact with wine,
so too [should one avoid] that Ekādaśī which is complete and on which the Dvādaśī likewise follows.
A householder should fast on the preceding day when it is joined with the following [Ekādaśī],
provided that even a single digit (kalā) of Ekādaśī exists there and does not extend beyond the twelfth day.
In that regard, breaking the fast on the thirteenth day yields the merit of a hundred sacrifices, provided the eleventh day has been omitted and the [thirteenth] is conjoined with the twelfth. (36)
One who desires the supreme goal should fast on the full twelve-day period (dvādaśī) when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) is complete and that same [eleventh day] recurs at dawn. (37)

If the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is slightly less than the following day, then for those men whose minds are fully intent upon the vow of Ekādaśī, all [the preceding days] must be treated as the subsequent [Ekādaśī]. 38.
For them, there is indeed residence in heaven, and then they go to the abode of Hari;
there is no means for the world beyond superior to Ekādaśī.
Even one joined with many sins who observes the day of Hari shall be liberated from all sins and go to the abode of Hari. 40.
A woman who observes the day of Hari together with her husband becomes possessed of excellent sons, a fortunate mistress, and after death goes to the abode of Hari. 41.
O best of the twice-born, there is no way to calculate the merit of one who, with a spirit of devotion, offers a lamp before Hari on the day of Hari. 42.
O twice-born one, she who, together with her husband and kinsmen, observes the vigil for Hari, shall dwell for a long time in the abode of Hari along with her husband.
O twice-born one, whatever object a person offers with devotion to Hari on His day, his merit shall indeed be inexhaustible forever. (44)
Formerly, in a city named Kāñcanā, there was a man named Vallabha;
though possessing abundant wealth, he shone like the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) himself. ||45||
O Hemaprabha, there his beloved wife named Mahārūpā was present;
however, the fault of being talkative (mukharatva) greatly obstructed the virtues of that Cakravartin. ||46||
O ascetic, she would constantly engage in quarrels with her husband and perpetually revile her elders at will with vulgar speech. (47)
She should always eat from the same cooking vessel, remaining hidden, alone, and pure;
and she should daily give the remnants of her food to her elders. 48.
O Brahmin, my mind was always fixed on her paramour, and she would constantly say, "I am a virtuous wife," while she was perpetually causing mental distress to her husband through quarrels. (49)
O twice-born one, once seeing her arrive, her husband rebuked her and struck her, for she was possessed of every sin.
Filled with intense anger, she went to an empty house;
there she remained, sleeping and unnoticed, and she did not eat even water or food. (51)
O Brahmin, by fate, on that day Viṣṇu performed his side-turning;
it was the Ekādaśī vow, which destroys all sins.
Then, at dawn, that woman arrived there on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī) conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, her mind overflowing with intense anger.
Having fasted for two days, she became free from impurity;
and at night, O twice-born one, she attained death on that very day.
Then, by the command of Yama, messengers arrived in that manner to lead her away;
they were terrifying, with nooses and mallets in their hands.
And when he bound his mind and set out for the abode of Kṛtānta,
then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Then, having severed his bonds,
those sinless ones led him, freed from all taint, and caused him to ascend to the divine abode of Hari.
O bull among the twice-born, you have heard the greatness of Viṣṇu’s day, which is auspicious and difficult to attain, as it was recounted by the gods who had gathered there. 58.
Even if one acts without desire,
that mortal who gives a lamp in the abode of Hari on the Ekādaśī day shall go to the temple of Hari.

He who goes [to the shrine] on every single step obtains a fruit even greater than that of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). Those who listen to or recite the Purāṇas on the day of Hari obtain for every syllable the fruit born from the gift of a tawny cow (kapilā-dāna).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Day of Hari," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. ||15||
Chapter Sixteen.
Śaunaka said: "O Sūta, by what action and by what expiation (cainasa) would the destruction of sins occur?"
May the grace of Śrī Hari be upon me; therefore, please speak out of compassion.
Sūta said:
Listen, O Śaunaka; I shall speak that which destroys the sins of those who hear it, by which the grace of Viṣṇu may be obtained, which brings about the destruction of all evil. 2.
On the full moon day, however, one who is endowed with a spirit of devotion should perform various kinds of worship for the glorious Lord of the Universe. ||3||
O Sage, the defilement accumulated by that person over ten million births shall surely perish;
for it will certainly arise from the grace born of the mouth of this Śrīramaṇa. 4.
Whoever with devotion offers food to a twice-born on the twelfth lunar day,
his sins are utterly destroyed at the rising of the sun on the following morning.

O twice-born one, if a person performs the ritual bathing of Śrī Hari with milk, Śrī Hari is immediately pleased; on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), he is likewise pleased by offerings such as sugar and other sweets.
Indeed, he who offers a flower to Śrī Hari without the mantra is like one offering a stone; such a giver goes to a downward state.
If a man indeed gives a gift that is like a stone to one who is as foolish as a block of earth, no merit whatsoever accrues to him. ||8||
A twice-born man devoid of knowledge who, out of delusion, accepts a gift with a foolish mind,
goes to hell along with him, just as one might consume old fire from the end of time.
Just as an elephant or a deer made of wood, or as one made of painting, so too are those who bear the name of "Brahmin" while being devoid of knowledge—mere carriers of the title. (10)
Just as water situated in a vessel is purified by wind, sun, and fire, so too one's impurity perishes upon seeing a pārṣada with devotion. ||11||
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvina, a person should offer ghee, parched rice, and cowries for the sake of play to Śrī Hari. (12)

If a man, out of delusion, does not give [the merit] to Hari—the remover of suffering—who, through devotion, reaches the station from which there is no return, then Hari will find no satisfaction in him. 13.
Whoever offers even a single cowrie shell on the full moon day shall certainly dwell for that many days in the abode of Hari during the month of Āśvina.
O best of the twice-born, in former times there was a Śūdra named Kāladvija in Karavīrapura; he was merciless, sinful, and a source of terror. (15)
Though he was intent on his own affairs, he was a destroyer of his master's work;
once, when he passed away, the messengers of Yama, with terrifying hands, arrived.
They arrived to bring him to the abode of Yama;
having seen him bound, they brought him there, and Yama questioned his minister.
Yama said:
"O wise Citragupta, tell me in full detail what office this man holds and whatever good or evil deeds he has performed."
Citragupta said:
"This man is a sinner of evil conduct who has failed in his master's service;
he possesses not even an atom of merit, so let him be cooked in hell. (19)
O King, for a hundred manvantaras, that cruel man shall dwell in the womb of a serpent;
having attained birth as a stone, he shall remain there incessantly within his home.
Sūta said:
For that length of time, O Brahmin, he then fell into hell;
after that, he was born in an extremely miserable state as a serpent in a house of stone.
Once, O twice-born one, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvina,
she caused parched grain and cowries to be thrown outside from the mouth of a serpent.
The fallen [sins] fell before Hari; the compassionate Hari, the destroyer of suffering, himself quickly destroyed this man's sin. ||23||
Once, when his time had come, he departed for the state of the ancestors;
O twice-born one, the messengers of Yama arrived many times to bring him back.
When they set out to bind [him] and lead him toward the abode of Yama,
the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing conchs, discs, and maces.
Having cut the noose, he ascended to heaven, swift and freed from all sin;
there the messengers of Yama fled, and they placed him [upon the celestial vehicle].
Then the serpent, surrounded by them, went to the abode of Viṣṇu;
there he stood before Hari, forever free from rebirth.
O twice-born one, if one were to remove iron with devotion and offer it along with parched grain and ghee, I do not know what certain merit would accrue from even a single cowrie shell! (28)
Whoever should hear this chapter, which destroys sin, their sins shall perish through the grace of Śrī Hari as well. (29)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka," in the Brahma-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.
The Seventeenth Chapter.
Śaunaka said:
[Please tell me] the greatness of the water from Viṣṇu’s feet, which destroys all sins.
O ocean of compassion, O one of great wisdom, tell me [this] together with its root.
Sūta said:
The auspicious water from the feet of Viṣṇu destroys all sins;
he who carries even a single drop of it obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
O Brahmin, the water from Viṣṇu’s feet destroys sin through mere touch;
there is no untimely death, and one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. (3)
Even a most sinful person who drinks the water from Viṣṇu’s feet—O Brahmin, there is no doubt that the evil karma residing within his body shall go to destruction. ||4||
O twice-born one, he who carries with devotion on his head the water from Viṣṇu’s feet joined with a tulasī leaf shall go to the abode of Hari.
The fruit that is obtained by giving gold equal in weight to Mount Meru is attained by men simply by touching the water from the feet of Hari.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through giving thousands of millions of cows,
that same fruit is certainly attained by touching the water used for washing the feet.
Whatever fruit is obtained by performing thousands of millions of sacrifices,
that is surpassed ten millionfold for men who touch the water from the feet of Hari.
Whatever fruit is obtained by people through the gift of ten million maidens, the fruit of touching the water from Viṣṇu’s feet is greater than that, O twice-born one. (9)
