Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Entry of Raghunātha into the City," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||3||
(4) The Fourth Chapter.
Vātsyāyana said:
O Lord of the sovereign of serpents, capable of bearing the burden of the earth, please listen to one doubt of mine and explain it out of compassion. (1)
Ever since Raghunātha’s departure for the forest occurred, she has remained with a body but with a vacant mind. ||2||
Distraught by separation from him, her body emaciated and deeply afflicted with grief, she heard from the fair-faced ministers that the Lord of the Raghus had arrived. (3)
How did she rejoice? What happened there? What was the sign?
And what did she say to the bearer of Rāmacandra’s message? (4)
Cut through this doubt of mine regarding the arising of the qualities of the Lord of the Raghus;
please explain it correctly to me as I listen with devotion. (5)
Śeṣa said:
Well asked, O highly fortunate one, honored by the best of the twice-born!
Listen with a single-minded focus as I relate that to you directly. (6)
Having drunk again and again that nectar of Rāma’s arrival, which had fallen from the lotus of her face,
she indeed became overwhelmed, her limbs paralyzed with joy.
Is this a dream of mine, deluded as I am, or is it a deceptive word?
For how could I, unfortunate as I am, behold Rāma’s face again? (8)
Having performed much austerity, this infant son was indeed obtained;
yet, due to some sin of mine, he has once again met with separation. (9)
O good minister, is Rāma well, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa? How does that hero remember me, who am so deeply distressed, while he himself dwells as a forest-dweller? (10)
Thus she lamented loudly, her mind fixed on the memory of Raghunātha;
utterly bewildered, she did not perceive anything of her own, nor of another.
Sumukha, too, seeing his mother thus deeply distressed, [was overcome with grief].
Fanned by the fierce breezes, he regained consciousness once more;
he repeatedly spoke gentle and joy-inducing words to his mother.
He made her joyful once again by reminding her of Raghunātha’s arrival:
"O Mother, know that Raghunātha has reached home along with Lakṣmaṇa. (13)
"Behold him together with Sītā and honor him with blessings"—having heard these truthful words spoken by Sumukha, [he did so]. ||14||
I do not know such joy as she experienced when she rose up in the courtyard, her body covered with horripilation. 15.
While he was beholding Tārām, overwhelmed with joy and shedding tears, the lord of kings, Rāma, arrived mounted upon a celestial chariot. ||16||
The wise one reached his mother Kaikeyī’s residence and stood before her; there he saw Rāma standing before him, bowed down by the burden of shame for having caused his father's death.
Seeing his mother repeatedly overcome by great anxiety and filled with shame, Rāma, the banner of the solar dynasty, said nothing.
He spoke to her with words imbued with humility;
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Mother, having gone to the forest, I have performed everything in that manner."
O Mother, alas! What misdeed have I committed now, or what have I done contrary to your command?
I have done nothing wrong; why will you not look upon me again? (20)
"Having greeted him with blessings, look upon both Bharata and me.
O sinless one, having heard these words of her father, she lowered her face.
He replied very slowly, "O Rāma, go to your own home.
Having heard these words of his mother, Rāma, the best of men, [prepared to depart].
Having paid his respects, that ocean of compassion, the high-minded one, went home;
having seen Rāma together with the son of Sumitrā.
"Live long! Live long! he exclaimed with blessings;
and Cārāmbabhadra also prostrated himself at his mother's feet.
Embracing him with great joy, he spoke these words again:
"O Ratnagarbha, nothing of this kind has ever been done for me by any of my other brothers."
Just as the wise Yama brought about the removal of my suffering. ||26||
O Mother, know that whatever is recovered by me after Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa is entirely due to the efforts of Lakṣmaṇa. ||27||
Having accepted the blessing bestowed by Sumitrā upon his head with his own hands, he,
surrounded by the gods, departed for the palace of his mother.
Seeing his mother thrilled with joy and longing for the sight of him,
Hari descended from his vehicle and took hold of her pure feet.
Her mind overwhelmed by the longing to see him,
the mother embraced Rāma again and again and attained great joy.
Then his body's hair stood on end, his speech became faltering, and warm tears of joy flowed forth in a continuous stream. (31)
Seeing his mother devoid of her two bracelets, her body lacking its usual ornaments for the hands and feet, and bearing a form stripped of all finery.
Seeing that emaciated Gī, who was somewhat cheered by her own vision [of him] yet still possessed of sorrow, he—
perceiving that she had not yet reached the limit of her suffering— spoke to her.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Mother, I have not served your feet for a long time;
therefore, forgive this offense of mine, who am devoid of fortune. (34)
Those sons who are not eager to serve their mother and father should be considered, O supreme mother, as mere insects born from semen. (35)
What shall I do, having gone to the Daṇḍaka forest by the command of Janaka?
Even there, having become an object of your compassion, I have crossed the ocean of suffering. (36)
Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa and taken to Laṅkā;
through your grace, she has been recovered by me after I slew that lord of the Rākṣasas. (37)
O Sītā, this devoted wife has fallen at your feet;
please show favor to her, who is fearful of impurity and whose mind is fixed upon your feet.
Having heard those words, they prostrated at the feet of their daughter-in-law;
bestowing blessings upon her, they spoke to that devoted wife. (39)
O beautiful lady, sport for a long time with Śītānātha;
O purifying one, give birth to a son and sanctify your own lineage.
Women like you, devoted to their husbands and following after their husband’s joys and sorrows, become sharers in his suffering; this is not a falsehood in the three worlds. (41)
O daughter of Videha, your own family has been sanctified by you yourself;
I shall follow you to the great forest to the pair of Rāma’s lotus feet.
What is surprising about those men who possess wives as radiant as ten million suns—wives who are virtuous and desire the welfare of their own husbands? (43)
Having spoken thus to the lotus-eyed wife of Raghunātha, she became silent, thrilled, with the hair on her body standing on end. 44.
Then his brother Bharata presented to the wise Rāmacandra his own great kingdom, which had been granted by their father.
Those ministers, being greatly delighted, summoned astrologers who were experts in counsel and,
with the utmost reverence, asked them for an auspicious moment.
On an auspicious moment, on a favorable day joined with a propitious lunar mansion, they zealously performed his consecration for the great kingship. (47)
Having drawn the earth with its seven islands upon a beautiful tiger skin, the great king, the lord of kings, stood upon it. (48)
From that very day, the minds of the virtuous attained great joy, while the hearts of the wicked, who torment others, were filled with dejection. (49)
But women, O Sage, devoted to their husbands through their devotion to them and dedicated to the vow of fidelity, never commit a sin even in their minds. (50)
Then the Daityas, Devas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Mahoragas—all of them, standing on the path of righteousness, received the King’s command upon their heads. (51)
Devoted to helping others, contented in the happiness of their own dharma, and spending every moment of day and night in the diversion of learning—such people are auspicious. (52)
Even a mighty wind could not forcibly carry away the fine garments of those standing on the path; and there, indeed, was no talk of thieves.
Rāma, the bestower of wealth upon those who seek it, a compassionate treasury of mercy, together with his brothers, constantly performed the praise of his guru and the gods. (54)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Royal Consecration of the Best of the Raghus," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||4||
(5) Fifth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then the gods, bowing down with hearts gladdened by the slaying of the lord of demons named Rāvaṇa, praised Rāma who had been consecrated. ||1||

The gods said: Victory, O son of Daśaratha, destroyer of the afflictions of the gods! Victory, victory, O burner of the lineage of the Dānavas! Victory, O slayer of enemies, whose hands are ever busy in seizing the hosts of the best of gods and the throngs of serpents! 2.

O Lord of the World, while poets are eager to describe Your destruction of the lords of the Danujas, You effortlessly swallow the multitudes of worlds once again at the time of universal dissolution. 3.
Victory to you, who are liberated from the sufferings of birth, old age, and the like; O most powerful one, lift us up!
Victory to you, born in the ocean of the lineage of those whose hands uphold Dharma, O Acyuta, free from old age and death! 4.
O best of gods, even those who have committed many sins are purified by your names;
how much more so those preceded by virtuous brahmins, who have attained this fair-bodied human state? (5)

We long in our minds for that pair of your feet, praised by Hara and Viriñci, which grants the fulfillment of all desired wishes, and which is beautifully adorned upon our hearts with marks such as the sacred barley-grains. 6.
If you, who possess a splendor that eclipses the very form of Madana, do not grant fearlessness to the earth,
how indeed can the hosts of gods be happy?
Are they not indeed purifiers full of compassion? ||7||
Whenever the demons and serpents cause us suffering,
at those times you take birth upon this earth,
O Lord, though you are unborn, immutable, and yet appearing as a hunter.
Abiding in his own intrinsic nature, he is worshipped by his own [devotees]. ||8||

Having strewn the surface of the earth with virtuous deeds that destroy evil and are like nectar for the dead, and being praised by non-human beings who proclaim your virtues, enter quickly once more into your own abode. 9.

May he who is beginningless yet the first-born, who assumes the form of an old man, who wears a garland and a crown, who resembles the god whose banner bears the makara, and whose lotus feet are served by the enemy of Smara—may he, having forcibly destroyed his foes, grant victory! (10)
Having spoken thus, all those gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, repeatedly bowed to the Lord of the Raghus, who was gratified by the destruction of his enemy. ||11||
Thus, greatly delighted by the praise, the highly illustrious Lord of the Raghus looked upon those gods who stood with bowed heads and spoke to them as they prostrated. (12)
Śrī Rāma said: "O gods, choose from me some boon that is very difficult to obtain— a boon which no god, demon, or yakṣa has ever received with such devotion."
The Suras said:
"O Lord, everything most excellent has been obtained by us from the Blessed One, since this enemy of ours, the Ten-faced one, has been slain. (14)
"O, whenever an asura inflicts harm upon us, at that very time this must be done; this alone is the destruction of the enemy. (15)
Having said "So be it," the heroic joy of the Raghus spoke again.
Śrī Rāma said: "O gods, listen to my words with full attention. (16)
A person who shall repeatedly recite this wonderful hymn composed by you and woven from my own defects—in the morning or once at night—[shall attain his desires]. (17)
For him, there shall be no terrible defeat by enemies;
nor shall there be union with poverty, nor defeat by disease. (18)
But their devotion to my two feet shall be even greater, as they joyfully recite [this] to other men. (19)
Having spoken thus, that crest-jewel of kings became silent; all the gods, greatly delighted, departed each to his own world.
Raghunātha, the leader of the world, protected those wise brothers like a father, and he protected his subjects like his own sons until their dissolution. 21.
While he rules over the worlds, there is no untimely death for men; nor is there any great affliction by disease or other misfortunes within their homes. (22)
No enemy shall ever cause fear;
the trees shall always bear fruit, and the earth shall abound with grain. (23)
Their lives were made secure by the company of sons, grandsons, and kinsmen; what joy did they not find from the pleasures born of such union, which dispelled the weariness of separation? (24)
Constantly eager for discourse on the lotus feet of Śrī Raghunātha,
never do they utter words of censure against others.
Even the artisans, alas, never committed a sin in their minds, for they were foretelling the suffering of the blow from the hand of Raghunātha. ||26||
With their eyes fixed motionlessly upon the face of Sītā’s husband, the people remained constantly filled with compassion. ||27||
He obtained a kingdom free from rivals, with abundant forces and vehicles, and made delightful by sages who were joyful and well-nourished and adorned with golden ornaments. ||28||
It was fully nourished by those who constantly performed their duties of sacrifice and charitable works;
it always possessed abundant crops and was endowed with excellent wealth and fertile fields. (29)
It was a beautiful country with excellent offspring, healthy, abundant in fine grass, rich in cattle and wealth, and adorned with rows of temples dedicated to the deities.
There, indeed, the villages were completely full, resplendent with an abundance of wealth;
they possessed artificial gardens of beautiful flowers and trees bearing delicious fruits. ||31||
There the lands shine with lotus-filled lakes;
there the rivers are full of deceit; and nowhere at all is there any crowd of people. (32)
These alone are the true lineages of the noble-born and the castes—not those who are destitute—in which there is never any lapse regarding women nor any among the learned. (33)
In that realm, the rivers do not flow in crooked ways, nor are the subjects crooked in their conduct;
there, the nights are joined with darkness only during the dark fortnights, and men are bowed only before the gods. (34)
There, women were not joined with passion, men were not full of unrighteousness, and there was no one who was blinded by wealth, nor anyone who was gluttonous in eating.
Where there was no chariot without a driver, nor any man other than a Vaiśya;
where the rod of punishment was applied only to axes, mattocks, plows, and rows of fans. (36)
In the assemblies of kings, there is never anywhere any obstruction born of anger, except among the crowds of gamblers;
nor is there ever any lamentation. (37)
Only gamblers are seen there, with dice in their hands; only those weak women who live amidst the waters of gossip about stupidity are found there. (38)
Where women with firm hearts are the boundary-markers, and where the application of *kuṣṭha* is found only among medicinal herbs, not among men. (39)
Where there is piercing in the case of fine jewels, and indeed the chisel in the hands of sculptors;
where, moreover, due to the arising of a sattvic state of being, no one anywhere has fear of anything. (40)
There is the fever born of desire, poverty, and impurity, as well as the constant difficulty of obtaining desirable objects through the lack of merit. (41)
Only elephants are vigilant in battle; only the waters of the ocean are free from waves;
only among elephants is there a loss of ichor; and only on trees are there sharp thorns. (42)
In arrows, there is the separation from the string; in books, firm binding; and in the wicked alone is the abandonment of affection—not so among people in general. (43)
They protected that land, cherishing the subjects who were themselves cherished;
they established righteousness in the country like a wielder of the rod of punishment over the wicked. (44)
While the lord was thus protecting the land and the surface of the earth according to dharma,
eleven thousand years passed by.
There, having heard from low-born people of Sītā’s humiliation and his own reproach from the washerman, the scion of Raghu became distressed. (46)
At that time, while the king was ruling the earth according to dharma,
Sītā remained alone, strictly guarded by his command.
Once, while that one of great intelligence was seated in the midst of the assembly, the great sage Kumbhotpatti, the best of munis, arrived. 48.
Taking the water of honor (*arghya*), the great king, accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, rose up as the people beheld the drier of the ocean who had arrived. (49)
Having welcomed him with great hospitality and inquired after his well-being,
the descendant of Raghu spoke to him once he was comfortably seated and rested.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Meeting with Agastya," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||5||
The Sixth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
Thus [he spoke to] him who was satisfied by his welcome, a treasure-house of celibacy and austerity.
The wise hero, the teacher of all the worlds, spoke to the sage. ||1||
Welcome to you, O illustrious one, born from a jar and treasure-house of austerity!
By the sight of you, we, together with our entire households, have been purified. (2)
I hope your devotion remains fixed upon the Vedas and the Shastras; I hope that no one anywhere on this earth will cause obstacles to your ascetic penance. (3)
O highly fortunate Lopāmudrā, you are a practitioner of dharma; through the power of your devotion to your husband, everything becomes auspicious. (4)
O great-souled one, embodiment of the Dharma, treasure-house of compassion, O Lord of Sages, what task can I perform for you who are free from all worldly desire? (5)

"O Lord of Sages, although everything occurs in great abundance according to your own will through the power of your asceticism, nevertheless, having shown compassion toward me, please grant me instruction."
Śeṣa said:
Having been addressed thus by the wise king of kings, the teacher of the world,
he spoke to Rāma, the lord of the worlds, in a most humble tone.
Agastya said:
"O Lord, who are difficult even for the gods to behold, yet a joy to behold;
O King of kings, O ocean of mercy, know that I have come here with this thought. (8)
The asura known as Rāvaṇa, a thorn to the worlds, has been slain by you. By good fortune the gods are now happy; by good fortune King Vibhīṣaṇa [is established]. (9)
O Rāma, O best of gods, by the sight of you today, my evil deeds have indeed vanished;
O supreme deity, the treasury of my mind is now filled with bliss.
Having spoken thus, the one born from a jar (Agastya) immediately became silent,
his mind overwhelmed with the joy of beholding Rāma.
Rāma questioned that sage, who was expert in knowledge:
"You know everything—pertaining to the past and the future—transcending the world, in its entirety. (12)
O Sage, tell all this in great detail to me who asks; who was this Rāvaṇa, the tormentor of the gods, who was slain by me? (13)
Kumbhakarṇa also asked: "O great sage, what is the species of this one? Is he a god, a demon, a piśāca, or a rākṣasa? (14)
O Omniscient One, tell me everything; you know all things in detail. Therefore, having shown compassion toward me, explain it all to me. (15)
Having heard these words, the pitcher-born Agastya, a treasury of asceticism,
began to speak that which had been asked by the king of the Raghus.
O King, Brahmā is the creator; Pulastya was his son. From him was born Viśravas, who was highly proficient in the knowledge of the Vedas. (17)
Two wives were born to him, both upholding the conduct of devoted wives; one was named Aṅkā and the second was known as Ākaiṣī. (18)
In the eastern quarter, he who was born from the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) and bore the splendor of a world-protector, made his residence in Laṅkā by the grace of Śiva. (19)
To the daughter of Vidyunmālin, however, there were three great sons:
Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and the meritorious Vibhīṣaṇa. ||20||
O Mahāmati, because she was born from the womb of a Rākṣasī and because her birth occurred at the time of twilight, the minds of both were skilled in unrighteousness.
On one occasion, he traveled in the exceedingly beautiful Puṣpaka chariot,
which was fashioned of gold and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells.
Having ascended [the chariot] to behold his father, he set forth endowed with splendor,
being praised by his own attendants who were adorned with various jewel ornaments.
Having arrived and fallen at the feet of his parents, the son remained for a long time,
his soul overwhelmed with joy and the hair on his body standing on end.
He said to me: "Today is a most auspicious day, the dawning of the fruit of great fortune, since I have beheld your feet, which are so meritorious to behold. (25)
Having praised him with these and other words of praise, he went to his own palace;
and his parents also became filled with joy through their affection for their son. (26)
Seeing him, the wise Rāvaṇa said to his own mother:
"Who is this man—is he a god, or a yakṣa, or perhaps the best of men? (27)
He who had once attended upon the feet of my father has now returned, a treasure-house of great fortune, well-surrounded by his own attendants. (28)
By what merit was this celestial chariot, swift as the wind, obtained through austerity—a supreme abode for the pleasures of gardens, groves, and amorous pastimes? (29)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, the mother, distressed by anger and with a troubled mind, spoke to her son while slightly changing the expression of her eyes. (30)
O son, listen to my words, which are endowed with much instruction and are superior in their skillful analysis of his birth, deeds, and so forth. (31)
"O co-wife, the destined time has arrived for the one dwelling within my womb, by whom your mother's stainless and great lineage shall be made to blaze forth. (32)
You are a sinful insect born from her womb, merely filling your own belly;
just as a donkey knows its own burden but not its value.
Likewise, you appear to be ignorant, possessing beds, seats, and enjoyments; it is possible for you to be asleep, or to have gone somewhere, or to have fallen [from your state]. (34)
By this austerity, which brought satisfaction to Śiva, he obtained residence in Laṅkā, a celestial chariot swift as thought, and the riches of sovereignty. (35)
How fortunate is this mother Sudhanvā, and how great her merit and compassion, since her son, through his own virtues, has attained the station of the great! (36)
Having heard these words spoken in distress by her whose vital breaths were nearly exhausted, that most wicked soul,
harboring anger within himself, spoke again to her regarding her ascetic resolve.
Rāvaṇa said: "O Mother, listen to my words filled with pride:
you alone are Ratnagarbhā (the one whose womb contains jewels), from whom we three sons have been born."
Who is that worm? One who possesses wealth. Where is his penance? It is indeed very slight. And what is his kingdom? It is joined with only a few servants. (39)
O Mother, endowed with compassion, listen to my vow made out of zeal;
it has never been made by anyone else before, O you who are uniquely fortunate in this world. (40)
If I were to bring the entire world under my control by means of austerities performed with difficulty that cause satisfaction to Brahmā; ||41||
If, having always renounced food, water, sleep, and likewise play, there should still be sin for me due to the destruction of the world of my ancestors; [then let it be so]. (42)
Kumbhakarṇa also, accompanied by Vibhīṣaṇa and his brother Rāvaṇa, having spoken thus, went to the mountain forest.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Birth of Rāvaṇa," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
[Verse 6]
(7) The Seventh Chapter.
Agastya said:
Then the Daitya Sata performed severe penance for ten thousand years,
standing on his tiptoes and gazing at the sun with his eyes.
Kumbhakarṇa also performed a most difficult penance;
the righteous-souled Vibhīṣaṇa, however, practiced supreme austerity.
Then the Blessed One, the God of gods, the Lord of creatures, who is served by the crowns of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and others, became pleased. ||3||
He bestowed a vast kingdom that illumines the three worlds,
and he made his body beautiful, frequented by gods and dānavas.
Then his brother Dhanada, who possessed a righteous mind, was distressed;
however, the celestial chariot was then led away from here by force to the city of Laṅkā.
The entire world was scorched, as were the gods dwelling in heaven;
he struck down the community of Brahmins and became the root-destroyer of the sages.
Then the gods, including Indra, being exceedingly distressed, approached Brahmā;
those high-souled ones offered hymns of praise and prostrated themselves like a staff.
All the gods, filled with reverence, praised him with meaningful words;
thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, said to him, "I shall do this."
Then the gods reported before Brahmā the distress caused by the Ten-necked one, as well as their own defeat.
Having meditated for a moment, Brahmā went to Kailāsa together with the gods;
on the side of that mountain, it was filled with various wonders.
Standing there, the gods, led by Śakra, offered praise for the sake of well-being:
"Homage to Bhava, to Śarva; homage to him who has a blue neck. (11)
"Salutations to you who are gross and subtle, to you of manifold forms; salutations to you!
Having heard these words spoken with every mouth, Śaṅkara [listened]. (12)
He said to Nandin, "Bring the gods here to me.
Immediately thereafter, the gods were summoned by Nandin.
Having entered the inner apartments, the gods beheld him with eyes wide with wonder;
then Brahmā, having arrived, saw Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
It was attended by thousands of millions of joyful followers—naked, deformed, crooked, soiled, and likewise hideous. (15)
Having prostrated and stood before him along with the gods, the Grandfather spoke to the Lord of the God of Gods: "Behold the condition of the inhabitants of heaven."
O Great God, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, show mercy;
O Lord, exert yourself for the sake of slaying the wicked Daityas. 17.
Having heard those words filled with wretchedness and grief, he too,
accompanied by all the gods, went to the abode of Hari.
All the sages, along with the gods, serpents, and kinnaras, offered praise:
"Victory to you, Mādhava, Lord of Gods! Victory to you, the destroyer of the suffering of your devotees! (19)
"Behold, O Great God! Look upon your own servants!
Thus all the gods, led by Śarva, cried out loudly.

Having heard what was said and having perceived the affliction of the gods, Viṣṇu reflected upon it; then, as if bringing their sorrow to an end, he addressed the gods with a voice like a mass of clouds. (21)
O gods, led by Brahmā, Śiva, and Indra, listen to these words intended for your welfare:
I know the fear caused to you by the Ten-necked One; having now undertaken this incarnation, I shall destroy it today.

This city of Ayodhyā, the ornament of the earth, has been protected by kings born of the solar lineage who performed noble deeds such as great gifts and sacrifices; it shines with its silvered grounds. (23)
In that city, King Daśaratha, endowed with glory and victorious over the circle of all directions, now rules the kingdom as a sovereign lord, though he remains childless. (24)

Desiring a son, the sacrificer, endowed with great strength, performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice according to the prescribed rites, having requested the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who was worthy of praise and worship.
Then, O gods, I was previously entreated by that ascetic: "O Lord, out of affection for my three wives, please become fourfold for their sake. (26)
Accompanied by those named Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, I shall effect the eradication of Rāvaṇa along with his roots, his army, and his vehicles.
"You all, too, descend by means of your own respective powers and wander here throughout the entire surface of the earth in the form of bears and monkeys. (28)
Having spoken thus, O Sage, he quickly ceased his speech;
and the gods, having heard these great words, were all filled with joy in their hearts. (29)
They performed exactly as instructed by the wise God of gods,
each assuming his own respective form as a mountain, a monkey, or a bear.
O great king, he who is that Viṣṇu, the great god and the destroyer of the suffering of the gods— he is indeed the Blessed One who has assumed a physical form.
"O high-minded one, this Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna are your sons, as is the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, the oppressor of the gods. (32)
Driven by the persistence of former enmity, he abducted Jānakī once more;
however, that Daitya, who belonged to the species of Brahmarākṣasa, was slain by you.
The lord of the Daityas, the son of Pulastya and the sole thorn of all the worlds, has been cast down; O Maheśvara, may you obtain happiness throughout the entire earth. 34.
Today there is happiness for the Brahmins and strength for the sages and ascetics;
all sacred fords are auspicious, and all sacrifices are well-performed. (35)
O Supreme among Men, O Soul of the Universe, O Source of the World, while you were king, the entire world—including gods, asuras, and humans—attained happiness. (36)
All this that I was asked by you, O sinless one, has been told to you by me according to my understanding—
both the origin and the dissolution.
Having thus heard this news, which resembled that of the lineage of the lords of the Daityas, the Great Person, the Lord and Sovereign,
his lotus-like face had its flow of tears checked.
His power was renowned in the assemblies of those born on the [divine] planes. ||38||

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin and Fall of Rāvaṇa," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(8) The Eighth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
This [work] destroys the sins of those who hear the story of Vātsyāyana, the best of sages;
it belongs to the God of gods, the protector of Brahman, the sole guardian of all dharma. ||1||
Seeing the king unconscious, the pot-born Agastya, a treasury of asceticism, slowly touched him with his hand and spoke these words through his tears: ||2||
O Bhairava, arise quickly; why do you despair?
You are the eternal Mahāviṣṇu, the destroyer of the race of Daityas. ||3||
The past, the future, and the present—indeed, the entire world, both stationary and moving—has no other mover besides you; for what reason, then, have you fainted here? (4)
Having heard the words uttered by the one born from a jar (Agastya), the great king rose up, his face filled with tears streaming from his eyes. ||5||
With his body bowed down by the weight of shame and turned away from any thought of betraying Brahmanas, he spoke in a most piteous manner, with words uttered indistinctly and at length.
Śrī Rāma said:
Alas! Behold the ignorance of me, a deluded and evil-minded man, who, greedy for sensual pleasure, has slain one born into a family of brāhmaṇas. (7)
For the sake of a woman, O Brahmin, I—who possess discernment through the Vedas and Shastras—destroyed the Vāḍava clan like one devoid of intellect and extremely wicked-minded. (8)
A Brahmin born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus would not be one to utter harsh words;
by performing such an act, this [lineage] has been most grievously defiled. (9)
Those Brahmins who were worthy of worship through gifts, honors, and meals—those priests have been slain by me with volleys of arrows. (10)
To what worlds shall I go? Even the hell of Kumbhīpāka is unbearable;
there is no such sacred ford (tīrtha) that is capable of purifying me. 11.
Neither knowledge of the scriptures, nor austerity, nor charity, nor even speech, nor vows and the like, can be the means of my purification, for I am a hater of Brahmins. (12)
Those men who have provoked the family of Brahmins and are destined for hell will, having gone to hell, experience manifold suffering. (13)
The Veda is the root of the dharmas for those who distinguish between the castes and stages of life;
the Brāhmaṇa family is its root, being the sole branch of all the Vedas. 14.
What will be the consequence for me, who have cut down the root through arrogance?
What indeed must be done today so that there may be welfare for me? (15)
Śeṣa said:
To Rāma, the lord of kings and the bull among the Raghus, who was lamenting intensely, the pot-born sage (Agastya) spoke these words concerning his illusory human form. 16.
Agastya said:
"O great sage, O king of noble intellect, do not despair!
Since you desire the destruction of the wicked, you shall incur no sin of Brahmin-slaughter. (17)

You are the ancient Puruṣa, the manifest Lord beyond primordial nature (prakṛti); the creator, the destroyer, the protector, and the witness; devoid of qualities, yet by Your own will possessing qualities.
The drinker of liquor, the committer of Brahman-murder, the thief of gold, and the perpetrator of great sins—all indeed become quickly purified by the utterance of your name. (19)
O Great-minded One, this goddess, the daughter of Janaka, is the Great Vidyā;
by the mere remembrance of her, those who are liberated shall go to the supreme destination. (20)
O destroyer of demons, Rāvaṇa was indeed not a Daitya; he was a servant of yours in Vaikuṇṭha who attained the state of a Daitya due to the curse of the sages.
"You are the benefactor of that twice-born man, not his slayer;
reflecting thus, you ought not to grieve for yourself any further. (22)
Having heard these words, Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities,
spoke sweet words with a voice faltering with emotion.
Śrī Rāma said:
Sin is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being intentional or unintentional; that which is committed intentionally is "jñāta," while that which is devoid of such intent is "ajñāta. (24)
Action performed intentionally perishes only through its experience;
other [action] perishes through remorse—this is determined by the scriptures. (25)
Since I intentionally committed the highly censurable murder of a Brahmin, the praise of the virtuous is not sufficient to dispel my suffering. (26)
Tell me of such a thing that burns away my sin—be it a vow, a gift, a sacrifice, some sacred ford, or a great act of worship. (27)
By which my stainless fame shall indeed purify the worlds—those who have attained turbidity through sinful conduct and whose radiance has been destroyed by the murder of a Brahmin. (28)
Śeṣa said:
To Rāma, who had spoken thus and whose feet were illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of the gods and demons bowing down, that treasure-house of asceticism replied.
Listen, O Rāma, great hero, benefactor of the worlds! I shall speak these words for the purpose of removing the sin of killing a Brahmin. (30)
One should indeed perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice, which removes all sins; therefore, O Soul of the Universe, you should perform the beautiful Aśvamedha sacrifice. 31.
This was accomplished by you, O lord of the earth, who are wise, endowed with great prosperity, and distinguished by great strength. ||32||
O Brahmins, your ancestor, the great king Dilīpa, performed that horse sacrifice which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, Śatakratu, that bull among men,
attained his station in Amarāvatī, which is well-served by gods and daityas.
Manu, King Sagara, Marutta, and the son of Nahuṣa—all these were your ancestors who, having performed sacrifices, attained the supreme state. ||35||
Therefore, O Indra among the Kuru kings, you are capable;
accordingly, your brothers, who are like the guardians of the world, will conduct themselves as your well-wishers.
Having heard these words of the sage,
that fortunate best of the Raghus, fearing the slaughter of a brahmin and desiring to perform the sacrifice with wisdom, questioned him.
The ancient ritual being fully proclaimed. ||37||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Agastya to Raghunātha," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||8||
(9) The Ninth Chapter. Śrī Rāma said:
What kind of horse should be present there, and what is the procedure for its worship?
How can it be accomplished, and who are the enemies to be conquered therein? (1)
Agastya said: With a beautiful body whose color was like the water of the Gaṅgā, he was dark at the ears, red in the face, and marked as yellow at the tail. ||2||
Possessing the speed of thought, capable of traveling everywhere, and equal in splendor to Uccaiḥśravas,
he was declared to be the horse for the horse-sacrifice, marked with auspicious characteristics.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite on the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
one should write down one's own name, marked with one's strength, upon a leaf.
The sacrificial horse, though guarded with great effort by its protectors, must be released;
wherever the horse goes, there the well-guarded [protector] should follow.
Therefore, the horse must be brought back by force by those who provide protection, for someone might bind it by force, arrogant in the strength of his own prowess.
In these [periods] consisting of the *karts*, one should abide according to the rule, observing the restraints and so forth;
having become a bearer of the deer-horn, one should be endowed with celibacy (*brahmacarya*). ||7||
While he is observing his vow, as long as a year elapses, he should satisfy the poor and the wretched with wealth and other gifts. (8)
O noble one, food or wealth should be given abundantly;
for whatever the wise man requests, that very thing one indeed bestows upon him. (9)
For one who acts in this manner, the sacrifice of action attains completion;
it effects the destruction of all sins and the destruction of enemies. 10.
Therefore, O King, you are capable of establishing, protecting, and honoring [the Dharma]; having cleared away your own stainless infamy, purify other people as well.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of the twice-born, look now at my horse-stable;
are there any such horses there that are marked with auspicious characteristics? (12)
Having heard those words, Agastya, the mine of compassion, rose up while looking for auspicious horses worthy of the sacrifice. (13)
Then, having gone there to that hall accompanied by Rāmacandra,
he beheld horses of various kinds, swift as thought and possessed of great strength.
"Are these the descendants of Jirāja descended upon the surface of the earth? Or are they the consolidated masses of the fame of the lords of the Raghu dynasty gathered together?
Or is this a mass of nectar from the ocean in the form of a horse?"—seeing him thus, the sage was filled with wonder in his mind. (15)
On one side was an excellent row of horses with crimson bodies; on the other were those with black ears, possessing a luster like that of musk.
On one side were horses with the luster of gold, on another were those of blue color; on yet another side they were surrounded by steeds distinguished by variegated hues. (17)
Seeing all this, the sage, his mind filled with curiosity,
went to where those horses fit for sacrifice were to be seen.
There he saw hundreds of bound [images] of such colors;
seeing them, the sage, his hair standing on end with joy, was filled with wonder. (19)
All the cows had one ear black, their bodies resembled the color of milk,
they had yellow tails and red mouths, and were marked with auspicious characteristics.
Beholding on all sides those sinless ones, who resembled pure streams of water, who were graced by the speed of thought, and who possessed the splendor of the blossoms of stainless fame,
the sage— who had dried up the ocean— spoke to the Lord of Sītā, his eyes, face, and radiance brightened by the sight of the wondrous horse.
Agastya said:
"O best of the Raghus, as I behold these many auspicious sacrificial horses fit for the horse-sacrifice, my eyes find no satiety today."
"O illustrious Rāmacandra, honored by gods and asuras, perform the great horse sacrifice, O Great King, in its most extensive form. (23)
Like the Lord of the Gods performing all the assemblies of sacrifices, and like the Sun drying up the waters of the enemies of the gods;
having conquered that supreme city whose leaders of enemy hosts have been slain, provide for this highly fortunate one the enjoyment of happiness upon the surface of the earth. (24)
Thus, with all his senses satisfied by this discourse of words,
he gathered all the charming materials required for the sacrifice.
Accompanied by his ministers, the great king arrived at the bank of the Sarayū and ploughed a vast expanse of earth with golden-tipped ploughs.
Having repeatedly measured out the ground to the extent of four yojanas,
that best of men constructed pavilions for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having constructed the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules, provided with a womb-chamber and a girdle, adorned with many jewels, and endowed with every beauty; ||28||
The lord of sages, the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha, possessed of great ascetic power,
caused all of that to be performed in accordance with the injunctions of the Vedas and the Śāstras.
Sent by that sage to the hermitages of the best of sages,
his disciples reported that the foremost of the wicked was intent upon performing a horse sacrifice.
Then all those sages, the best among ascetics, being summoned, arrived, being exceedingly eager for a vision of the Supreme Lord. ||31||
Nārada, Asita, the mountain (Parvata), the sage Kapila, Jātūkarṇya, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Atri, and Āsuri; ||32||
Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Saṃvarta, and he known as Śuka—
these and others went to Rāma’s excellent horse sacrifice.
The high-minded descendant of Raghu honored them all with rising to meet them and salutations, as well as with offerings of water for the feet, seats, and other hospitable rites.
Having witnessed his prowess, he generally gave them cows and gold, saying:
"Great indeed is your good fortune, that you have come into my sight. (35)
Śeṣa said: O Brahmin, when the assembly of the best of sages was thus agitated,
there arose a discourse on dharma that was highly esteemed by those of all social classes and stages of life.
Vātsyāyana said:
What was that wonderful discourse on dharma that occurred there?
And what did the virtuous ones say out of compassion for all the worlds? (37)
Śeṣa said:
Seeing those lords of sages assembled together, the great Rāma, son of Daśaratha,
inquired about all the dharmas appropriate for all the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas).
Being thus questioned by Rāma, they proclaimed the dharmas of great merit;
I shall declare all of them to you—listen to them according to the rule. (39)
The sages said:
A brahmin must always perform sacrifices, study, and so forth;
having studied the Vedas, one who is free from passion should not enter the householder stage of life. (40)
A Brahmin must always avoid living by serving the low-born;
even when fallen into distress, he should never live by the livelihood of a dog.
Approaching one's wife during her fertile period is the supreme duty of a householder; or he may do so out of a desire for offspring, keeping in mind the boon granted to women. 42.
Approaching [a woman] during the day is considered detrimental to the longevity of men;
therefore, the day of a Śrāddha ceremony and all festival days (parvan) should be avoided by a wise man.
If one goes there to a woman out of delusion, he falls away from the supreme Dharma;
whereas he who approaches his wife during her fertile period and remains devoted to his own spouse [is not so hindered]. ||44||
A householder who engages in sexual union only during the fertile period is to be known here as one who always practices celibacy (*brahmacārī*).
The fertile period consists of sixteen nights; among these, four are censured. (45)
Among those [nights], the even ones grant sons, while the odd ones grant daughters;
one should avoid the evil moon and exclude the asterisms Maghā and Mūla. (46)
Being pure, he should approach his wife, especially under a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) named after a male;
thus she shall give birth to a pure son who accomplishes the goals of human existence.
In the *ārṣa* form of marriage, the giving of a pair of cattle that has been prescribed is praised;
even a small bride-price for a girl makes the buyer of the girl a sinner. (48)
Trade, service to a king, neglecting the study of the Vedas, improper marriage, and the omission of sacred rites are the causes of the downfall of a family. (49)
Whether by means of food, water, milk, roots, or fruits, the merit that a householder gains from the gift of a cow to a worthy recipient according to the prescribed rite—[that merit he attains]. (50)
If a guest departs from one's house unhonored and with his hopes shattered, he is instantly excluded from the merit accumulated by that person since birth. (51)
Having given to the ancestors, the gods, and men, the householder should eat the nectar;
he who cooks for his own sake eats only sin, being merely a filler of his own belly. (52)
Sin enters [the body] on the sixth and eighth lunar days through oil and meat respectively;
likewise, one should avoid using a razor and engaging in sexual intercourse on the fourteenth day. (53)
One should not approach a woman during her menses, nor eat together with one's wife;
one should not eat while wearing only a single garment, nor eat while seated on a high seat.
A man of noble character who desires spiritual luster should not look at a woman while she is eating;
he should not blow on fire with his mouth, nor should he look at a naked woman. (55)
One should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one cast impure things into it;
one should not commit violence against living beings, nor should one eat during the two twilights.
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor display Indra’s bow (a rainbow);
nor should one consume curd that has risen in its strength during the night. 57.

One should not greet a woman who is observing her menstrual period, nor should one eat until satiety during the nights; one should not be fond of the triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music), and one should not wash one's feet in a vessel of bell-metal.
One should not wear clothing or even sandals that have been used by another;
one should not eat from a broken vessel, nor should one eat food that has been defiled. (59)
One should not go to sleep with wet feet, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from food;
nor should one eat while lying down, nor should one touch the head while impure from food.
A man should not behave like a non-human; he should not despise himself.
He should not bow down before one who is arrogant, nor should he speak of the vital secrets of others.

Having thus relied upon the householder stage, one should proceed to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage; whether accompanied by his wife or having left her behind, he should thereafter become dispassionate.
Thus, these and other such teachings were proclaimed by the Ṛṣis at that time,
by the great Śrutārāma, who desired the welfare of all the world.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on All Dharmas," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||9||
(10) The Tenth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
While he was thus hearing the teachings, the spring season arrived, wherein the commencement of great-souled sacrificial rites and other ceremonies takes place. (1)
Perceiving that moment, the wise Vasiṣṭha, born from a water-jar,
spoke appropriately to the great king Rāmacandra.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed Rāmacandra, the time has now arrived for you, when the horse, having been duly consecrated for the sake of the sacrifice, is to be released. (3)
"O best of the twice-born, let the preparations be made there; having summoned her, let the Blessed One perform the worship of the brahmins as is appropriate. (4)
One should give gifts according to the prescribed rule to those who are distressed and wretched, having honored them with great respect, so that their own [merit] may arise for them.
"O Lord, having been initiated here by Kanaka’s virtuous wife, observe this vow:
sleep upon the ground, remain celibate, and abstain from all sensual enjoyments."
Wearing a deer horn at his waist and carrying a girdle, an antelope skin, and a staff,
he prepares the sacrificial requisites provided with all necessary materials.
Having heard these significant words of Vasiṣṭha, which were consistent with the facts,
the wise [Rāma] spoke to Lakṣmaṇa in a manner enriched by various meanings.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, listen to my words; having heard them, perform them immediately.
Bring with effort a horse suitable for the performance of the horse sacrifice."
Śeṣa said:
Having heard the words of the Lord of the Raghus, Lakṣmaṇa, the conqueror of enemies,
then spoke these words of various descriptions to the commander-in-chief.
Lakṣmaṇa said:
O hero, listen to these very sweet words; having heard them, act with haste again at the command of Rāma, whose feet are rubbed by the crowns of the crest-jewels of the lords of the earth.
Prepare the army, which is powerful due to the force of time and the strength of the wind, and which is equipped with excellent chariots, elephants, infantry, and cavalry riders. (11)

Let the horses, swift as the wind, be readied—those whose beautiful hoof-strikes resemble a garland of waves—and let them be mounted by excellent horsemen who carry many weapons and strike down the enemy forces. (12)
Behold the elephants, resembling mountains, with their mahouts holding spears and pikes in their hands;
they are accompanied by heroic warriors bearing weapons, who offer abundant gifts and are filled with all manner of arms and missiles. (13)
O son of the Wind, my chariots, resplendent with the abundance of outstretched banners and yoked to horses possessing the speed of a forest fire,
are equipped with various weapons and missiles that call to mind the destruction of diverse enemies.
Let the divisions of the supported roof-ridges be led away by the throngs of charioteers. ||14||
Hundreds of foot soldiers, with bows and fire-arms in their hands,
rushed toward me, exerting themselves to protect the horse worthy of the horse-sacrifice.
Having heard these words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, he summoned his army commander named Alajin and ordered him to prepare for battle.
Adorned with the beauty of ten firm water-pots and fine hair, bearing a conch-shell on his neck within an expansive throat-cavity like a jewel,
he possesses clear luster in his face and bears white radiance upon his ears.
It shone brightly, as it were, with the mass of rays from the tips of its upraised hands. ||17||
With its face adorned with decorative patterns, beautified by shimmering jewels, and graced with garlands of pearls, the horse emerged. 18.
Adorned with a white parasol and beautified by white chowries, the king of horses then emerged from the city, surrounded by a great radiance.
Some soldiers were in front, some in the middle, and others at the rear; thus they served Hari in a manner appropriate for service, just as the gods did in former times.
Then, having summoned the entire army, he issued this command at that time:
[an army] densely crowded with vast multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Then, from those assembled armies, a great clamor was heard;
thereafter, the sound of kettledrums arose in that best of cities.
Then, by that great and beloved roar of the heroes,
the mountain peaks trembled and the palaces shook.
O King, there arose a great neighing from the horses as they became bewildered;
the earth trembled violently, resounded by the clatter of chariots.
Then, as the herds of elephants moved about, the earth was covered with dust; rising up in great abundance, it caused the disappearance of the people there.
A great army, crowded with people and led by the commander-in-chief named Kālajit, marched forth, obscuring the sun with its umbrellas.
Roaring and creating a tumultuous commotion in the battle, those foremost of the Talavīra heroes set out with joy, fully prepared for the sacrifice of Raghunātha.
All of them bore musk-paste as body-unguents upon their limbs,
their heads were adorned with garlands of pure flowers,
and their bodies were decorated with ornaments such as crowns and bracelets.
Impelled by the lord of the earth, they all likewise set forth. ||28||
Thus did those lowly soldiers, bow-bearers, noose-bearers, and sword-bearers of clear prowess, advance toward the great king. (29)
Thus, gradually reaching the pavilion marked by the signs of sacrifice,
the horse leaped into the sky, causing the surface of the earth to be scarred by his hooves.
Seeing that Hari had arrived, Rāma, with a heart full of great satisfaction,
urged Vasiṣṭha toward the performance of the necessary rites.
Vasiṣṭha summoned Rāma, accompanied by his golden wife,
and caused him to perform the ritual for the removal of the sin of Brahman-slaughter.
Observing the vow of celibacy and carrying a deer-horn, Rāma,
the conqueror of enemy cities, caused that task to be performed.
For the purpose of performing the sacrificial rite, he prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) commensurate with the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
Therein was the wise preceptor (ācārya), a knower of the Vedas and an investigator of the Śāstras.
The sage Vasiṣṭha, the ancient family preceptor of Raghunātha,
performed his sacred rites there, while Agastya, a treasury of asceticism, practiced penance.
The sage Vālmīki was the Adhvaryu priest, and the sage Kaṇva was the gatekeeper;
there were eight gates there, truly adorned with beautiful archways.
At each of the two gates, there are two gatekeepers who are learned Brahmins skilled in incantations;
at the eastern gate are the two foremost sages known as Udevala and Asita.
At the southern gate were Bhūmā, Atri, Kaśyapa, and the treasure-house of asceticism; at the western gate were Ṛṣabha, Aujāta, Karṇya, and Jājali.
At the northern gate were two sages, each accompanied by two ascetics;
having thus performed the ritual for the gates, Vasiṣṭha, who was born from a water-jar, [proceeded].
O twice-born one, when Hayavara began to perform the proper worship, women who were well-dressed and adorned with garments and ornaments were there. (40)

They worshipped the honored one with turmeric, unbroken rice, perfumes, and other offerings; then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), they incensed him with moments of agallochum smoke.
Then, by the command of Tāḍavāja, the courtesans performed the birthday celebration for Vimalabhāla, who had been thus honored and anointed with sandalwood paste.
In that place, rich with fragrances such as saffron and endowed with every splendor,
he fastened a radiant leaf fashioned from refined gold.
There he painted the exalted power and might of the Ten-headed One (Rāvaṇa),
as well as the bow-bearing Guru, the preceptor of the initiation into archery and the banner of the Solar dynasty.
The son of him whom all the gods, together with the asuras, bow to with their jeweled crowns—the upholder of the Raghu lineage, who strips away the pride of the strength of heroes—[is here]. (45)
The highly fortunate Rāmacandra is the crest-jewel of all heroes;
his mother was born from the womb of the queen of the King of Kosala. 46.
Rāma, the destroyer of his enemies, who is a jewel born from her womb,
performs the horse sacrifice, being well-instructed by the Brāhmaṇa.
For the removal of the sin incurred from the slaughter of that eminent lord of Brahmins named Rāvaṇa,
he released that foremost of horses, the best among steeds.
It is well-protected by moats filled with a great army and its retinue;
its guardian is his brother Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa. ||49||
Accompanied by a host of an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, that best of kings might become arrogant due to the intoxication of his own power. (50)
"We are archers, heroes, the most excellent and fierce here;
therefore, seize by force this horse adorned with a jewel-garland. (51)
Then his brother Śatrughna, the slayer of enemies, effortlessly subdued that horse, which possessed the speed of thought, the swiftness of desire, and was more radiant than all other movements.
With those sharp-pointed arrows released from his bow, he [struck] the calves. ||53||
Thus spoke the great lord of sages with these and other words,
[praising] the blazing majesty of the heroic power of Śrī Rāmacandra’s arms.
He released [the arrow] which was a treasury of beauty, possessing the exceeding speed of the wind, and capable of traversing the specific realms of the netherworld and the earth. ||54||
Then Rāma, the best among wielders of weapons, commanded Śatrughna:
"Go behind this horse that moves at its own will, for the sake of protecting it. (55)
O Śatrughna, may your path be auspicious as you go;
may your two arms be victorious over enemies and capable of drawing out the foe. (56)
Those warriors who have gone forth to battle must be warded off by you; remaining endowed with the multitude of your own virtues, O Great One, protect me upon the earth.

By that [deed], those who perform meritorious actions praise the work of the Great Goddess, [who delivers] those who are asleep, fallen, stripped of their garments, terrified, and bowed down in supplication. ||57||
"Terrified like those deprived of their chariot, they say, 'We belong to you.
Therefore, you who desire the merit of Śatrughna, must not abandon them here. (58)
He who speaks thus to one who is free from pride, intoxicated, asleep, submerged [in delusion], or afflicted by fear—"I am yours"—goes to the lowest state. (59)
O you who are filled with all excellent virtues, do not harbor thoughts of another's property or another's wife, nor should you indulge in base pleasures. (60)
Do not first urge the elders to flee; conquer them with arrows. O compassionate one, do not neglect the worship of those worthy of honor. (61)
One should pay homage to a cow, a Brahmin, and a Vaiṣṇava endowed with righteousness;
by saluting them as one departs, one shall attain perfection.
Viṣṇu is the Lord of all, the witness, whose body pervades everything;
O mighty-armed one, those who belong to Him indeed wander about in His very form.
O scion of the Raghus, those who remember Mahāviṣṇu, who dwells in the hearts of all beings, should be considered equal in form to Mahāviṣṇu himself. 64.
Those for whom there is no "one's own" and no "another's," and for whom an enemy is equal to a friend—they are indeed Vaiṣṇavas who purify even a sinner in an instant. (65)
Those for whom the Bhāgavata is dear and for whom the Brāhmaṇas are indeed dear have been sent here from Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of purifying the world.
He in whose mouth is the name of Hari, in whose heart is the eternal Viṣṇu,
and in whose belly is the food-offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu— he is a Vaiṣṇava, even if he is an outcaste dog-cooker.
I bow here with devotion to those for whom the Vedas are most dear, who do not seek the pleasures born of saṃsāra, and who are devoted to their own dharma.
There is no difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu, nor between Brahmā and Maheśvara;
I carry that which is purified by the dust of their feet, which destroys all sin. (69)
All those men for whom Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and Mahālakṣmī are not distinct [from one another] should be considered as having come here from the heavenly world. (70)

One who protects those who have come for refuge, who is devoted to honoring and giving, and who acts according to his ability for the pleasure of Hari—he indeed should be known as the best of Vaiṣṇavas. (71)
He whose name quickly burns away a great heap of sins, and who possesses devotion to His two feet—he indeed is a Vaiṣṇava. (72)
Having paid homage to those whose senses are under control and whose minds also contemplate Hari, one shall indeed be purified from birth until the end of death. (73)
Abandoning another's wife as you would a sword,
you shall become a ground for the prosperity of fame and ornaments;
thus, act according to my command.
May I attain the supreme abode, the praiseworthy state of perfect yoga.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Instruction to Śatrughna," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||10||
(11) Chapter Eleven. Śeṣa said:
Having thus commanded, the Blessed One, Rāma, the subduer of enemies,
looked again at the heroes and spoke with a grave voice.
I, following his command, protected the flank of my brother Śatrughna,
who was indeed guarding the horse.

May he who shall utterly defeat all the foremost heroes who have come against him with multitudes of weapons piercing the vital organs, take this single betel-roll, thereby spreading his own fame most extensively upon the earth. (3)
When Rāma had spoken thus, Puṣkala, the son of Bharata,
took the betel-roll from that lotus-like hand of the King of the Raghus.
"O Lord, I shall go every day to protect Śatrughna from behind, O Master, fully equipped and bearing all weapons, missiles, bows, and arrows. (5)
"O noble-minded Rāmacandra, by this [act] serving as the omen, your majesty shall conquer the entire surface of the earth."
By your grace, I am now capable of forbidding all those—including gods, asuras, and humans—who have assembled here for battle. (7)
"My master will come to know everything from witnessing my prowess;
therefore, O Śatrughna, I shall go as one who provides protection for your back. (8)
As the son of Bharata was speaking thus, the lordly monkey, expressing his approval with "Excellent!
and "Well said!", praised all the chief heroes among the monkeys, whose faces were as bright as the wind-god.
O great hero Bhīma-Nūman, listen to my words with respect:
through your grace, this kingdom has been obtained by me, free from all thorns. (10)
"O Lord of Monkeys, I know all that deed of yours, O Hari, by which you crossed the ocean during your union with Sītā."
"Go, acting as the protector of my army at my command;
Śatrughna, my own brother, must be protected by you just as I am. (12)
O high-minded one, wherever a lapse of judgment arises in Śatrughna, there my brother must be awakened. 13.
Having heard these great words of the wise Rāmacandra,
he then placed them upon his head and offered his salutation.
Then the great king commanded Jambavan, the lord of monkeys,
who possessed the supreme splendor of the foremost of monkeys, for the service of Raghunātha.
Aṅgada, Gavaya, Mainda, as well as the monkey Dadhimukha;
Sugrīva, the lord of the monkeys, and the two monkeys Śatavali and Akṣika. ||16||
"O you, become prepared! For the elephant has attained such speed that its hair and breath have turned blue. Thus did he speak, and so forth. 17.
Adorned with all kinds of elephants and excellent horses decorated with refined gold, as well as armor and helmets, they were quickly arrayed.
Śeṣa said:
Then Rāma, resplendent with strength and valor, summoned his wise minister Sumantra and arrived at the presence of the chief counselor;
he called for men capable of protecting the kingdom. (19)
Having heard this, the slayer of enemy heroes spoke thus:
"Alas! Here are powerful lords of men who ought to be protected. (20)
O Raghunātha, listen to these nine heroes who are well-united, wielders of the bow, possessors of great knowledge, and experts in all weapons and missiles. (21)
[He will be] foremost in valor like a sapphire, as well as a king who is a treasury of fortune;
he will be a scorcher of enemies and a king skilled in weapons. ||22||
This kṣatriya, a great hero with sapphire-blue jewels, the foremost of chariot-warriors—he alone shall protect the hundred thousand [soldiers] and fight them fearlessly. (23)
With ten akṣauhiṇīs for the protection of Yātudhāna’s vehicle,
and with my uplifted arms, sharp and equipped with helmets.
For he, whose prowess is supreme, has shattered the pride of the best of warriors;
he is the discharger of arrows from both the left and right hands, and the most eminent knower of all weapons. (25)
Here comes he who, equipped with a staff-like bow, has arrived with twenty akṣauhiṇīs for the protection of the sacrificial horse, girded for the destruction of his enemies.
Likewise, this best of kṣatriyas was Lakṣmīnidhi,
who, having propitiated Śata-dhṛti through austerities, practiced the divine weapons.
The Brahmāstra, the Pāśupatyastra, the Gāruḍa known as the Nāga, the Māyūra, the Nākula, the Raudra, the Vaiṣṇava, and that known as the Megha. ||28||
He is one who knows the application and withdrawal of the weapons beginning with the Vajra known as Pārśvata, as well as that designated as Vāyavya, and so forth. 29.
Accompanied by one akṣauhiṇī of his own troops, he set forth—he who is the crest-jewel of heroes and the destroyer of all enemies. (30)
This very one, skilled in all weapons and missiles, a forest fire for the lineage of his enemies, has today become the foremost among archers and the scorcher of his foes. (31)
Let them depart with a vast army accompanied by fourfold forces;
let those who are fierce in strength today place the command of Śatrughna upon their heads. (32)
King Ugrāśva was likewise skilled in weapons;
all of them were well-armored protectors of the horse. (33)
Having heard these words spoken by the minister, he rejoiced greatly and commanded those soldiers described by the wise counselor.
Having obtained the permission of the Lord of the Raghus, they attained great joy;
for a long time they had desired that supreme goal, yet they were fierce in battle.
Equipped with armor and the like, as well as by means of various weapons and missiles,
they went to the camp of Śatrughna, urged on by the husband of Sītā.

Śeṣa said: Then Rāma, having been thus addressed by the Ṛṣi, worshipped in due order all the sages, beginning with the preceptor, according to the prescribed rites and with the sacrificial fees as directed.
Rāma gave to the teacher an elephant sixty years of age,
a single horse with the speed of thought, adorned with a jewel necklace.
A single chariot made of gold, adorned with jewels and gems, yoked to four horses, and equipped with all necessary implements. ||39||
One hundred thousand mani-gems were visibly present,
along with one hundred *tulās* of pearls and one thousand *tulās* of coral of brilliant luster.
A single village, well-prosperous and crowded with various people, abounding in diverse crops and filled with many kinds of mansions. (41)
He likewise gave to the Brahman priest, and he also gave to the Hotṛ and the Adhvaryu;
having bestowed abundant gifts upon the officiating priests, the best of the Raghus bowed down to them.
All of them honored him with various words of blessing:
"Live long, O great king Rāmacandra, upholder of the Raghu lineage! (43)
The gift of a maiden, the gift of land, and likewise the gift of an elephant;
the gift of a horse, the gift of gold, and the gift of sesame seeds along with pearls. ||44||
The Great One ordained for the Brahmins the gift of food, the gift of water, the supreme gift of fearlessness, and all kinds of gifts of precious gems. 45.
Say to someone: "Give! Give wealth! Give! Do not withhold!
[And say: "May he give food, may he give food, endowed with every enjoyment! (46)
In this manner, the wise Lord of the Raghus proceeded with all auspicious rites, accompanied by excellent brahmins and provided with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). ||47||
Then Rāma’s younger brother went and prostrated before his mother, saying:
"O beautiful lady, give me your command; I am going for the sake of protecting the horse. (48)
Having conquered the host of enemies through your grace, I shall return endowed with splendor, accompanied by great kings and the preeminent horse. (49)
The mother said: "Son, go, O great hero; may your paths be auspicious.
Having conquered all the hosts of enemies, return again, O you of noble mind. (50)
Protect Puṣkala, your own brother, who is most skilled in dharma, exceedingly powerful, and even now endowed with childlike playfulness. 51.
"O son, if you come endowed with Puṣkala and possessed of auspiciousness, then I shall have joy; otherwise, I shall be a partaker of grief. (52)
Being thus addressed, he replied to his own mother:
"Remembering the pair of your feet, I shall attain what is auspicious. (53)
"O beautiful lady, having protected Puṣkala and made my own lineage glorious, I shall return again full of joy, having acted in a manner worthy of my name. (54)
Having spoken thus, the hero departed for the sacrificial pavilion where the excellent Rāma sat, clad in the attire of a sacrificer, surrounded by the foremost of the best of sages. (55)
The wise hero, endowed with every splendor, said:
"O Rāma, command me for the protection of the horse, with your permission. (56)
Raghunātha, having heard that, said, "May it not be so!
You must not strike a child, a woman, one who is intoxicated, or one who is unarmed. (57)
Then Lakṣmaṇa, the brother of Jānakī and son of Janaka,
smiling slightly and winking with his eye, spoke to Rāma.
Lakṣmīnidhi said:
O Rāmacandra, mighty-armed one, devoted to all dharma, instruct Śatrughna in such a way that he may become extraordinary among men. (59)
Performing actions appropriate to his lineage and likewise following the conduct of his predecessors,
he shall go to the supreme abode, endowed with splendor, energy, and strength.
"O Great King, it was said by you that one should not insult a Brahmin;
yet your father, devoted to his father, killed a Brahmin. (61)
You too have committed a very great deed censured by the world;
for you have slain a woman who certainly should not have been killed. (62)
His elder brother, the great king,
previously performed a feat of valor by gradually cutting off the ears of the Rākṣasī.
"King Śatrughna will act in this manner according to your instruction;
for if he were to act otherwise, it would be unworthy of his lineage. (64)
To him who had spoken thus, Rāma, who was skilled in all forms of speech, replied as if smiling with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Furthermore, let the peaceful yogins, who are equal in suffering and happiness, listen;
they understand the means for crossing over and emerging from the shoreless cycle of existence. (66)
Those heroes, who are great archers and experts in all weapons and missiles, they alone understand the ways of war, but not those like you. (67)
Those who cause suffering to others and those who wander onto the wrong path must be restrained by all kings who desire the welfare of the entire world. (68)
Having heard this spoken, all those present in the assembly smiled at the subduer of enemies;
then Agastya released that well-adorned horse which had been duly honored.
Having recited this mantra, Vasiṣṭha, born from a water-jar,
touched the horse with the tip of his hand and released it with a desire for victory.
Come quickly, O Vājin, as if in play, to every part of the earth's surface;
you have been released for the sake of the sacrifice, so return here with haste.
Released from his horse by all the soldiers skilled in weapons and missiles,
he set out toward the eastern direction, surrounded by them and endowed with the speed of the wind.
The entire force of his movement caused the surface of the earth to tremble;
even Śeṣa supported the world with his hood slightly bent down.
The quarters of the sky became serene, and the surface of the earth was endowed with splendor;
gentle breezes blew from behind that Śatrughna.
As Śatrughna prepared for his departure, his right arm throbbed, foretelling auspiciousness and becoming a source of victory.
Puṣkala entered his own beautiful and prosperous home,
which was adorned with white balconies and jeweled altars.
There he saw his own wife, who was devoted to her husband;
she was somewhat delighted by the sight of him and longed for the sight of her husband.

With her lotus-face, she was chewing betel leaf mixed with fine camphor; from her nostrils issued a great fragrance, and upon her arms, which resembled lotus stalks, there was a beautiful mark on her ear.

Alas! Her breasts resemble *kucautu* and *mālūra* fruits, her waist is adorned with a beautiful girdle, and her feet are exceedingly tender, marked by the impressions of anklets; yet she bears her own husband, who has been slain. 79.
Embracing his beloved, who spoke with a voice faltering from grief,
he made his own body one with her by the intense pressure of their embrace upon her breasts.
He said, "O auspicious lady, by the command of Rāma, I am going as the protector of Śatrughna's rear, guarding the horse while mounted on a chariot; please grant me permission. (81)
These mothers of mine must be honored by you with the massaging of their feet and other services; for you should eat their leftovers, showing respect in the performance of such tasks. (82)
O fearless one, you must not insult any of the auspicious noble women devoted to their husbands, such as Lopāmudrā and others, for they are adorned by the power of their own asceticism. 83.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Reunion of Puṣkala with His Wife after the Release of the Horse," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||11||
The Twelfth Chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having seen her husband speak thus with overflowing love, she [spoke].
She replied, as if smiling, speaking with a somewhat faltering voice. ||1||
O Lord, may victory be mine everywhere on the field of battle;
let the command of Śatrughna be carried out so that the protection of the horses may be ensured. 2.
Your servant, who follows at your feet, is to be remembered everywhere;
for my mind never goes anywhere other than to you, O Lord. (3)
I am never to be remembered as one who is exclusively intent on battle;
as long as I am present, there is doubt regarding victory for you in war.
O lotus-eyed one, you must act in such a way that Ūrmilā and the others do not mock me upon seeing me with their hand-strikes. ||5||
This is the wife of one who is greatly afraid and flees from battle; for cowards do not fight—where is the occasion for heroes? (6)
Therefore, just as the hosts of gods shouted loudly in joy at the slaying of Medin, so too must you act for the protection of the horse of the mighty-armed Rāma. (7)
O warrior, you must go at the very front everywhere;
let the powerful enemies strike your back with their bows like deaf mutes. (8)
May the army of your enemies quickly become agitated by mutual fear, due to the terror of your uplifted hand and the swords of the Bhojas. 9.
A great family is to be honored by you as you conquer your enemies;
go, O Lord of mighty arms, and may prosperity attend you here.
"Take this bow, adorned with a great and excellent string, at the roar of which the host of enemies becomes overcome with fear. (11)
Let these two quivers of arrows be filled with ten million arrows capable of crushing ten million enemies, so that they may be slain by the hero as is fitting. (12)
Now, place this armor upon your body, which is most beautiful;
it is firm, with a great brilliance like a thunderbolt, destroying all dense darkness. 13.
He placed his own helmet upon his head, which was exceedingly beautiful and charming,
adorned with excellent gems and jewels.
Beholding that daughter of a hero whose speech was so pure,
he gazed upon her face with the lotus-like vision of his eyes.
Having attained the burden of supreme liberation, the conqueror of enemies, capable of engaging in battle, spoke to her with great fortitude. (15)
Puṣkala said: "What extent do you describe for me? I shall carry out all of that accordingly.
Your fame, O beloved, shall become that of a hero's wife—resplendent and desired. (16)
The valiant one accepted everything bestowed by Itikāntimatī: the armor, the excellent crown, the great bow, the sword of wisdom, and all else. (17)
Having put on all that, the excellent warrior, who was endowed with great splendor and skilled in all weapons and missiles, shone exceedingly. ||18||
Richly adorned with the splendor of various weapons and missiles, decorated with garlands of heroes, and anointed with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and other fragrant substances. (19)
There, the virtuous Kāntimatī repeatedly performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for him, who was adorned from his feet up to his knees with various flower garlands.
Having performed the lustration ceremony many times, scattering pearls repeatedly,
with her eyes streaming with falling tears, she embraced her own husband.
Then, embracing her firmly for a long time, he consoled her, saying:
"O beloved wife of a hero, do not suffer this great separation from me."
"O devoted wife, I am going into your presence. Having said this to his own wife, the lord ascended the chariot. (23)
Then, devoted solely to her husband's welfare, she gazed with unblinking eyes at her excellent husband as he departed.
He went to see his father, King Janaka, and his mother, who was overwhelmed with affection; having approached his father, he saluted him joyfully with his head.
Then, having embraced her son, she placed him upon her lap; shedding a flood of bitter tears, she said, "May it be well with you. (26)
Rāma, the supreme performer of sacrifices, said to his father Bharata:
"He must be protected by Lakṣmaṇa and by you, the high-souled ones. (27)
Commanded by his mother and by his father with joyful words,
he went to Śatrughna’s camp, which was adorned by great heroes.
Surrounded by chariot-warriors, heroic infantry, excellent horses, and cavalrymen,
that leader of great sacrifices went joyfully to the Udāraghuṭṭa mountain.
Proceeding through the regions of Pāñcāla, Kuru, and Uttarakuru,
as well as Daśārṇa and Śrīviśāla, he was endowed with every splendor.
There, as he listened everywhere to the entire glory of the hero of the Raghus— glory which effects the protection of devotees through the slaying of the demon Rāvaṇa— (31)
Furthermore, by undertaking purifying rites such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*),
Rāma will spread his fame throughout the world and protect the people from fear.
To them, the great and preeminent Śatrughna gave necklaces, various jewels, immense wealth, and garments. (33)
Named Sumati, he was radiant with splendor, proficient in all branches of knowledge, the minister of Raghunātha, and the excellent follower of Śatrughna. (34)
That great hero traveled through many villages and provinces with him;
yet, due to the majesty of the Lord of the Raghus, no one seized the horse. ||35||
Many rulers of the land, possessing great strength and prowess, were equipped with the fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. ||36||
Having repeatedly brought many riches joined with pearls and rubies,
they bowed down again and again to Śatrughna, who had arrived for the purpose of guarding the horse.
