"O descendant of Raghu, this kingdom, all this wealth, along with my sons, cattle, and kinsmen—all this belongs to Rāmacandra; it is not mine. (38)
Having thus heard what was said by him, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
took leave of his own command there and set out on the road accompanied by them.
O Brahmin, having thus arrived in due course accompanied by his horse, Śatrughna reached the city of Ahicchatrā, which was crowded with various kinds of people. (40)
It was crowded with Brahmins and twice-born men, adorned with various jewels, and beautifully decorated with golden and crystal palaces and gate-towers. ||41||
There, in every palace, lotus-faced women endowed with the grace of lovely ladies were seen, casting aside their brilliance. (42)
There, those who delight in their own proper conduct and enjoy every kind of pleasure, are endowed with such playfulness as the attendants of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). ||43||
Wherever there are heroes with bows in hand, skilled in the fitting of arrows, they make King Sumada exceedingly joyful. 44.
The Lord beheld such a city from afar;
by its side was that best of cities, an enchanting garden endowed with splendor.
With *punnāgas*, *nāgacampas*, *tilakas*, and *devadārus*; with *aśokas*, *pāṭalas*, mango trees, *mandāras*, and *kovidāras*. ||46||
With mangoes, jackfruit, and *damba* trees, as well as *priyāla* and *panasa* trees;
with *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, and with *mallikā*, *jāti*, and *yūthī* jasmine. ||47||
Then Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, beheld that place adorned with nīpa, kadamba, bakula, campaka, madana, and other trees. 48.
Then, by means of his yogic power, the hero went right after him into the middle of that forest, which was beautifully adorned with *tamāla*, *tāla*, and other trees.
The lotus of whose feet is served by those who wield the bow. ||49||
There he beheld a marvelous temple constructed of sapphire, beryl, and likewise emerald. (50)
It was radiant, worthy of being served by the gods, resembling a plateau of Mount Kailāsa, and beautified by pillars made of gold—truly the best among dwellings. 51.
Having seen that excellent temple of Raghunātha’s brother,
he questioned his own minister Sumati, the best among speakers.
Śatrughna said:
"O best of ministers, tell me what this is, whose temple it is, and why is it being worshipped here? For what reason does it stand here, O sinless one? (53)
Having heard this, the omniscient knower of mantras spoke:
"Listen with one-pointed mind, O hero, as I tell you everything in its entirety. (54)
Know that the supreme abode of Kāmākṣā bestows the sole bliss of the universe;
O Lord of Creatures, by the mere sight of it, all perfections are attained. 55.
Having praised and bowed to her, the gods and asuras attained complete prosperity;
she is the bestower of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, and is compassionate toward her devotees. (56)
Formerly requested here by the intoxicated King of Ahicchatra, she remains and performs everything that removes the suffering of her devotees. 57.
Pay homage to her, O Śatrughna, crest-jewel of all heroes!
By bowing down, you shall swiftly attain a perfection difficult even for gods and asuras to obtain. (58)
Having heard those words, Śatrughna, the scorcher of enemies and bull among men,
questioned Bhavānī regarding the entire account.
Śatrughna said: Who was the king Ahicchatrāpati Sumada, and what penance did he perform, by which this Mother of all the worlds remained pleased and stayed here? (60)
Tell everything, O Great Minister, augmented by various meanings;
speak as you know it to be, therefore, O one of great intelligence. (61)
Sumati said:
"The Hemakūṭa mountain is pure and adorned by all the gods;
there exists a stainless sacred ford (tīrtha) well-served by hosts of sages. (62)
Having lost his father-in-law, his wife, and his children,
and being oppressed on all sides by his enemies, Sumada went to the forest to perform penance.
For three years, with his mind focused on a single point,
Dadhīca meditated upon the Mother of the Worlds, his eyes fixed and motionless upon the tip of his nose.
For three years, subsisting on dry leaves,
he performed a most fierce and extremely difficult supreme penance.
For three years during the cold season, he remained submerged in water;
in the summer, he practiced the penance of the five fires; and in the rainy season, he stood facing the clouds.
Restraining his breath for three years and keeping Bhavānī in mind,
the wise man perceives nothing else within the range of his own consciousness.
When twelve years had passed, Śakra, beholding this supreme austerity and perceiving it intensely with his mind, trembled with fear.
He commanded him, who was surrounded by his retinue and accompanied by Apsarases, as he prepared for victory over Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods.
O deluder, act so that an obstacle to Sumada’s asceticism may arise, performing a pleasing service for me who desires to go. (70)
Having heard these great words, the Lord Turāsāha himself,
O descendant of Raghu, spoke with intense pride regarding his universal conquest.
Kāma said:
"O Lord, who is this Hisumāda? What insignificant penance does he perform?
I can bring about the destruction of the penance of Brahmā and the other gods; what need is there to mention him? (72)
In former times, the moon, pierced by the power of my arrows, went to Tārā;
you too went to Ahalyā, and Viśvāmitra to Menakā.
"Do not worry while I, the servant of the Lord of the Gods, am present.
Here I go against Sumada; protect the gods, O noble one! (74)
Having spoken thus, Ākāmadeva went to Mount Hemakūṭa,
accompanied by his friend Vasanta as well as by hosts of Apsarases.
There, spring rendered all the trees endowed with flowers and fruits,
and caused them to be resounded by flocks of cuckoos and swarms of bees.
A very cool breeze blew, taking refuge in the southern direction and carrying the fragrance of *lavaṅga* flowers from the banks of the Kṛtamālā river.
Thus,
at the end of her forest-dwelling, that most excellent of apsarases, surrounded by her companions, went there to the presence of Sumadantika.

There, she was skilled in the art of singing with a voice as beautiful as that of the Kinnaras, and she was proficient in various types of musical instruments, such as the mṛdaṅga and the paṇava drums. (79)
Having heard that song and beholding the enchanting spring, that lord of men—
Likewise, the wise one made his eyes turn toward the charming warbling of the cuckoos. (80)
O sinless one, seeing that the king had awakened, the flower-armed god of love hurriedly and swiftly strung his bow behind him.
There, a certain Apsaras, with her sprout-like eyes dancing, massaged the feet of the king.
Another cast a side-long glance; yet another made intense gestures with her limbs. (82)
Surrounded by apsarases, his mind overwhelmed by desire,
he whose senses were the crest-jewel of those who have mastered them began to reflect.
"All these excellent apsarases, sent by Śakra to create obstacles for his asceticism, will act exactly as they have been instructed. (84)
Having reflected thus, the ascetic spoke to those excellent women:
"Who are you? Where do you dwell? What is it that you intend to do? (85)
Oh, what a great marvel has occurred, that you, who are so difficult to attain even through austerities, have come before my eyes by virtue of my own penance! (86)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Kāmākṣā," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(13) Chapter Thirteen. Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Sumada, that treasure-house of asceticism,
the celestial nymphs, led by Rambhā, spoke to him with joy.
"O beloved, through your ascetic penances we have become women endowed with every excellence;
enjoy the entirety of our youth—renounce the fruit of your austerities! (2)
May this fortunate Ghṛtācī, whose body possesses the luster of a campaka flower, enjoy the nectar of your mouth, which is as delightful as the fragrance of camphor. (3)
O highly fortunate one, by virtue of your own formidable merit, quickly enjoy this woman, who possesses most beautiful grace, enchanting limbs, and firm, full, and excellent breasts.
Furthermore, you must abandon the mass of suffering that has already been attained. ||4||
Me too, adorned with priceless ornaments,
my chest graced by a garland of Mandāra flowers.
Speak so that you may firmly embrace her, whose hair is like a chowrie of various wonderful tales.
"Drink the nectar issuing from my mouth;
having ascended an excellent celestial chariot, he shall go with me."
Having reached the peak of Sumeru, frequented by many merits,
he enjoys the fruit of his excellent austerities.
Adorned with the beauty of the youth of Tilottamā,
may she take up the sunshade over your head.
Marked by the continuous flow of beautiful whisks, they were like two streams of the Gaṅgā, O most excellent one upon the earth. 7.
Listen, O sir, to this captivating tale of love;
drink it like the nectar desired even by the hosts of gods.
Having reached the excellent garden named Candana, O Lord of the Kurus, sport there with the most beautiful women. (8)
Having heard what was thus said, the king of great intelligence reflected: "From where indeed have they arrived?"
By my ascetic power, the celestial nymphs have been well-created;
what obstacle is there here that must be dealt with? (9)
Thus, the wise and heroic king, anxious with thought as he reflected upon himself and them, spoke to Sumada and the celestial women.
You are the very form of the Mother of the World residing within my heart;
she whom I contemplate is likewise considered to be of your own nature.
This trivial heavenly bliss described by you is full of conceptual construction;
my mistress, when served with devotion by me, will grant a boon. (12)
By whose grace Brahmā attained the great Satyaloka;
she alone will bestow everything, for she is the one who brings an end to the suffering of her devotees. 13.
What is Nandana, and what is the mountain beautifully adorned with gold?
What is that which, though easily attainable through even slight merit, bestows the suffering of a demon? (14)
Having heard these words, Kāma struck the god of men with various arrows, yet he was truly not able to cause him even the slightest harm.
Neither by side-long glances, nor by the tinkling of their anklets, nor by embraces, nor by their gazes were the celestial nymphs able to distract his mind. (16)
Having gone back as they had come, the king of steadfast intellect told Śakra what had happened;
hearing that, Indra became afraid and began his own service.
Then, having observed that he was undisturbed, Abikā appeared in person before the great king, who had conquered his senses, and was deeply gratified.
Behind the five-faced one, she is gracefully poised, holding a noose and a kusha grass;
bearing a bow and arrows, the Mother is the purifier of the purifiers of the world. 19.
Beholding his mother, who possessed the splendor of ten million suns and held a bow, arrows, a goad, and a noose, the wise one was filled with joy.
Having bowed his head many times to his mother, who was filled with devotion,
she laughed and repeatedly touched her own limbs with her hands.
The one of great intelligence offered praise with a mental disposition overflowing with devotion, his voice faltering and his throat adorned with horripilation. (22)
O sinless one, whose pair of feet is served by the hosts of devotees of the Great Goddess Jayadevi, and whose feet are worshipped by the lords of gods such as Brahmā and Rudra! 23.
O Mother, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings shines as being permeated by your portions;
apart from you, nothing exists. O Auspicious Mother, salutations to you! 24.
O Earth, you have been established by me through my sustaining power (ādhāra-śakti) so that you do not waver;
you are adorned with mountains, forests, groves, and the elephants of the quarters. 25.
The sun blazes, scorching the earth with its sharp rays;
by your power, it releases the moisture residing in the soil, drawing it up.
May the fire situated within and without bring peace to the worlds, O Great Goddess, who are honored by gods and asuras, through your majesty! 27.
You are knowledge; you are the great illusion (mahāmāyā) of Viṣṇu, the sole protector of the world. By your own power, you create this universe, and you protect it, O deluder. 28.
Having attained perfection from you, all the gods indeed proceed happily; protect me, O Lord of Compassion, who are saluted by all and beloved by your devotees. (29)
O Mother, O first-born of the Great Puruṣa, make me, your servant, who takes refuge at your feet, achieve my desired perfection. (30)
Sumati said:
"The Mother of the World, thus gratified, said to her devotee Sumada, whose body was emaciated by asceticism: 'Choose an excellent boon.'"
Having heard these words, King Sumada was overjoyed and chose his own kingdom back, now that its thorns— the wicked— had been destroyed.
May there be unswerving devotion to the pair of feet of Maheśī, which further grants liberation that carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (33)
Kāmākṣā said:
"May you obtain a kingdom that is exceedingly joyful and free from all thorns;
may you become one whose two lotus-feet are served by jewels among women. (34)
O you who are named Sumada, may there never be such humiliation by enemies as occurred when the highly illustrious Lord of the Raghus, having slain the afflicted Rāvaṇa, [was mocked]. (35)
For he will perform the horse sacrifice, adorned with every requisite;
his brother is the great hero Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy warriors.
"Protecting [the kingdom], he will come here surrounded by heroes and others;
you must hand over to him the entire prosperous kingdom, wealth, and so forth. (37)
You shall protect [it] with your own formidable archer-warriors;
thereafter, O high-minded one, you will wander everywhere upon the earth. (38)
Then, having paid homage to Rāma, who is served by Brahmā, Indra, Īśa, and the others,
you shall attain liberation, which is difficult even for yogis to reach through the practice of self-restraint.
I shall remain here for as long as it takes for the arrival of Rāma’s horse;
thereafter, having rescued you, I shall go to the supreme abode.
Having spoken thus, the goddess, who is saluted by gods and asuras, vanished;
and Sumada also, having slain his enemies in Ahicchatrā, became king.
Although this king is incapable, being merely joined with an army and vehicles, I, well-trained in great illusions, shall not be captured by him. (42)
Having heard that the supreme horse of the horse-sacrifice had arrived at the vicinity of the city, and that you, the high-minded one whose feet are served by all great kings, were there as well; 43.
The All-Knowing King, the bearer of the name Sumada, will grant everything now through the majesty of the great king Rāmacandra. ||44||
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this account of Sumada, the highly illustrious, exceedingly powerful, and noble-minded [Bali] exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and rejoiced greatly. 45.
The lord of Ahicchatrā, surrounded by all his own attendants and served by many kṣatriyas, sat comfortably in the assembly hall.
Brahmins learned in the Vedas and Vaiśyas abundant in wealth waited upon the king, who was full of joy and endowed with splendor. 47.
The excellent Brahmins, who follow the path of justice and delight in the knowledge of the Vedas, bestow their blessings upon that king, the sole protector of all the worlds. 48.
At that time, someone arrived and said to the king: "O Lord, a certain horse belonging to Ajāneka stands at the gate with a message."
Having heard that, he quickly dispatched his chief attendant, saying:
"Find out whose horse this is near my city."
Having gone there, the palace attendant learned the events from the beginning and reported them to the king, who was served by great kings. (51)
Having heard this, the wise King, constantly remembering the horse of the Lord of the Raghus,
commanded all his people.
All those who possess worldly pleasures, who are filled with wealth and grain, and who place auspicious arches and other ornaments upon their houses—may they all attain this here. (53)
Thousands of beautiful maidens, adorned with every ornament, mounted upon elephants, [waited] in front of Śatrughna. ||54||
Then, having issued all these commands himself, the king was surrounded by his retinue of sons, grandsons, queens, and others. ||55||
Accompanied by his great ministers and excellent warriors such as Puṣkala and others, Śatrughna beheld the heroic king named Sumada.
It was joined by elephants yoked with riders, by foot soldiers who tormented the enemy, and by adorned horses; it was filled with heroes and graced by the heroic.
Then the great king, having arrived, joyfully bowed to Śatrughna:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; my body has been truly honored. (58)
"Accept this kingdom, O illustrious Great King, adorned with horses and elephants, and well-filled with great wealth such as rubies and pearls. (59)
"O Lord, I have long been waiting for the arrival of the horse;
what was previously foretold by Kāmākṣā has now come to pass—alas! (60)
Behold my city and make its people fulfilled;
O King Rāmānuja, purify our entire lineage.
Having said this, he caused Kuñjara, who was as radiant as the moon, to mount [the chariot], and likewise the great hero Puṣkala; then he himself ascended.
Then, O Great King, the sound of kettledrums, cymbals, trumpets, lutes, and other instruments,
impelled by Sumada, pervaded everything.
The maidens approached the great lord of men,
Śatrughna, whose feet are served by Indra and the other gods.
Seated upon elephants, they offered congratulations with heaps of pearls, though they were not [actually] employed [for that purpose]. ||64||
Gradually returning to the city with joyful people,
they were honored with festive greetings and reached their home, which was adorned with arched gateways and other decorations.
Accompanied by his jewel-like horse and likewise graced by heroes,
King Śatrughna, honored by the king, reached the palace.
Then, having worshipped the younger brother of Raghunātha with offerings such as *arghya* and other honors,
they presented everything to the wise Rāmacandra.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Entrance of Śatrughna into the City of Ahicchatrā," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||13||
Chapter Fourteen. Śeṣa said:
Then the king spoke to Śatrughna, who was satisfied with his welcome.
That bull among men was desirous of hearing the most excellent narrative of Raghunātha. ||1||
Sumada said:
"Is Rāma, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, dwelling in happiness? He is this very incarnation for the protection of his devotees and the one who bestows grace upon me. (2)
Blessed are these people in this city, who, filled with supreme joy, incessantly drink from the lotus-face of Raghunātha with the cups of their eyes. (3)
O bull among men, O great-minded one, my entire collection of wealth, as well as the various objects belonging to my family, land, and so forth, has been fully accomplished for its purpose. (4)
Previously, by her compassionate grace, Kāmākṣī bestowed upon me this favor:
that the crane shall behold the face of Raghunātha, which is like a lotus, together with his family.
When the heroic Sumada, the best of kings, had spoken thus,
they related everything concerning the arising of the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus.
Having stayed there for three nights, the younger brother of the Lord of the Raghus,
possessed of great intelligence, resolved to depart along with the king.
Having understood that, Sumada quickly consecrated his son in the kingdom, with the approval of the great king Śatrughna and Puṣkala. ||8||
There, that highly intelligent one bestowed garments, many jewels, and various kinds of wealth upon the servants of Śatrughna.
Then he began his departure with ministers who were most wealthy,
along with infantry, cavalry, elephants, excellent horses, and ten million chariots.
Accompanied by that archer Sumada, Śatrughna,
who bore the majesty of the Lord of the Raghus, proceeded along the path laughing.
Having reached the bank of the Payoṣṇī river, the best of horses proceeded;
all the warriors who protected the descendant of Vīhaya followed behind him.
Beholding the various hermitages of the sages who maintained great austerities,
he heard here and there of the arising of the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus.
This wise Hari goes forth, protected by tawny deer, and repeatedly guarded by tawny monkeys and the best of Hari’s devotees who follow him. 14.
Hearing these auspicious words of the sages on all sides,
the Great Lord, whose mental disposition was overflowing with devotion, was deeply gratified.
And he beheld the pure hermitage, crowded with people engaged in their duties, where the sound of the Vedas silenced all other noise for the men who were listening. (16)
The entire sky was purified by the smoke from the sacrificial offerings of the Agnihotra fire,
and it was beautifully adorned with the numerous sacrificial posts erected by the eminent sages.
Where cows accustomed to being tended by deer must be protected, and where mice dig burrows out of fear of the cat. (18)
Peacocks and mongooses play with serpents day and night;
elephants and lions, having attained friendship, dwell together constantly without fear. (19)
There, the black antelopes, intent on feeding upon the wild rice, felt no fear from predators, being protected by throngs of sages. (20)
The cows, whose udders are like jars and whose bodies are as radiant as the Nandini,
sanctify the mountain with the dust raised from their hooves.
Seeing him with lotus-like hands holding sacrificial fuel, the best of sages, accustomed to religious rites,
questioned the omniscient sage Rāma Sumati.
Śatrughna said: "O wise one, whose abode shines before us—this place free from enmity, worthy of service, and crowded with throngs of sages? (23)
I shall listen to the news of the sage and establish purity; I shall sanctify my own body through his accounts, descriptions, and so forth. (24)
Having heard these significant words of the high-souled Śatrughna,
the minister of the wise Lord of the Raghus spoke.
Sumati said:
"Know that Cyavana’s hermitage is adorned by great ascetics;
it is free from enmity, crowded with sages, and filled with the wives of the munis. (26)
That great sage, who established the shares for the gods and physicians at the great Svāyambhuva sacrifice, was one whose lineage remained undivided.
This power of the Great Sage cannot be exhausted by anyone;
for he is enriched by the strength of his asceticism and is indeed the very embodiment of the Vedas.
Having heard the news concerning the great sage Cyavana, Rāma’s younger brother questioned Sumati about everything, including Śakra, who was the foremost among those who eat.
Śatrughna said:
When did he assign a share to the two Aśvins among the rows of gods?
And what was done by the King of the Gods at this great sacrifice on earth? (30)
Sumati said: In the lineage of Brahmā, there was a sage renowned as Bhṛgu;
once, he went out in the evening to gather sacrificial fuel. (31)
Then, for the sake of utterly destroying him, the powerful Rākṣasa Damana arrived and spoke these words, which caused great terror. (32)
"Where is that sage? Where is his sinless wife?
Thus he spoke again and again, his voice agitated with rage. (33)
Then Agni, perceiving that danger had arisen from the Rākṣasa,
showed him his blameless wife who was pregnant.
The Rākṣasa seized her, like a female osprey, from Bhṛgu, the lord of the night-prowlers, the protector of the protectors, and the treasure-house of asceticism. (35)
Speaking thus, he took that distressed woman and went outside,
awakening that virtuous lady of Bhṛgu’s lineage with the blow of his wicked words.
Then, from the middle of her womb, the great being fell out with blazing eyes, like a fire-eating elephant. ||37||
He said: "Do not go quickly, O evil-minded one! You shall be reduced to ashes;
for having violated a virtuous woman, you will not attain any well-being. (38)
Thus addressed, he fell down, his body reduced to ashes;
then the mother, taking her child, returned to the hermitage with a distracted mind.
Bhṛgu, having learned that everything had been done by Vahni, was overcome with anger and cursed him:
"O you wicked betrayer of your enemies, may you become a devourer of all things! (40)
Then, afflicted by extreme suffering, he cursed him; the Fire-god quickly seized his feet and said:
"O Lord, O great-minded one, ocean of mercy, grant me your favor. (41)
Out of fear, I have spoken words that were untruthful, yet I am not a hater of my guru;
therefore, O crest-jewel of dharma, show compassion toward me. (42)
"By bestowing that favor upon me, you shall become pure even while consuming all things.
Thus spoke the compassionate ascetic-muni to the eater of oblations (Agni). 43.

Once the son had emerged from the womb, the pure and auspicious brahmin, with *darbha* grass in hand, performed the birth rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules. (44)
All the ascetics called him Cyavana because he had fallen from his celestial state;
he grew gradually, like the moon on the first day of the bright fortnight.
Accompanied by all his disciples, who were endowed with the power of asceticism, he went to the Revā river, the sole purifier of the world, in order to perform penance. ||46||
Having gone there, the great one performed austerities for ten thousand years;
were two parrots born from his nostrils, adorning the top of an anthill? (47)
Deer, coming there with eager longing, scratched their itching bodies against her;
yet no one recognized her at all, for she was shrouded in an irresistible ascetic glow.
Once, the lord Manu, being intent upon a pilgrimage to sacred fords, set out with his family and surrounded by a great force. ||49||
Having bathed there in the great river and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
That maiden wandered here and there within the Tīrthāvana grove,
accompanied by her friends and adorned with beautiful ornaments of refined gold.
There, having seen an anthill beautifully adorned by great trees,
he beheld a certain radiance that was devoid of blinking or winking.
Having gone there, she prodded him with sticks until blood flowed;
seeing the king's exhaustion, the queen became extremely distressed.
Nevertheless, overwhelmed by the reproach of her kinsmen,
she, afflicted by fear, lamented for herself by herself.
Then, O King, the earth trembled and a meteor fell from the sky;
all the directions became smoky and the sun was encircled by a halo. (55)
Then many horses, chariots, and elephants of the king perished;
wealth along with jewels was lost, and there was mutual strife at that time.
Seeing that, the king became afraid and, with a somewhat agitated mind, asked the people: "By whom has this sage been offended? (57)
Having learned from Pāraṇa about the conduct of his daughter,
he went there deeply distressed, accompanied by a vast army and vehicles.
Beholding that treasure-house of asceticism, endowed with great austerity, I praised him and sought his favor, saying: "O best of sages, have mercy! (59)
Therefore, being pleased, that best of sages, a man of great austerity, said to him:
"You have perceived all this, including the portents and other signs, which was brought about by your son."
"Your daughter has caused the eyes of the great king to burst open; they have bled profusely. Knowing this, she did not tell you. (61)
Therefore, this great princess should be given to me according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, the pacification of the portent will occur, without a doubt. ||62||
Having heard that, King Prajñācakṣus, being distressed, gave his daughter— who was endowed with noble lineage, youth, beauty, virtuous conduct, and auspicious marks— to him.
As soon as this lotus-eyed maiden was given away by the king,
all the portents arising from the sage’s wrath were pacified.
Having given his daughter to that sage, a treasure-house of asceticism, the king—
filled with compassion yet once again sorrowful— returned to his own city.

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Cyavana," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||14||
Fifteenth Chapter.
Sumati said:
Then the sage, having returned to his own hermitage together with Mānavī, the daughter of Manu, and his wife...
Having destroyed all sins through the practice of yoga, he attained liberation. ||1||
He chose as his husband from among his peers one who was deprived of sight and whose vital energy had been taken away by old age.
He served that supreme Harimedha as if he were his own family deity, the bestower of his heart's desires. ||2||
She, understanding his gestures, was devotedly serving her husband,
who was high-minded, a treasure-house of asceticism, and dear to her.
The virtuous Manoharā attained supreme joy, like Śacī intent upon serving Śakra. ||3||
The slender princess, endowed with all auspicious marks, served at his feet; she was beautiful and subsisted on fruits, roots, and water.
Constantly intent on carrying out his command and devoted to honoring him, she passes her time dedicated to the welfare of all living beings. (5)
Having abandoned sloth, malice, greed, sin, and pride, he,
ever vigilant and striving, gratified Cyavana.
Thus, as he performed service to him with the actions of speech and body for a thousand years, the Great King conceived a desire in his mind.
Once, the two physicians of the gods arrived at the hermitage of the sage; having honored them with a welcome, she performed worship for them.
His mental disposition was satisfied by the worship, including water for honor and water for the feet, performed by the daughter of Śaryāti.
Under the influence of affection, those two beautiful ones spoke these enchanting words: "Choose a boon. (9)
Having seen the physicians praising [him], and while the boon was being requested from the gods,
that daughter of the king, the best among the wise, formed a resolution.
Perceiving her husband's intention, the princess spoke these words:
"If you two gods are pleased, then my eyes have already been given to my husband."
Having heard these enchanting words of Sukanyā and having observed her virtuous conduct, the two best of physicians spoke as follows: (12)
If your husband, that lord of the gods, should now assign a portion [of the sacrifice] to us, he would grant us the clear vision of our eyes. (13)
Cyavana also said "Om" when the two heroes offered him a choice portion of their vital energy;
then, delighted, the Aśvins spoke to that best of ascetics.
"Plunge into this lake of worldly existence created by the Siddhas," thus addressed was he whose body was seized by old age and whose veins were filled with its flow. (15)
Having been led into the lake by the two Aśvins, while they themselves were bathing in the water, three men rose up—lovely and dear to women. (16)
Beholding those men of excellent form, who were radiant as the sun, wearing golden garlands and earrings, well-attired, and all of equal appearance, she of beautiful hips was struck with wonder.
Not knowing her husband's whereabouts, the virtuous woman sought refuge with the Aśvins;
pleased by her devotion to her husband, they revealed him to her. (18)
Having addressed the sage, the two departed for heaven by means of a celestial chariot,
intent on performing their own share of the sacrificial rites in the sacrifice they were about to perform.
After some time, seeing her emaciated by her ascetic observances, he was moved by compassion and spoke with a voice faltering with love. (20)
I am pleased today by this devotion of yours, O beautiful lady, who bestows honor, through your supreme service and singular devotion in your heart.
This body of embodied beings, which is their most intimate friend, has not been regarded as suitable to be sacrificed for my sake. (21)
For him who is detached from unwholesome dharmas, there are the graces of the Blessed One, won through austerity, meditative concentration, knowledge, and self-yoga.
By following these very same [teachings], which are non-contradictory, I grant you a vision that is fearless and free from sorrow. ||22||
But others [say]: "What need has the Lord of Wide Strides for the arrangement of purposes, which are merely the opening and closing of his eyebrows?"
They enjoyed the fruits of their own dharma, which were perfected and free from worldly power, divine and difficult for men to attain even through royal transformations. ||23||
Seeing him speaking thus, the woman— expert in all yogic arts and sciences— was freed from her anxiety.
With her voice overwhelmed by respectful affection, her face radiant with a smile and a bashful glance, she spoke. ||24||
Sukanyā said:
"O bull among the twice-born, O Lord, O Master, I realize that this has indeed been accomplished by you, the sovereign of unfailing yoga and māyā."
May that union with your body, which you have promised as a sacred vow, result in offspring of most excellent virtue for virtuous women. 25.
There, having trained himself in what was to be done according to the instruction,
by which means this [ascetic] had excessively emaciated his body through excessive desire for self-mortification.
"Success will be achieved for her who is tormented by the god of love;
therefore, O wretched one, look for a dwelling suitable for her that is like the abode of her lord. (26)
Sumati said:
O King, desiring to do what was pleasing to his beloved, he resorted to the yoga of Cyavana and immediately manifested a celestial chariot that travels at will.
It was delightful, yielding all desires, endowed with every kind of jewel,
resulting in the accumulation of all prosperity, and adorned with pillars of precious gems.
It was provided with divine coverings, bringing comfort at all times, and adorned with variegated bands and banners. ||29||
It was resplendent with garlands of various flowers, with bees humming sweetly, and with diverse garments such as fine linen, silk, and woven cloth. ||30||
In the dwellings arranged one above the other, each separately provided with prepared couches, it was made lovely with fans, garments, and other such items.
Adorned here and there with various crafts displayed in every place,
it was graced by great emerald plateaus and coral altars.
The entrance, with its threshold of beautiful coral, shone with diamond door-panels;
its sapphire peaks were adorned with golden water-pots.
It was graced with excellent lotus-red gems as bright as eyes, fashioned into diamond walls, and adorned with various canopies draped with strings of pearls. ||34||
There, amidst the warbling of flocks of pigeons here and there, I climbed up repeatedly,
taking them for artificial birds.
With its monasteries, resting places, pavilions, courtyards, and open squares arranged for one’s pleasure, it was as if to amaze even itself. (36)
Beholding the house in this manner with a mind that was not overly pleased, he who knows the inner intentions of all beings spoke to her himself: (37)
"O timid one, having bathed in this lake, ascend this celestial chariot," said the lotus-eyed woman of beautiful brows, taking her husband's word to heart.
Wearing garments covered in dust as if they were braided hair,
their bodies were smeared with foul mud and their breasts were spotted.
There, with joy, she entered the lake of auspicious waters;
meanwhile, the hundred daughters of Niśa remained within their dwellings inside the lotuses.
He saw that all of them were of youthful age and possessed the fragrance of blue lotuses;
seeing her, those women with uplifted faces rose quickly and spoke. (41)
"We are your servants; what shall we do for you?
Having bathed that high-minded lady with this most precious bath-water," [42]
O giver of joy, he gave him a pair of spotless, new *dukūla* garments for his chest, as well as most excellent, precious ornaments that were exceedingly splendid. 43.
There was food endowed with every excellence and a drink like the nectar of immortality;
then he beheld his own self in a mirror, wearing a garland, stainless, and most excellent.
Having had the rites for a safe journey performed by those maidens, he was honored by them and adorned with a necklace of great value and a golden ornament.
With a golden necklace upon her neck, wearing bracelets and jingling golden anklets,
she had a golden girdle set with many jewels fastened around her hips.
Her face shone with beautiful eyebrows, white and lustrous eyes reaching to the corners,
and dark locks of hair that vied with the beauty of a lotus bud.
When she remembered her beloved husband, the favorite of the sages,
she went to where that lord of sages dwelt together with his wives.
Then, seeing herself before her husband surrounded by a thousand women,
she fell into doubt regarding that course of yoga.
She shone with a splendor unprecedented, her form having been cleansed of all impurities by the virtuous;
she bore her own natural beauty, her lovely breasts well-veiled.
Attended by a thousand Vidyādharīs and beautifully dressed,
the slayer of enemies, his passion aroused, then caused her to ascend that celestial chariot.
In that celestial chariot, his majesty unimpaired, accompanied by his beloved, his body attended upon by Vidyādharīs;
Shining with its clusters of blooming white water-lilies, the lake appeared as beautiful as the moon situated in the sky, surrounded by stars.
Therefore, in the valleys of the lords of the kulaparvatas— the abodes of the eight world-guardians— which possess the charm of breezes that are companions to the god of love;
Accompanied by her host of women, she took delight for a long time like Kubera in the sounds of the *śiva* drum, which were being struck by the Siddhas.
In the Vaiśrambhaka, the celestial grove, the Nandana, the Puṣpabhadraka,
the Mānasa, and the Caitrarathya, he took delight with Rāmā, being devoted to her.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Cyavana’s Austerity and Enjoyment," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||15||
(16) The sixteenth chapter. Sumati said:
Thus sporting everywhere upon the surface of the earth,
he did not perceive that years had passed, measured by the count of hundreds.
Then, O Brahmin, having realized that his most excellent and beloved wife had reached her own destined time and was fulfilled by her desires, he [acted].
He returned to the excellent hermitage situated on the banks of the Payoṣṇī—a place free from enmity, crowded with people, and frequented by deer. ||3||
There that great ascetic dwelt with his disciples who were well-versed in the Vedas;
constantly served at his pair of feet, he performed supreme penance.
Then once, Śaryāti desired to sacrifice to those deities;
at that time, he dispatched his servants to bring Cyavana. (5)
Summoned by them, that best of the twice-born, a man of great austerity, arrived there together with his lawful wife Sukanyā, who was firmly established in virtuous conduct.
The one of great renown saw that best of sages arrive with his wife and daughter;
he beheld a man of solar brilliance standing beside his daughter.
The king spoke to the princess, who had performed a prostration at his feet,
without bestowing any blessings and appearing as if his mind were not particularly pleased.
"What is this you wish to do? You have insulted your husband, that sage honored by the world."
Having abandoned a husband who is not esteemed because he is seized by old age, you have taken to this traveler, a paramour. (9)
How has your mind come to understand this, that you, born of a noble family of the virtuous, bring such disgrace upon your lineage by supporting a paramour who is overwhelmed by shame?
She who is not even the least bit under the control of her father or her own husband. ||10||
To her father who was speaking thus, she, with a pure smile and a slight smirk, said: "O Father, this son of Bhrigu is your son-in-law. (11)
He reported all this—the attainment of youth and beauty—to his father;
amazed and exceedingly pleased, he embraced his daughter. (12)
By his own spiritual power, Cyavana caused the Soma sacrifice to be performed for the hero [Aśvin], and he took up a draught of Soma even for the two Aśvins, who were previously drinkers of no Soma.
Endowed with the power of asceticism, he caused Indra to seize him;
for Śakra, having taken up his thunderbolt, desired to strike that best of Brahmins.
Seeing Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt—who was about to strike him—making himself and the god who purifies the assembly (Agni) subjects of the same sacrificial row, the sage [spoke]. 15.
The wise one uttered the syllable *huṃ* and paralyzed his arm;
there, Indra was seen by all with his arm rendered motionless, O Mānava.
Panting with rage like a snake restrained by a mantra,
Śakra, his arms paralyzed, praised that sage, a treasure-house of asceticism.
To him who was offering a portion to the Aśvins with a fearless heart, they said, "O Lord, let the tribute for the Aśvins be given. (18)
"I do not forbid you, O father; forgive the great sin I have committed.
Thus addressed, the sage, a treasure-house of compassion, quickly abandoned his anger. (19)
At that time, O bull among men, even Indra’s arm was released;
seeing this, all the people were filled with wonder in their minds. (20)
They praised the power of the Brahmins, which is difficult even for the gods and others to attain;
then the great king bestowed much wealth upon the Brahmins.
The scorcher of his enemies performed the final purificatory bath at Lake Cakrā after his sacrifice;
O Cyavana, tell me that which was asked by you—what a great act of compassion!
Having paid homage to him whose form is asceticism, and having obtained blessings for victory, he was told everything regarding his vow, endowed as it was with austerity and yoga. ||23||
"O Rāma, O delightful one, please send [him] along with his wife to the sacrifice.
Śeṣa said: While they were thus conversing, the horse arrived at the hermitage.
Moving with the speed of the wind, he left the earth marked by his hooves;
in that great exertion, he grazed upon the dūrvā grass with the tip of his mouth.
While the sages had gone to the river to bathe, taking their darbha grass with them,
Śatrughna— the scorcher of enemy armies and esteemed by heroes— [arrived].
He reached the exceedingly beautiful dwelling of the sage Cyavana;
having gone to that hermitage, he saw the sage Cyavana.
Standing near Sukanyā, who appeared like the very embodiment of asceticism, he prostrated at his feet while uttering his own name. (28)
"I am Śatrughna, the younger brother of the Lord of the Raghus and the protector of his horse. ||29||
"I pay homage to you for the pacification of great sins"—having heard these words, the best of sages spoke. (30)
O best among the foremost of men, may there be prosperity for you through the destruction of your enemies;
as you protect the sacrifice, may your fame become vast.
O Brahmins, behold this wonder: even one who performs sacrifices becomes a delight to others;
for by the mere remembrance of his name, people perform acts that destroy their sins. (32)
Even men joined with great sins who take pleasure in the wives of others attain the supreme goal when they are intent on remembering his name at the time of death. (33)
By the dust arising from his lotus-feet,
she who bore a form of stone instantly became the companion of Gautama’s half-body, assuming a form that enchants the mind.
Māmakī, who was filled with love through meditation upon his form, burnt away the entire heap of her sins and attained a beautiful form. (35)
In the arena of battle, the Daityas, beholding his form which captivates the mind, attained that very form of his, free from all transformation.

Having meditated upon this, which is the culmination of the yogis' meditation, and having established themselves in yoga, they were liberated from the fear of saṃsāra and proceeded to the supreme state. ||37||
I am blessed today that I shall behold the beautiful face of Rāma—
its eyes with their lotus-petal-like corners, its fine nose, and its well-raised, lovely eyebrows.
She, whose tongue is like the tongue of a serpent, respectfully performs the chanting of the name of Raghunātha, which is contrary to her nature. 39.

Today we have attained the merit of asceticism, and today our desires are fulfilled, since we shall behold the face of Rāmacandra, which is difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain. (40)
With the dust of his feet, I shall make my own body pure;
and with most wonderful accounts, I shall purify my own tongue. 41.
Thus, with tears flowing and his voice faltering, he was overcome by the love awakened through the remembrance of the feet of Ādirāma, which had spread throughout the community of Vraja.
O Śrī Rāmacandra, bull among the Raghus, embodiment of dharma, compassionate toward devotees, deliver me from this cycle of worldly existence! 42.
Then, speaking before the sages with his eyes filled with streams of tears,
he did not perceive anything belonging to another there, as he remained absorbed in meditation upon his own self.
Śatrughna laughed at that sage and said, "O Lord,
let this best of sacrifices be rendered most pure by the dust of your feet."
It is a great fortune that the Lord of the Raghus, that mighty-armed one who is worshipped by all the worlds, dwells within the hearts of you all. (45)
Thus addressed, Cyavana, together with his retinue and surrounded on all sides by fires,
went there, immersed as if in a lake of joy.
Beholding that devotee of Rāma approaching on foot, Hanumān addressed Śatrughna with words full of humility.
"O Lord, if you would tell me of a most beautiful great soul, a supreme sage devoted to Rāma, I shall lead him to my own city. (48)
Having heard these significant words of the monkey hero, the slayer of enemies commanded Hanumān: "Go and deliver this message to the sage. (49)
The swift Hanumān, like the all-pervading wind, placed that sage along with his family upon his back and quickly carried them through the sky.
Seeing that sage who had arrived, Rāma, the best among the wise,
being pleased and overwhelmed with affection, offered him water for his hands and feet and other traditional honors.
I am blessed, O best of sages, for by the sight of you now, this sacrifice of mine, prepared with all its requisites, has been purified. (52)
Having heard these words, Acyuta, the best of sages, supremely delighted, spoke to Gopī, whose hair stood on end with love.
O Lord, O God who is the refuge of Brahmins, this worship of the submarine fire is fitting for you,
who thus protect the path of dharma, O Great King.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Horse to Cyavana’s Hermitage," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||16||
(17) Chapter Seventeen. Śeṣa said:
Then Śatrughna, beholding the inconceivable power of Cyavana’s asceticism, praised that Brahmanic austerity which is uniquely venerated by all the worlds. ||1||
"O best of Brahmins, behold the perfection of yoga, which in a mere instant has caused that celestial chariot—so difficult to obtain—to be fashioned! (2)
Where is the great attainment of enjoyments for sages of stainless soul?
And where is the desire for enjoyment in those of human nature who lack the power of austerity? (3)
Thus, having made this aspiration to himself at Cyavana’s hermitage, Śatrughna stayed for a moment, drank water, and attained a state of pleasant enjoyment. ||4||
The great horse, possessing the speed of the wind, drank the water of that river named Payoṣṇī, whose essence is holy, and proceeded on his way. (5)
Then, seeing his departure, the warriors followed after him—
some on elephants, some on foot, some on chariots, and others on horses.
Accompanied by his preeminent minister named Sumati, Śatrughna quickly followed behind on a chariot adorned with horses.
Traveling on, the horse reached the city named Ratnātaṭa, belonging to the king called Vimala, which was crowded with people who were joyful and well-nourished. (8)
Having heard from his servant that the excellent horse of Raghunātha had indeed arrived nearby in front of him, accompanied by all the warriors; ||9||
Then, with seventy elephants of moon-like hue,
along with ten thousand horses and chariots possessing the luster of gold— (10)
Accompanied by a thousand [chariots], he went forth toward Śatrughna;
having paid homage to Śatrughna and all the great car-warriors who had arrived, [he stood before them].
Having offered him his entire treasury, all his wealth, and his kingdom, the king stood before him and said, "What shall I do? (12)
The great king also firmly embraced him with both arms as he bowed at his feet,
and together with his son, he returned to his own kingdom.
Having set everything down, he was surrounded by many archers.
Having heard the name "Rāmacandra," which is enchanting to all the senses,
they all bowed down to him and gave him that horse along with great wealth.
Having honored the king with supreme joy, Śatrughna then departed behind the horse accompanied by his army.
As he was traveling thus, he beheld on that path a preeminent mountain, resplendent with rows of plateaus made of crystal, gold, and silver. (16)
The surface of the earth, abounding in various minerals, resounded with the roar of waterfalls and was resplendent with the colors of excellent ores such as red chalk and lac. ||17||
Where the hosts of Siddhas sport with the Siddhas, free from fear from any quarter; where Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Nāgas play with effortless ease. (18)
It was attended by a cool breeze touched by the waves of the Gaṅgā, resounded with the playing of the lute, and beautified by the charming warbling of parrots. ||19||
Beholding the mountain, Śatrughna, his mind filled with wonder arising from that sight, spoke thus to Sumati. (20)
"What is this great, excellent mountain that astonishes my mind?
This wonderful peak, consisting of a hundred prasthas of great silver, shines upon my path. (21)
Is this the dwelling place of the deities, a playground for the gods, which causes such agitation to the mind with its abundance of splendors? (22)
Having heard these words, Sumati then spoke, his mind fixed upon the lotus feet of Rāmacandra, who is the abode of the virtues about to be described. (23)
"O King, O protector of the earth, this blue mountain shines before us, surrounded on all sides by enchanting great peaks with crystal summits. (24)
Sinful men who take pleasure in the wives of others do not see this;
those lowest of men who indeed do not honor the multitude of Viṣṇu’s qualities [do not see it]. (25)
Those who, relying on investigations based on their own intellectual reasoning and arguments, do not accept the Dharma established by the virtuous as arising from the Śrutis and Smṛtis; ||26||
Those who sell indigo, those who sell lac, the Brāhmaṇa who sells clarified butter and other such items, and he who drinks liquor; ||27||

A father, deluded by sin and driven by greed for wealth, would not give his daughter—who is endowed with beauty—to one of noble family and good character; rather, he sells her out of avarice for material goods. (28)
That man who defiles his wife, who is of noble family and virtuous character, eats the sweet fruit himself and gives nothing to his kinsmen. (29)
That person of base intellect who makes a distinction in the cooking for a meal or for the sake of Brahmins—whether it be *kṛsara* or *pāyasa*—does not cause the seeker to receive it. (30)

Those who treat guests with contempt when they are tormented by the heat of the sun and other hardships, those who consume what belongs to the atmosphere, and those who are betrayers of trust—[these are the ones who suffer]. (31)
O Great King, those who have turned their backs on Raghunātha do not see this meritorious, best of mountains, which is graced by Puruṣottama. (32)
This captivating one purifies us all by his very sight;
here stands he whose feet are worshipped by the crowns of the gods. (33)
The Supreme Person, the giver of merit, is worthy of being seen by those who possess merit;
yet the Vedas, though declaring "not this, not this," do not fully know Him.
The dust of whose feet is sought after by Indra and the other gods and is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
whom the wise know through the Vedānta and other scriptures that are complete in their expression. (35)
Thus, the glorious Puruṣottama dwells here upon the Blue Mountain (Nīla-śaila).
Ascend it after having paid homage and worshipped Him with virtuous deeds and other offerings. (36)
O King, by consuming the food offering (naivedya), one indeed becomes four-armed;
in this regard, they also cite this ancient history (itihāsa). ||37||
Listen to that, O Great King, which is endowed with every wonder—the account of what happened to King Ratnagrīva and his family. (38)
Having obtained [the boon] of four arms and so forth, which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to attain, there was a great royal city named Kāñcī, renowned throughout the worlds. (39)
Abounding in a great multitude of people and rich in forces and vehicles,
it is there that the foremost of Brahmins dwell, intensely devoted to the six duties.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings and longing for devotion to Rāma, they were performers of the *araṇa-kṣatriya* rites and never fled even in battle. ||41||
The Vaiśyas are averse to adultery, the property of others, and malice toward others; their auspicious livelihoods consist of usury, agriculture, and trade.
Śūdras, for whom the distinction between night and day has vanished through their service to Brāhmaṇas, always cultivate devotion for the lotus feet of Raghunātha. (43)
O Rāma, some common folk indeed utter "Rāma, Rāma" from the tips of their tongues, yet they do not commit sin even with their minds here. ||44||
Generosity, compassion, self-restraint, and truthfulness—these always abide there.
No sinless man there utters a word that causes harm to others. (45)
They do not harbor greed for the wealth of others, nor do they commit sin;
thus, O Great King, is the people protected by Ratnagrīva.
Free from greed, he takes only the sixth part as tax there and nothing else;
thus does the king protect his subjects in accordance with dharma. (47)
Many years passed while he enjoyed every luxury;
then one day, O Great King, he spoke thus to Viśālākṣī.
O large-eyed one, sons have been born to you—a devoted wife, a lawful partner, and one solely dedicated to her husband—who are now the bearers of the burden of protecting the subjects. (49)
My retinue is vast and free from all distress;
my elephants are like mountains, and my horses are like the wind. (50)
Chariots yoked with excellent horses are always at my disposal;
by the grace of Mahāviṣṇu, there is nothing lacking for me. (51)
Thus, O most beautiful one, this single desire alone remains in my mind: that today I have not yet visited a supreme sacred ford. (52)
It is fit for putting an end to dwelling in the womb and is graced by Govinda;
yet I have become old, with a body marked by wrinkles and grey hair. (53)
I shall devotedly perform the service of the heart-stealing holy places (tīrthas) for as long as a man remains filled only with the concerns of his own belly throughout his life. (54)
That man who does not perform worship of Hari is considered a bull among cows;
therefore, O auspicious lady, my dear, I am going on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Having resolved thus, "He whose burden was borne by his son, the king," he meditated upon Hari at twilight and during the intervals of the night.
Having risen in the morning and performed his morning prayers and other rites, that king saw a single dream of a brahmin ascetic. (57)
The great king, having comfortably entered the assembly hall together with his ministers,
then beheld a brahmin ascetic whose body was emaciated by penance.
Wearing matted hair, bark garments, and a loincloth, holding a staff in his hand,
his body was made meritorious through service at many sacred fords.
Seeing him, the mighty-armed king bowed his head in salutation; with a joyful heart, the lord of the earth offered him water for the hands, water for the feet, and other traditional honors.
When the twice-born one was seated comfortably and rested, he questioned the learned man:
"O Master, by the sight of you today, the sin of my body has been removed. (61)
"Since that great one has respectfully gone to the house of that wretched woman to protect her,
therefore, O elder of the Brahmins, tell me about this now."
"O gods, what sacred site (tīrtha) might be capable of destroying this embryo?
You are all-pervading, supreme, and devoted to meditative absorption and contemplation. (63)
Just as those of pure self, having performed merit by bathing in all sacred fords, become stainless,
so too, listen to me in detail as I speak to you who are full of faith.
"O expert in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), please speak out of your grace.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Listen, O Indra among kings; I shall describe the service of sacred fords (*tīrthasevana*) as you have asked. (65)
By whose grace might there be an avoidance of rebirth?
This Śrī Rāmacandra, the destroyer of the fever of saṃsāra, is to be served.
That very Blessed One, known as Puruṣottama, is worthy of worship;
various cities have been seen by me which bring about the destruction of all sins. (67)
Ayodhyā, the Sarayū, the Tāpī, as well as the supreme gateway of Hari (Prayāga), the Avanti, the Narmadā, the Kāverī, and the river that flows to the ocean (the Gaṅgā). 68.
Gokarṇa and the one called Hāṭaka destroy even ten million acts of killing;
the great mountain named Mallika grants liberation to those men who behold it. (69)
Wherever the water among men becomes dark or stainless, I have seen that very place to be a holy ford (tīrtha) capable of removing sin. (70)
I have seen Dvāravatī, frequented by gods and asuras,
where the Gomatī flows, its waters being the very embodiment of Brahman and auspicious.
Where sleep is declared to be dissolution and death is liberation—so says the Śruti—and where no strife whatsoever arises among men dwelling therein. (72)
Wherever there are wheels—whether they belong to stones, humans, or even those who possess wheels—beasts, insects, birds, and so forth, all are embodied beings of the wheel (cakras). ||73||
That city, in which Trivikrama—the sole protector of all the worlds—resides, has been brought within the range of my vision through great merits. (74)
I have beheld Kurukṣetra, which removes all slaughter;
there lies the Syama Tapaḥka, which destroys even the greatest sins.
I beheld Vārāṇasī, where Viśvanātha has made his abode, and where he imparts the liberating mantra known as Brahman. (76)
In which [state] die insects, birds, bees,
or animals, as well as those of asura birth.
Having abandoned the happiness of enjoying their own karma, they go to Kailāsa, their sufferings having passed away. ||77||
Where the Maṇikarṇika holy site is located, and where the river flows northward,
it effects the severing of the bonds of saṃsāra even for those who have committed sins.
Wearing matted hair and earrings, adorned with excellent ornaments of serpents,
and clothed in elephant hides, they dwell there, free from all suffering.
The mere name of Kālabhairava carries out the command of Yama;
the Lord Yama, though bearing his staff, does not even concern himself with the affairs of men. (80)
Such was the city of Kāśī marked by the Lord of the Universe that I beheld;
O King, many other holy places were also seen by me. (81)
But there was one supreme and great wonder seen on Mount Nīla in the presence of Puruṣottama, which has never come within the range of my eyes elsewhere. (82)

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Meeting with the Brāhmaṇas," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||17||
(18) Chapter Eighteen.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O King, listen to what occurred on Nīla, the best of mountains;
by having faith in which, men attain the eternal Brahman. 1.
While wandering there, I went to the mountain named Nīla,
where the peaks were repeatedly washed by the waters of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
There, on the mountain peak, I saw Bhillas bearing bows, who had dispelled their fatigue with the roots and fruits that served as their food. (3)
Then, a very great doubt quickly arose within me:
"Are these four-armed men, bearing bows and arrows, [deities]? (4)
The form of those who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha and have conquered their selves is now visible;
how was it obtained by these [beings], which is difficult even for Brahmā and others to attain? (5)
With their hands resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, bow, and lotus,
their bodies encircled by forest garlands, they stood nearby like devotees of Viṣṇu.
O King, with a mind filled with doubt, I then asked:
"Who are you, and how was this four-armed form obtained by you? (7)
Then, having laughed at me profusely, they replied:
"This Brahmin does not know the wonderful greatness of the *piṇḍa*. (8)
Having heard this, I said: "O most righteous ones who possess four-armed bodies, tell me: what is this *piṇḍa*, and to whom is it being given? (9)
Then, having heard my words spoken by those great-souled ones,
they [related] everything that had occurred there, beginning with the birth of the Four-Armed One.
The Kirātas said:
"Listen to the account of our Brāhmaṇa; he was a young child who, while playing, used to wander about constantly eating jambū fruits and other such things. (11)
Once, while playing, he climbed a beautiful mountain peak together with his young companions, surrounded by them.
Then, I beheld there a wonderful temple of the gods, its golden walls inlaid with emeralds and other precious gems. (13)
Seeing it violently tearing apart his own mass of darkness like the sun, he was struck with wonder: "What is this? Whose house is this? (14)
"Having gone there, I shall see: what is this state of the great ones?"—thinking thus, he entered his home with great fortune. (15)
There he beheld the Lord of Gods, who is saluted by both gods and asuras, resplendent with a crown, necklaces, armlets, a neck-ornament, and other jewels. (16)
He wore two very pure, heart-stealing earrings,
while his lotus-feet were intoxicated by the fragrance of *tulasī* that delighted the six-legged bees.
[I bow to] the embodiment of Śrī, whose feet are worshipped by those endowed with forms such as the conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga bow, and lotus, and who is well-served by Nārada and others.
Some sang, danced, and laughed most wonderfully;
they delighted the great king, who is uniquely venerated by all the worlds. (19)
O Sage, having beheld Hari there, he approached him;
meanwhile, the gods, having performed an extensive worship there consisting of incense and other offerings, [remained present].
Having offered the food oblation for the sake of the Beloved of Śrī and performed the lustration ceremony (anīrājana),
they then went each to their own home, O King, beholding His grace with great reverence.
By virtue of great fortune, he obtained a single grain of the food offering, which is difficult to attain even for Brahmā, the gods, and other celestial or human beings. (22)
Then, having consumed that and beheld the form of Śrī,
he attained the state of having four arms, becoming exceedingly beautiful through his son Pṛthu.
Then, as soon as we reached home, the boy was repeatedly observed by us;
he had attained the state of having four arms and was bearing the conch, the discus, and other [emblems]. (24)
When we asked him, "What is this wonderful thing that has occurred?", the boy then related to us all a most marvelous account. (25)
Previously, the Lord of the Gods was seen there at the very peak of the mountain;
there, a beautiful morsel of food offering was obtained by me. (26)
Merely by eating that, and for no other reason,
he immediately attained the state of having four arms, filled with wonder.
Having heard those words of his, we too were immediately struck with wonder;
thus, even by us was that god seen, who is exceedingly difficult to encounter.
There, food and other provisions, endowed with every delicious flavor, were enjoyed;
and we, moreover, by the grace of the Four-Armed One himself, [attained this].
Having gone there as well, O best of the gods, you too should behold the Lord. ||29||
O bull among Brahmins, having eaten a morsel of food there, the four-armed Bhava spoke that wonder which was asked by you.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Brahmin," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||18||
(19) The Nineteenth Chapter: The Greatness of Puruṣottama
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Having heard those wonderful words of the Bhillas, and considering this to be a great marvel, I became exceedingly joyful. (1)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, his body sanctified by merit,
he ascended the peak there, which was adorned with jewels and rubies.
There, O Great King, I beheld the God who is worshipped by gods and others;
having paid homage, I became one who has achieved his purpose through the first feeding of solid food. (3)
Having attained a four-armed form marked with the conch, discus, and other signs through the vision of Puruṣottama, I shall not enter a womb again. ||4||
O King, you too should go quickly to that mountain named Nīla;
thus make yourself successful and free from the suffering of pregnancy.
Having heard these words of that wise one whose speech was eloquent, he,
with his limbs thrilled with joy, questioned the sage regarding the procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites.
The king said: "Excellent, O foremost of Brahmins! Well spoken by you, O sinless one, regarding the majesty of Puruṣottama, which destroys the sins of those who hear it. (7)
Tell me the procedure for the pilgrimage to the sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) as it is ordained in the Vedas;
by what ritual may men obtain the full fruit of their journey? (8)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious procedure for the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrtha-yātrā), by which the God who is saluted by gods and demons is attained. (9)
Whether one’s body is wrinkled and grey-haired, or even endowed with youth, having recognized that death is unavoidable, one should take refuge in Hari. (10)
One's mind should be directed solely toward his glorification, his hearing, his salutation, and his worship; it should not be directed elsewhere, such as toward women and the like. 11.

Having observed that everything is perishable, momentary, and a source of great suffering, [one should seek] the Imperishable One, who transcends birth, death, and old age, and is beloved by devotion. 12.
If a person distributes [wealth] in any manner whatsoever—whether out of anger, desire, fear, hatred, greed, or hypocrisy—he does not experience suffering. ||13||
That person becomes virtuous through association with the saintly who are free from sin;
by whose grace men become devoid of suffering. (14)
O Great King, that which those holy ones—who are tranquil in passion and free from desire and greed—proclaim brings about the cessation of saṃsāra. (15)
In sacred fords, one may find a saint who is devoted to Rāmacandra;
the sight of whom is like a fire that instantly consumes the heap of men's sins. (16)
Therefore, men who fear the cycle of existence should constantly go to sacred fords that possess meritorious waters and are resplendent with rows of virtuous people. (17)
When those sacred fords are visited according to the prescribed rite, they destroy evil;
O tiger among kings, perform that rite as it is found within the scope of the Vedas.
One should first generate detachment toward one's wife, family, and so forth;
having realized that they are unreal, one should instead remember Hari with the mind. (19)
Having gone from there for the distance of one krośa while uttering "Rāma,
Rāma," one who knows the ritual procedure should bathe in the holy fords and other sacred waters and have his head shaved.
The sins of men who go to sacred fords (tīrtha) remain clinging to their hair; therefore, one should perform the shaving of the head.
Then, free from greed and wearing the attire of a holy place, that man should carry a staff without a knot, a water-pot, and a deerskin. (22)
For men who travel according to the prescribed rule, there is especially the attainment of fruit;
therefore, one should perform the ritual for pilgrimage to sacred sites with every effort. (23)
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord who is affectionate toward His devotees, O Master of the cows!
O Blessed Viṣṇu, the ultimate refuge, protect me from this manifold cycle of birth and death. 25.
Speaking thus, remembering Hari with his tongue and mind,
the highly fortunate one should proceed on foot toward the sacred ford.
A man traveling by vehicle obtains an equal share of the fruit [of his actions];
by means of sandals, a fourth part; and by means of a bullock-cart, the sin of killing a cow and so forth. (27)
One who engages in worldly transactions receives a third part; one who eats [there] receives an eighth part.
Going there to a sacred site (tīrtha) without desire, one obtains half the fruit. ||28||
A pilgrimage to sacred fords should be performed according to the rules;
indeed, the destruction of evil occurs especially when it is done in accordance with the prescribed ritual. (29)
There, one should pay homage to the virtuous through prostrations at their feet and service;
for by that means, devotion to Hari, the Supreme Person, is attained. (30)
Thus has the procedure for the sacred ford been declared in brief and not in detail.
Having thus adopted this ritual, go to Puruṣottama. (31)
O Great King, Acyuta, being pleased with you, will grant you such devotion that the crossing over of saṃsāra will occur in an instant. (32)
O bull among men, having heard the procedure for pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā), which destroys all sins, one is liberated from all terrible evils. 33.
Sumati said:
Having heard these words, the great sage, his mind overwhelmed by the longing to behold that sacred ford, prostrated at [his] feet. (34)
Intent on leading everyone along with him out of a desire for pilgrimage to sacred sites, he commanded his own minister, Uttama, who was most skilled in counsel. (35)
O minister, by my command, you must instruct all the citizens for the sake of the joy of beholding the lotus feet of Puruṣottama. (36)
"Those people who are in my city and those who carry out my word—all you best of men, let them depart from my city along with me. (37)
But those men who, transgressing my word, shall remain at home, they—being sinners and causes of unrighteousness—are to be punished with the rod of Yama. ||38||
What is the use of your multitude of sons, or what use are kinsmen of such wicked conduct, by whom Puruṣottama—the bestower of merit—has not been seen with their own eyes? (39)
The offspring of those whose sons or grandsons have not gone to Hari for refuge are like a herd of sows that feed upon excrement. (40)
O my people, quickly bow down to that God who is capable of purifying all by his name alone. (41)
Thus, the great minister named Uttama, who bore a name true to his character, rejoiced at these words which were captivating and filled with the virtues of the Blessed One. 42.
Having mounted an excellent elephant, he caused a proclamation to be made by means of a drum,
as commanded by the king who desired to undertake this pilgrimage to the sacred ford.
Then, departing in haste with the King of the World, I went to the Great Mountain;
let the one named Puruṣottama, the destroyer of sins, be beheld. 44.
Let the entire ocean of saṃsāra once again become as insignificant as a puddle in a cow's hoofprint;
let men adorn their respective bodies with the marks of the conch, the discus, and other such symbols. (45)
Thus the minister, whose fatigue was dispelled by meditation on the feet of Raghunātha, caused that wonderful proclamation ordered by the king to be heard. 46.
Having heard that, all those subjects were flooded with the essence of bliss;
they set their minds upon their own deliverance through the sight of the Supreme Person.
There, the brahmins, well-attired along with their disciples, went forth,
bestowing blessings rich with the granting of boons upon the lord of the earth.
The Kṣatriyas were archers and heroes; the Vaiśyas were intent on trade and commerce;
and the Śūdras, delighted by the prospect of crossing over the cycle of existence, had their own bodies [prepared for service]. (49)
Washermen, leather-workers, honey-makers, Kirātas,
and wall-painters lived by the profession of needlework and by the trade of selling betel-leaf.
Those who carry palm-clappers as musical instruments, those who live by tending cattle, as well as sellers of oil and sellers of cloth; ||51||
Filled with joy, the citizens and the bards recounted the ancient legends; then, by the king's command, the Magadha bards departed from there.
They lived by the profession of physicians, as well as those skilled in gambling; they were experts in the delicious flavors of cooked food and delighted others with humorous speech. (53)
Then the vidyādharas skilled in magic arts, as well as those proficient in the arts of livelihood, went forth from the middle of the city, praising the great king. ||54||
The king also, having performed there the morning twilight rituals and other duties,
summoned that most pure brahmin, the best of ascetics.
At his command, the great king went out from the city;
followed by the people, the king shone like the moon among the stars. (56)
Having traveled for the distance of one *krośa* and having shaved his head according to the prescribed rite,
he carried a staff, a water-pot, and a beautiful deer-skin.
Endowed with an auspicious appearance and devoted to the meditation on Hari, he possessed great renown, maintaining a mind free from desire, anger, and other such passions. ||58||
Then, kettledrums, war-drums,
large drums, and small drums, as well as conchs, lutes, and other instruments, were repeatedly sounded by their players.
"O Lord of the gods, O Jayadeva, O Puruṣottama who destroys suffering! Reveal Your form to me!"—saying this, the people went forth. (60)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of Ratnagrīva for the Sacred Fords," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(20) The twentieth chapter. Sumati said:
Then, as the king set forth accompanied by all his people, the Vaiṣṇavas of great fortune and the singers performed the glorification of Kṛṣṇa. ||1||
On the way, that great king heard the praise of Govinda:
"Victory to Mādhava! O Supreme Person, refuge for the devotees! (2)
Seeking out many sacred fords, performing his ablutions and beholding their great majesty, he then heard from the ascetics and brahmins about their greatness.
With his mind delighted by various accounts of Viṣṇu,
the king had the singers sing of the Great Viṣṇu at every stage along the way.
The wise Great King, who had conquered his senses, gave gifts to the poor, the wretched, the helpless, and those accustomed to the impressions of their past lives. ||5||
Making himself free from the dust of various sectarian doctrines and having attained a state of spiritual fitness,
he departed with his own people, devoted solely to meditation upon Hari.
As the king went along, he saw before him a river that destroys sins,
filled with stones marked by the discus-sign, and as pure as the minds of sages.
It was graced by many rows of numerous groups of sages and beautified by the warbling of birds such as cranes.
Having seen him, he questioned that foremost of brahmins, an ascetic learned in dharma,
whose knowledge was strengthened by his specialized understanding of the greatness of many sacred fords (tīrthas).
"O Lord, who is this meritorious river, frequented by throngs of sages, that fills my heart with an abundance of joy? (10)
Having heard these words of that wise king of kings,
the learned man began to speak of the supreme majesty of the sacred fords (tīrthas).
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, this Gaṇḍakī is a queen of rivers, frequented by gods and asuras;
she destroys the accumulation of sins through the flow of her meritorious waters. (12)
By seeing it, one burns away mental sin; by touching it, the sin born of action;
and by drinking it, the accumulation of sin arising from one's own speech.
Having previously seen that all his subjects were impure, the Lord of Creatures created this [Ganges], which destroys manifold sins, from the drops of sweat upon his own cheek.
Those men who touch this river, which possesses meritorious waters and is easy to cross, shall never again be subject to the womb, even if they are doers of evil. (15)
And the stones found here, adorned with the marks of wheels, are indeed the supreme Bhagavāns themselves, bearing their own true forms. (16)
That man who constantly worships the stone marked with the discus shall never again enter the womb of a mother. 17.
The wise man who worships the excellent śālagrāma stone should become possessed of right conduct and free from greed and delusion. (18)
Indeed, by a man who has turned away from the wives and wealth of others, the Śālagrāma stone marked with a discus should be worshipped with great effort. (19)
The discus found in Dvāravatī and the stone originating from the Gaṇḍakī river indeed remove, in an instant, the sins of men accumulated over hundreds of births. (20)
Even if a man should be the perpetrator of thousands of sins, by drinking the water from the Śālagrāma stone, he becomes purified in an instant. (21)
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, a householder established on the path of the Vedas shall attain liberation after worshipping the Śālagrāma. ||22||
A woman should never perform the worship of the Śālagrāma, whether she is widowed or fortunate, if she desires the welfare of the heavenly realm. (23)
Even if she is endowed with birth, character, and virtue, a woman who, out of delusion, touches [a man], abandons her mass of merit and quickly goes to hell. (24)
The best of Brahmins declare that flowers released from the hand of a woman onto a Śālagrāma stone fall with greater force than a thunderbolt. (25)
Sandalwood becomes like poison, a flower becomes like a thunderbolt, and an offering made for the Blessed One becomes like the deadly Kālakūṭa venom. (26)
Therefore, the touch of a woman upon a stone slab must be avoided with one's whole being;
she who performs it goes to hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
