Even one of evil conduct, or even one joined with the murder of a Brahmin, attains the supreme goal after drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone. (28)
Tulasī, sandalwood paste, water, a conch shell, a bell, and a discus; a stone slab, a copper vessel, and the nectar of the name and feet of Viṣṇu. (29)
The sages, who are peaceful and proficient in the meaning of all scriptures, declare that the nectar of the verses, consisting of nine [lines], is the burner of the heap of sins. (30)
O King, whatever merit arises from bathing at all sacred fords and from performing all sacrifices—that is found, wondrously, in every single drop [of this water]. (31)
Wherever the Śālagrāma stone is worshipped by the most excellent of men, that area for a distance of one yojana is endowed with ten million sacred sites (tīrthas). ||32||
Śālagrāmas that are equal in size should be worshipped, but not two among those that are equal;
those that are unequal should be worshipped, but not three among those that are unequal. (33)
The Cakra that originates at Dvārāvatī, as well as that which originates at the Gaṇḍakī—
wherever there is a confluence of these two, there is the Gaṅgā-Samudragā.
Harsh women make men destitute of longevity, fortune, and strength;
therefore, those who are affectionate and possess enchanting forms bestow prosperity.
Whatever man desires long life, and whatever person indeed desires wealth, by honoring [this], he obtains everything pertaining to both this world and the next. (36)
O King, at the time of death, for a fortunate man, the merit of reciting the names of Hari resides in the stone [liṅga] near his heart. (37)

If, even through mere confidence in him, the manifestation of the Śālagrāma stone occurs within the channels of one's vital breath as they move, there is liberation for him; of this there is no doubt. (38)
Formerly, it was declared by the Blessed One to the wise Ambarīṣa: "Brahmins who have renounced worldly life and are affectionate, as well as Śālagrāma stones," (39)
Indeed, these three forms of mine on the circle of the earth were assumed with great compassion in order to effect the removal of the sins of the sinful. (40)
Those sinners who even once revile the Śālagrāma stone are quickly cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell until the dissolution of all beings. 41.
The foolish-minded person who prevents another from preparing to perform worship causes his mother, father, and circle of kinsmen to share in the fate of hell. (42)
Or whoever says: "O dear one, perform the worship of Śālagrāma;
by doing so once, you will quickly lead your ancestors to Vaikuṇṭha, thereby fulfilling your purpose. (43)
In this very context, O sages who are free from passion and devoid of desire and anger, I shall relate this ancient history as an illustration. 44.
Formerly, in the land known as Kīkaṭa, which was devoid of righteousness, there lived a man of the Pulkasa caste named Śabara. ||45||
Constantly intent on slaying living beings and repeatedly wielding his bow, he forcibly robs those desiring to go to a sacred ford of their very life. (46)

He was constantly intent on the slaughter of many living beings and devoted to the taking of others' property; he was always possessed by passion and the like, and joined with desire, anger, and so forth. ||47||
He wanders incessantly through the terrible forest, slaughtering living beings,
with the tip of his arrow smeared with poison and his hand drawn back upon the bowstring.
The hunter, who wanders about once and causes fear to all living beings, does not realize that the terrible time has arrived even though it is close at hand. (49)
The messengers of Yama arrived, holding nooses and mallets in their hands;
they had copper-colored hair and long nails, and were terrifying with their gaping mouths and fangs.
Bearing dark iron shackles, those who cause delusion bound this sinner,
who brings fear to all living beings.

Sometimes, though not even intending it in his mind, he may become a benefactor to all living beings; yet at other times, he may be intent upon another's wife, another's wealth, and the injury of others. (52)
And I shall pull out his large tongue from here;
and as for that one who speaks, I shall pluck out his eye.
One says, "I shall cut off the hands of this sinner," while another says, "I shall cut off the ears of this evil-minded one. (54)
Speaking thus and grinding their teeth together with great intensity,
they approached that evil-minded one and stood there, intoxicated and armed.
Then one messenger, assuming the form of a serpent, bit him on the foot;
as soon as he was bitten, he suddenly became lifeless.
Then those helpless ones bound him with iron chains;
they struck him with whips and angrily beat him with mallets.
"Alas, you wicked and evil-souled one! You have never performed a single virtuous deed, not even in thought; therefore, we shall cast you into the Raurava hells. (58)
Fierce and enraged crows and vultures will devour your skin and flesh;
for from birth until now, you have not performed service to Hari.
Having abandoned your wife, children, and others, you have lived well;
yet you never once remembered the Lord Janārdana, the remover of sins.
Therefore, by the command of Dharmarāja, we shall all lead you, O descendant of Ikṣvāku, to the hells of Bhīṣmaka and Raurava with many beatings.
When, having spoken thus, those powerless ones desired to bring him back,
at that moment Mahā-Viṣṇu, who is devoted solely to the lotus feet [of his master], arrived.
Then those hosts of Yama’s messengers, bearing wicked weapons such as nooses, mallets, and staffs, were seen by the high-souled Vaiṣṇava.
They prepared to seize the Pulkasa, binding him with iron shackles, shouting, "Bind!
Bind! Swallow! Cut! Pierce! Split! (64).
Then, seeing him, he who was devoted to Padmanābha became free from cruelty and directed his mind toward him with extreme compassion. (65)
"Let this great suffering from wicked beings not come near me;
I shall release him this very day even from the messengers of Yama."
Having formed this thought regarding him, the Lord of Sages, filled with compassion,
took a Śālagrāma stone in his hand and went into his presence.
Placing the meritorious water from his feet, mixed with *tulasī* leaves,
into his mouth, he chanted the name of Rāma with his ears.
The Vaiṣṇava placed Tulasī upon his head;
having held the stone of Mahā-Viṣṇu to his heart, that Vaiṣṇava laughed aloud.
As you go toward the hells, destined for various torments, may the touch of the Śālagrāma stone burn away your great sin. (70)
When he had spoken thus, the most wonderful hosts of Viṣṇu arrived in his presence; their laughter vanished upon touching the stone.
Clad in yellow garments and resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
they arrived and liberated him from the formidable iron fetters.
Having released the Pulkasa man who had committed great evil, they said: "For what reason has this Vaiṣṇava, a venerable bearer of a body, been bound? (73)
"Whose command do you follow that you act in such an unrighteous manner?
Release this Vaiṣṇava; for what purpose has he been held captive? (74)
Having heard these words, the servants of Yama,
who were prepared to bring the sinner at the command of Dharmarāja, spoke.
Never at any time did he benefit even a single living being with his mind;
rather, he was a bearer of a wicked body who committed the great sin of killing living beings. //76//
Devoted constantly to the wives of others and a perpetrator of every sin, he plundered many men as they were traveling on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Therefore, we had come to lead away this sinful Pulkasa man;
why has he been released by you soldiers who arrived here unexpectedly? (78)
The messengers of Viṣṇu said:
"The sin of killing a Brahmin and other such sins arising from the slaughter of millions of living beings—all these the touch of a Śālagrāma stone burns away in that very instant. (79)
If the name "Rāma," having entered the ear through trust, burns away one's sins just as a spark of fire consumes cotton, [then what need is there for other means? (80)
He who has the tulasī plant upon his head, the beautiful stone [of Śrī Rāma] upon his heart, and the name of Rāma in his mouth or his ear—he is liberated at that very moment. (81)
Therefore, he previously placed a tulasī leaf upon his head, quickly heard the name of Rāma, and firmly held it within his heart like nectar. (82)
Therefore, his mass of sins is burnt away and his body becomes meritorious;
he shall go to the supreme abode, which is very difficult for sinners to attain. (83)
Having enjoyed all heart-stealing pleasures there for ten thousand years,
he obtained birth in Bhārata and propitiated the Teacher of the World.
He shall attain the supreme state, which is very difficult even for gods and asuras to reach;
yet he has not fully realized the greatness of this stone of the Supreme Lord. ||85||
"By merely seeing, touching, or even worshipping [this], all sins are instantly destroyed.
Having spoken thus, all the hosts of Mahāviṣṇu became silent. (86)
O King, those servants of Yama related the wonder to him;
the devotee of Viṣṇu, who was solely devoted to Raghunātha, attained great joy. ||87||
"Released from this snare, he shall go to the supreme state. Then there arrived a pure [lotus], adorned with a multitude of golden lotuses (kiṃkiṇī). 88.
Having ascended a celestial chariot, enchanting and most wonderful, he went from the world of the gods to heaven, which is frequented by those of great merit. (89)
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he came down to the earth;
having attained birth in Kāśī within a pure and excellent Vāḍava family, [he was born]. (90)
Having worshipped the Lord of the worlds, that sinner attained the supreme state by touching the Śālagrāma stone through the company of the virtuous. (91)
Freed from great suffering, he went to the supreme state.
O King, I have thus related to you the great narrative of the Gaṇḍakī. 92.
Having heard it, one is liberated from sins and attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||93||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gaṇḍakī," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||20||
(21) Chapter Twenty-One. Sumati said:
Having brought this incomparable majesty of the Gaṇḍakī to his ears, that best of kings considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose. (1)
Having bathed at the sacred ford and offered libations to all his ancestors, the great man rejoiced while performing the worship of the Śālagrāma stone according to the words of the Brāhmaṇa.
There, that best of kings took twenty-four slabs and worshipped them with love, using offerings such as sandalwood paste and other honors. ||3||
Having bestowed gifts there, especially upon the poor and the blind, the king set out for the temple of Puruṣottama. ||4||
Thus proceeding by stages, he reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
having brought it within the range of his vision, he joyfully questioned that brahmin.
"O Lord, tell me, how far away is the great mountain named Nīla, the abode of Puruṣottama, which is saluted by gods and asuras? (6)
Having heard those great words of King Ratnagrīva, he was filled with wonder and spoke respectfully toward the king. (7)
O King, this place at the foot of the Nīla mountain is worthy of homage;
for what reason is it not seen, even though it bestows the fruit of great merit? (8)
Again and again he said this: "O King, why is this place, which bears the abode of Puruṣottama, not seen on the slopes of the Blue Mountain? (9)
"I have bathed here thoroughly; here, O King, my eyes fell upon the Bhillas, and by this very path I ascended to the top of the mountain. (10)
Having heard those words, the king was pained in his mind;
longing for the sight of the Blue Mountain, he made his heart full of yearning. (11)
He said: "O Brahmin, how can that Supreme Person be seen?
Or how is Nīla not seen? Tell me the means for this. (12)
Then, having heard the words of King Ratnagrīva,
the astonished king spoke these words to the ascetic brāhmaṇa.
O Lord of the Earth, having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, we must remain here until Nīla is seen. (14)
He who is known by the name Puruṣottama is sung of as the destroyer of sins; he who bears the name Bhaktavatsala will swiftly bestow his grace. 15.
This crest-jewel of the gods of gods never abandons his devotees;
many devotees have been protected by him—sing of that, O high-minded one! (16)
Having heard these words, the king, with a distressed heart,
bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and then undertook a fast unto death.
When the Supreme Person shows compassion toward me, I shall perform worship and take food, provided that it does not violate my vow of fasting. (18)
Having thus made this vow on the shore of the Ganges and the ocean,
he observed a fast while singing of the multitude of virtues of Hari.

The king said: Victory to you, O Lord who is the source of compassion for the miserable! Victory to you, whose auspicious name removes suffering! Victory to you, who destroy the afflictions of your devotees with your excellent form! Victory to you, the slayer of the wicked! 20.
Then, seeing Ambarīṣa distressed,
his every auspiciousness destroyed by the brāhmaṇa’s curse,
He granted him His vision, holding [the Lord] in His own hands.
He protected [her] while she resided within his belly. ||21||

Afflicted by the torments inflicted upon you by the Daitya king as your father through the hurling of spears, nooses, water, and fire, you were protected by Him who assumed the form of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, even as your father looked on. 22.

Seeing the lordly elephant, fallen with his foot into the mouth of a crocodile and tormented by extreme suffering, you—your mind moistened with noble compassion—performed the act of tearing him from it like Garuḍa. (23)
Having cast aside his bird-bannered chariot and taken up his discus with great speed, the Lord,
praised by the gods, is celebrated as the deliverer from the sacrifice of Amuṣya-nakra and the one who instantly brought about its destruction.
Wherever there is the destruction of Your servants' enemies, O Lord, there You, assuming a physical form, protect Your own people with Your enchanting deeds that remove all sins. (25)
O Beloved of Your Devotees, whose soles are rubbed by the diamonds in the crowns of the gods who are the lords of the distressed;
O Lord whose splendor burns away tens of millions of sins—reveal Your own vision to me! 26.

O Lord of the mind, if this person who has committed evil has come here, then show him [the way], for we have forgotten that destroyer of the flood of sins which is worshipped by gods and asuras. (27)
By chanting even so much of Your stainless name, people cross the entire ocean of evil;
if I have performed even a single recollection of it, then may that which wards off all suffering be attained. 28.
Sumati said:
Singing thus of his virtues day and night, the lord of the earth did not rest for even a moment; indeed, he found no pleasure in sleep.
Singing, walking, speaking, and standing—day and night he says this:
"O Lord of Compassion, O Supreme Person, reveal Your own form! (30)
Thus five days passed for the king at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
then the Lord of the Cowherds, that ocean of compassion, thought with mercy: ||31||
Having had his sins removed by this song composed by me, O King, behold my most beloved, who is saluted by gods and demons. 32.
Having thus reflected, the Lord, his mind filled with compassion,
assumed the guise of a renunciant and, being all-powerful, went into the presence of the king.
Having gone there, assuming the guise of a great royal ascetic with a triple staff,
he was seen by the ascetic out of compassion for his devotee.
Having uttered "Oṃ namo viṣṇave," the best of kings bowed down; with his mind fixed on Hari, he performed worship with offerings of water for the hands, water for the feet, and a seat.
He said: "It is incomparable good fortune that you have come within the range of my vision;
beyond this, Govinda will grant me his own sight. (36)
Having heard those words, the renunciant spoke to him:
"O King, listen to my speech as it issues forth from me. (37)
Through my knowledge, I know the past, the future, and all that is occurring at present;
therefore, I shall say something—listen with a one-pointed mind. (38)
Tomorrow at midday, Hari, the giver, will grant you that vision which is difficult even for Brahmā to attain;
together with your five kinsmen, you shall go to the supreme abode.
You were the minister, and Mahilāvatāpasa was the submarine fire; in the city you were known as Tava-kara, and Sādhu was Vāyaka. ||40||
By means of these five, you shall go to that most excellent Blue Mountain (Nīlaparvata), which is honored by the gods, worshipped by the deities, and saluted by Brahmā and Indra.
Having spoken thus, the ascetic vanished and was no longer seen anywhere;
hearing this, the king immediately attained a state of joy mixed with great wonder.
The king said: "O Master, who was that person who came and addressed me thus? That giver of joy to my heart is no longer seen; where has he gone? (43)
The ascetic said:
"O King, drawn by your great love, this one named Puruṣottama, the destroyer of all sins, has arrived. (44)
Tomorrow at midday, a great mountain will appear before you;
having ascended it and beheld Hari, you shall have accomplished your purpose.
With the fever of his heart extinguished by the nectar-filled words of "Thus [spoke the Lord]," the king attained a joy that even Brahmā could not know. 46.
Then the kettledrums resounded, as did the lutes, small drums, and horn-like instruments;
for at that time there was great joy in the mind of the king of kings.
Singing of Hari, whether standing, laughing, talking, speaking, or bowing, he attained a profound bliss that destroys all suffering. 48.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of the Renunciant," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||21||
(22) The twenty-second chapter. Sumati said:
Then, having spent the entire day in the remembrance and chanting of Hari's names,
he slept at night on the bank of the Gaṅgā, which bestows great fruit.
In the midst of a dream, however, he beheld himself as four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the Śārṅga bow. ||2||
He danced before Puruṣottama together with Śarva and the other gods, who were endowed with splendor and accompanied by their own forms, bearing maces, lotuses, conchs, discs, and other weapons.

Seeing him constantly worshipped by the excellent hosts of Viṣvaksena’s attendants with their beautiful forms, he was struck with wonder and experienced a most extraordinary joy regarding the objects of the world. ||3||
The high-minded one considered himself a vessel of compassion for Puruṣottama, who grants whatever is desired by the mind. ||4||
Having thus seen this dream regarding his kingdom, O best of Brahmins, that excellent king woke up in the morning and related the dream he had beheld.
Having heard that, the wise son of Aṅgiras spoke in wonder:
"O King, have you seen him who is named Puruṣottama? (6)
"Lord Hari will bestow his own body, marked with the signs of the conch, discus, and so forth.
Having heard those words, the high-minded Ratnagrīva [was filled with joy]. (7)
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and having offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he caused gifts to be bestowed upon the poor according to their mental desires.
Singing the multitude of Hari’s virtues, he beheld a vision;
then, at the time of midday, celestial drums resounded repeatedly in the sky.
They struck him, resounded with the great noise of the blows from the hands of the gods,
and suddenly a rain of flowers fell upon the king's head.
"You are blessed, O best of kings; behold Nīla now within the range of your vision."
When the king heard the words uttered by the god,
he then became marvelous, possessing a splendor exceeding that of ten million suns.
A great mountain named Nīla came within the range of the king's vision;
it shone brilliantly together with its peaks made of silver and gold. (13)
Is this fire blazing? Or is it a second sun? Is this a flash of lightning—a male being who has suddenly assumed a steady radiance? (14)
Having seen the beautifully adorned Nīlaprastha, the ascetic brāhmaṇa reported it to the king, saying, "This is a great, meritorious mountain. (15)
Having heard that, the best of kings bowed his head in salutation:
"I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, O Nīla, for you have come within the range of my vision. (16)
O bull among men, the ministers, the king’s wives, the kāravaṇas, and the vāyakas became thrilled upon seeing Nīla. 17.
These five, at the time of victory, ascended Mount Nīla while hearing the great sounds of kettledrums produced by the immortals.
Upon that mountain peak, which was adorned with various trees,
he beheld an unsurpassed temple constructed of gold.
Brahmā always comes there and performs worship of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin); he offers food-offerings (naivedya) which bring satisfaction to Hari. ||20||
Then, having seen there that supreme, stainless temple of the gods,
he entered it surrounded by his five attendants.
There, he saw him shining upon a lion-throne inlaid with gold and great jewels, four-armed and enchanting.
Accompanied by his wife and joined by the king’s attendants, he prostrated before [the deity] who is worshipped by Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Vijaya, Jaya, and others. ||23||
Having prostrated before the Supreme Self, the Great King bathed the Best of Gods according to the prescribed rites with the bathing mantras declared in the Vedas.
With a delighted mind, O King, the monarch offered him water for the hands and feet and other honors;
having anointed him with sandalwood paste, he presented him with excellent garments. (25)
Then the king, having performed the incense offering and the waving of lights (ārārtika), presented an offering of food that was entirely delicious and pleasing to the divine image. 26.
Having prostrated, the ascetic and the brahmin offered praise with collections of hymns composed of a multitude of virtues according to their respective intelligence. (27)
The King said:
You alone are the Supreme Person, the Lord manifest, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti);
you are distinct from both cause and effect, and are worshiped by the principles beginning with the Great Principle (mahat-tattva). ||28||
From the lotus of your navel was born Brahmā, who is expert in the work of creation;
likewise, Rudra, the agent of dissolution, was born from your eye.
Commanded by you, he performs all the activities of the universe;
from you was born this ancient world, both that which is stationary and that which moves.
O Lord of the Universe, for one who perceives You as entering into the power of consciousness, there is indeed no birth for them, nor is there an end.
O Lord, increase, decrease, and transformation indeed exist within you alone.
Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting devotees and for the purpose of establishing dharma, you indeed perform births, deeds, and qualities that are appropriate [to each occasion]. (32)
O Brahman, O progenitor of the Great Puruṣa, by assuming the body of a fish, you slew the demon Śaṅkha and the Vedas were well protected.
Even Śeṣa, Nārada, Brahmā, Bhāratī, and even Maheśvarī do not know [the truth];
how much less others, such as the great Viṣṇu or dull-witted people like me? (34)
Even the mind does not attain you, nor does this supreme goddess of speech;
therefore, O Lord, how could I be capable of praising you? (35)
Having thus praised him, he repeatedly prostrated with his head bowed, his voice choked with emotion and his body marked by the bristling of his hair. (36)
Thus, his soul delighted by this praise, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person,
spoke these truthful and meaningful words to the king.
The Blessed Lord said: O King of great intelligence, I have become greatly delighted by your hymn of praise.
Know me, O Great King, as being beyond material nature (prakṛti). 38.
Indeed, quickly partake of this delightful offering;
having attained the state of four arms, you shall go to the supreme abode. (39)
Any person who shall praise me with this jewel of a hymn composed by you, even to him I shall grant a vision that bestows the boons of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (40)
Having heard these words thus spoken by the Blessed One, the king partook of the food offering together with his four attendants. (41)
Then a celestial chariot arrived, adorned with networks of tinkling bells, attended by throngs of apsarases, and endowed with every object of enjoyment. ||42||
Beholding him who is named Puruṣottama, the righteous king, having made himself a vessel for his compassion, paid homage at his feet. 43.
Then, by his command, having ascended a celestial chariot accompanied by a woman, he went to the wonderful Vaikuṇṭha in the heavens while he was looking on. 44.
The minister, devoted to the Dharma of the king and the most excellent among those who know all dharmas,
departed together with him in a celestial chariot, attended by a multitude of women.
There, a brahmin ascetic who had bathed in all the sacred fords attained the state of having four arms and departed with the gods in their celestial chariots.
Karaṃba, too, having attained the vision [of the Lord] through the merit of his great royal songs, went to the abode of the gods, which is difficult for all the deities and others to attain. (47)
All of them set out for the most wonderful realm of Viṣṇu, possessing four arms and bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. ||48||
All the pure and majestic clouds, with food in their hands, adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, sang praises to the heavens. (49)
Then, upon seeing those rows of celestial chariots, the people of the world raised a clamor of drums that reached the ears of all.
At that time, there was a certain brāhmaṇa who was devoted to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu;
his mind drawn by the longing for separation from Him, he became four-armed.
Beholding that wonderful and great act of compassion, those people praised it;
having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, they returned toward that city.
Oh, what great fortune belongs to Ratnagrīva, the king of noble mind!
With this very body, he has gone to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (53)
O King, this is the Blue Mountain (Nīlagiri), honored by Puruṣottama;
merely upon seeing it, people go directly to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme refuge. 54.
He who hears this greatness of Nīla is fortunate;
indeed, he who causes others to hear it—both of them shall go to the supreme state. ||55||
Upon hearing this, however, the evil dream perishes by the mere remembrance [of it];
Puruṣottama bestows the crossing over from saṃsāra upon those who face him. ||56||
He who dwells in Nīlā is that Rāma, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
Sītā is Mahālakṣmī herself, the cause of all causes. ||57||
Having performed the horse sacrifice (hayamedha), he will indeed purify the worlds;
for his name is prescribed as the atonement for the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Now your horse has arrived at the most excellent Nīla mountain;
O high-minded one, pay homage to Lord Puruṣottama. (59)
Having become sinless therein, we shall go to the supreme state,
by whose grace many have crossed over the ocean of existence.
As he was speaking thus, the horse reached Mount Nīla,
crushing the earth into a flattened circle by the force of the wind it stirred up.
Then the king also, following upon his back, reached the mountain named Nīla at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; having bathed there, he went to Puruṣottama.
Having praised and bowed to the Lord of Gods, who is worshipped by both gods and asuras,
the slayer of enemies considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Nīlagiri," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||22||
(23) Chapter Twenty-Three. Śeṣa said:
Having stood for a moment and having eaten some grass, the horse, swift as thought,
went forth surrounded by a line of warriors, with a leaf held on its forehead and accompanied by chowries.
He was protected by Śatrughna, the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi, King Puṣkala, Ugravāha, and Pratāpāgrya. ||2||
O Lord, he followed, protected by many millions of heroes, toward that city which was well-guarded by Subāhu and equipped with its defensive walls and gates.
Then his great son, Damana, having gone out on a hunt,
saw a horse with a leaf-patterned forehead and smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents.
Seeing his servant, he said: "Whose horse has come within the range of my vision?
Why is there a leaf on its forehead, and why does it carry such a beautiful chowrie? (5)
Having heard these words of the king, the servant then departed for the place where that beautiful horse with the leaf-mark on its forehead was staying.
Having seized him by his mass of hair, which was adorned with a garland of jewels,
he led him before the king who belonged to the lineage of Subāhu.
They caused him to read the letter, which was adorned with beautiful characters:
"The powerful King Daśaratha was the sovereign of Ayodhyā. (8)
His own younger brother was Rāmabhadra, the crest-jewel of all heroes;
there was no other on earth equal to him in the prowess of wielding the bow.
Therefore, that horse, adorned with sandalwood paste and other unguents, was released by him;
the righteous Śatrughna, slayer of enemy heroes, protects it.
"Those who are brave and these heroes with bows in hand—they shall seize by force this horse adorned with a garland of jewels. (11)
And Śatrughna, the crest-jewel of all heroes, shall liberate him,
so that he may offer prostration at the feet of that archer.
Perceiving this intention, the prince said:
"Rāma alone is the wielder of the bow; we are not considered Kṣatriyas. (13)
"While my father still stands upon this earth, what is this great pride in the world?
Let him reap the fruit of his arrogance through the arrows released by me. (14)
Today, let these sharp arrows truly make Śatrughna like a flowering śuka tree, his body entirely covered with wounds. (15)
Let my arrows tear open the temples of my elephants, and let them see hundreds of horses drenched in floods of blood. (16)
May the hosts of Yoginīs drink blood from human skulls;
may the jackals be satisfied by devouring the flesh of my enemies. 17.
Let the brave warriors behold my great strength of arm as I discharge millions of arrows released from the staff of my bow. (18)
Having spoken thus to the king, the powerful son named Udamanā sent him back to his own city and became exceedingly joyful. (19)
He spoke thus to the commander: "O high-minded one, prepare for me a limited army to repel the hosts of enemies. (20)
Having prepared his army, while he stood in the circle of the battlefield facing [the enemy] swiftly, that most fierce one was reached by those who followed on horseback.
"Where is that horse of the great king, marked with a crest-leaf?
they asked one another repeatedly, being greatly agitated.
Then Pratāpāgrya beheld before him a supreme ascetic and a camp made ready, resounding with the shouts of heroes.
There, some people said: "O King, this horse has been led by him;
otherwise, how could that hero, followed by his army, stand facing us? (24)
Having heard this, Pratāpāgrya dispatched a servant;
having gone there, he asked, "Where is King Rāma, the thief? (25)
"By whom was he led away, and from where? Rama does not know;
he is free from anger—he before whom the gods, headed by Śakra, bowed down and presented offerings. (26)
If that great army of the King of Dharma does not bow down, it will surely devour him entirely, for it is enraged.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the powerful son of the king,
being deeply distressed, silenced him with a web of words.
I have brought away the sacrificial horse, adorned with the marks of feathers and other ornaments;
those who are heroes, defeat me and release it from my power.
Having heard those words, the servant went away laughing, filled with rage;
he reported to the king exactly as it had been described by Upavarṇita.
Hearing that, his eyes copper-red with rage, the immensely powerful Pratāpāgrya went forth to fight the prince who was preceded by great heroes.
The powerful one went forth in a chariot with golden poles, beautifully adorned with excellent horses,
possessing a fine pole, and filled with all kinds of weapons.
Endowed with great strength, he had that bow fashioned;
again and again he laughed loudly, his eyes overflowing with tears born of wrath.
Mounted on horses and elephants, with swords flashing in their hands,
they followed that foremost of heroes, whose eyes were agitated and filled with wrath.
Elephants and foot-soldiers by the millions were prepared for battle,
desiring for a long time to engage in combat brought about by the hero.
Then the prince, the foremost of heroes, surrounded by a great army, went forth to meet the enemy host that had been mobilized against him. (36)
Equipped with armor, a sword, and a bow, the youth went forth to fight with effortless ease, like a lion king against a herd of elephants.
Then those warriors, enraged and seeking to slay one another, skilled in the duties of battle, cried out to each other, "Cut! Pierce! Strike! ||38||

Foot soldiers with hosts of infantry, those mounted on elephants with their riders, those mounted on chariots with those staying in chariots, and those mounted on horses with those stationed on horses. ||39||
Elephants were split in two, and horses were cut into pieces;
indeed, the earth became filled with the brains of many men.
Then the king, Pratāpāgrya, possessed of great strength, became enraged upon seeing the prince intent on the slaughter of his own army. ||41||
There he said to his charioteer, "Drive the horses elsewhere from me,
for that prince, a great car-warrior, is intent on the slaughter of the army."
Then the heroic prince, whose feet were bowed to by the crest-jewels of warriors,
went directly to meet that powerful man, who was foremost in majesty.
The charioteer brought the horses, foremost in prowess, to the place where that hero of unassailable valor, the crest-jewel of all heroes, was located. (44)
Having gone there, they challenged that prince who was intent on battle;
he stood in his chariot, which was polished with gold, wielding his staff-like bow.
O little prince, you have bound this most excellent horse;
yet you do not know the great king who is served by all the lords of heroes. 46.
Having taken away the horse of that one whose wondrous majesty even the lord of the Daityas was unable to endure, you have come to this city. (47)
"Know me, who has arrived before you, to be your enemy in the form of Time. Release the horse and go, O child; engage in your auspicious play. (48)
Whose son are you? Whence have you come? Why were you, a horse, brought by us who lack foresight? O child, how has this lack of compassion arisen in you toward me?
Having heard this, the high-minded Damana smiled and spoke to Pratāpāgrya, treating his army as if it were a blade of grass.
Damana said:
"This horse was forcibly bound by me and brought to my own city;
I shall not surrender it today while I still have life. O one of great strength, fight with me! (51)
"What you said—that I am a child and should go play—behold that very play of a great king upon the front line of battle! (52)
Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus and having strung his excellent bow,
the elephant placed a hundred arrows upon the chest of Pratāpāgrya.
Aiming a hundred arrows, the majestic one blew his conch shell;
by that sound of the conch, fear indeed arose among the timid.
He struck him in the heart with a hundred arrows;
Pratāpāgrya, being light-handed, cut down those well-jointed shafts.
Seeing his arrows being cut down by every shot,
the powerful prince, filled with rage, discharged sharp, crescent-headed arrows equipped with heron feathers.
In the midst of the sky and the earth, arrows were seen released from the bow—inscribed with their own names and beautifully adorned by the falling of their sharp edges. (57)
The arrows, lodged in his arms and heart, emitted many sparks of fire, which caused a great conflagration among the army. (58)
Pratāpāgrya, becoming enraged, cried out, "Stay! Stay!
and struck him on the head with ten arrows.
They were fixed upon the forehead of that prince of Bāṇa,
shining like the ten branches of a tree upon the peak of Mount Meru.
By that blow from the arrow, the high-minded one was pained,
just as a seven-year-old elephant is when struck by a staff.
Fixing three hundred auspicious arrows upon his bow— arrows adorned with golden feathers and resembling the great fire of cosmic destruction— he released them.
Those arrows, having pierced his chest with supreme force,
fell downward drenched in blood, like those who have turned their backs on devotion to Rāmacandra.
Excelling in prowess and enraged, discharging arrows by the thousands,
he swiftly deprived Subāhu’s son of his chariot in that very instant.
With four [arrows] he struck down the four horses; with two he felled the standard; with one he caused the head of the charioteer to fall from his body to the earth. (65)
They struck that son of the king again with four [arrows], and at that very moment, he cut down a bow equipped with a string with a single one.
Mounting another chariot, beautifully adorned with excellent horses,
that high-minded one took a bow in his hand and made it ready by stringing it.
He replied to that foremost of the valiant: "A wonderful feat has been performed by you. Now, O noble warrior, behold the prowess of my bow! (68)
Having spoken thus, Damanaka took up ten arrows;
with four of them, he sent the four horses to the abode of Yama.
Having cut the chariot, complete with its wheels, into four pieces like sesame seeds,
he pierced the heart with one arrow and the charioteer with another.
Having filled his conch and accompanied by the sound of that conch, he,
the virtuous one of great strength, honored that deed as heroic.
Beholding such valor, filled with supreme indignation and fury, he mounted another chariot and went forth to fight the prince. (72)
"O hero, behold my wonderful prowess!
Having said this, he released a flood of sharp-jointed arrows.
Arrows were seen everywhere, upon the elephants and the horses; like the Supreme Brahman, they pervaded all things and remained within the range of perception. (74)
Having covered that prince with millions of sharp arrows, he who possessed the prowess of a roaring serpent acted swiftly.
Gladdening his own hosts and making his enemies great with sorrow, he rendered their hearts utterly void and deprived them of life.
Seeing himself completely covered by the multitude of the prince’s cold-tipped arrows, he was provoked to rage.
Possessing great prowess, he seized weapons and,
wielding a mighty bow with his staff-like arms, shook it.
The one of great strength shattered all missiles and weapons;
with eyes copper-red with rage, he discharged arrows that tore through his enemies.
Having shaken off that web of weapons, the prince said to him:
"O noble sir, if you are a hero, endure this one blow from me."
If I do not strike you down from your chariot with this [weapon], O hero, listen to the vow I have made out of pride. (79)
May the sin of those who, being experts in the doctrine of limited causality, revile the Veda, be like my own, causing them to sink into the ocean of hell. (80)
Having spoken thus, he drew from his quiver an excellent, sharp arrow that resembled the God of Death,
was wreathed in garlands of flames, and was fixed upon a bow like unto Time itself.
The arrow, aimed at the heart by the excellent king and released,
went with great speed toward him, possessing a brilliance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Seeing the arrow raised for his own downfall, Pratāpāgrya fixed arrows upon his bow, sharpened for the purpose of cutting that shaft. ||83||
Indeed, having covered the lord with all his arrows right in the middle, Sabāṇa went toward the heart of Pratāpāgrya, who was endowed with fortitude. 84.
The lotus-stalk, fixed in his heart, entered deep within him;
the king, having been struck, fell prostrate upon the surface of the earth.
Fainted and deprived of consciousness, he had fallen from the seat of the chariot onto the ground;
the charioteer, taking him up, carried him away from the circle of the battlefield.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the army was broken and fled from there, where that one named Śatrughna stood, surrounded by ten million warriors.
Having attained victory and supreme prowess, that prince, having conquered [all],
waited for King Śatrughna.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Battle of the Princes," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||23||
(24) The twenty-fourth chapter. Śeṣa said:
But Śatrughna, overcome with rage, crushed them with his teeth,
shaking his hands and repeatedly licking his lower lip with his tongue.
Again and again he asked them: "By whom was my horse led away? By whom was Pratāpāgrya conquered—he who is the crest-jewel of all heroes? (2)
Then the servants said: "O slayer of enemies, one named Damana, the son of Subāhu, having conquered Pratāpāgrya, has seized his horse. (3)
Having heard that his horse had been taken by his enemy Damana, he arrived with great speed at the place where the field of battle was located.
There, together with Śatrughna, he saw elephants with split temples,
resembling mountains with streams of blood flowing from them, arrogant with rut.
The horses there, along with their riders, were wounded;
they were seen by the enraged Śatrughna, the heroic slayer of enemies.
Beholding the men, chariots, and elephants shattered, that slayer of enemies became exceedingly enraged,
like the ocean of dissolution at the time of universal destruction.
Seeing before him the formidable leader of the cavalry, who had treated his own army as mere straw because he was the conqueror of Pratāpāgrya, [he was struck with wonder]. (8)
Then the king, his eyes agitated with anger, replied to the warriors:
"Who is this invincible one here, who wields every kind of weapon and missile? (9)
"Let him who, fearless and fully prepared, shall conquer this heroic prince, skilled in the arts of war, with his weapons—let that man stand ready. (10)
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes, prepared to conquer Damana and spoke this speech: ||11||
"O Master, where is this Damanaka, and where is your immeasurable power?
By your majesty I shall conquer; O high-minded one, I am going now. (12)
"By whom shall this horse be led while I stand ready for battle?
This majesty of the Lord of the Raghus will accomplish every task. (13)
O Lord, hear my vow, which bestows joy upon you:
I shall conquer this Arjuna, who is skilled in the arts of battle. (14)
If the sin that arises from being separated from tasting the honey of the lotus feet of Rāmacandra should ever overcome my mind, may it be destroyed. 15.

If one considers anyone other than the feet of one's father and mother to be a sacred ford (tīrtha), and should oppose them, that is my darkness; it would not conquer me if [the father] were to subdue him.
Alas, the elephant, having pierced the chests of kings with its first-drawn arrows, now adorns the battlefield ground by lying upon it. 17.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this vow of Puṣkala,
the illustrious scion of Raghu rejoiced in his heart and dispatched him toward the battlefield.
Commanded thus, he departed surrounded by many troops to where the prince Damana, born of a heroic lineage, was staying. (19)
Damana also, the foremost of heroes, surrounded by his own army, went forth to meet him who had arrived at the field of battle with that command. (20)
Those two, seated upon their chariots and gracing them with their splendor, met one another;
were they the lords of battle and the Daitya who had come to the field for the sake of combat? (21)
Puṣkala said to that mighty son of Vairāja, "Know that Prince Damana has arrived. (22)
O best of beings, know that the formidable son of Bharata, who was ready for battle, was marked by Puṣkala with his own name. 23.
O high-minded one, prepare yourself with the multitude of my weapons; I shall conquer you, who are like a bee constantly devoted to the lotus feet of Raghunātha.
Having heard these words, Adamana, the slayer of enemy heroes,
eloquent, fearless, and having witnessed his own prowess, replied while smiling.
Know me to be Damana, the son of Subāhu, whose sins were destroyed by devotion to his father, and who am now the horse-herder for King Śatrughna. (26)
Victory! This arrow has been released by fate; behold its power as it reaches the head of Meraṇa, upon whom it shall bestow its ornamentation.
Having spoken thus, he drew his bow back to his ear with an arrow fixed upon it and released sharp shafts that snatch away the lives of enemies. (28)
Those arrows, becoming a dense mass, covered the sky, wherein the radiance of the sun's rays was warded off by the shadow of the shafts. ||29||
The continuous stream of arrows clinging to the mass of the elephants' temples was like the various mineral pigments adorning the mountains.
There were seen fallen elephants, horses, and chariots, struck down by the multitude of arrows from the king’s son. (31)
Beholding that prowess and seeing the circle of the battlefield pervaded by the shadow of his arrows, Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes, [acted].
Having drawn an arrow charged with fire-mantras upon his bow,
he sipped water and, according to the proper rite, released the shaft.
Then fire appeared there at the head of the battle,
licking the sky with its flames like the fire of universal destruction that has arisen.
Then his army, scorched and seized with terror on the field of battle,
became intent on flight, oppressed by the flames of fire.
Moreover, the umbrellas of the archers, though consumed by fire, were seen there bearing a luster like that of gold and shaped like the moon.
The horses of the enemies, scorched by the fire, fled away;
even their chariots, though equipped with beautiful poles, were consumed by the flames.
Then, carrying heaps of jewels such as gems and rubies, the young elephants fled,
tormented by the garlands of flames from the fire of the king's arm.
In some places the elephants were not lost; in some places the horse-riders [remained];
in some places the foot-soldiers were not lost, their bodies consumed by fire. (39)
All the arrows discharged by the prince were brought to destruction;
they were instantly reduced to ashes by the flames of the fire. ||40||
Then, his own army having been consumed by fire, Damana, filled with rage, took up the Vāruṇa weapon in order to extinguish it with all his knowledge of missiles. ||41||
That Varuṇa-missile, released by the king for the purpose of extinguishing the fire,
flooded his army, which was crowded with chariots and horses.
The chariots of the adversaries were seen submerged in water, and even their elephants, having been drenched, attained a state of calm. (43)
The fire, released by the Agneya weapon, attained pacification;
its own strength, which had been oppressed by the flames of the fire, reached a state of calm. 44.
O Father, who would not shiver with cold from their enemies, being struck by showers of hailstones and tormented by the wind? (45)
Then, beholding his own army oppressed by a flood of water—
some parched, some agitated, some destroyed, or carried away by Varuṇa— [he saw it thus].
Then Puṣkala, the son of Bharata, his eyes copper-red with extreme anger,
fixed a single great arrow charged with the Vāyavya weapon upon his bow.
Then, impelled by the Vāyavya weapon, a great wind arose and with its force destroyed the approaching army of clouds. 48.
The elephants, struck by the wind and clashing against one another, and the horses, likewise crowded together with their respective riders, [were thrown into confusion]. (49)
Men, their hair disheveled by the force of the wind and devoid of strength, fell down as if they were vetālas inhabiting the earth, appearing terrifying to behold.
Seeing his entire army overwhelmed by the wind-god,
that prince fixed the mountain-weapon upon his bow.
Then mountains fell upon the heads of those who were fighting;
the wind, covered by them, did not move anywhere.
Puṣkala then fixed an arrow known as Vajra upon his bow;
by that Vajra, they were all cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds in an instant.
Having reduced mountains, men, and dust to nothing, the prince’s arrow— empowered by mantras— fell with a loud and violent roar.
With his mind agitated by grief, pierced in the heart, and severely wounded,
the powerful hero suffered intensely and fell into a state of extreme dejection.
Seeing him thus overwhelmed by dejection, the charioteer, skilled in policy,
drove the prince away from that place for a distance of one krośa.
Then the soldiers of the king’s son, being hard-pressed, fled away;
having reached the city, they reported that the prince was overcome by dejection. (57)
Having thus achieved victory at the forefront of the battle, Puṣkala, though he knew the dharma,
was no longer able to strike, as he remembered the words of the Lord of the Raghus.
Then a great sound of drumbeats and shouts of victory arose, and enchanting voices proclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (59)
Seeing the victorious Puṣkala, Śatrughna attained great joy;
surrounded by his ministers, headed by Sumati, he offered him praise.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Victory of Puṣkala," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||24||
(25) Chapter Twenty-Five.
Śeṣa said:
Then, seeing his own soldiers drenched in a flood of blood, the king did not attain happiness;
he grieved for them and inquired about their conduct.
Tell me how he performed all his deeds and how he captured that excellent horse;
furthermore, tell me what was his strength, and how many brave warriors came to fight him? (2)
Then, having launched his army against the enemy, how did my hero Udamanas wage war?
Having achieved victory over that invincible foe, alas, some person indeed struck down the hero. (3)
Having heard these words of the king, his servants— whose bodies, garments, and other belongings were drenched with blood— replied as follows.
O King, having gazed upon the horse adorned with leaf-marks and other ornaments,
he seized it out of pride, treating the best of the Raghus as if it were a blade of grass.
Then, followed by horses and surrounded by a small force of troops, he arrived;
with him there occurred a tumultuous battle that made one's hair stand on end.
Then, having rendered him unconscious with his own arrows, your son stood as Śatrughna, surrounded by his own forces, approached. ||7||
Then a great battle took place, augmented by weapons and missiles;
the mighty son of Tvaṣṭṛ achieved victory many times over.
Now, O King, having been addressed by that son of Śatrughna’s brother,
your heroic son was rendered unconscious in the battle.
Having heard these words, filled with rage and grief,
he became motionless like the ocean on a full-moon day.
Emaciated by grief, his lower lip quivering with rage, biting his lips with his teeth and licking them with his tongue, he spoke to the commander-in-chief.
"O General, quickly prepare my army;
I shall fight with Rāma’s great warriors, who have brought harm upon my son. (12)
Today, if I were to strike down this one who causes suffering to my son with sharpened arrows, even though Maheśvara is his protector; (13)
Having heard these words spoken by King Subhuja, the commander-in-chief acted accordingly and prepared himself.
They reported to the king that his fourfold army was ready— a force renowned for its timely might, which had already struck down tens of millions of wicked men.
Having heard the words of the commander-in-chief, Subāhu, the slayer of enemy heroes,
then went forth to where Śatrughna, the tormentor of his own son, was located.
With jars [of wine], with horses intoxicated by rut and swift as thought, and with chariots filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles that conquer the enemy; ||17||
Then, as that army advanced with its immense weight, the earth shook violently,
and a great commotion arose within the ranks.
Seeing the king gone forth in a golden chariot,
Śatrughna prepared his army, which was capable of striking down all enemies.
His brother Suketu, skilled in combat with the mace, arrived on a chariot drawn by horses, fully equipped with all weapons and missiles. (20)
Citrāṅgada, the son of Gasta, who was skilled in all forms of warfare,
quickly went with his own chariot to the army of Śatrughna, which was intoxicated with pride.
His younger brother, named Vicitra, who was skilled in diverse modes of combat,
departed in a golden chariot, tormented by grief for his brother.
On the following day, other great archers, experts in all weapons and missiles, commanded by the king, went to the battlefield filled with heroes. (23)
King Asubahu, having arrived at the battlefield out of rage,
beheld his son lying unconscious and tormented by arrows.
Seeing her own son, named Damana, standing on the floor of the chariot and bewildered, she repeatedly experienced great sorrow and fanned him with sprouts.
Sprinkled with water and touched by the king’s soft hand,
the hero Damana, an expert in supreme weapons, gradually regained consciousness.
"Where has my bow gone? Where has Puṣkala gone?
Having abandoned the battle, he has departed, tormented by the wounds from my arrows. (27)
Having heard these words spoken by his son,
Subāhu attained supreme joy and embraced his own son.
Beholding King Janaka, Damanaka, with his head bowed low, fell at his feet in devotion,
his body unharmed by the rows of weapons.
Then the king, skilled in the arts of war, spoke again to his son, the commander of the army, who was stationed upon his chariot.
"Form in battle the array known as Krauñca, which is difficult for enemies to conquer;
entering it, you shall defeat the army of King Śatrughna. (31)
Having heard those words of King Subāhu,
he formed a specific and excellent array known as the Krauñca.
Furthermore, your hosts of enemies are suddenly approaching—mighty warriors bearing a multitude of weapons. (32)
Mukheśuketu was his face, while the one named Citrāṅga was his throat; the two princes were his two wings, and Rājā was established as his tail.
Having placed his great army, adorned with elephants and horses, in the center,
the king formed another variegated array known as the *krauñca*.
Seeing the well-constructed Krauñca array, perfectly prepared and standing firm against the enemy's force, the king set his mind on battle with those stationed at Śatrughna’s front.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Encounter with Subāhu’s Army," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||25||
(26) The twenty-sixth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Śatrughna beheld that army, which was as formidable in appearance as a cloud and surrounded by many elephants, horses, chariots, and infantrymen. ||1||
Sumati replied with these words, endowed with profound sound, attended by scholars who were experts in the investigation of various doctrines. (2)
Śatrughna said:
"O wise one, whose city has this great being reached? I wish to behold this army, which is like the waves of the ocean or curdled milk."
Whose is this force, endowed with swift-footed horses, that shines resplendent before us, having approached with zeal for battle? (4)
Explain all of this to me exactly as I ask, so that,
having understood it, I may direct my own warriors to their positions in the battle.
Having heard these words, the wise and virtuous Sumati,
being pleased, spoke these words to Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies.
Sumati said: "O King, there exists nearby a beautiful city called Cakrāṅkā,
in which the people are free from sin due to their devotion to Viṣṇu."
This Subāhu, the lord of that city and the foremost among those who know the Dharma, stands here before you, O son, surrounded by his sons and grandsons. (8)
He was constantly devoted to his own wife and turned away from the wives of others;
the stories of Viṣṇu, which illuminate no other purpose, remained fixed in his ears.
The king does not seize the property of others, taking no more than a sixth part as tax; and those who are devoted to Viṣṇu, being worthy of worship by you, O righteous one, are honored by you.
Constantly devoted to the service of Viṣṇu’s lotus feet and faithful to his vow, he was intent on his own duty and turned away from the duties of others. 11.
Nowhere was there ever a force equal to his strength among those of inferior heroes;
yet, upon hearing of his son's fall, he became overwhelmed with rage and grief.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, he has arrived for battle;
you too have many heroes, headed by Lakṣmīnidhi, [to face] these men.
"They shall conquer all directions with their multitude of weapons for the supreme benefit of others.
Hearing those words, Śatrughna spoke to his excellent soldiers: (14)
Today, the Krauñca formation has been arrayed by the troops of Subāhu, their minds overflowing with the surge of exultation at having attained the field of battle. (15)
Who, skilled in weapons, will pierce those warriors stationed on the wings and face, he by whose division his own power is diminished and who is intent on conquering the hero? (16)
Then the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi took the betel-roll from my lotus-like hand for the purpose of breaking the Krauñca mountain.
Surrounded by many heroes skilled in all weapons and missiles, he spoke these words to the king: "I shall go to pierce Krauñca."
"Bhārgava was already here; indeed, I too am the piercer of Krauñca.
Furthermore, he spoke thus to another hero: 'Who shall go with you? (19)
Then Puṣkala,
Riputāpa, Nīlaratna, Ugrāśva, and Vīramardana set their minds on following behind him.
All of them set out at Shatrughna’s command to break through that Krauñca mountain;
Shatrughna also, standing upon his chariot and bearing all manner of supreme weapons, followed.
Then, followed by him and surrounded by many soldiers, they set out;
the two oceans of their respective forces were seen facing one another.
When the two heroes, intent on bringing about the dissolution of the world,
were engaged in battle, then the sturdy kettledrums of both armies were struck.
The sounds of battle-drums and the blasts of conchs were heard here and there;
the horses neighed and the elephants trumpeted loudly in that place.
The foremost heroes utter "huṃ, huṃ," and the rims of the chariot wheels roar;
there the brave warriors, enraged and proud of their strong arms, [stand ready].
"Cut them down! Break them! Be firm!"—thus many were seen shouting in the forest.
O slayer of enemies, such was the state of the two armies as they exerted themselves in the battle.
To Suketu, who was standing before him, Lakṣmīnidhi said:
"Know that this son of Janaka is known as Lakṣmīnidhi. (27)
"Release the horse of Rāmacandra, the subduer of all demons, who is skilled in all weapons and missiles and proficient in every mode of combat. (28)
"Once pierced by my arrows, you shall not go to the abode of Yama," said Suketu, rushing suddenly toward that foremost of heroes as he spoke.
Having strung his bow and discharging inauspicious arrows, he stood firm;
those arrows, with sharpened joints and golden feathers, were released simultaneously from there.
There, in the midst of the battle, were seen those all-pervading and most irresistible [arrows],
having struck down [the enemy] through the network of his shafts;
then Lakṣmīnidhi drew his bow with its string fully extended.
Having fixed six arrows to his chest,
he released them— sharp and adorned with polished joints.
Having pierced the heart of his strong-armed brother,
those arrows were seen upon the earth, stained dark with blood.
His heart pierced by that arrow, Suketu, filled with rage,
struck him with twenty sharp, straight-knotted shafts.
With their bodies pierced by arrows and drenched in blood, both were seen by the soldiers like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. (34)
Releasing millions of arrows and fitting swift shafts to the string,
those two of great strength and light-handedness could not be perceived by anyone.
With their excellent bows drawn into circles and raining down a torrent of arrows,
they acted like the two clouds Navāmbuda and Budabuda, executing the commands of Indra in the heavens.

They were seen merely cutting down the arrows, elephants, horses, and brave men of those two [heroes], leaving them headless, yet they were not observed in the acts of aiming or releasing their own weapons.
The earth was filled with excellent warriors wearing crowns and earrings, holding bows and arrows in their hands, and biting their lips in rage. ||38||
As those two, both experts in all weapons and missiles, fought out of pride, a great and terrible battle took place that caused amazement even to the gods. (39)
An extreme crush occurred, tearing apart tens of millions of heroes;
nowhere was anyone seen amidst the mass of arrows.
At that moment, the heroic Lakṣmīnidhi, the crusher of enemies,
fixed eight firm and sharpened arrows upon his bow.
With four [arrows], the hero brought Suketu’s horses to their destruction;
with one, he swiftly and forcefully severed his exceedingly fierce standard.
Filled with rage, he struck off the charioteer’s head from his body with one arrow, and with another he severed the strung bow.
The impetuous King pierced Suketu with a single arrow in the heart;
seeing that wonderful feat, the heroes were filled with amazement. (44)
With his bow severed, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he took up a great mace and approached, desiring to fight. (45)
Beholding him approaching, skilled in the art of mace-fighting and equipped with a massive mace,
he [Bhīma] descended from his chariot.
Taking up a massive mace made entirely of iron, variegated with gold and endowed with every splendor, he advanced. ||47||
Lakṣmīnidhi, becoming violently enraged,
quickly struck Suketu in the chest with a mace that resembled the fire of a thunderbolt.
O great sage, struck by the mace, the hero fell from heaven like one intoxicated with pride when struck on the head with a sharp blade and garlands. 49.
Then that foremost of heroes spoke to King Lakṣmīnidhi:
"O scorcher of foes, if you are a hero, endure this one blow from me."
Having said this, he struck him violently on the forehead with his mace.
Struck on the forehead by the mace, he vomited blood and became exceedingly enraged.
He struck him on the head with his mace, which was like the form of Death;
Suketu, who knew what was right, also struck him on the shoulder.
Thus, both being highly enraged and experts in mace-fighting,
they engaged in a duel with clubs, each desiring victory over the other.
Mutually attacking with discordant views and intent upon slaying one another, not a single person was defeated there in that battle, nor did anyone survive.
Upon their heads, foreheads, shoulders, chests, and all their limbs,
they were drenched by streams of blood— those two possessed of great strength and prowess.
Then the powerful Alakṣmīnidhi, enraged and impetuous, raised his mace and rushed with great force to strike the younger brother of the King in the chest.
Then, seeing him approaching and bearing a great mace,
the king’s brother went forth with force against that powerful one.
He seized with his own hand the mace hurled by him;
with that very mace, the one of great strength struck him in the heart.
Seeing his own mace taken away by him, King Lakṣmīnidhi desired to fight that most powerful man with a wrestling match.
Then the king’s younger brother, enraged, seized him with both arms and fought,
he who was the best among heroes and skilled in all forms of combat.
Then Alakṣmīnidhi struck him on the chest with his fist;
then he too, raising his fist, struck him on the head.
Enraged, with their lower lips bitten like tender sprouts, they struck one another with fists resembling thunderbolts and with terrible slaps of their palms.
Fighting fist-to-fist, biting one another, and tearing at each other's hair and scratching with their nails, a tumultuous battle occurred between the two that made the hair stand on end.
Then his brother, becoming enraged, seized the king by the foot,
whirled him around, and threw him down upon the ground.
Lakṣmīnidhi seized the younger brother of the king by the hand and,
having whirled him around a hundred times, struck him down upon the back of an elephant.
Having fallen upon the ground and regained consciousness a moment later,
the valorous one whirled about in the sky with such speed as before.
Thus fighting on, they engaged in hand-to-hand combat once more,
foot against foot, hand against hand, chest against chest, and face against face.
Thus, locked together and each desiring the other's death,
both of them, though full of prowess, fell into a swoon.
Seeing that, they were filled with wonder and praised him by the thousands:
"Blessed is this king, a treasure-house of Lakṣmī; blessed is the powerful younger brother of the king! (69)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Mace-Fight," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||26||
(27) The twenty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Seated upon a variegated chariot drawn by swans, with his neck adorned with a golden chain and graced by heroes,
he plunged into that army as a boar plunges into the ocean.
Drawing his very firm bow, which resounded like the roar of a thundercloud,
he released sharp arrows capable of incinerating millions of enemies.
With all their limbs pierced by his arrows, those great warriors lay prostrate,
still wearing their crowns and armor, their lips firmly bitten.
Thus, having set out for battle, he went with Puṣkala to fight,
taking up his bow adorned with jewels, which scorched his enemies.
The form of those two joined together appeared exceedingly beautiful,
like that of Skanda and Tāraka in the ancient battle between Tāraka and Skanda.
Swiftly drawing his bow, the ambidextrous Savyasācin, full of prowess,
quickly struck him with straight-knotted arrows.
Overcome with rage, Citra also took up arrows and bows and repeatedly discharged them upon the head of the battlefield.
There was no taking up [of weapons], nor joining together, nor even releasing;
those two alone were seen, with their bows drawn into circles.
Then that Puṣkala, filled with rage, pierced that great warrior and formidable hero in the center of his chest with a hundred arrows. 9.
In an instant, he cut all of Citrāṅgada’s arrows into pieces as small as sesame seeds;
then, he struck Puṣkala on his limbs with sharp shafts.
Puṣkala made that divine chariot whirl in the sky with his beautiful *bhrāmaka* weapon; it was like a marvel. ||11||
Having wandered for only a moment, he— along with his chariot and horses—
attained a precarious stand in the circle of battle, having been held fast.
Seeing his prowess, the wise Citrāṅgada, who was highly skilled in all weapons, became exceedingly enraged and spoke to Puṣkala. ||13||
Citrāṅgadā said:
"An evil deed has been committed by you, one condemned by brave warriors in battle;
my chariot, yoked with horses, was made to whirl in the sky for a moment. (14)
Behold my prowess, displayed by me even with these excellent warriors;
though you are a wanderer of the sky, let it be so, for you are honored by the gods. (15)
Having spoken thus, he who was the knower of supreme weapons and the best among those who know all dharmas released an exceedingly terrible missile from his bow in the battle. (16)
Pierced by that arrow, he whirled about in the sky like a bird,
along with his chariot, horses, banner, and charioteer, in the midst of the battle.
But while that best of charioteers was circling in the sky with great speed,
before he could regain his composure, another arrow was released.
Then, accompanied by his charioteer, he wandered about again;
beholding that deed of his son, the king was filled with wonder.
Somehow managing to regain his composure, Puṣkala, the slayer of enemy heroes,
struck his chariot with arrows, along with its driver and horses.
The hero, his chariot shattered, took refuge in another;
that one too was quickly broken by Puṣkala’s arrows on the field of battle. (21)
Furthermore, having stationed himself elsewhere until [the opponent] came directly before him,
he then again shattered that chariot with sharp arrows.
Thus, indeed, for the son of King Daśaratha, who was unbroken [in valor], there was a great battle with the heroic Puṣkala, who is distinguished in great combat. 23.
Then, standing upon a variegated chariot, Gaka approached with great speed toward Puṣkala to engage him in battle.
In that battle, he struck Puṣkala with five arrows;
struck by those arrows, the son of Bharata was exceedingly pained.
Enraged, the great [hero] raised his bow and released ten sharp arrows,
beautifully adorned with golden feathers, into his heart.
Those exceedingly terrible arrows drank his blood;
having drunk it, they fell upon the earth like ancestors who bear witness to falsehoods.
Then the enraged Gāṅgeya took up five broad-headed arrows (bhalla) and released them at the forehead of his son, the highly powerful Bhārata. ||28||
Struck by those bhalla-arrows, he became enraged; fixing an arrow to his excellent bow, he made a remarkable vow regarding the slaughter of Gani.
"O hero, listen quickly to my vow concerning your death;
having understood that, you must now fight with full attention."
If, by this arrow, I do not deprive you of life after you have defiled a virtuous woman so beautifully adorned with character and conduct— 31.
The world is attained by those people who remain under the sway of Yama;
may that world be mine as well—this is my solemn promise, spoken in truth. (32)
Having heard these excellent words, the slayer of enemy heroes laughed and,
being wise and brave, spoke these auspicious words to Puṣkala.
Death must inevitably occur for all living beings everywhere and at all times;
therefore, O crest-jewel of heroes, there is no sorrow in death. (34)
Since my vow was not fulfilled by one who possesses both valor and lack of valor, let this great declaration of mine, which has now become false, be heard once more. (35)
If I do not sever your arrow aimed at my destruction, then let all those who pride themselves on being heroes hear my vow! 36.
Indeed, he who would cause internal distraction for one desiring to go on a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrtha), considering any vow other than the Ekādaśī vow to be superior, [is a fool]. (37)
"May the sin of him who violates his vow be mine!
Having uttered these words, he became silent and took up his bow. (38)
Then, having drawn that excellent, sharp, and sweet-tasting arrow from his quiver,
he spoke these clear words which brought about the destruction of the enemy.
Puṣkala said:
"If the pair of Rāma’s feet have been worshipped by me with a mind free from deceit, then let my word come true. (40)
"If, having enjoyed my own wife, I have not known another woman even in my mind—by this truthful word, let it become true in battle. (41)
Having uttered these words, he discharged from his bow an inauspicious arrow,
resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, which was capable of severing the head of a hero.
Beholding that released arrow, the powerful son of the king fixed another sharp shaft,
resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, upon his bow.
Severed by that arrow, the shaft [of the enemy] was intent on killing him;
when that arrow was cut down, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose at that time.
The upper half fell to the ground, while the lower half remained joined with the fruit;
he instantly severed the neck as if it were a lotus stalk. (45)
Then, seeing him fallen upon the ground, all his soldiers cried out "Alas! Alas! and became intent on flight. ||46||
That head of his, excellent with its crown and earrings, shone exceedingly as it fell upon the earth, like the orb of the moon fallen from the sky. 47.
Seeing him fallen, the hero Puṣkala, son of Bharata, plunged into this array, which was graced by all the foremost warriors. (48)

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Citrāṅga," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||27||
(28) The twenty-eighth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then, beholding his son fallen, lifeless, and cast aside, the king, afflicted by the grief for his son, lamented intensely. ||1||
Deeply distressed, he struck his own head with both hands;
trembling violently, he shed tears from his lotus-like eyes. (2)
Having seized the fallen, curved, and most beautiful lunar disc, which was drenched with the blood of those struck among the Puṣkala warriors and adorned with earrings; ||3||
With his pair of curved eyebrows raised and his sprout-like lower lip bitten, he lamented with his lotus-face full of kisses and spoke these words:

Alas, O hero! Why do you not look upon me with your pair of bright eyes, I whose heart is so anxious for my son? O brave one!
Why are you devoid of conversation for my amusement? Indeed, you appear as if your mind is submerged in an ocean of anger. ||5||
"O son, why do you speak to me thus again and again with a smile?
O dear son, you delight me with words as sweet as nectar."
"O high-minded one, take Śatrughna’s horse, which is adorned with white chowries and enriched with the splendor of golden ornaments; it has not yet slept. (7)
This Puṣkala, the foremost in valor, radiant with majesty, and the supreme scorcher of enemies, stands before us holding his bow, slaying the heroes of the foe. (8)
Restrain him with sharp arrows discharged from your bow;
how is it that you, O hero, have become bewildered and sit here in the midst of battle? ||9||
Elephants, foot soldiers, and those mounted on chariots, afflicted by fear, have come to you for refuge; look upon them, O high-minded one! (10)
O son, how could you possibly endure the sharp arrows of Śatrughna, released from his fierce bow, upon the field of battle? (11)
Who indeed is capable of protecting the atoms that are devoid of you? When you shall cast off sleep, then I shall be capable for victory. (12)
Having lamented thus intensely, the king, distressed by grief for his son, struck his own heart many times with his hand. (13)
Then, seated upon their own various chariots,
they bowed at the feet of their father and spoke words appropriate for the occasion.
O King, tell us what grief dwells in our hearts while we still live;
for heroes, death in battle gives rise to great glory. (15)
Blessed indeed is this earth, which is beautified by the wonderful cow;
for the Lord, wearing a crown and biting his lips with his two teeth, shines here. (16)
"Speak quickly! Perform today itself the task you desire:
let us two destroy the entire army of Śatrughna, which is now without a protector."
This very day, having severed the head adorned with a crown from his chariot, strike down Puṣkala, the slayer of my brother, in battle.
"Abandon your grief; why do you appear so afflicted by great suffering, O high-minded one?
Command us, who are worthy of honor, and likewise set your mind upon battle. (19)
Having heard these words of his two sons who pride themselves on their heroism,
the great king cast aside his grief and resolved his mind upon battle.
Those two, intoxicated by the pride of battle, went forth as adversaries against you both toward the enemy's camp, which was filled with endless warriors.
The hero Yuyudhāna fought in battle with the other, Riputāpana, as two clouds clash during the rainy season, he with his sword and the other with his sapphire-blue jewel.
The powerful king, holding his bow, stood upon a chariot adorned with gold, variegated with jewels,
and enriched by the beauty of its gem-encrusted pole.
He went forth to fight Śatrughna, who was surrounded by millions of heroes,
treating as mere blades of grass those great warriors who were highly skilled in the science of archery.
Seeing Subāhu arrive to fight, filled with rage and intent on the slaughter of the entire army due to the loss of his son— ||25||
Hanumān, moving by the side of Śatrughna, rushed toward him in battle,
making a great roar like a cloud while using his claws as weapons.
Subāhu, his eyes filled with rage, laughed and spoke these words to Hanumān as he approached him, making that great roar: ||27||
"Where has Puṣkala gone? Today, on the field of battle, I shall swiftly strike down your son, his head adorned with glowing earrings. (28)
Where is Śatrughna, the protector of the army? Where is Rāma? And where are the warriors?
Let them behold me as I come to the battle, crying out loudly to take their lives.
Having heard those words, Hanumān said to him:
"Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa and protector of the army, is present. (30)
O King, how could he fight in the vanguard when his servant stands at the front?
O bull among men, having defeated me in battle, you shall go there. (31)
Having spoken thus, he pierced the exceedingly fierce monkey in the heart with ten arrows, as he stood firm like a great mountain peak.
Having seized all those sharp, enemy-piercing arrows that had come toward him with his hollowed palms, he crushed them into pieces as small as sesame seeds.
Having pulverized those arrows with roars like the thundering of clouds,
the one of great strength then wound him high up with his tail and carried him away.
Then that best of kings, remaining stationed in the sky,
repeatedly struck Lāngūla with sharp-pointed arrows.
Struck on the tip of his tail with straight-jointed arrows,
he released that divine chariot, which was variegated with gold.
With eyes filled with rage, he struck Hanūmat, the best of monkeys, with a volley of sharp arrows released with great force.
Pierced by arrows and drenched in blood on all sides, Hanumān,
the lord of monkeys, summoned a great rage toward the king.
Seizing his chariot together with its horses by means of their tusks, they crushed it with great force; that was like a marvel.
Seeing his own chariot being shattered,
the powerful king hurriedly mounted another chariot and fought that one of great strength.
Expert in aiming his arrows and a master of supreme weapons, the king struck him on the face, the mouth, the chest, the arms, and the feet. (41)
Then, enraged, that best of monkeys leaped up with speed and struck the chest of the king, who was graced by his excellent warriors, with his foot. (42)
Struck by a sudden blow to the ground, he fell down and fainted;
vomiting warm blood from his mouth, he trembled with gasping breaths. ||43||
Then Hanumān, becoming exceedingly enraged in that great battle,
