crushed horses, heroes, and elephants by his sheer force.
Then his brother Asukeśu and King Lakṣmīnidhi, both well-prepared for battle, approached the field. 45.
Seeing the king unconscious, the men who had fled were wounded here and there by the multitudes of arrows showered by Puṣkala. ||46||
Seeing his own army being broken, the powerful prince Damana checked it, as a dam holds back the surging ocean.
Then, having fainted from that blow, the king saw a single dream:
that he had been struck by the strike of the forefoot of the foremost of monkeys in the midst of battle. (48)
Rāmacandra, however, was in Ayodhyā at the pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū, surrounded by many brahmins who were the most eminent among sacrificial priests. ||49||
There, the gods beginning with Brahmā, as well as millions of cosmic eggs, stand with palms joined in reverence and repeatedly praise him with hymns of praise. (50)
Nārada and others, their hands radiant with lutes, sing of Rāma—the dark-hued one with beautiful eyes, who holds a deer-horn. ||51||
There the Apsarases, Ghṛtācī, Menakā, and others, dance;
assuming the forms of the Vedas, they wait upon Rāghava.
Whatever collection of objects exists endowed with every beauty, he is the giver of it all, bestowing enjoyments upon his devotees. ||53||
Perceiving these and other such things, he regained consciousness while still dreaming;
his knowledge struck down by the curse of Brahmā, he spoke, saying, "What have I seen? (54)
Having risen, he set out toward the battle on foot with Śatrughna,
surrounded by ten million servants and encircled by ten million chariots.
The knower of dharma restrained Suketu, Tusamāhūya, Vicitra, and Damana, who were prepared to engage in battle.
The great king, whose soul was righteous yet joined with unrighteousness, said to them:
"O brothers and sons, listen to these words endowed with righteousness. (57)
"Let us fight quickly, for a great calamity has occurred:
that you have seized the powerful horse of Rāmacandra! (58)
This Rāma is the Supreme Brahman, beyond cause and effect;
he is the Lord of the moving and unmoving world, assuming a human form.
O sinless ones, I have now realized this supreme knowledge of Brahman; previously, my wealth of wisdom was stolen by the curse of Aṅgiras.
Once, desiring to know the ultimate truth, I went on a pilgrimage to ancient sacred sites;
there I beheld many sages who were most eminent in their knowledge of Dharma. (61)
Desiring to know [the truth], I went to the sage Asita;
then that brahmin, showing compassion toward me, spoke.
He who is the lord of Ayodhyā is designated by the term "Supreme Brahman";
his consort, Queen Jānakī, is traditionally held to be the direct embodiment of consciousness itself.
Yogis, desiring to cross the ocean of saṃsāra which is difficult to traverse and shoreless, worship Him directly with offerings such as these. (64)
The one whose banner is Garuḍa removes great sins by being remembered even for a moment;
the wise man who serves him will cross over saṃsāra. ||65||
Then I said to the brahmin: "Who is this Rāma, a mere mortal?
And who is this lady Jānakī, overwhelmed by both joy and grief? (66)
How can there be birth for that which is unborn? What action can there be for that which is a non-doer?
O Sage, tell me how it is that you have transcended birth, suffering, and old age. (67)
When I had spoken thus, the lord of sages, filled with anger, cursed me:
"O lowest of men, you have replied to this [sage] without knowing his true nature! (68)
"You mock this Rāma, laughing that he is merely a human;
therefore, being utterly deluded regarding the truth, you shall become a mere filler of your belly. (69)
Then, filled with compassion, I grasped his feet;
seeing my humility, that ocean of mercy spoke to me. (70)
O King, when you create obstacles for Rāma during his sacrifice,
then Hanumān will strike your feet with great force.
O King, you will understand this present state according to your own intellect;
that which I was told by him in the past has now been seen by me.
When the enraged Hanumān struck me on the chest,
I then beheld the Lord of Ramā, whose true nature is the perfect Brahman.
Therefore, bring that horse which is rich in beauty; O you of great strength, I offer these riches, garments, and this very kingdom. (74)
"Having seen Rāma, may I become one who has fulfilled his purpose in this merit-bestowing sacrifice"; thus thinking, he brought a horse to me, saying, "This is pleasing to me. (75)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Defeat of Subāhu," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||28||
The twenty-ninth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words of their father, the warriors were filled with joy.
"So be it," they said to the great king, who was longing for a vision of Rāma. ||1||
The sons said:
"O King, we know nothing other than your lotus feet;
therefore, let that which has arisen from your heart come into being this very moment. (2)
"Let this horse be led there, adorned with white chowries, richly embellished with garlands of jewels, and anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents. (3)
O Lord, sovereignty has its fruit in the power of command; the treasury is abundant with great wealth;
and there are garments that are highly precious, fine, and of excellent quality. (4)
There were sandalwood trees and moon-like objects, as well as most enchanting horses;
there were elephants exuding rut and chariots with golden poles.
Adorned with various ornaments of most diverse colors and the like,
there were a hundred thousand female servants and likewise charming male servants.
There were jewels resembling the sun and various kinds of gems, as well as bright pearls originating from the frontal globes of elephants.
O King of great intellect, whatever object there may be, even hundreds of thousands of corals, give all that to Rāmacandra with a heart full of compassion.
"O Lord of the Earth, why do you not entrust us all—your sons and servants—to you? O King, why do you not hand over the royal throne to those who depend on you? (9)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of his son, the lord of the earth became joyful; he then spoke to his heroic sons, who were intent on carrying out his command.
The king said:
"Bring all of you, equipped with armor and weapons in hand, accompanied by various chariots; then we shall go toward the king."
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the king, the heroic Suketu, whose mind was thus filled with wonder, set out for the battle at his command, ready for action. (12)
Having gone there, the heroes mounted that most beautiful horse, which was equipped with white chowries and adorned with golden leaf-patterns and other ornaments. ||13||
Richly adorned with garlands of jewels, beautified by variegated leaves, enriched with ornaments of diverse gems, and well-decorated with nets of pearls. (14)
It was held by ropes by great heroes—soldiers in front and behind—who were equipped with great weapons and missiles and endowed with every splendor. ||15||
A white parasol shines high above the head of this horse, and a pair of beautiful whisks are held repeatedly before him. (16)
And he led the horse, perfumed with incense such as black aloe and other fragrances and swift as the wind,
before the king for the sake of the Horse Sacrifice, the excellent rite.
Seeing that horse brought before him—adorned with a jewel-garland, swift as thought, and able to assume any form at will—the king rejoiced exceedingly. (18)
Adorned with royal insignia and other ornaments, the supremely righteous king, accompanied by his sons and grandsons, went on foot toward Śatrughna. (19)
He went forth to perform the proper expenditure of his fleeting riches, considering them to be perishable and a source of suffering for those whose minds are attached to them. (20)
Then he beheld Śatrughna, adorned with a white parasol and being fanned with chowries by servants standing before him.
Ask Sumati about that narrative of Rāmacandra, which is free from reports of fear and adorned with the splendor of heroism. (22)
It was crowded with tens of millions of heroes, bustling with horse-keepers,
and surrounded on all sides by thousands of monkeys.
Seeing Śatrughna, he prostrated himself on the battlefield along with his sons;
filled with joy and with his mind fixed solely on Rāma, he exclaimed, "I am blessed! ||24||
Seeing the formidable king, Śatrughna rose from his seat out of affection and embraced him with both arms along with all the soldiers.
Having honored Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, with great reverence, the king,
filled with joy, spoke to him in a voice faltering with emotion.
Subāhu said:
"Today I am blessed, along with my sons, my family, and my mounts, since I behold your two feet, which are praised by millions of kings. (27)
This best of horses was seized by my ignorant son Damanaka;
O ocean of compassion, please forgive this transgression of his. (28)
He did not know that the descendant of Raghu was the supreme deity of all gods,
the creator of the universe who, by his mere play, is both the deliverer and the protector.
"This kingdom is prosperous, with abundant armies and vehicles; these treasuries are full of wealth; these are my sons, and here am I. (30)
"We are all devotees of Rāmanātha, the executors of your command; accept everything as fruitful, for there is nothing in me that is improper. (31)
Where is that Hanumān, the bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma, by whose grace I shall obtain a vision of the King of Kings? (32)
What indeed can be obtained on this earth by the company of the virtuous?
By whose grace I, though a fool, have crossed over the curse of a Brahmin. (33)
Having seen this great king today, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, I shall obtain here the entire fruit of birth, which is otherwise difficult to attain. (34)
My life has already passed away for me, who have been separated from Rāma for so long;
only a very small portion remains—how then shall I behold the best of the Raghus?
Show me Rāma, who is skilled in the performance of sacrificial rites,
by the dust of whose feet the beloved wife of the sage became purified like a stone.
The crow, that bird, attained the supreme state by the mere touch of his arrow;
and many others, upon beholding his lotus-like face, reached the state beyond reckoning.
But those who respectfully take up the name of this Lord of the Raghus attain that supreme abode which is meditated upon by yogis. (38)
How great is the compassion of that blessed Ayodhyā, which grants such happiness to its inhabitants by allowing them to drink in the lotus-face of Rāma with the cups of their own eyes! 39.
Having thus addressed the king, I said: "I offer you my kingdom, my wealth, and everything else; O Lord of the Earth, what shall I do? (40)
Having heard these words of the king, the conqueror of enemy cities, eloquent and skilled in speech, replied to that monarch. (41)
Śatrughna said:
"O King, how can you, my honored elder, speak thus?
Let this Damana rule over all that belongs to you and your kingdom. (42)
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas: that which prescribes battle.
By my command, you must all return with this entire kingdom and its wealth. 43.
O lord of the earth, just as Lord Śiva is always to be worshipped by me with speech and mind, so too shall you become worthy of my worship. 44.
"May you be ready today for the pursuit of that horse;
be equipped with armor and a sword, accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots. (45)
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, the lord of the earth,
having consecrated his son in the kingdom, was duly honored by Śatrughna.
Surrounded by great chariot-warriors, the king, having performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules for his own son slain on the field of battle by Puṣkala, [proceeded].
For a moment, that great chariot-warrior, the knower of reality, grieved according to the worldly perspective; then, recollecting the Lord of the Raghus, he dispelled his grief through knowledge. 48.
Fully prepared and standing upon his chariot, surrounded by a great army and preceded by the great car-warrior Śatrughna, he arrived.
Seeing that he had arrived with his entire army, the king formed the resolve to depart,
leaving the care of the excellent horse to him.
That horse, released by him and marked with a leaf upon its forehead,
proceeded toward many eastern regions, turning in a counter-clockwise direction.
In various places, even by kings who were honored as great heroes, prostrations were made to him; he did not accept anything, nor was he ever provoked to anger.
Some brought various garments, some their own great kingdom,
some wealth, and some their people, and having brought these, they bowed down before him.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Departure of Śatrughna and Subāhu," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||29||
The thirtieth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Then the horse, adorned with feathers, reached the city of Tejas.
In which [age] the truthful king protects his subjects with truth.
Then the younger brother of Raghunātha, surrounded by a crore of followers, went before him on horseback, he who is the subduer of cities. ||2||
Having seen that delightful city, adorned with variegated ramparts and illuminated on all sides by golden domes, [he entered]. (3)
It was resplendent on all sides with thousands of temples, and there the monasteries of ascetics shone, filled with those who had renounced the world. ||4||
Where the great goddess flows, resting upon the head of the one with the eye on his forehead (Śiva),
crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and frequented by throngs of sages.
Furthermore, the smoke arising from the *agnihotra* sacrifice in every house of the brahmins purifies those whose minds are submerged in even the most heinous sins.
King Aśvatthāman, the scorcher of enemies, his mind filled with joy and wonder arising from the sight of that city, spoke to Sumati. (7)
Śatrughna said: "O minister, tell me whose city this is that has come within the range of my vision,
which brings such delight to the mind and is protected by righteousness?"
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of King Śatrughna, Sumati spoke everything exactly as it was, without any arrogance. (9)
Sumati said:
"Listen attentively, O Master, to the auspicious stories of the Vaiṣṇavas, by hearing which one is liberated from sin even equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. (10)
He remains as one liberated while living, a bee at the lotus feet of Rāma;
he is truthful, a performer of sacrifices among the sacrificers, a knower of all duties, and a great protector.
Having propitiated the Cow of Plenty with many vows, his father, known in the world as Ṛtabhara, attained him;
he was renowned throughout the earth and supremely righteous.
Know that Satyavān, endowed with many virtues and great splendor, whom the cow Prasannā gave birth to as her son, is the best among kings. 13.
Śatrughna said:
Who was King Bharata, and for what purpose was the cow worshipped?
How did his son become a Vaiṣṇava and a servant of Viṣṇu? (14)
Relate all of this narrative concerning the non-Vaiṣṇava;
for hearing it removes the mountain of great sins born of the slaughter of cows. (15)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, which were full of great significance,
he related clearly that narrative of his origin.
In former times, King Bharata was childless;
although he had many wives, he did not obtain a son among them. (17)
Then, being intent on his welfare, he questioned the sage named Ajābāli, who had arrived by chance, regarding the cause for the birth of a son.
Ṛtabhara said:
"O Master, O blind one, tell me the words that cause the birth of a son;
by performing what may an excellent offspring be born who shall uphold my lineage? (19)
Having understood that, O best of sages, I shall certainly carry out your word—
whether it be a gift, a vow, a pilgrimage, or a fast.
Having heard these words of the king, the best of sages spoke words that would bring about the birth of a son to him who was bowed down and seeking offspring.
O Lord, there are indeed three means for one who desires to obtain offspring:
the grace of Viṣṇu, or that of a cow, or else that of Śiva.
Therefore, O King, you must indeed perform worship of the cow, who is the very body of the gods;
for upon her tail, mouth, horns, and back, the deities are established. (23)
Being pleased, she will swiftly grant what is desired, conjoined with Dharma.
Knowing this, O Ṛtambhara, perform the worship of the cow. (24)
Indeed, for one who constantly honors a cow in his home with fodder and other provisions, both the gods and the ancestors remain perpetually satisfied. (25)
Whoever, observing auspicious vows, gives the daily provision for a cow according to the rule—by that truth, may all his desires be fulfilled. (26)
A thirsty cow tied up in the house, a maiden in the home during her menstrual period, and a deity with its offerings removed destroy previously accumulated merit. (27)
If a man should indeed prevent a cow from eating her own grass while she is grazing, his ancestors of the past fall headlong into the Kampa hell. (28)
That mortal of deluded intellect who strikes a cow with a staff goes,
deprived of all merit, to the city of Dharmarāja.
"Those who indeed restrain this [child] shall fall into a lower state;
our son, being fortunate, will surely deliver us. (30)
In this very context, I shall relate this ancient history,
the wonderful account of Janaka that occurred long ago in the city of Dharmarāja.
Once, King Janaka voluntarily relinquished his life-breaths;
at that moment, a celestial chariot adorned with a network of tinkling bells arrived.
Then, having mounted it, the king, his body borne by servants,
proceeded along the road toward the city of Saṃyaminī, the capital of Dharma.
Then those evildoers, having been tormented in millions of hells, attained happiness upon reaching the wind from the body of their father. (34)
The suffering born of burning in hell brought about happiness for them;
thus, the great misery of their father was destroyed by the life-span of the cow. (35)
Seeing him thus departed, those people, afflicted by sin, cried out excessively in fear, unwilling to be separated from him. (36)
They spoke these compassionate words: "O doer of good deeds, do not go from here;
by the touch of the wind from your body, may we be happy and free from suffering. (37)
Having heard these words, the supremely righteous king,
filled with a flood of compassion, reflected within his mind.
If the happiness of living beings here were to arise from me, then I would remain right here in this city; this very place would be as delightful as heaven. (39)
Having done this, the king remained there as if at the very entrance of hell, his mind filled with compassion as he brought happiness to living beings. (40)
There, Dharmarāja, having arrived at the gate of hell that bestows suffering, inflicts intense torments upon those who have committed various sins. (41)
Then they beheld King Janaka standing at the gate,
possessing great merit and endowed with compassion, traveling in a celestial chariot.
The Lord of the Dead spoke to Janaka with a gentle voice: "O King, you who are the crest-jewel of all dharma, from where have you come? (43)
This place belongs to sinners, the wicked, and those who take the lives of others; such merit-performers as you do not come here even for ten generations of ancestors, O King. 44.
In this age, there will indeed be three types of men who are intent on harming others, devoted to slandering others, and preoccupied with the wealth of others. ||45||
Indeed, that man who would abandon a most virtuous wife who is devoted solely to his service, except for a transgression, shall fall into this hell. 46.
But that man who, enticed by greed for wealth, deceives a friend, shall come here and suffer terrible torment from me. (47)
Whether out of fear, or through hatred, or even out of derision, such a person of deluded intellect does not remember Rāma with their mind, speech, or actions, even while living. (48)
I bound him again and cast him into these very fires, cooking him;
yet he by whom the Lord of Men is remembered is the warder-off of the torments of hell. (49)
The sin of men remains within their bodies only so long as they do not utter the name of Rāma, O King, due to the wicked-mindedness of the Kali age. (50)
O Great-Minded One, there are kṣatriyas who commit great evils;
my servants bring them here, for they are unable even to look upon those like you. (51)
Therefore, O Great King, go and enjoy manifold pleasures;
having ascended the most excellent celestial chariot, enjoy the merit you have acquired. (52)
Having heard these words of his lord, the King of Dharma, he,
filled with a flood of compassion, spoke to the King of Dharma.
Janaka said:
"O Lord, I shall go out of compassion for these living beings;
indeed, they have attained happiness and remain at ease because of my bull. (54)
O King, if you release all these who are situated in hell, then I shall go happily to heaven, which is inhabited by meritorious people. (55)
Jābāli said: Having heard these words, he replied to Ajātaśatru,
pointing out one by one the many individual souls dwelling in hell.
Dharma said: "This man followed his friend's wife while she was trusting;
therefore, I have cooked him in the iron cauldron for ten thousand years."
Afterwards, having cast this offender into the womb of a sow,
he shall be brought down among humans, marked with the sign of a eunuch.
Because he repeatedly embraced another's wife by force,
he is therefore cooked here in Raurava for a hundred years.
But this evil-minded one, having stolen his own property belonging to another, consumed it;
therefore, having cut off his hands, I shall cook him in pus and blood. (60)
This evening, he did not offer even a word of welcome or honor to the guest who had arrived, though he was afflicted by hunger. (61)
Therefore, he should be cast into the Tāmisra hell, which is filled with wealth;
there, tormented by bees, he shall undergo torment for a hundred years.
First, this man was not ashamed while loudly reviling another;
furthermore, he listened to that [reviling] many times, pricking up his ears. (63)
Therefore, these two have fallen into a blind well, tormented by suffering;
this betrayer of friends, filled with anxiety, is being intensely cooked in the Raurava hell.
Therefore, having caused these beings to exhaust their karmic debts of suffering, I shall liberate them;
go now, O tiger among men, you who are the creator of a mass of merit! (65)
Jābāli said:
Having thus pointed out the living beings who remained silent while committing their deeds,
that devotee of Rāma, his eyes filled with compassion, spoke.
Janaka said:
"How may liberation from hell come about for living beings who are suffering? Please tell me that quickly, by doing which they might attain happiness. (67)
Dharma said: "Viṣṇu has not been propitiated by these, nor have the stories of Him been heard by them.
How can there be liberation from hell for those who commit such sins? (68)
If you release even these great evildoers, then, O Great King, bestow upon me that merit; I shall tell you what it is. (69)
Once, having risen in the morning with a mind of pure disposition, he meditated upon the illustrious Raghunātha, who is known as the remover of great sins. (70)
"Whatever you have uttered with a pure mind, saying 'Rāma, Rāma,' offer that merit to these [beings], so that there may be their deliverance from hell. (71)
Jābāli said:
Having heard these words of that wise Dharmarāja,
O great king, he gave him the merit he had accumulated since birth.
By the merits performed in previous births arising from the worship of the Lord of the Age (Aghunātha), may their liberation from these hells be beautiful and immediate. 73.
As he was speaking thus, those who were situated in the Jīva hell were instantly liberated from that hell and came to possess divine bodies. (74)
They said to Janaka, "O King, by your grace we shall, in an instant, be liberated from this sorrowful hell and go to the supreme abode. (75)
Seeing those men, who resembled the sun and had emerged from hell, he—
being devoted to compassion for all beings— rejoiced greatly in his heart.
They all departed for the celestial realm adorned by the gods, praising Janaka, the great king and ocean of compassion. ||77||

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Beings Residing in Hell by Janaka," within the Narrative of Satyavatī in the Rāmāśvamedha, occurring in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||30||
The thirty-first chapter.
Jābāli said:
Now, when those men who were situated in hell had departed...
The king questioned Kīnāśa, the best among those who know all dharmas.
The King said:
"O Dharmarāja, you have stated that those men who commit sins do not come to this abode, nor are they devoted to the discourse of dharma. (2)
"O righteous one, by what sin has my arrival here occurred?
Tell me all that, explaining the cause of this misfortune from the very beginning. (3)
Having heard those words, Dharmarāja, the supreme ascetic,
then related to her his arrival at the city of Yama.
The King of Dharma said:

O King, your merit is great; such as yours has never existed for anyone else upon the surface of the earth, you who are a bee at the honey of the nectar from the pair of feet of the Lord of the Raghus.
Your fame, like the celestial river Ganges, bestows supreme delight and delivers the wicked; it purifies all sinners who are burdened by impurity.
Nevertheless, O best of kings, a trace of sin still remains within him,
by which he has come to the vicinity of Saṃyaminī, though filled with merit.
Once, out of pride, he obstructed a cow while it was grazing;
by the ripening of that evil deed, he beheld the gateway to hell.
Now, freed from sin and endowed with abundant merit, enjoy the many vast pleasures acquired through your own merit. (9)
Raghunātha, whose ocean of compassion was stirred by these [words], removed their suffering and sent them along the great path to Saṃyaminī, the realm of Viṣṇu. 10.
O you of excellent vows, if you had not come by this wrong path, how could their liberation from hell have occurred? (11)
O one of great intelligence, those like you, who are pained by the suffering of others and are abodes of compassion, bring about the destruction of the suffering of living beings in this manner. (12)
Jābāli said:
Having thus spoken and bowed to that Śamana,
he departed for heaven in a divine celestial chariot, resplendent with hosts of Apsarases.
Therefore, cows should be worshipped constantly; one should not revile them even in thought.
By reviling them, one goes to hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras.
Therefore, O best of kings, perform the worship of the cow;
from her, when she is satisfied, you shall quickly obtain a son devoted to righteousness.
Sumati said:
Having heard that, he respectfully asked about the worship of the cow:
"How is she to be worshipped with diligence, and what does she do for a man? (16)
Jābāli explained the ritual worship of the cow according to the prescribed rules:
"The observer of the vow should go daily to the forest for the purpose of grazing the cow. (17)
O King, one who desires sons should collect barley grains that have been offered as food, consumed, or used as cow-dung, and which are fit for eating. 18.
When he drinks water, then that water to be drunk must be pure;
when he stands in a high place, then he must likewise be seated upon a seat. (19)
One should constantly restrain this dog and personally provide fodder for it;
to one who acts in this manner, a son devoted to righteousness will be granted. (20)
Sumati said: Having heard these words, Ṛtadhara, the righteous-souled one who desired a son,
performed a vow while practicing the worship of a cow.
Every day, he would offer grass to the cow, having gratified her with barley;
the wise man, devoted to the practice of eating only barley, restrained her from consuming grain.
Thus, as she worshipped the cow, many days passed;
she grazed on grass and other fodder in the middle of the forest, free from fear from any quarter.
Once, the king, casting his gaze about to behold the splendor of that forest, wandered around it with great curiosity.
Then, from the depths of the forest, a five-faced beast came and struck the cow,
who was crying out in many ways and distressed by the weight of the lion.
Then the king, having arrived and beholding his own mother slain by a lion, wept, utterly overwhelmed with grief.
Deeply distressed, he approached Jābāli, the best of sages,
and asked for an expiation for that killing of a cow committed through negligence.
Ṛtabhara said:
"O Master, by your command, while I was staying in the forest guarding the cow, a lion came from somewhere out of sight and killed her. (28)
By your command, what shall I do as an atonement for that sin?
Or how can there be the completion of the vow that bestows a son upon me? (29)
To the king who had spoken thus, the best of sages said:
"O protector of the earth, there are indeed means for the removal of this sin."
O high-minded one, for the slayer of a Brahmin, the ungrateful person, and the drinker of liquor, even those penances that remove all sins do not avail. 31.
Through difficult penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, through gifts, vows, observances, and restraints, sins go to their dissolution for one who practices these rules with constancy. (32)
And there is no atonement for these two who have committed the flowering of sin:
for one who intentionally kills a cow, and for one who reviles Nārāyaṇa. (33)
That lowest of beings who, through thought or deed, causes suffering to cows shall go to a place in hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Even that unfortunate man who should revile the god Hari but once shall see hell, surrounded by his sons and grandsons. (35)
Therefore, O lord of men, having known this, one who reviles Hari while inflicting suffering upon cows shall never attain liberation from hell. (36)
However, there exists an expiation for the unintentional killing of a cow;
O wise one, go therefore to Ṛtuparṇa, who is a devotee of Rāma.
Seeing all enemies as equal to friends, he will quickly tell you the atonement for this killing of a cow. (38)
In former times, you were exiled from that country by thieves;
having abandoned your state of enmity, go now to Ṛtuparṇa.
Whatever he shall quickly say, perform it without distraction, so that there may indeed be atonement for the sin committed by you. (40)
Having heard those words, he went to Ṛtuparṇa,
who was a devotee of Rāma and looked upon enemy and friend with an equal eye.
He related to him what had occurred, such as the killing of the cow and so forth;
he, too, reflected upon a means for the expiation of that sin.
Having reflected for a moment, the wise king Ṛtuparṇa, who was skilled in dharma, spoke these words with a smile to that Ṛta-bhara.
"O King, who am I in the presence of sages who know the scriptures? Why have I abandoned them to come to you, a fool who fancies himself a scholar? (44)
If you have faith in me, then I shall say something;
listen with respect, O tiger among men, to what I have to say. (45)
Worship Śrī Raghunātha with your actions, mind, and speech;
O great-minded one, being free from deceit in this world, bring an end to your distress. 46.
Being satisfied, he will grant every desire residing in your heart;
he will effect the destruction of the sin of cow-slaughter committed through ignorance. (47)
O best of beings, O righteous-souled one, protect the cow while remembering Rāma;
by giving gold to a twice-born, you will obtain atonement for your sin. 48.
Sumati said:
Having heard those words, King Bharata then accepted them as truth;
performing the remembrance of Rāma, he, with a purified soul, observed the vow.
Protecting the cow as before, he went to the great forest, constantly remembering the name of Rāma and devoted to the welfare of all living beings. (50)
Then Surabhi, being thoroughly gratified and pleased, said to him:
"O King, choose from me whatever boon is in your heart, whatever desire you cherish. (51)
Then Vairāja spoke to his son, who was handsome in body,
a devotee of Rāma, devoted to his father, and a protector of his own dharma.
Having granted that boon to the one who requested it, the compassionate goddess Kāmadhenu, smiling, vanished from sight even as she was being given away by her satisfied father.
At that time, his father obtained a son who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and a servant of Rāma;
there, the father gave him the name Satyavat.
Having obtained a son named Satyavān, who was devoted to his father and possessed valor equal to that of Śakra, the great king attained supreme joy.
Having obtained a righteous son, the king was filled with intense joy;
he entrusted the great kingdom to him and retired to the forest for ascetic practice.
There, having propitiated Hṛṣīkeśa with a mind endowed with devotion,
the king, his sins shaken off while still in his body, went to the abode of Hari.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dhenū Vrata," within the Narrative of Satyavatī in the Rāmāśvamedha, from the Dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana in the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||31||
Chapter Thirty-Two. Sumati said:
"O gentle one, this king is also well-known by the name Satyavat."
He gratified Lord of the World, Raghunātha, by means of his own dharma. ||1||
To him, the Lord Rāma, being pleased, granted unwavering devotion to his own lotus feet—a devotion difficult to attain even through millions of merits. ||2||
Endowed with compassion and free from worldly affliction, he constantly narrates the story of Śrī Raghunātha, which purifies all the worlds. ||3||
Whoever does not worship that god Raghunātha, the Lord of Ramā,
shall be struck with the staffs of Yama, which inspire even him with fear.
From the eighth year onwards until he reached eighty years of age,
the Ekādaśī vow was observed by all human beings through his influence.
The supreme garland from the lotus feet of the Lord of Ramā, which is ever dear to Tulasī, never left his neck.
He is worthy of worship even by the sages; how much more so by others?
Delighting in the remembrance of the Lord of the Raghus, his sins are cleansed and his misfortunes destroyed.
Having recognized that most wonderful horse of Rāmacandra,
he will come and hand over to you this kingdom free from all thorns.
O King, that which was spoken by you has been excellently related to you.
What more do you ask, O Lord? Command me; I shall do it.
Śeṣa said:
The horse entered that city, accompanied by various wonders;
seeing him, all the people went to the king and reported it. (10)
The people said:
"A certain horse, white in color like the water of the Gaṅgā, has arrived, shining with a golden plate upon its forehead. (11)
Having heard those delightful words spoken so pleasingly to the hearts of the people, the king laughed and replied to them: "Let it be known whose horse this is! (12)
And they said to him:
"The horse of King Rāma, protected by Śatrughna, is entering the middle of the city. (13)
Upon hearing the two-syllabled name of Rāma, which is so very beautiful, his heart rejoiced intensely, marked by a voice faltering with emotion. (14)
I am constantly meditating in my heart upon Yodhyāpati, who is like Rāma;
his horse has arrived at my city along with Śatrughna. (15)
There, Hanumān shall become a servant at the feet of Rāma;
he will never, even for a moment, forget Rāma within his mind. (16)
I am going where Śatrughna is, where the son of the Wind-god is, and where others who serve the lotus feet of that human-forest (Rāma) are also found. (17)
Then he commanded his minister: "Taking all the great royal wealth, come quickly with me. (18)
I shall go to protect the excellent horse of the Lord of the Raghus, in order to perform the service of His lotus feet, which is so very difficult to attain. (19)
Having spoken thus, he then went out with his troops against Śatrughna;
meanwhile, Rāma’s brother arrived at the city with his army.
The heroes roar, their powerful chariots thunder,
and the sounds of victory conchs resound there on all sides, along with the notes of flutes.
Having arrived accompanied by his ministers, King Satyavān prostrated at our feet and bestowed upon us a kingdom of great wealth.
Then Śatrughna, knowing that king to be devotedly loyal to Rāma,
gave that great kingdom to his son named Rukma.
Having embraced Hanumān, whose arms were strong, the servant of Rāma,
and having also embraced other great devotees of Rāma, he of great fame [departed].
Endowed with truth, he considered himself as one who had achieved his purpose;
accompanied by Śatrughna, his heart rejoiced at that time.
Meanwhile, Śatrughna, well-protected by heroes, went a great distance on horseback accompanied by those warriors and the king.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Meeting with Satyavatsa," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||32||
The thirty-third chapter. Śeṣa said:
While the many excellent kings, headed by Śatrughna, were departing...
And among all the great kings, each accompanied by ten million chariots. ||1||
Suddenly, an extremely dreadful darkness arose on the path,
in which one's own kin and strangers could no longer be distinguished by people.
The sky was shrouded in dust and filled with lightning and thunder;
in such a tumultuous and terrifying situation, [he remained] there. ||3||
The clouds rained down blood, pus, impurities, and much else;
those warriors, their supreme enemies, became utterly overwhelmed.
The world was thrown into confusion, and everyone wondered, "What is this? What is happening?
as the eyes of all people—even those of renowned power—were enveloped in darkness.
A friend of Rāvaṇa named Vidyunmālī, who was well-known and surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas, resided in Pātāla and carried off the horse.
Mounted upon a horse that moved at will through celestial mansions and was served by all the Yakṣas, he struck fear into the powerful enemies and indeed destroyed them.
Within a moment, that darkness vanished and the sky shone forth stainless;
the heroes, led by Śatrughna, asked, "Where is that horse? (8)
All of them, looking at the king of horses one after another, beheld Naya-dāvaha; then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
"Where has the horse of the Ashvamedha sacrifice been led by that evil-minded one?"— when they had spoken these words, O Lord of Anujas, he [the King] remained silent for a moment.
He was seen surrounded by all the brave warriors standing in their chariots, adorned with valor,
and by the foremost of the Rākṣasas mounted upon excellent celestial vehicles.
There, Rākṣasas were seen with faces distorted by frowns, mouths gaping wide, and terrifying tusks; they were intent on devouring the army. 12.
Then they informed Śatrughna, the best among the foremost of men, saying, "We do not know where this horse has gone; it has vanished from our sight like a celestial being sporting in the sky. (13)
Having thrown us heroes into confusion with darkness, he approached;
O tiger among kings, seize the horse as is fitting. (14)
Hearing those words, Śatrughna was overcome with great rage and asked:
"Who is this powerful Rākṣasa who has seized my horse? (15)
Let that celestial chariot fall today, struck down by my multitude of arrows;
let the head of that enemy of mine fall today, severed by my razor-sharp shafts.
Let all the chariots, equipped and filled with great weapons and missiles, go forth to counteract him—the stealer of horses—and let the warriors advance. (17)
Having spoken thus, his eyes copper-red with rage, he addressed his own minister—
one who knew right and wrong policy, was brave, and was skilled in the conduct of war.
Śatrughna said:
"O Minister, tell me who these are that are intent on slaying the Rākṣasa—those great warriors, wielders of mighty weapons, and supreme masters of the highest missiles. (19)
"Tell me quickly after due reflection; I shall do as you say. Name for her those heroes who are worthy of her and skilled in all weapons. (20)
Having heard this, the minister spoke words that were appropriate,
pointing out those heroes who were capable in the best of battles and possessed of great speed.
Sumati said: "Let Puṣkala, the scorcher of enemies, equipped with great weapons and missiles, go forth to conquer that Rākṣasa in battle, intent upon victory. (22)
Likewise, let Lakṣmīnidhi, accompanied by a multitude of weapons, cause the destruction of that vehicle with his own sharp arrows. (23)
Hanumān, whose deeds are bold, is capable of fighting the Rākṣasas;
O Lord, he can strike the demons with his mouth and his tail.
The monkeys too, who were heroes skilled in the deeds of the forest, set out to fight, all of them impelled by your word. (25)
Sumada, Subāhu, and Pratāpāgrya— the most excellent of beings—
went forth with their sharp arrows to fight those lowest of Rākṣasas.
You too, standing upon a chariot surrounded by great weapons, should achieve victory in battle, intent as you are on slaying the Rākṣasa. ||27||
O King, this is my opinion: those warriors who crush the enemy are the ones who should go swiftly; what is the use of many other soldiers? 28.
When the chief minister named Sumati had spoken thus,
Śatrughna addressed the heroes who were skilled in warfare.
"O heroes, Puṣkala and the others, you who are experts in all weapons and missiles!
Make this vow before me for the destruction of the Rākṣasa."
Having made a vast vow, resplendent with your own prowess, go quickly into the midst of the enemy, accompanied by your forces. (31)
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, those of great strength,
endowed with splendor, each made their own grand vow.
Thereupon, first of all, the hero Puṣkala, having heard the words of the lord of the earth, filled with supreme enthusiasm, uttered this vow: ||33||
Puṣkala said: "Listen, O tiger among kings, to my vow made through my prowess—most wonderful—to be heard by all the worlds. (34)
I would strike the Daitya—who was overcome by fainting and whose face was disheveled with tangled hair—with sharp, razor-tipped arrows released from my bow. (35)
Whatever sin belongs to one who consumes a maiden, and whatever sin belongs to one who reviles the gods—may that sin be mine if I should make my own word false. (36)
O great king, listen to my vow regarding this: if these soldiers of immense strength do not fall when pierced by my arrows. (37)
If I do not speak the truth, may that very sin which belongs to one who creates a distinction between Viṣṇu and Īśa, or even between Śiva and Śakti, be mine indeed. (38)
"Everything I have said regarding the lotus feet of Raghunātha shall be made true by her alone, whose devotion is unwavering. (39)
Having heard that vow of Puṣkala, King Lakṣmīnidhi made a true vow, adorned by his own prowess. ||40||
Lakṣmīnidhi said:
That man who, having heard the censure of the Vedas, delights in mental theft while remaining like a silent sage, is excluded from all dharma. (41)
That Brahmin who is of evil conduct, who sells lac, lac-dye, and the like,
and who, being a fool deluded by greed for wealth, sells even a cow— 42.

If I turn my face away [from you], may the sin of drinking water from a well belonging to a mleccha fall upon me; for one who does not perform atonement after drinking such water must undergo penance. (43)
Then, having heard that vow, Hanumān, skilled in battle,
performed remembrance of Rāma’s feet and spoke these auspicious words.
My Lord’s heart should indeed be meditated upon constantly and repeatedly by yogis—He whom all the gods, along with the asuras, bow down to with their jeweled crowns. (45)
Rāma, the illustrious lord of Ayodhyā, is worshipped by the lords of the world;
whatever word I speak after remembering him shall indeed become true. 46.
"O King, who is this insignificant and weak Daitya, stationed in a vehicle that moves at will? Tell me quickly; he must be destroyed by me alone. (47)
With the tip of my tongue, I shall lift up Mount Meru together with the Lord of the Gods;
I shall dry up the entire ocean, and I shall drink up its waters. 48.
By the grace of King Śrī Raghunātha and Jānakī, there is nothing on this earth that may ever be impossible for me to achieve. 49.
O Lord, if this word spoken by me should prove false, then and there may I be far removed from devotion to Raghunātha. (50)
If a Śūdra should tend a Kapilā cow with the intention that it be for sale, may his sin be equal to mine if he should speak a falsehood. (51)
If a Śūdra, deluded by passion, should out of ignorance approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, let his sin be as mine if he should utter a falsehood. (52)
He who, greedy for the taste on his tongue, drinks that wine by smelling which one goes to hell and by touching which one goes even to Raurava.
Whatever sin may arise from that, let it certainly be mine;
provided that, by the power of Rāma’s grace, I do not make my vow false. (54)
When this had been said by the great heroes, the warriors, joined together with speed, made a great vow characterized by their own prowess. ||55||
While the men looked on, Śatrughna also made a vow there, praising those heroes skilled in combat as "Excellent! Excellent! (56).
"I shall declare before you my own vow, adorned by its courage;
listen to it, O highly fortunate ones, endowed as you are with enthusiasm for battle. (57)
If he strikes down his head with my arrows,
his chariot wheel, shattered and severed, shall fall upon the earth.
Whatever sin there is from false testimony, whatever sin from the theft of gold, and whatever sin from the reviling of Brahmins—may that [sin] be mine today, for certain. (59)
Having heard these excellent words of Śatrughna, those heroes who were honored by the brave said:
"O brother of Rāghava, you are blessed; who else could be superior to you? (60)
By you alone has been slain the Daitya named Lavaṇa, the son of Madhu, who was of great strength and a source of suffering for the gods and Dānavas, O Lord of the World. (61)
Who is this wicked Vairākṣasa, and where is his meager strength?
O high-minded one, you shall bring about his destruction in an instant.
Having spoken thus, those great heroes prepared themselves on the battlefield and went joyfully toward the Rākṣasa to fulfill their own true vow.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of Vīra’s Vow," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(34) The thirty-fourth chapter. Śeṣa said:
They went toward the lowest of the Rākṣasas in chariots drawn by excellent horses, richly adorned, filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles, and equipped with various jewels. ||1||
Seeing them, the Rākṣasa, standing in his chariot that moved at will,
spoke many times as if threatening them with a voice deep as a thundercloud.
As Māyā was going to her own palace to fight with Subhata,
she did not abandon her own life-breaths, just as one would not release a noble horse before the race is finished.
Known as Vidyunmālin, he was a dear friend of Rāvaṇa;
I have come here to perform the funeral rites for my friend who has become a ghost.
Where is that Rāma who went forth having slain his own friend Rāvaṇa?
And where is his brother, that crest-jewel of all heroes? (5)
Having slain him, you shall obtain atonement for that [offense] against Rāma’s younger brother,
drinking his blood as it wells up with bubbles from the tube of his throat.
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the most excellent among the foremost of warriors,
spoke to him who was endowed with prowess and heroism.
Puṣkala said: "Noble warriors do not engage in boastful talk in battle;
they demonstrate their prowess by discharging showers of their own weapons and missiles. (8)
"Having seized the horse of him by whom Rāvaṇa was slain along with his friends and kinsmen, where will you go, O you who are difficult to subdue? (9)
"O Śatrughna, you shall fall by arrows discharged from the bow;
jackals will devour you when you have fallen upon the ground, deprived of life. (10)
Do not roar while I, the servant of the wicked Rāma, am present!
Subhata warriors roar in battle only after they have conquered the enemy—how wonderful! (11)
Śeṣa said:
As the hero Puṣkala, who was fierce in battle, was speaking thus,
that best of Rākṣasas struck him violently in the chest with a spear.
Then Sapuṣkala cut that great iron spear, which was of some indeterminate nature, with three exceedingly fierce and sharp arrows. ||13||
Struck by arrows and rendered lusterless, she fell to the earth in three parts; as she fell, did she not shine like the threefold power (Śakti-trayī) of Viṣṇu? ||14||
Seeing that spear shattered, the Rākṣasa, the scorcher of his enemies,
seized a three-pointed iron trident.
The lord of the rākṣasas released a sharp-pointed arrow resembling a blazing fire;
as it came toward him, the one named Puṣkala warded it off with his arrows. ||16||
Having severed the essence of the trident-wielder’s army, the servant of the Lord,
Puṣkala, took up his bow and fixed sharp arrows that were as swift as thought.
Those arrows, having struck his heart, quickly produced passion,
just as the captivating qualities of Viṣṇu produce their own devotion in a Vaiṣṇava.
Afflicted by the pain of being pierced by those arrows, the exceedingly arrogant Vidyunmālin seized a terrible mallet, intent on slaying Puṣkala.
A mallet was hurled at him by the thief named Vidyunmālin;
striking his heart, it quickly caused him to faint, thereby rendering him unconscious.
Struck by the mallet, the hero Puṣkala, the scorcher of enemies, trembled violently and fell onto the seat of his chariot. ||21||
Then Ugradaṃṣṭra, his brother,
fought Lakṣmīnidhi with many weapons and missiles discharged in various ways, which were capable of taking away the lives of heroes.
Regaining consciousness at that very moment, Puṣkala said to the Rākṣasa:
"O best of Rākṣasas, you are blessed; truly great is your prowess! (23)
Now behold my lofty vow, cherished by a hero:
today I shall strike you down from your celestial chariot to the earth with my sharp arrows.
Having spoken thus, he seized a sharp, irresistible arrow—
blazing with the brilliance of fire and endowed with great majesty.
Just as he prepares his own prowess to counter that [enemy], so too does the exceedingly fierce, sharp-edged arrow remain fixed within his heart. (26)
Stunned by that arrow, his mind reeling, the rākṣasa fell unconscious from the seat of Kāmagopa onto the ground.
His own elder brother, being seen by Ugradamṣṭra as he was falling,
seized him from that celestial chariot and carried him away, fearing his enemy.
With great fury, he spoke to Puṣkala, the best among the strong:
"O evil-minded one, where will you go after having struck down my brother? (29)
Having conquered me in battle, you have indeed achieved supreme victory;
since I stand here before you, let your hope for glory be turned back.
Speaking thus, his eyes filled with rage, he struck that wicked man in the heart with ten arrows. (31)
Struck by ten arrows by the high-souled Puṣkala,
the evil-minded one became enraged in his heart and proceeded to strike him.
Then, crushing them with fury and raising his fist,
he struck him in the heart, producing a sound like the falling of a thunderbolt.
Struck by the fist of that wicked-souled one, the heroic Puṣkala, a master of supreme weapons, did not feel even a slight pain from the impact. ||34||
Vatsadāman discharged those exceedingly sharp arrows at his heart;
pained by those shafts, the Daitya seized a trident.
Blazing fiercely, most terrifying with garlands of flames from its three points,
that dreadful [spear] struck the heart of the great hero Puṣkala.
Struck by that spear, that best of archers fainted;
overcome by extreme distress, he fell upon his chariot.
Perceiving that he had fallen into a swoon, Hanumān, the son of the Wind,
his own spirit agitated by anger, addressed that Rākṣasa.
"Where are you going, O fool, while I stand here as your deliverer? I shall strike you with blows from my feet, for you have come as a stealer of my horse! (39)
Having spoken thus, the great Daitya, stationed in the sky, struck the enemy soldiers while standing in their celestial chariots, tearing them apart with the tips of his claws.
Some were struck with his tail, some were struck with the soles of his feet, and some were torn apart by the arms of the son of the Wind-god. (41)
Some perished, some were struck down, and others, huddled together, fainted;
then, afflicted by the fear and pain of being trampled by his feet, they fled.
Many exceedingly dreadful rākṣasas were slain there,
indeed cut and split in two by the son of the Wind-god.
That celestial chariot, moving at will, with its walls and arches shattered, was surrounded by asuras crying out "Alas! Alas! in distress.
The great hero Hanumān was seen here and there, glancing at the ground and glancing at the sky, as he went toward Nandurāsada with longing. 45.
Wherever that celestial chariot was, there the monkey, born of the Wind, assuming any form at will, could be seen striking it. 46.
While the great multitude of celestial beings was thus thrown into confusion,
the lord of the Daityas, Ugradamṣṭra, approached Hanumān.
"Having struck down the enemy, you have performed a great deed; had you remained for even a moment longer, you would have brought about the severance of his life. (48)
Having spoken thus, that evil-minded one struck Hanumān with a very sharp trident that possessed the luster of a blazing fire.
Then the valiant one seized the approaching trident in his mouth and crushed it entirely,
for it was fashioned from all kinds of metal.
Having pulverized that iron trident released by the Daitya,
the mighty Hanumān struck him with many blows of his palms.
Struck here and there by the slaps of the lord of monkeys, he,
being pained, unleashed a magic power that causes terror to all the worlds.
Then a fierce darkness arose, in which neither one's own fire nor another's could be seen,
and in which many people could no longer distinguish between their own kin and strangers.
Rocks resembling mountain peaks fell upon the great warriors;
struck by them, they all became utterly distressed. ||54||
There, the clouds flash with lightning, roar fiercely, rain down pus and blood, and discharge foul water. (55)
Many headless trunks were seen falling from the sky, their heads severed yet still adorned with earrings. (56)
Naked, deformed, with disheveled hair and most hideous faces, the Daityas were seen everywhere, appearing terrible and causing fear. (57)
Then, with their vision clouded and agitated by mutual fear, they were intent on flight, crying out, "Alas! A great calamity! ||58||
Then the highly illustrious Aśatrughna, standing upon his chariot, arrived;
having performed the remembrance of Śrī Rāma, he fixed arrows upon his bow. (59)
Then, having dispelled that illusion with the mohana (stupefying) weapon,
the valiant one showered streams of arrows from the sky upon the god in battle.
Then the quarters of the sky became clear; the sun was surrounded by a halo, the clouds dispersed as they had come, and the lightning attained stillness. (61)
Then this great celestial chariot, filled with Rākṣasas and exceedingly agitated by cries of "Cut! and "Pierce!", appeared before him. 62.
And hundreds of thousands of arrows, adorned with golden nocks, fell repeatedly upon the celestial chariot situated in the sky, which could travel anywhere at will.
Then that celestial chariot was seen shattered; it did not remain aloft, but fell to the earth like a fragment of one's own city broken into pieces. 64.
Then the enraged Daitya fixed arrows upon his bow;
roaring loudly, he scattered them [at Rāma] with those shafts while assailing Rāma’s brother.
Hundreds of his arrows,
with their sharp points, having struck his body in great numbers, attained a beauty like that of streams of blood flowing from him.
Śatrughna, endowed with supreme power, fixed upon his bow the Vāyavya weapon, which causes the Rākṣasas to tremble.
By that weapon, beings moving through the sky were seen falling from their celestial chariots into the air with their hair disheveled, like throngs of *bhūtas* and *vetālas*.
Seeing that weapon discharged by the brother of the Lord of the Raghus,
the son of Danu took up the Pāśupata weapon upon his bow.
Then there arose Vetālas, Pretas, and night-stalkers,
equipped with skull-bowls and cleavers, drinking copious amounts of blood.
The blood of those three heroic Śatrughnas fell joyfully;
even while they were still alive, it was difficult to restrain, for their hands were adorned with scissor-weapons (kartarīs).
Seeing that weapon pervading and eclipsing the splendor of all the heroes,
he released the weapon named Nārāyaṇa in order to repel it.
The Nārāyaṇa weapon warded off all of them in that very instant;
those [missiles] sent forth by the night-stalkers met their destruction. ||73||
Then the enraged night-stalker Vidyunmālī took up a sharp,
terrible trident, fierce and capable of slaying his enemies.
As Vidyunmālin approached in battle with a trident in his hand,
he struck him with arrows as bright as the crescent moon, severing that arm.
With my hand covered by those arrows, I raised my head and said: "You are slain!
Come, O enemy! Who will be your protector? (76)
Having spoken thus, he immediately severed with sharp arrows the head of that powerful hero, along with its earrings.
Seeing his head severed, the powerful Ugradamṣṭra began to strike Śatrughna, who is served by heroes, with his fist.
But Śatrughna, with a razor-sharp arrow, severed the heads of those heroes who were rushing forward from the gateway, all of whom were experts in every weapon and missile. (79)
All the surviving Rākṣasas, deprived of their lord, approached Śatrughna;
having prostrated before him, they then presented the captured horse.
Then, the sounds of lutes and the blasts of conchs were heard together with the captivating shouts of victory from the brave warriors. (81)

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Rākṣasa Vidyunmālī," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||34||
The thirty-fifth chapter.
Śeṣa said: Having recovered that horse which had been seized by the Rākṣasas, King Aśvapati Śatrughna...
Endowed with Puṣkala, he attained extreme joy. ||1||
With their limbs drenched in blood, those warriors likewise praised that great king, a treasury of the goddess Lakṣmī, who was filled with martial zeal. ||2||
When that great Daitya Vidyutmālin, who was difficult to conquer, had been slain,
all the gods, casting off fear, attained great happiness.
The river, having become stainless from its birth, became utterly pure;
fragrant breezes blew, scented with pure and powerful waters.
Those great heroes, equipped with armor, standing upon their chariots with stainless limbs, all endowed with the fortune of victory, spoke to the king. ||5||
The heroes said:
"O high-minded one, by good fortune the Daitya Vidyunmālin has been slain by you—he from whose fear the gods were struck with terror and expelled from heaven. (6)
By good fortune, the magnificent great steed of Raghunātha has been recovered;
by good fortune, you have attained victory everywhere throughout the circle of the earth.
"O Lord, let this mount, swift as thought and delightful, release me;
for its speed has become equal to that of the wind, O high-minded one. (8)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the heroes, which were appropriate for the occasion, he praised them, saying "Excellent! Excellent! and released that best of horses.
Then, well-guarded and mounted, he wandered toward the northern direction,
accompanied by excellent chariots, infantry, and horses, all of whom were experts in every weapon and missile.
In that regard, O Vātsyāyana, listen to this captivating account of what occurred concerning Śatrughna, which burns away heaps of sin. (11)
Then he reached the Revā river, frequented by hosts of sages;
was it the essence of a mass of sapphires appearing under the guise of water? (12)
Having bowed down to all those excellent sages, he, attended by his heroic followers,
mounted the back of that jewel among horses which travels at will and followed behind it.
He went there to that dilapidated hermitage, constructed of palāśa leaves, sprinkled by the surging waves of the Revā river, and serving as a refuge that removes all sins. (14)
Seeing that Sumati, who was omniscient and skilled in policy, Śatrughna—himself an expert in all matters of dharma, worldly purpose, and the performance of duty—laughed. (15)
The king said:
"O minister, tell me whose hermitage is this, so holy in appearance?
Pray, explain this to me as I ask, for you are the most excellent among those skilled in deliberation. (16)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Sumati spoke to that king with a voice bright with a smile, demonstrating his own friendliness. (17)
Sumati said:
"O great king, having seen this best of sages who is devoted to all the scriptures, we shall indeed be cleansed of our sins. (18)
Therefore, having bowed to him, ask him; he will tell you everything, for he is eager to bestow the lotus-feet of Raghunātha.
He was known by the name Āraṇyaka, a servant of the feet of Raghunātha;
he was perfected through most intense austerity and was an expert in the meaning of all the scriptures. (20)
Having heard those words, which were enriched with righteousness and purpose, he then went to see him, accompanied by only a few attendants. ||21||
Hanumān, the heroic Puṣkala, Sumati the best of ministers, Lakṣmīnidhi, Pratāpāgrya, Subāhu, and likewise Sumada. ||22||
Surrounded by these, the noble-minded King Śatrughna reached the hermitage to pay homage to the excellent brahmin Āraṇyaka.
Having approached that best of ascetics, he then paid his respects along with all those heroes, bowing low with humility. (24)
Seeing all those kings, headed by Śatrughna, bowing down, he then offered them water for their hands and feet, as well as fruits, roots, and other honors.
He said to all those kings: "O sinless ones, where have you gathered? How have you come here? Tell me all of that."
Having heard those words of his, O best of sages, Sumati, the son of Vāḍava and an expert in debate, spoke these words: ||27||
Sumati said:
"This horse of the king of the Raghu dynasty is being protected by all;
the hero intends to perform a sacrifice for which every requisite has been gathered. (28)
Having heard those words of theirs, the best of sages spoke, dispelling all that terrible darkness as if with a tooth-stick. ||29||
The forest-dweller said:
What is the use of various other sacrifices, performed with all their requisite materials, which surely yield only a small amount of merit and bestow a perishable state? (30)
The deluded world, having abandoned Hari—
the hero of the Raghus, the Lord of Ramā, who bestows the station of eternal sovereignty— performs the worship of others.
Merely by being remembered, he removes the mountain of sins for men; yet, having abandoned him, the fool suffers through sacrifices, yogic practices, vows, and the like. (32)
Oh, behold the exceedingly strange delusion of people!
Having abandoned the easily accessible devotion to Rāma, they practice that which is difficult to attain. 33.
It is meditated upon by yogis both with desires and those free from desire;
it bestows liberation upon men and destroys all sins merely by being remembered. (34)
Formerly, desiring to know the truth and seeking out one possessed of knowledge through careful inquiry, I visited many sacred fords; yet no one instructed me in the truth. (35)
Then, by great good fortune, he encountered the sage Lomaśa,
who had come from the heavenly realm with the desire to perform a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Then, having prostrated before that Great Sage, whose two feet are served by great yogis and who possesses a long life, I questioned him. (37)
"O Master, I have obtained this human birth, which is marvelous and difficult to find.
Desiring to cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra, what should be done by me? (38)
Having reflected, he said: "Is there any vow, gift, recitation, sacrifice, or deity that can truly deliver one from this cycle of worldly existence? (39)

O Lord of Yoga, you who have reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, please tell me that [truth] by which, having known it from the ocean of your compassion, one may cross over this terrible and boundless cycle of existence. (40)
Having heard these words of mine, the best of sages spoke:
"Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Brahmin, endowed with supreme faith. (41)
There are gifts, sacred fords, vows, observances, and restraints; likewise, there are numerous yogas and sacrifices that bestow heaven. (42)
I shall proclaim the supreme secret that destroys all evil;
listen to it, O highly fortunate one, for it delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra. (43)
It should not be given to an atheist, nor to one who is untrustworthy; it should not be given to a slanderer, nor even to a rogue, nor to an enemy of devotion.
This supreme [teaching], which causes the destruction of all suffering, should be told to one who is a devotee of Rāma, who is peaceful, and who is free from desire and anger. 45.
There is no god higher than Rāma; there is no vow higher than Rāma. There is no yoga higher than Rāma; there is no sacrifice higher than Rāma. 46.
By remembering, reciting, and worshipping that supreme [mantra], a person attains the highest prosperity both in this world and in the next. ||47||
When remembered and meditated upon in the mind, he who bestows the fruit of all desires grants supreme devotion, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (48)
Even a dog-cooker (outcaste) attains the supreme goal by remembering Rāma;
what then need be said of those like you who are devoted to such scriptures? 49.
The secret of all the Vedas and Shastras has been revealed to you; therefore, act in such a way that their desire may be fulfilled. (50)
Rāmacandra is the one God; his worship is the one vow;
his name is the one mantra; his scripture is that alone; and his praise is that very same thing.
Therefore, with your whole being, worship the enchanting Rāmacandra.
May this ocean of saṃsāra become as insignificant as the water in a cow's hoofprint. ||52||
Having heard those words, I asked a question again:
"O Lord, how is he recited, and how is he worshipped by men? (53)
O Great Sage, O Knower of All, tell me in detail that by knowing which I may achieve my purpose within the three worlds, O Best of Munis. (54)
Having heard these words of mine and reflected upon them,
the peerless Lomaśa spoke everything to me, preceded by meditation upon Rāma.
Listen, O sinless one, best of Brahmins; I shall tell you that which you have asked, so that the Lord of Ramā, who burns away the fever of worldly existence, may be pleased. (56)
One should meditate at the foot of the Kalpa tree, which grants the fulfillment of all desires, within the delightful city of Ayodhyā, adorned with wonderful pavilions.
The lion throne, adorned with great emeralds, gold, sapphires, and other jewels, is captivating to the mind and destroys the darkness of ignorance through its splendor. (58)
Seated upon that was the charming King of the Raghus, his body dark like a blade of durva grass, worshipped by the god of gods and by Indra himself. ||59||
On the full moon night, his face was like the full cool orb, surpassing the luster of a parrot;
he bore upon his forehead a mark equal to a sliver of the eighth-day moon.
Abounding in the beauty of dark locks of hair, surpassed by the jewels of his crown, and resplendent with two earrings shaped like sea-monsters (makara) in their exquisite beauty. ||61||

It was resplendent with lips possessing the beautiful luster of coral, and it was beautifully adorned by the king of the twice-born (the teeth), which had the form of the hands of the Lord of Stars (the moon). ||62||
Her face is beautified by a tongue that has the luster of a hibiscus flower and is as red as the madhūka blossom;
within her dwell the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, together with all the Śāstras.
He was adorned with a neck possessing the beauty of a conch shell, and he bore excellent, high shoulders like those of a lion. (64)
His two arms were long and well-proportioned, marked with golden armlets and bracelets; their splendor was adorned by the brilliance of rings and diamonds, reaching down to his knees. (65)
His broad chest was adorned by the abode of Lakṣmī and was most enchanting,
marked with various signs such as the Śrīvatsa.
He has broad shoulders, a large navel, and is adorned with a beautiful waist;
he possesses a special splendor that surpasses even the Kaustubha jewel. (67)
He was graced with the splendor of two pure thighs joined at the knees,
and his feet were adorned with the marks of the thunderbolt, the barley-corn, and the auspicious goad.
Having meditated upon and remembered Him who shines with His two tender feet, which are the objects of meditation for yogis, you shall cross over the ocean of saṃsāra.
By constantly worshipping him with sandalwood and other offerings according to one's desire,
one attains the supreme prosperity, both of this world and the next.
O great king, you have asked about the supreme meditation of Rāma;
that has now been told to you—cross over this ocean of saṃsāra by means of it. 71.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Lomaśa and Āraṇyaka," within the Āraṇyaka episode of the Rāmāśvamedha, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. ||35||
Chapter Thirty-Six. Śeṣa said:
Having heard this most great [account] from Lomaśa, O best of Brahmins, [the king was filled with wonder].
Again he questioned that omniscient sage, the best among yogis.
The forest-dweller said:
O high-minded one, I ask you this as one would a most excellent sage; may you, being endowed with compassion, explain everything to me, your servant. (2)
O highly fortunate one, who is this Rāma who is constantly meditated upon by you?
O bull among the twice-born, tell me of his various deeds.
For what purpose has he descended, and why has he assumed human form?
Tell me all of that quickly, so as to dispel my doubt.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these most excellent words of the sage, Lomaśa narrated the wonderful life-story of Rāma. (5)
Having perceived that the worlds were submerged in hell, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga will enter into the womb of Yajñā for the sake of spreading his fame throughout the world.
Knowing this, the Supreme Lord, an ocean of compassion and enchanting,
assumed four incarnations here tonight, accompanied by Śrī.
When the previous Tretā Yuga had arrived, Rāma, the delighter of the Raghus,
the lotus-eyed one, was born in the solar dynasty as the full moon.
Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, wearing side-locks of hair, and still young, we two followed Viśvāmitra at his word, devoted to him. (9)
For the purpose of protecting the sacrifice, the king gave the two boys—
tamed, heroic archers who were devoted followers of Viśvāmitra.
As they were traveling along that path, the formidable Rākṣasī Tāṭakā encountered them there for the purpose of creating an obstacle for the two of them.
With the permission of the sage, Rāghava caused Tāṭakā, who was like a second Yama, to enter the forest for the practice of the science of archery. 12.
By the touch of whose soles Ahalyā, Gautama’s wife, who had been turned into stone through the power of a curse, was restored to her original form. (13)
While Viśvāmitra’s sacrifice was proceeding well,
that most wicked one struck Mārīca and Subāhu with supreme arrows.
In his fifteenth year, Rāma broke the bow of Īśvara that was kept in the house of Janaka, and he took the six-year-old daughter of Mithilā as his wife.
He married the beautiful Sītā, who was not born from a womb;
having obtained Sītā, Rāghava then felt his purpose in life was fulfilled.
Then he sported with her for twelve years;
in the twenty-seventh year, he appointed him as the crown prince.
Then Kaikeyī urged the king for two boons;
by one of them, Rāma was to depart along with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Let Jaṭādhara go forth as a wandering ascetic here for fourteen years;
meanwhile, O Bharata, may you remain the sovereign heir-apparent for the second [period]. (19)
The king sent Rāma, accompanied by Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa, into exile;
for three nights he subsisted on water, and on the fourth day he ate fruit.
In the fifth year, Rāma established his residence at Citrakūṭa;
then, O great sage, in the thirteenth year, he stayed at Pañcavaṭī.
While he was wandering in the forest together with Jānaki, Rāma disfigured the night-stalker Śūrpaṇakhā.
Then, due to the ripening of his evil karma, a rākṣasa arrived to seize her;
this occurred on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, during the muhūrta known as Vṛnda.
Daśagrīva abducted Sītā in the absence of the two Rāghavas;
while being carried away by him, she cried out like a female cakravāka bird.
"Rāma, Rāma! Protect me, protect me, who have been seized by a demon!
Just as a hawk overcome by hunger might carry off a quail from its nest. (25)
Just as Rāvaṇa, having fallen under the power of lust, was carrying away the daughter of Janaka,
so too did Jaṭāyu, the king of birds, then act toward that daughter of Janaka.
He fought with the lord of the Rākṣasas and, struck by Rāvaṇa, fell down;
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, he was dwelling in the abode of Rāvaṇa.
On the tenth day of the month, Sampāti informed the monkeys of her;
on the eleventh day, he leaped from Mount Mahendra for a distance of one hundred yojanas.
Hanumān searched throughout that sharp-edged Laṅkā;
at the end of that night, there was indeed no sight of Sītā for Hanumān.
On the twelfth day, Hanumān stationed himself on the Śiṃśapā tree;
during that night, a conversation took place for the sake of Jānakī’s confidence.
The battle continued with Akṣa and the others until the thirteenth day;
on the fourteenth day, the monkey was bound by Śakrajit using the Brahmāstra.
The burning of Laṅkā by means of the fire-tail was accomplished;
on the full moon day, the monkey returned once more to Mount Mahendra.
On the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, after five days had passed on the road, he returned; it is said that on the sixth day, Madhuvana was destroyed.
On the seventh [tithi], the offering of recognition and the presentation of all [the requisites] should be performed;
on the eighth, under Uttaraphalgunī and during the muhūrta named Vijaya.
When the thousand years had reached their midpoint, Rāghava made his vow and set forth;
having made that promise, Rāma departed toward the southern direction.
"Even after crossing the ocean, I shall slay the lord of the rākṣasas;
Sugrīva also became my friend as I set out for the southern quarter. (36)
Within seven days, from the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa until the third, the camp was established on the bank of the Sindhu river on a Wednesday.
Vibhīṣaṇa, accompanied by his army, arrived as an attendant for that descendant of Raghu on the fourth day, having joined with Rāma.
Intent upon crossing the ocean, Rāma remained engaged in mantras on the fifth day and undertook a fast unto death for four days.
Then there is the attainment of the excellent ocean and the simultaneous manifestation of the path;
thereafter, the beginning occurs on the tenth day and the completion on the thirteenth.
On the fourteenth day, Rāma encamped his army on Mount Suvela;
by the end of the second day following the full moon, the crossing of the army was completed in three days.
Having crossed the ocean, Rāma, accompanied by the army of the lord of the monkeys and together with Lakṣmaṇa, besieged Laṅkā for the sake of Sītā.
From the third day until the tenth, that encampment lasted for eight days;
on the eleventh day, Śuka and Sāraṇa arrived there.
On the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, there was a counting of the army,
as well as a sudden description by Śārdūla of the arrival of the monkey leaders.
On the thirteenth day after the new moon, Rāvaṇa spent three days in Laṅkā enumerating his army and rousing them for the battle.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, he set out on the mission of Aṅgada;
thereafter, he witnessed the illusory head and other [limbs] of Sītā’s husband.
From the second day of the month of Māgha until the eighth, for seven days, there was a tumultuous battle between the Rākṣasas and the monkeys. ||47||
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, during the night, it is said that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa were bound with serpent-nooses by Indrajit in battle.
When the leaders of the monkeys were agitated and utterly devoid of energy,
Pavana recited prayers on the tenth day for the sake of releasing them from the serpent-noose.
Then the true nature of Karṇa and the arrival of Garuḍa for Rāma;
on the eleventh and twelfth days, the slaying of Dhūmrākṣa was accomplished. ||50||
On the thirteenth day, he was indeed slain by him in the battle at Kaṃpana;
[this occurred] from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the first day of the dark fortnight.
Within three days, his slaughter was carried out by Nīla on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, starting from the second day.
In that tumultuous battle, Rāvaṇa was driven from the gateway by Rāma;
he remained there until he was awakened by Rāvaṇa on the eighth day from the fifth.
Then Kumbhakarṇa took his food for four days, from the ninth day until the fourteenth day. ||54||
Slain in battle by Rāma, that devourer of many monkeys was withdrawn from the field out of grief on the day of the new moon.
From the first day of the month of Phālguna until the fourth, those five rākṣasas, beginning with Bisataṃtu, were slain within four days. (56)
From the fifth [day] until the seventh, there was likewise the slaying of Atikāya;
from the eighth until the twelfth, five days were passed in combat.
Nikumbha, Kuṃbha, Ūrdhvabāhu, Tumburu, Makarākṣa, and Ajita— the conqueror of Indra— were slain within three days on the second day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna.
From the third day until the seventh, for those five days,
there was indeed a suspension of all activity because they were preoccupied with bringing the medicinal herbs.
Then, within five days from the thirteenth day, Indrajit—
renowned for his strength and prowess— was slain by Lakṣmaṇa in battle.
On the fourteenth day, the Ten-necked one received his initiation through the withdrawal of his powers;
on the new moon day, the Supporter of the Ten headed forth for battle.
During the five days from the first to the fifth of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
while Rāvaṇa was engaged in battle, there occurred a great slaughter of the rākṣasas.
From the sixth until the eighth day of the month of Caitra, there was the slaying of Mahāpārśva and others;
