on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, however, occurred the piercing of Saumitri’s spear.
Overcome with anger, Rāma drove away Daśakaṃdhara,
by whom Droṇādri was brought for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa and offered to him.
On the tenth day, there was a withdrawal at night due to the protection of the Rākṣasas;
on the eleventh day, however, Mātali became the charioteer for Rāma’s chariot.
Then, urged by Vāsava,
the King, though filled with anger, offered [the animal] with devotion from the twelfth day until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
In eighteen days, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa in a duel of chariots;
in that tumultuous battle, Rāma achieved victory.
From the second day of the bright fortnight of Māgha until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra—
thus, within eighty-seven days, there is an intermediate period of fifteen days.
The withdrawal from battle and the combat lasted for seventy-two days; the funeral rites for Rāvaṇa and the others took place on the new moon day.
On the lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha,
Rāma consecrated Vibhīṣaṇa in the sovereignty of Laṅkā on the second day.
On the third day, the purification of Sītā was accomplished; having slain the Lord of Laṅkā before long, he, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, obtained a boon from the gods.
Having taken the virtuous Jānakī, who was suffering at the hands of the Rākṣasa, he returned with her,
carrying her with the greatest joy.
On the fourth day of Vaiśākha, Rāma, mounted upon the Puṣpaka chariot,
returned once more through the air toward the city of Ayodhyā.
When his fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth day of the month of Mādhava, Rāma,
accompanied by his followers, sat down in the hermitage of Bharadvāja.
On the sixth day, he met with Bharata at Nandigrāma;
on the seventh day, that scion of Raghu was consecrated in Ayodhyā.
For ten months and one additional month— totaling fourteen days— the daughter of Mithilā dwelt in Rāvaṇa’s residence, deprived of Rāma.
Rāma ruled for forty-two years;
at that time, thirty-three years of Sītā’s life had passed. (77)
Having slain Rāvaṇa in battle, the Lord Rāma joyfully entered the city of Ayodhyā when he was fourteen years of age.
There, Rāma, together with his brothers, then ruled the kingdom;
while he was governing the realm, there was a family priest, the best among those who speak. (79)
Agastya, born from a jar, approached that lord of the stars, the moon;
at his word, this Lord of the Raghus will perform the horse sacrifice.
O you of excellent vows, he will come to your hermitage with his horses;
his joyful warriors shall also come to your hermitage.
Before them, you shall tell captivating stories of Rāma;
with them, O bull among the twice-born, you shall go to Ayodhyā. (82)
Upon seeing Rāma in Ayodhyā, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, you shall at that very moment become one who has crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra. 83.
Having spoken thus to me, the best of sages, Lomaśa, who possesses all wisdom, said, "What do you wish to ask? Then I spoke what was beneficial.
Through your grace, the entire wonderful life-story of Rāma has been known;
by your favor, may I attain the lotus-feet of Rāma. (85)
After I had paid my obeisance, the lord of sages departed;
by his grace, I obtained the worship of Rāma’s feet.
Thus, I remember the feet of him who is charming to the mind day after day,
and I sing his deeds again and again with great haste.
I rejoice as I purify other people with this song that captivates the heart,
remembering again and again the words of that sage while gazing upon him.
I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, and I am fortunate upon this earth, for I shall behold the lotus feet of Rāmacandra. (89)
Therefore, he who delights in the self, who is enchanting to behold, and who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, should be worshipped by all; indeed, he is worthy of veneration. (90)
Therefore, for what purpose have you arrived here, and who is this lord of monkeys?
This righteous-souled one is performing the horse sacrifice, a great ritual. (91)
Relating all of that while protecting you on the path,
he repeatedly remembered again and again the feet of the Lord of the Raghus.
Having heard these words of the sage, they were filled with wonder;
remembering Raghunātha, they spoke to the sage Āraṇyaka. (93)

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Life of Rāma," in the dialogue between Lomaśa and Āraṇyaka within the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, during the conversation between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The thirty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
Thus questioned by the best of sages regarding the wonderful life-story of Rāma, he spoke.
Considering themselves blessed and fortunate, they spoke with reverence of their own selves. ||1||
The people said:
"We have all been purified now by the sight of you,
since you purify us people with the stories of Rāma."
Listen to these truthful words; you are the most excellent of brahmin-sages.
Whatever you have asked us, we shall relate all of that to you. (3)
At the word of Agastya, the illustrious Rāma, for the sake of removing the sin of killing a brahmin, performed a very great sacrifice provided with all necessary materials. (4)
O high-minded one, know that all those brahmins, while protecting him, have come to your hermitage together with the horse.
Having heard these words, which were like a captivating elixir,
the Brahmin, a devotee of Rāma, attained extreme joy.
Today this tree has borne fruit, endowed with the glory of my heart's desire; today my mother is blessed, she who gave birth to me.
Today I have obtained a kingdom free from thorns;
today my treasuries are well-filled; today the gods are thoroughly propitiated.
The fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice that you have obtained today by offering oblations of my poison shall be realized when you behold the pair of lotus-feet of Rāmacandra.
That lord and master who constantly meditates upon his own Ayodhyā will surely become visible to my eyes as one who captivates the mind.
Hanumān will embrace me and inquire after my welfare;
seeing my great devotion, that most excellent being will attain satisfaction. (11)
Having heard these words, Hanumān, the best of monkeys,
grasped the pair of feet of the sage Āraṇyaka.
"O Lord, O brahmin-sage, know me, who stand before you, to be Hanumān, the servant of Rāma’s disciple, who am like a mere speck of dust, O lord of sages. (13)
When he had spoken thus, the son of Vāyu, filled with supreme joy, embraced Hanumān, who was resplendent with devotion to Rāma. (14)
Both were pierced by love and both were drenched in nectar; they remained there as if covered over, like figures in a painting. (15)
Seated there, their minds overflowing with love for the lotus feet of the Lord of the Raghus, they engaged in most enchanting conversation. (16)
Hanumān spoke these various beautiful words to that best of sages,
the forest-dweller, who was absorbed in meditation upon the feet of Rāma.
"O Lord, this is the great jewel of Daśaratha’s lineage;
this is the great hero Śatrughna, the brother of Rāma, who bows before you. (18)
Lavaṇa, who caused fear to all the worlds, was slain by Lavana-oda; and all the sages, whose wealth is their excellent asceticism, were made happy. ||19||
This one named Puṣkala, served by the most eminent warriors, bows down to you, by whom the great heroes have now been defeated on the field of battle. (20)
Know this minister of Rāma to be possessed of many virtues and great strength;
he is dearer to the Lord of the Raghus than life itself, omniscient, and skilled in dharma.
This Subāhu, exceedingly fierce and a forest fire to the lineage of Vaira, has now come to you, O one of great fame, as a bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma. 22.
Even this Sumada, by serving the supreme feet of Pārvatī, has now attained the great means of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. (23)
This Satyavān, who upon hearing from his servant that the horse had been recovered, offered you the kingdom and prostrated himself upon the ground. (24)
Having heard these words,
the forest-dwelling sage embraced him with respect and welcomed him with fruits and other offerings.
Delighted, they took up residence there in the hermitage of the best of sages; having performed their daily rites at dawn, those illustrious ones went to the Revā river.
Then Śatrughna, having placed the sage together with his attendants upon the Nārāyaṇa chariot, brought him to Ayodhyā, the city where Rāma had made his abode. (27)
Seeing from afar the city inhabited by the kings of the Solar dynasty,
he quickly became a pedestrian out of a longing to behold the Lord of the Raghus.
Having reached the beautiful city of Ayodhyā, which was adorned by its people,
his longing for the sight of Rāma had grown intense through thousands of desires.
There, on the bank of the Sarayū, adorned with pavilions, he beheld Rāma, dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, whose eyes possessed the luster of a blue lotus.
He held the beautiful deer-horn, endowed with splendor;
he was surrounded by hosts of sages headed by Vyāsa, and well-served by heroes.
He was surrounded by Bharata, the son of Sumitrā,
as he bestowed upon the destitute and the needy the gifts they had requested.
Beholding him, he who was called Āraṇyaka thought, "I have achieved my purpose, since these two eyes of mine,
resembling lotus petals, have beheld him."
Today, his mastery of all the scriptures has become truly meaningful, since by knowing Śrī Rāma he has reached this city of Ayodhyā. (34)
Thus, with many such words, he was filled with joy;
his body shone with the great delight of beholding the feet of Rāma.
He proceeded toward the vicinity of Rameśvara, a place extremely remote and inaccessible even to other masters of yoga who are devoted to inquiry. ||35||
"I am blessed today, for I shall bring Rāma’s two feet within the range of my vision," he said, gazing intently at Rāma alone. (36)
Rāma, too, seeing that best of Vāḍavas blazing with his own splendor and bearing the very form of asceticism, then rose to meet him. (37)
The great Rāmacandra bowed for a long time at his feet, saying:
"O God who is devoted to Brahmanas, you have today purified me. (38)
Speaking these words, the Lord fell at his feet—he whose feet are illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of the gods and asuras who bow before him. (39)
The great ascetic Vāḍavendra took that best of kings, who was prostrate before him, by the middle of his arms and embraced his beloved lord. 40.
The Lord, the son of Kausalyā, having seated him upon a high throne made of jewels,
washed his pair of feet with water.
Hari himself placed the water for washing the feet upon his head,
saying, "Today my entire host, along with my family, has been purified."
Then, having anointed himself with sandalwood paste, he gave away a milch cow;
and, served by the gods and Indra, the lord of the gods spoke these charming words.
"O Lord, let the horse-sacrifice known as the Vājimedha be performed by me;
this very sacrifice shall become complete today through your arrival at my feet. (44)
"Today this horse-sacrifice, purified by your foot, shall effect the destruction of the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin. (45)
To him who was speaking these words, the sage Āraṇyaka, laughing, spoke this with the voice of Mādhavī, he who is served by the lords of kings of kings.
O Lord of the Earth, let the Brahmins, who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, praise you with appropriate words, for they are the very embodiments of the Brahman, O Great King. (47)
O protector of the earth, when you perform auspicious deeds such as the worship of Brahmins, then all kings, including the Brahmins, will honor you.
"That you have said, 'I shall perform a pure sacrifice for the removal of the great sin of killing a king'—those words are indeed laughable. (49)
By remembering your name, even a fool devoid of all sacred scriptures, having crossed the ocean of all sins, shall attain the supreme state. ||50||
It is clear that this—the remembrance of the name of Rāma, which delivers one from sin—is the essential meaning of all the Vedas and Itihāsas. (51)
Sins equal to the killing of a Brahmin roar only so long as the name "Rāmacandra" is not clearly uttered by you. 52.
O Great King, hearing the thundering roar of your name, the jars of great sins flee here and there, desiring a place to hide. (53)
Therefore, O Rāma, how could there be for you even the sight of the great merit of killing? Upon hearing your auspicious story, one shall immediately become purified. (54)
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, I heard these words from the mouths of the sages dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā, who were knowers of the past.
Men who are cowardly and great sinners remain afraid of sin only so long as the Name, which is enchanting to the mind, does not speak within their speech. 56.
Therefore, I am blessed now; for me, the destruction of this cycle of worldly existence has become easily attainable through the sight of you, O Rāmacandra. (57)
When the sage had spoken thus, all the ascetics there honored him, exclaiming, "Excellent! Excellent! (sādhu-sādhu).
Śeṣa said:
A great marvel occurred there; listen as I recount it to you, O best of sages, descendant of Vatsya, who are solely devoted to devotion for Rāma. (59)
Upon seeing the great king Rāma, who was the very object of his meditation, he experienced extreme joy and spoke to the lords of sages: 60.
O lords of sages, listen to my most enchanting words:
who else in this world will ever be as fortunate as I?
"There has never been, nor will there ever be, anyone like me who is so angry,
that Rāmabhadra, having bowed to me, should inquire after my welfare."
He whose lotus-feet’ dust is ever sought by the Vedas has today drunk the pure water from my feet and attained purification.
As he was speaking thus, a burst of Brahma-energy occurred;
that radiant splendor emerged from his being and entered the Lord of the Raghus.
While all the worlds were looking on at the pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū, she attained the power of *sāyujya*, which is difficult even for yogis to obtain. (65)
Then there arose the sound of celestial instruments and the resonance of lutes;
a rain of flowers fell before them as they beheld this wondrous and marvelous sight.
Even the sages, having beheld this, praised the Lord of Sages:
"This best of sages has achieved his life's purpose, since he has beheld the form of Rāma. (67)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Departure of the Forest Sage to the World of Viṣṇu," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||37||
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard this narrative, the noble-minded Vātsyāyana—
He attained supreme joy and spoke to the Lord of Serpents.
Vātsyāyana said:
O Lord of Serpents, I am not satiated as I listen to the story of Raghunātha, whose fame dispels the suffering of his devotees. 2.
The forest-dwelling sage named Dhanya, a supreme upholder of the Vedas, beheld Raghunātha and cast off his transient body. ||3||
Then [the king asked]: "O Lord of Serpents, where has the horse of the king gone? By whom was it led away?
And how did the fame of the Lord of Ramā arise there?"
Tell me all this truthfully,
since you are omniscient and are the very embodiment of Him who bears the form of the mountain-sustainer (Śiva).
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, with a heart full of joy,
he spoke of the life of Rāma, giving rise to accounts of his various virtues.
Śeṣa said:
O brahmin-sage, you ask well as you repeatedly inquire about the virtues of the Lord of the Raghus;
though you have heard them before, you treat them as if unheard, maintaining a longing for them.
Then the horse emerged, surrounded by many soldiers,
to graze on the delightful bank of the Revā, which is frequented by hosts of sages.
Then all the soldiers, experts in warfare, advanced here and there toward wherever the horse went, keeping watch and following its path. ||9||
Having reached the Atharvā river, which possesses unfathomable waters,
the bull of the gods, honored by all, stood upon its bank bearing a golden leaf from Mount Bhāla.
Then the noble Jālaśaurāmacandra, the best of horses, [crossed] the water;
at that time, all the great heroes there were struck with wonder. ||11||
They said to one another: "How can there be a meeting with the horse?
Who among us is able to go here and bring that great jewel from the water? (12)
While they were thus conversing with one another, filled with agitation,
the Lord of the Rākṣasas arrived together with hundreds of heroes.
Seeing them all thus dejected, he who was named Śatrughna,
the crest-jewel of heroes, questioned them with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Why have you all remained here today in the water in such a multitude?
Where is the horse of the Lord of Raghu, adorned with its golden leaf? (15)
"Is he submerged in water, or has he been devoured by some arrogant creature?
Tell me that quickly; how have you all become so bewildered? (16)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the king, the best of the Raghus, those heroes related everything to that crest-jewel of warriors. (17)
The people said:
"O Lord, we did not know that for a moment the water rose; consequently, your horse, so enchanting to the mind, has not returned from where it plunged. (18)
"Go there yourself and bring this horse back with speed;
O high-minded one, we must go there along with you. (19)
Having heard these words of the soldiers, the scion of Raghu felt distress upon seeing the people intent on crossing the Jalasanta river.
He said to the chief minister: "What should be done after this?
Tell me how the recovery of the horse will come about. (21)
"Who are the heroes there that can be employed to search for the horse in the water? Or who will bring the horse back? Tell me by what means this shall be done. (22)
Having heard these words of the king, Sumati, the best of ministers,
spoke words appropriate for the occasion, as if gladdening Śatrughna.
O Lord, you whose deeds are marvelous, the power of your majesty is evident here:
the ability to go to the netherworld while remaining clearly within the midst of water. 24.
Furthermore, even for the great-souled Hanumān—who was Puṣkala and devoted to the service of Rāma’s feet—there was still power remaining. (25)
Therefore, you three must go and certainly bring a horse, so that there may be a mount for the wise Lord of the Raghus. 26.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes,
himself entered the midst of the waters accompanied by Hanumān and Puṣkala.
As soon as he entered the water, an immeasurable city appeared, enriched with the beauty of many gardens. (28)
There, on a pillar fashioned from rubies,
they saw Rāma’s horse tied, adorned with beautiful golden leaf-patterns.
There, excellent women possessing enchanting forms were waiting upon that one beautiful woman as she sat comfortably on a couch. (30)
Seeing them, all those women said to their mistress:
"These men are small in stature and age, yet they possess well-nourished bodies. (31)
The fruit of this excellent food for you will be great:
the blood of these men, whose lives have come to an end, shall be sweet. (32)
Having heard these words of her maidservants, the excellent woman,
the sinless one, laughed slightly while making her face dance with her eyebrows.
Then those three arrived, adorned with the splendor of their armor,
wearing helmets, and endowed with heroism and valor.
Seeing those women there, endowed with the glory of beauty, the brahmin spoke in amazement: "O what is this great sight that is seen? (35)
Then all those high-souled hosts of gods, their pairs of feet illuminated by the radiance of the jewels in their crowns, paid homage to the best of deities.
That beautiful woman questioned all those excellent men, saying: "Who are you that have arrived here, and how is it that you are men bearing weapons? (37)
My place is inaccessible to all the gods; it is a great delusion.
Indeed, for one who has reached this state, there is no turning back at all. 38.
"To whom does this horse belong, and why is it being fanned with a chowrie? It is adorned with a golden plate; tell me, who is its master? (39)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of his, which were filled with delusive conduct, Hanumān, free from fear, replied to her as if laughing. (40)
We are the subjects of King Vaikuntha, the crest-jewel of the three worlds;
this triple world bows down to him, the crown jewel of all the gods. ||41||
"Know me to be the one who will initiate the horse sacrifice for the noble Rāma;
O beautiful woman, release my horse—how has it been bound? (42)
We are skilled in all missiles and experts in all weapons and arms;
we shall forcibly lead away the horse after slaying its obstructors. (43)
Having heard these words of the monkey, the excellent woman, staying within the cave, replied as if laughing, she being skilled in speech. (44)
"I have brought this vehicle; no one is capable of releasing it, even with ten thousand years of sharp, flaming millions of arrows. (45)
"However, as one who performs the service of Rāma’s lotus feet, I shall not accept the vehicle of that wise king of kings. (46)
A great new challenge has arisen for my steed, the excellent horse of my leadership;
may Rāmacandra, the refuge of all and affectionate toward his devotees, forgive this. 47.
O best of gods, you who are distressed, for the sake of that man named Ikṣvāku, beg a boon from that protector, even one unattainable by the gods themselves. 48.
Just as the Supreme Person may forgive my exceedingly fierce arrogance, so you all, casting aside all shame, should choose this most excellent boon. 49.
Having heard her words, Hanumān spoke to her:
"By the grace of the Lord of the Raghus, everything is powerful for us. (50)
Nevertheless, I beg for one final, supreme boon:
fulfill the desire cherished in my heart.
In birth after birth, the Lord of Raghus is our Master; we are His servants—what else could we do? (51)
Having heard these words of the monkey, the daughter of the mountain then spoke sweet words, honored for their excellence, while smiling. (52)
"O servants, whatever you have requested— which is indeed difficult even for all the gods to obtain—
that shall come to pass without doubt under the rule of the Lord of the Raghus."
"Or rather, though I have committed an offense, I shall grant one boon; may these words of mine come true for the sake of pleasing the Lord of the Raghus. (54)
The king Agrevīramaṇi, accompanied by great heroes and protected by Śiva, will seize your mount. (55)
O you of great strength, take up that great weapon for the sake of conquering him;
you must fight that great one against Śatrughna in a duel of chariots.
When you discharge this weapon in battle, by means of it, Rāma’s true nature will be known once again. (57)
Having recognized him and bowed at his feet, he will prostrate himself;
therefore, take up that weapon of mine which tears asunder enemies.
Having heard that, the brother of Raghunātha, facing northward, took up the wonderful, purifying weapon bestowed by Goyoginī. 59.
Having obtained that weapon, he of great splendor became the destroyer of his enemies;
he was difficult to assail, difficult to propitiate, and indeed a goad for the elephants that were his foes.
Having bowed to her, Śatrughna, the best of the descendants of Raghu, took that excellent horse from the water and went to the bank of the Revā, which was suitable for his pleasure.
Seeing her, all the soldiers were delighted and filled with joy; praising her, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", they asked about the departure of the horse.
Hanumān related the great arrival of the horse and the attainment of boons from those [goddesses]; having heard this, they too were filled with joy.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Horse from the Midst of the Water upon Seeing the Yoginīs by Śatrughna," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Thirty-nine.
Śeṣa said: While the drums were resounding and the sounds of lutes were heard everywhere, [the Lord appeared].
Then, with his vehicle released, he went to the city of the gods, constructed by the gods. ||1||
There, with the arrangements of crystal walls in the houses of the people,
they mock the pure Vindhya mountain frequented by serpents.
There, even from a distance, royal palaces are seen, adorned with various jewels and featuring gate-towers of rubies. (3)
There, the lotus-women, enchanting in every house of the people, captivate the hearts of men as they are gazed upon with eyes like lotus-petals. (4)
In every house and upon every beautiful ground,
the ruby is seen set there as if in rivalry with the lips of those wise men.
In every house, pleasure-mountains fashioned from sapphire gems bring auspiciousness to the crested peacocks, as if they were clouds.
Alas! Wherever that [cloud] is constantly obstructed by the crystal palaces in the houses of men, it causes fear among the clouds and they do not even remember Lake Mānasa.
In the abode of Śiva, darkness is perpetually dispelled by moonlight;
indeed, for men there, no distinction between the bright and dark fortnights exists.
There, King Vīramaṇi, the foremost among the righteous and great, rules a vast kingdom endowed with every enjoyment. ||9||
His son, a great hero named Rukmāṅgada,
powerful and possessed of a beautiful body, went to the forest to sport with women.
The jingling of their anklets and the sound of their bracelets—what need is there for further description of that which captivates even the God of Love? O Lord! ||11||
He went to a vast forest filled with trees in full bloom, a place eternally established by Śiva, resplendent with all six seasons. ||12||
Where campaka trees abound, beautified by their blossoming buds, they cause the pain of love in the hearts of longing men when beheld. (13)
Mango trees were bent low by their fruit, joined at the tips of their branches;
likewise there were *nāga*, *punnāga*, *śāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees. ||14||
Where the cries of cuckoos are constantly within the range of hearing, and where the beautiful jasmine flowers have their sleep dispelled by the humming of bees.
There were groves of pomegranate trees interspersed with karṇikāra trees, resplendent with rows of wild ketaka, kānaki, and various other trees. ||16||
In that forest, his mental state filled with joy, singing sweetly and loudly with a desire to compose [his song],
he whose body was a treasury of beauty entered, free from fear, surrounded by women with swelling breasts.
Some delighted that beautiful man with their arts of dance;
some with the arts of song, and others with words appropriate to their cleverness. (18)
Others, intoxicated with passion, gratified him with gestures of their eyebrows;
other women made him joyful by their skill in embracing and speaking. (19)
Having gathered flowers with them, those women adorned him;
and he, assuming the form of Kāma, spoke with tender words, saying, "May you rejoice."
Thus, at the time of the departure of the wise king of kings, that most magnificent horse proceeded toward that forest region. (21)
His forehead was adorned with a single ornament fashioned from gold leaf, and his hair,
dyed with saffron and red sandalwood paste, was as white as the Ganges.
Seeing women whose bodies were the very source of supreme curiosity, with a gait equal to the wind and surpassing it in speed; (22)
They spoke to their husband, whose complexion was like the interior of a lotus,
and who surpassed the luster of coral with the brilliance of his copper-red lips.
Their faces were beautifully adorned with smiles as charming as the rays of the moon, possessing a power that deludes the eyes and mind like the arrows of Kāma. ||23||
The women said:
"Whose is this beautiful great necklace, adorned with a single golden leaf?
To whom does it belong, so rich in splendor? Take it yourself, O lady. (24)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words, he whose eyes were charming with playfulness effortlessly seized the horse with one lotus-like hand.
Having read the golden leaf inscribed with clear letters, he laughed in the midst of the women and spoke these words again: ||26||
Rukmāṅgada said:
"On this earth, there is no one equal to my father in valor or in prosperity; how is it that King Rāma displays such arrogance toward him? (27)
Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, always provides protection for him;
he whom gods, dānavas, and yakṣas honor with their jeweled crowns. (28)
"Let the mighty Janaka indeed perform the horse-sacrifice;
let his warriors go to the stable and bind my horse there. (29)
Having heard these words, those enchanting women,
their faces filled with great joy, addressed their beloved with these [verses].
Having taken the horse, the great son of King Vīramaṇi entered the city with his wife amidst great festivities.
Then, as the drums were struck loudly and evenly on all sides,
he, being praised by the gods, went to the great palace of his father.
He told him that the horse of the Lord of the Raghus,
which had been released for the Horse Sacrifice, was pure, swift, and wonderful.
It was protected by Śatrusūdana, who was joined by a great force;
having heard those words of his, the great King Vīramaṇi—
The one of great intelligence did not praise that deed excessively, as it was like the conduct of a thief returning after having carried something away. (35)
He spoke to his son-in-law Śiva, the performer of wondrous deeds,
who bears half of the Lord of Ganas and wears the crescent moon as his ornament.
Thereupon, the great King Vīramaṇi deliberated with him, censuring the great deed performed by his son as something blameworthy in the eyes of the great. (37)
Śiva said:
"O King, a most wonderful deed has been performed by your son;
he has slain the great steed of the wise Rāmacandra. (38)
Today a great battle appears, which will bewilder both gods and asuras,
fought by the great king Śatrughna, the sole protector of ten million heroes.
O son, that Rāma, whose very name is uttered by my tongue and whom I hold dear, has carried away your sacrificial horse.
A most supreme and great gain will surely come to us in battle, that we shall behold the lotus-feet of Rāma, served by our own [Lord]. (41)
"Here is a great task requiring no effort; they will forcibly lead away this horse, even though it is protected by me. (42)
Therefore, O Great King, having bowed down along with your kingdom, and having given food to this horse, look upon its pair of hooves. (43)
Having heard these words of Śiva, that best of kings spoke to him whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by the lords of the gods and others.
Vīramanī said:
"This is the duty of Kṣatriyas, namely the protection of their majesty;
therefore, he has prepared to invade that [territory] by means of the sacrifice known as the horse-sacrifice."
Therefore, every person who possesses pride must protect his own majesty by performing whatever actions are possible, even at the cost of his body's destruction. (46)
"O Lord of the Kurus, everything has been accomplished by this son, since he has captured the horse; therefore, act with propriety toward King Rāma, whom you have provoked. (47)
This deed would not be worthy for Kṣatriyas to perform:
that one, overwhelmed by fear, should suddenly prostrate at the feet of an enemy. (48)
The enemies laugh at him, saying, "This lowest of kings is a coward;
he is base, vulgar, lowly, humble, and overwhelmed by fear. (49)
Therefore, when the occasion for battle has arrived, you must first deliberate upon what ought to be done and then protect your devotees as is appropriate. (50)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, the Moon-crested Lord spoke these words, laughing with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, bewildering the mind. (51)
Even though thirty-three crores of gods have assembled here, who among them can seize the horse from me, its protector? (52)
If Rāma comes here and reveals his own self to me, then I shall bow down to his most tender feet. (53)
The Master alone must be fought; this is declared by Mahānanda.
Other heroes are like blades of grass; they are truly incapable of accomplishing anything. (54)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, fight while I stand ready as your protector; for who could seize your horse by force, even if the three worlds were united against you? (55)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these supreme words of the moon-crested Lord, the king, who was eager for the act of battle, rejoiced exceedingly in his heart. (56)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Seizing of the Horse by Vīramaṇiputra," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padmapurāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
The fortieth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
O great king, the army attendants were endowed with great strength.
They gathered there, beholding that horse of King Rāma. ||1||
Where is that horse, by whom was it led, and how is he not seen? Where has that extremely dull-witted man gone, having stolen the bride from the city? (2)
While he was observing that path until the tumultuous roar of the army was heard,
the great king arrived, surrounded by a vast host.
He questioned all his servants: "Where is my horse now?
Why is the steed, so beautifully adorned with golden plates, not to be seen? (4)
Having heard those words, the attendants following him said to their lord: "O Master, whose mind is as swift as the wind, by whom has your horse been taken in the forest?"
Therefore, O Lord, since he has been carried off and is not seen by us who are experts in the ways of horses,
an effort must be made here toward his recovery.
Having heard their words, King Śatrughna, the destroyer of enemies who had assumed a form that bewilders others, questioned Sumati.
Śatrughna said:
"Who is the king who dwells here, and how did you come to meet him? What is the strength of this lord of the earth, by whom this horse has been taken today? (8)
Sumati said:
"O King, this is indeed the city of the gods, fashioned by the God himself;
like Kailāsa, it is impregnable even to hosts of enemies joined together."
In this Vīramaṇī, the king is a great hero, powerful and majestic;
protected by Śiva, he rules the kingdom with righteousness. ||10||
He who brings about the dissolution of the world remained there, brought under control by devotion;
the moon-crested Lord, always showing partiality toward his devotee.
Therefore, if a great battle should occur here once [the enemy] has been seized, let those who are vigilant indeed provide protection for the camp. 12.
Having heard this, that illustrious crest-jewel of all kings, accompanied by Śatrughna, drew up his army in battle array and took his stand. (13)
Then, while he was seated comfortably and consulting with his excellent minister, the divine sage arrived, filled with curiosity for the battle.
Seeing that sage, a treasure-house of asceticism, arrive, Śatrughna rose from his seat, offered him a place to sit, and then presented him with the madhuparka.
And, being pleased by the welcome, he who was skilled in the art of speech spoke with pleasing words to Nārada, the best of sages.
Śatrughna said:
"O highly intelligent brahmin, tell me where my horse is;
its track cannot be found by my skilled servants. (17)
"Tell us by which proud kṣatriya he was carried off;
O one whose wealth is asceticism, how will the recovery of the horses come about here? (18)
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, Nārada spoke while repeatedly playing his lute and singing the stories of Rāma.
Nārada said:
O King, this is Devapura;
there, the great monarch Vīramaṇi’s preeminent horse was seized by his son while he was dwelling in the forest.
In that place, a great and most terrible battle will take place for you today;
heroes endowed with strength and valor will fall therein.
Therefore, O one of great strength, you must remain here with great effort;
arrange a formation that is difficult for the enemy forces to penetrate. (22)
O King, victory shall be yours over this best of men through great hardship;
for who indeed in all the world could defeat Rāma? (23)
Having spoken thus, the Brahmin vanished and remained stationed in the sky,
desiring to witness a most terrible battle like that between the gods and the dānavas.
Śeṣa said: Then King Vīramaṇi, the crest-jewel of all heroes,
caused a great-sounding drum to be beaten within his own city.
He summoned the commander of the army, the great and exalted hero of his enemies,
and spoke to him quickly with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Vīramaṇi said:
"O General, give me the command of the drum in this beautiful city.
Having heard that, those well-prepared men set out toward Śatrughna.
Having heard these words of King Vīramaṇi at that time, he had a drum beaten, resounding with a great noise. ||28||
The sound of kettledrums was heard in every house along the street; all the heroes residing in the royal city went forth to slay Śatrughna. (29)
Those who, considering themselves heroes, openly disregard the command of the King—even if they be his sons or brothers—should be put to death by the king’s order. (30)
"Let the heroes listen once more to the sound of the beaten drums;
having heard it, let that which is to be done quickly be performed without delay. (31)
Śeṣa said:
Having thus brought the sound of the drum within the range of his own ears,
the best of men approached the foremost of kings, the most excellent of heroes.
Their own bodies were adorned with golden armor, and the depths of their hearts rejoiced at the great festival of battle. ||32||
Some went forth wearing beautiful helmets upon their heads,
richly adorned with armor and graced by hundreds of millions of ornaments.
At the king’s command, they went in a chariot yoked with a pair of horses, resplendent with jewels and gold, to the abode of that best of men, full of excitement. (34)
Some went on intoxicated elephants, others on beautiful horses;
all of them, carrying out the king's command, proceeded to the royal palace.
Adorned with a beautiful golden armor and helmet,
Rukmāṅgada also stood upon his own chariot, which was as swift as thought.
His younger brother Śubhāṅgada, wearing upon his excellent body his own armor made of great jewels, set out for the festival of battle. (37)
The king’s brother, Vīrasiṃha, who was skilled in all weapons and missiles, went there by the king's command, for such was the sovereign's decree. (38)
The king’s nephew, known as Balamitra,
also went to the royal palace, equipped with armor and a sword.
Then the great commander-in-chief, though himself an enemy-slayer, having fully prepared that fourfold army, informed the king.
Then King Vīramaṇi mounted an excellent chariot, filled with all kinds of weapons and missiles, which was lofty with a great wheel set with jewels. 41.
Then, from that ocean of heroes, the sound of conchs was heard simultaneously,
as if urging on the timid warriors in the battle.
Then, drums sounded together, played by skilled musicians,
where his armies stood ready to advance for battle.
Having all performed rites for auspiciousness and being adorned with every ornament, they went to the field of battle fully equipped with all weapons and missiles. (44)
The mountain caves were filled with the sound of kettledrums and conchs;
did he go to summon those dwelling in heaven? Or was it his own roar that went there? (45)
In that tumultuous situation, the great King Vīramaṇi, filled with martial zeal, went to the field of battle. 46.
Having arrived and stationed himself there for a while, he then brought forth men from that place, as numerous as an ocean, consisting of chariots and infantry, to overwhelm them.
Seeing that approaching force, which had raised a great clamor by charioteers skilled in weaponry, the king spoke to Sumati: ||48||
Śatrughna said:
"The powerful Vīramaṇi has arrived as my horse-guard, along with a great army and cavalry, to fight me once again. (49)
"How should the battle be waged? Who among those of superior strength will exert themselves?
[Tell me] so that all those heroic ones may attain their desired victory. (50)
Sumati said:
"O Lord, this great king has arrived, surrounded by a vast army;
he has come for the sake of battle, yet he is endowed with devotion to Śiva. (51)
Now let the hero Puṣkala, who is skilled in the highest weapons, fight;
and let other warriors as well, such as Nīlaratna and others, who are experts in warfare, also engage. ||52||
O sinless one, you must either fight with Śiva or with the king;
he of great strength and prowess must be defeated in a duel.
"O King, by this method you shall achieve victory here;
afterwards, O high-minded Lord, do whatever pleases you. (54)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, having resolved upon battle, then commanded his brave warriors. (55)
All you kings, skilled in weapons, together with your armies, must strive once again so that Meñjaya may quickly prevail in battle. (56)
Having heard of Rāghava’s victory, those experts in crossing waters, filled with great enthusiasm, went forth to fight with his soldiers. ||57||

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Resolve for Battle with Vīramaṇi," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-one. Śeṣa said:
The mighty forces of Śatrughna were fully prepared for battle.
Endowed with valor, they went into the midst of Vīramaṇi’s army. ||1||
Discharging arrows with those [weapons], they were seen standing within the range of the arrows, men wielding bows who had struck down many soldiers. ||2||
There, many elephants and chariots made of jewels were struck down; they were seen on the field of battle with their vehicles and horses broken. ||3||
Hearing that their slaughter had been carried out, the powerful Rukmāṅgada,
standing upon a chariot adorned with jewels, went forth with his troops to fight.
Placing arrows upon his bow and holding two inexhaustible quivers, he was terrifying with the corners of his red eyes, filled with great wrath. ||5||
Agitating thousands of heroes with many arrows and causing them to cry out "Alas! Alas!", the powerful Gada, son of Ugrasena, advanced.
The powerful prince, equal to him in strength, fame, and splendor,
challenged Śatrughna, Bhārati, and Puṣkala.
Rukmāṅgada said:
"Come, O you of heroic deeds, great strength, and prowess!
Fight with me, the powerful and radiant prince. (8)
O hero, what is the use of these other terrified men slain by the millions?
Achieve victory by engaging in a great battle with me! 9.
Having spoken thus, the powerful Puṣkala, laughing in the meantime, struck him in the broad center of his chest with sharp-jointed arrows. (10)
Unable to endure that, the prince took up arrows on his great bow and struck the hero Puṣkala in the chest with ten shafts.
Both equally impetuous and both desiring victory, those two shone in battle like the two princes, Kumāra and Tāraka.
Fixing ten great, sharp arrows upon his bow,
the hero Puṣkala rendered the prince chariotless.
With four [arrows] he struck down his four horses; with two, he felled the charioteer;
with one, his standard; and with two, the two protectors of the chariot.
Vegavān pierced the prince with a single arrow in the heart;
seeing that miraculous feat, all the heroes were greatly delighted. (15)
With his bow severed, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed,
he was overcome with extreme anger and mounted another chariot.
Having mounted his excellent chariot, adorned with jewels,
he took up his great bow, which was very firm and strung with a cord.
Having displayed great prowess, Rukmāṅgada spoke these words to the hero Puṣkala:
"O supreme ascetic, where will you go after performing such a great feat? (18)
Behold today my prowess, which has been fashioned by my own strength;
O hero, stay firm with effort, for I shall not allow your chariot to reach the sky.
Having spoken thus, he fixed a most fierce arrow upon his bow;
then, having consecrated it with mantras, he discharged that whirling weapon at the chariot of Pauṣkali.
He discharged a sharp arrow, uniquely adorned with golden feathers;
by that arrow, his chariot was driven a distance of one yojana.
Held with great difficulty by his charioteer, the chariot reeled upon the earth;
having regained its steadiness with effort, Puṣkala, the supreme knower of weapons, [remained firm].
Holding that arrow of Vāṇa upon his bow, he spoke these words to him:
"O foremost of heroes, attain heaven, which is served by all the gods."
O best of kings, those like you are worthy of the earth, yet you are also worthy of the assembly of Śatakratu; therefore, go to the abode of the gods.
Having said this, he discharged a great weapon capable of reaching the sky;
by that arrow, he [the opponent], along with his chariot, went upward according to the natural course.
Transcending all the worlds, he went toward the orb of the sun;
by its flame, his chariot—along with the horses and the charioteer—was consumed.
With his body mostly consumed by those [flames], he fell down in great misery,
clutching the moon-crested Lord who removes the suffering of the heart.
Having fallen there upon the ground, his body scorched by the fire,
he fell into extreme agony and fainted within the circle of the charnel ground.
When that prince had fallen to the ground and fainted, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there at the front of the battle.
Those enemies, Puṣkala and the others, attained the goddess of victory;
while the horse-protectors, their enemies, were defeated and fled.
Then, seeing his son's fainting spell, King Vīramaṇi, filled with grief,
went into the midst of the battle toward Puṣkala.
Then this earth, along with its mountains and excellent forests, trembled;
the brave attained joy, while the cowards were oppressed by fear.
Bearing a great bow and even two inexhaustible quivers,
he did not challenge his enemy, though he was emitting sighs of rage.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Victory of Puṣkala and the Defeat of Rukmāṅgada," in the *Rāmāśvamedha* section of the *Pātālakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||41||
Chapter Forty-two. Śeṣa said:
Having challenged that King Puṣkala, who was like a vast ocean of a great army, [he spoke].
Even Hanumān, having clearly perceived the lord of monkeys, rushed toward him.
Raising his massive body like a club,
he let out a roar that echoed with the sound of thundering clouds.
The lord of monkeys went from those excellent heroes stationed on the battlefield to that jewel among heroes, the king of men.
Seeing Hanumān approaching, the heroic Puṣkala gazed at him with eyes deeply reddened by anger toward his enemy.
Puṣkala, the knower of supreme missiles, spoke thus to Hanumān, making the entire battlefield resound with his voice as deep as a thundercloud. ||4||
Puṣkala said:
"O great monkey, why have you come to fight in this battle?
How small is your strength compared to the vast power of King Vīramaṇi? (5)
Where all the inhabitants of the three worlds have assembled face to face, do you wish to go there to fight in sport, or not? 6.
Who is this King Vīramaṇi, and how insignificant is his strength?
Your arrival here, O hero, is considered most formidable. (7)
Having crossed the difficult-to-traverse ocean of Raghunātha’s grace,
I shall in an instant bring the Lord of the Yakṣas to his senses in the battle with the Kauravas.
Just as you crossed the ocean of Rākṣasas through the abundance of Rāma’s compassion,
so too shall I cross over this difficult-to-traverse [ocean] by remembering Rāma well.
Whoever, having encountered some insurmountable difficulty, remembers the Lord of the Raghus, for them the ocean of suffering will dry up; of this there is no doubt. ||10||
Therefore, O mighty one, go to the presence of Śatrughna, the great hero of Vraja;
having defeated King Vīramaṇi in an instant, he shall arrive here. ||11||
Śeṣa said: Having heard these wise words spoken by Puṣkala,
the slayer of enemy heroes spoke again to Puṣkala.
Hanumān said:
"O son, do not act with such rashness toward King Vīramaṇi;
he is a giver of gifts, a protector of those seeking refuge, and endowed with strength and heroism."

"You are but a child, yet you have become an aged king and the most eminent among all those skilled in weapons and missiles; numerous heroes, resplendent with valor, have been conquered by you in battle. (14)
Know that Sadāśiva is his protector, ever by his side;
Sthāṇu, who has been brought under control by devotion, and Soma are situated here in this city. (15)
Therefore, O Puṣkala, I shall fight with this king alone;
you, having conquered the other heroes, shall attain abundant fame.
Puṣkala said:
"Śiva is to be won over through devotion; he was established by him in his own city.
However, Maheśvara remains with a heart that is not quickly won. (17)
This Sadāśiva, having attained the supreme state, is to be worshipped;
that Rāma, having abandoned my mind, does not go anywhere else. (18)
Where Rāma is, there is the entire universe, both the stationary and the moving;
therefore, I shall conquer King Raṇavīramaṇi.
Go forth to fight other noble kings in battle, those headed by Vīrasiṃha; O Lord, do not harbor anxiety for me, O monkey.
Having heard these words, which were spoken with great composure, Hanumān went to the battle to fight Vīrasiṃha, the younger brother of the king.
Lakṣmīnidhi engaged in a duel with his son, named Gada,
who was skilled in the knowledge of great weapons and missiles.
Urged by his own prowess and strength, Prince Sumada, equipped with weapons, advanced into the battle to fight against Balamitra. (23)
Seeing that king challenging him, Puṣkala, who was skilled in single combat,
stood upon his gold-inlaid chariot and advanced toward him.
Seeing Puṣkala, who was skilled in battle, arrive there,
the king spoke with fearless words in the midst of the forest, his speech being well-composed.
Vīramaṇi said:
"Go, desiring to save your life, for this boy is a serpent of illusion, enraged and possessing fierce wrath in battle; he will surely fight me. (26)
For kings like me show compassion toward children such as you;
they do not strike them down. Therefore, go outside this refuge.
"As long as you were seen by my eyes, so long was my mind free from agitation;
now, my mind is eager to strike you down. (28)
That you pierced my son with arrows and rendered him unconscious— all that has been forgiven by me today, for your intellect is as great as that of a child.
Having heard these words, Puṣkala spoke to him:
Puṣkala said:
"I am a child, while you are very old and an expert in all weapons and missiles. (30)

And as for the opinion of the Kṣatriyas: those who are endowed with a preponderance of strength are themselves the elders among the foremost of kings, having attained the status of being advanced in age. (31)
By me was that son, who was arrogant with valor and strength, rendered unconscious;
now I shall strike you down with weapons in battle.
Therefore, O King, stand with effort at the head of the battle;
no one who is devoted to Rāma shall conquer me while I remain in the position of Indra. (33)
Having heard these words spoken by Puṣkala, the foremost of kings laughed;
then, looking at Bāla, he became enraged and spoke again.
Perceiving him to be enraged, the son of Bharata, driven by madness,
struck the king in the heart with twenty sharp arrows.
Seeing those arrows released by the thief approaching him, the king,
becoming exceedingly enraged, cut them into many pieces with his own sharp shafts.
Seeing his arrows cut down, the son of Bharata, the slayer of enemy heroes, became exceedingly enraged in his heart and struck that king with three shafts.
The prince named Puṣkala pierced him in the forehead;
there they shone like the peaks of Mount Trikūṭa fixed together.
Afflicted by those arrows, the king,
filled with great wrath, struck the heroic Puṣkala in the heart with nine shafts.
By those calf-toothed arrows, the many-colored blood of Rāma’s younger brother’s son was drunk up. ||39||
Just as angry venomous serpents reside within their own bodies, so too Puṣkala,
having fallen into a state of supreme rage, [addressed] the king once again.
With a hundred sharp-jointed arrows, he pierced Aśu;
by those arrows, his armor was shattered, as were his crown and helmet.
His great chariot bow, strung and ready, was shattered by him who was overwhelmed with rage;
his body, pierced by arrows, was drenched in blood.
Mounting another chariot, he went to the son of Bharata and said:
"O bee at the lotus-feet of the heroic Rāma, you are blessed! (43)
"O hero, a great deed has been performed by you today, in that I have been deprived of my chariot;
protect your life now while I am fighting. (44)
"Life is easily lost when one stands in the form of Time.
Having said this, he who was skilled in weapons struck [his opponent] with countless arrows. (45)
On the ground, arrows were seen scattered in every direction;
there, thousands of elephants and horses were likewise pierced and struck down.
Chariots, joined with their charioteers, were cut and split asunder by him.
There, a river of streams of blood flowed across the courtyard. ||47||
For there, intoxicated elephants are seen like mountain peaks, and their hair, appearing like moss, repeatedly rests upon the heads of living beings. 48.
There, the severed fingers of heroes, smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents, were seen like snakes, beautiful with the splendor of their rings. (49)
There, the heroes indeed bore the heads of the foremost soldiers, which resembled tortoises, as they were covered with flesh and blood that appeared like mud. ||50||
When such a conflict had thus occurred, hundreds of yoginīs drank the blood of living beings fallen in battle from their vessels in the arena.
Filled with joy and curiosity, they indeed devoured me;
having drunk my blood there and eaten my flesh, they became utterly intoxicated.
In that battle, the Piśācas danced, laughed loudly, and sang loudly in the midst of the hosts, [seizing] as it were the heads of living beings.
Holding intoxicated cows with both hands and intent on beating them like cymbals,
the Śivās [ate] the great flesh of those fallen there upon the battlefield.
Having devoured [them], they roared, intoxicated and striking fear into the cowardly;
the cowards, overcome with terror, entered the hollow of the kuñjara tree.
The sinners were devoured by the yoginīs; they had no place of refuge anywhere.
Observing this slaughter of his own army, the leader of the chariots [acted].
Puṣkala also wrought a slaughter there upon the field of battle;
as the heads of elephants were split asunder, pearls fell like rain.
Covered with hair, that river appears like the Tāmraparṇī;
it has joined the bodies of men struck by the arrows discharged by Puṣkala.
They bring about the severance of life for even heroes on every side. ||58||
All were seen with their bodies drenched in blood, all with their limbs severed;
what indeed [could be more] than these brave warriors in the midst of the battle-host? (59)
At that moment, enraged and overwhelmed by a flood of anger, he addressed the lord of the earth and struck him with many arrows.
King Gośīrṇakavaca, perceiving him to be possessed of great strength, struck that [demon] Mahābala with millions of arrows, which pierced him as he was already split by the king's shafts.
By those arrows, much blood flowed from his armor; his body, though beautiful, became like the withered wood of an old forest tree pierced by a shower of shafts.
Standing in the midst of the arrow-storm, his mind was overwhelmed;
and that son of Bharata was unable either to take up more arrows or to join them together.
Remembering Rāma, he took up his great and firm bow and made it ready;
he then released sharpened arrows capable of repelling hosts of enemies.
O best of sages, having dispersed that net of arrows with those shafts,
he blew his conch in battle and fearlessly approached the king.
Puṣkala said:
"O hero, you have performed a great deed in that you brought me, the fierce scorcher of heroes, within the range of Bāṇa’s arrows."
"Because of my seniority, you are now worthy of my respect on this battlefield;
O King Vīramaṇi, behold today my great prowess. (67)
"O hero, do not cause me to faint with three arrows;
otherwise, listen to my vow which shall stupefy all heroes. (68)
Even having reached the Gaṅgā, which removes all sins, that great sinner who, acting with the conduct of a great fool, does not bathe there after disparaging her [is lost]. (69)
O King Bhava, if his sin were like mine—had he not struck you down on the field of battle—then I would have rendered him unconscious; therefore, remain prepared for war.
Having heard these words of Puṣkala, the best of kings became greatly enraged and agitated; he drew his bow and fixed sharp arrows upon it. (71)
Having pierced the heart of those enemies, they fell upon the great Bhārata like those who have turned their backs on devotion to Rāma, falling headlong to the earth.
Then he released a sharpened arrow, blazing like fire,
aiming it at his broad chest which was as expansive as the surface of a door-panel.
Severed in two by a shaft from the lord of the earth, he fell in the midst of the chariot, blazing like the orb of the sun. (74)
Then he took up another arrow born of devotion to his mother;
having fixed that meritorious shaft, he again cut it down with a great [arrow].
Then, undaunted and mindful of what ought to be done,
that master of supreme weapons released Rāma— who destroys one's own suffering— into his heart.
That arrow, resembling a venomous serpent and blazing with a radiance equal to the sun, struck his heart and indeed caused him to fall into a swoon.
Then, everything was raised in cries of "Alas! Alas! and everyone became intent on flight;
when the king's army had fallen into a state of utter confusion, Puṣkala achieved victory.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Defeat of Vīramaṇi," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Forty-three. Śeṣa said:
Having approached Vīrasiṃha, Hanumān spoke these words.
Stay here for a moment; O Vīraja, from where will I go to you? ||1||
Having heard these great words of the monkey, [Rāvaṇa],
overwhelmed by a flood of anger, [took up] his bow which sounded like a rain-cloud.
Shouting fiercely and discharging sharp arrows in battle,
he appeared as beautiful as a rain-cloud pouring down torrents during the month of Āṣāḍha.
Seeing those sharp arrows deeply embedded in his own body,
Hanumān, the son of Añjanī, became exceedingly enraged in his heart.
He struck him in the heart with a fist as hard as a diamond;
struck by that fist, the hero fell upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing his paternal uncle unconscious,
Śubhāṅgada and Gada also abandoned their swoon and returned to the field of battle.
Raining down arrows like two great-sounding clouds,
they wrought a terrible slaughter and advanced against the monkey.
Seeing those two heroes arrived in battle, the lord of the monkeys enveloped them,
along with their chariots and their bows, with his tail.
We shall burst open this place on the earth; at that very moment, both of them became unconscious, motionless, and their bodies turned crimson with blood.
Having engaged in battle for a long time with Sumada, Balamitra rendered him unconscious with arrows of very sharp joints. ||10||
Puṣkala was struck by an arrow and fell into a swoon devoid of consciousness; meanwhile, Jayanta reached Kaṭaka, which harassed the soldiers of Śatrughna.
At that time, Sāmba, mounted upon an excellent chariot and stretching his divine bow, rushed toward these warriors.
The Great One, bearing the crescent moon within his mass of matted locks, wearing ornaments of serpents that are painful to the touch of the mind, and holding the Ājagava bow; ||13||
Seeing his own kinsmen unconscious, Maheśvara, the destroyer of the suffering of his devotees,
set out with a great army to fight these soldiers of Śatrughna.
Accompanied by my attendants and retinue, treading upon the surface of the earth,
I came for the sake of protecting my devotees, just as Śiva [came] to Tripura.
With eyes reddened by anger, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who brings about the dissolution of the world and is worshipped by the gods, beheld the highly esteemed heroes as he proceeded.
Seeing that Maheśāna had arrived,
the powerful younger brother of Rāma went forth in battle to fight the crest-jewel of all the gods.
Then, seeing that Śatrughna had arrived, Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
who holds a bow of excellent qualities, became overcome with supreme anger and spoke.
Puṣkala, who serves the feet of Rāma, has performed a great deed;
having slain my devotee in the arena of battle, he has come here. (19)
Today there stands the heroic Puṣkala, a master of supreme missiles;
having slain him in battle, I shall obtain happiness after afflicting my devotee.
Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus, he dispatched Vīrabhadra toward Puṣkala, saying,
"Go and fight Puṣkala, the subduer of his own servants, in battle."
They dispatched the mighty Hanumān, along with Nandin,
Kuśadhvaja, Pracaṇḍa, Bhṛṅgin, and Subāhu.
And Puṣkala commanded his own group named Caṇḍa, headed by Sumada;
meanwhile, Vīrabhadra approached with a great host.
Beholding Mahārudra, the high-minded Puṣkala advanced to fight;
in the battle, he struck him with five arrows.
With his limbs wounded by those arrows, he hurled a trident;
having cut down that trident in an instant, the one of great strength roared aloud.
O twice-born one, seeing his own trident severed, the powerful follower of Rudra swiftly struck Bhāratī on the head with a khaṭvāṅga staff.
Struck by the blows of the mace, that formidable warrior fainted for a moment; then, regaining consciousness, the noble hero Puṣkala, an expert in supreme weapons, [prepared for battle].
With arrows, he instantly severed the khaṭvāṅga staff held in the hand of Vīrabhadra;
Vīrabhadra, his own khaṭvāṅga staff having been cut, [acted] while it remained in his hand.
Having fallen into a state of supreme wrath, he shattered Jarathin’s chariot;
having broken the chariot of Tuvīra, he left the son of Vidhāsa as a mere foot-soldier.
He fought with the high-souled Puṣkala in a hand-to-hand struggle;
then Puṣkala, having abandoned his chariot, crushed it with great force.
The one of great strength struck Vīrabhadra with his fist;
thus they struck each other with fists, as well as with thighs and knees.
Intent on slaying one another and desiring victory over each other,
this state of the two lords continued thus for four days and nights.
Neither he nor the one of great strength was defeated there;
on the fifth day having passed, the mighty Vīrabhadra [prevailed].
Having seized the great hero Puṣkala, who did not flee,
a battle took place between the two of them that bewildered both gods and asuras.
Then, highly enraged, Puṣkala struck Vīrabhadra violently with his fists, kicks, arms, and excellent knees. (35)
Seizing him by the neck, he struck him against the ground;
by that blow, the mighty Vīrabhadra was pained.
Seizing Puṣkala by the foot, he struck him repeatedly;
having beaten Puṣkala upon the ground, that one of great strength— ||37||
And with his trident, the immensely powerful Vīrabhadra swiftly struck off the head of Kartas'u, whose earrings were blazing, and let out a great roar. 38.
As that formidable son of Śarva roared and unleashed his weapons, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the soldiers of Puṣkala’s army in the battle.
All the people in the midst of the battle, though highly skilled, were seized with terror;
they beheld Śatrughna and Puṣkala fallen on the field of combat.
Having heard that Puṣkala had been slain by Vīrabhadra, the attendant of Maheśvara, the great hero [Rāvaṇa] then [acted]. ||41||
Seeing him who had attained extreme suffering in battle, the great Śiva, overcome with grief, recognized that Śatrughna was distressed and spoke these words: 42.
O Puṣkala, do not grieve for that heroic Śatrughna who has been slain in battle;
O one of great strength, do not harbor sorrow for Śatrughna in this conflict.
The downfall of heroes in the midst of battle is remembered for the sake of fame;
blessed is the hero named Puṣkala, who [performed] the five-fold sacrifice for the Brahmins. 44.
He fought as it were with Vīrabhadra, the bringer of the great dissolution, by whom Dakṣa—who had acted with pride and contempt—was struck down in an instant. (45)
"O great king, O mighty one, abandon your grief and fight, for by him the Daityas and the soldiers of Tripura were destroyed in an instant."
O foremost of heroes, stand with effort in this state of being established as the conqueror of Māyā;
having completely abandoned grief, the heroic Śatrughna became enraged at Śaṅkara. 47.
With bows and arrows drawn and ready, they covered Maheśvara;
those arrows struck his divine head and body, leaving them wounded and mangled.
As he performed a great marvel, having arrived for the sake of protecting his devotees, Śaṅkara’s arrows remained suspended in the sky, swallowing their [the enemies'] arrows. 49.
Having pervaded this entire universe, even the sage Citrakārin,
upon seeing the strength of those two in battle, considered it to be everywhere present.
Residing in their own cities, they took refuge in celestial chariots that reached the sky, which cause the dissolution of the world, bring about its destruction, and delude all beings. (51)
Having come to behold them, they praise those two greatly:
"This one is the cause of the dissolution and creation of these three worlds. (52)
"This one too is the younger brother of the great king Rāmacandra; what will happen now, or who will conquer the circle of the earth? (53)
The hero of speech shall suffer defeat at the head of the battle;
thus did the mutual combat continue for eleven days.
When the twelfth day arrived, the lord of men, filled with rage, discharged the weapon known as Brahmā in order to slay Mahādeva. ||55||
O Śatrughna, that great weapon, the Savijñāya, was released by the enemy;
yet even as he laughed, he drank up that great Brahmaśiras which had been discharged.
Having attained extreme amazement, he thought, "What should be done beyond this?
Thus occupied with reflection, there arose in his heart something like a blazing fire.
The crest-jewel of the gods discharged an arrow, by which Śatrughna was rendered unconscious at the archway. 58.
The entire camp, frequented by soldiers, became a scene of "Alas!
Alas! cries; all the heroes were struck down to the surface of the earth by the hosts of Rudra.
Subāhu, Sumada, and others, proud of the strength of their own arms,
beheld Śatrughna fallen and unconscious, tormented by arrows.
While Puṣkala was being guarded by his attendants stationed on the chariot,
Hanumān arrived to fight Śiva, the agent of universal destruction.
O brāhmaṇa, while causing his own warriors to remember Śrī Rāma with great joy,
he became intensely enraged and began to lash his tail violently.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Defeat of Puṣkala and Śatrughna," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||43||
(44) The forty-fourth chapter. Śeṣa said:
Having approached Rudra, who was at the head of his hosts on the battlefield, the heroic Hanumān spoke, desiring to subdue the lord of the gods. ||1||
Hanumān said:
"Since you have acted in opposition to the dharma of Rudra, I desire to punish you for being intent on slaying a devotee of Rāma. (2)
"O Lord, I have heard this previously stated in many ways by the divine sages:
Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is one who constantly remembers the feet of the Lord of the Raghus. (3)
All that was false regarding Śatrughna as he fought back;
though Puṣkala struck him, the hero Śatrughna too fell unconscious.
Therefore, I shall cast you down to where the dissolution of the world is imminent; stay here with effort, O wretch, you who are averse to devotion to Śarva! 5.
Śeṣa said:
To the monkey who had spoken thus, the Great Lord replied:
"Blessed are you, O best of heroes; what you say is not false."
This Lord Rāmacandra of mine is saluted by gods and asuras;
therefore, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, brought back his horse.

He has arrived for the sake of protecting that [disciple], being completely won over by devotion to him; for such is the established principle: "In whatever way possible, a devotee must be protected as one's own self. (8)
May the great Raghunātha, showing some slight anger due to the intense suffering of his devotee, look upon me with compassion despite my shamelessness.
Śeṣa said:
While Caṇḍīśa was speaking thus, Hanumān became exceedingly enraged;
seizing a massive rock, he struck his chariot.
Struck by that stone, his chariot—along with its driver, horses, and its standards and banners—was shattered into pieces. (11)
Remaining in the sky, they all praised the lord of monkeys:
"O Lord of Monkeys, you are blessed; a great deed has been performed by you. (12)
Seeing Śrī Śiva deprived of his chariot, Nandin rushed toward him and said to the illustrious Mahādeva, "Please mount upon my back. (13)
Then Hanumān, becoming exceedingly enraged, uprooted a rock with great force and struck the Lord of the Bhūtas, who was seated upon his bull, in the chest.
Then the Lord of Beings, having been struck, took up his sharp trident,
which was blazing with three points and possessed a radiance equal to the flames of fire.
Seeing that great trident approaching with a blazing radiance,
Jaṭilaśas quickly seized it in his hand and shattered it in an instant.
When the lord of monkeys had broken his trident, Śiva instantly took up in his hand a spear fashioned entirely of iron.
That spear, released by Śiva, struck the heart of that wise one;
in an instant, the lord of monkeys became overwhelmed with distress there. ||18||
In an instant, having crossed over that [ocean] as it were and seized a formidable tree,
he struck him in the heart, which was adorned with great serpents.
Struck by that hero, the lords of serpents were overcome with terror;
abandoning him, they fled here and there and quickly departed for the netherworld (pātāla).
When that mountain was released from his chest, Śiva looked at it and,
becoming enraged, took up a terrible mace with both his hands.
"O lowest of monkeys, you have fled from the battle; go!
I shall take away your life with this mace right now."
Seeing the pestle released by the enraged Śiva, the monkey,
remembering Hari, evaded it with great speed.
That great iron club, released by Śiva, fell downward;
having rent asunder the entire earth, it went to the netherworld (rasātala). ||24||
Then Hanumān, the servant of Rāma, becoming exceedingly enraged,
seized a mountain in his hand and struck him on the chest.
Just as the husband of Satī resolved to cut down the mountain,
he was struck by the lord of monkeys with a many-branched śāla tree.
While he was still intent on cutting that darkness, he was struck by a stone;
then Śiva, exerting himself, began to split his own heart with those very stones.
Then he caused a rain of stones and mountain peaks;
and having enveloped him with a net of creepers, he struck that lord of spirits.
With rocks, mountains, and trees, and by repeatedly lashing his tail, Nandin caused great terror and even split the moon into fragments. (29)
The wrathful Maheśāna became utterly overwhelmed;
with a blow at every moment, he caused him to be greatly distressed.
He said to the lord of the monkeys: "O follower of the descendant of Raghu, you are blessed!
A great deed has been performed by you today; I am well-pleased with your effort. (31)
I am not easily attained through mere gifts, nor through lack of discipline, nor through slight austerity;
I possess great speed. Therefore, pray for a boon.
Śeṣa said:
Seeing him speaking thus, Hanumān spoke to that well-pleased Great Lord (Aheśāna), laughing with a fearless voice. (33)
Hanumān said:
"O Great Lord, by the grace of the Lord of the Raghus, everything is mine;
nevertheless, I beg a boon from you, who have been gratified by my combat. (34)
This one named Puṣkala has fallen, slain in battle;
likewise, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Rāma, has fainted on the gateway.
Many other heroes have fallen, wounded by arrows;
some have fainted and collapsed—protect them along with your hosts. (36)
And just as these great elements, vetālas, piśācas, and others do not carry them off nor devour them, so too do dogs, jackals, and the like. (37)
Act in such a way that there shall be no injury to their bodies,
until I have conquered the host of Indra and brought him to Mount Droṇa.
In that place, having sown medicinal herbs and stationed the soldiers, you must protect them all in every way by reviving them with your power. (39)
"I am going there to bring Drona, the best of mountains, upon which dwell medicinal herbs that restore life to living beings. (40)
Having heard these words, he said to him, "So be it":
"Go quickly to that mountain to protect you from your enemies who have killed your soldiers. (41)
Having heard those words of the Lord, he went to Mount Droṇa;
crossing all the continents, he reached the Ocean of Milk.
But here, the great Śiva protected this cremation ground with his own hosts, who possessed immense strength and prowess. (43)
Hanumān, having approached Mount Droṇa— the great mountain named Droṇa—
and having quickly placed that Linga within it, set out for the field of battle.
When the wicked Caka prepared to lead him away, the mountain Pāriyātra saw him and, out of compassion for his protector, [stood as a barrier] so that the hosts of gods could not [approach]. 45.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they said: "What is this that has happened on the mountain?
For who is this hero of great strength and prowess who is leading him away? (46)
Having done this, all the asuras, gathering together, beheld the monkey;
crying out, "Release him!", they struck him with millions of weapons and missiles. (47)
Seeing them all being slaughtered, the heroic Hanumān became exceedingly enraged;
in an instant, he slew them all, just as Śakra destroyed all the Asuras.
Some there were struck by his feet, some crushed by his hands;
some were beaten with his tail, and others struck by his horn. ||49||
Struck by that monkey, they all instantly lost their composure;
some fell upon the ground, drenched in blood. ||50||
Some, terrified by the fear of the monkey, went to Śakra, the lord of the gods;
they were drenched by their wounds, their bodies mangled and covered in blood.
Seeing them agitated by fear and drenched in blood,
Śakra, the best of all the gods, spoke to the deities with a troubled mind.
"How are you all here? Why are you drenched in blood? By which Daitya or by which vile Rākṣasa have you been struck down? (53)
"Having understood this entire matter to be entirely true, I shall go immeasurably;
having slain and bound that intoxicated slayer of yours, I shall return. (54)
Having heard these words, the best of gods spoke with piteous voices to Turāsāha, who is honored by both gods and asuras. (55)
The gods said:
"Having come here, we do not know who this being is, assuming the form of a monkey;
he is intent on carrying away Mount Lāṅgūlaveṣṭita, having prepared to take Droṇa."
Having thus resolved their minds, we all, well-united and fully armored, waged war, raining down a shower of all kinds of weapons and missiles. ||57||
Therefore, we were all defeated in battle by that one who was powerful; many among us, the best of gods, were slain there and fell to the ground. (58)
We have returned here from death by virtue of our many merits;
we are covered all over with blood and afflicted by the pain of our wounds. (59)
Having heard these words of the gods,
Śiva commanded all the gods, who were endowed with great strength, to go to their city.
"Go and bind the immensely powerful monkey who has reached Mount Mahādroṇa;
having bound him, bring him here—you who are the cause of the gods' defeat in battle. (61)
Thus commanded, they went to that best of mountains, Droṇa,
where the powerful hero Hanumān, the foremost of monkeys, was staying.
Having gone there, they all struck the exceedingly powerful Hanumān;
however, he was struck down by Hanumān with his fists and blows from his palms.
Falling there in an instant with their bodies wounded by blood,
others fled from the Lord of the Three Heavens.
Having heard that, Śakra, the best of the gods, became enraged and commanded all the foremost of the immortals regarding the heroic lord of monkeys.
Commanded by him, they indeed went to where the powerful lord of monkeys was;
seeing all of them arrived, that best of monkeys spoke to them.
"O you of many heroes, I shall now forcibly bring Māyā, the destroyer in battle, along with Himā,
into the vicinity of the city of Saṃyaminī."
Thus addressed, they all returned and, fully armored and endowed with great strength, struck the monkey with many kinds of weapons and missiles discharged from afar. (68)
Some with spears and axes, some with swords and sharp-edged spears,
and some with clubs and javelins— rendered turbid by rage.
Struck by the various weapons of the foremost immortals,
that powerful one quickly struck all those best of gods with boulders.
Some fled and went into the presence of Śakra;
having heard the words spoken by them, the lord of the gods became afraid.
Having approached and bowed to Bṛhaspati, the excellent preceptor of the gods and the counselor of the inhabitants of heaven, he questioned him.
Indra said: "O Lord, who is this man who has come to lead Droṇa away—he by whom these heroic immortals, bearing weapons, have been slain? (73)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard those words spoken by Gīrasa, the great [serpent] spoke to Turāsāha, the lord of the gods, who was agitated with fear. (74)
Bṛhaspati said:
"He who slew Rāvaṇa in battle and consumed Kumbhakarṇa—he by whom all enemies were slain, his servant I am. (75)
By him, the fire from whose tail burnt down the three peaks of Laṅkā,
Akṣa was slain, and Hanumān was disregarded.
Therefore, all have been struck down for the sake of Droṇa;
this great king, the best of the strong, now prepares to perform a horse sacrifice.
But the great king Vīramaṇi, a devotee of Śiva, seized his horse;
thereupon a battle ensued that bewildered even the gods. (78)
"Śiva has slain those many heroes of Vīrārāma in battle;
that one of great power will surely lead Droṇa there to bring them back to life. (79)
"This [demon] cannot be conquered by you, even in hundreds of years, unless you are endowed with strength. Therefore, propitiate the monkey and give him that medicinal herb. (80)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Gods on Mount Droṇa," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||44||
Chapter Forty-Five. Śeṣa said:
Having heard the words spoken by his preceptor, the self-ruling Vṛṣaparvan, the enemy of the gods, [spoke].
Having learned that the son of the Wind had arrived for the sake of Rāma’s mission. ||1||
