Fearing that danger had arrived from the monkey who harbored evil intent,
he rejoiced greatly in his heart and spoke to Vācaspati.
Indra said:
"O Lord of the Gods, if this Droṇa is led away, how should it be done?
Tell me how the gods may once again have life."
Now, pacify this wind-blown [calamity] exactly as it is;
thus Rāma will attain supreme joy and the gods shall find happiness. (4)
Having heard the words of the lord of the gods, Vācaspati then placed Śakra at the forefront, surrounded by all the deities.
He went to that place where the fearless monkey Hanumān was, who,
having forcibly conquered all the asuras, remained seated at ease while roaring loudly.
Having approached his presence, those gods, led by Bṛhaspati,
fell at the feet of the son of the Wind-god.
Urged by that lord of the gods, the preceptor of the world, Bṛhaspati, the best among speakers, spoke to that hero. (8)
O high-minded one, the gods performed this deed against you out of ignorance of your prowess; you are a servant of the feet of Śrī Rāma.
"For what purpose has this host of Māras come, and how did their assembly here occur?
We shall all do exactly as you have commanded. (10)
Becoming enraged and casting aside compassion, look toward the Lord of the Gods;
assuming a terrifying form, he shall strike fear into the Daityas and the son of the Wind-god. 11.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words spoken by the gods along with their preceptor, the one of great fame spoke to all the gods and the preceptor as well. (12)
"Many soldiers of King Vīramaṇi were slain by Śarva in battle;
indeed, I shall lead Droṇa to the mountain in order to restore them to life. (13)
Those who, arrogant in the strength of their own prowess, shall attempt to obstruct him—
I will send them at that very moment to the abode of Yama.
Therefore, speak, you all, of that medicine, whether it be from Droṇa or elsewhere, by which I shall restore to life the heroes who have died upon the field of battle.
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled son of Vāyu, they all bowed down and gave him the life-restoring herb (saṃjīvanauṣadha). ||16||
Greatly rejoicing, those Asuras, having themselves abandoned their dwellings in heaven, went forth filled with happiness, placing the Lord of the Gods at their head. (17)
Hanumān, having taken that medicine, arrived at the gateway,
while being praised by all the hosts of gods who were eager for his great feat.
Seeing Hanumān arrive, all the enemies praised him, saying "Excellent! Excellent!", and they regarded that bird as truly marvelous.
The monkey, filled with great joy, approached Puṣkala,
who had arrived before him as a fallen warrior, dead.
O Śivā, though it was not protected within the fierce maṇḍala,
the mind of Śrī Rāma indeed went near him.
And having summoned the minister Sumati, who held the opinion of the great ones, he said:
"Today I shall restore to life all the heroes who have died in battle."
Having spoken thus, Bheṣaja joined his head to Puṣkala’s body with his own body, and spoke these auspicious words: ||22||
If I have pleased my husband Rāghava with my mind, my speech, and my actions,
then by this medicine let him live quickly.
As soon as these words were spoken, Puṣkala,
that crest-jewel of heroes, rose up and, out of rage, bit them on the field of battle.
"Where has that Vīrabhadra gone? Having fainted on the courtyard of my feet, I shall strike him down this very moment; where is my excellent bow? (25)
To Vaiprāśravīra, who was speaking thus, the Lord of Monkeys said:
"You are blessed, O hero; speak further to him on the field of battle. (26)
"By the grace of Raghunātha, you who were slain by Vīrabhadra have been restored to life; come now to Śatrughna, who has fainted. (27)
Having spoken thus, he departed for that foremost of battlefields;
there Śatrughna remained panting, tormented by Śiva’s arrow. (28)
Having gone there into the presence of the high-souled Śatrughna, and having placed the medicine upon his chest once he had regained his breath, [she departed].
Hanumān said to him, "O best of Śatrughna’s sons, why have you fainted on the battlefield, O you of great strength and prowess? (30)
"If I maintain this celibacy with diligence until the end of my life, then let the hero Śatrughna live again this very moment. (31)
By his mere speaking, this [world] was restored to life for a moment;
but where is Śiva? Where has Śiva gone, abandoning the field of battle? (32)
Those many who had been slain in battle by the illustrious Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
were all restored to life by the high-souled lord of monkeys.
Then all of them, well-armored and their minds filled with rage,
mounted their respective chariots and advanced against the enemies, their bodies wounded in battle.
Puṣkala [fought] Vīrabhadra, Kuśadhvaja [fought] Caṇḍa, and the heroic Hanūmat [fought] Nandin; Śatrughna [fought] Śiva in the battle.
The king approached Śatrughna, the best among the strong, who was drawing his bow and standing in battle having invoked Śiva for his welfare. (36)
The heroic King Vīramaṇi and the powerful Śatrughna engaged in a battle that caused wonder even to the sages. ||37||
O twice-born one, more than a hundred chariots were shattered in an instant by King Vīramaṇi, the slayer of enemies, like sesame seeds. 38.
Then, becoming exceedingly enraged on the field of battle, Śatrughna discharged the Agneya weapon to burn him along with his army. (39)
Seeing that great, burning weapon released by the enemy,
the king became exceedingly enraged and took up the Vāruṇa weapon.
Seeing him afflicted by the cold due to the Vāruṇa weapon, the powerful younger brother of Rāma discharged the Vāyavya weapon at him;
by that, a great wind arose.
Driven by the wind, the clouds dispersed in all directions;
having scattered here and there, that entire army shone with happiness.
When his army was afflicted by the wind, the great king Vīramati took up the mountain-weapon (parvatāstra) against the enemy in his bow.
The wind, obstructed by the mountains, did not stir in that battle;
seeing this, Rāma’s younger brother took up the vajra-weapon.
Struck by the Vajra-weapon, all the mountains were reduced to pieces like sesame seeds;
they reached a state of powder in that battle honored by the best of heroes.
The cows, pierced by the Vajra-weapon, became beautiful with blood; the battle-fronts turned crimson, and the combat became a marvel. ||46||
Then the great King Vīramaṇi, becoming exceedingly enraged,
fixed upon his bow the wonderful Brahmāstra, which consumes all enemies.
Śatrughna took up an arrow and recalled that enchanting weapon,
granted by the Yoginī, which bewilders all enemies.
Just as that Brahmāstra, released from his hand, was approaching the enemy,
Śatrughna discharged the Mohana weapon at him.
In an instant, that Brahmāstra was split in two by the Mohanāstra;
it immediately struck the king's heart, causing the monarch to fall into a swoon.
Hundreds of arrows were discharged by King Śatrughna;
all those heroic hosts belonging to Rudra were once again rendered unconscious.
The fools fell upon the ground at the feet of Śiva;
then Śiva, enraged, proceeded toward the king while standing upon his chariot.
Śatrughna, having arrived suddenly on the field of battle to fight with Śiva,
engaged in combat after making his bow ready and its string drawn tight.
Between the two of them there occurred a terrible battle, shattering their enemies, in which the quarters of the sky were set ablaze by various weapons and missiles hurled in many ways. (54)
With the clashing of missiles and counter-missiles, and with blows and counter-blows,
such a circle of battle had never been seen even among the gods and the Daityas.
Then, utterly distressed in that battle with Śiva,
Śatrughna remembered his Lord there, following the instruction of Pāvana.
"O brother Hānātha, the most fierce Śiva, having raised his bow, is taking away our lives; protect us on the field of battle! (57)
O Rāma, O ocean of compassion, may you, who have crossed the vast sea of manifold sufferings by means of the name "Rāma-tapas," likewise deliver me, who am situated in misery! 58.
Thus she speaks: "When, upon beholding him within the circle of the arched gateway, Rāma—the lotus-eyed one, dark as the petal of a blue water-lily—appears... (59)
Carrying a deer-horn on his shoulder and bearing a consecrated body,
Śatrughna was filled with wonder upon seeing him in the midst of the battle host.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Meeting with Śrī Rāma," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||45||
Chapter Forty-Six. Śeṣa said:
Having seen that Śrī Rāma, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, had arrived, Śatrughna [welcomed him].
O best of the twice-born, his brother was liberated from all suffering.
Hanumān, seeing Rāma bewildered,
joyfully prostrated at his feet and spoke to him who had come for the sake of protecting his devotees.
O Lord, this protection of Your own devotees is indeed fitting:
that You have liberated all those conquered in battle and bound by fetters. (3)
But we, O descendant of Raghu, are indeed fortunate that we shall behold your feet;
by your grace alone, we shall conquer our enemies in an instant.
Śeṣa said:
Then Sthāṇu, having prostrated at the feet of Rāma— who had arrived there and was the object of meditation for yogis— spoke to him who grants fearlessness to those who do not bow.
You alone are the manifest Puruṣa, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), whom they praise; you who, by means of a portion of yourself, create, preserve, and destroy the universe.
You are formless, yet the supreme cause of the entire universe;
though you are one alone, you assume a threefold form, endowed with illusion.
In creation, I exist in the form of the Creator; in preservation, I am myself;
and at the dissolution of the universe, I directly assume the name of Śarva.
The performance of the horse-sacrifice by the Supreme Lord, for the sake of removing the sin of Brahmin-slaughter, was a wondrous forest of his prowess. 9.

Since I carry upon my head that very water which, when used for washing his feet, is called the Gaṅgā and flows between my ears for the sake of pacifying my sins—how can there be any sin remaining for you? (10)
I have clearly committed many harmful deeds; O compassionate one, may you forgive that which has caused you distress. (11)
"What shall I do? This was done by me for the sake of upholding the truth;
knowing your power, I have come for the purpose of protecting your devotee. (12)
Formerly, in Ujjayinī, at the abode of Mahākāla,
he bathed in the river named Śiprā and performed a most wonderful penance.
Then, having become pleased, I said to the lord of the earth:
"O great king, ask for this wonderful kingdom along with all its subjects. (14)
I declared, "O King, this excellent kingdom shall remain in Devapura until the sacrificial horse of Rāma arrives in the city. (15)
"From this moment forth, I shall remain here, intent on protecting you; what else can I do, O Rāma, for whom a boon has been granted, other than to remain true to my own word? (16)
"I have now been favored by the king, along with my sons, cattle, and kinsmen;
the horse is being surrendered, and the king will perform service at your feet. (17)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Maheśa, the best of the Raghus, his eyes filled with compassion, spoke with a steady voice. (18)
Rāma said:
"This indeed is the duty of the gods: the protection of their devotee.
You have performed a noble deed in that your devotee has now been protected."
"You are in my heart, O Śarva, and I am in your heart; there is no difference between us, yet the foolish perceive this with their perverted intellects. (20)
Those men who truly create a distinction between us two, who are of one and the same form,
shall be cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells for a thousand kalpas.
Yet those who were your devotees became my devotees endowed with righteousness;
even my devotees, through great devotion, performed prostrations before you. (22)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words spoken thus, the Lord Śarva restored King Vīramaṇi,
who had fainted, to life by the touch of his hand.
The prosperous, capable, and powerful Lord also restored to life his other sons who had fainted and were tormented by arrows.
The Lord of Beings caused the king—who was prepared for that purpose and surrounded by his sons and grandsons—to perform prostration at the feet of Śrī Rāma. 25.
Blessed was King Vīramaṇi, who beheld the best of the Raghus, who is difficult to attain even for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of yogis established in yoga. 26.
O best of the twice-born, having thus honored that Raghunātha, those whose bodies had been rendered purposeful became most worthy of worship by Brahmā and the other gods.
Praised by Śatrughna, Hanumān, Puṣkala, and other eminent warriors,
the king gave that supreme horse to Rāma.
Then, impelled by Śarva, King Vīramaṇi gave away everything, including his kingdom, along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen.
Then Rāma was praised by all his enemies and by his own servants,
especially by Śatrughna and the others who were exceedingly eager.
Standing upon the jewel-studded chariot, he remained invisible;
when Rāmabhadra had vanished from sight, everyone was struck with great wonder.
Do not recognize that Rāma, who is worshipped as the sole refuge of the world;
he always exists, established everywhere, both in water and on land.
Then the heroes, exceedingly joyful, embraced one another;
with the sounding of musical instruments and cymbals, there was a truly great festival. (33)
Then the horse, released by all those heroes skilled in weapons and missiles,
was followed by them all with affection and filled with wonder.
Śarva, whose vow is true, having obtained the permission of his servant, declared Śrī Rāma—the one who is uniquely difficult for the world to attain—to be his refuge. (35)
Having himself vanished there, Śarva, the cause of dissolution and creation,
went to Kailāsa, adorned by his attendants.
King Vīramaṇi, meditating upon the lotus-feet of Śrī Rāma,
set out together with Śatrughna and his powerful army.
Those best of men who hear this life-story of Rāma shall never again experience the suffering born of worldly existence. (38)

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Departure of the Horse," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||46||
The forty-seventh chapter. Śeṣa said:
O twice-born one, from Hayagotra [he went] to Hemakūṭa, and from there to Bhārata.
He was protected by many thousands of soldiers and adorned with tied chowries. ||1||
It is indeed ten thousand yojanas in extent, equal in width and length,
and possesses beautiful peaks made of silver, gold, and other precious substances.
There was a great and excellent garden, adorned on all sides with trees— śālas, tālas, tamālas, and karṇikāras.
Indeed, [it was filled] with *tāla*, *nāga-punnāga*, *kovidāra*, and *bilvaka* trees;
with *campaka*, *bakula*, *megha*, *madana*, *kuṭaja*, and others. ||4||
The forest was adorned with *jātikā* and *yūthikā* jasmine, as well as *navamālikā*, mangoes, *mādhava* grapes, and pomegranates. (5)
Resounding with the cries of many flocks of birds, made to ring out by the humming of bees,
filled with the calls of peacocks, that horse brings happiness in all seasons.
Accompanied by Śatrughna and endowed with the speed of thought, he entered,
bearing upon his broad forehead a beautiful golden leaf.
O best of the twice-born, listen to that wonderful event which occurred suddenly at that time as he was proceeding with his horse-sacrifice.
His limbs became stiff, and though he stood upon the path of motion,
that best of horses became as immovable as Mount Hemakūṭa.
Then all his keepers struck him with lashes of whips;
yet even when beaten, that best of horses did not move, his limbs remaining rigid.
Approaching Śatrughna who was nearby, the horse-keepers cried out:
"O Lord, we do not know what has happened to that most excellent of horses! (11)
O high-minded one, as that king, whose speed was like that of thought, proceeded on his excellent steed, there suddenly occurred a paralysis of his limbs.
"Though we struck him with whips, he did not move at all there;
having reflected thus, O best of kings, perform whatever action is required. (13)
Then the king, no longer filled with wonder, went together with all his troops and attendants into the presence of that great being.
Puṣkala then seized his feet with both arms and tried to lift him from the ground; however, he did not move at all. ||15||
Then the horse, being overwhelmed by the strength of the powerful one, did not tremble;
the high-minded Hanumān then resolved to lift it up.
Wrapping his tail around the horse with his strength, that best among the powerful pulled the mount with force; yet even so, the horse did not move.
Then Hanumān, the best of monkeys, filled with wonder,
spoke to Śatrughna, the foremost of the strong, while the heroes were listening.
"Just now, Droṇa was effortlessly uprooted by me with my tail;
yet here is a great marvel: even this tiny horse does not tremble. (19)
For the cause of this was seen by powerful and arrogant heroes;
yet, even though he was pulled, he did not move from his place even by the measure of a sesame seed. (20)
Having heard the speech of the monkey, Śatrughna, filled with wonder, spoke to Sumati, the best among ministers and the most eloquent of speakers. (21)
Śatrughna said:
"O sinless minister, what caused this paralysis of the horse's body?
What remedy should be applied here so that the horse may regain its gait? (22)
Sumati said:
"O Master, some sage who is expert in all branches of knowledge must be sought.
I know the origin of the country through direct perception, not through hearsay. (23)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words of Sumati, he who was skilled in dharma sought out the auspicious sage together with his servants. (24)
Having gone everywhere, all those soldiers searched for the sage who knows the Dharma, yet they did not see the Lord of Sages anywhere.
But one attendant, who was merely a common person following the Brahmin,
exerted himself toward the eastern direction and beheld a great hermitage.
There, all creatures and people alike were free from enmity;
having had all their sins destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā, they were exceedingly beautiful.
There, some performed supreme austerities with fires;
with smoke they remained face-downward, and with leaves they filled their own bellies, subsisting on air.
There, the smoke born of the fire-sacrifice constantly purifies [the air], where many sages rejoice and the excellent creepers have shed their leaves. (29)
Having learned of that charming hermitage of the sage Śaunaka,
they informed the king, whose mind was filled with wonder.
Having heard that, Śatrughna was exceedingly delighted; accompanied by his servants and joined by Hanumān, Puṣkala, and others, he then went to that hermitage.
There, having beheld the best of sages who had properly offered oblations into the fire,
he prostrated himself like a staff at his feet, which destroy all sins.
Knowing that Śatrughna, the best among the strong, had arrived, he offered him the guest-offering, water for the feet, and other honors; he became delighted by the sight of him.
When the king was comfortably seated and rested, the lord of sages said to him: "O King, for what purpose are you wandering? Why are you traveling such a great distance? (34)
If kings like you were to roam throughout the entire earth, then wicked people would no longer harass the virtuous who are free from distress. (35)
Speak, O best among the powerful slayers of kings;
may everything concerning your wandering and other activities lead to auspiciousness for all. (36)
Śeṣa said:
To the Brahmin who had spoken thus, the Lord of the Earth replied with a voice faltering with emotion, his own body thrilled with joy. (37)
Śatrughna said:
"O best among the knowers of truth, listen: it was a wondrous thing that occurred suddenly; Rāma’s horse, having stolen its heart's desire, was not far from your dwelling. (38)
While he was wandering at will through that garden, rich in the beauty of its trees,
his horse’s limbs suddenly became paralyzed for a moment.
Then the powerful heroes, Puṣkala and others, fierce with intoxication,
forcibly pulled at the vehicle, yet even so, it did not move.
"You are remembered as the one who ferries us across the ocean of boundless suffering;
having been seen by good fortune, tell us the cause [of this]. (41)
Śeṣa said:
Thus questioned, the best of sages, possessed of great intelligence, meditated for a moment;
then, through reflection, he established two [conclusions] supported by reason.
In an instant, having attained that state of knowledge, his eyes blossomed with wonder;
he spoke to the king, who was distressed and filled with doubt.
Śaunaka said:
Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of the pillar of horses;
by hearing this most wonderful narrative, one is liberated from suffering. 44.
In the great forest of the Gauḍa country, adorned by the banks of the Kāverī,
a Brāhmaṇa named Sātvata performed supreme austerity.
For one day he consumed milk, for one day he subsisted on air, and for one day he remained entirely without food; in this manner, he should carry it out for three days.
While he was thus engaged in his vow, Time, the destroyer of all, seized him with its fangs; the great ascetic met his death.
In a celestial palace rich with every splendor and adorned with all kinds of jewels,
I remained upon the peak of Mount Meru, sporting together with the Apsarases.
There, on Mount Jambū, there was a Jambū tree whose juice was worthy of being consumed;
it was joined with the river named Āvatī, which was filled with liquid gold. 49.
In that [place], sages endowed with the merit of manifold austerities and possessed of all happiness sported with their desires, filled with curiosity. (50)
There, sporting at his own will with the celestial nymphs and filled with joy,
he acted in opposition to them, arrogant with the intoxication of his own self-conceit.
Then, cursed by the sages, the Rākṣasa became deformed;
thereafter, being exceedingly distressed, he spoke to the sages whose wealth was their learning and austerity.
"May all of you, O compassionate brahmins, show me favor;
for when you have favored me, then you will have favored me. (53)
Then, through the forceful hearing of the story of Rāma, you will be restrained;
subsequently, liberation from this most terrible curse of Īśa shall come to pass.
"O Lord, the god has been declared by the sages to have attained the state of a rākṣasa;
therefore, O you of stainless fame, paralyze Rāma’s horse and release [the captive]. (55)

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Curse," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana. ||47||
The forty-eighth chapter. Śeṣa said: Having heard what was thus spoken by the sage, the slayer of enemy heroes [replied].
Honoring his astonishment, he spoke to Śaunaka within his heart.
Śatrughna said:
"O you who bear the name Sātvata, the course of action is profound and mysterious;
for even though you have attained heaven through great deeds, you have been turned into a Rākṣasa by another deed. (2)
O Lord, O Great Sage, please explain the destiny resulting from one's actions, and by what ripening of karma such-and-such a hell comes to be. (3)
Śaunaka said:
"O best of the Raghavas, you are blessed that such an auspicious thought has arisen in you; for though you already know the truth, O Lord, you speak it for the sake of the world."
I shall describe the various destinies resulting from diverse karmas;
listen to them, O Great King, for by hearing them one may attain liberation. (5)
That evil-minded person who, with the intent to enjoy them, forcibly seizes another's wealth, offspring, wife, or whatever belongs to another. (6)
Bound by the noose of Time and led by the mighty messengers of Yama,
he is cast into Tāmisra for as long as a thousand years.
There, the servants of Yama, brandishing their weapons, inflict beatings upon those tormented by the experience of their sins; thereafter, they enter the womb of a sow.
Having experienced great suffering there, he will return to human status, marked by diseases and the like, and bringing ill repute upon himself. (9)
He who, devoted to sin, nourishes only his own family by practicing malice toward living beings, shall fall into the Andhatāmisra hell.
Those who falsely commit the slaughter of human beings and noble kinsmen shall be cast down into the Raurava hell;
they shall be split apart by those [beings] with great ferocity.
He who clearly commits the slaughter of living beings for the sake of his own belly is cast down by my command into the hell named Mahāraurava. (12)
That evildoer who indeed hates his own biological father, a Brāhmaṇa,
is cast into the great and wicked Kālasūtra hell, which extends for ten thousand yojanas.
For as many hairs as there are on the bodies of the cattle against whom one harbors hatred,
for that many thousands of years one is tormented by the Yama-wardens.
Having become a sovereign on earth, he would punish even those who do not deserve punishment; being greedy, he would even inflict corporal punishment upon a Brāhmaṇa. (15)
This [world] is oppressed by wicked ones with the faces of boars who are incapable of doing anything;
later, for the sake of liberation from sin, one is born into wicked wombs.
Those men who, out of delusion, forcibly seize the livelihood or even a small amount of the property and means of subsistence belonging to Brahmins or cows, are destroyers of their own merit. ||17||
Furthermore, those who, being greedy for sweets, personally bring food [to others] shall be cast into the Andhakūpa hell and be greatly tormented there. (18)
One who gives no hospitality to a guest, even a friend, falls indeed into the hell known as Kṛmibhojana (the feeding of worms). ||19||
But one who, in times of distress, takes away gold and other such things,
or the property of a Brahmin, unless he is extremely wicked, shall fall into the Sandaṃśa hell.
He who nourishes only his own body and knows no other, being of deluded intellect,
falls into the most dreadful hell called Kumbhīpāka, which is heated with oil.
If one should, out of delusion, desire a woman who is not to be approached because of her female nature, what can they do with her? They cause him to embrace a glowing iron pillar. (22)
Those who, arrogant in their own strength, violate the boundaries of the Vedas, fall into the Vaitaraṇī river and become eaters of blood. (23)
He who, having made a *vṛṣalī* his wife, practices the life of a householder with her, falls into the Pūyoda hell, overwhelmed by great suffering. (24)
Those fools who, relying on this delusion, deceive the world, fall into the Vaiśasana hell, struck by Yama.
Those fools who cause their own semen to be drunk by a woman of their own caste—
those sinners, intent on drinking semen, [beget] sons born from a stream of semen.
Those who are thieves, arsonists, wicked men, poisoners, or plunderers of villages— endowed with such sins, they are cast down like dogs into the Sārameyādana hell.
A man burdened by sin speaks false testimony;
he who is powerful forcibly seizes the wealth belonging to another. (28)
That sinner falls headlong down into the Avīci hell;
having experienced great suffering there, he enters a most wicked womb. (29)
The fool-minded man drinks wine from the taste of the tongue of a woman;
yet what can those who act according to the nature of iron do to make him drink that [iron]? (30)
A man who, arrogant due to his own learning and conduct, disregards those who are disciplined in yoga,
falls headlong into the Kṣāra hell when he dies.
Those men devoid of dharma who commit treachery against those who trust them are cast into the Śūlaprota hell, where they endure many torments.
The slanderer causes all people to tremble with his speech;
having fallen among scorpions, he is bitten by scorpions. (33)
Thus, O King, there are many hells for evildoers;
having committed sin, they go to these places of most terrible torment. (34)
For those who have not listened to the discourses on the Arāma and have failed to perform service for others, all manner of sufferings arise within the midst of hell. (35)
In this regard, for one who has attained happiness, it is as if they have crossed over [the ocean of existence] to heaven;
whereas those who are suffering and afflicted by disease have come from hell. (36)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, the protector of the earth, feeling perplexed from moment to moment,
questioned that brahmin once again for the sake of dispelling all his doubts.
O great sage, tell me the signs of each respective sin;
by what sin does what sign arise in the world of mortals? (38)
Having heard these words, the sage spoke to the king:
"Listen, O King, I shall describe the signs of those who commit evil deeds. (39)
Śaunaka said:
A drinker of spirituous liquor is born as a Śyāmadantaka (one with black teeth) in hell;
and one who eats what is forbidden to be eaten is born as one suffering from abdominal tumors.
By eating food looked upon by a woman in her courses, one is born with worms in the stomach;
by eating food touched by dogs, cats, or the like, one becomes foul-smelling. (41)
A man who eats without first offering [food] to the gods and others becomes afflicted with diseases of the stomach, miserable, and tormented by great maladies. (42)
From creating obstacles to others' food, indigestion arises; one becomes afflicted with chronic stomach ailments and possesses a weak digestive fire, eating only a single meal at a time. (43)
One who steals the path shall be afflicted with vomiting and disease;
a slanderer is born in hell and suffers from asthma and cough.
One who causes pain to others will become a rogue, afflicted by epilepsy, and suffering from colic;
furthermore, one who sets forest fires will suffer from bloody dysentery. ||45||
He who throws wine, water, or even excrement into a temple shall suffer from a most terrible anal disease, which is the very form of his sin. (46)
Those who cause the destruction of a fetus suffer from diseases such as consumption, urinary disorders, and dropsy;
and one who destroys an image is born without a stable foundation.
One who speaks wickedly shall indeed be afflicted with a skin disease; one who reviles others becomes bald;
and one who takes sides in an assembly suffers from wing-palsy (hemiplegia). 48.
One who mocks others becomes one-eyed; a stealer of a Brahmin’s gold has deformed nails;
a thief of a blue lotus becomes a leper; a thief of copper becomes a dwarf; and a stealer of a conch shell becomes one with white spots on his body.
A man who steals earrings is born with hair as yellow as a pigeon;
and a man who steals a head is born suffering from diseases of the head.
A man who steals ghee is born with eye disease;
and a man who steals iron is born among the barbarians.
A man is born covered with fat, like a leather bag;
yet another man is born as a stealer of honey, possessing the odor of a bladder.
By stealing oil, a man becomes afflicted with severe itching; and by taking uncooked food, he is born deficient in teeth. (53)
From stealing cooked food, one will suffer from diseases of the tongue;
and a man who approaches his mother is born devoid of a penis. ||54||
From approaching the wife of one's guru, urinary distress arises;
and from approaching a sister, yellow leprosy arises. ||55||
By approaching one's own daughter, one is born with red leprosy;
by approaching the wife of a brother, one is born with glandular leprosy. ||56||
By approaching the wife of one's master and others [forbidden women], a ringworm eruption arises;
by approaching a trusting wife, one is born with elephantiasis. //57//
By approaching one's paternal aunt, one shall have a wound on the right limb;
by approaching the wife of a maternal uncle, one shall have a wound on the left limb. ||58||
By approaching the wife of one's paternal uncle, leprosy arises on the hips;
by approaching the wife of a friend, one becomes widowed. ||59||
Through indulgence with women of one's own kin, a fistula of the perineum arises;
through indulgence with female ascetics, urinary disorder (prameha) arises in a man. (60)
Through sexual union with the wife of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one is born with a nasal deformity;
through sexual union with the wife of one initiated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), one is born with foul-flowing blood. (61)
By approaching a wife of one's own caste, one suffers a wound of the heart;
by approaching a woman of a higher caste, one suffers a wound of the head. (62)
And from engaging in sexual intercourse with an animal, urinary obstruction arises;
these defects shall befall men at the end of their stay in hell, without a doubt. (63)
These very same [symptoms] occur in women as well through contact with various men;
thus, O King, have the signs of great sinners been proclaimed. (64)
Through the merit of giving, through ritual acts such as visiting sacred fords, or likewise by hearing the life-story of Rāma or by ascetic penance, one shall attain destruction [of karma]. (65)
For all people, the river of Hari’s fame washes away the mire of the sins of sinners; no deliberation is required in this matter. (66)
If one should consider Hari to be in the womb, for such a person the sacrifices prescribed by the rules and even the most meritorious sacred fords are not capable of purifying him. (67)
He who, weak in knowledge, laughs at the life-story being recited, shall not find liberation from the hells even at the end of a kalpa. (68)
O King, for the sake of the horse's liberation, cause the life-story of the Lord of Śrī to be heard along with his attendants, so that the horse may find its way. (69)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard this, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, became overjoyed;
having bowed to him and circumambulated him, he departed accompanied by his attendants.
Having gone there, together with Hanumān, he spoke of the life of Rāma— which destroys even the most grievous misfortunes— by the side of that excellent horse.
By the merit of chanting the glories of Rāma, ascend to your own celestial mansion; wander freely in the world and be liberated from an evil rebirth. (72)
Having heard these words, just as Śatrughna stood there,
he beheld a stainless, excellent deity seated in a celestial chariot.
He said: "O King, O high-minded one, I am liberated through the hearing of the glorification of Rāma; I shall go to my own abode—give me your command. (74)
Having spoken thus, the god departed, seated upon his own celestial chariot;
then those followers, together with Śatrughna, were filled with wonder.
Then, released from the paralysis of his limbs and from the surface of the earth,
the horse went wandering through that entire forest, which was teeming with birds.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Release of the Horse," in the Rāmāśvamedha section of the Pātālakhaṇḍa within the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana.
(49) The forty-ninth chapter.
Śeṣa said:
Seven months passed for that excellent horse as it wandered with ease through the land of Bhārata, which was filled with many kings.
Honored by the best of kings as he traveled throughout the excellent land of Bhārata, he was surrounded by the most eminent heroes, such as the formidable Śatrughna and others. ||2||
He wandered through many lands near the Himalayas,
subduing provoked elephants while remembering the power of Rāma.
Oṃ! Praised by kings, the horse Gakali, the best of steeds, went to the enchanting city of King Suratha. 4.
There was a city named Kuṇḍala,
where the earring of Aditi fell to the earth from the ears of the two [sons] who were joyful and terrified.
Wherein he never at any time transgressed the Dharma, and every day he performed the remembrance of Śrī Rāma with love. ||6||
Furthermore, where the Aśvattha and Tulasī are worshipped daily by men who are free from sin and are servants of the Lord of the Raghus; ||7||
Where there are temples, beautiful with images of Rāghava, which are worshipped daily by those of pure mind and free from deceit. (8)
Where there is no talk of strife concerning Hari, where there is meditation upon Him in the heart, and no recollection of the fruits of desire; ||9||
There, among those whose bodies were purified by the news of Rāma, there was never any lack of devotion to truth among men who prided themselves on their addiction to truthfulness. (10)
In that place dwelt the righteous-souled Asuratha, who was truthful, powerful, and supremely intoxicated with joy, his heart gladdened by the remembrance of the feet of the Lord of the Raghus. ||11||
How can I describe the excellent Suratha, the servant of Rāma?
Upon him, who is a field of all virtues, these [virtues] are spread wide, purifying all sin. 12.
Once, while wandering about, the servants of that king saw the horse of the horse-sacrifice, adorned with sandalwood paste.
Seeing this, they were struck with wonder and looked at the horse's hoof-print, which was inscribed with clear syllables and smeared with sandalwood paste and other substances. (14)
Having learned that the horse, which was captivating to the eye, had been captured by Rāma, those present in the royal assembly, filled with excitement, joyfully reported it to the king. (15)
"O Lord, the master of the city of Ayodhyā is Rāghava;
a horse fit for the horse-sacrifice has been released by him and is wandering about. (16)
Accompanied by his servants, he arrived near Satepura and said, "O Great King, please accept this most beautiful horse. (17)
Śeṣa said:
Having heard these words spoken by himself, he was overwhelmed with joy and spoke to his powerful heroes in a voice as deep as a thundercloud: 18.
Suratha said:
"Blessed are we, along with our attendants, that we behold the face of Rāma;
I shall seize his horse, though it be surrounded by ten million warriors. (19)
Then I shall surely release him when Ārāma approaches—my devoted follower who has long been intent on meditation and has now accomplished his purpose. (20)
Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus, the protector of the earth himself commanded his servants:
"Seize the horse by force; he must be released once he is no longer within the range of sight. (21)
"It is my opinion that a very great gain will be yours, in that you shall behold the feet of Rāma, which are difficult even for Brahmā, Śakra, and others to obtain. (22)
He alone is fortunate—whether he be a kinsman, a son, a friend, or even an animal or a mount—by whom the attainment of Rāma may be brought about. (23)
Therefore, having taken the sacrificial horse, adorned with a golden plate, he tied up that beautiful steed, swift as desire, in the stable.
Having been told this, they then went and, taking Rāma’s beautiful horse,
they swiftly gave it all to the auspicious king.
Having obtained the horse of Rāma, the king, the subduer of demons and expert in the performance of dharma,
spoke to his powerful servants.
O Vātsyāyana of great intelligence, listen with a one-pointed mind: there is no man who indulges in another's wife who does not fall within its sphere. 27.
He is not intent on the wealth of others, nor is he a libertine in sensual desires;
his tongue does not wander onto the wrong path because of the chanting of Rāma’s glories. (28)
The king said to his servants: "You have come for the sake of service; tell me of your activities, for you are experts in the performance of righteous deeds. (29)
They observed the vow of having only one wife, were not covetous of the property of others, did not delight in slandering others, and had not strayed from the path of the Vedas. ||30||
The soldiers perform the remembrance of Śrī Rāma and other such rites every day;
I, possessing fierce anger, protect them for the sake of their service to Rāma. (31)
Those men who possess qualities contrary to this and are joined with evil— I dwell in my own domain, not those of wicked mind.
By his instruction, even the most wicked cease committing sins in their minds, becoming filled with the joy of having all their transgressions destroyed through meditation on Hari. (33)
When the ruler of the land was thus endowed with righteousness, then all the inhabitants of that place, having died, attained final liberation. (34)
At that time, there was no one in the city of Sauratha who could rival Yama;
therefore, assuming the form of a sage, he approached the lord of the earth.
Wearing garments of bark and with his head adorned by matted locks, he beheld Suratha, a servant of Hara, in the midst of the assembly hall. ||36||

He who places the supreme name of Hari upon the head of a *tulasī* plant and causes his own people to hear news concerning those devoted to dharma and sacred rites—[him I consider a true devotee]. (37)
Then, seeing the sage standing like the very embodiment of asceticism,
the king paid homage at his feet and offered him water for washing the feet and other honors.
To the sage who was seated comfortably and at rest, the foremost of kings said: "Blessed is my birth today; blessed is my home today. (39)
Tell me various excellent stories of Rāma,
by listening to which there shall be a destruction of sins at every step.
Having heard what was thus spoken, the sage laughed heartily,
displaying his teeth while clapping his hands together.
To that laughing sage he said, "Why are you laughing without cause?
Please tell me out of grace so that there may be peace for my mind. (42)
Then the sage said to the king: "Listen, O King, with an attentive mind, to that supreme cause which I shall declare to you, for which you have smiled. (43)
"You have spoken; now describe the glory of Hari before me. Who is Hari, and whose is his glory? All men are subject to their own karma. (44)
By action heaven is attained; by action one goes to hell;
by action alone all things—sons, grandsons, and many others—come to be. (45)
Śakra, having performed a hundred sacrifices, went to the supreme state;
Brahmā also, through his ritual action, attained the wonderful world known as Satya.
The lords, such as the Maruts and others, perfected through manifold karmas, enjoy the happiness of sensory pleasures while being served by hosts of celestial nymphs. ||47||
Therefore, perform sacrifices and other rites, and worship the gods;
in this way, your stainless fame shall spread across the surface of the earth. 48.
Having heard those words, his mind agitated by anger, he spoke to the Brahmin who was skilled in ritual action and solely intent on Rāma. (49)
Do not speak of the matter of ritual action, which yields only perishable fruits;
go outside the vicinity of this city, for you are despised by the world.
Indra will soon fall, and the lotus-born Brahmā will fall;
those who are eager for the worship of the grove of men (the Buddha) shall not fall.
Behold Prahlāda, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others who are truly wonderful;
those who are devotees of Rāma never fall at any time.
Those wicked ones who have committed offenses against the Jaina community will strike them with iron hammers and with bonds of nooses. ||53||
"O lowest of the twice-born, because you are a Brāhmaṇa, I shall not inflict corporal punishment upon you;
go, go away from my sight, lest I beat you! (54)
When the excellent king named Suratha had spoken thus,
his servants seized him by the arm and prepared to cast him out.
Then, assuming his own form which is worshipped by the whole world, he said to the king:
"I am well-pleased; ask for a boon, O servant of Hari. (56)
O you of excellent vows, though tempted by me with many words, you—served by the virtuous—did not waver from your service to the Lord of Men. (57)
Then the lord of the earth, seeing Yama well-pleased, spoke:
"If you are pleased, grant me an excellent boon. (58)
"Indeed, there shall be no death for me until my meeting with Rāma;
nor shall there ever be any fear for me here from the King of Dharma."
Then he said to the king: "This shall come to pass for you;
the Lord of Raghu will truly fulfill everything that you desire. (60)
Having spoken thus, Dharma vanished and departed toward his own city,
praising the conduct of that one whose soul was devoted to Hari.
The righteous king, a servant of Rāma, with supreme joy,
took the horse and spoke to his servants, who were themselves servants of Hari.
"I have seized this mount of King Rāghava;
you who are skilled in battle, prepare yourselves in every way! (63)
Thus addressed, all those mighty warriors of the Lord immediately prepared themselves and went to the assembly hall with eager anticipation.
From King Vīra were born ten sons: Campaka, Mohaka, Ripuñjaya, Atidurvāra, Pratāpin, and Balamodaka. ||65||
Haryakṣa, Sahadeva, Bhūrideva, and Sutāpana—these ten sons of the king stood ready on the field of battle. (66)
"Alas, we have become possessed by such rashness that we desired to go;
even the king [prepared] his own wonderful chariot, fashioned with the splendor of gold. (67)
Surrounded by his entire army and filled with martial zeal for battle, he summoned him [to combat] with well-adorned, swift horses.
The lord of the earth sat in the assembly hall, issuing commands to all his servants.
Thus, in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the Pātāla-khaṇḍa, within the dialogue between Śeṣa and Vātsyāyana, in the section concerning Rāma’s horse-sacrifice, [the account of] Suratha—
